accompany someone on a journey.monolingual: 1. [for someone] to go with someone on a trip, journey, adventure, etc. _Would you please accompany me on my next trip?
examples: Would you please accompany me on my next trip? 2.

accompany someone with something.monolingual: to use a particular musical instrument to play music that goes along with someone else’s musical performance. _ She accompanied Mary with her f lute.
examples: She accompanied Mary with her f lute.

accord with something.monolingual: to agree with or match up with something; to jibe with something. _Does this accord with what you heard?

according to hoyle.monolingual: according to the rules; in keeping with the way something is normally done. (Alludes to the rules for playing games. Edmond Hoyle wrote a widely used book with rules for card games. This expression is usually used for something other than games.) _ T
examples: That’s wrong. According to Hoyle, this is the way to do it.

according to one’s own lights.monolingual: according to the way one believes; according to the way one’s conscience or inclinations lead one. _ John may have been wrong, but he did what he did according to his own lights.
examples: John may have been wrong, but he did what he did according to his own lights.

according to someone or something.monolingual: as said or indicated by someone or something. _ According to the weather forecast, this should be a beautiful day.
examples: According to the weather forecast, this should be a beautiful day.

according to something.monolingual: in proportion to something. _ You will get paid according to the number of hours that you work.
examples: You will get paid according to the number of hours that you work.

account for someone or something.monolingual: to know the state of or whereabouts of someone or something. (Usually in reference to some person or thing placed in one’s charge.) _ They cannot account for three of the passengers.
examples: They cannot account for three of the passengers.

account for something.monolingual: to explain something. _Your explanation accounts for everything that has happened.
examples: Your explanation accounts for everything that has happened.

accredit something to someone.monolingual: to assign or attribute a deed to someone; to assign or attribute praise to someone. (Often passive.) _We can accredit this great success to Fred and his committee.
examples: We can accredit this great success to Fred and his committee.

accrue to someone or something.monolingual: [used of interest paid on money] to be credited to an account or to a person’s account. _ Interest will accrue to your account as long as the account is active.
examples: Interest will accrue to your account as long as the account is active.

accuse someone of something.monolingual: to charge someone with a crime, a violation of rules or instructions, or doing something wrong. _ Please don’t accuse me of forgetting to lock the door.
examples: Please don’t accuse me of forgetting to lock the door.

ace out.monolingual: to be fortunate or lucky. _ Freddy aced out at the dentist’s office with only one cavity.
examples: Freddy aced out at the dentist’s office with only one cavity.

ace someone out†.monolingual: to maneuver someone out; to win out over someone. _Martha aced out Rebecca to win the first place trophy.
examples: Martha aced out Rebecca to win the first place trophy.

achilles’ heel.monolingual: Fig. a weak point or fault in someone or something otherwise perfect or excellent. (From the legend of Greek hero Achilles, who had only one vulnerable part of his body, his heel; as an infant his mother had held him by one heel to dip him in the Riv
examples: He was very brave, but fear of spiders was his Achilles’ heel.

aching heart.monolingual: Fig. the feeling of pain because of love that is lost or has faded away. (Described as being in the heart, where love is said to reside.) _I try to tell my aching heart that I don’t love him.
examples: I try to tell my aching heart that I don’t love him.

the acid test.monolingual: Fig. a test whose findings are beyond doubt or dispute. _The senator doesn’t look too popular just now, but the acid test will be if he gets reelected.
examples: The senator doesn’t look too popular just now, but the acid test will be if he gets reelected.

acknowledge someone as something.monolingual: to agree or announce publicly that a person holds a particular office or station, or that a person has particular qualities. _ She found it difficult to acknowledge herself as a failure.
examples: She found it difficult to acknowledge herself as a failure.

acknowledge someone to be right.monolingual: to admit or state that someone is correct about something. _ Bill said that the car was useless, and the mechanic acknowledged him to be right.
examples: Bill said that the car was useless, and the mechanic acknowledged him to be right.

acknowledge something as something.monolingual: to agree or announce publicly that something is as previously stated. _ The president acknowledged the statement as the truth.
examples: The president acknowledged the statement as the truth.

acquaint someone with something.monolingual: to introduce someone to an unfamiliar thing; to become familiar with something; to get to know something; to tell someone the facts [about someone or something]. _ It took a month for the new attorney to acquaint herself with the facts in the case.
examples: It took a month for the new attorney to acquaint herself with the facts in the case.

*acquainted with someone.monolingual: [of a person] known to someone; [of a person] having been introduced to someone. (*Typically: be ~; become ~; get ~.) _We are only acquainted with each other. We are certainly not what you would call close friends.
examples: We are only acquainted with each other.

*acquainted with something.monolingual: familiar with something; able to understand or recognize something. (*Typically: be ~; become ~; get ~.) _ Tom is fully acquainted with the way we do things.
examples: Tom is fully acquainted with the way we do things.

acquiesce to someone or something.monolingual: to give in to someone or someone’s wishes; to agree, perhaps reluctantly, to someone’s ideas or requests. _We are willing to acquiesce to your demands.
examples: We are willing to acquiesce to your demands.

acquit someone of something.monolingual: to establish someone’s innocence of a criminal charge or the blame for some wrongdoing. _ The investigator acquitted Wally of the charges.
examples: The investigator acquitted Wally of the charges.

across the board.monolingual: Fig. [distributed] equally for everyone or everything. _ The school board raised the pay of all the teachers across the board.
examples: The school board raised the pay of all the teachers across the board.

act as someone.monolingual: to perform in the capacity of someone, temporarily or permanently; to serve in some special capacity, possibly temporarily. _ This is Mr. Smith. He’ll act as manager from now on.
examples: This is Mr. Smith.

act for someone.monolingual: 1. to represent someone in an official capacity; to represent the interests of someone. _ Don’t worry. I am acting for the owner. I am his real estate agent.
examples: Don’t worry. I am acting for the owner.

an act of faith.monolingual: an act or deed demonstrating religious faith; an act or deed showing trust in someone or something. _ For him to trust you with his safety was a real act of faith.
examples: For him to trust you with his safety was a real act of faith.

an act of god.monolingual: an occurrence or an event for which no human is responsible; an act of nature such as a storm, an earthquake, or a wildfire. _ Will your insurance com- pany pay for damage caused by earthquakes and other acts of God?

an act of war.monolingual: 1. Lit. an international act of warlike violence for which war is considered a suitable response. _ To bomb a ship is an act of war.
examples: To bomb a ship is an act of war.

act out.monolingual: to behave badly. (Usually used to describe young people.) _ Your son has been acting out in the classroom, and his teacher feels that professional intervention is desirable.
examples: Your son has been acting out in the classroom, and his teacher feels that professional intervention is desirable.

act something out†.monolingual: 1. to perform in real life a role that one has imagined in a fantasy. _ When I was onstage, I was really acting an old fantasy out. _ I acted out an old fantasy onstage.
examples: When I was onstage, I was really acting an old fantasy out.

act up.monolingual: [for a thing or a person] to behave badly. _This car is acting up again.
examples: This car is acting up again.

act your age!.monolingual: Behave more maturely! (A rebuke for someone who is acting childish. Often said to a child who is acting like an even younger child.) _ Child: Aw, come on! Let me see your book! Mary: Be quiet and act your age. Don’t be such a baby!
examples: Child: Aw, come on! Let me see your book! Mary: Be quiet and act your age.

actions speak louder than words..monolingual: Prov. Cliché What you do is more significant than what you say. _ You keep saying that you’ll do your fair share of the housework. Remember that actions speak louder than words.
examples: You keep saying that you’ll do your fair share of the housework.

adapt something for something.monolingual: to change or alter something for use with something else. _ Has this furnace been adapted for natural gas?

adapt something from something.monolingual: to derive something from something else; to create by modifying something else. _ I adapted my new musical from a novel.
examples: I adapted my new musical from a novel.

adapt something to something.monolingual: to convert something to fit or work with something else. _We converted our furnace to natural gas.
examples: We converted our furnace to natural gas.

adapt to something.monolingual: to adapt or get used to someone or something. _ Please try to adapt to our routine.
examples: Please try to adapt to our routine.

add insult to injury.monolingual: Fig. Cliché to make a bad situation worse; to hurt the feelings of a person who has already been hurt. _First, the basement f looded, and then, to add insult to injury, a pipe burst in the kitchen. _My car barely started this morning, and to add insu
examples: First, the basement f looded, and then, to add insult to injury, a pipe burst in the kitchen.

add something together.monolingual: to sum or total two or more things. _ Add these two together and tell me what you get.
examples: Add these two together and tell me what you get.

add something up†.monolingual: to sum or total a set of figures. _ Please add these figures up again. _ I didn’t add up these figures!
examples: Please add these figures up again.

addict someone to something.monolingual: to cause someone to become habituated to something, usually alcohol or some another drug. _ The hospital personnel were thought to have addicted John to morphine. _ She ended up addicting herself to the substance.
examples: The hospital personnel were thought to have addicted John to morphine.

address oneself to someone.monolingual: to speak directly to a particular person, rather than someone else. _I did not address myself to you!

address oneself to something.monolingual: to turn one’s complete attention to something, such as a problem or an issue. _ Please address yourself to these current, pressing problems.
examples: Please address yourself to these current, pressing problems.

address something to someone.monolingual: to write someone’s name and address on an envelope, package, letter, etc. _Gilbert addressed the envelope to Walter.
examples: Gilbert addressed the envelope to Walter.

adhere to something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to stick to something. _ The stamp won’t adhere to the envelope.
examples: The stamp won’t adhere to the envelope.

adjourn for a time.monolingual: to bring a meeting to a temporary close so the participants can take part in some other activity. _ We must adjourn for the day.
examples: We must adjourn for the day.

adjourn to some place.monolingual: to bring a meeting to a temporary close so the participants can move to another place (where the meeting will be started again). _We adjourned to the sitting room.
examples: We adjourned to the sitting room.

adjust something to something.monolingual: to make something fit something else; to alter something to make it suitable for something else. _ The builder adjusted the plans for the new house to the requirements of the fire marshal.
examples: The builder adjusted the plans for the new house to the requirements of the fire marshal.

admire someone for something.monolingual: to have a positive feeling toward someone because of something. _ I really admire you for your courage.
examples: I really admire you for your courage.

admire to do something.monolingual: Rur. to want to do something, to be happy to do something. _ He asked her to the dance. She said she would admire to go with him.
examples: He asked her to the dance.

admit something into something.monolingual: to allow something to be introduced into something else. _ You cannot admit this document into the body of evidence!

admit something to someone.monolingual: to confess something to someone. _ Harry admitted his error to his uncle.
examples: Harry admitted his error to his uncle.

admit to something.monolingual: to acknowledge or confess something; to acknowledge or confess to having done something. _ Max would not admit to anything.
examples: Max would not admit to anything.

admonish someone for something.monolingual: to warn or scold someone mildly for doing something. _The nurse admonished the patient for not eating her dinner.
examples: The nurse admonished the patient for not eating her dinner.

adopt someone as something.monolingual: to choose someone as something. _ The committee will adopt Jane as its candidate.
examples: The committee will adopt Jane as its candidate.

adopt something as something.monolingual: to take on something, such as a policy or principle, as one’s own. _ I will adopt this policy as my own.
examples: I will adopt this policy as my own.

adore someone for doing something.monolingual: to be in awe of someone for doing something well. _Everyone adores Sally for her wonderful sense of humor.
examples: Everyone adores Sally for her wonderful sense of humor.

adore someone for having something.monolingual: to be in awe of someone because of a particular trait or feature. _ Robert adores Mary for her smiling eyes.
examples: Robert adores Mary for her smiling eyes.

adulterate something with something.monolingual: to dilute or taint something with some other substance. _ They adulterated the wine with some sort of drug.
examples: They adulterated the wine with some sort of drug.

advertise for someone or something.monolingual: to advertise one’s intention to purchase something or hire a particular type of person. _ Did you advertise for a new receptionist?

advertise something for a price.monolingual: to make known by public notice that something is to be sold at a particular price. _ Is this the one that was advertised for a dollar?

advertise something for something.monolingual: to make known by public notice, such as broadcast or print notice, that something is available for purchase or rent. _ Was this apartment advertised for rent?

advise against something.monolingual: to suggest that something not be done. _ Lisa always advises against hasty actions.
examples: Lisa always advises against hasty actions.

advise someone against doing something.monolingual: to encourage or counsel someone not to do something. _ I advised Bill against quitting his job.
examples: I advised Bill against quitting his job.

advise someone of something.monolingual: to inform someone of specific facts or some other information. _ I hope you will advise Larry of the details of the proposal.
examples: I hope you will advise Larry of the details of the proposal.

affinity for someone or something.monolingual: a strong preference for something; a strong liking for something. _Mary’s affinity for classical music accounts for her large collection of recordings.
examples: Mary’s affinity for classical music accounts for her large collection of recordings.

affix one’s signature to something.monolingual: to sign one’s name on something. _ I affixed my signature to each of the documents.

afflict someone with someone.monolingual: to burden someone with an annoying person. _I was foolish enough to aff lict myself with my young cousin for the weekend.
examples: I was foolish enough to aff lict myself with my young cousin for the weekend.

afflict someone with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to cause someone to suffer from a disease or disability. _ The virus has aff licted everyone in the valley.

afraid of one’s own shadow.monolingual: Fig. easily frightened; always frightened, timid, or suspicious. (An exaggeration.) _ After Tom was robbed, he was even afraid of his own shadow.

after all.monolingual: 1. anyway; in spite of what had been decided. (Often refers to a change in plans or a reversal of plans.) _ It looks like Tom will go to law school after all.

after hours.monolingual: after the regular closing time; after any normal or regular time, such as one’s bedtime. _ John got a job sweeping f loors in the library after hours.

after the fact.monolingual: after something has happened; after something, such as a crime, has taken place. (Originally a legal phrase.) _ John is always making excuses after the fact.

after you..monolingual: Please go ahead of me.; Please pass through ahead of me. _Bob stepped back and made a motion with his hand indicating that Mary should go first. “After you,” smiled Bob.

again and again.monolingual: repeatedly; again and even more [times]. _ He knocked on the door again and again until I finally answered.

against all odds.monolingual: despite very low probability; in a most unlikely way. _ Against all odds, she managed to win the trophy.
examples: Against all odds, she managed to win the trophy.

against someone’s will.monolingual: without a person’s consent or agreement. _You cannot force me to come with you against my will!

against the clock.monolingual: Fig. in a race with time; in a great hurry to get something done before a particular time. _In a race against the clock, they rushed the accident victim to the hospital.
examples: In a race against the clock, they rushed the accident victim to the hospital.

agitate for something.monolingual: to stir up active support for something. _ The committee agitated for a change, but nothing was done.
examples: The committee agitated for a change, but nothing was done.

agree to disagree.monolingual: Cliché [for two or more parties] to calmly agree not to come to an agreement in a dispute. _ We have accomplished nothing except that we agree to disagree.

agree to something.monolingual: to consent to something; to allow something to be done; to approve something. _ If you don’t agree to my leaving early, I’ll just do it anyway.

agree with someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to hold the same opinion or judgment as someone else. _ I simply do not agree with you!
examples: I simply do not agree with you! 2.

agree with something.monolingual: 1. Fig. [for something] to look good or go well with something else. _This dress does not agree with these shoes, does it?
examples: This dress does not agree with these shoes, does it? 2.

examples: I want to be able to finish the job ahead of schedule.

examples: By the end of the week, I usually can get ahead of my duties, but not by much.

examples: If you show up ahead of time, you will have to wait.

aid and abet someone.monolingual: Cliché to help someone; to incite someone to do something, possibly something that is wrong. (Originally a legal phrase.) _ He was scolded for aiding and abetting the boys who were fighting.
examples: He was scolded for aiding and abetting the boys who were fighting.

aid someone in doing something.monolingual: to help someone do something. _ He aided her in fixing up the back bedroom.
examples: He aided her in fixing up the back bedroom.

aid someone in something.monolingual: to help someone in some kind of trouble. _ Will you aid me in this difficulty?

aim to do something.monolingual: Rur. to intend to do something. _ I didn’t aim to hurt your feelings, sugar, you know I didn’t.
examples: I didn’t aim to hurt your feelings, sugar, you know I didn’t.

ain’t it the truth?.monolingual: Rur. or Jocular That is true.; Isn’t that true? (Used to agree with a statement someone has made.) _Jane: I swear, life can be a trial sometimes. Bill: Yes, Lordy. Ain’t it the truth?
examples: Jane: I swear, life can be a trial sometimes.

ain’t particular.monolingual: 1. Rur. doesn’t or don’t care. _ Tom: Would you rather have ice cream or cheese on your apple pie? Mary: Whatever you’re having. I ain’t particular.

examples: Whenever I get around Tom, I end up getting the air.

air one’s belly.monolingual: Fig. Sl. to empty one’s stomach; to vomit. _I had a bad case of food poisoning and was airing my belly for most of the night.

air one’s grievances.monolingual: Fig. to complain; to make a public complaint. _ I know how you feel, John, but it isn’t necessary to air your grievances over and over.

air one’s lungs.monolingual: 1. Rur. to swear. _Don’t pay those old cowboys no mind. They’re just airin’ the lungs. _ I could tell John was working on his old car ’cause I could hear him out in the garage, airin’ his lungs.
examples: Don’t pay those old cowboys no mind.

air one’s paunch.monolingual: Sl. to vomit. _ He got so nauseous that he spent much of the night airing his paunch.
examples: He got so nauseous that he spent much of the night airing his paunch.

air one’s pores.monolingual: Sl. to undress oneself; to become naked. _ Me and Wilbur, that’s my brother, both fell in the creek and had to air our pores a while so our pants could dry out.
examples: Me and Wilbur, that’s my brother, both fell in the creek and had to air our pores a while so our pants could dry out.

air out.monolingual: [for something] to remain in the fresh air and become fresher. _ The pillows are airing out on the balcony.
examples: The pillows are airing out on the balcony.

air something out†.monolingual: to freshen something up by placing it in the open air; to freshen a room by letting outside air move through it. _ I’ll have to air out the car. Someone has been smoking in it.
examples: I’ll have to air out the car.

alert someone to something.monolingual: to make someone aware of trouble or potential trouble. _ The auditors alerted us to some problems with the accounts.
examples: The auditors alerted us to some problems with the accounts.

alight from something.monolingual: to get off something; to get down off something. _ Almost three hundred people alighted from the plane.
examples: Almost three hundred people alighted from the plane.

align something with something.monolingual: to adjust, straighten, or arrange something in reference to something else. _ Try to align this piece with the one next to it.
examples: Try to align this piece with the one next to it.

alive with people or things.monolingual: Fig. covered with, filled with, or active with people or creatures. _ Look! Ants everywhere. The f loor is alive with ants!
examples: Look! Ants everywhere.

all agog.monolingual: surprised and amazed. _He sat there, all agog, as the master of ceremonies read his name as the winner of first prize.
examples: He sat there, all agog, as the master of ceremonies read his name as the winner of first prize.

all and sundry.monolingual: Cliché everyone; one and all. _Cold drinks were served to all and sundry.
examples: Cold drinks were served to all and sundry.

all around robin hood’s barn.monolingual: going somewhere by an indirect route; going way out of the way [to get somewhere]; by a long and circuitous route. _We had to go all around Robin Hood’s barn to get to the little town.
examples: We had to go all around Robin Hood’s barn to get to the little town.

all at once.monolingual: 1. Lit. all at the same time. _The entire group spoke all at once.
examples: The entire group spoke all at once.

all by one’s lonesome.monolingual: Rur. all alone; by oneself. _Mary’s folks went out and left her all by her lonesome.
examples: Mary’s folks went out and left her all by her lonesome.

all day long.monolingual: throughout the day; during the entire day. _ We waited for you at the station all day long.
examples: We waited for you at the station all day long.

all ears.monolingual: Fig. listening eagerly and carefully. _ Well, hurry up and tell me. I’m all ears.
examples: Well, hurry up and tell me.

all eyes and ears.monolingual: Fig. listening and watching eagerly and carefully. _ Be careful what you say. The children are all eyes and ears. _ Tell us quick. We are all eyes and ears!
examples: Be careful what you say.

all gone.monolingual: used up; finished; over with. _Oh, the strawberry jelly is all gone. _ We used to have wonderful parties, but those days are all gone.
examples: Oh, the strawberry jelly is all gone.

all hell broke loose.monolingual: all sorts of wild or terrible things happened. _ When the boss left early for the weekend, all hell broke loose.
examples: When the boss left early for the weekend, all hell broke loose.

all in a day’s work.monolingual: part of what is expected; typical or normal. _ I don’t particularly like to cook, but it’s all in a day’s work. _Cleaning up after other people is all in a day’s work for a busboy.
examples: I don’t particularly like to cook, but it’s all in a day’s work.

all in all.monolingual: considering everything that has happened; in summary and in spite of any unpleasantness. _ All in all, it was a very good party. _ All in all, I’m glad that I visited New York City.
examples: All in all, it was a very good party.

all in good time.monolingual: at some future time; in the near future; in good time; soon. (This phrase is used to encourage people to be patient and wait quietly.) _ When will the baby be born? All in good time. _Mary: I’m starved! When will Bill get here with the pizza? Tom: Al
examples: When will the baby be born? All in good time.

all in one piece.monolingual: Fig. safely; without damage. _ Her son came home from school all in one piece, even though he had been in a fight. _ The package was handled carelessly, but the vase inside arrived all in one piece.
examples: Her son came home from school all in one piece, even though he had been in a fight.

all night long.monolingual: throughout the whole night. _ I couldn’t sleep all night long. _ John was sick all night long.
examples: I couldn’t sleep all night long.

all of a size.monolingual: Rur. all of the same size. _ I tried to pick out the biggest tomato, but they were pretty much all of a size. _ The houses in that neighborhood are all of a size.
examples: I tried to pick out the biggest tomato, but they were pretty much all of a size.

all of a sudden.monolingual: suddenly. _ All of a sudden lightning struck the tree we were sitting under. _ I felt a sharp pain in my side all of a sudden.
examples: All of a sudden lightning struck the tree we were sitting under.

all or nothing.monolingual: 1. Lit. everything or nothing at all. _Sally would not accept only part of the money. She wanted all or nothing. _ I can’t bargain over trif les. I will have to have all or nothing.
examples: Sally would not accept only part of the money.

all over town.monolingual: 1. Lit. in many places in town. _ Our dog got loose and ran all over town. _Jane looked all over town for a dress to wear to the party.
examples: Our dog got loose and ran all over town.

all right for you!.monolingual: That’s the end of being friendly with you!; That’s the last chance for you! (Usually said by a child who is angry with a playmate.) _ All right for you, John. See if I ever play with you again. _ All right for you! I’m telling your mother what you di
examples: All right for you, John.

all right with someone.monolingual: agreeable to someone. _ If you want to ruin your life and marry Tom, it’s all right with me. _ I’ll see if using the car is all right with my father.
examples: If you want to ruin your life and marry Tom, it’s all right with me.

all righty..monolingual: Inf. All right.; OK. _ Tom: Let’s go to the state fair. Bill: All righty, let’s do that. _ Everybody ready? All righty, then, let’s get started.
examples: Tom: Let’s go to the state fair.

all roads lead to rome..monolingual: Prov. There are many different routes to the same goal. _ Mary was criticizing the way that Jane was planting the f lowers. John said, “Never mind, Mary, all roads lead to Rome.” _ Some people learn by doing. Others have to be taught. In the long run
examples: Mary was criticizing the way that Jane was planting the f lowers.

all’s well that ends well..monolingual: Prov. Cliché An event that has a good ending is good even if some things went wrong along the way. (This is the name of a play by Shakespeare.) _ I’m glad you finally got here, even though your car had a f lat tire on the way. Oh, well. All’s well th
examples: I’m glad you finally got here, even though your car had a f lat tire on the way.

*all shook up.monolingual: Sl. excited; disturbed and upset. _ She stole my heart, and I’m all shook up. _ They were all shook up after the accident.
examples: She stole my heart, and I’m all shook up.

all show and no go.monolingual: Sl. equipped with good looks but lacking action or energy. (Used to describe someone or something that looks good but does not perform as promised.) _That shiny car of Jim’s is all show and no go. _He’s mighty handsome, but I hear he’s all show and n
examples: That shiny car of Jim’s is all show and no go.

*all spruced up.monolingual: freshened up; tidied up; cleaned up. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; get someone or something ~.) _ Let’s get the yard all spruced up for spring.
examples: Let’s get the yard all spruced up for spring.

all sweetness and light.monolingual: Cliché very kind, innocent, and helpful. _ She was mad at first, but after a while, she was all sweetness and light. _ At the reception, the whole family was all sweetness and light, but they argued and fought after the guests left.
examples: She was mad at first, but after a while, she was all sweetness and light.

all the livelong day.monolingual: all day long. _ Well, of course you get to feeling stiff, sitting in front of a computer all the livelong day. _ I’d go crazy if I had to stay at home all the livelong day.
examples: Well, of course you get to feeling stiff, sitting in front of a computer all the livelong day.

*all the marbles.monolingual: Fig. all the winnings, spoils, or rewards. (*Typically: end up with ~; get ~; win ~; give someone ~.) _Somehow Fred always seems to end up with all the marbles. I don’t think he plays fair.
examples: Somehow Fred always seems to end up with all the marbles.

all the rage.monolingual: Fig. in current fashion; being a current fad. _ A new dance called the “f loppy disc” is all the rage. _ Wearing a rope instead of a belt was all the rage in those days.
examples: A new dance called the “f loppy disc” is all the rage.

all the time.monolingual: 1. Lit. throughout a specific period of time. _ Bill was stealing money for the last two years, and Tom knew it all the time. _ All the time through December and January, Jane held down two jobs.
examples: Bill was stealing money for the last two years, and Tom knew it all the time.

all the way.monolingual: 1. Lit. from the beginning to the end; the entire distance, from start to finish. _ The ladder reaches all the way to the top of the house. _ I walked all the way home.
examples: The ladder reaches all the way to the top of the house.

all the way live.monolingual: Sl. very exciting; excellent. _ Man, this place is all the way live. _ Oh, Tiffany is just, like, all the way live!
examples: Man, this place is all the way live.

all there.monolingual: Fig. alert, aware, and mentally sound. (Usually negative.) _ After talking with Larry today, I get the feeling that he’s not quite all there. _You do such foolish things sometimes! I wonder if you’re all there.
examples: After talking with Larry today, I get the feeling that he’s not quite all there.

all thumbs.monolingual: Fig. very awkward and clumsy, especially with one’s hands. _Poor Bob can’t play the piano at all. He’s all thumbs. _Mary is all thumbs when it comes to gardening.
examples: Poor Bob can’t play the piano at all.

all to the good.monolingual: for the best; to one’s benefit. _He missed the train, but it was all to the good because the train had a wreck. _ It was all to the good that he died without suffering.
examples: He missed the train, but it was all to the good because the train had a wreck.

all told.monolingual: Fig. totaled up; including all parts. _ All told, he earned about $700 last week. _ All told, he has many fine characteristics.
examples: All told, he earned about $700 last week.

all vine and no taters.monolingual: Rur. to be all display with no real value. _ She’s a good-looking woman, but really she’s all vine and no taters. _ Don’t be fooled by Jim’s f lowery promises. They’re all vine and no taters.
examples: She’s a good-looking woman, but really she’s all vine and no taters.

all walks of life.monolingual: Fig. all social, economic, and ethnic groups. _ We saw people at the airport from all walks of life. _The people who came to the street fair represented all walks of life.
examples: We saw people at the airport from all walks of life.

all wet.monolingual: 1. Lit. completely wet. _ I fell in and got all wet.
examples: I fell in and got all wet.

all wool and no shoddy.monolingual: Rur. one hundred percent good quality. _Everything Mary sells is the best there is, all wool and no shoddy. _John’s a good man through and through— all wool and no shoddy.
examples: Everything Mary sells is the best there is, all wool and no shoddy.

all year round.monolingual: Fig. throughout all the seasons of the year; during the entire year. _ The public swimming pool is enclosed so that it can be used all year round. _In the South they can grow f lowers all year round.
examples: The public swimming pool is enclosed so that it can be used all year round.

*an all-out effort.monolingual: a very good and thorough effort. (*Typically: begin ~; have ~; make ~; start ~.) _We need to make an all-out effort to get this job done on time. _ The government began an all-out effort to reduce the federal budget.
examples: We need to make an all-out effort to get this job done on time.

all-out war.monolingual: total war, as opposed to limited military actions or threats of war. _ We are now concerned about all-out war in the Middle East. _ Threats of all-out war caused many tourists to leave the country immediately.
examples: We are now concerned about all-out war in the Middle East.

allow for someone or something.monolingual: 1. to plan on having enough of something (such as food, space, etc.) for someone. _Mary is bringing Bill on the picnic, so be sure to allow for him when buying the food. _ Allow for an extra person when setting the table tonight.
examples: Mary is bringing Bill on the picnic, so be sure to allow for him when buying the food.

allow something for something.monolingual: 1. to allocate a share or a suitable amount of something, such as time, money, space, etc., for some activity or goal. _ I allowed only an hour for lunch. _ They did not allow enough money for their expenditures this month.
examples: I allowed only an hour for lunch.

alloy something with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to combine one molten metal into another molten metal. _ Is it possible to alloy copper with nickel? _ The copper has been alloyed with nickel.
examples: The copper has been alloyed with nickel.

allude to someone or something.monolingual: to refer to someone or something; to make an implication about someone or something. _I did not mean to allude to someone you disliked so much. _ I alluded to the accident only once.
examples: I did not mean to allude to someone you disliked so much.

the almighty dollar.monolingual: Fig. the U.S. dollar, or the acquisition of money, when viewed as more important than anything else. _ Bill was a slave to the almighty dollar. _ It’s the almighty dollar that drives Wall Street thinking.
examples: Bill was a slave to the almighty dollar.

almost lost it.monolingual: Fig. to nearly lose one’s temper, composure, or control, as out of anger. _ I was so mad, I almost lost it. _ When he saw the dent in his fender, he almost lost it.
examples: I was so mad, I almost lost it.

along with someone or something.monolingual: in addition to someone or something; together with someone or something. _ Jane went to the mall along with David. _I ate some chocolates along with some fruit.
examples: Jane went to the mall along with David.

*aloof from someone or something.monolingual: being remote or distant from someone or something. (*Typically: be ~; keep ~; remain ~; stay ~.) _She tends to keep aloof from the rest of us. _Ken stays aloof from other committee members between meetings.
examples: She tends to keep aloof from the rest of us.

alpha and omega.monolingual: both the beginning and the end; the essentials, from the beginning to the end; everything, from the beginning to the end. _ He was forced to learn the alpha and omega of corporate law in order to even talk to the lawyers. _He loved her deeply. She wa
examples: He was forced to learn the alpha and omega of corporate law in order to even talk to the lawyers.

alphabet soup.monolingual: initialisms and acronyms, especially when used excessively. _ The names of these government agencies are just alphabet soup. _Just look at the telephone book! You can’t find anything because it’s filled with alphabet soup.
examples: The names of these government agencies are just alphabet soup.

also-ran.monolingual: someone of no significance. (From horse racing, used of a horse that finishes a race but that does not finish among the money winners.) _ Oh, he’s just another also-ran. _ Ignore the also-rans.
examples: Oh, he’s just another also-ran.

alternate with something.monolingual: 1. [for someone] to serve as a substitute for someone. _I alternated with Fred as the lead in the school play. _ They asked Harry to alternate with Ron on the team.
examples: I alternated with Fred as the lead in the school play.

always chasing rainbows.monolingual: tending to look for something (more) exciting and (more) rewarding but without realistic expectations. _ He can’t seem to settle down and enjoy life. He’s always chasing rainbows.
examples: He can’t seem to settle down and enjoy life.

am i right?.monolingual: Inf. Isn’t that so? Right? (A way of demanding a response and stimulating further conversation.) _ John: Now, this is the kind of thing we should be doing. Am I right? Sue: Well, sure. I guess. _ Fred: You don’t want to do this for the rest of your l
examples: John: Now, this is the kind of thing we should be doing.

amalgamate something with something.monolingual: to unite something with something else; to merge two things. _We will amalgamate this company with another firm. _ How long has our local been amalgamated with the national union?
examples: We will amalgamate this company with another firm.

amalgamate with something.monolingual: to join with something; to merge with something. _ Our group decided to amalgamate with another group. _ The groups did not amalgamate after all.
examples: Our group decided to amalgamate with another group.

ambulance chaser.monolingual: a lawyer who hurries to the scene of an accident to try to get business from injured persons. _ The insurance companies are cracking down on ambulance chasers.
examples: The insurance companies are cracking down on ambulance chasers.

*american as apple pie.monolingual: Cliché quintessentially American. (*Also: as ~.) _ A small house with a white picket fence is supposed to be as American as apple pie.
examples: A small house with a white picket fence is supposed to be as American as apple pie.

amount to much.monolingual: to be as good as something; to be any good. _His fine plans don’t amount to much, since he won’t work for them. (Usually negative.) _ She’s a nice girl, but she’ll never amount to much.
examples: His fine plans don’t amount to much, since he won’t work for them.

amuse someone with something.monolingual: to entertain or interest someone with something. _ Try to amuse the child with this little toy. _She was able to amuse herself with the puzzle for a while.
examples: Try to amuse the child with this little toy.

ancient history.monolingual: Fig. someone or something from so long ago as to be completely forgotten or no longer important, as a former relationship. _ Bob? I never think about Bob anymore. He’s ancient history. _ His interest in joining the army is now ancient history.
examples: Bob? I never think about Bob anymore.

and all that jazz.monolingual: and all that stuff; and all that nonsense. _ I need some glue, paper, string, and all that jazz to make a kite. _ She told me I was selfish, hateful, rude, ugly, and all that jazz.
examples: I need some glue, paper, string, and all that jazz to make a kite.

and change.monolingual: plus a few cents; plus a few hundredths. (Used in citing a price or other decimal figure to indicate an additional fraction of a full unit.) _This one only costs ten bucks and change. _The New York Stock Exchange was up seven points and change for th
examples: This one only costs ten bucks and change.

and how!.monolingual: Inf. I agree! _ I am really excited you are here. And how! _ Bill: I am pleased you are here. Bob: Me, too! And how!
examples: I am really excited you are here.

and that’s a fact.monolingual: Fig. and that is true. (Used to emphasize a statement.) _John ain’t no friend of mine, and that’s a fact. _ I’ll be glad when this day is over, and that’s a fact.
examples: John ain’t no friend of mine, and that’s a fact.

and that’s that..monolingual: That is final and nothing more needs to be said. _ I refuse to go with you and that’s that!

and the like.monolingual: and other similar things. _ Whenever we go on a picnic, we take potato chips, hot dogs, soda pop, and the like. _I’m very tired of being yelled at, pushed around, and the like.
examples: Whenever we go on a picnic, we take potato chips, hot dogs, soda pop, and the like.

and then some.monolingual: and even more; and more than has been mentioned. _ John is going to have to run like a deer and then some to win this race. _ The cook put the amount of salt called for into the soup and then some.
examples: John is going to have to run like a deer and then some to win this race.

and this and that.monolingual: and more; and other miscellaneous things. _ Mom sent me some pillowcases, some sheets, a couple of blankets, and this and that. _ The repairman tightened some screws, fiddled with some bolts, and this and that.
examples: Mom sent me some pillowcases, some sheets, a couple of blankets, and this and that.

and what have you.monolingual: and more things; and other various things. _ Their garage is full of bikes, sleds, old boots, and what have you. _ The merchant sells writing paper, pens, string, and what have you.
examples: Their garage is full of bikes, sleds, old boots, and what have you.

angle for something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to fish for something, as with a fishhook and line. _ Fred was angling for a big bass. _ I am angling for whatever I can catch.
examples: Fred was angling for a big bass.

annex something to something.monolingual: [for a governmental body of a town or city] to attach a parcel of land onto an existing parcel of land through legal proceedings. _ The village annexed some adjacent land to itself. _ The adjoining lot was annexed to the site to allow for a bigger bu
examples: The village annexed some adjacent land to itself.

annex to something.monolingual: [for the owner of a parcel of land] to have land attached to an adjacent town or city. _ Our community doesn’t want to annex to Adamsville. _ The town voted to annex to the neighboring city of Smithton.
examples: Our community doesn’t want to annex to Adamsville.

announce something to someone.monolingual: to tell something publicly to someone. _ The president announced his nominee for attorney general to the media. _ When was the news announced to the public?
examples: The president announced his nominee for attorney general to the media.

anoint someone with something.monolingual: to pour or rub oil on a person’s head as an honor or blessing; to put a liquid onto oneself. (Mostly in biblical references.) _ They anointed the king with oil and praised him greatly. _ He anointed himself with a menthol rub that was meant to help h
examples: They anointed the king with oil and praised him greatly.

another country heard from.monolingual: Fig. yet another person adds to the conversation. Used when someone joins a discussion other people are having, especially unexpectedly. (Used sarcastically, implying that the new speaker is not welcome in the discussion.) _ Alan: You ought to take a
examples: Alan: You ought to take a vacation tomorrow.

answer for someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to speak for another person. _ I can’t answer for Chuck, but I do have my own opinion. _I will answer for my friend in his absence.
examples: I can’t answer for Chuck, but I do have my own opinion.

answer for someone or something.monolingual: Fig. to explain or justify the actions of someone or some act; to take responsibility or blame for someone or something. _ You will have to answer for your children’s bad behavior. _ I will answer only for my own misdeeds.
examples: You will have to answer for your children’s bad behavior.

answer the door.monolingual: Fig. [after hearing the doorbell or a knock] to go to the door to see who is there. _Would you please answer the door. I am busy. _I wish someone would answer the door. I can’t stand to hear the knocking.
examples: Would you please answer the door.

answer to someone.monolingual: 1. Fig. to explain or justify one’s actions to someone. (Usually with have to.) _If John can- not behave properly, he’ll have to answer to me. _ The car thief will have to answer to the judge.
examples: If John can- not behave properly, he’ll have to answer to me.

*ants in one’s pants.monolingual: Fig. nervousness and agitation. (on the image of someone suffering great discomfort as if having actual ants in the pants. *Typically: get ~; have ~; give one ~.) _I always get ants in my pants before a test. _ I wonder if all actors get ants in thei
examples: I always get ants in my pants before a test.

any fool thing.monolingual: any ridiculous thing; anything that should be viewed as unimportant. _ He’ll buy his wife any fool thing she wants. _ Bill can get distracted by any fool thing.
examples: He’ll buy his wife any fool thing she wants.

any old thing.monolingual: Fig. just anything, not necessarily old. _ Just give me one. I don’t care which. Just give me any old thing.
examples: Just give me one.

any port in a storm.monolingual: Fig. when one is having serious trouble, one must accept any solution, whether one likes the solution or not. _I don’t want to live with my parents, but it’s a case of any port in a storm. I can’t find an apartment I can afford. _ He hates his job, b
examples: I don’t want to live with my parents, but it’s a case of any port in a storm.

anything new down your way?.monolingual: Rur. Has any interesting event happened where you live? _ Bill: Anything new down your way? Bob: Nothing worth talking about. _ Mary: Hi, Sally. Anything new down your way? Sally: No, what’s new with you? Mary: Nothing much.
examples: Bill: Anything new down your way? Bob: Nothing worth talking about.

anything you say..monolingual: Fig. Yes.; I agree. _ Mary: Will you please take these blouses over to the cleaners? Bill: Sure, anything you say. _ Mother: You’re going to finish your homework before you watch TV, right? Child: Anything you say, Mom.
examples: Mary: Will you please take these blouses over to the cleaners? Bill: Sure, anything you say.

appeal against something.monolingual: to ask a court of appeals to change a ruling made by a lower court. _ My lawyer appealed against the judgment. _ We will file an appeal against the court ruling.
examples: My lawyer appealed against the judgment.

appeal to someone.monolingual: to please or attract someone. _ Fast food doesn’t appeal to me. _ The idea of a vacation to Florida this winter appeals to me a lot.
examples: Fast food doesn’t appeal to me.

appear as something.monolingual: 1. to act a certain part in a play, opera, etc. _ Madame Smith-Franklin appeared as Carmen at the City Opera last season. _ The actor refused to appear as a villain in the play.
examples: Madame Smith-Franklin appeared as Carmen at the City Opera last season.

appear at some place.monolingual: to perform at a particular place. _ She is appearing at the Bijou all month. _ I will appear at Carnegie Hall soon.
examples: She is appearing at the Bijou all month.

appear at some time.monolingual: to arrive at a particular time. _ I am due to appear at the council at noon. _ I will appear at the meeting whenever my plane gets in.
examples: I am due to appear at the council at noon.

appear before someone.monolingual: 1. to show up in the presence of someone, suddenly. _The deer appeared before us with no sound or other warning. _ A frightful specter appeared before me.
examples: The deer appeared before us with no sound or other warning.

appear before something.monolingual: to arrive in advance of the appointed time or before some event. _ Please appear at least ten minutes before you are due. _ It is best to appear shortly before the time of your interview.
examples: Please appear at least ten minutes before you are due.

appear for someone.monolingual: to represent or substitute for a person who is absent. _ I will appear for you in the council. _ Who is going to appear for my lawyer, who is ill?
examples: I will appear for you in the council.

appear in court.monolingual: to go to a court of law as a participant. _ She has to appear in court tomorrow. _ I have to appear in court for my traffic violation.
examples: She has to appear in court tomorrow.

appear in something.monolingual: 1. to be seen in some performance. _ The singer will appear in the opera with the rest of the chorus. _ I will appear in Aida.
examples: The singer will appear in the opera with the rest of the chorus.

appear to someone.monolingual: [for something] to make an appearance before someone. _My late grandmother appeared to me in a dream.
examples: My late grandmother appeared to me in a dream.

appear to someone that....monolingual: Fig. to seem to someone that... _ It appears to me that you are always late.
examples: It appears to me that you are always late.

appearances can be deceiving..monolingual: Prov. Things can look different from the way they really are. _ Edward seems like a very nice boy, but appearances can be deceiving. _ Jane may look like she doesn’t understand you, but she’s really extremely bright. Appearances can be deceiving.
examples: Edward seems like a very nice boy, but appearances can be deceiving.

appertain to something.monolingual: [of a responsibility or privilege] to belong to something as a right. _Do these rights appertain to a third cousin of the deceased? _ The statement doesn’t make sense. It appertains to no one as it is stated.
examples: The statement doesn’t make sense.

the apple of someone’s eye.monolingual: Fig. someone’s favorite person or thing; a boyfriend or a girlfriend. _Tom is the apple of Mary’s eye. She thinks he’s the greatest. _ John’s new car is the apple of his eye.
examples: Tom is the apple of Mary’s eye.

apple-polisher.monolingual: Fig. a flatterer. _ Doesn’t that wimpy apple-polisher know how stupid he looks? _ Everybody at my office seems to be an apple-polisher but me.
examples: Everybody at my office seems to be an apple-polisher but me.

apples and oranges.monolingual: Fig. two entities that are not similar. (Used especially in reference to comparisons of unlike things.) _ You can’t talk about Fred and Ted in the same breath! They’re like apples and oranges. _Talking about her current book and her previous bestsell
examples: You can’t talk about Fred and Ted in the same breath! They’re like apples and oranges.

apply oneself to something.monolingual: to work hard and diligently at something. _ You should apply yourself to your studies. _ She applied herself to her work and the time passed very rapidly.
examples: You should apply yourself to your studies.

apply something to something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to put something onto the surface of something. _ Apply the decal to the surface of the glass. _Apply the paint evenly to each surface.
examples: Apply the decal to the surface of the glass.

apply to someone or something.monolingual: [for rules, laws, etc.] to affect someone or something; to be relevant to someone or something. _ Does this rule apply to me? _ These policies apply only to very large companies.
examples: These policies apply only to very large companies.

apply within.monolingual: to ask about something [inside some place]. (Usually part of a sign or announcement posted outside a place.) _The sign outside the office read,“Apply within.” _If you are interested in working here, please apply within.
examples: The sign outside the office read,“Apply within.

appoint someone to something.monolingual: to select or assign someone to serve in a particular role. (Usually focusing on the role of the person or on a group of persons with similar roles.) _ I am going to appoint you to the position of treasurer. _ Fred tried to appoint himself to the boar
examples: I am going to appoint you to the position of treasurer.

appraise something at something.monolingual: to study something and place a monetary value on it. _ They appraised the house at twice what it is worth. _The diamond ring was appraised at a very high price.
examples: They appraised the house at twice what it is worth.

apprentice someone to someone.monolingual: to assign someone to work at a certain trade and learn it from someone experienced. _ She apprenticed her son to a local diesel mechanic. _ I apprenticed myself to a printer and learned what it means to get really dirty.
examples: She apprenticed her son to a local diesel mechanic.

apprise someone of something.monolingual: to inform someone of something. _I hope you will apprise me of any change. _Have you been apprised of the new rule?
examples: I hope you will apprise me of any change.

appropriate something for something.monolingual: 1. to allot a certain amount of money for a particular purpose. _ They will appropriate $10,000 for the exhibit at the fair. _ A large sum was appropriated for the expenses.
examples: They will appropriate $10,000 for the exhibit at the fair.

approve of someone or something.monolingual: to take a favorable view of someone or something. _I approve of the way you have remodeled the kitchen. _ I don’t approve of your foul language.
examples: I approve of the way you have remodeled the kitchen.

april showers bring may flowers..monolingual: Prov. Although rain in April is annoying, it starts the flowers growing. _ Child: I hate all this rain. Why does it have to rain? Mother: April showers bring May f lowers. _ Although it was a dreary, rainy day, we felt cheerful, since April showers b
examples: Child: I hate all this rain.

arbitrate in a dispute.monolingual: to mediate or negotiate a settlement in a dispute. _ She refuses to arbitrate in this dispute. _ I will arbitrate in this little disagreement.
examples: She refuses to arbitrate in this dispute.

arch over someone or something.monolingual: to bend or curve over someone or something; to stand or remain bent or curved over someone or something. _The trees arched gracefully over the walkway. _A lovely bower of roses arched over the bride.
examples: The trees arched gracefully over the walkway.

argue against someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for someone] to make a case against someone or something; to oppose the choice of someone or something in an argument. _ I am preparing myself to argue against the case. _Liz argued against Tom as the new president, but we chose him anyway.
examples: I am preparing myself to argue against the case.

argue back.monolingual: to argue with or oppose someone; to answer back (to someone); to talk back (to someone). (Usually said of persons who are supposed to listen and obey without comment.) _ Please don’t argue back all the time. _ I wish you children did not argue back s
examples: Please don’t argue back all the time.

argue for someone or something.monolingual: to make a case in favor of someone or something; to speak on behalf of someone or something in an argument. _ Are you prepared to argue strongly for this proposal? _ We will argue for our candidate in the debate.
examples: We will argue for our candidate in the debate.

argue someone down†.monolingual: to defeat someone in a debate. _ Sally could always argue him down if she had to. _She tries to argue down everyone she meets.
examples: Sally could always argue him down if she had to.

argue someone into doing something.monolingual: to convince or persuade someone to do something. _ She was unable to argue the manager into attending. _ She was unable to argue herself into doing something so unpleasant.
examples: She was unable to argue the manager into attending.

argue something down†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to reduce something, such as a bill or a price, by arguing. _ I tried to argue the price down, but it did no good. _ Tom could not argue down the bill.
examples: I tried to argue the price down, but it did no good.

argue something out†.monolingual: to settle something by discussing all the important points. _We are going to have to argue this out some other time. _Must we argue out every single detail of this contract?
examples: We are going to have to argue this out some other time.

argue with something.monolingual: to challenge or dispute something; to dispute someone’s statement of fact. _ I won’t argue with your conclusions. _ It is not a good idea to argue with the facts.
examples: I won’t argue with your conclusions.

*arm in arm.monolingual: Fig. [of persons] linked or hooked together by the arms. (*Typically: go ~; stroll ~; walk ~.) _ The two lovers walked arm in arm down the street. _They skated arm in arm around the rink.
examples: The two lovers walked arm in arm down the street.

*armed and dangerous.monolingual: Cliché [of someone who is suspected of a crime] having a gun or other lethal weapon and not being reluctant to use it. (This is part of a warning to police officers who might try to capture an armed suspect. *Typically: be ~; be regarded as ~; be pre
examples: The murderer is at large, presumed to be armed and dangerous.

armed to the teeth.monolingual: Fig. heavily armed with deadly weapons. _ The bank robber was armed to the teeth when he was caught. _ There are too many guns around. The entire country is armed to the teeth.
examples: The bank robber was armed to the teeth when he was caught.

arouse someone from something.monolingual: to activate a person out of a state of rest, sleep, or inaction. _ I could not arouse her from her sleep. _She aroused herself from a deep sleep.
examples: I could not arouse her from her sleep.

arrange for something.monolingual: to prepare or plan for something. _ We will arrange for a celebration. _ John arranged for it.
examples: We will arrange for a celebration.

arrange some music for something.monolingual: to prepare or adapt music for particular instruments or for a particular musical key. _ Paul arranged the piece for piano. _ This piece was arranged for the guitar by Frank’s brother.
examples: Paul arranged the piece for piano.

arrange something for some time.monolingual: to plan something for a particular time. _ We will arrange a picnic for the afternoon. _ I will arrange an appointment for the noon hour.
examples: We will arrange a picnic for the afternoon.

as a last resort.monolingual: as the last choice; if everything else fails. _ Call me at home only as a last resort. _ As a last resort, the doctor will perform surgery.
examples: Call me at home only as a last resort.

as a matter of course.monolingual: normally; as a normal procedure. _ The nurse takes your temperature as a matter of course. _ You are expected to make your own bed as a matter of course.
examples: The nurse takes your temperature as a matter of course.

as a matter of fact.monolingual: actually; in addition to what has been said; in reference to what has been said. _ As a matter of fact, John came into the room while you were talking about him. _ I’m not a poor worker. As a matter of fact, I’m very efficient.
examples: As a matter of fact, John came into the room while you were talking about him.

as a rule.monolingual: in general; usually. _As a rule, men should wear tuxedos at formal dinners. _ As a rule, the bus picks me up at 7:30 every morning.
examples: As a rule, men should wear tuxedos at formal dinners.

as all get out.monolingual: Rur. very much; as much as can be. _ I’m tired as all get out.
examples: I’m tired as all get out.

as an aside.monolingual: [said] as a comment that is not supposed to be heard by everyone. _ At the wedding, Tom said as an aside, “The bride doesn’t look well.” _ At the ballet, Billy said as an aside to his mother, “I hope the dancers fall off the stage!”
examples: At the wedding, Tom said as an aside, “The bride doesn’t look well.

as bad as all that.monolingual: as bad as reported; as bad as it seems. (Usually expressed in the negative.) _ Come on! Nothing could be as bad as all that. _ Stop crying. It can’t be as bad as all that.
examples: Come on! Nothing could be as bad as all that.

as far as it goes.monolingual: as much as something does, covers, or accomplishes. (Usually said of something that is inadequate.) _ Your plan is fine as far as it goes. It doesn’t seem to take care of everything, though. _ As far as it goes, this law is a good one. It should set
examples: Your plan is fine as far as it goes.

as good as one’s word.monolingual: obedient to one’s promise; dependable in keeping one’s promises. _ He was as good as his word. He lent me the books as he said he would. _ She said she would babysit and she was as good as her word.
examples: He was as good as his word.

as i live and breathe!.monolingual: Fig. How amazing! (Said on seeing or experiencing something surprising.) _As I live and breathe, here we are again! _ Well, as I live and breathe, it’s Harry Smith!

as it is.monolingual: the way things are; the way it is now. _ “I wish I could get a better job,” remarked Tom. “I’m just getting by as it is.” _ Mary: Can we afford a new refrigerator? Fred: As it is, it would have to be a very small one.
examples: “I wish I could get a better job,” remarked Tom.

as it were.monolingual: as one might say; as could be said. (Sometimes used to qualify an assertion that may not sound reasonable.) _ He carefully constructed, as it were, a huge submarine sandwich. _ The Franklins live in a small and, as it were, exquisite house.
examples: He carefully constructed, as it were, a huge submarine sandwich.

as luck would have it.monolingual: by good or bad luck; as it turned out; by chance. _ As luck would have it, we had a f lat tire. _ As luck would have it, the check came in the mail today.
examples: As luck would have it, we had a f lat tire.

as such.monolingual: in the way something is; as someone or something is. _I cannot accept your manuscript as such. It needs revisions. _ You are new to this job, and as such, I will have to train you.
examples: I cannot accept your manuscript as such.

as usual.monolingual: as is the normal or typical situation. _ John ordered eggs for breakfast, as usual. _ He stood quietly as usual, waiting for the bus to come.
examples: John ordered eggs for breakfast, as usual.

as well.monolingual: also; in addition. _ Could I have a second helping of potatoes as well? _ I’m feeling tired, and dizzy as well.
examples: I’m feeling tired, and dizzy as well.

aside from someone or something.monolingual: not including someone or something. _ Aside from a small bank account, I have no money at all. _ Aside from Mary, Nancy, Craig, and Phil, I have no friends on campus.
examples: Aside from a small bank account, I have no money at all.

ask after someone.monolingual: to inquire about the health and wellbeing of someone. _Hermione asked after you when I saw her today. _ I asked after Molly and her family.
examples: Hermione asked after you when I saw her today.

ask for someone or something.monolingual: to request someone or something; to ask that someone come forth. _ The police are at the door asking for Henry. _ The child asked for a glass of water.
examples: The police are at the door asking for Henry.

ask for the moon.monolingual: Fig. to make outlandish requests or demands for something, such as a lot of money or special privileges. _ She’s asking for the moon, and she’s not going to get it. _ Don’t ask for the moon. Be reasonable!
examples: She’s asking for the moon, and she’s not going to get it.

ask someone back.monolingual: 1. [for a host or hostess] to invite someone to come again (at a later time or to another similar event). _ After the way you behaved, they’ll never ask us back. _ They had been asked back a number of times, but they never came.
examples: After the way you behaved, they’ll never ask us back.

ask someone down†.monolingual: to invite someone to come to one’s home [for a visit]. (Usually said when someone must go to a lower level, travel south, down a hill, or into the country for the visit.) _Sam asked us down for Friday evening. Shall we go? _We asked down some old fri
examples: Sam asked us down for Friday evening.

ask someone over.monolingual: to invite someone who lives close by to come to one’s home [for a visit]. (Either to a house or apartment.) _Can we ask Tom over? _He has been asked over a number of times.
examples: He has been asked over a number of times.

ask someone up†.monolingual: to ask someone to come to one’s home for a visit. (Usually said when someone must travel north, up a hill, or to an apartment on a higher floor for the visit.) _ Let’s ask Judy up for the weekend. _ We asked up a few old friends.
examples: Let’s ask Judy up for the weekend.

asking price.monolingual: the price that someone puts on an item being offered for sale. _ I think your asking price is a little high.
examples: I think your asking price is a little high.

*asleep at the switch.monolingual: Fig. not attending to one’s job; failing to do one’s duty at the proper time. (Alludes to a technician or engineer on a train sleeping instead of turning whatever switches are required. *Typically: be ~; fall ~.) _The security guard fell asleep at th
examples: The security guard fell asleep at the switch and a robber broke in.

aspire to something.monolingual: to seek or aim for something better. _ She aspires to a job more challenging than her current position. _ I aspire to far greater things.
examples: She aspires to a job more challenging than her current position.

assail someone with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to attack someone with something, such as a weapon. _ The crook assailed the officer with the officer’s own club. _The riot police were assailed with stones and bottles.
examples: The crook assailed the officer with the officer’s own club.

assault and battery.monolingual: a violent attack [upon someone] followed by a beating. (A technical legal charge.) _ Richard was charged with two counts of assault and battery. _ Dave does not go out at night because he does not want to be a victim of assault and battery.
examples: Richard was charged with two counts of assault and battery.

assault the ear.monolingual: Fig. [for sound or speech] to be very loud or persistent. _That loud music assaults the ears! _I can’t hear you with all that traffic noise assaulting my ears.
examples: I can’t hear you with all that traffic noise assaulting my ears.

assent to something.monolingual: to agree to something. _ I assent to what you suggest. _ She will not assent to our request.
examples: I assent to what you suggest.

assess something at something.monolingual: to estimate or value something at some figure. _ They assess the value of our house at half what it would sell for. _ The house was assessed at far more than its true worth.
examples: They assess the value of our house at half what it would sell for.

assign something to someone.monolingual: to attribute something to someone; to blame something on someone. _ We were forced to assign the blame to Robert. _ They assigned the responsibility for the accident to the driver of the car.
examples: We were forced to assign the blame to Robert.

assimilate with some people.monolingual: to join or mix in with people and become accepted by them. _ It’s easy for Karen to assimilate with new people. _ I want to assimilate rapidly with the other people in my class.
examples: It’s easy for Karen to assimilate with new people.

assist in something.monolingual: to help with something. _May I assist in this? _ Please assist in this task.
examples: Please assist in this task.

assist someone in something.monolingual: to help a particular person working on a task. _ Please assist Greg in the committee’s assignment. _ We assisted him in the whole procedure.
examples: Please assist Greg in the committee’s assignment.

associate with someone.monolingual: to be friendly with someone; to be acquainted with someone socially in a work setting. _ We seek to associate with persons like ourselves. _ I like to associate with interesting people.
examples: We seek to associate with persons like ourselves.

assume liability for something.monolingual: to accept the responsibility for paying a cost. _ Mr. Smith assumed liability for his son’s student loans. _ The store assumed liability for the injured customer’s hospital bills.
examples: Mr. Smith assumed liability for his son’s student loans.

assure someone of something.monolingual: to guarantee something to someone; to promise someone that something will happen or that a particular state exists. _I want to assure you of our good intentions. _Frequently, she had to assure herself of her basic worth.
examples: I want to assure you of our good intentions.

astound someone with something.monolingual: to shock or amaze someone with something. _ She astounded us with her skill. _ He astounded himself with his sudden burst of strength.
examples: She astounded us with her skill.

at a dead end.monolingual: Fig. having reached an impasse; able to go no further forward. _ I can’t go on. I’m at a dead end. _ We are at a dead end; the project is hopelessly stalled.
examples: I can’t go on. I’m at a dead end.

at a premium.monolingual: at a high price; priced high because of something special. _ Sally bought the shoes at a premium because they were of very high quality. _ This new sports car sells at a premium because so many people want to buy it.
examples: Sally bought the shoes at a premium because they were of very high quality.

at a set time.monolingual: at a particular time; at an assigned time. _ Each person has to show up at a set time. _ Do I have to be there at a set time, or can I come whenever I want?
examples: Each person has to show up at a set time.

at a sitting.monolingual: at one time; during one period. (Usually refers to an activity that takes place while a person is seated.) _ The restaurant could feed only sixty people at a sitting. _ I can read about three hundred pages at a sitting.
examples: The restaurant could feed only sixty people at a sitting.

at a stretch.monolingual: continuously; without stopping. _We all had to do eight hours of duty at a stretch. _ The baby doesn’t sleep for more than three hours at a stretch.
examples: We all had to do eight hours of duty at a stretch.

at all times.monolingual: constantly; continuously. _ You must keep your passport handy at all times when you are traveling in a foreign country. _ When you’re in a crowd, you must watch your child at all times.
examples: You must keep your passport handy at all times when you are traveling in a foreign country.

at an early date.monolingual: soon; some day soon. _ The note said, “Please call me at an early date.” _ You are expected to return the form to the office at an early date.
examples: The note said, “Please call me at an early date.

at an end.monolingual: having come to a stop; having reached the end. _ Things are now at an end. _ It’s over between us. It’s at an end. Good-bye.
examples: Things are now at an end.

at any rate.monolingual: in any case; anyway. _ At any rate, what were we talking about? _ At any rate, I don’t think you should quit your job.
examples: At any rate, I don’t think you should quit your job.

*at bay.monolingual: Fig. at a distance. (*Typically: be ~; keep someone or something ~; remain ~.) _I have to keep the bill collectors at bay until I get my paycheck. _The mosquitoes will not remain at bay for very long.
examples: I have to keep the bill collectors at bay until I get my paycheck.

at close range.monolingual: very near; in close proximity. (Usually used in regard to shooting.) _The hunter fired at the deer at close range. _ The powder burns tell us that the gun was fired at close range.
examples: The hunter fired at the deer at close range.

at cross-purposes.monolingual: with opposing viewpoints; with goals that interfere with each other. _ We are arguing at crosspurposes. We aren’t even discussing the same thing. _ Bill and Tom are working at cross-purposes. They’ll never get the job done right.
examples: We are arguing at crosspurposes.

at death’s door.monolingual: very near the end of one’s life. (Often an exaggeration.) _ I was so ill that I was at death’s door for three days. _ The family dog was at death’s door for three days, and then it finally died.
examples: I was so ill that I was at death’s door for three days.

at ease.monolingual: without worry or anxiety. _ The performer is at ease on the stage. _ After she had met a few people, Mary felt at ease with the group.
examples: The performer is at ease on the stage.

at every turn.monolingual: everywhere; everywhere one looks. _There is a new problem at every turn. _Life holds exciting adventures at every turn.
examples: There is a new problem at every turn.

at face value.monolingual: from outward appearance; from what something first appears to be. (From the value printed on the “face” of a coin or bank note.) _Don’t just accept her offer at face value. Think of the implications. _Joan tends to take people at face value and so sh
examples: Don’t just accept her offer at face value.

at fault.monolingual: to blame [for something]; serving as the cause of something bad. _ I was not at fault in the accident. You cannot blame me.
examples: I was not at fault in the accident.

at first.monolingual: initially; at the very beginning. _ He was shy at first. Then he became more friendly. _At first we chose the red one. Later we switched to the blue one.
examples: He was shy at first.

at first light.monolingual: at dawn; when the first light of dawn appears. _ We will be ready to leave at first light.
examples: We will be ready to leave at first light.

*at full blast.monolingual: using full power; as loudly as possible. (*Typically: be on ~; play ~; play something ~; run ~; run something ~.) _ The neighbors had their televisions on at full blast. _ The car radio was on at full blast. We couldn’t hear what the driver was sayin
examples: The neighbors had their televisions on at full blast.

at full strength.monolingual: at the strongest amount, dilution, power, loudness, etc. _ You should use this medicine at full strength, even if it tastes bad.
examples: You should use this medicine at full strength, even if it tastes bad.

*at great length.monolingual: for a long period of time. (*Typically: explain ~; question someone ~; speak ~.) _ The lawyer questioned the witness at great length.
examples: The lawyer questioned the witness at great length.

at hand.monolingual: close by in time or space. _I don’t happen to have your application at hand at the moment. _ With the holiday season at hand, everyone is very excited.
examples: I don’t happen to have your application at hand at the moment.

at hazard.monolingual: in danger; at risk. _ He is not willing to have much of his money at hazard in the stock market. _ Your life is at hazard unless you wear a helmet when you ride your motorcycle.
examples: He is not willing to have much of his money at hazard in the stock market.

at home.monolingual: at or in one’s dwelling. _ Is Mary at home, or is she still at work? _ What time will she be at home?

at it again.monolingual: doing something again. _ I asked Tom to stop playing his trumpet, but he’s at it again. _ They are at it again. Why are they always fighting?
examples: I asked Tom to stop playing his trumpet, but he’s at it again.

at large.monolingual: 1. free; uncaptured. (Usually said of criminals not in custody.) _At noon, the day after the robbery, the thieves were still at large. _There is a murderer at large in the city!
examples: At noon, the day after the robbery, the thieves were still at large.

at last.monolingual: finally; after a long wait. _ The train has come at last. _ At last, we have gotten something to eat.
examples: The train has come at last.

at least.monolingual: anyway; in spite of difficulties. _ At least we had a good evening, even though the afternoon was rainy. _ At least we came away with some of our money left.
examples: At least we had a good evening, even though the afternoon was rainy.

at least so many.monolingual: no less than; no fewer than. _There were at least four people there that I knew. _ I want to spend at least three weeks in Mexico.
examples: There were at least four people there that I knew.

at liberty.monolingual: free; unrestrained. _The criminal was set at liberty by the judge. _ You’re at liberty to go anywhere you wish. _ I’m not at liberty to discuss the matter.
examples: The criminal was set at liberty by the judge.

*at loose ends.monolingual: restless and unsettled; unemployed. (*Typically: be ~; leave someone ~.) _ Just before school starts, all the children are at loose ends. _ Jane has been at loose ends ever since she lost her job.
examples: Just before school starts, all the children are at loose ends.

at night.monolingual: during the night. _ Most people sleep at night. _ Mary studies at night.
examples: Most people sleep at night.

at once.monolingual: immediately; right now. _We must leave at once! _ You must come here at once; it is an emergency.
examples: You must come here at once; it is an emergency.

at one’s wit ’s end.monolingual: Fig. at the limits of one’s mental resources. _ I’m at my wit’s end with this problem. I cannot figure it out. _ Tom could do no more. He was at his wit’s end.
examples: I’m at my wit’s end with this problem.

at peace.monolingual: 1. relaxed and happy. _ I am always at peace when I sit in my rocking chair. _ When the warm breeze is blowing, I am at peace.
