examples: I am always at peace when I sit in my rocking chair.

at play.monolingual: [at this moment] involved in playing. _ The children are at play, and I am doing household chores. _ Whether I am at work or at play, I try to be pleasant to people.
examples: The children are at play, and I am doing household chores.

at present.monolingual: now; at this point in time. _ We are not able to do any more at present. _ We may be able to lend you money next week, but not at present.
examples: We are not able to do any more at present.

at random.monolingual: by chance; haphazard. _ The lottery numbers are chosen at random. _ As a prank, the children dialed phone numbers at random.
examples: The lottery numbers are chosen at random.

at regular intervals.monolingual: [of things in a series] at points that are equally distant from each other. _ You will find service stations at regular intervals along the highway. _There are street lights at regular intervals on the main street of town.
examples: You will find service stations at regular intervals along the highway.

at rest.monolingual: 1. not moving; not active. _ After the hectic day, the office was finally at rest at 8:00 p.m. _ When the car is at rest, you can get into the backseat.
examples: After the hectic day, the office was finally at rest at 8:00 p.

*at risk.monolingual: in a situation where there is risk or hazard; in danger. (*Typically: be ~; put someone or something ~.) _ I refuse to put my family’s welfare at risk by quitting my job. _ Your whole future is at risk if you don’t stop smoking.
examples: I refuse to put my family’s welfare at risk by quitting my job.

at sea.monolingual: 1. Lit. on the sea; away on a voyage on the ocean. _The ship is at sea now, and you can’t disembark. _I spent many happy days at sea on my cruise.
examples: The ship is at sea now, and you can’t disembark.

at sea level.monolingual: at the level of the surface of the ocean. _ It is easier to breathe at sea level than in the mountains. _ Boats on the ocean are at sea level, but those on rivers are not.
examples: It is easier to breathe at sea level than in the mountains.

at sixes and sevens.monolingual: lost in bewilderment; at loose ends. _ Mrs. Smith is at sixes and sevens since the death of her husband. _Bill is always at sixes and sevens when he’s home by himself.
examples: Mrs. Smith is at sixes and sevens since the death of her husband.

at some time sharp.monolingual: exactly at the time named. _ You must be here at noon sharp. _ The plane is expected to arrive at seven forty-five sharp.
examples: You must be here at noon sharp.

at someone’s beck and call.monolingual: ready to obey someone. _ What makes you think I wait around here at your beck and call? I have to leave for work, you know! _ It was a fine hotel. There were dozens of maids and waiters at our beck and call.
examples: It was a fine hotel.

at someone’s earliest convenience.monolingual: as soon as it is possible for someone to do something. (This is also a polite way of saying immediately.) _ Please stop by my office at your earliest convenience. _Bill, please have the oil changed at your earliest convenience.
examples: Please stop by my office at your earliest convenience.

at someone’s request.monolingual: due to someone’s request; on being asked by someone. _At his mother’s request, Tom stopped playing the saxophone. _ At the request of the police officer, Bill pulled his car over to the side of the road.
examples: At his mother’s request, Tom stopped playing the saxophone.

at someone’s service.monolingual: Fig. ready to help someone in any way. _ The count greeted me warmly and said, “Welcome to my home. Just let me know what you need. I’m at your service.” _ The desk clerk said, “Good morning, madam. I’m at your service.”
examples: The count greeted me warmly and said, “Welcome to my home.

at stake.monolingual: Fig. ready to be won or lost; at risk; hanging in the balance. _ That’s a very risky investment. How much money is at stake? _I have everything at stake on this wager.
examples: That’s a very risky investment.

at that rate.monolingual: in that manner; at that speed. _If things keep progressing at that rate, we’ll be rich by next year. _At that rate we’ll never get the money that is owed us.
examples: If things keep progressing at that rate, we’ll be rich by next year.

at the appointed time.monolingual: at the expected or assigned time. _The cab pulled up in the driveway at the appointed time. _ We all met at the hotel at the appointed time.
examples: The cab pulled up in the driveway at the appointed time.

at the eleventh hour.monolingual: Fig. at the last possible moment. (Just before the last clock hour, 12) _ She always turned her term papers in at the eleventh hour. _ We don’t worry about death until the eleventh hour.
examples: She always turned her term papers in at the eleventh hour.

at the end of nowhere.monolingual: Fig. at a remote place; at some distance from civilization. (An exaggeration.) _They live way out in the country at the end of nowhere. _ The police will never find us here, at the end of nowhere.
examples: They live way out in the country at the end of nowhere.

at the height of something.monolingual: Fig. at the most intense or forceful aspect of something. _At the height of his career, Tom was known around the world. _ At the height of the party, there were 50 people present.
examples: At the height of his career, Tom was known around the world.

at the last gasp.monolingual: Fig. at the very last; at the last chance; at the last minute. (Refers to someone’s last breath before death.) _ She finally showed up at the last gasp, bringing the papers that were needed. _We got there at the last gasp, just before our names were
examples: She finally showed up at the last gasp, bringing the papers that were needed.

at the last minute.monolingual: Fig. at the last possible chance; in the last few minutes, hours, or days. (Often an exaggeration.) _Please don’t make reservations at the last minute. _Why do you ask all your questions at the last minute?
examples: Please don’t make reservations at the last minute.

at the latest.monolingual: not beyond the time mentioned. _ Please pay this bill in ten days at the latest. _I’ll be home by midnight at the latest.
examples: Please pay this bill in ten days at the latest.

at the outset.monolingual: Fig. at the very beginning. _ At the outset, we were told everything we had to do. _I learned at the outset of the project that I was to lead it.
examples: At the outset, we were told everything we had to do.

at the rear of something.monolingual: located at the back part of something. _I keep my tools at the rear of my garage. _There’s a stream at the rear of my property.
examples: I keep my tools at the rear of my garage.

at the same time.monolingual: 1. Lit. during the same moment; simultaneously. _ We arrived at the same time. _ Too many things are happening at the same time, and I am confused.
examples: We arrived at the same time.

at the wheel.monolingual: 1. operating the wheel that turns a ship’s rudder; at the helm. _The cabin boy was at the wheel with the captain close by.
examples: The cabin boy was at the wheel with the captain close by.

at the zenith of something.monolingual: Fig. at the highest point of something; at the pinnacle of something. _ Tragically, at the zenith of his career, the teacher died suddenly. _ The scientist was at the zenith of her career when she made her discovery. avenge at this juncture at this p
examples: Tragically, at the zenith of his career, the teacher died suddenly.

at this rate.monolingual: at this speed; if things continue in the same way. (Usually of a pessimistic view.) _ Hurry up! We’ll never get there at this rate. _ At this rate, all the food will be gone before we get there.
examples: Hurry up! We’ll never get there at this rate.

at will.monolingual: whenever one wants; freely. _ You’re free to come and go at will. _ The soldiers were told to fire their guns at will. _ You can eat anything you want at will.
examples: You’re free to come and go at will.

at work.monolingual: 1. at one’s place of work. _ I’m sorry to call you at work, but this is important. _ She’s at work now. She’ll be home at supper time.
examples: I’m sorry to call you at work, but this is important.

atone for something.monolingual: to make amends for an error. _ You must atone for the bad things you have done.
examples: You must atone for the bad things you have done.

attach oneself to someone.monolingual: 1. Fig. to become emotionally involved with someone. _ Fred seems to have attached himself to a much older woman, who has captured his attention. _ Somehow, Susan has attached herself emotionally to Tom, and she is distraught over his being away.
examples: Fred seems to have attached himself to a much older woman, who has captured his attention.

attach oneself to something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to connect or secure oneself to something. _ During the storm, Tony attached himself to the helm and proceeded to steer the boat. _ The caterpillar attached itself to a branch and began to spin its cocoon.
examples: During the storm, Tony attached himself to the helm and proceeded to steer the boat.

attach to someone.monolingual: Fig. [for blame, importance, guilt, fault, etc.] to become “fixed” onto someone or an organization. _A lot of guilt attaches to Henry for his part in the plot. _ Most of the blame for the accident attaches to Roger.
examples: A lot of guilt attaches to Henry for his part in the plot.

attach to something.monolingual: [for something] to be meant to fit onto or into something. _ This one attaches to this other one right at this point. _ This part should have attached to the back of the desk, but it didn’t fit.
examples: This one attaches to this other one right at this point.

attached to someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. connected to someone or something. _The patient has a tube attached to his arm. _ A little shelf is attached to the wall.
examples: The patient has a tube attached to his arm.

attend to someone.monolingual: to listen to someone. _ Please attend to your teacher’s instructions. _ Attend to the announcement of the new f light departure time.
examples: Please attend to your teacher’s instructions.

attend to someone or something.monolingual: to take care of the needs of someone or something; to respond to a request or demand from someone or something. _ Please attend to your wounded friend. _ Would you please attend to the action points of this memo?
examples: Please attend to your wounded friend.

attest to something.monolingual: to certify or bear witness to a fact. _ I cannot attest to what you have reported. _ The witness attested to the suspect’s presence at the scene of the crime.
examples: I cannot attest to what you have reported.

attire someone in something.monolingual: to dress someone in something. _ The mother attired her children in new, clean clothes. _ She attired herself in her finest garments.
examples: The mother attired her children in new, clean clothes.

auction something off†.monolingual: to sell something [to the highest bidder] at an auction. _ He auctioned his home off. _ He auctioned off his home. _ The duke was forced to auction off his ancestral home to pay his taxes.
examples: He auctioned his home off.

audition for something.monolingual: to try out for a part in something. (In a setting in which one’s singing, speaking, or playing is heard and judged.) _ I plan to audition for the lead role in the school play. _ Liz auditioned for The Mikado.
examples: I plan to audition for the lead role in the school play.

audition someone for something.monolingual: to allow someone to try out for a part in a performance; to judge someone’s singing, speaking, or playing potential for a part in a performance. _Will you audition anyone else for the part? _ Have you been auditioned for a part in the school play?

avail oneself of something.monolingual: to help oneself by making use of something that is available. _We availed ourselves of Tom’s goodwill and let him repair the fence. _ The campers availed themselves of the first chance in a week to take a shower.
examples: We availed ourselves of Tom’s goodwill and let him repair the fence.

avenue of escape.monolingual: Fig. the pathway or route along which someone or something escapes. _ The open window was the bird’s only avenue of escape from the house. _ Bill saw that his one avenue of escape was through the back door.
examples: The open window was the bird’s only avenue of escape from the house.

average something up†.monolingual: to calculate the average of a set of figures. _ Please add these figures and average them up. _ Please average up all the monthly expenses for the previous year. _ Will you please average these figures up on the calculator?
examples: Please add these figures and average them up.

*away from it all.monolingual: at a place where one can avoid completely what one is leaving behind. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _I need a few days off to get away from it all. _Everyone needs to get away from it all every now and then.
examples: I need a few days off to get away from it all.

*away from one’s desk.monolingual: Fig. not available for a telephone conversation; not available to be seen or spoken to. (Sometimes said by the person who answers a telephone in an office. It means that the person whom the caller wants is not immediately available due to personal or
examples: I’m sorry, but Ann is away from her desk just now.

a babe in arms.monolingual: 1. Lit. a very young baby that is carried by an adult. _I have known that since I was a babe in arms! _ A young mother with a babe in arms stood in line with the rest of the students.
examples: A young mother with a babe in arms stood in line with the rest of the students.

a babe in the woods.monolingual: Fig. a naive or innocent person; an inexperienced person. (Like a child lost in the woods.) _ Bill is a babe in the woods when it comes to dealing with plumbers. _ As a painter, Mary is fine, but she’s a babe in the woods as a musician.
examples: Bill is a babe in the woods when it comes to dealing with plumbers.

back and fill.monolingual: Fig. to act indecisively; to change one’s direction repeatedly; to reverse one’s course. (Originally nautical, referring to trimming the sails so as to alternately fill them with wind and release the wind, in order to maneuver in a narrow space.) _ T
examples: The president spent most of his speech backing and filling on the question of taxation.

back and forth.monolingual: in one direction and then the other repeatedly; from one place to another repeatedly. _ We tossed the ball back and forth between us. _The tiger paced back and forth in its cage.
examples: We tossed the ball back and forth between us.

back east.monolingual: to or from the eastern United States, especially the northeastern or New England states. (Used even by people who have never been in the East.) _ Sally felt that she had to get back East for a few days. _Tom went to school back East, but his brother
examples: Sally felt that she had to get back East for a few days.

back into someone or something.monolingual: to move backwards, bumping into someone or something; to move a car backwards into something, such as a garage or a parking space. _ I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to back into you. _ I backed into the potted plant.
examples: I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to back into you.

the back of the beyond.monolingual: the most remote place; somewhere very remote. _ John hardly ever comes to the city. He lives at the back of the beyond. _Mary likes city life, but her husband likes to live in the back of the beyond.
examples: John hardly ever comes to the city.

*back on one’s feet.monolingual: 1. Lit. standing up again after a fall. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ She struggled to get back on her feet after she fell.
examples: She struggled to get back on her feet after she fell.

*back on track.monolingual: Fig. running according to schedule again. (*Typically: get ~; get something ~; have something ~; put something ~.) _ I hope we can have this project back on track by the end of the week.
examples: I hope we can have this project back on track by the end of the week.

back oneself into a corner.monolingual: Fig. to manage to get oneself into a position where there is limited escape. (Ranging from literal to figurative.) _He tells different stories to different people. Finally he backed himself into a corner and had to admit his lies.
examples: He tells different stories to different people.

back onto someone or something.monolingual: to go backwards, moving or rolling onto someone or something. _ The motorcycle backed onto my toe. _ Don’t back onto anything as you go down the driveway!
examples: The motorcycle backed onto my toe.

back-order something.monolingual: [for a merchant] to order something that is not in stock and make delivery to the customer when the goods become available. _The store didn’t have the replacement part for my vacuum cleaner, so the manager back-ordered it for me. _ The shop had to ba
examples: The store didn’t have the replacement part for my vacuum cleaner, so the manager back-ordered it for me.

back over someone or something.monolingual: [for a car or other vehicle] to roll backwards over someone or something. _ Sandy backed over her brother’s bicycle. _ She almost backed over her brother.
examples: Sandy backed over her brother’s bicycle.

back someone for something.monolingual: to support or endorse someone for something, such as a public office. _ We all back Tom for president. _ I am backing Jane for treasurer.
examples: We all back Tom for president.

back someone up†.monolingual: to provide someone with help in reserve; to support someone. _ Don’t worry. I will back you up when you need me. _ Will you please back up Nancy over the weekend?
examples: Don’t worry. I will back you up when you need me.

back something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to drive a car backwards. _Will you back your car up a little? _I will back up the car.
examples: I will back up the car.

back the wrong horse.monolingual: Fig. to support someone or something that cannot win or succeed. _ I don’t want to back the wrong horse, but it seems to me that Jed is the better candidate. _ Fred backed the wrong horse in the budget hearings.
examples: I don’t want to back the wrong horse, but it seems to me that Jed is the better candidate.

back to basics.monolingual: return to basic instruction; start the learning process over again. _ Class, you seem to have forgotten the simplest of facts, so it’s back to basics for the first week of classes.
examples: Class, you seem to have forgotten the simplest of facts, so it’s back to basics for the first week of classes.

back to square one.monolingual: Fig. back to the beginning. (As with a board game.) _ Negotiations have broken down, and it’s back to square one. _We lost our appeal of the lower court decision, so back to square one.
examples: Negotiations have broken down, and it’s back to square one.

back to the drawing board.monolingual: Fig. time to start from the start; it is time to plan something over again. (Plans or schematics are drawn on a drawing board. Note the variations shown in the examples.) _ It didn’t work. Back to the drawing board. _I flunked English this semester.
examples: It didn’t work.

back to the salt mines.monolingual: Cliché time to return to work, school, or something else that might be unpleasant. (The phrase implies that the speaker is a slave who works in the salt mines.) _It’s one o’clock and lunch break is over. Back to the salt mines. _School starts in the
examples: It’s one o’clock and lunch break is over.

back up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for objects] to obstruct and accumulate in a pathway or channel. _ Something clogged the sewer and it backed up.
examples: Something clogged the sewer and it backed up.

backfire on someone.monolingual: Fig. [for something, such as a plot] to fail unexpectedly; to fail with an undesired result. _ Your plot backfired on you. _ I was afraid that my scheme would backfire on me.
examples: Your plot backfired on you.

backseat driver.monolingual: Fig. an annoying passenger who tells the driver how to drive; someone who tells others how to do things. _ I don’t need any backseat driver on this project. _ Stop pestering me with all your advice. Nobody likes a backseat driver!
examples: I don’t need any backseat driver on this project.

back-to-back.monolingual: 1. Lit. adjacent and touching backs. _They started the duel by standing back-to-back. _ Two people who stand back-to-back can manage to see in all directions.
examples: They started the duel by standing back-to-back.

a bad hair day.monolingual: a bad day in general. (As when one’s inability to groom one’s hair in the morning seems to color the events of the day.) _I’m sorry I am so glum. This has been a real bad hair day. _ It’s just one bad hair day after another.
examples: I’m sorry I am so glum.

bad money drives out good..monolingual: Prov. If there is counterfeit or inflated currency in circulation, people will hoard their genuine currency; worthless things will drive valuable things out of circulation. (This principle is also known as Gresham’s Law.) _ When the government reduce
examples: When the government reduced the amount of copper in the pennies it produced, we saw that bad money drives out good; everyone saved copper pennies and only spent the less pure ones.

bad news travels fast..monolingual: Prov. Information about trouble or misfortune disseminates quickly (more quickly than good news). _ John: Hi, Andy. I’m sorry to hear you got fired. Andy: How did you know about that already? It only happened this morning. John: Bad news travels fast
examples: John: Hi, Andy.

a bad penny.monolingual: a worthless person. _ Wally is a bad penny. Someday he’ll end up in jail. _ My little brother is a real bad penny. Every time he shows up, he wants to borrow money.
examples: Wally is a bad penny.

badger someone into something.monolingual: Fig. to pester someone into doing something. _Don’t try to badger us into doing it. _ My brother and I were badgered into cleaning out the garage.
examples: Don’t try to badger us into doing it.

bad-mouth someone or something.monolingual: to say negative things about someone or something. _ Mr. Smith was always bad-mouthing Mrs. Smith. They just didn’t get along. _ John bad-mouths his car constantly because it is too small for him.
examples: Mr. Smith was always bad-mouthing Mrs.

bag of bones.monolingual: an extremely skinny person or animal with bones showing. (The skin is the figurative bag.) _I’ve lost so much weight that I’m just turning into a bag of bones. _ Get that old bag of bones off the racetrack!
examples: I’ve lost so much weight that I’m just turning into a bag of bones.

bag of tricks.monolingual: Fig. a collection of special techniques or methods. _ What have you got in your bag of tricks that could help me with this problem? _Here comes Mother with her bag of tricks. I’m sure she can help us.
examples: Here comes Mother with her bag of tricks.

bag on someone.monolingual: Sl. to criticize someone. _ Stop bagging on me! I’m tired of all your complaining. _If you are going to bag on everyone all the time, I don’t want to hear about it.
examples: Stop bagging on me! I’m tired of all your complaining.

bag that!.monolingual: Sl. Forget that! _ Bag that! The number I gave you was wrong. _There are four—no, bag that!—six of the red ones and three blue ones.
examples: Bag that! The number I gave you was wrong.

bail someone or something out†.monolingual: Fig. to rescue someone or something from trouble or difficulty. (Based on bail someone out of jail.) _ The proposed law was in trouble, but Senator Todd bailed out the bill at the last minute. _ I was going to be late with my report, but my roommate
examples: The proposed law was in trouble, but Senator Todd bailed out the bill at the last minute.

bail something out†.monolingual: 1. to remove water from the bottom of a boat by dipping or scooping. _ Tom has to bail the boat out before we get in. _ You should always bail out a boat before using it.
examples: Tom has to bail the boat out before we get in.

bait and switch.monolingual: Fig. a deceptive merchandising practice where one product is advertised at a low price to get people’s attention [the bait], but pressure is applied to get the customer to purchase a more expensive item. _ Walter described how the store used bait and
examples: Walter described how the store used bait and switch, since they never seemed to have in stock the bargains that they advertised.

a baker’s dozen.monolingual: thirteen. (Bakers often added an extra item to an order for a dozen.) _ We ended up with a baker’s dozen each of socks and undershirts on our shopping trip.
examples: We ended up with a baker’s dozen each of socks and undershirts on our shopping trip.

the balance of power.monolingual: the situation where the power held by one governing body or adversary is balanced by the power of another. _ The balance of power was threatened when China captured our airplane.
examples: The balance of power was threatened when China captured our airplane.

balance out.monolingual: to equal out; to become even or fair. _These things all balance out in the end. _Don’t worry. Things will balance out.
examples: These things all balance out in the end.

balance something against something else.monolingual: to consider one thing in reference to another; to weigh one possibility against another possibility. _ We will have to balance all the good he did against all the bad. _The good will be balanced against the bad in the final reckoning.
examples: We will have to balance all the good he did against all the bad.

balance something with something else.monolingual: to offset something with something else; to balance something against something else. _ The teacher tends to balance a harsh grading scheme with a strong sense of fair play. _Roger balanced the spicy soup with a bland first course. _They balanced his
examples: The teacher tends to balance a harsh grading scheme with a strong sense of fair play.

*baleful as death.monolingual: promising evil; very threatening. (*Also: as ~.) _The wind’s moan was as baleful as death. _ His voice sounded baleful as death.
examples: The wind’s moan was as baleful as death.

balk at something.monolingual: to resist and object to something; to shy away from doing something. _ I hope they don’t balk at finishing their work. _ They will probably balk at it.
examples: I hope they don’t balk at finishing their work.

ball and chain.monolingual: 1. a wife. (Mostly jocular.) _ I’ve got to get home to my ball and chain. _My ball and chain is mad at me.
examples: I’ve got to get home to my ball and chain.

ball someone or something up†.monolingual: to interfere with someone or something; to mess someone or something up. _ Who balled this television up? _ Someone balled up the television.
examples: Someone balled up the television.

ball something up†.monolingual: to roll something up into a ball. (Alluding to something, such as rope, being tangled up and so useless.) _She balled the clay up and stuck it to the clown’s face as a nose. _ Why are you balling up the paper?
examples: She balled the clay up and stuck it to the clown’s face as a nose.

a ballpark figure.monolingual: Fig. an estimate; an off-the-cuff guess. _ I don’t need an exact number. A ballpark figure will do.
examples: I don’t need an exact number.

the balls of one’s feet.monolingual: the bottom part of the feet just behind the toes. _Mary got blisters on the balls of her feet from playing tennis. _ The dancer balanced on the balls of his feet.
examples: Mary got blisters on the balls of her feet from playing tennis.

ban someone from something.monolingual: 1. to prohibit someone from doing something. _We banned everyone from smoking. _ Everyone has been banned from smoking.
examples: We banned everyone from smoking.

bandage someone or something up†.monolingual: to wrap bandages on someone or on someone’s wounds. _ We should bandage the wounds up first. _ We should bandage up the wounds first. _ I have to bandage him up before we can move him. _She bandaged herself up with the supplies she kept in her backpa
examples: We should bandage the wounds up first.

bandy something about†.monolingual: to spread something, such as someone’s good name, around in an unfavorable context; to toss words around in a gossipy fashion. (Bandy means to toss or hit something back and forth.) _ Just stop bandying words about and start telling the truth! _ Ther
examples: There is no need to keep bandying about those rumors.

bandy with someone.monolingual: to argue [with someone]; to argue by “playing catch with words.” (Bandy means to toss or hit something back and forth.) _ Why are you bandying with me? _ She has been bandied with enough. Give her a straight answer.
examples: She has been bandied with enough.

bang against someone or something.monolingual: to knock or strike against someone or something. _ The shutter banged against the side of the house. _ The board banged against me and hurt my shin.
examples: The shutter banged against the side of the house.

bang for the buck.monolingual: value for the money spent; excitement for the money spent; a favorable cost-to-benefit ratio. (Expressed as an amount of bang for the buck.) _I didn’t get anywhere near the bang for the buck I expected. _How much bang for the buck did you really thin
examples: I didn’t get anywhere near the bang for the buck I expected.

bang into someone or something.monolingual: to knock or bump into someone or something. _Why did you bang into me with your car? _ I banged into the door by accident.
examples: I banged into the door by accident.

bang on someone or something.monolingual: to strike someone or something repeatedly. (Especially to beat on a person or a drum.) _ Please stop banging on that drum! _ Max was banging on Lefty when the cops arrived.
examples: Max was banging on Lefty when the cops arrived.

bang someone or something around†.monolingual: to knock someone or something about; to beat or strike someone or something. _ Let’s bang him around a little and see if that will change his mind. _ Why are you banging around my friend? _ Don’t bang those pans around. _He banged himself around badl
examples: Let’s bang him around a little and see if that will change his mind.

bang someone up†.monolingual: to beat someone up; to assault someone; to damage someone. _ The crooks banged him up a little bit. _ The crash banged up the passengers in the car. _ She banged herself up badly.
examples: The crooks banged him up a little bit.

bang something in†.monolingual: to crush something; to dent or collapse something. _Who banged the side of the washing machine in? _ Who banged in the side of the washing machine?

bang something out†.monolingual: to play something on the piano, loudly, banging on the keys; to type something on a keyboard by pounding on the keys. _Let me bang this melody out and see if you can guess who wrote it. _ Please bang out the school song good and loud. _I banged out t
examples: Let me bang this melody out and see if you can guess who wrote it.

bang something up†.monolingual: to crash or wreck something; to damage something. _ Don’t bang my best skillet up! _ Who banged up my best skillet?

bank on something.monolingual: Fig. to be so sure of something that one can trust it as one might trust a bank with one’s money. _ I will be there on time. You can bank on it. _ I need a promise of your help. I hope I can bank on it.
examples: I will be there on time.

banker’s hours.monolingual: Fig. short work hours: 10:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. _When did you start keeping banker’s hours? _There aren’t many bankers who keep banker’s hours these days.
examples: There aren’t many bankers who keep banker’s hours these days.

baptism of fire.monolingual: Fig. a first experience of something, usually something difficult or unpleasant. _My son’s just had his first visit to the dentist. He stood up to this baptism of fire very well. _Mary’s had her baptism of fire as a teacher. She was assigned to the w
examples: My son’s just had his first visit to the dentist.

bar none.monolingual: with no exceptions. (Follows an assertion.) _ This is the best of all, bar none.
examples: This is the best of all, bar none.

bar someone from some place.monolingual: to prevent someone from entering some place. _ Please don’t bar me from the movie theater. I will be quiet from now on. _ They were barred from the concert for smoking.
examples: Please don’t bar me from the movie theater.

the bare something.monolingual: the smallest or least possible. _ Bob did the bare minimum of work to pass the class. _ Food, clothing, and shelter are the bare necessities of life.
examples: Bob did the bare minimum of work to pass the class.

bare something to someone.monolingual: to reveal or disclose something to someone. _I have to know a guy pretty well before I will bare my innermost thoughts to him. _ Our criminal involvement was bared to the judge.
examples: I have to know a guy pretty well before I will bare my innermost thoughts to him.

bare-bones.monolingual: Cliché limited; stripped down; lacking refinements or extras. _This one is the bare-bones model. It has no accessories at all.
examples: This one is the bare-bones model.

barf out.monolingual: Sl. to become deranged, to a greater or lesser degree. _ Terry barfed out when he heard about the damage Nick had done to his car. _ Yuck! I thought I was going to barf out.
examples: Terry barfed out when he heard about the damage Nick had done to his car.

barf someone out.monolingual: Sl. to disgust someone. (Fixed order.) _ You just barf me out! _ I barf myself out every time I look in the mirror.
examples: I barf myself out every time I look in the mirror.

bargaining chip.monolingual: Fig. something to be used (traded) in negotiations. _I want to use their refusal to meet our terms as a bargaining chip in future negotiations. _I need to have a few bargaining chips ready when we get down to drawing up the contract.
examples: I want to use their refusal to meet our terms as a bargaining chip in future negotiations.

barge into someone or something.monolingual: Fig. to bump or crash into someone or something, possibly on purpose. _ She just barged into me and nearly knocked me over. _Tom tripped, barged into the water cooler, and hurt his knee.
examples: She just barged into me and nearly knocked me over.

bark at someone.monolingual: Fig. to speak harshly to someone. _Don’t bark at me like that over such a trivial mistake! _ Ken barked at the children for being noisy.
examples: Ken barked at the children for being noisy.

bark at someone or something.monolingual: Lit. [for a dog] to make a characteristic sharp sound at someone or something. _ The dog is barking at the traffic again. _ Their guard dog was barking at me.
examples: The dog is barking at the traffic again.

bark up the wrong tree.monolingual: Fig. to make the wrong choice; to ask the wrong person; to follow the wrong course. (Alludes to a dog in pursuit of an animal, where the animal is in one tree and the dog is barking at another tree.) _ If you think I’m the guilty person, you’re barki
examples: If you think I’m the guilty person, you’re barking up the wrong tree.

a barking dog never bites..monolingual: Prov. Someone who makes threats all the time seldom carries out the threats. _ Old Mrs. Smith keeps saying she’ll call the police if we walk on her lawn, but don’t worry. A barking dog never bites. _My boss threatens to fire me at least once a week,
examples: Old Mrs. Smith keeps saying she’ll call the police if we walk on her lawn, but don’t worry.

barrel along.monolingual: to move along rapidly. _ The car was barreling along at a fairly rapid clip. _ Don’t barrel along so fast that you miss the turn.
examples: The car was barreling along at a fairly rapid clip.

a barrel of fun.monolingual: Fig. a tremendous amount of fun. _ Jill is just a barrel of fun in class. _ We had a barrel of fun at your party.
examples: Jill is just a barrel of fun in class.

barter something away†.monolingual: to trade something away; to lose something of value in a trade. _Don’t barter my car away! _ Don’t barter away anything of such high value.
examples: Don’t barter away anything of such high value.

barter something for something else.monolingual: to trade something for something else. _ He sought to barter the car for a large computer. _ She bartered the piano for a settee.
examples: He sought to barter the car for a large computer.

barter something off†.monolingual: to get rid of something by trading it for something else. _ See if you can barter that old desk off. _ She bartered off the used bookshelf.
examples: See if you can barter that old desk off.

barter with someone.monolingual: to enter into trading with someone without using money; to bargain with someone. _Are you willing to barter with me, or is this strictly a cash transaction?

base one’s opinion on something.monolingual: to make a judgment or form an opinion from something. _ You must not base your opinion on one bad experience. _ I base my opinion on many years of studying the problem.
examples: You must not base your opinion on one bad experience.

bash someone or something around†.monolingual: to treat someone or something roughly (physically or figuratively); to beat on or abuse someone or something (physically or otherwise). _ Stop bashing me around, and let’s talk. _ The robber acted as though he was about to bash around his victims.
examples: Stop bashing me around, and let’s talk.

bash something in†.monolingual: to crush something inward or to the inside. _ Don’t bash the door in! _ It sounds like someone is bashing in the door.
examples: It sounds like someone is bashing in the door.

bash something up†.monolingual: to crash something; to strike something and damage it. _She bashed the car up badly. _How did she bash up the car?
examples: She bashed the car up badly.

bask in something.monolingual: Fig. to enjoy or revel in something, such as praise, fame, etc. (Alludes to a person or animal resting in the warming rays of the sun.) _Alice enjoyed basking in her newfound fame. _ Lily loves basking in praise.
examples: Alice enjoyed basking in her newfound fame.

a basket case.monolingual: Fig. a person who is a nervous wreck. (Formerly referred to a person who is physically disabled in all four limbs because of paralysis or amputation.) _ After that all-day meeting, I was practically a basket case. _ My weeks of worry were so intense
examples: After that all-day meeting, I was practically a basket case.

bat something around†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to knock something around with a bat or something similar. _Terry spent a little time batting a ball around, then he went home. _ Let’s bat around some balls before we go home.
examples: Terry spent a little time batting a ball around, then he went home.

batten down the hatches.monolingual: Fig. to prepare for difficult times. (From a nautical expression meaning, literally, to seal the hatches against the arrival of a storm. The word order is fixed.) _ Here comes that contentious Mrs. Jones. Batten down the hatches! _Batten down the hat
examples: Here comes that contentious Mrs.

batter someone or something up†.monolingual: to damage or harm someone or something. _ Max threatened to batter Lefty up within an inch of his life. _ Who battered up this desk?
examples: Max threatened to batter Lefty up within an inch of his life.

batter something down†.monolingual: to smash or break down something, such as a wall, door, or any defensive structure. _ Do they have to batter anything down as part of the construction project? _ They battered down the wall as a first step in enlarging the house.
examples: They battered down the wall as a first step in enlarging the house.

battle against someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to wage a fight against someone or something; to attempt to defeat someone or something. _ The army battled against the enemy until both sides were exhausted.
examples: The army battled against the enemy until both sides were exhausted.

battle for something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to fight to gain something. _ The army battled for the town until they had defeated its defenders.
examples: The army battled for the town until they had defeated its defenders.

battle of the bulge.monolingual: the attempt to keep one’s waistline slim. (Jocular. Alludes to a World War II battle.) _ She appears to have lost the battle of the bulge. _I’ve been fighting the battle of the bulge ever since I turned 35.
examples: She appears to have lost the battle of the bulge.

a battle royal.monolingual: a classic, hard-fought battle or argument. _ The meeting turned into a battle royal and everyone left angry.
examples: The meeting turned into a battle royal and everyone left angry.

battle something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to fight about something to a conclusion. _ They battled the matter out and came to an agreement. _ The two young toughs went into the alley to battle out their differences.
examples: They battled the matter out and came to an agreement.

bawl someone out†.monolingual: to scold someone in a loud voice. _ The teacher bawled the student out for arriving late. _Principals don’t usually bawl out students.
examples: The teacher bawled the student out for arriving late.

bay at something.monolingual: to howl at something. (Usually said of a dog, wolf, or coyote.) _The dogs were baying at the moon. _ We heard a coyote in the distance, baying at the moon.
examples: The dogs were baying at the moon.

be careful..monolingual: 1. an instruction to take care in a particular situation. _ Bill: I’m going to the beach tomorrow. Sally: Be careful. Use lots of sunscreen! _ Jane: Well, we’re off to the Amazon. Mary: Heavens! Be careful!
examples: Bill: I’m going to the beach tomorrow.

be game.monolingual: to be ready for action; to be agreeable to participating in something. _ “I’m game,” David replied when I suggested we go for a long hike. _We’re going to the park to play football. Are you game?
examples: “I’m game,” David replied when I suggested we go for a long hike.

be in aid of.monolingual: to be intended to help, cure, or resolve. _ What is all this in aid of ? _ I don’t understand what your comments are in aid of.
examples: I don’t understand what your comments are in aid of.

be just before you’re generous..monolingual: Prov. Do what you ought to do before you do things that you want to do; pay your debts before you give money away. _Jill: It’s payday! I can’t wait to go out and buy my niece that nice toy train set for her birthday. Jane: But, Jill, we have bills to
examples: Jill: It’s payday! I can’t wait to go out and buy my niece that nice toy train set for her birthday.

be my guest..monolingual: Help yourself.; After you. (A polite way of indicating that someone else should go first, help himself or herself to something, or take the last one of something.) _Mary: I would just love to have some more cake, but there is only one piece left. Sal
examples: Mary: I would just love to have some more cake, but there is only one piece left.

be one’s brother’s keeper.monolingual: to be responsible for someone else. (Used of others besides just real brothers.) _ I can’t force these kids to go to school and get an education so they can get jobs. I am not my brother’s keeper. _You can’t expect me to be my brother’s keeper. Each
examples: I can’t force these kids to go to school and get an education so they can get jobs.

be quiet!.monolingual: Stop talking or making noise. (Regarded as a bit harsh or overbearing, but made polite with please.) _ Bill (entering the room): Hey, Tom! Tom: Please be quiet! I’m on the phone. _ Tom: Hey, Bill! Bill: Be quiet! You’re too loud. Tom: Sorry.
examples: Bill (entering the room): Hey, Tom! Tom: Please be quiet! I’m on the phone.

be that as it may.monolingual: Cliché even if what you say is true. _ I am sorry to hear about your troubles, but, be that as it may, you still must carry out your responsibilities. _ Be that as it may, I still cannot help you.
examples: I am sorry to hear about your troubles, but, be that as it may, you still must carry out your responsibilities.

be there or be square..monolingual: Sl. Attend or be at some event or place or be considered uncooperative or not “with it.” _ There’s a bunch of people going to be at John’s on Saturday. Be there or be square.
examples: There’s a bunch of people going to be at John’s on Saturday.

beam me up, scotty!.monolingual: Get me out of here!; Take me away from this mess! (From the late 1960s television program Star Trek.) _This place is really crazy! Beam me up, Scotty! _ I’ve heard enough! Beam me up, Scotty!

beam up.monolingual: Sl. to die. (Alluding to the television program Star Trek.) _ Pete Dead? I didn’t think he was old enough to beam up. _I was so exhausted after climbing four f lights that I was afraid I would beam up.
examples: Pete Dead? I didn’t think he was old enough to beam up.

bear fruit.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a plant or tree] to yield fruit. _ Our apple tree didn’t bear fruit this year.
examples: Our apple tree didn’t bear fruit this year.

bear in mind that....monolingual: to remember [something]; to consider [something]. _ Bear in mind that the trip will be expensive. _ I asked the teacher to bear in mind that I am just a beginner.
examples: Bear in mind that the trip will be expensive.

bear someone or something up†.monolingual: to hold someone or something up; to support someone or something. _ Will this bench bear me up? _ This bench is so sturdy it would bear up an elephant.
examples: This bench is so sturdy it would bear up an elephant.

bear someone up†.monolingual: to sustain or encourage someone. _Your encouragement bore me up through a very hard time. _ I will bear up the widow through the funeral service as well as I can.
examples: Your encouragement bore me up through a very hard time.

bear something out†.monolingual: [for facts or evidence] to support or confirm a story or explanation. _The facts don’t bear this out. _ Her story bears out exactly what you said.
examples: The facts don’t bear this out.

bear watching.monolingual: to need close, attentive observation or monitoring. _ This problem will bear watching. _ This is a very serious disease, and it will bear watching for further developments.
examples: This problem will bear watching.

bear with someone or something.monolingual: to be patient with someone or something; to wait upon someone or something. (Especially through difficulties.) _ Please bear with me for a moment while I try to get this straightened out. _Can you bear with the committee until it reaches a decision?
examples: Please bear with me for a moment while I try to get this straightened out.

beat against someone or something.monolingual: to strike against someone or something. _The wind beat against the sides of the house. _ Max beat against Lefty’s jaw with his quick jabs.
examples: The wind beat against the sides of the house.

beat at something.monolingual: to strike out at something. _ He beat at his attacker to no avail. _ Lily beat at the snake, but didn’t harm it.
examples: He beat at his attacker to no avail.

beat it!.monolingual: Inf. Go away!; Get out! _ Bill: Sorry I broke your radio. Bob: Get out of here! Beat it! _ “Beat it, you kids! Go play somewhere else!” yelled the storekeeper.
examples: Bill: Sorry I broke your radio.

beat on someone or something.monolingual: to pound or hammer on someone or something. _ She beat on him until he let her go. _ Stop beating on that drum!
examples: She beat on him until he let her go.

beat one’s gums.monolingual: to waste time talking a great deal without results. (As if one were toothless.) _I’m tired of beating my gums about this over and over. _ You’re just beating your gums. No one is listening.
examples: I’m tired of beating my gums about this over and over.

beat oneself up.monolingual: Fig. to be overly critical of one’s behavior or actions; to punish oneself with guilt and remorse over past actions. (Not a physical beating. Fixed order.) _ It’s over and done with. There’s no need to beat yourself up. _ He’s beating himself up over
examples: It’s over and done with.

beat someone down†.monolingual: Fig. to defeat or demoralize someone. _ The constant bombing finally beat them down. _ The attackers beat down the defenders.
examples: The constant bombing finally beat them down.

beat someone into something.monolingual: Fig. to beat a person until the person turns into a particular physical state, such as a pulp, a mess, etc. _ Fred threatened to beat Mike into a pulp if he didn’t do as he was asked. _ Mike beat Fred into a bloody mess.
examples: Fred threatened to beat Mike into a pulp if he didn’t do as he was asked.

beat someone or something back†.monolingual: to drive someone or something back to where it came from. _ We beat them back to where they were before the war started. _The army beat back the defenders and saved the town. _ They were able to beat the wolves back and make an escape.
examples: We beat them back to where they were before the war started.

beat someone or something off†.monolingual: to drive someone or something away by beating. _ They beat the enemy off. _ The army beat off the savage attack, saving the town. _ I was able to beat off the intruder.
examples: They beat the enemy off.

beat someone or something out†.monolingual: to beat someone or something; to win over someone or something. _ The other team beat us out readily. _ They beat out every other team in the league, too. _ I will win! You will not beat me out!
examples: The other team beat us out readily.

beat someone out†.monolingual: to outdistance someone; to perform better than someone. _We have to beat the other company out, and then we’ll have the contract. _ I beat out Walter in the foot race.
examples: We have to beat the other company out, and then we’ll have the contract.

beat someone’s brains out.monolingual: 1. to hit or batter someone severely. _ She threatened to beat my brains out. _ Those thugs nearly beat his brains out.
examples: She threatened to beat my brains out.

beat someone to something.monolingual: to get to something before someone else; to claim something before someone else does. _ You beat me to it and took the last cookie. _ Ken beat John to the door.
examples: You beat me to it and took the last cookie.

beat someone up†.monolingual: to harm or subdue a person by striking him. _ The robber beat me up and took my money. _ I really wanted to beat up that intruder.
examples: The robber beat me up and took my money.

beat something down†.monolingual: 1. to break something in; to break through something. _Don’t beat the door down! I’m coming! _Please don’t beat down the door!
examples: Please don’t beat down the door! 2.

beat something into something.monolingual: to beat or whip something with a utensil, until it changes into something else. _Beat the white of the egg into stiff peaks. _ Beat the batter into a smooth consistency.
examples: Beat the white of the egg into stiff peaks.

beat something up†.monolingual: 1. to whip up something, such as an egg. _ Beat the egg up and pour it in the skillet. _ Beat up another egg and do the same.
examples: Beat the egg up and pour it in the skillet.

beat the clock.monolingual: Fig. to do something before a deadline; to finish before the time is up. (Alludes to accomplishing something before a clock reaches a specific time.) _ Sam beat the clock, arriving a few minutes before the doors were locked. _ They were afraid they w
examples: Sam beat the clock, arriving a few minutes before the doors were locked.

beat the gun.monolingual: Fig. to manage to do something before the ending signal. (Originally from sports, referring to scoring in the last seconds of a game just before the referee fires a gun to signal the end of the game.) _The field goal beat the gun and was in the air j
examples: The field goal beat the gun and was in the air just in time.

beat the rap.monolingual: Sl. to evade conviction and punishment (for a crime). _He was charged with drunk driving, but he beat the rap. _ The police hauled Tom in and charged him with a crime. His lawyer helped him beat the rap.
examples: He was charged with drunk driving, but he beat the rap.

beat up on someone.monolingual: to batter someone, usually physically. _ Lefty beat up on Max and made a mess of him. _ Don’t beat up on me, you bully!
examples: Lefty beat up on Max and made a mess of him.

beauty is only skin-deep..monolingual: Prov. A person who looks beautiful may not have a pleasing personality; a person’s good looks may not last. _ Fred: I hope Nancy will go out with me. She’s so beautiful! Jane: I hate to disappoint you, but in Nancy’s case, beauty is definitely only s
examples: Fred: I hope Nancy will go out with me.

beckon to someone.monolingual: to signal someone to come. _ Wally beckoned to Sally, and she came over to him. _ Lily beckoned to Max and he turned his back on her.
examples: Wally beckoned to Sally, and she came over to him.

become of someone or something.monolingual: to happen or occur to someone or something. _Whatever became of Joe and his friends? _I don’t know what became of my other plaid sock.
examples: I don’t know what became of my other plaid sock.

*becoming on someone.monolingual: [of clothing] complimentary to someone; [of clothing] enhancing one’s good looks. (*Typically: be ~; look ~.) _ The dress you wore last night is not becoming on you. _ That color is very becoming on you.
examples: The dress you wore last night is not becoming on you.

bed down some place.monolingual: to sleep somewhere; to find a place to sleep somewhere. _ I need to bed down somewhere for the night. _ Can I bed down here with you?
examples: I need to bed down somewhere for the night.

a bed of roses.monolingual: a luxurious situation; an easy life. _ Who said life would be a bed of roses? _If I had a million bucks, I would be in a bed of roses.
examples: If I had a million bucks, I would be in a bed of roses.

bed-and-breakfast.monolingual: a type of lodging for travelers or tourists offering a place to sleep and breakfast the next morning, typically in a small inn or private home. _ We visited six European countries and stayed in a bed-andbreakfast every night. _ I had to take a bed-an
examples: We visited six European countries and stayed in a bed-andbreakfast every night.

*a bee in one’s bonnet.monolingual: a single idea or a thought that remains in one’s mind; an obsession. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give one ~.) _ I have a bee in my bonnet over that cool new car I saw, and I can’t stop thinking about it. _ I got a bee in my bonnet about swimming. I j
examples: I have a bee in my bonnet over that cool new car I saw, and I can’t stop thinking about it.

beef about someone or something.monolingual: Sl. to complain about someone or something. _Stop beefing about Karen. _He is always beefing about his working conditions.
examples: Stop beefing about Karen.

beef something up†.monolingual: to add strength or substance to something. _ Let’s beef this music up with a little more on the drums. _ They beefed up the offer with another thousand dollars.
examples: Let’s beef this music up with a little more on the drums.

beer up.monolingual: Sl. to drink a lot of beer. _Those guys are out there beering up like mad. _ Stop beering up and go home!
examples: Those guys are out there beering up like mad.

before long.monolingual: soon. _Billy will be grown-up before long. _ If we keep spending so much, before long we’ll be without any money.
examples: Billy will be grown-up before long.

*before someone’s time.monolingual: happening before someone was born or old enough to know what was going on. (*Typically: be ~; happen ~; occur ~.) _Of course I don’t remember it. It was before my time. _ All that happened before your time.
examples: Of course I don’t remember it.

before you know it.monolingual: almost immediately. _ I’ll be there before you know it. _If you keep spending money like that, you’ll be broke before you know it.
examples: I’ll be there before you know it.

beg for someone or something.monolingual: to plead to be given someone or something. _He missed Jane a lot and was just begging for her to return to him. _ Jane begged for another helping of ice cream.
examples: He missed Jane a lot and was just begging for her to return to him.

beg of someone.monolingual: to request earnestly of someone. (Usually added to a request.) _ Please help me. I beg of you. _ I beg of you to help me.
examples: Please help me.

beg something from someone.monolingual: to plead for something from someone. _She begged the amount of a telephone call from someone who walked by. _ I begged a dollar from a kind lady who went by.
examples: She begged the amount of a telephone call from someone who walked by.

beg something of someone.monolingual: to request earnestly that someone do something or grant something. _ Please help me. I beg it of you. _ She begged a favor of Max.
examples: Please help me.

beg something off†.monolingual: to decline an invitation politely. _ She begged the trip to the zoo off. _ We all begged off the dinner invitation.
examples: She begged the trip to the zoo off.

beg the question.monolingual: 1. to carry on a false argument where one assumes as proved the very point that is being argued, or more loosely, to evade the issue at hand. (Essentially a criticism of someone’s line of argument.) _ Stop arguing in circles. You’re begging the quest
examples: Stop arguing in circles.

beggars can’t be choosers..monolingual: Prov. If someone gives you something you asked for, you should not complain about what you get. _ I asked Joe to lend me his bicycle, and he sent me this old, rusty one. But beggars can’t be choosers. _ Jill: Let me wear your green dress; I don’t lik
examples: I asked Joe to lend me his bicycle, and he sent me this old, rusty one.

begin by doing something.monolingual: to start out by doing something first. _ We will begin by painting the house. _ She began by opening the door.
examples: We will begin by painting the house.

begin to see daylight.monolingual: Fig. to begin to see the end of a long task. _ I’ve been working on my thesis for two years, and at last I’m beginning to see daylight. _I’ve been so busy. Only in the last week have I begun to see daylight.
examples: I’ve been working on my thesis for two years, and at last I’m beginning to see daylight.

begin to see the light.monolingual: Fig. to begin to understand something. _ My algebra class has been hard for me, but I’m beginning to see the light. _ I was totally confused, but I began to see the light after your explanation.
examples: My algebra class has been hard for me, but I’m beginning to see the light.

begin with someone or something.monolingual: to start off a sequence with someone or something. _ Let’s have dinner begin with a nice clear soup. _ I will begin with Liz and take Frank next.
examples: Let’s have dinner begin with a nice clear soup.

beginner’s luck.monolingual: absolute luck; the luck of an inexperienced person. (Referring to surprisingly good luck.) _ I could never have accomplished this if I had practiced a lot. My win was just beginner’s luck.
examples: I could never have accomplished this if I had practiced a lot.

the beginning of the end.monolingual: Fig. the start of the termination of something or of someone’s death. _ When he stopped coughing and grew still, I knew it was the beginning of the end. _ The enormous debt we ran up marked the beginning of the end as far as our standard of living wa
examples: When he stopped coughing and grew still, I knew it was the beginning of the end.

beguile someone into something.monolingual: to charm someone into doing something. _ You can’t beguile me into stealing for you! _ I beguiled Tom into driving me to the airport.
examples: I beguiled Tom into driving me to the airport.

beguile someone out of something.monolingual: 1. to charm someone out of doing something. _I will try to beguile them out of doing it. _ He beguiled her out of leaving.
examples: I will try to beguile them out of doing it.

beguile someone with something.monolingual: to charm or fascinate someone with something. _ She beguiled her date with tales of her luxurious lifestyle. _ He spent the evening beguiling her with stories of the Old West.
examples: She beguiled her date with tales of her luxurious lifestyle.

*behind bars.monolingual: in jail. (*Typically: be ~; put someone ~.) _ Very soon, you will be behind bars for your crimes. _Max should be behind bars soon for his conviction on burglary charges.
examples: Very soon, you will be behind bars for your crimes.

behind closed doors.monolingual: in secret; away from observers, reporters, or intruders, usually in a closed room. _ They held the meeting behind closed doors, as the law allowed. _ Every important issue was decided behind closed doors.
examples: They held the meeting behind closed doors, as the law allowed.

*behind schedule.monolingual: having failed to do something by the appointed time, especially the time given on a written plan. (*Typically: be ~; fall ~; get ~.) _We have to hurry and finish soon or we will fall behind schedule. _The project is behind schedule by six months.
examples: We have to hurry and finish soon or we will fall behind schedule.

behind someone’s back.monolingual: without someone’s knowledge; secret from someone. _Please don’t talk about me behind my back. _ She sold the car behind his back, while he was away on vacation.
examples: Please don’t talk about me behind my back.

*behind the eight ball.monolingual: 1. Fig. in trouble; in a weak or losing position. (Alludes to the eight ball in pool, which in certain games cannot be touched without penalty. *Typically: be ~; get ~; have someone ~; put someone ~.) _I’m behind the eight ball again and can’t see ho
examples: I’m behind the eight ball again and can’t see how to relieve my dilemma.

behind the scenes.monolingual: without receiving credit or fame; out of public view. (Referring originally to those who worked on a theatrical piece but do not appear on the stage.) _ The people who worked behind the scenes are the real heroes of this project. _ I worked behind th
examples: The people who worked behind the scenes are the real heroes of this project.

behind the times.monolingual: old-fashioned. _ Sarah is a bit behind the times. Her clothes are quite old-fashioned. _ Our 90- year-old state senator is a bit behind the times.
examples: Sarah is a bit behind the times.

behind you!.monolingual: Look behind you!; There is danger behind you! _ “Behind you!” shouted Tom just as a car raced past and nearly knocked Mary over. _ Alice shouted, “Behind you!” just as the pickpocket made off with Fred’s wallet.
examples: “Behind you!” shouted Tom just as a car raced past and nearly knocked Mary over.

behoove one to do something.monolingual: Cliché [for someone] to be obliged to do something. _ It behooves you to apologize to her for how you insulted her. _ It behooves me to make up for all the help you have given me.
examples: It behooves you to apologize to her for how you insulted her.

belabor the point.monolingual: to spend too much time on one item of discussion. _ I don’t want to belabor the point, but the sooner we get this matter settled, the better. _If the speaker would agree not to belabor the point further, I will place it on the agenda for resolution a
examples: I don’t want to belabor the point, but the sooner we get this matter settled, the better.

belch out.monolingual: to burst, billow, or gush out. _ Smoke belched out of the chimney.
examples: Smoke belched out of the chimney.

belch something up†.monolingual: to cause the release of something that goes upward. _ The fire belched flames and smoke up. _ The volcano belched up clouds of poison gasses.
examples: The fire belched flames and smoke up.

believe in someone or something.monolingual: to trust or have faith in someone or something; to accept a fact or what someone says as truth. _ You must believe in your own abilities. _ I believe in myself and my talent.
examples: You must believe in your own abilities.

believe it or not.monolingual: (you may) choose to accept something as true or not; it may seem amazing but it’s true. _ It’s late, but believe it or not, I just got home from work. _ I’m over fifty years old, believe it or not.
examples: It’s late, but believe it or not, I just got home from work.

believe something of someone.monolingual: to accept a statement about someone as truth. _ What a terrible thing for Jill to do. I can’t believe it of her. _I can believe anything of Max. He’s such a conniving person.
examples: What a terrible thing for Jill to do.

believe you me!.monolingual: Inf. You really should believe me!; You’d better take my word for it! _ Alice: Is it hot in that room? Fred: It really is. Believe you me! _ Sue: How do you like my cake? John: Believe you me, this is the best cake I’ve ever eaten!
examples: Alice: Is it hot in that room? Fred: It really is.

bell, book, and candle.monolingual: things that are miraculous or that signal that something unusual or bizarre may soon happen. (Alluding originally to the items used when performing the rite of excommunication from the Roman Catholic Church.) _ Look, I can’t work miracles! Do you exp
examples: On the top shelf of the tiny used-book store, Jim saw a bell, book, and candle sitting in a row, and he knew he was going to find some very interesting reading material.

bellow something out†.monolingual: to cry something out loudly with great force. _ Don’t just say it. Bellow it out! _ Bellow out your name so we know who you are!
examples: Don’t just say it.

bells and whistles.monolingual: Fig. extra, fancy add-ons or gadgets. _ I like cars that are loaded with all the bells and whistles. _ All those bells and whistles add to the cost.
examples: I like cars that are loaded with all the bells and whistles.

belly out.monolingual: [for a sheet of fabric, such as a ship’s sail] to fill out in the wind. _ The sails bellied out as the ship turned to catch the wind. _ When the sails bellied out, we began to move forward.
examples: The sails bellied out as the ship turned to catch the wind.

belly up.monolingual: 1. intoxicated by alcohol. _ Fred was boiled— belly up—glassy-eyed. _After four beers, I was belly up, for sure.
examples: Fred was boiled— belly up—glassy-eyed.

belong to someone or something.monolingual: to be owned by someone or something. _ This one belongs to me. _ This desk belongs to the company. You can’t take it home!
examples: This one belongs to me.

belong under something.monolingual: to be classified under some general category. _This one belongs under the other category. _ This file belongs under A.
examples: This one belongs under the other category.

below average.monolingual: lower or worse than average. _ Tom’s strength is below average for a child his size. _ Dad asked why my grades are below average.
examples: Tom’s strength is below average for a child his size.

below par.monolingual: not as good as average or normal. _I feel a little below par today. I think I am getting a cold. _ His work is below par, and he is paid too much money.
examples: I feel a little below par today.

below someone.monolingual: ranking below someone. _ I am below Terri, but my scores are better than Carol’s. _ I am below everyone in the class.
examples: I am below Terri, but my scores are better than Carol’s.

*below someone or something.monolingual: positioned under or lower than someone or something. (*Typically: be ~; lie ~; sink ~; sit ~.) _ The sun is below the horizon. _ The swimming hole is below the dam.
examples: The sun is below the horizon.

belt a drink down†.monolingual: Fig. to drink an alcoholic drink rapidly. _ She belted a couple of drinks down and went out to face her guests. _ How many drinks did Gloria belt down?
examples: She belted a couple of drinks down and went out to face her guests.

belt someone or something down†.monolingual: to secure someone or something with a belt or strap. _Please belt the child’s seat down and put the child in it. _Did you belt down the kids?
examples: Please belt the child’s seat down and put the child in it.

belt someone up†.monolingual: to secure someone with a belt, such as a seat belt in a car. _I had to belt her up because the seat belt was so complicated. _ We belted up the kids securely.
examples: I had to belt her up because the seat belt was so complicated.

belt something out†.monolingual: Fig. to sing or play a song loudly and with spirit. _When she’s playing the piano, she really belts the music out. _ She really knows how to belt out a song.
examples: When she’s playing the piano, she really belts the music out.

belt the grape.monolingual: Sl. to drink wine or liquor heavily and become intoxicated. _ He has a tendency to belt the grape—every afternoon after work. _She’s been belting the grape more than her husband wants.
examples: He has a tendency to belt the grape—every afternoon after work.

bend back.monolingual: to lean or bend backwards. _ He bent back to pick up the book, and he fell. _ When she bent back, she ripped something.
examples: He bent back to pick up the book, and he fell.

bend before something.monolingual: to bend under the pressure of moving air. _ The trees bent before the wind. _ Our roses bent gracefully before the breeze.
examples: The trees bent before the wind.

bend down.monolingual: to curve downward; [for someone] to lean down. _ Please bend down and pick up the little bits of paper you just dropped. _ The snow-laden bushes bent down.
examples: Please bend down and pick up the little bits of paper you just dropped.

bend forward.monolingual: to lean forward; to curve forward. _ The tree bent forward in the wind. _ I bent forward to pick up the pencil.
examples: The tree bent forward in the wind.

bend in.monolingual: to curve or turn inward. _The shore bent in about a mile to the west. _ The side of the shed bent in under the force of the wind.
examples: The shore bent in about a mile to the west.

bend over.monolingual: [for someone] to bend down at the waist. _ I bent over and picked up the coin. _ When he bent over, something ripped.
examples: I bent over and picked up the coin.

bend someone or something back†.monolingual: to curve or arch someone or something backward. _ We bent the child back a little so we could examine the spider bite. _ Ouch! Don’t bend back my hand! _ Bend the branch back so we can get a better view.
examples: We bent the child back a little so we could examine the spider bite.

bliss out.monolingual: Sl. to be overcome with happiness. _She blissed out at the concert, because she loves that kind of music.
examples: She blissed out at the concert, because she loves that kind of music.

bliss someone out†.monolingual: Sl. to cause someone to be overcome with happiness. _ This kind of sunny weather just blisses me out. _The lovely weather blissed out everyone after the long winter.
examples: This kind of sunny weather just blisses me out.

blitz someone out†.monolingual: Sl. to shock or disorient someone. _ The accident blitzed her out for a moment. _ The second act blitzed out the audience and thrilled them to pieces.
examples: The accident blitzed her out for a moment.

blitzed out.monolingual: Sl. shocked or disoriented. _ Ann was totally blitzed out by the events of the day. _ They were totally blitzed out by the bad news.
examples: Ann was totally blitzed out by the events of the day.

block someone up†.monolingual: to constipate someone. _ That food always blocks me up. _ He blocked himself up by eating something he shouldn’t. _ That vile stuff would block up anybody!
examples: That food always blocks me up.

block something off†.monolingual: to prevent movement through something by putting up a barrier; to close a passageway. _ Sam blocked the corridor off with a row of chairs. _He used some chairs to block off the hallway.
examples: Sam blocked the corridor off with a row of chairs.

block something out†.monolingual: 1. to obscure a clear view of something. _ The trees blocked the sun out. _ The bushes blocked out my view of the car that was approaching.
examples: The trees blocked the sun out.

block something up†.monolingual: to obstruct something; to stop the flow within a channel. _ The heaps of debris blocked the channel up. _ The leaves blocked up the drain.
examples: The heaps of debris blocked the channel up.

blood and guts.monolingual: 1. Fig. strife; acrimony. _ There is a lot of blood and guts around here, but we get our work done anyway. _ Cut out the blood and guts and grow up.
examples: There is a lot of blood and guts around here, but we get our work done anyway.

blood, sweat, and tears.monolingual: Fig. the signs of great personal effort. _ There will be much blood, sweat, and tears before we have completed this project. _ After years of blood, sweat, and tears, Timmy finally earned a college degree.
examples: There will be much blood, sweat, and tears before we have completed this project.

blood will have blood..monolingual: Prov. People will use violence to get revenge for violent acts; murderers will themselves be murdered. _ Although no one suspected him of the murder he had committed, Parker lived in fear. He had heard that blood will have blood. _I am afraid that th
examples: Although no one suspected him of the murder he had committed, Parker lived in fear.

blood will tell..monolingual: Prov. A person whose ancestors had certain characteristics, often bad ones, will eventually turn out to be similar. _ Lisa’s father was a gambler, and now Lisa has started to gamble, too. Blood will tell. _ William went to all the best schools, but h
examples: Lisa’s father was a gambler, and now Lisa has started to gamble, too.

bloody but unbowed.monolingual: Fig. showing signs of a struggle, but not defeated. (Originally referring to the head. From the poem Invictus by William Earnest Henley.) _ Liz emerged from the struggle, her head bloody but unbowed. _ We are bloody but unbowed and will fight to the
examples: Liz emerged from the struggle, her head bloody but unbowed.

blossom forth.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a plant] to burst into flower. _ All the trees blossomed forth at the same time. _ Each spring my tulips blossom forth in all their glory.
examples: All the trees blossomed forth at the same time.

blossom into something.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a plant] to develop into full bloom. _ The bush blossomed into beautiful red roses. _ Imagine this brown old bulb blossoming into a lovely f lower.
examples: The bush blossomed into beautiful red roses.

blossom out.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a plant or tree] to become covered with flowers. _ The apple tree blossomed out for the last time.
examples: The apple tree blossomed out for the last time.

a blot on the landscape.monolingual: Fig. a sight that spoils the look of a place. _ That monstrosity you call a house is a blot on the landscape. You should have hired a real architect!
examples: That monstrosity you call a house is a blot on the landscape.

blot someone or something out†.monolingual: Fig. to forget someone or something by covering up memories or by trying to forget. _ I try to blot those bad thoughts out. _ I tried to blot out those unhappy days.
examples: I try to blot those bad thoughts out.

blot someone out†.monolingual: Sl. to kill someone. (Originally underworld slang.) _ Sorry, chum, we got orders to blot you out. _ The gang blotted out the only living witness before the trial.
examples: Sorry, chum, we got orders to blot you out.

blot something out†.monolingual: to make something invisible by covering it. _ Don’t blot the name out on the application form. _ Who blotted out the name on this form?
examples: Don’t blot the name out on the application form.

blow away.monolingual: [for something light] to be carried away by the wind. _ The leaves blew away on the autumn winds. _ My papers blew away!
examples: The leaves blew away on the autumn winds.

blow hot and cold.monolingual: Fig. to be changeable or uncertain (about something). _ He keeps blowing hot and cold on the question of moving to the country. _ He blows hot and cold about this. I wish he’d make up his mind.
examples: He keeps blowing hot and cold on the question of moving to the country.

blow in.monolingual: [for something] to cave in to the pressure of moving air. _ The door blew in during the storm. _ The window blew in from the wind.
examples: The door blew in during the storm.

blow into something.monolingual: to force air into something. _He blew into the balloon. _ I blew into the box, hoping to get some of the little bits of paper out.
examples: He blew into the balloon.

blow it out your ear!.monolingual: Sl. Go away!; Leave me alone! _ Oh, blow it out your ear, you cornball! _ You are not cool, you’re just weird! Blow it out your ear!

blow itself out.monolingual: [for a storm or a tantrum] to lose strength and stop; to subside. (Fixed order.) _The storm blew itself out. _ Eventually, the hurricane blew itself out.
examples: The storm blew itself out.

blow on it!.monolingual: Sl. Cool it!; Take it easy! _ It’s all right, Tom. Blow on it! _ Hey, man. Relax. Blow on it!
examples: It’s all right, Tom.

blow on something.monolingual: to force air across something especially with a puff of breath. _ Jill blew on the hot soup. _ Blow on the fire to make it burn hotter.
examples: Jill blew on the hot soup.

blow one’s nose.monolingual: to expel mucus and other material from the nose using air pressure from the lungs. _ Excuse me, I have to blow my nose. _ Bill blew his nose into his handkerchief.
examples: Excuse me, I have to blow my nose.

blow over.monolingual: Fig. [for something] to diminish; to subside. (As with a storm or a temper tantrum.) _ Her display of temper finally blew over. _ The storm will blow over soon, I hope.
examples: Her display of temper finally blew over.

blow someone a kiss.monolingual: to pantomine the sending of a kiss to a person visible nearby by kissing one’s hand and “blowing” the kiss off the hand toward the person. _ As she boarded the train she blew him a kiss, and he waved back.
examples: As she boarded the train she blew him a kiss, and he waved back.

blow someone away.monolingual: 1. Sl. [for something shocking or exciting] to overwhelm a person; to excite a person very much. _ The amount of the check blew me away. _ The loud noise from the concert blew me away.
examples: The amount of the check blew me away.

blow someone or something away†.monolingual: [for the wind] to carry someone or something away. _ The wind almost blew her away. _ It nearly blew away all the houses.
examples: The wind almost blew her away.

blow someone or something down†.monolingual: [for a rush of air] to knock someone or something over. _ The wind blew Chuck down. _ The tornado blew down many buildings.
examples: The wind blew Chuck down.

blow someone or something over.monolingual: [for the wind] to move strongly and upset someone or something. _ The wind almost blew us over. _ The tornado blew the shed over.
examples: The wind almost blew us over.
