blow someone or something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to destroy someone or something by explosion. _The terrorists blew the building up at midday. _ They blew up the bridge.
examples: The terrorists blew the building up at midday.

blow someone out.monolingual: Sl. to kill someone, especially with gunshots. (Fixed order.) _ Lefty set out to blow Max out once and for all. _ Lefty wanted to blow Max out too.
examples: Lefty set out to blow Max out once and for all.

blow someone over†.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for the wind or an explosion] to knock someone over. _ The force of the wind nearly blew me over. _ The wind blew over the old tree.
examples: The force of the wind nearly blew me over.

blow someone’s brains out†.monolingual: Sl. to kill someone with a gun. _ Careful with that gun, or you’ll blow your brains out. _ Max was so depressed that he wanted to blow out his brains.
examples: Careful with that gun, or you’ll blow your brains out.

blow someone’s cover.monolingual: Sl. to reveal someone’s true identity; to ruin someone’s scheme for concealment. _ The dog recognized me and blew my cover. _ I didn’t mean to blow your cover by calling out to you.
examples: The dog recognized me and blew my cover.

blow someone’s doors off†.monolingual: Sl. [for a driver] to speed past another vehicle. _ Wow, he almost blew my doors off! _ The truck passed us and blew off our doors!

blow someone’s mind.monolingual: 1. Sl. to disturb or distract; to destroy the function of one’s brain. _ It was a terrible experience. It nearly blew my mind. _ She blew her mind on drugs.
examples: It was a terrible experience.

blow someone to something.monolingual: Sl. to pay for something or someone, such as a meal, a movie, a drink, etc. _ Let me blow you to a meal. _ I think I’ll blow myself to a fancy dessert.
examples: Let me blow you to a meal.

blow something out†.monolingual: to extinguish a flame with a puff of breath. _ I blew the candle out. _ I blew out the candles one by one.
examples: I blew the candle out.

blow something up†.monolingual: 1. to inflate something. _ He didn’t have enough breath to blow the balloon up. _They all blew up their own balloons.
examples: He didn’t have enough breath to blow the balloon up.

blow the joint.monolingual: Sl. to get out of a place, usually in a hurry or without delay. _ Come on, let’s blow the joint before there’s trouble. _ They blew the joint about an hour ago.
examples: Come on, let’s blow the joint before there’s trouble.

blow up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to explode. _ The bomb might have blown up if the children had tried to move it. _ The firecracker blew up.
examples: The bomb might have blown up if the children had tried to move it.

blow up in someone’s face.monolingual: 1. Lit. to blow up or explode suddenly. _The bomb blew up in the terrorist’s face. _The firecracker blew up in his face and injured him.
examples: The bomb blew up in the terrorist’s face.

blue blood.monolingual: 1. Fig. the blood [heredity] of a noble family; aristocratic ancestry. _ The earl refuses to allow anyone who is not of blue blood to marry his son. _ Although Mary’s family is poor, she has blue blood in her veins.
examples: The earl refuses to allow anyone who is not of blue blood to marry his son.

blue collar.monolingual: of the lower class or working class; of a job or a worker, having to do with manual labor. (Also, when used as an attributive adjective, often blue-collar. Com- pare this with white collar. Alludes to the typical color of work shirts worn by mechanic
examples: His parents were both blue-collar workers.

*the blues.monolingual: 1. sadness; a mood of depression. (*Typically: get ~; have ~.) _ You’ll have to excuse Bill. He’s getting the blues thinking about Jane. _ I get the blues every time I hear that song.
examples: You’ll have to excuse Bill.

bluff someone into something.monolingual: to mislead or deceive someone into doing something. _ Are you trying to bluff me into giving up without a fight? _ I won’t be bluffed into revealing the whereabouts of the safe.
examples: I won’t be bluffed into revealing the whereabouts of the safe.

blush with something.monolingual: [for someone’s cheeks] to redden from a particular emotion or reaction. _She blushed with shame. _ You could see that Lily was blushing with anger, even though she tried to conceal it.
examples: She blushed with shame.

board something up†.monolingual: to enclose or seal a building or part of a building with boards or panels. _ We will have to board this house up if we can’t sell it. _ Should I board up the house while I am away that season?
examples: We will have to board this house up if we can’t sell it.

board with someone.monolingual: to live with someone temporarily, usually while paying to do so. _I will board with my aunt when I go to school in Adamsville. _I do not wish to board with relatives.
examples: I will board with my aunt when I go to school in Adamsville.

bodily functions.monolingual: Euph. anything the body does automatically or as a normal occurrence, especially urinating and defecating. _ The dog needed to go outside and perform her bodily functions. _ It is not polite to discuss bodily functions at the dinner table.
examples: The dog needed to go outside and perform her bodily functions.

the body politic.monolingual: the people of a country or state considered as a political unit. _ The body politic was unable to select between the candidates.
examples: The body politic was unable to select between the candidates.

bog down.monolingual: to become encumbered and slow. (As if one were walking through a bog and getting stuck in the mud. Often preceded by a form of get.) _ The process bogged down and almost stopped. _The truck got bogged down in the mud soon after it started.
examples: The process bogged down and almost stopped.

*bogged down.monolingual: stuck; prevented from making progress. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; become ~.) _The students became bogged down with the algebra problems. _ The Smiths really got bogged down in decorating their house.
examples: The students became bogged down with the algebra problems.

boggle at something.monolingual: to be amazed at something, particularly something large or surprising. _ The audience boggled at the size of the loss. _ I boggled at the damage to my car.
examples: The audience boggled at the size of the loss.

boggle someone’s mind.monolingual: to confuse someone; to overwhelm someone; to blow someone’s mind. _The immense size of the house boggles my mind. _She said that his arrogance boggled her mind.
examples: The immense size of the house boggles my mind.

boil over.monolingual: [for a liquid] to overflow while being boiled. _ The sauce boiled over and dripped onto the stove. _ Don’t let the stew boil over!
examples: The sauce boiled over and dripped onto the stove.

boil something away†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to boil a liquid until it is gone altogether. _ She left the kettle on and boiled the water away. _ Boil away some of that water.
examples: She left the kettle on and boiled the water away.

boil something down†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to condense or thicken something, such as a liquid. _I have to boil this gravy down for a while before I can serve it. _You boil down the sauce and I’ll set the table.
examples: I have to boil this gravy down for a while before I can serve it.

boil something up†.monolingual: Rur. to cook a batch of food by boiling. _ She boiled some beans up for dinner. _ She boiled up some potatoes.
examples: She boiled some beans up for dinner.

boil with something.monolingual: Fig. to show the heat or intensity of one’s anger. _ You could see that she was just boiling with anger. _ Tom was boiling with rage when we got there.
examples: You could see that she was just boiling with anger.

*bold as brass.monolingual: very bold; bold to the point of rudeness. (*Also: as ~.) _ Lisa marched into the manager’s office, bold as brass, and demanded her money back. _ The tiny kitten, as bold as brass, began eating the dog’s food right under the dog’s nose.
examples: Lisa marched into the manager’s office, bold as brass, and demanded her money back.

bollix something up†.monolingual: Inf. to ruin something; to mess something up. _ Please don’t bollix my stereo up. _ Who bollixed up the folded laundry?
examples: Please don’t bollix my stereo up.

bolster someone up†.monolingual: Fig. to give someone emotional support and encouragement. _ We bolstered her up the best we could, but she was still unhappy. _ I don’t mind bolstering up people who are depressed.
examples: We bolstered her up the best we could, but she was still unhappy.

bolster something up†.monolingual: to give added support to something. _ The carpenter bolstered the shelf up with a nail or two. _ I had to bolster up the door or it would have fallen in.
examples: The carpenter bolstered the shelf up with a nail or two.

a bolt from the blue.monolingual: Fig. a sudden surprise. (Alludes to a stroke of lightning from a cloudless sky.) _ Joe’s return to Springfield was a bolt from the blue. _ The news that Mr. and Mrs. King were getting a divorce struck all their friends as a bolt from the blue.
examples: Joe’s return to Springfield was a bolt from the blue.

bolt something down†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to fasten something down securely with bolts. _ Did anyone bolt the washing machine down? _ Someone should bolt down this washing machine.
examples: Someone should bolt down this washing machine.

bomb someone out†.monolingual: to cause people to flee by bombing their homes and towns. _The planes bombed the villagers out. _ The attack bombed out everyone for miles around.
examples: The planes bombed the villagers out.

bomb something out†.monolingual: to destroy a place by bombing. _ I hope they don’t bomb the village out. _The planes bombed out the factory.
examples: I hope they don’t bomb the village out.

bombard someone with questions.monolingual: Fig. to ask someone many questions, one after another. _The press bombarded the president with questions. _The company spokesperson was bombarded with leading questions.
examples: The press bombarded the president with questions.

bone of contention.monolingual: Fig. the subject or point of an argument; an unsettled point of disagreement. _We’ve fought for so long that we’ve forgotten what the bone of contention is. _The question of a fence between the houses has become quite a bone of contention.
examples: We’ve fought for so long that we’ve forgotten what the bone of contention is.

booby prize.monolingual: a mock prize given to the worst player or performer. _Bob should get the booby prize for the worst showing in the race.
examples: Bob should get the booby prize for the worst showing in the race.

book someone on something.monolingual: to reserve a place for someone on some travel conveyance. _ They booked us on a direct f light to San Juan. _ He booked himself on a f light to Manaus.
examples: They booked us on a direct f light to San Juan.

book something up†.monolingual: to reserve all the available places. _ The travel agency booked all the good seats up. _ Who booked up all these seats?
examples: The travel agency booked all the good seats up.

boom out.monolingual: [for a loud sound] to sound out like thunder. _ His voice boomed out such that everyone could hear. _ An explosion boomed out and frightened us all.
examples: His voice boomed out such that everyone could hear.

boom something out†.monolingual: [for someone] to say something very loud; to shout. _Will someone with a loud voice boom the names out? _ The announcer boomed out the names of the players.
examples: The announcer boomed out the names of the players.

boost someone up†.monolingual: to give someone a helpful lift up to something. _She boosted me up so I could get into the window. _ They boosted up the child for a better view.
examples: She boosted me up so I could get into the window.

*the boot.monolingual: dismissal from employment or from a place that one is in. (*Typically: get ~; give someone ~.) _I guess I wasn’t dressed well enough to go in there. They gave me the boot. _ I’ll work harder at my job today. I nearly got the boot yesterday.
examples: I guess I wasn’t dressed well enough to go in there.

boot something up†.monolingual: to start up a computer. _ She booted her computer up and started writing. _ Please go boot up your computer so we can get started.
examples: She booted her computer up and started writing.

boot up.monolingual: [of a computer] to begin operating; to start up one’s computer. _He turned on the computer and it booted up. _ Try to boot up again and see what happens.
examples: He turned on the computer and it booted up.

booze it up.monolingual: Sl. to drink heavily; to drink to get drunk. (Fixed order.) _ She wanted to get home and booze it up by herself. _ He boozes it up every Friday after work.
examples: She wanted to get home and booze it up by herself.

booze up.monolingual: Sl. to drink heavily. _ Those guys are always boozing up. _ Stop boozing up and go home.
examples: Those guys are always boozing up.

bore through someone.monolingual: Fig. [for someone’s gaze] to seem to penetrate the person being gazed or stared at. _ Her stare bored right through me.
examples: Her stare bored right through me.

bore through something.monolingual: to pierce or drill through something. _The drill bit could not bore through the steel plate.
examples: The drill bit could not bore through the steel plate.

born out of wedlock.monolingual: born to an unmarried mother. _ The child was born out of wedlock. _In the city many children are born out of wedlock.
examples: The child was born out of wedlock.

borrow something.monolingual: Euph. to steal something. _ The bank robber borrowed a car to drive out of state. _ I discovered that my office mate had been borrowing money out of my wallet when I wasn’t looking.
examples: The bank robber borrowed a car to drive out of state.

borrow something from someone.monolingual: to request and receive the use of something from someone. _ Can I borrow a hammer from you? _ Sorry, this hammer was borrowed from my father.
examples: Sorry, this hammer was borrowed from my father.

borrow trouble.monolingual: Fig. to worry needlessly; to make trouble for oneself. _ Worrying too much about death is just borrowing trouble. _ Do not get involved with politics. That’s borrowing trouble.
examples: Worrying too much about death is just borrowing trouble.

boss someone around†.monolingual: to give orders to someone; to keep telling someone what to do. _Stop bossing me around. I’m not your employee. _ Captain Smith bosses around the whole crew. That’s his job.
examples: Stop bossing me around.

botch something up†.monolingual: to mess something up; to do a bad job of something. _ You really botched this up. _ I did not botch up your project.
examples: You really botched this up.

both sheets in the wind.monolingual: intoxicated. (A ship’s sheets are the ropes or lines that control the sails. See also three sheets in the wind.) _She’s both sheets in the wind at the moment. _ She’s not just both sheets in the wind—they’re all in the wind.
examples: She’s both sheets in the wind at the moment.

bother about something.monolingual: to care about something; to take the trouble to deal with something. _ Please don’t bother about this mess. I’ll clean it up. _ Don’t bother about it.
examples: Please don’t bother about this mess.

bother with someone or something.monolingual: to take the time or trouble to deal with someone or something. (Usually negative.) _ Please don’t bother with Jill. She can take care of herself. _ Don’t bother me with your problems.
examples: Please don’t bother with Jill.

the bottle.monolingual: drinking alcohol. _ His friends thought he was a bit too fond of the bottle. _ She tried to stay away from the bottle, but she never could manage it for long.
examples: His friends thought he was a bit too fond of the bottle.

the bottom line.monolingual: 1. Lit. the last figure on a financial profitand- loss statement, or on a bill. _What’s the bottom line? How much do I owe you? _ Don’t tell me all those figures! Just tell me the bottom line.
examples: Don’t tell me all those figures! Just tell me the bottom line.

bottom out.monolingual: Fig. to reach the lowest or worst point of something. _ All my problems seem to be bottoming out. They can’t get much worse. _ Interest rates bottomed out last February.
examples: All my problems seem to be bottoming out.

bounce along.monolingual: 1. Lit. to move along bouncing. (As might be done by a ball.) _ The ball bounced along and finally came to rest. _ The beach ball sort of bounced along until it came to the water.
examples: The ball bounced along and finally came to rest.

bounce something back and forth.monolingual: 1. Lit. to bat, toss, or throw something alternately between two people. (Usually a ball.) _The two guys bounced the ball back and forth. _ John and Timmy bounced it back and forth.
examples: The two guys bounced the ball back and forth.

bounce up and down.monolingual: to spring up and down due to natural elasticity or from being jostled or thrown. _The ball bounced up and down for an amazingly long time. _ I bounced up and down in the back of that truck for almost an hour.
examples: The ball bounced up and down for an amazingly long time.

bound and determined.monolingual: Cliché very determined; very committed or dedicated (to something). _We were bound and determined to get there on time. _ I’m bound and determined that this won’t happen again.
examples: We were bound and determined to get there on time.

bound for somewhere.monolingual: headed for a specific goal or destination. _ Bill accidentally got on a bus bound for Miami. _ Our baseball team is bound for glory.
examples: Bill accidentally got on a bus bound for Miami.

bound hand and foot.monolingual: with hands and feet tied up. _ The robbers left us bound hand and foot. _ We remained bound hand and foot until the police found us and untied us.
examples: The robbers left us bound hand and foot.

bound to do something.monolingual: certain to do something; destined to do something. _ Jill’s bound to do a good job. _ We are bound to tell the truth.
examples: Jill’s bound to do a good job.

bow and scrape.monolingual: Fig. to be very humble and subservient. _Please don’t bow and scrape. We are all equal here. _The salesclerk came in, bowing and scraping, and asked if he could help us.
examples: Please don’t bow and scrape.

bow before someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to bend or curtsy in respect to someone or something. _ I will not bow before any king or queen. _Henry insisted that I bow before him.
examples: I will not bow before any king or queen.

bow to someone’s demands.monolingual: Fig. to yield to someone’s demands; to agree to do something that someone has requested. _ In the end, they had to bow to our demands. _We refused to bow to their demands that we abandon the project.
examples: In the end, they had to bow to our demands.

bow to the porcelain altar.monolingual: Sl. to vomit, especially as a result of drinking too much alcohol. (The porcelain altar is a euphemism for a toilet bowl.) _ He spent the whole night bowing to the porcelain altar. _I have the feeling that I will be bowing to the porcelain altar befo
examples: He spent the whole night bowing to the porcelain altar.

bowl someone over.monolingual: 1. Lit. to knock someone over. (Fixed order.) _ We were bowled over by the wind. _ Bob hit his brother and bowled him over.
examples: We were bowled over by the wind.

bowl up.monolingual: to fill a pipe bowl with smokable material. _The detective bowled up and struck a match. _ Roger bowled up, but forgot to light his pipe.
examples: The detective bowled up and struck a match.

box someone in†.monolingual: Fig. to put someone into a bind; to reduce the number of someone’s alternatives. _ I don’t want to box you in, but you are running out of options. _ I want to box in the whole staff, so they’ll have to do it my way.
examples: I don’t want to box you in, but you are running out of options.

box someone or something in†.monolingual: to trap or confine someone or something. _ He boxed her in so she could not get away from him. _ They tried to box in the animals, but they needed more space. _ Don’t try to box me in.
examples: He boxed her in so she could not get away from him.

box someone up†.monolingual: to confine someone in a small area. _ Please don’t box me up in that little office. _The boss boxed up Fred in a tiny office. _ Why the president boxes himself up in such a little office is beyond me.
examples: Please don’t box me up in that little office.

box something up†.monolingual: to place something in a box. _ Please box the books up and put them into the trunk of the car. _ Please box up four of these for me.
examples: Please box the books up and put them into the trunk of the car.

boxed in.monolingual: Fig. in a bind; having few alternatives. _ I really feel boxed in around here. _ I got him boxed in. He’ll have to do it our way.
examples: I really feel boxed in around here.

boxed on the table.monolingual: Sl. died on the (operating) table. (Medical.) _ The surgeon did the best job possible, but the patient boxed on the table. _ Another patient boxed on the table. That’s three this month.
examples: The surgeon did the best job possible, but the patient boxed on the table.

boy howdy!.monolingual: Rur. an exclamation of excited surprise. _ Bob: Well, I finally got here. Fred: Boy howdy! Am I glad to see you! _ Bill: How do you like my horse? Fred: That’s one fine-looking filly! Boy howdy!
examples: Bob: Well, I finally got here.

boys will be boys..monolingual: Prov. Boys are expected to be irresponsible or boisterous. (Also said ironically about men.) _ You can’t blame David for breaking the window with his baseball. Boys will be boys. _My husband can’t resist driving eighty miles an hour in his new sports
examples: You can’t blame David for breaking the window with his baseball.

brace oneself for something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to hang onto something or prop oneself against something in preparation for something that might cause one to fall, blow away, wash away, etc. _ Hold onto the rail. Brace yourself. Here comes another huge wave.
examples: Hold onto the rail.

brace someone or something up†.monolingual: to prop up or add support to someone or something. _ They braced the tree up for the expected windstorm. _ They braced up the tree again after the storm.
examples: They braced the tree up for the expected windstorm.

brace up.monolingual: to take heart; to be brave. _ Brace up! Things could be worse. _ I told John to brace up because things would probably get worse before they got better.
examples: Brace up! Things could be worse.

brag about someone or something.monolingual: to boast about someone or something; to talk proudly about someone or something. _ He bragged about how selfish he was. _ Jill brags a lot about her kids.
examples: He bragged about how selfish he was.

brain someone.monolingual: Fig. to strike a person hard on the skull as if to knock out the person’s brains. (Often said as a vain threat.) _ I thought he was going to brain me, but he only hit me on the shoulder. _ If you don’t do it, I’ll brain you.
examples: I thought he was going to brain me, but he only hit me on the shoulder.

brainwash someone with something.monolingual: to drive specific knowledge or propaganda into someone’s brain, by constant repetition and psychological conditioning. _ The dictator brainwashed his people with lie after lie. _You have brainwashed yourself with your own propaganda.
examples: The dictator brainwashed his people with lie after lie.

brass someone off†.monolingual: Sl. to make someone angry. (Primarily military. As angry as the “brass,” or officers, might get about something.) _ You really brass me off. _ The private brassed off the sergeant.
examples: You really brass me off.

brave something out†.monolingual: to endure something; to put up with something courageously. _I don’t know if all the men can brave the attack out. _ The soldiers braved out the attack.
examples: I don’t know if all the men can brave the attack out.

bread and water.monolingual: Fig. the most minimal meal possible; a meal as once was given to prisoners. (Usually used in reference to being in prison or jail.) _ Wilbur knew that if he got in trouble again it would be at least a year on bread and water. _ This dinner is terribl
examples: Wilbur knew that if he got in trouble again it would be at least a year on bread and water.

bread-and-butter letter.monolingual: a letter or note written to follow up on a visit; a thank-you note. _ When I got back from the sales meeting, I took two days to write bread-andbutter letters to the people I met. _ I got sort of a breadand- butter letter from my nephew, who wants to
examples: When I got back from the sales meeting, I took two days to write bread-andbutter letters to the people I met.

break a code.monolingual: to figure out a code; to decipher a secret code. _ The intelligence agents finally broke the enemy’s code. _ When they broke the code, they were able to decipher messages.
examples: The intelligence agents finally broke the enemy’s code.

break a leg!.monolingual: Fig. Good luck! (A special theatrical way of wishing a performer good luck. Saying “good luck” is considered by actors to be a jinx.) _“Break a leg!” shouted the stage manager to the heroine. _Let’s all go and do our best. Break a leg!
examples: “Break a leg!” shouted the stage manager to the heroine.

break a record.monolingual: to destroy a previously set high record by setting a new one. _ The athlete broke all the school records in swimming. _The league record was broken after thirty years.
examples: The athlete broke all the school records in swimming.

break a story.monolingual: [for a media outlet] to be the first to broadcast or distribute the story of an event. _ The Tribune broke the story before the Herald could even send a reporter to the scene.
examples: The Tribune broke the story before the Herald could even send a reporter to the scene.

break against something.monolingual: [for something] to crash against something. _ The waves broke against the barrier. _ The glass broke against the side of the sink.
examples: The waves broke against the barrier.

break bread with someone.monolingual: Fig. to eat a meal with someone. _ Please come by and break bread with us sometime. _ I would like to break bread with you.
examples: Please come by and break bread with us sometime.

break camp.monolingual: to close down a campsite; to pack up and move on. _ Early this morning we broke camp and moved on northward. _ Okay, everyone. It’s time to break camp. Take those tents down and fold them neatly.
examples: Early this morning we broke camp and moved on northward.

break down.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to fall apart; [for something] to stop operating. _ The air-conditioning broke down, and we got very warm. _ The car broke down on the long trip.
examples: The air-conditioning broke down, and we got very warm.

break even.monolingual: for income to equal expenses. (This implies that money was not made or lost.) _ Unfortunately, my business just managed to break even last year. _ I made a bad investment, but I broke even.
examples: Unfortunately, my business just managed to break even last year.

break for something.monolingual: 1. to stop working for something else, such as lunch, coffee, etc. _We should break now for lunch. _ I want to break for coffee.
examples: We should break now for lunch.

break into a gallop.monolingual: [for a horse] to begin to gallop; [for a horse] to speed up to a gallop. _ The pony broke into a gallop, racing to get home. _ Near the stables, the horse broke into a fast gallop.
examples: The pony broke into a gallop, racing to get home.

break into something.monolingual: to begin to perform or utter suddenly, especially with song, speech, chattering, tears, etc. _ Suddenly, she broke into song. _ As soon as the movie started, the people behind me broke into loud chattering.
examples: Suddenly, she broke into song.

break it up!.monolingual: Stop fighting!; Stop arguing! (Fixed order.) _Tom: I’m going to break your neck! Bill: I’m going to mash in your face first! Bob: All right, you two, break it up! _ When the police officer saw the boys fighting, he came over and hollered, “Break it u

break new ground.monolingual: Fig. to begin to do something that no one else has done; to pioneer [in an enterprise]. _ Dr. Anderson was breaking new ground in cancer research. _ They were breaking new ground in consumer electronics.
examples: Dr. Anderson was breaking new ground in cancer research.

break one’s stride.monolingual: to deviate from a rhythmic stride while walking, running, or marching. _ After I broke my stride, I never could pick up enough speed to win the race.
examples: After I broke my stride, I never could pick up enough speed to win the race.

break one’s word.monolingual: not to do what one said one would do; not to keep one’s promise. (Compare this with keep one’s word.) _ Don’t say you’ll visit your grandmother if you can’t go. She hates people to break their word. _If you break your word, she won’t trust you again.
examples: Don’t say you’ll visit your grandmother if you can’t go.

break out.monolingual: 1. to burst forth suddenly, as with a fire, a riot, giggling, shouting, etc. _ A fire broke out in the belfry. _ A round of giggling broke out when the teacher tripped.
examples: A fire broke out in the belfry.

break out in a rash.monolingual: [for the skin] to erupt with a rash. _I knew Dan had the chicken pox, because he broke out in a rash and had a dry cough. _ The baby breaks out in a rash all the time.
examples: I knew Dan had the chicken pox, because he broke out in a rash and had a dry cough.

break out with something.monolingual: to utter or emit laughter, a shout, or a cry. _ The kids broke out with a cheer. _ They broke out with laughter every time they saw the lady with the red wig.
examples: The kids broke out with a cheer.

break over something.monolingual: [for waves] to lift high and tumble over a barrier. _The waves broke over the rocks at the shore. _ Huge waves broke over the bow of the ship.
examples: The waves broke over the rocks at the shore.

break silence.monolingual: to give information about a topic that no one was mentioning or discussing. _ The press finally broke silence on the question of the plagiarized editorial.
examples: The press finally broke silence on the question of the plagiarized editorial.

break someone down†.monolingual: to force someone to give up and tell secrets or agree to do something. _After threats of torture, they broke the spy down. _They broke down the agent by threatening violence.
examples: After threats of torture, they broke the spy down.

break someone in†.monolingual: to train someone to do a new job; to supervise someone who is learning to do a new job. _ Who will break the new employee in? _ I have to break in a new receptionist.
examples: I have to break in a new receptionist.

break someone’s fall.monolingual: to cushion a falling person; to lessen the impact of a falling person. _ When the little boy fell out of the window, the bushes broke his fall. _The old lady slipped on the ice, but a snowbank broke her fall.
examples: When the little boy fell out of the window, the bushes broke his fall.

break someone’s heart.monolingual: Fig. to cause someone great emotional pain. _ It just broke my heart when Tom ran away from home. _ Sally broke John’s heart when she refused to marry him.
examples: It just broke my heart when Tom ran away from home.

break someone up†.monolingual: to cause a person to laugh, perhaps at an inappropriate time. _ John told a joke that really broke Mary up. _ The comedian’s job was to break up the audience by telling jokes.
examples: John told a joke that really broke Mary up.

break something down†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to tear something down; to destroy something. _They used an ax to break the door down. _We broke down the wall with big hammers.
examples: They used an ax to break the door down.

break something in†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to crush or batter something to pieces; to break something down. _Why are you breaking the door in? Here’s the key! _ Who broke in the door?
examples: Who broke in the door? 2.

break something loose from something.monolingual: to loosen a part of something; to loosen and remove a part of something. _ The mechanic broke the strap loose from the tailpipe. _ The bracket was broken loose from the wall.
examples: The mechanic broke the strap loose from the tailpipe.

break something on something.monolingual: to strike and break something against something else. _ She broke the glass on the countertop. _ He broke his arm on the steps.
examples: She broke the glass on the countertop.

break something to pieces.monolingual: to shatter something. _I broke my crystal vase to pieces. _ I dropped a glass and broke it to pieces.
examples: I broke my crystal vase to pieces.

break something to someone.monolingual: to disclose some news or information to someone. (Often said of unpleasant news.) _I hate to be the one to break this to you, but there is trouble at home. _ We broke the bad news to Ken gently.
examples: I hate to be the one to break this to you, but there is trouble at home.

break something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to destroy something. _ The storm broke the docks up on the lake. _The police broke up the gambling ring.
examples: The storm broke the docks up on the lake.

break the back of something.monolingual: Fig. to end the domination of something; to reduce the power of something. _ The government has worked for years to break the back of organized crime. _ This new medicine should break the back of the epidemic.
examples: The government has worked for years to break the back of organized crime.

break the bank.monolingual: Fig. to use up all one’s money. (Alludes to casino gambling, in the rare event when a gambler wins more money than the house has on hand.) _It will hardly break the bank if we go out to dinner just once. _ Buying a new dress at a discount price won’t
examples: It will hardly break the bank if we go out to dinner just once.

break the ice.monolingual: 1. Fig. to attempt to become friends with someone. _ He tried to break the ice, but she was a little cold. _ A nice smile does a lot to break the ice.
examples: He tried to break the ice, but she was a little cold.

break the silence.monolingual: to make a noise interrupting a period of silence. _The wind broke the silence by blowing the door closed.
examples: The wind broke the silence by blowing the door closed.

break the spell.monolingual: to put an end to a magic spell. _ The wizard looked in his magic book to find out how to break the spell.
examples: The wizard looked in his magic book to find out how to break the spell.

break up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to fall apart; to be broken to pieces. (Typically said of a ship breaking up on rocks.) _In the greatest storm of the century, the ship broke up on the reef. _ It broke up and sank.
examples: In the greatest storm of the century, the ship broke up on the reef.

break wind.monolingual: Euph. to expel gas from the anus. _Someone in the bus broke wind. It smelled terrible. _ He broke wind with an embarrassing noise.
examples: Someone in the bus broke wind.

breaking and entering.monolingual: the crime of forcing one’s way into a place. (A criminal charge.) _ Wilbur was charged with four counts of breaking and entering. _ It was not an act of breaking and entering. The thief just opened the door and walked right in.
examples: Wilbur was charged with four counts of breaking and entering.

the breaking point.monolingual: 1. Lit. the point at which something will break. _ The mule’s back was strained to the breaking point with masses of bundles and straw.
examples: The mule’s back was strained to the breaking point with masses of bundles and straw.

a breath of fresh air.monolingual: 1. Lit. an influx of air that is not stale or smelly, especially from outdoors. _ You look ill, John. What you need is a breath of fresh air.
examples: You look ill, John.

breathe a sigh of relief.monolingual: 1. Lit. to sigh in a way that signals one’s relief that something has come to an end. _ At the end of the contest, we all breathed a sigh of relief.
examples: At the end of the contest, we all breathed a sigh of relief.

breathe down someone’s neck.monolingual: 1. Fig. to keep close watch on someone; to watch someone’s activities intently. (Alludes to someone standing very close behind a person.) _ I can’t work with you breathing down my neck all the time. Go away. _ I will get through my life without your
examples: I can’t work with you breathing down my neck all the time.

breathe easy.monolingual: to assume a relaxed state after a stressful period. _After this crisis is over, I’ll be able to breathe easy again. _ He won’t be able to breathe easy until he pays off his debts.
examples: After this crisis is over, I’ll be able to breathe easy again.

breathe in.monolingual: to inhale; to take air into the lungs. _ Now, relax and breathe in. Breathe out. _Breathe in deeply; enjoy the summer air.
examples: Now, relax and breathe in.

breathe into something.monolingual: to exhale into something; to expel one’s breath into something. _ I was told to breathe into a tube that was connected to a machine of some type.
examples: I was told to breathe into a tube that was connected to a machine of some type.

breathe one’s last.monolingual: Euph. to die. _ She breathed her last at about two o’clock that afternoon. _ Cradled in his wife’s arms, he breathed his last.
examples: She breathed her last at about two o’clock that afternoon.

breathe out.monolingual: to exhale. _ Now, breathe out, then breathe in. _ The doctor told me to breathe out slowly.
examples: Now, breathe out, then breathe in.

breathe something in†.monolingual: to take something into the lungs, such as air, medicinal vapors, gas, etc. _Breathe the vapor in slowly. It will help your cold. _ Breathe in that fresh air!
examples: Breathe the vapor in slowly.

breathe something into something.monolingual: to revive something; to introduce something new or positive into a situation. _ Her positive attitude breathed new life into the company. _ The project breathed a new spirit into the firm.
examples: Her positive attitude breathed new life into the company.

breathe something out†.monolingual: to exhale something. _ At last, he breathed his last breath out, and that was the end. _ Breathe out your breath slowly.
examples: At last, he breathed his last breath out, and that was the end.

breeding will tell..monolingual: Prov. One’s character or lack of it will become known. _ From the beginning, he appeared to be courteous, and now he clearly has proven himself to be so. Breeding will tell.
examples: From the beginning, he appeared to be courteous, and now he clearly has proven himself to be so.

breeze along.monolingual: Fig. to travel along casually, rapidly, and happily; to go through life in a casual and carefree manner. _ Kristine was just breezing along the road when she ran off onto the shoulder. _We just breezed along the highway, barely paying attention to wh
examples: Kristine was just breezing along the road when she ran off onto the shoulder.

breeze away.monolingual: to leave quickly or abruptly. _She said nothing more. She just breezed away. _ I breezed away without stopping to say good-bye.
examples: She said nothing more.

breeze off.monolingual: to leave quickly or abruptly. _Don’t just breeze off! Stay and talk. _ Lily breezed off in a huffy manner.
examples: Don’t just breeze off! Stay and talk.

brew a plot.monolingual: Fig. to plot something; to make a plot. _The children brewed an evil plot to get revenge on their teacher. _We brewed a plot so that we would not have to help with dinner.
examples: The children brewed an evil plot to get revenge on their teacher.

brew something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to brew something, as in making coffee or tea. _Can somebody brew some coffee up? _ Let me brew up a pot of tea, and then we’ll talk.
examples: Let me brew up a pot of tea, and then we’ll talk.

brew up.monolingual: Fig. to build up; [for something] to begin to build and grow. (Typically said of a storm.) _ A bad storm is brewing up in the west. _ Something serious is brewing up in the western sky.
examples: A bad storm is brewing up in the west.

bribe someone into doing something.monolingual: to pay money to get someone to do something. _You can’t bribe me into doing anything! _ Max bribed Lily into leaving early.
examples: Max bribed Lily into leaving early.

brick something up†.monolingual: to fill up an opening with bricks. _ He bricked the doorway up. _ Why did he brick up the opening?
examples: He bricked the doorway up.

bricks and mortar.monolingual: buildings; the expenditure of money on buildings rather than something else. (The buildings referred to can be constructed out of anything.) _ The new president of the college preferred to invest in new faculty members rather than bricks and mortar.
examples: The new president of the college preferred to invest in new faculty members rather than bricks and mortar.

bridge over something.monolingual: to make a bridge or passage over something. _They bridged over each of the streams as they came to them. _ I think we can bridge over this little river in a few days if we work hard.
examples: They bridged over each of the streams as they came to them.

bridge the gap.monolingual: 1. Lit. to make a bridge that reaches across a space. _ The engineers decided to bridge the gap with a wooden structure.
examples: The engineers decided to bridge the gap with a wooden structure.

bridle at someone or something.monolingual: Fig. to show that one is offended by someone or something. _ She bridled at the suggestion that she should go. _Tony bridled at Max. Max was going to have to be dealt with.
examples: She bridled at the suggestion that she should go.

bright and breezy.monolingual: cheery and alert. _You look all bright and breezy this morning. _ Bright and breezy people on a gloomy day like this make me sick.
examples: You look all bright and breezy this morning.

bright and early.monolingual: very early in the morning or the workday. _Yes, I’ll be there bright and early. _I want to see you here on time tomorrow, bright and early, or you’re fired!
examples: Yes, I’ll be there bright and early.

*bright as a button.monolingual: intelligent; quick-minded. (Usually used to describe children. *Also: as ~.) _ Why, Mrs. Green, your little girl is as bright as a button. _ You can’t fool Jane. She may be only six years old, but she’s bright as a button.
examples: Why, Mrs. Green, your little girl is as bright as a button.

*bright as a new pin.monolingual: bright and clean; shiny. (*Also: as ~.) _After Joe cleaned the house, it was as bright as a new pin. _My kitchen f loor is bright as a new pin since I started using this new f loor wax.
examples: After Joe cleaned the house, it was as bright as a new pin.

*a bright idea.monolingual: a clever thought or new idea. (*Typically: have ~; get ~; give someone ~.) _ Now and then I get a bright idea. _ John hardly ever gets a bright idea.
examples: Now and then I get a bright idea.

brighten up.monolingual: to become brighter; to lighten, especially with sunshine. _The sky is brightening up a little. _When the morning sky brightens up just a little, the birds begin to sing.
examples: The sky is brightening up a little.

bright-eyed and bushy-tailed.monolingual: Fig. awake and alert. (Often used ironically, as in the first example. The idea is that one is like a frisky animal, such as a squirrel.) _ Jill: Hi, Jane! How are you on this beautiful morning? Jane: Bright-eyed and bushy-tailed, just as you might e
examples: Jill: Hi, Jane! How are you on this beautiful morning? Jane: Bright-eyed and bushy-tailed, just as you might expect, since I’ve only had three hours of sleep.

brimming with something.monolingual: Fig. full of some kind of happy behavior. _ The volunteer workers were brimming with goodwill. _ The smiling children were brimming with joy.
examples: The volunteer workers were brimming with goodwill.

bring a dog to heel.monolingual: to make a dog heel; to make a dog stand or follow close to one’s heels. _ A quiet command from his owner brought Fido to heel.
examples: A quiet command from his owner brought Fido to heel.

bring a verdict in†.monolingual: [for a jury] to deliver its decision to the court. _Do you think they will bring a verdict in today? _ The jury brought in their verdict around midnight.
examples: The jury brought in their verdict around midnight.

bring home the bacon.monolingual: Fig. to earn a salary; to bring home money earned at a job. _ I’ve got to get to work if I’m going to bring home the bacon. _ Go out and get a job so you can bring home the bacon.
examples: I’ve got to get to work if I’m going to bring home the bacon.

bring one to one’s senses.monolingual: to cause someone to return to normal [after being out of control or irrational]. _A gentle slap in the face brought him to his senses. _ Liz was brought to her senses quickly.
examples: A gentle slap in the face brought him to his senses.

bring one to oneself.monolingual: to cause one to become rational; to cause one to act normal. _ A glass of ice water thrown in her face brought Sally to herself. _ I was brought to myself by some smelling salts.
examples: A glass of ice water thrown in her face brought Sally to herself.

bring someone back out.monolingual: [for an applauding audience] to succeed in bringing a performer back onto the stage for a curtain call or encore. _ They brought her back out about seven times, cheering and applauding. _ She was brought back out repeatedly for curtain calls.
examples: They brought her back out about seven times, cheering and applauding.

bring someone back to reality.monolingual: to force someone to face reality. _ The rain shower brought her back to reality. _ Liz was brought back to reality by a rude shock.
examples: The rain shower brought her back to reality.

bring someone down†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to assist or accompany someone from a higher place to a lower place. _ Please bring your friends down so I can meet them. _She brought down her cousin, who had been taking a nap upstairs. _ Aunt Mattie was brought down for supper.
examples: Please bring your friends down so I can meet them.

bring someone down to earth.monolingual: Fig. to help someone face reality; to help someone who is euphoric become more realistic. _ The events helped bring us all down to earth. _I hate to be the one to bring you down to earth, but things aren’t as good as you think.
examples: The events helped bring us all down to earth.

bring someone into the world.monolingual: Fig. to deliver a baby; to attend the birth of someone. _ The doctor who brought me into the world died last week. _ I was brought into the world by a kindly old doctor.
examples: The doctor who brought me into the world died last week.

bring someone on†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to bring someone out onto the stage. _ Now, for the next act, I’m going to bring a chorus on, and I’m sure you’ll love them. _ Bring on the clowns!
examples: Now, for the next act, I’m going to bring a chorus on, and I’m sure you’ll love them.

bring someone or something back†.monolingual: to make someone or something return. _Would you please bring the child back? _ Bring back my child!

bring someone or something forth†.monolingual: to present or produce someone or something. _ Bring the roast turkey forth! _ Bring forth the roast turkey!

bring someone or something forward.monolingual: to introduce someone or something; to move someone or something into a more visible position. _ Please bring him forward so that we can examine him. _ Please bring your chair forward so I can see you.
examples: Please bring him forward so that we can examine him.

bring someone or something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to cause someone or something to go up with one from a lower place to a higher place. _We brought them up and let them view the city from the balcony. _Why did you bring up Tom? Wasn’t he comfortable down there?
examples: We brought them up and let them view the city from the balcony.

bring someone or something up-to-date.monolingual: to modernize someone or something. _We brought the room up-to-date with a little paint and some modern furniture. _I can bring you up-to-date with a new hairdo.
examples: We brought the room up-to-date with a little paint and some modern furniture.

bring someone over† to something.monolingual: to bring someone for a visit and a meal or other event. _ Please bring your friend over to dinner sometime. _ I want to bring over my husband sometime.
examples: Please bring your friend over to dinner sometime.

bring someone through something.monolingual: to help someone endure something, such as a disease, an emotional upset, or a stressful period. _ The doctor brought Tom through the sickness. _ Liz was brought through the ordeal by her friends.
examples: The doctor brought Tom through the sickness.

bring someone to.monolingual: to help someone return to consciousness. _ We worked to bring him to before he went into shock. _ He was finally brought to by the smelling salts.
examples: We worked to bring him to before he went into shock.

bring someone to a boil.monolingual: Fig. to make someone very angry. _This really brought her to a boil. She was fit to be tied. _ Lily was really brought to a boil by the news.
examples: This really brought her to a boil.

bring someone to account.monolingual: Fig. to confront someone with a record of misdeeds and errors. _The committee decided to bring Martha to account. _ Martha was brought to account by the committee.
examples: The committee decided to bring Martha to account.

bring someone to do something.monolingual: to cause someone to do something; to encourage someone to do something. _ What brought you to do this? _ I was brought to do this by a guilty conscience.
examples: I was brought to do this by a guilty conscience.

bring someone to heel.monolingual: Fig. to cause someone to act in a disciplined fashion; to force someone to act in a more disciplined manner. _She tried to bring her husband to heel, but he had a mind of his own. _ He was brought to heel by his demanding wife.
examples: She tried to bring her husband to heel, but he had a mind of his own.

bring someone to justice.monolingual: Fig. to punish someone for a crime. _ The police officer swore she would not rest until she had brought the killer to justice. _Years later, the rapist was found out and finally brought to justice.
examples: The police officer swore she would not rest until she had brought the killer to justice.

bring someone together.monolingual: 1. Lit. to cause people to gather into a group. _ He brought everyone together in the drawing room. _ They were brought together in a large conference room.
examples: He brought everyone together in the drawing room.

bring someone up† for something.monolingual: 1. to suggest someone’s name for something. _ I would like to bring Beth up for vice president. _ I will bring up Beth for this office if you don’t.
examples: I would like to bring Beth up for vice president.

bring someone up† on something.monolingual: to provide something while raising a child to adulthood. _She brought her children up on fast food. _ You shouldn’t bring up your children on that kind of entertainment!
examples: She brought her children up on fast food.

bring something about†.monolingual: to make something happen. _ Is she clever enough to bring it about? _Oh, yes, she can bring about anything she wants.
examples: Oh, yes, she can bring about anything she wants.

bring something all together.monolingual: to organize something; to coordinate something or some event. _ The party was a great success. Janet was the one who brought it all together. _It was a difficult conference to organize, but Sam brought it all together.
examples: The party was a great success.

bring something back†.monolingual: to restore an earlier style or practice. _ Please bring the good old days back. _ Bring back good times for all of us.
examples: Please bring the good old days back.

bring something back to life.monolingual: Fig. to restore vitality to something, such as a performance, a story, etc. _ The third act of the play had a clever twist that brought the whole drama back to life.
examples: The third act of the play had a clever twist that brought the whole drama back to life.

bring something down†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to move something from a higher place to a lower place. _ Bring that box down, please. _ And while you’re up there, please bring down the box marked “winter clothing.”
examples: Bring that box down, please.

bring something down to something.monolingual: to make a concept simpler to understand by bringing it to a simpler level of understanding. _Why don’t you bring all this down to my level? _ Everything was brought down to the child’s level.
examples: Everything was brought down to the child’s level.

bring something home to someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to return home with a gift for someone. _ I brought a box of candy home to the children. _ The candy was brought home to Lily by Ken.
examples: I brought a box of candy home to the children.

bring something into being.monolingual: to cause something to be; to create something. _ How can I bring my new scheme into being? _ The new scheme was brought into being by a lot of hard work.
examples: The new scheme was brought into being by a lot of hard work.

bring something into blossom.monolingual: to make a plant or tree bloom. _ The special plant food brought the rosebush into blossom. _The roses were brought into blossom by the lovely weather.
examples: The special plant food brought the rosebush into blossom.

bring something into focus.monolingual: 1. Lit. to make something seen through lenses sharply visible. _I adjusted the binoculars until I brought the bird sharply into focus. _The flowers were brought into focus by adjusting the controls.
examples: I adjusted the binoculars until I brought the bird sharply into focus.

bring something into play.monolingual: 1. Lit. [in a ball game] to put the ball into the action of the game, such as after a timeout. _ Fred brought the ball into play when he bounced it in from the sidelines.
examples: Fred brought the ball into play when he bounced it in from the sidelines.

bring something into question.monolingual: to cause something to be doubted; to cause something to be questioned. _ What you have just told me seems to bring the wisdom of the trip into question. _ Your presence here has been brought into question.
examples: What you have just told me seems to bring the wisdom of the trip into question.

bring something into service.monolingual: to begin to use something; to start something up. _ They are bringing a much larger boat into service next month. _ A newer machine will be brought into service next year.
examples: They are bringing a much larger boat into service next month.

bring something off†.monolingual: to cause something to happen; to carry out a plan successfully. _Do you think you can bring it off ? _ She brought off her plan without a hitch!

bring something on†.monolingual: 1. to cause something to happen; to cause a situation to occur. _ What brought this event on? _ What brought on this catastrophe?
examples: What brought on this catastrophe? 2.

bring something on someone.monolingual: to cause something to go wrong for someone. _ You brought it on yourself. Don’t complain. _ Max brought this problem on all of us.
examples: You brought it on yourself.

bring something out of mothballs.monolingual: Fig. to bring something out of storage and into use; to restore something to active service. _They were going to bring a number of ships out of mothballs, but the war ended before they needed them.
examples: They were going to bring a number of ships out of mothballs, but the war ended before they needed them.

bring something to a boil.monolingual: to heat liquid to its boiling point; to make something boil. _ First, you must bring the soup to a boil.
examples: First, you must bring the soup to a boil.

bring something to a head.monolingual: to cause something to come to the point when a decision has to be made or action taken. _The latest disagreement between management and the union has brought matters to a head. There will be an all-out strike now. _ It’s a relief that things have bee
examples: The latest disagreement between management and the union has brought matters to a head.

bring something to a standstill.monolingual: to cause a process or a job to reach a point at which it must stop. _ The accident brought the work to a standstill. _ The strike brought construction to a standstill.
examples: The accident brought the work to a standstill.

bring something to fruition.monolingual: to make something come into being; to achieve a success. _ Do you think you can bring this plan to fruition? _ The plan was brought to fruition by the efforts of everyone.
examples: The plan was brought to fruition by the efforts of everyone.

bring something to light.monolingual: Fig. to make something known. _The scientists brought their findings to light. _We must bring this new evidence to light.
examples: The scientists brought their findings to light.

bring something to rest.monolingual: to cause a machine, vehicle, or process to stop. _ Jill brought the car to rest against the curb. _ The car was brought to rest against the curb.
examples: Jill brought the car to rest against the curb.

bring something to someone’s aid.monolingual: to bring something with which to help someone. _The officer brought medical supplies to our aid. _An ambulance was brought to the injured man’s aid.
examples: The officer brought medical supplies to our aid.

bring something to someone’s attention.monolingual: to make someone aware of something; to mention or show something to someone. _ I would like to bring this problem to your attention. _ If there is something I should know about, please bring it to my attention.
examples: I would like to bring this problem to your attention.

bring something to the fore.monolingual: to move something forward; to make something more prominent or noticeable. _ All the talk about costs brought the question of budgets to the fore. _The question of budget planning was brought to the fore.
examples: All the talk about costs brought the question of budgets to the fore.

bring something together†.monolingual: to assemble things; to gather things together. _ Thank you for bringing everything together so we can begin work. _ We brought together all the tools that we needed.
examples: Thank you for bringing everything together so we can begin work.

bring something up†.monolingual: Lit. to vomit something up; to cough something up. _ See if you can get him to bring the penny up. _ I did, and he brought up a nickel instead!
examples: See if you can get him to bring the penny up.

bring something with.monolingual: (Inf. or regional.) to carry something along with [oneself]. _ Are you going to bring your umbrella with? _ I brought it with. Don’t worry.
examples: I brought it with.

bring something within a range.monolingual: to adjust something into a particular range; to adjust a parameter. _ Let’s try to bring your cholesterol within the normal range with diet. _ It was brought within the normal range by an expensive drug.
examples: Let’s try to bring your cholesterol within the normal range with diet.

bring the house down†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to cause a house to collapse. _The most severe earthquake in years finally brought the house down. _ The earthquake brought down all the houses on the hillside.
examples: The most severe earthquake in years finally brought the house down.

bring up the rear.monolingual: to move along behind everyone else; to be at the end of the line. (Originally referred to marching soldiers. Fixed order.) _Here comes John, bringing up the rear. _ Hurry up, Tom! Why are you always bringing up the rear?
examples: Here comes John, bringing up the rear.

bristle at something.monolingual: Fig. to show sudden anger or other negative response to something. (Alludes to a dog or cat raising the hair on its back in anger or as a threat.) _ She bristled at the suggestion. _ I knew Lily would bristle at the appearance of Max.
examples: She bristled at the suggestion.

*broad as a barn door.monolingual: very broad or wide. (*Also: as ~.) _ Jim’s backside is as broad as a barn door. _ The weight lifter’s chest is broad as a barn door.
examples: Jim’s backside is as broad as a barn door.

broad in the beam.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of a ship] wide at amidships. _ This old tub is broad in the beam and sits like a ball in the water, but I love her.
examples: This old tub is broad in the beam and sits like a ball in the water, but I love her.

broaden out.monolingual: to become wider; to expand. _ The river broadened out and became deeper. _ The road broadens out here.
examples: The river broadened out and became deeper.

broaden something out†.monolingual: to make something wider; to expand something. _ Now, broaden this part out a little, so it looks like a cloud, not a painted pillow. _Broaden out the river in your painting so it looks very wide. _ The photographic view of the valley can be broadened
examples: Now, broaden this part out a little, so it looks like a cloud, not a painted pillow.

broken dreams.monolingual: wishes or desires that cannot be fulfilled. _ We all have our share of broken dreams, but they were never all meant to come true anyway.
examples: We all have our share of broken dreams, but they were never all meant to come true anyway.

a broken reed.monolingual: an unreliable or undependable person. (On the image of a useless, broken reed in a reed instrument.) _You can’t rely on Jim’s support. He’s a broken reed. _Mr. Smith is a broken reed. His deputy has to make all the decisions.
examples: You can’t rely on Jim’s support.

browbeat someone into something.monolingual: Fig. to bully or intimidate someone into something. _ It won’t do any good to try to browbeat me into it. _ I was browbeaten into doing it once. I refuse to do it again.
examples: It won’t do any good to try to browbeat me into it.

*brown as a berry.monolingual: very brown from the sun; quite suntanned. (*Also: as ~.) _ She was out in the sun so much that she became as brown as a berry.
examples: She was out in the sun so much that she became as brown as a berry.

brown out.monolingual: [for the electricity] to diminish in power and dim the lights, causing a brownout. (Something less than a blackout, when there is no power.) _ The power kept browning out. _ The lights started to brown out, and I thought maybe there was a power short
examples: The power kept browning out.

brown someone off†.monolingual: Sl. to make someone angry. _ You really brown me off!

browse among something.monolingual: 1. [for an animal] to wander about among plants and trees, selecting and eating some. _The deer were browsing among the vegetables in my garden. _ The cows were browsing among the grasses in the field.
examples: The deer were browsing among the vegetables in my garden.

browse on something.monolingual: [for an animal] to feed on some kind of plant material. _The deer browsed on the tender shoots in my garden. _ The rabbit browsed on my carrots.
examples: The deer browsed on the tender shoots in my garden.

bruit something about.monolingual: to spread a rumor around; to gossip something around. _ You really shouldn’t bruit that incident about, you know. _ The story was bruited about all over the office.
examples: You really shouldn’t bruit that incident about, you know.

brush over someone or something.monolingual: Fig. to deal lightly with an important person or matter; to just barely mention someone or something. _ I want to hear more. You only brushed over the part I was interested in. _ You only brushed over the bit about your girlfriend. Tell us more about
examples: I want to hear more.

brush someone off†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to remove something, such as dust or lint, from someone by brushing. _ The bathroom attendant brushed Mr. Harris off and was rewarded with a small tip. _The porter had never brushed off such a miserly man before.
examples: The bathroom attendant brushed Mr.

brush someone or something aside†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to push or shove someone or something out of the way. _ Don’t just brush me aside. I almost fell over. _ I brushed aside the branch, not realizing it was poison ivy.
examples: Don’t just brush me aside.

brush something down†.monolingual: to clean and groom fur or fabric by brushing. _ Why don’t you brush your coat down? It’s very linty. _ I brushed down my trousers, and they looked much better.
examples: Why don’t you brush your coat down? It’s very linty.

brush something up†.monolingual: to improve one’s knowledge of something or one’s ability to do something. _ I need to brush my French up a little bit. _ I need to brush up my French.
examples: I need to brush my French up a little bit.

a brush with death.monolingual: Fig. an instance of nearly dying. _ After a brush with death, Claire seemed more friendly and outgoing.
examples: After a brush with death, Claire seemed more friendly and outgoing.

*the brush-off.monolingual: Fig. rejection; being cast aside and ignored. (*Typically: get ~; give someone ~.) _ Don’t talk to Tom. He’ll just give you the brush-off. _ I went up to her and asked for a date, but I got the brush-off.
examples: Don’t talk to Tom.

bubble over.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for boiling or effervescent liquid] to spill or splatter over the edge of its container. _ The pot bubbled over and put out the f lame on the stove. _The stew bubbled over.
examples: The pot bubbled over and put out the f lame on the stove.

buck for something.monolingual: Sl. to work ambitiously for something, such as a promotion. _ I’m just bucking for recognition and, of course, a 20 percent raise. _ You can tell by her attention to the boss that she’s bucking for promotion.
examples: I’m just bucking for recognition and, of course, a 20 percent raise.

buck someone off†.monolingual: [for a horse or similar animal] to rear up in an attempt to shake off its rider. _ The horse tried to buck Sharon off, but she held on tight. _ The horse bucked off its rider.
examples: The horse tried to buck Sharon off, but she held on tight.

the buck stops here..monolingual: The need to act or take responsibility, that other people pass on to still other people, ulti- mately ends up here. (An expression made famous by U.S. President Harry Truman, about the finality of decisions a president must make. See also pass the bu
examples: After everyone else has avoided making the decision, I will have to do it.

buck up.monolingual: to cheer up; to perk up. _Come on, now, buck up. Things can’t be all that bad. _ She began to buck up when I showed her the results of the tests.
examples: Come on, now, buck up.

buckle someone in†.monolingual: to attach someone securely with a vehicle’s seat belts. (This includes airplane seat belts.) _ Don’t forget to buckle the children in. _ Did you buckle in the children?
examples: Don’t forget to buckle the children in.

buckle someone or something down†.monolingual: to attach someone or something down with straps that buckle together. _ They stopped to buckle the load down again. _ Did you buckle down the kids?
examples: They stopped to buckle the load down again.

buckle someone or something up†.monolingual: to attach someone or something securely with straps that buckle together. (This emphasizes the completeness and secureness of the act.) _Buckle the children up before we leave. _Buckle up your shoes.
examples: Buckle the children up before we leave.

buckle under.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to collapse. _With heavy trucks on it, the bridge buckled under. _ The table buckled under.
examples: With heavy trucks on it, the bridge buckled under.

buckle under something.monolingual: to collapse under or from the weight of something. _ The bridge buckled under the weight of the truck and collapsed. _The table finally buckled under.
examples: The bridge buckled under the weight of the truck and collapsed.

bud out.monolingual: [for a flowering plant or tree] to develop buds. _ How early in the spring do the trees bud out around here? _ The trees bud out in early spring.
examples: The trees bud out in early spring.

a budding genius.monolingual: a very bright and promising young person. _Harry is a budding genius, but he seems like a fairly normal teenager.
examples: Harry is a budding genius, but he seems like a fairly normal teenager.

buff something down†.monolingual: to polish or smooth something by buffing. _ I buffed the newly waxed table down with a cloth. _ I’m going to go out and buff down the car.
examples: I buffed the newly waxed table down with a cloth.

buff something up†.monolingual: to polish something to a shine. _ He buffed his shoes up and went out for the evening. _ He buffed up the antique silver platter.
examples: He buffed his shoes up and went out for the evening.

bug off.monolingual: 1. Sl. to cease bothering [someone]. _ Hey, bug off! Your comments are annoying. _ I wish you would bug off!
examples: Hey, bug off! Your comments are annoying.

bug out.monolingual: 1. Sl. to pack up and leave or retreat. _Orders are to bug out by oh-nine-hundred. _ Okay, everybody, move it! We’re bugging out.
examples: Orders are to bug out by oh-nine-hundred.

bug someone.monolingual: to irritate someone; to bother someone. _Go away! Stop bugging me! _ Leave me alone. Go bug someone else.
examples: Leave me alone.

build a better mousetrap.monolingual: to develop or invent something superior to a device that is widely used. (From the old saying, “If you build a better mousetrap, the world will beat a path to your door.”) _Harry thought he could build a better mousetrap, but everything he “invented”
examples: Harry thought he could build a better mousetrap, but everything he “invented” had already been thought of.

build down.monolingual: [for traffic] to reduce in volume or diminish. _ At about six, the going-home traffic begins to build down. _ When traffic builds down, I leave for home.
examples: At about six, the going-home traffic begins to build down.

build out onto something.monolingual: to extend a building onto a particular space. _We can build out onto the adjacent lot after we purchase it. _ We built out onto the area over the old patio.
examples: We can build out onto the adjacent lot after we purchase it.

build someone or something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to make someone or something bigger or stronger. _ Tom is lifting weights to build himself up for basketball. _ Tom needs to build up his upper body.
examples: Tom is lifting weights to build himself up for basketball.

build something out of something.monolingual: to construct something from parts or materials. _ She built a tower out of the blocks. _ They will build the bridge out of reinforced concrete.
examples: She built a tower out of the blocks.

build something to order.monolingual: to build an individual object according to a special set of specifications. _I am having them build a new house to order—just for us. _The car will be built to order.
examples: I am having them build a new house to order—just for us.

build something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to add buildings to an area of land or a neighborhood. _ They are really building this area up. There is no more open space. _ They built up the area over the years.
examples: They are really building this area up.

build up.monolingual: to increase; to develop. _ The storm clouds are building up. Better close the windows.
examples: The storm clouds are building up.

build up to something.monolingual: 1. [for a person] to lead up to something or advance to doing or saying something. _ I can tell you are building up to something. What is it?
examples: I can tell you are building up to something.

bulge out.monolingual: to swell outward; to extend out into a lump or mound. _ The puppy’s tummy bulged out, full of food. _ The bag of grass clippings bulged out heavily.
examples: The puppy’s tummy bulged out, full of food.

bulge with something.monolingual: to be swollen with something. _The bag was bulging with gifts and candy. _ The chipmunk’s cheeks bulged with the nuts it had found.
examples: The bag was bulging with gifts and candy.

bulldoze into something.monolingual: Fig. to move clumsily into something. _ Don’t just bulldoze into me! Watch where you are going! _ Todd bulldozed into the wall, denting it badly.
examples: Todd bulldozed into the wall, denting it badly.

bulldoze through something.monolingual: Fig. to push clumsily and carelessly through something. _ Don’t just bulldoze through your work! _I wish you wouldn’t bulldoze through the room.
examples: I wish you wouldn’t bulldoze through the room.

bully for you!.monolingual: 1. an expression that praises someone or someone’s courage. (Dated, but still heard.) _ The audi- ence shouted, “Bravo! Bully for you!” _ Bob: I quit my job today. Sally: Bully for you! Now what are you going to do? Bob: Well, I need a little loan to
examples: Bob: I quit my job today.

bully someone into something.monolingual: to harass or threaten someone into doing something. _The coach tried to bully them into agreeing to stay late and practice. _ Don’t try to bully me into your way of doing things.
examples: The coach tried to bully them into agreeing to stay late and practice.

bum out.monolingual: Sl. to have a bad experience. (Originally referred to a bad experience with drugs.) _ Are you going to bum out again tonight? _ Man, is he bummed out!

*the bum’s rush.monolingual: hurrying someone out of a place. (As someone might quickly escort a vagrant from a fancy restaurant. *Typically: get ~; give someone ~.) _ The young customer in the jewelry store was getting the bum’s rush until he pulled out an enormous roll of bill
examples: The young customer in the jewelry store was getting the bum’s rush until he pulled out an enormous roll of bills.

bum someone out†.monolingual: Sl. to disappoint someone. _ This menial job really bums me out. _ The bad movie bummed out the entire audience.
examples: This menial job really bums me out.

bum something off someone.monolingual: Sl. to beg or borrow something from someone. _ Can I bum a cigarette off you? _ You can’t bum anything off me that I don’t have.
examples: You can’t bum anything off me that I don’t have.

*a bum steer.monolingual: misleading instructions or guidance; a misleading suggestion. (Bum= false; phony. Steer = guidance, as in the steering of a car. *Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _Wilbur gave Ted a bum steer and Ted ended up in the wrong town. _ I got a bu
examples: Wilbur gave Ted a bum steer and Ted ended up in the wrong town.

bumble through something.monolingual: to get through something clumsily. _I guess I will have to bumble through this speech again. _ Lily bumbled through her song and f led from the stage.
examples: I guess I will have to bumble through this speech again.

bump someone or something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to damage or batter someone or something. _ The crash into the wall bumped the race driver up a little. _ The accident bumped up the passengers a little.
examples: The crash into the wall bumped the race driver up a little.

bump that!.monolingual: Sl. Forget that! _ Bump that! I was wrong. _ I gave you the wrong number. Bump that!
examples: Bump that! I was wrong.

bumper to bumper.monolingual: [of traffic] close together and moving slowly. _The traffic is bumper to bumper from the accident up ahead.
examples: The traffic is bumper to bumper from the accident up ahead.

a bunch of fives.monolingual: Sl. a punch from a closed fist. _ How would you like a bunch of fives right in the kisser? _ He ended up with a bunch of fives in the gut.
examples: He ended up with a bunch of fives in the gut.

bunch someone or something up†.monolingual: to pack or cluster things or people together. _ Bunch them up so you can squeeze them into the sack. _ Kelly bunched up the roses and put them in a vase.
examples: Bunch them up so you can squeeze them into the sack.

bunch up.monolingual: to pack together or cluster. _ Spread out. Don’t bunch up!

a bundle of nerves.monolingual: a very nervous person. _I was a bundle of nerves before my dental appointment.
examples: I was a bundle of nerves before my dental appointment.

bundle off.monolingual: to leave in a hurry; to take all one’s parcels or baggage and leave in a hurry. _ She got ready and bundled off after her bus. _ Her arms full, Lily bundled off in a rush.
examples: She got ready and bundled off after her bus.

bung something in†.monolingual: to cram or bang something into something. _He bunged the cork into the barrel. _With a heavy blow, he bunged in the cork.
examples: He bunged the cork into the barrel.

bung something up†.monolingual: to damage someone or something by blows. _Don’t let the watermelon roll around in the trunk of your car. You don’t want to bung it up. _ Last time I put up the storm windows, I really bunged up my hands.
examples: Don’t let the watermelon roll around in the trunk of your car.

bunged up.monolingual: battered or bruised. _It used to be a nice table, but it got all bunged up. _What happened to Jane? Her face was bunged up.
examples: It used to be a nice table, but it got all bunged up.

bungle something up†.monolingual: to botch something; to mess something up. _ Please don’t bungle this job up. _ Tom was careless and he bungled up the job.
examples: Please don’t bungle this job up.

buoy someone or something up†.monolingual: to keep someone or something afloat. _Use this cushion to buoy yourself up. _The log buoyed up the swimmer until help came. _ The air trapped in the hull buoyed the boat up.
examples: Use this cushion to buoy yourself up.

buoy someone up†.monolingual: Fig. to support, encourage, or sustain someone. _ The good news buoyed her up considerably. _ Her good humor buoyed up the entire party.
examples: The good news buoyed her up considerably.

burden someone with something.monolingual: to give unpleasant information to someone; to give someone some bad news. _ I hate to burden you with this, but your cat ran away. _ I wish I had not been burdened with all the facts.
examples: I hate to burden you with this, but your cat ran away.

burgeon out.monolingual: to develop and grow rapidly; to burst forth. _ The flowers burgeoned out and made the garden beautiful again. _ When the trees have burgeoned out, spring is really here.
examples: The flowers burgeoned out and made the garden beautiful again.

burn something to a crisp.monolingual: to burn something totally or very badly. _ The cook burned the meat to a crisp.
examples: The cook burned the meat to a crisp.

burn away.monolingual: 1. [for something] to burn until there is no more of it. _ All the oil burned away. _ The logs burned away and the fireplace was cooling down.
examples: All the oil burned away.
