burn down.monolingual: 1. [for a building] to be destroyed by fire. _ The barn burned down. _There was a fire, and the old factory was burned down.
examples: The barn burned down.

burn for someone or something.monolingual: to desire someone or something very much. _ Jim said he was burning for Sally. _ I was just burning for another look at her.
examples: Jim said he was burning for Sally.

burn off.monolingual: [for some excess volatile or flammable substance] to burn away or burn up. _ A film of oil on the surface of the water was burning off, making dense black smoke. _ The alcohol burned off and left a delicious f lavor in the cherries jubilee.
examples: A film of oil on the surface of the water was burning off, making dense black smoke.

burn someone at the stake.monolingual: 1. Lit. to set fire to a person tied to a post (as a form of execution). _They used to burn witches at the stake.
examples: They used to burn witches at the stake.

burn someone down†.monolingual: Sl. to humiliate someone. _ Man, don’t you ever burn me down like that again! _ You just want to burn down everybody to make yourself seem better.
examples: You just want to burn down everybody to make yourself seem better.

burn someone in effigy.monolingual: to burn a dummy or other figure that represents a hated person. _ For the third day in a row, they burned the king in effigy. _ Until they have burned you in effigy, you can’t really be considered a famous leader.
examples: For the third day in a row, they burned the king in effigy.

burn someone up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to destroy someone by fire. _ The house fire burned the victims up. _ The fire burned up both of them.
examples: The house fire burned the victims up.

burn something away†.monolingual: to remove or destroy something by burning. _ The doctor burned the wart away. _ The doctor burned away the wart.
examples: The doctor burned the wart away.

burn something down†.monolingual: [for a fire] to destroy a building completely. _The fire burned the barn down. _It burned down the barn.
examples: The fire burned the barn down.

burn something out†.monolingual: 1. to burn away the inside of something, getting rid of excess deposits. _ The mechanic burned the carbon out of the manifold. _ He burned out all of the carbon deposits.
examples: The mechanic burned the carbon out of the manifold.

burn something up†.monolingual: to destroy something by fire; [for fire] to consume something. _Take this cardboard and burn it up. _ The fire burned up the papers and left no trace.
examples: Take this cardboard and burn it up.

burn the midnight oil.monolingual: Fig. to stay up working, especially studying, late at night. (Alludes to working by the light of an oil lamp late in the night.) _ I have a big exam tomorrow so I’ll be burning the midnight oil tonight. _ If you burn the midnight oil night after nigh
examples: I have a big exam tomorrow so I’ll be burning the midnight oil tonight.

burn up.monolingual: to become destroyed or consumed by fire. _The wood burned up and left only ashes. _The deed burned up in the fire.
examples: The wood burned up and left only ashes.

burn with something.monolingual: 1. [for a fire] to burn with a particular quality. _ The building burned with great ferocity. _ The fire burned with a lot of crackling and popping.
examples: The building burned with great ferocity.

burned to a cinder.monolingual: burned very badly. [Very often used figuratively.] _ I stayed out in the sun too long, and I am burned to a cinder. _ This toast is burnt to a cinder.
examples: I stayed out in the sun too long, and I am burned to a cinder.

burned up.monolingual: Fig. very angry. (From the heat of anger. See also burn someone up.) _ My new assistant’s mistakes are so maddening! I’ve never been so burned up in my life. _ I’m really burned up at Bob’s behavior.
examples: My new assistant’s mistakes are so maddening! I’ve never been so burned up in my life.

burst at the seams.monolingual: 1. Fig. to be very full and burst, perhaps at the seams. (Alludes to something that would burst at the seams if overfilled.) _ I am so full from dinner! I’m ready to burst at the seams. _ The room was so full it was bursting at the seams.
examples: I am so full from dinner! I’m ready to burst at the seams.

burst forth.monolingual: to come forth explosively. _ The words burst forth and frightened everyone. _ The blossoms burst forth in the first warm days of the year.
examples: The words burst forth and frightened everyone.

burst into sight.monolingual: Fig. to come into view suddenly. (As if the sight appeared as suddenly as an explosion.) _ The sun finally burst into sight at the horizon. _ Suddenly, a tiger burst into sight and caught the hunter off guard.
examples: The sun finally burst into sight at the horizon.

burst onto the scene.monolingual: Fig. to appear suddenly in a location. _When Charles burst onto the scene, no one was prepared for the news he brought. _The police suddenly burst onto the scene and arrested everyone in the room.
examples: When Charles burst onto the scene, no one was prepared for the news he brought.

burst out.monolingual: to explode outward; to break open under force. _ The door burst out and released the trapped people. _ When the glass burst out, Gerald was cut by some splinters.
examples: The door burst out and released the trapped people.

burst out doing something.monolingual: to begin to do something suddenly, such as cry, laugh, shout, etc. _Suddenly, she burst out singing. _Ted burst out laughing when he read the joke.
examples: Suddenly, she burst out singing.

burst out laughing.monolingual: to begin to laugh suddenly. _ The entire audience burst out laughing when the clown took a fall. _Every time I think of you sitting there with a lap full of spaghetti, I burst out laughing.
examples: The entire audience burst out laughing when the clown took a fall.

burst out with something.monolingual: Fig. to utter something loudly and suddenly. (Compare this with burst in (with something).) _ The child burst out with a scream. _ Lily burst out with song.
examples: The child burst out with a scream.

burst someone’s bubble.monolingual: Fig. to destroy someone’s illusion or delusion; to destroy someone’s fantasy. _I hate to burst your bubble, but Columbus did not discover Canada. _ Even if you think I am being foolish, please don’t burst my bubble.
examples: I hate to burst your bubble, but Columbus did not discover Canada.

burst through something.monolingual: to break through or penetrate something with force. _ The tank burst through the barrier easily. _ The workers burst through the wall after a lot of hard work.
examples: The tank burst through the barrier easily.

burst with excitement.monolingual: Fig. to have a strong feeling of excitement. _Joe was just bursting with excitement because of his triumph. _ The new toys had the children all bursting with excitement.
examples: Joe was just bursting with excitement because of his triumph.

burst with joy.monolingual: Fig. [for someone] to be full to the bursting point with happiness. (To be so filled with joy as if to burst.) _When I got my grades, I could have burst with joy. _ Bill was not exactly bursting with joy when he got the news.
examples: When I got my grades, I could have burst with joy.

burst with pride.monolingual: to be full as if to the bursting point with pride. _My parents were bursting with pride when I graduated from college. _ I almost burst with pride when I was chosen for the first prize.
examples: My parents were bursting with pride when I graduated from college.

bury oneself in something.monolingual: 1. Fig. to become very busy with something. _ She stopped taking phone calls and buried herself in her work. _He tended to bury himself in his work.
examples: She stopped taking phone calls and buried herself in her work.

bury the hatchet.monolingual: Fig. to make peace. _ Let’s stop arguing and bury the hatchet. _ Tom and I buried the hatchet and we are good friends now.
examples: Let’s stop arguing and bury the hatchet.

bush out.monolingual: [for a plant, bush, beard, head of hair] to develop many small branches or hairs. _His beard bushed out and really needed trimming. _I hope the hedge bushes out nicely this year.
examples: His beard bushed out and really needed trimming.

business as usual.monolingual: having things go along as usual. _ Even right after the f lood, it was business as usual in all the stores. _ Please, everyone, business as usual. Let’s get back to work.
examples: Even right after the f lood, it was business as usual in all the stores.

business before pleasure..monolingual: Prov. You should finish your work before starting to relax and enjoy yourself. _ Alan: Hi, Ted. Shall we get something to drink? Ted: Business before pleasure, Alan. Do you have the reports I asked you to bring? _ I’d love to go water-skiing with you
examples: Alan: Hi, Ted. Shall we get something to drink? Ted: Business before pleasure, Alan.

the business end of something.monolingual: the part or end of something that actually does the work or carries out the procedure. _ Keep away from the business end of the electric drill so you won’t get hurt. _ Don’t point the business end of that gun at anyone. It might go off.
examples: Keep away from the business end of the electric drill so you won’t get hurt.

a busman’s holiday.monolingual: leisure time spent doing something similar to what one does at work. (Alludes to a bus driver going on a bus tour for his vacation or on a day off.) _ Tutoring students in the evening is a busman’s holiday for our English teacher. _ It’s a bit of a b
examples: Tutoring students in the evening is a busman’s holiday for our English teacher.

bust a bronco.monolingual: to ride and thus tame a wild horse so that it can be ridden. (Bust is a nonstandard form of burst.) _ In them days, I made my living busting broncos. _That was the meanest bronco I ever seen. Nobody could bust ’im.
examples: In them days, I made my living busting broncos.

bust a move.monolingual: Sl. to leave (a place.) _Let’s go. Time to bust a move. _ Let’s bust a move. Lots to do tomorrow.
examples: Let’s go. Time to bust a move.

bust out laughing.monolingual: Fig. to start laughing suddenly. _I busted out laughing when I saw him in that getup. _ The bridegroom was so nervous, it was all he could do not to bust out laughing.
examples: I busted out laughing when I saw him in that getup.

bust someone one.monolingual: Sl. to punch someone; to give someone a punch, probably in the face. (Bust is a nonstandard form of burst meaning ‘hit’ here.) _ You better shut up, or I’ll bust you one! _ You want me to bust you one? I will if you do that again.
examples: You want me to bust you one? I will if you do that again.

bust someone up†.monolingual: 1. Sl. to cause lovers to separate; to break up a pair of lovers, including married persons. ’ here.) _ Mary busted Terri and John up. _ Mary busted up Terri and John.
examples: Mary busted Terri and John up.

bust someone wide open.monolingual: Sl. to beat someone severely. (An exaggeration. Bust is a nonstandard form of burst.) _If you ever take a step onto my property, I’ll bust you wide open. _ Jim threatened to bust Bill wide open.
examples: If you ever take a step onto my property, I’ll bust you wide open.

bust something up†.monolingual: 1. Inf. to break or ruin something; to break something into smaller pieces. (Bust is a nonstandard form of burst meaning ‘break’ here.) _ Who busted this plate up? _ Don’t bust up the plates! Be careful!
examples: Don’t bust up the plates! Be careful! 2.

bust up.monolingual: 1. Sl. [for lovers] to separate or break up. (Bust is a nonstandard form of burst meaning ‘break’ here.) _ Tom and Alice busted up for good. _ They busted up last week.
examples: Tom and Alice busted up for good.

bustle about doing something.monolingual: to go about doing something busily and energetically. _Greg bustled about all day, doing the chores. _ Lily bustled about, getting dinner ready.
examples: Greg bustled about all day, doing the chores.

bustle about some place.monolingual: to move about some place very busily, or as if busy. _ They were all bustling about the kitchen, getting the feast ready. _ Veronica was bustling about outside, cleaning up the yard.
examples: They were all bustling about the kitchen, getting the feast ready.

bustle around.monolingual: to move about very busily. _ The people were bustling around, trying to get things ready for the picnic. _ I wish you would stop bustling around.
examples: The people were bustling around, trying to get things ready for the picnic.

bustle off.monolingual: to leave in haste. _ Well, I have to bustle off or I’ll miss my f light. _ I hate to bustle off so soon.
examples: Well, I have to bustle off or I’ll miss my f light.

bustle someone off†.monolingual: to help someone leave; to send someone out or away. _ The cops bustled the crook off. _ They bustled off the three men who were fighting.
examples: The cops bustled the crook off.

*busy as a hibernating bear.monolingual: not busy at all. (*Also: as ~.) _ Tom: I can’t go with you. I’m busy. Jane: Yeah. You’re as busy as a hibernating bear. _ He lounged on the sofa all day, busy as a hibernating bear.
examples: Tom: I can’t go with you.

but for someone or something.monolingual: if it were not for someone or something. _ But for the railing, I’d have fallen down the stairs. _ But for the children, Mrs. Smith would have left her husband years ago.
examples: But for the railing, I’d have fallen down the stairs.

but good.monolingual: severely; thoroughly. _She told him off but good. _ Joe beat up Bill but good.
examples: She told him off but good.

butt into something.monolingual: to intrude upon something; to break into a conversation. _ Please don’t butt into my conversation; I’m on the phone. _I don’t like my conversations being butted into by perfect strangers!
examples: Please don’t butt into my conversation; I’m on the phone.

the butt of a joke.monolingual: the reason for or aim of a joke, especially when it is a person. _Poor Fred was the butt of every joke told that evening.
examples: Poor Fred was the butt of every joke told that evening.

butt out.monolingual: to exit [as abruptly as one has intruded]. (Compare this with butt in (on someone or something). Usually a command.) _ Butt out! Leave me alone! _ Please butt out of my life!

*butterflies in one’s stomach.monolingual: a nervous feeling in one’s stomach. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ Whenever I have to speak in public, I get butterf lies in my stomach. _ She always has butterf lies in her stomach before a test. _It was not frightening enough to giv
examples: Whenever I have to speak in public, I get butterf lies in my stomach.

button something down†.monolingual: to fasten something down with buttons. _ Button your collar down. You look too casually dressed. _ Please button down your collar.
examples: Button your collar down.

button something up†.monolingual: to fasten something with buttons. _Button your shirt up, please. _I will button up my shirt.
examples: Button your shirt up, please.

button up.monolingual: 1. Lit. to fasten one’s buttons. _ Your jacket’s open. You’d better button up. It’s cold. _ I’ll button up in the car.
examples: Your jacket’s open.

buttress something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to brace something; to provide architectural support for something. _ We have to buttress up this part of the wall while we work on it. _ The workers buttressed the wall up with heavy timbers.
examples: We have to buttress up this part of the wall while we work on it.

buy someone off†.monolingual: to bribe someone to ignore what one is doing wrong. _ Do you think you can buy her off ? _ The mobster tried to buy off the jury.
examples: The mobster tried to buy off the jury.

buy someone or something out†.monolingual: to purchase full ownership of something from someone or a group. _ We liked the company, so we borrowed a lot of money and bought it out. _ Carl bought out the owners of the company.
examples: We liked the company, so we borrowed a lot of money and bought it out.

buy someone’s wolf ticket.monolingual: Sl. to challenge someone’s boast or taunt. _ He wants me to buy his wolf ticket bad. _ He’s such a fighter. He’ll buy anybody’s wolf ticket.
examples: He wants me to buy his wolf ticket bad.

buy something at something.monolingual: 1. to purchase something at a particular place or at a particular type of sale, such as a store, an auction, a clearance sale, etc. _I bought this table at an auction. _This was bought at an auction.
examples: I bought this table at an auction.

buy something on credit.monolingual: to purchase something now and pay for it later (normally plus interest). _ Almost everyone who buys a house buys it on credit. _ I didn’t have any cash with me, so I used my credit card and bought a new coat on credit.
examples: Almost everyone who buys a house buys it on credit.

buy something on time.monolingual: to buy something on credit. _ Tom: That’s an awful fancy TV. Are you sure you can afford it? Jane: I’m buying it on time. _I bought the sofa on time, but I paid cash for the chairs.
examples: Tom: That’s an awful fancy TV.

buy something out†.monolingual: to buy all that is available of a particular item. _ The kids came in and bought all our bubble gum out. _ They bought out the bubble gum in a single hour.
examples: The kids came in and bought all our bubble gum out.

buy something sight unseen.monolingual: to buy something without seeing it first. _ I bought this land sight unseen. I didn’t know it was so rocky. _It isn’t usually safe to buy something sight unseen.
examples: I bought this land sight unseen.

buy something up†.monolingual: to buy all of something; to buy the entire supply of something. _ He bought the oranges up from all the groves. _ He bought up all the oranges and drove up the price.
examples: He bought the oranges up from all the groves.

buy the big one.monolingual: Euph. to die. _ I don’t plan to buy the big one for at least another thirty years. _ She conked out for good—you know, bought the big one.
examples: I don’t plan to buy the big one for at least another thirty years.

buy time.monolingual: to postpone an event hoping that the situation will improve. _You are just stalling to buy time. _Maybe I can buy some time by asking the judge for a continuance.
examples: You are just stalling to buy time.

buy trouble.monolingual: Fig. to encourage trouble; to bring on trouble. (As if certain acts would pay for or cause difficulties that would have to be suffered through.) _ I don’t want to buy trouble. I have enough already. _ Saying something insulting to him is just buying
examples: I don’t want to buy trouble.

buzz along.monolingual: to move or drive along fast. _ The cars were buzzing along at a great rate. _Traffic is sure buzzing along.
examples: The cars were buzzing along at a great rate.

buzz for someone.monolingual: to sound a signal for someone. _ Please buzz for the bell captain. _ I buzzed for my secretary and waited for a reply.
examples: Please buzz for the bell captain.

buzz off.monolingual: Fig. to leave quickly. _I’ve got to buzz off. Bye. _ It’s time for me to buzz off.
examples: I’ve got to buzz off.

buzz with something.monolingual: Fig. [for a place] to be busy or filled with something. _ The room buzzed with excitement. _ The office had better be buzzing with moneymaking activity when I get there.
examples: The room buzzed with excitement.

by a mile.monolingual: Fig. by a great distance. (Usually an exaggeration.) _ You missed the target by a mile. _ Your estimate of the budget deficit was off by a mile.
examples: You missed the target by a mile.

by a show of hands.monolingual: [of a vote taken] expressed by people raising their hands. _We were asked to vote for the candidates for captain by a show of hands. _Bob wanted us to vote on paper, not by a show of hands, so that we could have a secret ballot.
examples: We were asked to vote for the candidates for captain by a show of hands.

by all appearances.monolingual: apparently; according to what one sees or how things seem. _She is, by all appearances, ready to resume work. _ By all appearances, we ought to be approaching the airport.
examples: She is, by all appearances, ready to resume work.

by all means.monolingual: certainly; yes; absolutely. _ I will attempt to get there by all means. _ Bob: Can you come to dinner tomorrow? Jane: By all means. I’d love to.
examples: I will attempt to get there by all means.

by all means of something.monolingual: trying to do something by the use of every possible manner of something. _ People will be arriving by all means of transportation. _ The surgeon performed the operation by all means of instruments.
examples: People will be arriving by all means of transportation.

by and by.monolingual: at some time in the future; as time passes. _ The weather’s sure to clear up by and by. _ You may think your heart is broken, but you’ll feel better by and by.
examples: The weather’s sure to clear up by and by.

by and large.monolingual: generally; usually. (Originally a nautical expression.) _ I find that, by and large, people tend to do what they are told to do. _ By and large, rosebushes need lots of care.
examples: I find that, by and large, people tend to do what they are told to do.

by ankle express.monolingual: Fig. on foot. _ After my horse was stolen, I had to go by ankle express. _ It’s a five-minute drive, forty minutes by ankle express.
examples: After my horse was stolen, I had to go by ankle express.

by any means.monolingual: by any way possible. _ I need to get there soon by any means. _I must win this contest by any means, fair or unfair.
examples: I need to get there soon by any means.

by brute strength.monolingual: by great muscular strength. _ The men moved the heavy door by brute strength.
examples: The men moved the heavy door by brute strength.

by chance.monolingual: accidentally; randomly; without planning. _I found this book by chance at a book sale. _ We met by chance in a class in college.
examples: I found this book by chance at a book sale.

by check.monolingual: by using a check for payment. _ He paid for the book by check. _ You will be paid by check.
examples: He paid for the book by check.

by choice.monolingual: due to conscious choice; on purpose. _I do this kind of thing by choice. No one makes me do it. _ I didn’t go to this college by choice. It was the closest one to home.
examples: I do this kind of thing by choice.

by coincidence.monolingual: by an accidental and strange similarity; by an unplanned pairing of events or occurrences. _ We just happened to be in the same place at the same time by coincidence. _By coincidence, the circus was in town when I was there. I’m glad because I love c
examples: We just happened to be in the same place at the same time by coincidence.

by cracky!.monolingual: Rur. By God! (A mild oath, often used to express surprise or approval.) _Jim said he’d get the whole house painted this weekend, and by cracky, that’s just what he did. _ By cracky! That thunder sure was loud.
examples: Jim said he’d get the whole house painted this weekend, and by cracky, that’s just what he did.

by dint of something.monolingual: because of something; due to the efforts of something. (Dint is an old word meaning ‘force,’ and it is never used except in this phrase.) _ They got the building finished on time by dint of hard work and good organization. _By dint of much studying,
examples: They got the building finished on time by dint of hard work and good organization.

by force of habit.monolingual: owing to a tendency to do something that has become a habit. _ After I retired, I kept getting up and getting dressed each morning by force of habit.
examples: After I retired, I kept getting up and getting dressed each morning by force of habit.

by godfrey!.monolingual: By God! (A mild oath.) _ By godfrey, Jim’s brother is a big man! _ Those cats sure do make a lot of noise, by godfrey.
examples: Those cats sure do make a lot of noise, by godfrey.

by hand.monolingual: made by human hands and handheld tools as opposed to a machine. _ This fine wooden cabinet was made by hand. _ I carved this figurine by hand.
examples: This fine wooden cabinet was made by hand.

by itself.monolingual: with the help of nothing else; without the addition of anything else. _ Will this food be enough by itself for all of us? _ Can the dog get out of the house by itself ?

by leaps and bounds.monolingual: Fig. rapidly; by large movements forward. _ The brush we cut back last fall is growing by leaps and bounds. _The profits of my company are increasing by leaps and bounds. _ He is gaining by leaps and bounds.
examples: The brush we cut back last fall is growing by leaps and bounds.

by main strength and awkwardness.monolingual: Rur. by force or brute strength. _ Tom: How did you get that piano up the stairs? Mary: By main strength and awkwardness. _ By main strength and awkwardness, we got all the luggage crammed into the car.
examples: Tom: How did you get that piano up the stairs? Mary: By main strength and awkwardness.

by means of something.monolingual: using something; with the use of something. _ I opened the bottle by means of a bottle opener. _ I was able to afford a car by means of a loan.
examples: I opened the bottle by means of a bottle opener.

by mistake.monolingual: in error; accidentally. _I’m sorry. I came into the wrong room by mistake. _ I chose the wrong road by mistake. Now we are lost.
examples: I’m sorry. I came into the wrong room by mistake.

by myself.monolingual: 1. with no one else present; alone. _ I sat at the table by myself. _ I will not be at the party. I will be at home by myself tonight.
examples: I sat at the table by myself.

by no means.monolingual: absolutely not; certainly not. _ I’m by no means angry with you. _ Bob: Did you put this box here? Tom: By no means. I didn’t do it, I’m sure.
examples: I’m by no means angry with you.

by oneself.monolingual: 1. with no one else present; alone (of two or more people). _ Must one sit by oneself or may one join another group? _ One just hates eating by oneself, doesn’t one?
examples: One just hates eating by oneself, doesn’t one? 2.

by ourselves.monolingual: 1. with no one else present; alone. _Do we have to sit here by ourselves? Can’t we sit with Mary and Max? _We like to eat by ourselves, so we can talk about private matters.
examples: We like to eat by ourselves, so we can talk about private matters.

by rote.monolingual: [of learning or memorizing] done as habit and without thinking. _I simply memorized the speech by rote. I don’t know what it means. _ The student learns everything by rote and doesn’t really understand the concepts.
examples: I simply memorized the speech by rote.

by shank’s mare.monolingual: Fig. by foot; by walking. (Shank refers to the shank of the leg.) _My car isn’t working, so I’ll have to travel by shank’s mare. _ I’m sore because I’ve been getting around by shank’s mare.
examples: My car isn’t working, so I’ll have to travel by shank’s mare.

by the day.monolingual: one day at a time. _I don’t know when I’ll have to leave town, so I rent this room by the day.
examples: I don’t know when I’ll have to leave town, so I rent this room by the day.
Eggs are normally sold by the dozen.

by the dozens.monolingual: Fig. many; by some fairly large, indefinite number. (Similar to but implying less than hundreds. Compare this with by the dozen.) _ Just then people began showing up by the dozens. _I baked cookies and pies by the dozens for the charity bake sale.
examples: Just then people began showing up by the dozens.

by the handful.monolingual: in amounts equal to a handful; in quantity. _Billy is eating candy by the handful. _People began leaving by the handful at midnight.
examples: Billy is eating candy by the handful.

by the hour.monolingual: at each hour; once each hour. _It kept growing darker by the hour. _I have to take this medicine by the hour.
examples: It kept growing darker by the hour.

by the month.monolingual: one month at a time. _ Not many apartments are rented by the month. _I needed a car for a short while, so I rented one by the month.
examples: Not many apartments are rented by the month.

by the same token.monolingual: Cliché a phrase indicating that the speaker is introducing parallel or closely contrasting information. _Tom: I really got cheated! Bob: You think they’ve cheated you, but, by the same token, they believe that you’ve cheated them. _ Some say he is a
examples: Tom: I really got cheated! Bob: You think they’ve cheated you, but, by the same token, they believe that you’ve cheated them.

by the week.monolingual: one week at a time. _I plan my schedules by the week. _ Where can I rent a room by the week?
examples: I plan my schedules by the week.

by the year.monolingual: one year at a time. _ Most apartments are available by the year. _ We budget by the year.
examples: Most apartments are available by the year.

by themselves.monolingual: 1. with help from no one else. _ Do you think they can do it by themselves? _ Mike and Max cannot lift the piano by themselves.
examples: Mike and Max cannot lift the piano by themselves.

by virtue of something.monolingual: because of something; due to something. _She’s permitted to vote by virtue of her age. _They are members of the club by virtue of their great wealth.
examples: She’s permitted to vote by virtue of her age.

by way of something.monolingual: 1. passing through something (as a place); via something. _ He came home by way of Toledo. _She went to the bank by way of the drugstore.
examples: He came home by way of Toledo.

by word of mouth.monolingual: by speaking rather than writing. _ I learned about it by word of mouth. _ I need it in writing. I don’t trust things I hear about by word of mouth.
examples: I learned about it by word of mouth.

by yourself.monolingual: 1. with no one else present; alone. _ Do you want to sit here by yourself, or can I sit here too? _ Don’t sit at home by yourself. Come to the movie with me.
examples: Don’t sit at home by yourself.

by yourselves.monolingual: 1. with no one else present; alone (of two or more people). _Are you two going to stand here by yourselves all evening? _ Don’t sit home by yourselves. Come to the party.
examples: Don’t sit home by yourselves.

cage someone or something in†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to enclose someone or something in a cage. _ We caged the monkey in, but it threw a fit. _ We are going to have to cage in the dogs.
examples: We caged the monkey in, but it threw a fit.

cajole someone into something.monolingual: to coax or persuade someone to do something. _ They tried to cajole us into helping them move. _ You can’t cajole me into doing that!
examples: They tried to cajole us into helping them move.

cajole someone out of something.monolingual: 1. to coax or persuade someone not to do something. _ Try and cajole her out of going there. _I cajoled her out of leaving so soon.
examples: Try and cajole her out of going there.

calculate on something.monolingual: Rur. to think about or plan on something. _ Let me calculate on this a little bit. _ He’s busy calculating on a serious problem.
examples: Let me calculate on this a little bit.

call a halt to something.monolingual: to demand that something be stopped. _We must call a halt to this childish behavior. _ The manager called a halt to all overtime.
examples: We must call a halt to this childish behavior.

call a meeting.monolingual: to ask that people assemble for a meeting; to request that a meeting be held. _ The mayor called a meeting to discuss the problem. _ I’ll be calling a meeting of the library board to discuss the new building project.
examples: The mayor called a meeting to discuss the problem.

call a spade a spade.monolingual: Fig. to call something by its right name; to speak frankly about something, even if it is unpleasant. (Considered offensive by some. Use only with discretion.) _Well, I believe it’s time to call a spade a spade. We are just avoiding the issue. _ Let’
examples: Well, I believe it’s time to call a spade a spade.

call again..monolingual: Please visit this shop again sometime. (Said by shopkeepers and store clerks.) _ “Thank you,” said the clerk, smiling, “Call again.” _ Clerk: Is that everything? John: Yes. Clerk: That’s ten dollars even. John: Here you are. Clerk: Thanks. Call again
examples: “Thank you,” said the clerk, smiling, “Call again.

call at some place.monolingual: to visit some place; [for a ship] to put into port at a place. _ I called at the druggist’s for some medicine. _Our ship will call at seven ports during the voyage.
examples: I called at the druggist’s for some medicine.

call back.monolingual: 1. to call [someone] again on the telephone at a later time. _Call back later, please. _I will call back when you are not so busy.
examples: Call back later, please.

call for someone or something.monolingual: 1. to need, require, or demand something or the services of someone. _ The recipe calls for two cups of f lour. _ This job calls for someone with experience.
examples: The recipe calls for two cups of f lour.

call hogs.monolingual: Rur. to snore. _ I couldn’t sleep at all last night, with Cousin Joe calling hogs in the next room. _ Joe calls hogs so loud the windows rattle.
examples: I couldn’t sleep at all last night, with Cousin Joe calling hogs in the next room.

call in sick.monolingual: to call one’s place of work to say that one is ill and cannot come to work. _ Four of our office staff called in sick today. _ I have to call in sick today.
examples: Four of our office staff called in sick today.

call it a day.monolingual: to quit work and go home; to say that a day’s work has been completed. _ I’m tired. Let’s call it a day. _ The boss was mad because Tom called it a day at noon and went home.
examples: I’m tired. Let’s call it a day.

call it a night.monolingual: to end what one is doing at night and go [home] to bed. _At midnight, I called it a night and went to bed. _ Guest after guest called it a night, and at last we were alone.
examples: At midnight, I called it a night and went to bed.

call it quits.monolingual: to quit; to resign from something; to announce that one is quitting. _ Okay! I’ve had enough! I’m calling it quits. _ Time to go home, John. Let’s call it quits.
examples: Okay! I’ve had enough! I’m calling it quits.

call my service..monolingual: Please don’t call me directly, but through my answering service. (Not a friendly or encouraging invitation.) _ Good to talk to you, but I gotta go now. Call my service. _ I can’t talk now. Call my service.
examples: Good to talk to you, but I gotta go now.

the call of nature.monolingual: Euph. the need to go to the lavatory. _ Stop the car here! I have to answer the call of nature. _ There was no break in the agenda, not even for the call of nature.
examples: Stop the car here! I have to answer the call of nature.

call on someone.monolingual: to court someone. _ Jim’s calling on the new cook over at the Browns’. _ In the old days, a boy had to ask a girl’s father for permission to come call on her.
examples: Jim’s calling on the new cook over at the Browns’.

call on something.monolingual: Fig. to draw on something, such as a particular quality or talent. _ This project calls on all the creative skills you can gather together. _ It calls on everything you’ve got.
examples: This project calls on all the creative skills you can gather together.

call someone about something.monolingual: to call someone on the telephone, seeking information about someone or something. _I’ll call Maggie about Ted and see what she knows. _Let me call the manager about this.
examples: I’ll call Maggie about Ted and see what she knows.

call someone back†.monolingual: 1. to call someone again on the telephone. _ Since she is not there, I will call her back in half an hour. _ Carl called back Mary after his meeting was over.
examples: Since she is not there, I will call her back in half an hour.

call someone by a name.monolingual: to address someone by a particular kind of name. _ They call me by my first name. _ Don’t call me by my nickname!
examples: They call me by my first name.

call someone down†.monolingual: to reprimand a person; to bawl someone out. _ The teacher had to call down Sally in front of everybody. _ “I wish you wouldn’t call me down in public,” cried Sally.
examples: The teacher had to call down Sally in front of everybody.

call someone forth†.monolingual: to call to someone to come out or come forward. _ The principal called Wally forth. _ Please call forth Wally again.
examples: The principal called Wally forth.

call someone forward.monolingual: to call to someone to the front, and to the attention of everyone present. _ The teacher called the student forward to recite. _Don’t call me forward. I am not prepared.
examples: The teacher called the student forward to recite.

call someone names.monolingual: to call someone by an abusive or insulting name. _Billy cried when the other kids called him names. _ John was punished for calling his teacher names.
examples: Billy cried when the other kids called him names.

call someone or something back†.monolingual: to call out that someone or something should come back. _ As she left, the clerk called her back. _ The clerk called back the customer.
examples: As she left, the clerk called her back.

call someone or something out†.monolingual: to request the services of someone or a group. _Things got bad enough that the governor called the militia out. _ The governor called out the militia.
examples: Things got bad enough that the governor called the militia out.

call someone or something up†.monolingual: to call someone, a group, or a company on the telephone. _ I will call them up and see what they have to say. _ Please call up the supplier.
examples: I will call them up and see what they have to say.

call someone out†.monolingual: to challenge someone to a fight. _ Wilbur wanted to call him out, but thought better of it. _ Why did you call out that guy? He used to be a prizefighter!
examples: Wilbur wanted to call him out, but thought better of it.

call someone’s bluff.monolingual: to demand that someone prove a claim or is not being deceptive. _ All right, I’ll call your bluff. Show me you can do it! _Tom said, “You’ve made me really angry, and I’ll punch you if you come any closer!” “Go ahead,” said Bill, calling his bluff.
examples: All right, I’ll call your bluff.

call someone to account.monolingual: to ask one to explain and justify one’s behavior, policy, performance, etc. _ The sergeant called the police officer to account. _I called my workers to account for the accident.
examples: The sergeant called the police officer to account.

call someone to attention.monolingual: to demand that someone assume the formal military stance of attention. _The officer called the platoon to attention. _ The sergeant called us to attention.
examples: The officer called the platoon to attention.

call someone together.monolingual: to request that people come together for a meeting. _Please call everyone together and we’ll discuss this. _ I called all the players together.
examples: Please call everyone together and we’ll discuss this.

call someone up†.monolingual: to request that someone or a group report for active military service. _The government called the reserve units up for active service. _ They called up another battalion.
examples: The government called the reserve units up for active service.

call something forth†.monolingual: [for an event] to draw a particular quality or induce a particular behavior. _The battle called extraordinary courage forth from the soldiers. _ It called forth great courage.
examples: The battle called extraordinary courage forth from the soldiers.

call something off†.monolingual: to cancel an event. _ It’s too late to call the party off. The first guests have already arrived. _ Because of rain, they called off the baseball game.
examples: It’s too late to call the party off.

call something out†.monolingual: 1. to draw on something, such as a particular quality or talent. _ It’s times like these that call the best out in us. _ These times call out our best effort.
examples: It’s times like these that call the best out in us.

call something square.monolingual: to pronounce a debt or obligation to have been paid, balanced, or ended. _ Thanks for the hundred bucks. I think we can call it square now.
examples: Thanks for the hundred bucks.

call something up†.monolingual: to summon information from a computer. _ John used his laptop to call the information up. _ With a few strokes on the computer keyboard, Sally called up the figures she was looking for.
examples: John used his laptop to call the information up.

call the dogs off†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to order hunting or watch dogs to abandon their quarry. _ They robber gave up and the guard called the dogs off. _Call off the dogs!
examples: They robber gave up and the guard called the dogs off.

call to someone.monolingual: to shout to get someone’s attention. _ I called to Fred, but he didn’t hear me. _ Did you hear me call to you?
examples: I called to Fred, but he didn’t hear me.

called to straw.monolingual: Rur. about to begin labor and childbirth. _ Susan was called to straw when she was only seven months along. _ Nancy’s nine months pregnant and could be called to straw any day now.
examples: Susan was called to straw when she was only seven months along.

calm down.monolingual: to relax; to become less busy or active. _Now, now, calm down. You look so nervous. _Please calm down. Nothing bad is going to happen.
examples: Now, now, calm down.

camp it up.monolingual: [for performers] to overact or behave in an affected manner. _The cast began to camp it up in the second act, and the critics walked out. (Fixed order.) _ There is no need to camp it up. Play it the way it was written.
examples: The cast began to camp it up in the second act, and the critics walked out.

camp out.monolingual: to live out of doors temporarily in a tent or camping vehicle, as on a vacation or special camping trip. _ I love to camp out in the winter.
examples: I love to camp out in the winter.

campaign against someone or something.monolingual: 1. to crusade or battle against someone or something. _ Currently, I am campaigning against littering. _ Sarah is campaigning against crooked politicians.
examples: Currently, I am campaigning against littering.

campaign for someone or something.monolingual: to support actively someone or someone’s candidacy for political office. _ I would be very happy to campaign for you. _I want to campaign for the winning candidate.
examples: I would be very happy to campaign for you.

*a can of worms.monolingual: Fig. a very difficult issue or set of problems; an array of difficulties. (*Typically: be ~; open ~.) _This political scandal is a real can of worms. _Let’s not open that can of worms!
examples: This political scandal is a real can of worms.

can you imagine?.monolingual: Can you believe that?; Imagine that! _She wore jeans to the wedding. Can you imagine? _Billy was eating the houseplant! Can you imagine?
examples: She wore jeans to the wedding.

cancel each other out†.monolingual: [for the opposite effects of two things] to balance each other. _ The cost of the meal you bought and what I owed you cancel each other out, so we’re even. _ They canceled out each other.
examples: The cost of the meal you bought and what I owed you cancel each other out, so we’re even.

cancel someone’s christmas.monolingual: Sl. to kill someone; to destroy someone. (Underworld or jocular; the idea is that the dead person will not live until Christmas.) _ If he keeps bugging me, I’m gonna cancel his Christmas. _Willie threatened to cancel Richard’s Christmas if Richard di
examples: If he keeps bugging me, I’m gonna cancel his Christmas.

cancel something out†.monolingual: to balance the effects of something. _Sending f lowers might cancel the bad feelings out. _The last payment canceled out the debt.
examples: Sending f lowers might cancel the bad feelings out.

cannot help doing something.monolingual: not able to refrain from doing something; not able not to do something. _ Anne is such a good cook, I can’t help eating everything she serves. _ Since John loves to shop, he can’t help spending money.
examples: Anne is such a good cook, I can’t help eating everything she serves.

can’t hack it.monolingual: unable to do the job. _ I thought delivering papers would be an easy job, but I just can’t hack it. _If you can’t hack it, let me know, and I’ll help you out.
examples: I thought delivering papers would be an easy job, but I just can’t hack it.

can’t help but do something.monolingual: [to be] unable to choose any but one course of action. (Also with cannot.) _ Her parents live nearby, so she can’t help but go there on holidays. _ Bob is a tennis fan and can’t help but travel to Wimbledon each year.
examples: Her parents live nearby, so she can’t help but go there on holidays.

can’t see straight.monolingual: Fig. cannot function (often because of strong emotion). _I am so mad I can’t see straight. _She left me so frustrated that I couldn’t see straight.
examples: I am so mad I can’t see straight.

cap and gown.monolingual: the academic cap or mortarboard and the robe worn in formal academic ceremonies. _ We all had to rent cap and gown for graduation. _ I appeared wearing my cap and gown, but I had shorts on underneath because it gets so hot at that time of year.
examples: We all had to rent cap and gown for graduation.

capable of doing something.monolingual: having the ability to do something. _Do you think Tom is capable of lifting 200 pounds? _ No one I know is capable of such a crime!

capitalize on something.monolingual: Fig. to build on something; to exploit something, such as an opportunity of talent, to one’s own benefit. _ Let’s try to capitalize on the strength of the economy and invest for the future. _ Capitalize on your experience in the field and you’ll do w
examples: Let’s try to capitalize on the strength of the economy and invest for the future.

capitulate to someone or something.monolingual: to surrender or submit to someone or something. _The general finally capitulated to the enemy. _ I won’t capitulate in this argument.
examples: The general finally capitulated to the enemy.

captain of industry.monolingual: Fig. a high-ranking corporation officer; a wealthy and successful capitalist. _The captains of industry manage to hang on to their money no matter what. _ It’s fun to see those captains of industry drive up in their limousines.
examples: The captains of industry manage to hang on to their money no matter what.

capture someone’s imagination.monolingual: Fig. to intrigue someone; to interest someone in a lasting way; to stimulate someone’s imagination. _ The story of the young wizard has captured the imagination of the world’s children.
examples: The story of the young wizard has captured the imagination of the world’s children.

*a card.monolingual: Fig. an entertaining and clever person who says or does funny things. (*Typically: act like ~; be ~.) _ He is such a card. Always making jokes. _ Mary is a card, and she has to learn to take things seriously sometimes.
examples: He is such a card.

card-carrying member.monolingual: Fig. an official member of some group, originally, the communist party. _ Bill is a cardcarrying member of the electricians union.
examples: Bill is a cardcarrying member of the electricians union.

care about someone or something.monolingual: 1. to hold someone or something dear; to prize someone or something. _I really care about you. _ I care very much about my family.
examples: I really care about you.

care for someone.monolingual: to feel tenderly toward someone; to love someone. _ I care for you a great deal, Walter. _ I care for you too, Alice.
examples: I care for you a great deal, Walter.

care for someone or something.monolingual: to take care of someone or something. _Will you care for my cat while I am away? _ I would be happy to care for your child.
examples: I would be happy to care for your child.

care for something.monolingual: to like the taste of some kind of food or drink. (Usually used with a negative.) _ I don’t care for sweet potatoes. _ I don’t care for sweet desserts.
examples: I don’t care for sweet potatoes.

care to do something.monolingual: to want to do something; to be willing to do something. _I really don’t care to see that movie. _ Would you care to go out for dinner?
examples: I really don’t care to see that movie.

careful not to do something.monolingual: using care to avoid some difficulty or difficulties. _Please be careful not to discuss politics with Mr. Brown. _ Please be careful not to leave the house unlocked.
examples: Please be careful not to discuss politics with Mr.

carp about someone or something.monolingual: to complain about someone or something. _You are always carping about all your petty problems at work. _ Stop carping about Randy!
examples: You are always carping about all your petty problems at work.

carp at someone or something.monolingual: to criticize someone or something. _ Poor Clara is carping at Bill’s carelessness again. _ Please stop carping at me.
examples: Poor Clara is carping at Bill’s carelessness again.

carry coals to newcastle.monolingual: Prov. to do something unnecessary; to do something that is redundant or duplicative. (Newcastle is an English town from which coal was shipped to other parts of England.) _Mr. Smith is so rich he doesn’t need any more money. To give him a gift certif
examples: Mr. Smith is so rich he doesn’t need any more money.

carry on.monolingual: to behave badly or mischievously. _The children always carry on when the teacher’s out of the room. _Stop carrying on and go to sleep!
examples: The children always carry on when the teacher’s out of the room.

carry on somehow.monolingual: to manage to continue or endure, in spite of problems. _ Even though we did not have a lot of money, we managed to carry on somehow. _ Don’t worry about us. We will carry on somehow.
examples: Even though we did not have a lot of money, we managed to carry on somehow.

carry over.monolingual: to extend into another time period or location. _ I don’t like for bills to carry over into the next month. _ Please do not let the paragraph carry over.
examples: I don’t like for bills to carry over into the next month.

carry someone away†.monolingual: [for someone or something] to cause a person to lose control. _ The excitement of the parade carried us all away. _The fervor of the speech carried away the whole crowd.
examples: The excitement of the parade carried us all away.

carry someone or something away†.monolingual: to take or steal someone or something. _ Someone carried our lawn furniture away while we were on vacation. _The kidnappers carried away the child when no one was looking.
examples: Someone carried our lawn furniture away while we were on vacation.

carry someone or something off†.monolingual: to take or steal someone or something. _ The kidnappers carried the child off. _ They carried off the child.
examples: The kidnappers carried the child off.

carry someone or something out†.monolingual: to lift up and move someone or something out. _ Help me carry the baby and her things out. _ Let’s carry out the dishes and set the table.
examples: Help me carry the baby and her things out.

carry something back†.monolingual: to take something back to where it came from. _ Did you bring this here? If so, carry it back. _ Please carry back the empty box after you take out all the books.
examples: Did you bring this here? If so, carry it back.

carry something down†.monolingual: to take something from a higher to a lower place. _Would you go up to the attic and carry the trunk down? _ Why should I carry down the trunk?

carry something forward.monolingual: to take a figure from one column or category to another. _ Now, carry this figure forward into the tens column.
examples: Now, carry this figure forward into the tens column.

carry something off†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to take something away with oneself; to steal something. _ Someone carried off my books! _ I think someone carried off the lawn chairs last night.
examples: I think someone carried off the lawn chairs last night.

carry something out†.monolingual: to perform a task; to perform an assignment. _ “This is a very important job,” said Jane. “Do you think you can carry it out?” _ The students didn’t carry out their assignments.
examples: “This is a very important job,” said Jane.

carry something over†.monolingual: to let something like a bill extend into another period of time. _ We’ll carry the amount of money due over into the next month. _ Yes, please carry over the balance.
examples: We’ll carry the amount of money due over into the next month.

carry the ball.monolingual: 1. Lit. to be the player who is relied on to gain yardage, especially in football. _ It was the fullback carrying the ball. _Yes, Tom always carries the ball.
examples: It was the fullback carrying the ball.

carry the torch.monolingual: Fig. to lead or participate in a (figurative) crusade. _ The battle was over, but John continued to carry the torch. _ If Jane hadn’t carried the torch, no one would have followed, and the whole thing would have failed.
examples: The battle was over, but John continued to carry the torch.

cart someone or something off†.monolingual: to take or haul someone or something away. (When used with someone the person is treated like an object.) _ The police came and carted her off. _ Let’s cart off these boxes.
examples: The police came and carted her off.

*carte blanche.monolingual: Fig. freedom or permission to act as one wishes or thinks necessary. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ He’s been given carte blanche with the reorganization of the workforce. _ The manager has been given no instructions about how to trai
examples: He’s been given carte blanche with the reorganization of the workforce.

carve someone or something up†.monolingual: to damage someone or something by careless or purposeful cutting (of a person, can be figurative). _Someone carved the tabletop up. Who did it and why? _ The boxer wanted to carve up his opponent.
examples: Someone carved the tabletop up.

carve something from something.monolingual: to shape by cutting something off or out of something with a knife. _ Can you carve an elephant from a bar of soap?

carve something in stone.monolingual: Fig. to fix some idea permanently. _ No one has carved this one approach in stone; we have several options.
examples: No one has carved this one approach in stone; we have several options.

carve something out†.monolingual: to hollow something out by carving; to make something hollow by carving. _ Can he carve a bowl out of such soft wood? _ He carved out the bowl of the pipe and then began to sand it.
examples: He carved out the bowl of the pipe and then began to sand it.

carve something up†.monolingual: to divide something up, perhaps carelessly. _The peace treaty carved the former empire up into several countries. _You can’t just carve up one country and give the pieces away.
examples: The peace treaty carved the former empire up into several countries.

the case.monolingual: the [current] instance; an actual situation. _ I think Bill is a vegetarian, and if that is the case, we should not serve him meat. _Susie believes trees can talk, but that is not the case.
examples: I think Bill is a vegetarian, and if that is the case, we should not serve him meat.

a case in point.monolingual: a specific example of what one is talking about. _ Now, as a case in point, let’s look at nineteenthcentury England. _Fireworks can be dangerous. For a case in point, look at what happened to Bob Smith last Fourth of July.
examples: Now, as a case in point, let’s look at nineteenthcentury England.

a case of mistaken identity.monolingual: the incorrect identification of someone. _ I am not the criminal you want to arrest. This is a case of mistaken identity.
examples: I am not the criminal you want to arrest.

*a case of something.monolingual: 1. an instance of something. (*Typically: be ~; have ~.) _ This is a case of police brutality. They should not have injured the suspect.
examples: This is a case of police brutality.

case someone or something out†.monolingual: Sl. to look someone or something over carefully, with a view to additional activity at a later time. _ He came into the room and cased all the lighting fixtures out. _ He cased out the fixtures to see which ones to replace. _ John cased the girls out
examples: He came into the room and cased all the lighting fixtures out.

case the joint.monolingual: 1. Sl. to look over some place to figure out how to break in, what to steal, etc. (Underworld.) _ First of all you gotta case the joint to see where things are. _You could see he was casing the joint the way he hung around.
examples: First of all you gotta case the joint to see where things are.

cash flow problem.monolingual: a lack of hard currency. _ My real estate business has a temporary cash flow problem. _ Due to his cash flow problem, he was unable to pay his employees that month.
examples: My real estate business has a temporary cash flow problem.

cash is king..monolingual: Prov. It is best to keep one’s investment money in cash. (Said when the prices in the securities markets are too high. It is better to build up cash and wait for a break in the market.) _ Things look a little pricey now. I’d say that cash is king for
examples: Things look a little pricey now.

cash is trash..monolingual: Prov. It is unwise to keep one’s investment money in cash. (Said when there are good opportunities in securities and it is foolish not to invest cash.) _If you’ve got money sitting around in savings while the market is steaming ahead, you are losing
examples: If you’ve got money sitting around in savings while the market is steaming ahead, you are losing dollars.

cash money.monolingual: Rur. money in bills and coins. _ You could make cash money selling your quilts, you really could. _ Joe wants cash money for his old TV set. He won’t let me have it on credit.
examples: You could make cash money selling your quilts, you really could.

cash or credit.monolingual: [a purchase made] either by paying cash or by putting the charges on a credit account. _ When Fred had all his purchases assembled on the counter, the clerk asked, “Cash or credit?” _That store does not give you a choice of cash or credit. They want
examples: That store does not give you a choice of cash or credit.

cash something in†.monolingual: to exchange something with cash value for the amount of money it is worth. _ I should have cashed my insurance policy in years ago. _ It’s time to cash in your U. S. savings bonds.
examples: I should have cashed my insurance policy in years ago.

cash-and-carry.monolingual: a method of buying and selling goods at the retail level where the buyer pays cash for the goods and carries the goods away. (As opposed to paying on credit or with the cost of delivery included.) _ Sorry, we don’t accept credit cards. This is strict
examples: Sorry, we don’t accept credit cards.

cast aspersions on someone.monolingual: to make a rude and insulting remark. _ I resent your casting aspersions on my brother and his ability! _ It is rude to cast aspersions on people in general.
examples: It is rude to cast aspersions on people in general.

cast in the same mold.monolingual: Fig. [of two or more people or things] very similar. _ The two sisters are cast in the same mold—equally mean. _ All the members of the family are cast in the same mold and they all had success as entertainers.
examples: The two sisters are cast in the same mold—equally mean.

cast one’s eyes down†.monolingual: Fig. to tilt one’s head or gaze downward. (Usually a sign of shame or to appear not to have seen someone.) _ She cast her eyes down as they saw each other again. _ He cast down his eyes in shame.
examples: She cast her eyes down as they saw each other again.

cast one’s vote.monolingual: to vote; to place one’s ballot in the ballot box. _ The citizens cast their votes for president. _ The wait in line to cast one’s vote was almost an hour.
examples: The citizens cast their votes for president.

cast someone as something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to choose someone to play a particular role in a play, opera, film, etc. _ The director cast her as the young singer. _ They cast me as a villain.
examples: The director cast her as the young singer.

cast someone or something up†.monolingual: [for the waves] to bring up and deposit someone or something on the shore. _ The waves cast the wreckage up, and it was found on the shore. _ The waves cast up the wreckage of a boat.
examples: The waves cast the wreckage up, and it was found on the shore.

cast something down†.monolingual: to hurl or throw something down. _She cast the glass down, breaking it into a thousand pieces. _ She cast down the tray and all that was on it.
examples: She cast the glass down, breaking it into a thousand pieces.

cast-iron stomach.monolingual: Fig. a very strong stomach that can withstand bad food or anything nauseating. _ If I didn’t have a cast-iron stomach, I couldn’t eat this stuff. _Fred— known for his cast-iron stomach—ate ten whole hot peppers.
examples: If I didn’t have a cast-iron stomach, I couldn’t eat this stuff.

a cat has nine lives..monolingual: Prov. Cats can survive things that are severe enough to kill them. (You can also refer to a particular cat’s nine lives.) _ Jill: My cat fell off a thirdf loor balcony and just walked away. How can he do that? Jane: A cat has nine lives. _ I think my
examples: Jill: My cat fell off a thirdf loor balcony and just walked away.

catch it.monolingual: to get into trouble and receive punishment. _ I know I’m going to catch it for denting mom’s car when I get home. _ Bob hit Billy in the face. He really caught it from the teacher for that.
examples: I know I’m going to catch it for denting mom’s car when I get home.

catch one’s breath.monolingual: Fig. to struggle for normal breathing after strenuous activity. _ The jogger stopped to catch her breath. _ It took Jimmy a minute to catch his breath after being punched in the stomach.
examples: The jogger stopped to catch her breath.

catch onto something.monolingual: [for something] to snag on or get grabbed by something else. _ This little piece has to catch onto this gear each time it comes around. _ A few threads of my shirt caught onto the cactus needles and ruined the whole thing.
examples: This little piece has to catch onto this gear each time it comes around.

catch someone out†.monolingual: to discover the truth about someone’s deception. _ The investigator tried to catch me out, but I stuck to my story. _The teacher caught out the student and punished him immediately.
examples: The investigator tried to catch me out, but I stuck to my story.

catch someone up in something.monolingual: [for excitement or interest] to extend to and engross someone. _ The fireworks caught everyone up in the excitement. _ The accident caught us all up in the resultant confusion.
examples: The fireworks caught everyone up in the excitement.

catch someone with something.monolingual: 1. to discover or apprehend someone with something—usually something stolen or illicit. _ They caught Elizabeth with the earrings she shoplifted. _Don’t let them catch you with the money!
examples: They caught Elizabeth with the earrings she shoplifted.

catch something from someone.monolingual: to get a disease from someone. _ I hope my children catch the chicken pox in kindergarten. Better to have it while you are young. _I don’t want to catch a cold from you.
examples: I hope my children catch the chicken pox in kindergarten.

catch something on something.monolingual: to snag something on something. _ I caught the pocket of my trousers on the drawer pull and almost ripped it off. _ He caught the sleeve of his uniform on a branch.
examples: I caught the pocket of my trousers on the drawer pull and almost ripped it off.

catch something up† in something.monolingual: to ensnare and capture something in something. _ We caught a large number of fish up in the net. _ We caught up many fish in the net.
examples: We caught a large number of fish up in the net.

a catch to it.monolingual: a hidden problem associated with it. _ It sounds good at first, but there’s a catch to it. You have to pay all costs up front.
examples: It sounds good at first, but there’s a catch to it.

catch-as-catch-can.monolingual: the best one can do with whatever is available. _ We went hitchhiking for a week and lived catch-as-catch-can. _ There were ten children in our family, and every meal was catch-as-catch-can.
examples: We went hitchhiking for a week and lived catch-as-catch-can.

cater to someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to provide for or care for someone or something. _ I believe that we can cater to you in this matter. _Our company caters to larger firms that do not wish to maintain a service department.
examples: I believe that we can cater to you in this matter.

caught short.monolingual: 1. left without any money temporarily. _ I’m caught a little short. Can I borrow a few bucks?
examples: I’m caught a little short.

cave in.monolingual: [for a roof or ceiling] to collapse. _The roof of the mine caved in when no one was there. _ The tunnel caved in on the train.
examples: The roof of the mine caved in when no one was there.

cavil at someone.monolingual: to find fault with someone; to complain about someone constantly. _ Will you never cease caviling at all of us? _ There is no need to cavil at me day and night!

cease and desist.monolingual: to completely stop doing something. (A legal phrase.) _The judge ordered the merchant to cease and desist the deceptive practices. _ When they were ordered to cease and desist, they finally stopped.
examples: The judge ordered the merchant to cease and desist the deceptive practices.

cede something to someone.monolingual: to grant a parcel of land to someone. _ We refuse to cede that land to you. _ They ceded the land to the city for a park.
examples: We refuse to cede that land to you.

celebrate someone for an accomplishment.monolingual: to honor someone for having done something. _ The people celebrated the astronaut for a successful journey. _She was celebrated widely for her discovery.
examples: The people celebrated the astronaut for a successful journey.

cement something together.monolingual: to fasten something together with glue or household cement. _Use this stuff to cement the vase together. _ Will you cement these parts together?
examples: Use this stuff to cement the vase together.

center around someone or something.monolingual: to make someone or something the central point in something; to be based on someone or something. _ Your salary increases center around your ability to succeed at your job. _ The success of the picnic centers around the weather next week.
examples: Your salary increases center around your ability to succeed at your job.

the center of attention.monolingual: the focus of people’s attention; the thing or person who monopolizes people’s attention. _ She had a way of making herself the center of attention wherever she went.
examples: She had a way of making herself the center of attention wherever she went.

center on someone or something.monolingual: to focus on someone or something in particular. _Let us center on the basic problem and try to solve it. _ I want to center on Liz and her contributions to the firm.
examples: Let us center on the basic problem and try to solve it.

a certain party.monolingual: someone you know but whom I do not wish to name. _ I spoke to a certain party about the matter you mentioned. _If a certain party finds out about youknow- what, what on earth will you do?
examples: I spoke to a certain party about the matter you mentioned.

certain sure.monolingual: Rur. very sure. _ Tom: Are you sure you saw Bill at work today? Mary: Certain sure. _If you keep hanging around with them no-good kids, you’ll get in a heap of trouble for certain sure.
examples: Tom: Are you sure you saw Bill at work today? Mary: Certain sure.

chafe at something.monolingual: Fig. to be irritated or annoyed at something. _ Jane chafed at the criticism for a long time afterward. _ Jerry chafed for a while at what Ken had said.
examples: Jane chafed at the criticism for a long time afterward.

the chain of command.monolingual: Fig. the series or sequence of holders of responsibility in a hierarchy. _ The only way to get things done in the military is to follow the chain of command. Never try to go straight to the top.
examples: The only way to get things done in the military is to follow the chain of command.

chain someone or something down†.monolingual: to fasten someone or something down with chains. _ They chained down the bicycle rack so no one could steal it. _We chained the toolshed down so a strong wind would not blow it over.
examples: They chained down the bicycle rack so no one could steal it.

chain something to something.monolingual: to connect things together with chains. _ We chained all the bicycles to one another so no one could steal them. _We will have to chain the lawn furniture to a tree if we leave it out while we are on vacation.
examples: We chained all the bicycles to one another so no one could steal them.

chain something up†.monolingual: to lock or secure a door or gate with chains. _ Please chain the gate up again when you come through. _ Yes, chain up the gate.
examples: Please chain the gate up again when you come through.

chalk something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to draw a picture of something in chalk, especially to illustrate a plan of some type. _The coach chalked the play out so the players could understand what they were to do. _ Our team captain chalked out the play.
examples: The coach chalked the play out so the players could understand what they were to do.

chalk something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to write something on a chalkboard. _ Let me chalk this formula up so you all can see it. _ I’ll chalk up the formula.
examples: Let me chalk this formula up so you all can see it.

challenge someone on something.monolingual: to dispute someone’s statement, remarks, or position. _ I think Fred is wrong, but I won’t challenge him on his estimate.
examples: I think Fred is wrong, but I won’t challenge him on his estimate.

challenge someone to something.monolingual: to dare someone to do something; to invite someone to compete at something. _ I challenge you to a round of golf. _ Jerry challenged us to a debate of the issues.
examples: I challenge you to a round of golf.

chance something.monolingual: to risk doing something; to try doing something while being aware of the risk involved. _ I don’t usually ride horses, but this time I will chance it. _ Bob didn’t have a ticket, but he went to the airport anyway, chancing a cancellation.
examples: I don’t usually ride horses, but this time I will chance it.

chances are.monolingual: the likelihood is (followed by a clause stating what is likely). _Chances are that she would have been late even if she had left on time.
examples: Chances are that she would have been late even if she had left on time.

change hands.monolingual: [for something] to be sold or passed from owner to owner. (From the “point of view” of the object that is passed on.) _How many times has this lot changed hands in the last ten years? _ We built this house in 1970, and it has never changed hands.
examples: We built this house in 1970, and it has never changed hands.

change into someone or something.monolingual: to alter one’s or its state to another state. _ The ugly witch changed into a lovely maiden. _ An insect larva changes into a cocoon.
examples: The ugly witch changed into a lovely maiden.

a change of pace.monolingual: an addition of some variety in one’s life, routine, or abode. _ Going to the beach on the weekend will be a change of pace. _ The doctor says I need a change of pace from this cold climate.
examples: Going to the beach on the weekend will be a change of pace.

a change of scenery.monolingual: a move to a different place, where the surroundings are different. _ I thought I would go to the country for a change of scenery. _ A change of scenery would help me relax and organize my life.
examples: I thought I would go to the country for a change of scenery.

change off.monolingual: [for people] to alternate in doing something. _Tom and I changed off so neither of us had to answer the phone all the time. _ Let’s change off every 30 minutes.
examples: Tom and I changed off so neither of us had to answer the phone all the time.

change out of something.monolingual: to take off a set of clothing and put on another. _I have to change out of these wet clothes. _ You should change out of your casual clothes and put on something more formal for dinner.
examples: I have to change out of these wet clothes.

change places with someone.monolingual: to trade or exchange situations or locations with someone. _He has a much higher salary, but I wouldn’t change places with him for the world. _ Juan decided to change places with Ken in the bus.
examples: He has a much higher salary, but I wouldn’t change places with him for the world.

change someone’s mind.monolingual: to cause a person to think differently (about someone or something). _ Tom thought Mary was unkind, but an evening out with her changed his mind. _I can change my mind if you convince me that you are right.
examples: Tom thought Mary was unkind, but an evening out with her changed his mind.

change someone’s tune.monolingual: to change the manner of a person, usually from bad to good, or from rude to pleasant. _The teller was most unpleasant until she learned that I’m a bank director. Then she changed her tune. _ “I will help change your tune by fining you $150,” said the
examples: The teller was most unpleasant until she learned that I’m a bank director.

change something back†.monolingual: to cause something to return to the original or a previous form. _ Whoever changed the television channel should change it back. _ Change back the channel to the game!
examples: Whoever changed the television channel should change it back.

change something with someone.monolingual: to trade or exchange something with someone. _I changed coats with Fred and his is much warmer. _ Will you change seats with me?
examples: I changed coats with Fred and his is much warmer.

change the channel.monolingual: Sl. to switch to some other topic of conversation. _ Just a minute. I think you changed the channel. Let’s go back to the part about you owing me money. _ Let’s change the channel here before there is a fight.
examples: Just a minute. I think you changed the channel.

change the subject.monolingual: to begin talking about something different. _ They changed the subject suddenly when the person whom they had been discussing entered the room. _ We’ll change the subject if we are embarrassing you.
examples: They changed the subject suddenly when the person whom they had been discussing entered the room.

change to something.monolingual: to convert to something; to give up one and choose another. _We will change to standard time in the fall. _I decided to change to gas for heating and cooking.
examples: We will change to standard time in the fall.

channel something off†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to drain off water or some other liquid through a channel. _ The front yard is flooded, and we will have to channel the water off. _ Let’s channel off the water before it gets too deep.
examples: The front yard is flooded, and we will have to channel the water off.

chapter and verse.monolingual: Fig. very specifically detailed, in reference to sources of information. (A reference to the method of referring to biblical text.) _ He gave chapter and verse for his reasons for disputing that Shakespeare had written the play. _ The suspect gave ch
examples: He gave chapter and verse for his reasons for disputing that Shakespeare had written the play.

character assassination.monolingual: Fig. seriously harming someone’s reputation. _ The review was more than a negative appraisal of his performance. It was total character assassination.
examples: The review was more than a negative appraisal of his performance.

charge at someone or something.monolingual: to move quickly forward to attack someone or something. _ The elephant charged at the hunter. _ I was afraid that the water buffalo was going to charge our vehicle.
examples: The elephant charged at the hunter.

charge off.monolingual: to move quickly or run away. _ He got angry and charged off. _ Juan charged off to talk to the boss.
examples: He got angry and charged off.

charge someone up†.monolingual: to excite someone; to make a person enthusiastic about something. _ The speaker charged up the crowd. _ He reread the report, hoping to charge himself up enough to make some positive comments.
examples: The speaker charged up the crowd.

charge someone with something.monolingual: 1. to place criminal charges against someone. _ The police charged Max with robbery.
examples: The police charged Max with robbery.

charge something against something.monolingual: to debit or assign the cost of something against something. _ Can I charge this item against the entertainment account? _ Don’t even try to charge it against your business expenses.
examples: Don’t even try to charge it against your business expenses.

charge something off as something.monolingual: to consider something a legitimate expense and deduct it from one’s taxes; to assign something to the tax loss category in accounting. _ I will have to charge this off as a loss. _ Try to charge it off as a business expense.
examples: I will have to charge this off as a loss.

charge something on something.monolingual: 1. to put the cost of something on a credit card or credit account. _ I would like to charge this purchase on my credit card. _What card do you want to charge it on?
examples: I would like to charge this purchase on my credit card.

charged up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of something such as a battery] full of electrical power. _ The battery is completely charged up. _If the battery isn’t charged, the car won’t start.
examples: The battery is completely charged up.

charity begins at home..monolingual: Prov. You should take care of family and people close to you before you worry about helping others. _ I don’t think our church should worry so much about a foreign relief fund when there are people in need right here in our city. Charity begins at ho
examples: I don’t think our church should worry so much about a foreign relief fund when there are people in need right here in our city.

*a charley horse.monolingual: a painful, persistent cramp in the arm or leg, usually from strain. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ Don’t hike too far or you’ll get a charley horse.
examples: Don’t hike too far or you’ll get a charley horse.

charm someone with something.monolingual: to enchant or fascinate someone with something. _ He charmed her with stories of his house on the beach. _ She charmed him with her bright smile.
