examples: He charmed her with stories of his house on the beach.

charm the pants off someone.monolingual: Fig. to use very charming behavior to persuade someone to do something. (Use with caution.) _She is so nice. She just charms the pants off you. _ He will try to charm the pants off you, but you can still refuse to take the job if you don’t want to do
examples: She is so nice. She just charms the pants off you.

chase someone or something around†.monolingual: to follow someone or something around in pursuit. (There is an implication that the person or thing pursued is attempting to elude whatever is in pursuit.) _ The dog chased us around in play. _ It chased around all the children.
examples: The dog chased us around in play.

chase someone or something down†.monolingual: to track down and seize someone or something. _ Larry set out to chase the pickpocket down. _ The police chased down the suspect.
examples: Larry set out to chase the pickpocket down.

chase someone or something up†.monolingual: to seek someone or something out; to look high and low for someone or something. _ I will chase Tom up for you. _ I will try to chase up a buyer for your car.
examples: I will chase Tom up for you.

chat about someone or something.monolingual: to talk idly or informally about someone or something. _ We need to chat about Molly. _ I want to chat about your expenditures a little.
examples: We need to chat about Molly.

chatter about someone or something.monolingual: to talk idly and actively about someone or something. _All the guests were chattering about something or other. _ People are chattering about you and Claire. Do you want to know what they are saying?
examples: All the guests were chattering about something or other.

chatter from something.monolingual: [for one’s teeth] to shake noisily with a chill from the cold, the dampness, a fever, etc. _ My teeth were chattering from the extreme cold. _ It was a terrible illness. My teeth chattered from the chills that followed the fever.
examples: My teeth were chattering from the extreme cold.

cheat at something.monolingual: to use deception while competing [against someone]. _ They say she cheats at cards. _ The mob is likely to cheat at getting the contracts.
examples: They say she cheats at cards.

cheat on someone.monolingual: to commit adultery; to be unfaithful to one’s spouse or lover. _ “Have you been cheating on me?” cried Mrs. Franklin. _ He was caught cheating on his wife.
examples: “Have you been cheating on me?” cried Mrs.

cheat someone out of something.monolingual: to get something from someone by deception. _ Are you trying to cheat me out of what is rightfully mine? _ She cheated herself out of an invitation because she lied about her affiliation.
examples: She cheated herself out of an invitation because she lied about her affiliation.

check on someone or something.monolingual: to look into the legitimacy or condition of someone or something. _Sarah will check on the matter and report to us. _ I will check on Jeff while he’s not feeling well.
examples: Sarah will check on the matter and report to us.

check out.monolingual: [for someone or something] to prove to be correctly represented. _ Everything you told me checks out with what other witnesses said.
examples: Everything you told me checks out with what other witnesses said.

check out the plumbing.monolingual: Euph. to go to the bathroom. (The order is fixed.) _ I think I’d better check out the plumbing before we get on the highway.
examples: I think I’d better check out the plumbing before we get on the highway.

check someone in†.monolingual: to record the arrival of someone. _Ask the guard to check you in when you get there. _ Tell the guard to check in the visitors as they arrive.
examples: Ask the guard to check you in when you get there.

check someone or something off†.monolingual: to mark or cross out the name of a person or thing on a list. _I am glad to see that you were able to come. I will check you off. _ I checked the items off. _ I checked off the recent arrivals.
examples: I am glad to see that you were able to come.

check someone or something out†.monolingual: to evaluate someone or something. _ That stock sounds good. I’ll check it out. _ I’ll check out the competition.
examples: That stock sounds good.

check someone or something over†.monolingual: to examine someone or something closely. _You should have the doctor check you over before you go back to work. _ The doctor checked over the children who had shown the worst symptoms. _ The mechanic checked the car over.
examples: You should have the doctor check you over before you go back to work.

check something in†.monolingual: 1. to record that someone has returned something. _ I asked the librarian to check the book in for me. _Did the librarian check in the book?
examples: I asked the librarian to check the book in for me.

check something out†.monolingual: to examine or try something; to think about something. _ It’s something we all have to be concerned with. Check it out. _ Check out the new comedy show on tonight.
examples: It’s something we all have to be concerned with.

check that.monolingual: cancel that; ignore that (last remark). _Check that. I was wrong. _At four, no, check that, at three o’clock this afternoon, the shipment arrived and was signed for.
examples: Check that. I was wrong.

check through something.monolingual: to examine something or a collection of things. (Usually refers to papers or written work, or to details in the paperwork.) _ Check through this and look for missing pages. _ I’ll check through it for typographical errors also.
examples: Check through this and look for missing pages.

checks and balances.monolingual: a system, as in the U.S. Constitution, where power is shared between the various branches of government. _ The newspaper editor claimed that the system of checks and balances built into our Constitution has been subverted by party politics.
examples: The newspaper editor claimed that the system of checks and balances built into our Constitution has been subverted by party politics.

*a checkup.monolingual: a physical examination by a physician. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ She got a checkup yesterday. _ I’m going to have a checkup in the morning. I hope I’m okay.
examples: She got a checkup yesterday.

cheek by jowl.monolingual: Fig. side by side; close together. _ The pedestrians had to walk cheek by jowl along the narrow streets. _The two families lived cheek by jowl in one house.
examples: The pedestrians had to walk cheek by jowl along the narrow streets.

cheer for someone or something.monolingual: to give a shout of encouragement for someone or something. _ Everyone cheered for the team. _ I cheered for the winning goal.
examples: Everyone cheered for the team.

cheer someone or something on†.monolingual: to encourage someone or a group to continue to do well, as by cheering. _ We cheered them on, and they won. _We cheered on the team. _ Sam cheered Jane on.
examples: We cheered them on, and they won.

cheer someone up†.monolingual: to make a sad person happy. _ When Bill was sick, Ann tried to cheer him up by reading to him. _ Interest rates went up, and that cheered up all the bankers.
examples: When Bill was sick, Ann tried to cheer him up by reading to him.

cheer up.monolingual: [for a sad person] to become happy. _ After a while, she began to cheer up and smile more. _ Cheer up! Things could be worse.
examples: After a while, she began to cheer up and smile more.

cheese someone off†.monolingual: Sl. to make someone very angry. _ You sure know how to cheese Laurel off. _ Bobby cheesed off every person in the club.
examples: You sure know how to cheese Laurel off.

*cheesed off.monolingual: Sl. angry; disgusted. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; get someone ~.) _ Clare was really cheesed off at the waiter. _ The waiter was cheesed off at the cook.
examples: Clare was really cheesed off at the waiter.

cherry-pick something.monolingual: Fig. to choose something very carefully. (As if one were closely examining cherries on the tree, looking for the best.) _ We have to cherry-pick the lumber we want to use for the cabinetry. Nothing but the best will do.
examples: We have to cherry-pick the lumber we want to use for the cabinetry.

chew one’s own tobacco.monolingual: Rur. to mind one’s own business. _Sally: You seem awfully happy all of a sudden. How come? Tom: Chew your own tobacco. _I’m just sitting here chewing my own tobacco, not bothering anybody.
examples: Sally: You seem awfully happy all of a sudden.

chew one’s.monolingual: cud Fig. to think deeply; to be deeply involved in private thought. (Alludes to the cow’s habit of bringing food back from the first stomach into the mouth to chew it, called chewing the cud.) _ He’s chewing his cud about what to do next.
examples: He’s chewing his cud about what to do next.

chew someone or something up†.monolingual: to damage or ruin someone or something by pinching, grinding, biting, etc. _ Stay away from the mower blade or it will chew you up. _ The lawn mower chewed up the f lowers.
examples: Stay away from the mower blade or it will chew you up.

chew something away†.monolingual: to gnaw something off; to gnaw at something until it’s all gone. _ You can see what’s left of it. Most of it has been chewed away by some animal. _Your puppy chewed away the top of my shoe!
examples: You can see what’s left of it.

chew something up†.monolingual: to grind food with the teeth until it can be swallowed. _You had better chew that stuff up well. _ Please chew up your food well.
examples: You had better chew that stuff up well.

chicken feed.monolingual: Fig. a small amount of anything, especially of money. _ Of course I can afford $800. That’s just chicken feed. _ It may be chicken feed to you, but that’s a month’s rent to me.
examples: Of course I can afford $800.

chicken out on someone.monolingual: Inf. to decide not to do something for or with someone. _ Come on, don’t chicken out on me now! _ Ken chickened out on us and won’t be going with us.
examples: Ken chickened out on us and won’t be going with us.

chicken-hearted.monolingual: cowardly. _ Yes, I’m a chicken-hearted softie. I never try anything too risky.
examples: Yes, I’m a chicken-hearted softie.

chide someone for something.monolingual: to tease or scold someone for doing something. _ Maria chided Gerald for being late.
examples: Maria chided Gerald for being late.

chief cook and bottle washer.monolingual: Fig. the person in charge of practically everything (such as in a very small business). _ I’m the chief cook and bottle washer around here. I do everything.
examples: I’m the chief cook and bottle washer around here.

child’s play.monolingual: something very easy to do. _ The test was child’s play to those who took good notes. _Finding the right street was child’s play with a map.
examples: The test was child’s play to those who took good notes.

chill someone’s action.monolingual: Sl. to squelch someone; to prevent someone from accomplishing something. _Freddie is trying to chill my action, and he’d better stop and leave me alone.
examples: Freddie is trying to chill my action, and he’d better stop and leave me alone.

*chilled to the bone.monolingual: Fig. very cold. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ I got chilled to the bone in that snowstorm. _ The children were chilled to the bone from their swim in the ocean.
examples: I got chilled to the bone in that snowstorm.

chin music.monolingual: Fig. Inf. talk; conversation. _ Whenever those two get together, you can be sure there’ll be plenty of chin music. _Bill just loves to hear himself talk. He’ll make chin music for hours at a time.
examples: Whenever those two get together, you can be sure there’ll be plenty of chin music.

a chink in one’s armor.monolingual: Fig. a special weakness that provides a means for attacking or impressing someone otherwise invulnerable. (Alludes to an opening in a suit of armor that allows a weapon to penetrate.) _ Jane’s insecurity is the chink in her armor. _ The boss seems me
examples: Jane’s insecurity is the chink in her armor.

chip away.monolingual: [for something] to break off or break away in small chips. _ The edges of the marble step chipped away over the years. _Some of the stone figures had chipped away so badly that we couldn’t see what they were.
examples: The edges of the marble step chipped away over the years.

*a chip on one’s shoulder.monolingual: Fig. a bad attitude that tends to get someone easily upset. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give one ~.) _Why did you get so angry at the slightest criticism? You seem to have a chip on your shoulder.
examples: Why did you get so angry at the slightest criticism? You seem to have a chip on your shoulder.

chips and dip.monolingual: potato chips, or some other kind of crisp snack food, and a sauce or dressing to dip them into before eating them. _ There were tons of chips and dip and all kinds of cold drinks available for everyone.
examples: There were tons of chips and dip and all kinds of cold drinks available for everyone.

chock full of something.monolingual: Fig. very full of something. _ These cookies are chock full of big chunks of chocolate.
examples: These cookies are chock full of big chunks of chocolate.

choke on something.monolingual: to gag and cough on something stuck in the throat. _The dog choked on the meat. _The restaurant patron began to choke on a fish bone.
examples: The dog choked on the meat.

choke someone off†.monolingual: to prevent someone from continuing to talk. (A figurative use; does not imply physical choking.) _The opposition choked the speakers’ debate off before they finished. _ Why did they want to choke off the speakers?
examples: The opposition choked the speakers’ debate off before they finished.

choke someone up†.monolingual: Fig. to cause someone to feel like starting to cry. _ Sad stories like that always choke me up. _ The movie was sad and it choked up most of the audience.
examples: Sad stories like that always choke me up.

choke something back†.monolingual: to fight hard to keep something from coming out of one’s mouth, such as sobs, tears, angry words, vomit, etc. _ I tried to choke the unpleasant words back, but I could not. _ She choked back her grief, but it came forth nonetheless. _ I could hardly
examples: I tried to choke the unpleasant words back, but I could not.

choke something down†.monolingual: to eat something, even though it is hard to swallow or tastes bad. _ The cough medicine tasted terrible, but I managed to choke it down. _ She choked down four of those pills all at once.
examples: The cough medicine tasted terrible, but I managed to choke it down.

choke something off†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to restrict or strangle a living creature’s windpipe. _The tight collar on the cat tended to choke its airstream off. _The collar choked off its airstream.
examples: The tight collar on the cat tended to choke its airstream off.

choke something up†.monolingual: 1. to clog something up; to fill up and block something. _ Branches and leaves choked the sewer up. _Rust choked up the pipes.
examples: Branches and leaves choked the sewer up.

choke up.monolingual: 1. to feel like crying. _I choked up when I heard the news. _He was beginning to choke up as he talked.
examples: I choked up when I heard the news.

choose among someone or something.monolingual: to make a choice of a person or thing from a variety of possibilities. _We will choose among the names on the list you gave us. _ I need to choose among the car models available.
examples: We will choose among the names on the list you gave us.

choose from someone or something.monolingual: to make a selection from a group of persons or things. _ You will have to choose from these people only. _ Ron chose from the items in the catalog.
examples: You will have to choose from these people only.

choose someone as something.monolingual: to select someone to be something. _ We will choose her as our representative. _ I chose Sam as my assistant.
examples: We will choose her as our representative.

choose something for someone.monolingual: to select something for someone, perhaps as a gift. _ I will probably choose f lowers for your mother. _I chose a funny card for his birthday.
examples: I will probably choose f lowers for your mother.

chop someone off†.monolingual: Fig. to stop someone in the middle of a sentence or speech. (Abruptly, as if actually chopping or cutting.) _ I’m not finished. Don’t chop me off! _ The moderator chopped off the speaker.
examples: I’m not finished.

chop something back†.monolingual: to prune vegetation; to reduce the size of plants by cutting. _ Why don’t you chop those bushes back while you have the shears out? _Chop back the bushes, please.
examples: Chop back the bushes, please.

chop something down†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to cut down something, such as a tree, with an ax. _ Please don’t chop my favorite tree down. _ Don’t chop down this tree!
examples: Please don’t chop my favorite tree down.

chuck it in.monolingual: Inf. to quit; to give up. (Fixed order.) _ I was so depressed, I almost chucked it in. _ If I didn’t have to keep the job to pay my bills, I’d have chucked it in long ago.
examples: I was so depressed, I almost chucked it in.

chuck someone or something away†.monolingual: to push or shove someone or something out of the way quickly or roughly. _She chucked the children away and ran to lock the door to protect them. _ He chucked away his clothes in a drawer. _ The rock star approached, and the guard chucked the teenage
examples: She chucked the children away and ran to lock the door to protect them.

chuck someone under the chin.monolingual: to tap someone, as a child, lightly under the chin, as a sign of affection. _ He said hello to little Mary and chucked her under the chin. _ Please don’t chuck me under the chin! I am not a child, you know!
examples: He said hello to little Mary and chucked her under the chin.

chuck something away†.monolingual: to throw something away; to dispose of something. _Would you please just chuck this garbage bag away? _ I don’t want to chuck away any paper that’s been used on only one side.
examples: I don’t want to chuck away any paper that’s been used on only one side.

chuck something down†.monolingual: Sl. to eat something very quickly. _ Don’t just chuck your food down. Enjoy it! _ I’ll be with you as soon as I chuck down this hamburger.
examples: Don’t just chuck your food down.

chuck something over something.monolingual: to throw something over something. _ Here, chuck this over the wall, and let’s go. _If you chuck another can over the fence, I will file a complaint.
examples: Here, chuck this over the wall, and let’s go.

chuck something up†.monolingual: to vomit something up. _ Don’t give chocolate to the dog. It will just chuck it up later. _The dog chucked up the grass it had eaten.
examples: Don’t give chocolate to the dog.

chug along.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a train engine] to labor along slowly. (Steam locomotives made the sound “chug, chug.”) _ The train chugged along to the top of the hill.
examples: The train chugged along to the top of the hill.

chum up to someone.monolingual: to try or seem to become friendly with someone. _ Todd chummed up to Martin. _ I don’t want to have to chum up to anyone I don’t want to work with.
examples: Todd chummed up to Martin.

chum up with someone.monolingual: to become friendly with someone. _ He seems to have chummed up with Fred. _ Juan quickly chummed up with all the guys in his class.
examples: He seems to have chummed up with Fred.

a chunk of change.monolingual: Fig. a lot of money. _Tom’s new sports car cost a real big chunk of change!

chunk something.monolingual: Rur. to throw something. _The kids were out chunking rocks into the lake. _ Somebody chunked a snowball at me!
examples: The kids were out chunking rocks into the lake.

church key.monolingual: a two-ended device used to remove bottle tops and to pierce a hole in can lids. _I’m looking for the church key so I can open this beer. _ She opened the can of tomato juice with the church key.
examples: I’m looking for the church key so I can open this beer.

churn something out†.monolingual: to produce something in large numbers, perhaps carelessly. _We churn toys out by the thousand. _ This factory can churn out these parts day and night.
examples: We churn toys out by the thousand.

churn something up†.monolingual: to stir up a liquid; to mix up material suspended in water. _ The oars of our boat churned the shallow water up, leaving little clouds of sediment in our wake. _ The oars churned up the mud.
examples: The oars of our boat churned the shallow water up, leaving little clouds of sediment in our wake.

circulate among someone or something.monolingual: to move at random within a gathering of people or things. _ Karen circulated among the guests, serving drinks. _ The guests circulated among the various rooms in the house.
examples: Karen circulated among the guests, serving drinks.

circulate something through something.monolingual: to route something through something; to make something travel through something. _ Walter circulated the memo from the boss through the department. _ I would like for you to circulate this through the members of the club.
examples: Walter circulated the memo from the boss through the department.

circulate through something.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a fluid in a closed system of pipes or tubes] to flow through the various pathways of pipes and tubes. _ Cold water circulates through the entire building and keeps it cool. _ Blood circulates through the veins and arteries, reaching all
examples: Cold water circulates through the entire building and keeps it cool.

circumstances alter cases..monolingual: Prov. In unusual situations, people are allowed to do unusual things. _ Cashier: I’m sorry, this store does not accept personal checks. Customer: But I need this medicine, and I don’t have any cash. I’ve shopped at this store for fifteen years. Surel
examples: Cashier: I’m sorry, this store does not accept personal checks.

cite someone for something.monolingual: 1. to honor someone for doing something; to give someone a citation of honor for doing something good. _The town council cited her for bravery. _They cited Maria for her courageous act.
examples: The town council cited her for bravery.

city slicker.monolingual: someone from the city who is not familiar with country ways. _Them city slickers think we’re stupid just because we talk different. _The city slicker didn’t know the first thing about fishing for trout.
examples: Them city slickers think we’re stupid just because we talk different.

claim a life.monolingual: Fig. [for something] to take the life of someone. _ The killer tornado claimed the lives of six people at the trailer park. _ The athlete’s life was claimed in a skiing accident.
examples: The killer tornado claimed the lives of six people at the trailer park.

claim something for something.monolingual: to make a claim for money in payment for damages. _ David claimed one thousand dollars for the damaged car. _ She claimed a lot of money for the amount of harm she experienced.
examples: David claimed one thousand dollars for the damaged car.

clam up.monolingual: to say nothing. (Closing one’s mouth in the way that a clam closes up.) _ The minute they got him in for questioning, he clammed up. _ You’ll clam up if you know what’s good for you.
examples: The minute they got him in for questioning, he clammed up.

clamor against someone or something.monolingual: to raise a great outcry against someone or something. _The protestors clamored against the mayor. _The citizens clamored against the new taxes.
examples: The protestors clamored against the mayor.

clamor for someone or something.monolingual: to raise a great outcry for someone or something. _ Everyone was clamoring for Mark. They just loved him. _The children were clamoring for ice cream.
examples: Everyone was clamoring for Mark.

clap something out†.monolingual: to clap the rhythmic beat of something in order to learn it. (Said of music.) _All right, now. Let’s clap the rhythm out. _ We’ll clap out the rhythm in time with our singing.
examples: All right, now. Let’s clap the rhythm out.

clap something together.monolingual: to slap two things, usually hands, together so that they make a noise. _ The boys clapped their hands together whenever a goal was scored. _ One of the orchestra members clapped two blocks of wood together periodically, making a very loud noise.
examples: The boys clapped their hands together whenever a goal was scored.

clash against something.monolingual: to wage a battle or attack against someone or something. _ The troops clashed against the enemy. _We clashed against the opposite side for over three days.
examples: The troops clashed against the enemy.

clash with something.monolingual: [for the color of something] to conflict with or mismatch another color. _ This red carpet clashes with the purple of the drapes. _ This red does not clash with purple. It looks gorgeous.
examples: This red carpet clashes with the purple of the drapes.

*a clean bill of health.monolingual: Fig. a physician’s determination that a person is in good condition, especially following an illness, surgery, etc. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ Sally got a clean bill of health from the doctor. _ Now that Sally has a clean bill of
examples: Sally got a clean bill of health from the doctor.

clean one’s act up†.monolingual: to reform one’s conduct; to improve one’s performance. _ We were told to clean our act up or move out. _ I cleaned up my act, but not in time. I got kicked out.
examples: We were told to clean our act up or move out.

clean someone or something down†.monolingual: to clean someone or something by brushing or with flowing water. _ He was covered with mud, and we used the garden hose to clean him down. _ Please clean down the sidewalk.
examples: He was covered with mud, and we used the garden hose to clean him down.

clean someone or something up†.monolingual: to get someone or something clean. _Please go into the bathroom and clean yourself up. _ I’ll clean up the kids before we leave for dinner. _ Can you clean this place up a little?
examples: Please go into the bathroom and clean yourself up.

clean someone out†.monolingual: 1. Fig. to get or use up all of someone’s money. _ The bill for supper cleaned me out, and we couldn’t go to the f lick. _ The robbers cleaned out all the bank’s cash.
examples: The bill for supper cleaned me out, and we couldn’t go to the f lick.

clean someone’s plow.monolingual: Rur. to beat someone up. _ If Joe crosses me one more time, I’ll clean his plow for sure. _ Somebody must have really cleaned Bill’s plow last night. He had two black eyes this morning!
examples: If Joe crosses me one more time, I’ll clean his plow for sure.

clean something out†.monolingual: to remove dirt or unwanted things from the inside of something. _Someone has to clean the garage out. _ I’ll clean out my closet tonight.
examples: Someone has to clean the garage out.

a clean sweep.monolingual: a broad movement clearing or affecting everything in its pathway. _ The manager and everybody in accounting got fired in a clean sweep of that department. _ Everybody got a pay rise. It was a clean sweep.
examples: The manager and everybody in accounting got fired in a clean sweep of that department.

clean-cut.monolingual: having to do with a person (usually male) who is neat and tidy. _He’s a very clean-cut guy, and polite too. _ He’s sort of clean-cut looking, but with curly hair.
examples: He’s a very clean-cut guy, and polite too.

cleaned out.monolingual: 1. Fig. broke; with no money. _ I’m cleaned out. Not a cent left. _ Tom’s cleaned out. How will he pay his bills now?
examples: I’m cleaned out.

cleanliness is next to godliness..monolingual: Prov. It is very important to keep yourself clean. _ Child: How come I have to take a bath? Mother: Cleanliness is next to godliness. _ The woman sitting next to me on the bus had obviously never heard that cleanliness is next to godliness.
examples: Child: How come I have to take a bath? Mother: Cleanliness is next to godliness.

*clear as a bell.monolingual: very clear, as with the sound of a bell. (*Also: as ~.) _ I fixed the radio, so now all the stations come in clear as a bell. _ Through the wall, I could hear the neighbors talking, just as clear as a bell.
examples: I fixed the radio, so now all the stations come in clear as a bell.

*clear as crystal.monolingual: 1. Cliché very clear; transparent. (*Also: as ~.) _The stream was as clear as crystal. _She cleaned the windowpane until it was clear as crystal.
examples: The stream was as clear as crystal.

*clear as mud.monolingual: 1. Cliché not clear at all. (*Also: as ~.) _ Your swimming pool needs cleaning; the water is clear as mud.
examples: Your swimming pool needs cleaning; the water is clear as mud.

*clear of something.monolingual: without touching something; away from something. (*Typically: keep ~; move ~; remain ~; stand ~.) _ Please stand clear of the doors while the train is moving. _Make sure the dog moves clear of the driveway before backing the car up.
examples: Please stand clear of the doors while the train is moving.

clear someone of something.monolingual: to show that a person is innocent; to exonerate someone of a crime. _ An investigation cleared me of any wrongdoing. _ They were unable to clear themselves of the charges.
examples: An investigation cleared me of any wrongdoing.

clear someone’s name.monolingual: to prove that someone is not guilty of a crime or misdeed. _ I was accused of theft, but the real thief confessed and I cleared my name.
examples: I was accused of theft, but the real thief confessed and I cleared my name.

clear something away†.monolingual: to take something away. _ Please clear the children’s toys away. _ Would you clear away the dishes?
examples: Please clear the children’s toys away.

clear something for publication.monolingual: to approve the release of something so it can be published. _ The government refused to clear the story for publication. _ I want to clear this for publication as soon as possible.
examples: The government refused to clear the story for publication.

clear something from some place.monolingual: to take something away from a place. _ Please clear all these papers from the desk. _ Would you clear the dishes from the table?
examples: Please clear all these papers from the desk.

clear something up†.monolingual: 1. to make something more clear. _ Let the muddy water stand overnight so it will clear up. _ A strong wind blew in and cleared up the smoke in the air.
examples: Let the muddy water stand overnight so it will clear up.

clear the air.monolingual: 1. Lit. to get rid of stale or bad air. _ Open some windows and clear the air. It’s stuffy in here.
examples: Open some windows and clear the air.

clear the decks.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for everyone] leave the deck of a ship and prepare for action. (A naval expression urging seaman to stow gear and prepare for battle or other action.) _ An attack is coming. Clear the decks.
examples: An attack is coming.

clear the table.monolingual: to remove the dishes and other eating utensils from the table after a meal. (Compare this with set the table.) _ Will you please help clear the table? _ After you clear the table, we’ll play cards.
examples: After you clear the table, we’ll play cards.

clear the way!.monolingual: Please get out of the way, because someone or something is coming through and needs room! _ The movers were shouting, “Clear the way!” because they needed room to take the piano out of the house.
examples: The movers were shouting, “Clear the way!” because they needed room to take the piano out of the house.

clear up.monolingual: 1. [for the sky] to become more clear or sunny. _Suddenly, the sky cleared up. _When the sky cleared up, the breeze began to blow.
examples: Suddenly, the sky cleared up.

cleave to someone.monolingual: to be sexually faithful, usually to one’s husband. (Biblical. As in the traditional marriage ceremony, “And cleave only unto him.”) _ She promised to cleave only to him for the rest of her life.
examples: She promised to cleave only to him for the rest of her life.

click with someone.monolingual: 1. [for something] to be understood or comprehended by someone suddenly. _ His explanation clicked with Maggie at once.
examples: His explanation clicked with Maggie at once.

cling to someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to hold on tight to someone or something. _ The child clung tightly to his mother. _ As she drifted in the sea, she clung to a f loating log.
examples: The child clung tightly to his mother.

cling together.monolingual: [for two or more people or animals] to hold on tightly to each other. _ The two children clung together throughout the ordeal. _The baby baboon and its mother clung together and could not be separated.
examples: The two children clung together throughout the ordeal.

clip someone’s wings.monolingual: Fig. to restrain someone; to reduce or put an end to someone’s privileges. (Alludes to clipping a bird’s wings to keep it from flying away.) _You had better learn to get home on time, or I will clip your wings. _ My mother clipped my wings. I can’t g
examples: You had better learn to get home on time, or I will clip your wings.

clip something from something.monolingual: to cut something out of or away from something; to cut something off something. _ I clipped the picture from the magazine. _ I clipped the straggly hairs from his head.
examples: I clipped the picture from the magazine.

cloak-and-dagger.monolingual: involving secrecy and plotting. _ A great deal of cloak-and-dagger stuff goes on in political circles. _ A lot of cloak-and-dagger activity was involved in the appointment of the director.
examples: A great deal of cloak-and-dagger stuff goes on in political circles.

clock in.monolingual: to record one’s time of arrival, usually by punching a time clock. _ What time did she clock in? _ She forgot to clock in today.
examples: She forgot to clock in today.

clock out.monolingual: to record one’s time of departure, usually by punching a time clock. _ I will clock out just before I go home. _ Jim clocked out early Tuesday to go to the doctor.
examples: I will clock out just before I go home.

clock someone in.monolingual: to observe and record someone’s time of arrival. _ The manager says he clocked you in at noon. That’s a bit late, isn’t it?
examples: The manager says he clocked you in at noon.

clock someone out.monolingual: to observe and record someone’s time of departure. _ Jane clocked herself out and went home.
examples: Jane clocked herself out and went home.

clock something up†.monolingual: 1. to record the accumulated hours, miles, etc., of some device or machine. (The recording is usually done by a meter of some type such as a speedometer, an elapsed time meter, etc. _ She must have clocked two hundred f lying hours up in six months.
examples: She must have clocked two hundred f lying hours up in six months.

clock-watcher.monolingual: someone—a worker or a student—who is always looking at the clock, anticipating when something will be over. _ There are four clock-watchers in our office. _ People who don’t like their jobs can turn into clockwatchers.
examples: There are four clock-watchers in our office.

clog someone up†.monolingual: [for some kind of food] to constipate someone. _ This cheese clogs me up. I can’t eat it. _ This food clogs up people who eat it.
examples: This cheese clogs me up.

clog something up†.monolingual: [for something] to obstruct a channel or conduit. _ The leaves clogged the gutters up. _ They clogged up the gutter.
examples: The leaves clogged the gutters up.

clog something with something.monolingual: to block or obstruct a channel or conduit with something. _ The neighbors clogged the creek with their brush and leaves. _ Please don’t clog the drain with garbage.
examples: The neighbors clogged the creek with their brush and leaves.

clog up.monolingual: [for a channel or conduit] to become blocked. _ The canal clogged up with leaves and mud.
examples: The canal clogged up with leaves and mud.

close at hand.monolingual: within reach; handy. _ I’m sorry, but your letter isn’t close at hand. Please remind me what you said in it. _When you’re cooking, you should keep all the ingredients close at hand.
examples: I’m sorry, but your letter isn’t close at hand.

close, but no cigar..monolingual: Cliché Some effort came close to succeeding, but did not succeed. (Alludes to not quite winning a cigar as a prize.) _ Jill: How did you do in the contest? Jane: Close, but no cigar. I got second place.
examples: Jill: How did you do in the contest? Jane: Close, but no cigar.

close on something.monolingual: to formally complete the sale and transfer of property, especially real estate. _ We closed on the new house on April
examples: We closed on the new house on April 16.

close ranks.monolingual: to move closer together in a military formation. _The soldiers closed ranks and marched on the enemy in tight formation.
examples: The soldiers closed ranks and marched on the enemy in tight formation.

close someone or something down†.monolingual: to force someone or someone’s business, office, shop, etc., to close permanently or temporarily. _The health department closed the restaurant down. _ They closed down the same place last year, too.
examples: The health department closed the restaurant down.

close someone up†.monolingual: to close a surgical wound at the end of a surgical procedure. _ Fred, would you close her up for me? _ Fred closed up the patient.
examples: Fred closed up the patient.

close something off†.monolingual: to prevent entrance into something; to block something off. _Please don’t close this passageway off. _ They closed off the passageway anyway.
examples: Please don’t close this passageway off.

close something out†.monolingual: 1. to sell off a particular kind of merchandise with the intention of not selling it in the future. _ These are not selling. Let’s close them out. _ They closed out all of last season’s merchandise.
examples: These are not selling.

close something to someone.monolingual: to prevent someone or some type of person from participating in or attending something. _ We closed membership to anyone who signed up late. _ They had to close the registration to nonresidents.
examples: We closed membership to anyone who signed up late.

close something up†.monolingual: 1. to close someone’s business, office, shop, etc., temporarily or permanently. _ Tom’s restaurant nearly went out of business when the health department closed him up. _The health department closed up the restaurant.
examples: Tom’s restaurant nearly went out of business when the health department closed him up.

close to home.monolingual: Fig. affecting one personally and intimately. _ Her remarks were a bit too close to home. I took her review as a personal insult.
examples: Her remarks were a bit too close to home.

*close to someone.monolingual: friendly or intimate with someone. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ She is very shy and really won’t let anyone get close to her. _ It is difficult to get close to a loner like Wally.
examples: She is very shy and really won’t let anyone get close to her.

*close to someone or something.monolingual: 1. near someone or something. (*Typically: get ~; stand ~; sit ~; move ~.) _ Don’t get close to me. I have a cold. _ If you get close to the fire, you may get burned.
examples: Don’t get close to me.

close up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for an opening] to close completely. _ The door closed up and would not open again. _The wound will close up completely in a day or so.
examples: The door closed up and would not open again.

close up shop.monolingual: Fig. to quit working, for the day or forever. (Fixed order.) _ It’s five o’clock. Time to close up shop. _ I can’t make any money in this town. The time has come to close up shop and move to another town.
examples: It’s five o’clock.

close with someone or something.monolingual: to end a performance with a particular act or event. _ The show is almost over and we will close with Sarah Miles, who will announce her own song title. _ The evening closed with a magic act.
examples: The show is almost over and we will close with Sarah Miles, who will announce her own song title.

closet someone with someone.monolingual: to put someone into a private room with someone else for the purposes of conducting business. _ She closeted herself with the president and finally, once and for all, had her say.
examples: She closeted herself with the president and finally, once and for all, had her say.

clothe someone in something.monolingual: to dress someone in something. _She clothed her children in the finest garments. _ He clothed himself in his tuxedo for the wedding.
examples: She clothed her children in the finest garments.

clothes make the man..monolingual: Prov. People will judge you according to the way you dress. _ Jim was always careful about how he dressed. He believed that clothes make the man.
examples: Jim was always careful about how he dressed.

cloud over.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for the sky] to fill with clouds; [for the sun] to be obscured by clouds. _ It was beginning to cloud over, so we went inside. _ The sky clouded over and it began to get chilly.
examples: It was beginning to cloud over, so we went inside.

cloud up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for the sky] to get cloudy, as if it were going to rain. _All of a sudden it clouded up and began to rain. _ It usually clouds up at the top of the mountain.
examples: All of a sudden it clouded up and began to rain.

clunk down.monolingual: [for something] to drop or fall, making the sound “clunk.” _A large piece of metal clunked down right in front of me. _ A tree branch clunked down on the roof and damaged a few shingles.
examples: A large piece of metal clunked down right in front of me.

clunk something down†.monolingual: to drop or place something heavily on something so that it makes a clunking noise. _ He clunked the big box down on the table. _ He clunked down all his school books on the table.
examples: He clunked the big box down on the table.

cluster around someone or something.monolingual: [for a group of people or things] to bunch together, surrounding someone or something. _ The birds clustered around the chimney top to keep warm. _ The kids clustered around the police officer.
examples: The birds clustered around the chimney top to keep warm.

cluster together.monolingual: to bunch or group together. _All of the bats clustered together on the roof of the cave. _ The children clustered together in small groups here and there on the playground.
examples: All of the bats clustered together on the roof of the cave.

clutch at someone or something.monolingual: to grasp at or grab for someone or something. _ He clutched at the roots of the trees along the bank, but the f lood swept him away. _ Karen clutched at me, but lost her grip.
examples: He clutched at the roots of the trees along the bank, but the f lood swept him away.

clutch at straws.monolingual: Fig. to continue to seek solutions, ideas, or hopes that are insubstantial. _ When you talk of cashing in quick on your inventions, you are just clutching at straws. _ That is not a real solution to the problem. You are just clutching at straws.
examples: When you talk of cashing in quick on your inventions, you are just clutching at straws.

clutter something up†.monolingual: to mess something up; to fill something or some place up with too many things. _ Heaps of newspapers cluttered the room up and made it a fire hazard. _ Who cluttered up this house?
examples: Heaps of newspapers cluttered the room up and made it a fire hazard.

coach someone for something.monolingual: to train or drill someone in preparation for doing something. _ Elliott coached his roommate every night for the contest. _Juan coached Alice for the play.
examples: Elliott coached his roommate every night for the contest.

coalesce into something.monolingual: [for two or more things] to blend or fuse and become one thing. _ The fading colors coalesced into a gray blur. _ In the distance, the crowd coalesced into a single blob.
examples: The fading colors coalesced into a gray blur.

coast along.monolingual: to roll or move along with little or no effort. _ We just coasted along on the f lat prairie. _ We coasted along until we came to the bottom of the hill.
examples: We just coasted along on the f lat prairie.

the coast is clear..monolingual: There is no visible danger. _I’m going to stay hidden here until the coast is clear. _ You can come out of your hiding place now. The coast is clear.
examples: I’m going to stay hidden here until the coast is clear.

coast-to-coast.monolingual: from the Atlantic to the Pacific Oceans (in the continental U.S.A.); all the land between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans (considered in either direction). _My voice was once heard on a coast-to-coast radio broadcast. _Our car made the coast-to-coast
examples: My voice was once heard on a coast-to-coast radio broadcast.

coat and tie.monolingual: [for men] a jacket or sports coat and necktie. (A respectable but less than formal standard of dress.) _ My brother was not wearing a coat and tie, and they would not admit him into the restaurant. _ I always carry a coat and tie in my car just in ca
examples: My brother was not wearing a coat and tie, and they would not admit him into the restaurant.

coax someone to do something.monolingual: to urge someone to do something. _ The kids coaxed her to let them go swimming. _ Can I coax you to try some of this pie?
examples: The kids coaxed her to let them go swimming.

cock a snook at someone.monolingual: to show or express defiance or scorn at someone. _ He cocked a snook at the traffic cop and tore up the ticket. _The boy cocked a snook at the park attendant and walked on the grass.
examples: He cocked a snook at the traffic cop and tore up the ticket.

cock of the walk.monolingual: someone who acts more important than others in a group. _ The deputy manager was cock of the walk until the new manager arrived. _He loved acting cock of the walk and ordering everyone about.
examples: The deputy manager was cock of the walk until the new manager arrived.

cock-and-bull story.monolingual: a hard-to-believe, made-up story; a story that is a lie. _ Don’t give me that cock-and-bull story. _ I asked for an explanation, and all I got was your ridiculous cock-and-bull story!
examples: Don’t give me that cock-and-bull story.

coexist with someone or something.monolingual: to exist agreeably or tolerably with or at the same time as someone or something. _ I decided that I would have to coexist with your policies, despite my objections. _ It is hard for cats to coexist with dogs.
examples: I decided that I would have to coexist with your policies, despite my objections.

coffee and.monolingual: coffee and a doughnut or a pastry. _ I’ll have coffee and. _ We stopped at a little shop for coffee and.
examples: I’ll have coffee and.

coffee and danish.monolingual: a cup of coffee and a Danish sweet roll. _ A few of us like to have coffee and Danish before we start work. _ Coffee and Danish is not my idea of a good breakfast!
examples: A few of us like to have coffee and Danish before we start work.

coffee-table book.monolingual: a book that is more suitable for display than for reading, typically, an oversize, illustrated book left on the coffee table for visitors to examine. _ This book is more of a coffee-table book than an art book. I prefer something more scholarly. _ We
examples: This book is more of a coffee-table book than an art book.

cogitate on something.monolingual: Rur. to think about something. _ Cogitate on this idea for a while. _ I will have to cogitate on this for a few days. I’ll get back to you.
examples: Cogitate on this idea for a while.

cohabit with someone.monolingual: 1. [for an unmarried person] to live with a person of the opposite sex. _They were cohabiting with one another for several years.
examples: They were cohabiting with one another for several years.

coil something up†.monolingual: to roll or twist something into a coil. _ Maria coiled the strip of stamps up and put them in the little dispenser. _ Please coil up the rope.
examples: Maria coiled the strip of stamps up and put them in the little dispenser.

coin a phrase.monolingual: Fig. to create a new expression that is worthy of being remembered and repeated. (Often jocular.) _ He is “worth his weight in feathers,” to coin a phrase.
examples: He is “worth his weight in feathers,” to coin a phrase.

coincide with something.monolingual: to agree with or match something; [for something] to happen at the same time as something else. _ This pattern coincides with the pattern we see in the carpet. _ My birthday sometimes coincides with Thanksgiving Day.
examples: This pattern coincides with the pattern we see in the carpet.

coldcock someone.monolingual: to knock someone unconscious. _ He hit him once and looks like he coldcocked him. _ She coldcocked him with her walking stick.
examples: He hit him once and looks like he coldcocked him.

cold comfort.monolingual: no comfort or consolation at all. _ She knows there are others worse off than her, but that’s cold comfort. _It was cold comfort to the student that others had failed as he had done.
examples: She knows there are others worse off than her, but that’s cold comfort.

*cold feet.monolingual: Fig. fear of doing something; cowardice at the moment of action. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ The bridegroom got cold feet on the day of the wedding. _ Sally said I should try skydiving, but I had cold feet.
examples: The bridegroom got cold feet on the day of the wedding.

*a cold fish.monolingual: Fig. a person who is distant and unfeeling. (*Typically: act like ~; be ~.) _Bob is so dull—a real cold fish. _ She hardly ever speaks to anyone. She’s a cold fish.
examples: Bob is so dull—a real cold fish.

cold hands, warm heart..monolingual: Prov. People whose hands are usually cold have kind and loving personalities. _Nancy: I don’t like holding hands with Joe. His hands are so cold. Jane: Cold hands, warm heart.
examples: Nancy: I don’t like holding hands with Joe.

cold, hard cash.monolingual: cash, not checks or credit. _I want to be paid in cold, hard cash, and I want to be paid now! _ Pay me now! Cash on the barrelhead—cold, hard cash.
examples: Pay me now! Cash on the barrelhead—cold, hard cash.

cold-shoulder.monolingual: to ignore someone; to give someone a cool reception. _ The hostess cold-shouldered me, so I spilt my appetizers in the swimming pool. _Tiffany cold-shouldered the guy who was trying to f lirt with her.
examples: The hostess cold-shouldered me, so I spilt my appetizers in the swimming pool.

*the cold shoulder.monolingual: Fig. an attitude of rejection. (*Typically: get ~; give someone ~.) _ If you greet her at a party, you’ll just get the cold shoulder. _I thought that Sally and I were friends, but lately I’ve been getting the cold shoulder.
examples: If you greet her at a party, you’ll just get the cold shoulder.

cold turkey.monolingual: Sl. immediately; without tapering off or cutting down gradually. _ Tom stopped smoking cold turkey. _ She gave up her drinking habit cold turkey and had no ill effects.
examples: Tom stopped smoking cold turkey.

collaborate with someone or something.monolingual: to work together on something with someone or a group. _ I will collaborate with Amy on this research. _ I was forced to collaborate with a totally uninformed committee.
examples: I will collaborate with Amy on this research.

collapse into something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to fall down into something with suddenness, as if out of energy. _ She was so tired, she collapsed into the chair. _ Juan collapsed into a chair and fell fast asleep.
examples: She was so tired, she collapsed into the chair.

collapse under someone or something.monolingual: to cave in under the weight of someone or something. _ The grandstand collapsed under the weight of the spectators. _The bridge collapsed from the force of the f lood.
examples: The grandstand collapsed under the weight of the spectators.

collar-and-tie men.monolingual: Rur. businessmen who wear dress shirts and ties. _After Jim graduated from college, he went off to join the collar-and-tie men. _ Us working folks at the plant have an awful time getting the collar-and-tie men to see our point of view.
examples: After Jim graduated from college, he went off to join the collar-and-tie men.

collate something with something.monolingual: to compare or match something with something. _ Try to collate these figures with that other list. _I can’t collate these notations with the spreadsheet they go with.
examples: Try to collate these figures with that other list.

collect around someone or something.monolingual: to gather around someone or something; to accumulate around someone or something. _ The guests collected around the table that held the birthday cake. _The children collected around the birthday boy.
examples: The guests collected around the table that held the birthday cake.

collect on something.monolingual: to take or receive payment on a debt or promise. _ I have come to collect on your debt. _ I will have to assign your account to an agency to collect on this bill.
examples: I have come to collect on your debt.

collect one’s thoughts.monolingual: Fig. to take time to think through an issue; to give some thought to a topic. _ I’ll speak to the visitors in a moment. I need some time to collect my thoughts.
examples: I’ll speak to the visitors in a moment.

collect something from someone.monolingual: 1. to gather up something from someone; to gather money from someone. _ I’m here to collect used clothing from you. _ She is out collecting donations from the neighbors.
examples: I’m here to collect used clothing from you.

collect something up†.monolingual: to gather something up. _ Collect your things up, and let’s go. _ I collected up all my luggage and left.
examples: Collect your things up, and let’s go.

collide with someone or something.monolingual: to crash with or bump into someone or something. _ The bus collided with a truck. _ Maria collided with Alice, but neither was hurt.
examples: The bus collided with a truck.

collude with someone or something.monolingual: to plot or conspire with someone or a group. _ The CEO colluded with the board of directors in the stock scandal.
examples: The CEO colluded with the board of directors in the stock scandal.

color something in†.monolingual: to paint or draw color on a pattern or outline. _ Here is a sketch. Please color it in. _ Color in the sketch, please.
examples: Here is a sketch.

comb through something.monolingual: Fig. to look through something, examining it thoroughly. _ I combed through all my belongings, looking for the lost papers. _ The vet combed through the dog’s coat, looking for tick bites.
examples: I combed through all my belongings, looking for the lost papers.

combine something with something.monolingual: to mix something with something else. _ I want to combine the red f lowers with the pink ones for a bouquet. _ First, combine the eggs with the sugar.
examples: I want to combine the red f lowers with the pink ones for a bouquet.

come a cropper.monolingual: Fig. to have a misfortune; to fail. (Meaning ‘fall off one’s horse.’) _ Bob invested all his money in the stock market just before it fell. Boy, did he come a cropper. _ Jane was out all night before she took her final. She really came a cropper.
examples: Bob invested all his money in the stock market just before it fell.

come about.monolingual: 1. to happen. _ How did this damage come about? _ This came about due to the windstorm.
examples: This came about due to the windstorm.

come across.monolingual: 1. to be compliant. _Oh, she’ll come across, just you wait; she’ll do what we want.
examples: Oh, she’ll come across, just you wait; she’ll do what we want.

come again..monolingual: 1. Please come back again sometime. _ Mary: I had a lovely time. Thank you for asking me. Sally: You’re quite welcome. Come again. _ “Come again,” said Mrs. Martin as she let Jimmy out the door.
examples: Mary: I had a lovely time.

come again?.monolingual: ) I didn’t hear what you said. Please repeat it. _ Sally: Do you want some more carrots? Mary: Come again? Sally: Carrots. Do you want some more carrots?
examples: Sally: Do you want some more carrots? Mary: Come again? Sally: Carrots.

come apart.monolingual: to break apart; to break up. _ The missile came apart in midair. _ I was afraid our car would come apart on that rough road.
examples: The missile came apart in midair.

come as no surprise.monolingual: will not be surprising [for someone] to learn [something]. _It will come as no surprise for you to learn that the company is losing money this year. _ It came as no surprise that the president had been lying.
examples: It will come as no surprise for you to learn that the company is losing money this year.

come at someone or something.monolingual: 1. to make a threatening move toward someone or something. _ The gorilla came at the cage and shook the bars. _ Walter came at the cake as if he were going to snatch the whole thing.
examples: The gorilla came at the cage and shook the bars.

come away empty-handed.monolingual: to return without anything. _ All right, go gambling. Don’t come away empty-handed, though. _ Go to the bank and ask for the loan again. This time don’t come away empty-handed.
examples: All right, go gambling.

come away with someone.monolingual: to go away or travel away with someone. _ Come away with me for a ride in the country. _ Come away with me and we’ll find a nice place to eat.
examples: Come away with me for a ride in the country.

come back.monolingual: to return; to return to an advantageous or favorable state or condition. _Walter practiced every day, hoping to come back from his injury. _When will the good old days come back?
examples: Walter practiced every day, hoping to come back from his injury.

come back anytime..monolingual: Please come and visit us again. You’re always welcome. (Often said by a host or hostess to departing guests.) _ Mary: So glad you could come. Bill: Thank you. I had a wonderful time. Mary: Come back anytime. _ Bob: Thanks for the coffee and cake. Bye
examples: Mary: So glad you could come.

come before someone or something.monolingual: 1. [of persons or things in an order or a line] to be in front of or in advance of someone or something. _ This one comes before that one. _ She comes before me.
examples: This one comes before that one.

come by something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to travel by a specific means, such as a plane, a boat, or a car. _ We came by train. It’s more relaxing. _Next time, we’ll come by plane. It’s faster.
examples: We came by train.

come by something honestly.monolingual: 1. Fig. to get something honestly. _ Don’t worry. I came by this Swiss watch honestly. _ I have a feeling she didn’t come by it honestly.
examples: Don’t worry. I came by this Swiss watch honestly.

come down.monolingual: 1. Sl. to happen. _ Hey, man! What’s coming down? _ When something like this comes down, I have to stop and think things over.
examples: When something like this comes down, I have to stop and think things over.

come down in the world.monolingual: to lose one’s social position or financial standing. _ Mr. Jones has really come down in the world since he lost his job. _ If I were unemployed, I’m sure I’d come down in the world, too.
examples: Mr. Jones has really come down in the world since he lost his job.

come down to earth.monolingual: 1. Lit. to arrive on earth from above. _ An angel came down to earth and made an announcement.
examples: An angel came down to earth and made an announcement.

come down to some place.monolingual: to come to some place in the south or in a lower altitude for a visit. (Assumes a perspective of a visitor from a northern state of the U.S.) _ Come down to our place in Florida this winter if you want.
examples: Come down to our place in Florida this winter if you want.

come down to something.monolingual: to be reduced to something; to amount to no more than something. _ It comes down to whether you want to go to the movies or stay at home and watch television. _ It came down to either getting a job or going to college.
examples: It comes down to whether you want to go to the movies or stay at home and watch television.

come down with something.monolingual: to become or to be sick with some illness. _Susan came down with a bad cold and had to cancel her trip. _I didn’t go to work because I came down with the f lu.
examples: Susan came down with a bad cold and had to cancel her trip.

come for someone.monolingual: to arrive to get someone. _I have come for Amy. Is she ready? _ The mothers came for their children at about five o’clock.
examples: I have come for Amy.

come forth.monolingual: to come out; to move forward and appear. _ Please come forth and meet your cousins. _ All the stage crew came forth and received some applause.
examples: Please come forth and meet your cousins.

come forward.monolingual: 1. Lit. to move oneself forward. _ Come forward and stand before the whole class.
examples: Come forward and stand before the whole class.

come from behind.monolingual: to advance from a losing position. (Alludes to being behind in a score or in a race.) _ Our team came from behind to win the game. _ The horse I bet on came from behind and almost placed second.
examples: Our team came from behind to win the game.

come from far and wide.monolingual: to arrive from everywhere; to arrive from many directions and great distances. _ People came from far and wide to attend the annual meeting. _The deer came from far and wide to lick the salt block we had put out.
examples: People came from far and wide to attend the annual meeting.

come from nowhere.monolingual: to come as a surprise with no warning. _ The dogs came from nowhere and attacked my cat. _The whole set of problems came from nowhere. There was no way we could have foreseen them.
examples: The dogs came from nowhere and attacked my cat.

come from someone or something.monolingual: to arrive from someone or something; [for something] to have originated with someone or something. _ Did this letter come from Alice? _ A notice came from the Internal Revenue Service.
examples: A notice came from the Internal Revenue Service.

come full circle.monolingual: Fig. to return to the original position or state of affairs. _The family sold the house generations ago, but things have come full circle and one of their descendants lives there now.
examples: The family sold the house generations ago, but things have come full circle and one of their descendants lives there now.

come hell or high water.monolingual: Fig. no matter what happens. (Use hell with caution.) _I’ll be there tomorrow, come hell or high water. _ Come hell or high water, I intend to own my own home.
examples: I’ll be there tomorrow, come hell or high water.

come home from some place.monolingual: to arrive home from another place. _ The soldiers came home from the war. _ When will you come home from the office?
examples: The soldiers came home from the war.

come home to someone.monolingual: Fig. [for a fact] to be recognized suddenly by someone. _Suddenly, it came home to me that you thought I was Ronald. _ The importance of the events of the day finally came home to me.
examples: Suddenly, it came home to me that you thought I was Ronald.

come in for something.monolingual: to be eligible for something; to be due something. _ You are going to come in for a nice reward. _ Your report came in for a lot of criticism at the last board meeting.
examples: You are going to come in for a nice reward.

come in handy.monolingual: [for something] to be useful. _ I think that this gadget will come in handy in the kitchen.
examples: I think that this gadget will come in handy in the kitchen.

come in useful.monolingual: to be useful. _ Your report has come in useful a number of times.
examples: Your report has come in useful a number of times.

come into being.monolingual: to begin existence. _ This idea came into being during the last decade. _ When did this organization come into being?
examples: This idea came into being during the last decade.

come into conflict.monolingual: [for things or people] to conflict or to be at odds with one another. _The various policies came into conf lict at the last moment. _ Bill and Bob came into conf lict over almost everything.
examples: The various policies came into conf lict at the last moment.

come into effect.monolingual: to become valid, effective, or operable. _When did these rules come into effect? _They came into effect while you were on vacation.
examples: They came into effect while you were on vacation.

come into existence.monolingual: to begin existence; to begin to be. _ This country came into existence in the early part of the fifteenth century. _ When did this little town come into existence?
examples: This country came into existence in the early part of the fifteenth century.

come into fashion.monolingual: to become stylish or fashionable. _ Do you think that a design like this will ever come into fashion? _ That kind of dance will never come into fashion.
examples: That kind of dance will never come into fashion.

come into play.monolingual: to become an important factor in something; to go into force. _All your hard practice and preparation will now come into play in the finals.
examples: All your hard practice and preparation will now come into play in the finals.

come into prominence.monolingual: to become notable; to become renowned. _She first came into prominence during the late forties, when she starred in a few movies. _Wally came into prominence when he won the state championship.
examples: She first came into prominence during the late forties, when she starred in a few movies.

come into season.monolingual: [for a game animal] to be subject to legal hunting. _When do ducks come into season around here? _ Deer came into season just yesterday.
examples: Deer came into season just yesterday.

come into service.monolingual: to begin to be used; to begin to operate and function as designed. _ When did this elevator come into service? _ I think that this machine came into service during World War II.
examples: I think that this machine came into service during World War II.

come into the world.monolingual: Fig. to be born. _ I came into this world nearly seventy years ago. _ Little Timmy came into the world on a cold and snowy night.
examples: I came into this world nearly seventy years ago.

come monday.monolingual: Rur. when Monday comes. (Can be used with other expressions for time, as in come next week, come December, come five o’clock. See the second example.) _ Joe plays so hard on the weekend that come Monday, he’s all worn out. _ You may think that puttin
examples: Joe plays so hard on the weekend that come Monday, he’s all worn out.

come off.monolingual: Inf. to happen; to take place. _ What time does this party come off ? _ How did your speech come off ? _ It came off very well.
examples: It came off very well.

come off it!.monolingual: 1. Inf. Stop acting arrogantly! ) _ Come off it, Tiff. You’re not the Queen of England.
examples: Come off it, Tiff.

come off second best.monolingual: to be second to someone or something; to get the poorer end of a bargain. _As usual, he came off second best with a little less prize money than the winner. _ I don’t want to come off second best again.
examples: As usual, he came off second best with a little less prize money than the winner.

come on as something.monolingual: to appear to be something; to project one’s image as something. _ The senator comes on as a liberal, but we all know better. _He comes on as a happy guy, but he is miserable.
examples: The senator comes on as a liberal, but we all know better.

come out.monolingual: 1. Lit. to exit; to leave the inside of a place. _ Please come out. We have to leave. _ When do you think they will all come out?
examples: Please come out.

come out ahead.monolingual: to end up with a profit, benefit, or advantage. _ It was a tricky deal, and no one came out ahead of anyone else. _ I never come out ahead after paying my bills.
examples: It was a tricky deal, and no one came out ahead of anyone else.

come out badly.monolingual: [for efforts at something] to have a bad result. _I hope trying to get back together with Joan doesn’t come out badly.
examples: I hope trying to get back together with Joan doesn’t come out badly.

come out in something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to come outside wearing something in particular. _ You shouldn’t come out in that skimpy jacket. _I didn’t mean to come out in my pajamas. I just wanted to get the newspaper.
examples: You shouldn’t come out in that skimpy jacket.

come out in the wash.monolingual: Fig. to work out all right. (Alludes to a clothing stain that can be removed by washing.) _ Don’t worry about that problem. It’ll all come out in the wash. _This trouble will go away. It’ll come out in the wash.
examples: Don’t worry about that problem.

come out of left field.monolingual: [for a problem or dilemma] to come from an unexpected place. _ This new problem came out of left field. We were really surprised. _ Your remarks came out of left field. I can’t understand your complaint.
examples: This new problem came out of left field.

come out of one’s shell.monolingual: Fig. to become more friendly; to be more sociable. (Alludes to a shy turtle putting its head out of its shell.) _ Come out of your shell, Tom. Go out and make some friends.
examples: Come out of your shell, Tom.

come out on something.monolingual: [for someone] to do well or poorly on a business venture. _ How did you come out on the Adams project? _ We came out ahead on the Adams project, but for the quarter we came out with a loss overall.
examples: We came out ahead on the Adams project, but for the quarter we came out with a loss overall.

come out on top.monolingual: Fig. to end up being the winner. _ I knew that if I kept trying, I would come out on top. _Harry came out on top as I knew he would.
examples: I knew that if I kept trying, I would come out on top.

come out to be.monolingual: to end up being a certain way. _I do not know what this sculpture will come out to be. _When I start writing a poem, I never know what it will come out to be.
examples: I do not know what this sculpture will come out to be.

come out well.monolingual: to end up well. _ I hope things come out well. _ Everything will come out well in the end.
examples: I hope things come out well.

come out with something.monolingual: 1. to publish something. _ When are you going to come out with a new edition? _The publisher decided not to come out with the book.
examples: The publisher decided not to come out with the book.

come over.monolingual: 1. to join this party or side; to change sides or affiliation. _Tom was formerly an enemy spy, but last year he came over. _I thought that Bill was a Republican. When did he come over?
examples: Tom was formerly an enemy spy, but last year he came over.

come over someone.monolingual: [for something] to affect a person, perhaps suddenly. _I just don’t know what came over me. _Something came over her just as she entered the room.
examples: I just don’t know what came over me.

come over someone or something.monolingual: to move over and above someone or something. _ A cloud came over us and rained like fury. _ Darkness came over the city and streetlights blinked on.
examples: A cloud came over us and rained like fury.

come right in..monolingual: Come in, please, you are very welcome here. _Fred (opening door): Well, hi, Bill. Bill: Hello, Fred. Good to see you. Fred: Come right in. Bill: Thanks.
examples: Fred (opening door): Well, hi, Bill.

come short of something.monolingual: Fig. to do something almost; to fail to achieve something completely. _The workers came short of finishing the job on time. _ We came short of our goal for the year.
examples: The workers came short of finishing the job on time.

come someone’s way.monolingual: [for something] to come to someone. _ I wish a large sum of money would come my way. _ I hope that no bad luck comes my way.
examples: I wish a large sum of money would come my way.

come to a bad end.monolingual: Fig. to have a disaster, perhaps one that is deserved or expected; to die an unfortunate death. _My old car came to a bad end. Its engine seized up. _The dishonest merchant came to a bad end.
examples: My old car came to a bad end.

come to a boil.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a liquid] to reach the boiling point. _ The soup came to a boil and the chef reduced the f lame.
examples: The soup came to a boil and the chef reduced the f lame.

come to a conclusion.monolingual: 1. to reach a decision. _ We talked for a long time but never came to any conclusion. _ Can we come to a conclusion today, or do we have to meet again?
examples: We talked for a long time but never came to any conclusion.

come to a halt.monolingual: to stop; to slow down and stop. _ Slowly, the train came to a halt. _After the bus came to a halt, more people got on.
examples: Slowly, the train came to a halt.

come to a head.monolingual: Fig. [for a problem] to reach a critical or crucial stage. _At the end of the week, everything came to a head and Sam was fired.
examples: At the end of the week, everything came to a head and Sam was fired.

come to a pretty pass.monolingual: Fig. to encounter a difficult situation. (This pretty expresses irony.) _ This project has come to a pretty pass. I don’t know how we can possibly finish on time. _ Mary had come to a pretty pass. She quit her job to be with her husband, and then he
examples: This project has come to a pretty pass.

come to a standstill.monolingual: [for something] to slow down and finally stop; to stop completely. (Usually refers to something that is progressing, such as work, traffic, negotiations.) _ As the strike began, the production line came to a standstill. _ At the height of rush hour,
examples: As the strike began, the production line came to a standstill.

come to a stop.monolingual: [for someone or something] to stop moving or happening. _ The bus finally came to a stop so I could get off. _ The dog’s barking finally came to a stop.
examples: The bus finally came to a stop so I could get off.

come to an impasse.monolingual: Fig. to reach a deadlock, stalemate, etc., in a situation. (Alludes to a blocked roadway.) _The committee has come to an impasse in its deliberations.
examples: The committee has come to an impasse in its deliberations.

come to an untimely end.monolingual: Fig. to come to an early death. _ Poor Mr. Jones came to an untimely end in a car accident. _ Cancer caused Mrs. Smith to come to an untimely end.
examples: Poor Mr. Jones came to an untimely end in a car accident.

come to attention.monolingual: to assume a formal military posture, standing very straight. _ Almost immediately, the soldiers came to attention.
examples: Almost immediately, the soldiers came to attention.

come to fruition.monolingual: Fig. to occur or turn out as suspected or intended. _ When will all of these good things come to fruition? _Our hard work and the end we planned for will soon come to fruition.
examples: Our hard work and the end we planned for will soon come to fruition.

come to grief.monolingual: Fig. to experience something unpleasant or damaging. _ In the end, he came to grief because he did not follow instructions.
examples: In the end, he came to grief because he did not follow instructions.

come to harm.monolingual: to experience something bad; to get damaged or harmed. _ I sincerely hope that you do not come to harm. _ I hope no one comes to harm.
examples: I sincerely hope that you do not come to harm.

come to life.monolingual: 1. Lit. to act as if alive after a period of seeming not to be alive. _As the anesthetic wore off, the patient came to life. _ After CPR, the child came to life.
examples: As the anesthetic wore off, the patient came to life.

come to light.monolingual: Fig. [for something] to become known or to be discovered. _Many surprises have come to light since then. _ Nothing new has come to light since we talked last.
examples: Many surprises have come to light since then.

come to mind.monolingual: Fig. [for a thought or idea] to enter into one’s consciousness or be remembered. _ Do I know a good barber? No one comes to mind right now. _ Another idea comes to mind. Why not check in the phone book?
examples: Do I know a good barber? No one comes to mind right now.

come to much.monolingual: 1. to amount to a large amount of money. (Usually used with a negative.) _ The bill did not come to much, considering what we had for dinner and drinks.
examples: The bill did not come to much, considering what we had for dinner and drinks.

come to no good.monolingual: to end up badly; to come to a bad end. _ The street gang leaders came to no good in the end.
examples: The street gang leaders came to no good in the end.

come to one’s feet.monolingual: to stand up. _ The audience came to its feet, cheering. _ Fred came to his feet to greet Roger.
examples: The audience came to its feet, cheering.

come to one’s senses.monolingual: to begin thinking sensibly. _ I’m glad he finally came to his senses and went on to college. _ I wish you would come to your senses and look for a better job.
examples: I’m glad he finally came to his senses and went on to college.

come to pass.monolingual: to happen; to take place. _ And when do you think all these good things will come to pass? _ Do you think it will really come to pass?

come to rest.monolingual: to stop; to slow down and stop. _ The ball rolled and rolled and finally came to rest. _ Where did the ball come to rest?
examples: The ball rolled and rolled and finally came to rest.

come to someone’s assistance.monolingual: to arrive and provide assistance to someone. _A kindly truck driver came to our assistance, and we were able to call for help. _I hope someone will come to my assistance soon.
examples: A kindly truck driver came to our assistance, and we were able to call for help.

come to the fore.monolingual: Fig. to become prominent; to become important. _ The question of salary has now come to the fore. _Since his great successes as a prosecutor, he has really come to the fore in city politics.
examples: The question of salary has now come to the fore.

come to think of it.monolingual: I just remembered. _ Come to think of it, I know someone who can help. _ I have a screwdriver in the trunk of my car, come to think of it.
examples: Come to think of it, I know someone who can help.

come to this.monolingual: to result in this situation. (Usually said out of surprise.) _ Who would believe it would come to this? _ So, it has come to this?

come together.monolingual: 1. to touch together; to meet. _The ends of the boards just came together. They were almost too short. _We came together in the park, just as we had agreed.
examples: The ends of the boards just came together.
