come true.monolingual: to materialize as expected or hoped. _ Jane’s wishes had come true. _ Dave wondered if his dreams would ever come true.
examples: Jane’s wishes had come true.

come under something.monolingual: to be classed in the category of something. _ This request comes under the category of a plain nuisance. _ Your proposal comes under the heading of new business and is out of order.
examples: This request comes under the category of a plain nuisance.

come unglued.monolingual: Fig. to lose emotional control; to break out into tears or laughter. _ When Sally heard the joke, she almost came unglued. _When the bank took away my car, I came unglued and cried and cried.
examples: When Sally heard the joke, she almost came unglued.

come up.monolingual: 1. Lit. to come from a lower place to a higher one. _ You can come up now. They are gone. _ Come up and enjoy the view from the tallest rooftop in the county.
examples: You can come up now.

come up a storm.monolingual: Rur. to become stormy. _ It came up a storm as I was on my way home, and I got soaked to the skin.
examples: It came up a storm as I was on my way home, and I got soaked to the skin.

come up for air.monolingual: 1. Lit. to lift one’s head out of the water to breathe. _After staying under water for almost a minute, Jason had to come up for air.
examples: After staying under water for almost a minute, Jason had to come up for air.

come up for something.monolingual: to be eligible for something; to be in line or sequence for something. _ She comes up for reelection in April. _ How soon does your driver’s license come up for renewal?
examples: She comes up for reelection in April.

come up through the ranks.monolingual: Fig. to rise to a position of leadership by working up through the sequence of lower positions. _He came up through the ranks to become a corporate executive. _The general came up through the ranks. There is no other way to become a general.
examples: He came up through the ranks to become a corporate executive.

come up to someone’s expectations.monolingual: to be as good as someone expected. _Sorry, but this product does not come up to my expectations and I want to return it.
examples: Sorry, but this product does not come up to my expectations and I want to return it.

come up to someone’s standards.monolingual: to meet or be equal to someone’s standards or requirements. _ Does this ice cream come up to your standards? _ Ann’s concert recital did not come up to her own standards.
examples: Ann’s concert recital did not come up to her own standards.

come what may.monolingual: Cliché no matter what might happen. _ I’ll be home for the holidays, come what may. _ Come what may, the mail will get delivered.
examples: I’ll be home for the holidays, come what may.

come within something.monolingual: 1. to be in the category of something; to be under the domain of someone or something. _ This comes within the domain of the treasurer. _ This matter doesn’t come within my area of expertise.
examples: This comes within the domain of the treasurer.

come-hither look.monolingual: an alluring or seductive look or glance, usually done by a woman. _She blinked her bedroom eyes and gave him a come-hither look. _ She had mastered the come-hither look, but was not ready for the next part.
examples: She blinked her bedroom eyes and gave him a come-hither look.

*comfortable as an old shoe.monolingual: Cliché very comfortable; very comforting and familiar. (*Also: as ~.) _ My old house may seem small to you, but I think it’s cozy. It’s as comfortable as an old shoe.
examples: My old house may seem small to you, but I think it’s cozy.

coming out of one’s ears.monolingual: Fig. very numerous or abundant. (As if people or things were coming in great numbers from many sources including unlikely ones.) _ I’ve got phone and e-mail messages coming out of my ears. _ We are very busy at the factory. We have orders coming out
examples: I’ve got phone and e-mail messages coming out of my ears.

coming up a cloud.monolingual: Rur. getting ready to rain. _ Look at that sky! It’s comin’ up a cloud!

commence with someone or something.monolingual: to start a procedure affecting a number of people or things by choosing a particular person or thing first. _ Each meeting commences with a reading of the minutes of the last meeting. _ The doctor interviews with Lynn and took everyone else in the or
examples: Each meeting commences with a reading of the minutes of the last meeting.

commend someone for something.monolingual: to praise someone for doing something. _The committee commended Ralph for his good work.
examples: The committee commended Ralph for his good work.

commiserate with someone.monolingual: to share one’s misery with another person who is also miserable. _ I stopped by Bruce’s house to commiserate with him on being laid off.
examples: I stopped by Bruce’s house to commiserate with him on being laid off.

commit oneself on something.monolingual: to agree to something; to promise or pledge to do something. _I’m sorry, but I can’t commit myself on this matter until I know more details.
examples: I’m sorry, but I can’t commit myself on this matter until I know more details.

commit oneself to something.monolingual: 1. to agree to something; to promise or pledge to do something. _ Yes, I will commit myself to the repair of the door frame. _ Will you commit yourself to finishing on time?
examples: Yes, I will commit myself to the repair of the door frame.

commit something to memory.monolingual: to memorize something. _Do we have to commit this poem to memory? _The dress rehearsal of the play is tomorrow night. Please make sure you have committed all your lines to memory by that time.
examples: The dress rehearsal of the play is tomorrow night.

commit to someone.monolingual: to marry or enter into an exclusive relationship with another person. _Jane says she loves me, but she’s not ready to commit to any one person. _ If you can’t commit to me, then this relationship is over.
examples: Jane says she loves me, but she’s not ready to commit to any one person.

commode-hugging drunk.monolingual: Sl. heavily alcohol intoxicated; drunk and vomiting. _Willie got commode-hugging drunk in the space of two hours.
examples: Willie got commode-hugging drunk in the space of two hours.

commune with something.monolingual: Fig. to experience wordless or spiritual communication with something. _ She went on long walks to commune with nature. _He enjoyed going off on a retreat to commune with his inner self.
examples: She went on long walks to commune with nature.

communicate something to someone.monolingual: to say or write something to someone; to tell someone something. _Will you please communicate my regards to her? _ I intend to communicate your request to the front office this morning.
examples: I intend to communicate your request to the front office this morning.

communicate with someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to correspond or talk with a person. _ I have to communicate with Wally first. _As soon as I have communicated with Fred, I can give you an answer.
examples: I have to communicate with Wally first.

commute between places.monolingual: to travel between the place where one works and the place where one lives. _ I have to commute between Chicago and Detroit every week. _ Mary has commuted between New York City and New Jersey for years.
examples: I have to commute between Chicago and Detroit every week.

commute from some place.monolingual: to travel to work from some place. _ I commute from way out in the country. _ Betty commutes from only a few miles away and will be here very soon.
examples: I commute from way out in the country.

commute something into something.monolingual: to change something into something. _ No one, as it turns out, can commute lead into gold. _ I had hoped to commute this argument into a sensible discussion, but it is hopeless.
examples: No one, as it turns out, can commute lead into gold.

compartmentalize something into somethin.monolingual: to segment or divide something into smaller things; to assign the parts of something into categories. _We will have to compartmentalize this large area into a number of smaller offices. _ His brain seems to be compartmentalized into a number of diffe
examples: We will have to compartmentalize this large area into a number of smaller offices.

compel someone to do something.monolingual: to force someone to do something; to drive someone to so something. _You can’t compel me to do that. _ She compelled herself to try, even though she was ill.
examples: You can’t compel me to do that.

compensate for something.monolingual: to counterbalance or counteract something; to make up for something. _ Your present kindness will not compensate for your previous rudeness.
examples: Your present kindness will not compensate for your previous rudeness.

compensate someone for something.monolingual: to pay someone [back] money for something. _ Don’t worry. I will compensate you for your loss. _ Let us compensate you for your expenses.
examples: Don’t worry. I will compensate you for your loss.

compete against someone.monolingual: to contend against someone; to play against someone in a game or contest. _ I don’t see how I can compete against all of them. _ She refused to compete against her own brothers.
examples: I don’t see how I can compete against all of them.

compete against something.monolingual: to struggle against something; to seem to be in a contest with something. _It was hard to be heard. I was competing against the noise of construction. _ Please stop talking. I do not wish to compete against the audience when I lecture.
examples: It was hard to be heard.

compete for someone or something.monolingual: to contend against or contest [someone] for someone or something; to struggle for someone or something [against a competitor]. _They are competing for a lovely prize. _ Ed and Roger are competing for Alice’s attention.
examples: They are competing for a lovely prize.

compete in something.monolingual: to enter into a competition. _ I do not want to compete in that contest. _ Ann looked forward to competing in the race.
examples: I do not want to compete in that contest.

compete with someone or something.monolingual: to contend against someone, something, or a group; to play in a competition against someone, something, or a group. _ I can’t compete with all this noise. _ We always compete closely with our crosstown rivals, Adams High School.
examples: I can’t compete with all this noise.

compile something from something.monolingual: to make up something from something; to collect and consolidate something from something. _ She compiled a book of poetry from verses written by her friends. _ Lynn compiled a picture book from family photographs going back almost a century.
examples: She compiled a book of poetry from verses written by her friends.

complain about someone or something.monolingual: to protest someone or something; to grouch about someone or something. _ Oh, stop complaining about the weather. _ You are always complaining about me.
examples: Oh, stop complaining about the weather.

complain of something.monolingual: to moan and suffer from a disease; to report the symptoms of a disease or health condition. _ Kenneth complained of a headache and general weakness. _ The patient was complaining of a headache.
examples: Kenneth complained of a headache and general weakness.

complain to someone.monolingual: to grouch or protest to someone. _ Don’t complain to me. _ I will complain to the manager.
examples: Don’t complain to me.

compliment someone on something.monolingual: to say something nice to someone about something connected to that person. _ I was pleased with Alice’s work and complimented her on it. _ They complimented me on my new tie.
examples: I was pleased with Alice’s work and complimented her on it.

comply with something.monolingual: to conform to something; to obey guidelines or regulations; to agree to something. _I hope you decide to comply with our rules. _ I am happy to comply with your request.
examples: I hope you decide to comply with our rules.

comport oneself with some manner.monolingual: to behave in a certain manner. _I hope you are able to comport yourself with better behavior next time. _The old man was able to comport himself with dignity.
examples: I hope you are able to comport yourself with better behavior next time.

composed of something.monolingual: assembled or made out of something. _ This cloth is composed of a number of different kinds of fibers. _The committee is composed of people from every department.
examples: This cloth is composed of a number of different kinds of fibers.

compound something with something.monolingual: to unite some substance with another; to mix something with something else. _Can this unpleasant medicine be compounded with something to make it palatable?

compress something into something.monolingual: 1. to squeeze or press something into something, such as a mold or container. _We compressed the tomatoes into the jar. _I cannot compress any more clothing into the suitcase.
examples: We compressed the tomatoes into the jar.

comprised of someone or something.monolingual: made up of someone or something. (The use of of after comprise is regarded as bad grammar by some.) _ The committee was comprised of representatives from all areas. _ The dessert was comprised of a number of different delicious substances.
examples: The committee was comprised of representatives from all areas.

compute something at something.monolingual: to calculate the total of something to be a certain figure. _ I compute the total at nearly three thousand dollars. _ The tax department computed the penalty at an enormous amount.
examples: I compute the total at nearly three thousand dollars.

con someone into something.monolingual: to deceive someone into doing something. _ The dishonest contractor conned her into buying a new furnace even when her old one was fine. _ You are just conning yourself into believing your plan will work.
examples: The dishonest contractor conned her into buying a new furnace even when her old one was fine.

con someone out of something.monolingual: to trick someone out of money or something of value. _Anne conned her little sister out of her allowance. _Dave conned me out of my autographed baseball.
examples: Anne conned her little sister out of her allowance.

concede to someone or something.monolingual: to yield to someone or a group; to give in to someone or a group. _In the end we conceded to the demands of the petition. _ I will not concede to you.
examples: In the end we conceded to the demands of the petition.

*conceited as a barber’s cat.monolingual: Rur. very conceited; vain. (*Also: as ~.) _ Ever since he won that award, he’s been as conceited as a barber’s cat.
examples: Ever since he won that award, he’s been as conceited as a barber’s cat.

conceive of someone or something.monolingual: to think of or invent the notion of someone or something. _ Who on earth ever conceived of doing this? _ Edison conceived of many very useful things that we now use every day.
examples: Edison conceived of many very useful things that we now use every day.

concentrate at some place.monolingual: to gather thickly at a place. _ The moths concentrated at the window at night, attracted by the light. _ All the thirsty children concentrated at the water fountain.
examples: The moths concentrated at the window at night, attracted by the light.

concern someone in something.monolingual: to bring someone into some matter; to engage someone in something; to occupy someone with something. _ Don’t concern Dave in our party planning. He doesn’t know anything about entertaining. _ The wrong committee was concerned in this from the very be
examples: Don’t concern Dave in our party planning.

condemn someone as something.monolingual: to blame or judge someone as being something bad. _The team condemned Larry as a traitor. _ Max was condemned as a common thief.
examples: The team condemned Larry as a traitor.

condemn someone for something.monolingual: to blame or judge someone for something or for having done something. _ I really can’t condemn her for doing it. I would have done the same too. _Don’t condemn yourself for the accident. It was no one’s fault.
examples: I really can’t condemn her for doing it.

condemn someone to something.monolingual: [for a judge] to sentence someone to something; to relegate someone to a particular punishment. _By confessing, he condemned himself to many years in prison. _ I don’t want to condemn you to a life of unpleasantness.
examples: By confessing, he condemned himself to many years in prison.

condescend to do something.monolingual: to agree to do something that is humbling or belittling. _ I will not condescend to respond to that remark. _ “Will you condescend to join us for dinner?” teased Bob.
examples: I will not condescend to respond to that remark.

condescend to someone.monolingual: to talk down to someone; to treat people as if they were below oneself; to patronize someone. _ Please do not condescend to me. _ There is no need to condescend to the children. They are just small, not stupid.
examples: Please do not condescend to me.

confederate with someone or something.monolingual: to organize, join, or unite with someone or a group. _ A number of states confederated with one another and formed a loose association. _ I confederated with the neighbors and we filed a joint complaint.
examples: A number of states confederated with one another and formed a loose association.

confess to something.monolingual: to admit having done something. _ He will not confess to the crime. _ In the end, Max confessed to it.
examples: He will not confess to the crime.

confide in someone.monolingual: to trust someone with one’s secrets or personal matters. _Sally always confided in her sister Ann. _ She didn’t feel that she could confide in her mother.
examples: Sally always confided in her sister Ann.

confirm someone in something.monolingual: to perform a religious rite that ties one more closely to one’s religion. _ They confirmed her in the church this morning.
examples: They confirmed her in the church this morning.

conflict with something.monolingual: to clash with something. (Does not refer to fighting.) _ This date conf licts with my doctor’s appointment. _ As far as I can tell, the date you suggest does not conf lict with anything.
examples: This date conf licts with my doctor’s appointment.

conform to something.monolingual: to agree with or behave within guidelines or regulations. _ I hope that your policies will conform to our guidelines. _Does my casual dress conform to your regulations?
examples: I hope that your policies will conform to our guidelines.

conform with something.monolingual: to match or agree with a model, plan, or set of specifications. (Compare this with conform to something.) _ Does this part conform with the specifications? _ This one conforms with them quite well.
examples: This one conforms with them quite well.

confront someone with something.monolingual: to face someone with incriminating evidence, charges of wrongdoing, or criticism. _ The angry husband confronted his wife with the evidence of her financial irresponsibility. _The police confronted Wilson with the witness’s statement.
examples: The angry husband confronted his wife with the evidence of her financial irresponsibility.

confuse someone about something.monolingual: to cause someone to be puzzled or bewildered about something. _ She confused me about the time of the concert. _ I wish you wouldn’t confuse me about those things.
examples: She confused me about the time of the concert.

conjure someone or something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to make someone or something appear, seemingly by the use of magic. _ The magician conjured seven white doves up. _ Then an old wizard conjured up a horse.
examples: The magician conjured seven white doves up.

consarn it!.monolingual: Rur. Damn it! (A mild oath.) _ Consarn it! I can’t find my keys. _That’s the second batch of muffins I’ve burned today, consarn it!
examples: Consarn it! I can’t find my keys.

conscript someone into something.monolingual: to call someone into military service; to draft someone. _ The war-torn country was even conscripting children into the army. _ Fred was conscripted into the army.
examples: The war-torn country was even conscripting children into the army.

consent to something.monolingual: to agree to permit something to happen. _ I will not consent to your marriage. _ There is no need for you to consent to anything.
examples: I will not consent to your marriage.

consider someone for something.monolingual: to think about offering someone a job, office, or other responsibility. _ Would you consider David for the job? _ I could not possibly consider you for the position.
examples: I could not possibly consider you for the position.

consist of someone or something.monolingual: to include people or things; to be made up of people or things. _ This bread consists of f lour, water, sugar, oil, and yeast. _ The U.S. Senate consists of two elected officials from each state.
examples: This bread consists of f lour, water, sugar, oil, and yeast.

console someone on something.monolingual: to comfort someone about something. _ I want to console you on your recent loss. _ They consoled Fred on the continuing difficulties he was having.
examples: I want to console you on your recent loss.

console someone with something.monolingual: to use something to comfort someone. _We consoled her with a sympathy card and f lowers. _ He sat down and consoled himself with a beer or two.
examples: We consoled her with a sympathy card and f lowers.

consort with someone.monolingual: 1. to associate with someone. _It is said that she consorts with thieves. _ No one worth anything would consort with Max.
examples: It is said that she consorts with thieves.

*conspicuous by one’s absence.monolingual: Cliché noticeably absent (from an event). (*Typically: be ~; made ~.) _ How could the bride’s father miss the wedding? He was certainly conspicuous by his absence.
examples: How could the bride’s father miss the wedding? He was certainly conspicuous by his absence.

constrain someone from doing something.monolingual: to prevent someone from doing something; to hold someone back from doing something. _ I hope this doesn’t constrain you from trying out for the play. _ His handicap did not constrain him from finishing the race.
examples: I hope this doesn’t constrain you from trying out for the play.

construe something as something.monolingual: to interpret something to mean something. _ Please do not construe this as criticism. _ We mistakenly construed her comments as positive.
examples: Please do not construe this as criticism.

*contact with someone.monolingual: a link to someone resulting in communication. (*Typically: be in ~; have ~; make ~.) _I have had no contact with Bill since he left town. _ Tom made contact with a known criminal last month.
examples: I have had no contact with Bill since he left town.

contend against someone or something.monolingual: to fight or compete against someone or something. _Do we have to contend against all this criticism? _ Ed refuses to have to contend against Eric.
examples: Ed refuses to have to contend against Eric.

contend with a problem.monolingual: to put up with a difficulty; to struggle with the problems caused by someone or something. _ I cannot contend with your temper anymore. _ I wish we did not have to contend with this changeable weather.
examples: I cannot contend with your temper anymore.

continue by doing something.monolingual: to keep going by starting to do something else or the next step. _ You are doing very well in this piano lesson. Please continue by playing the other sonata. _ After the interruption, Wally continued by explaining his position on the trade negotiatio
examples: You are doing very well in this piano lesson.

continue with something.monolingual: to keep doing whatever was being done before. _ Oh, please continue with your discussion. _ Do you mind if I continue with my knitting as we talk?
examples: Oh, please continue with your discussion.

contract something out†.monolingual: to make an agreement with someone to do a specific amount of work. (Rather than doing it oneself or in one’s own place of business.) _I will contract this out and have it done by consultants. _ I contracted out this kind of job the last time.
examples: I will contract this out and have it done by consultants.

a contradiction in terms.monolingual: a statement containing a seeming contradiction. _ A wealthy pauper is a contradiction in terms. _ A straight-talking politician may seem to be a contradiction in terms.
examples: A wealthy pauper is a contradiction in terms.

contrary to something.monolingual: in spite of something that seems to suggest otherwise; regardless of something else. _ Contrary to what you might think, I am neat and tidy. _ Contrary to public opinion, my uncle is well and healthy.
examples: Contrary to what you might think, I am neat and tidy.

contrast with someone or something.monolingual: 1. to be different from someone or something. _Bill’s cheery attitude really contrasts with the gloom of his twin brother, Bob. _This stiped tie really contrasts with that polka-dot shirt.
examples: Bill’s cheery attitude really contrasts with the gloom of his twin brother, Bob.

contribute to something.monolingual: 1. to donate something to some cause. _ Please contribute to the fund for the needy.
examples: Please contribute to the fund for the needy.

*control over someone or something.monolingual: the power to direct or manage someone or something. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ I have no control over Mary. I can’t stop her from running away. _Who gave you control over what goes on in this house?
examples: I have no control over Mary.

convalesce from something.monolingual: to recuperate from a disease, operation, or injury. _ I spent three weeks in bed convalescing from the f lu. _ Donna needed some time to convalesce from her surgery.
examples: I spent three weeks in bed convalescing from the f lu.

convict someone of something.monolingual: to pronounce someone guilty of something. _ In the end, they convicted her of theft. _ The police wanted to convict Max of the crime.
examples: In the end, they convicted her of theft.

convince someone of something.monolingual: to persuade someone that something is true. _ You will never convince me of what you say. _ I will probably convince myself of the need to find a better job.
examples: You will never convince me of what you say.

convulse someone with something.monolingual: to cause someone to quake or jerk because of pain or emotion. (Can be physical or figurative; see examples.) _ He convulsed with abdominal pain from something he ate. _The audience was convulsed with laughter.
examples: He convulsed with abdominal pain from something he ate.

cook someone’s goose.monolingual: Fig. to damage or ruin someone. _ I cooked my own goose by not showing up on time. _ Sally cooked Bob’s goose for treating her the way he did.
examples: I cooked my own goose by not showing up on time.

cook something to perfection.monolingual: to cook something perfectly. _ John cooked my steak to perfection. _ The entire dinner was cooked to perfection!
examples: John cooked my steak to perfection.

cook something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to prepare a batch of some kind of food by cooking. _ Fred cooked a batch of beans up for the ranch hands. _ He cooked up some food for dinner.
examples: Fred cooked a batch of beans up for the ranch hands.

cooked up.monolingual: contrived. (This is hyphenated before a nominal.) _ The whole thing seems so cooked up. _ What a cooked-up story! Of course, you don’t believe it.
examples: The whole thing seems so cooked up.

cooking with gas.monolingual: doing [something] exactly right. _ That’s great! Now you’re cooking with gas! _I knew she was finally cooking with gas when she answered all the questions correctly.
examples: I knew she was finally cooking with gas when she answered all the questions correctly.

*cool as a cucumber.monolingual: extremely calm; imperturbable. (*Also: as ~.) _ Joan felt nervous, but she acted as cool as a cucumber. _ The politician kept cool as a cucumber throughout the interview with the aggressive journalist.
examples: Joan felt nervous, but she acted as cool as a cucumber.

cool, calm, and collected.monolingual: Cliché [of a person] very calm and poised. _ James did very well in his TV appearances. He stayed cool, calm, and collected. _ The bad news didn’t seem to distress Jane at all. She remained cool, calm, and collected.
examples: James did very well in his TV appearances.

cool it!.monolingual: Inf. Calm down!; Take it easy! _ Don’t get mad, Bob. Cool it! _ Cool it, you guys! No fighting around here.
examples: Don’t get mad, Bob.

cool one’s heels.monolingual: Fig. to wait (for someone); to wait for something to happen. _ I spent an hour cooling my heels in the waiting room while the doctor saw other patients. _ All right, if you can’t behave properly, just sit down here and cool your heels until I call yo
examples: I spent an hour cooling my heels in the waiting room while the doctor saw other patients.

cool someone out†.monolingual: Sl. to calm someone; to appease someone. _ Cool yourselves out, you people. We gotta be sensible. _ The manager appeared and tried to cool out everybody, but that was a waste of time.
examples: Cool yourselves out, you people.

cooled out.monolingual: Sl. calm; unabashed. _ Ted is a really cooled out kind of guy. _ When she’s cooled out, she’s great.
examples: Ted is a really cooled out kind of guy.

cooler heads prevail.monolingual: Fig. the ideas or influence of less emotional people prevail. (Used of a tense situation.) _ One hopes that cooler heads will prevail and soon everything will calm down.
examples: One hopes that cooler heads will prevail and soon everything will calm down.

coop someone or something up†.monolingual: to confine someone or something in a small place. _ Don’t coop me up. I can’t stand small places. _We had to coop up the dogs for a while.
examples: Don’t coop me up.

co-opt someone into something.monolingual: to convince someone of a differing view to adopt one’s position or philosophy. _ They tried to co-opt the students into rioting. _There is no point in trying to co-opt them into it. They are too clever.
examples: They tried to co-opt the students into rioting.

coordinate something with something.monolingual: 1. to make something harmonize with something else. _I want to coordinate my hat with my shoes. _ Is this tie coordinated with my jacket?
examples: I want to coordinate my hat with my shoes.

cop a packet.monolingual: to become badly injured; to be wounded severely. (Originally military.) _My uncle copped a packet in Normandy. _ If you want to cop a packet or worse, just stand up in that shallow trench, son.
examples: My uncle copped a packet in Normandy.

cop a plea.monolingual: Fig. to plead guilty to a lesser charge to avoid a more serious charge or lessen time of imprisonment. _ He copped a plea and got off with only two months in the slammer.
examples: He copped a plea and got off with only two months in the slammer.

cop a squat.monolingual: Sl. to sit down. _ Hey, man! Come in and cop a squat here next to me. _Cop a squat and crack a tube.
examples: Hey, man! Come in and cop a squat here next to me.

cop an attitude.monolingual: Sl. to take a negative or opposite attitude about something. _ My teenage son copped an attitude when I asked why he seemed to be sneaking around.
examples: My teenage son copped an attitude when I asked why he seemed to be sneaking around.

cop onto something.monolingual: Sl. to understand or become aware of something. _ I think I’m copping onto the significance of this at last. _ Try to cop onto what I’m saying, Otto.
examples: I think I’m copping onto the significance of this at last.

cope with someone or something.monolingual: to endure someone or something; to manage to deal with someone or something. _ I don’t think I can cope with any more trouble. _ I can’t cope with your being late for work anymore.
examples: I don’t think I can cope with any more trouble.

copulate with someone.monolingual: [for someone] to have sexual intercourse with someone. _ He said he wanted to copulate with whom?

cordon something off†.monolingual: to mark off an area where people should not go with a rope, tape, ribbon, etc. _ The police cordoned the scene of the crime off, and we could not even get close. _ They cordoned off the area.
examples: The police cordoned the scene of the crime off, and we could not even get close.

cork high and bottle deep.monolingual: Rur. very drunk. _ By the time the party was over, he was cork high and bottle deep.
examples: By the time the party was over, he was cork high and bottle deep.

cork something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to close and seal a bottle with a cork. _ I think we should cork this up and save it for later. _ Cork up the bottle for later.
examples: I think we should cork this up and save it for later.

corral someone or something.monolingual: Fig. to herd someone or something into a corral or other enclosed space. _ It took the cowboys two hours to corral the mustangs. _ The nursery school teacher herded the kids off the playground and corraled them in the classroom.
examples: It took the cowboys two hours to corral the mustangs.

correlate something with something.monolingual: to match or equate something with something else. _ Can you correlate her comment with what she said yesterday? _ The scientist could not correlate the new data with his hypothesis.
examples: The scientist could not correlate the new data with his hypothesis.

correlate with something.monolingual: to match or equate with something. _ This does not correlate with your earlier story. _ What she said yesterday does not correlate with what she is saying today.
examples: This does not correlate with your earlier story.

correspond to something.monolingual: to match up with something; to harmonize with something. _This pin on this part corresponds to the receptacle on the other part it fits into.
examples: This pin on this part corresponds to the receptacle on the other part it fits into.

cost something out†.monolingual: to figure out the total cost of some set of costs or a complex purchase of goods or services. _ Give me a minute to cost this out, and I will have an estimate for you. _ Do you have time to cost out these specifications this week?
examples: Give me a minute to cost this out, and I will have an estimate for you.

cotton up to someone.monolingual: Rur. to try to make friends with someone; to flatter or fawn on someone in hopes of favorable treatment. _ James set out to cotton up to the parents of his friends. _ Just watch her cotton up to the teacher!
examples: James set out to cotton up to the parents of his friends.

a couch potato.monolingual: a lazy individual, addicted to televisionwatching. _All he ever does is watch TV; he’s become a real couch potato. _ Couch potatoes can tend to become very fat and unhealthy, you know.
examples: All he ever does is watch TV; he’s become a real couch potato.

couch something in something.monolingual: to express something in carefully chosen or deceptive words. _He tended to couch his explanations in arcane vocabulary. _She couched her words in an overly polite manner.
examples: He tended to couch his explanations in arcane vocabulary.

cough one’s head off.monolingual: Fig. to cough long and hard. _ I had the f lu. I nearly coughed my head off for two days.
examples: I had the f lu.

cough something out†.monolingual: to say something while coughing. _ He coughed the words out, but no one could understand him. _ He coughed out the name of his assailant.
examples: He coughed the words out, but no one could understand him.

cough something up†.monolingual: 1. to get something out of the body by coughing. _She coughed some matter up and took some more medicine. _ She coughed up phlegm all night.
examples: She coughed some matter up and took some more medicine.

could i be excused?.monolingual: Would you give me permission to leave?; Would you give me permission to leave the table? (Also used with can or may in place of could.) _ Bill: I’m finished, Mom. Could I be excused? Mother: Yes, of course, when you use good manners like that.
examples: Bill: I’m finished, Mom.

could i call you?.monolingual: 1. I am too busy to talk to you now. Do you mind if I telephone you later on? (Usually in a business context. Also used with can in place of could. May is too polite here.) _ Sally: I can’t talk to you right now. Could I call you? Tom: Sure, no probl
examples: Sally: I can’t talk to you right now.

could i come in?.monolingual: Do you mind if I enter? (A polite request. Also used with can or may in place of could.) _ Tom (standing in the doorway): Hello, I’m with the Internal Revenue Service. Could I come in? _ Bill: Hi, Tom. What are you doing here? Tom: Could I come in? I
examples: Tom (standing in the doorway): Hello, I’m with the Internal Revenue Service.

could i get by, please?.monolingual: Would you please allow me space to pass by? (Also used with can or may in place of could. May is almost too polite.) _ Poor Bill, trapped at the back of the elevator behind a huge man, kept saying, “Could I get by, please?” _ “Can I get by, please?”
examples: “Can I get by, please?” Jane said, squeezing between passengers on the crowded bus.

couldn’t be happier.monolingual: totally happy. _They both couldn’t be happier since they got married.
examples: They both couldn’t be happier since they got married.

councils of war never fight..monolingual: Prov. A group of people charged with crucial decisions often cannot act decisively. _ We tried to convince the boss not to form a committee, but to decide himself. We knew that councils of war never fight.
examples: We tried to convince the boss not to form a committee, but to decide himself.

counsel someone about something.monolingual: to give advice to someone about something. _ Will you counsel George about which tires to buy?

counsel someone against something.monolingual: to advise someone against doing something. _ The lawyer counseled her against suing the government. _ I was counseled against going for a walk alone at night.
examples: The lawyer counseled her against suing the government.

count against someone.monolingual: [for something] to be held against someone; [for something] to weigh against someone. _ I hope this mistake doesn’t count against me. _Don’t worry, it won’t count against you at all.
examples: I hope this mistake doesn’t count against me.

count down.monolingual: to count backwards to an event that will start when zero is reached. _ The project manager was counting down—getting ready for the launch of the rocket. _ I can still hear the captain counting down: “Five, four, three, two, one, zero, blast off!”
examples: The project manager was counting down—getting ready for the launch of the rocket.

count for something.monolingual: to be valid for something; to be worth something. _ Doesn’t all my work count for anything? _ Your positive attitude counts for a lot as far as I’m concerned.
examples: Your positive attitude counts for a lot as far as I’m concerned.

count off.monolingual: [for a series of people, one by one] to say aloud the next number in a fixed sequence. _ The soldiers counted off by threes. _The sergeant told them to count off.
examples: The soldiers counted off by threes.

count on someone or something.monolingual: to rely on someone or something; to depend on someone or something. _ We can count on Bill to get the job done. _ Can I count on this car to start every morning of the year?
examples: We can count on Bill to get the job done.

count someone among something.monolingual: to consider someone as a particular type of person or part of a particular group. _ I count her among my closest friends. _ Rachel counted herself among the luckiest people alive.
examples: I count her among my closest friends.

count someone or something off†.monolingual: to count people or things, to see if they are all there. _ Let’s count them off to see who’s missing. _ Count off each person, one by one. _ I counted each one off.
examples: Let’s count them off to see who’s missing.

count someone or something up†.monolingual: to count things or people to see how many there are. _ Let’s count them up and see how many we have. _I counted all the guests up, and there are too many to seat. _ Please count up all these books and tell me how many there are.
examples: Let’s count them up and see how many we have.

count something against someone.monolingual: to regard something in a negative way against someone. _ I’m afraid we must count this against you as an unexcused absence. _ Don’t count that last strike against the batter.
examples: I’m afraid we must count this against you as an unexcused absence.

count something as something.monolingual: to treat or think of something as being a certain thing. _ I count this as a win. _ Did you count that one as a fair ball?
examples: I count this as a win.

count something in†.monolingual: to include something in a count of something. _ Did you count the tall ones in? _ Did you count in the tall ones in the corner?

count something out†.monolingual: 1. to disregard something; to eliminate a possibility. _ We’ll have to count out the possibility of his being elected. _ Never count it out. It can always happen.
examples: We’ll have to count out the possibility of his being elected.

count up to something.monolingual: 1. to say or list the numbers from zero on up to a certain number. _ Can you count up to a million? _ I can count up to any number you name, and I will do it if you will stay around to listen.
examples: I can count up to any number you name, and I will do it if you will stay around to listen.

count with someone.monolingual: to be important to someone. _ Your cooperation really counts with me. _ All my efforts do not count with her.
examples: Your cooperation really counts with me.

counter with something.monolingual: to say something in refutation of something; to strike back with something. _ Aren’t you going to counter with an argument? _ He countered with a punch in the jaw.
examples: He countered with a punch in the jaw.

a country mile.monolingual: Rur. a great distance. _The batter knocked that ball a country mile. _ I had to walk a country mile to the next gas station.
examples: The batter knocked that ball a country mile.

a couple of.monolingual: two; two or three; a few; some; not many. _ Bill grabbed a couple of beers from the refrigerator. _I hung a couple of pictures on the wall.
examples: Bill grabbed a couple of beers from the refrigerator.

couple someone with someone.monolingual: to join one person with another to make a pair. _I coupled Todd with Amy for the dinner party.
examples: I coupled Todd with Amy for the dinner party.

couple something together.monolingual: to attach two parts of something together. _ Couple these two cars together and put them on track seven. _ You have to couple the ends of the two hoses together before you turn on the water.
examples: Couple these two cars together and put them on track seven.

couple something with something.monolingual: to join one thing with another to make a pair. _We coupled the budget issue with the staffing issue for our agenda.
examples: We coupled the budget issue with the staffing issue for our agenda.

couple with someone.monolingual: Euph. to have sexual intercourse with someone. _ They coupled with each other in a night of passion.
examples: They coupled with each other in a night of passion.

couple with something.monolingual: to connect or join to something. _ This railroad car will couple with the engine. _ These cars did not couple with the others properly, and there was almost an accident.
examples: This railroad car will couple with the engine.

course of action.monolingual: the procedures or sequence of actions that someone will follow to accomplish a goal. _ I plan to follow a course of action that will produce the best results. _ The board planned a course of action that would reduce costs and eliminate employees.
examples: I plan to follow a course of action that will produce the best results.

course through something.monolingual: to run, race, or flow rapidly through something. _ I believe, sometimes, that ice water courses through your veins. _No, perfectly red blood courses through them.
examples: I believe, sometimes, that ice water courses through your veins.

cover a lot of ground.monolingual: 1. Lit. to travel over a great distance; to investigate a wide expanse of land. _ The prospectors covered a lot of ground, looking for gold. _ My car can cover a lot of ground in one day.
examples: The prospectors covered a lot of ground, looking for gold.

cover for someone.monolingual: 1. to make excuses for someone; to conceal someone’s errors. _If I miss class, please cover for me. _ If you’re late, I’ll cover for you.
examples: If I miss class, please cover for me.

cover someone in something.monolingual: to place something over someone or something to serve as clothing or concealment. _ The designer had covered her in see-through fabric that was very revealing.
examples: The designer had covered her in see-through fabric that was very revealing.

cover someone or something up†.monolingual: to place something on someone or something for protection or concealment. _ Cover the pie up, so Terry won’t see it. _ Cover up Jimmy so he doesn’t get cold.
examples: Cover the pie up, so Terry won’t see it.

cover something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to place some sort of cover on something. _ Please cover up that mess with a cloth. _ Cover it up.
examples: Please cover up that mess with a cloth.

cover the territory.monolingual: 1. Lit. to travel or deal with a specific large area. _The sales manager was responsible for all of the eastern states and personally covered the territory twice each year.
examples: The sales manager was responsible for all of the eastern states and personally covered the territory twice each year.

cover the waterfront.monolingual: to deal with every detail concerning a specific topic. _ Her talk really covered the waterfront. By the time she finished, I knew much more than I wanted to know.
examples: Her talk really covered the waterfront.

cow paste.monolingual: Rur. butter. _ Would you kindly pass the cow paste?

cow someone into something.monolingual: to intimidate someone into doing something through the use of guilt or shame. _You can’t cow me into doing it. Those tricks don’t work on me. _ You can cow Wally into almost anything.
examples: You can’t cow me into doing it.

cower from something.monolingual: to draw back from the fear of something. _ The wolves cowered from the f lames. _ Some excited hyenas cowered from the lions as they passed by.
examples: The wolves cowered from the f lames.

crack a book.monolingual: Fig. to open a book to study. (Usually used with a negative.) _ I never cracked a book and still passed the course. _ Sally didn’t crack a book all semester.
examples: I never cracked a book and still passed the course.

crack a bottle open†.monolingual: Fig. to open a bottle of liquor. _ Let’s crack open a bottle and celebrate. _ He cracked a bottle open and poured a little for everyone to try.
examples: Let’s crack open a bottle and celebrate.

crack a joke.monolingual: to tell a joke. _ She’s never serious. She’s always cracking jokes. _ Every time Tom cracked a joke, his buddies broke up laughing.
examples: She’s never serious.

crack a smile.monolingual: to grin; to smile. _I was tellin’ my best jokes, but Jim never cracked a smile. _ She looked surprised, and then cracked a big, beautiful smile.
examples: I was tellin’ my best jokes, but Jim never cracked a smile.

crack open.monolingual: [for something brittle] to break or split open. _ The egg cracked open and a chick worked its way out. _ The side of the mountain cracked open and molten lava flowed out.
examples: The egg cracked open and a chick worked its way out.

crack some suds.monolingual: Sl. to drink some beer. _ Let’s go out tonight and crack some suds. _ The guys wanted to watch the game and crack some suds.
examples: Let’s go out tonight and crack some suds.

crack someone or something up†.monolingual: to damage someone or something. _ Who cracked my car up? _ Who cracked up my car? Who was driving? _ The accident cracked him up a little.
examples: The accident cracked him up a little.

crack someone up†.monolingual: to make someone laugh very hard; to make someone break out laughing. _ You and your jokes really crack me up. _ That comedian really knows how to crack up an audience.
examples: You and your jokes really crack me up.

crack something up†.monolingual: to crash something; to destroy something (in an accident). _ The driver cracked the car up in an accident. _ The pilot cracked up the plane.
examples: The driver cracked the car up in an accident.

crack under the strain.monolingual: Fig. to have a mental or emotional collapse because of continued work or stress. _He worked 80-hour weeks for a month and finally cracked under the strain.
examples: He worked 80-hour weeks for a month and finally cracked under the strain.

crack up.monolingual: 1. to have a wreck. _ The plane cracked up and killed two of the passengers. _Whose car cracked up on the expressway?
examples: The plane cracked up and killed two of the passengers.

cracked.monolingual: Fig. solved; understood. (*Typically: get something ~; have something ~.) _ I’ve got the mystery cracked! _ After I get it cracked, the rest’ll be easy.
examples: After I get it cracked, the rest’ll be easy.

cramp someone’s style.monolingual: Fig. to limit someone in some way. _I hope this doesn’t cramp your style, but could you please not hum while you work? _To ask Bob to keep regular hours would really be cramping his style.
examples: To ask Bob to keep regular hours would really be cramping his style.

crank someone up†.monolingual: Fig. to motivate; to get someone started. _ See if you can crank up your brother and get him going on time today. _ Some mornings, I can’t crank myself up enough to get to work on time.
examples: See if you can crank up your brother and get him going on time today.

crank something out†.monolingual: Fig. to produce something quickly or carelessly; to make something in a casual and mechanical way. _John can crank a lot of work out in a single day. _ The automated production line could really crank out parts, but the quality was shoddy.
examples: John can crank a lot of work out in a single day.

crank something up†.monolingual: 1. to get a machine or a process started. (Alludes to turning the starting crank of an early automobile.) _ Please crank the machinery so the workers can start working. _Let’s crank up the drill and make a few holes here in the wall.
examples: Please crank the machinery so the workers can start working.

crap out.monolingual: Sl. to die. _ Max almost crapped out from the beating he took. _The old dog just crapped out. What shall we do?
examples: Max almost crapped out from the beating he took.

crash and burn.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a plane or car] to crash and burst into flames. _ The small plane crashed and burned just after it took off.
examples: The small plane crashed and burned just after it took off.

crash around.monolingual: to move around in a noisy way _ Stop crashing around. I’m trying to study. _The people upstairs were crashing around and I couldn’t get any sleep.
examples: Stop crashing around.

a crash course in something.monolingual: a short and intense training course in something. _ I took a crash course in ballroom dancing so we wouldn’t look stupid on the dance f loor.
examples: I took a crash course in ballroom dancing so we wouldn’t look stupid on the dance f loor.

crash into someone or something.monolingual: to bump or ram into someone or something accidentally or roughly. _The student crashed into the door when it opened suddenly. _ The car crashed into a bus.
examples: The student crashed into the door when it opened suddenly.

crash something together.monolingual: to bring things together with great force, making a loud noise. _ Fred crashed the cymbals together and the sound could have wakened the dead. _ Don’t crash those pans together. It drives me crazy.
examples: Fred crashed the cymbals together and the sound could have wakened the dead.

crash through something.monolingual: to break through something forcefully. _ The cows crashed right through the fence.
examples: The cows crashed right through the fence.

crash to the floor.monolingual: to fall onto the floor and make a crashing sound. _ The tray of dishes crashed to the f loor. _ Everything crashed to the f loor and was broken.
examples: The tray of dishes crashed to the f loor.

crash together.monolingual: to ram or move together with great force. _ The two cars crashed together, making a loud noise. _ The ships crashed together, opening a gaping hole in the side of one of them.
examples: The two cars crashed together, making a loud noise.

crash with someone.monolingual: Sl. to spend the night at someone’s place. _ I don’t need a hotel room. I can crash with Tom. _ There is no room for you to crash with me.
examples: I don’t need a hotel room.

crave to do something.monolingual: Rur. to want to do something eagerly. _ I don’t crave to ride the roller coaster, thank you. _ The kids have been craving to see that movie for weeks.
examples: I don’t crave to ride the roller coaster, thank you.

crawl back to someone.monolingual: Fig. to go back to someone humbly, perhaps asking for forgiveness. _ I knew you would come crawling back to me! _ I wouldn’t crawl back to him for all the tea in China.
examples: I wouldn’t crawl back to him for all the tea in China.

crawl out.monolingual: to get out by crawling. _The bears finally woke up and crawled out. _ In the cave, I injured my leg and I had to crawl out.
examples: The bears finally woke up and crawled out.

crawl over something.monolingual: to cross over something by crawling. _We crawled over the pile of boxes. _Timmy crawled over the carpet and stood up at the coffee table.
examples: We crawled over the pile of boxes.

crawling with someone.monolingual: Fig. [of a surface] covered with many people or members of a class of people moving about. _The place was crawling with police and FBI agents. _ The city was crawling with tourists making it almost impossible to go from place to place.
examples: The place was crawling with police and FBI agents.

crazy in the head.monolingual: stupid or insane. _ Be quiet, Jed. You are just crazy in the head. _ Am I crazy in the head, or did I just see someone walking a leopard on a leash?
examples: Be quiet, Jed. You are just crazy in the head.

the cream of the crop.monolingual: Fig. the best of all. _ This particular car is the cream of the crop. _ These three students are very bright. They are the cream of the crop in their class.
examples: This particular car is the cream of the crop.

crease something up†.monolingual: to get creases or folds into something that is supposed to be flat; to wrinkle one’s clothing. (Very similar to messed up.) _ You will crease your jacket up if you don’t sit up straight. _I was sitting so long that I creased up my pants.
examples: You will crease your jacket up if you don’t sit up straight.

creature comforts.monolingual: things that make people comfortable. _The hotel room was a bit small, but all the creature comforts were there.
examples: The hotel room was a bit small, but all the creature comforts were there.

creep across something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to move across something slowly and carefully; to sneak across something. _ The soldiers crept slowly across the rope bridge. _ The cat crept across the f loor, stalking the mouse.
examples: The soldiers crept slowly across the rope bridge.

creep along something.monolingual: to move along something slowly and carefully; to sneak along something. _ Creep along the side of the building until you reach the door. _ The cat crept along the narrow kitchen counter.
examples: Creep along the side of the building until you reach the door.

creep away.monolingual: to travel away slowly and carefully; to sneak away. _The boys were completely ashamed and crept away. _ The cat crept away quietly.
examples: The boys were completely ashamed and crept away.

creep by.monolingual: Fig. [for time] to pass slowly. _The minutes crept by as I awaited Mrs. Barron’s telephone call. _ I know the days will creep by until we finally get our test results.
examples: The minutes crept by as I awaited Mrs.

creep over someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something, such as an insect] to walk or crawl over someone or something. _ A huge ant crept over me, and I just lay there.
examples: A huge ant crept over me, and I just lay there.

creep under something.monolingual: to move slowly and carefully underneath something; to sneak underneath something. _ The dog crept under the table to escape punishment. _ The chipmunk crept under a pile of leaves and disappeared.
examples: The dog crept under the table to escape punishment.

creep up.monolingual: [for darkness] to move gradually and slowly [toward someone or something]. _ Dusk crept up and swallowed us in darkness.
examples: Dusk crept up and swallowed us in darkness.

a crick in one’s back.monolingual: a twisted or cramped place in the back that causes pain. _I can’t move! I’ve got a crick in my back! _ I had a crick in my back all night and I couldn’t sleep.
examples: I had a crick in my back all night and I couldn’t sleep.

a crick in one’s neck.monolingual: Fig. a twisted place or a cramp in the neck that causes pain. _ I got a crick in my neck from sleeping in a draft. _When I read on the plane, I get a crick in my neck.
examples: I got a crick in my neck from sleeping in a draft.

crime doesn’t pay..monolingual: Prov. Crime will ultimately not benefit a person. _ No matter how tempting it may appear, crime doesn’t pay.
examples: No matter how tempting it may appear, crime doesn’t pay.

cringe before someone or something.monolingual: to cower or recoil in the presence of someone or something. _ Jeff cringed before the wrath of the policeman.
examples: Jeff cringed before the wrath of the policeman.

crinkle up.monolingual: to wrinkle up. _Her nose crinkled up when she laughed.
examples: Her nose crinkled up when she laughed.

criticize someone for something.monolingual: to reprimand or censure someone for something. _I hope you don’t criticize me too severely for my part in this matter. _ Maria criticized Ken for not being there on time.
examples: I hope you don’t criticize me too severely for my part in this matter.

crock someone or something up†.monolingual: Sl. to damage or harm someone or something. _ The accident crocked me up a bit. _ I really crocked up my car last night.
examples: The accident crocked me up a bit.

crop out.monolingual: to appear on the surface; [for something] to reveal itself in the open; to begin to show above the surface. _A layer of rock cropped out at the edges of the desert.
examples: A layer of rock cropped out at the edges of the desert.

crop someone or something out†.monolingual: [for a photographer] to cut or trim out someone or something from a photograph. _ The photographer cropped Mr. Jones out of the picture. _ See if you can crop out the ugly fence at the side of the house.
examples: The photographer cropped Mr.

crop up.monolingual: to appear without warning; to happen suddenly; [for something] to begin to reveal itself in the open. _ Some new problems cropped up at the last minute.
examples: Some new problems cropped up at the last minute.

cross over.monolingual: 1. to cross something such as a river or a street. _This is a very wide river. Where do we cross over? _Let’s cross over here where it’s shallow.
examples: This is a very wide river.

cross over into some place.monolingual: to go from one place into another, by crossing a border, river, mountain range, etc. _The refugees crossed over into Switzerland. _We crossed over into Missouri at dawn.
examples: The refugees crossed over into Switzerland.

cross over something.monolingual: to go some place by crossing a border, river, mountain range, etc. _Do we want to cross over the river at this point? _How do we cross over the highway?

cross someone.monolingual: to oppose someone. _You best not cross Jim. He has a very bad temper. _ This is the last time you cross me, you hear?
examples: You best not cross Jim.

cross someone or something out†.monolingual: to draw a line through the name of someone or something on a list or record. _You can cross me out. I’m not going. _ Please cross out Sarah’s name. _ I crossed the sweater out. It was an error.
examples: You can cross me out.

cross someone’s palm with silver.monolingual: Fig. to pay money to someone in payment for a service. (A fortune-teller might ask for a potential customer to cross her palm with silver. Used in that sense or jocularly for something like tipping a porter.) _I crossed his palm with silver, but he s
examples: I crossed his palm with silver, but he still stood there.

cross someone up†.monolingual: to give someone trouble; to defy or betray someone; to spoil someone’s plans. (Also without up.) _ You really crossed up Bill when you told Tom what he said. _ Please don’t cross me up again.
examples: You really crossed up Bill when you told Tom what he said.

cross something with something.monolingual: 1. to go across something, using a particular type of vehicle. _ The explorers crossed the river with their Jeep. _ We can’t cross this stream with the canoes. It’s too fast.
examples: The explorers crossed the river with their Jeep.

cross the rubicon.monolingual: Fig. to do something that inevitably commits one to following a certain course of action. (Alludes to the crossing of the River Rubicon by Julius Caesar with his army, which involved him in a civil war in B.C. 49.) _ Jane crossed the Rubicon by signi
examples: Jane crossed the Rubicon by signing the contract.

cross-examine someone.monolingual: to question someone in court who has already been questioned by the opposing side; to question a suspect or a witness at great length. _ The lawyer plans to cross-examine the witness tomorrow morning. _The police cross-examined the suspect for three
examples: The lawyer plans to cross-examine the witness tomorrow morning.

crouch around.monolingual: [for people or other creatures] to stoop or squat within an area. _Everyone crouched around, hoping the bomb would fall somewhere else. _ The baboons crouched around, grooming one another.
examples: Everyone crouched around, hoping the bomb would fall somewhere else.

crouch down.monolingual: to stoop or huddle down. _ Crouch down here, next to me. _ Suddenly, Tex crouched down and reached for his pistol.
examples: Crouch down here, next to me.

crow bait.monolingual: Rur. someone or an animal that is likely to die; a useless animal or person. _ That old dog used to hunt good, but now he’s just crow bait.
examples: That old dog used to hunt good, but now he’s just crow bait.

crowd around someone or something.monolingual: to flock or swarm around someone or something. _ The children crowded around the department store Santa, eager for their chance at talking to him. _ Everyone crowded around the radio to listen.
examples: The children crowded around the department store Santa, eager for their chance at talking to him.

crowd someone or something together.monolingual: to push or squeeze people or things together. _ See if you can crowd them together and get more in the row. _ I am afraid that I crowded the plants together too much.
examples: See if you can crowd them together and get more in the row.

crowd together.monolingual: to pack tightly together. _ The tenants crowded together in the lobby. _ All the kittens crowded together to keep warm.
examples: The tenants crowded together in the lobby.

crown someone with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to place a crown on someone’s head. _ They crowned the prince with the heavily jeweled royal crown.
examples: They crowned the prince with the heavily jeweled royal crown.

crown something with something.monolingual: Fig. to place something on the very top of something. (As if crowning royalty.) _ The chef crowned the cake with golden icing.
examples: The chef crowned the cake with golden icing.

cruise around in something.monolingual: to drive or ride around in something. _Would you like to cruise around in a car like that? _They really liked cruising around in the motorboat.
examples: They really liked cruising around in the motorboat.

crumble away.monolingual: to break away in little pieces. _ The marble pillar was crumbling away because of the acidic rain. _ One of my teeth is just crumbling away.
examples: The marble pillar was crumbling away because of the acidic rain.

crumble into something.monolingual: to break apart and fall down into bits and pieces. _ The base of the pillar suddenly crumbled into dust. _ The bones crumbled into dust as the body was lifted from the box.
examples: The base of the pillar suddenly crumbled into dust.

crumble up.monolingual: to break up into little pieces. _ The cake, which was very dry, crumbled up when I tried to cut it. _ The paper of the old book crumbled up when I turned the pages.
examples: The cake, which was very dry, crumbled up when I tried to cut it.

crumped out.monolingual: Sl. intoxicated. _ She was too crumped out to drive herself home. _ Are you crumped out again?
examples: She was too crumped out to drive herself home.

crumple something up†.monolingual: to fold up or crush someone or something. _Walter crumpled the paper up. _ He crumpled up the paper.
examples: Walter crumpled the paper up.

crumple up.monolingual: to fold up; to collapse. _ She was so frightened that she just crumpled up. _ Fran crumpled up in a dead faint.
examples: She was so frightened that she just crumpled up.

crunch someone or something up†.monolingual: to break someone or something up into pieces. _That machine will crunch you up. Stay away from it! _A number of blows with the hammer crunched up the rocks into pebbles. _Try to crunch the larger chunks up.
examples: That machine will crunch you up.

crunch something down†.monolingual: to press or crush something down, breaking it with a crunching noise. _ Sally crunched the flower pot down, breaking it. _She crunched down the fragile glass in the box accidentally.
examples: Sally crunched the flower pot down, breaking it.

crusade against someone or something.monolingual: to campaign or demonstrate against someone or something. _ You are always crusading against one cause or another. _Ed started crusading against Eric and the latter threatened suit.
examples: You are always crusading against one cause or another.

crusade for someone or something.monolingual: to campaign or demonstrate for someone or something. _ I can hardly crusade for the defeat of a friend. _ Ed went on a crusade for Eric, hoping to get him elected.
examples: I can hardly crusade for the defeat of a friend.

*a crush on someone.monolingual: infatuation with someone. (*Typically: get ~; have ~.) _ Mary thinks she’s getting a crush on Bill. _Sally says she’ll never have a crush on anyone again.
examples: Mary thinks she’s getting a crush on Bill.

crush someone or something down†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to press or force someone or something down. _ Crush the leaves down so you can put more into the basket. _ Crush down the leaves and fill the basket higher.
examples: Crush the leaves down so you can put more into the basket.

crush something in†.monolingual: to force something inward; to break something in. _ The beam nearly crushed Jason’s head in. _ He tried to crush in the door.
examples: The beam nearly crushed Jason’s head in.

crush something up†.monolingual: to reduce the mass of something by crushing. _Crush this up and put it in the sauce. _Crush up a clove of garlic and put it in the sauce.
examples: Crush this up and put it in the sauce.

crushed by something.monolingual: Fig. demoralized; having hurt feelings. _ The whole family was completely crushed by the news. _ I was just crushed by your attitude. I thought we were friends.
examples: The whole family was completely crushed by the news.

cry before one is hurt.monolingual: Fig. to cry or complain needlessly, before one is injured. _ Bill always cries before he’s hurt. _ There is no point in crying before one is hurt.
examples: Bill always cries before he’s hurt.

cry bloody murder.monolingual: Fig. to scream as if something very serious has happened, especially unnecessarily. _ Now that Bill is really hurt, he’s crying bloody murder. _ There is no point in crying bloody murder about the bill if you knew the restaurant was expensive.
examples: Now that Bill is really hurt, he’s crying bloody murder.

cry for someone or something.monolingual: 1. to weep for the absence or loss of someone or something. _ No need to cry for me. Take care of yourself. _She cried for her lost cat.
examples: No need to cry for me.

cry in one’s beer.monolingual: Fig. to feel sorry for oneself. _ She calls up, crying in her beer, and talks on and on about her problems. _ Don’t cry in your beer. Get yourself straightened out.
examples: She calls up, crying in her beer, and talks on and on about her problems.

cry one’s eyes out.monolingual: Fig. to cry very hard. _When we heard the news, we cried our eyes out with joy. _She cried her eyes out after his death.
examples: When we heard the news, we cried our eyes out with joy.

cry oneself to sleep.monolingual: to weep until sleep overtakes one. _ The baby finally cried herself to sleep.
examples: The baby finally cried herself to sleep.

cry over someone or something.monolingual: to weep because of someone or something. _ There’s no need to cry over it. Things will work out. _ She is still crying over her lost love.
examples: There’s no need to cry over it.

cry over spilled milk.monolingual: Fig. to be unhappy about what cannot be undone. _ He is always crying over spilled milk. He cannot accept reality. _ It can’t be helped. Don’t cry over spilled milk.
examples: He is always crying over spilled milk.

cry wolf.monolingual: Fig. to cry or complain about something when nothing is really wrong. (From the story wherein a child sounds the alarm frequently about a wolf when there is no wolf, only to be ignored when there actually is a wolf.) _ Pay no attention. She’s just cr
examples: Pay no attention.

a crying shame.monolingual: Fig. a very unfortunate situation; a real shame. _It’s a crying shame that people cannot afford adequate housing. _ That your father could not attend graduation was a crying shame.
examples: It’s a crying shame that people cannot afford adequate housing.

cue someone in†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to give someone a cue; to indicate to someone that the time has come. _Now, cue the orchestra director in. _ All right, cue in the announcer.
examples: Now, cue the orchestra director in.

culminate in something.monolingual: to climax in something; to end with something. _ The contest culminated in a victory for the best band. _ The play-offs culminated in a big win for the Chicago team.
examples: The contest culminated in a victory for the best band.

culturally advantaged.monolingual: Euph. rich; upper-class. _I can’t deny I had a culturally advantaged upbringing. _The charity appealed to culturally advantaged people to donate time and money to those less fortunate.
examples: I can’t deny I had a culturally advantaged upbringing.

culture vulture.monolingual: someone whom one considers to be excessively interested in the (classical) arts. _ She won’t go to a funny film. She’s a real culture vulture. _They watch only highbrow television. They’re culture vultures.
examples: She won’t go to a funny film.

cup one’s hands together.monolingual: to put one’s hands together to form a sort of cup. _ He cupped his hands together and scooped up the water. _You have to cup your hands together if you want a drink.
examples: He cupped his hands together and scooped up the water.

curdle someone’s blood.monolingual: Fig. to frighten or disgust someone severely. _ The story was scary enough to curdle your blood. _ The terrible scream was enough to curdle my blood.
examples: The story was scary enough to curdle your blood.

cure someone of something.monolingual: to rid someone of a disease, ailment, bad habit, or obsession. _I hope that the doctor prescribes something to cure him of that chronic cough. _Will you please try to cure yourself of your constant interrupting?
examples: I hope that the doctor prescribes something to cure him of that chronic cough.

cure something of something.monolingual: to eliminate the cause of a malfunction in a machine or a device. _I think I have cured the stapler of jamming all the time. _ I can’t seem to cure the committee of procrastination.
examples: I think I have cured the stapler of jamming all the time.

curiosity killed the cat..monolingual: Prov. Being curious can get you into trouble. (Often used to warn someone against prying into other’s affairs.) _ Jill: Where did you get all that money? Jane: Curiosity killed the cat.
examples: Jill: Where did you get all that money? Jane: Curiosity killed the cat.

curl something up†.monolingual: to roll something up into a coil. _ She curled the edges of the paper up while she spoke. _ Why did she curl up the paper?
examples: She curled the edges of the paper up while she spoke.

curl up and die.monolingual: Fig. to die. (Often jocular.) _ When I heard you say that, I could have curled up and died. _ No, it wasn’t an illness. She just curled up and died.
examples: When I heard you say that, I could have curled up and died.

curry favor with someone.monolingual: to try to win favor from someone. _ The lawyer tried to curry favor with the judge. _ It’s silly to curry favor with the boss. Just act yourself.
examples: The lawyer tried to curry favor with the judge.

curse at someone or something.monolingual: to swear at someone or something; to use foul language at someone or something. _He cursed at the jammed toaster and pounded his fist on the counter in anger. _ Please don’t curse at me.
examples: He cursed at the jammed toaster and pounded his fist on the counter in anger.

curse someone for something.monolingual: to damn someone for doing something; to invoke evil upon someone for doing something. _ She cursed her mother for ever having borne her. _ Over and over, she cursed herself for ever having come there.
examples: She cursed her mother for ever having borne her.

curtain something off†.monolingual: to separate something or some place with a drape, screen, or curtain. _We curtained this part of the room off, so please sleep over there. _ We will curtain off part of the room.
examples: We curtained this part of the room off, so please sleep over there.

curtains for someone or something.monolingual: the death, end, or ruin of someone or something. (From the lowering or closing of the curtains at the end of a stage performance.) _ If the car hadn’t swerved, it would have been curtains for the pedestrians. _ If they can’t get into the export marke
examples: If the car hadn’t swerved, it would have been curtains for the pedestrians.

curtsy to someone.monolingual: [for a woman] to dip or bow in deference to someone. _ Of course, I curtsied to the queen! Do you think I’m an anarchist? _ The little girls curtsied after they did their dance number.
examples: The little girls curtsied after they did their dance number.

curve to something.monolingual: to bend or bow toward something, some direction, or some place. _ The road curved to the left. _ One of her toes curves to the right.
examples: The road curved to the left.

cuss a blue streak.monolingual: Rur. to curse a great deal. _ When she dropped the brick on her toe, she cussed a blue streak. _Bill could cuss a blue streak by the time he was eight years old.
examples: When she dropped the brick on her toe, she cussed a blue streak.

cuss someone out†.monolingual: to curse at someone. _ Dad cussed me out for losing the money he gave me. _The little kid cussed out his brother, shocking his grandmother.
examples: Dad cussed me out for losing the money he gave me.

the customer is always right..monolingual: Prov. In order to keep customers happy, the people who serve them should always obey their wishes. (Often cited as a principle of good business dealings; customers sometimes say it to the people serving them in order to try to get good service.) _ Wh
examples: When I began working at the gift shop, my boss told me, “Remember, the customer is always right, no matter how stupid or rude you may think he is being.

cut a deal.monolingual: to arrange a deal; to negotiate an agreement. _ Maybe we can cut a deal. Let’s talk. _ The two lawyers cut a deal that left me with my car, although she got the house.
examples: Maybe we can cut a deal.

cut a fine figure.monolingual: to look good; to look elegant. (Usually said of a male.) _Tom really cuts a fine figure on the dance f loor. _ Bill cuts a fine figure since he bought some new clothes.
examples: Tom really cuts a fine figure on the dance f loor.

a cut above average.monolingual: better than average. _John isn’t the best mechanic in town, but he’s a cut above average.
examples: John isn’t the best mechanic in town, but he’s a cut above average.

a cut above something.monolingual: a measure or degree better than something else. _ Your shirt is beautiful, but mine is a cut above yours.
examples: Your shirt is beautiful, but mine is a cut above yours.

cut along something.monolingual: to make a cut following a line or guide. _ Please cut along the dotted line. _My hand is too shaky to cut along the line neatly.
examples: Please cut along the dotted line.

cut and dried.monolingual: fixed; determined beforehand; usual and uninteresting. (Can be hyphenated before nominals.) _ I find your writing quite boring. It’s too cut and dried. _ The lecture was, as usual, cut and dried.
examples: I find your writing quite boring.

cut and paste.monolingual: 1. Lit. to cut something out of paper with scissors and paste it onto something else. _ The teacher told the little children that it was time to cut and paste, and they all ran to the worktables. _ Mary made a tiny house by cutting and pasting little
examples: The teacher told the little children that it was time to cut and paste, and they all ran to the worktables.

cut and run.monolingual: Sl. to run away quickly. (Alludes to cutting loose a ship’s or boat’s anchor and sailing away in a hurry.) _ Wilbur decided to cut and run when he heard the police sirens. _As soon as I finish what I am doing here, I’m going to cut and run. I’ve got
examples: Wilbur decided to cut and run when he heard the police sirens.

cut around something.monolingual: to move rapidly around something, such as a corner, pole, beam, etc. _ The cat cut around a corner and escaped from the dog. _ The speeding car cut around the light pole and almost hit it.
