examples: The cat cut around a corner and escaped from the dog.

cut back.monolingual: to turn back; to reverse direction. _ Suddenly, the bull cut back in our direction and began chasing us. _ The road cuts back about a mile ahead, and it goes west again.
examples: Suddenly, the bull cut back in our direction and began chasing us.

cut both ways.monolingual: to affect both sides of an issue equally. _ Remember that your suggestion that costs should be shared cuts both ways. Your division will have to reduce its budget as well. _ If our side cannot take along supporters to the game, then yours cannot eith
examples: Remember that your suggestion that costs should be shared cuts both ways.

cut corners.monolingual: Fig. to take shortcuts; to save money or effort by finding cheaper or easier ways to do something. _ They’re always finding ways to cut corners. _ I won’t cut corners just to save money. I put quality first.
examples: They’re always finding ways to cut corners.

cut it out!.monolingual: Inf. Stop doing that!; Stop saying that! (Fixed order.) _Sue: Why, I think you have a crush on Mary! Tom: Cut it out! _ “Cut it out!” yelled Tommy as Billy hit him again.
examples: “Cut it out!” yelled Tommy as Billy hit him again.

cut off.monolingual: 1. to stop by itself or oneself. _ The machine got hot and cut off. _Bob cut off in midsentence.
examples: The machine got hot and cut off.

cut one’s eyeteeth on something.monolingual: Fig. to grow up experiencing something; to have had the experience of dealing with something [successfully] at a very early age. _ My grandfather taught me how to fish, so I cut my eyeteeth on fishing. _ Fred cut his eyeteeth on writing; both his par
examples: My grandfather taught me how to fish, so I cut my eyeteeth on fishing.

cut one’s losses.monolingual: to do something to stop a loss of something. _ I knew I had to do something to cut my losses, but it was almost too late. _ Sell some of the high-priced stuff to cut your losses.
examples: I knew I had to do something to cut my losses, but it was almost too late.

cut one’s wolf loose.monolingual: Sl. to go on a drinking bout; to get drunk. _ I’m gonna go out and cut my wolf loose tonight. _You’re going to cut your wolf loose too often and really get into trouble.
examples: I’m gonna go out and cut my wolf loose tonight.

cut oneself on something.monolingual: to slice one’s flesh with something accidentally. _ Careful, you will cut yourself on that knife. _ Careful! Don’t cut yourself on that broken glass.
examples: Careful, you will cut yourself on that knife.

cut out.monolingual: to depart; to leave in a hurry. _ Good-bye. I have to cut out now. _It’s time I was cutting out. I’m late already.
examples: Good-bye. I have to cut out now.

cut out for something.monolingual: suited for something. _ She was bright and she loved to read. Her folks thought she was cut out for being a schoolteacher. _ He did his best, but he just wasn’t cut out for farming.
examples: She was bright and she loved to read.

cut out to be something.monolingual: destined to be something or a particular type of person. _ I don’t think I was cut out to do this. _ We weren’t cut out to be laborers.
examples: I don’t think I was cut out to do this.

cut someone dead.monolingual: to ignore someone totally. _ Joan was just about to speak to James when he walked away and cut her dead. _ Jean cut her former husband dead.
examples: Joan was just about to speak to James when he walked away and cut her dead.

cut someone down†.monolingual: to kill someone with a weapon, such as a sword, or with gunfire, etc. _ The bandits cut the bystanders down and f led. _ The gunman cut down an innocent pedestrian.
examples: The bandits cut the bystanders down and f led.

cut someone or something out†.monolingual: to eliminate someone or something. _They cut out the free coffee with lunch at the cafeteria. _We have to cut Chuck out. There are too many better men on the team.
examples: They cut out the free coffee with lunch at the cafeteria.

cut someone or something up†.monolingual: Fig. to criticize someone or something severely. _ Jane is such a gossip. She was really cutting Mrs. Jones up. _ The professor really cut up my essay.
examples: Jane is such a gossip.

cut someone’s water off†.monolingual: Fig. to squelch someone; to thwart someone. (Fixed order.) _ Well, I guess that cuts your water off! _ That sure cuts off my water!

cut someone to ribbons.monolingual: 1. Lit. to cut or slice someone severely. _ He broke a mirror and the glass cut his hand to ribbons.
examples: He broke a mirror and the glass cut his hand to ribbons.

cut someone up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to gash or carve on someone by cutting. _The thugs cut him up badly, just for talking back. _ They cut up their victim into pieces.
examples: The thugs cut him up badly, just for talking back.

cut someone up.monolingual: Fig. to make someone laugh. _That comedian’s routine really cut me up. _ Tommy’s rude noises cut the whole class up, but not the teacher.
examples: That comedian’s routine really cut me up.

cut something back†.monolingual: to prune plants; to reduce the size of plants, bushes, etc. _ Let’s cut these bushes back. They’re getting in the way. _ Don’t cut back my roses!
examples: Let’s cut these bushes back.

cut something down†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to chop something down; to saw or cut at something until it is felled. _Stop cutting the banners down! _ Don’t cut down that tree!
examples: Don’t cut down that tree! 2.

cut something down† to something.monolingual: to reduce something to a manageable size. _ We cut the program down to size and it was very enjoyable. _ We cut down the program to a half hour.
examples: We cut the program down to size and it was very enjoyable.

cut something from something.monolingual: to remove something from something by cutting. _She carefully cut the blossoms from the bush. _ A few blossoms were cut from the bush.
examples: She carefully cut the blossoms from the bush.

cut something off†.monolingual: 1. to shorten something. _ Cut this board off a bit, would you? _ Cut off this board a little, please.
examples: Cut off this board a little, please.

cut something on something.monolingual: 1. to slice something on or against something, accidentally. _ I cut my finger on the knife. _ Maria cut her foot on the broken glass.
examples: I cut my finger on the knife.

cut something to the bone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to slice deep to a bone. _The knife cut John to the bone. He had to be sewed up. _ Cut each slice of ham to the bone. Then each slice will be as big as possible.
examples: The knife cut John to the bone.

cut something with something.monolingual: to dilute something with something else. _ They cut the liquor with cold water. _ Please cut this with some soda. It’s too sweet, otherwise.
examples: They cut the liquor with cold water.

cut teeth.monolingual: [for a baby or young person] to have new teeth emerging through the gums. _Billy is cranky because he’s cutting teeth. _ Ann cut her first tooth this week.
examples: Billy is cranky because he’s cutting teeth.

cut the deadwood out.monolingual: 1. Lit. to prune away and remove the dead branches from a tree or bush. _They cut a lot of the deadwood out to save the tree. _ You have to cut out the deadwood to make room for new growth.
examples: They cut a lot of the deadwood out to save the tree.

cut the dust.monolingual: Fig. to take a drink of liquor. _ I think I’ll stop in here and cut the dust. _ I want to cut the dust. Can I have a snort?
examples: I think I’ll stop in here and cut the dust.

cut the pie up†.monolingual: Fig. to divide something up. (Can refer to an actual pie or anything that can be divided into varying portions.) _ It all depends on how you cut the pie up. _ How should I cut up the pie?
examples: It all depends on how you cut the pie up.

cut through red tape.monolingual: Fig. to eliminate or neutralize something complicated, such as bureaucratic rules and procedures. _ I will try to cut through all the red tape for you so you get your visa on time. _ I am sure someone can help us cut through all this red tape.
examples: I will try to cut through all the red tape for you so you get your visa on time.

cut through something.monolingual: to penetrate something by cutting; to slice through something. _ The worker cut through the steel door with a torch. _ Walter cut through the rind of the watermelon.
examples: The worker cut through the steel door with a torch.

cut to someone or something.monolingual: to shift the radio, movie, or television audience’s attention abruptly to someone or something new. _ Suddenly, the engineer cut to the announcer. _ The technical director cut to a remote unit that was covering an accident. _ The camera cut to scenes
examples: Suddenly, the engineer cut to the announcer.

cut to the chase.monolingual: Sl. to focus on what is important; to abandon the preliminaries and deal with the major points. _ All right, let’s stop the idle chatter and cut to the chase. _ After a few introductory comments, we cut to the chase and began negotiating.
examples: All right, let’s stop the idle chatter and cut to the chase.

cut up.monolingual: to act wildly; to show off and be troublesome; to act like a clown. _ Tom, Billy! Stop cutting up, or I’ll send you to the principal’s office. _ If you spent more time studying than cutting up, you’d get better grades.
examples: Tom, Billy! Stop cutting up, or I’ll send you to the principal’s office.

cut your peaches.monolingual: Rur. go on with what you were doing. _ Stop gawking and cut your peaches. _ There’s no need for you to follow me around. Go cut your peaches.
examples: Stop gawking and cut your peaches.

*cute as a bug’s ear.monolingual: very cute. (*Also: as ~.) _ That little baby is cute as a bug’s ear.
examples: That little baby is cute as a bug’s ear.

the cutting edge.monolingual: Fig. the most forward part of a trend; the leading part of a trend. (Alludes to the edge of a sword. See also on the cutting edge. See also on the bleeding edge.) _ Fred’s invention put him on the cutting edge of the computer chip business.
examples: Fred’s invention put him on the cutting edge of the computer chip business.

dab at something.monolingual: to touch or pat something. _The painter dabbed at the canvas, making little changes here and there. _ Don’t just dab at the wall, spread the paint on!
examples: The painter dabbed at the canvas, making little changes here and there.

dabble at something.monolingual: to play at doing something; to do something halfheartedly. _ Don’t just dabble at your history paper. Settle down and do it right. _ She dabbles at painting.
examples: Don’t just dabble at your history paper.

dabble in something.monolingual: to be involved in something in a casual manner. _ She dabbled in local politics for a while. _ I want to dabble in something new for a while.
examples: She dabbled in local politics for a while.

dad fetch my buttons!.monolingual: Rur. What a surprise!; Goodness me! _ Dad fetch my buttons! It’s a letter from Aunt Rita! _ Dad fetch my buttons, I never was so happy in all my life!

daily dozen.monolingual: Fig. physical exercises done every day. _ My brother always feels better after his daily dozen. _ She would rather do a daily dozen than go on a diet.
examples: My brother always feels better after his daily dozen.

the daily grind.monolingual: [someone’s] everyday work routine. _I’m getting very tired of the daily grind. _ When my vacation was over, I had to go back to the daily grind.
examples: I’m getting very tired of the daily grind.

dally over something.monolingual: to waste time or take too long doing something. _ Don’t dally over your food. Eat your dinner. _ I wish you wouldn’t dally over your homework.
examples: Don’t dally over your food.

dally with someone.monolingual: to flirt with someone; to waste time with someone of the opposite sex. (Old.) _ Sam is dallying with that Johnson girl again. _ Stop dallying with her and get back to your studies!
examples: Sam is dallying with that Johnson girl again.

dam something up†.monolingual: to erect a barrier in a river, stream, brook, etc. _ We are going to have to dam this stream up to make a pond for the cattle. _ Let’s dam up this stream. _ Why is this river dammed up?
examples: We are going to have to dam this stream up to make a pond for the cattle.

damn it to blue blazes!.monolingual: Rur. Damn it. (An oath.) _ Damn it to blue blazes, I told you I can’t lend you any more money! _ “Damn it to blue blazes! I give up!” Joe shouted, f linging his tools aside.
examples: “Damn it to blue blazes! I give up!” Joe shouted, f linging his tools aside.

damn someone with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to curse someone with words. _ She damned him with curse after curse. _ Maria damned Joe with the worst curses she could think of.
examples: She damned him with curse after curse.

damp off.monolingual: [for seedlings] to die from too much water. _ All the new plants damped off, and we had to buy some from the nursery. _ The little seedlings damped off and withered away.
examples: All the new plants damped off, and we had to buy some from the nursery.

damp something down†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to make something damp. _ Damp the clothes down before you iron them. _ Please damp down the clothes first.
examples: Damp the clothes down before you iron them.

dance at someone’s wedding.monolingual: to celebrate in honor of someone at someone’s wedding. _ I will dance at your wedding—if you invite me, of course. _ If you think I will dance at your wedding, you had better be nicer to me!
examples: I will dance at your wedding—if you invite me, of course.

dance on air.monolingual: Fig. to be very happy; to be euphoric enough as if to dance on air. _I was so happy, I could have danced on air. _ She was just dancing on air, she was so happy.
examples: I was so happy, I could have danced on air.

dance to something.monolingual: to respond to music or rhythm with dancing. _ I can’t dance to that fast beat! _ That music is horrible. No one can dance to that.
examples: That music is horrible.

dance with death.monolingual: Fig. to attempt to do something that is very risky. _ The crossing of the border into enemy territory was like dancing with death. _You are dancing with death in your effort to cross that narrow ledge.
examples: The crossing of the border into enemy territory was like dancing with death.

dance with someone.monolingual: to perform social dancing with another person. _ Do you think you would like to dance with Wally? _ Would you please dance with me?

dangle from something.monolingual: to hang from something. _ A number of colorful glass balls dangled from the branches of the tree. _ Some loose threads dangled from the bottom of his jacket.
examples: A number of colorful glass balls dangled from the branches of the tree.

dangle something from something.monolingual: to hang something loosely from something else. _ She dangled a few small bells from the bottom of her skirt during the holidays. _ I dangled a bit of fish from the window so I could see how high the cat would jump.
examples: She dangled a few small bells from the bottom of her skirt during the holidays.

dark horse.monolingual: Fig. someone or something whose abilities, plans, or feelings are little known to others. (From a race horse about which little or nothing is known.) _ It’s difficult to predict who will win the prize—there are two or three dark horses in the tournam
examples: It’s difficult to predict who will win the prize—there are two or three dark horses in the tournament.

darken someone’s door.monolingual: Fig. [for an unwelcome person] to come to someone’s door seeking entry. (As if the visitor were casting a shadow on the door. Formal, or even jocular.) _ Who is this who has come to darken my door? _She pointed to the street and said, “Go and never d

dart about.monolingual: to move about quickly. _ The little fish were darting about everywhere. _ People were darting about, to and fro, during the noon rush hour.
examples: The little fish were darting about everywhere.

dart across something.monolingual: to run quickly over something. _ A small animal darted across the road in front of the car. _ I tried to dart across the street, but the traffic was too heavy.
examples: A small animal darted across the road in front of the car.

dart in and out.monolingual: [for something moving] to move quickly between two things, or into a number of things, and move away again. _ On the highway, a small car was darting in and out of the two right lanes of traffic. _ A small bird darted in and out of the bush, probably
examples: On the highway, a small car was darting in and out of the two right lanes of traffic.

dash across something.monolingual: to run quickly across some area. _ John dashed across the busy street and ran in the door. _ The dog dashed across the yard and confronted the meter reader.
examples: John dashed across the busy street and ran in the door.

dash someone’s hopes.monolingual: Fig. to ruin someone’s hopes; to put an end to someone’s dreams or aspirations. _Mary dashed my hopes when she said she wouldn’t marry me.
examples: Mary dashed my hopes when she said she wouldn’t marry me.

dash something off†.monolingual: to make or do something quickly. _ I will dash this off now and try to take more time with the rest of them. _I will see if I can dash off a cherry pie before dinner.
examples: I will dash this off now and try to take more time with the rest of them.

dash something to pieces.monolingual: to break something into small pieces. _ She dashed the glass to pieces on the f loor—she was so mad. _The potter dashed the imperfect pot to pieces.
examples: She dashed the glass to pieces on the f loor—she was so mad.

date from something.monolingual: to have an existence that extends from a particular time. _ This building dates from the beginning of the last century. _ These books date from the 1920s.
examples: This building dates from the beginning of the last century.

daub something with something.monolingual: to smear or paint something with something sticky, such as paint, grease, makeup, etc. _ The mechanic daubed the part with grease and put it back where it came from. _ The end of the chair leg was daubed with glue and set into place.
examples: The mechanic daubed the part with grease and put it back where it came from.

davy jones’s locker.monolingual: the bottom of the sea, especially when it is a grave. _ They were going to sail around the world, but ended up in Davy Jones’s locker. _ Most of the gold from that trading ship is in Davy Jones’s locker.
examples: They were going to sail around the world, but ended up in Davy Jones’s locker.

dawdle about.monolingual: to waste time in a place; to waste time talking idly. _ Don’t dawdle about. Get moving. _ Tim has been dawdling about all morning.
examples: Don’t dawdle about.

dawdle along.monolingual: to move along slowly and casually. _ The boys dawdled along on their way to school. _ We were just dawdling along, talking about life. We didn’t know we were late.
examples: The boys dawdled along on their way to school.

dawdle over something.monolingual: to waste time when one should be doing a particular task; to loaf while doing something. _ Don’t dawdle over your hamburger. The lunch period ends in two minutes. _ Don’t dawdle over it. Get it done.
examples: Don’t dawdle over your hamburger.

dawdle something away†.monolingual: to waste a particular amount of time; to let a period of time slip away, wasted. _You didn’t finish your work because you dawdled most of your time away. _ You dawdle away too much time daydreaming.
examples: You didn’t finish your work because you dawdled most of your time away.

day after day.monolingual: every day; daily; all the time. _ He wears the same clothes day after day. _ She visits her husband in the hospital day after day.
examples: He wears the same clothes day after day.

*the day off.monolingual: a day free from working. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~; take ~.) _ The next time I get a day off, we’ll go to the zoo. _ I have the day off. Let’s go hiking.
examples: The next time I get a day off, we’ll go to the zoo.

*day one.monolingual: the very beginning; the very first day. (*Typically: from ~; since ~.) _ You haven’t done anything right since day one! You’re fired! _ She was unhappy with her new car from day one.
examples: She was unhappy with her new car from day one.

a day person.monolingual: a person who prefers to be active during the daytime. (Compare this with a night person.) _I am strictly a day person. Have to be in bed early.
examples: I am strictly a day person.

daydream about someone or something.monolingual: to have daytime fantasies about someone or something. _ Poor Alice is always daydreaming about Albert. _ John is daydreaming about running away to Tahiti.
examples: Poor Alice is always daydreaming about Albert.

daylight robbery.monolingual: Fig. the practice of blatantly or grossly overcharging. _It’s daylight robbery to charge that amount of money for a hotel room! _ The cost of renting a car at that place is daylight robbery.
examples: The cost of renting a car at that place is daylight robbery.

day-tripper.monolingual: a tourist who makes excursions lasting just one day. _ At about 4:00 p.m. the day-trippers start thinning out. _ Being a day-tripper is hard on your feet sometimes.
examples: At about 4:00 p.

dead ahead.monolingual: straight ahead; directly ahead. _ Look out! There is a cow in the road dead ahead. _ The farmer said that the town we were looking for was dead ahead.
examples: Look out! There is a cow in the road dead ahead.

dead and buried.monolingual: 1. Lit. dead and interred, and soon to be forgotten. _ Now that Uncle Bill is dead and buried, we can read his will.
examples: Now that Uncle Bill is dead and buried, we can read his will.

dead and gone.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of a person] long dead. _ Old Gert’s been dead and gone for quite a spell. _ When I’m dead and gone, I hope folks remember me at my best.
examples: Old Gert’s been dead and gone for quite a spell.

dead broke.monolingual: completely broke; without any money. _I’m dead broke—not a nickel to my name. _ I’ve been dead broke for a month now.
examples: I’m dead broke—not a nickel to my name.

dead center.monolingual: at the exact center of something. _ The arrow hit the target dead center. _ When you put the f lowers on the table, put them dead center.
examples: The arrow hit the target dead center.

dead certain.monolingual: very sure. (Dead means absolutely.) _ I’m dead certain that horse will win. I bet two hundred on it myself. _ I didn’t believe the rumor at first, but Bill’s dead certain that it’s true.
examples: I’m dead certain that horse will win.

dead drunk.monolingual: very intoxicated; totally inebriated. _ They were both dead drunk. They could only lie there and snore. _ Marty stumbled off the bar stood dead drunk.
examples: They were both dead drunk.

a dead duck.monolingual: Fig. someone or something that is certain to die or fail. _ If I fail that test, I’m a dead duck. _ When the outlaw drew his pistol, the sheriff knew he was a dead duck.
examples: If I fail that test, I’m a dead duck.

dead easy.monolingual: very easy. _ This whole job is dead easy. _ It was so dead easy, Frank did it with one hand.
examples: This whole job is dead easy.

dead from the neck up.monolingual: 1. Fig. stupid. (With a “dead” head.) _ She acts like she is dead from the neck up.
examples: She acts like she is dead from the neck up.

a dead giveaway.monolingual: something that reveals a fact or an intention completely. _The car in the driveway was a dead giveaway that someone was at home.
examples: The car in the driveway was a dead giveaway that someone was at home.

dead in the water.monolingual: stalled; immobile. (Originally nautical.) _ This whole company is dead in the water. _ The project is out of funds and dead in the water for the time being.
examples: This whole company is dead in the water.

dead letter.monolingual: 1. a piece of mail that is returned to the post office as both undeliverable and unreturnable. _ At the end of the year, the post office usually has bushels of dead letters. _ Some of the dead letters are opened to see if there is an address inside.
examples: At the end of the year, the post office usually has bushels of dead letters.

a dead loss.monolingual: a total loss. _ My investment was a dead loss. _ This car is a dead loss after the accident.
examples: My investment was a dead loss.

dead meat.monolingual: Fig. dead; as good as dead. (Usually an exaggeration.) _ If you don’t do exactly as I say, you are dead meat!

dead men tell no tales..monolingual: Prov. Dead people will not betray any secrets. _ The club members liked to hold their secret meetings in a graveyard, since dead men tell no tales. _Gangster: Mugsy is going to tell the police that we robbed the bank. How can we stop him? Henchman: D
examples: The club members liked to hold their secret meetings in a graveyard, since dead men tell no tales.

dead on.monolingual: exactly right; on target. _ That’s a good observation, Tiffany. You are dead on. _ Your criticism is dead on!
examples: That’s a good observation, Tiffany.

dead serious.monolingual: absolutely serious; not joking. _Tom: You’re funning me. Bill: No, I’m dead serious. _Mary has threatened divorce a hundred times, but this time she says she’s dead serious.
examples: Tom: You’re funning me.

dead to the world.monolingual: 1. sound asleep. _After all that exercise, he’s dead to the world. _ He’s dead to the world, and I can’t rouse him.
examples: After all that exercise, he’s dead to the world.

dead wrong.monolingual: completely wrong. _ I’m sorry. I was dead wrong. I didn’t have the facts straight.
examples: I’m sorry. I was dead wrong.

deaden something with something.monolingual: to dull or anesthetize pain with something. _The doctor deadened the area with an injection before she began to stitch. _ I will deaden the pain with a local anesthetic.
examples: The doctor deadened the area with an injection before she began to stitch.

deadly dull.monolingual: very dull. _ The lecture was deadly dull, and I went to sleep. _ Her story was really deadly dull. I am sorry I was awake for part of it.
examples: The lecture was deadly dull, and I went to sleep.

deaf and dumb.monolingual: unable to hear or speak. (Used without any intended malice, but no longer considered polite. Sometimes euphemized as “hearing and speech impaired.”) _ Fred objected to being called deaf and dumb. _ Aunt Clara—she was deaf and dumb, you know—lived to
examples: Fred objected to being called deaf and dumb.

*deaf as a post.monolingual: deaf. (*Also: as ~.) _ When my cousin was a teenager, she played her drum set without ear protection, and she was as deaf as a post by the age of twentyfive. _ Mark can’t hear you even if you shout; he’s deaf as a post.
examples: When my cousin was a teenager, she played her drum set without ear protection, and she was as deaf as a post by the age of twentyfive.

deal in something.monolingual: to buy and sell something. _ My uncle is a stockbroker. He deals in stocks and bonds. _ My aunt deals in antiques.
examples: My uncle is a stockbroker.

deal something out†.monolingual: to pass something out piece by piece, giving everyone equal shares. _ The manager dealt the proposals out, giving each person an equal number to read. _ I’ll deal out some more proposals.
examples: The manager dealt the proposals out, giving each person an equal number to read.

deal with someone.monolingual: Sl. to kill someone. _ “Spike, you deal with that cop,” said the crime boss. _ The agent planned how best to deal with the rebel leader without getting caught.
examples: “Spike, you deal with that cop,” said the crime boss.

deal with someone or something.monolingual: to manage someone or something. _ This is not a big problem. I think I can deal with it. _ I am sure I can deal with Jill.
examples: This is not a big problem.

dear departed.monolingual: Euph. a dead person, as referred to at a funeral. _Let’s take a moment to meditate on the life of the dear departed. dedicate a Dear John letter a letter a woman writes to her boyfriend telling him that she does not love him anymore. _ Bert got a Dea
examples: Let’s take a moment to meditate on the life of the dear departed.

dear me!.monolingual: an expression of mild dismay or regret. _ Sue: Dear me, is this all there is? Mary: There’s more in the kitchen. _ “Oh, dear me!” fretted John, “I’m late again.”
examples: Sue: Dear me, is this all there is? Mary: There’s more in the kitchen.

death is the great leveler..monolingual: Prov. Death makes everyone equal, because it does not spare anyone, not even the wealthy, famous, or talented. (Also the cliché: the great leveler, death.) _ The wealthy tycoon lived as though he were exempt from every law, but death is the great lev
examples: The wealthy tycoon lived as though he were exempt from every law, but death is the great leveler and came to him the same as to everyone else.

death on something.monolingual: 1. Fig. very harmful; very effective in acting against someone or something. _ This road is terribly bumpy. It’s death on tires. _ The sergeant is death on lazy soldiers.
examples: This road is terribly bumpy.

debate on something.monolingual: to hold a long and disciplined discussion on a particular subject. _ We can debate on this all night if you think we will settle anything in the end. _ Are they still debating on the question?
examples: We can debate on this all night if you think we will settle anything in the end.

debit something with something.monolingual: to charge something for something. _ They debited Fred’s account with the whole expense. _The bank debited my checking account with the cost of the new checks.
examples: They debited Fred’s account with the whole expense.

deceive someone into something.monolingual: to trick someone into doing something. _She deceived me into giving her my car keys. _ You can’t deceive me into doing what I don’t want to do.
examples: She deceived me into giving her my car keys.

deceive someone with something.monolingual: to cheat someone with something or with deceptive words. _You cannot deceive me with your promises. _ You are just deceiving yourself with fancy talk.
examples: You cannot deceive me with your promises.

decide against someone or something.monolingual: to rule against someone or something; to make a judgment against someone or something. _We decided against Tom and chose Larry instead. _ Jane decided against the supplier.
examples: We decided against Tom and chose Larry instead.

decide for someone or something.monolingual: to rule in favor of someone or something; to make a judgment for someone or something. _ The jury decided for the plaintiff. _ The judge decided for me.
examples: The jury decided for the plaintiff.

decorate someone for something.monolingual: to award someone a medal or ribbon for doing something important or brave. _The town decorated her for her heroic act. _She was decorated for her heroism.
examples: The town decorated her for her heroic act.

decorate something with something.monolingual: to adorn or ornament something with something. _I will decorate the cake with roses made of sugar. _Can I decorate your car with streamers for the parade?
examples: I will decorate the cake with roses made of sugar.

deduce something from something.monolingual: to infer or conclude something from a set of facts. _Can I deduce a bit of anger from your remarks? _ I deduce nothing from everything I have heard today.
examples: I deduce nothing from everything I have heard today.

deduct something from something else.monolingual: to subtract an amount from another amount. _ Are you going to deduct this from your income taxes? _ Mr. Wilson deducted the discount from the bill.
examples: Mr. Wilson deducted the discount from the bill.

deep-six someone or something.monolingual: Sl. to get rid of someone or something; to dispose of someone or something. (Refers originally to burying someone or something six feet deep, the standard depth of a grave.) _ Take this horrible food out and deep-six it. _ That guy is a pain. Deep-si
examples: Take this horrible food out and deep-six it.

deface something with something.monolingual: to mutilate or spoil the appearance of something with something. _ Someone defaced the wall with spray paint. _Please don’t deface the facilities.
examples: Someone defaced the wall with spray paint.

default on something.monolingual: to fail to act in some way regarding something, such as failing to make a payment, thereby losing one’s right to the thing in question. _You are not going to default on your loan, are you? _ She defaulted on her mortgage payments and lost the house.
examples: She defaulted on her mortgage payments and lost the house.

defect from something.monolingual: to run away from something; to forsake something. _ Thousands of soldiers defected from the army. _ Roger would never think of defecting from the armed services.
examples: Thousands of soldiers defected from the army.

defect to something.monolingual: to forsake one group and take up with another. _ Will he defect to the other side? _ David defected to a small East European country.
examples: David defected to a small East European country.

defend someone with something.monolingual: to repel danger from someone with something. _ Here, defend yourself with this club. _ Mary defended herself with karate.
examples: Here, defend yourself with this club.

define something as something.monolingual: to label something as being something. _ I define that kind of behavior as just plain rude! _ We have to define that comment as careless and unthinking.
examples: We have to define that comment as careless and unthinking.

defraud someone out of something.monolingual: to cheat someone out of something. _ The crooked contractor defrauded the town out of a fortune. _ The clerk defrauded the employer out of a great deal of money.
examples: The crooked contractor defrauded the town out of a fortune.

degenerate into something.monolingual: to decay into something; to break down into something. _ The peace rally degenerated into a riot. _I was afraid that the party would degenerate into a drinking contest.
examples: The peace rally degenerated into a riot.

deign to do something.monolingual: to lower oneself to do something. _She will never deign to join in with us. _I expect that he will not deign to have dinner with us.
examples: She will never deign to join in with us.

delegate someone to something.monolingual: to appoint someone to something; to appoint someone to be something. _I will delegate Jane to be our representative. _ Donna was delegated to attend the conference.
examples: I will delegate Jane to be our representative.

delegate something to someone.monolingual: to assign a task to someone; to appoint someone to do a specific task. _I will have to delegate this job to Sam, who knows how to do these things. _ The job was delegated to Sally.
examples: I will have to delegate this job to Sam, who knows how to do these things.

delete something from something.monolingual: to remove something from something; to cross something out from something. _ Will you please delete this paragraph from the contract? _ The line was deleted from the sales agreement.
examples: The line was deleted from the sales agreement.

deliberate over someone or something.monolingual: to discuss and argue about someone or something. _ We will deliberate over this question tomorrow. _ We have been deliberating over Karen long enough.
examples: We will deliberate over this question tomorrow.

delight in someone or something.monolingual: to take great pleasure in someone or something. _ I delight in your interest in my work. _ We all delight in James. What a fine boy!
examples: I delight in your interest in my work.

delight someone by something.monolingual: to please someone with something; to please someone by doing something. _ You delighted me by agreeing to join us. _ I was delighted by your proposal.
examples: You delighted me by agreeing to join us.

delight someone with something.monolingual: to please someone with something, such as a gift. _We delighted Alice with a gift of money. _ She was delighted with the gift.
examples: We delighted Alice with a gift of money.

deliver someone of something.monolingual: to free someone from some burden or problem; to liberate someone from some confinement. _ He was looking for someone to deliver him of his burdensome responsibility. _ He was delivered of his burden.
examples: He was looking for someone to deliver him of his burdensome responsibility.

deliver something up† to someone.monolingual: to render or yield something to someone. _Will you please deliver the documents up to Jane? _ Will you please deliver up the documents to Jane?

delude someone into something.monolingual: to fool someone into thinking something. _ You can’t delude me into believing you. _ Todd deluded himself into believing he was back at home.
examples: You can’t delude me into believing you.

delude someone with something.monolingual: to fool or trick someone with something. _ She deluded us with her clever talk. _ Don’t delude yourself with false hopes.
examples: She deluded us with her clever talk.

delve into something.monolingual: to examine or study something carefully; to enter into the examination or study of something. _He delved into the solution of the problem facing him. _ I am just now delving into a study of the Trojan War.
examples: He delved into the solution of the problem facing him.

demonstrate against someone or something.monolingual: to make a public show against someone or something. _ The citizens demonstrated against the new policies. _A number of protestors demonstrated against the mayor.
examples: The citizens demonstrated against the new policies.

demonstrate for someone or something.monolingual: to make a public show in favor of someone or something. _ We will all demonstrate for Walter’s candidacy. _ A number of supporters demonstrated for the mayor.
examples: We will all demonstrate for Walter’s candidacy.

demonstrate something to someone.monolingual: to show someone how something works. _ Would you please demonstrate this DVD player to me? I may want to buy it. _ The new products were demonstrated to the board of directors in advance.
examples: Would you please demonstrate this DVD player to me? I may want to buy it.

demur at something.monolingual: to dispute something; to challenge something. _ I fear I must demur at your suggestion that I am aloof and condescending. _Alice demurred at the suggestion that she was late.
examples: I fear I must demur at your suggestion that I am aloof and condescending.

a den of iniquity.monolingual: a place filled with criminal activity or wickedness. _The town was a den of iniquity and vice was everywhere. _ Police raided the gambling house, calling it a den of iniquity.
examples: The town was a den of iniquity and vice was everywhere.

denounce someone as something.monolingual: to criticize someone as something; to publicly call someone something bad. _ The mayor denounced her opponent as a crook. _Anne was denounced as a cheater.
examples: The mayor denounced her opponent as a crook.

denounce someone for something.monolingual: to criticize someone publicly for doing something. _The candidate denounced the governor for raising taxes. _ Donna denounced the mayor for incompetence.
examples: The candidate denounced the governor for raising taxes.

dent something up†.monolingual: to mar or make depressions in something. _I don’t want to dent my car up. It’s still new. _He dented up my new bike!
examples: I don’t want to dent my car up.

depart for some place.monolingual: to leave for some place. _When shall we depart for the airport? _ When do we depart for St. Petersburg?
examples: When do we depart for St.

depart from some place.monolingual: to leave from some place or something; to set out from some place or something. _ When will you depart from here? _ We departed from Moscow on time.
examples: We departed from Moscow on time.

depart this life.monolingual: Euph. to die. _ He departed this life on April 20th,
examples: He departed this life on April 20th, 1973.

depict someone as something.monolingual: to show someone as something; to make someone appear to be something. _He did report the fire, but it is going too far to depict him as a hero. _The artist depicted himself as a much younger man than he really was.
examples: He did report the fire, but it is going too far to depict him as a hero.

deplete something of something.monolingual: to use up all of a certain thing that something has. _They will deplete the soil of its nutrients by planting the same crop over and over.
examples: They will deplete the soil of its nutrients by planting the same crop over and over.

deprive someone of something.monolingual: to take something away from someone. _ If you don’t behave, I will deprive you of your driving rights. _ They deprived themselves of a good time by pouting.
examples: If you don’t behave, I will deprive you of your driving rights.

deputize someone as something.monolingual: to assign someone the temporary power to act in some official capacity. _ The sheriff deputized Chuck as an aid during the uprising. _ Chuck was deputized as an officer of the law.
examples: The sheriff deputized Chuck as an aid during the uprising.

derive from something.monolingual: to come from something; to evolve from something. (Usually in reference to a word and its etymological history.) _This word derives from an ancient Celtic word. _ What does the English word skirt derive from?
examples: This word derives from an ancient Celtic word.

derive something from something.monolingual: to show how something is descended from something else. _Is it possible to derive this word from Greek? _ Is this word derived from Latin?

descend from something.monolingual: to move down from something. _ The bird descended from the top of the tree to a lower branch. _ Take care when you descend from the ladder.
examples: The bird descended from the top of the tree to a lower branch.

descend into something.monolingual: to go down into something. _ The butler descended into the cellar for another bottle of wine. _ Fred descended into the canyon on an organized tour.
examples: The butler descended into the cellar for another bottle of wine.

descend to something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to go down to something. _ I must descend to the lower level to greet the guests. _ Gerald descended to the front door to see who was there.
examples: I must descend to the lower level to greet the guests.

desensitize someone to something.monolingual: to make someone less sensitive to something. _The doctor wanted to desensitize the allergic child to pollen. _ I took injections to desensitize me to house dust.
examples: The doctor wanted to desensitize the allergic child to pollen.

deserve credit for something.monolingual: [for someone] to be owed recognition for doing something. _ He certainly deserves credit for the work he did on the project.
examples: He certainly deserves credit for the work he did on the project.

design something for someone.monolingual: to conceive of something for someone; to draw up plans of something for someone. _ Ann designed a new kitchen for us. _ Would you design a book cover for me?
examples: Ann designed a new kitchen for us.

design something for something.monolingual: to conceive of something that is to be part of something else; to draw up plans for something that is to be part of something else. _The engineers designed a cure for the rattling problem. _ Bob, the computer programmer, designed a fix for the bug in
examples: The engineers designed a cure for the rattling problem.

desires are nourished by delays..monolingual: Prov. The longer you have to wait for something you want, the more eager you will be to get it. _ The longer I had to postpone my trip to San Francisco, the more eagerly I wanted to go. Desires are nourished by delays.
examples: The longer I had to postpone my trip to San Francisco, the more eagerly I wanted to go.

desist from something.monolingual: to stop doing something. _ You must desist from further attempts to contact your wife. _ I wish you would desist from calling me Willie.
examples: You must desist from further attempts to contact your wife.

despair of something.monolingual: to give up all hope of something. _ Do not despair of his returning; I think we will see him again. _ I despair of ever seeing her again.
examples: Do not despair of his returning; I think we will see him again.

despise someone for something.monolingual: to hate someone for something or for doing something. _I just despise him for running away! _She despised herself for her dishonest actions.
examples: She despised herself for her dishonest actions.

despoil something of something.monolingual: to make something, such as a town, tomb, or building, lose value by stealing from it; to rob something of something. _ The vandals despoiled the castle of much of its furnishings. _ The land was despoiled of its fertility by overplanting.
examples: The vandals despoiled the castle of much of its furnishings.

destine someone for something.monolingual: to determine that someone should receive or achieve something in the future. _ Her many talents destined her for a distinguished career. _ Larry’s intelligence destined him for big things.
examples: Her many talents destined her for a distinguished career.

destined for something.monolingual: predetermined to achieve or become something. _ I know I am destined for a job that is better than this. _ We are destined for death in the long run.
examples: I know I am destined for a job that is better than this.

detail someone for something.monolingual: to choose someone to do a particular task. (Originally military.) _Sam detailed Private Bailey for guard duty. _ Donna was detailed for some extra work.
examples: Sam detailed Private Bailey for guard duty.

detect something in something.monolingual: to recognize or identify something in something. _ Can you detect the anger in her voice? _ I detect a bit of sarcasm in your comments.
examples: I detect a bit of sarcasm in your comments.

detract from someone or something.monolingual: to lessen or diminish someone or something. _ The large pieces of furniture detracted from the lovely design in the carpet. _Alice’s quiet demeanor did not detract from her grace and beauty.
examples: The large pieces of furniture detracted from the lovely design in the carpet.

deviate from something.monolingual: to wander away from something, such as a path, road, etc.; to vary from the normal procedure. _Please do not deviate from the path. You will crush the wildf lowers. _I will not deviate one inch from the route you have prescribed. _ They did not devia
examples: Please do not deviate from the path.

*the devil.monolingual: Fig. a severe scolding. (*Typically: get ~; catch ~; give someone ~.) _ Bill is always getting the devil about something. _I’m late. If I don’t get home soon, I’ll catch the devil!
examples: Bill is always getting the devil about something.

dialogue with someone.monolingual: to talk with someone. _ I look forward to dialoguing with you tomorrow. _ The supervisor sets aside time to dialogue with each and every person in the department once a week.
examples: I look forward to dialoguing with you tomorrow.

a diamond in the rough.monolingual: Fig. a person who has good qualities despite a rough exterior; a person with great potential. _ Sam looks a little scruffy, but he’s a diamond in the rough. _ He’s a diamond in the rough—a little hard to take at times, but very smart and helpful.
examples: Sam looks a little scruffy, but he’s a diamond in the rough.

dibs on something.monolingual: a claim on something. _ I’ve got dibs on the yellow one! _ Dibs on the front seat!

diddle someone out of something.monolingual: to cheat someone into giving up something. _ The boys diddled the old man out of a few bucks. _ He was diddled out of his last dime.
examples: The boys diddled the old man out of a few bucks.

diddle something out of someone.monolingual: Sl. to get something from someone by deception. _We diddled about forty bucks out of the old lady who runs the candy shop. _ They diddled Larry’s last dime out of him.
examples: We diddled about forty bucks out of the old lady who runs the candy shop.

diddle with something.monolingual: to play with something; to toy with something. _ Here, don’t diddle with that watch. _ Stop diddling with your nose, Jimmy!
examples: Here, don’t diddle with that watch.

didn’t care too hard.monolingual: Rur. didn’t mind. _ Dad said he didn’t care too hard if I took the dog out with me. _ If you don’t care too hard, I’ll shut this window.
examples: Dad said he didn’t care too hard if I took the dog out with me.

didn’t invent gunpowder.monolingual: Rur. did not do anything terribly important. _ He may be the class president, but he didn’t invent gunpowder. _ What’s all this fuss about a movie star? She didn’t invent gunpowder!
examples: He may be the class president, but he didn’t invent gunpowder.

die a natural death.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for someone] to die by disease or old age rather than by violence or foul play. _ I hope to live to 100 and die a natural death. _The police say she didn’t die a natural death, and they are investigating.
examples: I hope to live to 100 and die a natural death.

die away.monolingual: Fig. to fade away. _ The sound of the waterfall finally died away. _When the applause died away, the tenor sang an encore.
examples: The sound of the waterfall finally died away.

die back.monolingual: [for vegetation] to die back to the stems or roots. _ The hedge died back in the winter but regenerated leaves in the spring. _ This kind of grass dies back every year.
examples: The hedge died back in the winter but regenerated leaves in the spring.

die behind the wheel.monolingual: to die in an automobile accident in a car that one is driving. _ Poor Fred died behind the wheel in a horrible collision.
examples: Poor Fred died behind the wheel in a horrible collision.

die by one’s own hand.monolingual: Euph. to commit suicide. _Jane: I just heard that Bill died. I didn’t know he was sick. Dan: He wasn’t sick. He died by his own hand. _ She died at the age of fifty, by her own hand.
examples: Jane: I just heard that Bill died.

die by something.monolingual: to perish by a particular cause or device. (Often refers to execution as a death sentence.) _He died by electrocution. _ She was condemned to die by hanging.
examples: He died by electrocution.

die down.monolingual: to fade to almost nothing; to decrease gradually. _The fire died down and went out. _As the applause died down, a child came on stage with an armload of roses for the singer.
examples: The fire died down and went out.

die for someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to perish for the benefit or glory of someone or something. _ He said he was willing to die for his country. _ She would die for her child if necessary.
examples: He said he was willing to die for his country.

die in something.monolingual: to perish in a particular calamity or accident. _They both died in an automobile accident. _Wally did not want to die in the war.
examples: They both died in an automobile accident.

the die is cast..monolingual: Prov. A process is past the point of no return. (The die is one of a pair of dice. The cast means thrown. This phrase [in Latin] was said by Julius Caesar when he crossed the Rubicon with his legions, starting a civil war.) _ After that speech favori
examples: After that speech favoring reform of the education system, the die is cast.

die laughing.monolingual: 1. Lit. to meet one’s death laughing—in good spirits, revenge, or irony. _ Sally is such an optimist that she’ll probably die laughing. _ Bob tried to poison his rich aunt, who then died laughing because she had taken Bob out of her will.
examples: Sally is such an optimist that she’ll probably die laughing.

die of a broken heart.monolingual: Fig. to die of emotional distress. _I was not surprised to hear of her death. They say she died of a broken heart. _ In the movie, the heroine appeared to die of a broken heart, but the audience knew she was poisoned.
examples: I was not surprised to hear of her death.

die of boredom.monolingual: Fig. to be very bored. _ No one has ever really died of boredom. _We sat there and listened politely, even though we almost died of boredom.
examples: No one has ever really died of boredom.

die of throat trouble.monolingual: Sl. to be hanged. (Old.) _He died of throat trouble after the posse caught up with him. _The cattle rustler died of throat trouble.
examples: He died of throat trouble after the posse caught up with him.

die off.monolingual: [for a living thing] to perish one by one until there are no more. _Most of the larger lizards died off eons ago. _ It would be really bad if all the owls died off. _ The cucumber blossoms all died off.
examples: Most of the larger lizards died off eons ago.

die on someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a patient] to die under the care of someone. _Get that medicine over here fast, or this guy’s gonna die on me. _ Come on, mister, don’t die on me!
examples: Get that medicine over here fast, or this guy’s gonna die on me.

die out.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a species or family] to perish totally because of the failure to produce offspring. _I am the last one in the family, so I guess our line will die out with me. _ The owls might die out if you ruin their nesting area.
examples: I am the last one in the family, so I guess our line will die out with me.

differ from something.monolingual: [for something] to be different from something else. _No, this one differs from the one you saw because it has a bigger handle. _ How does this one differ from that one?
examples: No, this one differs from the one you saw because it has a bigger handle.

differ in something.monolingual: [for people or things] to be different in a specific way or in specific ways. _ They differ only in the color of their eyes and the size of their shoes. _They differ in size and shape.
examples: They differ only in the color of their eyes and the size of their shoes.

*different as night and day.monolingual: Cliché completely different. (*Also: as ~.) _Although Bobby and Billy are twins, they are as different as night and day. _ Birds and bats appear to be similar, but they are different as night and day.
examples: Although Bobby and Billy are twins, they are as different as night and day.

different strokes for different folks..monolingual: Prov. Different people like different things.; Different people live in different ways. _ My neighbor spends all his free time working in his garden. I would never want to do that, but different strokes for different folks.
examples: My neighbor spends all his free time working in his garden.

diffuse something through something else.monolingual: to distribute or scatter something through something else. _ The chemical process diffused the purple color through the liquid. _ Let us try to diffuse the medication through the bloodstream as rapidly as possible.
examples: The chemical process diffused the purple color through the liquid.

diffuse through something.monolingual: to spread or scatter through something. _The smell diffused through the office through the ventilating system. _The dye diffused through the water rapidly.
examples: The smell diffused through the office through the ventilating system.

dig at someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to poke or jab at someone or something. _ Don’t dig at me all the time. My side is getting sore where you jabbed me. _ Stop digging at the wall! Look at the hole you’ve made!
examples: Don’t dig at me all the time.

dig for something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to excavate to find something that is buried. _They are digging along the river bank for a special kind of clay. _ I want to dig for gold in Alaska.
examples: They are digging along the river bank for a special kind of clay.

dig one’s heels in†.monolingual: Fig. to refuse to alter one’s course of action or opinions; to be obstinate or determined. _ The student dug her heels in and refused to obey the instructions. _ I’m digging in my heels. I’m not going back.
examples: The student dug her heels in and refused to obey the instructions.

dig one’s own grave.monolingual: Fig. to be responsible for one’s own downfall or ruin. _ If you try to cheat the bank, you will be digging your own grave. _ Those politicians have dug their own grave with their new tax bill. They won’t be reelected.
examples: If you try to cheat the bank, you will be digging your own grave.

dig someone or something up†.monolingual: Fig. to go to great effort to find someone or something. (There is an implication that the thing or person dug up is not the most desirable, but is all that could be found.) _ Mary dug a date up for the dance next Friday. _ I dug up a recipe for roas
examples: Mary dug a date up for the dance next Friday.

dig something out†.monolingual: Fig. to work hard to locate something and bring it forth. _ They dug the contract out of the file cabinet. _ I dug out an old dress and wore it to the Fifties party.
examples: They dug the contract out of the file cabinet.

dig up!.monolingual: Sl. Listen carefully! _John: All right, you guys! Dig up! You’re going to hear this one time and one time only! _ Bill: Dig up! I’m only going to say this once. Bob: What was that? Bill: I said listen!
examples: Bill: Dig up! I’m only going to say this once.

dig up one’s tomahawk.monolingual: Rur. to get angry. (A jocular reversal of bury the tomahawk. Fixed order.) _ When Joe saw the mess we made, he dug up his tomahawk and went looking for us.
examples: When Joe saw the mess we made, he dug up his tomahawk and went looking for us.

digress from something.monolingual: [for a speaker or writer] to stray from the subject. _I am going to digress from my prepared text. _ You will pardon me if I digress from my point a little.
examples: I am going to digress from my prepared text.

dilate on something.monolingual: Fig. to speak or write in great detail on some subject. _I am sure you do not wish me to dilate further on this matter. _ If you do not see my point, I would be pleased to dilate on this matter further.
examples: I am sure you do not wish me to dilate further on this matter.

dim down.monolingual: [for the lights] to go dim. _The lights dimmed down for a few seconds. _Open the stage curtain when the house lights dim down.
examples: The lights dimmed down for a few seconds.

dim out.monolingual: [for a light] to grow dim and go out altogether. _ The lights dimmed out twice during the storm. _ I was afraid that the lights would dim out completely.
examples: The lights dimmed out twice during the storm.

dim something down†.monolingual: to make lights dim; to use a dimmer to make the lights dimmer. _Why don’t you dim the lights down and put on some music? _Let me dim down the lights and put on some music.
examples: Let me dim down the lights and put on some music.

dim something up†.monolingual: to use a dimmer to make the lights brighter. (Theatrical. A dimmer is a rheostat, variable transformer, or something similar. The expression, a seeming contradiction, is the opposite of dim something down.) _ As the curtain rose, the electrician dimm
examples: As the curtain rose, the electrician dimmed the lights up on a beautiful scene.

a dime a dozen.monolingual: Fig. abundant; cheap and common. _ People who can write good books are not a dime a dozen. _ Romantic movies are a dime a dozen.
examples: People who can write good books are not a dime a dozen.

dine at some place.monolingual: to eat at a place. _We really like to dine at the small cafe on the corner. _ I hope we can dine at a fine restaurant for our anniversary.
examples: We really like to dine at the small cafe on the corner.

dine in.monolingual: to eat at home rather than at a restaurant. _I think we will dine in tonight. _ I am tired of dining in. Let’s go out.
examples: I think we will dine in tonight.

dine off something.monolingual: to make a meal of something; to make many meals of something. _Do you think we can dine off the leg of lamb for more than one meal? _ I hope we dine off the turkey only one more time.
examples: I hope we dine off the turkey only one more time.

dine on something.monolingual: to eat something. _ We are dining on roast beef tonight. _ What will we be dining on tonight?
examples: We are dining on roast beef tonight.

dinged out.monolingual: Sl. intoxicated. _Gary is dinged out and can’t drive.
examples: Gary is dinged out and can’t drive.

dink someone off†.monolingual: Sl. to make someone angry. _Whatever you do, don’t dink her off! _ Why did you have to start out your speech by dinking off the entire audience?

dinner is served..monolingual: It is time to eat dinner. Please come to the table. (As if announced by a butler; often jocular.) _ Sue: Dinner is served. Mary (aside): Aren’t we fancy tonight? _ “Dinner is served,” said Bob, rather formally for a barbecue.
examples: Sue: Dinner is served.

dip into one’s savings.monolingual: Fig. to take out part of the money one has been saving. _ I had to dip into my savings in order to pay for my vacation. _I went to the bank and dipped into savings. There wasn’t much left.
examples: I had to dip into my savings in order to pay for my vacation.

dip to something.monolingual: to decline to a lower level quickly or briefly. _ The temperature dipped into the lower twenties overnight. _ The stock market dipped to a very low level during the day Friday.
examples: The temperature dipped into the lower twenties overnight.

direct something to someone.monolingual: to address, designate, or send something to someone. _Shall I direct the inquiries to you? _Please direct all the mail to the secretary when it is delivered.
examples: Please direct all the mail to the secretary when it is delivered.

dirt cheap.monolingual: extremely cheap. _ Buy some more of those plums. They’re dirt cheap. _ In Italy, the peaches are dirt cheap.
examples: Buy some more of those plums.

dirty crack.monolingual: a rude remark. _ Who made that dirty crack? _ Another dirty crack like that and I’ll leave.
examples: Another dirty crack like that and I’ll leave.

dirty deal.monolingual: an unfair deal. _ That was a dirty deal. I feel cheated. _ I got a dirty deal at that shop, and I won’t go back.
examples: That was a dirty deal.

dirty dog.monolingual: a low and sneaky person. _That dirty dog tried to cheat in the card game!

*a dirty look.monolingual: Fig. an angry face or a frown. (*Typically: get ~; give someone ~.) _ Anne gave me a dirty look. _ I got a dirty look from the teacher when I cracked a joke in class.
examples: Anne gave me a dirty look.

dirty old man.monolingual: a lecherous old man. (Usually jocular.) _ Jimmy, what you call f lirting will make some girls call you a dirty old man! _What a terrible joke. You are a dirty old man!
examples: What a terrible joke.

dirty something up†.monolingual: Rur. to get something dirty. _ Those pants are brand-new! Don’t dirty them up! _ Don’t dirty up your brand-new pants!

a dirty word.monolingual: 1. a swearword; an obscene or blasphemous word; a four-letter word. _You are not allowed to use dirty words in your school essays. _ My aunt is offended by the use of dirty words.
examples: You are not allowed to use dirty words in your school essays.

dirty work.monolingual: 1. Fig. unpleasant or uninteresting work. _ My boss does all the traveling. I get all the dirty work to do. _She’s tired of doing all the dirty work at the office.
examples: My boss does all the traveling.

disabuse someone of something.monolingual: to rid someone of an incorrect idea. _ Please allow me to disabuse you of that assumption. _ Please disabuse yourself of the notion that you are perfect.
examples: Please allow me to disabuse you of that assumption.

disagree with someone.monolingual: [for food or drink] to upset someone’s stomach. _Milk always disagrees with me. _Onions disagree with my husband, so he never eats them.
examples: Milk always disagrees with me.

disappear from something.monolingual: to vanish from something or some place, especially from sight, view, or the face of the earth; to have been taken away from something. _ Jack disappeared all of a sudden last week, as if from the face of the earth. _ The car pulled away and disappear
examples: Jack disappeared all of a sudden last week, as if from the face of the earth.

disapprove of someone or something.monolingual: to object to someone or something. _ I disapprove of her choice for maid of honor. _ Do you disapprove of me?
examples: I disapprove of her choice for maid of honor.

a disaster of epic proportions.monolingual: Cliché a very large disaster. (Often jocular.) _ The earthquake was responsible for a disaster of epic proportions. _Your late arrival caused a disaster of epic proportions.
examples: The earthquake was responsible for a disaster of epic proportions.

disbar someone from something.monolingual: to take the right to practice law away from a lawyer. _ The state board disbarred Todd from practicing law in his own state. _Sally was also disbarred from practicing law.
examples: The state board disbarred Todd from practicing law in his own state.

discharge someone from something.monolingual: 1. to fire someone from a job. _ The manager discharged Walter from his position with the bank. _ Walter was discharged from his job.
examples: The manager discharged Walter from his position with the bank.

discharge something from something.monolingual: to fire a round from a gun. _I discharged two bullets from the gun accidentally. _ Randy discharged about twenty rounds from his automatic rif le.
examples: I discharged two bullets from the gun accidentally.

discharge something into something.monolingual: to let something out of something into something else. _ She discharged some nitrogen from the tank into the laboratory by accident. _ The technician discharged oxygen into the atmosphere.
examples: She discharged some nitrogen from the tank into the laboratory by accident.

discipline someone for something.monolingual: to punish or chastise someone for doing something. _ I will have to discipline you for fighting. _ Mary was disciplined for taking part in the fiasco.
examples: I will have to discipline you for fighting.

disclose something to someone.monolingual: to tell or reveal something to someone. _ Tony refused to disclose the location of the papers to me. _ Please disclose the names to me at once.
examples: Tony refused to disclose the location of the papers to me.

discourage someone from something.monolingual: to dissuade someone from doing something. _I hope I can discourage Tom from leaving. _ I do not want to discourage you from further experimentation.
examples: I hope I can discourage Tom from leaving.

discriminate against someone or somethin.monolingual: to single out a type of person or thing for special negative treatment or denial of equal treatment; to act in a prejudicial manner against someone or something. _ This law discriminates against short people. _ You discriminate against people in whee
examples: This law discriminates against short people.

the disease to please.monolingual: an obsessive need to please people. _I, like so many, am aff licted with the disease to please. I am just too nice for my own good.
examples: I, like so many, am aff licted with the disease to please.

disembark from something.monolingual: to get off a ship, plane, or train. _We disembark from the ship in Manaus. _At what time do we expect to disembark from the plane?
examples: We disembark from the ship in Manaus.

disengage something from something.monolingual: to detach something from something. _ Sally disengaged the locking mechanism from the cupboard door and peeked in. _ The coupling was disengaged from the boxcar, and the car separated and rolled away.
examples: Sally disengaged the locking mechanism from the cupboard door and peeked in.

disguise someone in something.monolingual: to conceal someone’s identity in a costume or makeup. _ We disguised her in men’s clothing and got her across the border. _She disguised herself in a clown suit.
examples: We disguised her in men’s clothing and got her across the border.

*disgusted at someone or something.monolingual: severely disappointed at someone or something. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; grow ~.) _ We were disgusted at her incessant lying. _ Sam was disgusted at her.
examples: We were disgusted at her incessant lying.

*disgusted with someone or something.monolingual: severely disappointed over someone or something. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; grow ~.) _ I am totally disgusted with Ellen. _ We are all disgusted with the fall in the company’s profits.
examples: I am totally disgusted with Ellen.

dish on someone.monolingual: Sl. to gossip about or slander someone. _ Stop dishing on her. She never hurt you! _ They spent an hour dishing on Wally.
examples: Stop dishing on her.

dish something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to serve up food to people. _ I’ll dish it out, and you take it to the table. _ Careful how you dish out the mashed potatoes. There may not be enough.
examples: I’ll dish it out, and you take it to the table.

dish the dirt.monolingual: Sl. to spread gossip; to gossip. _ Let’s sit down, have a drink, and dish the dirt. _ David goes down to the tavern to dish the dirt.
examples: Let’s sit down, have a drink, and dish the dirt.

disinclined to do something.monolingual: unwilling to do something. _I am disinclined to allow you to leave class early. _They were disinclined to allow us to enter the country.
examples: I am disinclined to allow you to leave class early.

dismiss something as something.monolingual: to put something out of one’s mind or ignore something as something. (The second something can be a noun or an adjective.) _ I dismissed the whole idea as foolishness. _ It was not possible to dismiss the whole matter as a one-time happening. _ Molly
examples: I dismissed the whole idea as foolishness.

dismount from something.monolingual: to get down from something, such as a horse, bicycle, etc. _ She dismounted from her horse and f led into the house. _ Please dismount from the bicycle and wheel it into the shed.
examples: She dismounted from her horse and f led into the house.

dispatch someone from some place.monolingual: to send someone from some place. _ I dispatched a messenger from here over an hour ago. _ A telegram will be dispatched from my office first thing in the morning.
examples: I dispatched a messenger from here over an hour ago.

dispense with someone or something.monolingual: to get rid of someone or something; to brush someone or something aside. _ I think we will dispense with that subject for the rest of the day. _We will have to dispense with the expensive gifts this year.
examples: I think we will dispense with that subject for the rest of the day.

display something to someone.monolingual: to show something to someone. _ The peacock displayed his tail feathers to the other birds. _ Would you please display the artwork to the committee?
examples: The peacock displayed his tail feathers to the other birds.

dispose of someone.monolingual: Sl. to kill someone. _ Max suggested that he would dispose of Lefty if Lefty continued to be a pest. _ The boss ordered Max to dispose of Lefty.
examples: Max suggested that he would dispose of Lefty if Lefty continued to be a pest.

dispose of someone or something.monolingual: to get rid of someone or something. _ How can I dispose of this bothersome customer? _ Where shall I dispose of this wastepaper?

dispossess someone of something.monolingual: to separate someone from a possession. _ Do you intend to dispossess us of our home? _They were dispossessed of the only possessions they had.
examples: They were dispossessed of the only possessions they had.

dispute something with someone.monolingual: to argue with someone about something, such as an amount of money. _The customer disputed the amount of the check with the waiter. _ Please don’t feel like you have to dispute every bill with the supplier.
examples: The customer disputed the amount of the check with the waiter.

*dissatisfied with someone or something.monolingual: unhappy with someone or something. (*Typically: be ~; grow ~.) _We are quite dissatisfied with the service provided by the dealer. _ I am not dissatisfied with you.
examples: We are quite dissatisfied with the service provided by the dealer.

dissent from something.monolingual: to disagree with something. _We have chosen to dissent from the decision the rest of you made. _Fred dissented from almost everything that everyone else agreed on.
examples: We have chosen to dissent from the decision the rest of you made.

dissolve in something.monolingual: [for a substance] to break down in a liquid and disperse in the liquid. (Compare this with dissolve into something.) _ Salt will dissolve in warm water. _ This material will not dissolve in oil.
examples: Salt will dissolve in warm water.

dissolve into something.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a substance to change from a solid state into another state; [for a substance] to melt or liquefy something. (Compare this with dissolve in something.) _In a hot pan, the sugar dissolved into syrup.
examples: In a hot pan, the sugar dissolved into syrup.

dissolve something in something.monolingual: to cause a substance to break down in a liquid and disperse in the liquid. _ First, dissolve the salt in some warm water. _ Dissolve this medicine in water.
examples: First, dissolve the salt in some warm water.

dissolve something into something.monolingual: to cause a film or television picture to fade away into some other picture. _ The director dissolved the picture into the next scene. _ At this point, the opening scene should be dissolved into a side shot of the exterior.
examples: The director dissolved the picture into the next scene.

dissuade someone from something.monolingual: to discourage someone from (doing) something. _ I hope to dissuade her from getting married until she graduates. _I could not dissuade him from his plan.
examples: I hope to dissuade her from getting married until she graduates.

distill something from something.monolingual: to derive product from something by heating and condensation. _ They distilled the lighter components from the raw oil. _The alcohol was distilled from fermented grain.
examples: They distilled the lighter components from the raw oil.

distinguish oneself among someone.monolingual: to make oneself stand out from other people because of one’s achievements. _ I hope someday to distinguish myself among my peers. _ He distinguished himself among his classmates by his many talents.
examples: I hope someday to distinguish myself among my peers.

distract someone from something.monolingual: to turn or divert someone’s attention from something. _ I hate to distract you from your work, but I have some important news. _ You haven’t distracted me from anything.
examples: I hate to distract you from your work, but I have some important news.

distribute something between someone.monolingual: to give out shares of something to two people. _He distributed the remaining cake between Dave and Don. _ Please distribute the magazines between the two boys.
examples: He distributed the remaining cake between Dave and Don.

distribute something over something.monolingual: to spread something over something or over an area. _Distribute the icing over the entire cake. _ Walter distributed the sand over the icy spots.
examples: Distribute the icing over the entire cake.

distribute something to someone.monolingual: to give out something to someone. _ Can you distribute this clothing to the needy people who live around here? _ I will distribute the ice cream to the party guests.
examples: I will distribute the ice cream to the party guests.

diverge from something.monolingual: to move in a different direction from something. _Her line of thinking diverged from generally accepted thought on this point. _ The driveway diverges from the main road beyond the fence, straight ahead.
examples: Her line of thinking diverged from generally accepted thought on this point.

diverge to something.monolingual: to turn to a particular direction. _ A narrow road diverged to the left. _ A narrower channel diverged to the left of the island.
examples: A narrow road diverged to the left.

divert something into something.monolingual: 1. to channel something into something. _ We will have to divert the runoff water into the culvert. _ Let’s divert this stream into the ditch.
examples: We will have to divert the runoff water into the culvert.

divert something onto something.monolingual: to channel something onto the surface of something. _ Temporarily, they diverted the southbound traffic onto the side streets.
examples: Temporarily, they diverted the southbound traffic onto the side streets.

divide and conquer.monolingual: to cause the enemy to divide and separate into two or more factions, and then move in to conquer all of them. _Mary thought she could divide and conquer the board of directors, but they had survived such tactics many times, and her efforts failed. _
examples: Mary thought she could divide and conquer the board of directors, but they had survived such tactics many times, and her efforts failed.

divide by something.monolingual: to perform mathematical division by a particular number. _Can you divide by sixteens? _Add this figure to the next column and divide by twenty.
examples: Add this figure to the next column and divide by twenty.

divide something by something.monolingual: to perform mathematical division on something, using a particular number. _Now, divide this sum by the figure in column seven. _ Can you divide 1,400 by 59?
examples: Now, divide this sum by the figure in column seven.

divide something with someone.monolingual: to share something with someone. _ I will divide a piece of cake with you. _ They refused to divide the ice cream with us.
examples: I will divide a piece of cake with you.

divided between something.monolingual: separated into different categories. _ The applicants for the job seemed to be divided between the overqualified and the underqualified. _ The dogs were divided evenly between terriers and poodles.
examples: The applicants for the job seemed to be divided between the overqualified and the underqualified.

divided on someone or something.monolingual: having differing opinions about someone or something. _ Our opinions are divided on what is going to happen. _ We were divided on Ann. Some of us wanted to choose her; some did not.
examples: Our opinions are divided on what is going to happen.

divorce oneself from something.monolingual: to separate oneself from something, such as an idea, policy, philosophy, etc. _She was not able to divorce herself from long-held prejudice. _ You should divorce yourself from those limiting ideas.
examples: She was not able to divorce herself from long-held prejudice.
