divulge something to someone.monolingual: to reveal something to someone. _ Promise that you will not divulge any of this to anyone. _ She refused to divulge their names to us.
examples: Promise that you will not divulge any of this to anyone.

do a double take.monolingual: to react with surprise; to have to look twice to make sure that one really saw correctly. _ When the boy led a goat into the park, everyone did a double take. _ When the nurse saw that the man had six toes, she did a double take.
examples: When the boy led a goat into the park, everyone did a double take.

do a fade.monolingual: Sl. to leave; to sneak away. _ Richard did a fade when he saw heard the police siren. _ It’s time for me to do a fade.
examples: Richard did a fade when he saw heard the police siren.

do a land-office business.monolingual: Fig. to do a large amount of buying or selling in a short period of time. _ The icecream shop always does a land-office business on a hot day. _The tax collector’s office did a land-office business on the day that taxes were due.
examples: The icecream shop always does a land-office business on a hot day.

do a slow burn.monolingual: Fig. to be quietly angry. _ I did a slow burn while I was waiting in line for a refund.
examples: I did a slow burn while I was waiting in line for a refund.

do away with oneself.monolingual: Euph. to commit suicide. _ The doctor was afraid that Betty would do away with herself. _ I wouldn’t think of doing away with myself.
examples: The doctor was afraid that Betty would do away with herself.

do away with something.monolingual: to get rid of something. _ This chemical will do away with the stain in your sink. _ The time has come to do away with that old building.
examples: This chemical will do away with the stain in your sink.

do business with someone.monolingual: to trade or bargain with someone; to conduct commerce with someone. _ You sound reasonable. I think I can do business with you. _ I am sure we can do business with one another.
examples: You sound reasonable.

do for someone.monolingual: 1. to provide for someone; to take care of or serve someone. _ Do you expect me to stay home and do for you for the rest of my life? _I can’t do for all of them!
examples: I can’t do for all of them! 2.

do for something.monolingual: to serve as something; to substitute as something. _ I think that this stone will do nicely for a doorstop. _ This stick will just not do for a stirring spoon.
examples: I think that this stone will do nicely for a doorstop.

do justice to something.monolingual: 1. Fig. to do something well; to represent or portray something accurately. _Sally did justice to our side in the contract negotiations. _ This photograph doesn’t do justice to the beauty of the mountains.
examples: Sally did justice to our side in the contract negotiations.

do one’s business.monolingual: Euph. to defecate or urinate. _ Do you need to do your business before we get in the car? _ The cat did her business on the sofa again.
examples: The cat did her business on the sofa again.

do one’s duty.monolingual: 1. to do one’s job; to do what is expected of one. _ Please don’t thank me. I’m just doing my duty. _ Soldiers who fight in wars are doing their duty.
examples: Please don’t thank me.

do oneself proud.monolingual: to have done a very fine job. _ That’s super! You’ve done yourself proud! _ I feel like I’ve done myself proud by earning high honors.
examples: I feel like I’ve done myself proud by earning high honors.

do or die.monolingual: Fig. trying as hard as one can. _ I was determined to get there—do or die. _ (Used as an attributive) He has the obsessive do-or-die attitude.
examples: I was determined to get there—do or die.

do’s and don’ts.monolingual: the rules; the things that should be done and those that should not be done. _ I must admit that a lot of do’s and don’ts at this company are hard for me to understand. _Better learn the do’s and don’ts immediately.
examples: I must admit that a lot of do’s and don’ts at this company are hard for me to understand.

do sit down..monolingual: Don’t stand on ceremony.; Please sit down. (A polite phrase encouraging people to resume their seats after rising for an introduction or out of deference.) _ Tom rose when Mary approached the table, but she said graciously, “Do sit down. I just wante
examples: Tom rose when Mary approached the table, but she said graciously, “Do sit down.

do some fine coin.monolingual: Sl. to make a large sum of money. _ When I get my big break, I’m going to do some fine coin. _ Richard did some fine coin on that last housepainting job.
examples: When I get my big break, I’m going to do some fine coin.

do somehow by someone.monolingual: to treat someone in a particular manner. (Do not confuse this with a passive construction. The someone is not the actor but the object.) _ Tom did all right by Ann when he brought her red roses. _I did badly by Tom. I fired him without good reason.
examples: Tom did all right by Ann when he brought her red roses.

do somehow for someone.monolingual: to benefit or harm someone in some degree. _ This jacket does fine for me. I don’t need a different one. _ This meal does okay for me. I’m satisfied.
examples: This jacket does fine for me.

do someone a kindness.monolingual: to do a kind deed for a person. _My neighbor did me a kindness when he cut my grass. _ I am always happy to have the opportunity of doing someone a kindness.
examples: My neighbor did me a kindness when he cut my grass.

do someone damage.monolingual: Fig. to harm someone, physically or otherwise. _ I hope she doesn’t plan to do me damage. _ They did us damage by telling the whole story to the newspapers.
examples: I hope she doesn’t plan to do me damage.

do someone good.monolingual: to benefit someone. _ A nice hot bath really does me good. _ A few years in the army would do you good.
examples: A nice hot bath really does me good.

do someone or something up†.monolingual: to make someone or something attractive; to decorate or ornament someone or something. _Sally did Jane up for the party. _Would you do up this present for Jane? It’s her birthday.
examples: Sally did Jane up for the party.

do someone out of something.monolingual: to swindle something away from someone; to defraud someone of a right or of property. _Are you trying to do me out of what’s mine? _Max tried to do her out of everything she had. _ I did myself out of a week’s vacation by quitting when I did.
examples: Max tried to do her out of everything she had.

do someone proud.monolingual: to make someone proud. _ Bill’s kids sure did him proud at the boat race. _ Mary resolved she would do her friends proud.
examples: Bill’s kids sure did him proud at the boat race.

do someone’s bidding.monolingual: to do what is requested. _ The servant grumbled but did his employer’s bidding. _ Am I expected to do your bidding whenever you ask?
examples: The servant grumbled but did his employer’s bidding.

do someone’s heart good.monolingual: Fig. to make someone feel good emotionally. _ It does my heart good to hear you two are back together. _When she sent me a get-well card, it really did my heart good.
examples: It does my heart good to hear you two are back together.

do something by hand.monolingual: to do something with one’s hands rather than with a machine. _ The calculator was broken so I had to do the calculations by hand. _All this tiny stitching was done by hand. Machines cannot do this kind of work.
examples: The calculator was broken so I had to do the calculations by hand.

do something the hard way.monolingual: to accomplish something in the most difficult manner, rather than by an easier way. _ I made it to this job the hard way. I came up through the ranks. _ She did it the hard way. She had no help from her parents.
examples: I made it to this job the hard way.

do something to excess.monolingual: to do too much of something; to consume too much of something. _ Anne often drinks to excess at parties. _ John smokes to excess when he works.
examples: Anne often drinks to excess at parties.

do something up†.monolingual: 1. to fasten, zip, hook, or button some item of clothing. _ Would you do my buttons up in back? _Please do up my buttons.
examples: Please do up my buttons.

do something up brown.monolingual: to do something just right or with great effect. (Fixed order.) _Whenever they put on a party, they do it up brown. _ He was determined to cause a scandal, and he really did it up brown.
examples: Whenever they put on a party, they do it up brown.

do something with a vengeance.monolingual: Fig. to do something with vigor; to do something energetically as if one were angry. _ Bob is building that fence with a vengeance. _ Mary is really weeding her garden with a vengeance.
examples: Bob is building that fence with a vengeance.

do tell..monolingual: a response to one of a series of statements by another person. (The expression can indicate disinterest. Each word has equal stress. See also You don’t say.) _ Bill: The Amazon basin is about ten times the size of France. Mary: Do tell.
examples: Bill: The Amazon basin is about ten times the size of France.

do the dishes.monolingual: to wash the dishes; to wash and dry the dishes, knives, forks, glasses, etc., after a meal. _Bill, you cannot go out and play until you’ve done the dishes. _Why am I always the one who has to do the dishes?
examples: Bill, you cannot go out and play until you’ve done the dishes.

do the honors.monolingual: to act as host or hostess and serve one’s guests by pouring drinks, slicing meat, making (drinking) toasts, etc. _ All the guests were seated, and a huge juicy turkey sat on the table. Jane turned to her husband and said, “Bob, will you do the honors
examples: All the guests were seated, and a huge juicy turkey sat on the table.

do the trick.monolingual: to do exactly what is needed. _ This new paint scraper really does the trick. _ Is this envelope large enough to do the trick?
examples: This new paint scraper really does the trick.

do time.monolingual: Sl. to serve a sentence in prison; to serve a specific amount of time in prison. _ Lefty had done time on a number of occasions. _ You’d better talk and talk fast if you don’t want to do time.
examples: Lefty had done time on a number of occasions.

do what?.monolingual: What did you say?; You want me to do what? _ Charlie: My mama’s coming to visit, so I want you to cook a fancy dinner. Mary: Do what? _A: Let’s perambulate. B: Do what? A: Let’s take a walk.
examples: Charlie: My mama’s coming to visit, so I want you to cook a fancy dinner.

do with someone or something.monolingual: to do as well as possible with someone or something; to make do with someone or something. _ I will just have to do with the car I now have. _ Can she do with just one chair for a while?
examples: I will just have to do with the car I now have.

do you follow?.monolingual: Fig. Do you understand what I am saying?; Do you understand my explanation? _ Mary: Keep to the right past the fork in the road, then turn right at the crossroads. Do you follow? Jane: No. Run it by me again.
examples: Mary: Keep to the right past the fork in the road, then turn right at the crossroads.

do you mind?.monolingual: 1. You are intruding on my space!; You are offending me! (Impatient or incensed. Essentially, “Do you mind stopping what you are doing?”) _ The lady behind her in line kept pushing against her every time the line moved. Finally, Sue turned and said s
examples: The lady behind her in line kept pushing against her every time the line moved.

do you read me?.monolingual: 1. Fig. an expression used by someone communicating by radio, asking if the hearer understands the transmission clearly. _Controller: This is Aurora Center, do you read me? Pilot: Yes, I read you loud and clear. _ Controller: Left two degrees. Do you
examples: Controller: This is Aurora Center, do you read me? Pilot: Yes, I read you loud and clear.

dock something from something.monolingual: to withhold money from an amount due to someone. _I will have to dock this from your paycheck. _ The boss docked ten dollars from my monthly pay.
examples: I will have to dock this from your paycheck.

doctor livingstone, i presume?.monolingual: Jocular You are who I think you are, are you not? _ Oh, there you are. Doctor Livingstone, I presume?
examples: Oh, there you are.

doctor ’s orders.monolingual: something that one is strongly advised to do as ordered or as if ordered by a doctor. _ I have to spend a month in Arizona. Doctor’s orders. _I’m doing this on doctor’s orders, but I don’t like it.
examples: I have to spend a month in Arizona.

doctor someone up†.monolingual: to give someone medical treatment, especially first aid. _ Give me a minute to doctor Fred up, and then we can continue our walk. _ I’ll doctor up Fred with a bandage; you can go on ahead.
examples: Give me a minute to doctor Fred up, and then we can continue our walk.

dodder along.monolingual: to walk along unsteadily, as in old age. _ Both of the elderly ladies doddered along very slowly. _We dodder along because we can’t go any faster.
examples: Both of the elderly ladies doddered along very slowly.

dodge behind something.monolingual: to duck behind something; to move quickly and evasively behind something. _ She dodged behind a tree to hide from Mark. _ The turkey dodged behind a tree to elude the hunter.
examples: She dodged behind a tree to hide from Mark.

does it work for you?.monolingual: Is this all right with you?; Do you agree? (Can be answered by (It) works for me.) _ Bill: I’ll be there at noon. Does it work for you? Bob: Works for me. _Mary: We’re having dinner at eight. Does it work for you? Jane: Sounds just fine.
examples: Bill: I’ll be there at noon.

doesn’t care who knows it.monolingual: doesn’t try to conceal something. (Also with don’t. Don’t used with all persons is folksy.) _ Jane dyes her hair, and she doesn’t care who knows it. _ Yeah, my old man’s in jail. I don’t care who knows it!
examples: Jane dyes her hair, and she doesn’t care who knows it.

dog and pony show.monolingual: Fig. a display, demonstration, or exhibition of something—such as something one is selling. (As in a circus act where trained dogs leap onto and off of trained ponies.) _ Gary went into his standard dog and pony show, trying to sell us on an upgrade
examples: Gary went into his standard dog and pony show, trying to sell us on an upgrade to our software.

the dog ate my homework..monolingual: a poor excuse for something that someone has failed to do on time. (From an excuse a student might give for failing to turn in homework on time. Occurs in many variations.) _ The dog ate my homework, so I have nothing to turn in. _ (Used as an attrib
examples: The dog ate my homework, so I have nothing to turn in.

dog days.monolingual: the hottest days of summer, usually during July and August. (Named for Sirius, the ‘dog star.’) _Bill spent the dog days lying out in his hammock. _I hate doing yard work in the dog days.
examples: Bill spent the dog days lying out in his hammock.

dog does not eat dog..monolingual: Prov. One disreputable person will not harm other disreputable people. _ Ellen: My lawyer did such a bad job that I want to hire another lawyer to sue him. Jane: You’ll never find a lawyer to take on that job. Dog does not eat dog.
examples: Ellen: My lawyer did such a bad job that I want to hire another lawyer to sue him.

dog in the manger.monolingual: one who unreasonably prevents other people from doing or having what one does not wish them to do or have. (From one of Aesop’s fables in which a dog—which cannot eat hay—lay in the hayrack [manger] and prevented the other animals from eating the hay
examples: Jane is a real dog in the manger.

dog my cats!.monolingual: Rur.My goodness!; What do you know! (An exclamation of surprise.) _ Dog my cats! Somebody painted my house green! _ Well, dog my cats—it hasn’t rained once all month!

dog-eat-dog.monolingual: Fig. a situation in which one has to act ruthlessly in order to survive or succeed; ruthless competition. _ It is dog-eat-dog in the world of business these days. _ Universities are not quiet peaceful places. It’s dog-eat-dog to get a promotion.
examples: It is dog-eat-dog in the world of business these days.

dog-faced liar.monolingual: Rur. a terrible liar. _Suzy said Jimmy was a dog-faced liar. _ If Joe says that, he’s a dog-faced liar.
examples: Suzy said Jimmy was a dog-faced liar.

a doggy bag.monolingual: a bag or other container used to carry uneaten food home from a restaurant. (As if it is for the dog.) _I can’t eat all of this. Can I have a doggy bag, please?
examples: I can’t eat all of this.

doll someone up†.monolingual: to dress someone up in fancy clothes. _ She dolled her children up for church each Sunday. _ She dolls up all her kids once a week.
examples: She dolled her children up for church each Sunday.

dollar for dollar.monolingual: considering the amount of money involved; considering the cost or value. (Often seen in advertising.) _ Dollar for dollar, you cannot buy a better car. _ Dollar for dollar, this laundry detergent washes cleaner and brighter than any other product on
examples: Dollar for dollar, you cannot buy a better car.

done and gone.monolingual: Rur. gone. _She’s not here. She’s done and gone. _ Jed was done and gone before dawn.
examples: She’s not here. She’s done and gone.

a done deal.monolingual: a completed deal; something that is settled. _ It’s too late. It’s a done deal. _ The sale of the property is a done deal. There is nothing that can be done now.
examples: It’s too late. It’s a done deal.

done for.monolingual: finished; dead. _ I’m afraid that animal hit by the car is done for. _ The goldfish looked as if it was either done for or sunning its tummy.
examples: I’m afraid that animal hit by the car is done for.

*done in.monolingual: exhausted. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ I’m really done in! I think I’ll go to bed. _ After all that lifting, Gerald was done in and breathing hard.
examples: I’m really done in! I think I’ll go to bed.

done ’n’ did.monolingual: Rur. already did. _ Tom: Guess I better take the garbage out. Bill: No need. I done ’n’ did it. _Mary done ’n’ did the chores for you.
examples: Tom: Guess I better take the garbage out.

done over.monolingual: Sl. beat; outscored. _The other team was done over, and they showed it in their lackluster play.
examples: The other team was done over, and they showed it in their lackluster play.

done to a t.monolingual: cooked just right. _Yummy! This meat is done to a T. _ I like it done to a T, not too done and not too raw.
examples: Yummy! This meat is done to a T.

done to a turn.monolingual: 1. well-cooked; nicely cooked. _ The entire meal was done to a turn. _ The turkey was done to a turn.
examples: The entire meal was done to a turn.

done told you.monolingual: Rur. have already told you something. _ I done told you not to touch that pan, and you went and did it anyhow. _Sally done told you to leave that dog alone.
examples: I done told you not to touch that pan, and you went and did it anyhow.

done with someone or something.monolingual: finished with someone or something. _Mary is done with Bill. She has found another boyfriend. _ I can’t wait until I’m done with school forever. _ I agree. I’ll be glad when we are done with all these exams.
examples: Mary is done with Bill.

don’t ask..monolingual: It is so bad, I do not wish to be reminded or talk about it, so do not ask about it. _John: How was your class reunion? Alice: Oh, heavens! Don’t ask. _ Tom: What was your calculus final exam like? Mary: Don’t ask.
examples: John: How was your class reunion? Alice: Oh, heavens! Don’t ask.

don’t be too sure..monolingual: I think you are wrong, so do not sound so certain.; You may be wrong. (Compare this with Don’t speak too soon.) _ Bill: I think I’ve finally saved up enough money to retire. John: Don’t be too sure. Inf lation can ruin your savings.
examples: Bill: I think I’ve finally saved up enough money to retire.

don’t bother..monolingual: Please don’t do it. It is not necessary, and it is too much trouble. _ Mary: Should I make some dinner for you? Bill: No, don’t bother; it’s late. _Sue: Do you want me to save this spoonful of mashed potatoes? Jane: No, don’t bother. It isn’t worth i
examples: Mary: Should I make some dinner for you? Bill: No, don’t bother; it’s late.

don’t bother me!.monolingual: Go away!; Leave me alone! _ Tom: Hey, Bill! Bill: Don’t bother me! I’m busy. Can’t you see? _ “Don’t bother me! Leave me alone!” the child shouted at the dog.
examples: Tom: Hey, Bill! Bill: Don’t bother me! I’m busy.

don’t even look like something!.monolingual: Do not even appear to be doing something! (The something can be thinking about something or actually doing something.) _ Mary: Are you thinking about taking that last piece of cake? Bob: Of course not. Mary: Well, don’t even look like you’re doing it
examples: Mary: Are you thinking about taking that last piece of cake? Bob: Of course not.

don’t give a continental.monolingual: Rur. does not care at all. (Also with doesn’t. Don’t used with all persons is folksy.) _ I don’t give a continental if I never see him again. _ Mary’s kids can do whatever they want. She doesn’t give a continental.
examples: I don’t give a continental if I never see him again.

don’t give up!.monolingual: Do not stop trying!; Keep trying! _ John: Get in there and give it another try. Don’t give up! Bill: Okay. Okay. But it’s hopeless. _ Jane: I asked the boss for a raise, but he said no. Tom: Don’t give up. Try again later.
examples: John: Get in there and give it another try.

don’t give up the ship!.monolingual: Fig. Do not give up yet!; Do not yield the entire enterprise! (Fixed order. Alludes to the words on a flag made by Captain Oliver Hazard Perry in the Battle of Lake Erie during the War of 1812.) _ Bill: I’m having a devil of a time with calculus. I t
examples: Bill: I’m having a devil of a time with calculus.

don’t have a cow!.monolingual: Calm down!; Don’t get so excited! (Made famous in the television show, The Simpsons.) _ Chill out, man! Don’t have a cow! _ Aw, don’t have a cow, Dad!

don’t hold your breath..monolingual: Fig. Do not stop breathing waiting for something to happen that won’t happen. (Meaning that it will take longer for it to happen than you can possibly hold your breath.) _ Tom: The front yard is such a mess. Bob: Bill’s supposed to rake the leaves. T
examples: Tom: The front yard is such a mess.

don’t i know it!.monolingual: I know that very well! _ Mary: Goodness gracious! It’s hot today. Bob: Don’t I know it! _ Sue: You seem to be putting on a little weight. John: Don’t I know it!
examples: Mary: Goodness gracious! It’s hot today.

don’t knock it..monolingual: Don’t criticize it. _ You don’t want any okra? Don’t knock it.
examples: You don’t want any okra? Don’t knock it.

don’t make me laugh!.monolingual: That is a stupid suggestion! _ You a judge? Don’t make me laugh! _Don’t make me laugh. Tom could never do that.
examples: Don’t make me laugh.

don’t mention it..monolingual: You are welcome and your thanks are not necessary. _ A: Thank you so much! B: Don’t mention it.
examples: A: Thank you so much! B: Don’t mention it.

don’t mind me..monolingual: Don’t pay any attention to me.; Just ignore me. (Sometimes sarcastic.) _ Bill and Jane were watching television when Jane’s mother walked through the room, grabbing the newspaper on the way. “Don’t mind me,” she said.
examples: Bill and Jane were watching television when Jane’s mother walked through the room, grabbing the newspaper on the way.

don’t rush me!.monolingual: Don’t try to hurry me! _ Bill: Hurry up! Make up your mind! Bob: Don’t rush me! Bill: I want to get out of here before midnight. _Bill: The waiter wants to take your order. What do you want? Jane: Don’t rush me! I can’t make up my mind. Waiter: I’ll
examples: Bill: Hurry up! Make up your mind! Bob: Don’t rush me! Bill: I want to get out of here before midnight.

don’t say it!.monolingual: I don’t want to hear it!; I know, so you don’t have to say it. _ John (joking): What is that huge pile of stuff on your head? Bill: Don’t say it! I know I need a haircut.
examples: John (joking): What is that huge pile of stuff on your head? Bill: Don’t say it! I know I need a haircut.

don’t speak too soon..monolingual: I think you may be wrong. Don’t speak before you know the facts. (Compare this with Don’t be too sure.) _ Bill: It looks like it’ll be a nice day. Mary: Don’t speak too soon. I just felt a raindrop. _ Tom: It looks like we made it home without any pr
examples: Bill: It looks like it’ll be a nice day.

don’t stand on ceremony..monolingual: Do not wait for a formal invitation.; Please be at ease and make yourself at home. (Some people read this as “Don’t remain standing because of ceremony,” and others read it “Don’t be totally obedient to the requirements of ceremony.”) _ Come in, Tom.
examples: Come in, Tom. Don’t stand on ceremony.

don’t stay away so long..monolingual: Rur. Please visit more often. (Said upon the arrival or departure of a guest.) _ John: Hi, Bill! Long time no see. Don’t stay away so long! Bill: Thanks, John. Good to see you. _ Mary: I had a nice time. Thanks for inviting me. Sally: Good to see you
examples: John: Hi, Bill! Long time no see.

don’t sweat it!.monolingual: Inf. Don’t worry about it! _ No problem. Don’t sweat it! _ Don’t sweat it! We’ll take care of it.
examples: Don’t sweat it! We’ll take care of it.

don’t take any wooden nickels..monolingual: Prov. Be careful and do not let anyone cheat you. (Often used as a jocular way of saying good-bye.) _ Tom: So long. Bill: Don’t take any wooden nickels. _ Good luck in college. Don’t take any wooden nickels.
examples: Tom: So long. Bill: Don’t take any wooden nickels.

don’t tell a soul..monolingual: Please do not tell anyone this gossip. _ Bill: Is your brother getting married? Sally: Yes, but don’t tell a soul. It’s a secret. _Mary: Can you keep a secret? John: Sure. Mary: Don’t tell a soul, but Tom is in jail.
examples: Bill: Is your brother getting married? Sally: Yes, but don’t tell a soul.

don’t touch that dial!.monolingual: 1. Lit. Do not change your radio or television dial, but continue to listen to this station. (From broadcasts in the days when tuning was done with a dial.) _Don’t touch that dial. Stay tuned for The Adventures of Blondie.
examples: Don’t touch that dial.

don’t waste my time..monolingual: Do not take up my valuable time with a poor presentation.; Do not waste my time trying to get me to do something. _Bob: I’d like to show you our new line of industrial-strength vacuum cleaners. Bill: Beat it! Don’t waste my time. _“Don’t waste my tim
examples: Bob: I’d like to show you our new line of industrial-strength vacuum cleaners.

don’t waste your breath..monolingual: You will not get a positive response to what you have to say, so don’t even say it.; Talking will get you nowhere. _ Alice: I’ll go in there and try to convince her otherwise. Fred: Don’t waste your breath. I already tried it. _ Sally: No, I won’t ag
examples: Alice: I’ll go in there and try to convince her otherwise.

don’t waste your time..monolingual: You will not get anywhere with it, so don’t waste time trying. _ Mary: Should I ask Tom if he wants to go to the convention, or is he still in a bad mood? Sally: Don’t waste your time. Mary: Bad mood, huh? _ Jane: I’m having trouble fixing this doork
examples: Mary: Should I ask Tom if he wants to go to the convention, or is he still in a bad mood? Sally: Don’t waste your time.

don’t work too hard..monolingual: an expression said at the end of a conversation after or in place of good-bye. _ Mary: Bye, Tom. Tom: Bye, Mary. Don’t work too hard.
examples: Mary: Bye, Tom.

don’t you know it!.monolingual: You can be absolutely sure about that!; You’re exactly right, and I agree with you. (This is not a question.) _ Alice: Man, is it hot! Fred: Don’t you know it! _ Bob: This is the best cake I have ever eaten. The cook is the best in the world! Bill: D
examples: Bob: This is the best cake I have ever eaten.

don’t you wish!.monolingual: Don’t you wish that what you have just said were really true? _ Mary: I’m going to get a job that lets me travel a lot. Sally: Don’t you wish! _Sally: Sorry you lost the chess game. It was close, but your opponent was topnotch. Bob: Next time, I’ll d
examples: Mary: I’m going to get a job that lets me travel a lot.

doomed to something.monolingual: condemned to something; facing something as a future or as a consequence [of something]. _The project was doomed to failure from the start. _I am doomed to a life of hard work and low pay.
examples: The project was doomed to failure from the start.

door-to-door.monolingual: 1. Lit. having to do with movement from one door to another or from one house to another. _John is a door-to-door salesman. _ We spent two weeks making a door-to-door survey.
examples: John is a door-to-door salesman.

dope something out†.monolingual: 1. Sl. to figure something out. _ He spent a lot of time trying to dope the assignment out so he could understand it. _It’s hard to dope out a physics assignment after midnight.
examples: He spent a lot of time trying to dope the assignment out so he could understand it.

dork off.monolingual: Sl. to waste time; to goof off. _ Stop dorking off and get busy. _ The whole class was dorking off and the teacher got furious.
examples: Stop dorking off and get busy.

dot something with something.monolingual: to put little bits or dots of something on something. _ She dotted her face with red marks to make it look as if she had measles. _The chef dotted the cake with blobs of buttery icing.
examples: She dotted her face with red marks to make it look as if she had measles.

double as someone or something.monolingual: [for someone] to serve in two capacities. _The chairman will have to double as CEO until we find a new one. _This table doubles as a desk during busy times.
examples: The chairman will have to double as CEO until we find a new one.

double dutch.monolingual: 1. language or speech that is difficult or impossible to understand. _ This book on English grammar is written in double Dutch. I can’t understand a word. _ Try to find a lecturer who speaks slowly, not one who speaks double Dutch.
examples: This book on English grammar is written in double Dutch.

double over.monolingual: [for a person] to bend at the waist. _ Suddenly, he doubled over and collapsed. _ The people in the audience doubled over with laughter.
examples: Suddenly, he doubled over and collapsed.

double someone over†.monolingual: to cause someone to bend at the waist. _ The blow to the back of the head doubled Steve over. _ The wind almost doubled over the children running for home.
examples: The blow to the back of the head doubled Steve over.

double something over†.monolingual: to fold something over. _ Double the paper over twice, then press it f lat. _ Double over the cloth a few times before you pack it away.
examples: Double the paper over twice, then press it f lat.

a double whammy.monolingual: a double dose of something; a strong or powerful helping of something. _ When the Federal Reserve Board raised the interest rates, I got a double whammy. My stocks went down and my bonds did too.
examples: When the Federal Reserve Board raised the interest rates, I got a double whammy.

double-cross someone.monolingual: to betray someone. (Originally a more complicated switching of sides in a conspiracy wherein the double-crosser sides with the victim of the conspiracy—against the original conspirator.) _ Don’t even think about double-crossing me! _ Richard doublecr
examples: Richard doublecrossed Mr.

doubting thomas.monolingual: someone who will not easily believe something without strong proof or evidence. (Can be said of a man or a woman. From the biblical account of the apostle Thomas, who would not believe that Jesus had risen from the dead until he actually touched the
examples: Mary won’t believe that I have a dog until she sees it.

dovetail something into something.monolingual: Fig. to fit something neatly into something; to make something interlock nicely with something else. _ She dovetailed her story into mine perfectly and the police let us go.
examples: She dovetailed her story into mine perfectly and the police let us go.

dovetail with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to interlock tightly with something using a dovetail joint. _The side of the drawer dovetails with the front of the drawer.
examples: The side of the drawer dovetails with the front of the drawer.

down and dirty.monolingual: crude and carelessly done. _ (Used as an attributive.) The last time he painted the kitchen, it was a down and dirty job because he thought we were moving. Fig. coarse; mean-spirited. _ The campaign for governor really got down and dirty in the final
examples: (Used as an attributive.

down by some amount.monolingual: having a score that is lower, by the specified amount, than someone else’s score or the other team’s score. _ At halftime, the home team was down by 14 points. _Down by one run, the team scored two runs in the ninth inning and won the game.
examples: At halftime, the home team was down by 14 points.

down for something.monolingual: having one’s name written down for something. _ Am I down for an evening appointment? _ You are down for Friday.
examples: You are down for Friday.

*down in the dumps.monolingual: Fig. sad or depressed. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _I’ve been down in the dumps for the past few days. _ Try to cheer Jane up. She’s down in the dumps for some reason.
examples: I’ve been down in the dumps for the past few days.

down in the mouth.monolingual: Fig. sad-faced; depressed and unsmiling. _ Since her dog died, Barbara has been down in the mouth. _ Bob has been down in the mouth since he was laid off from his job.
examples: Since her dog died, Barbara has been down in the mouth.

down on one’s luck.monolingual: without any money; unlucky. _Can you lend me twenty dollars? I’ve been down on my luck lately. _ The gambler had to get a job because he had been down on his luck and hadn’t won enough money to live on.
examples: Can you lend me twenty dollars? I’ve been down on my luck lately.

*down pat.monolingual: learned or memorized perfectly. (*Typically: get something ~; have something ~.) _I have practiced my speech until I have it down pat. _ Tom has his part in the play down pat. He won’t make any mistakes.
examples: I have practiced my speech until I have it down pat.

down south.monolingual: to or at the southeastern United States. _ I used to live down South. _We are going down South for the winter.
examples: I used to live down South.

down the chute.monolingual: Fig. gone; wasted; ruined. _ A lot of money went down the chute on that deal, and all for nothing. _ I just hate to see all that effort go down the chute.
examples: A lot of money went down the chute on that deal, and all for nothing.

down the drain.monolingual: Fig. gone; wasted. _ Well, there’s 400 bucks down the drain. _ A lot of money went down the drain in that Wilson deal.
examples: Well, there’s 400 bucks down the drain.

down the hatch..monolingual: I am about to drink this.; Let’s all drink up. (Said as one is about to take a drink, especially of something bad-tasting or potent. Also used as a jocular toast.) _Bob said, “Down the hatch,” and drank the whiskey in one gulp. _ Let’s toast the brid
examples: Bob said, “Down the hatch,” and drank the whiskey in one gulp.

down the little red lane.monolingual: Fig. down someone’s throat; down a child’s throat. _ This really tasty medicine has to go down the little red lane. _The last spoonful of that stuff that went down the little red lane came right back up.
examples: This really tasty medicine has to go down the little red lane.

down the road.monolingual: 1. Lit. farther along on this same road. _ Just continue down the road until you come to a little church. Turn left there.
examples: Just continue down the road until you come to a little church.

down the street.monolingual: a short distance away on this same street. _Sally lives just down the street. _There is a drugstore down the street. It’s very convenient.
examples: Sally lives just down the street.

down to a gnat’s eyebrow.monolingual: Fig. down to the smallest detail. _ He described what the thief was wearing down to a gnat’s eyebrow. _ No use trying to sneak anything out of the refrigerator. Mom knows what’s in there, down to a gnat’s eyebrow.
examples: He described what the thief was wearing down to a gnat’s eyebrow.

down to chili and beans.monolingual: Rur. very poor; down to one’s last penny. _Mary and Tom aren’t doing too well. They’re down to chili and beans. _ Many’s the time I was down to chili and beans, but I always pulled through.
examples: Mary and Tom aren’t doing too well.

down to the last detail.monolingual: considering all of the details. _ Jean planned the party very carefully, down to the last minute. _Mary wanted to be in charge of everything right down to the last detail.
examples: Jean planned the party very carefully, down to the last minute.

down under.monolingual: Australia and New Zealand. _ I’ve always wanted to visit down under. _ We spent Christmas down under.
examples: I’ve always wanted to visit down under.

*down with a disease.monolingual: ill; sick at home. (Can be said about many diseases. *Typically: be ~; come ~; get ~.) _ Tom isn’t here. He’s down with a cold. _ Sally is down with the f lu.
examples: Tom isn’t here.

down with someone or something!.monolingual: Do away with someone or something!; I am opposed to someone or something! _Down with higher taxes! Down with corporate tax breaks! _ Down with tyrants!

down-and-out.monolingual: 1. having no money or means of support. _ There are many young people down-and-out in the city. _John gambled away all his fortune and is now completely down-and-out.
examples: There are many young people down-and-out in the city.

*down-at-the-heels.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of shoes] worn on the bottom of the heels. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _This pair is a little down-at-the-heels, but I only use them for gardening.
examples: This pair is a little down-at-the-heels, but I only use them for gardening.

downhill all the way.monolingual: Fig. easy the entire way. _ Don’t worry about your algebra course. It’s downhill all the way after this chapter. _ The mayor said that the job of mayor is easy—in fact, downhill all the way.
examples: Don’t worry about your algebra course.

downhill from here on.monolingual: Fig. easy from this point on. _ The worst part is over. It’s downhill from here on. _ The painful part of this procedure is over. It’s downhill from here on.
examples: The worst part is over.

down-home.monolingual: as one would find in rural, especially southern, America. _ She speaks with a kind of down-home accent that sounds more friendly than the typical, urban northener.
examples: She speaks with a kind of down-home accent that sounds more friendly than the typical, urban northener.

downtime.monolingual: the time when a computer or some other system is not operating. (Computer jargon.) _ I can’t afford a lot of downtime in the system I buy. _ We had too much downtime with the other machine.
examples: I can’t afford a lot of downtime in the system I buy.

down-to-earth.monolingual: 1. Fig. direct, frank, and honest. _ You can depend on Ann. She’s very down-to-earth. _ It’s good that she’s down-to-earth and will give us a frank response.
examples: You can depend on Ann.

*down-to-the-wire.monolingual: Fig. waiting until the very last moment; right up to the deadline. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ It came down-to-the-wire before I turned the proposal in. _ We went right down-to-the-wire on that one.
examples: It came down-to-the-wire before I turned the proposal in.

draft someone for something.monolingual: to select someone for something or to do something. _We drafted a bunch of the boys for moving tables. _ The committee drafted some of the members for kitchen work.
examples: We drafted a bunch of the boys for moving tables.

draft someone into something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to conscript someone into the armed services. _ The draft board drafted Scott into the army. _ Todd was drafted into the army.
examples: The draft board drafted Scott into the army.

drag behind.monolingual: to follow along close behind someone. _His little brother came along, dragging behind. _Stop dragging along behind!
examples: His little brother came along, dragging behind.

drag someone or something down†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to pull someone or something to the ground or to a lower level. _The lions dragged the antelope down and made dinner out of it. _ They dragged down the boxes from the closet shelf.
examples: The lions dragged the antelope down and made dinner out of it.

drag someone through the mud.monolingual: Fig. to insult, defame, and debase someone. _The newspapers dragged the actress through the mud week after week. _ The columnist felt it was her duty to drag people through the mud.
examples: The newspapers dragged the actress through the mud week after week.

drag someone up†.monolingual: to force someone to come up or to come and stand nearby. _ He wouldn’t come on his own, so I dragged him up. _ You will have to drag him up. He is too tired to walk by himself. _The reporter dragged up a homeless man to interview.
examples: He wouldn’t come on his own, so I dragged him up.

drag something behind one.monolingual: to pull something that is behind one. _ The child dragged the wooden toy behind him. _ What is that you are dragging behind you?
examples: The child dragged the wooden toy behind him.

drag something up†.monolingual: to pull something close, such as a chair, stool, etc., to sit in. _ Please drag a chair up and sit down. _ Drag up a chair and sit for a while.
examples: Please drag a chair up and sit down.

dragged out.monolingual: Sl. exhausted; worn out. _ I feel so dragged out. I think I need some sleep. _ After the game, the whole team was dragged out.
examples: I feel so dragged out.

dragoon someone into something.monolingual: to force someone into doing something. _ We dragooned the boys into helping us. _ She was trying to dragoon some of the men into setting up the banquet tables.
examples: We dragooned the boys into helping us.

drain away.monolingual: [for something] to flow away. _All the water drained away and exposed the mud and rocks on the bottom of the pond. _When the water drained away, we found three snapping turtles in the bottom of the pond.
examples: All the water drained away and exposed the mud and rocks on the bottom of the pond.

drain from something.monolingual: to flow out of something. _ All the dirty oil drained from the engine. _The milk drained from the leaky container and covered the bottom of the refrigerator.
examples: All the dirty oil drained from the engine.

drain out.monolingual: to flow out or empty. _All the milk drained out of the container onto the bottom of the refrigerator. _ All the oil drained out of the crankcase.
examples: All the milk drained out of the container onto the bottom of the refrigerator.

drain something of something.monolingual: to empty something out of something. _ He drained the glass of the remaining beer.
examples: He drained the glass of the remaining beer.

drape oneself over something.monolingual: to sprawl on a piece of furniture. _He draped himself over the armchair and dropped off to sleep. _He came in and casually draped himself over grandmother’s antique chair.
examples: He draped himself over the armchair and dropped off to sleep.

draw a blank.monolingual: 1. Fig. to get no response; to find nothing. _ I asked him about Tom’s financial problems, and I just drew a blank. _ We looked in the files for an hour, but we drew a blank.
examples: I asked him about Tom’s financial problems, and I just drew a blank.

draw blood.monolingual: 1. Lit. to hit or bite (a person or an animal) and make a wound that bleeds. _ The dog chased me and bit me hard, but it didn’t draw blood. _ The boxer landed just one punch and drew blood immediately.
examples: The dog chased me and bit me hard, but it didn’t draw blood.

draw interest.monolingual: 1. to appear interesting and get (someone’s) attention. (Note the variation in the examples.) _ This kind of event isn’t likely to draw a lot of interest. _ What kind of show will draw public interest?
examples: This kind of event isn’t likely to draw a lot of interest.

draw people or things together†.monolingual: to pull people together; to pull things together. _ She drew her toys together in preparation for leaving. _ She drew together all the people she wanted to talk to.
examples: She drew her toys together in preparation for leaving.

draw someone aside†.monolingual: to pull or steer someone aside. _ The teacher drew Bob aside to have a word with him. _ Harry drew aside someone he could trust and expressed his fears.
examples: The teacher drew Bob aside to have a word with him.

draw someone together.monolingual: to make people seek one another for emotional support. _The tragic accident drew the family all together. _Do you think the crisis actually will draw us closer together?
examples: The tragic accident drew the family all together.

draw something apart†.monolingual: to pull something, such as curtains or drapes, open or apart. _ She drew the curtains apart and looked out the window. _ She drew apart the curtains a little bit.
examples: She drew the curtains apart and looked out the window.

draw something down†.monolingual: to pull something down. _ She drew the shades down to cut off the bright sunlight. _ She drew down the shades.
examples: She drew the shades down to cut off the bright sunlight.

draw something forth†.monolingual: to pull something forward or where it can be seen. _ Carl drew a booklet forth and began to show it to the people sitting on either side of him. _ She drew forth her pocketknife and threatened the bandit.
examples: Carl drew a booklet forth and began to show it to the people sitting on either side of him.

draw something to.monolingual: to close or nearly close something, such as curtains, drapes, etc. _ She drew the drapes to and turned on the lights. _Please draw the door to as you leave, but don’t shut it all the way.
examples: She drew the drapes to and turned on the lights.

draw something to a close.monolingual: to make something come to an end. _ It is time we drew this evening to a close. _ Ann drew the meeting to a close with a few words of encouragement.
examples: It is time we drew this evening to a close.

draw something to someone’s attention.monolingual: to make someone aware of something. _ Please draw this error to the clerk’s attention.
examples: Please draw this error to the clerk’s attention.

draw something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to pull something close by, such as a chair, stool, etc. _ Draw a chair up and sit down. _ She drew up a pillow and sat on the f loor.
examples: Draw a chair up and sit down.

draw straws for something.monolingual: Fig. to decide who gets something or must do something by choosing straws from an unseen set of straws of different lengths. (The person who gets the shortest straw is chosen. See also draw lots.) _ We drew straws for the privilege of going first. _L
examples: We drew straws for the privilege of going first.

draw to a close.monolingual: to end; to come to an end. _ This evening is drawing to a close. _ It’s a shame that our vacation is drawing to a close.
examples: This evening is drawing to a close.

draw up.monolingual: to pull up more tightly; to shrink up. _ When they got wet, his trunks drew up and became very tight. _ This cheap underwear has a tendency to draw up.
examples: When they got wet, his trunks drew up and became very tight.

a drawing card.monolingual: Fig. an attraction that helps bring patrons to a place of entertainment. _ The comedian was a real drawing card at the night club.
examples: The comedian was a real drawing card at the night club.

*drawn and quartered.monolingual: Fig. to be dealt with very severely. (Now fig. except in historical accounts; refers to a former practice of torturing someone guilty of treason, usually a male, by disembowling and dividing the body into four parts. *Typically: be ~; have someone ~.
examples: Todd was practically drawn and quartered for losing the Wilson contract.

a dream come true.monolingual: Fig. a wish or a dream that has become a reality. _ My vacation to Hawaii was like a dream come true. _Having you for a friend is a dream come true.
examples: My vacation to Hawaii was like a dream come true.

dream of doing something.monolingual: Fig. to have a fantasy of doing something. _ I dream of owning a house like that. _ Clara dreamed of sailing off into the sunset with Roger.
examples: I dream of owning a house like that.

dream on..monolingual: What you are expecting or wanting to happen is nothing but fantasy. _You want to get promoted to general manager? Dream on. _ You, an opera singer? Dream on.
examples: You want to get promoted to general manager? Dream on.

dream something away†.monolingual: Fig. to waste away a period of time having fantasies. _ I just want to sit in the sun and dream the day away. _ Don’t dream away your life!
examples: I just want to sit in the sun and dream the day away.

dream something up†.monolingual: Fig. to invent something; to fabricate something. (The something can be the word something.) _ I don’t know what to do, but I’ll dream something up. _ Please dream up a solution for this problem.
examples: I don’t know what to do, but I’ll dream something up.

dredge someone or something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to scoop something up from underwater. _The workers dredged the lifeless body up from the cold black water. _ They dredged up the mud from the riverbed.
examples: The workers dredged the lifeless body up from the cold black water.

dress for someone.monolingual: to clothe oneself to please someone. _ I don’t dress for you! Don’t tell me how I should look! _Sally says she dresses for her friends, but she really dresses for herself.
examples: Sally says she dresses for her friends, but she really dresses for herself.

dress for something.monolingual: to clothe oneself suitably for some occasion or activity, or for success. _ Finally, I learned to dress for success. _I can wear my tuxedo if you want me to dress for the formal dinner.
examples: Finally, I learned to dress for success.

dress someone down†.monolingual: to bawl someone out; to give someone a good scolding. _The drill sergeant dressed down the entire squadron for failing inspection. _ I’m really late. I know my parents will dress me down when I get home.
examples: The drill sergeant dressed down the entire squadron for failing inspection.

dress someone or something up†.monolingual: to make someone or something appear fancier than is actually so. _ The publicity specialist dressed the actress up a lot. _ They dressed up the hall so it looked like a ballroom.
examples: The publicity specialist dressed the actress up a lot.

a dressing-down.monolingual: a harsh scolding. _ The boss gave the entire sales crew a powerful dressing-down for missing their forecast.
examples: The boss gave the entire sales crew a powerful dressing-down for missing their forecast.

drift along.monolingual: to float along; to be carried along on no particular course. _The boat just drifted along lazily with the current. _ The project drifted along until we received the leadership we needed.
examples: The boat just drifted along lazily with the current.

drift off.monolingual: to move slowly away. _ The boat slowly drifted off and was gone. _The clouds drifted off and the sun came out.
examples: The boat slowly drifted off and was gone.

drift off to sleep.monolingual: Fig. to fall asleep gradually. _ At last, he drifted off to sleep. _During that boring lecture, I drifted off to sleep a number of times.
examples: At last, he drifted off to sleep.

drift out.monolingual: to move out of a place slowly. _ After there was no more food, the people drifted out, one by one. _The boat drifted out and almost got away.
examples: After there was no more food, the people drifted out, one by one.

drift toward someone or something.monolingual: to move slowly and gradually toward someone or something. _ The clouds drifted toward us, and we could see that a storm was coming. _ As the clouds drifted toward us, we could feel the humidity increase.
examples: The clouds drifted toward us, and we could see that a storm was coming.

drift with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to float along with something; to be carried along at the same rate as something. _ He paddled the canoe into the center of the stream and let it drift with the current.
examples: He paddled the canoe into the center of the stream and let it drift with the current.

drill someone in something.monolingual: to give someone practice in something. _ Now, I am going to drill you in irregular verbs. _ The teacher drilled the students in the use of the passive.
examples: Now, I am going to drill you in irregular verbs.

drink like a fish.monolingual: Fig. to drink alcohol excessively; to be in the habit of drinking alcohol excessively. _ Jeff really drank like a fish at the party on Saturday. _ I worry about Nancy; she drinks like a fish.
examples: Jeff really drank like a fish at the party on Saturday.

drink someone under the table.monolingual: Fig. to be able to drink more alcohol than someone else. _ I bet I can drink you under the table.
examples: I bet I can drink you under the table.

drink something down†.monolingual: to drink something; to consume all of something by drinking it. _ Here, drink this down, and see if it makes you feel better. _Drink down this medicine.
examples: Here, drink this down, and see if it makes you feel better.

drink something in†.monolingual: Fig. to absorb something; to take in information, sights, a story, etc. _ Terry and Amy drove up to the top of the hill to drink the sights in. _They drank in the beautiful view.
examples: Terry and Amy drove up to the top of the hill to drink the sights in.

drink something up†.monolingual: to drink all of something that is served or that is on hand. _ Who drank all the root beer up? _ I drank up the root beer.
examples: I drank up the root beer.

drink to excess.monolingual: Euph. to drink too much alcohol; to drink alcohol continually. _Mr. Franklin drinks to excess. _ Some people drink to excess only at parties.
examples: Mr. Franklin drinks to excess.

drink to someone or something.monolingual: to toast someone or something; to take an alcoholic drink in honor of someone or something. _I’ll drink to that! _Let us drink to our guest of honor, Wallace J. Wilson!
examples: Let us drink to our guest of honor, Wallace J.

drink up!.monolingual: Finish your drink!; Finish that drink, and we’ll have another! _Okay, drink up! It’s closing time. _Drink up, and let’s get going.
examples: Okay, drink up! It’s closing time.

drip with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to be heavy or overloaded with something to the point of overflowing. _ The foliage dripped with the heavy morning dew. _ Her clothing dripped with seawater as she climbed back onto the deck.
examples: The foliage dripped with the heavy morning dew.

drive a hard bargain.monolingual: to work hard to negotiate prices or agreements in one’s own favor. _All right, sir, you drive a hard bargain. I’ll sell you this car for $12,450. _You drive a hard bargain, Jane, but I’ll sign the contract.
examples: All right, sir, you drive a hard bargain.

drive a price down†.monolingual: Fig. to force the price of something down. _ The lack of buyers drove the price down. _ The lack of buyers drove down the price.
examples: The lack of buyers drove the price down.

drive at something.monolingual: to be making a point; to be hinting at something; to work up to making a point. _What are you driving at? What’s the point? _ I could tell Mary was driving at something, but I didn’t know what it was.
examples: I could tell Mary was driving at something, but I didn’t know what it was.

drive away.monolingual: to leave some place driving a vehicle. _ They got in the car and drove away. _ They drove away and left us here.
examples: They got in the car and drove away.

drive back.monolingual: to go in a vehicle back to where it started. _ Mary drove back and parked the car where it had been when she started. _ You drive us there and I’ll drive back.
examples: Mary drove back and parked the car where it had been when she started.

drive into someone or something.monolingual: to strike someone or something while driving. _ She drove into the garage and damaged the wall. _ Accidentally, Fred drove into Max.
examples: She drove into the garage and damaged the wall.

drive off.monolingual: to leave somewhere, driving a vehicle. _ She got in her car and drove off. _ Please don’t drive off and leave me!
examples: She got in her car and drove off.

drive on.monolingual: to continue driving; to continue with one’s journey. _ We drove on for a little while. _ The traffic jam is breaking up, so we can drive on.
examples: We drove on for a little while.

drive safely..monolingual: an expression used to advise a departing person to be careful while driving. _ Mary: Good-bye, Sally. Drive safely. Sally: Good-bye. I will. _“Drive safely!” everyone shouted as we left on our trip.
examples: Mary: Good-bye, Sally.

drive someone around something.monolingual: to transport a person in a vehicle on a tour of something or some place. _ Fred will drive you around the city to see the sights. _ He spent an hour driving himself around town.
examples: Fred will drive you around the city to see the sights.

drive someone around the bend.monolingual: Fig. to make someone angry or very frustrated. _ This tax stuff is about to drive me around the bend. _ Gert will drive us all around the bend with her constant complaining.
examples: This tax stuff is about to drive me around the bend.

drive someone back on something.monolingual: to force someone to tap reserves of something. _ The hard times drove them back on their life savings. _ The challenges of being a corporate executive drove her back on all her personal resources.
examples: The hard times drove them back on their life savings.

drive someone back to someone.monolingual: to force someone to return to someone, such as a spouse, lover, parent, etc. _ Her bad experience with her new friend drove her back to her husband. _Being homeless was no fun, and soon Wally was driven back to his parents.
examples: Her bad experience with her new friend drove her back to her husband.

drive someone into a corner.monolingual: 1. Lit. to force someone into the place where two walls intersect. _They drove him into a corner and captured him there. _ When he is driven into a corner, he will fight.
examples: They drove him into a corner and captured him there.

drive someone or something back†.monolingual: to force someone or something away; to force someone or something to retreat. _ The infantry drove the attackers back into the desert. _ They drove back the invading army. _ We drove them back to the border.
examples: The infantry drove the attackers back into the desert.

drive someone or something off†.monolingual: to repel or chase away someone or something. _ The campers drove the cows off before the animals trampled the tents. _They drove off the cows.
examples: The campers drove the cows off before the animals trampled the tents.

drive someone to despair.monolingual: Fig. to depress someone; to frustrate someone. _ Sometimes raising an infant drives me to despair! _ The recent problems drove her to despair.
examples: The recent problems drove her to despair.

drive someone to distraction.monolingual: Fig. to confuse or perplex someone. _Can’t you see you’re driving her to distraction? _ The problems I am having with my boss are driving me to distraction.
examples: The problems I am having with my boss are driving me to distraction.

drive someone to do something.monolingual: to force someone to do something. _Poverty drove him to steal. _She drove herself to earn a living.
examples: Poverty drove him to steal.

drive someone to drink.monolingual: Fig. [for someone or something] to cause someone to turn to alcohol as an escape from frustration. _ Being a Cubs fan is enough to drive you to drink. _ She was driven to drink by the problems she had with her teenage son.
examples: Being a Cubs fan is enough to drive you to drink.

drive someone up the wall.monolingual: Fig. to annoy or irritate someone. _ Stop whistling that tune. You’re driving me up the wall. _All his talk about moving to California nearly drove me up the wall.
examples: Stop whistling that tune.

drive something around something.monolingual: 1. to steer or propel something around something. _Wally drove the small car around the post easily. _Please drive your truck around the corner carefully.
examples: Wally drove the small car around the post easily.

drone something out†.monolingual: to make a loud and low-pitched noise; to say something in a low-pitched and monotonous manner. _ The announcer droned the winning numbers out. _ She droned out the winning numbers.
examples: The announcer droned the winning numbers out.

drop a hint.monolingual: Fig. to give a tiny or careful hint about something. _ Mary dropped a hint that she wanted a new ring for her birthday.
examples: Mary dropped a hint that she wanted a new ring for her birthday.

drop across someone or something.monolingual: [for something long or wide] to fall on and lay on someone or something. _ A snake dropped across the hood of the tourist bus as it passed under a tree. _ As I lay sleeping, a ceiling panel dropped across me and woke me up.
examples: A snake dropped across the hood of the tourist bus as it passed under a tree.

drop away.monolingual: 1. Lit. to fall off; to fall away. _The leaves were still dropping away from the trees in November. _The dead branches dropped away from the tree.
examples: The leaves were still dropping away from the trees in November.

drop back.monolingual: 1. to fall back to an original position. _ His arm raised up and then dropped back. _ The lid dropped back to its original position as soon as we let go of it.
examples: His arm raised up and then dropped back.

drop below someone or something.monolingual: to fall to a point lower than someone or something. _ The gunman dropped below the cowboy’s hiding place and got ready to take a shot. _ The temperature dropped below the freezing point.
examples: The gunman dropped below the cowboy’s hiding place and got ready to take a shot.

drop dead.monolingual: 1. to die suddenly. _ I understand that Tom Anderson dropped dead at his desk yesterday. _ No one knows why Uncle Bob suddenly dropped dead.
examples: I understand that Tom Anderson dropped dead at his desk yesterday.

drop down.monolingual: 1. [for someone] to fall down or stoop down. _ Suddenly, Ted dropped down, trying not to be seen by someone in a passing car. _ I dropped down as soon as I heard the loud sounds.
examples: Suddenly, Ted dropped down, trying not to be seen by someone in a passing car.

drop everything.monolingual: Fig. to stop doing whatever you are doing. _ Drop everything and go outside. The house is on fire. _ Do you expect me to drop everything and come and pick you up at school?
examples: Drop everything and go outside.

drop in one’s tracks.monolingual: 1. to collapse from exhaustion. _ I was so tired, I dropped in my tracks. _Kelly almost dropped in her tracks from overwork.
examples: I was so tired, I dropped in my tracks.

drop in sometime..monolingual: Visit my home or office sometime when you are nearby. _Bob: Bye, Bill, nice seeing you. Bill: Hey, drop in sometime. Bob: Okay. _ “Drop in sometime,” said Bob to his uncle.
examples: Bob: Bye, Bill, nice seeing you.

drop like flies.monolingual: Fig. to faint, sicken, collapse, or die, in great numbers like houseflies dying in a large group. _ It was a terrible year for the f lu. People were dropping like f lies.
examples: It was a terrible year for the f lu.

drop off.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a part of something] to break away and fall off. _ The car’s bumper just dropped off—honest. _ I lifted boxes until I thought my arms would drop off.
examples: The car’s bumper just dropped off—honest.

drop one’s drawers.monolingual: to lower one’s pant or underpants. _ The boys dropped their drawers and jumped in the creek.
examples: The boys dropped their drawers and jumped in the creek.

drop one’s teeth.monolingual: Fig. to react with great surprise. _ I almost dropped my teeth when she told me her news. _They dropped their teeth when I told them I was married.
examples: I almost dropped my teeth when she told me her news.

drop out of sight.monolingual: 1. Lit. to fall behind something and be seen no longer. _ The pen dropped out of sight behind the sofa nevermore to be seen.
examples: The pen dropped out of sight behind the sofa nevermore to be seen.

drop over.monolingual: to come for a casual visit. _ We would love for you to drop over. _ I would really like to drop over soon.
examples: We would love for you to drop over.

drop someone or something down†.monolingual: to let someone or something fall. _ He dropped his pants down, revealing the swimming trunks beneath. _The rescuer dropped down the baby and the doctor caught it. _ Sam went to the well and dropped a rock down.
examples: He dropped his pants down, revealing the swimming trunks beneath.

drop something across something.monolingual: to let something fall in such a way that a span is bridged; to let something fall in such a way that a pathway is blocked. _ Let’s drop a little rug across the threshold. _ They dropped a huge boulder across the road so no one could pass.
examples: Let’s drop a little rug across the threshold.

drop something on someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to let something fall on someone. _ The bricklayer dropped some mortar on me.
examples: The bricklayer dropped some mortar on me.

drop the ball.monolingual: 1. Lit. [in a ball game of some type] to let the ball get away or fall out of one’s grasp. _ Good grief! Bill dropped the ball, just as he was about to score!
examples: Good grief! Bill dropped the ball, just as he was about to score! 2.

drop the other shoe.monolingual: Fig. to do the deed that completes something; to do the expected remaining part of something. _Mr. Franklin has left his wife. Soon he’ll drop the other shoe and divorce her. _Tommy has just failed three classes in school. We expect him to drop the o
examples: Mr. Franklin has left his wife.

drop-dead gorgeous.monolingual: Sl. very good-looking. _ Perry’s girlfriend is drop-dead gorgeous. How can a twit like him hold onto a looker like that?
examples: Perry’s girlfriend is drop-dead gorgeous.

drown in something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to be asphyxiated in some liquid. _ Wouldn’t you hate to drown in that nasty, smelly water? _I am not choosy about what I don’t want to drown in.
examples: I am not choosy about what I don’t want to drown in.

drown someone in something.monolingual: Fig. to inundate someone with something. _ I will drown you in money and fine clothes. _Mike drowned the nightclub singer in fancy jewels and furs.
examples: I will drown you in money and fine clothes.

drown someone or something out†.monolingual: [for a sound] to be so loud that someone or something cannot be heard. _ The noise of the passing train drowned out our conversation. _ The train drowned us out.
examples: The noise of the passing train drowned out our conversation.

drum on something.monolingual: to tap, thump, or beat on something in rhythm. _Who is drumming on the table? _Please stop drumming on the wall.
examples: Please stop drumming on the wall.

drum something out†.monolingual: to beat a rhythm, loudly and clearly, as if teaching it to someone. _Drum the rhythm out before you try to sing this song. _ Drum out the rhythm first.
examples: Drum the rhythm out before you try to sing this song.

drum something up†.monolingual: to obtain something by attracting people’s attention to one’s need or cause. _I shall try to drum up support for the party. _ You shall have to drum up new business by advertising. _ I need to do something to drum some business up.
examples: I shall try to drum up support for the party.

drunk and disorderly.monolingual: a criminal charge for public drunkenness accompanied by bad or offensive behavior. _ The judge fined Richard for being drunk and disorderly. _ In addition to being convicted for driving while intoxicated, Richard was found guilty of being drunk and d
examples: The judge fined Richard for being drunk and disorderly.

dry out.monolingual: 1. Lit. to become dry. _ The clothes finally dried out in the wet weather.
examples: The clothes finally dried out in the wet weather.

dry run.monolingual: Fig. an attempt; a practice or rehearsal. _We had better have a dry run for the official ceremony tomorrow. _ The children will need another dry run before their procession in the pageant.
examples: We had better have a dry run for the official ceremony tomorrow.

dry someone or something off†.monolingual: to remove the moisture from someone or something. _ Please dry your feet off before coming in. _ Dry off your feet before you come in here!
examples: Please dry your feet off before coming in.

dry someone out†.monolingual: Fig. to cause someone to become sober; to cause someone to stop drinking alcohol to excess. _ If the doctor at the clinic can’t dry him out, no one can. _The hospital will dry out Mary and start treatment.
examples: If the doctor at the clinic can’t dry him out, no one can.

dry something out†.monolingual: to make something become dry. _Dry this out and put it on immediately. _ Dry out your jacket in the clothes dryer.
examples: Dry this out and put it on immediately.

dry something up†.monolingual: 1. to cause moisture to dry away to nothing. _Dry this spill up with the hair dryer. _Will the hair dryer dry up this mess?
examples: Dry this spill up with the hair dryer.

dry spell.monolingual: Rur. a period with no rain. _The dry spell killed the crops. _ We ain’t had such a long dry spell since 1988.
examples: The dry spell killed the crops.

dry up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to dry away to nothing. _ Finally, the water on the track dried up, and the race was able to continue. _ When will the fields dry up so we can plant?
examples: Finally, the water on the track dried up, and the race was able to continue.

dry-gulch someone.monolingual: to ambush someone. _ The outlaw dry-gulched the traveler and took everything he had. _The posse planned to dry-gulch the outlaw by waiting outside his favorite saloon.
examples: The outlaw dry-gulched the traveler and took everything he had.

dub something in†.monolingual: to mix a new sound recording into an old one. _ The actor messed up his lines, but they dubbed the correct words in later. _ They dubbed in his lines.
examples: The actor messed up his lines, but they dubbed the correct words in later.

dub something over†.monolingual: to record a replacement sound over another sound in a recording. _They had dubbed over all the dialog in the movie. _It doesn’t matter if you say a word wrong on the tape. We can dub it over.
examples: They had dubbed over all the dialog in the movie.

duck and cover.monolingual: 1. Lit. to bend down and seek protection against an attack. _ When the gunfire started, we had to duck and cover or get killed.
examples: When the gunfire started, we had to duck and cover or get killed.

duck down.monolingual: to stoop down quickly, as if to avoid being hit. _ He ducked down when he heard the gunshot. _ Duck down and get out of the way.
examples: He ducked down when he heard the gunshot.

duck soup.monolingual: Fig. very easy; an easy thing to do. _For Maria, knitting a sweater is duck soup. _ Jill: This jar is stuck. Could you open it for me? Jane: Sure. Duck soup.
examples: For Maria, knitting a sweater is duck soup.

duded up.monolingual: Sl. dressed up. _She got all duded up in her fanciest dancing dress. _He hates fancy clothes. He didn’t even get duded up for his own wedding.
examples: She got all duded up in her fanciest dancing dress.

duke it out.monolingual: Sl. to have a fistfight. _ John told George to meet him in the alley so they could duke it out.
examples: John told George to meet him in the alley so they could duke it out.

duke someone out†.monolingual: Sl. to knock someone out. _ Wilbur tried to duke the guy out first. _ Bob duked out the mugger with a jab to the cheek.
examples: Wilbur tried to duke the guy out first.

dummy up.monolingual: Sl. to refuse to talk. _ Jill dummied up when they got her into the station. _John dummied up right away when the police arrived.
examples: Jill dummied up when they got her into the station.

dump something on someone.monolingual: Fig. to pour out one’s troubles to someone. _She dumped all her grief on her friend, Sally. _I wish you wouldn’t dump all your problems on me.
examples: She dumped all her grief on her friend, Sally.

dumped on.monolingual: 1. snowed on. _ The entire Midwest was dumped on with about ten inches of snow. _ Our town really got dumped on last night.
examples: The entire Midwest was dumped on with about ten inches of snow.

dun someone for something.monolingual: to harass someone to pay a bill or deliver something. _ If you don’t pay the bill, they will dun you for it day and night. _ My job is to dun people for payment of their bills.
examples: If you don’t pay the bill, they will dun you for it day and night.

dust someone off†.monolingual: Sl. to punch or beat someone. _ We dusted them off one by one. _ We had to dust off all those big guys.
examples: We dusted them off one by one.

dust someone or something off†.monolingual: to wipe or brush the dust off someone or something. _ Dust this vase off and put it on the shelf. _ Please dust off this vase.
examples: Dust this vase off and put it on the shelf.

dust someone’s pants.monolingual: Sl. to spank someone, usually a child. _ My dad will dust my pants if he hears about this. _ I’m too old for somebody to dust my pants.
examples: My dad will dust my pants if he hears about this.

dust something out†.monolingual: to brush the dust out of something. _Dust this cabinet out and put the china back in. _Please dust out this cabinet.
examples: Dust this cabinet out and put the china back in.

dutch auction.monolingual: an auction or sale that starts off with a high asking price that is then reduced until a buyer is found. (Viewed by some as insulting to the Dutch.) _ Dutch auctions are rare—most auctioneers start with a lower price than they hope to obtain. _My rea
examples: Dutch auctions are rare—most auctioneers start with a lower price than they hope to obtain.

dutch courage.monolingual: unusual or artificial courage arising from the influence of alcohol. (Viewed by some as insulting to the Dutch.) _ It was Dutch courage that made the football fan attack the policeman. _ It will take a bit of Dutch courage to make an after-dinner spe
examples: It was Dutch courage that made the football fan attack the policeman.

dutch treat.monolingual: a social occasion where one pays for oneself. (Viewed by some as insulting to the Dutch.) _ “It’s nice of you to ask me out to dinner,” she said, “but could we make it a Dutch treat?” _ The office outing is always a Dutch treat.
examples: The office outing is always a Dutch treat.

dutch uncle.monolingual: a man who gives frank and direct advice to someone. (In the way an uncle might, but not a real relative.) _ I would not have to lecture you like a Dutch uncle if you were not so extravagant. _He acts more like a Dutch uncle than a husband. He’s forev
examples: I would not have to lecture you like a Dutch uncle if you were not so extravagant.

dyed-in-the-wool.monolingual: [of someone] permanent or extreme. _ My uncle was a dyed-in-the-wool farmer. He wouldn’t change for anything. _ Sally is a dyed-in-the-wool socialist.
examples: My uncle was a dyed-in-the-wool farmer.

dying to do something.monolingual: Fig. very eager to do something. _ I’m just dying to go sailing in your new boat. _After a long hot day like this one, I’m just dying for a cool drink.
examples: I’m just dying to go sailing in your new boat.

eager beaver.monolingual: someone who is very enthusiastic; someone who works very hard. _ New volunteers are always eager beavers. _The young assistant gets to work very early. She’s a real eager beaver.
examples: New volunteers are always eager beavers.

eagle eye.monolingual: acute eyesight; an intently watchful eye. (From the sharp eyesight of the eagle.) _The students wrote their essays under the eagle eye of the headmaster. _The umpire kept his eagle eye on the tennis match.
examples: The students wrote their essays under the eagle eye of the headmaster.

*an earful.monolingual: Fig. a great amount of discussion, criticism, gossip, or complaint. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ She was really mad about something, and I sure got an earful. _ Sue was standing around the corner while Jim and Mary were arguing and
examples: She was really mad about something, and I sure got an earful.

early bird.monolingual: 1. Fig. a person who gets up early. _ I never miss sunrise. I’m an early bird. _ The early birds were up at dawn and ready for breakfast.
examples: I never miss sunrise.

early on.monolingual: early; at an early stage. _We recognized the problem early on, but we waited too long to do something about it. _ This doesn’t surprise me. I knew about it early on.
examples: We recognized the problem early on, but we waited too long to do something about it.

earn one’s keep.monolingual: to help out with chores in return for food and a place to live; to earn one’s pay by doing what is expected. _ I earn my keep at college by shoveling snow in the winter. _ Tom hardly earns his keep around here. He should be fired.
examples: I earn my keep at college by shoveling snow in the winter.

earn one’s spurs.monolingual: Fig. to prove oneself. _ After that rodeo, all the cowboys agreed that Sally had earned her spurs. _ He felt that he had earned his spurs when he received his Ph.D.
examples: After that rodeo, all the cowboys agreed that Sally had earned her spurs.

ease off.monolingual: [for something] to diminish. _ The rain began to ease off. _ The storm seems to have eased off a little.
examples: The rain began to ease off.

ease someone or something along.monolingual: to help someone or something to move along, very carefully. _ Just ease the piano along little by little. _ She eased the shy child along.
examples: Just ease the piano along little by little.

easier said than done.monolingual: Cliché said of a task that is easier to talk about than to do. _ Yes, we must find a cure for cancer, but it’s easier said than done. _ Finding a good job is easier said than done.
examples: Yes, we must find a cure for cancer, but it’s easier said than done.

easy come, easy go.monolingual: Cliché said to explain the loss of something that required only a small amount of effort to acquire in the first place. _ Ann found twenty dollars in the morning and spent it foolishly at noon. “Easy come, easy go,” she said. _John spends his money a
