examples: Ann found twenty dollars in the morning and spent it foolishly at noon.

easy does it..monolingual: 1. Move slowly and carefully. _ Bill (holding one end of a large crate): It’s really tight in this doorway. Bob (holding the other end): Easy does it. Take your time. _ Nurse (holding Sue’s arm): Easy does it. These first few steps are the hardest. S
examples: Bill (holding one end of a large crate): It’s really tight in this doorway.

easy pickings.monolingual: [of things] easy to get or steal; [of people] easy to get or persuade. _ The pickpockets found lots of easy pickings at the state fair.
examples: The pickpockets found lots of easy pickings at the state fair.

easy, there!.monolingual: Calm down! _ “Easy, there!” said Arizona Slim, patting his horse’s neck. _Easy, there! Before you start yellin’, tell me what you’re yellin’ about.
examples: “Easy, there!” said Arizona Slim, patting his horse’s neck.

easy to come by.monolingual: easily found; easily purchased; readily available. _Please be careful with that phonograph record. It was not easy to come by. _A good dictionary is very easy to come by.
examples: Please be careful with that phonograph record.

eat crow.monolingual: 1. Fig. to display total humility, especially when shown to be wrong. _ Well, it looks like I was wrong, and I’m going to have to eat crow. _ I’ll be eating crow if I’m not shown to be right.
examples: Well, it looks like I was wrong, and I’m going to have to eat crow.

eat humble pie.monolingual: to act very humble when one is shown to be wrong. _ I think I’m right, but if I’m wrong, I’ll eat humble pie. _ You think you’re so smart. I hope you have to eat humble pie.
examples: I think I’m right, but if I’m wrong, I’ll eat humble pie.

eat in.monolingual: to eat a meal at home. _ I really don’t want to eat in tonight. _ Let’s eat in. I’m tired.
examples: I really don’t want to eat in tonight.

eat like a bird.monolingual: Fig. to eat only small amounts of food; to peck at one’s food. _ Jane is very slim because she eats like a bird. _ Bill is trying to lose weight by eating like a bird.
examples: Jane is very slim because she eats like a bird.

eat like a horse.monolingual: Fig. to eat large amounts of food. _ No wonder he’s so fat. He eats like a horse. _ John works like a horse and eats like a horse, so he never gets fat.
examples: No wonder he’s so fat.

eat my shorts!.monolingual: Sl. Leave me alone!; Nonsense!; Drop dead! _You’re nuts! Eat my shorts! _You think I’m going to clean up after you? Eat my shorts!

eat one’s fill.monolingual: to eat as much as one can hold; to eat as much as one wants. _Please eat your fill. There’s plenty for everyone.
examples: Please eat your fill.

eat one’s hat.monolingual: Fig. a phrase telling the kind of thing that one would do if a very unlikely event really happens. _ If we get there on time, I’ll eat my hat. _I’ll eat my hat if you get a raise. _ He said he’d eat his hat if she got elected.
examples: If we get there on time, I’ll eat my hat.

eat one’s heart out.monolingual: 1. Fig. to grieve; to be sorrowful. (Fixed order.) _She has been eating her heart out over that jerk ever since he ran away with Sally. _ Don’t eat your heart out. You really didn’t like him that much, did you?
examples: She has been eating her heart out over that jerk ever since he ran away with Sally.

eat one’s words.monolingual: Fig. to have to take back one’s statements; to confess that one’s predictions were wrong. _ You shouldn’t say that to me. I’ll make you eat your words. _ John was wrong about the election and had to eat his words.
examples: You shouldn’t say that to me.

eat out.monolingual: to eat a meal away from home, as at a restaurant. _ I just love to eat out every now and then. _ Let’s eat out tonight. I’m tired.
examples: I just love to eat out every now and then.

eat out of someone’s hand.monolingual: Fig. to do exactly as someone says; to grovel to someone. _ I’ve got her eating out of my hand. She’ll do anything I ask. _ He will be eating out of your hand before you are finished with him.
examples: I’ve got her eating out of my hand.

eat someone’s lunch.monolingual: Sl. to best someone; to defeat, outwit, or win against someone. (Like a school bully taking away children’s lunches and eating them.) _ The upstart ABC Computer Company is eating IBM’s lunch.
examples: The upstart ABC Computer Company is eating IBM’s lunch.

eat someone’s salt.monolingual: Rur. to be someone’s guest. _ The least you can do when you’re eating someone’s salt is to help them out around the house. _ That good-for-nothing Jim was f lirting with Bill’s wife at the same time he was eating Bill’s salt.
examples: The least you can do when you’re eating someone’s salt is to help them out around the house.

eat someone up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to consume the flesh of someone. _ The big bad wolf said he was going to eat you up! _ The bear ate up the fish.
examples: The bear ate up the fish.

eat something away†.monolingual: to erode something; to consume something bit by bit. _ The acid ate the finish away. _ It ate away the finish.
examples: The acid ate the finish away.

eat something out†.monolingual: 1. to eat some kind of meal or a particular food away from home, as at a restaurant. _We eat fish out, but we don’t cook it at home. _ We may eat out a meal or two, but certainly not every meal.
examples: We eat fish out, but we don’t cook it at home.

eat up!.monolingual: to eat everything; to eat eagerly. (Usually a command to begin eating. Compare this with Drink up!.) _ Come on, let’s eat up and get going. _ Eat up, you guys, and get back to work!
examples: Come on, let’s eat up and get going.

eavesdrop on someone.monolingual: to listen in on people having a private conversation. _ I saw her eavesdropping on them. _ Please don’t eavesdrop on me.
examples: I saw her eavesdropping on them.

eavesdrop on something.monolingual: to listen in on a private conversation. _ She was eavesdropping on their conversation. _ Maria was eavesdropping on the telephone call.
examples: She was eavesdropping on their conversation.

ebb and flow.monolingual: to decrease and then increase, as with tides; a decrease followed by an increase, as with tides. _ The fortunes of the major political parties tend to ebb and flow over time. _ The ebb and flow of democracy through history is a fascinating subject.
examples: The fortunes of the major political parties tend to ebb and flow over time.

ebb away.monolingual: to recede; to subside; to flow back. _ His life ebbed away little by little. _As the sunlight ebbed away, the sky took on a grayish color.
examples: His life ebbed away little by little.

echo back to something.monolingual: [for something] to recall something similar in the past. _This idea echoes back to the end of the last century, when people thought this way.
examples: This idea echoes back to the end of the last century, when people thought this way.

echo with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a large space] to resound with the echoing sounds of a loud noise. _ The cathedral echoed with the sounds of the organ. _ The valley echoed with the sound of horses’ hooves.
examples: The cathedral echoed with the sounds of the organ.

economical with the truth.monolingual: Euph. untruthful. _ The mayor was known to be economical with the truth. _I discovered that my boss had been economical with the truth when she said that the company was making money.
examples: The mayor was known to be economical with the truth.

economize on something.monolingual: to save money by cutting the cost of something. _We will have to economize on our food budget. _ We can only economize on a few things.
examples: We will have to economize on our food budget.

edge someone out of something.monolingual: to pressure someone gradually to leave something; to put gradual pressure on someone to retire from a job. _We grasped the child’s hand and edged her out of the stable without frightening the horses. _The board tried to edge him out of the job by lim
examples: We grasped the child’s hand and edged her out of the stable without frightening the horses.

edge something with something.monolingual: to put an edging or border of something onto something. _The tailor edged the hem with lace, making the skirt appear longer. _ The hem was edged with lace.
examples: The tailor edged the hem with lace, making the skirt appear longer.

educate someone for something.monolingual: to train someone for something or to do something. _ I wasn’t educated for doing this kind of thing. _ He had spent many years educating himself for just this kind of job.
examples: I wasn’t educated for doing this kind of thing.

educate someone in something.monolingual: to train someone about something; to school someone in something. _ Her parents educated her in the ways of the old country. _She had educated herself in the ways of big business.
examples: Her parents educated her in the ways of the old country.

egg someone on.monolingual: to encourage, urge, or dare someone to continue doing something, usually something unwise. _ John wouldn’t have done the dangerous experiment if his brother hadn’t egged him on. _ The two boys kept throwing stones because the other children were eggi
examples: John wouldn’t have done the dangerous experiment if his brother hadn’t egged him on.

eighty-six something.monolingual: Sl. to throw something away. _ Let’s eighty-six this stew and go out and get some decent pizza.
examples: Let’s eighty-six this stew and go out and get some decent pizza.

eject someone from some place.monolingual: to use force to make someone leave a place; to throw someone out of some place. _ The management ejected Sam from the theater. _ He was ejected from the theater.
examples: The management ejected Sam from the theater.

eke something out†.monolingual: to extend something; to add to something. _ He worked at two jobs in order to eke his income out. _ He managed to eke out a living.
examples: He worked at two jobs in order to eke his income out.

elaborate on someone or something.monolingual: to give additional details about someone or something. _ Would you care to elaborate on that? _ I want to know more about Kelly. Could you elaborate on her?
examples: I want to know more about Kelly.

elbow grease.monolingual: Fig. hard scrubbing. _ Tom: What did you use to get your car so shiny? Mary: Just regular wax and some elbow grease. _Joe put a lot of elbow grease into cleaning the kitchen.
examples: Tom: What did you use to get your car so shiny? Mary: Just regular wax and some elbow grease.

elbow someone aside†.monolingual: to push someone aside with one’s elbow or arm. _ She elbowed the other woman aside and there was almost a fight. _The rude woman elbowed aside all the other people.
examples: She elbowed the other woman aside and there was almost a fight.

elect someone to something.monolingual: to select someone to be a member of something by ballot; to select someone to be an officer in something by ballot. _ We elected you to office, so do your job. _ Tom was elected to the congress.
examples: We elected you to office, so do your job.

eleventh-hour decision.monolingual: Fig. a decision made very late in a process, or at the last possible moment. _ Eleventhhour decisions are seldom satisfactory. _ The president’s eleventh-hour decision was made in a great hurry, but it turned out to be correct.
examples: Eleventhhour decisions are seldom satisfactory.

elicit something from someone.monolingual: to obtain information from someone. _ I hoped to elicit a statement from the mayor, but I could not reach her. _Larry was not able to elicit anything new from Jane.
examples: I hoped to elicit a statement from the mayor, but I could not reach her.

elope with someone.monolingual: to sneak away with someone and get married without much ceremony. _ Sally eloped with Tom, and everyone was surprised. _ I don’t want to elope with Juan. I want a church wedding.
examples: Sally eloped with Tom, and everyone was surprised.

emanate from someone or something.monolingual: to arise from or come out of someone or something. _A strange smell emanated from the basement. _ Some kind of eerie light emanated from the eyes of the statue.
examples: A strange smell emanated from the basement.

embark for some place.monolingual: to leave for some place, usually in a ship or an airplane. _ We are embarking for Denver tomorrow morning. _Maria is embarking for Honolulu in just a few minutes.
examples: We are embarking for Denver tomorrow morning.

embark on something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to begin a journey by boarding a ship, airplane, etc. _ They embarked on their journey from San Juan.
examples: They embarked on their journey from San Juan.

embarrass someone into doing something.monolingual: to shame someone into doing something. _ They tried to embarrass me into doing it, but I resisted. _ Juan tried to embarrass Fred into going home early.
examples: They tried to embarrass me into doing it, but I resisted.

embarrass someone with something.monolingual: to use something to make someone feel bad or ashamed. _Please don’t embarrass me with that old story again. _ Maria embarrassed Henry with a reminder of what had happened.
examples: Please don’t embarrass me with that old story again.

embed something in something.monolingual: to stick something into something. _ The mugger only embedded his knife in the cloth of the victim’s coat. _ A ring was embedded in the bread dough by accident.
examples: The mugger only embedded his knife in the cloth of the victim’s coat.

embellish something with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to ornament something with something. _ He embellished the painting with too many little decorations. _ The room has been embellished with too many baroque sconces.
examples: He embellished the painting with too many little decorations.

emblazon something with something.monolingual: to decorate something with writing or symbols. _ They emblazoned the wall with pictures of past triumphs. _His shield was emblazoned with the family crest.
examples: They emblazoned the wall with pictures of past triumphs.

embody something in something.monolingual: to actualize something in something; to make something represent something else in actuality. _ I tried to embody both good and evil in my painting. _ A strong sense of morality is embodied in her writing.
examples: I tried to embody both good and evil in my painting.

embroil someone in something.monolingual: Fig. to entangle someone in something; to get someone involved in something. _ Please do not embroil me in your squabbles. _I wish I could keep from embroiling myself in this kind of mess.
examples: Please do not embroil me in your squabbles.

empathize with someone or something.monolingual: to have an understanding about the way someone feels; to feel emotional pain with someone. _ I can really empathize with what you must be going through. I’ve been through the same thing. _ I empathize with people who have the same family problems tha
examples: I can really empathize with what you must be going through.

employ someone as something.monolingual: to pay someone to work in some capacity. _ I employed Fred as a personal secretary for about three months. _ Can you employ me as a stock clerk?
examples: I employed Fred as a personal secretary for about three months.

employ someone for something.monolingual: to hire someone for a particular purpose. _ I employ him for special chores around the factory. _ Kelly employed Walter for emergency repairs on the night shift.
examples: I employ him for special chores around the factory.

employ someone in something.monolingual: to pay someone to work in a particular type of work. _ I employ Tom in machine maintenance. _ Laura is employed in accounting.
examples: I employ Tom in machine maintenance.

empower someone to do something.monolingual: to authorize someone to do something; to grant someone the power to do something. _I will empower you to collect the dues of the members. _ The prime minister empowered a special office to oversee tax collection.
examples: I will empower you to collect the dues of the members.

emptier than a banker’s heart.monolingual: Rur. completely empty. _My wallet was emptier than a banker’s heart. _His pockets were emptier than a banker’s heart.
examples: My wallet was emptier than a banker’s heart.

empty into something.monolingual: [for a river, stream, or man-made conduit] to pour its contents into something. _The Amazon River empties into the Atlantic Ocean. _ The drainage pipe empties into the river.
examples: The Amazon River empties into the Atlantic Ocean.

empty someone out†.monolingual: to cause someone to empty the bowels, stomach, or bladder. _This medication will empty you out. _This stuff could empty out an army! _He fasted for two days to empty himself out.
examples: This medication will empty you out.

empty something out†.monolingual: to remove or pour all of the contents from something. _Please empty this drawer out and clean it. _ She emptied out the aquarium and cleaned it well.
examples: Please empty this drawer out and clean it.

enable someone to do something.monolingual: to make it possible for someone to do something. _ This money will enable me to open my own business. _ My uncle enabled me to open my own candy shop.
examples: This money will enable me to open my own business.

*enamored of someone or something.monolingual: to feel love for someone or something. (Often an exaggeration. *Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ She is hopelessly enamored of Tom. _ Tom is enamored of chocolate ice cream.
examples: She is hopelessly enamored of Tom.

enchant someone with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to bewitch someone or something with a magic spell. _The children were enchanted with a spell that made them forget.
examples: The children were enchanted with a spell that made them forget.

encourage someone in something.monolingual: to give support to someone about something in particular. _We want to encourage her in her musical career. _ Ted encouraged me in my efforts to become a baseball player.
examples: We want to encourage her in her musical career.

encourage someone to do something.monolingual: to inspire or stimulate someone to do something; to give someone the courage to do something. _We encouraged her to develop her musical talents. _He encouraged himself to study hard so he could make it into medical school.
examples: We encouraged her to develop her musical talents.

*an end in itself.monolingual: existing for its own sake; existing for no clear purpose. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ For Bob, art is an end in itself. He doesn’t hope to make any money from it. _ Learning is an end in itself. Knowledge does not have to have a practical applica
examples: For Bob, art is an end in itself.

end in something.monolingual: [for something, such as a play, film, opera, etc.] to end in a particular way. _ The opera ended in a lengthy duet before the death of the heroine. _ The party ended in a champagne toast.
examples: The opera ended in a lengthy duet before the death of the heroine.

the end justifies the means..monolingual: Prov. You can use bad or immoral methods as long as you accomplish something good by using them. (Not everyone agrees with this idea.) _ Lucy got money for the orphanage by embezzling it from the firm where she worked. “The end justifies the means,”
examples: Lucy got money for the orphanage by embezzling it from the firm where she worked.

end of story..monolingual: Inf. That completes the story, and I will say no more. _ I did it because I wanted to. End of story.
examples: I did it because I wanted to.

end something up†.monolingual: to terminate something; to bring something to an end. _He ended his vacation up by going to the beach. _ She ended up her speech with a poem.
examples: He ended his vacation up by going to the beach.

end up.monolingual: to come to an end. _ When will all this end up? _ I think that the party will have to end up about midnight.
examples: I think that the party will have to end up about midnight.

end up at something.monolingual: to be at something or some place at the end. _ The plane ended up at Denver airport because of a storm in Colorado Springs. _We ended up at home for the evening because the car broke down.
examples: The plane ended up at Denver airport because of a storm in Colorado Springs.

end with something.monolingual: to make something the final element, just before the end. _ We will end with the singing of the school song. _ The concert ended with a vigorous march.
examples: We will end with the singing of the school song.

endeavor to do something.monolingual: to try to do something. _ Whenever I endeavor to console her, she breaks down again. _ Maria endeavored to comfort Henry.
examples: Whenever I endeavor to console her, she breaks down again.

enfold someone in something.monolingual: to wrap or contain someone in something. _ He enfolded the tiny baby in a soft blanket. _ Sarah enfolded herself in the silk sheets and giggled with glee.
examples: He enfolded the tiny baby in a soft blanket.

enforce something on someone.monolingual: to make a law effective with regard to someone. _ I can’t enforce this on her if I don’t enforce it on you. _ This law can’t be enforced on anyone.
examples: I can’t enforce this on her if I don’t enforce it on you.

engage in small talk.monolingual: to talk only about minor matters rather than important matters or personal matters. _ All the people at the party were engaging in small talk. _They chatted about the weather and otherwise engaged in small talk.
examples: All the people at the party were engaging in small talk.

engage someone as something.monolingual: to hire someone to serve as something. _ Yes, I engaged her as a secretary just last month. _ Will you engage me as a general troubleshooter?
examples: Yes, I engaged her as a secretary just last month.

engage someone to someone.monolingual: to betroth someone to someone. _ Her parents engaged her to the man she ended up marrying. _ She engaged herself to some guy she met at a singles bar.
examples: Her parents engaged her to the man she ended up marrying.

engrave something into something.monolingual: to cut symbols into something. _She engraves a lovely design into the soap that she puts out for guests. _ Todd engraved his initials into the bark of the tree.
examples: She engraves a lovely design into the soap that she puts out for guests.

engrave something with something.monolingual: 1. to carve something, such as letters, into something. _ He engraved the soft pewter with an old motto. _ Can you engrave my watch with a date?
examples: He engraved the soft pewter with an old motto.

engross someone in something.monolingual: to occupy someone’s time or thinking with something. _ You can’t expect me to engross Tom in my work. _ We were all engrossed in what the speaker had to say.
examples: You can’t expect me to engross Tom in my work.

enjoin someone to do something.monolingual: to order someone to do something. _ We sought to enjoin her to remain in office. _ Sally wants to enjoin the committee to finish its work on time.
examples: We sought to enjoin her to remain in office.

enjoy your meal..monolingual: an expression used by food servers after the food has been served. _ The waiter set the plates on the table, smiled, and said, “Enjoy your meal.” _ Waiter: Here’s your dinner. Jane: Oh, this lobster looks lovely! Tom: My steak looks just perfect. Wai
examples: The waiter set the plates on the table, smiled, and said, “Enjoy your meal.

enlist someone for something.monolingual: to enroll someone for something; to seek help for something from someone. _ I enlisted all of them for the understudy parts. _Can I enlist you for the committee?
examples: I enlisted all of them for the understudy parts.

enlist someone in something.monolingual: to recruit someone into something; to recruit someone into the armed services. _They tried to enlist me in the army, but I decided against it. _ David enlisted his brother in an organization that gave assistance to peasants in South America.
examples: They tried to enlist me in the army, but I decided against it.

enough and some to spare.monolingual: Fig. plenty. _ Would you like some more pie? We’ve got enough and some to spare. _ Mary: Can I borrow a cup of milk? Tom: Don’t worry about borrowing. Take it. I have enough and some to spare.
examples: Would you like some more pie? We’ve got enough and some to spare.

enough is enough..monolingual: Prov. That is enough, and there should be no more.; Stop! _Stop asking for money! Enough is enough! _ I’ve heard all the complaining from you that I can take. Enough is enough!
examples: I’ve heard all the complaining from you that I can take.

ensconce oneself in something.monolingual: Fig. to establish oneself in something; to settle oneself into something; to place oneself firmly into something. _ He ensconced himself in the most comfortable chair. _ Sally ensconced herself in the huge throne and pretended she was a queen.
examples: He ensconced himself in the most comfortable chair.

enshrine something in something.monolingual: to honor someone or something by placement in a shrine. _ Bill enshrined his grandfather’s watch in a glass dome.
examples: Bill enshrined his grandfather’s watch in a glass dome.

ensue from something.monolingual: to result from someone or something. _ What ensued from the change in policy was not anticipated at all. _ A very serious problem ensued from the events of the day.
examples: What ensued from the change in policy was not anticipated at all.

enter in something.monolingual: to enroll as a participant in something, such as a contest, competition, etc. _ She was not ready to enter in the competition. _ I can’t enter in that contest. I’m not prepared.
examples: She was not ready to enter in the competition.

enter into something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to get into something. _ She entered into the house and immediately went to work. _ As the people entered into the cathedral, they became quiet.
examples: She entered into the house and immediately went to work.

enter one’s mind.monolingual: Fig. [for an idea or memory] to come into one’s consciousness; to be thought of. _ Leave you behind? The thought never even entered my mind. _A very interesting idea just entered my mind. What if I ran for Congress?
examples: Leave you behind? The thought never even entered my mind.

enter the lists.monolingual: Fig. to begin to take part in a contest or argument. _ He had decided not to stand for Parliament, but entered the lists at the last minute. _ The family disagreement had almost been resolved when the grandfather entered the lists.
examples: He had decided not to stand for Parliament, but entered the lists at the last minute.

entertain someone with something.monolingual: to provide something for amusement or refreshment to someone. _Will you try to entertain the children with a game or two, please? _ She entertained herself with the puzzle.
examples: She entertained herself with the puzzle.

enthrall someone with something.monolingual: to charm or captivate someone with something. _ They enthralled us with the beauty of their singing. _ The children enthralled us with their rustic dances.
examples: They enthralled us with the beauty of their singing.

entitle someone to do something.monolingual: [for something] to qualify someone to do something. _This ticket entitles you to go in and take a seat. _ Does this paper entitle me to get a discount?
examples: This ticket entitles you to go in and take a seat.

entreat someone to do something.monolingual: to beg someone to do something. _They entreated us to come back as soon as we could. _ I entreat you to think it over again.
examples: They entreated us to come back as soon as we could.

entwine around someone or something.monolingual: to weave or wind around someone or something. _ The snake entwined around the limb of the tree. _ The huge python entwined around the horrified farmer.
examples: The snake entwined around the limb of the tree.

enunciate something to someone.monolingual: to say something to someone very clearly and distinctly. _ Now, enunciate it to everyone, because they probably did not understand you the first time. _ I will enunciate it to you one more time, slowly.
examples: Now, enunciate it to everyone, because they probably did not understand you the first time.

equal to someone.monolingual: as good or as accomplished as someone else. _I certainly feel equal to Randy. He’s nothing special. _I don’t think that Bill feels equal to Bob, even though they are twins.
examples: I certainly feel equal to Randy.

equal to someone or something.monolingual: able to handle or deal with someone or something. _ I’m afraid that I’m not equal to Mrs. Smith’s problem right now. Please ask her to come back later. _That’s a very difficult task, but I’m sure Bill is equal to it.
examples: I’m afraid that I’m not equal to Mrs.

equip something with something.monolingual: to add a piece of equipment to something. _We will equip our truck with a plow blade and plow snow this winter. _ This car is equipped with air-conditioning.
examples: We will equip our truck with a plow blade and plow snow this winter.

erase something from something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to delete or wipe something from something. _ Please erase the writing from the blackboard. _ I will erase the incorrectly spelled word from my paper.
examples: Please erase the writing from the blackboard.

erupt from something.monolingual: to burst out of something or some place. _ A billow of smoke erupted from the chimney. _ A mass of ashes and gasses erupted from the volcano.
examples: A billow of smoke erupted from the chimney.

erupt into something.monolingual: [for something] to become a serious problem suddenly. _ The argument erupted into a terrible fight. _ They were afraid the fight would erupt into a riot.
examples: The argument erupted into a terrible fight.

escalate into something.monolingual: to intensify into something; to increase gradually into something. _ This argument is going to escalate into something serious very soon. _ These cases of the f lu could escalate into a real epidemic.
examples: This argument is going to escalate into something serious very soon.

escalate something into something.monolingual: to cause something to intensify. _He escalated the argument into a vicious fight. _ The dictator tried to escalate the disagreement into a cause for war.
examples: He escalated the argument into a vicious fight.

escape someone’s notice.monolingual: Fig. to go unnoticed; not to have been noticed. (Usually a way to point out that someone has failed to see or respond to something.) _I suppose my earlier request escaped your notice, so I’m writing again. _ I’m sorry. Your letter escaped my notice.
examples: I suppose my earlier request escaped your notice, so I’m writing again.

*estranged from someone.monolingual: to be alienated from someone. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _Toward the end, they were estranged from each other, so a separation was perfectly natural. _She had been estranged from her husband for a number of years.
examples: Toward the end, they were estranged from each other, so a separation was perfectly natural.

eternal life.monolingual: Euph. life after death. _He passed on into eternal life, leaving us behind to mourn. _She is now at rest in eternal life.
examples: He passed on into eternal life, leaving us behind to mourn.

the eternal triangle.monolingual: a sexual or emotional relationship involving two women and one man or two men and one woman. (Typically, a couple [man and woman] and another man or woman.) _ Henry can’t choose between his wife and his mistress. It’s the eternal triangle. _I’m surpr
examples: Henry can’t choose between his wife and his mistress.

evacuate one’s bowels.monolingual: Euph. to defecate. _ After taking a jog around the block, Jill felt the need to evacuate her bowels. _ I am afraid my little boy is sick. He has not evacuated his bowels for several days.
examples: After taking a jog around the block, Jill felt the need to evacuate her bowels.

evaluate someone as something.monolingual: to judge someone’s performance as something. _ I will have to evaluate you as a new student. _We must evaluate ourselves as teachers and leaders.
examples: I will have to evaluate you as a new student.

even a worm will turn..monolingual: Prov. Even a meek person will become angry if you abuse him or her too much. _ You’d better stop maltreating Amy. She’s a mild-mannered woman, but even a worm will turn.
examples: You’d better stop maltreating Amy.

*an even break.monolingual: a fair chance; a fair judgment. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ Please give me an even break! I need some help here!

even if it kills me.monolingual: Fig. [pledging to do something] even if [doing it] is very difficult. _ Don’t worry. I will get it done even if it kills me.
examples: Don’t worry. I will get it done even if it kills me.

even something out†.monolingual: to make something even or level. _ Please even the gravel out. _ They evened out the surface of the road.
examples: Please even the gravel out.

even something up†.monolingual: to make something even, square, level, equal, balanced, etc. _ I’ll even the table up. _ See if you can even up the legs of this table. It wobbles.
examples: I’ll even the table up.

even steven.monolingual: to be even (with someone or something) by having repaid a debt, replied in kind, etc. _ Bill hit Tom; then Tom hit Bill. Now they are even steven. _ Mary paid Ann the $100 she owed her. Ann said, “Good, we are even steven.”
examples: Bill hit Tom; then Tom hit Bill.

the evening of life.monolingual: Euph. old age. _ As she approached the evening of life, Sarah looked back on her accomplishments with satisfaction. _ The residents of this rest home are all in the evening of life.
examples: As she approached the evening of life, Sarah looked back on her accomplishments with satisfaction.

ever and anon.monolingual: now and then; occasionally. (Literary and archaic.) _Ever and anon the princess would pay a visit to the sorcerer in the small walled garden directly behind the castle.
examples: Ever and anon the princess would pay a visit to the sorcerer in the small walled garden directly behind the castle.

every fool thing.monolingual: every ridiculous or insignificant thing. _Every fool thing seems to go wrong with this car. _I don’t want to hear about every fool thing you did on your vacation.
examples: Every fool thing seems to go wrong with this car.

every jack has his jill..monolingual: Prov. Every man will eventually find a woman to be his romantic partner. _Bill: I’ll never have a girlfriend. None of the girls I take out will agree to a second date. Fred: Cheer up; every Jack has his Jill.
examples: Bill: I’ll never have a girlfriend.

every last one.monolingual: every one; every single one. _ You must eat all your peas! Every last one! _Each of you—every last one—has to take some medicine.
examples: Each of you—every last one—has to take some medicine.

every little bit helps..monolingual: Prov. Even the smallest amount is helpful. _ Tom: I can only give a dollar to your charity. Mary: That’s OK. Every little bit helps. _ Jane gave me a pair of booties for my new baby. It’s not much, but every little bit helps.
examples: Tom: I can only give a dollar to your charity.

every living soul.monolingual: Fig. every person. _ I expect every living soul to be there and be there on time. _ This is the kind of problem that affects every living soul.
examples: I expect every living soul to be there and be there on time.

every man has his price..monolingual: Prov. It is possible to bribe anyone as long as you know how much or what to bribe him or her with. _ Henchman: I’ve offered the judge half a million dollars to give you a light sentence, but he says he can’t be bought. Gangster: Keep trying. Every m
examples: Henchman: I’ve offered the judge half a million dollars to give you a light sentence, but he says he can’t be bought.

every man to his taste..monolingual: Prov. Everyone likes something different, and you should not condemn people because of what they like. (Can be used to remark that someone’s tastes are different from yours, as in the first example.) _ Jill: Why don’t you get some decent neckties, Fr
examples: Jill: Why don’t you get some decent neckties, Fred? Fred: What do you mean, decent? My ties are perfectly fine! Jill: Oh, well.

every nook and cranny.monolingual: Fig. every small, out-of-the-way place or places where something can be hidden. _ We looked for the tickets in every nook and cranny. They were lost. There was no doubt. _The decorator had placed flowers in every nook and cranny.
examples: We looked for the tickets in every nook and cranny.

every other person or thing.monolingual: every second or alternate person or thing. _The magician turned every other card over. _ Every other table had an ashtray on it.
examples: The magician turned every other card over.

every time one turns around.monolingual: Fig. frequently; at every turn; with annoying frequency. _ Somebody asks me for money every time I turn around. _ Something goes wrong with Bill’s car every time he turns around.
examples: Somebody asks me for money every time I turn around.

every walk of life.monolingual: every status and occupation. _ We invited people from every walk of life, but only those who could afford the long drive could possibly come.
examples: We invited people from every walk of life, but only those who could afford the long drive could possibly come.

everybody loves a lord..monolingual: Prov. People are attracted to the wealthy and powerful. _Although the prince was vulgar and unpleasant, he always received plenty of invitations to social gatherings; everybody loves a lord.
examples: Although the prince was vulgar and unpleasant, he always received plenty of invitations to social gatherings; everybody loves a lord.

everything an’ all.monolingual: Rur. everything. _ The thieves broke into Mary’s house and took the television, the silver, her jewelry, everything an’ all. _ I had to write a report about my trip to Memphis, what I did, what I ate, what I saw, and everything an’ all.
examples: The thieves broke into Mary’s house and took the television, the silver, her jewelry, everything an’ all.

everything but the kitchen sink.monolingual: Cliché almost everything one can think of. _ When Sally went off to college, she took everything but the kitchen sink. _ John orders everything but the kitchen sink when he goes out to dinner, especially if someone else is paying for it.
examples: When Sally went off to college, she took everything but the kitchen sink.

everything humanly possible.monolingual: everything that is in the range of human powers. _ The rescuers did everything humanly possible to find the lost campers. _ The doctor tried everything humanly possible to save the patient.
examples: The rescuers did everything humanly possible to find the lost campers.

everything’s coming up roses..monolingual: Fig. Everything is really just excellent. Life is prosperous. _ Life is wonderful. Everything is coming up roses. _ Q: How are things going? A: Everything’s coming up roses.
examples: Life is wonderful.

evict someone from some place.monolingual: to force someone to move out of something or some place. _They evicted the squatters from the building. _They were evicted from their home for not paying their mortgage.
examples: They evicted the squatters from the building.

exact something from someone.monolingual: to demand something from someone; to take something from someone. _The bill collector sought to exact payment from them for a debt that had been paid off long ago. _You cannot exact a single cent from me.
examples: The bill collector sought to exact payment from them for a debt that had been paid off long ago.

examine someone in something.monolingual: to give someone an examination in a particular subject or covering certain material. _ The committee examined her in her knowledge of history. _ I was examined in math.
examples: The committee examined her in her knowledge of history.

examine someone on something.monolingual: to give someone an examination covering certain material. _ I will have to examine you on this chapter myself. _ The teacher examined Larry on his understanding of phonetics.
examples: I will have to examine you on this chapter myself.

example is better than precept..monolingual: Prov. You will teach people more effectively by being a good example than you will by telling them what to do. _ Mother never lectured us; she just tried her best to be a good person, and we tried hard to be like her. She was living proof that exampl
examples: Mother never lectured us; she just tried her best to be a good person, and we tried hard to be like her.

the exception proves the rule..monolingual: Prov. Something that does not follow a rule shows that the rule exists. (Often used facetiously, to justify some rule you have proposed but which someone else has listed exceptions to. From a Latin phrase meaning that an exception tests a rule.) _ El
examples: Ellen: Men are always rude.

excerpt something from something.monolingual: to select a part of something from the whole. _ We excerpted a few short scenes from the play and performed them for the class. _ A few paragraphs had been excerpted from the film as an example.
examples: We excerpted a few short scenes from the play and performed them for the class.

exchange something for something.monolingual: to trade something for something else. _ I will exchange this one for a larger size. _ Can this be exchanged for something more suitable?
examples: I will exchange this one for a larger size.

exchange something with someone.monolingual: to trade something with someone. _I exchange Christmas presents with him, but I never see him otherwise. _ Let’s exchange coats with each other.
examples: I exchange Christmas presents with him, but I never see him otherwise.

excite someone about something.monolingual: to stimulate someone about something. _ I thought our vacation stories would excite her about going, but they did not. _ She was excited about the trip to Moscow.
examples: I thought our vacation stories would excite her about going, but they did not.

excite something in someone.monolingual: to arouse something in someone; to arouse someone with something. _ The horror movie excited a lot of fear in Mike. _ The smell of jasmine in the warm air excited a romantic streak in me.
examples: The horror movie excited a lot of fear in Mike.

excuse someone.monolingual: 1. to forgive someone. (Usually with me. Said when interrupting or when some other minor offense has been committed. There are many mannerly uses of this expression.) _John came in late and said, “Excuse me, please.” _ John said “excuse me” when he i
examples: John came in late and said, “Excuse me, please.

excuse someone for something.monolingual: to pardon someone for something or for (doing) something. _ Please excuse me for this mess. I’ve not been able to clean the house. _I can’t excuse myself for not doing it.
examples: Please excuse me for this mess.

excuse someone from something.monolingual: to permit a person not to do something; to exempt someone from something. _ Please excuse me from attending the meeting. _ I must excuse myself from the discussion.
examples: Please excuse me from attending the meeting.

exemplify something by something.monolingual: to use something to explain or illustrate something. _ He exemplifies wisdom by his decisions. _ Roger exemplifies virtue by the way he treats his employees.
examples: He exemplifies wisdom by his decisions.

exempt someone from something.monolingual: to release someone from the obligation to do something; to allow a person not to be affected by a rule or law. _I cannot exempt anyone from this rule. _The members of Congress exempted themselves from the wage freeze.
examples: I cannot exempt anyone from this rule.

exercised about something.monolingual: Fig. upset about something. _ Mary: You lost a hundred dollars playing poker!? Bill: Now don’t get exercised about it. _ I can’t tell Ma I’m failing English class. She gets exercised about every dumb thing I do.
examples: Mary: You lost a hundred dollars playing poker!? Bill: Now don’t get exercised about it.

exhort someone to do something.monolingual: to urge or pressure someone to do something. _ She exhorted us to do better, but we only did worse. _ The boss exhorted the workers to increase productivity.
examples: She exhorted us to do better, but we only did worse.

expand into something.monolingual: to grow into something; to enlarge into something. _ The little problem expanded into a big one in no time at all. _ In no time at all, the vegetable garden had expanded into a small farm.
examples: The little problem expanded into a big one in no time at all.

expand one’s horizons.monolingual: Fig. to experience and learn new things. _Read more! Travel! Go out and expand your horizons!

expand something into something.monolingual: to enlarge something into something; to make something grow into something. _ She expanded her business into a national company. _ I would like to build on an addition to expand this room into a more usable space.
examples: She expanded her business into a national company.

expatiate on someone or something.monolingual: to say or write many words about someone or something. _ She expatiated endlessly on the evils of tobacco. _ I have heard you expatiate on Harry quite enough, thank you.
examples: She expatiated endlessly on the evils of tobacco.

expectant mother.monolingual: a pregnant woman. _ The doctor’s waiting room was filled with expectant mothers. _ The magazine has articles of interest to young parents and expectant mothers.
examples: The doctor’s waiting room was filled with expectant mothers.

expel someone from something.monolingual: to force someone to leave something or some place; to eject someone from something or some place. _ The two men expelled the fighters from the tavern. _ Ken was expelled from school for disciplinary reasons.
examples: The two men expelled the fighters from the tavern.

expel something from something.monolingual: to force or eject something out of something. _ The machine expelled cup after cup from its opening. _ The volcano expelled huge globs of molten lava.
examples: The machine expelled cup after cup from its opening.

expend something for something.monolingual: to pay a certain amount for something. _I expended an enormous amount for skin creams. _How much money did you expend for this gaudy tie?
examples: I expended an enormous amount for skin creams.

expend something in something.monolingual: to use or consume something in some activity. _ You expend too much energy in talking. _ Harry expended a lot of time in the preparation of his speech.
examples: You expend too much energy in talking.

experience is the best teacher..monolingual: Prov. You will learn more from things that happen to you in real life than you will from hearing about or studying things that happen to other people. _I don’t care how many books you read about how to run a business; experience is the best teacher.
examples: I don’t care how many books you read about how to run a business; experience is the best teacher.

experiment in something.monolingual: to conduct research or experiments about something. _ The research group is experimenting in the field of biomechanics. _We want to experiment in thermodynamics.
examples: The research group is experimenting in the field of biomechanics.

experiment with someone or something.monolingual: to try different experiments on someone or something; to use different people or things as key variables in an experiment. _They are supposed to be experimenting with new drugs. _ We no longer experiment with animals.
examples: They are supposed to be experimenting with new drugs.

explain oneself.monolingual: 1. to explain what one has said or done or what one thinks or feels. (Formal and polite.) _ Please take a moment to explain yourself. I’m sure we are interested in your ideas. _ Yes, if you will let me explain myself, I think you’ll agree with my ide
examples: Please take a moment to explain yourself.

explain something away†.monolingual: to explain something so that it is no longer a problem. _ You can try to explain it away if you want, but that won’t solve the problem. _You can’t just explain away all your problems.
examples: You can try to explain it away if you want, but that won’t solve the problem.

explode with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to make a loud noise upon exploding or releasing energy. _ The bomb exploded with a thunderous roar. _When the joke was finished, the audience exploded with laughter.
examples: The bomb exploded with a thunderous roar.

export something to some place.monolingual: to sell something abroad to a particular country. _ They are now exporting their products to Hungary. _ We are exporting all our product line to Eastern Europe.
examples: They are now exporting their products to Hungary.

express one’s anger.monolingual: to allow a release or expression of anger, such as through angry words, violence, or talking out a problem. _ Don’t keep your emotions inside of you. You have to learn to express your anger. _ Bob expresses his anger by yelling at people.
examples: Don’t keep your emotions inside of you.

expunge something from something.monolingual: to erase something from something. _The judge ordered the clerk to expunge the comment from the record. _Please expunge the lawyer’s remark from the transcript.
examples: The judge ordered the clerk to expunge the comment from the record.

expurgate something from something.monolingual: to cleanse something by removing something. (Often refers to editing objectionable material from written or broadcast material.) _ They expurgated the most graphic passages from the novel. _ We will expurgate the offensive matter from the article.
examples: They expurgated the most graphic passages from the novel.

extend across something.monolingual: to spread across something. _ The shadows extended across the whole land. _ The fog extended across the low-lying land.
examples: The shadows extended across the whole land.

extend over someone or something.monolingual: to spread over someone or something. _ The smoke extended over Tom and his friends, who were having a picnic. _The cloud extended over the entire valley.
examples: The smoke extended over Tom and his friends, who were having a picnic.

extend something to something.monolingual: 1. to lengthen something to reach something. _We extended the antenna to its full length. _Extend your arm to the wall and see how straight you can make it.
examples: We extended the antenna to its full length.

extend to someone or something.monolingual: to reach all the way to someone or something. _ This policy extends to you also. _ The road extends to Los Angeles.
examples: This policy extends to you also.

extenuating circumstances.monolingual: special (but otherwise unspecified) circumstances that account for an irregular or improper way of doing something. _ Mary was permitted to arrive late because of extenuating circumstances. _ Due to extenuating circumstances, the teacher will not mee
examples: Mary was permitted to arrive late because of extenuating circumstances.

extrapolate something from something.monolingual: to reason out the answer from the known facts. _I cannot extrapolate what he meant from these notes. _ Can you extrapolate the annual total from the company’s sales so far this year?
examples: I cannot extrapolate what he meant from these notes.

exult in something.monolingual: to take great pleasure in something; to enjoy something immensely. _ I exult in the beauty of a spring day. _ We exulted in the glory of summer.
examples: I exult in the beauty of a spring day.

eyeball-to-eyeball.monolingual: Fig. face-to-face and often very close; in person. _They approached each other eyeball-to-eyeball and frowned. _ Let’s talk more when we are eyeball-toeyeball.
examples: They approached each other eyeball-to-eyeball and frowned.

eyes like saucers.monolingual: Fig. eyes opened widely as in amazement. _Our eyes were like saucers as we witnessed another display of the manager’s temper.
examples: Our eyes were like saucers as we witnessed another display of the manager’s temper.

face off.monolingual: 1. to begin a hockey game with two players facing one another. _ They faced off and the match was on.
examples: They faced off and the match was on.

face someone down†.monolingual: to make a face-to-face stand with someone who eventually backs down. _Chuck succeeded in facing Tom down. _ Facing down Tom wasn’t difficult for Chuck.
examples: Chuck succeeded in facing Tom down.

face someone or something forward.monolingual: to turn someone or something to the front. (Also with many other directions— backward, to the right, to the left, etc.) _Please face your brother forward now. _ Face the book forward so we can read the title.
examples: Please face your brother forward now.

face someone with something.monolingual: to present evidence of something to someone. _ When I faced him with the evidence, he confessed immediately. _The police faced Max with the witness’s story. _ The CEO was faced with the problem of bringing the bankrupt firm back to profitability.
examples: When I faced him with the evidence, he confessed immediately.

face something down.monolingual: to turn something face downward. _ Ted drew a card and faced it down. _ Face your cards down when you leave the card table.
examples: Ted drew a card and faced it down.

face something head-on.monolingual: Fig. to confront a problem directly and openly. _Let’s face this problem head-on and try to solve it quickly and painlessly.
examples: Let’s face this problem head-on and try to solve it quickly and painlessly.

face something with something.monolingual: to install something on the surface of something. _ We faced the kitchen walls with yellow tile. _ The wall was faced with tile.
examples: We faced the kitchen walls with yellow tile.

face the music.monolingual: Fig. to receive punishment; to accept the unpleasant results of one’s actions. _ Mary broke a dining- room window and had to face the music when her father got home. _ After failing a math test, Tom had to go home and face the music.
examples: Mary broke a dining- room window and had to face the music when her father got home.

face-to-face.monolingual: 1. Fig. in person; in the same location. (Said only of people. An adverb.) _Let’s talk about this face-toface. I don’t like talking over the telephone. _ Many people prefer to talk face-to-face.
examples: Let’s talk about this face-toface.

the facts of life.monolingual: 1. Euph. the facts of sex and reproduction, especially human reproduction. _My parents told me the facts of life when I was nine years old. _ Bill learned the facts of life from his classmates.
examples: My parents told me the facts of life when I was nine years old.

fade down.monolingual: [for sound] to diminish. _ The roar of the train faded down as it passed and f led into the night. _ As the thunder faded down, the sun began to break through the clouds.
examples: The roar of the train faded down as it passed and f led into the night.

fade from something.monolingual: [for something] to leave something gradually, such as one’s consciousness, memory, view, etc. _ The image faded from her memory at last.
examples: The image faded from her memory at last.

fade from view.monolingual: [for a sight] to fade away, typically owing to loss of light or distance. _ The scene faded from view as the stage lights dimmed. _My house faded from view as we drove down the long road to town.
examples: The scene faded from view as the stage lights dimmed.

fade into something.monolingual: to diminish or change into something. _The light of dusk faded into blackness. _In the corner of the painting, the deep reds faded into lavender.
examples: The light of dusk faded into blackness.

fade something down†.monolingual: to turn down a sound. (Broadcasting.) _ The radio engineer faded the music down and the announcer’s voice began. _ She faded down the music.
examples: The radio engineer faded the music down and the announcer’s voice began.

fade something in†.monolingual: to bring a picture, sound, or both into prominence. (Broadcasting.) _ The technician faded the picture in and the program began. _ Fade in the picture a little faster next time.
examples: The technician faded the picture in and the program began.

fade something out†.monolingual: to diminish something altogether. (Broadcasting.) _ At the end, you should fade the music out completely. _ Fade out the music earlier.
examples: At the end, you should fade the music out completely.

fade something up†.monolingual: to increase the sound gradually. (Broadcasting.) _The director faded the music up and then down again before the announcer spoke. _ Fade up the music when the announcer stops talking.
examples: The director faded the music up and then down again before the announcer spoke.

fag someone out.monolingual: Sl. to tire someone out. _ All that work really fagged me out. _ The hard climb fagged the hikers out.
examples: All that work really fagged me out.

fagged out.monolingual: Sl. exhausted. _ I’m really fagged out after all that running. _ John, you sure look fagged out.
examples: I’m really fagged out after all that running.

fail in something.monolingual: to have not earned passing or satisfactory grades in some school subject. _George is failing in geometry. _ I hope I do not fail in math.
examples: George is failing in geometry.

fail someone on something.monolingual: to give someone an unsatisfactory grade on an assignment or test. _ She failed us all on the math assignment. _The teacher failed half the class on the assignment.
examples: She failed us all on the math assignment.

faint dead away.monolingual: Fig. to faint and fall unconscious. _ I almost fainted dead away. _ David will faint dead away when he reads this.
examples: I almost fainted dead away.

faint from something.monolingual: to faint because of something. _ I nearly fainted from fear! _ Three people along the parade route fainted from the heat.
examples: Three people along the parade route fainted from the heat.

the faint of heart.monolingual: Fig. people who are squeamish; someone who is sickened or disturbed by unpleasantness or challenge. _ The pathway around the top of the volcano, near the crater, is not for the faint of heart.
examples: The pathway around the top of the volcano, near the crater, is not for the faint of heart.

fair and impartial.monolingual: just and unbiased. (Usually referring to some aspect of the legal system, such as a jury, a hearing, or a judge.) _ Gary felt that he had not received a fair and impartial hearing. _We demand that all of our judges be fair and impartial in every inst
examples: Gary felt that he had not received a fair and impartial hearing.

fair and square.monolingual: completely fair(ly); justly; within the rules. _She won the game fair and square. _The division of the money should be fair and square.
examples: She won the game fair and square.

*a fair shake.monolingual: an instance of fair treatment. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ He’s unpleasant, but we have to give him a fair shake. _ He got a fair shake from us. Don’t worry!
examples: He’s unpleasant, but we have to give him a fair shake.

fair something out†.monolingual: Rur. to distribute something fairly. _ She faired the meager stew out the best she could. _Walter faired out the pie.
examples: She faired the meager stew out the best she could.

fair to middlin’.monolingual: Rur. mediocre; not bad but not good. (Middling means ‘of average quality.’) _ Tom: How are you feeling today? Bill: Fair to middlin’. _ My sewing is excellent, but my cooking is only fair to middlin’.
examples: Tom: How are you feeling today? Bill: Fair to middlin’.

fair-haired boy.monolingual: Fig. a favored person. (Not necessarily young or a boy.) _ The teacher’s fair-haired boy always does well on tests. _The supervisor’s son was the fair-haired boy on the construction site.
examples: The teacher’s fair-haired boy always does well on tests.

fair-weather friend.monolingual: Fig. someone who is your friend only when things are pleasant or going well for you. _Bill stayed for lunch but he wouldn’t help me with the yard work. He’s just a fair-weather friend. _A fair-weather friend isn’t much help in an emergency.
examples: Bill stayed for lunch but he wouldn’t help me with the yard work.

faith will move mountains..monolingual: Prov. If you believe in what you are doing, you can overcome any obstacle. (Sometimes refers to faith in God.) _ Jane’s faith in her cause could move mountains. _You may feel disheartened sometimes, but remember that faith will move mountains.
examples: Jane’s faith in her cause could move mountains.

fake it.monolingual: to pretend (to do something). _ If you don’t know the right notes, just fake it. _ I can’t fake it anymore. I’ve got to be honest with you.
examples: If you don’t know the right notes, just fake it.

fake off.monolingual: Sl. to waste time; to goof off. _ Hey, you guys, quit faking off! _ All you clowns do is fake off. Now, get busy!
examples: All you clowns do is fake off.

fake someone out†.monolingual: to deceive someone; to fool someone. _You really faked me out. I never would have guessed it was you. _ The student tried to fake out the teacher.
examples: You really faked me out.

fake someone out of something.monolingual: Sl. to get something from someone by deception. _ He faked Tom out of his place in line. _ She faked me out of a lot of money.
examples: He faked Tom out of his place in line.

fall all over someone.monolingual: Fig. to give a lot of attention, affection, or praise to someone. _ My aunt falls all over me whenever she comes to visit. _ I hate for someone to fall all over me. It embarrasses me.
examples: My aunt falls all over me whenever she comes to visit.

fall asleep.monolingual: Fig. to go to sleep. _ I fell asleep while reading the very dull book. _ I got in bed and fell asleep at once.
examples: I fell asleep while reading the very dull book.

fall away toward something.monolingual: to slant downward toward something. _ The yard fell away toward the shore of the lake. _The broad expanse of prairie land fell away toward the river bottomland, and beyond that, the river itself.
examples: The yard fell away toward the shore of the lake.

fall back.monolingual: to move back from something; to retreat from something. _ The gang members fell back, and I took that opportunity to get away. _ The troops fell back to regroup.
examples: The gang members fell back, and I took that opportunity to get away.

fall below something.monolingual: to drop to a lower level than something. _ The temperature has fallen below freezing again. _ When the audience fell below two hundred a night, they closed the play.
examples: The temperature has fallen below freezing again.

fall beneath something.monolingual: to drop under something. _ The thimble fell beneath the sofa. _ The gift that Bob had purchased for Maggie fell beneath the wheels of a truck.
examples: The thimble fell beneath the sofa.

fall between two stools.monolingual: Fig. to come somewhere between two possibilities and so fail to meet the requirements of either. _ The material is not suitable for an academic book or for a popular one. It falls between two stools. _ He tries to be both teacher and friend, but fall
examples: The material is not suitable for an academic book or for a popular one.

fall by some amount.monolingual: [for an asset] to drop in value by a certain amount. _ The gas stocks fell by nearly 10 percent today. _ If the stock market falls by four hundred points, I’m going to jump off a cliff.
examples: The gas stocks fell by nearly 10 percent today.

fall down.monolingual: to drop or topple. _The baby fell down. _Walk carefully on this ice or you will fall down.
examples: The baby fell down.

fall down on the job.monolingual: Fig. to fail to do something properly; to fail to do one’s job adequately. _ The team kept losing because the coach was falling down on the job. _Tom was fired because he fell down on the job.
examples: The team kept losing because the coach was falling down on the job.

fall for someone.monolingual: Fig. to fall in love with someone. _ I fell for her in a big way. She’s gorgeous! _ Ted fell for Alice and they decided to get married.
examples: I fell for her in a big way.

fall for something.monolingual: Fig. to believe something without reservation. _Surely, you don’t expect me to fall for that! _She fell for the excuse I gave her about getting stuck in traffic.
examples: She fell for the excuse I gave her about getting stuck in traffic.

fall from grace.monolingual: 1. Lit. to sin and get on the wrong side of God. (A Christian concept.) _ It was either fall from grace or starve from lack of money. That’s how thieves are made. _ Given the choice between falling from grace and starving, few people choose to starve
examples: It was either fall from grace or starve from lack of money.

fall from power.monolingual: Fig. to go out of power; to go out of office. _ The dictator fell from power after the riots. _ Every ruler will fall from power sooner or later.
examples: The dictator fell from power after the riots.

fall from someone or something.monolingual: to fall off of someone or something. _The books fell from the top shelf in the earthquake. _The eggs rolled and fell from the counter and broke on the f loor.
examples: The books fell from the top shelf in the earthquake.

fall head over heels.monolingual: Fig. to fall down, perhaps turning over or rolling. _Fred tripped on the rug and fell head over heels into the center of the room. _ Slow down or you will fall down—head over heels.
examples: Fred tripped on the rug and fell head over heels into the center of the room.

fall heir to something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to inherit something; to end up with certain possessions of someone who has died. _ I fell heir to all my grandmother’s old photographs.
examples: I fell heir to all my grandmother’s old photographs.

fall ill.monolingual: Fig. to become ill. _ Tom fell ill just before he was to perform. _ We both fell ill after eating the baked fish.
examples: Tom fell ill just before he was to perform.

fall in.monolingual: to line up in a row, standing shoulder to shoulder. _ The Boy Scouts were told to fall in behind the leader. _ The soldiers fell in quickly.
examples: The Boy Scouts were told to fall in behind the leader.

fall in with something.monolingual: to concur with something; to harmonize with something. _ We had to fall in with her wishes. _ The statement falls in exactly with my view.
examples: We had to fall in with her wishes.

fall into decay.monolingual: to degenerate; to rot. _The house was very old and had fallen into decay. _ The small town fell into decay, and people moved out.
examples: The house was very old and had fallen into decay.

fall into disfavor.monolingual: to lose one’s influence; to be preferred less and less. _ This style of government fell into disfavor some years ago. _ Poor Lee fell into disfavor with the boss and lost all his special privileges.
examples: This style of government fell into disfavor some years ago.

fall into disgrace.monolingual: to become without honor. _ The mayor fell into disgrace because of his financial dealings. _We fell into disgrace because of our criminal affiliations.
examples: The mayor fell into disgrace because of his financial dealings.

fall into disuse.monolingual: to be used less and less. _The pump had fallen into disuse and the joints had rusted solid. _ Since my books had fallen into disuse, I sold them to a used-book dealer.
examples: The pump had fallen into disuse and the joints had rusted solid.

fall into one’s lap.monolingual: Fig. [for something of great value or usefulness] to be given or granted to someone without having been requested. _ Some valuable antique jewelry just fell into his lap. His late mother had kept it hidden for years.
examples: Some valuable antique jewelry just fell into his lap.

fall into the wrong hands.monolingual: Fig. to become associated with the wrong person; to become the possession of the wrong person. _ I don’t want these plans to fall into the wrong hands. _ This could be dangerous if it fell into the wrong hands.
examples: I don’t want these plans to fall into the wrong hands.

fall off.monolingual: to decline or diminish. _ Business falls off during the summer months. _My interest in school fell off when I became twenty.
examples: Business falls off during the summer months.

fall on deaf ears.monolingual: Fig. [for talk or ideas] to be ignored by the persons they were intended for. _ Her pleas for mercy fell on deaf ears; the judge gave her the maximum sentence. _ All of Sally’s good advice fell on deaf ears. Walter had made up his own mind.
examples: Her pleas for mercy fell on deaf ears; the judge gave her the maximum sentence.

fall on hard times.monolingual: Fig. to experience difficult times, especially financially. _Since the war, her family had fallen on hard times. _We fell on hard times during the recession.
examples: Since the war, her family had fallen on hard times.

fall on one’s sword.monolingual: 1. Lit. to fall down and be penetrated by one’s own sword, accidentally or on purpose. _ He tripped and fell on his sword.
examples: He tripped and fell on his sword.

fall out.monolingual: 1. to happen; to result. _As things fell out, we had a wonderful trip. _ What fell out of our discussion was a decision to continue.
examples: As things fell out, we had a wonderful trip.

fall out of bed.monolingual: 1. Lit. to roll out of one’s bed onto the floor. _ I fell out of bed and broke my arm. _ Billy fell out of bed and started to cry.
examples: I fell out of bed and broke my arm.

fall outside something.monolingual: to be beyond someone’s power, responsibility, or jurisdiction. _ This matter falls outside my bailiwick. _ Her offense fell outside of the manager’s jurisdiction.
examples: This matter falls outside my bailiwick.

fall over.monolingual: to topple over and fall down. _The fence fell over and dented the car. _ I felt faint and almost fell over.
examples: The fence fell over and dented the car.

fall over someone or something.monolingual: to stumble over someone or something. _ Sam came into the house and fell over a kitchen chair. _Walter fell over Roger, who was napping on the f loor.
examples: Sam came into the house and fell over a kitchen chair.

fall overboard.monolingual: to fall from a boat or a ship into the water. _ Someone fell overboard and they had to stop the boat and go back. _ The lady’s sunglasses fell overboard.
examples: Someone fell overboard and they had to stop the boat and go back.

fall short.monolingual: to lack something; to lack enough of something, such as money, time, etc. _ We fell short of money at the end of the month. _ Tom fell short of cash and had to borrow from me.
examples: We fell short of money at the end of the month.

fall through.monolingual: [for something, such as plans] to fail. _Our party for next Saturday fell through. _ I hope our plans don’t fall through.
examples: Our party for next Saturday fell through.

fall through something.monolingual: to fall and break through something. _ One of the skaters fell through the thin ice. _ A number of hailstones fell through the roof of the greenhouse.
examples: One of the skaters fell through the thin ice.

fall to.monolingual: to begin doing something; to prepare to do something and go to work on it. _She asked for help, and everyone fell to. _ Fall to, you guys!
examples: She asked for help, and everyone fell to.

fall to pieces.monolingual: 1. Lit. to break into pieces. _The road was so rough the car almost fell to pieces. _ I was afraid that my bicycle would fall to pieces before I got there.
examples: The road was so rough the car almost fell to pieces.

fall to someone.monolingual: Fig. to become the responsibility of someone. _ It always falls to me to apologize first. _ Why does it fall to me to answer the telephone every time it rings?
examples: It always falls to me to apologize first.

fall toward something.monolingual: to drop or fall in the direction of something. _ She fell toward the curb rather than toward the traffic. _ The tree fell toward the garage rather than toward the house.
examples: She fell toward the curb rather than toward the traffic.

fall under someone or something.monolingual: to drop down and end up beneath someone or something. _The old man fell under the wheels of the truck, but he suffered only minor injuries. _The child tripped and fell under Mrs. Rogers, who almost did not see her.
examples: The old man fell under the wheels of the truck, but he suffered only minor injuries.

fall under someone’s spell.monolingual: 1. Lit. to come under the magical control of a magician or similar person. _The damsel fell under the wizard’s spell and sat there speechless. _ As the children fell under the witch’s spell, they went to sleep.
examples: The damsel fell under the wizard’s spell and sat there speechless.

fall within something.monolingual: to belong to a specific category or classification. _ This falls within the realm of the medical profession. There’s no more I can do for you. _Does this fall within your area of expertise?
examples: This falls within the realm of the medical profession.

falter in something.monolingual: to fail in doing something; to exhibit a lack of something, such as faith, loyalty, perseverance, etc. _ He did not falter in his effort to see the project through to the end. _ I promised not to falter in my loyalty.
examples: He did not falter in his effort to see the project through to the end.

*familiar with someone or something.monolingual: to have a good knowledge of someone or something. (*Typically: be ~; become ~; get ~.) _ Are you familiar with changing a f lat tire? _ I can’t speak German fluently, but I’m somewhat familiar with the language.
examples: I can’t speak German fluently, but I’m somewhat familiar with the language.

familiarity breeds contempt..monolingual: Prov. People do not respect someone they know well enough to know his or her faults. _ The movie star doesn’t let anyone get to know him, because he knows that familiarity breeds contempt.
examples: The movie star doesn’t let anyone get to know him, because he knows that familiarity breeds contempt.

familiarize someone with something.monolingual: to help someone get to know or understand someone or something. _ I hope you will take the time to familiarize yourself with the instructions before you set out to operate this device. _ Let me take a moment to familiarize myself with the facts of th
examples: I hope you will take the time to familiarize yourself with the instructions before you set out to operate this device.

famous last words.monolingual: Fig. assertions that are almost immediately countered. (Sarcastic.) _ A: I said I would never speak to her again in my entire life! B: Famous last words! You just said hello to her.
examples: A: I said I would never speak to her again in my entire life! B: Famous last words! You just said hello to her.

*a fan of someone.monolingual: to be a follower of someone; to idolize someone. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _My mother is still a fan of the Beatles. _ I’m a great fan of the mayor of the town.
examples: My mother is still a fan of the Beatles.

fan out.monolingual: Fig. to spread out over a wide area. _The searchers fanned out, looking for the child lost in the woods. _ Let’s fan out and search a wider area.
examples: The searchers fanned out, looking for the child lost in the woods.

fan something out†.monolingual: to spread something out so that all parts can be seen better. (As one opens a wood and paper fan.) _ Todd fanned the cards out so we could see which ones he held. _ He fanned out the cards.
examples: Todd fanned the cards out so we could see which ones he held.

fan the breeze.monolingual: Fig. to chat or gossip. _ We’re just fanning the breeze, so you didn’t interrupt anything. _ Stop fanning the breeze and get to work.
examples: We’re just fanning the breeze, so you didn’t interrupt anything.

fancy footwork.monolingual: 1. Lit. clever and intricate dance steps. _ The old man was known for his fancy footwork when he was on Broadway.
examples: The old man was known for his fancy footwork when he was on Broadway.

fancy meeting you here!.monolingual: I am very surprised to meet you here! _ Tom: Hi, Sue! Fancy meeting you here! Sue: Hi, Tom. I was thinking the same thing about you. _“Fancy meeting you here,” said Mr. Franklin when he bumped into the company president at the racetrack.
examples: Tom: Hi, Sue! Fancy meeting you here! Sue: Hi, Tom.

fancy someone’s chances.monolingual: to have confidence in someone’s [including one’s own] ability to be successful. _ We all think she will refuse to go out with him, but he certainly fancies his own chances. _The other contestants are so talented that I don’t fancy his chances at all.
examples: We all think she will refuse to go out with him, but he certainly fancies his own chances.

far and away the best.monolingual: unquestionably the best. _ This soap is far and away the best I’ve ever used. _Sally is good, but Ann is far and away the best artist in our school.
examples: This soap is far and away the best I’ve ever used.

a far cry from something.monolingual: a thing that is very different from something else. _ What you did was a far cry from what you said you were going to do. _ The song they played was a far cry from what I call music.
examples: What you did was a far cry from what you said you were going to do.

far from it.monolingual: not it at all; not at all. _ Do I think you need a new car? Far from it. The old one is fine. _ Bill: Does this hat look strange? Tom: Far from it. It looks good on you.
examples: Do I think you need a new car? Far from it.

far from the madding crowd.monolingual: in a quiet, restful place. (From Thomas Gray’s poem, “Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard.”) _ Julia sat daydreaming at her desk, wishing she were far from the madding crowd. _ Jane: Where shall we go this weekend? Alan: Anywhere, as long as it’s f
examples: Julia sat daydreaming at her desk, wishing she were far from the madding crowd.

far gone.monolingual: 1. in an extreme state, usually an irrational or intoxicated state. _ Wow, that chick is far gone. Listen to her rave. _He was too far gone to make any sense.
examples: Wow, that chick is far gone.

far into the night.monolingual: late into the night; until very late. _ She sat up and read far into the night. _ The party went on far into the night.
examples: She sat up and read far into the night.

far out.monolingual: 1. Lit. far from the center of things; far from town. _ The Smiths live sort of far out. _ The restaurant is nice, but too far out.
examples: The Smiths live sort of far out.
