farm someone out†.monolingual: 1. [for someone in control] to send someone to work for someone else. _ I have farmed my electrician out for a week, so your work will have to wait. _ We farmed out the office staff.
examples: I have farmed my electrician out for a week, so your work will have to wait.

farm something out†.monolingual: 1. to deplete the fertility of land by farming too intensely. _ They farmed their land out through careless land management. _ They farmed out their land.
examples: They farmed their land out through careless land management.

fart around.monolingual: Fig. to waste time playing around. (Caution with fart, which is considered coarse.) _ Stop farting around and get the job started.
examples: Stop farting around and get the job started.

fashion something into something.monolingual: to make, form, or convert something into something else. _ He fashioned the newspaper into a temporary rain hat. _ Sarah fashioned the clay into a little bowl.
examples: He fashioned the newspaper into a temporary rain hat.

fashion something on something.monolingual: to model something on something else; to pattern something after something else. _ She fashioned her dress on something she had seen in a history book. _Donna fashioned the plan on the one Robert had used.
examples: She fashioned her dress on something she had seen in a history book.

fashion something out of something.monolingual: to make something from something; to convert something into something else. _ He tried to fashion a dog out of balloons. _ Elaine was expert at fashioning a bow out of chocolate.
examples: He tried to fashion a dog out of balloons.

fast and furious.monolingual: Cliché very rapidly and with unrestrained energy. _ Her work in the kitchen was fast and furious, and it looked lovely when she finished. _ Everything was going so fast and furious at the store during the Christmas rush that we never had time to eat
examples: Her work in the kitchen was fast and furious, and it looked lovely when she finished.

fast friends.monolingual: good, loyal friends. _ The two of them had been fast friends since college.
examples: The two of them had been fast friends since college.

a fast one.monolingual: a clever and devious trick. (Compare this with pull a fast one.) _ That was a fast one. I didn’t know you were so devious. _ This was the last fast one like that you’ll ever catch me with.
examples: That was a fast one.

fasten something up†.monolingual: to close something up, using buttons, a zipper, snaps, hooks, a clasp, or other things meant to hold something closed. _ Please fasten this up for me. I can’t reach the zipper. _ Please fasten up my buttons in back.
examples: Please fasten this up for me.

faster and faster.monolingual: at an increasing rate of speed; fast and then even faster. _The car went faster and faster and I was afraid we would crash. _ The cost of education goes up faster and faster every year.
examples: The car went faster and faster and I was afraid we would crash.

fast-talk someone into something.monolingual: to use deceitful talk to get someone to do something. _You can’t fast-talk me into giving you money. How dumb do you think I am? _ Max tried to fast-talk Lefty into robbing a bank with him.
examples: You can’t fast-talk me into giving you money.

fast-talk someone out of something.monolingual: to use deceitful talk to get someone not to do something or to give something up. _ Don’t try to fast-talk me out of my share.
examples: Don’t try to fast-talk me out of my share.

fat and happy.monolingual: Fig. content, as if from being well-fed. _ Since all the employees were fat and happy, there was little incentive to improve productivity. _You look fat and happy. Has life been treating you well?
examples: Since all the employees were fat and happy, there was little incentive to improve productivity.

fat and sassy.monolingual: Fig. in good health and spirits. _She came back from her vacation all fat and sassy. _Under Joe’s care, the runt of the litter grew up fat and sassy.
examples: She came back from her vacation all fat and sassy.

*fat as a pig.monolingual: exceptionally fat; grotesquely fat. (*Also: as ~.) _ If I don’t stop eating this cake, I’ll be fat as a pig! _ You really ought to go on a diet; you’re as fat as a pig.
examples: You really ought to go on a diet; you’re as fat as a pig.

fat cat.monolingual: Fig. someone who is ostentatiously and smugly wealthy. _ I like to watch the fat cats go by in their BMWs. _ I’m no fat cat. I can’t even pay my normal bills!
examples: I like to watch the fat cats go by in their BMWs.

fat chance.monolingual: Fig. very little likelihood. _ Fat chance he has of getting a promotion. _ You think she’ll lend you the money? Fat chance!
examples: Fat chance he has of getting a promotion.

*the fat hit the fire.monolingual: Fig. a situation that suddenly becomes frantic and unpleasant. (*Typically: suddenly ~; then ~; when ~.) _ Things were looking bad in the stock market, then the fat hit the fire and I lost everything.
examples: Things were looking bad in the stock market, then the fat hit the fire and I lost everything.

a fate worse than death.monolingual: Fig. a terrible fate. (Usually an exaggeration.) _ Having to sit through one of his lectures is a fate worse than death.
examples: Having to sit through one of his lectures is a fate worse than death.

father something on someone.monolingual: Fig. to regard someone as the author or originator of something. _ Do not attempt to father that stupid idea on me! _We fathered the whole plan on the president. And we learned later she had nothing to do with it.
examples: We fathered the whole plan on the president.

faunch around.monolingual: Rur. to fuss and complain. _Stop faunching around about your problems and go to sleep. _ Aunt Bess is always faunching around about something.
examples: Stop faunching around about your problems and go to sleep.

fear for someone or something.monolingual: to be afraid for the safety of someone or something; to worry about someone or something. _ I fear for Tom. He has gone to a very dangerous place. _ I don’t want to go down that rocky trail. I fear for my car.
examples: I fear for Tom.

a feather in one’s cap.monolingual: Fig. an honor; a reward for something. _Getting a new client was really a feather in my cap. _John earned a feather in his cap by getting an A in physics.
examples: Getting a new client was really a feather in my cap.

feature someone as something.monolingual: 1. to imagine someone to be something or a particular type of person. _ I really can’t feature you as a ship’s captain. _Alice had always featured Fred as a fairly even-tempered person.
examples: I really can’t feature you as a ship’s captain.

feature someone in something.monolingual: 1. to imagine someone wearing something. _I can’t feature you in that ridiculous dress. _ Can you feature Fran in that hat?
examples: I can’t feature you in that ridiculous dress.

feed one’s face.monolingual: Inf. to put food in one’s mouth; to eat (something). _ You’re always feeding your face. You’re going to get fat. _ Stop feeding your face and listen to me.
examples: You’re always feeding your face.

feed something back into something.monolingual: to return something back to where it came. _ I tried to feed the stamps back into the machine, but, of course, they wouldn’t go. _ The machine made too many boxes, but you can’t feed them back into it!
examples: I tried to feed the stamps back into the machine, but, of course, they wouldn’t go.

feed something back† to someone.monolingual: to give or hand something back to someone. _We fed the rope back to those in line behind us. _ Feed back the papers to the clerk.
examples: We fed the rope back to those in line behind us.

feed something into something.monolingual: to put something into something; to push a supply of something into something. _ I fed all the coins into the telephone and waited to be connected. _ I will feed every coin I have into the phone and see what it does for me. _ Did you feed the data in
examples: I fed all the coins into the telephone and waited to be connected.

feed something to someone.monolingual: Fig. to tell someone lies. _Don’t try to feed that nonsense to me! I know it isn’t so. _ Please don’t feed any of those lies to Mark.
examples: Don’t try to feed that nonsense to me! I know it isn’t so.

feed the kitty.monolingual: Fig. to contribute money. (A kitty here is a small collection of money.) _Please feed the kitty. Make a contribution to help sick children. _ Come on, Bill. Feed the kitty. You can afford a dollar for a good cause.
examples: Please feed the kitty.

a feeding frenzy.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of sharks] a vicious, competitive feeding attack on prey animals. _ One of the sharks was fatally bitten during a feeding frenzy amongst his own kind.
examples: One of the sharks was fatally bitten during a feeding frenzy amongst his own kind.

feel a draft.monolingual: to sense that one is being rejected; to sense that someone is cool toward one, possibly for racial reasons. _Oh, man, I feel a draft in here. Let’s leave. _What a reception! I sure felt a draft.
examples: Oh, man, I feel a draft in here.

feel at home.monolingual: to feel as if one belongs; to feel as if one were in one’s home; to feel accepted. _ I liked my dormitory room. I really felt at home there. _We will do whatever we can to make you feel at home.
examples: I liked my dormitory room.

feel blue.monolingual: Fig. to feel sad. _ You look like you feel blue. What’s wrong?
examples: You look like you feel blue.

feel fit.monolingual: to feel well and healthy. _If you want to feel fit, you must eat the proper food and get enough rest. _I hope I still feel fit when I get old.
examples: If you want to feel fit, you must eat the proper food and get enough rest.

feel for someone.monolingual: to feel the emotional pain that someone else is feeling; to empathize or sympathize with someone. _ I really feel for you. I’m so sorry it turned out this way. _ Fred felt for Dave, but there was nothing he could do for him.
examples: I really feel for you.

*a feel for something.monolingual: a natural or learned ability to do something. (*Typically: get ~; have ~.) _ I will do better with this work as soon as I get a feel for it. _ He doesn’t have a feel for this kind of careful work.
examples: I will do better with this work as soon as I get a feel for it.

feel like a new person.monolingual: Fig. to feel refreshed and renewed, especially after getting well or getting dressed up. _I bought a new suit, and now I feel like a new person. _ Bob felt like a new person when he got out of the hospital.
examples: I bought a new suit, and now I feel like a new person.

feel like doing something.monolingual: to want to do something; to be in the mood to do something; to feel well enough to do something. _ Do you feel like stopping work to eat something? _ I feel like going on a vacation.
examples: I feel like going on a vacation.

feel like someone or something.monolingual: to have the feel of someone or something; to seem to be someone or something according to feel or touch. _Whoever this is feels like Tom. Sort of soft and pudgy. _This thing feels like a rubber hose, not a hot dog.
examples: Whoever this is feels like Tom.

*the feel of something.monolingual: Fig. a sense for how something feels when it is being used correctly. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ I haven’t yet got the feel of this bat. I hope I don’t strike out. _ I can drive better now that I have the feel of this car’s steeri
examples: I haven’t yet got the feel of this bat.

feel one’s gorge rise.monolingual: Fig. to sense that one is getting very angry. _ I felt my gorge rise and I knew I was going to lose my temper. _ Bob could feel his gorge rise as he read his tax bill.
examples: I felt my gorge rise and I knew I was going to lose my temper.

feel one’s oats.monolingual: Fig. to be very lively. _ Careful with that horse. He’s feeling his oats today. _ Mary was feeling her oats and decided to go out dancing.
examples: Careful with that horse.

feel out of things.monolingual: to feel alienated from something. _ I feel out of things lately. Are people ignoring me? _ I feel a little out of things at this party, but I will try to join in the fun.
examples: I feel out of things lately.

feel someone up†.monolingual: to feel someone sexually. (Use discretion with topic.) _I heard him say he really wanted to feel her up. _ He wanted to feel up the girl.
examples: I heard him say he really wanted to feel her up.

feel something with something.monolingual: to touch and explore something with something. _ I felt the soft little creature with my hand. _ Don’t feel that thing with your bare hands.
examples: I felt the soft little creature with my hand.

feel up to something.monolingual: to feel well enough or prepared enough to do something. (Often in the negative.) _I don’t feel up to jogging today. _Aunt Mary didn’t feel up to making the visit.
examples: I don’t feel up to jogging today.

feeling no pain.monolingual: numbed by alcohol and feeling nothing; intoxicated. _She fell off the wagon and is feeling no pain. _ He drank the whole thing, and he’s feeling no pain.
examples: She fell off the wagon and is feeling no pain.

fence an animal in†.monolingual: to enclose an animal and its area within a fence or barrier. _We fenced the dog in to keep it at home. _ We had to fence in the dog.
examples: We fenced the dog in to keep it at home.

fence someone in†.monolingual: to restrict someone in some way. _ I don’t want to fence you in, but you have to get home earlier at night. _Don’t try to fence me in. I need a lot of freedom. _ Your last stupid move fenced in the department, making us less effective.
examples: I don’t want to fence you in, but you have to get home earlier at night.

fence something in†.monolingual: to enclose an area within a fence. _ When they fenced the garden in, they thought the deer wouldn’t be able to destroy the f lowers. _ We fenced in the yard to make a safe place for the children.
examples: When they fenced the garden in, they thought the deer wouldn’t be able to destroy the f lowers.

fend someone or something off†.monolingual: to hold someone or something off; to fight someone or something off. _ We knew we could fend them off only a little while longer. _ They could not fend off the attackers.
examples: We knew we could fend them off only a little while longer.

fender bender.monolingual: Fig. a minor car accident. _A small fender bender tied up traffic on the expressway for hours!

ferry someone around†.monolingual: to transport people here and there in small groups. _ I really don’t want to spend all my days ferrying children around. _ Why am I ferrying around a bunch of kids all day?
examples: I really don’t want to spend all my days ferrying children around.

fetch something in†.monolingual: to bring or pull something in. _Would you please fetch some more firewood in? _ Can you fetch in the paper?

fetch up.monolingual: Sl. to empty one’s stomach; to vomit. _ I really felt like I was going to fetch up. _ Somebody fetched up in here and didn’t clean it up.
examples: I really felt like I was going to fetch up.

fetch up at some place.monolingual: to reach a place; to end up at a place. _ We fetched up at Sam’s house at about midnight. _ The car fetched up at the cabin and everyone got out.
examples: We fetched up at Sam’s house at about midnight.

few and far between.monolingual: very few; few and widely scattered. _ Get some gasoline now. Service stations on this highway are few and far between. _ Some people think that good movies are few and far between.
examples: Get some gasoline now.

fiddle something away†.monolingual: to waste something. _She fiddled the afternoon away. _Don’t fiddle away the afternoon. Get to work.
examples: She fiddled the afternoon away.

fiddle while rome burns.monolingual: Fig. to do nothing or something trivial while knowing that something disastrous is happening. (From a legend that the Roman emperor Nero played the lyre while Rome was burning.) _The lobbyists don’t seem to be doing anything to stop this tax bill. Th
examples: The lobbyists don’t seem to be doing anything to stop this tax bill.

fiddle with someone or something.monolingual: to tinker or play with someone or something. _ Please don’t fiddle with the stereo controls. _ Leave your brother alone. Don’t fiddle with him. He’s cranky.
examples: Please don’t fiddle with the stereo controls.

fidget around.monolingual: to wiggle and twitch nervously. _The child sat there, fidgeting around for over ten minutes. _ Please don’t fidget around so.
examples: The child sat there, fidgeting around for over ten minutes.

fidget with something.monolingual: to play with something nervously. _ Please don’t fidget with your zipper. _ Carl is always fidgeting with his left ear.
examples: Please don’t fidget with your zipper.

a fifth wheel.monolingual: Fig. an unwelcome or extra person. _I don’t like living with my son and daughter-in-law. I feel like a fifth wheel. _ Bill always begs to come on camping trips with us, but really, he’s a fifth wheel.
examples: I don’t like living with my son and daughter-in-law.

fifty-fifty.monolingual: even or equal. _The chances of success are about fifty-fifty. _Even at fifty-fifty, it’s probably worth it, you know.
examples: The chances of success are about fifty-fifty.

fight about someone or something.monolingual: to have a battle or argue about someone or something. _ Why do we always have to fight about money? _ Let’s not fight about Ed.
examples: Let’s not fight about Ed.

fight against someone or something.monolingual: to battle against someone or something. _ The general refused to fight against the enemy, which was much stronger. _ He fought against the disease to the very end.
examples: The general refused to fight against the enemy, which was much stronger.

fight against time.monolingual: Fig. to hurry to meet a deadline or to do something quickly. _ The ambulance sped through the city to reach the accident, fighting against time. _ All the students fought against time to complete the test.
examples: The ambulance sped through the city to reach the accident, fighting against time.

fight fire with fire..monolingual: Prov. Use against your opponent the same methods he or she is using against you. _ After her opponent had spent several weeks slandering her, the candidate decided to fight fire with fire. _ When evangelists would come to our house and try to convert
examples: After her opponent had spent several weeks slandering her, the candidate decided to fight fire with fire.

fight for someone or something.monolingual: to go to battle for the benefit of someone or something; to go to battle in the name of someone or something. _ They all went off to fight for their country. _ The soldiers fought for the queen and the survival of the empire. _I guess I will have to
examples: They all went off to fight for their country.

fight on.monolingual: to continue to fight. _ The boys fought on until one of them was down. _ They fought on until they were exhausted.
examples: The boys fought on until one of them was down.

fight over someone or something.monolingual: to fight a battle that decides who gets someone or something. _Well, let’s not fight over Tom. You can have him. I can make a better team without him. _The children were fighting over who would get the largest piece of cake.
examples: Well, let’s not fight over Tom.

fight someone or something down†.monolingual: to fight against and defeat someone or something. _We fought the opposition down and got our bill through the committee. _We had to fight down Fred, who wanted something entirely different.
examples: We fought the opposition down and got our bill through the committee.

fight someone or something off†.monolingual: to repel an attack from someone or something. _We fought the enemy attack off, but they returned almost immediately. _She fought off the mosquitoes all evening. _ Jed fought the attacker off.
examples: We fought the enemy attack off, but they returned almost immediately.

fight something down†.monolingual: 1. to struggle to hold something back; to struggle to keep from being overwhelmed by something. _ She fought her anger down and managed to stay calm. _ She fought down the urge.
examples: She fought her anger down and managed to stay calm.

fight something out†.monolingual: to settle something by fighting. _Do we have to fight this out? Can’t we use reason? _ I prefer to fight out this matter once and for all.
examples: I prefer to fight out this matter once and for all.

fight the good fight.monolingual: to fight a noble and wellintentioned battle. _ He fought the good fight and left the meeting with a clear conscience.
examples: He fought the good fight and left the meeting with a clear conscience.

fight to the death.monolingual: to engage in a battle that isn’t finished until one opponent is dead. _ The two men looked as though they were going to fight to the death. _ These eviltempered dogs will fight to the death.
examples: The two men looked as though they were going to fight to the death.

a fighting chance.monolingual: a good possibility of success, especially if every effort is made. _ They have at least a fighting chance of winning the race. _The patient could die, but he has a fighting chance since the operation.
examples: They have at least a fighting chance of winning the race.

figure in something.monolingual: [for someone or something] to play a role in something. _ Tom figures in our plans for future office management. _ I don’t wish to figure in your future.
examples: Tom figures in our plans for future office management.

figure on doing something.monolingual: to plan on something. _ I figured on arriving at the party around eight o’clock. _ Jane figured on spending $25 on dinner.
examples: I figured on arriving at the party around eight o’clock.

figure on someone or something.monolingual: to count on someone or something; to assume something about someone or something. _I am figuring on twelve people for dinner next Friday. _We are figuring on you and your wife for dinner next weekend.
examples: I am figuring on twelve people for dinner next Friday.

figure someone as something.monolingual: to think of a person as a particular type of person. _I figured her as a reliable worker. _ We figured them all as good credit risks.
examples: I figured her as a reliable worker.

figure someone or something out†.monolingual: to begin to comprehend someone or something; to come to understand someone or something better. _I just can’t figure you out. _I can’t figure out quiet people readily.
examples: I just can’t figure you out.

figure something up†.monolingual: to add up the amount of something. _ Please figure the bill up. We have to go now. _ I will figure up the bill right away.
examples: Please figure the bill up.

file for something.monolingual: to submit an application or document for something. _The company filed for bankruptcy. _Let’s file for reorganization.
examples: The company filed for bankruptcy.

file something against someone.monolingual: to lodge a criminal charge against someone. _ Sally filed a charge of assault against Max. _ The old man filed charges against the attacker.
examples: Sally filed a charge of assault against Max.

file something down†.monolingual: to level off a protrusion by filing. _ File this edge down so no one gets cut on it. _ Please file down this edge.
examples: File this edge down so no one gets cut on it.

fill in.monolingual: [for an indentation, hole, etc.] to become full. _The scar filled in after a few months. _ Will this hole in the ground fill in by itself, or should I put some dirt in?
examples: The scar filled in after a few months.

fill in the blanks..monolingual: You can figure out the rest.; You can draw a conclusion from that. (Fixed order. See also fill something in.) _Mary: What happened at Fred’s house last night? Bill: There was a big fight, then the neighbors called the police. Mary: Then what happened
examples: Mary: What happened at Fred’s house last night? Bill: There was a big fight, then the neighbors called the police.

fill out.monolingual: to become full; to gain weight. _ About a month after her debilitating illness, Maggie began to fill out again. _ The fruit on the trees began to fill out, and we knew it was going to ripen soon.
examples: About a month after her debilitating illness, Maggie began to fill out again.

fill someone full of lead.monolingual: Sl. to shoot someone. _The shopkeeper bought a gun and swore the next time someone broke into the shop, he’d fill him full of lead. _Don’t move, or I’ll fill you full of lead.
examples: The shopkeeper bought a gun and swore the next time someone broke into the shop, he’d fill him full of lead.

fill someone’s head with something.monolingual: Fig. to put some kind of ideas into someone’s head. _ Who’s been filling your head with ideas like that? _Mary has been filling my head with ideas about how to get rich.
examples: Mary has been filling my head with ideas about how to get rich.

fill someone’s shoes.monolingual: Fig. to take the place of some other person and do that person’s work satisfactorily. (As if you were wearing the other person’s shoes.) _ I don’t know how we’ll be able to do without you. No one can fill your shoes. _ It’ll be difficult to fill Jane
examples: I don’t know how we’ll be able to do without you.

fill something in†.monolingual: 1. to add material to an indentation, hole, etc., to make it full. _ You had better fill the crack in with something before you paint the wall. _You should fill in the cracks first.
examples: You had better fill the crack in with something before you paint the wall.

fill something out†.monolingual: Fig. to complete a form by writing in the blank spaces. _Please fill this form out and send it back to us in the mail. _ I will fill out the form as you asked.
examples: Please fill this form out and send it back to us in the mail.

fill something to something.monolingual: to add material to something up to a certain point. _ Fill the barrel up to here and no higher. _ Please fill the glass to the top.
examples: Fill the barrel up to here and no higher.

fill the gap.monolingual: to serve temporarily. _ I think that the temp will fill the gap until a new person can be hired.
examples: I think that the temp will fill the gap until a new person can be hired.

fill up.monolingual: 1. to become full. _ The creek filled up after the heavy rain yesterday. _The rain barrel began to fill up during the storm.
examples: The creek filled up after the heavy rain yesterday.

filled to the brim.monolingual: filled all the way full; filled up to the top edge. _ I like my coffee cup filled to the brim. _ If the glass is filled to the brim, I can’t drink without spilling the contents.
examples: I like my coffee cup filled to the brim.

film over.monolingual: [for something] to develop a film on its surface. _ The windows had filmed over because of all the humidity. _ Her eyes filmed over with the cold.
examples: The windows had filmed over because of all the humidity.

filthy lucre.monolingual: money. _ I sure could use a little of that filthy lucre. _ I don’t want to touch any of your filthy lucre.
examples: I sure could use a little of that filthy lucre.

filthy rich.monolingual: 1. Fig. very wealthy. _ I wouldn’t mind being filthy rich. _ There are too many filthy rich people now.
examples: I wouldn’t mind being filthy rich.

a final fling.monolingual: Fig. the last act or period of enjoyment before a change in one’s circumstances or lifestyle. _ You might as well have a final f ling before the baby’s born. _ Mary’s find (something) out (about going out with her girlfriends for a final f ling. She’

financially embarrassed.monolingual: Euph. broke. _ I’m a bit financially embarrassed at the moment. _Gary found himself financially embarrassed when the time came to pay the bill.
examples: I’m a bit financially embarrassed at the moment.

find against someone or something.monolingual: [for a jury or a judge] to announce a decision against one side of a lawsuit. _ The jury found against the defendant, who was a horrible witness. _ The court found against the corporation and levied a fine.
examples: The jury found against the defendant, who was a horrible witness.

find favor with someone.monolingual: to win the praise of someone. _ The maid found favor with the family and was given a large salary increase. _Mary found favor with her employer because of her good ideas.

find someone in.monolingual: to learn or discover that one is at home; to learn or discover that one is in one’s office. _ I never expected to find you in at this time of night. _ Did you really expect to find me in on a Friday night?

find someone out.monolingual: 1. to discover that someone is not at home. _We knocked on their door and found them out. _ Sam found Frank out when he arrived to collect the debt.

follow the crowd.monolingual: to do what everyone else is doing. _ I am an independent thinker. I could never just follow the crowd. _When in doubt, I follow the crowd. At least I don’t stand out like a fool.
examples: I am an independent thinker.

*fond of someone or something.monolingual: liking someone or something. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ I’m fond of chocolate. _ Mary isn’t fond of me, but I’m fond of her.
examples: I’m fond of chocolate.

food for thought.monolingual: Fig. something for someone to think about; issues to be considered. _ Your essay has provided me with some interesting food for thought. _ My adviser gave me some food for thought about job opportunities.
examples: Your essay has provided me with some interesting food for thought.

fool around.monolingual: to waste time doing something unnecessary or doing something amateurishly. _ Stop fooling around and clean your room as I told you. _I wish you didn’t spend so much time fooling around.
examples: Stop fooling around and clean your room as I told you.

a fool’s paradise.monolingual: Fig. a state of being happy for foolish or unfounded reasons. _I’m afraid that Sue’s marital happiness is a fool’s paradise; there are rumors that her husband is unfaithful. _ Fred is confident that he’ll get a big raise this year, but I think he’s l
examples: I’m afraid that Sue’s marital happiness is a fool’s paradise; there are rumors that her husband is unfaithful.

fool someone into something.monolingual: to deceive someone or oneself into doing something. _ You’ll never fool me into believing you. _We fooled the boss into giving us all the day off.
examples: You’ll never fool me into believing you.

*a foot in both camps.monolingual: Fig. an interest in or to support each of two opposing groups of people. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _The shop steward had been promised a promotion and so had a foot in both camps during the strike—workers and management. _Mr. Smith
examples: The shop steward had been promised a promotion and so had a foot in both camps during the strike—workers and management.

foot-in-mouth disease.monolingual: the tendency to say the wrong thing at the wrong time. _I suffer a lot from foot-in-mouth disease. _ Well, Ralph has foot-in-mouth disease again.
examples: I suffer a lot from foot-in-mouth disease.

footloose and fancy-free.monolingual: Fig. without long-term responsibilities or commitments. _ All the rest of them have wives, but John is footloose and fancy-free. _ Mary never stays long in any job. She likes being footloose and fancy-free.
examples: All the rest of them have wives, but John is footloose and fancy-free.

for a living.monolingual: [of work] done to earn enough money to live. _ John paints houses for a living. _ What do you do for a living?
examples: John paints houses for a living.

*for a song.monolingual: Fig. cheaply. (As if the singing of a song were payment. *Typically: buy something ~; get something ~; pick up someone ~.) _No one else wanted it, so I picked it up for a song. _I could buy this house for a song, because it’s so ugly.
examples: No one else wanted it, so I picked it up for a song.

for all i care.monolingual: I don’t care if (something happens). _ For all I care, the whole city council can go to the devil. _ They can all starve for all I care.
examples: For all I care, the whole city council can go to the devil.

for all i know.monolingual: according to the information I have; I think; probably. (Usually implies uncertainty.) _ For all I know, the mayor has resigned already. _ She may have gone to town for all I know.
examples: For all I know, the mayor has resigned already.

for all intents and purposes.monolingual: Cliché seeming as if; looking as if. _Tom stood there, looking, for all intents and purposes, as if he could strangle Sally, but, being the gentleman that he is, he just glowered. _Mary: Is the car washed now? John: For all intents and purposes, yes,
examples: Tom stood there, looking, for all intents and purposes, as if he could strangle Sally, but, being the gentleman that he is, he just glowered.

for all practical purposes.monolingual: as might be reasonably expected; essentially. _ For all practical purposes, this is simply a matter of right and wrong. _ This should be considered final, for all practical purposes.
examples: For all practical purposes, this is simply a matter of right and wrong.

for all someone’s problems.monolingual: in spite of a person’s problems (as specified). _ For all her complaining, she still seems to be a happy person. _ For all my aches and pains, I’m still rather healthy.
examples: For all her complaining, she still seems to be a happy person.

for all the world.monolingual: 1. exactly; precisely. (Especially with look.) _ She sat there looking for all the world as if she was going to cry. _ It started out seeming for all the world like a beautiful day. Then a storm came up.
examples: She sat there looking for all the world as if she was going to cry.

for better or for worse.monolingual: under any conditions; no matter what happens. _ I married you for better or for worse. _ For better or for worse, I’m going to quit my job.
examples: I married you for better or for worse.

for days on end.monolingual: Fig. for many days. _ We kept on traveling for days on end. _ Doctor, I’ve had this pain for days on end.
examples: We kept on traveling for days on end.

for fear of something.monolingual: out of fear for something; because of fear of something. _He doesn’t drive for fear of an accident. _They lock their car doors for fear of being attacked.
examples: He doesn’t drive for fear of an accident.

for free.monolingual: for no charge or cost; free of any cost. _ They let us into the movie for free. _ I will let you have a sample of the candy for free.
examples: They let us into the movie for free.

for good.monolingual: forever; permanently. _ I finally left home for good. _They tried to repair it many times before they fixed it for good.
examples: I finally left home for good.

for good measure.monolingual: as extra; (adding) a little more to make sure there is enough. _ When I bought a pound of nails, the clerk threw in a few extra nails for good measure. _ I always put a little extra salt in the soup for good measure.
examples: When I bought a pound of nails, the clerk threw in a few extra nails for good measure.

for hours on end.monolingual: Fig. for many hours. _ We sat and waited in the emergency room for hours on end. _The children were happy to play video games for hours on end.
examples: We sat and waited in the emergency room for hours on end.

for instance.monolingual: for example. _ I’ve lived in many cities, for instance, Boston, Chicago, and Detroit. _ Jane is very generous. For instance, she volunteers at the hospital and gives money to charities.
examples: I’ve lived in many cities, for instance, Boston, Chicago, and Detroit.

for keeps.monolingual: forever. _Does that mean I’m going to have this scar for keeps? _ This is yours for keeps. Enjoy it.
examples: This is yours for keeps.

for life.monolingual: for the remainder of one’s life. _ The accident caused me to become blind for life. _She will stay in prison for life.
examples: The accident caused me to become blind for life.

for miles.monolingual: Fig. to or in a distance extending two or more miles. _ The huge field of wheat extends for miles. _ We traveled for miles without stopping.
examples: The huge field of wheat extends for miles.

for my money.monolingual: in my opinion (as regards value or worth). _ That’s the best brand of tools there is, for my money. _ For my money, you can’t go wrong with a pure wool sweater.
examples: That’s the best brand of tools there is, for my money.

for real.monolingual: Inf. genuine; not imaginary. _Ken is really strange. Is he for real? _ This whole day has been weird, it just isn’t for real.
examples: Ken is really strange.

for safekeeping.monolingual: for the purpose of keeping someone or something safe. _ I put my jewelry in the vault for safekeeping. _ I checked my fur coat at the entrance to the bar for safekeeping.
examples: I put my jewelry in the vault for safekeeping.

for sale.monolingual: available for purchase; buyable. _ Is this item for sale? _ How long has this house been for sale? _ My car is for sale. Are you interested?
examples: My car is for sale.

for shame!.monolingual: That is shameful! _ Sue: Did you hear that Tom was in jail? Fred: For shame! What did he do? Sue: Nobody knows. _ Mary: I’ve decided not to go to the conference. John: For shame! Who will represent us?
examples: Sue: Did you hear that Tom was in jail? Fred: For shame! What did he do? Sue: Nobody knows.

for short.monolingual: as an abbreviation. _ The Internal Revenue Service is known as the IRS for short. _ David goes by Dave for short.
examples: The Internal Revenue Service is known as the IRS for short.

for sure.monolingual: for certain. _ I will be there for sure. _ Sally: Are you ready to go? Bob: For sure. Sally: Then, let’s go.
examples: I will be there for sure.

for that matter.monolingual: besides; in addition. _ If you’re hungry, take one of my doughnuts. For that matter, take two. _ I don’t like this house. The roof leaks. For that matter, the whole place is falling apart. _ Tom is quite arrogant. So is his sister, for that matter.
examples: If you’re hungry, take one of my doughnuts.

for the asking.monolingual: if one just asks (for something); simply by asking; on request. _ Do you want to use my car? It’s yours for the asking. _ I have an extra winter coat that’s yours for the asking.
examples: Do you want to use my car? It’s yours for the asking.

*for the better.monolingual: to be an improvement. (*Typically: be ~; be a change ~.) _ A change of government would be for the better. _A new winter coat would certainly be for the better.
examples: A change of government would be for the better.

for the birds.monolingual: worthless; undesirable. _This television program is for the birds. _ Winter weather is for the birds.
examples: This television program is for the birds.

for the duration.monolingual: for the whole time that something continues; for the entire period of time required for something to be completed; for as long as something takes. _ We are in this war for the duration. _However long it takes, we’ll wait. We are here for the duration
examples: We are in this war for the duration.

for the fun of it.monolingual: just for the entertainment value of doing it. _ We went on a picnic just for the fun of it.
examples: We went on a picnic just for the fun of it.

for the life of me.monolingual: at all; even one little bit. (Used with a negative.) _ For the life of me, I can’t figure this out. _ I can’t for the life of me climb up a mountain.
examples: For the life of me, I can’t figure this out.

for the most part.monolingual: mostly; in general. _For the most part, the class is enjoying geometry. _ I like working here for the most part.
examples: For the most part, the class is enjoying geometry.

for the record.monolingual: so that (one’s own version of ) the facts will be known; for open, public knowledge. (This often is said when there are reporters present.) _ I’d like to say—for the record—that at no time have I ever accepted a bribe from anyone. _ For the record, I
examples: I’d like to say—for the record—that at no time have I ever accepted a bribe from anyone.

for your information.monolingual: a phrase that introduces or follows a piece of information. (Can be spoken with considerable impatience.) _Mary: What is this one? Sue: For your information, it is exactly the same as the one you just asked about. _Bob: How long do I have to wait her
examples: Mary: What is this one? Sue: For your information, it is exactly the same as the one you just asked about.

forbidden fruit.monolingual: Fig. someone or something that one finds attractive or desirable partly because having the person or thing is immoral or illegal. (Biblical; from the apple in the Garden of Eden that was forbidden to Adam by God.) _ Jim flirts with his sister-in-law
examples: Jim flirts with his sister-in-law only because she’s forbidden fruit.

force someone or something down†.monolingual: to press or push someone or something downward. _ I forced him down and slipped the handcuffs on him. _ The cop forced down the thug and handcuffed him. _I forced the dog down and held it there.
examples: I forced him down and slipped the handcuffs on him.

force someone’s hand.monolingual: to force a person to reveal plans, strategies, or secrets. (Alludes to a handful of cards in card playing.) _We didn’t know what she was doing until Tom forced her hand. _ We changed our game plan after we forced the other team’s hand in the first pe
examples: We didn’t know what she was doing until Tom forced her hand.

force something down†.monolingual: to force oneself to swallow something. _ I can’t stand sweet potatoes, but I manage to force them down just to keep from making a scene. _ She forced down the sweet potatoes.
examples: I can’t stand sweet potatoes, but I manage to force them down just to keep from making a scene.

force something through something.monolingual: to press or drive something through something that resists. _ They forced the bill through the legislature. _We were not able to force the matter through the board of directors.
examples: They forced the bill through the legislature.

fore and aft.monolingual: at the front and the back, usually of a boat or ship. _They had to attach new lights fore and aft because the old ones were not bright enough to meet the new regulations. _ The captain ordered a watch stationed fore and aft.
examples: They had to attach new lights fore and aft because the old ones were not bright enough to meet the new regulations.

foreclose on something.monolingual: to take the property on which a mortgage is held; to satisfy an unpaid loan by taking ownership of the property put up for security on the loan. _ If you don’t pay, we will be forced to foreclose on your house. _ The bank foreclosed on our property.
examples: If you don’t pay, we will be forced to foreclose on your house.

a foregone conclusion.monolingual: Cliché a conclusion already reached; an inevitable result. _ That the company was moving to California was a foregone conclusion. _That the mayor will win reelection is a foregone conclusion.
examples: That the company was moving to California was a foregone conclusion.

forewarned is forearmed..monolingual: Prov. If you know about something beforehand, you can prepare for it. _ Before you meet Lily, I should tell you that she’s a little eccentric. Forewarned is forearmed, right? _ Check the temperature before you go outside. Forewarned is forearmed.
examples: Before you meet Lily, I should tell you that she’s a little eccentric.

forget about someone or something.monolingual: 1. to put someone or something out of one’s mind. _ Don’t forget about me! _ You ought to forget about all that.
examples: You ought to forget about all that.

forget one’s manners.monolingual: to do something ill-mannered. _ Jimmy! Have we forgotten our manners?

forget oneself.monolingual: to forget one’s manners or training. (Said in formal situations in reference to belching, bad table manners, and, in the case of very young children, pantswetting.) _ Sorry, Mother, I forgot myself. _ John, we are going out to dinner tonight. Please
examples: Sorry, Mother, I forgot myself.

forget you!.monolingual: Sl. Drop dead!; Beat it! _ Oh, yeah! Forget you! _ Forget you! Get a life!

forgive and forget..monolingual: Prov. You should not only forgive people for hurting you, you should also forget that they ever hurt you. _ When my sister lost my favorite book, I was angry at her for weeks, but my mother finally convinced me to forgive and forget. _Jane: Are you g
examples: When my sister lost my favorite book, I was angry at her for weeks, but my mother finally convinced me to forgive and forget.

forgive someone for something.monolingual: to pardon someone for something. _ Please forgive me for being late. _ He never forgave himself for harming her.
examples: Please forgive me for being late.

form an opinion.monolingual: to think up or decide on an opinion. (Note the variations in the examples.) _ I don’t know enough about the issue to form an opinion. _ Don’t tell me how to think! I can form my own opinion. _ I don’t form opinions without careful consideration.
examples: I don’t know enough about the issue to form an opinion.

form and substance.monolingual: structure and meaningful content. _ The first act of the play was one screaming match after another. It lacked form and substance throughout. _ Jane’s report was good. The teacher commented on the excellent form and substance of the paper.
examples: The first act of the play was one screaming match after another.

form from something.monolingual: [for something] to develop from something; [for something] to assume a shape, using something else as raw material. _Suddenly, an idea began to form from the things that you had said. _It seemed that a figure was forming from the mists arising from t
examples: Suddenly, an idea began to form from the things that you had said.

form something out of something.monolingual: to shape something from something. _ He formed a tiny elephant out of the clay. _ Wally formed a mound out of the sand.
examples: He formed a tiny elephant out of the clay.

forty winks.monolingual: Fig. a nap; some sleep. _ I could use forty winks before I have to get to work. _ I need forty winks before I get started again.
examples: I could use forty winks before I have to get to work.

foul one’s own nest.monolingual: Fig. to harm one’s own interests; to bring disadvantage upon oneself. (Alludes to a bird excreting into its own nest. See also It’s an ill bird that fouls its own nest.) _He tried to discredit a fellow senator with the president, but just succeeded i
examples: He tried to discredit a fellow senator with the president, but just succeeded in fouling his own nest.

foul play.monolingual: illegal activity; bad practices. _The police investigating the death suspect foul play. _ Each student got an A on the test, and the teacher imagined it was the result of foul play.
examples: The police investigating the death suspect foul play.

foul someone or something up†.monolingual: to cause disorder and confusion for someone or something; to tangle up someone or something; to mess someone or something up. _ Go away! Don’t foul me up any more. _ You’ve fouled up my whole day. _ Watch out! You’re going to foul up my kite strings.
examples: Go away! Don’t foul me up any more.

foul up.monolingual: to blunder; to mess up. _Please don’t foul up this time. _The quarterback fouled up in the first quarter, and that lost us the game.
examples: Please don’t foul up this time.

fouled up.monolingual: messed up; ruined; tangled up. (Usually as fouled-up when attributive.) _ This is sure a fouled-up mess. _ You sure are fouled up, you know.
examples: This is sure a fouled-up mess.

found money.monolingual: money that has come to someone with such ease or surprise that one might have just as well found it by accident. _ The money he got from his uncle’s estate is all found money except for the taxes. He did nothing to earn it.
examples: The money he got from his uncle’s estate is all found money except for the taxes.

fraidy cat.monolingual: Fig. a coward; a person who is frightened of everything. (Used in children’s taunts.) _Don’t be a fraidy cat. Go ahead, jump! _ Carl is such a fraidy cat. He runs inside when it starts to rain.
examples: Don’t be a fraidy cat.

frame something in something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to place a frame of something around something. _ Let us frame the photograph in a wood frame rather than a metal one. _ Alice chose to frame the painting in a simple, unmatted frame.
examples: Let us frame the photograph in a wood frame rather than a metal one.

frame something out†.monolingual: to build the basic wood structure of a building, such as a house. _The carpenters, working fast, framed the whole house out in a day. _They framed out the house.
examples: The carpenters, working fast, framed the whole house out in a day.

fraternize with someone or something.monolingual: to associate with someone or a group; to consort with someone or a group. _ They were instructed not to fraternize with the opposing team before the game. _ Don’t fraternize with Lefty “Fingers” Moran.
examples: They were instructed not to fraternize with the opposing team before the game.

fraught with danger.monolingual: Cliché [of something] full of something dangerous or unpleasant. _ The spy’s trip to Russia was fraught with danger. _My escape from the kidnappers was fraught with danger.
examples: The spy’s trip to Russia was fraught with danger.

freak someone out†.monolingual: to shock or disorient someone. _The whole business freaked me out. _I didn’t mean to freak out everybody with the bad news.
examples: The whole business freaked me out.

free and clear.monolingual: without encumbrance, particularly in regard to the ownership of something. _ After the last payment, Jane owned the car free and clear. _ If you can’t prove that you own the house and the land it stands on free and clear, you can’t sell it.
examples: After the last payment, Jane owned the car free and clear.

free and easy.monolingual: casual. _ John is so free and easy. How can anyone be so relaxed? _ Now, take it easy. Just act free and easy. No one will know you’re nervous.
examples: John is so free and easy.

free gift.monolingual: something extra given to you when you buy something else. _ When you order your magazine subscription, this book is yours to keep as our free gift. _ This canvas tote is a free gift for everyone who opens an account at our bank today!
examples: When you order your magazine subscription, this book is yours to keep as our free gift.

free lunch.monolingual: Fig. something of value that is free. (Often negative. See also There’s no such thing as a free lunch.) _ There’s always somebody who’ll do anything to get a free lunch.
examples: There’s always somebody who’ll do anything to get a free lunch.

a free ride.monolingual: 1. Lit. a ride to somewhere for which no payment is demanded. _ I got a free ride from a truck driver who was headed for town. _ I won’t call a taxi when I can get a free ride.
examples: I got a free ride from a truck driver who was headed for town.

a freeze on doing something.monolingual: Fig. a policy that put a temporary end to something. _ The company put a freeze on hiring as soon as they took us over.
examples: The company put a freeze on hiring as soon as they took us over.

freeze one’s tail off.monolingual: Fig. Inf. to freeze; to get very cold. _ Don’t stand out there in the cold wind! You’ll freeze your tail off! _ It’s as cold as a welldigger’s nose today. I about froze my tail off walking to work.
examples: It’s as cold as a welldigger’s nose today.

freeze over.monolingual: [for a body of water] to get cold and form a layer of ice on top. _The pond froze over, so we went skating.
examples: The pond froze over, so we went skating.

freeze someone out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to make it too cold for someone, usually by opening windows or through the use of air-conditioning. _ Turn up the heat unless you’re trying to freeze us out. _ Are you trying to freeze out everybody? Close the door.
examples: Turn up the heat unless you’re trying to freeze us out.

freeze someone’s wages.monolingual: Fig. to hold someone’s pay at its current level. _The company froze everyone’s wages as soon as the economy went sour.
examples: The company froze everyone’s wages as soon as the economy went sour.

freeze something into something.monolingual: 1. to use cold to solidify something into a different state, usually water into ice. _ The extreme cold froze the water of the river into solid ice. _ The cold snap froze the water in the puddles into hard sheets of ice.
examples: The extreme cold froze the water of the river into solid ice.

freeze up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to freeze and stop functioning. _ The joint froze up and wouldn’t move anymore.
examples: The joint froze up and wouldn’t move anymore.

fresh and sweet.monolingual: 1. very clean and fresh smelling. _Now the baby is changed and she is all fresh and sweet.
examples: Now the baby is changed and she is all fresh and sweet.

*fresh as a daisy.monolingual: Cliché very fresh; [of a person] always alert and ready to go. (*Also: as ~.) _ How can you be fresh as a daisy so early in the morning? _I always feel fresh as a daisy after a shower.
examples: I always feel fresh as a daisy after a shower.

*a fresh start.monolingual: a new start; an act of starting over. (*Typically: get ~; get off to ~; give someone ~; have ~; make ~.) _ After our apologies and a little discussion, we decided to make a fresh start.
examples: After our apologies and a little discussion, we decided to make a fresh start.

freshen someone or something up†.monolingual: to revive or restore the appearance or vitality of someone or something. _What can we do to freshen this room up? _ A cold shower freshened up the runner.
examples: A cold shower freshened up the runner.

freshen up.monolingual: to get cleaned up, rested up, or restored. _ I need a few minutes to freshen up before dinner.
examples: I need a few minutes to freshen up before dinner.

fret not!.monolingual: Inf. Don’t worry!; Do not fret about it! _Mary: Oh, look at the clock! I’m going to be late for my appointment! Bob: Fret not! I’ll drive you. _ “Fret not!” said Sally. “We’re almost there!”
examples: Mary: Oh, look at the clock! I’m going to be late for my appointment! Bob: Fret not! I’ll drive you.

friend or foe.monolingual: a friend or an enemy. _ I can’t tell whether Jim is friend or foe. _“Who goes there? Friend or foe?” asked the sentry.
examples: I can’t tell whether Jim is friend or foe.

*friends with someone.monolingual: a friend of someone. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _Sally is friends with Bill. _Mary and Bill are friends with one another.
examples: Sally is friends with Bill.

*a frog in one’s throat.monolingual: Fig. a feeling of hoarseness or a lump in one’s throat. (Often regarded as a sign of fear. *Typically: get ~; have ~.) _ I feel like I’m getting a frog in my throat when I have to speak in public. _She says she gets a frog in her throat when she is n
examples: I feel like I’m getting a frog in my throat when I have to speak in public.

from a to z.monolingual: Fig. of a complete and wide variety. _ We have just about everything from A to Z. _ She ordered everything on the menu from A to Z.
examples: We have just about everything from A to Z.

from dawn to dusk.monolingual: Fig. during the period of the day when there is light; from the rising of the sun to the setting of the sun. _I have to work from dawn to dusk on the farm. _The factory runs from dawn to dusk to produce hats and gloves.
examples: I have to work from dawn to dusk on the farm.

from day to day.monolingual: on a daily basis; one day at a time; occasionally. _ We face this kind of problem from day to day. _ I’ll have to check into this matter from day to day.
examples: We face this kind of problem from day to day.

from door to door.monolingual: moving from one door to another— typically, from one house to another. _ The candidate went from door to door, campaigning for town council. _ The children went from door to door, saying “Trick or treat!” at each one.
examples: The candidate went from door to door, campaigning for town council.

from giddy-up to whoa.monolingual: Rur. all the way from the beginning to the end. _ The road is paved from giddy-up to whoa. _ The play stinks. It is dull from giddy-up to whoa.
examples: The road is paved from giddy-up to whoa.

from hand to hand.monolingual: Fig. from one person to a series of other persons. _The book traveled from hand to hand until it got back to its owner. _ By the time the baby had been passed from hand to hand, it was crying.
examples: The book traveled from hand to hand until it got back to its owner.

from head to toe.monolingual: Fig. from the top of one’s head to one’s feet. _ She was decked out in f lowers from head to toe. _ The huge parka covered the small child from head to toe, assuring that she would be well-protected against the cold.
examples: She was decked out in f lowers from head to toe.

from hell to breakfast.monolingual: Rur. from one end of the earth to the other; all over; everywhere. (Use with caution.) _ We searched from hell to breakfast, but never did find the runaway kid. _ I tracked that deer from hell to breakfast, but never got a shot at it.
examples: We searched from hell to breakfast, but never did find the runaway kid.

from here till next tuesday.monolingual: Rur. for a great distance; for a long time. _If you try that again, I’ll knock you from here till next Tuesday. _ You can lecture him from here till next Tuesday, but he won’t listen.
examples: If you try that again, I’ll knock you from here till next Tuesday.

from missouri.monolingual: requiring proof; needing to be shown something in order to believe it. (From the nickname for the state of Missouri, the Show Me State.) _ You’ll have to prove it to me. I’m from Missouri. _She’s from Missouri and has to be shown.
examples: You’ll have to prove it to me.

from overseas.monolingual: from a location on the other side of the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean, according to the point of view of someone located in the U.S. _ The latest word from overseas is that the treaty has been signed. _ Is there any news from overseas about the war?
examples: The latest word from overseas is that the treaty has been signed.

from pillar to post.monolingual: Fig. from one place to a series of other places; (figuratively) from person to person, as with gossip. _ My father was in the army, and we moved from pillar to post year after year. _ After I told one person my secret, it went quickly from pillar to
examples: My father was in the army, and we moved from pillar to post year after year.

from rags to riches.monolingual: Fig. from poverty to wealth; from modesty to elegance. _ The princess used to be quite poor. She certainly moved from rags to riches. _After I inherited the money, I went from rags to riches.
examples: The princess used to be quite poor.

*from scratch.monolingual: Fig. [making something] by starting from the beginning with the basic ingredients. (*Typically: bake something ~; do something ~; make something ~; start (something) ~.) _ We made the cake from scratch, using no prepared ingredients. _I didn’t have a
examples: We made the cake from scratch, using no prepared ingredients.

from sea to shining sea.monolingual: Fig. from coast to coast. (Taken from the lyrics of the song “America the Beautiful”.) _ The new insect pest spread from sea to shining sea in a matter of months.
examples: The new insect pest spread from sea to shining sea in a matter of months.

from side to side.monolingual: moving first to one side and then to the other, repeatedly. _ The pendulum of the clock swings from side to side. _ The singers swayed from side to side as they sang.
examples: The pendulum of the clock swings from side to side.

from start to finish.monolingual: Fig. entirely; throughout. _ I disliked the whole business from start to finish. _Mary caused problems from start to finish.
examples: I disliked the whole business from start to finish.

from stem to stern.monolingual: 1. Lit. from the front of a boat or ship to the back. _He inspected the boat from stem to stern and decided he wanted to buy it.
examples: He inspected the boat from stem to stern and decided he wanted to buy it.

from the ground up.monolingual: Fig. from the very beginning. _ We must plan our sales campaign carefully from the ground up. _ Sorry, but you’ll have to start all over again from the ground up.
examples: We must plan our sales campaign carefully from the ground up.

from the heart.monolingual: Fig. from a deep and sincere emotional source. _I know that your kind words come from the heart. _ We don’t want your gift unless it comes from the heart.
examples: I know that your kind words come from the heart.

from the outset.monolingual: throughout, from the very beginning. _ I felt from the outset that Lisa was the wrong one for the job. _ From the outset, I felt unwelcome in the group.
examples: I felt from the outset that Lisa was the wrong one for the job.

from the top.monolingual: Fig. from the beginning of something, such as a song or a script. _Okay, let’s try it again from the top. _ Play it from the top one more time.
examples: Okay, let’s try it again from the top.

from the word go.monolingual: Cliché from the very beginning. _ I knew about the problem from the word go. _ She was failing the class from the word go.
examples: I knew about the problem from the word go.

from time to time.monolingual: irregularly; now and then; occasionally; sometimes; not predictably. _ From time to time, I like to go fishing instead of going to work. _ Bob visits us at our house from time to time.
examples: From time to time, I like to go fishing instead of going to work.

from tip to toe.monolingual: Fig. from the top to the bottom. _ She is wearing all new clothes from tip to toe. _ The house needs to be cleaned thoroughly from tip to toe.
examples: She is wearing all new clothes from tip to toe.

from top to bottom.monolingual: Fig. from the highest point to the lowest point; throughout. _I have to clean the house from top to bottom today. _ We need to replace our elected officials from top to bottom.
examples: I have to clean the house from top to bottom today.

from way back.monolingual: from far in the past; from a much earlier time. _Grandfather comes from way back. _This antique clock is from way back.
examples: Grandfather comes from way back.

front for someone or something.monolingual: to serve as the public contact or public “face” for someone or something. _ Her publicity agent fronted for her most of the time. _ Max fronted for a gang of thieves.
examples: Her publicity agent fronted for her most of the time.

front on something.monolingual: [for a building or a piece of land] to face out on something. _ The property fronts on a lovely boulevard that has very little traffic. _Our house fronts on a lake.
examples: The property fronts on a lovely boulevard that has very little traffic.

the front-runner.monolingual: the person or thing thought most likely to win or succeed. _The press found out some juicy secrets about the front-runner and made them all public. _ Who is the front-runner in the race to be governor?
examples: The press found out some juicy secrets about the front-runner and made them all public.

frost over.monolingual: to become covered with frost. _ The windows had all frosted over in the night. _The car windows frosted over.
examples: The windows had all frosted over in the night.

froth something up†.monolingual: to whip or aerate something until it is frothy. _ Froth the milk up before you add it to the sauce. _ Froth up the milk before you pour it in.
examples: Froth the milk up before you add it to the sauce.

froth up.monolingual: [for something] to build up a froth when whipped, aerated, or boiled. _The mixture began to froth up as Dan beat it. _The milk frothed up as the steam went through it.
examples: The mixture began to froth up as Dan beat it.

frown at someone or something.monolingual: to scowl at someone or something. _ Please don’t frown at me. I didn’t do anything. _ Frank frowned at the dog and gave it a kick.
examples: Please don’t frown at me.

frown on someone or something.monolingual: to disapprove of someone or something; to show displeasure or disapproval of someone or something. _ The Internal Revenue Service frowns on tax cheaters. _ Aunt Clara always seemed to frown on my cousin for some reason.
examples: The Internal Revenue Service frowns on tax cheaters.

fry something up†.monolingual: to cook something by frying. _ Let’s fry some chicken up for dinner. _ We fried up some chicken.
examples: Let’s fry some chicken up for dinner.

fuck you!.monolingual: a strong condemnation. (Taboo.) _ Fuck you! Why did you have to do that? _ Fuck you! I don’t care any more!

fudge factor.monolingual: Fig. a margin of error. _ I never use a fudge factor. I measure correctly, and I cut the material exactly the way I measured it. _ I built in a fudge factor of three percent.
examples: I never use a fudge factor.

fuel up.monolingual: to fill one’s tank with fuel. _ Let’s stop here and fuel up. _ I need to fuel up at the next little town.
examples: Let’s stop here and fuel up.

*full as a tick.monolingual: very full of food or drink. (Alludes to a tick that has filled itself full of blood. See also tight as a tick. *Also: as ~.) _Little Billy ate and ate until he was as full as a tick. _ Our cat drank the cream until he became full as a tick.
examples: Little Billy ate and ate until he was as full as a tick.

full of holes.monolingual: Fig. [of an argument or plan] that cannot stand up to challenge or scrutiny. _Your argument is full of holes. _ This plan is full of holes and won’t work.
examples: Your argument is full of holes.

*full of oneself.monolingual: Fig. conceited; self-important. (*Typically: act ~; be ~.) _ Mary is very unpopular because she’s so full of herself. _She doesn’t care about other people’s feelings. She’s too full of herself.
examples: Mary is very unpopular because she’s so full of herself.

a full plate.monolingual: Fig. a full schedule; a lot to do. _I’m very busy at work, and I’ve got a full plate at home too.
examples: I’m very busy at work, and I’ve got a full plate at home too.

full steam ahead.monolingual: Fig. onward with determination. _We started moving full steam ahead on the project. _Full steam ahead! Let’s see how fast this will go!
examples: We started moving full steam ahead on the project.

full up.monolingual: Rur. full. _ I ate till I was full up. _ I can’t get any more gas in the tank. It’s full up.
examples: I ate till I was full up.

fulminate against someone or something.monolingual: to denounce someone or something. _ The workers were fulminating against their employer. _They are fulminating against the president of the union.
examples: The workers were fulminating against their employer.

fumble for something.monolingual: to try to grasp awkwardly for something. _He fumbled for his wallet, hoping Wally would pay the bill. _ Tex was shot while fumbling for his gun.
examples: He fumbled for his wallet, hoping Wally would pay the bill.

fume at someone.monolingual: Fig. to rage at someone. _She was really fuming at Sam, who had broken her table leg.
examples: She was really fuming at Sam, who had broken her table leg.

fun and games.monolingual: Fig. playing around; doing worthless things. _All right, Bill, the fun and games are over. It’s time to get down to work. _This isn’t a serious course. It’s nothing but fun and games.
examples: All right, Bill, the fun and games are over.

funked out.monolingual: Sl. intoxicated. _ Do you think you can go through life funked out all the time? _ Are you funked out again?

*funny as a crutch.monolingual: not funny at all. (Sarcastic. *Also: as ~.) _ Your trick is about as funny as a crutch. Nobody thought it was funny. _The lame joke Ron told was as funny as a crutch, and we all yawned.
examples: Your trick is about as funny as a crutch.

funny ha-ha.monolingual: amusing; comical. (As opposed to funny peculiar.) _I didn’t mean that Mrs. Peters is funny ha-ha. She’s weird—funny peculiar in fact. _Mike thinks his jokes are funny ha-ha, but we laugh because they are so silly.
examples: I didn’t mean that Mrs.

funny money.monolingual: 1. Sl. counterfeit money. _The bank teller spotted the funny money in the man’s deposit almost immediately.
examples: The bank teller spotted the funny money in the man’s deposit almost immediately.

funny peculiar.monolingual: odd; eccentric. (As opposed to funny haha.) _ I didn’t mean that Mrs. Peters is funny ha-ha. She’s weird—funny peculiar in fact. _His face is sort of funny— funny peculiar, that is.
examples: I didn’t mean that Mrs.

a fur piece.monolingual: Rur. a long distance. (Fur = far.) _ It’s a fur piece to the library. You’d best take the bus instead of walking. _ It’s a pretty fur piece to the nearest big town.
examples: It’s a fur piece to the library.

furnish something for something.monolingual: to provide something to be used as something. _ Could you furnish the salad for our picnic? _ We can’t furnish enough glassware for the whole party.
examples: We can’t furnish enough glassware for the whole party.

a furtive glance.monolingual: a secret or quick glance, quickly averted. _ He made a furtive glance in the direction of the closet when the robbers asked where the jewelery was hidden.
examples: He made a furtive glance in the direction of the closet when the robbers asked where the jewelery was hidden.

fuse something with something.monolingual: to bond something together with something. _ You have to fuse the upper layer to the lower layer with heat. _ He used heat and pressure to fuse the patch with the soft rubber of the raft.
examples: You have to fuse the upper layer to the lower layer with heat.

fuse with something.monolingual: to bond with something. _The metal has fused with the glass coating on the tank. _I didn’t know that metal could fuse with glass.
examples: The metal has fused with the glass coating on the tank.

fuss about someone or something.monolingual: to complain about someone or something. _ What are you fussing about now? _ Are you still fussing about Tony?

fuss and feathers.monolingual: Rur. fancy addictions that are overdone or troublesome. _ A truly elegant dress doesn’t have a lot of fuss and feathers. _ They ruined a nice room with all that fuss and feathers.
examples: A truly elegant dress doesn’t have a lot of fuss and feathers.

fuss at someone or something.monolingual: to complain at someone. _ Stop fussing at me! _ The squirrel is fussing at the dog.
examples: The squirrel is fussing at the dog.

fuss over someone or something.monolingual: to go to a lot of bother about someone or something. _ My aunt always fusses over me and my sister. _You spend a lot of time fussing over your hair.
examples: My aunt always fusses over me and my sister.

futz around.monolingual: Sl. to waste time. _ Stop futzing around and get the job done. _ I wish you would stop futzing around!
examples: Stop futzing around and get the job done.

futz something up†.monolingual: Sl. to mess something up. _Who futzed the computer up? _I don’t want to futz up the deal, so I will be quiet.
examples: I don’t want to futz up the deal, so I will be quiet.

gag on something.monolingual: to choke on something; to retch on something. _ The dog is gagging on whatever you gave her. _ This fish is good, but I hope I don’t gag on a bone.
examples: The dog is gagging on whatever you gave her.

gain from something.monolingual: to benefit from something. _ I hope you gain from this experience. _ What do you think I will gain from this?
examples: I hope you gain from this experience.

gain ground.monolingual: to make progress; to advance; to become more important or popular. _ Our new product is gaining ground against that of our competitor. _Since the government announced its new policies, the opposition has been gaining ground.
examples: Our new product is gaining ground against that of our competitor.

gain in something.monolingual: to advance in a particular quality. _Todd grew in stature and gained in wisdom. _ Mary gained in experience as the weeks went on.
examples: Todd grew in stature and gained in wisdom.

gain on someone or something.monolingual: to begin to catch up or move ahead of someone or something. _ We were gaining on them when they suddenly sped up. _ Our horse was gaining on the horse in front.
examples: We were gaining on them when they suddenly sped up.

gain something by doing something.monolingual: to achieve some benefit by doing something. _ What did he gain by dropping out of school? _ I will gain some degree of security by investing in U.S. Treasury bonds.
examples: I will gain some degree of security by investing in U.

gain something from something.monolingual: to earn or achieve something from something. _I hope you gain something worthwhile from all this. _I know I will gain some valuable experience from this job.
examples: I hope you gain something worthwhile from all this.

gallivant around.monolingual: to travel around aimlessly. _Why don’t you stop gallivanting around and come home for a while? _ Mary is off gallivanting around with her boyfriend.
examples: Mary is off gallivanting around with her boyfriend.

gallop through something.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a horse] to pass through something at a gallop. _ Her horse galloped through the garden and dumped her in the cabbages. _ A few horses galloped through the meadow.
examples: Her horse galloped through the garden and dumped her in the cabbages.

galumph around.monolingual: to move around looking for someone or something or transporting someone or something. _ I am so tired of galumphing around, dropping off and picking up kids. _ I have to stop galumphing around day after day.
examples: I am so tired of galumphing around, dropping off and picking up kids.

galvanize someone into action.monolingual: Fig. to stimulate someone into some activity. _The explosion galvanized Martha into action. _We were galvanized into action by the storm.
examples: The explosion galvanized Martha into action.

gamble on someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to make a wager on something concerning someone or something. _ I wouldn’t gamble on it happening. _ Don’t gamble on that horse. You’ll be sorry.
examples: I wouldn’t gamble on it happening.

gamble something away†.monolingual: to lose all of something by gambling. _ He gambled all his money away. _ He gambled away all his money.
examples: He gambled all his money away.

gape at someone or something.monolingual: to stare at someone or something in wonder. _ Don’t just stand there, gaping at me. Come in. _Stop gaping at the storm clouds and get in here.
examples: Don’t just stand there, gaping at me.

garb someone in something.monolingual: to dress someone in something. _He hoped that someday he wouldn’t have to garb his children in rags. _ She garbed herself in her finest clothes and got ready to meet her husband’s family.
examples: He hoped that someday he wouldn’t have to garb his children in rags.

garbage in, garbage out..monolingual: Prov. If you give nonsensical instructions to people or computers, those instructions will produce nonsensical results. _ Jill: Why is my computer generating all this gibberish? Jane: You must have made a mistake in the program. Garbage in, garbage o
examples: Jill: Why is my computer generating all this gibberish? Jane: You must have made a mistake in the program.

garbage something down†.monolingual: Sl. to gobble something up; to quickly swallow something down. _ Don’t garbage your food down! _That guy will garbage down almost anything.
examples: That guy will garbage down almost anything.

garnish something with something.monolingual: to embellish or decorate something, such as food, with something. _ For the final presentation, I will garnish the dish with a sprig of parsley. _ The roast was garnished with slices of apple.
examples: For the final presentation, I will garnish the dish with a sprig of parsley.

gas something up†.monolingual: to put gasoline into a vehicle. _ I have to gas this car up soon. _ I will stop and gas up the car at the next little town.
examples: I have to gas this car up soon.

gas up.monolingual: to fill up one’s gasoline tank with gasoline. _I have to stop at the next service station and gas up. _ The next time you gas up, try some of the gasoline with alcohol in it.
examples: I have to stop at the next service station and gas up.

gasp at someone or something.monolingual: to inhale sharply in surprise or shock at someone or something. _I gasped at the sight that lay before me. _ I saw how weary Denise looked and I gasped at her.
examples: I gasped at the sight that lay before me.

gasp for air.monolingual: to fight for a breath of air. (After one has been deprived of air.) _ Walter popped to the surface of the water and gasped for air. _The injured dog appeared to be gasping for air.
examples: Walter popped to the surface of the water and gasped for air.

gasp for breath.monolingual: to labor for one’s breath. (Usually because of physical exertion.) _She ran and ran until she was gasping for breath. _The diver finally came to the surface, gasping for breath.
examples: She ran and ran until she was gasping for breath.

gasp something out†.monolingual: to utter something, gasping. _ She gasped the words out haltingly. _Dan was just able to gasp out the instructions before he passed out.
examples: She gasped the words out haltingly.

gather around someone or something.monolingual: to collect around someone or something. _ Let’s all gather around her and hear her out. _ Please gather around the table for dinner.
examples: Let’s all gather around her and hear her out.

gather dust.monolingual: Fig. [for something] to sit unused for a long time. _ Most of my talent is just gathering dust because I don’t really have an opportunity to perform.
examples: Most of my talent is just gathering dust because I don’t really have an opportunity to perform.

gather someone or something together†.monolingual: to assemble people or things together in one place. _ Gather everyone together in the drawing room for a meeting. _Please gather together all the suspects so that they can be questioned again. _Would you gather all your papers together and put them a
examples: Gather everyone together in the drawing room for a meeting.

gather something from someone.monolingual: to collect something from someone. _ I will gather the papers from Wally, and you go get those that Ted is working on. _ Would you gather the pictures from everyone? We have to leave now and take them with us.
examples: I will gather the papers from Wally, and you go get those that Ted is working on.

gather something from something.monolingual: to collect something from something. _ Kristine gathered the honey from the beehives. _ I gathered my money from the cashier.
