examples: Kristine gathered the honey from the beehives.

gather something in†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to collect something and bring it in; to harvest something. _ We gathered the pumpkins in just before Halloween. _ We gathered in the pumpkins just in time.
examples: We gathered the pumpkins in just before Halloween.

gather something up†.monolingual: to collect something; to pick something up. _ Let’s gather our things up and go. _ Please gather up your things.
examples: Let’s gather our things up and go.

gather together.monolingual: to assemble together. _ We will gather together on the main deck for a meeting. _ Let’s all gather together this evening and sing.
examples: We will gather together on the main deck for a meeting.

*gaudy as a butterfly.monolingual: fancy; colorful. (*Also: as ~.) _Marie looked as gaudy as a butterf ly in her new dress. _ Michael’s scarf is gaudy as a butterf ly.
examples: Marie looked as gaudy as a butterf ly in her new dress.

gawk at someone or something.monolingual: to stare at someone or something, obviously and awkwardly. _ Why are you standing there, gawking at me? _ The tourists stood at the foot of the mountain and gawked at the top.
examples: The tourists stood at the foot of the mountain and gawked at the top.

gaze at someone or something.monolingual: to stare at someone or something. _I stood for an hour, gazing at the sea. _She gazed at me for a moment and then smiled.
examples: I stood for an hour, gazing at the sea.

gaze on someone or something.monolingual: to look at someone or something; to survey someone or something. _ She gazed sullenly on the ruin that had been her home. _ The teacher gazed on the student and frightened her.
examples: She gazed sullenly on the ruin that had been her home.

gaze out on something.monolingual: to look out on something, such as a lovely view, from inside a building or from a particular spot. _She gazed out on the flowering trees and knew that life would go on. _ Henry sat for hours, gazing out on the lake.
examples: She gazed out on the flowering trees and knew that life would go on.

generalize from something.monolingual: to assume a general pattern in something from specific observances of something. _You can hardly generalize from only two instances. _ You can’t generalize anything from the testimony of a single witness!
examples: You can hardly generalize from only two instances.

generous to a fault.monolingual: Cliché too generous; overly generous. _ My favorite uncle is generous to a fault. _ Sally— always generous to a fault—gave away her lunch to a homeless man.
examples: My favorite uncle is generous to a fault.

*gentle as a lamb.monolingual: Cliché [of someone] very gentle. (*Also: as ~.) _Don’t be afraid of Mr. Schaeffer. He may look fierce, but he’s as gentle as a lamb. _ Lisa was gentle as a lamb when dealing with children.
examples: Don’t be afraid of Mr.

the genuine article.monolingual: the real thing rather than a substitute. _ Is this the genuine article or some cheap imitation substitute? _ I’ll take the genuine article, thanks.
examples: I’ll take the genuine article, thanks.

get a laugh.monolingual: to do something that will create laughter. _ John will do almost anything to get a laugh.
examples: John will do almost anything to get a laugh.

get a life!.monolingual: Inf. Change your life radically! Find something interesting to do or say! _ You are such a twit! Get a life! _ Get a life, you clown!

get a ticket.monolingual: to receive a traffic ticket. _ If you keep racing along at this speed, you will get a ticket!

get aboard something.monolingual: to get onto a ship, a train, or an airplane. _ What time should we get aboard the ship? _ Everyone can get aboard at noon.
examples: Everyone can get aboard at noon.

get after someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to begin to chase someone. _ The other boys got after him and almost caught him. _ Henry got after Bill and almost caught up with him.
examples: The other boys got after him and almost caught him.

get ahead of oneself.monolingual: Fig. [for someone] to do or say something sooner than it ought to be done so that the proper explanation or preparations have not been made. _I have to stick to my notes or I will get ahead of myself in my lecture. _When he bought a new little bicycl
examples: I have to stick to my notes or I will get ahead of myself in my lecture.

get along.monolingual: 1. [for people or animals] to be amiable with one another. _Those two just don’t get along. _They seem to get along just fine.
examples: Those two just don’t get along.

get along on something.monolingual: Fig. to manage to survive with just something. _ I think we can get along on what I earn. _ I can’t get along on what they pay me.
examples: I think we can get along on what I earn.

get along with you!.monolingual: Rur. to go on; to depart; to go and “take oneself along.” (Only with you.) _ Get along with you, now. Get going! _ Get along with you, Sally!
examples: Get along with you, now.

get around someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to cluster around someone or something. _ Tell everyone to get around the cat so she won’t run away. _Let’s get around Mary and sing “Happy Birthday” to her.
examples: Tell everyone to get around the cat so she won’t run away.

get around to doing something.monolingual: to find time to do something; to do something after a long delay. to someone or something.) _ I finally got around to buying a new coat. _ It took Sally years to get around to visiting her aunt.
examples: I finally got around to buying a new coat.

get at someone.monolingual: Fig. to find a way to irritate someone; to manage to wound someone, physically or emotionally. _ Mr. Smith found a way to get at his wife. _ John kept trying to get at his teacher.
examples: Mr. Smith found a way to get at his wife.

get at something.monolingual: 1. Fig. to explain or understand something. _ We spent a long time trying to get at the answer. _ I can’t understand what you’re trying to get at.
examples: We spent a long time trying to get at the answer.

get away.monolingual: to move away. (Often a command.) _Get away! Don’t bother me! _ I tried to get away, but he wouldn’t let me.
examples: I tried to get away, but he wouldn’t let me.

get away with murder.monolingual: 1. Lit. to commit murder and not get punished for it. _ Don’t kill me! You can’t get away with murder!
examples: Don’t kill me! You can’t get away with murder! 2.

get axed.monolingual: Fig. to get fired. _ Betty and two of her friends got axed today.
examples: Betty and two of her friends got axed today.

get back to something.monolingual: to return to dealing with something. _ I will have to get back to my work now. _ I want to get back to my knitting.
examples: I will have to get back to my work now.

get better.monolingual: to improve. _ I had a bad cold, but it’s getting better. _ Business was bad last year, but it’s getting better. _ I’m sorry you’re ill. I hope you get better.
examples: I had a bad cold, but it’s getting better.

get busy.monolingual: to start working; to work or appear to work harder or faster. _The boss is coming. You’d better get busy. _ I’ve got to get busy and clean this house up.
examples: The boss is coming.

get carried away.monolingual: Fig. to be overcome by emotion or enthusiasm (in one’s thinking or actions). _ Calm down, Jane. Don’t get carried away. _ Here, Bill. Take this money and go to the candy store, but don’t get carried away.
examples: Calm down, Jane.

get cracking.monolingual: Rur. to get to work. _ If you want to finish that quilt by Labor Day, you best get cracking. _ Sit down to your homework and get cracking!
examples: If you want to finish that quilt by Labor Day, you best get cracking.

get down.monolingual: 1. Sl. to lay one’s money on the table. (Gambling.) _Okay, everybody get down. _Get down, and let’s get going!
examples: Okay, everybody get down.

get down to brass tacks.monolingual: Fig. to begin to talk about important things; to get down to business. _ Let’s get down to brass tacks. We’ve wasted too much time chatting. _ Don’t you think that it’s about time to get down to brass tacks?
examples: Let’s get down to brass tacks.

get down to cases.monolingual: to begin to discuss specific matters; to get down to business. _When we’ve finished the general discussion, we’ll get down to cases. _ Now that everyone is here, we can get down to cases.
examples: When we’ve finished the general discussion, we’ll get down to cases.

get down to the facts.monolingual: to begin to talk about things that matter; to get to the truth. _The judge told the lawyer that the time had come to get down to the facts. _Let’s get down to the facts, Mrs. Brown. Where were you on the night of January 16?
examples: The judge told the lawyer that the time had come to get down to the facts.

get down to the nitty-gritty.monolingual: to get down to the basic facts. _ Stop messing around and get down to the nittygritty. _ If we could only get down to the nitty-gritty and stop wasting time.
examples: Stop messing around and get down to the nittygritty.

get euchred out of something.monolingual: to get cheated out of something. (Alludes to losing in the card game euchre.) _Joe’s dad left him a farm, but he got euchred out of it by some city slicker real estate agent. _ I got euchred out of ten bucks by a con artist with a hard-luck story.
examples: Joe’s dad left him a farm, but he got euchred out of it by some city slicker real estate agent.

get going.monolingual: 1. to start moving. _ Let’s get going! We can’t stand here all day.
examples: Let’s get going! We can’t stand here all day.

get in deeper.monolingual: Fig. to get in more and more trouble; to get more deeply involved with someone or something. _ Everytime he opened his mouth to complain, he just got in deeper.
examples: Everytime he opened his mouth to complain, he just got in deeper.

get inside something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to go inside of something or some place. _Get inside the house and wait for me. _Get inside the car so you won’t get wet.
examples: Get inside the house and wait for me.

get into bed with someone.monolingual: Fig. to work closely as business partners; to merge businesses. _Have you heard? The company’s getting into bed with Acme Industries. _ I want you to get into bed with the other department supervisors and sort this problem out.
examples: Have you heard? The company’s getting into bed with Acme Industries.

get into one’s stride.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a runner] to reach a comfortable and efficient pace. _ I got into my stride right away, and that helped win the race. _She never got into her stride, and that’s why she lost.
examples: I got into my stride right away, and that helped win the race.

get it in the neck.monolingual: Sl. to receive trouble or punishment. _ You are going to get it in the neck if you are not home on time. _ I got it in the neck for being late.
examples: You are going to get it in the neck if you are not home on time.

get it off.monolingual: Sl. to achieve sexual release; to copulate. (Potentially offensive. Use only with discretion. Compare this with get it off with someone.) _Harry kept saying he had to get it off or die. What’s wrong with Harry? _ The entire crew of the yacht came ash
examples: Harry kept saying he had to get it off or die.

get it off with someone.monolingual: Sl. to have sexual intercourse with someone. _ She said she wanted to get it off with him. _ She said all he wanted was to get it off with just anybody.
examples: She said she wanted to get it off with him.

get it on.monolingual: 1. Sl. to begin something. _ Time to go back to work. Let’s get it on! _ Get it on, you guys! Time to start your engines.
examples: Time to go back to work.

get it out.monolingual: Fig. to tell someone about a problem; to pour out one’s grief. (Fixed order.) _ Come on, get it out. You’ll feel better. _ He would feel better if he could get it out.
examples: Come on, get it out.

get it wrong.monolingual: to misunderstand someone or something. _ Oh, Otto, you’ve got it wrong again! _ Why do you have to get it wrong every time?

get laid.monolingual: to have sexual intercourse. (Use caution.) _ Tommy wanted nothing more out of life than to get laid.
examples: Tommy wanted nothing more out of life than to get laid.

get lost.monolingual: 1. to become lost; to lose one’s way. _We got lost on the way home. _ Follow the path, or you might get lost.
examples: We got lost on the way home.

get married.monolingual: to become united as husband and wife. _Bill and Sally got married when they were in college. _ We got married in Texas just after we graduated from college.
examples: Bill and Sally got married when they were in college.

get moving.monolingual: to get busy; to get started; to work harder or faster. _ Come on, everybody. Get moving! _ The director is coming. You had better get moving.
examples: Come on, everybody.

get nowhere fast.monolingual: Fig. not to make progress; to get nowhere. _ I can’t seem to make any progress. No matter what I do, I’m just getting nowhere fast. _ Come on. Speed up this car. We’re getting nowhere fast.
examples: I can’t seem to make any progress.

get off.monolingual: 1. to start off (on a friendship). _ Tom and Bill had never met before. They seemed to get off all right, though. _ I’m glad they got off so well.
examples: Tom and Bill had never met before.

get off it!.monolingual: 1. Inf. Stop acting so arrogant! _ Get off it, you jerk! _Get off it! That’s too much!
examples: Get off it! That’s too much! 2.

get off my back!.monolingual: Inf. Stop harassing me!; Leave me alone about this matter! _Tom: You’d better get your paper written. Bill: I’ll do it when I’m good and ready. Get off my back! _ Alice: I’m tired of your constant criticism! Get off my back! Jane: I was just trying t
examples: Tom: You’d better get your paper written.

get off someone’s tail.monolingual: 1. Fig. to stop following someone closely, usually in an automobile. _ Get off my tail! Keep your distance! _I wish that car behind me would get off my tail.
examples: I wish that car behind me would get off my tail.

get off the dime.monolingual: Sl. to start moving; to get out of a stopped position. _ Why don’t you get off the dime and complete some of these projects that you started? _As soon as the board of directors gets off the dime on this proposal, we will have some action.
examples: As soon as the board of directors gets off the dime on this proposal, we will have some action.

get off to sleep.monolingual: to manage to get to sleep finally. _About midnight everyone finally got off to sleep. _ I wasn’t able to get off to sleep until dawn.
examples: About midnight everyone finally got off to sleep.

get on one’s horse.monolingual: Sl. to prepare to leave. (Usually fig., with no horse present.) _ It’s time to get on my horse and get out of here. _ I’ve got to get on my horse and go.
examples: It’s time to get on my horse and get out of here.

get on with something.monolingual: to continue doing something. _ Let’s get on with the game! _ We need to get on with our lives.
examples: We need to get on with our lives.

get one right here.monolingual: Fig. to affect one deeply in a specific way. (Usually accompanied with a hand gesture showing exactly where one is affected: the heart = lovingly, the stomach or bowels = sickeningly.) _That sort of thing gets me right here. _Pete clasped his hand to
examples: That sort of thing gets me right here.

get one’s act together.monolingual: to get oneself organized and on schedule. _I’ve got to get my act together and start getting my work done. _When I have my act together, I’ll get a job.
examples: I’ve got to get my act together and start getting my work done.

get one’s comeuppance.monolingual: to get a deserved punishment. _ I can’t wait till that snobbish girl gets her comeuppance. _ Joe got his comeuppance when the teacher caught him making fun of her.
examples: I can’t wait till that snobbish girl gets her comeuppance.

get one’s ears pinned back.monolingual: Fig. to experience a severe scolding. _ Jimmy was ordered to report to the principal’s office and got his ears pinned back.
examples: Jimmy was ordered to report to the principal’s office and got his ears pinned back.

get one’s feet wet.monolingual: Fig. to get a little first-time experience with something. (Obvious literal possibilities.) _ Of course he can’t do the job right. He’s hardly got his feet wet yet. _ I’m looking forward to learning to drive. I can’t wait to get behind the steering w
examples: Of course he can’t do the job right.

get one’s fingers burned.monolingual: Fig. to receive harm or punishment for one’s actions. (Normally fig.) _I had my fingers burned the last time I questioned the company policy. _I tried that once before and got my fingers burned. I won’t try it again.
examples: I had my fingers burned the last time I questioned the company policy.

get one’s head together.monolingual: to get one’s thoughts or attitude properly organized. _I’ve got to get my head together and get going. _ I need to take some time off and get my head together.
examples: I’ve got to get my head together and get going.

get one’s knuckles rapped.monolingual: 1. Lit. to get one’s knuckles struck with a ruler as a punishment. _ I got my knuckles rapped for whispering too much. _ You will have your knuckles rapped if you are not careful.
examples: I got my knuckles rapped for whispering too much.

get one’s lumps.monolingual: Inf. to get the result or punishment one deserves. _ If she keeps acting that way, she’ll get her lumps. _ We will see that Dave gets his lumps.
examples: If she keeps acting that way, she’ll get her lumps.

get one’s ticket punched.monolingual: Sl. to die; to be killed. (Literally, to be cancelled.) _ Poor Chuck got his ticket punched while he was waiting for a bus. _Watch out there, or you’ll get your ticket punched.
examples: Poor Chuck got his ticket punched while he was waiting for a bus.

get out.monolingual: 1. [for someone or an animal] to depart to the outside or to escape. _ When did your dog get out and run away? _ When did he get out of jail?
examples: When did he get out of jail? 2.

get out of a jam.monolingual: Fig. to get free from a problem or a bad situation. _Would you lend me five hundred dollars? I need it to get out of a jam. _ I need some help getting out of a jam.
examples: Would you lend me five hundred dollars? I need it to get out of a jam.

get out of a mess.monolingual: Fig. to get free of a bad situation. (Also with this, such a, etc.) _How can anyone get out of a mess like this? _ Please help me get out of this mess!

get out of my sight!.monolingual: Go away immediately! (Usually said in anger.) _ Get out of my sight! _ Please get out of my sight forever!

get out of one’s face.monolingual: Lit. Inf. to stop bothering or intimidating someone. _ Look, get out of my face, or I’ll poke you in yours! _He told you to get out of his face, you creep!

get out of someone’s hair.monolingual: Fig. Inf. to stop annoying someone. _ Will you get out of my hair! You are a real pain!

get out of town!.monolingual: Beat it!; Get out of here! _ Go away, you bother me! Get out of town! _ You’d better get out of town, my friend. You are a pest.
examples: You’d better get out of town, my friend.

get out with it!.monolingual: Get it said! _ Stop stuttering around! Get out with it! _ Get out with it! I don’t have all day to wait for you!

get out with one’s life.monolingual: Fig. to survive a serious or lifethreatening incident or an accident without dying. _ We were lucky to get out with our lives.
examples: We were lucky to get out with our lives.

get over it!.monolingual: Forget about it and be done with it! (Said to someone who is fretting and stewing over some kind of problem.) _ Forget about her. She’s gone. Get over it!
examples: Forget about her.

get over someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to move or climb over someone or something. _ I managed to get over the sand dunes and moved on toward the shoreline. _ I couldn’t get over the huge rock in the path, so I went around it.
examples: I managed to get over the sand dunes and moved on toward the shoreline.

get over something.monolingual: to recover from a disease. _It took a long time to get over the f lu. _ I thought I would never get over the mumps.
examples: It took a long time to get over the f lu.

get real!.monolingual: Inf. Start acting realistically! _ Hey, chum! You are way off base! Get real! _ Get real! Wake up to reality!

get religion.monolingual: Fig. to become serious (about something), usually after a powerful experience. (Sometimes literal.) _When I had an automobile accident, I really got religion. Now I’m a very safe driver.
examples: When I had an automobile accident, I really got religion.

get right on something.monolingual: to do something immediately. _ I know it has to be done today. I’ll get right on it. _ Please get right on these reports as soon as possible.
examples: I know it has to be done today.

get rolling.monolingual: Fig. to get started. _Come on. It’s time to leave. Let’s get rolling! _ Bill, it’s 6:30. Time to get up and get rolling!
examples: Come on. It’s time to leave.

get screwed.monolingual: 1. Sl. to have sexual intercourse. (Considered a crude usage.) _ A lot of the college kids on spring break in Florida do nothing but get drunk and get screwed.
examples: A lot of the college kids on spring break in Florida do nothing but get drunk and get screwed.

get serious!.monolingual: Inf. Get realistic!; Stop horsing around! _ Oh, come on! Get serious! You don’t really mean that!

get someone around the table.monolingual: Fig. to collect people together for discussion or bargaining. _ We have to get everyone around the table on this matter. _If I can get them around the table, I’m sure I can make them agree.
examples: We have to get everyone around the table on this matter.

get someone down.monolingual: to depress a person; to make a person very sad. _ My dog ran away, and it really got me down. _ Oh, that’s too bad. Don’t let it get you down.
examples: My dog ran away, and it really got me down.

get someone going.monolingual: to get someone excited; to get someone talking excitedly. _I guess I really got him going on the subject of politics. _The whole business really makes me mad. Don’t get me going.
examples: I guess I really got him going on the subject of politics.

get someone off.monolingual: 1. to get someone cleared of a criminal charge. _ Ted’s lawyer got him off, although we all knew he was guilty. _I hope someone can get her off. She is innocent no matter how it looks.
examples: Ted’s lawyer got him off, although we all knew he was guilty.

get someone or something back†.monolingual: to receive someone or something back; to recover someone who had been taken away; to recover something that had been taken away. _ Beth finally got her car back from the service station. _She got back her car.
examples: Beth finally got her car back from the service station.

get someone or something together.monolingual: to gather people or things together. _Let’s see if we can get both sides together and discuss this. _ I want to get Tom and Sharon together for a conference.
examples: Let’s see if we can get both sides together and discuss this.

get someone’s blood up.monolingual: Fig. to get someone or oneself angry. (Fixed order.) _ That kind of language really gets my blood up. _ That will really get his blood up!
examples: That kind of language really gets my blood up.

get someone’s drift.monolingual: Fig. to understand what someone is saying or implying. (Akin to if you get my drift.) _ I don’t want to hear anymore about her or you. Do you get my drift?
examples: I don’t want to hear anymore about her or you.

get someone’s goat.monolingual: Fig. to irritate someone; to annoy and arouse someone to anger. _I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to get your goat. _ Jean got Sally’s goat and Sally made quite a fuss about it.
examples: I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to get your goat.

get something for someone.monolingual: to obtain something for the use or benefit of someone. _ I will get a new book for you. Sorry I messed the old one up. _ Would you get a glass of water for me?
examples: I will get a new book for you.

get something for something.monolingual: to obtain a part or attachment for an object. _I need to get a part for the vacuum cleaner. _ Would you please get a bulb for my f lashlight?
examples: I need to get a part for the vacuum cleaner.

get something going with someone.monolingual: to start a romance or affair with someone. _ Todd got something going with Amy, and they both look pretty happy. _I want to get something going with Chuck.
examples: Todd got something going with Amy, and they both look pretty happy.

get something into a mess.monolingual: to cause something to become messy or untidy; to cause something to become unmanageable. _ When he made the spaghetti sauce, he got the kitchen into a real mess. _You have got these accounts into a mess!
examples: When he made the spaghetti sauce, he got the kitchen into a real mess.

get something off one’s chest.monolingual: to unburden oneself; to confess something; to criticize or make a personal complaint to someone. _You will feel better if you get it off your chest. _ I have to get this off my chest. I’m tired of your rudeness to me!
examples: You will feel better if you get it off your chest.

get something off the ground.monolingual: 1. Lit. to get something into the air. _ I’ll announce the weather to the passengers as soon as we get the plane off the ground. _I hope they get this plane off the ground soon.
examples: I’ll announce the weather to the passengers as soon as we get the plane off the ground.

get something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to remove or extricate something. _Please help me get this splinter out. _Would you help me get out this splinter? _ The tooth was gotten out without much difficulty.
examples: Please help me get this splinter out.

get something straight.monolingual: Fig. to understand something clearly. _ Now get this straight. You’re going to fail history. _ Let me get this straight. I’m supposed to go there in the morning?
examples: Now get this straight.

get something up†.monolingual: to organize, plan, and assemble something. _ Let’s get a team up and enter the tournament. _ I think we can get up a team quite easily.
examples: Let’s get a team up and enter the tournament.

get started on something.monolingual: to begin doing something; to take the first steps to do something. _ When do we get started on this project? _ I want to get started on this right away.
examples: I want to get started on this right away.

get the draw on someone.monolingual: Fig. to be faster than one’s opponent in a fight. (Alludes originally to an Old West gunfight.) _The sheriff got the draw on Arizona Slim and shot him in the arm. _ Bill’s competitor got the draw on him. She was the first one in town to start selling
examples: The sheriff got the draw on Arizona Slim and shot him in the arm.

get the drift of something.monolingual: Fig. to understand the general idea of something. _I knew enough German to get the drift of this article. _ I don’t get the drift of what you’re trying to tell me.
examples: I knew enough German to get the drift of this article.

get the drop on someone.monolingual: 1. Sl. [for person A] to manage to get a gun aimed at person B before person B can aim back at person A. (The gun is then “dropped” by person B.) _Fred got the drop on Wilbur in a f lash. _Wilbur was too stoned to get the drop on Fred.
examples: Fred got the drop on Wilbur in a f lash.

get the gate.monolingual: Inf. to be sent away; to be rejected. _ I thought he liked me, but I got the gate. _ I was afraid I’d get the gate, and I was right.
examples: I thought he liked me, but I got the gate.

get the go-by.monolingual: Inf. to be ignored or passed by. _ It was my turn, but I got the go-by. _ Tom stood on the road for fifteen minutes trying to get a ride, but all he could get was the go-by.
examples: It was my turn, but I got the go-by.

get the shaft.monolingual: Sl. to be cheated; to be taken advantage of; to be mistreated. _Why do I get the shaft when I did nothing wrong?

get the word.monolingual: Fig. to receive an explanation; to receive the final and authoritative explanation. _ I’m sorry, I didn’t get the word. I didn’t know the matter had been settled. _Now that I have gotten the word, I can be more effective in answering questions.
examples: I’m sorry, I didn’t get the word.

get to one’s feet.monolingual: Fig. to stand up. _ On a signal from the teacher, the students got to their feet. _ I was so weak, I could hardly get to my feet.
examples: On a signal from the teacher, the students got to their feet.

get under someone’s skin.monolingual: Fig. to bother or irritate someone. _ John is so annoying. He really gets under my skin. _ I know he’s bothersome, but don’t let him get under your skin.
examples: John is so annoying.

get under something.monolingual: to get beneath something. _ The cat came in and got under the sofa where she couldn’t be seen. _ Why don’t you get under the table where Billy won’t find you?
examples: The cat came in and got under the sofa where she couldn’t be seen.

get up.monolingual: to wake up and get out of bed. _ What time do you usually get up? _ I get up when I have to.
examples: I get up when I have to.

get up an appetite.monolingual: Fig. to do something to make one very hungry. (Usually in this order.) _ He can’t seem to get up an appetite these days. _Whenever I jog, I really get up an appetite.
examples: He can’t seem to get up an appetite these days.

get up something.monolingual: to manage to climb something. _ I was so tired I couldn’t get up the stairs. _ The entire group was able to get up the side of the mountain.
examples: I was so tired I couldn’t get up the stairs.

get up to something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to climb up to something, at a certain height or level. _ We finally got up to the top. _ How long will it take to get up to the tenth f loor?
examples: We finally got up to the top.

get well.monolingual: to become healthy again. _ Ann had a cold for a week, and then she got well. _ Hurry up and get well!
examples: Ann had a cold for a week, and then she got well.

get wet.monolingual: to become moist or soaked with water. _ Get out of the rain or you’ll get wet. _ Don’t get wet, or you’ll catch a cold.
examples: Get out of the rain or you’ll get wet.

get with it.monolingual: 1. Inf. to modernize one’s attitudes and behavior. _ Get with it, Martin. Go out and buy some new clothes! _ You really have to get with it, Ernie.
examples: Get with it, Martin.

get with something.monolingual: to become alert. (Often with it.) _Hey, stupid. Get with it! _ Wake up, Bill. Get with what’s going on!

get with the program.monolingual: Fig. follow the rules; do what you are supposed to do. (Implies that there is a clearly known method or “program” that is usually followed.) _ Come on, Mark. Get with the program. Do what you are told. _ Jane just can’t seem to get with the program.
examples: Come on, Mark. Get with the program.

a ghost of a chance.monolingual: even the slightest chance. (Usually negative.) _ She can’t do it. She doesn’t have a ghost of a chance. _ There is just a ghost of a chance that I’ll be there on time.
examples: She can’t do it.

giggle at someone or something.monolingual: to snicker or chuckle at someone or something. _ Are you giggling at me? _ Fran giggled at the antics of the clown.
examples: Fran giggled at the antics of the clown.

gild the lily.monolingual: Fig. to add ornament or decoration to something that is pleasing in its original state; to attempt to improve something that is already fine the way it is. (Often refers to flattery or exaggeration.) _Your house has lovely brickwork. Don’t paint it.
examples: Your house has lovely brickwork.

gird up one’s loins.monolingual: Fig. to get ready, especially for hard work; to prepare oneself (for something). _ Well, I guess I had better gird up my loins and go to work. _ Somebody has to do something about the problem. Why don’t you gird up your loins and do something?
examples: Well, I guess I had better gird up my loins and go to work.

give a little.monolingual: 1. Lit. to give a small amount of something, probably money. _If everyone will just give a little, we can have enough money to provide a nice Thanksgiving dinner for the needy.
examples: If everyone will just give a little, we can have enough money to provide a nice Thanksgiving dinner for the needy.

give cause for something.monolingual: to serve as a just cause for something; to warrant something. _Your comments give cause for further investigation. _ I didn’t give cause for you to worry so much.
examples: Your comments give cause for further investigation.

give currency to something.monolingual: to spread a story around. (With a negative if there is doubt about what is said.) _ I can’t give any currency to anything Ralph Jones says. _ We give no currency to those stories. _His actions gave currency to the rumor that he was about to leave.
examples: I can’t give any currency to anything Ralph Jones says.

give evidence of something.monolingual: to show signs of something; to give proof of something. _You are going to have to give evidence of your good faith in this matter. A nominal deposit would be fine. _ She gave evidence of being prepared to go to trial, so we settled the case.
examples: You are going to have to give evidence of your good faith in this matter.

give ground.monolingual: 1. Lit. to retreat, yielding land or territory. _I approached the barking dog, but it wouldn’t give ground.
examples: I approached the barking dog, but it wouldn’t give ground.

give in.monolingual: cave in; to push in. _The rotting door gave in when we pushed, and we went inside. _ The wall gave in where I kicked it.
examples: The rotting door gave in when we pushed, and we went inside.

give it a rest!.monolingual: Inf. Stop talking so much. Give your mouth a rest. (Familiar or rude. Compare this with Give me a rest!) _ Mary: So, I really think we need to discuss things more and go over all our differences in detail. Bill: Stop! I’ve heard enough. Give it a res
examples: Mary: So, I really think we need to discuss things more and go over all our differences in detail.

give it all you’ve got!.monolingual: Inf. Do your very best! _ Go out there and try. Give it all you’ve got!
examples: Go out there and try.

give it time..monolingual: Be patient.; In time, things will change. (Usually said to encourage someone to wait or be patient.) _ Things will get better. Don’t worry. Give it time. _ Of course, things will improve. Give it time.
examples: Things will get better.

give it up!.monolingual: Inf. Stop trying!; You are wasting your time! (Fixed order.) _Bob: I just can’t understand calculus! Bill: Give it up! Get out of that course and get into something less cruel. _ Tom: I’m just not a very good singer, I guess. Sue: It’s no good, Tom.
examples: Bob: I just can’t understand calculus! Bill: Give it up! Get out of that course and get into something less cruel.

give me a chance!.monolingual: 1. Please give me an opportunity to do something! _ Mary: I just know I can do it. Oh, please give me a chance! Sue: All right. Just one more chance. _ Bob: Do you think you can do it? Jane: Oh, I know I can. Just give me a chance!
examples: Mary: I just know I can do it.

give me a rest!.monolingual: Inf. Stop being such a pest!; Stop bothering me with this problem! (Compare this with Give it a rest!) _“Go away and stop bothering me!” moaned Bob. “Give me a rest!” _ Bob: I need an answer to this right away! Bill: I just gave you an answer! Bob: T
examples: “Go away and stop bothering me!” moaned Bob.

give of oneself.monolingual: to be generous with one’s time and concern. _ Tom is very good with children because he gives of himself. _ If you want to have more friends, you have to learn to give of yourself.
examples: Tom is very good with children because he gives of himself.

give one one’s freedom.monolingual: to set someone free; to divorce someone. _ Mrs. Brown wanted to give her husband his freedom. _ Well, Tom, I hate to break it to you this way, but I have decided to give you your freedom.
examples: Mrs. Brown wanted to give her husband his freedom.

give out.monolingual: 1. to wear out and stop; to quit operating. _ My old bicycle finally gave out. _ I think that your shoes are about ready to give out.
examples: My old bicycle finally gave out.

give rise to something.monolingual: to cause something; to instigate something. _ The attack gave rise to endless arguments. _Her ludicrous living gave rise to further speculation as to the source of her money.
examples: The attack gave rise to endless arguments.

give some thought to something.monolingual: to think about something; to devote some time to thinking about something. _ After I have had time to give some thought to the matter, I will call you.
examples: After I have had time to give some thought to the matter, I will call you.

give someone a dig.monolingual: Sl. to insult someone; to say something which will irritate a person. _ Jane gave Bob a dig about his carelessness with money. _ The headmaster’s daughter gets tired of people giving her digs about favoritism.
examples: Jane gave Bob a dig about his carelessness with money.

give someone a pain.monolingual: Fig. to annoy or bother someone. _ Please don’t give me a pain. I’ve had a hard day. _You give me a pain! _ She’s such a pest. She really gives me a pain.
examples: Please don’t give me a pain.

give someone a red face.monolingual: Fig. to make someone visibly embarrassed. _ We really gave him a red face when we caught him eavesdropping. _His error gave him a very red face.
examples: We really gave him a red face when we caught him eavesdropping.

give someone hail columbia.monolingual: Inf. to scold someone severely. _ The teacher gave her students Hail Columbia over their poor test scores. _ If Miss Ellen finds out I broke her window, she’ll give me Hail Columbia for sure!
examples: The teacher gave her students Hail Columbia over their poor test scores.

give someone odds that....monolingual: to propose a sham bet to someone, the implication being that even at favorable odds the outcome will defy the odds. (Often with a negative.) _ I’ll give you odds that you won’t be able to order a decent steak at this restaurant.
examples: I’ll give you odds that you won’t be able to order a decent steak at this restaurant.

give someone or something away†.monolingual: to reveal a secret about someone or something. _ I thought no one knew where I was, but my loud breathing gave me away. _We know that Billy ate the cherry pie. The cherry juice on his shirt gave him away. _ I had planned a surprise, but John gave awa
examples: I thought no one knew where I was, but my loud breathing gave me away.

give someone some lip.monolingual: Inf. to speak rudely or disrespectfully to someone; to sass someone. _ Billy gave me some lip, so I whupped him. _ Jane is always giving the teacher some lip.
examples: Billy gave me some lip, so I whupped him.

give someone some skin.monolingual: Sl. [for two people] to touch two hands together in a special greeting, like a handshake. (One hand may be slapped down on top of the other, or they may be slapped together palm to palm with the arms held vertically. Usually said as a command.) _ Hey
examples: Come over here, you guys.

give someone some sugar.monolingual: Rur. to give someone a kiss. _ Come here, honey, and give me some sugar. _ “Give me some sugar!” Grandma said when she saw me.
examples: Come here, honey, and give me some sugar.

give someone static.monolingual: Fig. to argue with someone; to give someone back talk. _ I want you to do it and do it now! Don’t give me any static!

give someone the eye.monolingual: Fig. to look at someone in a way that communicates romantic interest. _Ann gave John the eye. It really surprised him. _Tom kept giving Sally the eye. She finally got disgusted and left.
examples: Ann gave John the eye.

give someone the finger.monolingual: 1. Fig. to display the middle finger upright as a sign of derision. (The gesture is derisive and offensive. See also flip someone off, flip someone the bird.) _ Did one of you guys give Ted the finger? _ Somebody gave the cop the finger.
examples: Somebody gave the cop the finger.

give someone the gate.monolingual: Sl. to get rid of someone. _ The chick was a pest, so I gave her the gate. _ He threatened to give me the gate, so I left.
examples: The chick was a pest, so I gave her the gate.

give someone the go-by.monolingual: to bypass someone; to ignore someone. _ Gert gave us all the go-by when she took up with that rich boyfriend. _I didn’t mean to give you the goby. I’m preoccupied, that’s all.
examples: Gert gave us all the go-by when she took up with that rich boyfriend.

give someone the raspberry.monolingual: Inf. to make a rude noise with the lips at someone. _ The audience gave him the raspberry, which gave him some second thoughts about his choice of career. _Even after his grandstand play, they gave him the raspberry.
examples: The audience gave him the raspberry, which gave him some second thoughts about his choice of career.

give someone the shaft.monolingual: Sl. to cheat or deceive someone; to mistreat someone. _The boss really gave Wally the shaft. _ Somebody always gives me the shaft.
examples: The boss really gave Wally the shaft.

give someone the slip.monolingual: Sl. to escape from a pursuer. _ We were on his tail until he gave us the slip. _ I can give her the slip in no time at all.
examples: We were on his tail until he gave us the slip.

give someone tit for tat.monolingual: Fig. to give someone something equal to what was given you; to exchange a series of very similar things, one by one, with someone. _They gave me the same kind of difficulty that I gave them. They gave me tit for tat. _ He punched me, so I punched him
examples: They gave me the same kind of difficulty that I gave them.

give someone to understand something.monolingual: to explain something to someone; to imply something to someone. (Possibly misleading someone, accidentally or intentionally. See also given to understand.) _ Mr. Smith gave Sally to understand that she should be home by midnight. _The mayor gave the
examples: Mr. Smith gave Sally to understand that she should be home by midnight.

give someone up† for dead.monolingual: 1. Lit. to give up hope for someone who is dying; to abandon a dying person as already dead. _ The cowboys gave up their comrade for dead and rode off. _We gave up the poor old man for dead and went to telephone the police.
examples: The cowboys gave up their comrade for dead and rode off.

give something for something.monolingual: to exchange something for something. _I will give two brownies for that piece of cake in your lunch box. _ Jed gave two pigs for an old motorcycle.
examples: I will give two brownies for that piece of cake in your lunch box.

give something off†.monolingual: to release something, such as smoke, a noise, an odor, fragrance, etc. _ The little animal gave a foul smell off. _ The f lower gave off its heavy perfume at dusk.
examples: The little animal gave a foul smell off.

give something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to distribute something; to pass something out. _ The teacher gave the test papers out. _ The teacher gave out the papers.
examples: The teacher gave the test papers out.

give something to someone.monolingual: to bestow something, such as a gift, on someone. _Please give this to Sally Wilson. _Who gave this book to me? I want to thank whoever it was.
examples: Please give this to Sally Wilson.

give something up†.monolingual: 1. to forsake something; to stop using or eating something. _ I gave coffee up because of the caffeine. _They advised me to give up sugar in all forms.
examples: I gave coffee up because of the caffeine.

give the game away.monolingual: Fig. to reveal a plan or strategy. _ Now, all of you have to keep quiet. Please don’t give the game away. _ If you keep giving out hints, you’ll give the game away.
examples: Now, all of you have to keep quiet.

give the lie to something.monolingual: Fig. to show that something is a lie. _ The evidence gives the lie to your testimony. _ Your own admission of your part in the conspiracy gives the lie to your earlier testimony.
examples: The evidence gives the lie to your testimony.

give up.monolingual: to quit; to quit trying. _I give up! I won’t press this further. _ Are you going to give up or keep fighting?
examples: I give up! I won’t press this further.

give up the ghost.monolingual: Euph. to die. (Fixed order. Often used to describe machines breaking down.) _The old man gave up the ghost. _ My poor old car finally gave up the ghost.
examples: The old man gave up the ghost.

give vent to something.monolingual: Fig. to express anger. (The something is usually anger, ire, irritation, etc.) _John gave vent to his anger by yelling at Sally. _ Bill couldn’t give vent to his frustration because he had been warned to keep quiet.
examples: John gave vent to his anger by yelling at Sally.

give voice to something.monolingual: Fig. to express a feeling or an opinion in words; to speak out about something. _ The bird gave voice to its joy in the golden sunshine. _ The protestors gave voice to their anger at Congress.
examples: The bird gave voice to its joy in the golden sunshine.

give weight to something.monolingual: Fig. to attach importance to something. _I give a lot of weight to your opinion. _Kelly gave no weight at all to the comments by Betty.
examples: I give a lot of weight to your opinion.

give with something.monolingual: Inf. to give something to someone; to tell something to someone. _ Come on! Give with the money! _ You had better give with the information if you know what’s good for you.
examples: You had better give with the information if you know what’s good for you.

given to doing something.monolingual: likely to do something; inclined to do something habitually. _ Mary is given to singing in the shower. _Bob is given to shouting when things don’t go his way.
examples: Mary is given to singing in the shower.

given to understand.monolingual: [of someone] made to believe [something]. _ They were given to understand that there would be no tax increase, but after the election taxes went up. _ She was given to understand that she had to be home by midnight.
examples: They were given to understand that there would be no tax increase, but after the election taxes went up.

*the glad hand.monolingual: Fig. an overly friendly welcome; a symbol of insincere attention. (*Typically: get ~; give someone ~.) _ Whenever I go into that store, I get the glad hand. _ I hate to go to a party and get the glad hand.
examples: Whenever I go into that store, I get the glad hand.

glance at someone or something.monolingual: to look quickly at someone or something. _Sharon glanced at Todd to see if he looked as if he was ready to go. _ I glanced at my watch and realized how long all this had taken.
examples: Sharon glanced at Todd to see if he looked as if he was ready to go.

glance over someone or something.monolingual: to examine someone or something very quickly. _ I only glanced over the papers. They look okay to me. _The doctor glanced over the injured woman and called for an ambulance.
examples: I only glanced over the papers.

glance through something.monolingual: to look quickly at the contents of something. _ I glanced through the manuscript, and I don’t think it is ready yet. _Would you glance through this report when you have a moment?
examples: I glanced through the manuscript, and I don’t think it is ready yet.

glare at someone or something.monolingual: to scowl at someone or something. _Don’t glare at me! _I glared at the cat and thought mean thoughts.
examples: I glared at the cat and thought mean thoughts.

glass something in†.monolingual: to enclose something, such as a porch, in glass. _ I want to glass this porch in, so we can use it in the winter. _ We glassed in our porch last year.
examples: I want to glass this porch in, so we can use it in the winter.

glaze over.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to be covered over with a coat of something cloudy or ice. _The roads glazed over and became very dangerous. _ The street is glazed over badly.
examples: The roads glazed over and became very dangerous.

gleam with something.monolingual: to sparkle or shine with something. _ The crystal goblets gleamed with the sparkling candlelight. _ The glass gleamed with a bright ref lection.
examples: The crystal goblets gleamed with the sparkling candlelight.

glide across something.monolingual: to float or slide across something. _ The skaters glided across the frozen expanse of the river. _ The small plane glided across the sky.
examples: The skaters glided across the frozen expanse of the river.

glint with something.monolingual: to sparkle or shine with something. _ Her bright eyes glinted with the sunlight. _ The crystal goblet glinted with the orange firelight.
examples: Her bright eyes glinted with the sunlight.

glisten with something.monolingual: to sparkle or shimmer with something. _ The trees glistened with a thin coating of ice from the freezing rain. _ Fran’s eyes glistened with a few tears.
examples: The trees glistened with a thin coating of ice from the freezing rain.

glitter with something.monolingual: 1. to sparkle with something. _ Her earrings glittered with many tiny diamonds. _The tree glittered with tiny ice crystals.
examples: Her earrings glittered with many tiny diamonds.

gloat over something.monolingual: to rejoice smugly over something; to be glad that something unfortunate has happened to someone else. _He gloated over his good luck in a way that made all of us angry. _ Please don’t gloat over my misfortune.
examples: He gloated over his good luck in a way that made all of us angry.

glory be!.monolingual: Inf. an exclamation expressing surprise or shock. (A bit old-fashioned.) _ Mary: Glory be! Is that what I think it is? Sue: Well, it’s a kitten, if that’s what you thought. _Sally: First a car just missed hitting her, then she fell down on the ice. M
examples: Mary: Glory be! Is that what I think it is? Sue: Well, it’s a kitten, if that’s what you thought.

glory in something.monolingual: Fig. to take great pleasure in something; to revel in something. _He just glories in all the attention he is getting. _ Martha tends to glory in doing things just exactly right.
examples: He just glories in all the attention he is getting.

gloss over something.monolingual: to cover up, minimize, or play down something bad. _ Don’t gloss over your own role in this fiasco! _ I don’t want to gloss this matter over, but it really isn’t very important, is it?

the gloves are off..monolingual: Fig. There is going to be a serious dispute. (As if boxers had removed their gloves in order to inflict more damage. See also take the gloves off.) _Bob got mad and yelled, “Ok, the gloves are off!” and started cussing and pounding the table.
examples: Bob got mad and yelled, “Ok, the gloves are off!” and started cussing and pounding the table.

glow with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to put out light, usually because of high heat. _ The embers glowed with the remains of the fire. _ The last of the coals still glowed with fire.
examples: The embers glowed with the remains of the fire.

glower at someone or something.monolingual: to scowl intently at someone or something. _ The judge glowered at the irate wit- ness until order was restored. _Fred glowered at the painting of his uncle, hating the subject of the picture.
examples: The judge glowered at the irate wit- ness until order was restored.

glue something down†.monolingual: to fix something down onto something with cement. _Glue the edge of the rug down before someone trips over it. _ You should glue down the rug.
examples: Glue the edge of the rug down before someone trips over it.

glue something together†.monolingual: to attach the pieces of something together with glue. _ She glued the pieces of the model plane together. _ She glued together all the loose pieces.
examples: She glued the pieces of the model plane together.

glued to someone or something.monolingual: Fig. following someone everywhere; very close to or touching something. _ His little sister was glued to him all afternoon. Finally he sent her home.
examples: His little sister was glued to him all afternoon.

a glutton for punishment.monolingual: Fig. someone who is eager for a burden or some sort of difficulty; someone willing to accept a difficult task. _ Tom works too hard. He is a glutton for punishment. _ I enjoy managing difficult projects, but I am a glutton for punishment.
examples: Tom works too hard.

gnash one’s teeth.monolingual: Fig. to grind or bite noisily with one’s teeth. _ Bill clenched his fists and gnashed his teeth in anger. _ The wolf gnashed its teeth and chased after the deer.
examples: Bill clenched his fists and gnashed his teeth in anger.

a gnashing of teeth.monolingual: Fig. a show of anger or dismay. (Biblical: “weeping, wailing, and gnashing of teeth.”) _ After a little gnashing of teeth and a few threats, the boss calmed down and become almost reasonable.
examples: After a little gnashing of teeth and a few threats, the boss calmed down and become almost reasonable.

gnaw on something.monolingual: to chew on something. (Usually said of an animal.) _ The puppy has been gnawing on my slippers! _ This slipper has been gnawed on!

go about something.monolingual: to approach the doing of something in a particular way. _ How should I go about researching this topic? _ Would you tell me how to go about it?

go above someone or something.monolingual: to travel over someone or something. _ The model airplane swooped low right at us but went above us at the last minute.
examples: The model airplane swooped low right at us but went above us at the last minute.

go after someone.monolingual: to investigate someone or something for possible criminal prosecution. _The prosecutor went after Max first, knowing that Max was the gang leader. _ The police detectives went after the whole gang.
examples: The prosecutor went after Max first, knowing that Max was the gang leader.

go ahead..monolingual: Please do it.; You have my permission and encouragement to do it. _ Alice: I’m leaving. John: Go ahead. See if I care. _Jane: Can I put this one in the refrigerator? Sue: Sure. Go ahead.
examples: Alice: I’m leaving.

go along.monolingual: 1. to continue; to progress. _ Things are going along quite nicely in my new job. _ I hope everything is going along well.
examples: Things are going along quite nicely in my new job.

go around doing something.monolingual: to move around doing something. _ She keeps going around telling lies about me. _ Please stop going around knocking things over. _ She goes around helping whomever she can.
examples: She keeps going around telling lies about me.

go around someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to walk or travel in such a way as to avoid hitting or touching someone. _ I can’t move from this place right now. You’ll have to go around me.
examples: I can’t move from this place right now.

go astray.monolingual: 1. Lit. to wander off the road or path. _ Stick to the path and try not to go astray. _ I couldn’t see the trail and I almost went astray.
examples: Stick to the path and try not to go astray.

go at someone or something.monolingual: to attack someone or something; to move or lunge toward someone or something. _ The dog went at the visitor and almost bit him. _ He went at the door and tried to break it down.
examples: The dog went at the visitor and almost bit him.

go away!.monolingual: Leave me!; Get away from me! _ Mary: You’re such a pest, Sue. Go away! Sue: I was just trying to help. _ “Go away!” yelled the child at the bee.
examples: Mary: You’re such a pest, Sue.

go away empty-handed.monolingual: Fig. to depart with nothing. _ I hate for you to go away empty-handed, but I cannot afford to contribute any money. _ They came hoping for some food, but they had to go away empty-handed.
examples: I hate for you to go away empty-handed, but I cannot afford to contribute any money.

go awol.monolingual: to become absent without leave. (Originally military.) _ Private Smith went AWOL last Wednesday. Now he’s in a military prison. _Tom went AWOL and finally we had to fire him.
examples: Private Smith went AWOL last Wednesday.

go back.monolingual: to return to the place of origin. _ That’s where I came from, and I’ll never go back. _I don’t want to go back.
examples: That’s where I came from, and I’ll never go back.

go back to square one.monolingual: Fig. to return to the starting point. (Alludes to the squares of a board game.) _It’s back to square one. We have to start over. _It looks like it’s back to square one for you.
examples: It’s back to square one.

go bad.monolingual: to become rotten, undesirable, evil, etc. _ I’m afraid that this milk has gone bad. _ Life used to be wonderful. Now it has gone bad.
examples: I’m afraid that this milk has gone bad.

go bananas.monolingual: Sl. to go mildly crazy. _ Sorry, I just went bananas for a minute. _ I thought he was going to go bananas.
examples: Sorry, I just went bananas for a minute.

go before someone or something.monolingual: 1. to precede someone or something. _ Do you wish to go before me? _ I will go before the other waiters and clear the aisles.
examples: I will go before the other waiters and clear the aisles.

go begging.monolingual: Fig. to be left over, unwanted, or unused. (As if a thing were begging for an owner or a user.) _ There is still food left. A whole lobster is going begging. Please eat some more. _There are many excellent books in the library just going begging beca
examples: There is still food left.

go behind someone’s back.monolingual: 1. Lit. to move behind someone; to locate oneself at someone’s back. _ The mugger went behind my back and put a gun to my spine. _Bob went behind my back and pushed me through the opening.
examples: The mugger went behind my back and put a gun to my spine.

go below.monolingual: to go beneath the main deck of a ship. (Nautical.) _ I will have to go below and fiddle with the engine. _ The captain went below to escape the worst of the storm.
examples: I will have to go below and fiddle with the engine.

go berserk.monolingual: to go crazy. _ She went berserk and strangled her cat.
examples: She went berserk and strangled her cat.

go beyond someone or something.monolingual: to pass ahead of someone or something. _I went beyond the place where I should have turned off. _Fred went beyond me a half block before he remembered who I was. Then he came back and said hello.
examples: I went beyond the place where I should have turned off.

go beyond something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to do more of something than the expected amount; to go further with something than was required. _You clearly went beyond what was required of you. _ Sharon went beyond the basic requirements.
examples: You clearly went beyond what was required of you.

go broke.monolingual: to completely run out of money and other assets. _This company is going to go broke if you don’t stop spending money foolishly. _ I made some bad investments last year, and it looks as if I may go broke this year.
examples: This company is going to go broke if you don’t stop spending money foolishly.

go by the board.monolingual: Fig. to get ruined or lost. (This is originally a nautical expression meaning “to fall or be washed overboard.”) _ I hate to see good food go by the board. Please eat up so we won’t have to throw it out. _ Your plan has gone by the board. The entire
examples: I hate to see good food go by the board.

go cold turkey.monolingual: Inf. to stop (doing something) without tapering off. (Originally drug slang. Now concerned with breaking any habit.) _I had to stop smoking, so I went cold turkey. It’s awful! _ When heroin addicts go cold turkey, they get terribly sick.
examples: I had to stop smoking, so I went cold turkey.

go down.monolingual: 1. to sink below a normal or expected level or height. _The plane went down in f lames. _The ship went down with all hands aboard.
examples: The plane went down in f lames.

go down fighting.monolingual: Fig. to continue the struggle until one is completely defeated. _I won’t give up easily. I’ll go down fighting. _Sally, who is very determined, went down fighting.
examples: I won’t give up easily.

go down in flames.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a plane] to crash. _ The enemy fighter planes went down in f lames, ending the battle. _The pilot and crew went down in f lames near the airport.
examples: The enemy fighter planes went down in f lames, ending the battle.

go down on one’s knees.monolingual: to kneel down. _ The people went down on their knees and prayed. _ Larry went down on his knees and asked for forgiveness.
examples: The people went down on their knees and prayed.

go down something.monolingual: to descend something; to fall down something. _ She went down the ladder very carefully. _ I did not want to go down those steep stairs.
examples: She went down the ladder very carefully.

go down the line.monolingual: to go from person to person or thing to thing in a line of people or things. _ She went down the line, asking everyone for a dollar for a cup of coffee. _ Sam went down the line, passing out tickets.
examples: She went down the line, asking everyone for a dollar for a cup of coffee.

go down to something.monolingual: [for something] to decline or diminish to some level. _ His temperature has gone down to normal. _ Will the temperature go down to freezing tonight?
examples: His temperature has gone down to normal.

go down with something.monolingual: Fig. to be stricken with a disease. _ Beth went down with the f lu. _ She went down with a high fever.
examples: Beth went down with the f lu.

go downhill.monolingual: [for something] to decline and grow worse and worse. _ This industry is going downhill. We lose money every year. _As one gets older, one’s health tends to go downhill.
examples: This industry is going downhill.

go dutch.monolingual: [for each person in a pair or a group] to pay for himself or herself. _ I don’t want you to pay for my ticket. Let’s go Dutch. _Is it still considered a date if you go Dutch?
examples: I don’t want you to pay for my ticket.

go easy on something.monolingual: to use something sparingly. _ Go easy on the mustard. That’s all there is. _ Please go easy on the onions. I don’t like them very much.
examples: Go easy on the mustard.

go figure..monolingual: It’s really strange.; Just try to figure it out. _ She says she wants to have a conversation, but when I try, she does all the talking. Go figure.
examples: She says she wants to have a conversation, but when I try, she does all the talking.

go for broke.monolingual: to risk everything; to try as hard as possible. _ Okay, this is my last chance. I’m going for broke. _ Look at Mary starting to move in the final hundred yards of the race! She is really going for broke.
examples: Okay, this is my last chance.

go for it!.monolingual: Inf. Go ahead! Give it a good try! _ Sally: I’m going to try out for the basketball team. Do you think I’m tall enough? Bob: Sure you are! Go for it! _Bob: Mary can’t quit now! She’s almost at the finish line! Bill: Go for it, Mary!
examples: Sally: I’m going to try out for the basketball team.

go for nothing.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to be done for no purpose. _ All our work went for nothing. _ Our efforts at helping out went for nothing.
examples: All our work went for nothing.

go forward with something.monolingual: Fig. to continue with something; to do something that is planned. _ We will go forward with our plans. _ Let’s go forward with the plan.
examples: We will go forward with our plans.

go from bad to worse.monolingual: to progress from a bad situation to one that is worse. _ Things went from bad to worse in a matter of days. _ I’m afraid that things are going from bad to worse.
examples: Things went from bad to worse in a matter of days.

go fry an egg!.monolingual: Go away and stop bothering me! _ Go away and stop bothering me. Go fry an egg! _ Get out of my way! Go fry an egg!
examples: Go away and stop bothering me.

go haywire.monolingual: Rur. to go wrong; to malfunction; to break down. _I was talking to Mary when suddenly the telephone went haywire. I haven’t heard from her since. _ There we were, driving along, when the engine went haywire. It was two hours before the tow truck came
examples: I was talking to Mary when suddenly the telephone went haywire.

go hog wild.monolingual: Rur. to behave wildly. _ Have a good time at the party, but don’t go hog wild. _The teacher cannot control a class that is going hog wild.
examples: Have a good time at the party, but don’t go hog wild.

go home in a box.monolingual: Sl. to be shipped home dead. (Often said in exaggeration.) _ Hey, I’m too young to go home in a box. _ You had better be careful on this camping trip, or you’ll go home in a box.
examples: Hey, I’m too young to go home in a box.

go home to mama.monolingual: to give up something—such as a marriage— and return to one’s mother’s home. _ I’ve had it. I’m going home to mama. _Mary left him and went home to mama.
examples: I’ve had it. I’m going home to mama.

go hungry.monolingual: to miss a meal and end up hungry. _ The kids were late for dinner so they had to go hungry.
examples: The kids were late for dinner so they had to go hungry.

go in for something.monolingual: to take part in something; to enjoy (doing) something. _John doesn’t go in for sports. _None of them seems to go in for swimming.
examples: John doesn’t go in for sports.

go in someone’s favor.monolingual: [for something] to change to someone’s benefit. (Alludes to very changeable things like game scores, wind direction, or chance in general.) _ Things appear to be going in our favor—finally. _ The game was going in our favor during the first half.
examples: Things appear to be going in our favor—finally.

go in the right direction.monolingual: 1. Lit. to head or travel in the right direction. _ Are you sure we are going in the right direction? _ We were supposed to turn back there. We are not going in the right direction.
examples: We were supposed to turn back there.

go into a huddle.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for team members] to get into a small circle and plan what they are going to do next. _ They went into a huddle to plan their strategy. _The players will go into a huddle and decide what to do.
examples: They went into a huddle to plan their strategy.

go into a tailspin.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for an airplane] to lose control and spin to the earth, nose first. _ The plane shook and then suddenly went into a tailspin. _The pilot was not able to bring the plane out of the tailspin, and it crashed into the sea.
examples: The plane shook and then suddenly went into a tailspin.

go into hiding.monolingual: to conceal oneself in a hidden place for a period of time. _ The political dissident went into hiding. _ After robbing the bank, the bandits went into hiding for months.
examples: The political dissident went into hiding.

go into hock.monolingual: go into debt. _We will have to go into hock to buy a house. _I go further into hock every time I use my credit card.
examples: We will have to go into hock to buy a house.

go into one’s act.monolingual: Fig. to begin to behave in a way typical to oneself. _ The curtain opened and Steve went into his act.
examples: The curtain opened and Steve went into his act.

go into orbit.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a rocket, satellite, etc.] to rotate around a heavenly body in a fixed path. _ The satellite went into orbit just as planned. _ When did the moon go into orbit?
examples: The satellite went into orbit just as planned.

go into service.monolingual: to start operating. _ When will the new elevator go into service? _ It has already gone into service.
examples: It has already gone into service.

go into the service.monolingual: to enter one of the military services. _She went into the service when she got out of high school. _ I chose not to go into the service.
examples: She went into the service when she got out of high school.

go it alone.monolingual: to do something by oneself. _ Do you need help, or will you go it alone? _ I think I need a little more experience before I go it alone.
examples: I think I need a little more experience before I go it alone.

go like clockwork.monolingual: Fig. to progress with regularity and dependability. _The building project is progressing nicely. Everything is going like clockwork. _The elaborate pageant was a great success. It went like clockwork from start to finish.
examples: The building project is progressing nicely.

go off.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for an explosive device] to explode. _ The fireworks all went off as scheduled. _ The bomb went off and did a lot of damage.
examples: The fireworks all went off as scheduled.

go off half-cocked.monolingual: Fig. to go into action too early or without thinking. (Originally refers to a flintlock or matchlock gun firing prematurely, before the trigger was pulled.) _ Don’t go off half-cocked. Plan out what you’re going to do. _ Bill went off half-cocked and
examples: Don’t go off half-cocked.

go off on a tangent.monolingual: Fig. to pursue a somewhat related or irrelevant course while neglecting the main subject. _ Don’t go off on a tangent. Stick to your job. _ Just as we started talking, Henry went off on a tangent about the high cost of living.
examples: Don’t go off on a tangent.

go off on someone.monolingual: Sl. to berate someone. _ Don’t go off on me! I’m not the cause of your problems! _ The teacher went off on poor little Harry.
examples: The teacher went off on poor little Harry.

go on a binge.monolingual: to do too much of something, especially to drink too much. _ Jane went on a binge last night and is very sick this morning. _ Bill loves to spend money on clothes. He’s out on a binge right now—buying everything in sight.
examples: Jane went on a binge last night and is very sick this morning.

go on a rampage.monolingual: to get very disturbed or angry. _ The angry bull went on a rampage and broke the fence. _ My boss went on a rampage because the report wasn’t finished.
examples: The angry bull went on a rampage and broke the fence.

go on and on.monolingual: to (seem to) last or go forever. _ You talk too much, Bob. You just go on and on. _ The road to their house is very boring. It goes on and on with nothing interesting to look at.
examples: You talk too much, Bob.

go on the block.monolingual: Fig. [for something] to go up for auction; [for something] to be placed on the auction block. _ Our farm went on the block last week. Got a good price. _ When this painting goes on the block, I hope I get a lot for it.
examples: Our farm went on the block last week.

go on to something.monolingual: to advance to something or to doing something. _After a few years she went on to even greater heights. _ Larry went on to found his own company.
examples: After a few years she went on to even greater heights.

go on tour.monolingual: [for a performing group] to go from place to place, performing. _Our play went on tour across the state. _ If we make the play a success, we will go on tour.
examples: Our play went on tour across the state.

go out of business.monolingual: to stop doing commerce or business. _The new shop will probably go out of business if sales don’t get better. _ I have to work hard to keep from going out of business.
examples: The new shop will probably go out of business if sales don’t get better.

go out of service.monolingual: [for something] to stop working; [for something] to have been turned off so it cannot be used. _ This elevator went out of service last week. _ How long has it been since this thing went out of service?
examples: This elevator went out of service last week.

go out to someone.monolingual: [for one’s sympathy, heart, etc.] to be aimed toward someone. _All of my sympathy went out to her. I knew just how she felt. _My thanks go out to you all.
examples: All of my sympathy went out to her.

go out with something.monolingual: to go out of fashion at the same time as something else went out of fashion. _ That style of dress went out with the bustle. _ Your thinking went out with the horse and buggy.
examples: That style of dress went out with the bustle.

go over.monolingual: Euph. to leave one’s country and go to ideologically opposed or enemy country; to defect. _ When the ballet company visited New York, two of the dancers went over. _ He had been spying for the Americans for many years, and he finally went over.
examples: When the ballet company visited New York, two of the dancers went over.

go over someone or something.monolingual: to examine someone or something. _ The doctor will go over you very carefully, I’m sure. _I went over the papers and found nothing wrong.
examples: The doctor will go over you very carefully, I’m sure.

go over to some place.monolingual: to travel some distance or cross water to get to some place. _We went over to Cedar Point and spent the day having fun. _John went over to the other side of the stadium for the rest of the tournament.
examples: We went over to Cedar Point and spent the day having fun.

go over with a bang.monolingual: 1. Fig. [for something] to be funny or entertaining. _Our presentation was a success. It really went over with a bang. _ That’s a great joke. It went over with a bang.
examples: Our presentation was a success.

go overboard.monolingual: 1. Fig. to fall out of a boat or off of a ship; to fall overboard. _Be careful or you will go overboard. _ Someone went overboard in the fog.
examples: Be careful or you will go overboard.

go past someone or something.monolingual: to pass by someone or something. _You went right past Tom. Did you mean to? _Did I go past it?
examples: You went right past Tom.

go places.monolingual: to become very successful. _ I knew that Sally, with all her talent, would go places. _ I really want to go places in life.
examples: I knew that Sally, with all her talent, would go places.

go sky-high.monolingual: Fig. to go very high. _ Prices go sky-high whenever there is inf lation. _ Oh, it’s so hot. The temperature went sky-high about noon.
examples: Prices go sky-high whenever there is inf lation.

go sour.monolingual: Fig. to turn bad or unpleasant. _ It looks like all my plans are going sour. _My whole life is going sour right now.
examples: It looks like all my plans are going sour.

go stag.monolingual: to go to an event (which is meant for couples) without a member of the opposite sex. (Originally referred only to males.) _ Is Tom going to take you, or are you going stag? _ Bob didn’t want to go stag, so he took his sister to the party.
examples: Bob didn’t want to go stag, so he took his sister to the party.

go straight.monolingual: to stop breaking the law and lead a lawful life instead. _The judge encouraged the thief to go straight. _ After Bob was arrested, he promised his mother he would go straight.
examples: The judge encouraged the thief to go straight.

go the distance.monolingual: Fig. to do the whole amount; to play the entire game; to run the whole race. (Originally sports use.) _That horse runs fast. I hope it can go the distance. _This is going to be a long, hard project. I hope I can go the distance.
examples: That horse runs fast.

go the extra mile.monolingual: to try harder to please someone or to get the task done correctly; to do more than one is required to do to reach a goal. _I like doing business with that company. They always go the extra mile. _My teacher goes the extra mile to help us.
examples: I like doing business with that company.

go the limit.monolingual: Fig. to do as much as possible; to get as much as possible. _ Let’s plan to do everything we can. Let’s go the limit. _ We’ll go the limit. To heck with the cost.
examples: Let’s plan to do everything we can.

go there.monolingual: to begin a discussion of something; to take up a certain topic. (Similar to go into something. Often in the negative. This has nothing to do with traveling or going to a place.) _A: How are things going at your place of business? B: Please! I don’t w
examples: A: How are things going at your place of business? B: Please! I don’t want to go there.

go through.monolingual: to be approved; to succeed in getting through the approval process. _I sent the board of directors a proposal. I hope it goes through. _ We all hope that the new law goes through.
examples: I sent the board of directors a proposal.

go through someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to travel through someone’s body; to go (right) through someone. _ That medicine went right through me.
examples: That medicine went right through me.

go through someone or something.monolingual: [for something sharp] to penetrate someone or something. _ The sword went through the knight cleanly and quickly. _ The nail went through all three boards.
examples: The sword went through the knight cleanly and quickly.

go through something.monolingual: 1. to search through something. _ She went through his pants pockets, looking for his wallet. _ He spent quite a while going through his desk, looking for the papers.
examples: She went through his pants pockets, looking for his wallet.

go through the changes.monolingual: Fig. to experience life’s changes. _ A good day, a bad day—it’s all part of going through the changes. _ Nothing new with me, just going through the changes.
examples: A good day, a bad day—it’s all part of going through the changes.

go through the motions.monolingual: Fig. to make a feeble effort to do something; to do something insincerely or in cursory fashion. _Jane isn’t doing her best. She’s just going through the motions. _ Bill was supposed to be raking the yard, but he was just going through the motions.
examples: Jane isn’t doing her best.

go through the roof.monolingual: 1. Fig. Inf. to become very angry. _ She saw what had happened and went through the roof. _My father went through the roof when he saw what I did to the car.
examples: She saw what had happened and went through the roof.

go through with something.monolingual: to complete something the outcome of which is troubling or doubtful; to do something in spite of problems and drawbacks. _ I have to go through with it, no matter what. _I just couldn’t go through with it.
examples: I have to go through with it, no matter what.

go to any length.monolingual: Fig. to do whatever is necessary. _ I’ll go to any length to secure this contract. _ I want to get a college degree, but I won’t go to any length to get one.
examples: I’ll go to any length to secure this contract.

go to bat against someone.monolingual: Fig. to aid someone against someone else. _I would be happy to go to bat against Dan. _ We refused to go to bat against one of our friends.
examples: I would be happy to go to bat against Dan.

go to bat for someone.monolingual: Fig. to support or help someone. _I tried to go to bat for Bill, but he said he didn’t want any help. _ I heard them gossiping about Sally, so I went to bat for her.
