examples: I tried to go to bat for Bill, but he said he didn’t want any help.

go to bed.monolingual: to go to where one’s bed is, get into it, and go to sleep. _ It’s time for me to go to bed. _ I want to go to bed, but there is too much work to do.
examples: It’s time for me to go to bed.

go to it.monolingual: 1. Lit. to start something actively; to do something with vigor. _ Time to play ball. Go to it! _ Let’s go to it, you guys!
examples: Time to play ball.

go to pieces.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to fall apart into many pieces. _ The vase—which had been repaired many times—just went to pieces when I put it down. _When the window was hit by the ball, it went to pieces.
examples: The vase—which had been repaired many times—just went to pieces when I put it down.

go to press.monolingual: [for a publication] to be sent to the printing presses. _The book went to press last week. We expect finished books by the first of the month. _The book you want to order hasn’t even gone to press yet.
examples: The book went to press last week.

go to press with something.monolingual: [for someone] to cause something to be printed. _The columnist went to press with the rumor without checking any of her usual sources. _We are going to press with a series of books on textiles.
examples: The columnist went to press with the rumor without checking any of her usual sources.

go to sea.monolingual: to become a sailor. _ I went to sea at an early age. _ When I get older, I’m going to go to sea too.
examples: I went to sea at an early age.

go to someone’s head.monolingual: 1. Fig. [for something, such as fame or success] to make someone conceited. _Don’t let all this praise go to your head. _ Too much success will go to her head.
examples: Don’t let all this praise go to your head.

go to the bathroom.monolingual: 1. Fig. Euph. to go into and use a restroom, bathroom, or toilet. _ Bill: Where is Bob? Jane: He went to the bathroom. _ John went to the bathroom to brush his teeth.
examples: Bill: Where is Bob? Jane: He went to the bathroom.

go to the lavatory.monolingual: Euph. to go into a restroom and use a toilet. _Bob requested to leave the room to go to the lavatory. _ Please stop the car. I have to go to the lavatory.
examples: Bob requested to leave the room to go to the lavatory.

go to the limit.monolingual: to do as much as is possible to do. _Okay, we can’t afford it, but we’ll go to the limit. _ How far shall I go? Shall I go to the limit?
examples: Okay, we can’t afford it, but we’ll go to the limit.

go to the polls.monolingual: to go to a place to vote; to vote. _ What day do we go to the polls? _Our community goes to the polls in November.
examples: Our community goes to the polls in November.

go to the toilet.monolingual: Fig. Euph. to use a toilet for defecation or urination. _ Jimmy washed his hands after he went to the toilet. _ Excuse me, I have to go to the toilet.
examples: Jimmy washed his hands after he went to the toilet.

go to town.monolingual: 1. Lit. to travel into town or a city. _ I have to go to town today.
examples: I have to go to town today.

go to trial.monolingual: [for a case] to go into court to be tried. _When will this case go to trial? _ We go to trial next Monday.
examples: We go to trial next Monday.

go to waste.monolingual: [for something] to be wasted; to be unused (and therefore thrown away). _ Eat your potatoes! Don’t let them go to waste. _We shouldn’t let all those nice herbs go to waste. Let’s pick some before the first hard frost.
examples: Eat your potatoes! Don’t let them go to waste.

go together.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for two or more things] to look, sound, or taste good together. _ Do you think that this pink one and this purple one go together? _Milk and grapefruit don’t go together.
examples: Milk and grapefruit don’t go together.

go too far.monolingual: to do more than is acceptable. _ I didn’t mind at first, but now you’ve gone too far. _ If you go too far, I’ll slap you.
examples: I didn’t mind at first, but now you’ve gone too far.

go toward someone or something.monolingual: to move toward someone or something. _The child went toward the open door. _ The dog went toward the cat and the cat ran away.
examples: The child went toward the open door.

go under.monolingual: 1. to sink beneath the surface of the water. _ After capsizing, the ship went under very slowly. _ I was afraid that our canoe would go under in the rapidly moving water.
examples: After capsizing, the ship went under very slowly.

go under the knife.monolingual: Fig. to submit to surgery; to have surgery done on oneself. _She goes under the knife tomorrow for her gallbladder. _ Frank lives in constant fear of having to go under the knife.
examples: She goes under the knife tomorrow for her gallbladder.

go under the wrecking ball.monolingual: Fig. to be wrecked or torn down. _ That lovely old building finally went under the wrecking ball. _I hate to see good architecture go under the wrecking ball.
examples: That lovely old building finally went under the wrecking ball.

go up.monolingual: [for something] to go higher. _ Gasoline prices are still going up. _ Prices keep going up and up, no matter what.
examples: Gasoline prices are still going up.

go up against someone.monolingual: to compete with someone; to face someone in competition. _ She is going up against Rodney in the spelling bee. _ The champ went up against the challenger in a match last Friday.
examples: She is going up against Rodney in the spelling bee.

go up something.monolingual: to climb up something. _ The monkey went up the tree in no time. _ How fast can you go up this rope?
examples: The monkey went up the tree in no time.

go up the wall.monolingual: 1. Lit. to climb or run up the wall. _Look at that silly cat go up the wall! How can its claws hold onto the brick?
examples: Look at that silly cat go up the wall! How can its claws hold onto the brick? 2.

go whole hog.monolingual: to do everything possible; to be extravagant. _Let’s go whole hog. Order steak and lobster. _Show some restraint. Don’t go whole hog all the time.
examples: Let’s go whole hog.

go wild.monolingual: Fig. to get very excited. _ At the end of the football game, the kick was good and the crowd went wild.
examples: At the end of the football game, the kick was good and the crowd went wild.

go window-shopping.monolingual: to go about looking at goods in store windows without actually buying anything. _ The office workers go window-shopping on their lunch hour, looking for things to buy when they get paid. _ Joan said she was just going window-shopping, but she bought
examples: The office workers go window-shopping on their lunch hour, looking for things to buy when they get paid.

go with the tide.monolingual: Fig. to move along with the effect of outside forces. _ I just go with the tide. I never fight fate. _ She just goes with the tide, never giving a thought to thinking for herself.
examples: I just go with the tide.

go wrong.monolingual: to fail; [for something bad] to happen. _ The project failed. I don’t know what went wrong. _ I’m afraid that everything will go wrong.
examples: The project failed.

goad someone into something.monolingual: to urge or coerce someone into doing something. _Don’t try to goad me into it. I just won’t do it! _ We goaded Mary into going with us.
examples: Don’t try to goad me into it.

goad someone on.monolingual: to urge someone onward, possibly with jeers or challenges; to urge someone to continue. (Usually in this order.) _ The cheering crowd goaded the team on to victory. _ I goaded Jed on to taking the risk.
examples: The cheering crowd goaded the team on to victory.

gobble someone or something up†.monolingual: to eat someone or something completely and rapidly. _ The wolf said that he was going to gobble the little girl up. _ The wolf wanted to gobble up the little pig.
examples: The wolf said that he was going to gobble the little girl up.

gobble something down†.monolingual: to eat something very fast, swallowing large chunks. _ The dog gobbled the meat down in seconds. _ The cat gobbled down the sardines.
examples: The dog gobbled the meat down in seconds.

gobble something up†.monolingual: to use up, buy up, or occupy all of something. _ The shoppers gobbled all the sale merchandise up in a few hours. _ They gobbled up everything.
examples: The shoppers gobbled all the sale merchandise up in a few hours.

god only knows!.monolingual: Inf. Only God knows.; No one knows but God. _ Tom: How long is all this going to take? Alice: God only knows! _ Bob: Where are we going to find one hundred thousand dollars? Mary: God only knows!

god rest someone’s soul..monolingual: May God bless a previously mentioned person who has died. _ I remember what my mother, God rest her soul, used to say about that.
examples: I remember what my mother, God rest her soul, used to say about that.

god willing..monolingual: If God wants it to happen. (An expression indicating that there is a high certainty that something will happen, so high that only God could prevent it.) _ John: Please try to be on time. Alice: I’ll be there on time, God willing. _ Bob: Will I see yo
examples: John: Please try to be on time.

goggle at someone or something.monolingual: to stare at someone or something with bulging eyes. _Don’t stand there goggling at me! _ The child stood there and goggled at the newborn lamb.
examples: The child stood there and goggled at the newborn lamb.

going, going, gone.monolingual: 1. [in an auction] close to being sold, almost sold, sold. _ Going, going, gone. The new owner is the handsome gentleman in the back row.
examples: Going, going, gone.

going great guns.monolingual: Fig. going fast or energetically. _ I’m over my cold and going great guns. _ Business is great. We are going great guns selling ice cream.
examples: I’m over my cold and going great guns.

the going rate.monolingual: the current rate or the current charges for something. _The going interest rate for your account is 10 percent. _ Our babysitter charges us the going rate.
examples: The going interest rate for your account is 10 percent.

going strong.monolingual: functioning well or energetically. _ We are still well and going strong.
examples: We are still well and going strong.

a gold mine of information.monolingual: Fig. someone or something that is full of information. _ Grandfather is a gold mine of information about World War I. _ The new encyclopedia is a positive gold mine of useful information.
examples: Grandfather is a gold mine of information about World War I.

a golden opportunity.monolingual: Fig. an excellent opportunity that is not likely to be repeated. _ When I failed to finish college, I missed my golden opportunity to prepare myself for a good job.
examples: When I failed to finish college, I missed my golden opportunity to prepare myself for a good job.

gone but not forgotten.monolingual: Cliché gone or dead and still remembered. _The good days we used to have together are gone, but not forgotten. _ Uncle Harry is gone but not forgotten. The stain where he spilled the wine is still visible in the parlor carpet.
examples: The good days we used to have together are gone, but not forgotten.

gone goose.monolingual: someone or something that has departed or run away. _ Surely, the burglar is a gone goose by now. _ The child was a gone goose, and we did not know where to look for him.
examples: Surely, the burglar is a gone goose by now.

gone to meet one’s maker.monolingual: Euph. died. _ Poor old Bob has gone to meet his maker. _ After a long illness, Reggie went to meet his maker.
examples: Poor old Bob has gone to meet his maker.

gone with the wind.monolingual: Fig. gone as if taken away by the wind. (A phrase made famous by the Margaret Mitchell novel and subsequent film Gone with the Wind. The phrase is used to make gone have a stronger force.) _ Everything we worked for was gone with the wind.
examples: Everything we worked for was gone with the wind.

a goner.monolingual: a dead or dying creature or person. _ The boy brought the sick fish back to the pet store to get his money back. “This one is a goner,” he said. _ John thought he was a goner when his parachute didn’t open.
examples: The boy brought the sick fish back to the pet store to get his money back.

good and something.monolingual: very or completely something. (Something is a state of being.) _Joe never does anything till he’s good and ready. _ Mary’s good and mad, all right.
examples: Joe never does anything till he’s good and ready.

*good as done.monolingual: the same as being done; almost done. (*Also: as ~. Many different words can replace done in this phrase, according to context: cooked, dead, finished, painted, typed, etc.) _ This job is as good as done. It’ll just take another second. _ Yes, sir, if
examples: This job is as good as done.

*good as gold.monolingual: Cliché very good. (Usually used to describe children. *Also: as ~.) _ Mother: Thank you for taking care of Gretchen; I hope she hasn’t been too much trouble. Grandmother: Not at all; she’s been as good as gold. _ We knew that Daddy would not read us
examples: Mother: Thank you for taking care of Gretchen; I hope she hasn’t been too much trouble.

*good as new.monolingual: Cliché as good as when it was new; as well or as healthy as normal. (*Also: as ~.) _A little rest and I’ll be as good as new.
examples: A little rest and I’ll be as good as new.

a good bet.monolingual: Fig. a great likelihood. _It’s a good bet that he will be late because of the rain.
examples: It’s a good bet that he will be late because of the rain.

the good book.monolingual: the Bible. _I read some in the Good Book every day. _ Sally’s always quoting from the Good Book.
examples: I read some in the Good Book every day.

the good die young..monolingual: Prov. Good people tend to die at an early age. _Marshall’s twenty-year-old son died in a car crash; it did not comfort Marshall to think that the good die young. _ Jill: It doesn’t seem fair that Laurie is dead. She was such a wonderful person. Jane:
examples: Marshall’s twenty-year-old son died in a car crash; it did not comfort Marshall to think that the good die young.

a good egg.monolingual: Fig. a good and dependable person. _ He seems like a good egg. I’ll take a chance on him.
examples: He seems like a good egg.

good enough..monolingual: That’s good.; That’s adequate. _Bill: Well, now. How’s that? Bob: Good enough. _ Bob: I’ll be there about noon. Tom: Good enough. I’ll see you then.
examples: Bill: Well, now.

good fences make good neighbors..monolingual: Prov. It is easier to be friendly with your neighbor if neither of you trespasses upon the other’s property or privacy. _ Jane: The guy next door is letting his party guests wander across our lawn again. Alan: I guess we’ll have to build a fence ther
examples: Jane: The guy next door is letting his party guests wander across our lawn again.

good for what ails you.monolingual: Rur. able to cure any problem or illness. (Usually used to describe food or liquor.) _ Have a sip of this whiskey. It’s good for what ails you. _ Sally’s beef broth is good for what ails you.
examples: Have a sip of this whiskey.

good for you!.monolingual: a complimentary expression of encouragement for something that someone has done or received. _Sue: I just got a raise. Bill: Good for you! _Jane: I really told him what I thought of his rotten behavior. Sue: Good for you! He needs it.
examples: Sue: I just got a raise.

good golly, miss molly!.monolingual: Inf. Good grief !; Wow! _Good golly, Miss Molly! This place is a mess! _ Good golly, Miss Molly, that’s awful!

good grief!.monolingual: Inf. an exclamation of surprise, shock, or amazement. _ Alice: Good grief! I’m late! Mary: That clock’s fast. You’re probably okay on time. _ Bill: There are seven newborn kittens under the sofa! Jane: Good grief!
examples: Alice: Good grief! I’m late! Mary: That clock’s fast.

good luck!.monolingual: 1. a wish of good luck to someone. _ Mary: I have my recital tonight. Jane: I know you’ll do well. Good luck! _ Sally: I hear you’re leaving for your new job tomorrow morning. Bob: That’s right. Sally: Well, good luck!
examples: Mary: I have my recital tonight.

a good many.monolingual: quite a few. _ I have a good many kinfolk in Texas. _ Mary owns a good many acres of land.
examples: I have a good many kinfolk in Texas.

the good old days.monolingual: back in an earlier time which everyone remembers as a better time, even if it really wasn’t. _ Back in the good old days, during World War I, they used real cactus needles in record players. _ The good old days didn’t start until they had indoor bath
examples: Back in the good old days, during World War I, they used real cactus needles in record players.

a good sport.monolingual: someone who can accept a loss in a competition or can accept being the butt of a joke. _Bob is usually a good sport, but this time he didn’t seem to appreciate your joke.
examples: Bob is usually a good sport, but this time he didn’t seem to appreciate your joke.

good to go.monolingual: Inf. all ready to go; all checked and pronounced ready to go. _I’ve checked everything and we are good to go. _ Everything’s good to go and we will start immediately.
examples: I’ve checked everything and we are good to go.

good-bye and good riddance..monolingual: Cliché a phrase marking the departure of someone or something unwanted. _ Fred: Supposing I was to just walk out of here, just like that? Mary: I’d say good-bye and good riddance. _ As the garbage truck drove away, carrying the drab old chair that Ma
examples: Fred: Supposing I was to just walk out of here, just like that? Mary: I’d say good-bye and good riddance.

*the goods on someone.monolingual: something potentially damaging or embarrassing about someone. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ John beat me unfairly in tennis, but I’ll get even. I’ll get the goods on him and his cheating. _ The authorities are going to get the goods
examples: John beat me unfairly in tennis, but I’ll get even.

goof around.monolingual: to act silly. _ The kids were all goofing around, waiting for the bus. _ Stop goofing around!
examples: The kids were all goofing around, waiting for the bus.

goof off.monolingual: to waste time. _John is always goofing off. _Quit goofing off and get to work!
examples: John is always goofing off.

goof on someone.monolingual: Inf. to tease or kid someone. _ I don’t believe you. I think you’re just goofing on me.
examples: I don’t believe you.

goof someone or something up†.monolingual: Inf. to mess someone or something up; to ruin someone’s plans; to make something nonfunctional. _ Who goofed this machine up? _ Who goofed up the machine?

goose egg.monolingual: 1. Fig. a raised bump on the skull as when one’s head has been struck. _ I walked into the edge of the door and got a terrible goose egg.
examples: I walked into the edge of the door and got a terrible goose egg.

the gospel truth.monolingual: Fig. the undeniable truth. _ The witness swore he was telling the gospel truth. _ I told my parents the gospel truth about how the vase broke.
examples: The witness swore he was telling the gospel truth.

gossip about someone or something.monolingual: to talk maliciously about someone or something. _ Who are you gossiping about now? _They are gossiping about what happened last weekend.
examples: They are gossiping about what happened last weekend.

gouge something out of someone.monolingual: to cheat someone out of something. (Compare this with chisel something out of someone.) _ They gouged the money out of the old man. _ The crooks gouged the life savings out of the old lady.
examples: They gouged the money out of the old man.

grace something with something.monolingual: Fig. to adorn something or some place with something, especially a person’s presence. _The lovely lady graced our home with her presence. _ The stage was graced with f lowers and a few palm trees.
examples: The lovely lady graced our home with her presence.

graced with something.monolingual: made elegant by means of some ornament or decoration. _ The altar was graced with lovely white f lowers. _ The end of the beautiful day was graced with a beautiful sunset.
examples: The altar was graced with lovely white f lowers.

*graceful as a swan.monolingual: very graceful. (*Also: as ~.) _ The boat glided out onto the lake as graceful as a swan. _ Jane is graceful as a swan.
examples: The boat glided out onto the lake as graceful as a swan.

a grain of truth.monolingual: even the smallest amount of truth. _The attorney was unable to find a grain of truth in the defendant’s testimony. _ If there were a grain of truth to your statement, I would trust you.
examples: The attorney was unable to find a grain of truth in the defendant’s testimony.

a grandfather clause.monolingual: a clause in an agreement that protects certain rights granted in the past even when conditions change in the future. _ The contract contained a grandfather clause that protected my pension payments against claims such as might arise from a future law
examples: The contract contained a grandfather clause that protected my pension payments against claims such as might arise from a future lawsuit.

grandfather someone or something in†.monolingual: to protect someone or a right through the use of a grandfather clause. _ My payments were grandfathered in years ago.
examples: My payments were grandfathered in years ago.

grant something to someone.monolingual: to give or award something to someone. _The foundation granted a large sum of money to Jane for her research. _ They granted an award to Kelly.
examples: The foundation granted a large sum of money to Jane for her research.

graph something out†.monolingual: to draw a graph of something. _ Please take this data and graph it out. _Graph out this data, please.
examples: Please take this data and graph it out.

grapple with something.monolingual: Fig. to deal with a problem; to get a “good hold” on a problem. _ I have enough to grapple with now. No more problems, please. _ I cannot grapple with any additional problems.
examples: I have enough to grapple with now.

grasp at someone or something.monolingual: to try to seize someone or something. _ He grasped at the bar and held on tight. _ The beggar grasped at the pedestrian and lost his grip.
examples: He grasped at the bar and held on tight.

grasping at straws.monolingual: Fig. to depend on something that is useless; to make a futile attempt at something. _ John couldn’t answer the teacher’s question. He was just grasping at straws. _There I was, grasping at straws, with no one to help me.
examples: John couldn’t answer the teacher’s question.

grass widow.monolingual: a woman abandoned by her husband. (The origin of this is not clear.) _ Jane’s husband isn’t dead, but she’s a widow just the same—a grass widow. _ Bill ran off and left Mary a grass widow.
examples: Jane’s husband isn’t dead, but she’s a widow just the same—a grass widow.

grate on someone.monolingual: to annoy someone; to rub someone the wrong way. _Your negative attitude really grates on me. _ Everything you say grates on me.
examples: Your negative attitude really grates on me.

grate on something.monolingual: to rub, scrape, or abrade something. _ The tree branch is grating on the side of the house. _ The bottom of the door is grating on the threshold. Please fix it.
examples: The tree branch is grating on the side of the house.

gratify someone’s desires.monolingual: Euph. to have sex with someone. _ The prostitute promised to gratify her customer’s desires. _ That night, he gratified her desires.
examples: The prostitute promised to gratify her customer’s desires.

a gray area.monolingual: Fig. an area of a subject or question that is difficult to put into a particular category because it is not clearly defined and may have connections or associations with more than one category. _ The responsibility for social studies in the college i
examples: The responsibility for social studies in the college is a gray area.

gray matter.monolingual: Fig. intelligence; brains; power of thought. _ Use your gray matter and think what will happen if the committee resigns. _Surely they’ll come up with an acceptable solution if they use some gray matter.
examples: Use your gray matter and think what will happen if the committee resigns.

graze against someone or something.monolingual: to brush or scrape against someone or something. _ The car grazed against the side of the truck. _ I grazed against an old man as I was jogging this morning.
examples: The car grazed against the side of the truck.

graze on something.monolingual: 1. [for animals] to browse or forage in a particular location. _ The cattle are grazing on the neighbor’s land. _I wish they wouldn’t graze on other people’s land.
examples: The cattle are grazing on the neighbor’s land.

grease the skids.monolingual: Fig. to help prepare for or ease the way for the success or failure of someone or something. _Ray set out to grease the skids for the right things to happen. _ We need someone to grease the skids for the Wilson contract.
examples: Ray set out to grease the skids for the right things to happen.

a greasy spoon.monolingual: Fig. a cheap diner, where the silverware might not be too clean. _The corner greasy spoon is always busy at lunchtime.
examples: The corner greasy spoon is always busy at lunchtime.

great balls of fire!.monolingual: Inf. Good heavens!; Wow! _ Mary got up to play the fiddle, and great balls of fire! That girl can play! _Tom: Will you marry me? Jane: Yes, I will. Tom: Great balls of fire! I’m the happiest man on earth.
examples: Tom: Will you marry me? Jane: Yes, I will.

the great beyond.monolingual: Euph. life after death. _ The fortuneteller claimed to get messages from the great beyond. _ I often think of my loved ones in the great beyond, and long for the day I will see them again.
examples: The fortuneteller claimed to get messages from the great beyond.

a great deal.monolingual: much; a lot. _You can learn a great deal about nature by watching television. _ This is a serious problem and it worries me a great deal.
examples: You can learn a great deal about nature by watching television.

great minds think alike..monolingual: Prov. Very intelligent people tend to come up with the same ideas at the same time. (Used playfully, to commend someone for expressing the same thing you were thinking of; implies that you are congratulating that person for being as smart as you are.
examples: Jill: Let’s ride our bikes to the store instead of walking.

great scott!.monolingual: Inf. an exclamation of shock or surprise. _ “Great Scott! You bought a truck!” shrieked Mary. _ Fred: The water heater just exploded! Bill: Great Scott! What do we do now? Fred: Looks like cold showers for a while.
examples: “Great Scott! You bought a truck!” shrieked Mary.

the great unwashed.monolingual: Fig. the general public; the lower middle class. _ The Simpsons had a tall iron fence around their mansion—put there to discourage the great unwashed from wandering up to the door by mistake, I suppose. _ Maw says the great unwashed don’t know enough
examples: The Simpsons had a tall iron fence around their mansion—put there to discourage the great unwashed from wandering up to the door by mistake, I suppose.

greek to someone.monolingual: incomprehensible to someone; as mysterious as Greek writing. _ I don’t understand this. It’s all Greek to me. _She said it was Greek to her, and that it made no sense at all.
examples: I don’t understand this.

*green as grass.monolingual: very green. (*Also: as ~.) _ His face turned as green as grass just before he vomited.
examples: His face turned as green as grass just before he vomited.

green stuff.monolingual: Fig. money; U.S. paper money. _I’ve run out of green stuff. Can you loan me a few bucks?
examples: I’ve run out of green stuff.

*green with envy.monolingual: Fig. appearing jealous; appearing envious. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ My new car made my neighbor green with envy. _ Bill was green with envy that I won first place.
examples: My new car made my neighbor green with envy.

grieve for someone or something.monolingual: to mourn for someone or something. _Don’t grieve for me. I’m okay. _She grieved for her lost chances.
examples: Don’t grieve for me.

grieve over someone or something.monolingual: to lament and pine for someone or something. _Now, don’t grieve over a lost cat. _ There is no reason to continue grieving over him.
examples: Now, don’t grieve over a lost cat.

the grim reaper.monolingual: Fig. death. _ I think I have a few years to go yet before the grim reaper pays me a call.
examples: I think I have a few years to go yet before the grim reaper pays me a call.

grin and bear it.monolingual: Fig. to endure something unpleasant in good humor. _ There is nothing you can do but grin and bear it. _ I hate having to work for rude people. I guess I have to grin and bear it.
examples: There is nothing you can do but grin and bear it.

grin at someone or something.monolingual: 1. to smile a beaming smile at someone or something. _The entire class grinned at the camera. _ I grinned at her and she turned away quickly.
examples: The entire class grinned at the camera.

grin from ear to ear.monolingual: Fig. to smile a very wide, beaming smile. _ She was grinning from ear to ear as she accepted the prize. _ We knew Timmy was happy because he was grinning from ear to ear.
examples: She was grinning from ear to ear as she accepted the prize.

grind on.monolingual: Fig. [for something] to drag on endlessly. _ The hours ground on without anything happening. I was so tired of waiting. _ The lecture ground on, minute after minute.
examples: The hours ground on without anything happening.

grind someone down†.monolingual: Fig. to wear someone down by constant requests; to wear someone down by constant nagging. _ If you think you can grind me down by bothering me all the time, you are wrong. _ The constant nagging ground down the employees at last.
examples: If you think you can grind me down by bothering me all the time, you are wrong.

grind something away†.monolingual: to remove something by grinding. _ Grind the bumps away and make the wall smooth. _ Please grind away the bumps.
examples: Grind the bumps away and make the wall smooth.

grind something down†.monolingual: to make something smooth or even by grinding. _ Grind this down to make it smooth. _ Please grind down this rough spot.
examples: Grind this down to make it smooth.

grind something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to produce something by grinding. _Working hard, he ground the powder out, a cup at a time. _ He ground out the powder, a cup at a time.
examples: Working hard, he ground the powder out, a cup at a time.

grind something to something.monolingual: to keep grinding something until it is something. _I ground the fennel seeds to a powder and threw them in the simmering sauce. _ The wheels of the cars, trucks, and buses had ground the football to a broken mass.
examples: I ground the fennel seeds to a powder and threw them in the simmering sauce.

grind something together.monolingual: to rub things together. _ Stop grinding your teeth together. _ The stones ground together as we drove over them.
examples: Stop grinding your teeth together.

grind something up†.monolingual: to pulverize or crush something by crushing, rubbing, or abrasion. _ Please grind the fennel seeds up. _Grind up the fennel seeds and sprinkle them on the top.
examples: Please grind the fennel seeds up.

grind to a halt.monolingual: Fig. to slow down and stop. _ Every day about noon, traffic in town grinds to a halt. _ The bus ground to a halt at the corner and someone got off.
examples: Every day about noon, traffic in town grinds to a halt.

*a grip on oneself.monolingual: Fig. control of one’s emotions. (*Typically: get ~; have ~.) _ Calm down, man! Get a grip on yourself! _ I encouraged him to get a grip on himself.
examples: I encouraged him to get a grip on himself.

gripe at someone.monolingual: to complain to someone. _ Stop griping at me! _ There is no need to gripe at your little brother.
examples: There is no need to gripe at your little brother.

gripe one’s soul.monolingual: Inf. to annoy someone. _ That kind of thing really gripes my soul! _John, have I ever told you that you gripe my soul?

grit one’s teeth.monolingual: Fig. to grind or clench one’s teeth together in anger or determination. _ I was so mad, all I could do was stand there and grit my teeth. _ All through the race, Sally was gritting her teeth. She was really determined.
examples: I was so mad, all I could do was stand there and grit my teeth.

groan about someone or something.monolingual: to complain about someone or something. _ What are you groaning about? _ She is groaning about her work.
examples: She is groaning about her work.

groan something out†.monolingual: to say something with a groan. _He groaned the name out. _ He groaned out the name of his assailant before he passed out.
examples: He groaned the name out.

groan under something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to groan while bearing a heavy burden. _He groaned under the weight of the trunk. _The rafters groaned under the heavy weight of the pianos.
examples: He groaned under the weight of the trunk.

groan with something.monolingual: to groan because of something, such as pain. _ She groaned with pain, but no one helped her. _ I think the old man was groaning with boredom more than anything else.
examples: She groaned with pain, but no one helped her.

groom someone as something.monolingual: to prepare someone for a job or position. _ He was grooming his son as his successor. _ They groomed Charles as the next treasurer.
examples: He was grooming his son as his successor.

groom someone for something.monolingual: to prepare someone for something; to prepare someone to be someone. _The boss is grooming his son for the presidency of the company. _ They are grooming the vice president for the top position.
examples: The boss is grooming his son for the presidency of the company.

groove on someone or something.monolingual: to show interest in someone or something; to relate to someone or something. _ Fred was beginning to groove on new age music when he met Phil. _ Sam is really grooving on Mary.
examples: Fred was beginning to groove on new age music when he met Phil.

grope after someone or something.monolingual: to reach for a departing or fleeing person or thing awkwardly or ineffectually. _ The feeble hand groped after the departing form. _I groped after the cat as it ran under the bed.
examples: The feeble hand groped after the departing form.

grope at someone or something.monolingual: to reach for someone or something blindly. _ She groped feebly at the form she could hardly see. _ Sharon groped at Frank as he ran out to get the doctor.
examples: She groped feebly at the form she could hardly see.

gross someone out†.monolingual: to disgust someone. _ Those horrible pictures just gross me out. _ Jim’s story totally grossed out Sally.
examples: Those horrible pictures just gross me out.

ground someone in something.monolingual: Fig. to instruct someone in an area of knowledge. _ We grounded all our children in the basics of home cooking. _We were all grounded in basic cooking by the time we were six.
examples: We grounded all our children in the basics of home cooking.

ground something on something.monolingual: Fig. to build a firm basis for something on something else. _ He grounded his thinking on his detailed research. _ His thinking was grounded on years of reading.
examples: He grounded his thinking on his detailed research.

*grounds for something.monolingual: the basis or cause for legal action such as a lawsuit. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ Your negligence is grounds for a lawsuit. _ Is infidelity grounds for divorce in this state?
examples: Your negligence is grounds for a lawsuit.

group someone or something together.monolingual: to gather people or things together. _ Try to group all the smokers together at one table. _ Steve grouped all the dictionaries together.
examples: Try to group all the smokers together at one table.

group something under something.monolingual: to classify something under some category. _ They have now grouped the fungi under their own families. _ We should group all the older ones under a separate category.
examples: They have now grouped the fungi under their own families.

grouse about someone or something.monolingual: to complain about someone or something. _ What are you grousing about now? _ I am grousing about your carelessness!

grovel before someone or something.monolingual: to prostrate oneself before someone or something. _ The prisoner groveled before his accusers. _ The peasant groveled before the lord of the manor.
examples: The prisoner groveled before his accusers.

grovel to someone.monolingual: to kneel in deference to someone; to kowtow to someone. _ You don’t have to grovel to me! _ I refuse to grovel to anyone.
examples: I refuse to grovel to anyone.

grow away from someone.monolingual: [for someone] to become less intimate with someone; [for someone] to become independent of someone gradually. _ She has grown away from her husband over the years. _We expect our children to grow away from us.
examples: She has grown away from her husband over the years.

grow away from something.monolingual: [for something] to move away from something as it grows. _ The tree grew away from the house—thank heavens. _ See if you can train the vine to grow away from the fence.
examples: The tree grew away from the house—thank heavens.

grow back.monolingual: [for something that has come off] to grow back again. (Includes parts of plants and some animals, fingernails, toenails, etc.) _ The lizard’s tail grew back in a few months. _ The leaves will grow back in a month or so.
examples: The lizard’s tail grew back in a few months.

grow from something.monolingual: to develop and grow from a seed, bulb, corm, etc. _This huge tree grew from a little seed. _ What kind of plant grows from this bulb?
examples: This huge tree grew from a little seed.

grow in something.monolingual: 1. [for someone] to increase in some quality, such as wisdom, strength, stature, etc. _ As I got older, I was supposed to grow in wisdom and other good things. _ Sam grew in strength as he got over the disease.
examples: As I got older, I was supposed to grow in wisdom and other good things.

grow into something.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a child] to develop into a particular type of person. _ The child grew into a tall, powerful athlete. _ I hope I have grown into a person my parents can be proud of.
examples: The child grew into a tall, powerful athlete.

grow on someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a fungus, tumor, parasite, etc.] to live and grow on someone’s skin. _ I’ve got this stuff growing on me and I want to get rid of it. _ Is that an ink stain or is something growing on you?
examples: I’ve got this stuff growing on me and I want to get rid of it.

grow out.monolingual: [for something that has been cut back] to regrow. _ Don’t worry, your hair will grow out again. _ Will the grass grow out again, do you think?
examples: Don’t worry, your hair will grow out again.

grow out of something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to develop and grow outward from something. _ Soft green shoots grew out of the trunk of the tree. _A bush grew out of the gutter and hung down the front of the house.
examples: Soft green shoots grew out of the trunk of the tree.

grow over something.monolingual: [for vegetation] to cover over something as it grows. _The vines grew over the shed and almost hid it from view.
examples: The vines grew over the shed and almost hid it from view.

grow something from something.monolingual: to propagate a plant from a seed, bulb, corm, etc. _I grew these tomatoes from seeds. _ Can you grow a mango tree from a seed?
examples: I grew these tomatoes from seeds.

grow to do something.monolingual: to gradually begin to do certain things, using verbs such as feel, know, like, need, respect, sense, suspect, think, want, wonder, etc. _ I grew to hate Bob over a period of years. _As I grew to know Bob, I began to like him.
examples: I grew to hate Bob over a period of years.

grow together.monolingual: [for things] to join together as they grow and develop. _ Two of these trees grew together when they were much smaller. _ The broken ends of the bone grew together far more rapidly than Chuck had thought.
examples: Two of these trees grew together when they were much smaller.

grow up.monolingual: to become mature; to become adult. _ All the children have grown up and the parents are left with a lot of debts.
examples: All the children have grown up and the parents are left with a lot of debts.

growl at someone or something.monolingual: to snarl at someone or something. _ Don’t growl at me like that. _ The dog growled at the cat.
examples: Don’t growl at me like that.

growl something out†.monolingual: to say something with a sound like growling or snarling. _ Jane growled a few words out. _ She growled out a few words and the gates opened for us.
examples: Jane growled a few words out.

*gruff as a bear.monolingual: gruff; curt and unsociable. (*Also: as ~.) _ I hate to ask Erica questions; she’s always gruff as a bear. _I’m always as gruff as a bear before I’ve had my first cup of coffee.
examples: I hate to ask Erica questions; she’s always gruff as a bear.

grumble about someone or something.monolingual: to complain about someone or something. _ What are you grumbling about now? _ The students were grumbling about the teacher.
examples: The students were grumbling about the teacher.

grumble at someone.monolingual: to complain to someone. _Go grumble at someone else. I’m tired of listening. _Stop grumbling at me!
examples: Go grumble at someone else.

grunt something out†.monolingual: to say something with a snort or grunt. _ Jane grunted a command out to someone. _ She grunted out a curt command and the gate opened.
examples: Jane grunted a command out to someone.

grunt work.monolingual: Fig. work that is menial and thankless. _During the summer, I earned money doing grunt work. _ I did all of the grunt work on the project, but my boss got all of the credit.
examples: During the summer, I earned money doing grunt work.

guarantee against something.monolingual: to certify that something bad will not happen. _ No one can guarantee against that happening. _ I can’t guarantee against something going wrong.
examples: No one can guarantee against that happening.

guard against someone or something.monolingual: to take care to avoid someone or something. _ Try to guard against getting a cold. _ You should guard against pickpockets.
examples: Try to guard against getting a cold.

guess at something.monolingual: to estimate something; to give an opinion about what something might be. _ I hate to just guess at it, but if you insist: ten feet long. _ Go ahead, guess at the number of pennies in this jar.
examples: I hate to just guess at it, but if you insist: ten feet long.

guess what!.monolingual: Inf. a way of starting a conversation; a way of forcing someone into a conversation. _ Alice: Guess what! Bob: I don’t know. What? Alice: I’m going to Europe this summer. Bob: That’s very nice. _ John: Guess what! Jane: What? John: Mary is going to h
examples: Alice: Guess what! Bob: I don’t know.

guest of honor.monolingual: a guest who gets special attention from everyone; the person for whom a party, celebration, or ceremony is given. _ Bob is the guest of honor, and many people will make speeches about him. _ The guest of honor sits at the front of the room on the dai
examples: Bob is the guest of honor, and many people will make speeches about him.

guffaw at someone or something.monolingual: to laugh at someone or something very hard and raucously. _ The audience guffawed at the clown’s antics. _ The old man guffawed at the clown.
examples: The audience guffawed at the clown’s antics.

gulp for air.monolingual: Fig. to eagerly or desperately try to get air or a breath. _Tom gulped for air after trying to hold his breath for three minutes. _ Mary came up out of the water, gulping for air.
examples: Tom gulped for air after trying to hold his breath for three minutes.

gulp something back†.monolingual: Fig. to force or hold back tears, sobs, etc. _ He gulped his sobs back and clutched at his wound. _ He gulped back his sobs.
examples: He gulped his sobs back and clutched at his wound.

gulp something down†.monolingual: to drink all of something, usually quickly. _He gulped his coffee down and left. _He gulped down his coffee.
examples: He gulped his coffee down and left.

gun for someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to seek one out to shoot one. _ They say that Tex is gunning for the sheriff.
examples: They say that Tex is gunning for the sheriff.

gung ho.monolingual: Inf. enthusiastically in favor of something. _ Bobby is really gung ho on his plan to start his own company.
examples: Bobby is really gung ho on his plan to start his own company.

gush over someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for liquid] to flood over someone or something. _ The f loodwaters gushed over the farmland. _ The hot soup gushed over the cook as the huge pot tipped over.
examples: The f loodwaters gushed over the farmland.

gush with something.monolingual: [for something] to flow with something. _ The stream gushed with the sudden runoff of the storm. _The faucet gushed with brownish water, so I turned it off.
examples: The stream gushed with the sudden runoff of the storm.

gussied up.monolingual: Rur. dressed up fancy. _All the girls got gussied up for the dance, but the guys wore their regular clothes. _ Mary really got gussied up. She even curled her hair.
examples: All the girls got gussied up for the dance, but the guys wore their regular clothes.

gussy someone or something up†.monolingual: Rur. to dress someone or something up; to make someone or something fancy. _ She gussied the kids up for the wedding. _ See if you can gussy up this room a little before folks get here.
examples: She gussied the kids up for the wedding.

guzzle something down†.monolingual: to drink something rapidly and eagerly. _He guzzled the beer down and called for another. _ He guzzled down the beer and called for another.
examples: He guzzled the beer down and called for another.

gyp someone out of something.monolingual: to deceive someone in order to get something of value. _The salesclerk gypped me out of a dollar. _ The taxi driver tried to gyp me out of a fortune by driving all over the place.
examples: The salesclerk gypped me out of a dollar.

hack around.monolingual: Inf. to waste time. _I’m just hacking around and doing nothing. _Stop hacking around and get to work.
examples: I’m just hacking around and doing nothing.

hack one’s way through something.monolingual: Fig. to cut one’s way through something. _We had to hack our way through the jungle. _ The surveyors hacked a pathway through the undergrowth.
examples: We had to hack our way through the jungle.

hack someone or something apart†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to chop up someone or something. _ The murderer hacked the victim apart. _He hacked apart the victim. _The butcher hacked the chicken apart.
examples: The murderer hacked the victim apart.

hack something.monolingual: Inf. to endure something; to deal with something. (The something is usually it.) _ I don’t know if I can hack it. _ John works very hard, but he can’t seem to hack it.
examples: I don’t know if I can hack it.

hack something down†.monolingual: to chop something down. _ Who hacked this cherry tree down? _ Who hacked down this cherry tree?

hack something off†.monolingual: to chop something off. _I need to get up that tree and hack that big branch off before it bangs on the house. _ Please hack off that big branch.
examples: I need to get up that tree and hack that big branch off before it bangs on the house.

hack something to something.monolingual: to cut something up into something roughly or crudely, such as pieces, bits, smithereens. _The editor hacked my story to smithereens. _ Don’t hack the turkey to pieces!
examples: The editor hacked my story to smithereens.

hack something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to chop something up into pieces. (Refers often to wood.) _ Hack all this old furniture up, and we’ll burn it in the fireplace. _ Hack up this stuff, and we’ll burn it.
examples: Hack all this old furniture up, and we’ll burn it in the fireplace.

hadn’t oughta.monolingual: Inf. should not have. _ You hadn’t oughta teased me like that. _ I know I hadn’t oughta stolen that candy.
examples: You hadn’t oughta teased me like that.

haggle about something.monolingual: to bargain or negotiate about something. _ They are always willing to haggle about the price, so don’t take the first price you’re given. _I wish you wouldn’t try to haggle about everything when we shop.
examples: They are always willing to haggle about the price, so don’t take the first price you’re given.

hail from some place.monolingual: to come from some place as one’s hometown or birthplace; to originate in some place. _He hails from a small town in the Midwest. _ Where do you hail from?
examples: He hails from a small town in the Midwest.

hail someone as something.monolingual: to praise someone for being something. _The active members hailed him as fraternity brother of the year. _Sally was hailed as an effective leader.
examples: The active members hailed him as fraternity brother of the year.

hale and hearty.monolingual: Cliché healthy. _ The young infant was hale and hearty. _The calf—hale and hearty—ran around the barnyard.
examples: The young infant was hale and hearty.

hale-fellow-well-met.monolingual: Fig. friendly to everyone; falsely friendly to everyone. (Usually said of males.) _ Yes, he’s friendly, sort of hale-fellow-well-met. _He’s not a very sincere person. Hail-fellow-well-met—you know the type. _ What a pain he is. Good old Mr. Hail-fell
examples: Yes, he’s friendly, sort of hale-fellow-well-met.

half a bubble off plumb.monolingual: Fig. giddy; crazy. _She is acting about half a bubble off plumb. What is wrong with her? _ Tom is just half a bubble off plumb, but he is all heart.
examples: She is acting about half a bubble off plumb.

half in the bag.monolingual: intoxicated. _ Jerry was half in the bag when we found him. _They were all half in the bag by midnight.
examples: Jerry was half in the bag when we found him.

half the battle.monolingual: Fig. a significant part of an effort. _Getting through traffic to the airport was half the battle. The f light was nothing at all.
examples: Getting through traffic to the airport was half the battle.

half the time.monolingual: sometimes. _ I like that TV show, but half the time I forget to watch it when it’s on. _ She says she’s my friend, but she can’t remember my name, half the time.
examples: I like that TV show, but half the time I forget to watch it when it’s on.

half under.monolingual: 1. Lit. semiconscious. _ I was half under and could hear what the doctor was saying. _ I was afraid they would start cutting while I was only half under.
examples: I was half under and could hear what the doctor was saying.

ham something up†.monolingual: Fig. to make a performance seem silly by showing off or exaggerating one’s part. (A show-off actor is known as a ham.) _ Come on, Bob. Don’t ham it up! _ The play was going fine until Bob got out there and hammed up his part.
examples: The play was going fine until Bob got out there and hammed up his part.

hammer on someone or something.monolingual: to pound on someone or something. _ The cop hammered on the poor man over and over. _ Sharon hammered on the door for a long time.
examples: The cop hammered on the poor man over and over.

hammer something down†.monolingual: to pound something down even with the surrounding surface. _Hammer all the nails down so that none of them will catch on someone’s shoe. _ Hammer down all these nails!
examples: Hammer all the nails down so that none of them will catch on someone’s shoe.

hammer something home†.monolingual: Fig. to try extremely hard to make someone understand or realize something. _ The boss hopes to hammer the firm’s poor financial position home to the staff. _ I tried to hammer home to Anne the fact that she would have to get a job.
examples: The boss hopes to hammer the firm’s poor financial position home to the staff.

hammer something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to hammer a dent away; to make a dent even with the surrounding surface. _ I’m going to have to have someone hammer this dent in my fender out. _ It will take a while to hammer out the dent.
examples: I’m going to have to have someone hammer this dent in my fender out.

*hand in hand.monolingual: 1. Lit. holding hands. (*Typically: do something ~; sit ~; walk ~.) _ They walked down the street hand in hand. _Bob and Mary sat there quietly, hand in hand.
examples: They walked down the street hand in hand.

hand it over..monolingual: Give it to me. (Fixed order.) _ It’s mine. Hand it over! _ Come on. Give me the box of jewels. Hand it over!
examples: Come on. Give me the box of jewels.

hand over fist.monolingual: Fig. [for money and merchandise to be exchanged] very rapidly. _ What a busy day. We took in money hand over fist. _They were buying things hand over fist.
examples: What a busy day.

hand over hand.monolingual: Fig. [moving] one hand after the other (again and again). _ Sally pulled in the rope hand over hand. _ The man climbed up the rope hand over hand.
examples: Sally pulled in the rope hand over hand.

hand something around†.monolingual: to pass something around. _ Hand this around and let everyone look at it. _ Hand around each of these pictures so everyone gets to see them.
examples: Hand this around and let everyone look at it.

hand something in†.monolingual: to submit something by hand. _ Did you hand your application form in? _ I forgot to hand in my test paper.
examples: I forgot to hand in my test paper.

hand something over.monolingual: to give something (to someone); to relinquish something (to someone); to turn something over (to someone). _ Come on, John! Hand over my wallet. _ Please hand this over to the guard.
examples: Come on, John! Hand over my wallet.

hand something to someone.monolingual: to give something to someone by hand. _ The clerk handed her a message when she stopped at the desk. _This message was just handed to me.
examples: The clerk handed her a message when she stopped at the desk.

*a hand with something.monolingual: Fig. assistance with something, especially using the hands. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ Mary would really like to get a hand with that. It’s too much for one person. _ I’d like to have a hand with this.
examples: Mary would really like to get a hand with that.

*a handful.monolingual: Fig. someone, often a child, who is difficult to deal with. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _Bobby can be a real handful when he needs a nap.
examples: Bobby can be a real handful when he needs a nap.

*a handle on something.monolingual: Fig. a means of understanding something; an aid to understanding something. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ Let me try to get a handle on this. _ Now that I have a handle on the concept, I can begin to understand it.
examples: Let me try to get a handle on this.

handle someone with kid gloves.monolingual: Fig. to be very careful with a touchy person. _ Bill has become so sensitive. You really have to handle him with kid gloves. _You don’t have to handle me with kid gloves. I can take it.
examples: Bill has become so sensitive.

hands down.monolingual: easily; unquestionably. _ She won the contest hands down. _ They declared her the winner hands down.
examples: She won the contest hands down.

hands off!.monolingual: Do not touch someone or something. _Careful! Don’t touch that wire. Hands off! _ The sign says, “Hands off!” and you had better do what it says.
examples: Careful! Don’t touch that wire.

handsome is as handsome does..monolingual: Prov. It is more important to treat people well than to be good-looking.; Just because you are good-looking does not mean you are a good person. _ Jill: I’d like to get to know George better. Jane: Why? Jill: He’s so handsome. Jane: Handsome is as ha
examples: Jill: I’d like to get to know George better.

hang a few on†.monolingual: to take a few drinks; to have a few beers. _ They went out to hang a few on. _ Let’s hang on a few and then go on to the meeting.
examples: They went out to hang a few on.

hang a huey.monolingual: Sl. to make a U-turn. _ Hang a huey in the middle of the block. _ Right here! Hang a huey!
examples: Hang a huey in the middle of the block.

hang a left.monolingual: Inf. to turn left. _ He hung a left at the wrong corner. _ Hey, here! Hang a left here!
examples: He hung a left at the wrong corner.

hang a louie.monolingual: Sl. to turn left. _ You have to hang a louie at the stop sign. _ Go another block and hang a louie.
examples: You have to hang a louie at the stop sign.

hang a ralph.monolingual: Sl. to turn right. _ He skied down the easy slope and hung a ralph near a fir tree. _Don’t hang a ralph until you get past the traffic light.
examples: He skied down the easy slope and hung a ralph near a fir tree.

hang a right.monolingual: Inf. to turn right. _Hang a right about here. _ I told him to hang a right at the next corner, but he went on.
examples: Hang a right about here.

hang by something.monolingual: 1. to be suspended at the end of something, such as a rope, chain, string, etc. _ The bag is only hanging by a string. _ The food hung by a rope from a tree to protect it from the bears that wandered into camp now and then.
examples: The bag is only hanging by a string.

hang fire.monolingual: to delay or wait; to be delayed. _ I think we should hang fire and wait for other information. _ Our plans have to hang fire until we get planning permission.
examples: I think we should hang fire and wait for other information.

hang from something.monolingual: to be suspended from something. _ Colorful decorations hung from the branches of the tree. _ What is that hanging from the side of the building?
examples: Colorful decorations hung from the branches of the tree.

hang in there..monolingual: Be patient, things will work out. _ Bob: Everything is in such a mess. I can’t seem to get things done right. Jane: Hang in there, Bob. Things will work out. _ Mary: Sometimes I just don’t think I can go on. Sue: Hang in there, Mary. Things will work
examples: Bob: Everything is in such a mess.

hang it all!.monolingual: Inf. Damn it all! _ Oh, hang it all! I’m late. _ He’s late again! Hang it all!
examples: Oh, hang it all! I’m late.

hang it up.monolingual: Sl. to quit something. (Fixed order. See also hang something up.) _ I’ve had it with this job. It’s time to hang it up. _ Just hang it up. Don’t bother with it.
examples: I’ve had it with this job.

*the hang of something.monolingual: the knowledge or knack of doing something correctly. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; teach someone ~.) _As soon as I get the hang of this computer, I’ll be able to work faster. _Now that I have the hang of starting the car in cold weather, I won’t have t
examples: As soon as I get the hang of this computer, I’ll be able to work faster.

hang off.monolingual: to wait quietly to one side. _ The boys hung off a little, waiting to see what would happen next. _Hang off awhile and don’t do anything.
examples: The boys hung off a little, waiting to see what would happen next.

hang on.monolingual: 1. to wait awhile. _ Hang on a minute. I need to talk to you. _Hang on. Let me catch up with you.
examples: Hang on a minute.

hang on for dear life.monolingual: Cliché to hang on tight. _ As the little plane bounced around over the mountains, we hung on for dear life.
examples: As the little plane bounced around over the mountains, we hung on for dear life.

hang over someone or something.monolingual: 1. to be suspended over someone or something. _A fancy crystal chandelier hung over us. _An ornate ceiling fan hung over the table.
examples: A fancy crystal chandelier hung over us.

hang someone by the neck.monolingual: to execute someone or kill oneself by tying a noose around the neck and dropping the victim in order to break the neck or strangle the victim. _ The executioner hanged him by the neck until he died. _ He hanged himself by the neck.
examples: The executioner hanged him by the neck until he died.

hang someone for something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to execute someone by hanging for doing something. _ The state prosecutor will try to hang you for this crime. _The sheriff wanted to hang Jed for murder.
examples: The state prosecutor will try to hang you for this crime.

hang someone in effigy.monolingual: Fig. to hang a dummy or some other figure of a hated person. _ They hanged the dictator in effigy. _ The angry mob hanged the president in effigy.
examples: They hanged the dictator in effigy.

hang someone out to dry.monolingual: Fig. to defeat or punish someone. _ The boss was really angry at Billie. He yelled at him and hung him out to dry.
examples: The boss was really angry at Billie.

hang something on someone.monolingual: Sl. to blame something on someone; to frame someone for something. _Don’t try to hang the blame on me! _ The sheriff tried to hang the bank robbery on Jed.
examples: The sheriff tried to hang the bank robbery on Jed.

hang something up†.monolingual: to return the telephone receiver to its cradle. _ Please hang this up when I pick up the other phone. _ Please hang up the phone.
examples: Please hang this up when I pick up the other phone.

hang together.monolingual: 1. Fig. [for something or a group of people] to hold together; to remain intact. _I hope our bridge group hangs together until we are old and gray. _ I don’t think that this car will hang together for another minute.
examples: I hope our bridge group hangs together until we are old and gray.

hang up.monolingual: 1. [for a machine or a computer] to grind to a halt; to stop because of some internal complication. _ Our computer hung up right in the middle of printing the report. _I was afraid that my computer would hang up permanently.
examples: Our computer hung up right in the middle of printing the report.

hang with someone.monolingual: Sl. to spend or waste time with someone. _ Dave spent the afternoon hanging with Don, and neither one got anything done. _I’m going down to the corner and hang with the guys.
examples: Dave spent the afternoon hanging with Don, and neither one got anything done.

happen to someone or something.monolingual: to befall someone or something; to occur to someone or something. _What is going to happen to me? _ Something awful happened to your car.
examples: Something awful happened to your car.

a happy camper.monolingual: a happy person. _The boss came in this morning and found his hard disk trashed. He was not a happy camper.
examples: The boss came in this morning and found his hard disk trashed.

happy hour.monolingual: a time to drink a cocktail, starting at about 5:00 p.m. (Often bars have lower prices during “happy hour.”) _ I think that Mary has been starting happy hour a little early. Before noon I think.
examples: I think that Mary has been starting happy hour a little early.

*hard as nails.monolingual: Cliché [of someone] stern and unyielding. (*Also: as ~.) _ Don’t try to bargain with Liz. She’s as hard as nails. _Bob may seem sweet and easily swayed, but in fact he’s hard as nails.
examples: Don’t try to bargain with Liz.

*hard feelings.monolingual: Fig. feelings of resentment or anger. (*Typically: cause ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ The argument caused a lot of hard feelings, but finally we got over it.
examples: The argument caused a lot of hard feelings, but finally we got over it.

hard of hearing.monolingual: [of someone] unable to hear well or partially deaf. _ Please speak loudly. I am hard of hearing. _ Tom is hard of hearing, but is not totally deaf.
examples: Please speak loudly.

hard on someone.monolingual: harming someone’s feelings; demanding much from someone. _ I wish you wouldn’t be so hard on me. So I make mistakes. I never said I was perfect.
examples: I wish you wouldn’t be so hard on me.

*the hard sell.monolingual: high-pressure selling techniques. (*Typically: get ~; give someone ~.) _They gave me the hard sell, but I still wouldn’t buy the car. _ The clerk gave the customer the hard sell.
examples: They gave me the hard sell, but I still wouldn’t buy the car.

hard to take.monolingual: difficult or painful to accept. _ The news was hard to take, but we soon realized that it was all for the best.
examples: The news was hard to take, but we soon realized that it was all for the best.

hard words break no bones..monolingual: Prov. Verbal abuse does not physically hurt you, and therefore you should not be very upset by it. (Can be used to reply to someone who is verbally abusing you.) _ Jill: I can’t believe some of the names Fred called me. Jane: Well, hard words break n
examples: Jill: I can’t believe some of the names Fred called me.

harden oneself to something.monolingual: Fig. to make oneself capable of bearing something unpleasant. _You will have to learn to harden yourself to tragedies like this. They happen every day in a hospital. _ She had learned to harden herself to the kinds of poverty she had to work in.
examples: You will have to learn to harden yourself to tragedies like this.

harden something off†.monolingual: to accustom a young plant to normal weather so it can be moved from a protected environment to the out-of-doors. _ We put the plants by the open window to harden them off. _ We hardened off the plants.
examples: We put the plants by the open window to harden them off.

harden something up†.monolingual: to make something hard or strong. _ Put the meat in the freezer awhile to harden it up before you try to slice it thin. _Harden up the ice cream a little in the freezer.
examples: Put the meat in the freezer awhile to harden it up before you try to slice it thin.

hardly have time to think.monolingual: so busy that one can hardly think properly; very busy. _I’ve been so busy that I hardly have time to think. _ I hardly have time to think in the job that I do. We are just too busy.
examples: I’ve been so busy that I hardly have time to think.

hard-nosed.monolingual: Fig. stern and unforgiving. _ Mr. Howe was known to be very hard-nosed, but he could really be friendly if you got to know him.
examples: Mr. Howe was known to be very hard-nosed, but he could really be friendly if you got to know him.

harmonize with someone or something.monolingual: to blend with someone or something musically. _ Please try to harmonize with the rest of the singers! _Will you harmonize with the piano, please?

harness an animal up†.monolingual: to put a harness on an animal, such as a horse. _You had better harness the horses up so we can go. _ Please harness up the mare for me.
examples: You had better harness the horses up so we can go.

harp on someone or something.monolingual: Fig. to keep talking or complaining about someone or something; to refer to someone or something again and again. _I wish you would quit harping on Jeff all the time. He couldn’t be all that bad. _ Stop harping on my mistakes and work on your own.
examples: I wish you would quit harping on Jeff all the time.

has come and gone.monolingual: has already arrived and has already departed. _ No, Joy is not here. She’s come and gone. _ Sorry, you are too late for your appointment. The doctor has come and gone.
examples: No, Joy is not here.

hash something up†.monolingual: 1. to chop something up. _Now, hash the onion and garlic up and put it in the skillet. _Now, hash up the beef and brown it.
examples: Now, hash the onion and garlic up and put it in the skillet.

haste makes waste..monolingual: Prov. You do not save any time by working too fast; hurrying will cause you to make mistakes, and you will have to take extra time to do the job over again. _ Fred: Hurry up and get my car fixed. Alan: Don’t rush me. Haste makes waste.
examples: Fred: Hurry up and get my car fixed.

hatch an animal out†.monolingual: to aid in releasing an animal from an egg. _ They hatched lots of ducks out at the hatchery. _ The farmer hatched out hundreds of chicks each month.
examples: They hatched lots of ducks out at the hatchery.

hatchet man.monolingual: a man who does the cruel or difficult things for someone else; someone who does someone else’s dirty work. _He served as the president’s hatchet man and ended up doing all the dirty work.
examples: He served as the president’s hatchet man and ended up doing all the dirty work.

hate someone’s guts.monolingual: Fig. to hate someone very much. _ Oh, Bob is terrible. I hate his guts! _You may hate my guts for saying so, but I think you’re getting gray hair.
examples: Oh, Bob is terrible.

haul off and do something.monolingual: 1. Inf. to draw back and do something, such as strike a person. _ She hauled off and slapped him hard. _Max hauled off and poked Lefty in the nose.
examples: She hauled off and slapped him hard.

haul someone in†.monolingual: Fig. to arrest someone; [for a police officer] to take someone to the police station. _ The cop hauled the drunk driver in. _ They hauled in the suspects.
examples: The cop hauled the drunk driver in.

haul something down†.monolingual: to pull something down from a higher level. _Terry hauled the sail down and put it away. _ Please haul down the mainsail.
examples: Terry hauled the sail down and put it away.

have a bad attitude.monolingual: to have a negative outlook on things; to be uncooperative. _ Perry has a bad attitude and has nothing positive to contribute to the conversation.
examples: Perry has a bad attitude and has nothing positive to contribute to the conversation.

have a ball.monolingual: to have an exciting time. _ I plan to have a ball while I’m on vacation. _ Come on, everybody! Let’s have a ball!
examples: I plan to have a ball while I’m on vacation.

have a bellyful.monolingual: Inf. to have as much as one can stand. _ I’ve had a bellyful of your whining. Be quiet!
examples: I’ve had a bellyful of your whining.

have a big mouth.monolingual: to be a gossiper; to be a person who tells secrets. _ Mary has a big mouth. She told Bob what I was getting him for his birthday. _You shouldn’t say things like that about people all the time. Everyone will say you have a big mouth.
examples: Mary has a big mouth.

have a blast.monolingual: Inf. to have a great time; to have a lot of fun. _ The food was good and we had a blast. Thanks for inviting us to the party.
examples: The food was good and we had a blast.

have a blimp!.monolingual: Sl. Have a good year! (A reference to the Goodyear blimp, which is famous for being at notable events.) _ Good-bye. Have a blimp! _ Have a blimp! See you next summer.
examples: Have a blimp! See you next summer.

have a blowout.monolingual: 1. [for one’s car tire] to burst. _ I had a blowout on the way here. I nearly lost control of the car. _ If you have a blowout in one tire, you should check the other tires.
examples: I had a blowout on the way here.

have a brush with something.monolingual: to have a brief contact with something; to have an experience with something. (Especially with the law. Sometimes a close brush.) _ Ann had a close brush with the law. She was nearly arrested for speeding. _When I was younger, I had a brush with scar
examples: Ann had a close brush with the law.

have a buzz on.monolingual: Fig. to be intoxicated. (Fixed order.) _ Pete has a buzz on and is giggling a lot. _ Both of them had a buzz on by the end of the celebration.
examples: Pete has a buzz on and is giggling a lot.

have a change of heart.monolingual: Fig. to change one’s attitude or decision, usually from a negative to a positive position. _ I had a change of heart at the last minute and gave the beggar some money. _Since I talked to you last, I have had a change of heart. I now approve of your m
examples: I had a change of heart at the last minute and gave the beggar some money.

have a death wish.monolingual: Fig. to seem to be willing to take all sorts of needless risks. _ Look at the way that guy drives. He must have some sort of a death wish.
examples: Look at the way that guy drives.

have a field day.monolingual: Fig. to experience freedom from one’s usual work schedule; to have a very enjoyable time. (As with children who are released from classes to take part in sports and athletic contests.) _ The boss was gone and we had a field day today. No one got anyt
examples: The boss was gone and we had a field day today.

have a flair for something.monolingual: to have a talent for doing something; to have a special ability in some area. _ Alice has quite a f lair for designing. _ I have a f lair for fixing clocks.
examples: Alice has quite a f lair for designing.

have a glass jaw.monolingual: Fig. to be susceptible to a knockout when struck on the head. (Said only of boxers who are frequently knocked down by a blow to the head.) _ When the prizefighter was knocked out cold by a right to the chin in the first round, the newspapers said he
examples: When the prizefighter was knocked out cold by a right to the chin in the first round, the newspapers said he had a glass jaw.

have a good arm.monolingual: Fig. to have a strong and conditioned arm for sports, especially pitching in baseball. _Perry had a good arm, but he often pitched wide of the plate.
examples: Perry had a good arm, but he often pitched wide of the plate.

have a good thing going.monolingual: to have something of an ongoing nature arranged for one’s own benefit. _ Sally paints pictures and sells them at art fairs. She has a good thing going, and she makes good money. _ John inherited a fortune and doesn’t have to work for a living anymore
examples: Sally paints pictures and sells them at art fairs.

have a good time..monolingual: Enjoy yourself in what you are about to do. (Often said when someone is about to leave for an event.) _ Bill: I’m leaving for the party now. Father: Have a good time. _ Sue: Tonight is the formal dance at the Palmer House, and I’m going. Mary: Have a
examples: Bill: I’m leaving for the party now.

have a green thumb.monolingual: Fig. to have the ability to grow plants well. _ Just look at Mr. Simpson’s garden. He has a green thumb. _ My mother has a green thumb when it comes to houseplants.
examples: Just look at Mr.

have a head for something.monolingual: Fig. have the mental capacity for something. _ Jane has a good head for directions and never gets lost. _ Bill doesn’t have a head for figures and should never become an accountant.
examples: Jane has a good head for directions and never gets lost.

have a heart.monolingual: Fig. to be compassionate; to be generous and forgiving; to have an especially compassionate heart. _ Oh, have a heart! Give me some help! _If Anne had a heart, she’d volunteer to help us on the charity drive.
examples: If Anne had a heart, she’d volunteer to help us on the charity drive.

have a heart of gold.monolingual: Cliché to be generous, sincere, and friendly. _Mary is such a lovely person. She has a heart of gold. _You think Tom stole your watch? Impossible! He has a heart of gold.
examples: Mary is such a lovely person.

have a heart of stone.monolingual: Fig. to be cold and unfriendly. _ Sally has a heart of stone. She never even smiles. _The villain in the play had a heart of stone. He was cruel to everyone.
examples: Sally has a heart of stone.

have a kick to it.monolingual: Fig. to have a strong or spicy flavor; to have a high alcohol content. _I like that salsa. It has a kick to it. _ Tom’s moonshine sure has a kick to it—don’t drink too much of it, now!
examples: I like that salsa.

have a low boiling point.monolingual: Fig. to anger easily. _ Be nice to John. He’s upset and has a low boiling point. _Mr. Jones sure has a low boiling point. I hardly said anything, and he got angry.
examples: Be nice to John.

have a mind to.monolingual: to be inclined to do something. _ I have a mind to accept your challenge. _ Tom had a mind to call up Sally and ask her to dinner.
examples: I have a mind to accept your challenge.

have a near miss.monolingual: Fig. to nearly crash or collide. _ The airplanes—flying much too close—had a near miss. _I had a near miss with a bike while driving over here.
examples: The airplanes—flying much too close—had a near miss.

have a nice flight..monolingual: Please enjoy your flight. (Said when wishing someone well on an airplane trip. Often said by airline personnel to their passengers.) _Clerk: Here’s your ticket, sir. Have a nice f light. Fred: Thanks. _ As Mary boarded the plane, the f light attendan
examples: Clerk: Here’s your ticket, sir.

have a nose for something.monolingual: Fig. to have the ability to sense or find something, such as news, trouble, gossip, etc. _ She really has a nose for news. She’s a good reporter. _Fred has a nose for gossip.
examples: She really has a nose for news.

have a one-track mind.monolingual: Fig. to think entirely or almost entirely about one subject. _ Adolescent boys often have one-track minds. All they’re interested in is the opposite sex. _ Bob has a one-track mind. He can only talk about football.
examples: Adolescent boys often have one-track minds.

have a place in something.monolingual: to have a role in some plan or some activity. _ Do I have a place in the negotiations? _ Mary did not have a place in any of this.
examples: Mary did not have a place in any of this.

have a rare old time.monolingual: a fine and enjoyable time at a party or something similar. _ We had a rare old time at Tom’s the other night. _ I haven’t had a rare old time like that in years.
examples: We had a rare old time at Tom’s the other night.

have a roving eye.monolingual: Euph. to be flirtatious; to be interested in having sexual relations outside of marriage. (Usually used to describe men.) _ Poor Maria. Her husband has a roving eye. _ When they were first married, he had a roving eye.
examples: Poor Maria. Her husband has a roving eye.

have a run of something.monolingual: Fig. to have a continuous series of events. (Especially bad luck.) _ I had a run of bad luck at the casino. _ The city had a run of serious crimes that angered the citizens. _The company had a run of huge sales increases over the last few years.
examples: I had a run of bad luck at the casino.

have a seat.monolingual: to sit down. (Often a polite invitation to sit down.) _ Have a seat. I’ll be with you in a minute.
examples: Have a seat. I’ll be with you in a minute.

have a spaz.monolingual: Sl. to get angry or hysterical; to have a conniption (fit). (Spaz is short for a spastic attack or fit.) _ If my dad hears about this, he’ll have a spaz. _The teacher had a spaz when I came in so late.
examples: If my dad hears about this, he’ll have a spaz.

have a stake in something.monolingual: Fig. to have something at risk in something; to have a financial or other interest in something. _ I have a stake in that company. I want it to make a profit. _ I don’t have a stake in it, so I don’t care.
examples: I have a stake in that company.
