have a stroke.monolingual: to experience sudden unconsciousness or paralysis due to an interruption in the blood supply to the brain. (Also used as an exaggeration. See the last example.) _ The patient who received an artificial heart had a stroke two days after the operation.
examples: The patient who received an artificial heart had a stroke two days after the operation.

have a sweet tooth.monolingual: Fig. to desire to eat many sweet foods—especially candy and pastries. _ I have a sweet tooth, and if I don’t watch it, I’ll really get fat. _ John eats candy all the time. He must have a sweet tooth.
examples: I have a sweet tooth, and if I don’t watch it, I’ll really get fat.

have a thirst for something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to be thirsty for something to drink. _ I have a thirst for a tall glass of iced tea.
examples: I have a thirst for a tall glass of iced tea.

have a way with words.monolingual: to have talent in the effective or stylish use of words. _ Ask Perry to make the announcement. He has a way with words.
examples: Ask Perry to make the announcement.

have a weight problem.monolingual: Euph. to be fat; to be overweight. _ He had a weight problem when he was a teenager, but he slimmed down once he started exercising. _She has a weight problem, but she’s a lovely woman.
examples: He had a weight problem when he was a teenager, but he slimmed down once he started exercising.

have all one’s marbles.monolingual: Fig. to have all one’s mental faculties; to be mentally sound. (Very often with a negative or said to convey doubt.) _I don’t think he has all his marbles. _ Do you think Bob has all his marbles?
examples: I don’t think he has all his marbles.

have an accident.monolingual: 1. to experience something that was not foreseen or intended. _ Traffic is very bad. I almost had an accident. _ Drive carefully. Try to avoid having an accident.
examples: Traffic is very bad.

have an appetite for something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to have a desire to eat something in particular. _ I have an appetite for a nice big steak.
examples: I have an appetite for a nice big steak.

have an ear for something.monolingual: Fig. to have the ability to learn music or languages. _ Bill doesn’t have an ear for music. He can’t carry a tune. _Mary has a good ear for languages.
examples: Bill doesn’t have an ear for music.

have arrived.monolingual: to have reached a position of power, authority, or prominence. _ Jane saw her picture on the cover of the magazine and felt that she had finally arrived. _When I got an office with a window, I knew that I had arrived.
examples: Jane saw her picture on the cover of the magazine and felt that she had finally arrived.

have at it..monolingual: Start doing it.; Start eating your food. _ John: Here’s your hamburger. Have at it. Jane: Thanks. Where’s the mustard? _ John: Did you notice? The driveway needs sweeping. Jane: Here’s the broom. Have at it.
examples: John: Here’s your hamburger.

have at someone.monolingual: to go at someone; to attack someone. _ The boys had at the gang members and gave them a beating. _ I just knew John was going to have at Fred.
examples: The boys had at the gang members and gave them a beating.

have bats in one’s belfry.monolingual: Inf. Fig. to be crazy. _You must really have bats in your belfry if you think I’ll put up with that kind of stuff. _ Pay no attention to her. She has bats in her belfry.
examples: You must really have bats in your belfry if you think I’ll put up with that kind of stuff.

have been around.monolingual: to be experienced in life. (Use with caution since this can also be taken to mean to be promiscuous.) _Ask Sally about how the government works. She’s been around the state capital for years. _ They all know a lot about life. They’ve been around.
examples: Ask Sally about how the government works.

have broad shoulders.monolingual: 1. Lit. to have wide shoulders. _ She has broad shoulders because she exercises and lifts weights.
examples: She has broad shoulders because she exercises and lifts weights.

have carnal knowledge of someone.monolingual: Euph. to have had sex with someone. (Formal or jocular.) _ She had never before had carnal knowledge of a man.
examples: She had never before had carnal knowledge of a man.

have cause to do something.monolingual: to have a justifiable reason to do something. _Do you have cause to think that Mary took your money? _ He had no cause to yell at me like that.
examples: He had no cause to yell at me like that.

have clean hands.monolingual: Fig. to be guiltless. (As if a guilty person would have dirty or bloody hands.) _ Don’t look at me. I have clean hands. _ The police took him in, but let him go after questioning because he had clean hands.
examples: Don’t look at me.

have come a long way.monolingual: 1. Lit. to have traveled a long distance. _ You’ve come a long way. You must be tired and hungry. _ I’ve come a long way. Please let me rest.
examples: You’ve come a long way.

have confidence in someone.monolingual: to trust someone; to know that someone will be true. _I have confidence in you, and I know you will do well. _ Randy tends not to have confidence in anyone.
examples: I have confidence in you, and I know you will do well.

have dibs on something.monolingual: to reserve something for oneself; to claim something for oneself. (Often said by children.) _ I have dibs on the last piece of cake. _ John has dibs on the last piece again. It isn’t fair.
examples: I have dibs on the last piece of cake.

have egg on one’s face.monolingual: Fig. to be embarrassed by something one has done. (As if one went out in public with a dirty face.) _ I was completely wrong, and now I have egg on my face. _ She’s really got egg on her face!
examples: I was completely wrong, and now I have egg on my face.

have faith in someone.monolingual: to believe someone; to trust someone to do or be what is claimed. _ I have faith in you. I know you will try your best. _ We have faith in you and know you can do the job well.
examples: I have faith in you.

have feet of clay.monolingual: Fig. [for a strong person] to have a defect of character. _ All human beings have feet of clay. No one is perfect. _ Sally was popular and successful. She was nearly fifty before she learned that she, too, had feet of clay.
examples: All human beings have feet of clay.

have fun.monolingual: to experience enjoyment. _ Please forget your problems and have fun.
examples: Please forget your problems and have fun.

have growing pains.monolingual: 1. Fig. [for a child] to have pains— which are attributed to growth—in the muscles and joints. _ The doctor said that all Mary had were growing pains and that nothing was really wrong. _ Not everyone has growing pains.
examples: The doctor said that all Mary had were growing pains and that nothing was really wrong.

have had enough.monolingual: to have had as much of something as is needed or will be tolerated. _ Stop yelling at me. I’ve had enough. _ No more potatoes, please. I’ve had enough. _ I’m leaving you, Bill. I’ve had enough!
examples: Stop yelling at me.

have had its day.monolingual: to be no longer useful or successful. _ Streetcars have had their day in most American cities. _ Some people think that the fountain pen has had its day, but others prefer it to other kinds of pens.
examples: Streetcars have had their day in most American cities.

have i made myself clear?.monolingual: Do you understand exactly what I am telling you? (Indicates anger or dominance.) _ I don’t intend to warn you again. Have I made myself clear? _ I do not want you to hang around with Tim ever again! Have I made myself clear?
examples: I don’t intend to warn you again.

have intimate relations with someone.monolingual: Euph. to have sex with someone. _ I understand that Jim once had intimate relations with Sarah. _Rumor has it that she has had intimate relations with someone other than her husband.
examples: I understand that Jim once had intimate relations with Sarah.

have it both ways.monolingual: to have both of two incompatible things. _John wants the security of marriage and the freedom of being single. He wants to have it both ways. _ John thinks he can have it both ways—the wisdom of old age and the vigor of youth.
examples: John wants the security of marriage and the freedom of being single.

have it in for someone.monolingual: to be mad at someone; to wish to harm someone. _ Jane seems to have it in for Jerry. I don’t know why. _ Max has it in for his old girlfriend since she broke up with him.
examples: Jane seems to have it in for Jerry.

have it your way..monolingual: It will be done your way.; You will get your way. (Usually shows irritation on the part of the speaker.) _ Tom: I would like to do this room in blue. Sue: I prefer yellow. I really do. Tom: Okay. Have it your way. _ Jane: Let’s get a pie. Apple would
examples: Tom: I would like to do this room in blue.

have kittens.monolingual: to get extremely upset. _My mother pretty near had kittens when she found out I got fired. _ Calm down. Don’t have kittens.
examples: My mother pretty near had kittens when she found out I got fired.

have more luck than sense.monolingual: to be lucky but not intelligent. _ Jane went driving out into Death Valley without any water. She survived—she has more luck than sense. _ Tom: I like to drive ninety miles an hour on the freeway. Nobody’s ever caught me. Mary: You have more luck tha
examples: Jane went driving out into Death Valley without any water.

have no business doing something.monolingual: to be wrong to do something; to be extremely unwise to do something. _ You have no business bursting in on me like that! _You have no business spending money like that!

have no staying power.monolingual: to lack endurance; not to be able to last. _ Sally can swim fast for a short distance, but she has no staying power. _That horse can start fairly fast, but it has no staying power.
examples: Sally can swim fast for a short distance, but she has no staying power.

have no truck with something.monolingual: Rur. to have nothing to do with something. _ After the way Mary treated me, I’ll have no truck with her. _ We only show good, wholesome movies at this theater. We have no truck with most of that Hollywood trash.
examples: After the way Mary treated me, I’ll have no truck with her.

have none of something.monolingual: to tolerate or endure no amount of something. _ I’ll have none of your talk about quitting school. _ We’ll have none of your gossip. _ I wish to have none of the sweet potatoes, please.
examples: I’ll have none of your talk about quitting school.

have nothing on someone.monolingual: 1. to lack the evidence necessary to place a charge against someone. _ The police had nothing on Bob, so they let him loose. _ You’ve got nothing on me! Let me go!
examples: The police had nothing on Bob, so they let him loose.

have one in the oven.monolingual: Fig. to be pregnant with a child. _ She’s got three kids now and one in the oven.
examples: She’s got three kids now and one in the oven.

have one’s hand in something.monolingual: Fig. to exercise control over something; to play an identifiable role in doing something. _ She always has to have her hand in everything. _ I want to have my hand in the arrangement.
examples: She always has to have her hand in everything.

have one’s hands tied.monolingual: Fig. to be prevented from doing something. (As if one’s hands were made immobile.) _ I can’t help you. I was told not to, so I have my hands tied. _ John can’t help. He has his hands tied by his boss.
examples: I can’t help you.

have one’s heart stand still.monolingual: Fig. an expression said when one’s heart (figuratively) stops beating because one is shocked or is feeling strong emotions. _ I had my heart stand still once when I was overcome with joy. _ Lovers— at least the ones in love songs—usually say their he
examples: I had my heart stand still once when I was overcome with joy.

have one’s luck run out.monolingual: Fig. for one’s good luck to stop; for one’s good fortune to come to an end. _I had my luck run out when I was in South America. I nearly starved. _ I hate to have my luck run out just when I need it.
examples: I had my luck run out when I was in South America.

have one’s way with someone.monolingual: Euph. to have sexual relations with someone, possibly with that person being reluctant. _ He invited her up to his apartment, hoping to have his way with her. _ Now that you have had your way with me, do I mean nothing to you?
examples: He invited her up to his apartment, hoping to have his way with her.

have one’s wires crossed.monolingual: Fig. to have one’s mental processes in disarray; to be confused. _You don’t know what you are talking about. You’ve really got your wires crossed!s _ Joan got her wires crossed about who arrived first. It was Bob, not Gary.
examples: You don’t know what you are talking about.

have pull with someone.monolingual: to have influence with someone. (Also with some, much, lots, etc.) _ Let’s ask Ann to help us. She has pull with the mayor. _ Do you know anyone who has some pull with the bank president? I need a loan.
examples: Let’s ask Ann to help us.

have recourse to something.monolingual: to be able to use something for help; to be able to fall back on something. _ You will always have recourse to the money your grandfather left you. _ You will not have recourse to that money until you are over 21 years of age.
examples: You will always have recourse to the money your grandfather left you.

have relations with someone.monolingual: Euph. to have sexual relations with someone. _While engaged to Mary, he was having relations with at least two other women. _She was having relations with one of her employees, which was strictly against policy.
examples: While engaged to Mary, he was having relations with at least two other women.

have rocks in one’s head.monolingual: Fig. to be silly or crazy. _John is a real nut. He has rocks in his head. _ I don’t have rocks in my head—I’m just different.
examples: John is a real nut.

have seen better days.monolingual: Euph. to be in bad condition. _ My old car has seen better days, but at least it’s still running. _ She’s seen better days, it’s true, but she’s still lots of fun.
examples: My old car has seen better days, but at least it’s still running.

have someone back.monolingual: to invite someone for a return visit. _ We would love to have you back sometime. _ We want to have you back the next time you are in town.
examples: We would love to have you back sometime.

have someone by something.monolingual: to hold onto someone by something. _ She had me by the shoulder and I couldn’t get away. _ Timmy had Billy by the collar and was punching him on the shoulder.
examples: She had me by the shoulder and I couldn’t get away.

have someone dead to rights.monolingual: Fig. to have caught someone red-handed; to have irrefutable evidence about someone’s misdeed. _ We have you dead to rights on this one. _The cops had him dead to rights with damning testimony of two eyewitnesses.
examples: We have you dead to rights on this one.

have someone down.monolingual: to have someone for a visit to a place that is on a lower level or in the south. (Fixed order.) _ Why don’t we have Roger down for the weekend? _ They had us down to their place in Florida.
examples: They had us down to their place in Florida.

have someone for breakfast.monolingual: Fig. to defeat someone with ease. _ Careful, she’ll have you for breakfast if you’re not prepared to debate her. _ I’m afraid they had our team for breakfast again.
examples: Careful, she’ll have you for breakfast if you’re not prepared to debate her.

have someone in one’s corner.monolingual: Fig. to have someone supporting one’s position or goals. (Originally from boxing.) _As long as I have Mr. Howe in my corner, I feel confident about what I have to say.
examples: As long as I have Mr.

have someone in one’s pocket.monolingual: Fig. to have complete control over someone. _ Don’t worry about the mayor. She’ll cooperate. I’ve got her in my pocket. _John will do just what I tell him. I’ve got him and his brother in my pocket.
examples: Don’t worry about the mayor.

have someone on the string.monolingual: Fig. to have someone waiting for a decision. _ Sally has John on the string. He has asked her to marry him, but she hasn’t replied yet. _ Yes, it sounds like she has him on the string.
examples: Sally has John on the string.

have someone or something cornered.monolingual: 1. Lit. to have someone or something trapped as in a corner. _ We had the wild cat cornered, but it jumped over the wall and got away.
examples: We had the wild cat cornered, but it jumped over the wall and got away.

have someone’s eye.monolingual: Fig. [for someone] to establish and hold eye contact with someone; to attract someone’s attention. _ When Tom at last had her eye, he smiled at her. _ Once she had my eye, she began motioning toward the exit.
examples: When Tom at last had her eye, he smiled at her.

have someone’s hide.monolingual: Fig. to punish someone severely. _ The sheriff swore he’d have the outlaw’s hide. _ You lousy no-good so-and-so! I’ll have your hide!
examples: The sheriff swore he’d have the outlaw’s hide.

have something cinched.monolingual: Fig. Inf. to have something settled; to have the results of some act assured. _ Don’t worry. I’ve got it cinched. _ You just think you’ve got it cinched.
examples: Don’t worry. I’ve got it cinched.

have something in hand.monolingual: Fig. to have something under control. _ I thought I had my destiny in hand, but then fate played a trick on me. _ Don’t worry about me. I have everything in hand.
examples: I thought I had my destiny in hand, but then fate played a trick on me.

have something in stock.monolingual: to have merchandise available and ready for sale. _Do you have extra large sizes in stock? _ Of course, we have all sizes and colors in stock.
examples: Of course, we have all sizes and colors in stock.

have something made.monolingual: to hire someone to make something. _ Isn’t it a lovely coat? I had to have it made because I couldn’t find one I liked in a store. _We had the cake made at the bakery. Our oven isn’t big enough for a cake that size.
examples: Isn’t it a lovely coat? I had to have it made because I couldn’t find one I liked in a store.

have something on file.monolingual: to have a written record of something in storage. _ I’m sure I have your letter on file. I’ll check again. _We have your application on file somewhere.
examples: I’m sure I have your letter on file.

have something on the ball.monolingual: to have a particular amount of smartness or cleverness. _ Both John and Mary have a lot on the ball. They should go far. _ I think I’d do better in school if I had more on the ball. I learn slowly.
examples: Both John and Mary have a lot on the ball.

have something to burn.monolingual: Fig. to have lots of something, such as money, power, food, space, cars, etc.; to have more of something than one needs. _Look at the way Tom buys things. You’d think he had money to burn. _If I had all that acting talent to burn as he does, I’d have
examples: Look at the way Tom buys things.

have something to spare.monolingual: Fig. to have more than enough of something. _ Ask John for some firewood. He has firewood to spare. _ Do you have any candy to spare?
examples: Ask John for some firewood.

have sticky fingers.monolingual: Fig. to have a tendency to steal. _ The clerk—who had sticky fingers—got fired. _ The little boy had sticky fingers and was always taking his father’s small change.
examples: The clerk—who had sticky fingers—got fired.

have the hots for someone.monolingual: Sl. to be sexually aroused by someone. _ Perry has the hots for Earline.
examples: Perry has the hots for Earline.

have the makings of something.monolingual: Fig. to possess the qualities that are needed for something. _ The young boy had the makings of a fine baseball player. _My boss has all the makings of a prison warden.
examples: The young boy had the makings of a fine baseball player.

have the midas touch.monolingual: Fig. to have the ability to be successful, especially the ability to make money easily. (From the name of a legendary king whose touch turned everything to gold.) _ Bob is a merchant banker and really has the Midas touch. _ The poverty-stricken boy t
examples: Bob is a merchant banker and really has the Midas touch.

have the mullygrubs.monolingual: Rur. to feel depressed. _ She had the mullygrubs because her husband was out of town. _ Joe had the mullygrubs. We tried to cheer him up.
examples: She had the mullygrubs because her husband was out of town.

have the stomach for something.monolingual: 1. Fig. to be able to tolerate certain foods. _Do you have the stomach for Tex- Mex cooking? _ We just don’t have the stomach for onions anymore.
examples: We just don’t have the stomach for onions anymore.

have to do with something.monolingual: to be associated with or related to something. _Sally’s unhappiness has to do with the way you insulted her. _ My illness has to do with my stomach.
examples: Sally’s unhappiness has to do with the way you insulted her.

have to get married.monolingual: Euph. [for a couple] to get married because the woman is pregnant. _They didn’t have a long engagement. They had to get married, you see. _They had to get married, and their first baby was born seven months later.
examples: They didn’t have a long engagement.

have to live with something.monolingual: to have to endure something. _ I have a slight limp in the leg that I broke last year. The doctor says I’ll have to live with it. _We don’t like the carpeting in the living room, but since money is so tight we’ll have to live with it.
examples: I have a slight limp in the leg that I broke last year.

have two left feet.monolingual: Fig. to be very awkward with one’s feet. (Often refers to awkwardness at dancing.) _ I’m sorry, I can’t dance better. I have two left feet.
examples: I’m sorry, I can’t dance better.

have words.monolingual: Euph. to argue. _ From the sound of things, Bill and his father had words last night. _ We had words on the subject of money.
examples: From the sound of things, Bill and his father had words last night.

have you met someone?.monolingual: a question asked when introducing someone to someone else. (The question need not be answered. The someone is usually a person’s name.) _ Tom: Hello, Mary. Have you met Fred? Mary: Hello, Fred. Glad to meet you. Fred: Glad to meet you, Mary. _ Tom: H
examples: Tom: Hello, Mary.

hazard an opinion.monolingual: Fig. to give an opinion. _Anne asked the attorney to hazard an opinion about the strength of her lawsuit. _ Don’t feel like you have to hazard an opinion on something you know nothing about.
examples: Anne asked the attorney to hazard an opinion about the strength of her lawsuit.

he who hesitates is lost..monolingual: Prov. People should act decisively. _ Jill: Should I apply for that job? At first I thought I definitely should, but now I don’t know. . . . Jane: She who hesitates is lost. _ Call that girl and ask her out. Call her right now. He who hesitates is lo
examples: Jill: Should I apply for that job? At first I thought I definitely should, but now I don’t know.

head for someone or something.monolingual: to aim for or move toward someone or something. _ She waved good-bye as she headed for the door. _ Ann came in and headed for her mother.
examples: She waved good-bye as she headed for the door.

head for the last roundup.monolingual: Euph. to reach the end of usefulness or of life. (Originally said of a dying cowboy.) _ This ballpoint pen is headed for the last roundup. I have to get another one. _ I am so weak. I think I’m headed for the last roundup.
examples: This ballpoint pen is headed for the last roundup.

head on.monolingual: directly; head to head. _ I think we need to face this threat head on. Let’s be proactive not reactive!
examples: I think we need to face this threat head on.

head over heels in debt.monolingual: Fig. deeply in debt. _ Finally, when she was head over heels in debt, she cut up her credit cards. _ I couldn’t stand being head over heels in debt, so I always pay off my bills immediately.
examples: Finally, when she was head over heels in debt, she cut up her credit cards.

head someone or something off†.monolingual: Fig. to intercept and divert someone or something. _ I think I can head her off before she reaches the police station. _I hope we can head off trouble. _ We can head it off. Have no fear.
examples: I think I can head her off before she reaches the police station.

head something out†.monolingual: to aim something outward; to move something on its way, head or front first. _Head the boat out and pull out the throttle. _I headed out the car and we were on our way.
examples: Head the boat out and pull out the throttle.

head something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to get something pointed in the right direction. (Especially a herd of cattle or a group of covered wagons.) _Head those wagons up—we’re moving out. _ Head up the wagons!
examples: Head those wagons up—we’re moving out.

head toward someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to point at and move toward someone, something, or some place. _Head toward Mary and don’t stop to talk to anyone else. _Sharon headed toward the parking lot, hoping to get home soon.
examples: Head toward Mary and don’t stop to talk to anyone else.

headed for something.monolingual: destined for something. _Harry is headed for real trouble. _ She is headed for a breakdown.
examples: Harry is headed for real trouble.

heads or tails.monolingual: the face of a coin or the other side of a coin. (Often used in an act of coin tossing, where one circumstance is valid if the front of a coin appears and another circumstance is valid if the other side appears.) _ Jim looked at Jane as he f lipped th
examples: Jim looked at Jane as he f lipped the coin into the air.

heads up!.monolingual: Raise your head and look around you carefully for information or something that you need to see or avoid. _ Heads up! Watch out for that door! _ Heads up! There is a car coming.
examples: Heads up! There is a car coming.

heads will roll.monolingual: Fig. people will get into severe trouble. _ When the company’s year-end results are known, heads will roll. _ Heads will roll when the principal sees the damaged classroom.
examples: When the company’s year-end results are known, heads will roll.

heal over.monolingual: [for the surface of a wound] to heal. _ The wound healed over very quickly, and there was very little scarring. _ I hope it will heal over without having to be stitched.
examples: The wound healed over very quickly, and there was very little scarring.

heal someone of something.monolingual: to cure someone’s ailments. _ Are you the doctor who healed me of my wounds? _ Can any doctor heal us of a common cold?

heal up.monolingual: [for an injury] to heal. _ The cut healed up in no time at all.
examples: The cut healed up in no time at all.

a heap of something.monolingual: a great deal of something. _ Tom’s got a heap of money, but no one to spend it on. _A teacher has to have a heap of patience as well as a lot of smarts.
examples: Tom’s got a heap of money, but no one to spend it on.

a heap sight.monolingual: Rur. a lot; very much. _ This chair is a heap sight better than that one. _You got a heap sight more taters than I did.
examples: This chair is a heap sight better than that one.

heap something up†.monolingual: to make something into a pile. _ He heaped the mashed potatoes up on my plate, because he thought I wanted lots. _ Heap up the leaves in the corner of the yard.
examples: He heaped the mashed potatoes up on my plate, because he thought I wanted lots.

heap something with something.monolingual: to pile something onto something. _Karen heaped Jeff ’s plate with way too much food. _ We heaped the driveway with leaves and then put them into bags.
examples: Karen heaped Jeff ’s plate with way too much food.

hear about someone or something.monolingual: to learn about someone or something. (Not necessarily by hearing.) _ Have you heard about Tom and what happened to him? _ I heard about the accident.
examples: I heard about the accident.

hear from someone or something.monolingual: to get a message from someone or a group. _ I want to hear from you every now and then. _ We hear from the court every year or so about jury duty.
examples: I want to hear from you every now and then.

hear of someone or something.monolingual: to learn of the existence of someone or something. _ Did you ever hear of such a thing? _ I have heard of Sharon Wallace and I would like to meet her.
examples: I have heard of Sharon Wallace and I would like to meet her.

hear someone out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to hear all of what someone has to say. (Fixed order.) _ Please hear me out. I have more to say. _ Hear out the witness. Don’t jump to conclusions.
examples: Please hear me out.

hear something through.monolingual: to listen to all of something. _ I would like you to hear this explanation through before making your decision. _ I won’t have an opinion until I hear this through.
examples: I would like you to hear this explanation through before making your decision.

hearing impaired.monolingual: Euph. deaf or nearly deaf. _This program is closed-captioned for our hearing-impaired viewers. _ His mother happens to be hearing impaired, so he learned to sign at an early age.
examples: This program is closed-captioned for our hearing-impaired viewers.

hearken to someone or something.monolingual: Formal or stilted to listen to someone or something; to pay attention to someone or something. _ Please hearken to me. I speak the truth. _ Hearken to the call of the nightingale.
examples: Please hearken to me.

heart and soul.monolingual: Fig. the central core [of someone or something]. _ Now we are getting to the heart and soul of the matter. _ This feature is the heart and soul of my invention.
examples: Now we are getting to the heart and soul of the matter.

heat someone up†.monolingual: Fig. to make someone angry. (One old [now folksy] past tense is het.) _ This kind of nonsense really heats me up. _ Mean talk heats up the kids.
examples: This kind of nonsense really heats me up.

heat up.monolingual: 1. Lit. to get warmer or hot. _ It really heats up in the afternoon around here. _ How soon will dinner be heated up?
examples: It really heats up in the afternoon around here.

heave something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to lift something up. _ With a lot of effort, they heaved the heavy lid up. _ The workers heaved up the huge boulder.
examples: With a lot of effort, they heaved the heavy lid up.

heave to.monolingual: to stop a sailing ship by facing it directly into the wind. _ The captain gave the order to heave to. _ The ship hove to and everyone had a swim.
examples: The captain gave the order to heave to.

heaven help us!.monolingual: Fig. Good grief !; That’s awful. _ He fell and broke his hip! Heaven help us! What’s next?

heavens to betsy!.monolingual: Inf. My goodness! (A mild oath.) _ Heavens to Betsy! What was that noise? _Heavens to Betsy! It’s good to hear your voice!

heavy going.monolingual: difficult to do, understand, or make progress with. _ Jim finds math heavy going. _ Talking to Mary is heavy going. She has nothing interesting to say.
examples: Jim finds math heavy going.

heavy into someone or something.monolingual: Inf.much concerned with someone or something; obsessed with someone or something. _ Freddie was heavy into auto racing and always went to the races. _ Sam is heavy into Mary. He’s been out with her every night this week.
examples: Freddie was heavy into auto racing and always went to the races.

hedge against something.monolingual: to do something to lessen the risk of something happening; to bet against something bad happening. _I want to hedge against something going wrong in the stock market, so I have bonds in my portfolio, too. _ We will hedge against any risk we can detec
examples: I want to hedge against something going wrong in the stock market, so I have bonds in my portfolio, too.

hedge one’s bets.monolingual: Fig. to reduce one’s loss on a bet or on an investment by counterbalancing the loss in some way. _ Bob bet Ann that the plane would be late. He usually hedges his bets. This time he called the airline and asked about the plane before he made the bet.
examples: Bob bet Ann that the plane would be late.

hedge someone in†.monolingual: Fig. to restrict someone. _ Our decision hedged in the children so they could not have any f lexibility. _ She hedged herself in by her own behavior.
examples: Our decision hedged in the children so they could not have any f lexibility.

hedge someone or something in†.monolingual: to enclose someone or something in a hedge. _ Their overgrown yard has almost hedged us in. _ Their bushes hedged in our yard.
examples: Their overgrown yard has almost hedged us in.

hedge something against something.monolingual: Fig. to protect investments against a decline in value by making counterbalancing bets or investments. _The investor hedged his portfolio against a drop in stock prices by buying some bonds. _ I have to hedge my bets against losing.
examples: The investor hedged his portfolio against a drop in stock prices by buying some bonds.

hell around.monolingual: Sl. to go around making trouble or noise. _ Who are those kids who are out there helling around every night? _ They hell around because it’s fun.
examples: They hell around because it’s fun.

a hell of a mess.monolingual: Inf. a terrible mess. (Use caution with hell.) _ This is really a hell of a mess you’ve gotten us into. _ I never dreamed I’d come back to such a hell of a mess.
examples: This is really a hell of a mess you’ve gotten us into.

a hell of a note.monolingual: Inf. a surprising or amazing piece of news. (Use caution with hell.) _ So you’re just going to leave me like that? Well, that’s a hell of a note! _ You forgot what I asked you to bring? That’s a hell of a note.
examples: You forgot what I asked you to bring? That’s a hell of a note.

hell on a holiday.monolingual: Rur. a big commotion. (Use caution with hell.) _ It was hell on a holiday outside the stadium when the team won the big game. _ What’s going on down on Main Street? Sounds like hell on a holiday!
examples: It was hell on a holiday outside the stadium when the team won the big game.

hell on earth.monolingual: Fig. a very unpleasant situation, as if one were in hell. _That man made my life hell on earth! _The whole time I was there was just hell on earth.
examples: The whole time I was there was just hell on earth.

hell-bent for leather.monolingual: Inf.moving or behaving recklessly; riding a horse fast and recklessly. _They took off after the horse thief, riding hell-bent for leather. _ Here comes the boss. She’s not just angry; she’s hell-bent for leather.
examples: They took off after the horse thief, riding hell-bent for leather.

hell-bent for somewhere or something.monolingual: Fig. riding or drive somewhere very fast or recklessly. _Fred sped along, hellbent for home, barely missing another car.
examples: Fred sped along, hellbent for home, barely missing another car.

hellfire and damnation!.monolingual: Inf. Damn it! (An oath used to express anger or irritation.) _Hellfire and damnation! Turn that radio down! _ Hellfire and damnation! This is the second time our picnic’s been rained out.
examples: Hellfire and damnation! This is the second time our picnic’s been rained out.

help out some place.monolingual: to help [with the chores] in a particular place. _Would you be able to help out in the kitchen? _ Sally is downtown, helping out at the shop.
examples: Sally is downtown, helping out at the shop.

help someone along.monolingual: 1. to help someone move along. _ I helped the old man along. _ Please help her along. She has a hurt leg.
examples: I helped the old man along.

help someone in something.monolingual: to help someone with some task; to help someone in the doing of something. _Please help me in my efforts to win the contest. _ Will you help me in my reelection?
examples: Please help me in my efforts to win the contest.

help someone off with something.monolingual: to help someone take off an article of clothing. _Would you please help me off with my coat? _We helped the children off with their boots and put their coats in the hall.
examples: We helped the children off with their boots and put their coats in the hall.

help someone on with something.monolingual: to help someone put on an article of clothing. _ Would you help me on with my coat? _ Please help her on with her coat.
examples: Please help her on with her coat.

help yourself..monolingual: Please take what you want without asking permission. _ Sally: Can I have one of these doughnuts? Bill: Help yourself. _ Mother led the little troop of my friends to the kitchen table, which was covered with cups of juice and plates of cookies. “Help
examples: Sally: Can I have one of these doughnuts? Bill: Help yourself.

*a helping hand.monolingual: Fig. help; physical help, especially with the hands. (*Typically: get ~; need ~; give someone ~; offer ~; offer someone ~.) _ When you feel like you need a helping hand making dinner, just let me know.
examples: When you feel like you need a helping hand making dinner, just let me know.

hem someone or something in†.monolingual: Fig. to trap or enclose someone or something. _ The large city buildings hem me in. _ Don’t hem in the bird. Let it have a way to escape.
examples: The large city buildings hem me in.

herd someone or something together.monolingual: to bunch people or animals together. _Let’s herd all the kids together and take them in the house for ice cream and cake. _I herded all the puppies together and put them in a box while I cleaned their play area.
examples: Let’s herd all the kids together and take them in the house for ice cream and cake.

the here and now.monolingual: the present, as opposed to the past or the future. _ I don’t care what’s happening tomorrow or next week! I care about the here and now. _ The past is dead. Let’s worry about the here and now.
examples: I don’t care what’s happening tomorrow or next week! I care about the here and now.

here and there.monolingual: at this place and that; from place to place. _We find rare books in used-book stores here and there. _ She didn’t make a systematic search. She just looked here and there.
examples: We find rare books in used-book stores here and there.

here goes nothing..monolingual: Inf. I am beginning to do something that will fail or be poorly done. _ Sally stood on the diving board and said, “Here goes nothing.” _ As Ann walked onto the stage, she whispered, “Here goes nothing.”
examples: Sally stood on the diving board and said, “Here goes nothing.

here’s to someone or something..monolingual: an expression used as a toast to someone or something to wish someone or something well. _ Here’s to Jim and Mary! May they be very happy! _ Here’s to your new job!

here, there, and everywhere.monolingual: Fig. everywhere; at all points. _ Fred searched here, there, and everywhere, frantically looking for the lost check. _ She did not rest until she had been here, there, and everywhere, shopping for just the right gift.
examples: Fred searched here, there, and everywhere, frantically looking for the lost check.

here we go again..monolingual: We are going to experience the same thing again.; We are going to hear about or discuss the same thing again. _John: Now, I would like to discuss your behavior in class yesterday. Bill (to himself): Here we go again. _Fred: We must continue our discu
examples: John: Now, I would like to discuss your behavior in class yesterday.

here you go..monolingual: Inf. Here is what you asked for. _ “Here you go,” said the waiter as he put the plate on the table. _ Here you go. Here is your hamburger and your drink.
examples: “Here you go,” said the waiter as he put the plate on the table.

hesitate over something.monolingual: to pause before acting on something; to suspend action about someone or something. _ We are hesitating over the final decision because we have some doubts about the competitors. _ Do not hesitate too long over this matter.
examples: We are hesitating over the final decision because we have some doubts about the competitors.

hew something down†.monolingual: to fell something wooden, usually a tree. _ We will have to hew most of this forest down. _ They hewed down the tree.
examples: We will have to hew most of this forest down.

hew to something.monolingual: to conform to a rule or principle. _ I wish you would hew to the rules a little better. _ Sarah refuses to hew to the company policies.
examples: I wish you would hew to the rules a little better.

a hidden agenda.monolingual: Fig. a secret plan; a concealed plan; a plan disguised as a plan with another purpose. _I am sure that the chairman has a hidden agenda. I never did trust him anyway.
examples: I am sure that the chairman has a hidden agenda.

hide behind someone or something.monolingual: to conceal oneself behind someone or something. _The child hid behind his father. _ Rachel hid behind a tree.
examples: The child hid behind his father.

hide one’s face in shame.monolingual: Fig. to cover one’s face because of shame or embarrassment. _Mary was so embarrassed. She could only hide her face in shame. _ When Tom broke Ann’s crystal vase, he wanted to hide his face in shame.
examples: Mary was so embarrassed.

hide something in something.monolingual: to conceal something inside something. _She hid her money in a book. _Let’s hide the cake in this closet.
examples: She hid her money in a book.

high and dry.monolingual: Fig. safe; unbothered by difficulties; unscathed. (As if someone or something were safe from a flood. See also leave someone high and dry.) _ While the riot was going on down on the streets, I was high and dry in my apartment. _Liz came out of the ar
examples: While the riot was going on down on the streets, I was high and dry in my apartment.
Tom is really high on the idea of going to Yellowstone this summer.

a high roller.monolingual: Fig. a gambler who bets heavily. _They welcomed me at the casino because I had the same name as one of their high rollers.
examples: They welcomed me at the casino because I had the same name as one of their high rollers.

*the high sign.monolingual: Fig. a prearranged signal for going ahead with something. (Often refers to a hand signal or some other visual signal. *Typically: get ~; give someone ~.) _ When I got the high sign, I pulled cautiously out into the roadway. _The train’s engineer got
examples: When I got the high sign, I pulled cautiously out into the roadway.

high-and-mighty.monolingual: Fig. self-important and arrogant. _ I don’t know why William is so high-and-mighty. He’s no better than the rest of us. _ The boss acts high-and-mighty because he can fire us all.
examples: I don’t know why William is so high-and-mighty.

high-pressure someone into something.monolingual: Fig. to urge someone forcefully to do something. _ Here comes Jill. Watch out. She will try to high-pressure you into working on her committee. _ You can’t high-pressure me into doing anything! I’m too busy!
examples: Here comes Jill.

hightail it out of somewhere.monolingual: Rur. to run or ride a horse away from somewhere fast; to leave in a hurry. (Typically heard in western movies.) _ Here comes the sheriff. We’d better hightail it out of here. _Look at that guy go. He really hightailed it out of town.
examples: Here comes the sheriff.

highway robbery.monolingual: outrageous overpricing; a bill that is much higher than normally acceptable but must be paid. (As if one had been accosted and robbed on the open road or in broad daylight.) _ Four thousand dollars! That’s highway robbery for one piece of furniture!

highways and byways.monolingual: 1. major and minor roads. _ The city council voted to plant new trees along all the highways and byways of the town.
examples: The city council voted to plant new trees along all the highways and byways of the town.

hike something up†.monolingual: to raise something, such as prices, interest rates, a skirt, pants legs, etc. _ The grocery store is always hiking prices up. _ She hiked up her skirt so she could wade across the creek.
examples: The grocery store is always hiking prices up.

hind end.monolingual: Rur. the rump of someone or an animal. _ If you say that again, I’ll swat you right across the hind end. _ The mule slipped and came down right on her hind end.
examples: If you say that again, I’ll swat you right across the hind end.

the hind end of creation.monolingual: Rur. a very remote place. _ I wish I lived in the city. I’m tired of living here in the hind end of creation. _Joe moved out to a little shack at the hind end of creation.
examples: I wish I lived in the city.

hinder someone from something.monolingual: to prevent someone from doing something. _ Please don’t hinder me from my appointed tasks. _ You can’t hinder me from doing what I want!
examples: Please don’t hinder me from my appointed tasks.

hindside first.monolingual: Rur. backwards. _ You’ve got your shirt on hindside first. _ The horse came out of the trailer hindside first.
examples: You’ve got your shirt on hindside first.

hint at something.monolingual: to refer to something; to insinuate something. _ What are you hinting at? _ I am not hinting at anything. I am telling you to do it!
examples: I am not hinting at anything.

hint for something.monolingual: to give a hint that something is wanted. _ I could tell she was hinting for an invitation. _ Are you hinting for a second helping of fried chicken?
examples: I could tell she was hinting for an invitation.

hint something to someone.monolingual: to give a hint or clue to someone. _ I thought she was leaving. She hinted that to me. _ She wasn’t hinting anything to you! You made it all up!
examples: I thought she was leaving.

*hip to someone or something.monolingual: Inf. knowing about someone or something; adapting to someone or something. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; become ~.) _The boss began to get hip to Mary and her deviousness. _ She finally began to get hip to what was going on.
examples: The boss began to get hip to Mary and her deviousness.

hire someone or something out†.monolingual: to grant someone the use or efforts of someone or something for pay. _ I hired my son out as a lawn-care specialist. _I hire out my son to mow lawns.
examples: I hired my son out as a lawn-care specialist.

hiss at someone or something.monolingual: 1. [for a reptile] to make a hissing sound as a warning. _The snake hissed at me. Otherwise I wouldn’t have known it was there. _ The lizard hissed at the snake.
examples: The snake hissed at me.

hiss something out†.monolingual: Fig. to say something with a hissing voice, usually in anger or disgust. _ The disgusted manager hissed his appraisal out. _ He hissed out his criticism.
examples: The disgusted manager hissed his appraisal out.

history repeats itself..monolingual: Prov. The same kinds of events seem to happen over and over. _ It seems that history is about to repeat itself for that poor country; it is about to be invaded again. _ Alan: The country is headed for an economic depression. Jane: How do you know? Al
examples: It seems that history is about to repeat itself for that poor country; it is about to be invaded again.

hit a plateau.monolingual: Fig. to reach a higher level of activity, sales, production, output, etc., and then stop and remain unchanged for a time. _ When my sales hit a plateau, my boss gave me a pep talk. _ When production hit a plateau, the company built a new factory.
examples: When my sales hit a plateau, my boss gave me a pep talk.

hit a snag.monolingual: Fig. to run into an unexpected problem. _ We’ve hit a snag with the building project. _I stopped working on the roof when I hit a snag.
examples: We’ve hit a snag with the building project.

hit against someone or something.monolingual: to strike against someone or something. _ The door hit against me as I went through. _ The door hit against my foot as I went out.
examples: The door hit against me as I went through.

hit at someone or something.monolingual: to strike at someone or something. _ The injured man hit at the nurses who were trying to help him. _ I hit at the wall to see how solid it was.
examples: The injured man hit at the nurses who were trying to help him.

hit bottom.monolingual: Fig. to reach the lowest or worst point. _Our profits have hit bottom. This is our worst year ever. _When my life hit bottom, I began to feel much better. I knew that if there was going to be any change, it would be for the better.
examples: Our profits have hit bottom.

hit on someone.monolingual: Inf. to flirt with someone; to make a pass at someone. _ The women were all hitting on George, but he didn’t complain. _I thought he was going to hit on me— but he didn’t.
examples: The women were all hitting on George, but he didn’t complain.

hit on something.monolingual: to discover something. _She hit on a new scheme for removing the impurities from drinking water. _ I hit on it when I wasn’t able to sleep one night.
examples: She hit on a new scheme for removing the impurities from drinking water.

hit pay dirt.monolingual: 1. Fig. to discover something of value. (Alludes to discovering valuable ore.) _Sally tried a number of different jobs until she hit pay dirt. _ I tried to borrow money from a lot of different people. They all said no. Then when I went to the bank, I
examples: Sally tried a number of different jobs until she hit pay dirt.

hit someone below the belt.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a boxer] to strike an opponent below the belt. (An unfair blow.) _ The champ hit the contender below the belt and the crowd began to boo like fury. _ Fred was hit below the belt and suffered considerably.
examples: The champ hit the contender below the belt and the crowd began to boo like fury.

hit someone hard.monolingual: Fig. to affect someone’s emotions strongly. _ The death of his friend hit John hard. _ The investor was hit hard by the falling stock prices.
examples: The death of his friend hit John hard.

hit someone in something.monolingual: to strike someone on a particular part of the body. _ She hit him in the face by accident. _ Watch out or you’ll hit yourself in the arm with the hammer.
examples: She hit him in the face by accident.

hit someone with something.monolingual: 1. Fig. to charge someone with an amount of money. _ The government hit us with a big fine. _The tax people hit us with a huge tax bill.
examples: The government hit us with a big fine.

hit something off†.monolingual: to begin something; to launch an event. _ She hit off the fair with a speech. _ The mayor hit the fair off by giving a brief address.
examples: She hit off the fair with a speech.

hit the brakes.monolingual: 1. Lit. to step on a vehicle’s brakes hard and fast. _ I came around the curve too fast and had to hit the brakes immediately.
examples: I came around the curve too fast and had to hit the brakes immediately.

hit the bull’s-eye.monolingual: 1. Lit. to hit the very center of a circular target. _ The archer hit the bull’s-eye three times in a row. _ I didn’t hit the bull’s-eye even once.
examples: The archer hit the bull’s-eye three times in a row.

hit the deck.monolingual: 1. Fig. to fall down; to drop down to the floor or ground. _ Hit the deck. Don’t let them see you. _ I hit the deck the minute I heard the shots.
examples: Hit the deck. Don’t let them see you.

hit the fan.monolingual: Inf. Fig. to become publicly known; to become a scandal. (From the phrase when the shit hit the fan.) _ I wasn’t even in the country when it hit the fan. _It hit the fan, and within ten minutes the press had spread it all over the world.
examples: I wasn’t even in the country when it hit the fan.

hit the ground running.monolingual: Fig. to start the day very energetically. _ A decade ago I had a lot more energy. I would wake up, hit the ground running, and never stop until I went to bed again.
examples: A decade ago I had a lot more energy.

hit the high spots.monolingual: Fig. to do only the important, obvious, or good things. _I won’t discuss the entire report. I’ll just hit the high spots. _First, let me hit the high spots; then I’ll tell you the details.
examples: I won’t discuss the entire report.

hit the jackpot.monolingual: 1. Lit. to win a large amount of money gambling or in a lottery. _ I hit the jackpot in the big contest. _ Sally hit the jackpot in the lottery.
examples: I hit the jackpot in the big contest.

hit the road.monolingual: Fig. to depart; to begin one’s journey, especially on a road trip; to leave for home. _ It’s time to hit the road. I’ll see you. _ We have to hit the road very early in the morning.
examples: It’s time to hit the road.

hit the skids.monolingual: Fig. to decline; to decrease in value or status. _ Jed hit the skids when he started drinking. _ The firm hit the skids when the dollar collapsed.
examples: Jed hit the skids when he started drinking.

hit the spot.monolingual: Inf. to be exactly right; to be refreshing. _ This cool drink really hits the spot. _ That was a delicious meal, dear. It hit the spot.
examples: This cool drink really hits the spot.

hit the trail.monolingual: Inf. to leave. (As if one were hiking or riding a horse.) _ I have to hit the trail before sunset. _ Let’s hit the trail. It’s late.
examples: I have to hit the trail before sunset.

hit town.monolingual: Fig. to arrive in town. _The minute he hit town, he checked into a hotel and took a long nap.
examples: The minute he hit town, he checked into a hotel and took a long nap.

a hive of activity.monolingual: Fig. a location where things are very busy. _ The hotel lobby was a hive of activity each morning. _ During the holidays, the shopping center is a hive of activity.
examples: The hotel lobby was a hive of activity each morning.

hoard something up†.monolingual: to accumulate a large store of something against bad times. _ Scott was hoarding canned goods up for the hard times ahead. _ He hoarded up many pounds of canned tuna.
examples: Scott was hoarding canned goods up for the hard times ahead.

*hoarse as a crow.monolingual: very hoarse. (*Also: as ~.) _ After shouting at the team all afternoon, the coach was as hoarse as a crow. _ Jill: Has Bob got a cold? Jane: No, he’s always hoarse as a crow.
examples: After shouting at the team all afternoon, the coach was as hoarse as a crow.

hobnob with someone or something.monolingual: to associate with someone or a group, especially with those more wealthy, famous, etc. _I’m not used to hobnobbing with such luminaries. _Walter is spending a lot of time hobnobbing with the very rich.
examples: I’m not used to hobnobbing with such luminaries.

hobson’s choice.monolingual: the choice between taking what is offered and getting nothing at all. (From the name of a stable owner in the seventeenth century who always hired out the horse nearest the door.) _ We didn’t really want that particular hotel, but it was a case of Ho
examples: We didn’t really want that particular hotel, but it was a case of Hobson’s choice.

hoe one’s own row.monolingual: Rur. to mind one’s own business. _ Tom: You’re cutting up those carrots awful small. Jane: Hoe your own row! _ He didn’t get involved in other people’s fights. He just hoed his own row.
examples: Tom: You’re cutting up those carrots awful small.

hog wild.monolingual: wild; out of control. _I went hog wild at the sale and bought six new pairs of shoes. _ There were a dozen different desserts at the picnic. A person who liked sweets could go hog wild.
examples: I went hog wild at the sale and bought six new pairs of shoes.

hoist with one’s own petard.monolingual: Fig. to be harmed or disadvantaged by an action of one’s own which was meant to harm someone else. (From a line in Shakespeare’s Hamlet.) _ She intended to murder her brother but was hoist with her own petard when she ate the poisoned food intended f
examples: She intended to murder her brother but was hoist with her own petard when she ate the poisoned food intended for him.

hold a meeting.monolingual: to meet; to have a meeting (of an organization). _ We’ll have to hold a meeting to make a decision. _ Our club held a meeting to talk about future projects.
examples: We’ll have to hold a meeting to make a decision.

hold by something.monolingual: to stick by a promise. _ I hope that you will hold by our agreement. _ I will hold by everything I said.
examples: I hope that you will hold by our agreement.

hold everything!.monolingual: Inf. Stop everything!; Everyone, stop! _ “Hold everything!” cried Mary. “There’s a squirrel loose in the kitchen!” _ Bill: Hold everything! Let’s try this part again. Bob: But we’ve already rehearsed it four times.
examples: “Hold everything!” cried Mary.

hold it!.monolingual: Inf. Stop right there. _Tom: Hold it! Mary: What’s wrong? Tom: You almost stepped on my contact lens. _Bill: Hold it! Bob: What is it? Bill: Sorry. For a minute, that stick looked like a snake.
examples: Tom: Hold it! Mary: What’s wrong? Tom: You almost stepped on my contact lens.

hold on.monolingual: to be patient. _ Just hold on. Everything will work out in good time. _ If you will just hold on, everything will probably be all right.
examples: Just hold on. Everything will work out in good time.

*a hold on someone.monolingual: a strong and secure influence on someone. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ The strange religion seemed to have a strong hold on its followers. _The drug has a hold on the minds of those who use it.
examples: The strange religion seemed to have a strong hold on its followers.

hold one’s breath.monolingual: 1. Lit. to stop breathing for a short period, on purpose. _ Do you hold your breath when you dive into the water? _ I can’t hold my breath for very long.
examples: I can’t hold my breath for very long.

hold one’s end up†.monolingual: to carry one’s share of the burden; to do one’s share of the work. _ You’re not holding your end up. We’re having to do your share of the work. _ Get busy. You have to hold up your end.
examples: You’re not holding your end up.

hold one’s fire.monolingual: 1. Lit. to refrain from shooting (a gun, etc.). _ The sergeant told the soldiers to hold their fire. _ Please hold your fire until I get out of the way.
examples: The sergeant told the soldiers to hold their fire.

hold one’s head up†.monolingual: Fig. to be confident of the respect of other people; to hold up one’s head with pride rather than bowing one’s head. (A bowed head would indicate a lack of confidence.) _I am so embarrassed. I will never be able to hold my head up again. _ Now I can
examples: I am so embarrassed.

hold one’s liquor.monolingual: Fig. to be able to drink alcohol in quantity without ill effects. _Old Jed can sure hold his liquor— and a lot of it, too. _ I asked him to leave because he can’t hold his liquor.
examples: Old Jed can sure hold his liquor— and a lot of it, too.

hold one’s nose.monolingual: 1. Lit. to use one’s fingers to keep one’s nose closed to avoid a bad smell or to keep water out. _ The kid held his nose and jumped off the dock into the lake.
examples: The kid held his nose and jumped off the dock into the lake.

hold one’s own.monolingual: to do as well as anyone else. _ I can hold my own in a footrace any day. _ She was unable to hold her own, and she had to quit.
examples: I can hold my own in a footrace any day.

hold one’s peace.monolingual: to remain silent. _ Bill was unable to hold his peace any longer. “Don’t do it!” he cried. _ Quiet, John. Hold your peace for a little while longer.
examples: Bill was unable to hold his peace any longer.

hold one’s tongue.monolingual: Fig. to refrain from speaking; to refrain from saying something unpleasant. _ I felt like scolding her, but I held my tongue. _ Hold your tongue, John. You can’t talk to me that way!
examples: I felt like scolding her, but I held my tongue.

hold oneself together.monolingual: Fig. to maintain one’s calmness or sanity. _I don’t know if I can hold myself together through another horrible day like this one. _ I don’t know how she held herself together through all her troubles.
examples: I don’t know if I can hold myself together through another horrible day like this one.

hold out the olive branch.monolingual: Fig. to offer to end a dispute and be friendly; to offer reconciliation. (The olive branch is a symbol of peace and reconciliation. A biblical reference.) _ Jill was the first to hold out the olive branch after our argument. _ I always try to hold ou
examples: Jill was the first to hold out the olive branch after our argument.

hold someone for ransom.monolingual: to demand money for the return of a person who has been kidnapped. _ The kidnappers held me for ransom, but no one would pay. _ We will hold Timmy for ransom and hope that the police don’t find us.
examples: The kidnappers held me for ransom, but no one would pay.

hold someone hostage.monolingual: to keep someone as a hostage. _ The terrorists planned to hold everyone hostage in the airplane. _My neighbor was held hostage in his own home by a robber.
examples: The terrorists planned to hold everyone hostage in the airplane.

hold someone or something over†.monolingual: to retain someone or something (for a period of time). _ The storm held John over for another day. _The manager held over the hit movie for another week.
examples: The storm held John over for another day.

hold someone or something together.monolingual: to keep a group of people or things together. _She worked at two jobs in order to hold her family together. _ Our club was failing despite our efforts to hold it together.
examples: She worked at two jobs in order to hold her family together.

hold someone or something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to keep someone or something upright. _ Johnny is falling asleep. Please hold him up until I prepare the bed for him. _Hold up the window sash while I prop it open.
examples: Johnny is falling asleep.

hold someone’s attention.monolingual: Fig. to keep someone’s attention; to keep someone interested. _ The boring teacher could not hold the students’ attention. _The mystery novel held my attention and I couldn’t put it down.
examples: The boring teacher could not hold the students’ attention.

hold someone’s hand.monolingual: 1. Lit. to hold the hand of someone who is frightened, especially a child. _Please hold Jimmy’s hand when you cross the street.
examples: Please hold Jimmy’s hand when you cross the street.

hold someone to something.monolingual: Fig. to make someone adhere to an agreement. _ You promised me that you would buy six of them, and I’m going to hold you to your promise. _ It was difficult, but he held himself to the terms of the contract.
examples: You promised me that you would buy six of them, and I’m going to hold you to your promise.

hold someone up† to something.monolingual: to lift someone up to the level of something. _ I held up little Mary to the window so she could see out. _ She was held up to the window so she could see better.
examples: I held up little Mary to the window so she could see out.

hold something against someone.monolingual: Fig. to blame something on someone; to bear a grudge against someone; to resent someone. _ Your brother is mean to me, but I can’t hold it against you. _ You’re holding something against me. What is it?
examples: Your brother is mean to me, but I can’t hold it against you.

hold something for someone.monolingual: 1. to keep something safe for someone. _I will hold your money for you. _Do you want me to hold your wallet for you while you swim?
examples: I will hold your money for you.

hold something in abeyance.monolingual: to stall or postpone something. _ This is a good plan but not at this time. Let’s just hold it in abeyance until things get better. _ We will hold the matter in abeyance until we hear from you.
examples: This is a good plan but not at this time.

hold something together.monolingual: to keep the parts of an object together. _ Hold this broken vase together until I get back with the glue. _ What can I use to hold this together?
examples: Hold this broken vase together until I get back with the glue.

hold terror for someone.monolingual: [for something] to be frightening to a person. _ The thought of f lying to Rio by myself held great terror for me. _ Nothing holds terror for me. I am a daredevil.
examples: The thought of f lying to Rio by myself held great terror for me.

hold the fort.monolingual: Fig. to take care of a place while someone who is usually there is gone, such as a store or one’s home. (From western movies.) _I’m going next door to visit Mrs. Jones. You stay here and hold the fort. _ You should open the store at eight o’clock and
examples: I’m going next door to visit Mrs.

hold together.monolingual: [for something] to keep from falling apart. _ Don’t run the engine too fast because it won’t hold together. _ Do you think that this book will hold together much longer?
examples: Don’t run the engine too fast because it won’t hold together.

hold true.monolingual: [for something] to be true; [for something] to remain true. _Does this rule hold true all the time? _Yes, it holds true no matter what.
examples: Yes, it holds true no matter what.

hold your tongue!.monolingual: Inf. You have said enough!; You have said enough rude things. _ Bill: You’re seeing Tom a lot, aren’t you? You must be in love. Jane: Hold your tongue, Bill Franklin! _ After listening to the tirade against him for nearly four minutes, Tom cried out,
examples: Bill: You’re seeing Tom a lot, aren’t you? You must be in love.

hole in one.monolingual: 1. Lit. an instance of hitting a golf ball from the tee to the hole in only one try. (From the game of golf.) _ John made a hole in one yesterday. _ I’ve never gotten a hole in one.
examples: John made a hole in one yesterday.

a hole in the wall.monolingual: Fig. a tiny shop, room, etc., not much wider than its doorway. _ I went into this little hole in the wall where they had the nicest little gifts. _ His office is just a hole in the wall.
examples: I went into this little hole in the wall where they had the nicest little gifts.

holler something out†.monolingual: to yell something out. _ The guard hollered a warning out. _ They hollered out a warning.
examples: The guard hollered a warning out.

hollow something out†.monolingual: to make the inside of something hollow. _Martha hollowed the book out and put her money inside. _ She hollowed out a book.
examples: Martha hollowed the book out and put her money inside.

holy cow!.monolingual: Inf. Wow! _ Holy cow! I never expected such a nice gift! _ Give me a chance! Holy cow, don’t rush me!

holy joe.monolingual: 1. a chaplain; a cleric; a clergyman. _ I went to see the holy Joe, and he was a lot of help. _ Old holy Joe wants to see all of us at services.
examples: I went to see the holy Joe, and he was a lot of help.

holy mackerel!.monolingual: Inf.Wow! _Holy mackerel! What a beautiful day! _ Holy mackerel! What’s this? A new car?

holy moley!.monolingual: Inf.Wow! _Holy moley! A whole quarter! _ Look, here’s another one! Holy moley!

*home free.monolingual: safe and without problems. (Not necessarily about home or about money. *Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ Everyone else had a lot of trouble with the bureaucrats, but we got home free.
examples: Everyone else had a lot of trouble with the bureaucrats, but we got home free.

hone for someone or something.monolingual: Rur. to long for someone or something. _Tom: What’s wrong with Jane? Mary: She’s honing for her sweetheart. _ Jimmy was honing for the red bicycle in the toy store window.
examples: Tom: What’s wrong with Jane? Mary: She’s honing for her sweetheart.

honesty is the best policy..monolingual: Prov. You should always tell the truth, even when it seems as if it would be useful to tell a lie. _Jill: I borrowed Jane’s white blouse without asking her, and then I spilled tomato sauce on it. Should I tell her what happened, or should I just put
examples: Jill: I borrowed Jane’s white blouse without asking her, and then I spilled tomato sauce on it.

the honeymoon is over..monolingual: The early pleasant beginning (as at the start of a marriage) has ended. _Okay, the honeymoon is over. It’s time to settle down and do some hard work. _ I knew the honeymoon was over at my new job when they started yelling at me to work faster.
examples: Okay, the honeymoon is over.

honk at someone or something.monolingual: to sound a horn at someone or something. _ Is someone honking at me? _ The motorists honked at the sheep that were clogging the roadway.
examples: The motorists honked at the sheep that were clogging the roadway.

honor someone as something.monolingual: to praise someone as something; to praise someone for being something. _ Aren’t you going to honor Kevin as a hero? _We will honor Henry as the most promising scholar of the year.
examples: We will honor Henry as the most promising scholar of the year.

honor someone for something.monolingual: to praise someone for doing something. _ The committee agreed to honor Laurel for her role in the benefit dance. _I want to honor you for your efforts on behalf of our cause.
examples: The committee agreed to honor Laurel for her role in the benefit dance.

honor someone’s check.monolingual: to accept someone’s personal check in payment of an obligation. _The clerk at the store wouldn’t honor my check. I had to pay cash. _ The bank didn’t honor your check when I tried to deposit it. Please give me cash.
examples: The clerk at the store wouldn’t honor my check.

honor someone with something.monolingual: to show one’s respect for someone with something, such as a gift, party, ceremony, a response, etc. _ We would like to honor you with a little reception. _ We chose to honor you with a little gift.
examples: We would like to honor you with a little reception.

hoodwink someone into something.monolingual: Fig. to deceive someone into doing something. _She will try to hoodwink you into driving her to the airport. Watch out. _You can’t hoodwink me into doing that!
examples: She will try to hoodwink you into driving her to the airport.

hoodwink someone out of something.monolingual: Fig. to get something away from someone by deception. _ Are you trying to hoodwink me out of my money? _ Max tried to hoodwink the old lady out of all her money.
examples: Max tried to hoodwink the old lady out of all her money.

hoof it.monolingual: Inf. to walk. _ If nobody gives us a ride, we’ll have to hoof it. _She hoofed it home from the dance in her highheeled shoes.
examples: If nobody gives us a ride, we’ll have to hoof it.

hook, line, and sinker.monolingual: Fig. totally. _She fell for our story hook, line, and sinker. _ They believed every word hook, line, and sinker.
examples: She fell for our story hook, line, and sinker.

hook someone on something.monolingual: Fig. to addict someone to a drug or alcohol. _Careful, or you’ll hook yourself on those tranquilizers. _ Some friend at school hooked Roger on dope. _ Sharon has hooked herself on cocaine.
examples: Careful, or you’ll hook yourself on those tranquilizers.

hook something down†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to attach something and hold it down with a hook. _ Please hook the lid down so it doesn’t fall off. _Please hook down the lid.
examples: Please hook the lid down so it doesn’t fall off.

hook something into something.monolingual: to connect something to something. _ I want to hook another communication line into the system. _ Is it possible to hook my computer into your network?
examples: I want to hook another communication line into the system.

hook something up†.monolingual: to set something up and get it working. (The object is to be connected to a power supply, electronic network, telephone lines, etc.) _ Will it take long to hook the telephone up? _ As soon as they hook up the computer to the network, I can e-mail my
examples: As soon as they hook up the computer to the network, I can e-mail my friends.

hook up with someone.monolingual: 1. Fig. Inf. to meet with someone. _Fancy hooking up with you here, Bill. How have you been? _ Well, hello, Tom. I didn’t think I’d hook up with you again so soon.
examples: Fancy hooking up with you here, Bill.

hooked on something.monolingual: 1. Fig. addicted to a drug or something similar. _Jenny is hooked on cocaine. _She was not hooked on anything before that.
examples: Jenny is hooked on cocaine.

hoot and holler.monolingual: to shout in disapproval; to call and shout one’s displeasure. _After the umpire rendered his decision, the spectators hooted and hollered their thoughts on the matter. _ It’s hard to play a good game of basketball when the fans are hooting and holler
examples: After the umpire rendered his decision, the spectators hooted and hollered their thoughts on the matter.

hop something up†.monolingual: Sl. to make a machine, especially a car, run extra fast or give it extra power. _ He will take that junk heap home and hop it up. _He spent nearly every evening hopping up his old car.
examples: He will take that junk heap home and hop it up.

hop to it!.monolingual: Inf. Get started right now! _ Bill: I have to get these things stacked up before I go home. Bob: Then hop to it! You won’t get it done standing around here talking. _ “Hurry up! Hop to it!” urged Bill. “We’ve got to get this done!”
examples: Bill: I have to get these things stacked up before I go home.

hope for something.monolingual: to be optimistic that one’s wish for something will come true. _ I still hope for her return. _ We hope for good weather on Friday.
examples: I still hope for her return.

hope for the best.monolingual: to desire the best to happen. _ Good luck. You know we all hope for the best. _Mary is worried, but she hopes for the best.
examples: Good luck. You know we all hope for the best.

hopeless at doing something.monolingual: incapable of doing something. _Tom is hopeless at cooking. _Sally is hopeless at keeping her room clean, and it shows.
examples: Tom is hopeless at cooking.

hopped up.monolingual: 1. Sl. intoxicated with drugs or alcohol; stimulated by drugs or alcohol. _ The old man was hopped up again. He was addicted to opium. _ John usually gets hopped up on the weekends.
examples: The old man was hopped up again.

hopping mad.monolingual: Fig. very angry. _Joe got hopping mad when the salesclerk was rude to him. _ The student’s practical jokes made the teacher hopping mad.
examples: Joe got hopping mad when the salesclerk was rude to him.

horse sense.monolingual: Fig. common sense; practical thinking. _ Bob is no scholar but he has a lot of horse sense. _ Horse sense tells me I should not be involved in that project.
examples: Bob is no scholar but he has a lot of horse sense.

hose someone down†.monolingual: Sl. to kill someone. (Underworld. From the image of spraying someone with bullets.) _Mr. Big told Sam to hose Wilbur down. _The thugs tried to hose down the witness.
examples: Mr. Big told Sam to hose Wilbur down.

hose someone or something down†.monolingual: to wash something down with water from a hose. _Hose her down to cool her off and maybe she will do the same for you. _ Please hose down the driveway. _ Hose it down.
examples: Hose her down to cool her off and maybe she will do the same for you.

hot and bothered.monolingual: 1. Fig. excited; anxious. _ Now don’t get hot and bothered. Take it easy. _ John is hot and bothered about the tax increase.
examples: Now don’t get hot and bothered.

hot and heavy.monolingual: Fig. referring to serious passion or emotions. _ Things were getting a little hot and heavy so Ellen asked to be taken home. _The movie had one hot and heavy scene after another. Pretty soon it got to be a joke.
examples: Things were getting a little hot and heavy so Ellen asked to be taken home.

hot damn!.monolingual: Inf. Wow!; Hooray! (An exclamation of surprise and delight.) _ Hot damn! I just won a vacation trip to Florida!

hot off the press.monolingual: Fig. freshly printed; just released by a publisher. _Here is a copy of the new Perry Hodder novel. It’s hot off the press.
examples: Here is a copy of the new Perry Hodder novel.

hot on something.monolingual: Fig. enthusiastic about something; very much interested in something; knowledgeable about something. _Meg’s hot on animal rights. _ Jean is hot on modern ballet just now.
examples: Meg’s hot on animal rights.

a hot ticket.monolingual: Fig. something that is really popular and attractive at the moment. _ Singers who can dance are a hot ticket right now. Who knows what folks will like next month?
examples: Singers who can dance are a hot ticket right now.

hot under the collar.monolingual: Fig. very angry. _ The boss was really hot under the collar when you told him you lost the contract. _ I get hot under the collar every time I think about it.
examples: The boss was really hot under the collar when you told him you lost the contract.

a hotbed of something.monolingual: Fig. a nest of something; a gathering place of something. _ This office is a hotbed of lazy people. _ My class is a hotbed of nerds.
examples: This office is a hotbed of lazy people.

hotfoot it out of somewhere.monolingual: to run away from a place. _ Did you see Tom hotfoot it out of the office when the boss came in? _ Things are looking bad. I think we had better hotfoot it out of here.
examples: Things are looking bad.

hound something out of someone.monolingual: Fig. to force someone to give information. _ We are going to have to hound the information out of her. _ We hounded the combination to the safe out of them.
examples: We are going to have to hound the information out of her.

house of correction.monolingual: Euph. a prison. _He was sentenced to five years in the county’s house of correction. _The Jones House of Correction was built in the 1950s, when violent crime was much less common here.
examples: He was sentenced to five years in the county’s house of correction.

hover over someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to remain suspended over someone or something. _ The rescue helicopter hovered over the f loating sailor. _A huge blimp hovered over the football stadium.
examples: The rescue helicopter hovered over the f loating sailor.

how about that!.monolingual: Isn’t that surprising! _ A: My husband and I just celebrated our sixtieth anniversary. B: How about that!
examples: A: My husband and I just celebrated our sixtieth anniversary.

how about you?.monolingual: What do you think?; What is your choice?; What about you? _Bob: How are you, Bill? Bill: I’m okay. How about you? Bob: Fine, fine. Let’s do lunch sometime. _ Waiter: Can I take your order? Bill: I’ll have the chef ’s salad and ice tea. Waiter (turnin
examples: Bob: How are you, Bill? Bill: I’m okay.

how are you getting on?.monolingual: How are you managing?; How are you doing? _Jane: Well, Mary, how are you getting on? Mary: Things couldn’t be better. _Sue: Hey, John! How are you getting on? What’s it like with all the kids out of the house? John: Things are great, Sue!
examples: Jane: Well, Mary, how are you getting on? Mary: Things couldn’t be better.
