how come?.monolingual: How did that come about?; Why? _ Sally: I have to go to the doctor. Mary: How come? Sally: I’m sick, silly. _ John: I have to leave now. Bill: How come? John: I just have to, that’s all. _ Henry: How come you always put your right shoe on first? Rach
examples: Sally: I have to go to the doctor.

how do you do..monolingual: a standard inquiry and response on greeting or meeting someone. (This expression never has rising question intonation, but the first instance of its use calls for a response. Sometimes the response does, in fact, explain how one is.) _ Sally: Hello.
examples: Sally: Hello. How do you do.

how do you know?.monolingual: 1. How did you get that information? (A straightforward question. The stress in on know.) _ Bill: The train is about to pull into the station. Sue: How do you know? Bill: I hear it. _ Fred: I have to apologize for the coffee. It probably isn’t very g
examples: Bill: The train is about to pull into the station.

how do you like school?.monolingual: a phrase used to start a conversation with a school-age person. _Bob: Well, Billy, how do you like school? Billy: I hate it. Bob: Too bad. _ Mary: How do you like school? Bob: It’s okay. Almost everything else is better, though.
examples: Bob: Well, Billy, how do you like school? Billy: I hate it.

how do you like that?.monolingual: 1. Lit. Do you like that?; Is that to your liking? _Tom: There’s a bigger one over there. How do you like that? Bill: It’s better, but not quite what I want. _ Clerk: Here’s one without pleats. How do you like that? Fred: That’s perfect!
examples: Tom: There’s a bigger one over there.

how does that grab you?.monolingual: Inf. What do you think of that? (Pronounced more like HowZAT grab ya?.) _ Looks good, okay? How does that grab you? _How does that grab you? Enough salt?

how goes it?.monolingual: Inf. How are you?; How are things going? _ Nice to see you. How goes it? _ How goes it? Everything okay?
examples: Nice to see you.

how is someone getting along?.monolingual: How is someone feeling or progressing? _ How is your father getting along? Is he any better?

how is someone making out?.monolingual: How is someone doing?; How is someone surviving or getting along? _ How are you making out since your retirement?

how’s business?.monolingual: Inf. a question asked in a conversation about the state of someone’s business or job. _Tom: Hello, Sally. How’s business? Sally: Okay, I suppose. _ Bob: Good to see you, Fred. Fred: Hello, Bob. How’s business? Bob: Just okay.
examples: Tom: Hello, Sally.

how’s by you?.monolingual: Inf. a greeting inquiry. _ Fred: Hey, man! How’s by you? John: Just fine, Fred. _ Bob: Hello. What’s cooking? Bill: Nothing. How’s by you?
examples: Fred: Hey, man! How’s by you? John: Just fine, Fred.

how’s every little thing?.monolingual: Inf. How are you?; How are things with you? _Bill: Hello, Tom. Tom: Hi, Bill. How’s every little thing? Bill: Couldn’t be better. _Bill: Hi, Mary. How’s every little thing? Mary: Things are fine. How are you? Bill: Fine, thanks.
examples: Bill: Hello, Tom.

how’s that again?.monolingual: Inf. Please say that again.; I did not hear it all. _Sue: Would you like some coffee? Mary: How’s that again? Sue: I said, would you like some coffee? _ Tom: The car door is frozen closed. Bob: How’s that again? Tom: The car door is frozen closed.
examples: Tom: The car door is frozen closed.

how’s the wife?.monolingual: Inf. a phrase used by a man when inquiring about a male friend’s wife. _ Tom: Hi, Fred, how are you? Fred: Good. And you? Tom: Great! How’s the wife? Fred: Okay, and yours? Tom: Couldn’t be better. _Bill: Hi, Bob. How’s the wife? Bob: Doing fine. How
examples: Tom: Hi, Fred, how are you? Fred: Good.

how’s tricks?.monolingual: Inf. a greeting inquiry. _ Bob: Fred! How’s tricks? Fred: How are you doing, Bob? Bob: Doing great! _ Bill: What’s up? How’s tricks? Bob: I can’t complain. How are things going for you? Bill: Can’t complain.
examples: Bill: What’s up? How’s tricks? Bob: I can’t complain.

how so?.monolingual: Please explain your remark. _ A: You have to bring all the lawn furniture in. B: How so?
examples: A: You have to bring all the lawn furniture in.

how the mighty have fallen..monolingual: Prov. a jovial or mocking way of remarking that someone is doing something that he or she used to consider very demeaning. _Jill: Ever since Fred’s wife left him, he has had to cook his own meals. Jane: Well! How the mighty have fallen! _ When Dan lo
examples: Jill: Ever since Fred’s wife left him, he has had to cook his own meals.

how the other half lives.monolingual: Fig. how poorer people live; how richer people live. _ Now that I am bankrupt I am beginning to understand how the other half lives. _ Most people don’t care how the other half lives.
examples: Now that I am bankrupt I am beginning to understand how the other half lives.

a howdy and a half.monolingual: Rur. a short distance. _ Tom: Is it far to the dime store? Jane: Just a howdy and a half. _ Her house was a howdy and a half from the place where I grew up.
examples: Tom: Is it far to the dime store? Jane: Just a howdy and a half.

howl with something.monolingual: to yell or holler because of something, such as pain. _ Roger howled with pain as the needle went into his arm. _ Mary howled with grief when she saw what had happened to her roses.
examples: Roger howled with pain as the needle went into his arm.

how’re things going?.monolingual: Inf. a standard greeting inquiry. _ Bob: Hi, Fred! How’re things going? Fred: Could be better. How’s by you? _Bill: How are things going? Mary: Fine, but I need to talk to you.
examples: Bob: Hi, Fred! How’re things going? Fred: Could be better.

huddle around someone or something.monolingual: to gather or bunch around someone or something. _ The girls huddled around Mary to hear what she had to say. _ The kids huddled around the cake and consumed it almost instantaneously.
examples: The girls huddled around Mary to hear what she had to say.

huddle someone together.monolingual: to bunch people together. _ The scoutmaster huddled the boys together to give them a pep talk. _ Let’s huddle everyone together to keep warm.
examples: The scoutmaster huddled the boys together to give them a pep talk.

a hue and cry.monolingual: Fig. a loud public protest or opposition. _There was a hue and cry when the city government tried to build houses on the playing field. _ The decision to close the local school started a real hue and cry.
examples: There was a hue and cry when the city government tried to build houses on the playing field.

huff and puff.monolingual: Fig. to breathe very hard; to pant as one exerts effort. _ John came up the stairs huffing and puffing. _He huffed and puffed and finally got up the steep hill.
examples: John came up the stairs huffing and puffing.

hum with activity.monolingual: Fig. [for a place] to be busy with activity. _ The kitchen hummed with activity as usual. _ Our main office was humming with activity during the busy season.
examples: The kitchen hummed with activity as usual.

hunch over.monolingual: [for someone] to bend over. _ The wounded man hunched over and staggered to the window. _ He was hunched over with pain.
examples: The wounded man hunched over and staggered to the window.

hunch something up†.monolingual: to raise up or lift up some body part, usually the shoulders. _ He hunched his shoulders up in his effort to get warm. _ He hunched up his shoulders to keep warm.
examples: He hunched his shoulders up in his effort to get warm.

hunch up.monolingual: to squeeze or pull the parts of one’s body together. _ He hunched up in a corner to keep warm. _ Why is that child hunched up in the corner?
examples: He hunched up in a corner to keep warm.

hunger after something.monolingual: Fig. to crave for something, not necessarily food. _ I hunger after some old-fashioned gospel music. _ Mary hungered after something fattening, such as ice cream or even a baked potato with sour cream.
examples: I hunger after some old-fashioned gospel music.

hunger for someone or something.monolingual: to desire someone or something; to yearn for someone or something. _ I hunger for you. I want you madly. _ He looked at the cake and you could see he was hungering for it. _ The prisoner was consumed with a hunger for freedom.
examples: I hunger for you.

hunger is the best sauce..monolingual: Prov. Everything tastes especially good when you are hungry, because you are so eager to eat it. _ After our twenty-mile hike, we stopped at a little roadside restaurant. It may have been that they made the most delicious food in the world there, or
examples: After our twenty-mile hike, we stopped at a little roadside restaurant.

hungry for something.monolingual: Fig. desiring something, often something other than food. _ The orphan was hungry for the warmth of a family. _ Bill has become hungry for knowledge and is always studying.
examples: The orphan was hungry for the warmth of a family.

hunker down to something.monolingual: Fig. to apply oneself to something, to get started working at something. _ I hunkered down to my chores, hoping to get them done before noon. _ If you want to get a good grade on that report, you’d better hunker down to it.
examples: I hunkered down to my chores, hoping to get them done before noon.

hunt after someone or something.monolingual: to seek or pursue someone or something. _ I’m hunting after a tall man with straight black hair. _Elaine is hunting after a place to store her bicycle.
examples: I’m hunting after a tall man with straight black hair.

hunt for someone or something.monolingual: 1. to chase someone or something for sport. _ The hunter hunted for grouse on the game preserve. _Frank likes to hunt for deer.
examples: The hunter hunted for grouse on the game preserve.

hunt someone or something down†.monolingual: 1. to chase and catch someone or something. _ I don’t know where Amy is, but I’ll hunt her down. I’ll find her. _I will hunt down the villain.
examples: I don’t know where Amy is, but I’ll hunt her down.

hunt someone or something out†.monolingual: to find someone or something even if concealed. _ We will hunt them all out and find every last one of those guys. _ We will hunt out all of them. _ They hunted out the murderer.
examples: We will hunt them all out and find every last one of those guys.

hurl someone or something down†.monolingual: to throw or push someone or something downward to the ground. _ Roger hurled the football down and it bounced away wildly. _He hurled down the football in anger. _ The angry player hurled the ball down.

hurl something around†.monolingual: to throw something, such as words, around carelessly. _Don’t just go hurling foul words around like they didn’t mean anything. _You are just hurling around words!

hurry one on one’s way.monolingual: to help someone to hasten on. _ Mary hurried Joel on his way so he could catch his train. _ There is no need to hurry me on my way. I am leaving.

hurry someone or something along.monolingual: to make someone or something go faster. _Go hurry your mother along. We’re almost late. _ Why don’t you hurry the meeting along?

hurry someone or something up.monolingual: to make someone or something go or work faster. _Please hurry them all up. We are expecting to have dinner very soon. _ See if you can hurry this project up a little.
examples: Please hurry them all up.

hurry up and wait.monolingual: Fig. to do some things in a series fast and then have to wait a long time to do the next things in the series. (Originally military.) _ That’s all we ever do. Rush to stand in line somewhere. We just hurry up and wait all day long. _Hurry up and wait

hurt someone’s feelings.monolingual: to cause someone emotional pain. _It hurts my feelings when you talk that way. _I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to hurt your feelings.

hurtin’ for something.monolingual: Rur. in need of something. _ I went to fetch a bottle of cough syrup. My sick child was hurtin’ for it. _ Jim was hurting for a new set of tools.

hurtle through something.monolingual: to travel through something at great speed or with great force, possibly causing breakage. _A brick hurtled through the window and fell on the f loor. _ The rocket hurtled through space toward Mars.
examples: A brick hurtled through the window and fell on the f loor.

hush money.monolingual: Fig.money paid as a bribe to persuade someone to remain silent and not reveal certain information. _ Bob gave his younger sister hush money so that she wouldn’t tell Jane that he had gone to the movies with Sue. _ The crooks paid Fred hush money to k

hush someone up†.monolingual: 1. to make someone quiet. _ Please hush the children up. I have a telephone call. _ Hush up those kids!
examples: Please hush the children up.

hush something up†.monolingual: Fig. to keep something a secret; to try to stop a rumor from spreading. _ We just couldn’t hush it up. _ We wanted to hush up the story, but there was no way to do it.
examples: We just couldn’t hush it up.

hush up.monolingual: to be quiet; to get quiet; to stop talking. _ You talk too much. Hush up! _ I want you to hush up and sit down!
examples: You talk too much.

hush your mouth!.monolingual: Inf. Please be quiet. (Not very polite.) _I’ve heard enough of that talk. Hush your mouth! _Now, hush your mouth! You shouldn’t talk like that!
examples: I’ve heard enough of that talk.

hustle and bustle.monolingual: Fig. confusion and business. _I can’t stand the hustle and bustle of big cities. _ There is a lot of hustle and bustle in this office at the end of the fiscal year.
examples: I can’t stand the hustle and bustle of big cities.

hustle up.monolingual: to hurry up. _ Hustle up, you guys. We have to get moving. _ Hustle up. We are almost late.
examples: Hustle up, you guys.

hygienically challenged.monolingual: Euph. [of a person] dirty. (Jocular.) _Bill always smells terrible. He must be hygienically challenged. _ A couple of the kids in my class are, let us say, hygienically challenged.
examples: Bill always smells terrible.

hypothesize about something.monolingual: to speculate about something; to make guesses about something. _ Don’t waste time hypothesizing about what happened. _ There is no point in hypothesizing about what happened when we don’t know the actual truth.
examples: Don’t waste time hypothesizing about what happened.

hypothesize on something.monolingual: to conjecture on the origin or nature of something. _ We sat around hypothesizing on the origin of life.
examples: We sat around hypothesizing on the origin of life.

i am so sure!.monolingual: Inf. I am right! _ You are way rad! I am so sure! _ This is too much. I am so sure!
examples: This is too much.

i believe we’ve met..monolingual: a phrase suggesting that one has already met a person to whom one is being introduced. _ John: Alice, have you met Fred? Alice: Oh, yes, I believe we’ve met. How are you, Fred? Fred: Hello, Alice. Good to see you again. _Alice: Tom, this is my cousin
examples: John: Alice, have you met Fred? Alice: Oh, yes, I believe we’ve met.

i can accept that..monolingual: Inf. I accept your evaluation as valid. _ Bob: Now, you’ll probably like doing the other job much better. It doesn’t call for you to do the things you don’t do well. Tom: I can accept that. _Sue: On your evaluation this time, I noted that you need to
examples: Bob: Now, you’ll probably like doing the other job much better.

i can live with that..monolingual: Inf. That is something I can get used to.; That is all right as far as I’m concerned. _Sue: I want to do this room in green. Bill: I can live with that. _ Clerk: This one will cost twelve dollars more. Bob: I can live with that. I’ll take it.
examples: Sue: I want to do this room in green.

i can’t get over something!.monolingual: Fig. I am just so amazed! (The something can be a fact or a pronoun, such as that or it. Also with just, as in the examples.) _ “I just can’t get over the way everybody pitched in and helped,” said Alice. _Bob: The very idea, Sue and Tom doing someth
examples: “I just can’t get over the way everybody pitched in and helped,” said Alice.

i could eat a horse!.monolingual: Fig. I am very hungry! _ Where’s dinner? I could eat a horse!

i do believe..monolingual: a way of affirming or reaffirming one’s opinion. _Jim’s in love with that gal, I do believe. _Jane’s store will do well, I do believe.
examples: Jim’s in love with that gal, I do believe.

i don’t believe it!.monolingual: an expression of amazement and disbelief. _ Bob: Tom was just elected president of the trade association! Mary: I don’t believe it! _ Bob: They’re going to build a Disney World in Moscow. Sally: I don’t believe it!
examples: Bob: They’re going to build a Disney World in Moscow.

i don’t believe this!.monolingual: Inf. What is happening right now is unbelievable! _ It’s snowing in July! I don’t believe this! _ I don’t believe this! It can’t be happening.
examples: I don’t believe this! It can’t be happening.

i don’t care..monolingual: It doesn’t matter to me. _ Mary: Can I take these papers away? Tom: I don’t care. Do what you want. _ Bill: Should this room be white or yellow? Sally: I don’t care.
examples: Mary: Can I take these papers away? Tom: I don’t care.

i don’t mean maybe!.monolingual: Inf. I am very serious about my demand or order. _ Bob: Do I have to do this? Sue: Do it now, and I don’t mean maybe! _ Father: Get this place cleaned up! And I don’t mean maybe! John: All right! I’ll do it!

i don’t rightly know..monolingual: Rur. I do not know. _ Tom: When will Joe be getting back? Charlie: I don’t rightly know. _ Jane: What’s the difference between a first cousin and a first cousin once removed? Mary: I don’t rightly know.
examples: Tom: When will Joe be getting back? Charlie: I don’t rightly know.

examples: Tom: Think it will rain today? Sue: I doubt it.

examples: Bob: I’ll be there exactly on time.

i hope all goes well..monolingual: I hope there is success. _Good luck on your operation tomorrow. I hope all goes well.
examples: Good luck on your operation tomorrow.

i promise you!.monolingual: Inf. I am telling you the truth! (Compare this with Trust me!) _ John: Things will work out, I promise you! Jane: Okay, but when? _ Sue: I’ll be there exactly when I said. Bob: Are you sure? Sue: I promise you, I’m telling the truth!
examples: Sue: I’ll be there exactly when I said.

i rest my case..monolingual: 1. Lit. I have completed the presentation of my argument. (Said by a lawyer.) _ Clearly the defendant is guilty. I rest my case.
examples: Clearly the defendant is guilty.

i swan!.monolingual: Rur. What a surprise! _Well, I swan! I didn’t expect to see you here! _ Tom: I hear Charlie just won a thousand dollars! Jane: I swan!

examples: Mary: The weed of crime bears bitter fruit.

ice over.monolingual: [for water] to freeze and develop a covering of ice. _ I can’t wait for the river to ice over so we can do some ice fishing.
examples: I can’t wait for the river to ice over so we can do some ice fishing.

ice something down†.monolingual: to cool something with ice. _ They are icing the champagne down now. _They are icing down the champagne now.
examples: They are icing the champagne down now.

ice something up†.monolingual: to cause something to become icy. _ I hope the cold doesn’t ice the roads up. _The wind and rain iced up the roads.

ice up.monolingual: to become icy. _ Are the roads icing up?

the icing on the cake.monolingual: Fig. an extra enhancement. _Oh, wow! A tank full of gas in my new car. That’s icing on the cake! _ Your coming home for a few days was the icing on the cake.
examples: Oh, wow! A tank full of gas in my new car.

identify someone as someone.monolingual: 1. to determine that someone is a certain person. _Can you identify Fred as the perpetrator? _ Fred was identified as the thief.

idle about.monolingual: to loiter around, doing nothing. _Please don’t idle about. Get busy! _ Andy is idling about today.

idle something away†.monolingual: Fig. to waste one’s time in idleness; to waste a period of time, such as an afternoon, evening, one’s life. _She idled the afternoon away and then went to a party. _ Don’t idle away the afternoon.

ill at ease.monolingual: uneasy; anxious. _ I feel ill at ease about the interview. _ You look ill at ease. Please relax.
examples: I feel ill at ease about the interview.

examples: I tried to imbue my children with a strong sense of justice.

examples: This house is for immediate occupancy.

examples: I impressed the key into the wax, making a perfect copy.

examples: If I had the money, I would go back to college in a heartbeat.

in a jiffy.monolingual: Fig. very fast; very soon. _ Just wait a minute. I’ll be there in a jiffy. _ I’ll be finished in a jiffy.
examples: Just wait a minute.

examples: Now, calm down.

in a little bit.monolingual: Fig. in a small amount of time. _ I will be there in a little bit. Please wait. _ In a little bit, we can go outside and play.
examples: I will be there in a little bit.

in a mad rush.monolingual: Fig. in a hurry. _I ran around all day today in a mad rush, looking for a present for Bill. _Why are you always in a mad rush?
examples: I ran around all day today in a mad rush, looking for a present for Bill.

in a nutshell.monolingual: Fig. [of news or information] in a (figurative) capsule; in summary. _ This cable channel provides the latest news in a nutshell. _In a nutshell, what happened at work today?
examples: This cable channel provides the latest news in a nutshell.

in a pinch.monolingual: as a substitute. _A piece of clothing can be used as a bandage in a pinch. _ In a pinch, you can use folded paper to prop up the table leg so the table won’t rock.
examples: A piece of clothing can be used as a bandage in a pinch.

in a pique.monolingual: Fig. having a feeling of resentment; feeling that one’s pride has been hurt. _In a real pique, Anne insulted all of her friends. _ John’s found himself in a pique over Bob’s harsh criticism.
examples: In a real pique, Anne insulted all of her friends.

*in a quandary.monolingual: uncertain about what to do; perplexed. (*Typically: be ~; get [into] ~.) _ Mary was in a quandary about what college to go to. _ I couldn’t decide what to do. I was in such a quandary.
examples: Mary was in a quandary about what college to go to.

*in a rut.monolingual: Fig. in a type of boring habitual behavior. (As when the wheels of a buggy travel in the ruts worn into the ground by other buggies making it easiest to go exactly the way all the other buggies have gone before. *Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ My life ha
examples: My life has gotten into a rut.

in a sense.monolingual: in a way; in one way of looking at it. _ In a sense, cars make life better. _But, in a sense, they also make life worse.
examples: In a sense, cars make life better.

in a snit.monolingual: Fig. in a fit of anger or irritation. _ Don’t get in a snit. It was an accident. _ Mary is in a snit because they didn’t ask her to come to the shindig.
examples: Don’t get in a snit.

in a stage whisper.monolingual: Fig. in a loud whisper that everyone can hear. _ John said in a stage whisper, “This play is boring.” _ “When do we eat?” asked Billy in a stage whisper.
examples: John said in a stage whisper, “This play is boring.

in a stupor.monolingual: in a dazed condition; in a condition in which one cannot concentrate or think. _ The drunk driver walked away from the car accident in a stupor. _ In the morning, Mary remains in a stupor until she drinks coffee.
examples: The drunk driver walked away from the car accident in a stupor.

*in a tizzy.monolingual: Fig. in an excited and confused condition. (*Typically: be ~; get [into] ~.) _ John is in a tizzy because we’re an hour late. _Mary was in a tizzy when she couldn’t find her keys.
examples: John is in a tizzy because we’re an hour late.

in a twit.monolingual: upset; frantic. _ She’s all in a twit because she lost her keys. _Pete was in a twit and was quite rude to us.
examples: She’s all in a twit because she lost her keys.

in a twitter.monolingual: in a giddy state; silly. _ Don’t get yourself in a twitter. _ We were all in a twitter over the upcoming event.
examples: Don’t get yourself in a twitter.

*in a vicious circle.monolingual: Fig. in a situation in which the solution of one problem leads to a second problem, and the solution of the second problem brings back the first problem, etc. (*Typically: be ~; get [into] ~.) _ Life is so strange. I seem to be in a vicious circle mo
examples: Life is so strange.

in a word.monolingual: Fig. said simply; concisely said. _ Mrs. Smith is—in a word—haughty. _ In a word, the play f lopped.
examples: Mrs. Smith is—in a word—haughty.

in abeyance.monolingual: in reserve. _Until the judge determined that the evidence could be used in the trial, it was held in abeyance. _ I kept my opinion in abeyance.
examples: Until the judge determined that the evidence could be used in the trial, it was held in abeyance.

in accordance with something.monolingual: in agreement with something; in conformity with something. _ In accordance with our discussion, I have prepared a contract. _I did this in accordance with your request.
examples: In accordance with our discussion, I have prepared a contract.

in advance.monolingual: [of something given, paid, or provided] before it is due. _ The bill isn’t due for a month, but I paid it in advance. _ I want my pay in advance.
examples: The bill isn’t due for a month, but I paid it in advance.

in all my born days.monolingual: Rur. in my entire life. _ I’ve never seen such fireworks in all my born days. _ That’s the best party I was ever at in all my born days.
examples: I’ve never seen such fireworks in all my born days.

in all probability.monolingual: very likely; almost certainly. _ He’ll be here on time in all probability. _In all probability, they’ll finish the work today.
examples: He’ll be here on time in all probability.

in an age of years.monolingual: Rur. in a long time. _ How have you been? I haven’t talked to you in an age of years. _Jane hasn’t ridden a horse in an age of years.
examples: How have you been? I haven’t talked to you in an age of years.

*in an interesting condition.monolingual: Euph. pregnant. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ Young Mrs. Lutin is in an interesting condition. _ The bride appeared to be in an interesting condition.
examples: Young Mrs. Lutin is in an interesting condition.

*in an ivory tower.monolingual: Fig. in a place, such as a university, where one can be aloof from the realities of living. (*Typically: be ~; dwell ~; live ~; work ~.) _ If you didn’t spend so much time in your ivory tower, you’d know what people really think! _Many professors are
examples: Many professors are said to live in ivory towers.

in and of itself.monolingual: considering it alone. _ The idea in and of itself is not bad, but the side issues introduce many difficulties. _ Her action, in and of itself, caused us no problem.
examples: The idea in and of itself is not bad, but the side issues introduce many difficulties.

*in apple-pie order.monolingual: Fig. in very good order; very well organized. (*Typically: be ~; get something ~; put something ~.) _ Please put everything in apple-pie order before you leave. _ I always put my desk in apple-pie order every evening. _I’ve put my entire life into ap
examples: Please put everything in apple-pie order before you leave.

*in arrears.monolingual: [of debts; of an account] overdue. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ Jane’s student-loan payments are in arrears. _ The accounts of the bankrupt company were in arrears.
examples: Jane’s student-loan payments are in arrears.

in bad faith.monolingual: Fig. without sincerity; with bad or dishonest intent; with duplicity. _ It appears that you acted in bad faith and didn’t live up to the terms of our agreement. _ If you do things in bad faith, you’ll get a bad reputation.
examples: It appears that you acted in bad faith and didn’t live up to the terms of our agreement.

in bad sorts.monolingual: in a bad humor. _ Bill is in bad sorts today. He’s very grouchy. _ I try to be extra nice to people when I’m in bad sorts.
examples: Bill is in bad sorts today.

in between.monolingual: located in the middle of two things, states, or possibilities. _ The bath water is not hot or cold. It’s in between. _ A sandwich consists of two slices of bread with some other food in between.
examples: The bath water is not hot or cold.

*in black and white.monolingual: Fig. [of an agreement, contract, or statement] official, in writing or printing. (*Typically: be ~; get something ~.) _ I have it in black and white that I’m entitled to three weeks of vacation each year.
examples: I have it in black and white that I’m entitled to three weeks of vacation each year.

in brief.monolingual: briefly; concisely. _The whole story, in brief, is that Bob failed algebra because he did not study. _Please tell me in brief why you want this job.
examples: The whole story, in brief, is that Bob failed algebra because he did not study.

in broad daylight.monolingual: in the open light of day; clearly visible. _ The crime was committed in broad daylight. _ Bill stood there in broad daylight, but we never saw him.
examples: The crime was committed in broad daylight.

in bulk.monolingual: in large quantities or amounts, rather than smaller, more convenient quantities or amounts. _ Jane always bought office supplies in bulk to save money. _ Dave purchased cereal in bulk because his family used so much of it.
examples: Jane always bought office supplies in bulk to save money.

in business.monolingual: operating; equipped or ready to operate. _ We’re in business now, and things are running smoothly. _ Now it works. Now we’re in business.
examples: We’re in business now, and things are running smoothly.

in care of someone.monolingual: [to be delivered to someone] through someone or by way of someone. (Indicates that mail is to be delivered to a person at some other person’s address.) _Bill Jones is living at his father’s house. Address the letter to Bill in care of Mr. John Jones.
examples: Bill Jones is living at his father’s house.

in case of something.monolingual: if a problem occurs; if something happens; in the event that something happens. _What do we do in case of fire? _In case of an accident, call the police.
examples: In case of an accident, call the police.

in character.monolingual: Fig. typical of someone’s behavior. _ For Tom to shout that way wasn’t at all in character. He’s usually quite pleasant. _ It was quite in character for Sally to walk away angry.
examples: For Tom to shout that way wasn’t at all in character.

in clover.monolingual: Fig. having good fortune; in a very good situation, especially financially. _ If I get this contract, I’ll be in clover for the rest of my life. _ I have very little money saved, so when I retire I won’t exactly be in clover.
examples: If I get this contract, I’ll be in clover for the rest of my life.

in cold blood.monolingual: Fig. without feeling; with cruel intent. (Frequently said of a crime, especially murder.) _ The killer walked up and shot the woman in cold blood. _How insulting! For a person to say something like that in cold blood is just horrible.
examples: The killer walked up and shot the woman in cold blood.

in cold storage.monolingual: dead; in a state of death. (Alludes to the actual storage of certain things, such as fur coats, in cold storerooms.) _ Tom gets paid for putting his subjects in cold storage. _ Poor old Jed is in cold storage.
examples: Tom gets paid for putting his subjects in cold storage.

in consideration of something.monolingual: in return for something; as a result of something. _ In consideration of your many years of service, we are pleased to present you with this gold watch. _In consideration of your efforts, here is a check for $3,000.
examples: In consideration of your many years of service, we are pleased to present you with this gold watch.

in debt.monolingual: having debts; having much debt; owing money. _ Mary is deeply in debt. _ I am in debt to the bank for my car loan.
examples: Mary is deeply in debt.

in deep.monolingual: 1. Fig. deeply involved (with someone or something). _Mary and Sam are in deep. _Wilbur got in deep with the mob.
examples: Mary and Sam are in deep.

in deep water.monolingual: Fig. in a dangerous or vulnerable situation; in a serious situation, especially one that is too difficult or is beyond the level of one’s abilities; in trouble. _ John is having trouble with back taxes. He’s in deep water. _ Bill got in deep water in
examples: John is having trouble with back taxes.

in denial.monolingual: in a state of refusing to believe something that is true. _Mary was in denial about her illness and refused treatment. _ Tom doesn’t think he’s an alcoholic because he’s still in denial.
examples: Mary was in denial about her illness and refused treatment.

in detail.monolingual: with lots of details; giving all the details. (Often used with an adjective showing the level of detail, such as great, enormous, etc., as in the second example.) _ I explained the policy to the customer in detail. _We planned the entire project in g
examples: I explained the policy to the customer in detail.

in dire straits.monolingual: Fig. in a very serious, bad circumstance. _ We are nearly broke and need money for medicine. We are in dire straits.
examples: We are nearly broke and need money for medicine.

in disguise.monolingual: hidden behind a disguise; looking like something else. _ Santa Claus was really the little child’s father in disguise. _ What I thought was terrible turned out to be a blessing in disguise!
examples: Santa Claus was really the little child’s father in disguise.

in drag.monolingual: wearing the clothing of the opposite sex. (Usually refers to a man wearing women’s clothing.) _ Two actors in drag did a skit about life on the farm. _ Gary looks better in drag than he does in a suit.
examples: Two actors in drag did a skit about life on the farm.

in dribs and drabs.monolingual: in small portions; bit by bit. _ I’ll have to pay you what I owe you in dribs and drabs. _ The whole story is being revealed in dribs and drabs.
examples: I’ll have to pay you what I owe you in dribs and drabs.

in droves.monolingual: Fig. in large numbers. _ The settlers arrived on the prairie in droves.
examples: The settlers arrived on the prairie in droves.

*in earnest.monolingual: with sincerity. (*Typically: act ~; be ~; speak ~.) _ I’ve done all the research I need. I spent the day writing the paper in earnest. _Mary’s comments were in earnest. She really meant them.
examples: I’ve done all the research I need.

in effect.monolingual: producing a particular effect; effectively. _ In effect, this new law will raise taxes for most people. _ This policy harms domestic manufacturers. In effect, all our clothing will be made in foreign countries.
examples: In effect, this new law will raise taxes for most people.

in essence.monolingual: basically; essentially. _ I have lots of detailed advice for you, but in essence, I want you to do the best you can. _ In essence, lightning is just a giant spark of electricity.
examples: I have lots of detailed advice for you, but in essence, I want you to do the best you can.

in existence.monolingual: now existing; currently and actually being. _ The tiger may not be in existence in a few decades. _ All the oil in existence will not last the world for another century.
examples: The tiger may not be in existence in a few decades.

in fact.monolingual: in reality; really; actually. _ I’m over forty. In fact, I’m forty-six. _ This is a very good computer. In fact, it’s the best.
examples: I’m over forty.

in fashion.monolingual: in style; current and socially acceptable. _ Is that kind of thing still in fashion? _ It won’t be in fashion very long.
examples: It won’t be in fashion very long.

in favor of someone.monolingual: to someone, as when writing a check. _ Please make out a check for $300 in Tom’s favor. _ I’m making out the check in favor of Mr. Brown.
examples: Please make out a check for $300 in Tom’s favor.

in fear and trembling.monolingual: Cliché with anxiety or fear; with dread. _In fear and trembling, I went into the room to take the test. _The witness left the courtroom in fear and trembling.
examples: In fear and trembling, I went into the room to take the test.

in fine feather.monolingual: 1. Fig. well dressed; of an excellent appearance. (Alludes to a bird that has clean, bright, and flawless feathers.) _Well, you are certainly in fine feather today. _ I like to be in fine feather when I have to give a speech.
examples: Well, you are certainly in fine feather today.

in flight.monolingual: while flying. _A passenger became ill in f light and the pilot had to return to the airport. _ I really don’t care to eat in f light. I am too nervous.
examples: A passenger became ill in f light and the pilot had to return to the airport.

*in focus.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of an image] seen clearly and sharply. (*Typically: be ~; come [into] ~; get [into] ~; get something [into] ~.) _ I have the slide in focus and can see the bacteria clearly.
examples: I have the slide in focus and can see the bacteria clearly.

*in force.monolingual: 1. [of a rule or law] currently valid or in effect. (*Typically: be ~.) _Is this rule in force now? _The constitution is still in force.
examples: The constitution is still in force.

in general.monolingual: referring to the entire class being discussed; speaking of the entire range of possibilities; in most situations or circumstances. _ I like vegetables in general, but not beets. _ In general, I prefer a hotel room on a lower f loor, but will take a h
examples: I like vegetables in general, but not beets.

in glowing terms.monolingual: Fig. using words of praise; using complimentary expressions. _ The college president described his accomplishments in glowing terms and awarded him with an honorary degree.
examples: The college president described his accomplishments in glowing terms and awarded him with an honorary degree.

in good faith.monolingual: Fig. with good and honest intent; with sincerity. _ We are convinced you were acting in good faith, even though you made a serious error. _ I think you didn’t sign the contract in good faith. You never intended to carry out our agreement.
examples: We are convinced you were acting in good faith, even though you made a serious error.

in good hands.monolingual: Fig. in the safe, competent care of someone. _ Don’t worry. Your children are in good hands. Sally is an experienced baby-sitter. _ Your car is in good hands. My mechanics are factory-trained.
examples: Don’t worry. Your children are in good hands.

in good repair.monolingual: Fig. operating well; well taken care of. (Usually said of a thing rather than a person.) _The house is in good repair and ought to attract a number of potential buyers. _ If the car were in good repair, it would run more smoothly.
examples: The house is in good repair and ought to attract a number of potential buyers.

in good spirits.monolingual: Fig. happy and cheerful; positive and looking toward the future, despite unhappy circumstances. _ The patient is in good spirits and that will speed her recovery. _Tom wasn’t in very good spirits after he heard the bad news.
examples: The patient is in good spirits and that will speed her recovery.

in great demand.monolingual: wanted by many people. _ Liz is in great demand as a singer. _ Mary’s paintings are in great demand.
examples: Liz is in great demand as a singer.

in great haste.monolingual: very fast; in a big hurry. _ John always did his homework in great haste. _ Why not take time and do it right? Don’t do everything in great haste.
examples: John always did his homework in great haste.

*in hand.monolingual: in one’s possession or control. (*Typically: be ~; have something ~.) _It’s in hand. I have it right here. _ The papers are in hand. Have no fear.
examples: It’s in hand. I have it right here.

*in harm’s way.monolingual: Fig. liable to be harmed; subject to potential causes of harm. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; put someone ~.) _ Soldiers are expected to know what to do when they are in harm’s way.
examples: Soldiers are expected to know what to do when they are in harm’s way.

*in heat.monolingual: in a period of sexual excitement; in estrus. (Estrus is the period of time in which females are most willing to breed. This expression is usually used for animals. It has been used for humans in a joking sense. *Typically: be ~; get [into] ~; go [int
examples: Our dog is in heat.

in heaven.monolingual: Fig. in a state of absolute bliss or happiness. _ Lisa was in heaven after winning the lottery. _ Resting in his hammock, John was simply in heaven.
examples: Lisa was in heaven after winning the lottery.

in high dudgeon.monolingual: Fig. feeling or exhibiting great resentment; taking great offense at something. (Often with leave.) _ After the rude remarks, the person who was insulted left in high dudgeon. _ Dennis strode from the room in high dudgeon, and we knew he would get hi
examples: After the rude remarks, the person who was insulted left in high dudgeon.

in hock.monolingual: in debt. _ After buying the luxury car, Bob was in hock for years.
examples: After buying the luxury car, Bob was in hock for years.

in hog heaven.monolingual: Fig. very happy; having a wonderful time. _Bill’s a fan of Clark Gable, so when the movie theater had a Clark Gable movie festival, Bill was in hog heaven. _Jane loves to quilt, so she was in hog heaven when they opened that new store for quilters.
examples: Bill’s a fan of Clark Gable, so when the movie theater had a Clark Gable movie festival, Bill was in hog heaven.

in horror.monolingual: with intense shock or disgust. _ Mike stepped back from the rattlesnake in horror. _ The jogger recoiled in horror when she came upon a body in the park.
examples: Mike stepped back from the rattlesnake in horror.

in ink.monolingual: written or signed with a pen that uses ink, not with a pencil. _You should write your report in ink. _You must sign your checks in ink.
examples: You should write your report in ink.

in jeopardy.monolingual: to be at risk; to be at peril. _ John puts himself in jeopardy every time he goes skydiving. _ I was in jeopardy when my car broke down on the deserted road.
examples: John puts himself in jeopardy every time he goes skydiving.

in kind.monolingual: 1. in goods rather than in money. _ The country doctor was usually paid in kind. He accepted two pigs as payment for an operation. _Do you have to pay tax on payments made in kind?
examples: The country doctor was usually paid in kind.

in labor.monolingual: [of a woman] experiencing the pains and exertion of childbirth. _ Susan was in labor for nearly eight hours. _ As soon as she had been in labor for an hour, she went to the hospital.
examples: Susan was in labor for nearly eight hours.

in less than no time.monolingual: Fig. very quickly. _ I’ll be there in less than no time. _ Don’t worry. This won’t take long. It’ll be over with in less than no time.
examples: I’ll be there in less than no time.

in lieu of something.monolingual: Fig. in place of something; instead of something. (The word lieu occurs only in this phrase.) _ They gave me roast beef in lieu of ham. _ We gave money to charity in lieu of sending f lowers to the funeral.
examples: They gave me roast beef in lieu of ham.

*in limbo.monolingual: 1. Lit. a region of the afterlife on the border of hell. (In some Christian religions, there is a limbo set aside for souls that do not go to either heaven or hell. This sense is used only in this religious context. *Typically: be ~; remain ~; stay ~
examples: The baby’s soul was in limbo because she had not been baptized.

in low cotton.monolingual: Rur. depressed. _ She was in low cotton because her dress got torn. _ Jed is in low cotton because his favorite hound is dead.
examples: She was in low cotton because her dress got torn.

in luck.monolingual: fortunate; lucky. _ You want a red one? You’re in luck. There is one red one left. _ I had an accident, but I was in luck. It was not serious.
examples: You want a red one? You’re in luck.

in marching order.monolingual: organized and equipped; ready to go. (Originally military.) _ Is our luggage all packed and in marching order? _We’re in marching order and eager to go, sir.
examples: We’re in marching order and eager to go, sir.

in memory of someone.monolingual: to continue the good memories of someone; for the honor of a deceased person. _ Many streets were renamed in memory of John F. Kennedy. _ We planted roses in memory of my deceased father.
examples: Many streets were renamed in memory of John F.

in midair.monolingual: in a point high in the air. _ The planes crashed in midair. _ Extra fuel was released from the plane in midair.
examples: The planes crashed in midair.

*in mint condition.monolingual: Fig. in perfect condition. (*Typically: be ~; find something ~.) _This is a fine car. It runs well and is in mint condition. _We saw a house in mint condition and decided to buy it.
examples: This is a fine car.

in my humble opinion.monolingual: Cliché a phrase introducing the speaker’s opinion. _“In my humble opinion,” began Fred, arrogantly, “I have achieved what no one else ever could.” _ Bob: What are we going to do about the poor condition of the house next door? Bill: In my humble opin
examples: “In my humble opinion,” began Fred, arrogantly, “I have achieved what no one else ever could.

in name only.monolingual: nominally; not actual, only by terminology. _ The president is head of the country in name only. Congress makes the laws. _ Mr. Smith is the boss of the Smith Company in name only. Mrs. Smith handles all the business affairs.
examples: The president is head of the country in name only.

in neutral.monolingual: with the shift lever of a vehicle in the position where the motor is running but is not powering the wheels or other moving parts. _ The car rolled down the hill because I’d left it in neutral and did not put on the brake. _ If you are moving and in
examples: The car rolled down the hill because I’d left it in neutral and did not put on the brake.

in no uncertain terms.monolingual: Cliché in very specific and direct language. _ I was so mad. I told her in no uncertain terms to leave and never come back. _ I told him in no uncertain terms to stop calling me.
examples: I was so mad. I told her in no uncertain terms to leave and never come back.

*in on the act.monolingual: Fig. involved in something with someone else. (Often refers to an unwelcome attempt to join someone’s performance. *Typically: be ~; get ~; let someone ~.) _ Everybody wants to get in on the act. _ Why are you trying to get in on the act?
examples: Everybody wants to get in on the act.

*in on the ground floor.monolingual: Fig. involved at the very beginning of something. (Alludes to riding in an elevator that will become increasingly crowded as it ascends. You will be able to get in most easily at the lowest level. *Typically: be ~; get ~; let someone ~.) _ If you are
examples: If you are starting a new project, I want to get in on the ground floor.

*in one’s birthday suit.monolingual: Fig. naked; nude. (In the “clothes” in which one was born. *Typically: be ~; get [into] ~.) _I’ve heard that John sleeps in his birthday suit. _We used to go down to the river and swim in our birthday suits.
examples: I’ve heard that John sleeps in his birthday suit.

in one’s book.monolingual: Fig. according to one’s own opinion. _ He’s okay in my book. _ In my book, this is the best that money can buy.
examples: He’s okay in my book.

in one’s cups.monolingual: Euph. drunk. _She doesn’t make much sense when she’s in her cups. _ The speaker—who was in his cups—could hardly be understood.
examples: She doesn’t make much sense when she’s in her cups.

in one’s element.monolingual: Fig. in a natural or comfortable situation or environment. _Sally is in her element when she’s working with algebra or calculus. _Bob loves to work with color and texture. When he’s painting, he’s in his element.
examples: Sally is in her element when she’s working with algebra or calculus.

in one’s glory.monolingual: Fig. at one’s happiest or best. _ When I go to the beach on vacation, I’m in my glory. _ Sally is a good teacher. She’s in her glory in the classroom.
examples: When I go to the beach on vacation, I’m in my glory.

in one’s mind’s eye.monolingual: Fig. in one’s mind or imagination. (Alludes to visualizing something in one’s mind.) _In my mind’s eye, I can see trouble ahead. _ In her mind’s eye, she could see a beautiful building beside the river. She decided to design such a building.
examples: In my mind’s eye, I can see trouble ahead.

in one’s opinion.monolingual: according to one’s belief or judgment. _ In my opinion, that is a very ugly picture. _ That isn’t a good idea in my opinion.
examples: In my opinion, that is a very ugly picture.

in one’s or its prime.monolingual: Fig. at one’s or its peak or best time. _ Our dog—which is in its prime—is very active. _ The building was in its prime back in the Fifties, but it has not been well maintained. _ I could work long hours when I was in my prime.
examples: Our dog—which is in its prime—is very active.

in one’s own way.monolingual: 1. as the best one can do; using a personal and individual strategy. _ I don’t know the answer to the problem, but perhaps I can help in my own way. _ She couldn’t go to war and carry a gun, but she helped the war effort in her own way.
examples: I don’t know the answer to the problem, but perhaps I can help in my own way.

in one’s right mind.monolingual: Fig. sane; rational and sensible. (Often in the negative.) _ That was a stupid thing to do. You’re not in your right mind. _ You can’t be in your right mind! That sounds crazy!
examples: That was a stupid thing to do.

in one’s salad days.monolingual: Fig. in one’s youth. (Usually formal or literary. Comparing the greenness of a salad with the greenness, or freshness and inexperience, of youth.) _ I recall the joys I experienced on school vacations in my salad days. _ In our salad days, we were ap
examples: I recall the joys I experienced on school vacations in my salad days.

in one’s second childhood.monolingual: Fig. [of an adult] interested in things or people that normally interest children. _ My father bought himself a toy train, and my mother said he was in his second childhood. _ Whenever I go to the river and throw stones, I feel as if I’m in my second
examples: My father bought himself a toy train, and my mother said he was in his second childhood.

in one’s spare time.monolingual: in one’s extra time; in the time not reserved for work or doing something else. _I write novels in my spare time. _I’ll try to paint the house in my spare time.
examples: I write novels in my spare time.

*in one’s sunday best.monolingual: Rur. in one’s best clothes; in the clothes one wears to church. (*Typically: be ~; get [into] ~.) _All the children were dressed up in their Sunday best. _I like to be in my Sunday best whenever I go out. _ Let’s get into our Sunday best and go out f
examples: All the children were dressed up in their Sunday best.

*in orbit.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of something] circling a heavenly body. (*Typically: be ~; put something [into] ~.) _ The moon is in orbit around the earth. _ They put the satellite into orbit.
examples: The moon is in orbit around the earth.

*in order.monolingual: properly arranged. (*Typically: get something ~; have something ~; put something ~.) _ Please get your desk in order. _ I wish you would put things in order!
examples: Please get your desk in order.

in order to do something.monolingual: for the purpose of doing something; as a means of doing something. _ I went to college in order to further my education. _ I gave John three dollars in order to buy lunch.
examples: I went to college in order to further my education.

in other words.monolingual: a phrase introducing a restatement of what has just been said. _ Henry: Sure I want to do it, but how much do I get paid? Andrew: In other words, you’re just doing it for the money. _Bill: Well, I suppose I really should prepare my entourage for depa
examples: Henry: Sure I want to do it, but how much do I get paid? Andrew: In other words, you’re just doing it for the money.

in park.monolingual: [of an automobile transmission] having the gears locked so the automobile cannot move. _ The driver stopped the car and placed it in park. _ You have to be in park in order to start this car.
examples: The driver stopped the car and placed it in park.

in part.monolingual: partly; to a lesser degree or extent. _I was not there, in part because of my disagreement about the purpose of the meeting. I also had a previous appointment. _ I hope to win, in part because I want the prize money.
examples: I was not there, in part because of my disagreement about the purpose of the meeting.

in particular.monolingual: specifically; especially. _I’m not going anywhere in particular. _ Of the three ideas, there is one I like in particular.
examples: I’m not going anywhere in particular.

in passing.monolingual: casually; said or mentioned as an aside. _I just heard your name in passing. I didn’t hear more than that. _ The lecturer referred to George Washington in passing.
examples: I just heard your name in passing.

in pencil.monolingual: written or signed with a pencil. _ Why did you write your report in pencil? _You can’t sign a check in pencil!

in perpetuity.monolingual: for an indefinitely long period of time; eternally. _ My trust fund generates income in perpetuity. _ The right for the road to cross my land was granted in perpetuity to the county.
examples: My trust fund generates income in perpetuity.

in person.monolingual: [of someone] actually physically present in a place rather than appearing in a film, on a television or computer screen, on a telephone, or through a radio broadcast. _ All the famous movie stars were there in person. _ You must appear in our office
examples: All the famous movie stars were there in person.

*in perspective.monolingual: within a reasonable view or appraisal. (*Typically: be ~; get something ~; have something ~; put something [into] ~.) _ Let’s try to keep everything in perspective. _ If we put the matter into perspective, I think we can discuss it reasonably.
examples: Let’s try to keep everything in perspective.

*in place.monolingual: in (someone’s or something’s) proper place or location. (*Typically: be ~; put something [into] ~.) _ The maid came into the room and put everything into place. _ It’s good to see everything in place again.
examples: The maid came into the room and put everything into place.

*in play.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of a ball, in a game] under the effect of the rules of the game. (*Typically: be ~; get back ~; put something back ~.) _ The ball is in play again and the activity is furious. _ The ball is not in play yet.
examples: The ball is in play again and the activity is furious.

in point of fact.monolingual: just to point out a fact; in fact. _In point of fact, I am not late. You are simply way too early.
examples: In point of fact, I am not late.

*in power.monolingual: in control; in charge. (*Typically: be ~; come [into] ~; get [into] ~.) _Who is in power now? _No one is in power. _ The provisional government came into power six months ago.
examples: No one is in power.

in practice.monolingual: 1. in the actual doing of something; in reality. _Our policy is to be very particular, but in practice we don’t care that much. _The instructions say not to set it too high. In practice I always set it as high as possible.
examples: Our policy is to be very particular, but in practice we don’t care that much.

in press.monolingual: [of a book or other document] in the process of being printed. _This book is in press. It won’t be available for at least two months. _ This book has been in press for a long time.
examples: This book is in press.

in print.monolingual: [of a book, magazine, newspaper, or other written material] to be available from the publisher. _ Ten thousand copies of the first edition remain in print. _ The publisher listed all of its books in print.
examples: Ten thousand copies of the first edition remain in print.

in private.monolingual: privately; without others present. _ I’d like to speak to you in private. _ I enjoy spending the evening in private.
examples: I’d like to speak to you in private.

in progress.monolingual: under way; happening; developing or moving right now. _ Don’t enter the studio. There’s a show in progress. _ We now return you to the regularly scheduled show in progress.
examples: Don’t enter the studio.

in proportion.monolingual: showing the correct size or proportion relative to something else. _ That man’s large head is not in proportion to his small body. _The cartoonist drew the dog in proportion to its surroundings.
examples: That man’s large head is not in proportion to his small body.

in public.monolingual: in a place or way so that other people can see or know about something. _It’s illegal to walk naked in public. _ John always tries to embarrass me whenever we’re in public.
examples: It’s illegal to walk naked in public.

in pursuit of something.monolingual: chasing after something. _ Bill spends most of his time in pursuit of money. _ Every year Bob goes into the countryside in pursuit of butterf lies.
examples: Bill spends most of his time in pursuit of money.

in rags.monolingual: Fig. in worn-out and torn clothing. _ Oh, look at my clothing. I can’t go to the party in rags! _I think the new casual fashions make you look as if you’re in rags.
examples: Oh, look at my clothing.

in rare form.monolingual: 1. Fig. well prepared for a good performance; at one’s best. _ The goalie is in rare form today; that’s his third great save already. _ We are not exactly in rare form on Monday mornings.
examples: The goalie is in rare form today; that’s his third great save already.

in reality.monolingual: viewing things realistically; really. _ Jane dreamed it was snowing, but in reality, it was very warm. _ John looks happy, but in reality, he is miserable.
examples: Jane dreamed it was snowing, but in reality, it was very warm.

in receipt of something.monolingual: in a state of having received something. (Used in business correspondence.) _ We are in receipt of your letter of request. _ When we are in receipt of your check for the full balance, we will mark your bill as paid.
examples: We are in receipt of your letter of request.

in recent memory.monolingual: Fig. the period of time in which things are still remembered and discussed. _ Never in recent memory has there been this much snow! _ I haven’t been this happy in recent memory!

in reduced circumstances.monolingual: Euph. in poverty. _ After Frederick lost his position, we lived in reduced circumstances while waiting for my inheritance.
examples: After Frederick lost his position, we lived in reduced circumstances while waiting for my inheritance.

in rehearsal.monolingual: a stage of development in the production of a play, opera, or concert, involving many rehearsals. _ The play is in rehearsal now and will open next month. _ While the opera was still in rehearsal, the star developed a hatred for the director.
examples: The play is in rehearsal now and will open next month.

in remission.monolingual: [of a serious disease] not worsening or progressing. _ While the disease was in remission, John got to leave the hospital. _ The doctor said my cancer was in remission.
examples: While the disease was in remission, John got to leave the hospital.

*in ruins.monolingual: in a state of destruction. (*Typically: be ~; lay ~; leave something ~.) _The enemy army left the cities they attacked in ruins. _ The crops laid in ruins after the f lood.
examples: The enemy army left the cities they attacked in ruins.

in season.monolingual: 1. [of a game animal] subject to legal hunting. _ You cannot shoot ducks. They are not in season.
examples: You cannot shoot ducks.

in secret.monolingual: secretly. _ They planned in secret to blow up the bridge. _ I will tell her in secret so no one else will hear.
examples: They planned in secret to blow up the bridge.

in service.monolingual: [of something] operating or operable. service.) _Is this elevator in service?

in session.monolingual: [of a court, congress, or other organization] operating or functioning. _ Use of cameras is forbidden while the meeting is in session. _ The spectators must remain quiet while court is in session.
examples: Use of cameras is forbidden while the meeting is in session.

in seventh heaven.monolingual: Fig. in a very happy state. _Ann was really in seventh heaven when she got a car of her own. _ I’d be in seventh heaven if I had a million dollars.
examples: Ann was really in seventh heaven when she got a car of her own.

in short.monolingual: stated briefly. _At the end of the financial report, the board president said, “In short, we are okay.” _ My remarks, in short, indicate that we are in good financial shape.
examples: At the end of the financial report, the board president said, “In short, we are okay.

in short order.monolingual: very quickly. _ I can straighten out this mess in short order. _ The maids came in and cleaned the place up in short order.
examples: I can straighten out this mess in short order.

in short supply.monolingual: Fig. scarce. _Fresh vegetables are in short supply in the winter. _ Yellow cars are in short supply because everyone likes them and buys them. _ At this time of the year, fresh vegetables go into short supply.
examples: Fresh vegetables are in short supply in the winter.

in sight.monolingual: 1. Lit. within the range of vision; visible. _ The goal is in sight. _ The end of the road is in sight.
examples: The goal is in sight.

in so many words.monolingual: Fig. exactly; explicitly; in plain, clear language. _ I told her in so many words to leave me alone. _ He said yes, but not in so many words.
examples: I told her in so many words to leave me alone.

*in someone’s face.monolingual: Sl. in a provocative attitude, as if ready to fight or argue. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ Ted’s a real pain. He likes to get in your face. He’ll argue about anything. _ I know you are angry, but don’t get in my face. I had nothing to do with it.
examples: Ted’s a real pain.

in someone’s favor.monolingual: to someone’s advantage or credit. (Especially in sports scores, as in the examples.) _ The score was ten to twelve in our favor. _At the end of the second half, the score was forty to three in the other team’s favor.
examples: The score was ten to twelve in our favor.

*in someone’s good graces.monolingual: Fig. in good with someone; in someone’s favor. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ I’m not in her good graces so I shouldn’t be the one to ask her.
examples: I’m not in her good graces so I shouldn’t be the one to ask her.

*in someone’s hair.monolingual: 1. Lit. tangled in someone’s hair. (*Typically: be ~; get [into] ~.) _ My bubble gum got in my hair and I had to cut it out.
examples: My bubble gum got in my hair and I had to cut it out.

*in someone’s possession.monolingual: held by someone; owned by someone. (*Typically: be ~; come [into] ~.) _ The book is now in my possession. _ How long has this object been in your possession?
examples: The book is now in my possession.

in someone’s prayers.monolingual: [of someone] remembered and called by name when someone prays. _I am sorry to hear of your sickness. You will be in our prayers. _ The whole family is in my prayers because they have suffered so much.
examples: I am sorry to hear of your sickness.

in spades.monolingual: in the best or most extreme way possible; extravagantly. _ He f lunked the test in spades. _ He succeeded at life in spades—honors degree, great career, rich wife, lovely children, and early retirement.
examples: He f lunked the test in spades.

in stitches.monolingual: Fig. laughing very hard. _ Charlie had us in stitches with all his jokes. _ The movie sure was funny. I was in stitches!
examples: Charlie had us in stitches with all his jokes.

in stock.monolingual: to have merchandise available and ready for sale. _ Do you have extra-large sizes in stock? _ Of course, we have all sizes and colors in stock.
examples: Of course, we have all sizes and colors in stock.

in storage.monolingual: in a place where things are stored or kept. _ Mary placed her winter clothes in storage during the summer. _John’s furniture is in storage while he is in the army.
examples: Mary placed her winter clothes in storage during the summer.

in style.monolingual: 1. Lit. in fashion; fashionable. _This old coat isn’t in style anymore. _I don’t care if it’s not in style. It’s warm. _I hope this coat comes into style again.
examples: This old coat isn’t in style anymore.

in surgery.monolingual: to be involved in surgery. (Can refer to a doctor, nurse, or patients.) _ Dr. Smith is in surgery now. _ The patient is still in surgery.
examples: Dr. Smith is in surgery now.

in tandem.monolingual: [of two or more things] in single file. _ We marched to the door in tandem. _ They rode along in tandem.
examples: We marched to the door in tandem.

in tatters.monolingual: Fig. in torn pieces of cloth. _ The poor man’s clothes hung in tatters. _ The f lag was in tatters after the storm.
examples: The poor man’s clothes hung in tatters.

in terms of something.monolingual: regarding something; concerning something. _ I don’t know what to do in terms of John’s problem. _Now, in terms of your proposal, don’t you think you’re asking for too much?
examples: I don’t know what to do in terms of John’s problem.

in the affirmative.monolingual: in the form of an answer that means yes. _ The soldier answered in the affirmative by nodding his head “yes.” _ My manager’s response was in the affirmative.
examples: The soldier answered in the affirmative by nodding his head “yes.

in the air.monolingual: Fig. everywhere; all about. _There is such a feeling of joy in the air. _ We felt a sense of tension in the air.
examples: There is such a feeling of joy in the air.

in the back.monolingual: in the back part of a building; in the back room of a building. _ I don’t have your size here, but perhaps I can find it in the back. _ He’s not in the shop right now. I’ll see if he’s in the back.
examples: I don’t have your size here, but perhaps I can find it in the back.

*in the bag.monolingual: 1. Fig. cinched; achieved. (*Typically: be ~; have something ~.) _It’s in the bag—as good as done. _ The election is in the bag unless the voters find out about my past.
examples: It’s in the bag—as good as done.

*in the balance.monolingual: in an undecided state; at risk. (*Typically: be ~; hang ~.) _He stood on the edge of the cliff, his life in the balance. _ With his fortune in the balance, John rolled the dice.
examples: He stood on the edge of the cliff, his life in the balance.

in the ballpark.monolingual: Fig. within certain boundaries; [of an estimate] close to what is expected. _Your estimate is not even in the ballpark. Please try again.
examples: Your estimate is not even in the ballpark.

*in the best of health.monolingual: very healthy. (*Typically: be ~; get oneself ~.) _ Bill is in the best of health. He eats well and exercises. _I haven’t been in the best of health. I think I have the f lu.
examples: Bill is in the best of health.

in the black.monolingual: Fig. not in debt; in a financially profitable condition. (As opposed to in the red.) _ I wish my accounts were in the black. _Sally moved the company into the black.
examples: I wish my accounts were in the black.

*in the bull pen.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of a baseball pitcher to be] in a special place near the playing field, warming up to pitch. (*Typically: be ~; go [into] ~.) _ You can tell who is pitching next by seeing who is in the bull pen. _ Our best pitcher just went into the bull pe
examples: You can tell who is pitching next by seeing who is in the bull pen.

*in the cards.monolingual: Fig. in the future. (*Typically: be ~; see something ~.) _Well, what do you think is in the cards for tomorrow? _I asked the boss if there was a raise in the cards for me.
examples: I asked the boss if there was a raise in the cards for me.

in the catbird seat.monolingual: Sl. in a dominant or controlling position. _ Sally’s in the catbird seat—telling everybody where to go. _ I hold all the aces. I’m in the catbird seat.
examples: Sally’s in the catbird seat—telling everybody where to go.

in the chips.monolingual: Fig. wealthy; having lots of money. (Having lots of gambling chips.) _I’m in the chips this month. Let’s go squander it. _If I were in the chips, I’d buy a Rolls Royce.
examples: I’m in the chips this month.

*in the clear.monolingual: 1. Lit. not obstructed; not enclosed. (*Typically: be ~; get [into] ~; get someone or something [into] ~.) _ You’re in the clear. Go ahead and back up. _ Once the deer got into the clear, it ran away.
examples: You’re in the clear.

in the context of something.monolingual: in the circumstances under which something happens or has happened. _In the context of a funeral, laughing loudly is inappropriate. _In the context of an argument, it is fine to speak firmly.
examples: In the context of a funeral, laughing loudly is inappropriate.

*in the doghouse.monolingual: Fig. in trouble; in (someone’s) disfavor. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; find oneself ~; put someone [into] ~.) _ I’m really in the doghouse with my boss. I was late for an appointment. _ I hate being in the doghouse all the time. I don’t know why I can’t
examples: I’m really in the doghouse with my boss.

*in the doldrums.monolingual: Fig. sluggish; inactive; in low spirits. (*Typically: be ~; put someone [into] ~.) _He’s usually in the doldrums in the winter. _ I had some bad news yesterday, which put me into the doldrums.
examples: He’s usually in the doldrums in the winter.

*in the drink.monolingual: Fig. in the water; in the ocean. (*Typically: be ~; fall ~; throw someone ~.) _He fell in the drink and had to be rescued.
examples: He fell in the drink and had to be rescued.

in the driver’s seat.monolingual: Fig. in control; in charge of things. (As if one were driving and controlling the vehicle.) _ Now that Fred is in the driver’s seat, there is a lot less criticism about how things are being done. _ Joan can’t wait to get into the driver’s seat and do
examples: Now that Fred is in the driver’s seat, there is a lot less criticism about how things are being done.

in the event of something.monolingual: if something happens; on the chance that something happens. _ In the event of his late arrival, please call me. _ In the event of rain, the parade is canceled.
examples: In the event of his late arrival, please call me.

*in the fast lane.monolingual: Fig. in a very active or possible risky manner. _ Fred lives in the fast lane. It’s lucky he’s still alive.
examples: Fred lives in the fast lane.

in the flesh.monolingual: Fig. bodily present; in person; totally real. _ I’ve heard that the queen is coming here in the f lesh. _ I’ve wanted a f lat-screen TV for years, and now I’ve got one right here in the f lesh.
examples: I’ve heard that the queen is coming here in the f lesh.

*in the groove.monolingual: Sl. attuned to something. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ I was uncomfortable at first, but now I’m beginning to get in the groove. _ Fred began to get in the groove, and things went more smoothly.
examples: I was uncomfortable at first, but now I’m beginning to get in the groove.

*in the gutter.monolingual: Fig. [of a person] in a low state; poor and homeless. (*Typically: be ~; fall [into] ~; put someone [into] ~.) _ You had better straighten out your life, or you’ll end in the gutter. _ His bad habits put him into the gutter.
examples: You had better straighten out your life, or you’ll end in the gutter.

*in the hole.monolingual: Fig. in debt. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; go ~; put someone ~.) _ I’m $200 in the hole. _ We went into the hole on that deal.
examples: I’m $200 in the hole.

in the hopper.monolingual: Fig. in process; in line to be processed. (A hopper is a chute for incoming work or material to be processed.) _ It’s in the hopper. I’ll get to it. _ Your job is in the hopper, and your turn is next.
examples: It’s in the hopper.

in the know.monolingual: knowledgeable. _ Let’s ask Bob. He’s in the know. _ I have no knowledge of how to work this machine. I think I can get myself in the know very quickly though.
examples: Let’s ask Bob. He’s in the know.

in the lap of luxury.monolingual: Cliché in luxurious surroundings. _ John lives in the lap of luxury because his family is very wealthy. _ When I retire, I’d like to live in the lap of luxury.
examples: John lives in the lap of luxury because his family is very wealthy.

in the laundry.monolingual: with the clothes that are waiting to be washed. _ Is my blue shirt clean or is it in the laundry? _ All my socks are in the laundry. What shall I do?
examples: All my socks are in the laundry.

in the line of duty.monolingual: Fig. as part of one’s expected duties. _When soldiers fight people in a war, it’s in the line of duty. _ Police officers have to do things they may not like in the line of duty.
examples: When soldiers fight people in a war, it’s in the line of duty.

in the loop.monolingual: Fig. in the group of persons communicating regularly about a specific plan or project. _ I don’t know what’s going on with the Jones deal since I’m not in the loop. _ Bob and Jean are in the loop. They can tell you what’s happening.
examples: I don’t know what’s going on with the Jones deal since I’m not in the loop.

in the main.monolingual: basically; generally. _Mary: Everything looks all right—in the main. Sally: What details need attention? Mary: Just a few things here and there. Like on page
examples: Mary: Everything looks all right—in the main.

in the making.monolingual: in development; in the process of developing. _ This is a real problem in the making. Let’s try to keep it from getting any worse.
examples: This is a real problem in the making.

in the meantime.monolingual: the period of time between two things; the period of time between now and when something is supposed to happen. _ The movie starts at 6:00. In the meantime, let’s eat dinner. _ My f light was at 8:00. In the meantime, I played solitaire.
examples: The movie starts at 6:00.

*in the middle of nowhere.monolingual: Fig. in a very remote place. (*Typically: be ~; drive [into] ~; put someone or something [into] ~.) _ To get to my house, you have to drive into the middle of nowhere. _ We found a nice place to eat, but it’s out in the middle of nowhere.
examples: To get to my house, you have to drive into the middle of nowhere.

in the money.monolingual: 1. Fig. wealthy. _John is really in the money. He’s worth millions. _If I am ever in the money, I’ll be generous.
examples: John is really in the money.

in the near future.monolingual: Cliché in the time immediately ahead. _I don’t plan to go to Florida in the near future. _Today’s prices won’t be around in the near future.
examples: I don’t plan to go to Florida in the near future.

in the offing.monolingual: happening at some time in the future. _ There is a big investigation in the offing, but I don’t know when. _It’s hard to tell what’s in the offing if you don’t keep track of things.
examples: There is a big investigation in the offing, but I don’t know when.

*in the open.monolingual: in the outdoors; in an area that is not closed in. (*Typically: be ~; put something ~.) _ John’s bike was stolen because he left it out in the open. _ Mary loves gardening because she loves to be in the open.
examples: John’s bike was stolen because he left it out in the open.

*in the picture.monolingual: Fig. well-informed; aware of what is going on. (*Typically: be ~; keep someone ~; put someone ~.) _ Please, keep me fully in the picture. _ John found out about the plan. He’s in the picture, so take care.
examples: Please, keep me fully in the picture.

in the pipeline.monolingual: Fig. backed up somewhere in a process; in process; in a queue. _ There’s a lot of goods still in the pipeline. That means no more new orders will be shipped for a while. _Your papers are in the pipeline somewhere. You’ll just have to wait.
examples: There’s a lot of goods still in the pipeline.

*in the poorhouse.monolingual: 1. Lit. in a (historical) communal dwelling for impoverished persons. (*Typically: live ~; end up ~.) _ He couldn’t pay his debts and had to live in the poorhouse.
examples: He couldn’t pay his debts and had to live in the poorhouse.

in the prime of life.monolingual: Fig. in the best and most productive and healthy period of life. _The good health of one’s youth can carry over into the prime of life. _He was struck down by a heart attack in the prime of life.
examples: The good health of one’s youth can carry over into the prime of life.

*in the public eye.monolingual: Fig. publicly; visible to all; conspicuous. (*Typically: be ~; find oneself ~; get [into] ~.) _ Elected officials find themselves constantly in the public eye. _ The mayor made it a practice to get into the public eye as much as possible.
examples: Elected officials find themselves constantly in the public eye.

in the rear.monolingual: located in the space or area behind someone or something. _ The waiter told me that the bathrooms were in the rear. _ All deliveries must be made in the rear.
examples: The waiter told me that the bathrooms were in the rear.

*in the red.monolingual: Fig. losing money. (*Typically: be ~; go [into] ~; as opposed to in the black.) _ State government has been operating in the red for five straight years. _ What with all those car repairs, we’re going to be in the red this month.
examples: State government has been operating in the red for five straight years.

in the right.monolingual: correct; morally or legally correct. _ I know I’m in the right. _ You are not in the right on this point.
examples: I know I’m in the right.

in the road.monolingual: 1. Lit. on the roadway. _ What’s that in the road ahead?
examples: What’s that in the road ahead? 2.

in the running.monolingual: Fig. in competition; competing and having a chance to win. _ Is Tom still in the running? Does he still have a chance to be elected? _I don’t know about Tom, but Gladys is definitely still in the running.
examples: I don’t know about Tom, but Gladys is definitely still in the running.

in the same breath.monolingual: Fig. [stated or said] almost at the same time. _ He told me I was lazy, but then in the same breath he said I was doing a good job. _ The teacher said that the students were working hard and, in the same breath, that they were not working hard enough
examples: He told me I was lazy, but then in the same breath he said I was doing a good job.

in the second place.monolingual: secondly; in addition. (Usually said after one has said in the first place.) _ In the first place, you don’t have enough money to buy one. In the second place, you don’t need one. _ In the first place, I don’t have the time. In the second place, I’m
examples: In the first place, you don’t have enough money to buy one.
