*in the soup.monolingual: Fig. in a bad situation. (*Typically: be ~; get [into] ~.) _Now I’m really in the soup. I broke Mrs. Franklin’s window. _ I make a lot of mistakes. It’s easy for me to get into the soup.
examples: Now I’m really in the soup.

*in the swim of things.monolingual: Fig. involved in or participating in events or happenings. (*Typically: be ~; get [into] ~.) _ I’ve been ill, but soon I’ll be back in the swim of things. _ I can’t wait to settle down and get into the swim of things.
examples: I’ve been ill, but soon I’ll be back in the swim of things.

*in the trust of someone.monolingual: under the responsibility or in the care of someone. (*Typically: be ~; leave someone or something ~; place someone or something ~.) _ The state placed the orphan in the trust of the foster parents. _ Our bonds are left in the trust of our broker.
examples: The state placed the orphan in the trust of the foster parents.

in the wake of something.monolingual: Fig. after something; as a result of some event. (Alludes to a ship’s wake.) _ We had no place to live in the wake of the fire. _ In the wake of the storm, there were many broken tree limbs.
examples: We had no place to live in the wake of the fire.

in the way of something.monolingual: as a kind of something; as a style of something. _ What do you have in the way of dress shoes? _ We have nothing in the way of raincoats.
examples: We have nothing in the way of raincoats.

in the wind.monolingual: Fig. about to happen. _There are some major changes in the wind. Expect these changes to happen soon. _ There is something in the wind. We’ll find out what it is soon.
examples: There are some major changes in the wind.

in the works.monolingual: Fig. being prepared; being planned; being done. _ There are some new laws in the works that will affect all of us. _ I have some ideas in the works that you might be interested in.
examples: There are some new laws in the works that will affect all of us.

in the worst way.monolingual: Fig. very much. _ I want a new car in the worst way. _ Bob wants to retire in the worst way.
examples: I want a new car in the worst way.

in the wrong.monolingual: wrong; morally or legally incorrect. _I am not in the wrong, you are. _ No, you are in the wrong.
examples: I am not in the wrong, you are.

in theory.monolingual: according to a theory; theoretically. _In theory, if I take my medicine regularly, I will get well. _How things work in theory doesn’t always match with how things work in reality.
examples: In theory, if I take my medicine regularly, I will get well.

in there.monolingual: Sl. sincere; likeable. _ Martha is really in there. Everybody likes her. _ I like a guy who’s in there—who thinks about other people.
examples: Martha is really in there.

in there pitching.monolingual: Fig. trying very hard. _ Bob is always in there pitching. _ Just stay in there pitching. You’ll make some progress eventually.
examples: Bob is always in there pitching.

in these parts.monolingual: Rur. around here; in this area. _ There aren’t any big hospitals in these parts. _ Joe’s the richest man in these parts.
examples: There aren’t any big hospitals in these parts.

in this day and age.monolingual: Fig. now; in these modern times. _ Bill: Ted f lunked out of school. Mother: Imagine that! Especially in this day and age. _ Bill: Taxes keep going up and up. Bob: What do you expect in this day and age?
examples: Bill: Ted f lunked out of school.

in those parts.monolingual: Rur. around there; in that area. _ I’ve got a cousin who lives in those parts. _ We used to spend our vacations in those parts.
examples: I’ve got a cousin who lives in those parts.

in times past.monolingual: Fig. long ago; in previous times. _In times past, you would not have been able to wear casual clothing to work. _ In times past, the air always seemed fresher and cleaner.
examples: In times past, you would not have been able to wear casual clothing to work.

in top form.monolingual: 1. [of someone or some creature] in very good physical condition. _ The runners are in top form, so this should be a good race. _ I’m not in top form, but I’m not completely out of shape either.
examples: The runners are in top form, so this should be a good race.

in tow.monolingual: closely following; under someone’s control. _ The nanny walked into the park with three children in tow. _ The manager went to the meeting with her staff in tow.
examples: The nanny walked into the park with three children in tow.

in transit.monolingual: while in the process of being transported. _ Dave is in transit from London to Chicago. _The new stereo is now in transit from the manufacturer.
examples: Dave is in transit from London to Chicago.

in triplicate.monolingual: [of a document] produced in three copies. _ Mr. Smith asked me to copy his notes in triplicate. _ I completed each form in triplicate.
examples: Mr. Smith asked me to copy his notes in triplicate.

*in trouble.monolingual: 1. in danger; in difficulty; due for punishment. (*Typically: be ~; get [into] ~.) _ If you don’t be quiet, you’re going to be in trouble. _ The company was in trouble for months, and then went bankrupt.
examples: If you don’t be quiet, you’re going to be in trouble.

in tune.monolingual: in a state where musical notes are at their proper intervals so that none are flat or sharp. _ Your piano is in tune. _ The choir members all sang in tune.
examples: Your piano is in tune.

*in tune with the times.monolingual: Fig. up-to-date; in fashion. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _Look at that old jacket, Bill. You’re not in tune with the times.
examples: Look at that old jacket, Bill.

in turn.monolingual: in the appropriate point in the series or order; when one’s turn comes. _ Someone has to wash the dishes after every meal. All of us will have to do it in turn. _ All three of them shared the task of carrying water in turn.
examples: Someone has to wash the dishes after every meal.

in unison.monolingual: [of musical notes, instruments, or voices] having the same pitch. _ This part of the piece is performed in unison. _ The twins sang in unison.
examples: This part of the piece is performed in unison.

in use.monolingual: [of some facility or device] occupied or busy. _ Sorry, this room is in use. _ How long will it be in use?
examples: Sorry, this room is in use.

in vain.monolingual: for no purpose; [done] as a failure. _ They rushed her to the hospital, but they did it in vain. _ We tried in vain to get her there on time.
examples: They rushed her to the hospital, but they did it in vain.

in view of something.monolingual: in consideration of something; because of something. _ In view of the high cost of gasoline, I sold my car. _ I won’t invite John to the meeting in view of his attitude.
examples: In view of the high cost of gasoline, I sold my car.

*in vogue.monolingual: fashionable; faddish. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _This style of coat is no longer in vogue. _That word isn’t in vogue any longer.
examples: This style of coat is no longer in vogue.

*in writing.monolingual: in written form rather that spoken. (*Typically: get something ~; have something ~; put something ~.) _ Be sure to get their salary offer in writing.
examples: Be sure to get their salary offer in writing.

inaugurate someone as something.monolingual: to install or introduce someone as something. _ The club inaugurated Amy as the new president. _ We will inaugurate Ken as vice president.
examples: The club inaugurated Amy as the new president.

incarcerate someone in something.monolingual: to imprison someone in something. _The sheriff incarcerated Lefty in the county jail. _ He had wanted to incarcerate Max in the jail too.
examples: The sheriff incarcerated Lefty in the county jail.

inch back.monolingual: to move back very slowly. _ The trainer inched back from the angry tiger. _ The tiger inched back and sprang.
examples: The trainer inched back from the angry tiger.

inch by inch.monolingual: Fig. one inch at a time; little by little. _Traffic moved along inch by inch. _ Inch by inch, the snail moved across the stone.
examples: Traffic moved along inch by inch.

inch forward.monolingual: to move forward very slowly. _ Inch forward very slowly, and try not to make any noise. _ The cat inched forward, taking care not to alert the bird to its presence.
examples: Inch forward very slowly, and try not to make any noise.

inch over.monolingual: to move over a tiny bit. _ Could you inch over a little? I need just a little more room. _ Please inch over a little.
examples: Could you inch over a little? I need just a little more room.

incite someone to something.monolingual: to excite or provoke someone to something. _The radicals tried to incite the students to violence. _The students were incited to violent behavior by the lecturer.
examples: The radicals tried to incite the students to violence.

incline forward.monolingual: to lean forward; to slant forward. _The earthquake-ravaged building inclined forward a little bit more and looked as if it was going to fall. _ My chair inclined forward and I kept feeling as if I were going to fall off.
examples: The earthquake-ravaged building inclined forward a little bit more and looked as if it was going to fall.

incline something forward.monolingual: to lean something forward; to make something slant forward. _Incline the light forward a little bit, so you can see better. _ The fence had been inclined slightly forward to make it harder to climb.
examples: Incline the light forward a little bit, so you can see better.

incline toward someone or something.monolingual: 1. to lean or slant toward someone or something. _ The piece of scenery inclined toward Roger very slowly and he jumped out of the way just in time. _ The tree inclined toward the direction of the wind.
examples: The piece of scenery inclined toward Roger very slowly and he jumped out of the way just in time.

inclined to do something.monolingual: to tend to do something; to lean toward doing something. _ Tom is inclined to tell jokes when he is with a group of people. _ I’m inclined to go to the beach tomorrow if it doesn’t rain.
examples: Tom is inclined to tell jokes when he is with a group of people.

increase by leaps and bounds.monolingual: Fig. to increase or grow by large increments. _The price of our stock is increasing by leaps and bounds.
examples: The price of our stock is increasing by leaps and bounds.

increase in something.monolingual: to grow or expand in some quality. _He increased in stature and wisdom. _The tree increased in size every year.
examples: He increased in stature and wisdom.

increase something by something.monolingual: to enlarge something by an amount or degree. _They increased the size of the house by two hundred square feet. _ The engine size on the new model has been increased by a small amount.
examples: They increased the size of the house by two hundred square feet.

increment something by something.monolingual: to increase a sum by a supplement [of a certain figure]. _ Increment the numbering by ten so that 1, 2, 3 becomes 10, 20,
examples: Increment the numbering by ten so that 1, 2, 3 becomes 10, 20, 30.

inculcate someone with something.monolingual: to touch or impress someone with some specific knowledge. _ The teacher sought to inculcate the students with the knowledge they needed. _ Her parents inculcated her with good manners.
examples: The teacher sought to inculcate the students with the knowledge they needed.

indicate something to someone.monolingual: to signify something to someone. (By speech, writing, or some other sign.) _ Karen indicated her agreement to the lawyer. _ Fred indicated his assent to me.
examples: Karen indicated her agreement to the lawyer.

indict someone for something.monolingual: [for a legal body] to arraign someone for a crime or name someone formally as the one accused of a crime. _The grand jury indicted her for murder. _ Then they indicted Max for grand larceny.
examples: The grand jury indicted her for murder.

indoctrinate someone into something.monolingual: to teach someone the ways of a group or some activity. _ The staff sought to indoctrinate Walter into the ways of office procedure. _ Todd indoctrinated Ken into camp life.
examples: The staff sought to indoctrinate Walter into the ways of office procedure.

indoctrinate someone with something.monolingual: to teach someone the official or fundamental knowledge about something. _They indoctrinated all their spies with the importance of being loyal to the death. _Ken indoctrinated Todd with revolutionary thinking.
examples: They indoctrinated all their spies with the importance of being loyal to the death.

induce labor in someone.monolingual: to cause the onset of childbirth in a mother-to-be. _ They decided to induce labor in the mother-to-be. _ They decided not to induce labor in Alice.
examples: They decided to induce labor in the mother-to-be.

induct someone into something.monolingual: 1. to conscript someone into the armed services; to bring a nonvolunteer into the armed services. _ They inducted Wally into the army in a little ceremony.
examples: They inducted Wally into the army in a little ceremony.

indulge in something.monolingual: 1. to take pleasure in doing something; to do something habitually. _ No, I don’t indulge in contact sports anymore. _We don’t indulge in strenuous activity.
examples: No, I don’t indulge in contact sports anymore.

indulge someone with something.monolingual: to grant someone the favor or privilege of something. _ Please indulge me with this one favor. _ He always indulged himself with dinner at a nice restaurant when he went into town.
examples: Please indulge me with this one favor.

*infatuated with someone or something.monolingual: to be in love with someone or something. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ She is infatuated with John. _ John is infatuated with chocolate ice cream.
examples: She is infatuated with John.

infect someone with something.monolingual: 1. to transmit diseasecausing organisms to someone. (Someone includes oneself.) _ Please don’t infect me with your cold germs. _ Somehow, she infected herself with the virus she was studying.
examples: Please don’t infect me with your cold germs.

infer something from something.monolingual: to reach a conclusion from something; to deduce facts from something, such as someone’s words, a situation, etc. _ What can we infer from the experience we have just had? _You should not infer anything from Sue’s remarks.
examples: You should not infer anything from Sue’s remarks.

*infested with something.monolingual: to be contaminated with a swarm or throng of some pest. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ All the campers are infested with lice. _ The dog is infested with ticks.
examples: All the campers are infested with lice.

inflate something with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to fill up something with air or some other gas. _ Jerry has to inf late all the balloons with helium. _ Ken inf lated the balloons with gas.
examples: Jerry has to inf late all the balloons with helium.

inform on someone.monolingual: to tell the authorities about someone; to tattle on someone. _ I am going to have to inform on you. _ Liz informed on Ken to their mother.
examples: I am going to have to inform on you.

inform someone of something.monolingual: to tell someone a fact. _ Please inform Sally of my decision. _ Sally has been informed of your decision.
examples: Please inform Sally of my decision.

inform someone on someone.monolingual: to tattle (on someone) (to someone). _ I will inform the teacher on you! _ Billy informed his mother on Bobby.
examples: Billy informed his mother on Bobby.

infuse someone with something.monolingual: to teach someone a body of knowledge or a perspective on a body of knowledge. _ The schools sought to infuse the children with a sense of history. _ Children should be infused with a respect for the rights of others.
examples: The schools sought to infuse the children with a sense of history.

infuse something into someone.monolingual: to instill specific knowledge into a person; to teach someone something very well. _ The boss infused a lot of company information into the new assistant before she took another job. _ The teacher infused a lot of knowledge into the students in a sho
examples: The boss infused a lot of company information into the new assistant before she took another job.

infuse something into something.monolingual: to mix something into something. _ You should infuse this mixture into the tea. _ The tea was infused into the water very slowly.
examples: You should infuse this mixture into the tea.

infuse something with something.monolingual: to make something mix into some liquid. _ He infused the mixture with a strong solution of soap. _ The chemical mixture was infused with the other solution.
examples: He infused the mixture with a strong solution of soap.

ingratiate oneself into something.monolingual: to work hard to bring oneself into the favor of someone. _ Oh, how he fawns over the guests! Isn’t it terrible the way he tries to ingratiate himself into their favor? _ You will never succeed in ingratiating yourself into my good graces.
examples: You will never succeed in ingratiating yourself into my good graces.

ingratiate oneself with someone.monolingual: to work oneself into someone’s favor. _ Why do you have to ingratiate yourself with everyone? Don’t you know how to be just plain friends? _ She was very obvious in her effort to ingratiate herself with the boss.
examples: She was very obvious in her effort to ingratiate herself with the boss.

inherit something from someone.monolingual: 1. to receive something from the estate of a person who has died. _ I inherited this silver bowl from my aunt. _ Liz inherited her house from her parents.
examples: I inherited this silver bowl from my aunt.

inhibit someone from doing something.monolingual: to keep someone from doing something. _We will attempt to inhibit Karen from doing it, but we have no control over her. _ A serious case of shyness inhibited Harry from participating in things.
examples: We will attempt to inhibit Karen from doing it, but we have no control over her.

inhibit something from doing something.monolingual: to keep something from happening. _We need to inhibit the weeds from further growth. _ The weeds were inhibited from spreading by the application of a pesticide.
examples: We need to inhibit the weeds from further growth.

initiate someone into something.monolingual: 1. to induct someone into an organization or activity, usually in a ceremony. _They will initiate me into the fraternity next week. _ They initiated all their new members into the club at once.
examples: They will initiate me into the fraternity next week.

inject something into something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to squirt something, such as oil, water, etc., into something. _ The pump injected the oil into the wheel bearings when I squeezed the lever. _ The mechanic injected a solvent into the lock.
examples: The pump injected the oil into the wheel bearings when I squeezed the lever.

ink something in†.monolingual: 1. to fill in an outline with ink. _ Please ink the drawing in with care. _Ink in the drawing carefully.
examples: Please ink the drawing in with care.

inlay something with something.monolingual: to decorate something by cutting in a design and filling the cut with some decorative substance. _ The workers inlaid the tabletop with bits of polished seashell. _The tabletop was inlaid with a lovely design.
examples: The workers inlaid the tabletop with bits of polished seashell.

inoculate someone against something.monolingual: to immunize someone against a disease. _ We need to inoculate all the children against whooping cough. _ Have you been inoculated against measles?
examples: We need to inoculate all the children against whooping cough.

inoculate someone with something.monolingual: to use a particular substance in immunizing someone against a disease. _ Donna inoculated Richard and Nancy with yellow fever vaccine for their trip. _ She also inoculated Sam with something to prevent malaria.
examples: Donna inoculated Richard and Nancy with yellow fever vaccine for their trip.

inquire about someone or something.monolingual: to ask about someone or something. _ I inquired about Tom and was told that he doesn’t live here anymore. _You will have to inquire about that at the front desk.
examples: I inquired about Tom and was told that he doesn’t live here anymore.

inquire after someone.monolingual: to ask about the well-being of someone. _Jerry inquired after you when I saw him at the store today. _ I will inquire after his wife the next time I see him. creature
examples: Jerry inquired after you when I saw him at the store today.

inquire for someone.monolingual: to ask to see someone. _ Mr. Franklin, there is a man out here inquiring for you. What shall I tell him? _ Who is inquiring for me?
examples: Mr. Franklin, there is a man out here inquiring for you.

inquire into something.monolingual: to look into something; to investigate something by asking questions. _ I will inquire into your complaint. It sounds as if something is wrong. _ We have not inquired into it yet.
examples: I will inquire into your complaint.

inquire something of someone.monolingual: to ask some information of someone. _ I need to inquire something of you. _ May I inquire something personal of you?
examples: I need to inquire something of you.

inquire within.monolingual: to ask questions of a person inside [some place, such as a store or office]. (Formula. On a sign posted outside.) _“Help wanted. Inquire within,” read the sign on the door. _ If you want to apply, you must inquire within.
examples: “Help wanted. Inquire within,” read the sign on the door.

inscribe something into something.monolingual: to write or engrave a dedication on a gift to someone. (Emphasis is on the act of inscribing.) _ It was a lovely watch. I asked them to inscribe something into the back, so I could remember the occasion. _ My initials were inscribed into the wristban
examples: It was a lovely watch.

inscribe something with something.monolingual: to engrave something with a message. _ Could you please inscribe this trophy with the information on this sheet of paper? _ I inscribed the bracelet with her name.
examples: I inscribed the bracelet with her name.

inside a week.monolingual: in less than a week. _We must get all this sorted out inside a week; all right? _We’ve got inside a week to get it right.
examples: We’ve got inside a week to get it right.

inside information.monolingual: information known only by those most involved with the issue; secret information relating to an organization. _I have some inside information about the Smith Company.
examples: I have some inside information about the Smith Company.

an inside job.monolingual: a crime committed by someone working or living at the scene of the crime. _ There was little doubt that it was an inside job, thought the inspector. _It’s a particularly cunning way to carry out an inside job.
examples: There was little doubt that it was an inside job, thought the inspector.

an inside joke.monolingual: a joke that only certain people understand; a joke understood only by people who know certain facts and context. _ What you said must be an inside joke. It makes no sense to me.
examples: What you said must be an inside joke.

the inside story.monolingual: an explanation known only by those most involved with the issue. _Well, I’ve heard the inside story, and it isn’t what you were told at all!

*the inside track.monolingual: Fig. an advantage (over someone) gained through special connections, special knowledge, or favoritism. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ If I could get the inside track, I could win the contract. _The boss likes me. Since I’ve got the in
examples: If I could get the inside track, I could win the contract.

insinuate oneself into something.monolingual: to work oneself into a group or situation. _ She had sought for years to insinuate herself into Terry’s organization. _ Must you always insinuate yourself into my set of friends?
examples: She had sought for years to insinuate herself into Terry’s organization.

insinuate something to someone.monolingual: to hint at something to someone; to imply something to someone. _ You think I am interested in you for your money! Is that what you are insinuating to me? _ I did not insinuate anything to you!

inspire someone with something.monolingual: to use something to inspire someone; to stimulate or encourage someone with something. _ The president inspired us all with patriotic speeches. _ She inspired us all with her story of heroism.
examples: The president inspired us all with patriotic speeches.

inspire something in someone.monolingual: to stimulate a particular quality in someone. _You do not particularly inspire trust in me. _ She inspires fear in me.
examples: You do not particularly inspire trust in me.

install someone as something.monolingual: to inaugurate or launch someone into the role of something. _The board installed Jerry as the new parliamentarian. _She installed herself as the boss of the kitchen and wouldn’t allow anyone else in.
examples: The board installed Jerry as the new parliamentarian.

instigate someone to do something.monolingual: to prompt someone to do something; to urge or cause someone to do something. _Are you the one who instigated Terry to start all this trouble? _ Did you instigate the children to do this?

instill someone with something.monolingual: to imbue or impress someone with something. _ Her story instilled us all with courage. _ She instilled us with courage.
examples: Her story instilled us all with courage.

instruct someone in something.monolingual: to teach someone about something. _ Amy will instruct you in the way to hang paper. _ The manager instructed Ken in the best method of entering data into the computer.
examples: Amy will instruct you in the way to hang paper.

instrumental in doing something.monolingual: playing an important part in doing something. _ John was instrumental in getting the contract to build the new building. _ Our senator was instrumental in defeating the bill.
examples: John was instrumental in getting the contract to build the new building.

insure against something.monolingual: to guard or protect against something. _ You must insure against theft and fire. _ I will insure against all risks.
examples: You must insure against theft and fire.

integrate someone with someone.monolingual: to mix people together; to unify people into one group. _The new regional YMCA will help Hispanics integrate with others in our community. _ They integrated themselves with the people already in attendance.
examples: The new regional YMCA will help Hispanics integrate with others in our community.

integrate something with something.monolingual: to merge things together; to join things into one. _ I want to integrate the accounting department with the auditing department to save a little money. _They integrated your department with mine.
examples: I want to integrate the accounting department with the auditing department to save a little money.

intend something as something.monolingual: to mean something to serve as something. _ We intend this money as a gift. Do not even think about paying it back. _ This money is intended as a gift.
examples: We intend this money as a gift.

intent on doing something.monolingual: determined to do something. _ The children were intent on making a snowman. _ The prisoner was intent on escaping.
examples: The children were intent on making a snowman.

inter someone in something.monolingual: to bury someone in something or in some place. _ They chose to inter her in the family burial plot. _ She was interred in the vault with the rest of the family.
examples: They chose to inter her in the family burial plot.

interact with someone.monolingual: to converse with and exchange ideas with someone. _ In act two, I want Terri to interact with Amy a little more. They act as if they never even met each other. _ The students will interact with one another in their study projects.
examples: In act two, I want Terri to interact with Amy a little more.

interact with something.monolingual: to have a reciprocal action with something; to react with something. (Often refers to the negative consequences of interaction.) _ Will this drug interact with coffee? _This drug will not interact with your current medication.
examples: This drug will not interact with your current medication.

interchange someone with someone else.monolingual: to exchange one person for another. _ I interchanged Sally with Roger for the honor of being first speaker. _ Roger has been interchanged with Sally.
examples: I interchanged Sally with Roger for the honor of being first speaker.

interchange something with something.monolingual: to exchange one thing for another. _Please interchange the orange one with the purple one. _ The orange one has been interchanged with the red one.
examples: Please interchange the orange one with the purple one.

interest someone in something.monolingual: to cause someone to wish to purchase something. _ Could I interest you in something with a little more style to it? _ Can I interest you in some additional insurance on your life?

interface with someone or something.monolingual: to develop a connection or interaction with someone or something. _Call Walter and set up a meeting so we can interface with him. _This computer is meant to interface with as many as five others just like it.
examples: Call Walter and set up a meeting so we can interface with him.

interfere in something.monolingual: to meddle in something; to become involved in someone else’s business. _ Don’t interfere in my business! _ Are you interfering in this matter again?

interfere with someone or something.monolingual: to meddle with something or someone’s affairs. _ Please do not interfere with us. _ Are you interfering with my project?
examples: Please do not interfere with us.

interject someone into something.monolingual: to force someone into something, usually into someone else’s business. _ I am going to have to interject Fred into this matter before it gets out of hand. _ I hate to interject myself into your affairs, but I have something to say.
examples: I am going to have to interject Fred into this matter before it gets out of hand.

interject something into something.monolingual: to volunteer information or a comment into a conversation. _ We can always count on Liz to interject something sensible into our discussions. _At last, something sensible has been interjected into our discussions.
examples: We can always count on Liz to interject something sensible into our discussions.

interlace something with something.monolingual: to weave something into something else. _ I will interlace some silver thread with the white yarn. _ The manufacturer had interlaced a silver thread into the yarn.
examples: I will interlace some silver thread with the white yarn.

intermarry with someone.monolingual: [for members of a group] to marry into another group, race, or clan. _ Our people don’t intermarry with people of that clan. _ They do not intermarry with other groups on purpose.
examples: Our people don’t intermarry with people of that clan.

intermingle something with something.monolingual: to mingle or merge things with things. _Don’t intermingle the U.S. mail with the interoffice mail. _ The office mail had been intermingled with the regular mail!
examples: Don’t intermingle the U.

intermingle with someone.monolingual: to mingle or merge with people. _ The mugger intermingled with the people on the street and could not be recognized. _Let’s intermingle with the guests.
examples: The mugger intermingled with the people on the street and could not be recognized.

intern someone in something.monolingual: to detain or imprison a person in something. _ The government interned the enemy prisoners in the camps for a few months. _He was interned in a prison camp during the war.
examples: The government interned the enemy prisoners in the camps for a few months.

interpret for someone.monolingual: to translate speech in a foreign language for someone. (Interpreting is done in real time.) _ Nina interpreted for Michael, since he understood very little Russian. _ Is there someone who can interpret for me?
examples: Nina interpreted for Michael, since he understood very little Russian.

interpret something as something.monolingual: to assume that something means something. _Don’t interpret what I just said as criticism. _ It will be interpreted as criticism no matter what you say.
examples: Don’t interpret what I just said as criticism.

interpret something for someone.monolingual: 1. to translate a foreign language for someone. (Interpreting is done in real time.) _ Could you interpret the ambassador’s address for me? _ Nina interpreted the director’s greetings for the visitors.
examples: Nina interpreted the director’s greetings for the visitors.

intersperse something among something.monolingual: to place something among things at random. _ We interspersed a few chocolate doughnuts among all the plain ones. _Some chocolate ones had been interspersed among the plain ones.
examples: We interspersed a few chocolate doughnuts among all the plain ones.

join up.monolingual: to join some organization. _ The club has opened its membership rolls again. Are you going to join up? _ I can’t afford to join up.
examples: The club has opened its membership rolls again.

joined at the hip.monolingual: Sl. closely connected; always together. _Those two are joined at the hip. They are always together. _ Sam and Martha are joined at the hip.
examples: Those two are joined at the hip.

the joke is on someone..monolingual: 1. Someone is the butt of the joke. _ The joke is on Bob, so it’s good that he is a good sport.
examples: The joke is on Bob, so it’s good that he is a good sport.

jolt someone out of something.monolingual: to startle someone out of inertness. _ The cold water thrown in her face was what it took to jolt Mary out of her deep sleep. _ At the sound of the telephone, he jolted himself out of his stupor.
examples: The cold water thrown in her face was what it took to jolt Mary out of her deep sleep.

jostle someone around†.monolingual: to push or knock someone around. _ Please don’t jostle me around. _ Don’t jostle around everyone!
examples: Please don’t jostle me around.

jostle someone aside†.monolingual: to push or nudge someone aside. _ Poor little Timmy was jostled aside by the crowd every time he got near the entrance. _ The big kids jostled aside all the little ones.
examples: Poor little Timmy was jostled aside by the crowd every time he got near the entrance.

jostle with someone.monolingual: to struggle with someone. _ Andy jostled with Fred for access to the door. _Timmy and Bobby jostled with one another while they were waiting to get in.
examples: Andy jostled with Fred for access to the door.

jot something down†.monolingual: to make a note of something. _ This is important. Please jot this down. _ Jot down this note, please.
examples: This is important.

juggle someone or something around†.monolingual: to alter the position or sequence of someone or something. _ We will juggle everyone around so that the second round of interviews are in a different order. _ I think I can juggle my schedule around so I can have lunch with you. _Please juggle around
examples: We will juggle everyone around so that the second round of interviews are in a different order.

juice and cookies.monolingual: trivial and uninteresting snacks or refreshments. _The party was not much. Nothing but juice and cookies. _After juice and cookies, we all went back into the meeting room for another hour of talk, talk, talk.
examples: The party was not much.

juice something back†.monolingual: Sl. to drink all of something alcoholic, quickly. _He juiced a beer back. _Max juiced back another beer.
examples: He juiced a beer back.

juice something up†.monolingual: 1. Sl. to make something more powerful. _How much did it cost to juice this thing up? _Wally juiced up his car.
examples: Wally juiced up his car.

juice up.monolingual: Sl. to drink one or more alcoholic drinks. _Hey, man, let’s go out and juice up tonight. _ Stop juicing up every night.
examples: Hey, man, let’s go out and juice up tonight.

jumble someone or something together.monolingual: to mix people or things together randomly into a hodgepodge. _They just jumbled everything together and made a real mess. _ The army just jumbled everybody together, no matter what their skills and talents were.
examples: They just jumbled everything together and made a real mess.

jumble something together.monolingual: to assemble something clumsily and hastily. _ They just jumbled some holiday decorations together. It really wasn’t very well done. _ I hope this airplane wasn’t jumbled together as badly as this meal.
examples: They just jumbled some holiday decorations together.

jumble something up†.monolingual: to make a hodgepodge out of things. _ Who jumbled my papers up? _ Who jumbled up all my papers?

jump across something.monolingual: to leap over something that is broad rather than tall. _ The frog jumped across the puddle. _ Timmy tried but failed to jump across the puddle.
examples: The frog jumped across the puddle.

jump at someone or something.monolingual: to jump in the direction of someone or something. _ The frog jumped at me, but I dodged it. _ The cat jumped at the leaf as it fell from the tree.
examples: The frog jumped at me, but I dodged it.

jump at something.monolingual: Fig. to seize the opportunity to do something. .) _ When I heard about John’s chance to go to England, I knew he’d jump at it. _ If something you really want to do comes your way, jump at it.
examples: When I heard about John’s chance to go to England, I knew he’d jump at it.

jump clear of something.monolingual: Fig. to get out of the way of something; to leap off something before it crashes. _ I barely had time to jump clear of the oncoming truck. _ I jumped clear of the ball as it came my way.
examples: I barely had time to jump clear of the oncoming truck.

jump down something.monolingual: to leap downward into or through something. _ The rats jumped down the manhole. _ Timmy jumped down the stairs on the morning of his birthday party.
examples: The rats jumped down the manhole.

jump from something to something.monolingual: to leap from one place to another. _ A frog jumped from lily pad to lily pad. _ The child jumped from stone to stone.
examples: A frog jumped from lily pad to lily pad.

*the jump on someone.monolingual: a chance to do something before someone else. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ Each reporter is trying to get the jump on the others with the story about the earthquake. _ Kelly finally got the jump on Sam.
examples: Each reporter is trying to get the jump on the others with the story about the earthquake.

jump on someone or something.monolingual: to pounce on someone or something. _ The cat jumped on the mouse. _ Max jumped on the unsuspecting tourist and robbed him.
examples: The cat jumped on the mouse.

jump out of something.monolingual: to leap from something. _A mouse jumped out of the cupboard and scared me. _I jumped out of bed and ran to answer the telephone.
examples: A mouse jumped out of the cupboard and scared me.

jump over something.monolingual: to leap over or across something. _ The fellow named Jack jumped over a candle placed on the f loor. _Puddles are to be jumped over, not waded through.
examples: The fellow named Jack jumped over a candle placed on the f loor.

jump over the broomstick.monolingual: Rur. to get married. _ Jim and Jane have decided to jump over the broomstick. _ The happiest day of my life was when your mother said she’d jump over the broomstick with me.
examples: Jim and Jane have decided to jump over the broomstick.

jump ship.monolingual: 1. Lit. to leave one’s job on a ship and fail to be aboard it when it sails; [for a sailor] to go AWOL. _ One of the deckhands jumped ship at the last port.
examples: One of the deckhands jumped ship at the last port.

jump the gun.monolingual: Fig. to start before the starting signal. (Originally used in sports contests that are started by firing a gun.) _We all had to start the race again because Jane jumped the gun. _When we took the test, Tom jumped the gun and started early.
examples: We all had to start the race again because Jane jumped the gun.

jump the track.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to fall or jump off the rails or guides. (Usually said about a train.) _ The train jumped the track, causing many injuries to the passengers. _ The engine jumped the track, but the other cars stayed on.
examples: The train jumped the track, causing many injuries to the passengers.

jump with something.monolingual: Fig. to be very active with excitement or enthusiasm. _The crowd was jumping with enthusiasm. _ The bar was jumping with young people.
examples: The crowd was jumping with enthusiasm.

junk mail.monolingual: annoying, unsolicited mail, such as promotional letters, etc. _I am so incredibly tired of getting pound after pound of junk mail every day. I could just scream.
examples: I am so incredibly tired of getting pound after pound of junk mail every day.

just a minute.monolingual: only a short time; [wait] a short period of time. _ I’m almost done. I’ll be there in just a minute! _ Could I have just a minute of your time?
examples: I’m almost done.

just in case.monolingual: in the event that (something happens). _All right. I’ll take it just in case. _ I’ll take along some aspirin, just in case.
examples: All right. I’ll take it just in case.

just in time.monolingual: at the last possible time. _He got to the meeting just in time. They had just started the topic he was supposed to talk about.
examples: He got to the meeting just in time.

just like that.monolingual: in just the way it happened or was stated; without any [further] discussion or comment. _Sue: You can’t walk out on me just like that. John: I can too. Just watch! _ Mary: And then she slapped him in the face, just like that! Sally: She can be so rud
examples: Sue: You can’t walk out on me just like that.

just off the boat.monolingual: Fig. to be newly immigrated and perhaps gullible and naive. _I’m not just off the boat. I know what’s going on. _ He may act like he’s just off the boat, but he’s very savvy.
examples: I’m not just off the boat.

just one’s cup of tea.monolingual: Fig. to be something that one prefers or desires. _ This spy novel is just my cup of tea. _ Teaching children to read is just my cup of tea.
examples: This spy novel is just my cup of tea.

just passing through.monolingual: just moving through an area and not stopping. _We didn’t stop in Moose Jaw. We were just passing through.
examples: We didn’t stop in Moose Jaw.

just so.monolingual: 1. in perfect order; neat and tidy. _ Her hair is always just so. _ Their front yard is just so.
examples: Her hair is always just so.

just the ticket.monolingual: Fig. to be just the perfect thing. _ This soup is just the ticket for a quick lunch. _ A good, hot cup of coffee will be just the ticket.
examples: This soup is just the ticket for a quick lunch.

just what the doctor ordered.monolingual: Fig. exactly what is required, especially for health or comfort. _ That meal was delicious, Bob. Just what the doctor ordered. _ Bob: Would you like something to drink? Mary: Yes, a cold glass of water would be just what the doctor ordered.
examples: That meal was delicious, Bob.

justify something by something.monolingual: to try to explain why something needs doing or why it is acceptable to do something. _ You cannot justify violence by quoting proverbs. _ Your action was totally justified by the circumstances.
examples: You cannot justify violence by quoting proverbs.

justify something to someone.monolingual: to explain something to someone and show why it is necessary. _Please try to justify this to the voters. _ I can justify your action to no one.
examples: Please try to justify this to the voters.

a kangaroo court.monolingual: a bogus or illegal court. _Is this a staff meeting or a kangaroo court? _You have turned this interview into a kangaroo court.
examples: You have turned this interview into a kangaroo court.

katie bar the door.monolingual: Prepare immediately for an advancing threat. _Katie bar the door, the grandchildren are here and they all look hungry.
examples: Katie bar the door, the grandchildren are here and they all look hungry.

keel over.monolingual: [for a person] to fall over or fall down in a faint or in death. _ It was so hot in the room that two people just keeled over.
examples: It was so hot in the room that two people just keeled over.

keel something over†.monolingual: Rur. to push something over. _ He leaned on the f limsy wall and keeled it right over. _ The high wind keeled over that sorry old fence.
examples: He leaned on the f limsy wall and keeled it right over.

keen on doing something.monolingual: willing or eager to do something. _ Dave isn’t very keen on going to the opera. _ The children are keen on swimming this afternoon. Shall I take them?
examples: Dave isn’t very keen on going to the opera.

keep a secret.monolingual: to know a secret and not tell anyone. _ Please keep our little secret private. _ Do you know how to keep a secret?
examples: Please keep our little secret private.

keep a stiff upper lip..monolingual: Prov. Act as though you are not upset.; Do not let unpleasant things upset you. (English people are stereotypically supposed to be very good at keeping a stiff upper lip.) _Even though he was only three years old, Jonathan kept a stiff upper lip the
examples: Even though he was only three years old, Jonathan kept a stiff upper lip the whole time he was in the hospital recovering from his surgery.

keep at it!.monolingual: Keep doing what you are doing!; Keep trying! (Said as encouragement to keep working at something.) _ The boss told me to keep at it every time he passed my desk. _ Keep at it, Tom! You can do it!
examples: The boss told me to keep at it every time he passed my desk.

keep at something.monolingual: to persist at doing something; to continue trying to do something. _ John kept at his painting until the whole house was done. _ Keep at the job if you want to get it finished.
examples: John kept at his painting until the whole house was done.

keep banker’s hours.monolingual: Fig. to work or be open for business for less than eight hours a day. _ The advertising agency keeps banker’s hours. They are only open until four. _ James doesn’t really work full-time. He keeps banker’s hours.
examples: The advertising agency keeps banker’s hours.

keep body and soul together.monolingual: Fig. to manage to keep existing, especially when one has very little money. (Compare this with keep the wolf from the door.) _ We hardly had enough to keep body and soul together. _I don’t earn enough money to keep body and soul together.
examples: We hardly had enough to keep body and soul together.

keep cool.monolingual: Inf. to stay calm and undisturbed. _ Relax, man, keep cool! _If Sally could just keep cool before a race, she could probably win.
examples: If Sally could just keep cool before a race, she could probably win.

keep faith with someone.monolingual: to be loyal to someone. _ I intend to keep faith with my people and all they stand for. _ We could not keep faith with them any longer.
examples: I intend to keep faith with my people and all they stand for.

keep fit.monolingual: to keep in good physical condition. _ I do everything I can to keep fit.
examples: I do everything I can to keep fit.

keep from something.monolingual: to avoid doing something; to refrain from doing something. _ How could I keep from crying? It was so sad! _ Try to keep from falling off the ladder.
examples: Try to keep from falling off the ladder.

keep good time.monolingual: [for a watch or clock] to be accurate. _ I have to return my watch to the store because it doesn’t keep good time. _ Mine keeps good time.
examples: I have to return my watch to the store because it doesn’t keep good time.

keep harping on something.monolingual: to continue to talk or complain about something; to keep raising a topic of conversation. _Why do you keep harping on the same old complaint? _You keep harping on my problems and ignore your own!

keep house.monolingual: to manage a household. _ I hate to keep house. I’d rather live in a tent than keep house. _My grandmother kept house for nearly sixty years.
examples: I hate to keep house.

keep in good with someone.monolingual: to remain in someone’s favor. _ I always try to keep in good with the boss’s secretary. _ It’s also good to keep in good with the boss.
examples: I always try to keep in good with the boss’s secretary.

keep in there!.monolingual: Inf. Keep trying! _ Andy: Don’t give up, Sally. Keep in there! Sally: I’m doing my best! _ John: I’m not very good, but I keep trying. Fred: Just keep in there, John.
examples: Andy: Don’t give up, Sally.

keep in touch..monolingual: Good-bye. (Sometimes a sarcastic way of saying good-bye to someone one doesn’t care about.) _ Nice talking to you. Keep in touch. _ Sorry, we can’t use you anymore. Keep in touch.
examples: Nice talking to you.

keep in training.monolingual: to maintain oneself in good physical condition. _ I try to keep in training so I will live longer. _ Try to keep in training.
examples: I try to keep in training so I will live longer.

keep it up!.monolingual: 1. Keep up the good work!; Keep on doing it.; Keep (on) trying. _ Jane: I think I’m doing better in calculus. John: Keep it up! _Sally: I can now jog for almost three miles. Fred: Great! Keep it up!
examples: Jane: I think I’m doing better in calculus.

keep late hours.monolingual: to stay up or stay out until very late at night. _ I’m always tired because I keep late hours. _ If I didn’t keep late hours, I wouldn’t sleep so late in the morning.
examples: I’m always tired because I keep late hours.

keep on an even keel.monolingual: Fig. to remain cool and calm. (Originally nautical.) _ If Jane can keep on an even keel and not panic, she will be all right. _Try to keep on an even keel and not get upset so easily.
examples: If Jane can keep on an even keel and not panic, she will be all right.

keep on keeping on.monolingual: Inf. keep trying; keep doing what you are doing. _ I do my best. I just keep on keeping on.
examples: I do my best. I just keep on keeping on.

keep on trucking.monolingual: Inf. to continue to do well; to continue to try. _ Just keep on trucking, man. _ All I can do is keep on trucking.
examples: Just keep on trucking, man.

keep on with something.monolingual: to continue with something. _ Just keep on with your work. Don’t pay any attention to me. _ Can I keep on with this while you are talking?
examples: Just keep on with your work.

keep one in one’s place.monolingual: to make someone stay in the proper rank or station. _ I guess you want to keep me in my place, is that right? _ I know enough to keep myself in my place.
examples: I know enough to keep myself in my place.

keep one’s chin up.monolingual: Fig. to keep one’s spirits high; to act brave and confident. _ Keep your chin up, John. Things will get better. _ Just keep your chin up and tell the judge exactly what happened.
examples: Keep your chin up, John.

keep one’s cool.monolingual: Inf. to remain calm and in control. _ Relax, man! Just keep your cool. _ It’s hard to keep your cool when you’ve been cheated.
examples: Relax, man! Just keep your cool.

keep one’s hands to oneself.monolingual: Fig. to refrain from touching anything or anyone; to refrain from punching or poking someone. _Won’t you keep your hands to yourself ? _ Keep your hands to yourself while we are in the toy store. _ I want you boys to stop fighting and keep your hands
examples: Keep your hands to yourself while we are in the toy store.

keep one’s head.monolingual: Fig. to remain calm and sensible when in an awkward situation that might cause a person to panic or go out of control. _ She was very angry. We had to calm her down and encourage her to keep her head. _ Always try to keep your head when others are pa
examples: She was very angry.

keep one’s head above water.monolingual: 1. Lit. to keep from drowning when swimming or floating. _ I was so tired I could hardly keep my head above water.
examples: I was so tired I could hardly keep my head above water.

keep one’s nose clean.monolingual: Fig. to keep out of trouble, especially trouble with the law. _ I’m trying to keep my nose clean by staying away from those rough guys. _John, if you don’t learn how to keep your nose clean, you’re going to end up in jail.
examples: I’m trying to keep my nose clean by staying away from those rough guys.

keep one’s opinions to oneself.monolingual: to stop mentioning one’s own opinions, especially when they disagree with someone else’s. _ You ought to keep your opinions to yourself rather than upset our guests. _Please keep your rude opinions to yourself!
examples: You ought to keep your opinions to yourself rather than upset our guests.

keep one’s own counsel.monolingual: Fig. to keep one’s thoughts and plans to oneself; to withhold from other people one’s thoughts and plans. _ Jane is very quiet. She tends to keep her own counsel. _ I advise you to keep your own counsel.
examples: Jane is very quiet.

keep one’s place.monolingual: Fig. to exhibit only the behavior appropriate to one’s position or status in life. _ When I complained about the food, they told me to keep my place! _ I suggest you keep your place until you’re in a position to change things.
examples: I suggest you keep your place until you’re in a position to change things.

keep one’s weather eye open.monolingual: Fig. to watch for something (to happen); to be on the alert (for something); to be on guard. _Some trouble is brewing. Keep your weather eye open. _Try to be more alert. Learn to keep your weather eye open.
examples: Some trouble is brewing.

keep one’s wits about one.monolingual: Fig. to remain rational when threatened or under stress; to keep one’s mind operating in a time of stress. _If Jane hadn’t kept her wits about her during the fire, things would have been much worse. _ I could hardly keep my wits about me.
examples: If Jane hadn’t kept her wits about her during the fire, things would have been much worse.

keep one’s word.monolingual: to uphold one’s promise; to do as one says. (The opposite of break one’s word.) _ I told her I’d be there to pick her up, and I intend to keep my word. _ Keeping one’s word is necessary in the legal profession.
examples: I told her I’d be there to pick her up, and I intend to keep my word.

keep oneself to oneself.monolingual: to remain aloof. _ He does tend to keep himself to himself. _ Keep yourself to yourself, and you’ll be all right there.
examples: He does tend to keep himself to himself.

keep smiling..monolingual: a good-bye phrase encouraging someone to have good spirits. _ John: Things are really getting tough. Sue: Well, just keep smiling. Things will get better. _ Bill: What a day! I’m exhausted and depressed. Bob: Not to worry. Keep smiling. Things will c
examples: John: Things are really getting tough.

keep someone at something.monolingual: to make sure someone continues to work at something. _ Please keep Walter at his chores. _ I was so sick I couldn’t keep myself at my work.
examples: Please keep Walter at his chores.

keep someone company.monolingual: to sit or stay with someone, especially someone who is lonely. _ I kept my uncle company for a few hours. _He was very grateful for someone to keep him company. He gets very lonely.
examples: I kept my uncle company for a few hours.

keep someone down.monolingual: to prevent someone from advancing or succeeding. _ His lack of a degree will keep him down. _ I don’t think that this problem will keep her down.
examples: His lack of a degree will keep him down.

keep someone from doing something.monolingual: to prevent someone from doing something. _ I kept the child from falling in the lake by grabbing his collar. _ I try to keep myself from overeating, but I seem to fail frequently.
examples: I kept the child from falling in the lake by grabbing his collar.

keep someone honest.monolingual: to manage to make someone behave honestly and fairly and tell the truth. _ I love to tell about our vacations, and my wife is usually with me to keep me honest.
examples: I love to tell about our vacations, and my wife is usually with me to keep me honest.

keep someone in sight.monolingual: to make sure that a person is visible at all times. _ He looks suspicious. Keep him in sight at all times. _ I cannot keep him in sight day and night.
examples: He looks suspicious.

keep someone in stitches.monolingual: Fig. to cause someone to laugh loud and hard, for a period of time. _ The comedian kept us in stitches for nearly an hour. _The teacher kept the class in stitches, but the students didn’t learn anything.
examples: The comedian kept us in stitches for nearly an hour.

keep someone on.monolingual: Fig. to retain someone in employment longer than is required or was planned. _ She worked out so well that we decided to keep her on. _Liz was kept on as a consultant.
examples: She worked out so well that we decided to keep her on.

keep someone on tenterhooks.monolingual: Fig. to keep someone in suspense. _ Don’t keep me on tenterhooks! Tell me your news! _We were all kept on tenterhooks waiting to find out what happened.
examples: We were all kept on tenterhooks waiting to find out what happened.

keep someone or something apart.monolingual: to keep someone away from someone else; to keep something away from something else. _ Try to keep the dogs and cats apart. _ Can you keep Bill and Bob apart?
examples: Try to keep the dogs and cats apart.

keep someone or something back†.monolingual: to hold someone or something in reserve. _ Keep back some of the food for an emergency. _ We are keeping Karen back until the other players have exhausted themselves.
examples: Keep back some of the food for an emergency.

keep someone or something down.monolingual: to hold someone or something in a hidden or protected position. _Try to keep Sam down where no one can see him. _ Please keep the noise down so Fred won’t know it’s a party when he comes in.
examples: Try to keep Sam down where no one can see him.

keep someone or something going.monolingual: to sustain someone or something. _I try to eat just enough food to keep me going. Enjoying food is just not an issue any more.
examples: I try to eat just enough food to keep me going.

keep someone or something together.monolingual: to keep things or a group of people together; to keep something, including a group of people, from falling apart. _ I hope we can keep our club together for a few more years. _ We will keep it together for a while longer. _Keep your toys together. Do
examples: I hope we can keep our club together for a few more years.

keep someone posted.monolingual: Fig. to keep someone informed (of what is happening); to keep someone up to date. _ If the price of corn goes up, I need to know. Please keep me posted. _ Keep her posted about the patient’s status.
examples: If the price of corn goes up, I need to know.

keep someone up.monolingual: 1. Lit. to hold someone upright. _ Try to keep him up until I can get his bed made. _ Keep her up for a few minutes longer.
examples: Try to keep him up until I can get his bed made.

keep something by.monolingual: to keep something handy; to keep something in reserve, ready to be used. _ Keep this extra glue by in case you need it. _ This money had been kept by for just such an emergency.
examples: Keep this extra glue by in case you need it.

keep something down.monolingual: 1. Lit. to make the level of noise lower and keep it lower. _Please keep it down. You are just too noisy. _ Keep the noise down, or I will call the police.
examples: Please keep it down.

keep something from someone.monolingual: not to tell something to someone. _Why did you keep the news from me? I needed to know. _ This matter shouldn’t have been kept from me.
examples: Why did you keep the news from me? I needed to know.

keep something on†.monolingual: to continue to wear an article of clothing. _I’m going to keep my coat on. It’s a little chilly in here. _ I’ll keep on my coat, thanks.
examples: I’m going to keep my coat on.

keep something on its feet.monolingual: Fig. to keep something stable and viable. _ It takes a lot of effort to keep this old firm on its feet. We may have to go out of business. _ Can we keep this business on its feet another year?
examples: It takes a lot of effort to keep this old firm on its feet.

keep something to a minimum.monolingual: to make something as small, few, or little as possible. _Do what you can to keep construction dust to a minimum. _The dust should be kept to a minimum.
examples: Do what you can to keep construction dust to a minimum.

keep something to oneself.monolingual: to keep something a secret. _ I want you to keep this news to yourself. _This should be kept to yourself.
examples: I want you to keep this news to yourself.

keep something under one’s hat.monolingual: Fig. to keep something a secret; to keep something in one’s mind (only). (If the secret stays under your hat, it stays in your mind. Note the use of but in the examples.) _ Keep this under your hat, but I’m getting married. _I’m getting married, but
examples: Keep this under your hat, but I’m getting married.

keep something under wraps.monolingual: Fig. to keep something concealed (until some future time). _We kept the plan under wraps until after the election. _ The automobile company kept the new model under wraps until most of the old models had been sold.
examples: We kept the plan under wraps until after the election.

keep something until some time.monolingual: to retain something until a certain time. _ Can you keep this box until I call for it next week? _ The package will be kept until Monday.
examples: The package will be kept until Monday.

keep something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to hold or prop something up. _ Keep your side of the trunk up. Don’t let it sag. _ Keep up your side of the trunk.
examples: Keep your side of the trunk up.

keep something with someone.monolingual: to leave something in the care of someone. _ Can I keep my bicycle with you while I am gone? _ I can keep your bicycle with me.
examples: I can keep your bicycle with me.

keep the ball rolling.monolingual: 1. Lit. to keep a rolling ball moving. _ You have to throw hard enough to keep the ball rolling all the way to the bowling pins.
examples: You have to throw hard enough to keep the ball rolling all the way to the bowling pins.

keep the home fires burning.monolingual: Fig. to keep things going at one’s home or other central location. (From a World War I song.) _My uncle kept the home fires burning when my sister and I went to school. _ The manager stays at the office and keeps the home fires burning while I’m out
examples: My uncle kept the home fires burning when my sister and I went to school.

keep this to yourself..monolingual: a phrase introducing something that is meant to be a secret. _ Andy: Keep this to yourself, but I’m going to Bora Bora on my vacation. Henry: Sounds great. Can I go too? _John: Keep this to yourself. Mary and I are breaking up. Sue: I won’t tell a so
examples: Andy: Keep this to yourself, but I’m going to Bora Bora on my vacation.

keep time.monolingual: 1. Lit. to maintain a musical rhythm. _ Bob had to drop out of the band because he couldn’t keep time. _Since he can’t keep time, he can’t march, and he can’t play the drums.
examples: Bob had to drop out of the band because he couldn’t keep time.

keep to oneself.monolingual: to be solitary; to stay away from other people. _ Ann tends to keep to herself. She doesn’t have many friends. _ I try to keep to myself each morning so I can get some work done.
examples: Ann tends to keep to herself.

keep to something.monolingual: to adhere to an agreement; to follow a plan; to keep a promise. _ Please keep to the agreed-upon plan. _ Can you keep to what we agreed on?
examples: Please keep to the agreed-upon plan.

keep together.monolingual: to remain as a group. _ We will keep together to the very end. _ Our group decided to keep together.
examples: We will keep together to the very end.

keep under something.monolingual: to remain beneath something. _ Keep under the packing crate, Max. _ I ordered the dog to keep under the table.
examples: Keep under the packing crate, Max.

keep up appearances.monolingual: to make things look all right whether they are or not. _ We must keep up appearances even if it means little sacrifices here and there. _ Things may be unpleasant, but we will keep up appearances.
examples: We must keep up appearances even if it means little sacrifices here and there.

keep up the good work..monolingual: Please keep doing the good things that you are doing now. (A general phrase of encouragement.) _Father: Your grades are fine, Bill. Keep up the good work. Bill: Thanks, Dad. _ “Nice play,” said the coach. “Keep up the good work!”
examples: Father: Your grades are fine, Bill.

keep up with the joneses.monolingual: Fig. to try to match the lifestyle of one’s neighbors. _ I am tired of trying to keep up with the Joneses. Let’s just move if we can’t afford to live here. _ We never try to keep up with the Joneses.
examples: I am tired of trying to keep up with the Joneses.

keep up with the times.monolingual: Fig. to work to appear contemporary and fashionable. _ I am too old-fashioned. I have to keep up with the times better. _ I don’t care about keeping up with the times.
examples: I am too old-fashioned.

keep within something.monolingual: to remain within a thing or within the boundaries of something. _ If you keep within the tourist area, you will be safe. _Please keep within the yard.
examples: If you keep within the tourist area, you will be safe.

keep your chin up..monolingual: Fig. an expression of encouragement to someone who has to bear some emotional burdens. (Fixed order.) _Fred: I really can’t take much more of this. Jane: Keep your chin up. Things will get better. _ John: Smile, Fred. Keep your chin up. Fred: I guess
examples: Fred: I really can’t take much more of this.

keep your head down..monolingual: Fig. Lie low, try not to be noticed. _ My advice to you is to keep your head down for the moment. _ Keep your head down. It’ll blow over.
examples: My advice to you is to keep your head down for the moment.

keep your opinions to yourself!.monolingual: Fig. I do not want to hear your opinions! _ Jane: I think this room looks drab. Sue: Keep your opinions to yourself! I like it this way! _ Sally: You really ought to do something about your hair. It looks like it was in a hurricane. John: Keep your o
examples: Jane: I think this room looks drab.

key someone up†.monolingual: to cause someone to be anxious or excited. _ The excitement of the moment really keyed me up. _ Thoughts of their vacation keyed up the children so much they couldn’t sleep.
examples: The excitement of the moment really keyed me up.

the key to success.monolingual: Fig. the secret to someone’s success. _Bob said that the key to his success is working hard, being on time, and being extremely lucky.
examples: Bob said that the key to his success is working hard, being on time, and being extremely lucky.

kick about someone or something.monolingual: Fig. to complain about someone or something. _Why are you kicking about your cousin? What has he done now? _ They kicked about our regulations, but they finally accepted them. kick something kick against someone or something to give someone or someth
examples: They kicked about our regulations, but they finally accepted them.

kick at someone or something.monolingual: to make kicking motions toward someone or something. _ The horse kicked at me, but I knew it was just a threat. _ The boys kicked at the can aimlessly.
examples: The horse kicked at me, but I knew it was just a threat.

kick back.monolingual: 1. Inf. to relax; to lean back and relax. _ I really like to kick back and relax. _ It’s time to kick back and enjoy life.
examples: I really like to kick back and relax.

a kick in the guts.monolingual: Sl. a severe blow to one’s body or spirit. _ The news was a kick in the guts, and I haven’t recovered yet. _ I didn’t need a kick in the guts like that.
examples: The news was a kick in the guts, and I haven’t recovered yet.

kick one’s heels up†.monolingual: Fig. to act frisky; to be lively and have fun. (Somewhat literal when said of hoofed animals.) _ I like to go to an old-fashioned square dance and really kick up my heels. _ For an old man, your uncle is really kicking his heels up.
examples: I like to go to an old-fashioned square dance and really kick up my heels.

kick over the traces.monolingual: Fig. to do what one is meant not to do; to rebel against authority. (Alludes to a horse that steps on the wrong side of the straps that link it to whatever it is pulling.) _ At the age of sixty, Walter kicked over the traces and ran away to Brazil. _
examples: At the age of sixty, Walter kicked over the traces and ran away to Brazil.

kick someone or something aside†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to get someone or something out of the way by kicking. _The bully kicked Timmy aside and grabbed our cake. _I kicked aside the cats and came into the room.
examples: The bully kicked Timmy aside and grabbed our cake.

kick someone or something away†.monolingual: to force someone or something away by kicking. _ Fred kicked the intruder away from the gun he had dropped on the f loor. _ Then he kicked away the gun. _ The kickboxer kicked the mugger away.
examples: Fred kicked the intruder away from the gun he had dropped on the f loor.

kick something around†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to move something around by kicking it, as in play. _Kick the ball around awhile and then try to make a goal. _ The boys kicked a can around, making a lot of noise. _Don’t kick around all the dirt. You’ll make a mess.
examples: Kick the ball around awhile and then try to make a goal.

kick something down†.monolingual: to break down something by kicking. _ I was afraid they were going to kick the door down. _ Don’t kick down the door!
examples: I was afraid they were going to kick the door down.

kick something in†.monolingual: to break through something by kicking. _ Tommy kicked the door in and broke the new lamp. _ He kicked in the door by accident.
examples: Tommy kicked the door in and broke the new lamp.

kick up.monolingual: to cause trouble or discomfort. _ The ignition in my car is kicking up again. I will have to have it looked into. _ Aunt Jane’s arthritis is kicking up. She needs to see the doctor again.
examples: The ignition in my car is kicking up again.

kid’s stuff.monolingual: a very easy task. _ Climbing that hill is kid’s stuff. _ Driving an automatic car is kid’s stuff.
examples: Climbing that hill is kid’s stuff.

kill for something.monolingual: Sl. to be willing to go to extremes to get something that one really wants or needs. (An exaggeration.) _ I could kill for a cold beer.
examples: I could kill for a cold beer.

kill someone with kindness.monolingual: Fig. to be enormously kind to someone. _You are just killing me with kindness. Why? _ Don’t kill them with kindness.
examples: You are just killing me with kindness.

kill the fatted calf.monolingual: Fig. to prepare an elaborate banquet (in someone’s honor). (From the biblical story recounting the return of the prodigal son.) _When Bob got back from college, his parents killed the fatted calf and threw a great party. _ Sorry this meal isn’t much,
examples: When Bob got back from college, his parents killed the fatted calf and threw a great party.

kill time.monolingual: Fig. to use something up, especially time. _ I killed time reading a novel. _ The employees were not encouraged to kill time.
examples: I killed time reading a novel.

killed outright.monolingual: killed immediately. _The driver was killed outright in the accident. _ Twenty people were killed outright in the explosion.
examples: The driver was killed outright in the accident.

killer instinct.monolingual: Cliché an inborn desire or ability to be ruthless. _ Fred has a real killer instinct. He’s a difficult boss to work for.
examples: Fred has a real killer instinct.

*a king’s ransom.monolingual: Fig. a great deal of money. (To pay an amount as large as one might have to pay to get back a king held for ransom. *Typically: cost ~; pay ~; spend ~.) _ I would like to buy a nice watch, but I don’t want to pay a king’s ransom for it. _ It’s a love
examples: I would like to buy a nice watch, but I don’t want to pay a king’s ransom for it.

kink up.monolingual: [for something] to develop kinks or tangles. _The leather parts tend to shrink and kink up in the damp weather. _ My hair kinks up in this weather.
examples: The leather parts tend to shrink and kink up in the damp weather.

kiss and make up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for two people who have been arguing] to kiss each other and apologize. _ John apologized to his wife for disagreeing with her, and they finally kissed and made up.
examples: John apologized to his wife for disagreeing with her, and they finally kissed and made up.

kiss and tell.monolingual: Fig. to participate in something secret and private, and then tell other people about it. (In actual use, it usually refers to a person of the opposite sex even when it does not refer to actual kissing.) _The project was supposed to be a secret betwe
examples: The project was supposed to be a secret between Jane and me, but she spread it all around.

the kiss of death.monolingual: Fig. an act that puts an end to someone or something. _ The mayor’s veto was the kiss of death for the new law. _ Fainting on stage was the kiss of death for my acting career.
examples: The mayor’s veto was the kiss of death for the new law.

kiss off.monolingual: 1. Sl. to die. _ The cat is going to have to kiss off one of these days soon. _ The cat kissed off after eighteen years of joy and devotion.
examples: The cat is going to have to kiss off one of these days soon.

kiss someone off†.monolingual: Sl. to kill someone. _ Max kissed Lefty off with a small gun he carried in his boot. _ He kissed off Lefty with a small gun.
examples: Max kissed Lefty off with a small gun he carried in his boot.

kiss someone on something.monolingual: to kiss someone on a particular place. _He kissed her right on the tip of her nose. _She was kissed on the tip of her nose.
examples: He kissed her right on the tip of her nose.

kiss someone or something off†.monolingual: Fig. to dismiss someone or something lightly; to abandon or write off someone or something. _ I kissed off about $200 on that last deal. _ They kissed me off and that was the end of that job.
examples: I kissed off about $200 on that last deal.

kiss someone’s ass.monolingual: Sl. to fawn over someone; to flatter and curry favor with someone. (Potentially offensive. Use ass with discretion.) _ What does he expect me to do? Kiss his ass? _ I won’t kiss your ass for anything.
examples: I won’t kiss your ass for anything.

kiss something good-bye.monolingual: to anticipate or experience the loss of something. _ If you leave your camera on a park bench, you can kiss it good-bye. _ You kissed your wallet good-bye when you left it in the store.
examples: If you leave your camera on a park bench, you can kiss it good-bye.

kiss the dust.monolingual: Sl. to fall to the earth, because of death or because of being struck. _ I’ll see that you kiss the dust before sunset, cowboy! _ You’ll kiss the dust before I will, Sheriff.
examples: You’ll kiss the dust before I will, Sheriff.

kiss up to someone.monolingual: Sl. to flatter someone; to curry favor with someone. _ Edgar is in kissing up to the boss again. _ Stop kissing up to me.
examples: Edgar is in kissing up to the boss again.

kissing cousins.monolingual: relatives who know one another well enough to kiss when they meet. _ Joe and I are kissing cousins, though we ain’t seen one another since we was kids. _Technically, we’re second cousins once removed, but I just say we’re kissing cousins.
examples: Joe and I are kissing cousins, though we ain’t seen one another since we was kids.

kith and kin.monolingual: friends and relatives; people known to someone. _ I was delighted to find all my kith and kin waiting for me at the airport to welcome me home. _I sent cards to my kith and kin, telling them of my arrival.
examples: I was delighted to find all my kith and kin waiting for me at the airport to welcome me home.

klutz around.monolingual: Inf. to go about acting stupidly or clumsily. _ Stop klutzing around and get your act together. _ Why are you klutzing around so much?
examples: Stop klutzing around and get your act together.

*knee-deep in something.monolingual: 1. Fig. heavily involved in something. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ Right now, we are knee-deep in trouble.
examples: Right now, we are knee-deep in trouble.

a knee-jerk reaction.monolingual: Fig. an automatic or reflex reaction; an immediate reaction made without examining causes or facts. _ With one of his typical knee-jerk reactions, he said no immediately, citing some moral argument that no one understood.
examples: With one of his typical knee-jerk reactions, he said no immediately, citing some moral argument that no one understood.

kneel down.monolingual: to get down on one’s knees. _ Please kneel down and fold your hands. _You should at least kneel down and be quiet.
examples: Please kneel down and fold your hands.

knit one’s brow.monolingual: to cause one’s brow to wrinkle. _ Bob knitted his brow when he was confused. _ Jane knitted her brow because she was angry.
examples: Bob knitted his brow when he was confused.

knit something together†.monolingual: to join things together by knitting. _ Terry knitted the parts of the sweater together. _ Sally knitted together the two parts of the glove.
examples: Terry knitted the parts of the sweater together.

knit together.monolingual: [for broken bones] to join or grow together. _ The bones are knitting together exactly as expected. _ If the bones don’t knit together properly, we will have to do something a little more drastic.
examples: The bones are knitting together exactly as expected.

knock against someone or something.monolingual: to bump against someone or something. _ Mickey knocked against Mary and said he was sorry. _I didn’t mean to knock against your sore knee.
examples: Mickey knocked against Mary and said he was sorry.

knock at something.monolingual: to knock [on something] at a particular location. _I could hear someone knocking at the door next to mine. _ Who is knocking at the door?
examples: I could hear someone knocking at the door next to mine.

knock it off!.monolingual: Inf. Be quiet!; Stop that noise! Stop doing that! _ John: Hey, you guys! Knock it off! Bob: Sorry. Bill: Sorry. I guess we got a little carried away. _ Sue: All right. Knock it off! Bill: Yeah. Let’s get down to business.
examples: John: Hey, you guys! Knock it off! Bob: Sorry.
