knock on something.monolingual: to rap or tap, often with the knuckles, on something. _ She knocked on the door several times. _ Knock on it again. Maybe she didn’t hear you.
examples: She knocked on the door several times.

knock on wood.monolingual: to rap on something made of wood. (Said as a wish for good luck. Usually a phrase attached to another statement. Sometime said while knocking or rapping on real wood.) _ I think I am well at last—knock on wood. _ I knock on wood when I wish something
examples: I think I am well at last—knock on wood.

knock one’s knees together.monolingual: Fig. [for one’s knees] to shake together from fright. _I stood there freezing for ten minutes, knocking my knees together in the cold. _ It takes a lot of energy to knock your knees together.
examples: I stood there freezing for ten minutes, knocking my knees together in the cold.

knock over something.monolingual: 1. Sl. to steal something. (The over is usually before the object in this expression.) _The gang knocked over an armored car. _Some cheap crook knocked over a load of television sets.
examples: The gang knocked over an armored car.

knock some heads together.monolingual: Fig. to scold some people; to get some people to do what they are supposed to be doing. _ If you kids don’t quiet down and go to sleep, I’m going to come up there and knock some heads together. _ The government is in a mess. We need to go to Washingt
examples: If you kids don’t quiet down and go to sleep, I’m going to come up there and knock some heads together.

knock someone into something.monolingual: to strike one, sending one into something. _ The blow knocked him into the wall. _ Max knocked Lefty into a lamp post.
examples: The blow knocked him into the wall.

knock someone or something down†.monolingual: to thrust someone or something to the ground by hitting. _The force of the blast knocked us down. _It knocked down everyone in the room.
examples: The force of the blast knocked us down.

knock someone or something over†.monolingual: to push or strike someone or something, causing the person or the thing to fall. ; knock something over.) _ I am sorry. I didn’t mean to knock you over. Are you hurt? _ Who knocked over this vase?
examples: I am sorry. I didn’t mean to knock you over.

knock someone out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to knock someone unconscious. (Someone includes oneself.) _ Fred knocked Mike out and left him there in the gutter. _ Fred knocked out Mike.
examples: Fred knocked Mike out and left him there in the gutter.

knock someone’s block off.monolingual: Sl. to hit someone hard in the head. _Wilbur almost knocked Tom’s block off by accident. _He threatened to knock my block off if I didn’t do as I was told.
examples: Wilbur almost knocked Tom’s block off by accident.

knock someone some skin.monolingual: Sl. to slap hands with someone, a sign of friendship. _Hey, man, knock me some skin! _ Pete knocked Sam some skin, and they left the building together.
examples: Pete knocked Sam some skin, and they left the building together.

knock someone up†.monolingual: Inf. to make a woman pregnant. _ They say it was Willie who knocked her up. _ He did not knock up Sue. I did.
examples: They say it was Willie who knocked her up.

knock something against something.monolingual: to strike something against something. _ He knocked a chair against the table and tipped both pieces of furniture over. _ A chair was knocked against the table, upsetting a vase.
examples: He knocked a chair against the table and tipped both pieces of furniture over.

knock something back†.monolingual: Sl. to drink down a drink of something, especially something alcoholic. _ I don’t see how he can knock that stuff back. _ John knocked back two beers in ten minutes.
examples: I don’t see how he can knock that stuff back.

knock something down†.monolingual: 1. Sl. to drink a portion of liquor. _ Here, knock this down and let’s go. _ He knocked down a bottle of beer and called for another.
examples: Here, knock this down and let’s go.

knock something off†.monolingual: 1. to manufacture or make something, especially in haste. _ I’ll see if I can knock another one off before lunch. _ They knocked off four window frames in an hour.
examples: I’ll see if I can knock another one off before lunch.

knock something out†.monolingual: 1. to create something hastily. _He knocked a few out as samples. _ He knocked out a few of them quickly, just so we could see what they were going to look like.
examples: He knocked a few out as samples.

knock something out of someone.monolingual: to beat someone until something emerges or dissipates. _Max knocked the truth out of the spy. _ Lefty knocked the story out of Max.
examples: Max knocked the truth out of the spy.

knock something out of something.monolingual: to beat or knock on something until something comes out. _Timmy knocked the stuffing out of his pillow. _ Someone knocked the coins out of my piggy bank.
examples: Timmy knocked the stuffing out of his pillow.

knock something over†.monolingual: to tip something over. _ Someone knocked the chair over. _ Who knocked over the flower pot?
examples: Someone knocked the chair over.

knock something to someone.monolingual: to hit something, such as a ball, to someone. _ The coach knocked the ball to each player in turn. _The ball was knocked to the guy out in center field.
examples: The coach knocked the ball to each player in turn.

knock something together†.monolingual: to assemble something hastily. _ I knocked this model together so you could get a general idea of what I had in mind. _See if you can knock together a quick snack. _This thing has just been knocked together!
examples: I knocked this model together so you could get a general idea of what I had in mind.

knock the habit.monolingual: to stop using drugs; to break a drug addiction. _ I just can’t knock the habit. _ He tried to knock the habit by drinking lots of booze.
examples: I just can’t knock the habit.

knock through something.monolingual: to break through something. _ They knocked through the wall and put in a doorway. _The wall had to be knocked through before we could install a doorway.
examples: They knocked through the wall and put in a doorway.

knock-down, drag-out fight.monolingual: a serious fight; a serious argument. _ Boy, they really had a knock-down, drag-out fight. _ Stop calling each other names, or you’re going to end up with a real knock-down, drag-out fight.
examples: Boy, they really had a knock-down, drag-out fight.

knocked in.monolingual: Sl. arrested. (Underworld.) _ Would you believe that Larry has never been knocked in? _When Lefty was knocked in, they found his heat on him.
examples: When Lefty was knocked in, they found his heat on him.

knocked out.monolingual: 1. Lit. unconscious. _ The losing boxer lay on the canvas, knocked out.
examples: The losing boxer lay on the canvas, knocked out.

knocked up.monolingual: 1. Lit. battered; beaten. _ Sally was a little knocked up by the accident. _ This book is a little knocked up, so I’ll lower the price.
examples: Sally was a little knocked up by the accident.

knot something together†.monolingual: to tie something together in a knot. _ Knot these strings together and trim the strings off the knot. _ Are the ropes knotted together properly? _ Quickly knot together the two loose ends!
examples: Knot these strings together and trim the strings off the knot.

know a trick or two.monolingual: to know some special way of dealing with a problem. _ I think I can handle all of this with no trouble. I know a trick or two. _ I may be a senior citizen, but I still know a trick or two. I think I can help you with this.
examples: I think I can handle all of this with no trouble.

know about someone or something.monolingual: to have information or expertise about someone or something. _ I know about John and what he does. _ I know about cars, but I can’t fix this one!
examples: I know about John and what he does.

know all the angles.monolingual: to know all the tricks and artifices of dealing with someone or something. _Ask my accountant about taxes. He knows all the angles. _ Larry knows all the angles. That’s how he keeps out of the slammer.
examples: Ask my accountant about taxes.

know at a glance that....monolingual: to know [something] without much evidence; to know or understand something without a lot of observation. _ I knew at a glance that Bobbie was severely injured and had to be gotten to a hospital as soon as possible.
examples: I knew at a glance that Bobbie was severely injured and had to be gotten to a hospital as soon as possible.

know from something.monolingual: to know about something. (Used on the eastern seaboard.) _ Do you know from thermostats? _ You don’t know from anything!

know of someone or something.monolingual: to be aware of the existence of someone or something. _ I think I know of someone who can help you. _ I didn’t know of Wally’s arrival.
examples: I think I know of someone who can help you.

know one’s abcs.monolingual: Fig. to know the alphabet; to know the most basic things (about something). _Bill can’t do it. He doesn’t even know his ABCs. _ You can’t expect to write a letter when you don’t even know your ABCs.
examples: Bill can’t do it.

know one’s place.monolingual: to know the behavior appropriate to one’s position or status in life. _ I know my place. I won’t speak unless spoken to. _ People around here are expected to know their place. You have to follow all the rules.
examples: I know my place.

know someone as someone.monolingual: to know someone by a different name. _I know her as Candy La Tour. _She has been known as Mary Rogers since her marriage.
examples: I know her as Candy La Tour.

know someone by sight.monolingual: to recognize a person’s face, but not know the name. _I’m afraid I don’t know her by sight. _ I know all my employees by sight.
examples: I’m afraid I don’t know her by sight.

know someone from someone.monolingual: to tell the difference between one person and another. _I don’t know Fred from his twin brother. _ I know Bill from Bob, but I can’t tell most identical twins apart.
examples: I don’t know Fred from his twin brother.

know something by heart.monolingual: Fig. to know something perfectly; to have memorized something perfectly. _ I know my speech by heart. _ I went over and over it until I knew it by heart.
examples: I know my speech by heart.

know something from memory.monolingual: to have memorized something so that one does not have to consult a written version; to know something well from seeing it very often. (Almost the same as know something by heart.) _ Mary didn’t need the script because she knew the play from memory. _
examples: Mary didn’t need the script because she knew the play from memory.

know something from something.monolingual: to tell the difference between one thing and another. (Often with a negative.) _ You don’t know a smoked herring from a squid! _ She didn’t know a raven from a crow, and who does?

know something inside out.monolingual: to know something thoroughly; to know about something thoroughly. _ I know my geometry inside out. _I studied and studied for my driver’s test until I knew the rules inside out.
examples: I know my geometry inside out.

know something only too well.monolingual: to know something very well; to know something from unpleasant experience. (Note the variation in the examples.) _ I know the problem only too well. _ I know only too well the kind of problem you must face.
examples: I know the problem only too well.

know something through and through.monolingual: to know something very well. _ I want you to know this project through and through before the staff meeting. _ I know my part in the play through and through.
examples: I want you to know this project through and through before the staff meeting.

know thyself..monolingual: Prov. Be aware of your own limitations; know what you are capable of doing. (This was the motto inscribed on the temple of Apollo at Delphi.) _The motto of the ballet corps was “Know thyself ”; every dancer was expected to know how far she could stre
examples: The motto of the ballet corps was “Know thyself ”; every dancer was expected to know how far she could stretch, and not hurt herself by trying to exceed her limits.

know where it’s at.monolingual: to be alert and know how the world—or some part of it—really works. _Man, you just don’t know where it’s at! _ I don’t know where cool jazz is at.
examples: I don’t know where cool jazz is at.

know where something is at.monolingual: to know where something is located. (Without at, this sense is standard English. See also know where it’s at.) _Do you know where the hammer is at? _ I don’t know where my glasses are at.
examples: I don’t know where my glasses are at.

know whereof one speaks.monolingual: to know well the subject that one is speaking about. _ You are wrong! You do not know whereof you speak. _ He simply doesn’t know whereof he speaks.
examples: You are wrong! You do not know whereof you speak.

knowledge is power..monolingual: Prov. The more you know, the more you can control. _ Child: How come I have to study something) history? I don’t care what all those dead people did hundreds of years ago. Mother: Knowledge is power. If you know something about the past, it may help
examples: Child: How come I have to study something) history? I don’t care what all those dead people did hundreds of years ago.

known fact.monolingual: something that is generally recognized as a fact. _ That grass is green is a known fact. _ It is a known fact that John was in Chicago on the night of the murder.
examples: That grass is green is a known fact.

known quantity.monolingual: someone whose character, personality, and behavior are recognized and understood. _ We need not worry about how John will behave. He is a known quantity. _ Lisa is a known quantity and I am sure she will not surprise us by voting with the opposition.
examples: We need not worry about how John will behave.

*a knuckle sandwich.monolingual: Inf. a punch. (*Typically: ask for ~; get ~; give someone ~; want ~.) _A: Nyah! Your mother smokes cigars! B: You want a knuckle sandwich?

kowtow to someone or something.monolingual: to grovel to someone or something. _I won’t kowtow to anyone! _You don’t expect me to go in there and kowtow to that committee, do you?

labor at something.monolingual: to work hard at something. _ He is laboring at his gardening and won’t be back in the house until dinnertime. _ What are you laboring at so intensely?
examples: He is laboring at his gardening and won’t be back in the house until dinnertime.

labor for someone or something.monolingual: to work on behalf of someone or something. _ I labored for them all day, and they didn’t even thank me. _ I have labored for this cause for many years.
examples: I labored for them all day, and they didn’t even thank me.

labor for something.monolingual: to work in order to get something, such as money. _ I was laboring for a pittance, so I decided to get another job. _ I labor for the love of it.
examples: I was laboring for a pittance, so I decided to get another job.

a labor of love.monolingual: Fig. a task that is either unpaid or badly paid and that one does simply for one’s own satisfaction or pleasure or to please someone whom one likes or loves. _Jane made no money out of the biography she wrote. She was writing about the life of a frie
examples: Jane made no money out of the biography she wrote.

labor over someone or something.monolingual: to work hard on someone or something. _ The surgeon labored over the patient for four hours. _ I labored over this painting for months before I got it the way I wanted it.
examples: The surgeon labored over the patient for four hours.

labor under an assumption.monolingual: Fig. to function or operate believing something; to go about living while assuming something [that may not be so]. _ I was laboring under the idea that we were going to share the profits equally. _ Are you laboring under the notion that you are going
examples: I was laboring under the idea that we were going to share the profits equally.

lace someone into something.monolingual: to tighten the laces of something someone is wearing. _ Sally helped Billy lace himself into his boots. _ The maid laced Gloria into her corset.
examples: Sally helped Billy lace himself into his boots.

lace someone up†.monolingual: to tie someone’s laces; to help someone get dressed in a garment having laces. _Would you please lace me up? I can’t reach the ties in the back. _ I laced up Sally, as she requested.
examples: Would you please lace me up? I can’t reach the ties in the back.

lace something up†.monolingual: to tie the laces of something. _ Lace your shoes up, Tommy. _ Lace up your shoes.
examples: Lace your shoes up, Tommy.

lace something with something.monolingual: to adulterate something with something, often with something alcoholic. _Someone laced the punch with strong whiskey. _ Who laced my coffee with brandy?
examples: Someone laced the punch with strong whiskey.

lack for something.monolingual: to lack something. _ We don’t lack for new ideas. _ We lack for nothing, thank you.
examples: We don’t lack for new ideas.

ladies first..monolingual: an expression of courtesy indicating that women should go first, as in going through a doorway. _ Bob stepped back and made a motion with his hand indicating that Mary should go first. “Ladies first,” smiled Bob.
examples: Bob stepped back and made a motion with his hand indicating that Mary should go first.

a ladies’ man.monolingual: Fig. a man who likes the company of women and whose company is liked by women, the suggestion being that he likes to flirt with them. _ John is a real ladies’ man. He hates all-male parties. _The new boss is always f lirting with the women in the off
examples: John is a real ladies’ man.

ladle something up†.monolingual: to scoop something up in a ladle. _ Jerry ladled a cool dipper of water up and quenched his thirst. _ Please ladle up the soup and serve it.
examples: Jerry ladled a cool dipper of water up and quenched his thirst.

lady of the evening.monolingual: Euph. a prostitute. _ I saw several ladies of the evening down on Main Street. _ He was approached by a lady of the evening.
examples: I saw several ladies of the evening down on Main Street.

lag behind in something.monolingual: to fall behind in something. _ I am lagging behind in my car payments. _ She is lagging behind in her homework assignments.
examples: I am lagging behind in my car payments.

laid back.monolingual: 1. calm and relaxed. _Willie is not what I would call laid back. _You are really one laid-back guy!
examples: Willie is not what I would call laid back.

laid out.monolingual: 1. intoxicated. _ Man, you got yourself laid out! _ I’m too laid out to go to work today.
examples: I’m too laid out to go to work today.

laid up.monolingual: [of people or things] immobilized for recuperation or repairs. _I was laid up for two weeks after my accident. _ My car is laid up for repairs. _ I was laid up with the f lu for a week.
examples: I was laid up for two weeks after my accident.

lame duck.monolingual: 1. Fig. someone who is in the last period of a term in an elective office and cannot run for reelection. _ You can’t expect much from a lame duck. _ As a lame duck, there’s not a lot I can do.
examples: You can’t expect much from a lame duck.

land a blow.monolingual: 1. Lit. to strike someone. _ He kept moving, and I found it almost impossible to land a blow. _The boxer landed a blow to the face of his opponent.
examples: He kept moving, and I found it almost impossible to land a blow.

land a job.monolingual: to find a job and be hired. _ As soon as I land a job and start to bring in some money, I’m going to get a stereo. _ I managed to land a job at a factory.
examples: As soon as I land a job and start to bring in some money, I’m going to get a stereo.

land at some place.monolingual: 1. [for a ship] to come to port at a place. _ The ship landed at the wharf and the passengers got off. _ We landed at the island’s main city and waited for customs to clear us.
examples: The ship landed at the wharf and the passengers got off.

land in something.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for an airplane] to return to earth in or near a particular city. _ We landed in Chicago on time. _ They could not land in San Francisco, so they f lew on to Sacramento.
examples: We landed in Chicago on time.

land o’ goshen!.monolingual: Rur. My goodness gracious! (A mild oath. Goshen was an agricultural region in Egypt occupied by the Israelites before the Exodus.) _ Land o’ Goshen, it’s sure good to see you. _ Land o’ Goshen! Look at that rain come down!
examples: Land o’ Goshen, it’s sure good to see you.

the land of nod.monolingual: a state of sleep. (Humorous. From the fact that people sometimes nod when they are falling asleep.) _ The baby is in the land of Nod. _ Look at the clock! It’s time we were all in the land of Nod.
examples: The baby is in the land of Nod.

land someone in something.monolingual: to cause someone to end up in something. _ His criminal activity finally landed him in jail. _ You really landed yourself in a fine mess!
examples: His criminal activity finally landed him in jail.

land something at some place.monolingual: to bring a boat, ship, or airplane to rest or to port at or near a place. _ The captain landed the boat at a small island in hopes of finding a place to make repairs. _ They had to land the plane at a small town because of a medical emergency.
examples: The captain landed the boat at a small island in hopes of finding a place to make repairs.

land up somehow.monolingual: Fig. to end up in some way. _If you keep eating all those sweets, you’ll land up sick. _ Do you want to land up without a job?
examples: If you keep eating all those sweets, you’ll land up sick.

land up somehow or somewhere.monolingual: to finish somehow or somewhere; to come to be in a certain state or place at the end. _We set out for Denver but landed up in Salt Lake City. _ He’s so extravagant that he landed up in debt.
examples: We set out for Denver but landed up in Salt Lake City.

land-office business.monolingual: Fig. a large amount of business done in a short period of time. _ We always do a landoffice business at this time of year. _We keep going. Never do land-office business—just enough to make out.
examples: We always do a landoffice business at this time of year.

a landslide victory.monolingual: a victory by a large margin; a very substantial victory, particularly in an election. _ The mayor won a landslide victory in the election. _ The younger candidate won a landslide victory in the presidential election.
examples: The mayor won a landslide victory in the election.

language that would fry bacon.monolingual: Rur. profanity; swearing; curse words. (“Hot” language.) _ He carried on in language that would fry bacon. _ I was shocked when I heard that sweet little girl use language that would fry bacon.
examples: He carried on in language that would fry bacon.

languish in some place.monolingual: 1. to become dispirited in some place; to weaken and fade away in some place. _ Claire languished in prison for her crime. _I spent over three days languishing in a stuffy hotel room. _ We languished in the airport waiting room while they refueled th
examples: Claire languished in prison for her crime.

languish over someone or something.monolingual: to pine over someone or something. _There is no point in languishing over Tim. He’ll never come back. _ She wasted half her life languishing over her lost opportunities.
examples: There is no point in languishing over Tim.

the lap of luxury.monolingual: Fig. a luxurious situation. _ I rather enjoy living in the lap of luxury. _ You call this pigpen the lap of luxury?
examples: I rather enjoy living in the lap of luxury.

lap something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for an animal] to lick something up. _ The dog lapped the ice cream up off the f loor. _ The dog lapped up the ice cream.
examples: The dog lapped the ice cream up off the f loor.

lapse from grace.monolingual: 1. Lit. to fall out of favor with God. _ The child was told that if he ever smoked even one cigarette, he would lapse from grace for certain. _It is easy, these days, to lapse from grace.
examples: The child was told that if he ever smoked even one cigarette, he would lapse from grace for certain.

lapse into something.monolingual: to weaken or slip into something, especially a coma. _ The survivor of the crash lapsed into a coma. _Aunt Mary lapsed into unconsciousness and died.
examples: The survivor of the crash lapsed into a coma.

*large as life.monolingual: Fig. in person; actually, and sometimes surprisingly, present at a place. (*Also: as ~.) _ I thought Jack was away, but there he was as large as life. _ Jean was not expected to appear, but she turned up large as life.
examples: I thought Jack was away, but there he was as large as life.

larger than life.monolingual: Fig. [of someone] having an aura of greatness, perhaps not supported by the real person. _ Perry seemed larger than life to those who had only read about him. To the rest of us, he was a boor. _ To the children, the star athlete who spoke at the scho
examples: Perry seemed larger than life to those who had only read about him.

lash against something.monolingual: [for something, such as wind or water] to beat or whip heavily against something. _ The angry waves lashed against the hull of the boat, frightening the people huddled inside. _ The wind lashed against the house and kept us awake all night.
examples: The angry waves lashed against the hull of the boat, frightening the people huddled inside.

lash at someone or something.monolingual: to thrash or beat someone or something violently. _ The rain lashed at the windows. _ The mule driver lashed at his beasts with his whip.
examples: The rain lashed at the windows.

lash into something.monolingual: to begin to eat something with vigor. _ Mary lashed into the huge ice cream sundae, and ate almost the whole thing. _ The workers lashed into their lunches and did not say a word until they had finished.
examples: Mary lashed into the huge ice cream sundae, and ate almost the whole thing.

lash someone or something down†.monolingual: to tie someone or something down. _ The villain lashed Nell down to the railroad tracks. _He lashed down the innocent victim. _Lash that cask down so it doesn’t wash overboard.
examples: The villain lashed Nell down to the railroad tracks.

lash something about.monolingual: to whip or fling something about violently. _The big cat lashed its tail threateningly. _The strong wind lashed the tall grass about.
examples: The big cat lashed its tail threateningly.

lash something together.monolingual: to tie something or things together. _ Let’s lash these logs together and make a raft. _ Lash two or three of the poles together to make them stronger.
examples: Let’s lash these logs together and make a raft.

last but not least.monolingual: Cliché last in sequence, but not last in importance. (Often said when introducing people.) _The speaker said, “And now, last but not least, I’d like to present Bill Smith, who will give us some final words.” _ And last but not least, here is the fina
examples: The speaker said, “And now, last but not least, I’d like to present Bill Smith, who will give us some final words.

last for something.monolingual: 1. to exist for a period of time; to serve or function for a period of time. _ This condition has lasted for some time. _ Enjoy it while you can. It won’t last forever.
examples: This condition has lasted for some time.

the last hurrah.monolingual: Fig. a final appearance, as at the end of one’s career; the last time for doing something. _ Tom is retiring, and we are having a little party as his last hurrah right now. He won’t be here the next time you visit our offices.
examples: Tom is retiring, and we are having a little party as his last hurrah right now.

last out.monolingual: to hold out; to endure. _ How long can you last out? _ I don’t think we can last out much longer without food and water.
examples: I don’t think we can last out much longer without food and water.

the last roundup.monolingual: Fig. death. (Old West.) _ To everyone’s surprise, he clutched the wound and faced the last roundup with a smile. _ When I know I’m headed for the last roundup, I’ll write a will.
examples: To everyone’s surprise, he clutched the wound and faced the last roundup with a smile.

last something out†.monolingual: to endure until the end of something. _ Ed said that he didn’t think he could last the opera out and left. _ He couldn’t last out the first act.
examples: Ed said that he didn’t think he could last the opera out and left.

last will and testament.monolingual: a will; the last edition of someone’s will. _ The lawyer read Uncle Charles’s last will and testament to a group of expectant relatives. _Fred dictated his last will and testament on his deathbed.
examples: The lawyer read Uncle Charles’s last will and testament to a group of expectant relatives.

*last-ditch effort.monolingual: Fig. a final effort; the last possible attempt. (*Typically: be ~; have ~; make ~.) _ I made one last-ditch effort to get her to stay. _It was a lastditch effort. I didn’t expect it to work.
examples: I made one last-ditch effort to get her to stay.

latch onto something.monolingual: 1. Fig. to obtain something. _ I have to latch onto a hundred bucks by Friday night. _ I latched onto a good book about repairing plumbing.
examples: I have to latch onto a hundred bucks by Friday night.

a late bloomer.monolingual: 1. Lit. a plant that blooms later than similar plants or that blooms late in the season. _ There are a few late bloomers in the garden, but by fall, we don’t care much anymore about f lowers.
examples: There are a few late bloomers in the garden, but by fall, we don’t care much anymore about f lowers.

late in life.monolingual: Fig. when one is old. _ Grandma injured her hip running. She’s exercising rather late in life. _Isn’t it sort of late in life for your grandparents to buy a house?
examples: Grandma injured her hip running.

late in the day.monolingual: Fig. far along in a project or activity; too late in a project or activity for action, decisions, etc., to be taken. _It was a bit late in the day for him to apologize. _ It’s late in the day to try to change the plans.
examples: It was a bit late in the day for him to apologize.

the late unpleasantness.monolingual: Euph. the U.S. Civil War. (Old.) _The town courthouse was burned in the late unpleasantness. _ Many of my ancestors lost their lives in the late unpleasantness.
examples: The town courthouse was burned in the late unpleasantness.

lather something up†.monolingual: to apply thick soapsuds to something, such as part of the body or all of it. _ He lathered his face up in preparation for shaving. _ He lathered up his face.
examples: He lathered his face up in preparation for shaving.

laugh about someone or something.monolingual: to chuckle or giggle loudly about someone or something. _Please don’t laugh about Sue. It’s not funny. _ They were laughing about my haircut.
examples: Please don’t laugh about Sue.

laugh at someone or something.monolingual: to chuckle or giggle loudly at someone or something, perhaps in ridicule. _ Thank goodness, the audience laughed at all my jokes. _ Don’t laugh at me! I’m doing my best! _ Everyone laughed at the love scene because it was so badly done.
examples: Thank goodness, the audience laughed at all my jokes.

laugh in someone’s face.monolingual: to laugh in derision directly to someone’s face; to show displeasure or ridicule at something one has said by laughing directly into one’s face. _ It is very impolite to laugh in someone’s face! _After I heard what she had to say, I just laughed in h
examples: After I heard what she had to say, I just laughed in her face.

laugh one’s head off.monolingual: Fig. to laugh very hard and loudly, as if one’s head might come off. _The movie was so funny I almost laughed my head off. _ I laughed my head off at Mary’s joke.
examples: The movie was so funny I almost laughed my head off.

laugh oneself out of something.monolingual: to lose out on something because one has made light of it or laughed at it. _ While you were howling with laughter about my hat, you laughed yourself out of a ride to town. The bus just pulled away. _ You laugh too much. You just laughed yourself out
examples: While you were howling with laughter about my hat, you laughed yourself out of a ride to town.

laugh oneself silly.monolingual: Fig. to laugh very, very hard. _I laughed myself silly when I heard that Steven was really going to give the graduation address.
examples: I laughed myself silly when I heard that Steven was really going to give the graduation address.

laugh someone off the stage.monolingual: Fig. to laugh rudely, forcing a person to leave a stage. _The rude audience laughed the politician off the stage. _ The children laughed the soprano off the stage. She really wasn’t very good, you know.
examples: The rude audience laughed the politician off the stage.

laugh someone or something down†.monolingual: to cause someone to quit or cause something to end by laughing in ridicule. _ Her singing career was destroyed when the audience laughed her down as an amateur. _ The cruel audience laughed down the amateur singer. _ They laughed down the magic act a
examples: Her singing career was destroyed when the audience laughed her down as an amateur.

laugh someone out of something.monolingual: to force someone to leave a place by laughing in ridicule. _The citizens laughed the speaker out of the hall. _ We laughed the city council out of the auditorium.
examples: The citizens laughed the speaker out of the hall.

laugh something away†.monolingual: 1. to spend an amount of time laughing. _ We laughed the hour away listening to the comedian. _ We laughed away the evening.
examples: We laughed the hour away listening to the comedian.

laugh something off†.monolingual: to treat a serious problem lightly by laughing at it. _ Although his feelings were hurt, he just laughed the incident off as if nothing had happened. _ He laughed off the incident.
examples: Although his feelings were hurt, he just laughed the incident off as if nothing had happened.

laugh something out of court.monolingual: to dismiss something presented in earnest as ridiculous. _ The committee laughed the suggestion out of court. _Bob’s request for a large salary increase was laughed out of court.
examples: The committee laughed the suggestion out of court.

laugh up one’s sleeve.monolingual: to laugh secretly; to laugh quietly to oneself. _ Jane looked very serious, but I knew she was laughing up her sleeve. _I told Sally that her dress was darling, but I was laughing up my sleeve because her dress was too small.
examples: Jane looked very serious, but I knew she was laughing up her sleeve.

laugh with something.monolingual: to laugh in a particular manner. _ Everyone was laughing with glee at the antics of the clown. _ Max laughed with malice as he saw his plan beginning to work.
examples: Everyone was laughing with glee at the antics of the clown.

laughingstock.monolingual: someone or something that is the target of ridicule. _ After he passed out at the president’s dinner, he became the laughingstock of all his colleagues.
examples: After he passed out at the president’s dinner, he became the laughingstock of all his colleagues.

launch into something.monolingual: to start in doing something. _Now, don’t launch into lecturing me about manners again! _ Tim’s mother launched into a sermon about how to behave at the dinner table.
examples: Tim’s mother launched into a sermon about how to behave at the dinner table.

launch out on something.monolingual: to start out to do something or go somewhere. _When are you going to launch out on your expedition? _ Ted and Bill launched out on their trip through the mountains.
examples: Ted and Bill launched out on their trip through the mountains.

*a law unto oneself.monolingual: Fig. one who ignores laws or rules; one who sets one’s own standards of behavior. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ You can’t get Bill to follow the rules. He’s a law unto himself. _ Jane is a law unto herself. She’s totally unwilling to cooperate.
examples: You can’t get Bill to follow the rules.

lay alongside something.monolingual: [for a ship] to rest afloat next to something. _ The ship lay alongside a lovely island while a shore party searched for fresh water. _Our ship lay alongside the narrow wooden pier.
examples: The ship lay alongside a lovely island while a shore party searched for fresh water.

lay an egg.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a hen, etc.] to deposit an egg. _ Old Red stopped laying eggs, so we stewed her for Sunday dinner.
examples: Old Red stopped laying eggs, so we stewed her for Sunday dinner.

lay claim to something.monolingual: to place a claim on something. _ Do you really think you can lay claim to that money after all these years? _ Someone came by and laid claim to the wallet you found.
examples: Someone came by and laid claim to the wallet you found.

lay down.monolingual: to give up. _Do you expect me to just lay down? _You really think I should just lay down and let them walk all over me?

lay down one’s arms.monolingual: Fig. to put one’s gun, sword, club, etc., down; to stop fighting; to surrender. _ The prisoners were instructed to lay down their arms. _ The soldiers laid down their arms and surrendered.
examples: The prisoners were instructed to lay down their arms.

lay for someone or something.monolingual: to lie in wait for someone or something. _ The sheriff was laying for the outlaw. _ Bill was laying for me when I came out of the saloon.
examples: The sheriff was laying for the outlaw.

lay into someone or something.monolingual: to attack, consume, or scold someone or something. _ Bob laid into the big plate of fried chicken. _The bear laid into the hunter. _My father really laid into me when I got home.
examples: Bob laid into the big plate of fried chicken.

lay low and sing small.monolingual: Rur. to hide; to make oneself inconspicuous. _ After he robbed the bank, the outlaw decided to lay low and sing small awhile. _ Jane is looking for you, and she sure is angry. You’d best lay low and sing small.
examples: After he robbed the bank, the outlaw decided to lay low and sing small awhile.

the lay of the land.monolingual: 1. Lit. the arrangement of features on an area of land. (Also with lie, especially British English.) _ The surveyor mapped the lay of the land. _ The geologist studied the lay of the land, trying to determine if there was oil below.
examples: The surveyor mapped the lay of the land.

lay someone away†.monolingual: Euph. to bury someone. _ Yes, he has passed. We laid him away last week. _ He laid away his uncle in a simple ceremony.
examples: Yes, he has passed.

lay someone down.monolingual: to ease someone into a reclining position; to ease someone into bed. _The baby woke up when I tried to lay him down. _ The nurse laid the disturbed patient down time and time again.
examples: The baby woke up when I tried to lay him down.

lay someone out†.monolingual: 1. Sl. to knock someone down with a punch; to knock someone unconscious. _ Tom laid out Bill with one punch to the chin. _ The policeman laid the thief out.
examples: Tom laid out Bill with one punch to the chin.

lay someone out in lavender.monolingual: Fig. to scold someone severely. _ She was really mad. She laid him out in lavender and really put him in his place. _ If you ever feel like you need to lay me out in lavender again, just forget it.
examples: She was really mad.

lay someone to rest.monolingual: Euph. to bury a dead person. _ They laid her to rest by her mother and father, out in the old churchyard. _ We gather together today to lay our beloved son to rest.
examples: They laid her to rest by her mother and father, out in the old churchyard.

lay someone up†.monolingual: to cause someone to be ill in bed. _A broken leg laid me up for two months. _ Flu laid up everyone at work for a week or more.
examples: A broken leg laid me up for two months.

lay something against something.monolingual: to lean or place something against something. _They laid the Christmas tree against the house where they could get to it easily when the time came. _Lay this hot cloth against the sore and hold it there.
examples: They laid the Christmas tree against the house where they could get to it easily when the time came.

lay something aside†.monolingual: to set something aside; to place something to one side, out of the way. _He laid his papers aside and went out to welcome the visitor. _ He laid aside his papers.
examples: He laid his papers aside and went out to welcome the visitor.

lay something before someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to present something to someone. _ The cat laid the mouse before her mistress. _Dave laid the present before her as a peace offering.
examples: The cat laid the mouse before her mistress.

lay something in†.monolingual: to get something and store it for future use. _ They laid a lot of food in for the holidays. _ We always lay in a large supply of firewood each November.
examples: They laid a lot of food in for the holidays.

lay something on†.monolingual: to supply something in abundance. _ Look at him lay that butter on! What do you suppose the insides of his arteries look like? _ They laid on a beautiful buffet lunch.
examples: They laid on a beautiful buffet lunch.

lay something on someone.monolingual: 1. Sl. to present a plan or an idea to someone. _ Here is this century’s greatest idea. Let me lay it on you. _ I’m going to lay a great idea on you.
examples: Here is this century’s greatest idea.

lay something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to spread something out. _ The nurse laid the instruments out for the operation. _The valet laid out the clothing for his employer.
examples: The nurse laid the instruments out for the operation.

lay something to something.monolingual: to attribute something to something. _ I lay all our problems to the inadequacy of our training. _ Mary laid her success to a good upbringing.
examples: I lay all our problems to the inadequacy of our training.

lay something together.monolingual: to lay things side by side. _ Lay all the logs together and stack them as high as you can. _ Lay the red ones together and put all the others over there in a pile.
examples: Lay all the logs together and stack them as high as you can.

lay something under something.monolingual: to place something beneath something. _ Please lay a cloth under your workbench to catch the sawdust. _Would you mind laying a sheet of plastic over the table?
examples: Please lay a cloth under your workbench to catch the sawdust.

lay something up†.monolingual: 1. to acquire and store something. _Try to lay as much of it up as you can. _ I am trying to lay up some firewood for the winter.
examples: Try to lay as much of it up as you can.

lay to.monolingual: to begin doing something, such as fighting or eating. _ All right, you guys. Lay to. The stuff will get cold if you don’t eat it. _ Lay to! Let’s get on with it.
examples: All right, you guys.

laze something away†.monolingual: to spend a period of time being lazy. _ I just love to sit here and laze the day away. _ I will laze away the entire day.
examples: I just love to sit here and laze the day away.

leach away.monolingual: [for something] to erode or wash away gradually by leaching. _The soft sandstone leached away under the constant rains. _ The f lowerpots sat out in the rain, where all the nutrients in the soil leached away.
examples: The soft sandstone leached away under the constant rains.

leach out of something.monolingual: [for a substance] to seep or drain out of something. _All the nutrients leached out of the soil and nothing would grow. _ The phosphorus leached out of the soil after a few years.
examples: All the nutrients leached out of the soil and nothing would grow.

lead down to something.monolingual: [for a pathway or other trail] to run downward to something. _ The trail led down to a spring at the bottom of the hill. _ These stairs lead down to the furnace room.
examples: The trail led down to a spring at the bottom of the hill.

lead forth.monolingual: [for someone] to go on ahead; to precede someone. _You lead forth, and I will follow. _Wallace led forth, but no one came after him.
examples: You lead forth, and I will follow.

lead off.monolingual: to be the first one to go or leave. _ You lead off. I’ll follow. _ Mary led off and the others followed closely behind.
examples: You lead off. I’ll follow.

lead on.monolingual: to continue to lead onward. _ The guide led on and we followed. _Lead on, my friend. We are right behind you!
examples: The guide led on and we followed.

lead someone astray.monolingual: to direct or guide someone in the wrong direction. _ I am afraid that this young man has been leading you astray. I think you had better stop seeing him. _No one can lead me astray. I know what I am doing.
examples: I am afraid that this young man has been leading you astray.

lead someone by something.monolingual: to guide someone by grasping a part and moving. _Do you expect me to lead you around by the hand, showing you everything to do in your job? _ The cop grabbed Max and led him around by the collar.
examples: The cop grabbed Max and led him around by the collar.

lead someone by the nose.monolingual: 1. Fig. to force someone to go somewhere (with you); to lead someone by coercion. _ John had to lead Tom by the nose to get him to the opera. _ I’ll go, but you’ll have to lead me by the nose.
examples: John had to lead Tom by the nose to get him to the opera.

lead someone down to something.monolingual: to guide someone downward to something. _ She led us down to a little room in the cellar, where the old trunk had been kept for all these years. _ Would you please lead me down to the wine cellar?
examples: She led us down to a little room in the cellar, where the old trunk had been kept for all these years.

lead someone or something forth†.monolingual: to bring or usher someone or something forward. _ The captain led the soldiers forth to the parade ground. _ They led forth the army into battle.
examples: The captain led the soldiers forth to the parade ground.

lead someone or something off†.monolingual: to guide someone or something away. _ The guide led the hikers off on the adventure of their lives. _ The dog owners led off their animals and they awaited the decision of the judges.
examples: The guide led the hikers off on the adventure of their lives.

lead someone to believe something.monolingual: Fig. to imply something to someone; to cause someone to believe something untrue. _ But you led me to believe that this watch was guaranteed! _Did you lead her to believe that she was hired as a clerk?

lead someone to do something.monolingual: Fig. to cause someone to do something. _ This agent led me to purchase a worthless piece of land. _ My illness led me to quit my job.
examples: This agent led me to purchase a worthless piece of land.

lead someone up something.monolingual: to guide someone upward along some route. _ Would you please lead Tom up the path so he can leave his things at the cabin on the hill? _ Mary led the visitors up the stairs to the loft, which she had recently redecorated.
examples: Mary led the visitors up the stairs to the loft, which she had recently redecorated.

lead the way.monolingual: to lead (someone) along the proper pathway. _ You lead the way, and we’ll follow. _ I feel better when you’re leading the way. I get lost easily.
examples: You lead the way, and we’ll follow.

lead up to something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to aim at or route movement to something. _ A narrow path led up to the door of the cottage. _ This road leads up to the house at the top of the hill.
examples: A narrow path led up to the door of the cottage.

lead with someone or something.monolingual: to start out with someone or something. _ The coach led with Walter as pitcher and Sam on first base. _ We will lead with our best players.
examples: The coach led with Walter as pitcher and Sam on first base.

lead with something.monolingual: to tend to strike first with a particular fist—the right, the left, the best, etc. (Boxing.) _Watch that guy, Champ, he always leads with his right. _ Get in there and lead with your left.
examples: Watch that guy, Champ, he always leads with his right.

leading question.monolingual: a question that suggests the kind of answer that the person who asks it wants to hear. _ The mayor was angered by the reporter’s leading questions. _ “Don’t you think that the police are failing to stop crime?” is an example of a leading question.
examples: The mayor was angered by the reporter’s leading questions.

a lead-pipe cinch.monolingual: Fig. something very easy to do; something entirely certain to happen. _ I knew it was a leadpie cinch that I would be selected to head the publication committee.
examples: I knew it was a leadpie cinch that I would be selected to head the publication committee.

leaf out.monolingual: [for a plant] to open its leaf buds. _ Most of the bushes leaf out in mid-April. _ The trees leafed out early this year.
examples: Most of the bushes leaf out in mid-April.

leak out.monolingual: [for information] to become known unofficially. _ I hope that news of the new building does not leak out before the contract is signed. _ When the story leaked out, my telephone would not stop ringing.
examples: I hope that news of the new building does not leak out before the contract is signed.

leak something to someone.monolingual: Fig. to tell [otherwise secret] information to someone. _ The government leaked a phony story to the press just to see how far it would travel. _The government leaks things to the press occasionally, just to see the reaction.
examples: The government leaked a phony story to the press just to see how far it would travel.

leak through something.monolingual: [for a fluid] to seep through something. _ Rainwater leaked through the roof. _ I was afraid that the crushed orange would leak through the paper bag.
examples: Rainwater leaked through the roof.

lean across someone or something.monolingual: to incline oneself across someone or something. _ She leaned across me to reach the telephone and spilled my wine. _ Laura leaned across the table and knocked my coffee over.
examples: She leaned across me to reach the telephone and spilled my wine.

lean against someone or something.monolingual: to prop oneself against someone or something. _The child leaned against her sister to keep warm. _ I leaned against the back of the chair and went right to sleep.
examples: The child leaned against her sister to keep warm.

lean and mean.monolingual: Fig. fit and ready for hard, efficient work. _ Dave got himself lean and mean and is ready to play in Saturday’s game. _The management is lean and mean and looks to turn a profit next year.
examples: Dave got himself lean and mean and is ready to play in Saturday’s game.

lean back.monolingual: [for someone] to recline backwards, usually in a chair. _Lean back and make yourself comfortable. _Let’s lean back and be comfortable.
examples: Lean back and make yourself comfortable.

lean down.monolingual: to bend over. _ Lean down and tie your shoe before you trip. _ He leaned down and picked something up from the f loor.
examples: Lean down and tie your shoe before you trip.

lean forward.monolingual: to bend forward. _ Lean forward a minute so I can put a cushion behind your back. _ When Betsy leaned forward, she lost her balance and fell.
examples: Lean forward a minute so I can put a cushion behind your back.

lean on someone.monolingual: Fig. to try to make someone do something; to coerce someone to do something. (From lean on someone or something.) _ If she refuses to do it, lean on her a bit. _ Don’t lean on me! I don’t have to do it if I don’t want to.
examples: If she refuses to do it, lean on her a bit.

lean on someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to incline or press on someone or something. _Don’t lean on me. I’m not strong enough to support both of us. _ Lean on the wall and rest a little while.
examples: Don’t lean on me.

lean out of something.monolingual: to hang or bend out of something or some place. _She leaned out of the window so she could watch what was going on. _ Don’t lean out of the car window. You will fall.
examples: She leaned out of the window so she could watch what was going on.

lean over.monolingual: 1. to bend over. _ Lean over and pick the pencil up yourself! I’m not your servant! _As Kelly leaned over to tie her shoes, her chair slipped out from under her.
examples: As Kelly leaned over to tie her shoes, her chair slipped out from under her.

lean something forward.monolingual: to tilt or bend something forward. _ Lean the board forward a little bit, please. _ Someone leaned this panel forward a little too much.
examples: Lean the board forward a little bit, please.

lean toward doing something.monolingual: to tend toward doing something; to favor doing something. _ The union is leaning toward accepting the proposal. _My friends leaned toward swimming instead of shopping.
examples: The union is leaning toward accepting the proposal.

lean toward someone or something.monolingual: 1. to incline toward someone or something. _ Tom is leaning toward Randy. I think he is going to fall on him. _The tree is leaning toward the edge of the cliff. It will fall eventually.
examples: Tom is leaning toward Randy.

leap at someone or something.monolingual: 1. to jump toward someone or something. _ The grasshopper leapt at me and scared me to death. _ The cat leapt at the mouse and caught it.
examples: The grasshopper leapt at me and scared me to death.

leap forward.monolingual: to jump or hop forward. _ The little creature leapt forward and looked carefully at us. _ As the frog leapt forward, the kitten jumped straight up and f led.
examples: The little creature leapt forward and looked carefully at us.

*a leap of faith.monolingual: Fig. acceptance of an idea or conclusion largely on faith. (*Typically: be ~; make ~; require ~.) _ We had to make quite a leap of faith to accept his promise after the last time he let us down.
examples: We had to make quite a leap of faith to accept his promise after the last time he let us down.

leap over something.monolingual: to jump over something. _ The dog leapt over the hedge and chased the rabbit around the corner of the house. _ Please don’t leap over my roses. You’ll damage them.
examples: The dog leapt over the hedge and chased the rabbit around the corner of the house.

leap up.monolingual: to jump upwards. _ The dog leapt up and licked my cheek. _ I leapt up so I could see over the wall for just a second.
examples: The dog leapt up and licked my cheek.

learn about someone or something.monolingual: to find out about someone or something. _ What have you learned about Mr. Franklin and his business dealings? _I learned about what causes rain.
examples: What have you learned about Mr.

learn by something.monolingual: to learn [something] from some kind of actual experience. _The best way to learn is to learn by doing. _ The best way to learn to sail is to learn by sailing.
examples: The best way to learn is to learn by doing.

learn from someone or something.monolingual: to learn [something] from the experience of someone or something. _ Pay attention to what Sarah does. I think you can learn from her. _ This was quite an experience, and we all can learn from it.
examples: Pay attention to what Sarah does.

learn of someone or something.monolingual: to find out about someone or something. _ I’m not in the telephone book. How did you learn of me? _ How did you learn of our company?
examples: I’m not in the telephone book.

learn something by heart.monolingual: Fig. to learn something so well that it can be written or recited without thinking; to memorize something. _The director told me to learn my speech by heart. _ I had to go over it many times before I learned it by heart.
examples: The director told me to learn my speech by heart.

learn something by rote.monolingual: Fig. to learn something by memorizing without giving any thought to what is being learned. _ I learned history by rote; then I couldn’t pass the test that required me to think. _ If you learn things by rote, you’ll never understand them.
examples: I learned history by rote; then I couldn’t pass the test that required me to think.

learn to live with something.monolingual: Fig. to learn to adapt to something unpleasant or painful. _Finally the doctor told Marion that she was going to have to learn to live with her arthritis. _ The f loor plan of the house we bought is not as spacious as we had thought, but we will lear
examples: Finally the doctor told Marion that she was going to have to learn to live with her arthritis.

lease something back†.monolingual: to sell something, then rent it from the buyer. _ We sold the building to a real estate firm and then leased it back. There was some tax saving involved. _ We leased back the building.
examples: We sold the building to a real estate firm and then leased it back.

lease something from someone.monolingual: to rent something from someone. _ We decided to lease the building from the owner rather than buying it. _ The company always leases its cars from the dealership.
examples: We decided to lease the building from the owner rather than buying it.

the least little thing.monolingual: the smallest possible thing. _ He gets upset over the least little thing. _ When she was a girl, she would throw a tantrum over the least little thing.
examples: He gets upset over the least little thing.

least of all.monolingual: the thing of smallest importance. (Compare this with most of all.) _ There were many things wrong with the new house. Least of all, the water faucets leaked. _ What a bad day. Many things went wrong, but least of all, I tore my shirt.
examples: There were many things wrong with the new house.

leave for some place.monolingual: to depart for some place. _ We will leave for Denver at dawn. _ When do we leave for Grandmother’s house?
examples: We will leave for Denver at dawn.

leave it at that.monolingual: to leave a situation as it is. _ This is the best we can do. We’ll have to leave it at that. _ I can do no more. I will have to leave it at that.
examples: This is the best we can do.

leave it to someone.monolingual: to depend on someone to behave in a certain way. _ Leave it to Harry to mess things up. _ She did it wrong again. Leave it to Janet! _ Jane: Will you do this as soon as possible? Mary: Leave it to me.
examples: Leave it to Harry to mess things up.

leave me alone!.monolingual: Stop harassing me!; Don’t bother me! _ John: You did it. You’re the one who always does it. Bill: Leave me alone! I never did it. _Fred: Let’s give Bill a dunk in the pool. Bill: Leave me alone!
examples: John: You did it.

leave no stone unturned.monolingual: Fig. to search in all possible places. (As if one might search under every rock.) _Don’t worry. We’ll find your stolen car. We’ll leave no stone unturned. _ In searching for a nice place to live, we left no stone unturned.
examples: Don’t worry. We’ll find your stolen car.

a leave of absence.monolingual: a period of time away from one’s job, with the employer’s permission. _ Mr. Takaguchi is on leave of absence because he is going back to school. _ His leave of absence is expected to end next month.
examples: Mr. Takaguchi is on leave of absence because he is going back to school.

leave off something.monolingual: to quit something. _I have to leave off working for a while so I can eat. _I left off reading and went downstairs for supper.
examples: I have to leave off working for a while so I can eat.

leave one’s mark on someone.monolingual: Fig. [for someone like a teacher] to affect the behavior and performance of another person. _ The wise professor left her mark on her students. _My father left his mark on me, and I will always remember all his good advice.
examples: The wise professor left her mark on her students.

leave one to one’s fate.monolingual: to abandon someone to whatever may happen—possibly death or some other unpleasant event. _ We couldn’t rescue the miners and were forced to leave them to their fate. _ Please don’t try to help. Just go away and leave me to my fate.
examples: We couldn’t rescue the miners and were forced to leave them to their fate.

leave someone cold.monolingual: to leave someone unaffected or bored. _ He said it was dull, and it left him cold. _ The music’s good, but the story left the producer cold.
examples: He said it was dull, and it left him cold.

leave someone flat.monolingual: 1. Fig. to fail to entertain or stimulate someone. _ Your joke left me f lat. _We listened carefully to his lecture, but it left us f lat.
examples: Your joke left me f lat.

leave someone for dead.monolingual: to abandon someone as being dead. (The abandoned person may actually be alive.) _ He looked so bad that they almost left him for dead. _ As the soldiers turned—leaving the enemy captain for dead— the captain fired at them.
examples: He looked so bad that they almost left him for dead.

leave someone high and dry.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for water] to recede and leave someone untouched. _ The waters receded and left us high and dry.
examples: The waters receded and left us high and dry.

leave someone in peace.monolingual: to stop bothering someone; to go away and leave someone alone. (Does not necessarily mean to go away from a person.) _ Please go—leave me in peace. _ Can’t you see that you’re upsetting her? Leave her in peace.
examples: Please go—leave me in peace.

leave someone in the lurch.monolingual: Fig. to leave someone waiting for or anticipating your actions. _ Where were you, John? You really left me in the lurch. _I didn’t mean to leave you in the lurch. I thought we had canceled our meeting.
examples: Where were you, John? You really left me in the lurch.

leave someone or something behind.monolingual: to fail or forget to bring someone or something along. _ John was sick, so we had to leave him behind. _Oh, I left my money behind.
examples: John was sick, so we had to leave him behind.

leave someone to it.monolingual: to withdraw and allow someone to finish something alone. _ I hate to leave before the job is finished, but I’ll have to leave you to it. _ I will leave them to it. I have to go home now.
examples: I hate to leave before the job is finished, but I’ll have to leave you to it.

leave something aside†.monolingual: 1. to leave something in reserve. _Leave some of the sugar aside for use in the icing. _Leave aside some cookies too.
examples: Leave some of the sugar aside for use in the icing.

leave something down.monolingual: to leave something in a lowered or low position. _ Leave the window down, please. It’s hot in this car. _ Leave the window down. This house is cold enough as it is.
examples: Leave the window down, please.

leave something on†.monolingual: 1. to continue to wear some article of clothing. _I think I will leave my coat on. It’s chilly in here. _I’ll leave on my coat.
examples: I think I will leave my coat on.

leave something open.monolingual: to leave a date or time unscheduled. _ I left something open on Friday, just in case we want to leave work early. _ Please leave an appointment open for Mrs. Wallace next week. She will be calling in to our office for an appointment.
examples: I left something open on Friday, just in case we want to leave work early.

leave something to chance.monolingual: to allow something to be settled by chance. _ Plan your day. Don’t leave anything to chance. _It is not a good idea to leave any of this to chance.
examples: Plan your day. Don’t leave anything to chance.

leave something to someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to will something to someone. _My grandfather left his house to my mother. _ I will leave this watch to one of my grandchildren.
examples: My grandfather left his house to my mother.

leave something up†.monolingual: to leave something in a raised or high position. _ It’s still warm in here. Please leave the window up. _ Please leave up the window. It’s so hot!
examples: It’s still warm in here.

leave the room.monolingual: 1. to go out of the room. _I had to leave the room to get drinks for everyone.
examples: I had to leave the room to get drinks for everyone.

leave with someone.monolingual: to depart in the company of someone. _ I left with Frank early in the evening and did not see what happened to Tom and Edna. _ Mary is gone. She left with Gerald.
examples: I left with Frank early in the evening and did not see what happened to Tom and Edna.

lecture someone for something.monolingual: to give someone a talkingto about something. _ Please don’t lecture me for being late. It won’t help now, will it? _ There is no point in lecturing us for something we didn’t do.
examples: Please don’t lecture me for being late.

leer at someone.monolingual: to gaze at someone flirtatiously or with lust. _Why are you leering at that woman in the bikini? _ Stop leering at me!

*a leg up.monolingual: Fig. a kind of help where someone provides a knee or crossed hand as a support for someone to place a foot on to get higher, as in mounting a horse or climbing over something. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ I gave her a leg up, and so
examples: I gave her a leg up, and soon she was on her horse.

*a leg up on someone.monolingual: Fig. an advantage that someone else does not have. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ I have a leg up on Walter when it comes to getting around town, since I have a car. _ I want to practice indoors all winter and get a leg up on Ken, sin
examples: I have a leg up on Walter when it comes to getting around town, since I have a car.

legislate against something.monolingual: to prohibit something; to pass a law against something. _ You can’t just legislate against something. You have to explain to people why they shouldn’t do it. _ The Congress has just legislated against insolvent banks.
examples: You can’t just legislate against something.

legislate for something.monolingual: to pass a law that tries to make something happen. _The candidate pledged to legislate for tax relief. _ We support your efforts to legislate for lower taxes.
examples: The candidate pledged to legislate for tax relief.

legwork.monolingual: the physical work accompanying a task. _I don’t mind making the phone calls if you do the legwork. _I have a gopher to do the legwork for me.
examples: I don’t mind making the phone calls if you do the legwork.

lend color to something.monolingual: Fig. to provide an interesting accompaniment for something. _ Your clever comments lent a great deal of color to the slide show of your vacation. _ The excellent master of ceremonies will lend color to an otherwise dry panel discussion.
examples: Your clever comments lent a great deal of color to the slide show of your vacation.

lend something to someone.monolingual: to make a loan of something to someone. _ Never lend money to a friend. _ Would you be able to lend your coat to Fred?
examples: Never lend money to a friend.

lengthen out.monolingual: to stretch or grow longer. _The days began to lengthen out and we knew summer was upon us. _As we approached the end of the trail, the distance seemed to lengthen out.
examples: The days began to lengthen out and we knew summer was upon us.

less is more..monolingual: Cliché fewer or small is better. _ Simplicity now rules our lives. Less is more. Smaller houses and cars. The world will be a better place!
examples: Simplicity now rules our lives.

less than pleased.monolingual: displeased. _We were less than pleased to learn of your comments. _ Bill was less than pleased at the outcome of the election.
examples: We were less than pleased to learn of your comments.

the lesser of two evils.monolingual: the less bad thing of a pair of bad things. _ I didn’t like either politician, so I voted for the lesser of two evils. _Given the options of going out with someone I don’t like and staying home and watching a boring television program, I chose the le
examples: I didn’t like either politician, so I voted for the lesser of two evils.

let alone someone or something.monolingual: not to mention or think of someone or something; not even to take someone or something into account. (Fixed order.) _Do I have a dollar? I don’t even have a dime, let alone a dollar. _ I didn’t invite John, let alone the rest of his family.
examples: Do I have a dollar? I don’t even have a dime, let alone a dollar.

let bygones be bygones..monolingual: Cliché Forgive someone for something he or she did in the past. _ Jill: Why don’t you want to invite Ellen to your party? Jane: She was rude to me at the office picnic. Jill: But that was six months ago. Let bygones be bygones. _ Nancy held a grudge
examples: Jill: Why don’t you want to invite Ellen to your party? Jane: She was rude to me at the office picnic.

let down.monolingual: to relax one’s efforts or vigilance. _ Now is no time to let down. Keep on your guard. _ After the contest was over, Jane let down a bit so she could relax.
examples: Now is no time to let down.

let fly with something.monolingual: Fig. to throw or thrust something, such as a rock, ball, punch, etc. _ The pitcher wound up and let f ly with a strike—right over the plate. _ Max let f ly with a blow to Lefty’s chin.
examples: The pitcher wound up and let f ly with a strike—right over the plate.

let george do it..monolingual: Fig. Let someone else do it: it doesn’t matter who. _ Billie always says, “Let George do it.” She is unwilling to help with things that don’t interest her.
examples: Billie always says, “Let George do it.

let it all hang out.monolingual: Inf. to be yourself, assuming that you generally are not; to become totally relaxed and unpretentious. _ Come on. Relax! Let it all hang out. _ I tried to let it all hang out, but I still felt out of place.
examples: Come on. Relax! Let it all hang out.

let it be..monolingual: Leave the situation alone as it is. _ Alice: I can’t get over the way he just left me there on the street and drove off. What an arrogant pig! Mary: Oh, Alice, let it be. You’ll figure out some way to get even. _John: You can’t! Bill: Can too! John:
examples: Alice: I can’t get over the way he just left me there on the street and drove off.

let it go..monolingual: Forget it.; Stop worrying about it. _ Don’t get so angry about it. Let it go. _ Let it go. Stop fretting.
examples: Don’t get so angry about it.

let on something.monolingual: to pretend something. _ She let on that she was a college graduate. _He looked quite tired, but that wasn’t how he let on.
examples: She let on that she was a college graduate.

let one’s emotions show.monolingual: to be emotional, especially where it is not appropriate. _ I’m sorry for the outburst. I didn’t mean to let my emotions show. _ Please stop crying. You mustn’t let your emotions show.
examples: I’m sorry for the outburst.

let one’s guard down†.monolingual: Fig. to stop guarding oneself against trouble; to relax one’s vigilance. _He never lets his guard down because he trusts no one.
examples: He never lets his guard down because he trusts no one.

let one’s hair down.monolingual: 1. Lit. to undo one’s hair and let it fall freely. _ When she took off her glasses and let her hair down, she was incredibly beautiful.
examples: When she took off her glasses and let her hair down, she was incredibly beautiful.

let oneself go.monolingual: 1. Fig. to become less constrained; to get excited and have a good time. _ I love to dance and just let myself go. _ Let yourself go, John. Learn to enjoy life.
examples: I love to dance and just let myself go.

let oneself in for something.monolingual: to make oneself vulnerable to some difficulty. _ I don’t want to let myself in for a lot of extra work. _ You really let yourself in for some problems!
examples: I don’t want to let myself in for a lot of extra work.

let out.monolingual: [for an event that includes many people] to end. (The people are then permitted to come out.) _ What time does the movie let out? I have to meet someone in the lobby. _ The meeting let out at about seven o’clock. _ School lets out in June.
examples: What time does the movie let out? I have to meet someone in the lobby.

let’s bump this place!.monolingual: Sl. Let’s get out of this place!; Let’s leave! _ Time to go. Let’s bump this place! _ Let’s bump this place! It’s dead here.
examples: Let’s bump this place! It’s dead here.

let’s call it a day..monolingual: Fig. Let us end what we are doing for the day. _ Mary: Well, that’s the end of the reports. Nothing else to do. Sue: Let’s call it a day. _ Bob: Let’s call it a day. I’m tired. Tom: Me too. Let’s get out of here.
examples: Mary: Well, that’s the end of the reports.

let’s dump..monolingual: Sl. Let’s go. _ It’s late. Let’s dump. _ Let’s dump. I’ve still got a lot to do at home tonight.
examples: It’s late. Let’s dump.

let’s get down to business..monolingual: Fig. a phrase marking a transition to a business discussion or serious talk. _John: Okay, enough small talk. Let’s get down to business. Mary: Good idea. _“All right, ladies and gentlemen, let’s get down to business,” said the president of the board.
examples: John: Okay, enough small talk.

let’s get out of here..monolingual: Let us leave (and go somewhere else). _ Alice: It’s really hot in this room. Let’s get out of here. John: I’m with you. Let’s go. _ Bill: This crowd is getting sort of angry. Bob: I noticed that too. Let’s get out of here.
examples: Alice: It’s really hot in this room.

let’s rock and roll!.monolingual: Inf. Let’s get started!; Let’s get moving! _A: Everybody ready? B: Yeah. A: Good. Let’s rock and roll!
examples: A: Everybody ready? B: Yeah.

let’s say.monolingual: introduces an estimate or a speculation. _I need about—let’s say—twenty pounds. _ Let’s say I go over and talk to him. What do you think?
examples: I need about—let’s say—twenty pounds.

let’s shake on it..monolingual: Let us mark this agreement by shaking hands on it. _ Bob: Do you agree? Mary: I agree. Let’s shake on it. Bob: Okay. _Bill: Good idea. Sounds fine. Bob (extending his hand): Okay, let’s shake on it. Bill (shaking hands with Bob): Great!
examples: Bob: Do you agree? Mary: I agree.

let sleeping dogs lie..monolingual: Prov. Do not instigate trouble.; Leave something alone if it might cause trouble. _ Jill: Should I ask the boss if he’s upset at my coming in late in the mornings? Jane: If he hasn’t said anything about it, just let sleeping dogs lie. _ I thought I w
examples: Jill: Should I ask the boss if he’s upset at my coming in late in the mornings? Jane: If he hasn’t said anything about it, just let sleeping dogs lie.

let someone down.monolingual: to disappoint someone; to fail someone. _ I’m sorry I let you down. Something came up, and I couldn’t meet you. _ I don’t want to let you down, but I can’t support you in the election.
examples: I’m sorry I let you down.

let someone go.monolingual: Euph. to fire someone. _ They let Jane go from her job. _ I’m afraid we’re going to have to let you go.
examples: They let Jane go from her job.

let someone in for something.monolingual: to cause someone to be involved in something, usually something unpleasant. _ Fred had no idea what his brother had let him in for when he agreed to take his place in the race. _ Jack didn’t know what he was letting himself in for when he married tha
examples: Fred had no idea what his brother had let him in for when he agreed to take his place in the race.

let someone or something down†.monolingual: Fig. to fail someone or something; to disappoint someone or a group. _ Please don’t let me down. I am depending on you. _ I let down the entire cast of the play.
examples: Please don’t let me down.

let someone slide by.monolingual: Fig. to permit someone to get past a barrier or a challenge too easily. _ You let too many students slide by. You need to be more rigorous. _Don’t let even one unqualified person slide by!
examples: You let too many students slide by.

let something off†.monolingual: to release something; to give something off. _ The engine let some evil smelling smoke off. _ The f lower let off a wonderful smell.
examples: The engine let some evil smelling smoke off.

let something out†.monolingual: 1. Fig. to reveal something; to tell about a secret or a plan. _ It was supposed to be a secret. Who let it out? _ Who let out the secret?
examples: It was supposed to be a secret.

let something pass.monolingual: Fig. to let something go unnoticed or unchallenged. _ Bob let Bill’s insult pass because he didn’t want to argue. _Don’t worry, I’ll let this little incident pass.
examples: Bob let Bill’s insult pass because he didn’t want to argue.

let something ride.monolingual: Fig. to allow something to continue or remain as it is. _ It isn’t the best plan, but we’ll let it ride. _ I disagree with you, but I’ll let it ride.
examples: It isn’t the best plan, but we’ll let it ride.

let the buyer beware..monolingual: Prov. ClichéWhen you buy something, you must take precautions against being cheated, because you cannot trust merchants to be honest about what they sell. _ Let the buyer beware when shopping for a used car. _Several of the lamps among those Max offe
examples: Let the buyer beware when shopping for a used car.

let the chance slip by.monolingual: Fig. to lose the opportunity (to do something). _When I was younger, I wanted to become a doctor, but I let the chance slip by. _ Don’t let the chance slip by. Do it now!
examples: When I was younger, I wanted to become a doctor, but I let the chance slip by.

let them eat cake..monolingual: Prov. A joking disclaimer of responsibility for some group of people. (Supposed to have been said by Marie Antoinette when she heard that the common people had no bread.) _ Fred: The budget will allow each one of our managers to get a substantial hol
examples: Fred: The budget will allow each one of our managers to get a substantial holiday bonus.

let up.monolingual: 1. to diminish. _I hope this rain lets up a little soon. _When the snow lets up so I can see, I will drive to the store.
examples: I hope this rain lets up a little soon.

let us do something..monolingual: We will do something [together]. _ Let us go in peace. _ Let us bow our heads in prayer.
examples: Let us go in peace.

level a charge against someone.monolingual: Fig. to place a charge against someone; to accuse someone of something. _The neighbors leveled a disturbance of the peace charge against us. _ The cops leveled an assault charge against Max.
examples: The neighbors leveled a disturbance of the peace charge against us.

level off.monolingual: [for variation or fluctuation in the motion of something] to diminish; [for a rate] to stop increasing or decreasing. _ The plane leveled off at 10,000 feet. _ After a while the workload will level off. _ Things will level off after we get through th
examples: The plane leveled off at 10,000 feet.
