level out.monolingual: [for something that was going up and down] to assume a more level course or path. _The road leveled out after a while and driving was easier. _As we got down into the valley, the land leveled out and traveling was easier.
examples: The road leveled out after a while and driving was easier.

a level playing field.monolingual: Fig. a situation that is fair to all; a situation where everyone has the same opportunity. field.) _ If we started off with a level playing field, everyone would have an equal chance.
examples: If we started off with a level playing field, everyone would have an equal chance.

level something down.monolingual: to make something level or smooth. _ The soil is very uneven in this part of the garden. Would you please level it down? _ The huge earth-moving machines leveled the hill down in preparation for the building of the highway.
examples: The soil is very uneven in this part of the garden.

level something off†.monolingual: to make something level or smooth. _ You are going to have to level the f loor off before you put the carpet down. _ Please level off the f loor.
examples: You are going to have to level the f loor off before you put the carpet down.

level something out†.monolingual: to cause something to assume a more level course or path. _ Level this path out before you open it to the public. _ They have to level out this roadway.
examples: Level this path out before you open it to the public.

level something to the ground.monolingual: to crush or demolish something down to the ground. _They were forced to level the building to the ground, because they could not afford to maintain it. _ The house was leveled to the ground by the tornado.
examples: They were forced to level the building to the ground, because they could not afford to maintain it.

level something up†.monolingual: to move something into a level or plumb position. _ Use a piece of wood under the table’s leg to level it up. _ I will level up the table.
examples: Use a piece of wood under the table’s leg to level it up.

license to do something.monolingual: permission, right, or justification to do something. _ You have no license to behave in that manner! _Who granted you license to enter my house without knocking?

*a lick and a promise.monolingual: Fig. a hasty bit of work; a quick once-over. (*Typically: finish something with ~; give something ~.) _ I was pressed for time, so I just gave the housework a lick and a promise. _Mary spent so much time on her history paper that she had to finish he
examples: I was pressed for time, so I just gave the housework a lick and a promise.

lick at something.monolingual: to draw the tongue over something repeatedly. _ Jimmy was just licking at the ice-cream cone, and soon it began to melt and drip off his elbow. _ I don’t just lick at the ice cream. I take big bites of it.
examples: Jimmy was just licking at the ice-cream cone, and soon it began to melt and drip off his elbow.

a lick of work.monolingual: a bit of work. (Used with a negative.) _ I couldn’t get her to do a lick of work all day long! _The boys didn’t do a lick of work while you were away.
examples: The boys didn’t do a lick of work while you were away.

lick one’s chops.monolingual: Fig. to show one’s eagerness to do something, especially to eat something. _ We could tell from the way the boys were licking their chops that they really wanted a turn at riding the motorcycle. _Fred started licking his chops when he smelled the tur
examples: We could tell from the way the boys were licking their chops that they really wanted a turn at riding the motorcycle.

lick one’s lips.monolingual: Fig. to show eagerness or pleasure about a future event. (From the habit of people licking their lips when they are about to enjoy eating something.) _ The children licked their lips at the sight of the cake. _ The author’s readers were licking their
examples: The children licked their lips at the sight of the cake.

lick one’s wounds.monolingual: Fig. to recover from a defeat or a rebuke. (Also literal for an animal.) _ After the terrible meeting and all the criticism, I went back to my office to lick my wounds.
examples: After the terrible meeting and all the criticism, I went back to my office to lick my wounds.

lick something up†.monolingual: to clean up all of some substance by licking with the tongue. (Usually said of an animal.) _ Don’t worry about the spilled milk. The dog will lick it up. _ The dog licked up the milk.
examples: Don’t worry about the spilled milk.

*a licking.monolingual: a spanking; a beating in a fight. (*Typically: get ~; take ~; give someone ~.) _ Billy, you had better get in here if you don’t want to get a licking. _ Bob took a real licking in the stock market. _ Tom gave Harry a licking in the fight he was in.
examples: Billy, you had better get in here if you don’t want to get a licking.

*a lid on something.monolingual: 1. Lit. a cover on something, such as a pot, pan, etc. (*Typically: get ~; keep ~; put ~.) _ Keep the lid on the pot until the stew is almost done. _ Put the lid on the skillet for just a little while.
examples: Keep the lid on the pot until the stew is almost done.

lie about.monolingual: 1. [for someone] to recline lazily somewhere. _ She just lay about through her entire vacation. _ Don’t lie about all the time. Get busy.
examples: She just lay about through her entire vacation.

lie at anchor.monolingual: [for a ship] to wait or rest at anchor. _ The ship lay at anchor throughout the day while a shore party searched for the runaway. _ We lay at anchor overnight, waiting for the tide.
examples: The ship lay at anchor throughout the day while a shore party searched for the runaway.

lie at death’s door.monolingual: Fig. to be close to dying. _She lay at death’s door for over a month. _ I do not want to lie at death’s door suffering. I hope to pass on quickly.
examples: She lay at death’s door for over a month.

lie back.monolingual: to relax; to lean back in a chair and relax. _ Just lie back and try to get comfortable. _ I really need to get home and lie back and relax.
examples: Just lie back and try to get comfortable.

lie behind someone or something.monolingual: 1. [for something] to be positioned to the rear of someone or something. _A wide expanse of water lay behind the sentry, and a narrow road- way lay in front. _A vast field lies behind the house.
examples: A wide expanse of water lay behind the sentry, and a narrow road- way lay in front.

lie beyond someone or something.monolingual: 1. to be located on the other side of someone or something. _ The stream lies beyond those men you see working in the field. _ The village lies just beyond that hill there.
examples: The stream lies beyond those men you see working in the field.

lie doggo.monolingual: Fig. to remain unrecognized (for a long time). _ This problem has lain doggo since
examples: This problem has lain doggo since 1967.

lie down.monolingual: to recline. _ Why don’t you lie down for a while? _ I need to lie down and have a little snooze.
examples: I need to lie down and have a little snooze.

lie down on something.monolingual: to recline on something. _ Don’t lie down on that couch! _I will just lie down on my bed for a few minutes.
examples: I will just lie down on my bed for a few minutes.

lie down under something.monolingual: to lie down beneath something. _She was tired, so she lay down under a willow tree by the brook. _ The dog lay down under a lawn chair and slept.
examples: She was tired, so she lay down under a willow tree by the brook.

lie fallow.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for farmland] to exist unplanted for a period of time. _ The fields lay fallow under the burning sun. It had been too wet to plant last spring.
examples: The fields lay fallow under the burning sun.

lie in.monolingual: [for a woman] to lie in bed awaiting the birth of her child. _ The child is due soon, and the mother is lying in at the present time. _ She did not lie in at all. She worked right up to the onset of labor pains.
examples: The child is due soon, and the mother is lying in at the present time.

lie in ruins.monolingual: to exist in a state of ruin, such as a destroyed city, building, scheme, plan, etc. _ The entire city lay in ruins. _ My garden lay in ruins after the cows got in and trampled everything.
examples: The entire city lay in ruins.

lie in something.monolingual: to recline in something, such as a bed, a puddle, etc. _ I found my wallet lying in a puddle. My money was soaked! _ We found Jimmy lying in a pile of leaves, napping.
examples: I found my wallet lying in a puddle.

lie in state.monolingual: [for a dead body] to be on display for public mourning. _ The president will lie in state in the Capitol Rotunda. _ Mourners filed past the leader where he lay in state.
examples: The president will lie in state in the Capitol Rotunda.

lie like a rug.monolingual: Sl. to tell lies shamelessly. _He says he didn’t take the money, but he’s lying like a rug. _ I don’t believe her. She lies like a rug.
examples: He says he didn’t take the money, but he’s lying like a rug.

lie through one’s teeth.monolingual: Fig. to lie boldly. _ I knew she was lying through her teeth, but I didn’t want to say so just then. _If John denies it he’s lying through his teeth, because I saw him do it.
examples: I knew she was lying through her teeth, but I didn’t want to say so just then.

lie with someone.monolingual: 1. to recline with someone. _Come and lie with me and we will keep warm. _ Jimmy and Franny were lying with each other to keep warm.
examples: Come and lie with me and we will keep warm.

lie within something.monolingual: to remain within a defined area or domain. _ The boundaries of the village lie completely within the river valley. _ The cost you cited lies within the range I was considering.
examples: The boundaries of the village lie completely within the river valley.

life begins at forty..monolingual: Prov. By the time you are forty years old, you have enough experience and skill to do what you want to do with your life. (Often said as an encouragement to those reaching middle age.) _Alan: Why are you so depressed? Jane: Tomorrow’s my fortieth bir
examples: Alan: Why are you so depressed? Jane: Tomorrow’s my fortieth birthday.

life in the fast lane.monolingual: a very active or possible risky way to live. _ Life in the fast lane is too much for me.
examples: Life in the fast lane is too much for me.

life is too short..monolingual: Life is short and there is no point in wasting it on things like worry, hatred, vengeance, etc. _ I am not going to spend any more time trying to get even with Wally. Life’s too short. _ It’s a waste of time worrying about money. Life is too short fo
examples: I am not going to spend any more time trying to get even with Wally.

the life of the party.monolingual: Fig. a person who is lively and helps make a party fun and exciting. _ Bill is always the life of the party. Be sure to invite him. _ Bob isn’t exactly the life of the party, but he’s polite.
examples: Bill is always the life of the party.

lift off.monolingual: [for a plane or rocket] to move upward, leaving the ground. _ The rocket lifted off exactly on time.
examples: The rocket lifted off exactly on time.

lift someone or something up†.monolingual: to raise someone or something. _ I helped lift him up and put him on the stretcher. _ Please lift up Tommy.
examples: I helped lift him up and put him on the stretcher.

lift up.monolingual: to raise up. _ Suddenly, the top of the box lifted up and a hand reached out. _Bill’s hand lifted up and fell back again.
examples: Suddenly, the top of the box lifted up and a hand reached out.

light someone or something up†.monolingual: to shine lights on someone or something. _We lit Fred up with the headlights of the car. _ Light up the stage and let’s rehearse.
examples: We lit Fred up with the headlights of the car.

light something up†.monolingual: 1. to light a fire, a gas burner, etc. _ I lit the kindling up and soon the fire was going. _ You light up the stove and get dinner going.
examples: I lit the kindling up and soon the fire was going.

light something with something.monolingual: 1. to set something afire with something else. _Kelly lit the fire with her last match. _ I will light the fire with a cigarette lighter.
examples: Kelly lit the fire with her last match.

light up.monolingual: 1. to become brighter. _ Suddenly, the sky lit up like day. _ The room lit up as the fire suddenly came back to life.
examples: Suddenly, the sky lit up like day.

lighten something up†.monolingual: to make something lighter or brighter. _ Some white paint will lighten this room up a lot. _ The sunlight came in and lightened up the kitchen.
examples: Some white paint will lighten this room up a lot.

lighten up.monolingual: to become lighter or brighter. _We applied a new coat of white paint to the walls, and the room lightened up considerably. _ The sky is beginning to lighten up a little.
examples: We applied a new coat of white paint to the walls, and the room lightened up considerably.

like a can of corn.monolingual: Rur. very easy. _ Whipping up dinner for twelve is like a can of corn, as far as Jane is concerned. _ The championship game was like a can of corn for our team. We won easily.
examples: Whipping up dinner for twelve is like a can of corn, as far as Jane is concerned.

like a three-ring circus.monolingual: Fig. chaotic; exciting and busy. _ Our household is like a three-ring circus on Monday mornings. _ This meeting is like a three-ring circus. Quiet down and listen!
examples: Our household is like a three-ring circus on Monday mornings.

*like a ton of bricks.monolingual: Inf. like a great weight or burden. (*Typically: fall ~; hit ~; hit someone ~.) _Suddenly, the truth hit me like a ton of bricks. _ The sudden tax increase hit like a ton of bricks. Everyone became angry.
examples: Suddenly, the truth hit me like a ton of bricks.

like breeds like..monolingual: Prov. People tend to raise children who are like them; something tends to give rise to things that resemble it. _Jill: I think Fred’s little boy is going to be just as disagreeable as Fred. Jane: That’s no surprise. Like breeds like.
examples: Jill: I think Fred’s little boy is going to be just as disagreeable as Fred.

*like death warmed over.monolingual: Fig. very ill; appearing very sickly. (*Typically: feel ~; look ~.) _ Oh dear, I feel like death warmed over. _ Poor Carol said you look like death warmed over.
examples: Oh dear, I feel like death warmed over.

like father, like son.monolingual: Prov. Fathers and sons resemble each other, and sons tend to do what their fathers did before them. _ Jill: George’s father smoked all the time, and now George is smoking excessively, too. Jane: Like father, like son, eh? _ I think my son will grow u
examples: Jill: George’s father smoked all the time, and now George is smoking excessively, too.

like fighting snakes.monolingual: Rur. chaotic; challenging. (As if every time one snake is subdued, another one attacks.) _ It’s like fighting snakes to get anything done at this time of year. _ Arguing with you is like fighting snakes.
examples: It’s like fighting snakes to get anything done at this time of year.

like flies to manure.monolingual: Rur. eagerly gathering in large numbers. (Has unpleasant connotations because of the reference to manure.) _Look at all them folks going to the freak show like f lies to manure. _ The reporters hovered around the movie star like f lies to manure.
examples: Look at all them folks going to the freak show like f lies to manure.

like gangbusters.monolingual: with great excitement and speed. (From the phrase “Come on like gangbusters,” a radio show that “came on” with lots of noise and excitement.) _She works like gangbusters and gets the job done. _They are selling tickets like gangbusters.
examples: She works like gangbusters and gets the job done.

like greased lightning.monolingual: Rur. very fast. _ Once I get her tuned up, this old car will go like greased lightning. _ He’s a fat kid, but he can run like greased lightning.
examples: Once I get her tuned up, this old car will go like greased lightning.

like hell and high lightning.monolingual: Rur. very fast. _The snowmobiles came zooming down the trail like hell and high lightning. _ The powerboat sped up the river like hell and high lightning.
examples: The snowmobiles came zooming down the trail like hell and high lightning.

like herding frogs.monolingual: Rur. chaotic; disorderly. (On the image of trying to direct frogs, which will jump any which way.) _ Trying to get those kids to march into the auditorium is like herding frogs. _Trying to get everybody to cooperate is like herding frogs.
examples: Trying to get those kids to march into the auditorium is like herding frogs.

like it or lump it!.monolingual: Inf. There is no other choice. Take that or none. _ John: I don’t like this room. It’s too small. Bill: Like it or lump it. That’s all we’ve got. _ Jane: I don’t want to be talked to like that. Sue: Well, like it or lump it! That’s the way we talk ar
examples: John: I don’t like this room.

like mother, like daughter..monolingual: Prov. Daughters resemble their mothers.; Daughters tend to do what their mothers did before them. _My mother loved sweets, and every time my father saw me with a cookie in my hand, he would sigh, “Like mother, like daughter.” _ Jill: Gina’s beautiful
examples: My mother loved sweets, and every time my father saw me with a cookie in my hand, he would sigh, “Like mother, like daughter.

like nobody’s business.monolingual: Inf. very well; very much. _She can sing like nobody’s business. What a set of pipes! _ My mom can cook chocolate chip cookies like nobody’s business.
examples: She can sing like nobody’s business.

like nothing on earth.monolingual: 1. Fig. very untidy or very unattractive. _Joan arrived at the office looking like nothing on earth. She had fallen in the mud. _ Alice was like nothing on earth in that electric yellow dress.
examples: Joan arrived at the office looking like nothing on earth.

like one of the family.monolingual: as if someone (or a pet) were a member of one’s family. _We treat our dog like one of the family. _ We are very happy to have you stay with us, Bill. I hope you don’t mind if we treat you like one of the family.
examples: We treat our dog like one of the family.

like pigs to the slaughter.monolingual: Rur. obediently and in large numbers. _Look at all the people lining up to mail their tax forms on time, like pigs to the slaughter.
examples: Look at all the people lining up to mail their tax forms on time, like pigs to the slaughter.

*like stink.monolingual: Inf. rapidly. (As fast as a smell spreads. *Typically: go ~; move ~; run ~; swim ~.) _ Those kids moved through the whole test like stink. Real eagerbeavers. _ The wood chipper went through the brush like stink and turned it into a small pile in minu
examples: Those kids moved through the whole test like stink.

*like the wind.monolingual: Fig. very fast; as fast and easy as the wind. (*Typically: go ~; move ~; run ~.) _ Emily’s sleek new bicycle can really go like the wind. _ The racehorse ran like the wind, beating its nearest opponent by several lengths.
examples: Emily’s sleek new bicycle can really go like the wind.

like to hear oneself talk.monolingual: [for someone] to enjoy one’s own talking more than people enjoy listening to it. _ I guess I don’t really have anything to say. I just like to hear myself talk, I guess. _ There he goes again. He just likes to hear himself talk.
examples: I guess I don’t really have anything to say.

like, you know.monolingual: Inf. a combining of the (essentially meaningless) expressions like and you know. (Never used in formal writing.) _She is, well, like, you know, uncool. _This is, well, like, you know, too much!
examples: She is, well, like, you know, uncool.

*likely as not.monolingual: Fig. probably; with an even chance either way. (*Also: as ~.) _ He will as likely as not arrive without warning. _ Likely as not, the game will be canceled.
examples: He will as likely as not arrive without warning.

limber someone or something up†.monolingual: to make someone or something more flexible or loose. _Let me give you a massage; that will limber you up. _I need to limber up my arms.
examples: Let me give you a massage; that will limber you up.

limit someone to something.monolingual: 1. to restrict someone to a certain amount or number of something. _ I will have to limit you to two helpings of mashed potatoes. _ I limit myself to cola drinks only.
examples: I will have to limit you to two helpings of mashed potatoes.

limit something to something.monolingual: to restrict something to a limited set, a certain amount, or a specific number of something. _Please limit your comments to five minutes. _Can you limit your remarks to the subject at hand?
examples: Please limit your comments to five minutes.

the line of least resistance.monolingual: the course of action that will cause least trouble or effort. _ Jane won’t stand up for her rights. She always takes the line of least resistance. _ Joan never states her point of view. She takes the line of least resistance and agrees with everyone
examples: Jane won’t stand up for her rights.

line someone or something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to put people or things in line. _ Line everyone up and march them onstage. _ Line up the kids, please. _Please line these books up. _Hey, you guys! Line yourselves up!
examples: Line everyone up and march them onstage.

line something with something.monolingual: to place a layer of something over the inside surface of something. _You should line the drawers with clean paper before you use them. _ I want to line this jacket with new material.
examples: You should line the drawers with clean paper before you use them.

line up.monolingual: to form a line; to get into a line. _All right, everyone, line up!

line up for something.monolingual: to form or get into a line and wait for something. _ Everyone lined up for a helping of birthday cake. _ Let’s line up for dinner. The doors to the dining room will open at any minute.
examples: Everyone lined up for a helping of birthday cake.

line up on something.monolingual: to form a line oriented on something. _ Line up on the white line painted on the pavement. _ Please line up on the marks on the f loor.
examples: Line up on the white line painted on the pavement.

line up with someone.monolingual: to get into a line with someone. _ Go over and line up with the others. _ Would you please line up with the other students?
examples: Go over and line up with the others.

linger around.monolingual: to wait around; to be idle some place. _ Don’t linger around. Get going! _All the students were lingering around, waiting until the last minute to go into the building.
examples: Don’t linger around.

linger on.monolingual: to remain for a long time; to exist longer than would have been thought. _ This cold of mine just keeps lingering on. _Some of the guests lingered on for a long time after the party was over.
examples: This cold of mine just keeps lingering on.

linger on something.monolingual: to delay moving on to the next thing; to remain at something and not move on. _ Don’t linger on that one problem so long. _ I don’t want to waste a lot of time lingering on this question.
examples: Don’t linger on that one problem so long.

linger over something.monolingual: 1. to take too much time or idle over something, such as a meal, a cup of coffee, etc. _ I could linger over coffee all morning, given the chance. _ Don’t linger over your soup. It will get cold.
examples: I could linger over coffee all morning, given the chance.

liquor someone up†.monolingual: to get someone tipsy or drunk. _ He liquored her up and tried to take her home with him. _ They liquored up the out-of-town visitors.
examples: He liquored her up and tried to take her home with him.

liquor up.monolingual: to drink an alcoholic beverage, especially to excess. _Sam sat around all evening liquoring up. _They seem to liquor up almost every night of the week.
examples: Sam sat around all evening liquoring up.

list someone as something.monolingual: to categorize someone as something, usually in a written list. _ I will list you as a contributor to the Preservation Fund, if you don’t mind. _ Although she was not registered as such, she listed herself as a stockbroker.
examples: I will list you as a contributor to the Preservation Fund, if you don’t mind.

list someone or something off†.monolingual: to recite a list of people or things, one by one. _She listed everyone off in order without having to look at her notes. _ She listed off the names of the people who are always late. _ Dale listed each one off.
examples: She listed everyone off in order without having to look at her notes.

list to a direction.monolingual: to lean to one side or another; to lean toward a specific direction. (Usually of ships or boats.) _ The ship had listed to one side since being struck by the speedboat. _ The huge ship listed a tiny bit to starboard.
examples: The ship had listed to one side since being struck by the speedboat.

listen for someone or something.monolingual: to try to hear someone or something. _ I will have to let you in the front door if you come home late. I will listen for you. _ I am listening for the telephone.
examples: I will have to let you in the front door if you come home late.

listen to reason.monolingual: to yield to a reasonable argument; to take the reasonable course. _ Please listen to reason, and don’t do something you’ll regret. _ She got into trouble because she wouldn’t listen to reason.
examples: Please listen to reason, and don’t do something you’ll regret.

listen to someone or something.monolingual: 1. to pay attention to and hear someone or something. _ Listen to me! Hear what I have to say! _ I want to listen to his speech.
examples: I want to listen to his speech.

listen up.monolingual: to listen carefully. (Usually a command.) _Now, listen up! This is important. _ Listen up, you guys!
examples: Now, listen up! This is important.

litmus test.monolingual: 1. Lit. a test used to determine the acidity or alkalinity of chemical substances. (Acid turns litmus paper red and alkaline compounds turn it blue.) _ I used a litmus test to show that the compound was slightly acid.
examples: I used a litmus test to show that the compound was slightly acid.

litter something up†.monolingual: to mess something up with litter, trash, possessions, etc. _ Who littered this room up? _ Who littered up this room?

a little bird told me..monolingual: Fig. a way of indicating that you do not want to reveal who told you something. (Sometimes used playfully, when you think that the person you are addressing knows or can guess who was the source of your information.) _Jill: Thank you for the beautifu
examples: Jill: Thank you for the beautiful pre- sent! How did you know I wanted a green silk scarf ? Jane: A little bird told me.

little bitty.monolingual: very little. _ Can I have just a little bitty piece of that lemon meringue pie? _He was just a little bitty boy.
examples: He was just a little bitty boy.

little by little.monolingual: gradually, a little bit at a time. _ I earned enough money, little by little, to buy a car. _Jimmy crawled, little by little, until he reached the door.
examples: I earned enough money, little by little, to buy a car.

little old someone or something.monolingual: ordinary; harmless. (Said to downplay or minimize the importance of something.) _ Aw, honey, I wasn’t gambling. I just went to one little old poker game. _ Charlie: Did you eat that whole chocolate cake that I was saving for the party? Jane: Little o
examples: Aw, honey, I wasn’t gambling.

little pitchers have big ears..monolingual: Prov. Children like to listen to adult conversations and can understand a lot of what they hear. (Used to warn another adult not to talk about something because there is a child present.) _ I started to tell Mary about the date I had on Saturday, but

little shaver.monolingual: Rur. a child; a baby. _I think the little shaver needs her diaper changed. _Tom thinks his grandson is the cutest little shaver there ever was.
examples: I think the little shaver needs her diaper changed.

little strokes fell great oaks..monolingual: Prov. You can complete a large, intimidating task by steadily doing small parts of it. _ Jill: How can I possibly write a fifty-page report in two months? Jane: Just write a little bit every day. Little strokes fell great oaks.
examples: Jill: How can I possibly write a fifty-page report in two months? Jane: Just write a little bit every day.

a little white lie.monolingual: Fig. a small, usually harmless lie; a fib. _ Every little white lie you tell is still a lie and it is still meant to mislead people.
examples: Every little white lie you tell is still a lie and it is still meant to mislead people.

live a life of something.monolingual: to have a life of a certain quality or style. _ The movie star lived a life of luxury. _ After Anne won the lottery, she lived the life of a queen.
examples: The movie star lived a life of luxury.

live among someone.monolingual: to live in a community with someone or a community made up of certain people. _ The anthropologist lived among the small tribe for two years. _ They lived among the Jivaro Indians for a brief period.
examples: The anthropologist lived among the small tribe for two years.

live and learn.monolingual: Cliché to increase one’s knowledge by experience. (Usually said when one is surprised to learn something.) _ I didn’t know that snakes could swim. Well, live and learn! _ John didn’t know he should water his houseplants a little extra in the dry wint
examples: I didn’t know that snakes could swim.

live and let live.monolingual: Cliché not to interfere with other people’s business or preferences. _ I don’t care what they do! Live and let live, I always say. _ Your parents are strict. Mine just live and let live.
examples: I don’t care what they do! Live and let live, I always say.

live beyond one’s means.monolingual: to spend more money than one can afford. _ The Browns are deeply in debt because they are living beyond their means. _ I keep a budget so that I don’t live beyond my means.
examples: The Browns are deeply in debt because they are living beyond their means.

live by one’s wits.monolingual: Fig. to survive by being clever. _ When you’re in the kind of business I’m in, you have to live by your wits. _ John was orphaned at the age of ten and grew up living by his wits.
examples: When you’re in the kind of business I’m in, you have to live by your wits.

live by something.monolingual: 1. to live near something. _ We live by a lovely park that is filled with children in the summer. _ I would love to live by the sea.
examples: We live by a lovely park that is filled with children in the summer.

live for someone or something.monolingual: 1. to exist for the benefit of someone or something. _ She just lives for her children. _ Roger lives for his work.
examples: She just lives for her children.

live for the moment.monolingual: Fig. to live only for the pleasures of the present time without planning for the future. _ You need to make plans for your future. You cannot live just for the moment! _ He lives only for the moment.
examples: You need to make plans for your future.

live from day to day.monolingual: Fig. to survive on limited means one day at a time with no plans or possibilities for the future. _ The Simpsons just live from day to day. They never plan for the future. _ I can’t live from day to day. I have to provide for the future.
examples: The Simpsons just live from day to day.

live from hand to mouth.monolingual: Fig. to live in poor circumstances. _When both my parents were out of work, we lived from hand to mouth. _We lived from hand to mouth during the war. Things were very difficult.
examples: When both my parents were out of work, we lived from hand to mouth.

live happily ever after.monolingual: Cliché to live in happiness after a specific event. (A formulaic phrase at the end of fairy tales.) _The prince and the princess lived happily ever after. _ They went away from the horrible haunted castle and lived happily ever after.
examples: The prince and the princess lived happily ever after.

live in.monolingual: to live at the residence at which one works. _ In order to be here early enough to prepare breakfast, the cook has to live in. _ Mr. Simpson has a valet, but he doesn’t live in.
examples: In order to be here early enough to prepare breakfast, the cook has to live in.

live in sin.monolingual: to live with and have sex with someone to whom one is not married. (Sometimes serious and sometimes jocular.) _Would you like to get married, or would you prefer that we live in sin for a few more years? _ Let’s live in sin. There’s no risk of divorc
examples: Let’s live in sin.

live in something.monolingual: to dwell within something or some place. _They live in the village. _She lives in a large house in the country.
examples: They live in the village.

live in the past.monolingual: Fig. to live while dwelling on past memories without participating in the present or planning for the future. _ You are just living in the past. Join us in the twenty-first century. _Living in the past has its advantages.
examples: You are just living in the past.

live in the present.monolingual: Fig. to deal with contemporary events and not be dominated by events of the past or planning for the future. _ Forget the past; live in the present. _ It was no longer possible to get Uncle Herman to live in the present.
examples: Forget the past; live in the present.

live it up.monolingual: to have an exciting time; to do what one pleases—regardless of cost—to please oneself. _ At the party, John was really living it up. _ Come on! Have fun! Live it up!
examples: At the party, John was really living it up.

live large.monolingual: to live in luxury; to spend time in grand style. _ George loved to live large, dining at fine French restaurants.
examples: George loved to live large, dining at fine French restaurants.

live off the land.monolingual: to live by eating only the food that one produces from the land; to survive by gathering or stealing food, fruits, berries, eggs, etc., while traveling through the countryside. _ We lived off the land for a few years when we first started out farming
examples: We lived off the land for a few years when we first started out farming.

live on borrowed time.monolingual: Fig. to exist only because of good fortune; to live on when death was expected. _ The doc- tors told him he was living on borrowed time. _You are living on borrowed time, so make the best of it.
examples: The doc- tors told him he was living on borrowed time.

live on one’s own.monolingual: to live independently, in a separate dwelling. _ I moved out of my parents’ house because I wanted to live on my own for a while. _ It’s time you were out living on your own.
examples: I moved out of my parents’ house because I wanted to live on my own for a while.

live on something.monolingual: to depend on something for sustenance. (Compare this with live off someone or something.) _I can’t live on bread and water. _ We can hardly live on $500 a week.
examples: I can’t live on bread and water.

live out of a suitcase.monolingual: Fig. to stay very briefly in several places, never unpacking one’s luggage. _ I hate living out of a suitcase. For my next vacation, I want to go to just one place and stay there the whole time.
examples: I hate living out of a suitcase.

live out of cans.monolingual: Fig. to eat only canned food. _You have to have some fresh fruit and vegetables. You can’t just live out of cans. _ We lived out of cans for the entire camping trip.
examples: You have to have some fresh fruit and vegetables.

live something down†.monolingual: to overcome the shame or embarrassment of something. _ You’ll live it down someday. _ Wilbur will never be able to live down what happened at the party last night.
examples: You’ll live it down someday.

live something out†.monolingual: to act out something such as one’s fantasies. _ She tried to live her dreams out. _ He has a tendency to try to live out his fantasies.
examples: She tried to live her dreams out.

live something over.monolingual: to go back and live a part of one’s life again in order to do things differently. _ I wish I could go back and live those days over again. Boy, would I do things differently! _I would like to live that period of my life over again.
examples: I wish I could go back and live those days over again.

live through something.monolingual: to endure something; to survive an unpleasant or dangerous time of one’s life. _ I almost did not live through the operation. _ I know I can’t live through another attack.
examples: I almost did not live through the operation.

live to do something.monolingual: 1. to survive long enough to do something. _ I just hope I live to see them get married and have children. _ Bill wants to live to see his grandchildren grow up.
examples: I just hope I live to see them get married and have children.

live together.monolingual: 1. [for two people] to dwell in the same place. _ I live together with my sister in the house my parents left us. _ Henry and Jill live together in their parents’ house.
examples: I live together with my sister in the house my parents left us.

live under someone or something.monolingual: to dwell directly beneath someone or something. _We live under the Johnsons. They are fairly quiet. _ We lived under a law office for a few years.
examples: We live under the Johnsons.

live up to something.monolingual: to fulfill expectations; to satisfy a goal or set of goals. (Often with one’s reputation, promise, word, standards, etc.) _ I hope I can live up to my reputation. _ The class lives up to its reputation of being exciting and interesting.
examples: I hope I can live up to my reputation.

live with someone.monolingual: Euph. to live together with someone; to live in a romantic relationship with someone outside of marriage. _ I lived with my aunt when I was growing up. _Is Frank living with his girlfriend? _Sandy is living with her domestic partner.
examples: I lived with my aunt when I was growing up.

live with something.monolingual: to put up with something; to endure something. (Does not mean “to dwell with.”) _ That is not acceptable. I can’t live with that. Please change it. _ Mary refused to live with the proposed changes.
examples: That is not acceptable.

live within one’s means.monolingual: to spend no more money than one has. _ We have to struggle to live within our means, but we manage. _ John is unable to live within his means.
examples: We have to struggle to live within our means, but we manage.

live within something.monolingual: 1. to live within certain boundaries. _ Do you think you can live within your space, or are we going to argue over the use of square footage? _ Ted demanded again that Bill live within his assigned area.
examples: Ted demanded again that Bill live within his assigned area.

live without something.monolingual: to survive, lacking something. _ I just know I can’t live without my car. _ I am sure we can live without vegetables for a day or two.
examples: I just know I can’t live without my car.

liven something up†.monolingual: to make something more lively or less dull. _ Some singing might liven things up a bit. _ The songs livened up the evening.
examples: Some singing might liven things up a bit.

the living end.monolingual: Fig. the absolute best [person]. _We really like Ralph. He is the living end as far as his girlfriend is concerned.
examples: We really like Ralph.

lo and behold!.monolingual: Cliché Look here!; Thus! (An expression of surprise.) _ Lo and behold! There is Fred! He beat us here by taking a shortcut.
examples: Lo and behold! There is Fred! He beat us here by taking a shortcut.

load into something.monolingual: [for people] to get into something. _ Everyone loaded into the bus, and we set off for Denver. _ The kids all loaded into the station wagon for the trip.
examples: Everyone loaded into the bus, and we set off for Denver.

*a load off one’s feet.monolingual: Fig. the weight of one’s body no longer supported by one’s feet, as when one sits down. (*Typically: get ~; take ~.) _Come in, John. Sit down and take a load off your feet. _ Yes, I need to get a load off my feet. I’m really tired.
examples: Come in, John. Sit down and take a load off your feet.

load something with something.monolingual: to burden something with something; to put a lot of something onto or into something. _Load this box with all the clothing you can get into it. _ Don’t load these drawers with so much stuff.
examples: Load this box with all the clothing you can get into it.

loaded for bear.monolingual: 1. Inf. angry. _He left here in a rage. He was really loaded for bear. _ When I got home from work, I was really loaded for bear. What a horrible day!
examples: He left here in a rage.

loaf around.monolingual: to waste time; to idle the time away doing almost nothing. _ Every time I see you, you are just loafing around. _ I enjoy loafing around on the weekend.
examples: Every time I see you, you are just loafing around.

loaf something away†.monolingual: to waste away a period of time. _ You have loafed the entire day away! _ He loafed away the entire day.
examples: He loafed away the entire day.

loan something to someone.monolingual: to lend something to someone. (Considered to be an error for lend.) _Can you loan a few bucks to Sam and me? _ I will not loan anything to you.
examples: I will not loan anything to you.

lobby against something.monolingual: to solicit support against something, such as a piece of legislation or a government regulation. _ We sent a lot of lawyers to the state capital to lobby against the bill, but it passed anyway. _ They lobbied against the tax increase.
examples: We sent a lot of lawyers to the state capital to lobby against the bill, but it passed anyway.

lobby for something.monolingual: to solicit support for something among the members of a voting body, such as the Congress. _ Tom is always lobbying for some reform bill or other. _The manufacturers lobbied for tax relief.
examples: Tom is always lobbying for some reform bill or other.

local yokel.monolingual: a local resident of a rural place. (Mildly derogatory.) _ One of the local yokels helped me change the tire. _ The local yokels all listen to the same radio station.
examples: One of the local yokels helped me change the tire.

lock someone or something away†.monolingual: to put someone or something away in a locked container or space. _You will have to lock all the medications away when the grandchildren come to visit. _They locked away some cash for a rainy day. _ They locked it away.
examples: You will have to lock all the medications away when the grandchildren come to visit.

lock something in†.monolingual: to make something, such as a rate of interest, permanent over a period of time. _ You should try to lock in a high percentage rate on your bonds. _ We locked in a very low rate on our mortgage.
examples: You should try to lock in a high percentage rate on your bonds.

lock, stock, and barrel.monolingual: Cliché everything. _We had to move everything out of the house—lock, stock, and barrel. _We lost everything—lock, stock, and barrel—in the fire.
examples: We had to move everything out of the house—lock, stock, and barrel.

lodge someone with someone.monolingual: to have someone stay with someone as a guest. _ We lodged the visitor with George for the weekend. _Would it be possible for us to lodge Mary with you?
examples: We lodged the visitor with George for the weekend.

lodge something against someone.monolingual: to place a charge against someone. _ The neighbors lodged a complaint against us for walking on their grass. _ I want to lodge an assault charge against Randy.
examples: The neighbors lodged a complaint against us for walking on their grass.

lodge something against something.monolingual: to place or prop something against something. _We lodged the chest against the door, making it difficult or impossible to open. _Let’s lodge the stone against the side of the barn to help support it.
examples: We lodged the chest against the door, making it difficult or impossible to open.

lodge something in something.monolingual: to get something stuck in something or some place. _She lodged her coat in the door and tore it. _He lodged a screwdriver in the machine’s gears by accident.
examples: She lodged her coat in the door and tore it.

lodge with someone.monolingual: to stay or reside with someone. _ I lodged with my cousin while I was in Omaha. _Tricia plans to lodge with us while she is here.
examples: I lodged with my cousin while I was in Omaha.

log on.monolingual: to begin to use a computer system, as by entering a password, etc. (This action may be recorded, or logged, automatically in the computer’s memory.) _ What time did you log on to the system this morning? _ I always log on before I get my first cup of
examples: I always log on before I get my first cup of coffee.

log someone for something.monolingual: 1. to schedule someone for something. _ I am going to log you for sentry duty on the weekends. _ We will have to log Bill for service as a parking attendant.
examples: I am going to log you for sentry duty on the weekends.

log something up†.monolingual: to record an amount of something. _ The ship logged many nautical miles up on its last voyage. _ It logged up a lot of miles.
examples: The ship logged many nautical miles up on its last voyage.

loiter around.monolingual: to idle somewhere; to hang around. _Stop loitering around! Get going! _ The kids were loitering around for most of the summer.
examples: The kids were loitering around for most of the summer.

loiter over something.monolingual: to dawdle or linger over something. _Don’t loiter over your meal. I want to start the dishwasher. _ I wish you wouldn’t loiter over your chores.
examples: Don’t loiter over your meal.

loiter something away†.monolingual: to idle away a period of time. _ Those boys will loiter half their lives away. _ They loitered away their summer vacation.
examples: Those boys will loiter half their lives away.

loll around.monolingual: to roll, flop, or hang around. _ The dog’s tongue lolled around as it rolled on its back, trying to keep cool. _ Stop lolling around and get to work.
examples: The dog’s tongue lolled around as it rolled on its back, trying to keep cool.

loll back.monolingual: [for a head] to fall or droop backwards. _ As he passed out, his head lolled back and struck the corner of the table. _ Her head lolled back and suddenly she was fast asleep.
examples: As he passed out, his head lolled back and struck the corner of the table.

loll out.monolingual: [for a tongue] to hang or flop out. _ The dog’s tongue lolled out as it lay sleeping. _ Since the dog’s tongue lolled out every time it opened its mouth, it is a wonder it didn’t bite it when it closed its mouth.
examples: The dog’s tongue lolled out as it lay sleeping.

long for someone or something.monolingual: to desire or pine for someone or something. _ She is longing for her old friends. _ Walter longed for his hometown in the mountains.
examples: She is longing for her old friends.

long gone.monolingual: gone a long time ago; used up a long time ago. _The ice cream and cake are long gone. You are simply too late for the refreshments.
examples: The ice cream and cake are long gone.

long in the tooth.monolingual: Fig. old. _ That actor is getting a little long in the tooth to play the romantic lead. _I may be long in the tooth, but I’m not stupid.
examples: That actor is getting a little long in the tooth to play the romantic lead.

*a long shot.monolingual: Fig. a risky bet; an attempt, bet, or proposition that has a low probability of success. (*Typically: be ~; seem like ~.) _Your solution is a long shot, but we’ll try it and hope it works.
examples: Your solution is a long shot, but we’ll try it and hope it works.

long story short.monolingual: Sl. to make a long story short. _Okay, long story short: everything that goes up comes down, okay? _ Then the guy comes over, and—long story short—“You got a match?”

long time no see..monolingual: Cliché I have not seen you in a long time.; We have not seen each other in a long time. _Tom: Hi, Fred. Where have you been keeping yourself ? Fred: Good to see you, Tom. Long time no see. _John: It’s Bob! Hi, Bob! Bob: Hi, John! Long time no see.
examples: Tom: Hi, Fred. Where have you been keeping yourself ? Fred: Good to see you, Tom.

look after someone or something.monolingual: to take care of someone or something. _Please look after my little boy. _Will you look after my cat while I’m away? _Do you want me to look after your car?
examples: Please look after my little boy.

look ahead to something.monolingual: to try to foresee something; to think into the future about something. _She looked ahead to a bright future in sales. _I look ahead to a new job when I graduate.
examples: She looked ahead to a bright future in sales.

look alike.monolingual: to appear similar. _ All these cars look alike these days. _The twins look alike and not many people can tell them apart.
examples: All these cars look alike these days.

look alive!.monolingual: Act alert and responsive! _ “Come on, Fred! Get moving! Look alive!” shouted the coach, who was not happy with Fred’s performance. _Bill: Look alive, Bob! Bob: I’m doing the best I can.
examples: “Come on, Fred! Get moving! Look alive!” shouted the coach, who was not happy with Fred’s performance.

look aside.monolingual: to look to one side; to turn one’s head aside so as not to see someone or something. _ As I approached, he looked aside, pretending not to recognize me. _ She looked aside, hoping I wouldn’t see her.
examples: As I approached, he looked aside, pretending not to recognize me.

look at someone cross-eyed.monolingual: Fig. to merely appear to question, threaten, or mock someone. (Often in the negative.) _ You had better be on your best behavior around Tony. Don’t even look at him cross-eyed! _ If you so much as look at me cross-eyed, I will send you to your room.
examples: You had better be on your best behavior around Tony.

look before you leap..monolingual: Prov. Cliché Think carefully about what you are about to do before you do it. _ I’m not saying you shouldn’t sign the lease for that apartment. I’m just saying you should look before you leap. _ Jill: I’m thinking about going to night school. Jane: A
examples: I’m not saying you shouldn’t sign the lease for that apartment.

look beyond someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to try to see to a point farther than someone or something. _ Look beyond Claire at the forest in the distance. _ Look beyond the house and see what you can spot in the trees behind it.
examples: Look beyond Claire at the forest in the distance.

look daggers at someone.monolingual: Fig. to give someone a dirty look. _ Tom must have been mad at Ann from the way he was looking daggers at her. _ Don’t you dare look daggers at me! Don’t even look cross-eyed at me!
examples: Tom must have been mad at Ann from the way he was looking daggers at her.

look fit to kill.monolingual: Fig. [dressed up] to look very fancy or sexy. _Mary put on her best clothes and looked fit to kill. _John looked fit to kill in his new tuxedo.
examples: Mary put on her best clothes and looked fit to kill.

look forward to something.monolingual: to anticipate something with pleasure. _ I’m really looking forward to your visit next week. _ We all look forward to your new book on gardening.
examples: I’m really looking forward to your visit next week.

look good on paper.monolingual: to seem fine in theory, but not perhaps in practice; to appear to be a good plan. _ The plan looks good on paper, but it may not work. _This looks good on paper. Let’s hope it works in the real world.
examples: The plan looks good on paper, but it may not work.

look here.monolingual: a phrase emphasizing the point that follows. (Can show some impatience.) _Henry: Look here, I want to try to help you, but you’re not making it easy for me. Rachel: I’m just so upset. _ Andy: Look here, I just asked you a simple question! Bob: As I t
examples: Henry: Look here, I want to try to help you, but you’re not making it easy for me.

look on.monolingual: to be a spectator and watch what is happening without participating. _ The beating took place while a policeman looked on. _While the kittens played, the mother cat looked on contentedly.
examples: The beating took place while a policeman looked on.

look on someone as something.monolingual: to view or think of someone as something. _I look on you as a very thoughtful person. _ Mary looked on Jane as a good friend.
examples: I look on you as a very thoughtful person.

look on the bright side.monolingual: Fig. consider the positive aspects of a negative situation. _ Look on the bright side. Things could have been much worse than they are.
examples: Look on the bright side.

look someone or something over†.monolingual: to examine someone or something. _ I think you had better have the doctor look you over. _ Please look over these papers.
examples: I think you had better have the doctor look you over.

look the other way.monolingual: 1. Lit. to look in the opposite direction. _ To make sure it’s safe to cross the street, look the other way before you step off the curb.
examples: To make sure it’s safe to cross the street, look the other way before you step off the curb.

look through something.monolingual: 1. to gaze through something. _ Look through the window at what the neighbors are doing. _ Look through the binoculars and see if you can get a better view.
examples: Look through the window at what the neighbors are doing.

look to one’s laurels.monolingual: Fig. to take care not to lower or diminish one’s reputation or position, especially in relation to that of someone else potentially better. _With the arrival of the new member of the football team, James will have to look to his laurels to remain as
examples: With the arrival of the new member of the football team, James will have to look to his laurels to remain as the highest scorer.

look toward someone or something.monolingual: to face in the direction of someone or something. _ Look toward Sarah and see where she is standing. Isn’t that a lovely garden she’s in? _ Look toward the sea and see what a sunset is meant to look like.
examples: Look toward Sarah and see where she is standing.

look under the hood.monolingual: to examine the engine of a car; to check the oil, water, and other such routine items associated with the engine of a car. _ I finished putting gas in. I need to look under the hood. _ Do you want me to look under the hood, sir?
examples: I finished putting gas in.

look up.monolingual: to show promise of improving. _My prospects for a job are looking up. _ Conditions are looking up.
examples: My prospects for a job are looking up.

look up and down something.monolingual: to gaze up and then down something, such as a street. _We looked up and down the street and saw no cars, no houses, and no people. _ Mary looked up and down the highway, but she could not find her lost hubcap.
examples: We looked up and down the street and saw no cars, no houses, and no people.

look up to someone.monolingual: Fig. to view someone with respect and admiration. _ Bill really looks up to his father. _ Everyone in the class looked up to the teacher.
examples: Bill really looks up to his father.

look who’s here!.monolingual: an expression drawing attention to someone present or who just arrived at a place. _ Bill: Look who’s here! My old friend Fred. How goes it, Fred? Fred: Hi, there, Bill! What’s new? Bill: Nothing much. _Bill: Look who’s here! Mary: Yeah. Isn’t that F
examples: Bill: Look who’s here! My old friend Fred.

look who’s talking!.monolingual: Fig. You are guilty of doing the same thing that you have criticized someone else for doing or that you accused someone else of doing. _Andy: You criticize me for being late! Look who’s talking! You just missed your f light! Jane: Well, nobody’s perf
examples: Andy: You criticize me for being late! Look who’s talking! You just missed your f light! Jane: Well, nobody’s perfect.

looking over one’s shoulder.monolingual: Fig. keeping watch for danger or threats to oneself. _ Bob’s a little paranoid. He’s always looking over his shoulder.
examples: Bob’s a little paranoid.

*a look-see.monolingual: Rur. a look at someone or something; a peek. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~; take ~.) _ A: Do you think they have finished painting your office yet? B: Let’s go down there and take a look-see.
examples: A: Do you think they have finished painting your office yet? B: Let’s go down there and take a look-see.

loom out of something.monolingual: to appear to come out of or penetrate something. _ A truck suddenly loomed out of the fog and just missed hitting us. _ A tall building loomed out of the mists.
examples: A truck suddenly loomed out of the fog and just missed hitting us.

loom up.monolingual: to appear to rise up [from somewhere]; to take form or definition, usually threatening to some degree. _ A great city loomed up in the distance. It looked threatening in the dusky light. _ A ghost loomed up, but we paid no attention, since it had to
examples: A great city loomed up in the distance.

a loose cannon.monolingual: a person whose actions are unpredictable and uncontrollable. _As it turned out, he’s not just a loose cannon. He makes sense. _ Some loose cannon in the State Department has been leaking stories to the press.
examples: As it turned out, he’s not just a loose cannon.

loose lips sink ships..monolingual: Don’t talk carelessly because you don’t know who is listening. (From wartime. Literally, “Don’t reveal even the location of a loved one on a ship, because the location could be communicated to the enemy by a spy.”) _You never know who is going to hea
examples: You never know who is going to hear what you say and how they will use what they hear.

loosen someone or something up†.monolingual: to make someone’s muscles and joints move more freely by exercising them. _ The exercise loosened me up quite nicely. _ It loosened up my legs. _ I have to do some exercises to loosen myself up.
examples: The exercise loosened me up quite nicely.

loosen someone up†.monolingual: Fig. to make someone or a group more relaxed and friendly. _ I loosened up the audience with a joke. _ Loosen yourself up. Relax and try to enjoy people.
examples: I loosened up the audience with a joke.

loosen up.monolingual: to become loose or relaxed. _Loosen up. Relax. _We tried to get Mary to loosen up, but she did not respond.
examples: Loosen up. Relax.

lope along.monolingual: to move along, bounding. _ The dog loped along at a very even pace, answering to his master’s whistle. _ The horses loped along, eager to get home.
examples: The dog loped along at a very even pace, answering to his master’s whistle.

lord it over someone.monolingual: Fig. to dominate someone; to direct and control someone. _ Mr. Smith seems to lord it over his wife. _ The boss lords it over everyone in the office.
examples: Mr. Smith seems to lord it over his wife.

lord knows i’ve tried..monolingual: Fig. I certainly have tried very hard. _Alice: Why don’t you get Bill to fix this fence? Mary: Lord knows I’ve tried. I must have asked him a dozen times—this year alone. _Sue: I can’t seem to get to class on time. Rachel: That’s just awful. Sue: Lor
examples: Alice: Why don’t you get Bill to fix this fence? Mary: Lord knows I’ve tried.

lord love a duck!.monolingual: Fig.My goodness! (An exclamation of surprise.) _ Lord love a duck! How that rain is coming down! _Lord love a duck! Did you see that cat chasing that dog?

lose a bundle.monolingual: Sl. to lose a lot of money. _Don lost a bundle on that land purchase. _ I know I would lose a bundle if I went to a casino and gambled.
examples: Don lost a bundle on that land purchase.

lose at something.monolingual: to be defeated at a particular game or activity. _We lost at basketball but we won at football this weekend. _ I hate to lose at checkers.
examples: We lost at basketball but we won at football this weekend.

lose by something.monolingual: to be defeated by a certain amount. _ Our team lost by ten points. _ I only lost by a few points.
examples: Our team lost by ten points.

lose face.monolingual: Fig. to lose status; to become less respectable. _ John is more afraid of losing face than losing money. _ Things will go better if you can explain to him where he was wrong without making him lose face.
examples: John is more afraid of losing face than losing money.

lose heart.monolingual: Fig. to lose one’s courage or confidence. _Now, don’t lose heart. Keep trying. _What a disappointment! It’s enough to make one lose heart.
examples: Now, don’t lose heart.

lose it.monolingual: 1. Sl. to empty one’s stomach; to vomit. _Oh, God! I think I’m going to lose it! _ Go lose it in the bushes.
examples: Go lose it in the bushes.

lose money on something.monolingual: to have a net loss on something, such as an investment. _ I lost thousands on that deal. _ I don’t want to lose money on any investment.
examples: I lost thousands on that deal.

lose one’s appetite.monolingual: to lose one’s desire to eat. _After that gory movie, I’m afraid I’ve lost my appetite.
examples: After that gory movie, I’m afraid I’ve lost my appetite.

lose one’s reason.monolingual: Fig. to lose one’s power of reasoning, possibly in anger. _I was so confused that I almost lost my reason. _ Bob seems to have lost his reason when he struck John.
examples: I was so confused that I almost lost my reason.

lose one’s shirt.monolingual: Fig. to lose a lot of money; to lose all of one’s assets (as if one had even lost one’s shirt). _I almost lost my shirt on that deal. I have to invest more wisely. _ No, I can’t loan you $200. I just lost my shirt at the racetrack.
examples: I almost lost my shirt on that deal.

lose one’s train of thought.monolingual: Fig. to forget what one was talking or thinking about. _ Excuse me, I lost my train of thought. What was I talking about? _ Your question made the speaker lose her train of thought.
examples: Excuse me, I lost my train of thought.

lose out.monolingual: to lose in competition; to lose one’s expected reward. _Our team lost out because our quarterback broke his leg. _I ran my best race, but I still lost out.
examples: Our team lost out because our quarterback broke his leg.

lose some amount of time.monolingual: [for some amount of time] to be wasted. _ We lost a lot of time waiting for Hermione. _ He lost no time in getting out of there.
examples: We lost a lot of time waiting for Hermione.

lose something at something.monolingual: to lose a wager at playing something or at gambling. _I lost a fortune at gambling. _We lost all our money at dice.
examples: I lost a fortune at gambling.

lose something in something.monolingual: to misplace something in something. _ I lost my wallet in the barn. _ Did someone lose something in the dining room?
examples: I lost my wallet in the barn.

lose something to someone.monolingual: to yield or give up something in defeat to someone. _ We lost the case to the opposing lawyers. _ Mary lost her title to last year’s runner-up.
examples: We lost the case to the opposing lawyers.

lose the use of something.monolingual: to be deprived of the use of something. _ After the accident, I lost the use of my left arm for a few days. _Andy lost the use of the car for a week.
examples: After the accident, I lost the use of my left arm for a few days.

lose to someone or something.monolingual: to be defeated by someone or something. _ I lost to Wendy in the sales contest. _ Our team lost to the Adamsville Raiders for the seventh year in a row.
examples: I lost to Wendy in the sales contest.

lose touch with reality.monolingual: to began to think unrealistically; to become unrealistic. _ I am so overworked that I am losing touch with reality. _ The psychotic criminal had lost touch with reality.
examples: I am so overworked that I am losing touch with reality.

*a losing streak.monolingual: Fig. a series of losses [in sports, for instance]. (*Typically: be on ~; have ~; continue one’s ~.) _ The team was on a losing streak that started nearly three years ago.
examples: The team was on a losing streak that started nearly three years ago.

lost and gone forever.monolingual: lost; permanently lost. _My poor doggy is lost and gone forever. _ My money fell out of my pocket and I am sure that it is lost and gone forever.
examples: My poor doggy is lost and gone forever.

a lost cause.monolingual: a futile attempt; a hopeless matter. _ Our campaign to have the new party on the ballot was a lost cause. _ Todd gave it up as a lost cause.
examples: Our campaign to have the new party on the ballot was a lost cause.

*lost in something.monolingual: enveloped in something; engrossed in something. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ Ed sat under the tree, lost in reverie. _ Excuse me. I didn’t hear you. I was lost in my own thoughts.
examples: Ed sat under the tree, lost in reverie.

*lost on someone.monolingual: Fig. wasted on someone; not valued or appreciated by someone. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ My jokes are lost on him. He is too literal. _ The humor of the situation was lost on Mary. She was too upset to see it.
examples: My jokes are lost on him.

lost without someone or something.monolingual: unable to function without someone or something. _ I am just lost without you. _ The engineer is lost without his pocket computer.
examples: I am just lost without you.

lost-and-found.monolingual: an office or department that handles items that someone has lost that have been found by someone else. _The lost-and-found office had an enormous collection of umbrellas and four sets of false teeth! _ I found a book on the seat of the bus. I turned
examples: I found a book on the seat of the bus.

a lot of give-and-take.monolingual: 1. Fig. a lot of two-way discussion. _It was a good meeting. There was a lot of give-andtake, and we all learned.
examples: It was a good meeting.

*a lot of nerve.monolingual: 1. Fig. great rudeness; a lot of audacity or brashness. (*Typically: have ~; take ~.) _He walked out on her, and that took a lot of nerve! _ You have a lot of nerve! You took my parking place!
examples: You have a lot of nerve! You took my parking place! 2.

*a lot of promise.monolingual: much promise for the future. (*Typically: have ~; show ~.) _Sally is quite young, but she has a lot of promise. _This bush is small, but it shows a lot of promise.
examples: Sally is quite young, but she has a lot of promise.

lots of luck!.monolingual: 1. Good luck! _ I’m glad you’re giving it a try. Lots of luck! _Lots of luck in your new job!
examples: I’m glad you’re giving it a try.

loud and clear.monolingual: clear and distinctly. (Originally said of radio reception that is heard clearly and distinctly.) _ Tom: If I’ve told you once, I’ve told you a thousand times: Stop it! Do you hear me? Bill: Yes, loud and clear. _ I hear you loud and clear.
examples: Tom: If I’ve told you once, I’ve told you a thousand times: Stop it! Do you hear me? Bill: Yes, loud and clear.

louse someone or something up†.monolingual: Inf. to ruin something; to mess someone or something up. _ You really loused me up! You got me in a real mess! _ Who loused up my scheme?

lousy with someone or something.monolingual: Inf. having lots of someone or something. (Like an infestation of lice.) _Old Mr. Wilson is lousy with money. _ Tiffany is lousy with jewels and furs, but she’s got bad teeth.
examples: Old Mr. Wilson is lousy with money.

love at first sight.monolingual: Fig. love established when two people first see one another. _Bill was standing at the door when Ann opened it. It was love at first sight. _It was love at first sight when they met, but it didn’t last long.
examples: Bill was standing at the door when Ann opened it.

love begets love..monolingual: Prov. If you behave lovingly to other people, they will behave lovingly to you. _ Child: I hate Tammy! She’s always mean to me. Father: If you’re nicer to her, maybe she’ll change her ways. Love begets love.
examples: Child: I hate Tammy! She’s always mean to me.

love is blind..monolingual: Cliché If you love someone, you cannot see any faults in that person. _ Jill: I don’t understand why Joanna likes Tom. He’s inconsiderate, he’s vain, and he isn’t even good-looking. Jane: Love is blind.
examples: Jill: I don’t understand why Joanna likes Tom.

love me, love my dog..monolingual: Prov. If you love someone, you should accept everything and everyone that the person loves. _ Jill: I wish you’d keep your dog out of the house when I come over. Jane: Love me, love my dog. _ Most of Alice’s friends didn’t like her sister, but they a
examples: Jill: I wish you’d keep your dog out of the house when I come over.

love will find a way..monolingual: Prov. People who are in love will overcome any obstacles in order to be together. (Sometimes used ironically, to suggest that someone is in love with whatever he or she is struggling to be near, as in the second example.) _ Jill: I feel so sorry for
examples: Jill: I feel so sorry for Lily and Craig.

love you!.monolingual: Inf. You are great! (Often insincere.) _ See ya around, Martin. Let’s do lunch! Love ya! Bye-bye. _ Nice talking to you, babe. Love you!
examples: See ya around, Martin.

a love-hate relationship.monolingual: Fig. a relationship of any kind that involves both devotion and hatred. _ Tommy has a love-hate relationship with his teacher. Mostly, though, it’s hate lately.
examples: Tommy has a love-hate relationship with his teacher.

*a low profile.monolingual: Fig. a persona or character that does not draw attention. (*Typically: assume ~; have ~; keep ~; give oneself ~.) _I try to be quiet and keep a low profile. It’s hard because I just love attention.
examples: I try to be quiet and keep a low profile.

lower one’s sights.monolingual: Fig. to set one’s goals lower. (Alludes to pointing the barrel of a rifle lower to lower the aim of the rifle.) _ Even though you get frustrated, don’t lower your sights. _ I shouldn’t lower my sights. If I work hard, I can do what I want.
examples: Even though you get frustrated, don’t lower your sights.

lower one’s voice.monolingual: Fig. to speak more softly. _Please lower your voice or you’ll disturb the people who are working. _ He wouldn’t lower his voice, so everyone heard what he said.
examples: Please lower your voice or you’ll disturb the people who are working.

lower oneself to some level.monolingual: Fig. to bring oneself down to some lower level of behavior. _ I refuse to lower myself to your level. _ Has TV news lowered itself to the level of the tabloids?
examples: I refuse to lower myself to your level.

lower someone’s ears.monolingual: Rur. to cut someone’s hair. _I asked the barber to lower my ears. _Looks like somebody lowered Joe’s ears!
examples: I asked the barber to lower my ears.

lower the boom on someone.monolingual: Fig. to scold or punish someone severely; to crack down on someone; to throw the book at someone. _ If Bob won’t behave better, I’ll have to lower the boom on him. _ The teacher lowered the boom on the whole class for misbehaving.
examples: If Bob won’t behave better, I’ll have to lower the boom on him.

low-hanging fruit.monolingual: Fig. the easiest person(s) to sell something to, to convince of something, or to fool. (From the much older easy pickings.) _ People who always want to be the first to buy something, they’re low-hanging fruit for this product. _ Don’t be satisfied wi
examples: People who always want to be the first to buy something, they’re low-hanging fruit for this product.

luck into something.monolingual: to find something by luck; to get involved in something by luck. _ I lucked into this apartment on the very day I started looking. _ We lucked into a good deal on a used car.
examples: I lucked into this apartment on the very day I started looking.

the luck of the draw.monolingual: the results of chance; the lack of any choice. _ Why do I always end up with the luck of the draw? _The team was assembled by chance. It was just the luck of the draw that we could work so well together.
examples: The team was assembled by chance.

luck out.monolingual: to be fortunate; to strike it lucky. _I really lucked out when I ordered the duck. It’s excellent. _ I didn’t luck out at all. I rarely make the right choice.
examples: I really lucked out when I ordered the duck.

luck out of something.monolingual: to get out of something by luck alone. _ I lucked out of taking a driving test. I only had to pass a vision test to get my license. _ Man, I really lucked out of it.
examples: I lucked out of taking a driving test.

a lucky dog.monolingual: Fig. a lucky person. _ You won the lottery? You are a lucky dog!

lucky for you.monolingual: a phrase introducing a description of an event that favors the person being spoken to. _ Andy: Lucky for you the train was delayed. Otherwise you’d have to wait till tomorrow morning for the next one. Fred: That’s luck, all right. I’d hate to have to
examples: Andy: Lucky for you the train was delayed.

lumber along.monolingual: to lope or walk along heavily and awkwardly. _ The horses were lumbering along very slowly because they were tired out. _ They were lumbering along, hoping to get there on time.
examples: The horses were lumbering along very slowly because they were tired out.

lumber off.monolingual: to move or lope away heavily and awkwardly. _The frightened bear lumbered off, and we left in a hurry. _ He lumbered off, leaving us there alone.
examples: The frightened bear lumbered off, and we left in a hurry.

*a lump in one’s throat.monolingual: the feeling of something in one’s throat—as if one were going to cry. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give one ~.) _ Whenever they play the national anthem, I get a lump in my throat. _I have a lump in my throat because I’m frightened.
examples: Whenever they play the national anthem, I get a lump in my throat.

lump it!.monolingual: Inf. Forget it!; Go away! _Well, you can just lump it! _ Lump it! Drop dead!

the lunatic fringe.monolingual: the more extreme members of a group. _ Most of the members of that religious sect are quite reasonable, but Lisa belongs to the lunatic fringe. _Many people try to avoid eating a lot of fat, but Mary is part of the lunatic fringe and will eat anythin
examples: Most of the members of that religious sect are quite reasonable, but Lisa belongs to the lunatic fringe.

lunch off something.monolingual: to make a lunch by eating something or part of something. _ We will be able to lunch off the leftover turkey for days! _ I can lunch off what is in the refrigerator. Don’t worry about me.
examples: I can lunch off what is in the refrigerator.

lunch out.monolingual: to eat lunch away from one’s home or away from one’s place of work. _I think I’ll lunch out today. I’m tired of carrying lunches. _ I want to lunch out today.
examples: I think I’ll lunch out today.

lunge at someone or something.monolingual: to jump or dive at someone or something. _The dog lunged at the man, but he got out of the way without getting bitten. _ The dog lunged at the bicycle.
examples: The dog lunged at the man, but he got out of the way without getting bitten.

lunge for someone or something.monolingual: to charge or jump at someone or something; to attack someone or something. _The mugger lunged for her, but she dodged him. _ Ted lunged for the door, but Bill beat him to it.
examples: The mugger lunged for her, but she dodged him.

lurch forward.monolingual: to jerk or sway forward. _The car lurched forward and shook us around. _ When the train lurched forward, we were pushed back into our seats.
examples: The car lurched forward and shook us around.

lurk around.monolingual: to slink or sneak around somewhere. _Who is that guy lurking around the building? _ Stop lurking around.
examples: Stop lurking around.

lust for something.monolingual: Fig. to desire something. _ He says he lusts for a nice cold can of beer. _ Mary lusts for rich and fattening ice cream.
examples: He says he lusts for a nice cold can of beer.

luxuriate in something.monolingual: to indulge oneself in something; to enjoy the luxury of something. _ She stood in front of the mirror, luxuriating in her lovely new coat. _They were all luxuriating in the warm, bubbling waters of the hot tub.
examples: She stood in front of the mirror, luxuriating in her lovely new coat.

made for each other.monolingual: [of two people] very well suited romantically. _ Bill and Jane were made for each other. _ Mr. and Mrs. Smith were not exactly made for each other. They really don’t get along.
examples: Bill and Jane were made for each other.

made for someone.monolingual: created to please someone or look good on someone in particular. _ This hat was made for me. _ This suit was just made for me!
examples: This hat was made for me.

made for something.monolingual: to have been designed or manufactured for some purpose; to be very suitable for something or some purpose. _ This night was made for love. _ This wrench is manufactured from the strongest metal. It is made for jobs just like this one.
examples: This night was made for love.

made to measure.monolingual: [of clothing] made especially to fit the measurements of a particular person. _ Jack has his suits made to measure because he’s rather large. _Having clothes made to measure is rather expensive.
examples: Jack has his suits made to measure because he’s rather large.

made to order.monolingual: made to one’s own measurements and on request. _ This suit fits so well because it’s made to order. _ His feet are so big that all his shoes have to be made to order.
examples: This suit fits so well because it’s made to order.

maiden voyage.monolingual: Fig. the first voyage of a ship or boat. _ The liner sank on its maiden voyage. _ Jim is taking his yacht on its maiden voyage.
examples: The liner sank on its maiden voyage.

mail something from some place.monolingual: to send something by mail from a particular place. _ I mailed the check from my office. _ I will mail it from the main post office.
examples: I mailed the check from my office.

mail something to someone.monolingual: to send something to someone by mail. _ I mailed the check to you yesterday. _ I mailed a gift to my niece.
examples: I mailed the check to you yesterday.

main strength and awkwardness.monolingual: Fig. great force; brute force. _ They finally got the piano moved in to the living room by main strength and awkwardness. _ Lifting the antique table must be done carefully. This is not a job requiring main strength and awkwardness.
examples: They finally got the piano moved in to the living room by main strength and awkwardness.

maintain someone in something.monolingual: to keep or provide for someone in a certain style or condition. _I insist that you maintain me in the style to which I have become accustomed. _ He had hoped to maintain himself in comfort.
