examples: I insist that you maintain me in the style to which I have become accustomed.

maintain something at something.monolingual: to keep something at a certain level, setting, degree, amount, etc. _ You must maintain the temperature at 30 degrees Celsius. _We have to maintain the temperature at a very high level.
examples: You must maintain the temperature at 30 degrees Celsius.

major in something.monolingual: to specialize in a certain subject in college. _ I majored in history in college. _ I want to major in math.
examples: I majored in history in college.

make a clean sweep.monolingual: Fig. to do something completely or thoroughly, with no exceptions. _ The boss decided to change the direction of the company, so he made a clean sweep and fired all the top management. _ They made a clean sweep through the neighborhood, repairing all
examples: The boss decided to change the direction of the company, so he made a clean sweep and fired all the top management.

make a comeback.monolingual: to return to one’s former (successful) career. _ After ten years in retirement, the singer made a comeback. _ You’re never too old to make a comeback.
examples: After ten years in retirement, the singer made a comeback.

make a deal with someone.monolingual: to strike a bargain with someone. _I want to buy your car and I think I can make a deal with you. _ I will make a deal with you that you will like.
examples: I want to buy your car and I think I can make a deal with you.

make a dent in something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to make a depression in something. _ I kicked the side of the car and made a dent in it. _ Please don’t make a dent in the side of the house.
examples: I kicked the side of the car and made a dent in it.

make a difference to someone.monolingual: [for one choice or another] to matter to someone. _ The big one or the little one—does it really make a difference to anyone? _It makes quite a difference to me!

make a go of something.monolingual: to succeed at something. (Often with it.) _ She just didn’t have the energy or inclination to make a go of her marriage. _ I did everything I could to make a go of it.
examples: She just didn’t have the energy or inclination to make a go of her marriage.

make a habit of something.monolingual: to do something so often that it becomes a habit. _ You mustn’t make a habit of interrupting. _ I make a habit of counting my change.
examples: You mustn’t make a habit of interrupting.

make a hit with someone.monolingual: to please someone; to impress someone. _ The dessert you served really made a hit with the guests. _ Her talk made a hit with the audience.
examples: The dessert you served really made a hit with the guests.

make a killing.monolingual: Fig. to have a great success, especially in making money. _John has got a job selling insurance. He’s not exactly making a killing. _ Bill made a killing at the racetrack yesterday.
examples: John has got a job selling insurance.

make a lap!.monolingual: Sl. to sit down. _ Hey, make a lap and get out of the way! _ Pull up a chair and make a lap!

make a man of someone.monolingual: Fig. to make a young male into an adult male. _ The experience will make a man of Ted. _ Send Wally into the army. That’ll make a man of him.
examples: The experience will make a man of Ted.

make a meal of something.monolingual: 1. to eat something. _ The cat made a meal of the fish. _ They made a meal of the roast beef and enjoyed it very much.
examples: The cat made a meal of the fish.

make a mess of something.monolingual: Fig. to mess something up; to ruin something. _ Give it a try, but don’t make a mess of it. _ Jerry made a mess of the kitchen.
examples: Give it a try, but don’t make a mess of it.

make a mistake.monolingual: to commit an error; to do something wrong accidentally. _ I made a mistake and I am really sorry about it.
examples: I made a mistake and I am really sorry about it.

make a mockery of something.monolingual: to make a deliberate parody or a poor imitation of something. _What a mess. You made a mockery of the task. _ You have made a mockery of my position!
examples: What a mess. You made a mockery of the task.

make a move on someone.monolingual: to attempt to seduce someone. _ Was he making a move on me? I think he was. _ Jed is known for making moves on young women.
examples: Was he making a move on me? I think he was.

make a night of it.monolingual: Fig. to spend the entire evening or night doing something. (Especially when one had intended to devote only a little time to the outing.) _ We went out to have a bite to eat and were having such a good time that we decided to make a night of it. _I d
examples: We went out to have a bite to eat and were having such a good time that we decided to make a night of it.

make a note of something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to write something down as a reminder. _ Please make a note of it so you will remember. _ I will make a note of it and try to remember where I put the note.
examples: Please make a note of it so you will remember.

make a nuisance of oneself.monolingual: to be a constant bother. _ I’m sorry to make a nuisance of myself, but I do need an answer to my question. _ Stop making a nuisance of yourself and wait your turn.
examples: I’m sorry to make a nuisance of myself, but I do need an answer to my question.

make a pass at someone.monolingual: to flirt with or suggest sexual activity with someone. _ Can you believe it? Larry made a pass at me! _ No one ever makes a pass at me.
examples: No one ever makes a pass at me.

make a pass at something.monolingual: to fly over or close by something. _ The plane made a pass at the landing field and pulled up at the last minute. _ The bird made a pass at me because I got too close to its nest.
examples: The plane made a pass at the landing field and pulled up at the last minute.

make a pig of oneself.monolingual: Fig. to eat too much, too fast, or noisily; to eat more than one’s share. _ Don’t make a pig of yourself! _ Sam is making a pig of himself and taking more than his share.
examples: Sam is making a pig of himself and taking more than his share.

make a run for it.monolingual: Fig. to run fast to get away or get somewhere. _When the guard wasn’t looking, the prisoner made a run for it. _ In the baseball game, the player on first base made a run for it, but he didn’t make it to second base.
examples: When the guard wasn’t looking, the prisoner made a run for it.

make a secret of something.monolingual: to act as if something were a secret. _ I’m not making a secret of it. I am quitting this job. _ Mary made a secret of her intentions.
examples: I’m not making a secret of it.

make a start on something.monolingual: to set out to do something; to make a beginning on something. _ See if you can make a start on the project. _I will try to make a start on the cleaning before I leave today.
examples: See if you can make a start on the project.

make a virtue of necessity.monolingual: Prov. to do what you have to do cheerfully or willingly. _When Bill’s mother became sick, there was no one but Bill to take care of her, so Bill made a virtue of necessity and resolved to enjoy their time together.
examples: When Bill’s mother became sick, there was no one but Bill to take care of her, so Bill made a virtue of necessity and resolved to enjoy their time together.

make an appearance.monolingual: to appear; to appear in a performance. _We waited for thirty minutes for the professor to make an appearance, then we went home. _ The famous singing star made an appearance in Detroit last August.
examples: We waited for thirty minutes for the professor to make an appearance, then we went home.

make an entrance.monolingual: to enter [a place], in some formal or special way, as onto the stage in a play or opera. _ She made her entrance too early and threw everyone into confusion.
examples: She made her entrance too early and threw everyone into confusion.

make an example of someone.monolingual: to do something to someone that shows the bad results of bad behavior; to point to someone as a bad example. _ The judge said that he would make an example of Sally and would fine her the maximum amount. _The teacher made an example of me to the clas
examples: The judge said that he would make an example of Sally and would fine her the maximum amount.

make an exhibition of oneself.monolingual: to show off; to try to get a lot of attention for oneself. _She is not just dancing, she is making an exhibition of herself. _ Whenever Rudy drinks, he makes an exhibition of himself.
examples: She is not just dancing, she is making an exhibition of herself.

make an impression on someone.monolingual: to produce a positive memorable effect on someone while one is present. (Akin to leave an impression (on someone).) _Tom made quite an impression on the banker.
examples: Tom made quite an impression on the banker.

make arrangements for someone.monolingual: to plan accommodations for someone. _ John is coming for a visit next week. Please make arrangements for him at the hotel. _ I will make arrangements for everyone when I call the hotel.
examples: John is coming for a visit next week.

make arrangements to do something.monolingual: to plan to do something; to facilitate the doing of something. _Please make arrangements to have all this stuff hauled away. _ We will make arrangements to be there on time.
examples: Please make arrangements to have all this stuff hauled away.

make believe that....monolingual: to pretend that... _ Make believe that you have a million dollars. What would you do with it?
examples: Make believe that you have a million dollars.

make book on something.monolingual: 1. Sl. to make or accept bets on something. _ Well, she might. But I wouldn’t make book on it. _ Don’t make book on my success in this game.
examples: Well, she might.

make certain of something.monolingual: to check something in order to be sure. _ Please make certain of what you want to do. _ Would you please make certain of the number of things you want to order?
examples: Please make certain of what you want to do.

make chin music.monolingual: Fig. to talk or chatter. _We sat around all evening making chin music. _ You were making chin music when you should have been listening.
examples: We sat around all evening making chin music.

make eyes at someone.monolingual: Fig. to flirt with someone. _ Mother, he’s making eyes at me! _Jed tried to make eyes at all the young women.
examples: Jed tried to make eyes at all the young women.

make for somewhere.monolingual: to set out for somewhere; to run or travel to somewhere. _ Wilbur made for Philadelphia when he heard the police in the Big Apple were after him. _ Barlowe made for the stairs, but two shots rang out, and he knew it was all over for Mary.
examples: Wilbur made for Philadelphia when he heard the police in the Big Apple were after him.

make free with someone.monolingual: to exploit someone; to take advantage of someone. _ You shouldn’t make free with your employees. They are liable to take you to court. _ He was making free with his secretary, having her do his private business.
examples: You shouldn’t make free with your employees.

make free with something.monolingual: to use something freely; to exploit something. _You can make free with the hot water. We have a huge tank. _ Sally is making free with the sugar I was saving for breakfast cereal.
examples: You can make free with the hot water.

make friends with someone.monolingual: to work to become a friend of someone. _ I want to make friends with all the people I am going to be working with. _ Let’s try to make friends with each other.
examples: I want to make friends with all the people I am going to be working with.

make good as something.monolingual: to succeed in a particular role. _ I hope I make good as a teacher. _ John made good as a football player.
examples: I hope I make good as a teacher.

make good money.monolingual: to earn a sizable amount of money. _ Ann makes good money at her job. _ I don’t know what she does, but she makes good money.
examples: Ann makes good money at her job.

make good on something.monolingual: 1. to fulfill a promise. _ Tom made good on his pledge to donate $1,000. _Bill refused to make good on his promise.
examples: Tom made good on his pledge to donate $1,000.

make good time.monolingual: to proceed at a fast or reasonable rate. _ On our trip to Toledo, we made good time. _ I’m making good time, but I have a long way to go.
examples: On our trip to Toledo, we made good time.

make inroads into something.monolingual: Fig. to succeed in getting something done or at least started. _ George was unable to make inroads into solving the problem. _ We are making no inroads into the high-priority project.
examples: George was unable to make inroads into solving the problem.

make it big.monolingual: to become successful, especially financially. _ I always knew that someday I would make it big. _ My brother made it big, but it has just led to tax problems.
examples: I always knew that someday I would make it big.

make it hot for someone.monolingual: Fig. to make things difficult for someone; to put someone under pressure. _ Maybe if we make it hot for them, they’ll leave. _ John likes making it hot for people. He’s sort of mean.
examples: Maybe if we make it hot for them, they’ll leave.

make it snappy!.monolingual: Inf. Hurry up!; Move quickly and smartly. _Andy: Make it snappy! I haven’t got all day. Bob: Don’t rush me. _Mary: Do you mind if I stop here and get some film? Bob: Not if you make it snappy! Mary: Don’t worry. I’ll hurry.
examples: Andy: Make it snappy! I haven’t got all day.

make it two..monolingual: I wish to order the thing that someone else just now ordered. (Said to food or drink server.) _ Bill (speaking to the waiter): I’ll have the roast chicken. Mary: Make it two. _Waiter: Would you like something to drink? Tom: Just a beer. Waiter (turni
examples: Bill (speaking to the waiter): I’ll have the roast chicken.

make it worth someone’s while.monolingual: Euph. to tip or offer special (usually extra) payment to someone. _ I made it worth the waiter’s while to give us good service. _ If you’ll throw a few contracts my way, I’ll make it worth your while.
examples: I made it worth the waiter’s while to give us good service.

make life miserable for someone.monolingual: to give someone misery; to be a great nuisance to someone. _ This nagging backache is making life miserable for me. _ I wish you would stop making life miserable for me.
examples: This nagging backache is making life miserable for me.

make light of something.monolingual: to treat something as if it were unimportant or humorous. _ I wish you wouldn’t make light of his problems. They’re quite serious. _ I make light of my problems, and that makes me feel better.
examples: I wish you wouldn’t make light of his problems.

make like someone or something.monolingual: to act like someone or something. _ Why don’t you make like a bunny and run away? Beat it! _ Would you please make like a butler and hold the door open for me?

make merry.monolingual: to have fun; to have an enjoyable time. _ The guests certainly made merry at the wedding. _The children were making merry in the backyard.
examples: The guests certainly made merry at the wedding.

make mine something..monolingual: I wish to have the thing named. (The something can be a particular food or drink, a flavor of a food, a size of a garment, or a type of almost anything. Most typically used for food or drink.) _ Bill: I want some pie. Yes, I’d like apple. Tom: Make m
examples: Bill: I want some pie.

make mischief.monolingual: to cause trouble. _Bob loves to make mischief and get other people into trouble. _Don’t believe what Mary says. She’s just trying to make mischief.
examples: Bob loves to make mischief and get other people into trouble.

make money on something.monolingual: to make a certain amount of profit on something. _ I am sure I can make something on the deal. _ Can I make any money on this sale?
examples: I am sure I can make something on the deal.

make my day!.monolingual: Inf. Go ahead, do what you are going to do, and I will be very happy to do what I have to do! (A catchphrase from a movie scene of a police officer who has a gun pointed at a criminal. The police officer wants the criminal to do something that will j
examples: Make my day. Just try it.

make no bones about it..monolingual: to make no mistake (about it); no need to doubt it; absolutely. _ This is the greatest cake I’ve ever eaten. Make no bones about it. _ Make no bones about it, Mary is a great singer.
examples: This is the greatest cake I’ve ever eaten.

make nonsense of something.monolingual: to make something appear to be silly or nonsensical. _ You are just making nonsense of everything I have tried to do. _ Your statement makes nonsense of everything you have said before.
examples: You are just making nonsense of everything I have tried to do.

make nothing of something.monolingual: to ignore something as if it had not happened; to think no more about something. (Often with it.) _My father caught me throwing the snowball, but he made nothing of it. _ I made nothing of the remark, even though it seemed quite rude. _I saw him leav
examples: My father caught me throwing the snowball, but he made nothing of it.

make one’s mark.monolingual: to do something that allows one to receive appropriate recognition. _ Perry made his mark by inventing a special kind of holder for a cell phone.
examples: Perry made his mark by inventing a special kind of holder for a cell phone.

make one’s way along something.monolingual: to move along something slowly or carefully. _ Todd made his way along the slippery walk. _The old man made his way along the street carefully.
examples: Todd made his way along the slippery walk.

make oneself at home.monolingual: to make oneself comfortable as if one were in one’s own home. _ Please come in and make yourself at home. _I’m glad you’re here. During your visit, just make yourself at home.
examples: Please come in and make yourself at home.

make oneself conspicuous.monolingual: to attract attention to oneself. _ Please don’t make yourself conspicuous. It embarrasses me. _ Ann makes herself conspicuous by wearing brightly colored clothing.
examples: Please don’t make yourself conspicuous.

make oneself heard.monolingual: to speak loudly so that one will be heard above background noise. _ I had to shout to make myself heard. _ He screamed to make himself heard over the sound of the plane’s engines.
examples: I had to shout to make myself heard.

make oneself miserable.monolingual: to do things which cause one to be unhappy. _You’re just making yourself miserable by trying to do something you aren’t qualified to do. _ I’m not making myself miserable! You’re making me miserable.
examples: You’re just making yourself miserable by trying to do something you aren’t qualified to do.

make oneself scarce.monolingual: Fig. [for someone] to become difficult to find; [for someone to] go into hiding. _ Tom is mad and is looking for you. Better make yourself scarce. _ Make yourself scarce! Here comes the sheriff.
examples: Tom is mad and is looking for you.

make or break someone.monolingual: [of a task, job, career choice] to bring success to or improve, or ruin, someone. _ The army will either make or break him. _ It’s a tough assignment, and it will either make or break her.
examples: The army will either make or break him.

make out like a bandit.monolingual: Rur. to make a large profit. _ Joe’s making out like a bandit, selling expensive cameras. _ Mary made out like a bandit, playing twenty-one in Las Vegas.
examples: Joe’s making out like a bandit, selling expensive cameras.

make out that....monolingual: to pretend that [something is so]. _He made out that he hadn’t seen me. _ We all made out that we hadn’t heard the sound.
examples: He made out that he hadn’t seen me.

make overtures about doing something.monolingual: to give hints about something; to present or suggest ideas. _The company made overtures about hiring me. _ Tom is making overtures about inviting us to his country home next month.
examples: The company made overtures about hiring me.

make sense.monolingual: to be understandable. _ John doesn’t make sense. _ What John says makes sense to me.
examples: John doesn’t make sense.

make someone an offer.monolingual: to offer someone an amount of money for something. (Usually an invitation.) _ Do you like it? Make me an offer.
examples: Do you like it? Make me an offer.

make someone eat crow.monolingual: Fig. to cause someone to retract a statement or admit an error. _ Because Mary was completely wrong, we made her eat crow. _ They won’t make me eat crow. They can’t prove I was wrong.
examples: Because Mary was completely wrong, we made her eat crow.

make someone look good.monolingual: to cause someone to appear successful or competent (especially when this is not the case). _ John arranges all his affairs to make himself look good. _ The manager didn’t like the quarterly report because it didn’t make her look good.
examples: John arranges all his affairs to make himself look good.

make someone look ridiculous.monolingual: to make someone look foolish (not funny). _ This hat makes me look ridiculous. _ Please make me look good. Don’t make me look ridiculous!
examples: This hat makes me look ridiculous.

make someone or something tick.monolingual: Fig. to cause someone or something to run or function. (Usually with what. Tick refers to a watch or clock.) _ I don’t know what makes it tick. _What makes John tick? I just don’t understand him. _ I took apart the radio to find out what made it tick
examples: I don’t know what makes it tick.

make someone’s blood boil.monolingual: Fig. to make someone very angry. _It just makes my blood boil to think of the amount of food that gets wasted around here. _ Whenever I think of that dishonest mess, it makes my blood boil.
examples: It just makes my blood boil to think of the amount of food that gets wasted around here.

make someone’s blood run cold.monolingual: Fig. to shock or horrify someone. _ The terrible story in the newspaper made my blood run cold. _ I could tell you things about prisons that would make your blood run cold.
examples: The terrible story in the newspaper made my blood run cold.

make someone’s gorge rise.monolingual: Fig. to cause someone to become very angry. _ The unnecessary accident made my gorge rise. _ Getting his tax bill made Bob’s gorge rise.
examples: The unnecessary accident made my gorge rise.

make someone’s mind up†.monolingual: to decide; to do something that decides something for someone. _ Will you please make up your mind? _ I will help make up your mind.
examples: I will help make up your mind.

make someone’s mouth water.monolingual: to make someone hungry (for something); to cause saliva to flow in someone’s mouth. _ That beautiful salad makes my mouth water. _ Talking about food makes my mouth water.
examples: That beautiful salad makes my mouth water.

make someone’s position clear.monolingual: to clarify where someone stands on an issue. _ I don’t think you understand what I said. Let me make my position clear. _ I can’t tell whether you are in favor of or against the proposal. Please make your position clear.
examples: I don’t think you understand what I said.

make someone sick.monolingual: to disgust someone. _I am really tired of your vile talk. You make me sick! _ She screamed at him that he made her sick and then she ran out of the house.
examples: I am really tired of your vile talk.

make someone up†.monolingual: to put makeup on someone. _You have to make the clowns up before you start on the other characters in the play. _ Did you make up the clowns?
examples: You have to make the clowns up before you start on the other characters in the play.

make something at someone.monolingual: to make some sign or signal at or to a person. _ Carlo made a sign at Bill, who seemed to know just what to do. _ Jimmy made an obscene gesture at me!
examples: Carlo made a sign at Bill, who seemed to know just what to do.

make something clear to someone.monolingual: to help someone understand something. _Let me help make the contract clear to you. _I want to make it clear to you, so ask questions if you want.
examples: Let me help make the contract clear to you.

make something from something.monolingual: to make something from certain parts or ingredients. _ I made this cake from fresh butter and eggs. _ They made the fences from the stones of a ruined Roman fort.
examples: I made this cake from fresh butter and eggs.

make something in something.monolingual: to make money in a particular enterprise. _ She made a lot of money in real estate. _ I hope to make some money in the stock market.
examples: She made a lot of money in real estate.

make something out†.monolingual: to see, read, or hear something well enough to understand it. _ What did you say? I couldn’t quite make it out. _ Can you make out what he is saying?
examples: What did you say? I couldn’t quite make it out.

make something out of nothing.monolingual: 1. Lit. to create something of value from nearly worthless parts. _My uncle— he sells sand—made a fortune out of nothing. _ My model airplane won the contest even though I made it out of scrap.
examples: My uncle— he sells sand—made a fortune out of nothing.

make something to order.monolingual: to custom-make an item; to make an item to fit someone’s specifications. _ The tailor made the jacket to order for me. _ The carpenter made the built-in bookcase to order for us.
examples: The tailor made the jacket to order for me.

make something up†.monolingual: 1. to redo something; to do something that one has failed to do in the past. _ Can I make the lost time up? _ Can I make up the test that I missed?
examples: Can I make up the test that I missed? 2.

make something up† from something.monolingual: to create something from something. _ I will make some stew up from the ingredients available in the fridge. _ I will make up a stew from the leftovers.
examples: I will make some stew up from the ingredients available in the fridge.

make something up to someone.monolingual: to make amends to someone. _ I’m so sorry. I will do what I can to make it up to you. _ I will make it up to them. Don’t worry.
examples: I’m so sorry. I will do what I can to make it up to you.

make something with something.monolingual: to make something out of something. _ I will make the cake with margarine rather than butter. _ Can you make our coffee with spring water, please?
examples: I will make the cake with margarine rather than butter.

make the arrangements.monolingual: Euph. to arrange a funeral. _ A funeral services practitioner will be happy to help you make the arrangements. _ When my father died, I was the one who made the arrangements.
examples: A funeral services practitioner will be happy to help you make the arrangements.

make the best of something.monolingual: to do as well as possible with something that is not too promising. _ I don’t like it, but I will try to make the best of my summer landscaping job by getting a good tan. _I will make the best of it, for a while anyway.
examples: I don’t like it, but I will try to make the best of my summer landscaping job by getting a good tan.

make the grade.monolingual: to be satisfactory; to be what is expected. _ I’m sorry, but your work doesn’t exactly make the grade. _ This meal doesn’t just make the grade. It is excellent.
examples: I’m sorry, but your work doesn’t exactly make the grade.

make the most of something.monolingual: to make something appear as good as possible; to exploit something; to get as much out of something as is possible. _ Mary knows how to make the most of her talents. _ They designed the advertisements to make the most of the product’s features.
examples: Mary knows how to make the most of her talents.

make the scene.monolingual: 1. Sl. to attend an event. _ We plan to make the scene, but we may be a bit late. _ I hope everybody can make the scene.
examples: We plan to make the scene, but we may be a bit late.

make the team.monolingual: to have been qualified enough to be selected to play on a sports team. _I tried out, but I didn’t make the team.
examples: I tried out, but I didn’t make the team.

make trouble.monolingual: to cause trouble or additional work. _ I don’t want to make trouble, but I have a few suggestions that could make things work more smoothly.
examples: I don’t want to make trouble, but I have a few suggestions that could make things work more smoothly.

make up.monolingual: to put on makeup. _ I have to go make up before Joe comes to pick me up.
examples: I have to go make up before Joe comes to pick me up.

make up a foursome.monolingual: to assemble into a team of four people. _ We have three people now. Who can we get to make up a foursome? _ Let’s make up a foursome and play bridge.
examples: We have three people now.

make up for lost time.monolingual: to catch up; to go fast to balance a period of going slow or not moving. _ We drove as fast as we could, trying to make up for lost time. _ Hurry. We have to make up for lost time.
examples: We drove as fast as we could, trying to make up for lost time.

make up something.monolingual: to constitute something. _Two chapters make up this volume. _ Over forty freight cars made up the train.
examples: Two chapters make up this volume.

make water.monolingual: Euph. to urinate. _She’s got some kind of condition where it hurts when she makes water. _Can we stop at this here gas station? I need to make water.
examples: She’s got some kind of condition where it hurts when she makes water.

make waves.monolingual: Sl. to cause difficulty. (Often in the negative.) _Just relax. Don’t make waves. _If you make waves too much around here, you won’t last long.
examples: Just relax. Don’t make waves.

make way.monolingual: to make progress; to move ahead. (Originally nautical. See also make way (for someone or something).) _ Is this project making way? _ A sailboat can’t make way if there is no wind.
examples: A sailboat can’t make way if there is no wind.

make with something.monolingual: Sl. to deliver something. _Come on, make with the stuff you promised! _ Make with the information, Max, or you will stay in jail even longer! _ Come on, make with the cash. _ I want to know. Come on, make with the answers!
examples: Come on, make with the cash.

make your mind up†..monolingual: Fig. Please make a decision.; Please choose. _Henry: I don’t have all day. Make up your mind. Rachel: Don’t rush me. _Bob: Make your mind up. We have to catch the plane. Mary: I’m not sure I want to go.
examples: Henry: I don’t have all day.

make yourself at home..monolingual: Fig. Please make yourself comfortable in my home. (Also a signal that a guest can be less formal.) _ Andy: Please come in and make yourself at home. Sue: Thank you. I’d like to. _Bill: I hope I’m not too early. Bob: Not at all. Come in and make yours
examples: Andy: Please come in and make yourself at home.

man about town.monolingual: a fashionable man who leads a sophisticated life. _ He prefers a nightclub to a quiet night at home—a man about town. _ Bob’s too much of a man about town to go to a football game.
examples: He prefers a nightclub to a quiet night at home—a man about town.

the man in the street.monolingual: Fig. the ordinary person. _Politicians rarely care what the man in the street thinks. _ The man in the street has little interest in literature.
examples: Politicians rarely care what the man in the street thinks.

a man of few words.monolingual: Fig. someone, not necessarily a man, who speaks concisely or not at all. _ He is a man of few words, but he usually makes a lot of sense.
examples: He is a man of few words, but he usually makes a lot of sense.

a man of the cloth.monolingual: Fig. a clergyman. _ Father Brown is a man of the cloth and is welcome at our table for dinner every Sunday.
examples: Father Brown is a man of the cloth and is welcome at our table for dinner every Sunday.

man proposes, god disposes..monolingual: Prov. People may make plans, but they cannot control the outcome of their plans. _ Jill: Are you really going to be able to finish writing your novel by the end of the year? Bob: Man proposes, God disposes.
examples: Jill: Are you really going to be able to finish writing your novel by the end of the year? Bob: Man proposes, God disposes.

man’s best friend.monolingual: Fig. a dog; dogs in general. _ Man’s best friend just peed all over my shoes!

man’s inhumanity to man.monolingual: Fig. human cruelty toward other humans. _It doesn’t take a war to remind us of man’s inhumanity to man.
examples: It doesn’t take a war to remind us of man’s inhumanity to man.

manage with someone or something.monolingual: to do as well as possible with only someone or something (less than one had hoped for). _We wanted Kelly to help us, but we will manage with Larry. _I am sure we can manage with the money that we have.
examples: We wanted Kelly to help us, but we will manage with Larry.

manage without someone or something.monolingual: to do as well as possible without someone or something. _Carla said that she just can’t manage without Jerry. _ We just can’t manage without some more money.
examples: Carla said that she just can’t manage without Jerry.

maneuver for something.monolingual: to get into position for something. _ Sally is maneuvering for a shot at a promotion. _ Todd maneuvered for some attention, but they ignored him.
examples: Sally is maneuvering for a shot at a promotion.

maneuver someone into something.monolingual: to lure, position, or deceive someone into (doing) something. _ I will see if I can maneuver him into accepting the offer. _ He was maneuvered into accepting the offer.
examples: I will see if I can maneuver him into accepting the offer.

maneuver someone out of something.monolingual: to trick someone out of getting or achieving something. _ Are you trying to maneuver me out of the running for the job? _ The runner maneuvered her opponent out of first place.
examples: The runner maneuvered her opponent out of first place.

manna from heaven.monolingual: Fig. unexpected help or comfort. (A biblical reference.) _The arrival of the rescue team was like manna from heaven to the injured climber. _The offer of a new job just as she had been fired was manna from heaven to Joan.
examples: The arrival of the rescue team was like manna from heaven to the injured climber.

many hands make light work..monolingual: Prov. If everyone helps with a large task, it will get done easily and quickly. _ Cleaning up the banquet room won’t take long if we all help; many hands make light work. _You do have a lot of dishes to wash, but you also have all of us to help you,
examples: Cleaning up the banquet room won’t take long if we all help; many hands make light work.

map something out†.monolingual: to plot something out carefully, usually on paper. _ I have a good plan. I will map it out for you. _ I will map out the plan for you.
examples: I have a good plan.

mar something up†.monolingual: to dent or scratch something; to harm the smooth finish of something. _ Please don’t mar the furniture up. _ Don’t mar up my desk.
examples: Please don’t mar the furniture up.

march against someone or something.monolingual: to march in a demonstration against someone or something. _ The demonstrators marched against the mayor. _ The citizens got together and marched against crime and injustice.
examples: The demonstrators marched against the mayor.

march on.monolingual: 1. Lit. to continue marching. _ Please march on. Don’t stop here; there are other parts of the parade coming along behind you. _Let’s march on. We have a long way to go.
examples: Please march on.

march past someone or something.monolingual: to move in a file or formation past someone or something. _ The people in the parade marched past the children standing on the curb. _ The soldiers marched past the general.
examples: The people in the parade marched past the children standing on the curb.

mark someone down†.monolingual: [for a teacher] to give someone a low score. _ He’ll mark you down for misspelled words. _ I marked down Tom for bad spelling.
examples: He’ll mark you down for misspelled words.

mark someone for life.monolingual: Fig. to affect someone for life. _ The tragedy marked her for life and she was never the same. _ She was marked for life by her brother’s untimely death.
examples: The tragedy marked her for life and she was never the same.

mark something as something.monolingual: to make a mark next to the name of something on a list indicating what the thing is. _ I will mark this one as expired. _ This one is marked as needing repair work.
examples: I will mark this one as expired.

mark something down†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to write something down on paper. _ She marked the number down on the paper. _She marked down the number.
examples: She marked the number down on the paper.

mark something in†.monolingual: to write or make a mark on something, perhaps in a box or on a line. _ I will mark an X in the box by your name. _ I’ll mark in the X.
examples: I will mark an X in the box by your name.

mark something up†.monolingual: 1. to mess something up with marks. _ Don’t mark up your book! _ Who marked this book up?
examples: Who marked this book up? 2.

mark time.monolingual: Fig. to wait; to do nothing but wait. _ I’ll just mark time till things get better. _ Do you expect me to just stand here and mark time?
examples: I’ll just mark time till things get better.

*a marked man.monolingual: Fig. to be someone, usually a male, who is in danger from harm by someone else. (*Typically: be ~; live like ~.) _ Bob’s a marked man. His parents found out that he’s skipping school. _Fred’s a marked man, too. Jack is looking for him to get his mone
examples: Bob’s a marked man.

maroon someone on an island.monolingual: to strand someone on something; to abandon someone on something, such as an island. _ The pirate captain marooned his first mate on a small island in the Caribbean. _ Through a navigation error, I marooned myself on a tiny island east of Guam.
examples: The pirate captain marooned his first mate on a small island in the Caribbean.

marriages are made in heaven..monolingual: Prov. You cannot foretell who will marry whom.; Two people may love each other very much but may end up not marrying each other, and two people who do not even know each other may marry each other in the end. _ Tom and Eliza were childhood sweetheart
examples: Tom and Eliza were childhood sweethearts, had a happy family, and now are celebrating their fiftieth wedding anniversary.

marry above oneself.monolingual: Fig. to marry someone in a higher social class than oneself. _They say she married above herself, but who cares? _ Scott thought it would not be possible to marry above himself.
examples: Scott thought it would not be possible to marry above himself.

marry into something.monolingual: to become a part of a family or a fortune by marriage. _ She married into money, they say. _ I always wanted to marry into a large family until I found out what that means in terms of buying gifts.
examples: She married into money, they say.

marshal someone or something together.monolingual: to organize or gather someone or something together. _The leader marshaled all his people together in preparation for the parade. _ Let’s marshal the troops together for the attack.
examples: The leader marshaled all his people together in preparation for the parade.

marvel at someone or something.monolingual: Fig. to express wonder or surprise at someone or something. _ I can only marvel at Valerie and all she has accomplished. _We all marveled at the beauty of the new building.
examples: I can only marvel at Valerie and all she has accomplished.

a marvel to behold.monolingual: someone or something quite exciting or wonderful to see. _ Our new high-definition television is a marvel to behold. _ Mary’s lovely new baby is a marvel to behold.
examples: Our new high-definition television is a marvel to behold.

mash on something.monolingual: to press on something, such as a button. (Southern.) _ He kept mashing on the doorbell until someone responded. _Just mash on this button if you want someone to come.
examples: He kept mashing on the doorbell until someone responded.

mash something up†.monolingual: to crush something into a paste or pieces. _Mash the potatoes up and put them in a bowl. _ Mash up the potatoes and serve them to our guests.
examples: Mash the potatoes up and put them in a bowl.

mash something with something.monolingual: 1. to use something to mash something up. _ Vernon mashed the potatoes with a spoon because he couldn’t find the masher. _Gerald used the heel of his shoe to mash the wasp.
examples: Vernon mashed the potatoes with a spoon because he couldn’t find the masher.

mask something out†.monolingual: to conceal or cover part of something from view. _ The trees masked the city dump out, so it could not be seen from the street. _ The trees masked out the dump.
examples: The trees masked the city dump out, so it could not be seen from the street.

masquerade as someone or something.monolingual: to appear disguised as someone or something; to pretend to be someone or something. _ We decided to masquerade as ghosts for the party. _Mr. Wilson, who is a bit overweight, masqueraded as Cinderella’s coach.
examples: We decided to masquerade as ghosts for the party.

match up.monolingual: [for things or people] to match, be equal, or complementary. _ These match up. See how they are the same length? _ Sorry, but these two parts don’t match up.
examples: These match up.

match up to something.monolingual: [for something] to match, be equal to, or complementary to something. _ This sock does not match up to the other one. _This one matches up to all the others.
examples: This sock does not match up to the other one.

mate with an animal.monolingual: [for an animal] to copulate with its own kind. _The gander mated with the goose in the barnyard. _ The coyote acted as if it wanted to mate with the dog.
examples: The gander mated with the goose in the barnyard.

mate with someone.monolingual: to marry with someone, and presumably, to copulate with someone. _Did you meet anyone you would like to mate with and spend the rest of your life with?

a matter of opinion.monolingual: the question of how good or bad someone or something is. _ It’s a matter of opinion how strong the company is. John thinks it’s great and Fred thinks it’s poor.
examples: It’s a matter of opinion how strong the company is.

matter to someone.monolingual: to be important to someone. _ Does money really matter to you? _ Yes, it matters to me a lot.
examples: Yes, it matters to me a lot.

max out.monolingual: to reach one’s maximum in something, such as weight in weight lifting or credit on a credit card. _Andy finally maxed out at 300 pounds. _ Randy just knew when he had maxed out. Something in his body told him to stop.
examples: Andy finally maxed out at 300 pounds.

maxed out.monolingual: 1. Sl. exhausted; tired. _I am just maxed out. I haven’t been getting enough sleep. _ I had to stop work because I was too maxed out.
examples: I am just maxed out.

may i be excused?.monolingual: May I leave this place, please?; May I leave to use the toilet? _ Nature calls. May I be excused? _ The student raised her hand and said, “Teacher, may I be excused?”

mean business.monolingual: to be very, very serious. _Stop laughing! I mean business. _I could tell from the look on her face that she meant business.
examples: Stop laughing! I mean business.

mean by something.monolingual: to intend a certain meaning by words or deeds. _ What do you mean by that? _ I did not mean anything special by my remarks.
examples: I did not mean anything special by my remarks.

mean no offense.monolingual: not to intend to offend. _ I’m really sorry. I meant no offense. _ It was simply a slip of the tongue. He meant no offense by it.
examples: I’m really sorry.

mean something as something.monolingual: to intend something to be understood as something. _ Do you mean your remarks as criticism? _ I meant my comment as encouragement.
examples: I meant my comment as encouragement.

a mean streak.monolingual: Fig. a tendency for a person to do things that are mean. _ I think that Wally has a mean streak that no one ever saw before this incident.
examples: I think that Wally has a mean streak that no one ever saw before this incident.

mean well.monolingual: to intend to be nice, polite, helpful, etc., but fail in the effort. _ I know you mean well, but your comments are sort of insulting.
examples: I know you mean well, but your comments are sort of insulting.

meant to be.monolingual: destined to exist. _ Our love was meant to be! _ It was not meant to be.
examples: It was not meant to be.

meant to be something.monolingual: destined or fated to be something. _Jane was meant to be a chemist. _I was meant to be rich, but something didn’t work right!
examples: Jane was meant to be a chemist.

measure something off†.monolingual: to determine the length of something. _He measured the length of the room off and wrote down the figure in his notebook. _ Fred measured off the width of the house. _ Fred measured a few feet of string off, and cut it with a knife.
examples: He measured the length of the room off and wrote down the figure in his notebook.

measure something out†.monolingual: to measure and distribute something as it is being taken out, unwrapped, unfolded, etc. _ Carl measured the grain out a cup at a time. _ He measured out the grain little by little.
examples: Carl measured the grain out a cup at a time.

a mecca for someone.monolingual: Fig. a place that is frequently visited by a particular group of people because it is important to them for some reason. (From the city of Mecca, the religious center of Islam.) _New York City is a Mecca for theatergoers. _ St. Andrews is a Mecca for
examples: New York City is a Mecca for theatergoers.

meddle in something.monolingual: to intrude [oneself] into something. _ I wish you wouldn’t meddle in my affairs. _ Go meddle in someone else’s business.
examples: I wish you wouldn’t meddle in my affairs.

meddle with someone or something.monolingual: to interfere with someone or something; to mess around with someone or something. _Please don’t meddle with me. I am in a bad mood. _ Would you please stop meddling with my computer?
examples: Please don’t meddle with me.

meditate on someone or something.monolingual: to reflect on someone or something. _ Judy was instructed to meditate on a f lower. _ I will meditate on that happy thought.
examples: Judy was instructed to meditate on a f lower.

*meek as a lamb.monolingual: [of someone] shy, quiet, and docile. (*Also: as ~.) _ Only an hour after their argument, Joe went to Elizabeth and, meek as a lamb, asked her to forgive him. _Betsy terrorizes the other children, but she’s as meek as a lamb around her elders.
examples: Only an hour after their argument, Joe went to Elizabeth and, meek as a lamb, asked her to forgive him.

meet one’s match.monolingual: Fig. to meet one’s equal; to encounter someone who can match or outdo one in some activity, talent, etc. _ John played tennis with Bill yesterday, and it looks as if John has finally met his match. _ Listen to Jane and Mary argue. I always thought th
examples: John played tennis with Bill yesterday, and it looks as if John has finally met his match.

meet one’s waterloo.monolingual: Fig. to meet one’s final and insurmountable challenge. (Alludes to the final defeat of Napoleon at Waterloo.) _ The boss is being very hard on Bill. It seems that Bill has finally met his Waterloo. _ John was more than Sally could handle. She has fin
examples: The boss is being very hard on Bill.

meet someone halfway.monolingual: Fig. to compromise with someone. _No, I won’t give in, but I’ll meet you halfway. _They settled the argument by agreeing to meet each other halfway.
examples: No, I won’t give in, but I’ll meet you halfway.

meet with someone.monolingual: to have a meeting with someone. _ I will meet with all of them on Monday. _ When can I meet with you?
examples: I will meet with all of them on Monday.

meet with something.monolingual: 1. [for someone] to experience something, such as an accident. _ Poor Carlo met with a serious accident. _Henry always feared meeting with a horrible fate.
examples: Poor Carlo met with a serious accident.

a meeting of the minds.monolingual: the establishment of agreement; complete agreement. _ After a lot of discussion we finally reached a meeting of the minds. _ We struggled to bring about a meeting of the minds on the issues.
examples: After a lot of discussion we finally reached a meeting of the minds.

a mell of a hess.monolingual: Inf. a hell of a mess. (A deliberate spoonerism.) _What a mell of a hess you’ve gotten us into this time. _ Have you ever seen such a mell of a hess?
examples: What a mell of a hess you’ve gotten us into this time.

mellow out.monolingual: 1. to become less angry. _When you mellow out, maybe we can talk. _ Come on, man, stop yelling and mellow out!
examples: When you mellow out, maybe we can talk.

melt away.monolingual: to melt into a liquid. _ The ice cubes melted away quickly in the intense heat. _ When the wax candles melted away, they ruined the lace tablecloth.
examples: The ice cubes melted away quickly in the intense heat.

melt down.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something frozen] to melt. _ The glacier melted down little by little. _ When the ice on the streets melted down, it was safe to drive again.
examples: The glacier melted down little by little.

melt in one’s mouth.monolingual: 1. to taste very good. (Also can be literal.) _ This cake is so good it’ll melt in your mouth. _ John said that the food didn’t exactly melt in his mouth.
examples: This cake is so good it’ll melt in your mouth.

melt in something.monolingual: 1. [for something] to melt to a liquid at a high temperature. _ Surely the plastic cup will melt in such heat. _ This tray will melt in the oven, so keep it out of there.
examples: Surely the plastic cup will melt in such heat.

melt into something.monolingual: to melt and change into a different state. _ All the ice cream melted into a sticky soup. _ The candles melted into a pool of colored wax in all the heat we had last summer.
examples: All the ice cream melted into a sticky soup.

melt something away†.monolingual: to cause something to melt into a liquid. _ The sun melted the ice away. _ The sun melted away the ice.
examples: The sun melted the ice away.

melt something down†.monolingual: to cause something frozen to melt; to cause something solid to melt. _ The rays of the sun melted the candle down to a puddle of wax. _ The heat melted down the ice.
examples: The rays of the sun melted the candle down to a puddle of wax.

melt something into something.monolingual: to cause something to change its state when melting. _The ice melted into a cold liquid that we could drink. _ We melted the fat into a liquid that we could deep-fry in.
examples: The ice melted into a cold liquid that we could drink.

mend one’s ways.monolingual: Fig. to improve one’s behavior. _ John used to be very wild, but he’s mended his ways. _You’ll have to mend your ways if you go out with Mary. She hates people to be late.
examples: John used to be very wild, but he’s mended his ways.

mention something to someone.monolingual: to refer to something while talking to someone. _ Please mention it to your father. _ You had better not mention that to anyone.
examples: Please mention it to your father.

a mere trifle.monolingual: Fig. a tiny bit; a small, unimportant matter; a small amount of money. _But this isn’t expensive! It costs a mere trif le!

merge something with something else.monolingual: to join two things together. _The management merged the sales division with the marketing division. _ We merged the accounting department with the auditing department.
examples: The management merged the sales division with the marketing division.

merge with someone or something.monolingual: to join with someone or something. _ Ted merged with Fred and they created a very profitable partnership. _ Our company merged with a larger one, and we all kept our jobs. _This stream merges with a larger stream about two miles to the west.
examples: Ted merged with Fred and they created a very profitable partnership.

mesh together.monolingual: to fit together. _ Their interests and personalities mesh together perfectly. _Their ideas don’t mesh together too well.
examples: Their interests and personalities mesh together perfectly.

mesh with something.monolingual: to fit with something. _ Your idea just doesn’t mesh with my plans. _Currently, your proposed project doesn’t mesh at all well with our long-range planning.
examples: Your idea just doesn’t mesh with my plans.

mess someone over†.monolingual: Sl. to treat someone badly; to beat or harm someone. _ Max messed Lefty over and sent him to the hospital. _ Max messed over Lefty.
examples: Max messed Lefty over and sent him to the hospital.

mess someone’s face up†.monolingual: Sl. to beat someone about the face. _ The champ threatened to mess the challenger’s face up. _The champ broke the challenger’s nose and really did mess up his face.
examples: The champ threatened to mess the challenger’s face up.

mess someone up†.monolingual: Sl. to rough someone up; to beat someone up. _The robbers threatened to mess Bob up if he didn’t cooperate. _ John messed up Bill a little, but no real harm was done.
examples: The robbers threatened to mess Bob up if he didn’t cooperate.

mess something up†.monolingual: to make something disorderly; to create disorder in something; to throw someone’s plans awry. _ You really messed this place up! _ Who messed up my bed? mills mess up to make an error; to do something wrong; to flub up. _ I hope I don’t mess up on th
examples: Who messed up my bed? mills mess up to make an error; to do something wrong; to flub up.

messed up.monolingual: 1. confused. _ I’m sort of messed up since my divorce. _ Most kids are sort of messed up at this age.
examples: I’m sort of messed up since my divorce.

metamorphose into something.monolingual: to transform into something. _This ugly caterpillar will surely metamorphose into something beautiful. _At about eighteen, Wally metamorphosed into a reasonably handsome young man.
examples: This ugly caterpillar will surely metamorphose into something beautiful.

mete something out†.monolingual: to measure something out. _ She meted the solution out carefully into a row of test tubes. _ She meted out the cookies to each of them.
examples: She meted the solution out carefully into a row of test tubes.

*method in one’s madness.monolingual: Fig. a purpose in what one is doing, even though it seems to be crazy. (*Typically: be ~; have ~.) _ What I’m doing may look strange, but there is method in my madness. _ Wait until she finishes; then you’ll see that she has method in her madness.
examples: What I’m doing may look strange, but there is method in my madness.

a middle ground.monolingual: a position of compromise; a state of thinking where two opposing parties can discuss an issue politely and productively. _ If we could only reach a middle ground on this issue, things wouldn’t be so confrontational.
examples: If we could only reach a middle ground on this issue, things wouldn’t be so confrontational.

the middle of nowhere.monolingual: a very isolated place. _ I don’t want to stay out here in the middle of nowhere. _ I was stranded in the middle of nowhere for an hour with a f lat tire.
examples: I don’t want to stay out here in the middle of nowhere.

might and main.monolingual: Cliché great physical strength; great force. _ The huge warrior, with all his might and main, could not break his way through the castle gates. _ The incredible might and main of the sea crushed the ship against the cliff.
examples: The huge warrior, with all his might and main, could not break his way through the castle gates.

might could.monolingual: Rur. might be able to. _ Charlie: Can you come out with me after work? Tom: I might could. I’ll have to see if my wife has other plans. _ I might could help you, if you’ll tell me what’s the matter.
examples: Charlie: Can you come out with me after work? Tom: I might could.

might makes right..monolingual: Prov. Cliché The stronger of two opponents will always control the situation. _Child: How come the country with the biggest army always tells the other countries what to do? Father: Might makes right.
examples: Child: How come the country with the biggest army always tells the other countries what to do? Father: Might makes right.

*a mile a minute.monolingual: Fig. very fast. (*Typically: go ~; move ~; talk ~; travel ~.) _ She talks a mile a minute and is very hard to keep up with.
examples: She talks a mile a minute and is very hard to keep up with.

militate against something.monolingual: [for something] to work against something. _ Everything you have said today militates against an early settlement to our disagreement. _ This really militates against my going to college.
examples: Everything you have said today militates against an early settlement to our disagreement.

the milk of human kindness.monolingual: Fig. natural kindness and sympathy shown to others. (From Shakespeare’s play Macbeth, I. v.) _ Mary is completely hard and selfish—she doesn’t have the milk of human kindness in her. _ Roger is too full of the milk of human kindness and people take a
examples: Mary is completely hard and selfish—she doesn’t have the milk of human kindness in her.

milk someone for something.monolingual: Fig. to pressure someone into giving information or money. _ The reporter milked the mayor’s aide for information. _ The thief milked me for $20.
examples: The reporter milked the mayor’s aide for information.

*a million miles away.monolingual: Fig. lost in thought; [of someone] daydreaming and not paying attention. (Only one’s mind is far away. *Typically: be ~; look to be ~; seem ~.) _He was a million miles away during the entire lecture. _ Look at her. She is a million miles away, not pa
examples: He was a million miles away during the entire lecture.

a millstone about one’s neck.monolingual: a continual burden or handicap. _ This huge and expensive house is a millstone about my neck. _ Bill’s inability to control his temper is a millstone about his neck.
examples: This huge and expensive house is a millstone about my neck.

mind one’s own business.monolingual: Fig. to attend only to the things that concern one. _Leave me alone, Bill. Mind your own business. _I’d be fine if John would mind his own business.
examples: Leave me alone, Bill.

mind one’s p’s and q’s..monolingual: Prov. to behave properly; to display good manners. _ When you children go to visit Aunt Muriel, you’ll have to mind your p’s and q’s; not like at home, where I let you do as you please. _We’d better mind our p’s and q’s for this new teacher; I hear h
examples: When you children go to visit Aunt Muriel, you’ll have to mind your p’s and q’s; not like at home, where I let you do as you please.

mind over matter.monolingual: Fig. [an instance where there are] intellectual powers overriding threats, difficulties, or problems. _You need to concentrate harder. Pay no attention to your surroundings. This is a case of mind over matter.
examples: You need to concentrate harder.

mind you.monolingual: a phrase introducing something that should be taken into consideration. _ He’s very well dressed, but mind you, he’s got plenty of money to buy clothes. _ Lisa is unfriendly to me, but mind you, she’s never very nice to anyone.
examples: He’s very well dressed, but mind you, he’s got plenty of money to buy clothes.

mind your own beeswax..monolingual: to mind one’s own business. (Juvenile.) _ You just mind your own beeswax! _ Lay off! Mind your own beeswax!

mine for something.monolingual: to dig into the ground in search of a mineral, a metal, or an ore. _ The prospectors ended up mining for coal. _ What are they mining for in those hills?
examples: The prospectors ended up mining for coal.

a mine of information.monolingual: Fig. someone or something that is full of information. _ Grandfather is a mine of information about World War II. _ The new search engine is a positive mine of useful information.
examples: Grandfather is a mine of information about World War II.

mingle with someone.monolingual: to mix with people. _ Try to mingle with the guests. _I would like to get out and mingle with people more.
examples: Try to mingle with the guests.

minister to someone or something.monolingual: to take care of someone or someone’s needs. _ Sarah tried to minister to the people of the village. _He sought to minister to the grief of the widow.
examples: Sarah tried to minister to the people of the village.

minor in something.monolingual: to study a secondary subject in college. (Compare this with major in something.) _ I minored in math in college. _ I decided to minor in history.
examples: I minored in math in college.

a miscarriage of justice.monolingual: a wrong or mistaken decision, especially one made in a court of law. _Sentencing the old man on a charge of murder proved to be a miscarriage of justice. _ Punishing the student for cheating was a miscarriage of justice. He was innocent.
examples: Sentencing the old man on a charge of murder proved to be a miscarriage of justice.

misery loves company..monolingual: Prov. Unhappy people like other people to be unhappy too. _ Jill: Why is Linda criticizing everybody today? Jane: Her boss criticized her this morning, and misery loves company. _ I should probably feel bad because my sister is so depressed, but I’m
examples: Jill: Why is Linda criticizing everybody today? Jane: Her boss criticized her this morning, and misery loves company.

misfortunes never come singly..monolingual: Prov. Bad things tend to happen in groups. _I already told you that my wife lost her job. Well, misfortunes never come singly; our house was robbed last night.
examples: I already told you that my wife lost her job.

mislead someone about something.monolingual: to misrepresent something to someone. _ I hope you are not trying to mislead me about the price. _ I’m afraid I misled you on this matter.
examples: I hope you are not trying to mislead me about the price.

miss a trick.monolingual: Fig. to miss an opportunity or chance. (Typically with the negative.) _ She hardly ever misses a trick. _Mr. Big never misses a trick. _How did a smart guy like you miss a trick like that?
examples: She hardly ever misses a trick.

miss the boat.monolingual: 1. Lit. to miss out (on something); to be ignorant (of something). _ Pay attention, John, or you’ll miss the boat and not learn algebra. _ Tom really missed the boat when it came to making friends.
examples: Pay attention, John, or you’ll miss the boat and not learn algebra.

miss the point.monolingual: to fail to understand the important part of something. _ I’m afraid you missed the point. Let me explain it again. _You keep explaining, and I keep missing the point.
examples: I’m afraid you missed the point.

mission in life.monolingual: one’s purpose in life; the reason for which one lives. _ Bob’s mission in life is to make money. _ My mission in life is to help people live in peace.
examples: Bob’s mission in life is to make money.

mix and match.monolingual: 1. to assemble a limited number of items, usually clothing, in a number of different ways. _ Alice learned to mix and match her skirts, blouses, and sweaters so that she always could be attractively dressed on a limited budget. _Gary always bought bl
examples: Alice learned to mix and match her skirts, blouses, and sweaters so that she always could be attractively dressed on a limited budget.

mix someone up†.monolingual: to confuse someone. _ Please don’t ask questions now; you’ll mix me up! _ You mixed up the speaker with your question.
examples: You mixed up the speaker with your question.

mix someone up† in something.monolingual: to get someone involved in something. _ Please don’t mix me up in this problem. _ Walter mixed up his daughter in the sordid affair.
examples: Please don’t mix me up in this problem.

mix something up†.monolingual: to bring something into disorder; to throw something into a state of confusion. _ Don’t mix up the papers on my desk. _He mixes up things in his eagerness to speak.
examples: Don’t mix up the papers on my desk.

mix with someone or something.monolingual: to mix socially with someone or a group. _ Tom dislikes Bill and Ted so much that he could never mix with them socially. _ She finds it difficult to mix with friends.
examples: Tom dislikes Bill and Ted so much that he could never mix with them socially.

mix with something.monolingual: [for a substance] to combine with a substance. _ Will this pigment mix with water? _ Water will not mix with oil.
examples: Water will not mix with oil.

a mixed bag.monolingual: a varied collection of people or things. (Refers originally to a bag of game brought home after a day’s hunting.) _The new students in my class are a mixed bag—some bright, some positively stupid. _ The furniture I bought is a mixed bag. Some of it i
examples: The new students in my class are a mixed bag—some bright, some positively stupid.

*mixed up in something.monolingual: involved in something, especially something wrong or illegal. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ The youth has had problems ever since he got mixed up in a group of boys that stole a car.
examples: The youth has had problems ever since he got mixed up in a group of boys that stole a car.

*mixed up with someone else.monolingual: involved with another person, possibly romantically. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ I hear that Sam is mixed up with Sally. _ Who is Jerry mixed up with now?
examples: I hear that Sam is mixed up with Sally.

moan about something.monolingual: to complain about something. _ What are you moaning about? _ I am not moaning about anything.
examples: I am not moaning about anything.

moan something out†.monolingual: to say something in a moan. _ The injured woman moaned the name of her assailant out. _ She moaned out the name.
examples: The injured woman moaned the name of her assailant out.

moan with something.monolingual: to groan because of pain or pleasure. _ The patient moaned with pain and fear. _ Ken moaned with pleasure.
examples: The patient moaned with pain and fear.

mock something up†.monolingual: to make a model or simulation of something. _The engineers mocked the new car design up for the managers to see. _ They mocked up the new car design.
examples: The engineers mocked the new car design up for the managers to see.

model something in something.monolingual: to make a model of something in a particular substance. _ She modeled the figure in clay. _ I modeled a bear in modeling clay.
examples: She modeled the figure in clay.

moderation in all things..monolingual: Prov. Do not do anything too much or too little. _ Felicia always ate sparingly. “Moderation in all things,” she told herself. _ Jane: I think you watch too much TV. Jill: So you think I shouldn’t watch any? Jane: No, just watch a reasonable amount.
examples: Felicia always ate sparingly.

moist around the edges.monolingual: intoxicated. _Charlie is more than moist around the edges. He is soused. _ Didn’t that guy seem a little moist around the edges?
examples: Charlie is more than moist around the edges.

the moment of truth.monolingual: Fig. the point at which someone has to face the reality of a situation. _ The moment of truth is here. Turn over your exam papers and begin. _Now for the moment of truth when we find out whether we have got planning permission or not.
examples: The moment of truth is here.

money from home.monolingual: 1. easily gotten money. (Underworld.) _ There is nothing to a simple con job like this. It’s money from home. _ This job is like taking candy from a kid. It’s money from home.
examples: There is nothing to a simple con job like this.

money is power..monolingual: Prov. If you have money, you can get things and do things. _ Emily wanted a career that would make her a lot of money, since money is power.
examples: Emily wanted a career that would make her a lot of money, since money is power.

money talks..monolingual: Fig. Money gives one power and influence to help get things done or get one’s own way. _ Don’t worry. I have a way of getting things done. Money talks. _ I can’t compete against rich old Mrs. Jones. She’ll get her way because money talks.
examples: Don’t worry. I have a way of getting things done.

monkey see, monkey do..monolingual: Prov. Children imitate what they see other people doing. _I don’t let my children watch TV programs that show kids being disrespectful to their elders. I know what would happen if I did: monkey see, monkey do.
examples: I don’t let my children watch TV programs that show kids being disrespectful to their elders.

monkey suit.monolingual: a tuxedo. (Jocular. Possibly in reference to the fancy suit worn by an organ-grinder’s monkey.) _Do I have to wear a monkey suit to dinner? _All the men except me wore monkey suits at dinner on the cruise.
examples: All the men except me wore monkey suits at dinner on the cruise.

moon something away†.monolingual: Fig. to waste time pining or grieving. _ Don’t moon the whole year away! _ You have mooned away half the year. Now pull yourself together!
examples: You have mooned away half the year.

mop something down†.monolingual: to clean a surface with a mop. _ Please mop this f loor down now. _ Please mop down this f loor.
examples: Please mop this f loor down now.

mop something off†.monolingual: to wipe the liquid off something. _ Please mop the counter off with paper towels. _Mop off the counter.
examples: Please mop the counter off with paper towels.

mop something up†.monolingual: to clean up something, such as a spill, with a mop or with a mopping motion. _Please mop this mess up. _ I will mop up this mess.
examples: Please mop this mess up.

mop something up† with something.monolingual: to clean or remove something from something else using a mop, rag, towel, etc. _ I can mop the mess up with this old rag mop. _ She will mop up the mess with the rag.
examples: I can mop the mess up with this old rag mop.

mope around.monolingual: to go about in a depressed state. _ Since her dog ran away, Sally mopes around all day. _Don’t mope around. Cheer up!
examples: Since her dog ran away, Sally mopes around all day.

a mopping-up operation.monolingual: a clean-up operation; the final stages in a project where the loose ends are taken care of. _It’s all over except a small mopping-up operation. _The mopping-up operation from the hurricane should cost just under twenty million.
examples: It’s all over except a small mopping-up operation.

moralize about someone or something.monolingual: to utter moral platitudes about someone or something. _ There is no point in moralizing about Carlo. He can’t be changed. _Why are you moralizing about the election? The people are always right.
examples: There is no point in moralizing about Carlo.

more and more.monolingual: an increasing amount; additional amounts. _ As I learn more and more, I see how little I really know. _ Dad seems to be smoking more and more lately.
examples: As I learn more and more, I see how little I really know.

more dead than alive.monolingual: Fig. exhausted; in very bad condition; near death. (Almost always an exaggeration.) _ We arrived at the top of the mountain more dead than alive. _The marathon runners stumbled one by one over the finish line, more dead than alive.
examples: We arrived at the top of the mountain more dead than alive.

more often than not.monolingual: Fig. usually. _ These f lowers will live through the winter more often than not. _This kind of dog will grow up to be a good watchdog more often than not.
examples: These f lowers will live through the winter more often than not.

more or less.monolingual: somewhat; approximately; a phrase used to express vagueness or uncertainty. _ Henry: I think this one is what I want, more or less. Clerk: A very wise choice, sir. _ I spent more or less a half hour waiting for my f light to depart.
examples: Henry: I think this one is what I want, more or less.

more power to you!.monolingual: Well done!; You really stood up for yourself !; You really did something for your own benefit! (The stress is on to, and the you is usually “ya.”) _ Bill: I finally told her off, but good. Bob: More power to you! _ Sue: I spent years getting ready fo
examples: Bill: I finally told her off, but good.

more’s the pity.monolingual: Fig. it is a great pity or shame; it is sad. (Sometimes with the.) _ Jack can’t come, more’s the pity. _ Jane had to leave early, more’s the pity.
examples: Jack can’t come, more’s the pity.

more than one bargained for.monolingual: more than one thought one would get. (Usually in reference to trouble or difficulty.) _ When Betsy brought home the sweet little puppy for a companion, she got more than she bargained for. That animal has cost her hundreds of dollars in bills. _I got
examples: When Betsy brought home the sweet little puppy for a companion, she got more than she bargained for.

the more the merrier.monolingual: Cliché the more people there are, the happier the situation will be. _Of course you can have a ride with us! The more the merrier. _The manager hired a new employee even though there’s not enough work for all of us now. Oh, well, the more the merrier
examples: Of course you can have a ride with us! The more the merrier.

morning dreams come true..monolingual: Prov. If you dream something in the morning, it will really happen. (According to a superstition.) _ As I was sleeping through the sound of my alarm clock this morning, I dreamed I was late to work. That morning dream definitely came true.
examples: As I was sleeping through the sound of my alarm clock this morning, I dreamed I was late to work.

most of all.monolingual: of greatest importance; more than any other. (Compare this with least of all.) _ I wanted to go to that museum most of all. Why can’t I go? _There are many reasons why I didn’t use my car today. Most of all, it’s a lovely day for walking.
examples: I wanted to go to that museum most of all.

motherhood and apple pie.monolingual: Fig. an often parodied sentiment expressed about allegedly quintessential elements of American home life. _ Fred is so old-fashioned. Everything about old times is good to him. He’s all motherhood and apple pie.
examples: Fred is so old-fashioned.

motion someone aside†.monolingual: to give a hand signal to someone to move aside. _ He motioned her aside and had a word with her. _ I motioned aside the guard and asked him a question.
examples: He motioned her aside and had a word with her.

motion to someone.monolingual: to make some sort of hand signal to a person. _ Did you motion to me? What do you want? _ I did not motion to you.
examples: I did not motion to you.

mound something up†.monolingual: to form something into a mound. _Mound the dirt up around the base of the shrub. _Please mound up the leaves around the rosebushes.
examples: Mound the dirt up around the base of the shrub.

mount something on something.monolingual: to place or attach something onto something. _ Mount the butterf lies on plain white paper. _ Sue mounted her favorite stamps on a display board.
examples: Mount the butterf lies on plain white paper.

mount up.monolingual: 1. to get up on a horse. _ Mount up and let’s get out of here! _ Please mount up so we can leave.
examples: Please mount up so we can leave.

a mouth full of south.monolingual: Sl. a southern accent. _ You sure do have a mouth full of South. _ I just love to hear a man with a mouth full of South.
examples: You sure do have a mouth full of South.

mouth off.monolingual: to speak out of turn; to backtalk. _ If you mouth off, I will ground you for three weeks. _Don’t mouth off at me, buster!
examples: If you mouth off, I will ground you for three weeks.

mouth on someone.monolingual: to inform the authorities on someone; to tattle on someone. _ Max mouthed on his accomplice and got him arrested. _ You had better not mouth on me!
examples: Max mouthed on his accomplice and got him arrested.

a movable feast.monolingual: 1. Lit. a religious holiday that is on a different date from year to year. _ Easter is the best known movable feast.
examples: Easter is the best known movable feast.

move along.monolingual: to continue to move; to start moving out of the way. (Often a command.) _ The crowd moved along slowly. _ Please just move along. There is nothing to see here.
examples: The crowd moved along slowly.

move aside.monolingual: to step or move out of the way. _Please move aside. _Could you please move aside so we can get this cart through?
examples: Please move aside.

move down.monolingual: to move oneself farther down a line of things. _ Someone else needs to sit on this bench. Please move down. _Could you move down a little so we can have some more room?
examples: Someone else needs to sit on this bench.

move for something.monolingual: to make a parliamentary or legal motion in favor of something. _ I move for dismissal of the case against my client. _ My lawyer moved for a recess of the trial.
examples: I move for dismissal of the case against my client.

move forward with something.monolingual: to advance with something; to make progress with something. _ Let us try to move forward with this matter at once. _ I want to move forward with the project at a fast pace.
examples: Let us try to move forward with this matter at once.

move in with someone.monolingual: to take up residence with someone. _ Sally moved in with Sam. _ Jimmy moved in with his brother and shared expenses.
examples: Sally moved in with Sam.

move on.monolingual: to continue moving; to travel on; to move along and not stop or tarry. _Move on! Don’t stop here! _Please move on!

move on someone.monolingual: to attempt to pick up someone; to attempt to seduce someone. _ Don’t try to move on my date, old chum. _Harry is trying to move on Tiffany. They deserve each another.
examples: Don’t try to move on my date, old chum.

move on something.monolingual: to do something about something. _ I will move on this matter only when I get some time. _ I have been instructed to move on this and give it the highest priority.
examples: I will move on this matter only when I get some time.

move over.monolingual: to move a bit [away from the speaker]. _Move over. I need some space. _ Please move over. Part of this space is mine.
examples: Move over. I need some space.

move someone or something around.monolingual: to move someone or something from place to place. _ I wish that the army would stop moving me around. I have moved ten times in eight years. _Let’s move the furniture around and see how this room looks.
examples: I wish that the army would stop moving me around.

move someone or something down†.monolingual: to cause someone or something to move farther down or along [something]. _ Move Tom down a few seats. We need more space here. _ Move down all these chairs. We need more space.
examples: Move Tom down a few seats.
