move someone or something forward.monolingual: to cause someone or something to advance. _ Move her forward. She is too far back. _ Please move the chair forward.
examples: Move her forward.

move someone or something on.monolingual: to cause someone or something to move onward or out of the way. _ Please move those people on. They are in the way. _The officers worked hard to move the crowd on.
examples: Please move those people on.

move someone or something over.monolingual: to cause someone or something to move a little way away. _ Move Tom over a little bit. He is taking too much space. _ Would you move your foot over a little?
examples: Move Tom over a little bit.

move someone or something up.monolingual: to cause someone or something to go higher or more forward. _She is too far down. Move her up one step. _Would you move the sofa up a little? It is too far back.
examples: She is too far down.

move someone to tears.monolingual: to bring someone to the point of crying. _The story moved me to tears. _As she recounted the accident, she moved herself to tears.
examples: The story moved me to tears.

move someone up†.monolingual: to advance or promote someone. _We are ready to move you up. You have been doing quite well. _ It will be years before they move up the new people.
examples: We are ready to move you up.

move to some place.monolingual: to move one’s household to some place, perhaps permanently. _ When we retired, we moved to Arizona. _ I hope we can move to a larger house.
examples: When we retired, we moved to Arizona.

move toward someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to move in the direction of someone or something. _ The car is moving toward Roger!
examples: The car is moving toward Roger! 2.

move up.monolingual: to advance; to go higher. _Isn’t it about time that I move up? I’ve been an office clerk for over a year. _ I had hoped that I would move up faster than this.
examples: Isn’t it about time that I move up? I’ve been an office clerk for over a year.

move up into something.monolingual: to advance into something. _ I moved up into administration and I like it fine. _ When I move up into management, I will get a bigger office.
examples: I moved up into administration and I like it fine.

move up through something.monolingual: to advance through something. _ He moved up through the ranks at a very rapid pace. _ He moved up through every level of management to become CEO.
examples: He moved up through the ranks at a very rapid pace.

movers and shakers.monolingual: people who get things done; organizers and managers. _ The movers and shakers in this firm haven’t exactly been working overtime. _Who are the movers and shakers around here?
examples: The movers and shakers in this firm haven’t exactly been working overtime.

mow someone or something down†.monolingual: to cut, knock, or shoot someone or something down. _ The speeding car almost mowed us down. _ The car mowed down the pedestrian.
examples: The speeding car almost mowed us down.

mr. nice guy.monolingual: a friendly, forgiving fellow. _You’ll find that I am Mr. Nice Guy as long as you play fair with me. _ Oh, my boss is Mr. Nice Guy. He’ll give me the day off, I’m sure.
examples: You’ll find that I am Mr.

mr. right.monolingual: the one man who is right for a woman to marry. _ Some day Mr. Right will come along and sweep you off your feet. _I’m tired of waiting for Mr. Right. Where is Mr. Maybe?
examples: Some day Mr. Right will come along and sweep you off your feet.

much ado about nothing.monolingual: Cliché a furor over something unimportant. (The name of a Shakespeare play.) _All this arguing is much ado about nothing.
examples: All this arguing is much ado about nothing.

much in evidence.monolingual: Cliché very visible or evident. _ John was much in evidence during the conference. _ Your inf luence is much in evidence. I appreciate your efforts.
examples: John was much in evidence during the conference.

much obliged..monolingual: Rur. Thankful and owing a debt of gratitude. _ A: Sit down, Elmer, and have a drink on me. B: Much obliged.
examples: A: Sit down, Elmer, and have a drink on me.

much of a muchness.monolingual: too much of something that there is generally a lot of. _ All this talk about e-commerce and business-2-business is too much of a muchness.
examples: All this talk about e-commerce and business-2-business is too much of a muchness.

*much sought after.monolingual: Cliché wanted or desired very much. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ This kind of crystal is much sought after. It’s very rare. _Sally is a great singer. She’s much sought after.
examples: This kind of crystal is much sought after.

muck something up†.monolingual: to ruin something. _ I should never have trusted Jim with the repair work. He was bound to muck it up. _ I asked her to take over for me while I was gone, and she really mucked it up. _ She mucked up the whole deal.
examples: I should never have trusted Jim with the repair work.

muddle along.monolingual: to progress in confusion; to continue awkwardly. _I will just have to muddle along as best I can until things get straightened out. _ The project muddled along until the new manager got hold of it.
examples: I will just have to muddle along as best I can until things get straightened out.

muddle around.monolingual: to work inefficiently. _ I can’t get anything done today. I’m just muddling around. _ Jed is not doing his job well. He is muddling around and getting nothing done.
examples: I can’t get anything done today.

muddle something up†.monolingual: to mix something up; to make something confusing. _ You really muddled the language of this contract up. _ Who muddled up the wording?
examples: You really muddled the language of this contract up.
Don’t muddy the water up.

muddy the water.monolingual: Fig. to make something less clear; to make matters confusing; to create difficulty where there was none before. _Things were going along quite smoothly until you came along and muddied the water. _The events of the past month have muddied the water a
examples: Things were going along quite smoothly until you came along and muddied the water.

muffle something up†.monolingual: to deaden or stifle a sound. _ Betty tried to muff le the sounds up, but everyone heard what was going on. _ She muff led up the sounds.
examples: Betty tried to muff le the sounds up, but everyone heard what was going on.

mulct something out of someone.monolingual: to cheat something away from someone. _ Are you trying to mulct my inheritance out of me? _ Max tried to mulct every last cent out of his victim.
examples: Max tried to mulct every last cent out of his victim.

mull something over†.monolingual: to think about something; to ponder or worry about something. _ That’s an interesting idea, but I’ll have to mull it over. _ I’ll mull over your suggestions and reply to you next week.
examples: That’s an interesting idea, but I’ll have to mull it over.

multiply by something.monolingual: to use the arithmetic process of multiplication to expand numerically a certain number of times. _To get the amount of your taxes, multiply by .025. _ Can you multiply by sixteens?
examples: To get the amount of your taxes, multiply by .

multiply something by something.monolingual: to use the arithmetic process of multiplication to expand numerically a particular number a certain number of times. _ Multiply the number of dependents you are claiming by one thousand dollars. _ Multiply 12 by 16 and tell me what you get.
examples: Multiply the number of dependents you are claiming by one thousand dollars.

a multitude of sins.monolingual: Fig. many kinds of sins or errors. _ The term offensive covers a multitude of sins.
examples: The term offensive covers a multitude of sins.

mum’s the word..monolingual: Fig. a pledge not to reveal a secret or to tell about something or someone. _“Mum’s the word,” said Jane to ease Mary’s mind about her secret.
examples: “Mum’s the word,” said Jane to ease Mary’s mind about her secret.

munch out.monolingual: Sl. to overeat. _ I can’t help it. Whenever I see french fries, I just have to munch out. _ I try not to munch out more than once a week.
examples: I can’t help it.

mung something up†.monolingual: Sl. to mess something up. _ Don’t mung it up this time. _The team munged up the play, and the coach blasted them but good.
examples: Don’t mung it up this time.

murder on something.monolingual: very destructive or harmful to something. _ Running a marathon is murder on your knees. _ This dry weather is murder on my crops.
examples: Running a marathon is murder on your knees.

murder will out..monolingual: Prov.Murder will always be discovered.; A bad deed will be found out. _ Horace thought he had disposed of his victim in such a way that no one would ever discover his crime, but murder will out.
examples: Horace thought he had disposed of his victim in such a way that no one would ever discover his crime, but murder will out.

murmur against someone or something.monolingual: to grumble about someone or something. _ Everyone was murmuring against the manager. _ The citizens will begin murmuring about the government soon.
examples: Everyone was murmuring against the manager.

muse over someone or something.monolingual: to reflect or meditate on someone or something. _ We were just now musing over Sarah and the way she has changed. _ Tom is so strange. I was musing over his behavior just yesterday.
examples: We were just now musing over Sarah and the way she has changed.

mushroom into something.monolingual: Fig. to grow suddenly into something large or important. _The question of pay suddenly mushroomed into a major matter. _ The unpaid bill mushroomed into a nasty argument and, finally, a court battle.
examples: The question of pay suddenly mushroomed into a major matter.

music to someone’s ears.monolingual: Fig. a welcome sound to someone; news that someone is pleased to hear. _A: Here’s your paycheck for this month. B: Ah, that’s music to my ears!
examples: A: Here’s your paycheck for this month.

muss someone or something up†.monolingual: to put someone or something into disarray. _Don’t muss me up! _You mussed up my hair. _ I’m afraid I mussed myself up a little.
examples: You mussed up my hair.

muster out of something.monolingual: to be discharged from military service. _ He mustered out of the service before his time was up. _ I want to know how I can muster out too.
examples: He mustered out of the service before his time was up.

muster something up†.monolingual: to call up some quality, such as courage. _ Do you think you can muster enough courage up to do the job? _ Can you muster up enough strength to do the job?

mutiny against someone or something.monolingual: 1. to rebel against a ship’s captain or the captain’s authority. _ The crew mutinied against the officers. _ They know better than to mutiny against an authority as great as that held by Captain Bligh.
examples: The crew mutinied against the officers.

mutter about someone or something.monolingual: to grumble or complain about someone or something. _ Are you muttering about me? What is your complaint? _Why is everyone muttering about the food here? It is excellent.
examples: Why is everyone muttering about the food here? It is excellent.

my cup runneth over..monolingual: Prov. I have received so many benefits that I cannot contain them all. (Said when you feel overcome because many good things have happened to you.) _ This week, I finished paying off my mortgage, my arthritis improved, and my first grandchild was bor
examples: This week, I finished paying off my mortgage, my arthritis improved, and my first grandchild was born.

my foot!.monolingual: Inf. I do not believe it!; Like hell! (An exclamation of contradiction.) _ Your prices are the best in town, my foot! I know two places cheaper. _ She’s going to marry you? My foot!
examples: Your prices are the best in town, my foot! I know two places cheaper.

my lips are sealed..monolingual: Fig. I will tell no one this secret or this gossip. _Mary: I hope you don’t tell anyone about this. Alice: Don’t worry. My lips are sealed. _Bob: Don’t you dare tell her I told you. Bill: My lips are sealed.
examples: Mary: I hope you don’t tell anyone about this.

my one and only.monolingual: one’s spouse or lover. _ Look at the time. I’ve got to get home to my one and only. _You’re my one and only. There is no one else for me.
examples: Look at the time.

my pleasure..monolingual: 1. You’re welcome.; It is my pleasure to do so. (From It’s my pleasure. There is a stress on both words.) _Mary: Thank you for bringing this up here. Bill: My pleasure. _Jane: Oh, Doctor, you’ve really helped Tom. Thank you so much! Doctor: My pleasu
examples: Mary: Thank you for bringing this up here.

nail someone’s ears back†.monolingual: Fig. to scold someone severely. _ I’m going to nail your ears back for doing that! _ Who’s going to nail back my ears?

nail something back†.monolingual: to secure something back out of the way by nailing it. _ Please nail the shutters back so they won’t bang against the house. _ I’ll nail back the shutters.
examples: Please nail the shutters back so they won’t bang against the house.

nail something into something.monolingual: to drive a nail or something similar into something. _ She nailed the hanger into the wall to hold the picture up. _ Please nail in this tack.
examples: She nailed the hanger into the wall to hold the picture up.

nail something up†.monolingual: 1. to put something up, as on a wall, by nailing. _ Please nail this up. _ I’ll nail up this picture for you.
examples: Please nail this up.

*naked as a jaybird.monolingual: Cliché naked; bare. (*Also: as ~.) _ Two-year-old Matilda escaped from her nurse, who was bathing her, and ran out naked as a jaybird into the dining room. _ Uncle John sometimes spends a whole day walking around his house as naked as a jaybird.
examples: Two-year-old Matilda escaped from her nurse, who was bathing her, and ran out naked as a jaybird into the dining room.

*the naked eye.monolingual: the human eye, unassisted by optics, such as a telescope, microscope, or spectacles. (*Typically: appear to ~; look to ~; see with ~; visible to ~.) _I can’t see the bird’s markings with the naked eye. _ The scientist could see nothing in the liquid
examples: I can’t see the bird’s markings with the naked eye.

the naked truth.monolingual: the complete, unembellished truth. _ Sorry to put it to you like this, but it’s the naked truth. _ I can take it. Just tell me the naked truth.
examples: Sorry to put it to you like this, but it’s the naked truth.

the name of the game.monolingual: Inf. the way things are; the way things can be expected to be. _ The name of the game is money, money, money. _ I can’t help it. That’s the name of the game.
examples: The name of the game is money, money, money.

name someone as something.monolingual: to select someone as something. _ The mayor named Karen as corporate council. _ The president named himself as chairman of the new committee.
examples: The mayor named Karen as corporate council.

narrow squeak.monolingual: Fig. a success almost not achieved; a lucky or marginal success; a problem almost not surmounted. _ That was a narrow squeak. I don’t know how I survived. _ Another narrow squeak like that and I’ll give up.
examples: That was a narrow squeak.

nature abhors a vacuum..monolingual: Prov. If there is a gap, something will fill it. _ Jill: As soon as the beggar who used to work that corner left, another one showed up. Jane: Nature abhors a vacuum.
examples: Jill: As soon as the beggar who used to work that corner left, another one showed up.

a nature stop.monolingual: Fig. a stop to use the toilet, especially during road travel. _I think I need a nature stop when it’s convenient. _ I left my comb back at the last nature stop.
examples: I think I need a nature stop when it’s convenient.

nause someone out†.monolingual: Sl. to make someone ill; to disgust someone. (From nauseate.) _ That’s awful. I bet it nauses Jennifer out. _ This day naused out everybody I know. _ He naused himself out just thinking of the accident.
examples: That’s awful. I bet it nauses Jennifer out.

near at hand.monolingual: close or handy (to someone). _Do you have a pencil near at hand? _ My dictionary isn’t near at hand.
examples: My dictionary isn’t near at hand.

*neat as a pin.monolingual: Cliché neat and orderly. (*Also: as ~.) _ Brad is such a good housekeeper; his apartment is always as neat as a pin. _ Joanne certainly is well-organized. Her desk is neat as a pin.
examples: Brad is such a good housekeeper; his apartment is always as neat as a pin.

necessity knows no law..monolingual: Prov. If you are desperate, you may have to do illegal things. _ I’m an honest person by nature, but I lost my job, and my kids needed food and clothes, and it seemed like the best way to get money was to deal in illegal drugs. Necessity knows no law
examples: I’m an honest person by nature, but I lost my job, and my kids needed food and clothes, and it seemed like the best way to get money was to deal in illegal drugs.

neck and neck.monolingual: Fig. exactly even, especially in a race or a contest. _ John and Tom finished the race neck and neck. _ Mary and Ann were neck and neck in the spelling contest. Their scores were tied.
examples: John and Tom finished the race neck and neck.

neck with someone.monolingual: to engage in amorous kissing and caressing with someone. _ Ted is over there necking with Molly. _ Molly is necking with Ted and thinking of Ken.
examples: Ted is over there necking with Molly.

need i say more?.monolingual: Is it necessary for me to say any more? _ Mary: There’s grass to be mowed, weeds to be pulled, dishes to be done, carpets to be vacuumed, and there you sit! Need I say more? Tom: I’ll get right on it. _ “This project needs to be finished before anyon
examples: Mary: There’s grass to be mowed, weeds to be pulled, dishes to be done, carpets to be vacuumed, and there you sit! Need I say more? Tom: I’ll get right on it.

need something yesterday.monolingual: Inf. to require something in a very big hurry. _ Yes, I’m in a hurry! I need it yesterday! _ When do I need it? Now! Now! No, I need it yesterday!

needless to say.monolingual: It is so obvious that it doesn’t need to be said, but.... _Needless to say, I should have spent more time on the report, but I just didn’t have it.
examples: Needless to say, I should have spent more time on the report, but I just didn’t have it.

neglect to do something.monolingual: to fail to do something. _ I hope you do not neglect to lock the door. _He neglected to water the plants.
examples: I hope you do not neglect to lock the door.

neighbor on something.monolingual: to be directly adjacent to something. _Our house neighbors on a park. _The park neighbors on a stretch of beach.
examples: Our house neighbors on a park.

neither can i..monolingual: I cannot do that either. (Any subject pronoun can be used in place of I.) _ Bill: No matter what they do to them, I just can’t stand sweet potatoes! Bob: Neither can I. _ John: Let’s go. I cannot tolerate the smoke in here. Jane: Neither can I.
examples: Bill: No matter what they do to them, I just can’t stand sweet potatoes! Bob: Neither can I.

neither does someone.monolingual: [does] not either. _Susan does not own a cat, and neither does Mary. _Bill doesn’t want to see a movie tonight, and neither do I.
examples: Susan does not own a cat, and neither does Mary.

neither fish nor fowl.monolingual: Cliché not any recognizable thing. _ The car that they drove up in was neither fish nor fowl. It must have been made out of spare parts. _This proposal is neither fish nor fowl. I can’t tell what you’re proposing.
examples: The car that they drove up in was neither fish nor fowl.

neither here nor there.monolingual: Cliché of no consequence or meaning; irrelevant and immaterial. _ Whether you go to the movie or stay at home is neither here nor there. _ Your comment—though interesting—is neither here nor there.
examples: Whether you go to the movie or stay at home is neither here nor there.

*neither rhyme nor reason.monolingual: Cliché without logic, order, or planning. (Describes something disorganized. *Typically: be ~; have ~.) _There seems to be neither rhyme nor reason to Gerald’s filing system. _ The novel’s plot had neither rhyme nor reason.
examples: There seems to be neither rhyme nor reason to Gerald’s filing system.

nerves of steel.monolingual: Fig. very steady nerves; great patience and courage. _ I was scared to death, but Fred, who has nerves of steel, faced the thugs bravely.
examples: I was scared to death, but Fred, who has nerves of steel, faced the thugs bravely.

nest in something.monolingual: to build a nest in something and live in it. _Some mice nested in a corner of the garage. _The birds nested in the eaves.
examples: Some mice nested in a corner of the garage.

nest together.monolingual: to fit together or within one another compactly. _ These mixing bowls nest together. _ I want some of those Russian wooden dolls that nest together.
examples: These mixing bowls nest together.

never a dull moment.monolingual: [it’s] always exciting around here. (Describes an exciting or hectic situation.) _ Every time I visit Jean, she has dozens of things planned for us to do: parties and theaters to attend, restaurants to try, scenic places to see. Never a dull moment.
examples: Every time I visit Jean, she has dozens of things planned for us to do: parties and theaters to attend, restaurants to try, scenic places to see.

never fear.monolingual: do not worry; have confidence. _ I’ll be there on time—never fear. _ I’ll help you, never fear.
examples: I’ll be there on time—never fear.

never in my life.monolingual: an emphatic expression showing the depth of the speaker’s feelings. _ Sally: Never in my life have I seen such a mess! John: Well, it’s always this way. Where have you been all this time? Sally: I just never noticed before, I suppose. _Sue: Never wil
examples: Sally: Never in my life have I seen such a mess! John: Well, it’s always this way.

never mind!.monolingual: Forget it!; It’s not important! _ Sally: What did you say? Jane: Never mind! It wasn’t important. _John: I tried to get the book you wanted, but they didn’t have it. Shall I try another store? Mary: No, never mind.
examples: Sally: What did you say? Jane: Never mind! It wasn’t important.

never say die..monolingual: Prov. Do not give up. _ Jill: I don’t think I can finish this project in time. Jane: Never say die. _Alan: It’s no use. I can’t make my checkbook balance. Jane: Never say die!
examples: Jill: I don’t think I can finish this project in time.

never would have guessed.monolingual: 1. never would have thought something to be the case. (Not used in other tenses.) _ He was the one who did it? I never would have guessed. _ I never would have guessed that he wanted the job. He kept it a very good secret.
examples: He was the one who did it? I never would have guessed.

new kid on the block.monolingual: 1. Lit. a child who has just moved to a certain neighborhood. _ The new kid on the block turned out to be a really good baseball player.
examples: The new kid on the block turned out to be a really good baseball player.

a new lease on life.monolingual: Cliché a renewed and revitalized outlook on life. _Getting the job offer was a new lease on life. _When I got out of the hospital, I felt as if I had a new lease on life.
examples: Getting the job offer was a new lease on life.

new one on someone.monolingual: something that one has not heard before and that one is not ready to believe. _ Bob’s talk of poverty is a new one on me. He always seems to have plenty of money. _ The firm’s difficulties are a new one on me. I thought that it was doing very well.
examples: Bob’s talk of poverty is a new one on me.

next question..monolingual: Inf. That is settled, let’s move on to something else. (Usually a way of evading further discussion.) _Mary: When can I expect this construction noise to stop? Bob: In about a month. Next question. _ Bill: When will the board of directors raise the d
examples: Mary: When can I expect this construction noise to stop? Bob: In about a month.

next to nothing.monolingual: Fig. hardly anything; almost nothing. _ This car’s worth next to nothing. It’s full of rust. _I bought this antique chair for next to nothing.
examples: This car’s worth next to nothing.

next to someone or something.monolingual: near to someone or something; adjacent to someone or something. _ I live next to a bank. _ Please sit next to me.
examples: I live next to a bank.

the next world.monolingual: Euph. life after death. _ We will meet in the next world. _ He believed he had made contact with spirits from the next world.
examples: We will meet in the next world.

nibble at something.monolingual: to take tiny bites of some kind of food. _ The children nibbled at their dinner because they had eaten too much candy. _ Stop nibbling at that candy.
examples: The children nibbled at their dinner because they had eaten too much candy.

nibble away at something.monolingual: to eat at something in tiny bits; to erode away tiny bits of something. _The waves nibbled away at the base of the cliff, year after year. _The mice nibbled away at the huge wheel of cheese.
examples: The waves nibbled away at the base of the cliff, year after year.

nice and some quality.monolingual: [being or having] enough of some quality; adequately; sufficiently. _ It is nice and cool this evening. _ I think your steak is nice and done now, just the way you like it.
examples: It is nice and cool this evening.

nice guys finish last..monolingual: Prov. You will never be able to get what you want by being kind and considerate. _ The unscrupulous salesman advised his trainees, “Don’t worry if you have to lie about the product to get the customer to buy it. Nice guys finish last.”
examples: The unscrupulous salesman advised his trainees, “Don’t worry if you have to lie about the product to get the customer to buy it.

nice meeting you..monolingual: It is nice to have met you. (Said when leaving someone whose acquaintance you have just made.) _I must go now, Fred. Nice meeting you. _Well, nice meeting you. I must get home now.
examples: I must go now, Fred.

nice place you have here..monolingual: Your home is nice. (A compliment paid by a guest. The word place might be replaced with home, house, room, apartment, etc.) _ Jane came in and looked around. “Nice place you have here,” she said. _ Bob: Come in. Welcome. Mary: Nice place you have her
examples: Jane came in and looked around.

nice weather we’re having..monolingual: 1. Lit. Isn’t the weather nice? (Sometimes used to start a conversation with a stranger.) _Bill: Nice weather we’re having. Bob: Yeah. It’s great. _Mary glanced out the window and said to the lady sitting next to her, “Nice weather we’re having.”
examples: Bill: Nice weather we’re having.

nick something up†.monolingual: to make little dents or nicks in something, ruining the finish. _ Someone nicked the kitchen counter up. _ Who nicked up the coffeepot?
examples: Someone nicked the kitchen counter up.

niggle about something.monolingual: to make constant petty complaints about something. _ Please don’t niggle about little things like this. This is just not important. _Let’s not niggle about it.
examples: Please don’t niggle about little things like this.

a night on the town.monolingual: a night of celebrating (at one or more places in a town). _Did you enjoy your night on the town? _After we got the contract signed, we celebrated with a night on the town.
examples: After we got the contract signed, we celebrated with a night on the town.

night owl.monolingual: Fig. someone who stays up at night; someone who works at night. _ My roommate is a night owl and usually reads until 5:00 a.m. _ A few night owls stayed at the café all night long.
examples: My roommate is a night owl and usually reads until 5:00 a.

a night person.monolingual: Fig. someone who is more alert and active at night than in the daytime. (Compare this with a day person.) _ I’m really not efficient until after supper. I am the quintessential night person.
examples: I’m really not efficient until after supper.

a nine days’ wonder.monolingual: Fig. something that is of interest to people only for a short time. _ Don’t worry about the story about you in the newspaper. It’ll be a nine days’ wonder and then people will forget. _The elopement of Bob and Anne was a nine days’ wonder. Now people
examples: Don’t worry about the story about you in the newspaper.

nine times out of ten.monolingual: Fig. usually; almost always. _ Nine times out of ten people will choose coffee rather than tea.
examples: Nine times out of ten people will choose coffee rather than tea.

nineteen to the dozen.monolingual: Prov. very rapidly or energetically. _Whenever I get together with my cousins, we always gossip away nineteen to the dozen. _ While Alan got the other ingredients, Jane was chopping up potatoes nineteen to the dozen.
examples: Whenever I get together with my cousins, we always gossip away nineteen to the dozen.

nine-to-five job.monolingual: a job with normal daytime hours. _ I wouldn’t want a nine-to-five job. I like the freedom I have as my own boss. _ I used to work nights, but now I have a nine-to-five job.
examples: I wouldn’t want a nine-to-five job.

nip and tuck.monolingual: Fig. almost even; almost tied. _ The horses ran nip and tuck for the first half of the race. Then my horse pulled ahead. _ In the football game last Saturday, both teams were nip and tuck throughout the game.
examples: The horses ran nip and tuck for the first half of the race.

nip at someone or something.monolingual: to bite at someone or something. _The dog nipped at the visitor, but didn’t cause any real harm. _ A small dog nipped at my heels.
examples: The dog nipped at the visitor, but didn’t cause any real harm.

nip something in the bud.monolingual: Fig. to put an end to something before it develops into something larger. (Alludes to destroying a flower bud before it blooms.) _ I wanted to nip that little romance in the bud. _ The whole idea was nipped in the bud.
examples: I wanted to nip that little romance in the bud.

no can do..monolingual: Inf. It can’t be done.; I can’t do it. _ Sorry, John. No can do. I can’t sell you this one. I’ve promised it to Mrs. Smith. _ Bill: Please fix this clock today. Bob: No can do. It’ll take a week to get the parts.
examples: Sorry, John. No can do.

no comment..monolingual: I have nothing to say on this matter. _ Q: When did you stop beating your dog? A: No comment. _ Q: Georgie, did you chop down the cherry tree? A: No comment.
examples: Q: When did you stop beating your dog? A: No comment.

no contest.monolingual: 1. Lit. [in games] a situation where one team fails to appear for a competition. _It was declared no contest because the opposing team was stuck in traffic out on the expressway.
examples: It was declared no contest because the opposing team was stuck in traffic out on the expressway.

no dice.monolingual: Inf. no; not possible. _When I asked about a loan, he said, “No dice.” _ No. It can’t be done, no dice.
examples: When I asked about a loan, he said, “No dice.

no doubt.monolingual: a transitional or interpretative phrase strengthening the rest of a previous sentence. _ Sue: Mary is giving this party for herself ? Rachel: Yes. She’ll expect us to bring gifts, no doubt. _ Mary: All this talk about war has my cousin very worried.
examples: Sue: Mary is giving this party for herself ? Rachel: Yes.

no earthly reason.monolingual: no conceivable reason. _ There is no earthly reason for your rude behavior. _ I can think of no earthly reason why the repairs should cost so much.
examples: There is no earthly reason for your rude behavior.

no end of something.monolingual: an endless supply of something. _ Have some candy. I have no end of chocolate drops. _ I’ve had no end of trouble ever since I bought this car.
examples: Have some candy.

no fair!.monolingual: Inf. That isn’t fair! _Bill: No fair! You cheated! Bob: I did not! _ “No fair,” shouted Tom. “You stepped over the line!”
examples: “No fair,” shouted Tom.

no flies on someone.monolingual: Fig. someone is not slow; someone is not wasting time. (On the image of flies not being able to land on someone moving fast.) _ Of course I work fast. I go as fast as I can. There are no f lies on me. _ There are no f lies on Robert. He does his work
examples: Of course I work fast.

no go.monolingual: Inf. negative; inopportune. (This is hyphenated before a nominal.) _We’re in a no-go situation. _ Is it go or no go?
examples: We’re in a no-go situation.

no great shakes.monolingual: Inf. someone or something that is not very good. (There is no affirmative version of this.) _ Your idea is no great shakes, but we’ll try it anyway. _ Ted is no great shakes when it comes to brains.
examples: Your idea is no great shakes, but we’ll try it anyway.

no harm done..monolingual: It is all right. No one or nothing has been harmed. _ It’s okay. No harm done. _ A: I am sorry I stepped on your toe. B: No harm done.
examples: It’s okay. No harm done.

no holds barred.monolingual: Fig. with no restraints. (Alludes to a wrestling match in which all holds are legal.) _ I intend to argue it out with Mary, no holds barred. _ When Ann negotiates a contract, she goes in with no holds barred and comes out with a good contract.
examples: I intend to argue it out with Mary, no holds barred.

no joke.monolingual: a serious matter. _ It’s no joke when you miss the last train. _ It’s certainly no joke when you have to walk home.
examples: It’s no joke when you miss the last train.

no kidding!.monolingual: 1. Inf. You are not kidding me, are you? (An expression of mild surprise.) _Jane: I got elected vice president. Bill: No kidding! That’s great!
examples: Jane: I got elected vice president.

no laughing matter.monolingual: a serious issue or problem. _ Be serious. This is no laughing matter. _ This disease is no laughing matter. It’s quite deadly if not treated immediately.
examples: Be serious. This is no laughing matter.

no lie?.monolingual: Inf. You are not lying, are you? _ Bill: A plane just landed on the interstate highway outside of town! Tom: No lie? Come on! It didn’t really, did it? Bill: It did too! Tom: Let’s go see it! _ Bob: I’m going to take a trip up the Amazon. Sue: No lie
examples: Bob: I’m going to take a trip up the Amazon.

no news is good news..monolingual: Not hearing any news signifies that nothing is wrong. _ Fred: I wonder if Jill is doing all right in her new job. Jane: No news is good news. _ Jane: I’m worried about my sister. She hasn’t called me for months. Alan: No news is good news, right?
examples: Fred: I wonder if Jill is doing all right in her new job.

no nonsense.monolingual: without any tricks, deceit, or wasting of time. (Hyphenated before nominals.) _Let’s have no nonsense while we are rehearsing the presentation! _Elton is a no-nonsense kind of guy.
examples: Elton is a no-nonsense kind of guy.

no offense meant..monolingual: I did not mean to offend [you]. _Mary: Excuse that last remark. No offense meant. Susan: It’s okay. I was not offended.
examples: Mary: Excuse that last remark.

no offense taken..monolingual: I am not offended [by what you said]. _ Pete: Excuse that last remark. I did not want to offend you. Tom: It’s okay. No offense taken.
examples: Pete: Excuse that last remark.

no one is indispensable..monolingual: Prov. Anyone may become unnecessary; anyone may lose his or her job. _ Fred: You can’t fire me. I’m absolutely necessary to this company. Nancy: No one is indispensable, Fred. _ The housekeeper was sure that her employer would always need her, but sh
examples: Fred: You can’t fire me.

no pain, no gain..monolingual: Fig. If you want to improve, you must work so hard that it hurts. (Associated with sports and physical exercise.) _Player: I can’t do any more push-ups. My muscles hurt. Coach: No pain, no gain. _ Come on, everybody! Run one more lap! No pain, no gai
examples: Player: I can’t do any more push-ups.

no point in something.monolingual: no purpose in doing something. _ There is no point in locking the barn door now that the horse has been stolen. _ There’s no point is crying over spilled milk.
examples: There is no point in locking the barn door now that the horse has been stolen.

no questions asked.monolingual: no inquiries [to be] made to find out who did something. _ Fines at the library will be suspended, no questions asked, for all late books returned during the first week of July.
examples: Fines at the library will be suspended, no questions asked, for all late books returned during the first week of July.

no rest for the wicked..monolingual: Fig. It’s because you are wicked that you have to work hard. (Usually jocular.) _A: I can’t seem to ever get all my work done. B: No rest for the wicked.
examples: A: I can’t seem to ever get all my work done.

no sale.monolingual: no. _I wanted to go to Florida for the holidays, but my father said, “No sale.” _ No sale. You can’t do it.
examples: I wanted to go to Florida for the holidays, but my father said, “No sale.

no salesman will call.monolingual: a phrase indicating that no salesman will visit or contact you if you make an inquiry about a product. _All inquiries are confidential and no salesman will call.
examples: All inquiries are confidential and no salesman will call.

no shortage of something.monolingual: lots of something; plenty of something. _ Oh, don’t worry about that. I have no shortage of money! _We’ve no shortage of fried chicken, so help yourself.
examples: Oh, don’t worry about that.

no soap.monolingual: Inf. no. _I can’t do it. No soap. _No soap, I don’t lend anyone money.
examples: I can’t do it. No soap.

no sooner said than done.monolingual: an expression indicating that something has been done quickly and obediently. _ Jill: Can I help you out? Jane: Yes! Put these files in alphabetical order. Jill: No sooner said than done. _ The service at the hotel was really remarkable. Everything w
examples: Jill: Can I help you out? Jane: Yes! Put these files in alphabetical order.

no spring chicken.monolingual: Fig. a person well past youth; an old person. _ That actress is no spring chicken, but she does a pretty good job of playing a twenty-year-old girl. _ Jane: How old do you think Robert is? Jill: Well, he’s certainly no spring chicken.
examples: That actress is no spring chicken, but she does a pretty good job of playing a twenty-year-old girl.

no stress.monolingual: Inf. no problem; no bother. _Don’t worry, man, no stress. _ Relax. No stress. It doesn’t bother me at all.
examples: Don’t worry, man, no stress.

no thanks to you.monolingual: I cannot thank you for what happened, because you did not cause it.; I cannot thank you for your help, because you did not give it. _ Bob: Well, despite our previous disagreement, he seemed to agree to all our demands. Alice: Yes, no thanks to you. I
examples: Bob: Well, despite our previous disagreement, he seemed to agree to all our demands.

no trespassing.monolingual: do not enter. (Usually seen on a sign. Not usually spoken.) _ The sign on the tree said, “No Trespassing.” So we didn’t go in. _ The angry farmer chased us out of the field shouting, “Get out! Don’t you see the ‘No Trespassing’ sign?”
examples: The sign on the tree said, “No Trespassing.

no two ways about it.monolingual: no choice about it; no other interpretation of it. (Note the form there’s rather than there are.) _ You have to go to the doctor whether you like it or not. There’s no two ways about it. _This letter means you’re in trouble with the tax people. There
examples: You have to go to the doctor whether you like it or not.

no way!.monolingual: Inf. No! _Me join the Army? No way! _She can’t do that. No way!
examples: She can’t do that.

no way, josé!.monolingual: Inf. No! (An elaboration of No. José is pronounced with an initial H.) _ Bob: Can I borrow a hundred bucks? Bill: No way, José! _Sally: Can I get you to take this nightgown back to the store for me and get me the same thing in a slightly smaller size

no wonder.monolingual: [something is] not surprising. _ No wonder the baby is crying. She’s wet. _ It’s no wonder that plant died. You watered it too much.
examples: No wonder the baby is crying.

nobody’s fool.monolingual: Fig. a sensible and wise person who is not easily deceived. _ Mary is nobody’s fool. She watches out for people who might try to cheat her. _ Anne may seem as though she’s not very bright, but she’s nobody’s fool.
examples: Mary is nobody’s fool.

*the nod.monolingual: Fig. someone’s choice for a position or task. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ The manager is going to pick the new sales manager. I think Ann will get the nod. _ I had the nod for captain of the team, but I decided not to do it.
examples: The manager is going to pick the new sales manager.

nod at someone.monolingual: to make a motion to someone with one’s head indicating a greeting, agreement, or something else. _ I nodded at Fred, but I really didn’t agree. _Molly nodded at Fred, and Fred, knowing she wanted to leave the party, went for their coats. _ When she o
examples: I nodded at Fred, but I really didn’t agree.

nod off.monolingual: to fall asleep, usually while sitting up. _Jack nodded off during the minister’s sermon. _Father always nods off after Sunday lunch.
examples: Jack nodded off during the minister’s sermon.

nominate someone as something.monolingual: to suggest someone to be the candidate to serve as something. _ I would like to nominate Karen as our representative. _ She nominated herself as the one most likely to do the job.
examples: I would like to nominate Karen as our representative.

nominate someone for something.monolingual: to suggest someone as a candidate for a particular office. _ I will nominate Carolyn for president. _ You cannot nominate yourself for this office.
examples: I will nominate Carolyn for president.

nominate someone to something.monolingual: to suggest someone to become a member of a group. _ I am the one who nominated her to the board. _ The president nominated herself to the position of chairman of the board.
examples: I am the one who nominated her to the board.

none of someone’s beeswax.monolingual: Inf. none of someone’s business. (Jocular.) _ It’s none of your beeswax. I’m not telling. _ You’ll never know. The answer is none of your beeswax.
examples: It’s none of your beeswax.

none of someone’s business.monolingual: not of someone’s concern. (A gentle rebuke.) _ Q: When are you going to leave for home? A: None of your business. _How I managed to afford all this is none of your business.
examples: Q: When are you going to leave for home? A: None of your business.

none of your lip!.monolingual: Fig. Shut up!; I don’t want to hear anything from you about anything! _ A: You are being a real nuisance about the broken window. B: None of your lip! Just help me clean it up.
examples: A: You are being a real nuisance about the broken window.

none other than.monolingual: Cliché the very [person]. (Expresses surprise.) _ The new building was opened by none other than the president. _Bob’s wife turned out to be none other than my cousin.
examples: The new building was opened by none other than the president.

none the wiser.monolingual: not knowing any more in spite of events or exposure to facts. _ I was none the wiser about black holes after the lecture. It was a complete waste of time. _ Anne tried to explain the situation tactfully to Bob, but in the end, he was none the wiser.
examples: I was none the wiser about black holes after the lecture.

*none the worse for wear.monolingual: Fig. no worse because of use or effort. _I lent my car to John. When I got it back, it was none the worse for wear. _ I had a hard day today, but I’m none the worse for wear.
examples: I lent my car to John.

none too something.monolingual: not very something; not at all something. _ The towels in the bathroom were none too clean. _ It was none too warm in their house.
examples: The towels in the bathroom were none too clean.

noodle around.monolingual: to wander around; to fiddle around with something. _ I couldn’t find the instructions so I spent the afternoon noodling around, trying to find out how it worked. _I noodled around until I found the right address.
examples: I couldn’t find the instructions so I spent the afternoon noodling around, trying to find out how it worked.

noodle over something.monolingual: Inf. to think about something. _ Let’s noodle over this problem for a bit and discuss it at our next meeting.
examples: Let’s noodle over this problem for a bit and discuss it at our next meeting.

nosh on something.monolingual: to make a snack of something. _ After Thanksgiving, we noshed on turkey for three days. _Who’s been noshing on the chocolate cake?
examples: After Thanksgiving, we noshed on turkey for three days.

not a bit.monolingual: none at all; not at all. _Am I unhappy? Not a bit. _ I don’t want any mashed potatoes. Not a bit!
examples: Am I unhappy? Not a bit.

not a chance!.monolingual: Inf. There is no chance at all that something will happen. (A variation of (There is) no chance.) _ Sally: Do you think our team will win today? Mary: Not a chance! _ Jane: Can I have this delivered by Saturday? Clerk: Not a chance!

not a kid anymore.monolingual: Fig. no longer in one’s youth. _ You can’t keep partying all weekend, every weekend. You’re not a kid anymore. _ Kathy: Bill is just as wild as ever, I hear. Jane: Bill needs to realize that he’s not a kid anymore.
examples: You can’t keep partying all weekend, every weekend.

not a living soul.monolingual: Fig. nobody. (See some of the possible variations in the examples.) _I won’t tell anybody—not a living soul. _ I won’t tell a living soul.
examples: I won’t tell anybody—not a living soul.

not able to go on.monolingual: unable to continue (doing something— even living). (Not able to is often expressed as can’t.) _I just can’t go on this way. _Before her death, she left a note saying she was not able to go on.
examples: I just can’t go on this way.

not able to help something.monolingual: unable to prevent or control something. (Not able to is often expressed as can’t.) _I’m sorry about being late. I wasn’t able to help it. _ Bob can’t help being boring.
examples: I’m sorry about being late.

not able to wait.monolingual: to have to go to the bathroom urgently. (Also more broadly literal.) _ Mom, I can’t wait. _ Driver, stop the bus! My little boy can’t wait.
examples: Mom, I can’t wait.

not again!.monolingual: Inf. I cannot believe that it happened again! _ Mary: The sink is leaking again. Sally: Not again! Mary: Yes, again. _ Fred: Here comes Tom with a new girlfriend. Sue: Not again!
examples: Mary: The sink is leaking again.

not agree with someone.monolingual: [for food] to make someone ill; [for something that one has eaten] to give one stomach distress. _ Fried foods don’t agree with Tom. _ I always have onions in my garden, but I never eat them. They just don’t agree with me.
examples: Fried foods don’t agree with Tom.

not all there.monolingual: Fig. not mentally adequate; crazy or silly. _ Sometimes I think you’re not all there. _ Be nice to Sally. She’s not all there.
examples: Sometimes I think you’re not all there.

not always..monolingual: a conditional negative response. (See examples.) _ John: Do you come here every day? Jane: No, not always. _ John: Do you find that this condition usually clears up by itself ? Doctor: Not always.
examples: John: Do you come here every day? Jane: No, not always.

not anymore..monolingual: The facts you mentioned are no longer true.; A previous situation no longer exists. _Mary: This cup of coffee you asked me to bring you looks cold. Do you still want it? Sally: Not anymore. _ Tom: Do the Wilsons live on Maple Street? Bob: Not anymore
examples: Mary: This cup of coffee you asked me to bring you looks cold.

not believe one’s ears.monolingual: Fig. not believe the news that one has heard. _ I couldn’t believe my ears when Mary said I won the first prize.
examples: I couldn’t believe my ears when Mary said I won the first prize.

not believe one’s eyes.monolingual: Fig. not to believe what one is seeing; to be shocked or dumbfounded at what one is seeing. _ I walked into the room and I couldn’t believe my eyes. All the furniture had been stolen! _ When Jimmy opened his birthday present, he could hardly believe
examples: I walked into the room and I couldn’t believe my eyes.

not born yesterday.monolingual: Fig. experienced; knowledgeable in the ways of the world. _ I know what’s going on. I wasn’t born yesterday. _ Sally knows the score. She wasn’t born yesterday.
examples: I know what’s going on.

not buy something.monolingual: Fig. not accept something (to be true). _You may think so, but I don’t buy it. _The police wouldn’t buy his story.
examples: You may think so, but I don’t buy it.

not by a long shot.monolingual: Fig. not by a great amount; not at all. _ Did I win the race? Not by a long shot. _ Not by a long shot did she complete the assignment.
examples: Did I win the race? Not by a long shot.

not for a moment.monolingual: not at all; not even for a short amount of time; never. _ I don’t want you to leave. Not for a moment! _ I could not wish such a horrible punishment on anyone. Not for a moment!
examples: I don’t want you to leave.

not for hire.monolingual: [of a taxi] not available to take new passengers. _ The taxi was going to pick someone up at a nearby hotel and was not for hire. _ The taxi had a lighted sign that said it was not for hire.
examples: The taxi was going to pick someone up at a nearby hotel and was not for hire.

not for my money..monolingual: Not as far as I’m concerned. (Has nothing to do with money or finance.) _ Sue: Do you think it’s a good idea to build all these office buildings in this part of the city? Mary: Not for my money. That’s a real gamble. _John: We think that Fred is the
examples: Sue: Do you think it’s a good idea to build all these office buildings in this part of the city? Mary: Not for my money.

not for publication.monolingual: not to be talked about openly; secret. _ Please tell no one about this. It’s not for publication. _ This report is not for publication, so keep it to yourself.
examples: Please tell no one about this.

not get one’s hopes up.monolingual: Fig. [one] should not expect something to happen; [one] should not start hoping that something will happen. _The rain could stop so we can go to the beach, but you should not get your hopes up.
examples: The rain could stop so we can go to the beach, but you should not get your hopes up.

not give a tinker’s damn.monolingual: Fig. not to care at all. (A tinker’s damn or dam may be a worthless curse from a tinker or a small dam or barrier used to contain molten metal.) _ I don’t give a tinker’s damn whether you go or not!

not give it another thought.monolingual: not to worry about something anymore. (A polite way of accepting someone’s apology.) _ It’s okay. Please don’t give it another thought. _ You should not give it another thought. No one was bothered at all.
examples: It’s okay. Please don’t give it another thought.

not grow on trees.monolingual: Fig. not to be abundant; not to be expendable. (Usually said about money.) _ I can’t afford that. Money doesn’t grow on trees, you know. _Don’t waste the glue. That stuff doesn’t grow on trees, you know.
examples: I can’t afford that.

not have all one’s marbles.monolingual: Fig. not to have all one’s mental capacities. _ John acts as if he doesn’t have all his marbles. _ I’m afraid that I don’t have all my marbles all the time.
examples: John acts as if he doesn’t have all his marbles.

not hold water.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of a container] not able to contain water without leaking. _ This old wading pool won’t hold water any longer.
examples: This old wading pool won’t hold water any longer.

not hold with something.monolingual: Rur. to disagree with something; to not tolerate something. _I don’t hold with what you are saying. _We don’t hold with that kind of thing around here.
examples: I don’t hold with what you are saying.

not hurt a flea.monolingual: Fig. not to harm anything or anyone, even a tiny insect. (Also with other forms of negation.) _ Ted would not even hurt a f lea. He could not have struck Bill. _ Ted would never hurt a f lea, and he would not hit anyone as you claim.
examples: Ted would not even hurt a f lea.

not in my book..monolingual: Fig. Not according to my views. (Compare this with Not for my money.) _ John: Is Fred okay for the job, do you think? Mary: No, not in my book. _Sue: My meal is great! Is yours good, too? Bob: Not in my book.
examples: John: Is Fred okay for the job, do you think? Mary: No, not in my book.

not just whistling dixie.monolingual: Rur. not talking nonsense. (Alludes to a song titled “Dixie.”) _ Man, you are right! You’re not just whistling Dixie. _ When you say she is wrong, you’re not just whistling Dixie.
examples: Man, you are right! You’re not just whistling Dixie.

not know from nothing.monolingual: Inf. to be stupid, innocent, and naive. (This nothing is not replaced with something. Usually used with don’t, as in the examples.) _ Old John—he don’t know from nothing. _What do you expect from somebody who don’t know from nothing?
examples: Old John—he don’t know from nothing.

not know one’s own strength.monolingual: not to realize how destructive or harmful one’s strength can be. _ I didn’t mean to hurt you. I guess I don’t know my own strength. _ He might break the door down by accident. He doesn’t know his own strength and could end up pushing too hard against
examples: I didn’t mean to hurt you.

not know someone from adam.monolingual: Fig. not to know someone by sight at all. _I wouldn’t recognize John if I saw him up close. I don’t know him from Adam. _ What does she look like? I don’t know her from Adam.
examples: I wouldn’t recognize John if I saw him up close.

not likely..monolingual: Inf. That is probably not so; that probably will not happen. _ Mary: Is it possible that you’ll be able to fix this watch? Sue: Not likely, but we can always try. _ Sally: Will John show up on time, do you think? Bob: Not likely.
examples: Mary: Is it possible that you’ll be able to fix this watch? Sue: Not likely, but we can always try.

not long for this world.monolingual: Fig. about to die. _ Our dog is nearly twelve years old and not long for this world. _ I’m so tired. I think I’m not long for this world.
examples: Our dog is nearly twelve years old and not long for this world.

not made of money.monolingual: Fig. [of a person] not having a lot of money; not having an unlimited supply of money. _ I can’t afford a car like that. I’m not made of money you know. _ There is only so much they can pay. They’re not made of money.
examples: I can’t afford a car like that.

not move a muscle.monolingual: to remain perfectly motionless. _ Be quiet. Sit there and don’t move a muscle. _I was so tired I couldn’t move a muscle.
examples: Be quiet. Sit there and don’t move a muscle.

not one iota.monolingual: not even a tiny bit. _ I won’t give you any at all! Not one iota! _I did not get one iota of encouragement from any of those people.
examples: I did not get one iota of encouragement from any of those people.

not one’s cup of tea.monolingual: Fig. not one’s choice or preference. (Used to describe an activity you do not enjoy. Can sound somewhat affected.) _ You three visit the museum without me. Looking at fussy old paintings is not my cup of tea. _ Going to church, Mary said, was not her
examples: You three visit the museum without me.

not one’s place.monolingual: not one’s role to do something. _ It was not my place to criticize my boss. _ It was not Bill’s place to ask the questions; it’s my project.
examples: It was not my place to criticize my boss.

not put it past someone.monolingual: to think that someone would not dare to do something. _ He might run away from school. I wouldn’t put it past him. _I wouldn’t put it past Roger to arrive unannounced.
examples: He might run away from school.

not right now, thanks..monolingual: No for the present. (It is hoped that one will be asked again later. Usually used for a [temporary] refusal of a serving of food or drink. There is an implication that more will be wanted later.) _Waiter: Do you want some more coffee? Mary: Not right
examples: Waiter: Do you want some more coffee? Mary: Not right now, thanks.

not set foot somewhere.monolingual: not to go somewhere. _I wouldn’t set foot in John’s room. I’m very angry at him. _ He never set foot here.
examples: I wouldn’t set foot in John’s room.

not shed a tear.monolingual: Fig. not to show any emotion even when something is very sad. _ At his uncle’s funeral, he didn’t shed a tear. They never got along.
examples: At his uncle’s funeral, he didn’t shed a tear.

not show one’s face.monolingual: not to appear somewhere; not to go to some place. _ After what she said, she had better not show her face around here again. _ If I don’t say I’m sorry, I’ll never be able to show my face again.
examples: After what she said, she had better not show her face around here again.

not sleep a wink.monolingual: not to sleep at all. _ I couldn’t sleep a wink last night. _ Ann hasn’t been able to sleep a wink for a week.
examples: I couldn’t sleep a wink last night.

not so hot.monolingual: Inf. not very good. _ The service here is not so hot. This restaurant is highly overrated.
examples: The service here is not so hot.

not to touch a drop.monolingual: Fig. not to drink any of something, usually alcohol. _He pledged not to touch a drop all weekend, but he broke his pledge on Friday night.
examples: He pledged not to touch a drop all weekend, but he broke his pledge on Friday night.

not to worry..monolingual: Inf. Please do not worry. _ Bill: The rain is going to soak all our clothes. Tom: Not to worry, I put them all in plastic bags. _ Sue: I think we’re about to run out of money. Bill: Not to worry. I have some more travelers checks.
examples: Bill: The rain is going to soak all our clothes.

not too shabby.monolingual: 1. Inf. nice; well done. (With emphasis on shabby.) _Is that your car? Not too shabby! _That play was not too shabby.
examples: That play was not too shabby.

not with it.monolingual: not able to think clearly; not able to understand things. _Lisa’s mother is not really with it anymore. She’s going senile. _ Tom’s not with it yet. He’s only just come around from the anesthetic.
examples: Lisa’s mother is not really with it anymore.

not worth a damn.monolingual: Inf. worthless. _This pen is not worth a damn. _ When it comes to keeping score, she’s not worth a damn.
examples: This pen is not worth a damn.

not worth mentioning.monolingual: 1. not important enough to require a comment. _ There are others, but they are not worth mentioning. _ A small number of books hint at the phenomenon, but they aren’t worth mentioning.
examples: There are others, but they are not worth mentioning.

not worth one’s while.monolingual: not worth bothering with; not worth spending time on. _ It’s not worth my while to discuss it with you. _Don’t bother trying to collect money from them. It isn’t worth your while.
examples: It’s not worth my while to discuss it with you.

not worth the trouble.monolingual: not important enough to require a comment or any effort. _ Don’t bother with it. It isn’t worth the trouble. _ There is no point in trying to get the spot out of the carpet. It isn’t worth the trouble.
examples: Don’t bother with it.

notch something up†.monolingual: to count up something; to add up or score something. _ We notched yet another victory up in our efforts to regain the trophy. _ Well, it looks like we notched up another victory.
examples: We notched yet another victory up in our efforts to regain the trophy.

note something down†.monolingual: to write down a note about something. _ Please note these words down. _ Note down the following facts.
examples: Please note these words down.

*noted for something.monolingual: Fig. famed for something; memorable for something. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _We were all noted for our polite manners. _ The restaurant was noted for its traditional fare. _Tom was noted far and wide for his excellent pies and cakes.
examples: We were all noted for our polite manners.

nothing but.monolingual: only; just. _ Jane drinks nothing but milk. _ Dave buys nothing but expensive clothes.
examples: Jane drinks nothing but milk.

nothing comes of nothing..monolingual: Prov. If you contribute nothing, you will get nothing. _ Jill: Why are you so depressed today? Jane: No reason. Jill: There has to be a reason. Nothing comes of nothing. _I’m not surprised you did so poorly in school; you haven’t been putting in any
examples: Jill: Why are you so depressed today? Jane: No reason.

nothing doing!.monolingual: Inf. I will not permit it!; I will not participate in it! _ John: Can I put this box in your suitcase? Bill: Nothing doing! It’s too heavy now. _ Sue: We decided that you should drive us to the airport. Do you mind? Jane: Nothing doing! I’ve got work
examples: John: Can I put this box in your suitcase? Bill: Nothing doing! It’s too heavy now.

nothing down.monolingual: requiring no down payment. _ You can have this car for nothing down and $140 a month. _ I bought a winter coat for nothing down and no payments due until February.
examples: You can have this car for nothing down and $140 a month.

nothing for me, thanks..monolingual: I do not want any of what was offered. (Typically to decline a serving of food or drink.) _Waiter: Would you care for dessert? Bob: Nothing for me, thanks. _ Bob: We have beer and wine. Which would you like? Mary: Nothing for me, thanks.
examples: Waiter: Would you care for dessert? Bob: Nothing for me, thanks.

nothing much..monolingual: Inf. not much; hardly anything; nothing of importance. (Often a reply to a greeting asking what one has been doing.) _John: Hey, man! How’s by you? Bob: Hiya! Nothing much. _ Bill: What have you been doing? Tom: Nothing much.
examples: John: Hey, man! How’s by you? Bob: Hiya! Nothing much.

nothing of the kind.monolingual: 1. no; absolutely not. _I didn’t tear your jacket—nothing of the kind! _ Did I break your vase? Nothing of the kind!
examples: Did I break your vase? Nothing of the kind! 2.

nothing short of something.monolingual: more or less the same as something bad; as bad as something. _ His behavior was nothing short of criminal. _ Climbing those mountains alone is nothing short of suicide.
examples: His behavior was nothing short of criminal.

nothing succeeds like success..monolingual: Prov. If you have succeeded in the past, you will continue to be successful in the future. _ After Alan’s brilliant courtroom victory, everyone wanted to be his client. Nothing succeeds like success.
examples: After Alan’s brilliant courtroom victory, everyone wanted to be his client.

nothing to boast about.monolingual: not worth bragging about; mediocre. _In high school, my grades were acceptable, but they were nothing to boast about. _Jill: Does this town have a good library? Nancy: It’s nothing to boast about.
examples: In high school, my grades were acceptable, but they were nothing to boast about.

nothing to choose from.monolingual: no choice; no choice in the selection; not enough of something to make a choice. _ I went to the store looking for new shoes, but there was nothing to choose from. _ By the time I got around to selecting a team of helpers, there was nothing to choose
examples: I went to the store looking for new shoes, but there was nothing to choose from.

nothing to it!.monolingual: It is very easy! _ Look, anybody can do it! Nothing to it! _ Changing a lightbulb is easy. Nothing to it!
examples: Changing a lightbulb is easy.

nothing to speak of.monolingual: not many; not much. _ John: What’s happening around here? Bill: Nothing to speak of. _ Mary: Has there been any rain in the last week? Sally: Nothing to speak of.
examples: John: What’s happening around here? Bill: Nothing to speak of.

nothing to write home about.monolingual: Fig. mediocre; not as good as you expected. _I went to that new restaurant last night. It’s nothing to write home about. _ Jill: I went to see a movie last night. Jane: How was it? Jill: Nothing to write home about.
examples: I went to that new restaurant last night.

nothing upstairs.monolingual: Fig. no brains; stupid. _ Tom is sort of stupid. You know—nothing upstairs. _I know what’s wrong with you. Nothing upstairs.
examples: Tom is sort of stupid.

nothing ventured, nothing gained..monolingual: If you do not take risks, you will never accomplish anything. _ Bill: Should I ask my boss for a promotion? Jane: Nothing ventured, nothing gained. _I think I’ll audition for a part in that play. Nothing ventured, nothing gained.
examples: Bill: Should I ask my boss for a promotion? Jane: Nothing ventured, nothing gained.

notify someone of something.monolingual: to inform someone about something. _ Can you notify my parents of my arrival at the airport? _ We were notified of it last night.
examples: We were notified of it last night.

now and then.monolingual: sometimes; occasionally. now and then.) _ I like to go to a movie now and then. _ We visit my parents now and then, but we rarely see our other relatives.
examples: I like to go to a movie now and then.

now hear this!.monolingual: Pay attention to what is going to be said! (In the manner of an announcement over a public address system, especially in the military.) _ Now hear this! You have to turn off the television and go to bed! _ Now hear this! Now hear this! Everyone is or
examples: Now hear this! Now hear this! Everyone is ordered to abandon ship.

now, now.monolingual: Inf. a calming and consoling phrase that introduces good advice. _ “Now, now, don’t cry,” said the mother to the tiny baby. _ Jane: I’m so upset! Andy: Now, now, everything will work out all right.
examples: “Now, now, don’t cry,” said the mother to the tiny baby.

*now or never.monolingual: at this time and no other. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ This is your only chance, John. It’s now or never. _ I decided that it was now or never, and jumped.
examples: This is your only chance, John.

now then.monolingual: a sentence opener indicating that a new topic is being opened or that the speaker is getting down to business. (Expressions such as this often use intonation to convey the connotation of the sentence that is to follow. The brief intonation pattern ac
examples: “Now then, where’s the pain?” asked the doctor.

now you’re talking!.monolingual: Inf. Now you are saying the right things. _Tom: I won’t put up with her behavior any longer. I’ll tell her exactly what I think of it. Bill: Now you’re talking! _ John: When I get back to school, I’m going to study harder than ever. Mother: Now you’r
examples: Tom: I won’t put up with her behavior any longer.

nowhere near.monolingual: not nearly. _ We have nowhere near enough wood for the winter. _They’re nowhere near ready for the game.
examples: We have nowhere near enough wood for the winter.

no-win situation.monolingual: a situation where there is no correct or satisfactory solution. _ The general was too weak to fight and too proud to surrender. It was a no-win situation. _ The huge dog my father gave us as a gift eats too much. If we get rid of the dog, my father w
examples: The general was too weak to fight and too proud to surrender.

nudge someone or something aside†.monolingual: to push or bump someone or something out of the way. _ We nudged the old man aside and went on ahead. _ She nudged aside the cat to make room on the sofa.
examples: We nudged the old man aside and went on ahead.

null and void.monolingual: Cliché without legal force; having no legal effect. _ The court declared the law to be null and void. _ The millionaire’s will was null and void because it was unsigned.
examples: The court declared the law to be null and void.

number in something.monolingual: to total up to a certain figure. _The birds numbered in the thousands. _These pesky ants number in the hundreds. Let’s move to another picnic table.
examples: The birds numbered in the thousands.

number someone with something.monolingual: to include someone in a list of people. _ I number Clara Wilson with the all-time greats. _ Todd numbered himself with the top athletes at the school.
examples: I number Clara Wilson with the all-time greats.

nurse someone back to health.monolingual: to care for a sick person until good health returns. _ Sally was glad to help nurse her mother back to health. _ She nursed her children back to health when they all had the f lu.
examples: Sally was glad to help nurse her mother back to health.

nurse something along†.monolingual: Fig. to manage something with care and thrift. _ The board of directors agreed to nurse the firm along for a while and then sell it. _ She nursed along the failing business until it was showing a profit.
examples: The board of directors agreed to nurse the firm along for a while and then sell it.

a nut case.monolingual: Fig. a crazy person; an irrational person. _Bob is acting stranger and stranger. He is turning into a real nut case.
examples: Bob is acting stranger and stranger.

nut up.monolingual: Sl. to go crazy. _I knew I would nut up if I didn’t quit that job. _ I almost nutted up at the last place I worked.
examples: I knew I would nut up if I didn’t quit that job.

nuts and bolts.monolingual: 1. Fig. the mundane workings of something; the basics of something. _ I want you to learn how to write well. You have to know the nuts and bolts of writing. _ She’s got a lot of good, general ideas, but when it comes to the nuts and bolts of getting
examples: I want you to learn how to write well.

nuts to you!.monolingual: Inf. Go away!; Drop dead! _ Well, nuts to you! You are just plain rude! _Nuts to you! I will NOT lend you money!

object to someone or something.monolingual: to disapprove of someone or something. _ I object to him as your choice. _ I object to your opinion.
examples: I object to him as your choice.

oblige someone by something.monolingual: to accommodate someone by doing something. _ Please oblige me by closing the window. _ Would you oblige me by accompanying me to the dance?
examples: Please oblige me by closing the window.

oblige someone to do something.monolingual: to require someone to do something. _ You are obliged to arrive on time and enter by the side door. _ The lateness of the hour obliged Tony to enter by the back door.
examples: You are obliged to arrive on time and enter by the side door.

oblige someone with something.monolingual: to accommodate someone with something. _ He obliged her with a willing attitude. _ Please oblige me with a big piece of cake.
examples: He obliged her with a willing attitude.

*obsessed with someone or something.monolingual: preoccupied with someone or something. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _Kathy was obsessed with the kitten. _Roger was obsessed with Kathy.
examples: Kathy was obsessed with the kitten.

occupy oneself by something.monolingual: to keep busy by doing something. _ Don’t worry. I can occupy myself by knitting or sewing. _ While waiting, I occupied myself by knitting a scarf.
examples: Don’t worry. I can occupy myself by knitting or sewing.

occupy someone with something.monolingual: to keep someone busy with something. _Can you occupy the child with this toy? _ Here, occupy yourself with this crossword puzzle.
examples: Here, occupy yourself with this crossword puzzle.

occur to someone.monolingual: [for an idea or thought] to come into someone’s mind. _ It occurred to me that you might be hungry after your long journey. _ Would it ever occur to you that I want to be left alone?
examples: It occurred to me that you might be hungry after your long journey.

odd man out.monolingual: an unusual or atypical person or thing. _ I’m odd man out because I’m not wearing a tie. _ You had better learn to use the new system software unless you want to be odd man out.
examples: I’m odd man out because I’m not wearing a tie.

the odd something.monolingual: an extra or spare something; a chance something. _ The tailor repaired the odd loose button on my shirt. _ When I travel, I might buy the odd trinket or two, but I never spend much money.
examples: The tailor repaired the odd loose button on my shirt.

odds and ends.monolingual: miscellaneous things. _ There were lots of odds and ends in the attic, but nothing of real value. _ I had the whole house cleaned out except for a few odds and ends that you might want to keep.
examples: There were lots of odds and ends in the attic, but nothing of real value.

the odds are against one.monolingual: [for fate] to be against one generally. _ You can give it a try, but the odds are against you. _ I know the odds are against me, but I wish to run in the race anyway.
examples: You can give it a try, but the odds are against you.

the odds-on favorite.monolingual: the most popular choice of a wager. _ Fred is the odds-on favorite for president of the board of trustees.
examples: Fred is the odds-on favorite for president of the board of trustees.

odor of sanctity.monolingual: Fig. an atmosphere of excessive holiness or piety. _I hate their house. There’s such an odor of sanctity with Bibles and holy pictures everywhere. _ The huge, medieval Gothic cathedral had a distinct odor of sanctity.
examples: I hate their house.

*of age.monolingual: old enough to marry, buy alcohol, or to sign legal agreements. (*Typically: be ~; come ~.) _ Now that Mary is of age, she can buy her own car. _When I’m of age, I’m going to get married and move to the city.
examples: Now that Mary is of age, she can buy her own car.

of all things!.monolingual: Can you imagine?; Imagine that! (Usually said about something very strange.) _ She wore jeans to the dance. Of all things! _Billy, stop eating the houseplant! Of all things!
examples: She wore jeans to the dance.

of course.monolingual: yes; certainly; for sure. _ Sally: Are you ready to go? Bob: Of course. Sally: Then let’s go. _ Jane: Are you coming with us? John: Of course. I wouldn’t miss this for the world. _ “And you’ll be there, of course?” asked Alice. _ “I would be happy to
examples: Sally: Are you ready to go? Bob: Of course.

of late.monolingual: lately. _ Have you seen Sally of late? _ We haven’t had an opportunity to eat out of late.
examples: We haven’t had an opportunity to eat out of late.

of mature years.monolingual: Euph. old. _ My employer is a man of mature years. _ The professor, a woman of mature years, is planning to retire at the end of the school term.
examples: My employer is a man of mature years.

of the first water.monolingual: Fig. of the finest quality. _ This is a very fine pearl—a pearl of the first water. _ Tom is of the first water—a true gentleman.
examples: This is a very fine pearl—a pearl of the first water.

of the persuasion that....monolingual: holding a belief that something is true or is in existence. _Anne is of the persuasion that supports that candidate for mayor. _The paranoid was of the persuasion that aliens lived among us.
examples: Anne is of the persuasion that supports that candidate for mayor.

off and running.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of horses, dogs, or people] having started racing. _ It’s a beautiful day at the races, and, yes, they’re off and running!
examples: It’s a beautiful day at the races, and, yes, they’re off and running! 2.

*off base.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of a runner in baseball] not having a foot touching the base. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ The runner was off base but the first baseman didn’t tag him out.
examples: The runner was off base but the first baseman didn’t tag him out.

*off campus.monolingual: not located or present on the grounds of a college or university. (*Typically: be ~; live ~; move ~.) _ Tom has an apartment off campus. _ The dean is off campus and cannot be reached.
examples: Tom has an apartment off campus.

off center.monolingual: not exactly in the center or middle. _The arrow hit the target a little off center. _ The picture hanging over the chair is a little off center.
examples: The arrow hit the target a little off center.

off chance.monolingual: slight possibility. _I need your phone number on the off chance I need more help. _ There’s an off chance that we might be hiring next month.
examples: I need your phone number on the off chance I need more help.

*off course.monolingual: 1. Lit. not going in the right direction. (*Typically: be ~; drift ~; get ~.) _ The ship is off course and may strike the reef!
examples: The ship is off course and may strike the reef! 2.

off duty.monolingual: not working at one’s job. (The opposite of on duty.) _ I’m sorry, I can’t talk to you until I’m off duty. _ The police officer couldn’t help me because he was off duty.
examples: I’m sorry, I can’t talk to you until I’m off duty.

off like a shot.monolingual: away [from a place] very quickly. _ He finished his dinner and was off like a shot. _ The thief grabbed the lady’s purse and was off like a shot.
examples: He finished his dinner and was off like a shot.

*off on a sidetrack.monolingual: Fig. on a digression; discussing a topic that is not the main topic. (Alludes to a train waiting on a siding. *Typically: be ~; get ~; get someone ~.) _ Anne got off on a sidetrack and never returned to her topic. _ The ineffective committee got off
examples: Anne got off on a sidetrack and never returned to her topic.

off on someone or something.monolingual: in a rage about someone or something; on a tirade about someone or something. _ Are you off on Sally again? Why can’t you leave her alone?

*off one’s game.monolingual: Fig. not able to play a sport as well as normal. (*Typically: be ~; put one ~; throw one ~.) _ I’m a little tired, and that generally puts me off my game.
examples: I’m a little tired, and that generally puts me off my game.

off season.monolingual: not in the busy time of the year. _ We don’t have much to do off season. _Things are very quiet around here off season.
examples: We don’t have much to do off season.

off someone or something goes.monolingual: someone or something is leaving. (Said on the departure of someone or something.) _ It’s time to leave. Off I go. _ Sally looked at the airplane taking off and said, “Off it goes.”
examples: It’s time to leave.

off the air.monolingual: not broadcasting (a radio or television program). _The radio audience won’t hear what you say when you’re off the air. _ When the performers were off the air, the director told them how well they had done.
examples: The radio audience won’t hear what you say when you’re off the air.

*off the hook.monolingual: Fig. freed from an obligation. (Alludes to a fish freeing itself from a fishhook. *Typically: be ~; get ~; get someone ~; let someone ~.) _ Thanks for getting me off the hook. I didn’t want to attend that meeting. _ I couldn’t get myself off the hook
examples: Thanks for getting me off the hook.

off the mark.monolingual: Fig. not quite exactly right. _ Her answer was a little off the mark. _ You were off the mark when you said we would be a little late to the party. It was yesterday, in fact!
