examples: Her answer was a little off the mark.

off the record.monolingual: Fig. unofficial; informal. (Of comments to the press that one does not want reported.) _ This is off the record, but I disagree with the mayor on this matter. _ Although her comments were off the record, the newspaper published them anyway.
examples: This is off the record, but I disagree with the mayor on this matter.

off the shelf.monolingual: Fig. ready made for purchase; not custommade. (Hyphenated when prenominal.) _I generally buy off-the-shelf clothing. I am a perfect size eight.
examples: I generally buy off-the-shelf clothing.

off the subject.monolingual: not concerned with the subject being discussed. _ I got off the subject and forgot what I was supposed to be talking about. _ The speaker was off the subject, telling about his vacation in Hawaii.
examples: I got off the subject and forgot what I was supposed to be talking about.

off the track.monolingual: Fig. [of comments] irrelevant and immaterial. _I’m afraid you’re off the track, John. Try again. _ I’m sorry. I was thinking about dinner, and I got off the track.
examples: I’m afraid you’re off the track, John.

*off the wagon.monolingual: 1. Fig. drinking liquor after a period of abstinence. (*Typically: be ~; fall ~; get ~.) _ Poor John fell off the wagon again. Drunk as a skunk. _ He was off the wagon for a year the last time before he sobered up.
examples: Poor John fell off the wagon again.

off to a running start.monolingual: with a good, fast beginning, possibly a head start. _I got off to a running start in math this year. _ The horses got off to a running start.
examples: I got off to a running start in math this year.

off to one side.monolingual: beside something; (moved) slightly away from something. _Our garden has roses in the middle and a spruce tree off to one side. _He took me off to one side to tell me the bad news.
examples: Our garden has roses in the middle and a spruce tree off to one side.

off to the races.monolingual: Fig. an expression characterizing the activity or excitement that is just beginning; [we are] leaving for something interesting or exciting. _ The tour bus is out in front waiting and we’ve said goodbye to everyone. Looks like we’re off to the races.
examples: The tour bus is out in front waiting and we’ve said goodbye to everyone.

*off topic.monolingual: not on the topic of discussion; far from the general subject of a discussion; not part of the purpose of a particular communication channel, such as an Internet newsgroup. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; get someone ~.) _ The boys in the back of the room j
examples: The boys in the back of the room just love to get the teacher off topic.

off with you!.monolingual: Go away!; Get going! (Formal or pompous.) _ Off with you! We’ve had enough of your banter!

offend against someone or something.monolingual: to anger or affront someone or something. _We do not wish to offend against anyone. _ He didn’t realize that he offended against their cultural values.
examples: We do not wish to offend against anyone.

offend someone with something.monolingual: to anger or affront someone with something. _Don’t offend us with your bad jokes. _ I offended Ralph with my constant niggling.
examples: Don’t offend us with your bad jokes.

*an offer one cannot refuse.monolingual: Cliché a very attractive offer. (*Typically: give one ~; make ~; make one ~.) _ He made me an offer I could not refuse, so I sold him my car.
examples: He made me an offer I could not refuse, so I sold him my car.

offer something for something.monolingual: to suggest a certain amount of money as a purchase price for something. _ I’ll offer you ten bucks for that watch. _ They offered me very little for my car.
examples: I’ll offer you ten bucks for that watch.

off-key.monolingual: [of music or singing] off pitch; out of tune. _She always sings off-key and makes the rest of the choir sound like baying hounds.
examples: She always sings off-key and makes the rest of the choir sound like baying hounds.

off-line.monolingual: not connected to a computer, by direct connection or via the telephone system, etc. (Compare this with online.) _ When he’s off-line he’s sort of lost. _ The system was off-line all day, so we could get nothing done.
examples: When he’s off-line he’s sort of lost.

off-the-cuff.monolingual: Fig. spontaneous; without preparation or rehearsal. _ Her remarks were off-the-cuff, but very sensible. _ I’m not very good at making speeches off-the-cuff.
examples: Her remarks were off-the-cuff, but very sensible.

off-the-wall.monolingual: Fig. odd; silly; unusual. _Why are you so offthe- wall today? _ This book is strange. It’s really off-thewall.
examples: This book is strange.

oh, boy..monolingual: 1. Inf. Wow! (Usually Oh, boy! An exclamation. It has nothing to do with boys.) _ Bill: Oh, boy! An old-fashioned circus! _ “Oh, boy!” shouted John. “Dinner smells great! When do we eat?”
examples: “Oh, boy!” shouted John.

oh, ye of little faith..monolingual: Fig. You who trust no one. (Jocular; the word ye is an old form of you used in the Bible.) _ You thought I wouldn’t show up on time? Oh, ye of little faith.
examples: You thought I wouldn’t show up on time? Oh, ye of little faith.

oh, yeah?.monolingual: Inf. Is that what you think? (Rude and hostile.) _ Tom: You’re getting to be sort of a pest. Bill: Oh, yeah? Tom: Yeah. _Bob: This sauce tastes bad. I think you ruined it. Bill: Oh, yeah? What makes you think so? Bob: My tongue tells me!
examples: Tom: You’re getting to be sort of a pest.

oink out.monolingual: Sl. to overeat. _I oink out every time we have chocolate cake. _ This Thursday starts a four-day weekend, and I plan to oink out every day.
examples: I oink out every time we have chocolate cake.

*old as methuselah.monolingual: very old. (Of a person; refers to a biblical figure held to have lived to be
examples: Old Professor Stone is as old as Methusehah but still gets around with a cane.

*old as the hills.monolingual: very old; ancient. (*Also: as ~.) _ That’s not a new joke; it’s as old as the hills! _ Our family custom of eating black-eyed peas on New Year’s Day is old as the hills.
examples: Our family custom of eating black-eyed peas on New Year’s Day is old as the hills.

old battle-axe.monolingual: a bossy old woman. _ She is such an old battle-axe. I’ll bet she’s hell to live with.
examples: She is such an old battle-axe.

old college try.monolingual: a valiant effort. _ Will made the old college try, but that wasn’t enough to get the job done.
examples: Will made the old college try, but that wasn’t enough to get the job done.

old habits die hard..monolingual: Prov. People find it difficult to change their accustomed behavior. _Joan retired last year, but she still gets up as early as she used to when she had to go to work. Old habits die hard.
examples: Joan retired last year, but she still gets up as early as she used to when she had to go to work.

old hat.monolingual: Fig. old-fashioned; outmoded. _That’s a silly idea. It’s old hat. _ Hardly anybody uses typewriters anymore. That’s just old hat.
examples: That’s a silly idea.

the old one-two.monolingual: a series of two punches delivered quickly, one after another. _Tom gave Bill the old one-two, and the argument was ended right there. _Watch out for Tom. He’s a master of the old one-two.
examples: Tom gave Bill the old one-two, and the argument was ended right there.

*an old warhorse.monolingual: a performance piece that is performed often. (*Typically: be ~; become ~; perform ~; play ~.) _ The symphony orchestra played a few old warhorses and then some ghastly contemporary stuff that will never again see the light of day.
examples: The symphony orchestra played a few old warhorses and then some ghastly contemporary stuff that will never again see the light of day.

an old wives’ tale.monolingual: Fig. a myth or superstition. _ You really don’t believe that stuff about starving a cold do you? It’s just an old wives’ tale.
examples: You really don’t believe that stuff about starving a cold do you? It’s just an old wives’ tale.

*on a diet.monolingual: trying to lose weight by eating less food or specific foods. (*Typically: be ~; go ~; put someone ~; stay ~.) _ I didn’t eat any cake because I’m on a diet. _ I’m getting too heavy. I’ll have to go on a diet. _ I have a lot of trouble staying on a di
examples: I didn’t eat any cake because I’m on a diet.

*on a fool’s errand.monolingual: Fig. involved in a useless journey or task. (*Typically: be ~; go ~.) _Bill went for an interview, but he was on a fool’s errand. The job had already been filled. _ I was sent on a fool’s errand to buy some flowers. I knew the shop would be closed by
examples: Bill went for an interview, but he was on a fool’s errand.

*on a pedestal.monolingual: Fig. elevated to a position of honor or reverence. (Alludes to honoring someone on display on a pedestal like a statue. *Typically: place someone ~; put someone ~.) _ He puts his wife on a pedestal. She can do no wrong in his opinion. _ I was just do
examples: He puts his wife on a pedestal.

*on a power trip.monolingual: exercising power and authority, especially unduly. (*Typically: be ~; be off ~; go ~; have ~.) _ Old Molly is off on a power trip again. She loves ordering everyone about.
examples: Old Molly is off on a power trip again.

on a roll.monolingual: in the midst of a series of successes. _Don’t stop me now. I’m on a roll. _ Things are going great for Larry. He’s on a roll now.
examples: Don’t stop me now.

on a shoestring.monolingual: Fig. with a very small amount of money. _ We lived on a shoestring for years before I got a goodpaying job. _ John traveled to Florida on a shoestring.
examples: We lived on a shoestring for years before I got a goodpaying job.

*on a silver platter.monolingual: Fig. using a presentation [of something] that is appropriate for a very formal setting. (*Typically: give something to someone ~; present something ~; serve something ~; want something ~.) _ Aren’t paper plates good enough for you? You want dinner ma

*on a string.monolingual: Fig. under control, as one would control a marionette. (*Typically: get someone ~; have someone ~; keep someone ~.) _ She keeps him on a string so he won’t get involved with other women.
examples: She keeps him on a string so he won’t get involved with other women.

on a tight leash.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of an animal] on a leash, held tightly and close to its owner. _ I keep my dog on a tight leash so it won’t bother people.
examples: I keep my dog on a tight leash so it won’t bother people.

on account.monolingual: [money paid or owed] on a debt. _ I paid twelve dollars on account last month. Wasn’t that enough? _ I still have $100 due on account.
examples: I paid twelve dollars on account last month.

on active duty.monolingual: in battle or ready to go into battle. (Military.) _ The soldier was on active duty for ten months. _ That was a long time to be on active duty.
examples: The soldier was on active duty for ten months.

on all fours.monolingual: on one’s hands and knees. _I dropped a contact lens and spent an hour on all fours looking for it. _The baby can walk, but is on all fours most of the time anyway.
examples: I dropped a contact lens and spent an hour on all fours looking for it.

on any account.monolingual: for any purpose; for any reason; no matter what. _ On any account, I’ll be there on time. _ This doesn’t make sense on any account.
examples: On any account, I’ll be there on time.

on approval.monolingual: for examination, with the privilege of return. _ I ordered the merchandise on approval so I could send it back if I didn’t like it. _ Sorry, you can’t buy this on approval. All sales are final.
examples: I ordered the merchandise on approval so I could send it back if I didn’t like it.

on bended knee.monolingual: kneeling, as in supplication. (The verb form is obsolescent and occurs now only in this phrase.) _ Do you expect me to come to you on bended knee and ask you for forgiveness? _The suitors came on bended knee and begged the attention of the princess.
examples: The suitors came on bended knee and begged the attention of the princess.

on board.monolingual: 1. Lit. aboard (on or in) a ship, bus, airplane, etc. _ Is there a doctor on board? We have a sick passenger. _ When everyone is on board, we will leave.
examples: Is there a doctor on board? We have a sick passenger.

on broadway.monolingual: Fig. located in the Broadway theater district in New York City; performed in the Broadway theater district. (Regarded as having the best of American stage productions.) _ Our musical is the best thing on Broadway! _ I want to be a star on Broadway so
examples: I want to be a star on Broadway someday.

on call.monolingual: ready to serve when called. _I live a very hard life. I’m on call twenty hours a day. _ I’m sorry, but I can’t go out tonight. I’m on call at the hospital.
examples: I live a very hard life.

on campus.monolingual: located or being on the grounds of a college or university. _ Do you live on campus or off campus? _ I don’t think that Lisa is on campus right now.
examples: I don’t think that Lisa is on campus right now.

on cloud nine.monolingual: Fig. very happy. _ When I got my promotion, I was on cloud nine. _When the check came, I was on cloud nine for days.
examples: When I got my promotion, I was on cloud nine.

on consignment.monolingual: [of goods] having been placed in a store for sale, with payments made for the goods by the operator of the store only if they are sold. _ The artist placed his work in a gallery on consignment. _ I will attempt to sell your clothing on consignment.
examples: The artist placed his work in a gallery on consignment.

*on course.monolingual: 1. Lit. going in the right direction or on the right route. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; stay ~.) _ We are on course and should arrive at our port about noon.
examples: We are on course and should arrive at our port about noon.

on credit.monolingual: using credit; buying something using credit. _ I tried to buy a new suit on credit, but I was refused. _ The Smiths buy everything on credit and are very much in debt.
examples: I tried to buy a new suit on credit, but I was refused.

on dead center.monolingual: 1. Lit. at the exact center of something. _The arrow hit the target on dead center. _When you put the f lowers on the table, put them on dead center.
examples: The arrow hit the target on dead center.

on deck.monolingual: 1. Lit. on the deck of a boat or a ship. _ Everyone except the cook was on deck when the storm hit. _ Just pull up the anchor and leave it on deck.
examples: Everyone except the cook was on deck when the storm hit.

on duty.monolingual: at work; currently doing one’s work. (The opposite of off duty.) _I can’t help you now, but I’ll be on duty in about an hour. _Who is on duty here? I need some help.
examples: I can’t help you now, but I’ll be on duty in about an hour.

on easy street.monolingual: Fig. in a state of financial independence and comfort. _ I want to live on easy street when I grow up. _ When I get this contract signed, I’ll be on easy street.
examples: I want to live on easy street when I grow up.

on edge.monolingual: 1. Lit. on something’s own edge. _Can you stand a dime on edge? _ You should store these crates on edge, not lying f lat.
examples: You should store these crates on edge, not lying f lat.

on fire.monolingual: 1. Lit. burning; being burned with flames. _Help! My car is on fire! _ That house on the corner is on fire!
examples: That house on the corner is on fire! 2.

on foot.monolingual: [running or walking] using the feet. _ My car won’t work so I have to travel on foot. _ We go everywhere around the campus on foot.
examples: My car won’t work so I have to travel on foot.

on hold.monolingual: 1. Lit. waiting; temporarily halted. _ The building project is on hold while we try to find money to complete it. _ We put our wedding plans on hold until we finished school.
examples: The building project is on hold while we try to find money to complete it.

on horseback.monolingual: on the back of a horse. _ Anne rode on horseback across the field. _ Because they loved horses, the couple decided to marry on horseback.
examples: Anne rode on horseback across the field.

on ice.monolingual: 1. Lit. stored or preserved on ice or under refrigeration. _ I have a lot of root beer on ice for the picnic. _ All the soft drinks are on ice.
examples: I have a lot of root beer on ice for the picnic.

on impulse.monolingual: after having had an impulse or sudden thought. _On impulse, Bob decided to buy a car. _I didn’t need a cellular telephone. I just bought it on impulse.
examples: On impulse, Bob decided to buy a car.

*on its feet.monolingual: Fig. organized and functioning; started up and functioning. (*Typically: get something ~; have something ~; put something ~.) _Trying to get this company on its feet is harder than I thought. _What will it take to put this company on its feet again?
examples: Trying to get this company on its feet is harder than I thought.

on land.monolingual: on the ground; on the land and not at sea or in the air. _ The f light was rough and I feel better now that I am back on land. _ When I am at sea, I feel more relaxed than when I am on land.
examples: The f light was rough and I feel better now that I am back on land.

on location.monolingual: [of a movie] being filmed in a place distant from the studio. _ This movie was shot on location in Ontario. _ The actress went on location in Spain for her latest film.
examples: This movie was shot on location in Ontario.

on medication.monolingual: taking medicine for a current medical problem. _ I can’t drive the car since I am on medication. _ He is on medication and hopes to be well soon.
examples: I can’t drive the car since I am on medication.

on moral grounds.monolingual: considering reasons of morality. _ He complained about the television program on moral gounds. There was too much ridicule of his religion.
examples: He complained about the television program on moral gounds.

on occasion.monolingual: occasionally. _ I like to go to the movies on occasion. _On occasion, Mary would walk her dog through the park.
examples: I like to go to the movies on occasion.

on one’s best behavior.monolingual: being as polite as possible. _ When we went out, the children were on their best behavior. _ I try to be on my best behavior all the time.
examples: When we went out, the children were on their best behavior.

on one’s deathbed.monolingual: while one is in bed and dying. _While he lay on his deathbed, he told his lawyer that he wanted to give all his money to charity.
examples: While he lay on his deathbed, he told his lawyer that he wanted to give all his money to charity.

on one’s feet.monolingual: 1. Lit. standing up. _ Get on your feet. They are playing the national anthem. _I’ve been on my feet all day, and they hurt.
examples: Get on your feet.

on one’s high horse.monolingual: Fig. in a haughty manner or mood. _ Larry is on his high horse again, bossing people around. _ The boss is on her high horse about the cost of office supplies.
examples: Larry is on his high horse again, bossing people around.

on one’s honor.monolingual: Fig. on one’s solemn oath; sincerely. _On my honor, I’ll be there on time. _He promised on his honor that he’d pay me back next week.
examples: On my honor, I’ll be there on time.

on one’s mind.monolingual: Fig. occupying one’s thoughts; currently being thought about. _ You’ve been on my mind all day. _ Do you have something on your mind? You look so serious.
examples: You’ve been on my mind all day.

on one’s own.monolingual: independently. _Our baby can now walk on his own. _ I have lived on my own since I was 18.
examples: Our baby can now walk on his own.

on one’s own hook.monolingual: all by oneself. _I don’t need any help. I can do it on my own hook. _ She did it on her own hook without having to call on anyone.
examples: I don’t need any help.

on one’s own time.monolingual: not while one is at work. _ The boss made me write the report on my own time. That’s not fair. _ Please make your personal telephone calls on your own time.
examples: The boss made me write the report on my own time.

on one’s person.monolingual: [of something] carried with one. _ Always carry identification on your person. _ I’m sorry, I don’t have any money on my person.
examples: Always carry identification on your person.

*on one’s toes.monolingual: Fig. alert. (*Typically: be ~; keep ~; keep one ~; stay ~.) _ You have to be on your toes if you want to be in this business. _ I have to stay on my toes to keep from getting fired.
examples: You have to be on your toes if you want to be in this business.

on order.monolingual: ordered with delivery expected. _ Your car is on order. It’ll be here in a few weeks. _I don’t have the part in stock, but it’s on order.
examples: Your car is on order.

on pins and needles.monolingual: Fig. anxious; in suspense. _ I’ve been on pins and needles all day, waiting for you to call with the news. _ We were on pins and needles until we heard that your plane had landed safely.
examples: I’ve been on pins and needles all day, waiting for you to call with the news.

on probation.monolingual: 1. Lit. serving a period of probation, typically after conviction for a crime. _ While Anne was on probation, she reported to the police regularly. _ John was on probation for a year.
examples: While Anne was on probation, she reported to the police regularly.

on purpose.monolingual: intentionally; in a way that is meant or intended; not an accident. _ The bully stepped on my foot on purpose. _ Jealously, Jimmy destroyed Billy’s sand castle on purpose.
examples: The bully stepped on my foot on purpose.

on sale.monolingual: available for sale at a reduced price. (Always implies lower than usual sale price.) _ These pots are on sale for $20. _ I bought these pants on sale for half price.
examples: These pots are on sale for $20.

on schedule.monolingual: at the expected or desired time. _The plane came in right on schedule. _ Things have to happen on schedule in a theatrical performance.
examples: The plane came in right on schedule.

on second thought.monolingual: Fig. having given something more thought; having reconsidered something. _ On second thought, maybe you should sell your house and move into an apartment. _On second thought, let’s not go to a movie.
examples: On second thought, maybe you should sell your house and move into an apartment.

on short notice.monolingual: quickly and without a timely notification of other people; with very little lead time. _She called the meeting on such short notice that we had no time to prepare.
examples: She called the meeting on such short notice that we had no time to prepare.

on someone’s account.monolingual: because of someone. _ Don’t do it on my account. _ They were late on Jane’s account.
examples: Don’t do it on my account.

on someone’s head.monolingual: Fig. [for something negative] belonging only to one person or group. _ All the blame fell on their heads. _ I don’t think that all the criticism should be on my head.
examples: All the blame fell on their heads.

*on someone’s heels.monolingual: Fig. following someone very closely; following very closely at someone’s heels. (*Typically: hard ~; hot ~; right ~. See also on someone’s tail.) _ I ran as fast as I could, but the dog was still hard on my heels. _ Here comes Sally, and John is hot
examples: I ran as fast as I could, but the dog was still hard on my heels.

*on someone’s nerves.monolingual: Fig. annoying someone. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ Our noisy neighbors are beginning to get on my nerves. _ That radio is getting on my nerves.
examples: Our noisy neighbors are beginning to get on my nerves.

on someone’s say-so.monolingual: on someone’s authority; with someone’s permission. _I can’t do it on your say-so. I’ll have to get a written request. _ Bill: I canceled the contract with the A.B.C. Company. Bob: On whose say-so?
examples: I can’t do it on your say-so.

*on someone’s shoulders.monolingual: Fig. on someone’s own self. (*Typically: be ~; carry something ~; fall ~; have something ~; leave something ~; put something ~.) _ Why should all the responsibility fall on my shoulders? _ She carries a tremendous amount of responsibility on her shou
examples: She carries a tremendous amount of responsibility on her shoulders.

on someone’s tail.monolingual: Inf. Fig. following someone closely. _ There is a huge truck on my tail. What should I do? _ Keep on her tail and don’t let her out of your sight.
examples: There is a huge truck on my tail.

on someone’s watch.monolingual: while someone is on duty; while someone is supposed to be in charge of a situation. _ I am not responsible since it didn’t happen on my watch. _ I guess I have to bear the blame since it happened on my watch.
examples: I am not responsible since it didn’t happen on my watch.

on spec.monolingual: 1. using money risked in the hope of profit; on speculation. _He lives by buying and selling houses on spec. _ I think it might be an idea to build a few yachts on spec just now.
examples: He lives by buying and selling houses on spec.

on standby.monolingual: waiting for one’s turn, especially describing the status of travelers who wait at a soon-to-depart train, plane, or bus, hoping that a seat will become available. _ The passenger waited on standby for an available seat. _ The agent was able to seat a
examples: The passenger waited on standby for an available seat.

on tap.monolingual: 1. Lit. having to do with beer served from a barrel or keg. _ Do you have any imported beers on tap here? _ I like beer on tap. The canned stuff tastes funny to me.
examples: I like beer on tap.

on target.monolingual: on schedule; exactly as predicted. _ Your estimate of the cost was right on target. _ My prediction was not on target.
examples: Your estimate of the cost was right on target.

on the air.monolingual: broadcasting (a radio or television program). _ The radio station came back on the air shortly after the storm. _ We were on the air for two hours.
examples: The radio station came back on the air shortly after the storm.

*on the back burner.monolingual: Fig. [of something] on hold or suspended temporarily. (Alludes to putting a pot that needs less active attention on a back burner of a stove, leaving space for pots that need to be stirred. Compare this with on the front burner. *Typically: be ~; put
examples: The building project is on the back burner for now.

on the ball.monolingual: Inf. knowledgeable; competent; attentive. _ This guy is really on the ball. _ If you were on the ball, this wouldn’t have happened.
examples: This guy is really on the ball.

*on the bandwagon.monolingual: Fig. on the popular side (of an issue); taking a popular position. (*Typically: be ~; climb ~; get ~; hop ~; jump ~.) _ You really should get on the bandwagon. Everyone else is. _ Jane has always had her own ideas about things. She’s not the kind of
examples: You really should get on the bandwagon.

on the beam.monolingual: Fig. exactly right; thinking along the correct lines. _That’s the right idea. Now you’re on the beam! _ She’s not on the beam yet. Explain it to her again.
examples: That’s the right idea.

on the bench.monolingual: 1. [of a judge] directing a session of court. _ I have to go to court tomorrow. Who’s on the bench? _ It doesn’t matter who’s on the bench. You’ll get a fair hearing.
examples: I have to go to court tomorrow.

on the bias.monolingual: on a diagonal line; on a diagonal pathway or direction. _ The panels of the dress were cut on the bias. _ The seamstress sewed the fabric on the bias.
examples: The panels of the dress were cut on the bias.

on the bird.monolingual: available on satellite television. _ There is a whole lot of good stuff on the bird, but you need a receiving dish to get it. _ I get a huge book every month listing what programs are on the bird.
examples: There is a whole lot of good stuff on the bird, but you need a receiving dish to get it.

on the block.monolingual: 1. Lit. on a city or suburban block. _ John is the biggest kid on the block. _We had a party on the block last weekend.
examples: John is the biggest kid on the block.

on the borderline.monolingual: in an uncertain position between two statuses; undecided. _ Bill was on the borderline between an A and a B in biology. _ Jane was on the borderline of joining the navy.
examples: Bill was on the borderline between an A and a B in biology.

on the bright side.monolingual: Fig. [ignoring the bad for a moment] considering the positive aspects of a situation. _ On the bright side, the car you wrecked was covered by insurance.
examples: On the bright side, the car you wrecked was covered by insurance.

on the button.monolingual: exactly right; in exactly the right place; at exactly the right time. _ That’s it! You’re right on the button. _ He got here at one o’clock on the button.
examples: That’s it! You’re right on the button.

on the cutting edge.monolingual: Fig. [for someone] to be trendy and very up-to-date; [for something] to be of the latest design. (Akin to on the bleeding edge.) _ This technology is right on the cutting edge. It’s so new, it’s not available to the public yet.
examples: This technology is right on the cutting edge.

on the defensive.monolingual: weary and ready to defend oneself. _ John goes on the defensive when his athletic ability is questioned. _ The child was on the defensive when questioned about cheating.
examples: John goes on the defensive when his athletic ability is questioned.

on the dole.monolingual: receiving welfare money. _I spent six months on the dole, and believe me, it’s no picnic.
examples: I spent six months on the dole, and believe me, it’s no picnic.

*on the dot.monolingual: Fig. at exactly the right time. (*Typically: be somewhere ~; arrive (somewhere) ~; get somewhere ~; see someone ~; show up ~.) _ I’ll be there at noon on the dot. _ I expect to see you here at eight o’clock on the dot.
examples: I’ll be there at noon on the dot.

on the double.monolingual: very fast; twice as fast as normal. (Originally military. Alludes to “double time” in marching.) _ Get over here right now—on the double! _ She wants to see you in her office on the double.
examples: She wants to see you in her office on the double.

*on the edge.monolingual: Fig. very anxious and about to become distraught; on the verge of becoming irrational. (*Typically: be ~; live ~. See also on edge.) _ After the horrible events of the last week, we are all on the edge.
examples: After the horrible events of the last week, we are all on the edge.

on the eve of something.monolingual: Fig. just before something, possibly the evening before something. _John decided to leave school on the eve of his graduation. _The team held a party on the eve of the tournament.
examples: John decided to leave school on the eve of his graduation.

on the face of it.monolingual: Fig. superficially; from the way it looks. _This looks like a serious problem on the face of it. It probably is minor, however. _ On the face of it, it seems worthless.
examples: This looks like a serious problem on the face of it.

on the fast track.monolingual: Fig. following an expedited procedure; being acted upon sooner or more quickly than is typical. _ Let’s put this project on the fast track and maybe we’ll see results sooner.
examples: Let’s put this project on the fast track and maybe we’ll see results sooner.

on the fly.monolingual: [done] while something or someone is operating or moving. _ I’ll try to capture the data on the f ly. _ Please try to buy some aspirin somewhere on the f ly today.
examples: I’ll try to capture the data on the f ly.

on the fringe.monolingual: 1. Lit. at the outer boundary or edge of something. _ He doesn’t live in the city, just on the fringe.
examples: He doesn’t live in the city, just on the fringe.

*on the front burner.monolingual: Fig. receiving particular attention or consideration. (Compare this with on the back burner. *Typically: be ~; put something ~.) _ So, what’s on the front burner for us this week? _ Move this project to the front burner so it will get some attention.
examples: Move this project to the front burner so it will get some attention.

on the go.monolingual: busy; moving about busily. _ I’m usually on the go all day long. _ I hate being on the go all the time.
examples: I’m usually on the go all day long.

on the heels of something.monolingual: Fig. soon after something. _ There was a rainstorm on the heels of the windstorm. _The team held a victory celebration on the heels of their winning season.
examples: There was a rainstorm on the heels of the windstorm.

on the horizon.monolingual: 1. Lit. appearing at the boundary between the earth and the sky. _ There is a storm on the horizon.
examples: There is a storm on the horizon.

on the hour.monolingual: at each hour on the hour mark. _ I have to take this medicine every hour on the hour. _ I expect to see you there on the hour, not one minute before and not one minute after.
examples: I have to take this medicine every hour on the hour.

on the house.monolingual: [of something] given away free by a merchant. _ “Here,” said the waiter, “have a cup of coffee on the house.” _ I went to a restaurant last night. I was the ten thousandth customer, so my dinner was on the house.
examples: “Here,” said the waiter, “have a cup of coffee on the house.

on the job.monolingual: working; doing what one is expected to do. _ I’m always on the job when I should be. _ I can depend on my furnace to be on the job day and night.
examples: I’m always on the job when I should be.

on the lam.monolingual: running from the police. (Underworld.) _ Richard has been on the lam for a week now. _ The gang leader broke out of prison and is still on the lam.
examples: Richard has been on the lam for a week now.

on the level.monolingual: honest; straightforward. _Come on now, on the level, tell me the truth. _ Is the ad on the level?
examples: Come on now, on the level, tell me the truth.

on the loose.monolingual: running around free. _ Look out! There is a bear on the loose from the zoo. _ Most kids enjoy being on the loose when they go to college.
examples: Look out! There is a bear on the loose from the zoo.

on the make.monolingual: 1. building or developing; being made. _ There is a company that is on the make. _ That was a very good sales strategy, John. You’re a real-estate agent on the make.
examples: There is a company that is on the make.

on the mark.monolingual: Fig. right on the measurement point; showing just the right anount. _ It’s exactly one quart, right on the mark.
examples: It’s exactly one quart, right on the mark.

*on the market.monolingual: openly available for sale. (*Typically: be ~; get something ~; put something ~.) _ We put our house on the market last year and it still hasn’t sold.
examples: We put our house on the market last year and it still hasn’t sold.

on the mend.monolingual: getting better; becoming healthy again. _ I cared for my father while he was on the mend. _ I took a leave of absence from work while I was on the mend.
examples: I cared for my father while he was on the mend.

on the move.monolingual: 1. moving from place to place. _ Are the cattle on the move now, or are they still grazing?
examples: Are the cattle on the move now, or are they still grazing? 2.

on the off chance.monolingual: because of a slight possibility that something may happen or might be the case; just in case. _ I went to the theater on the off chance that there were tickets for the show left. _We didn’t think we would get into the football game, but we went on th
examples: I went to the theater on the off chance that there were tickets for the show left.

on the other hand.monolingual: Fig. a phrase introducing an alternate view. _ John: I’m ready to go; on the other hand, I’m perfectly comfortable here. Sally: I’ll let you know when I’m ready, then. _ Mary: I like this one. On the other hand, this is nice too. Sue: Why not get bot
examples: John: I’m ready to go; on the other hand, I’m perfectly comfortable here.

on the pill.monolingual: taking birth control pills. _Is it true that Mary is on the pill? _ She was on the pill, but she isn’t now.
examples: She was on the pill, but she isn’t now.

on the prowl.monolingual: looking for someone for sexual purposes. (Alludes to a prowling cat.) _ Tom looks like he is on the prowl again tonight. _ That whole gang of boys is on the prowl. Watch out.
examples: Tom looks like he is on the prowl again tonight.

on the qt.monolingual: quietly; secretly. (An abbreviation of quiet.) _ The company president was making payments to his wife on the QT. _ The mayor accepted a bribe on the QT.
examples: The company president was making payments to his wife on the QT.

on the rag.monolingual: 1. Sl.menstruating. (Potentially offensive. Use with caution.) _ Kim’s on the rag and in a bad mood. _ Sue doesn’t go swimming when she’s on the rag.
examples: Kim’s on the rag and in a bad mood.

on the right track.monolingual: 1. Lit. following the right track or trail; riding on the correct track, as with a train. _ The train was on the right track when it left the station. I can’t imagine how it got lost.
examples: The train was on the right track when it left the station.

on the rise.monolingual: Fig. increasing in frequency or intensity. _ The number of auto thefts in Cook County is on the rise again.
examples: The number of auto thefts in Cook County is on the rise again.

on the road.monolingual: Fig. traveling from place to place, not necessarily on the highways; working away from one’s home or office. _ I was on the road with the circus for six months. _ I don’t work in the main office anymore. Now I’m on the road.
examples: I was on the road with the circus for six months.

on the road to recovery.monolingual: Cliché recovering; getting better; improving. _It’s been two weeks since her surgery, and she is on the road to recovery.
examples: It’s been two weeks since her surgery, and she is on the road to recovery.

on the rocks.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of a ship] broken and marooned on rocks in the sea. _ The ship crashed and was on the rocks until the next high tide.
examples: The ship crashed and was on the rocks until the next high tide.

on the run.monolingual: 1. Fig. while one is moving from place to place. _ I will try to pick up some aspirin today on the run. _ I will think about it on the run.
examples: I will try to pick up some aspirin today on the run.

on the safe side.monolingual: Fig. taking the risk-free path. _Let’s be on the safe side and call first. _ I think you should stay on the safe side and call the doctor about this fever.
examples: Let’s be on the safe side and call first.

on the same wavelength.monolingual: Fig. thinking in the same pattern. _ We’re not on the same wavelength. Let’s try again. _ We kept talking until we got on the same wavelength.
examples: We’re not on the same wavelength.

on the sauce.monolingual: drinking regularly; intoxicated. _ Poor old Ron is on the sauce again. _ He is on the sauce most of the time.
examples: Poor old Ron is on the sauce again.

on the scene.monolingual: Fig. available or present where something is happening or where something has happened. _ The ambulance was on the scene almost immediately. _I wasn’t on the scene when it happened.
examples: The ambulance was on the scene almost immediately.

on the shelf.monolingual: 1. Fig. not active socially; left to oneself in social matters. (Alludes to being left or stored on a shelf.) _ I’ve been on the shelf long enough. I’m going to make some friends. _ She likes being on the shelf.
examples: I’ve been on the shelf long enough.

on the side.monolingual: 1. Lit. extra, such as with a job or an additional order of food. _ I would like an order of eggs with toast on the side, please. _She is a bank teller and works as a waitress on the side.
examples: I would like an order of eggs with toast on the side, please.

on the skids.monolingual: Sl. on the decline. _ My newly started business is on the skids. _ Her health is really on the skids, but she stays cheery anyway.
examples: My newly started business is on the skids.

on the sly.monolingual: Fig. secretly and deceptively. _ She was stealing little bits of money on the sly. _ Martin was having an affair with the maid on the sly.
examples: She was stealing little bits of money on the sly.

on the spot.monolingual: 1. Lit. at exactly the right place; at exactly the right time. _ It’s noon, and I’m glad you’re all here on the spot. Now we can begin. _I expect you to be on the spot when and where trouble arises.
examples: It’s noon, and I’m glad you’re all here on the spot.

*on the stick.monolingual: Inf. organized and busy. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ Get on the stick and get this job done! _ Come on, you guys. Let’s get on the stick!
examples: Come on, you guys.

on the street.monolingual: 1. Fig. widely known. _ Sue put it on the street, and now everyone knows. _ It’s on the street. There isn’t anyone who hasn’t heard it.
examples: Sue put it on the street, and now everyone knows.

on the strength of something.monolingual: Fig. because of the support of something, such as a promise or evidence; due to something. _ On the strength of your comment, I decided to give John another chance. _ On the strength of my testimony, my case was dismissed.
examples: On the strength of your comment, I decided to give John another chance.

on the table.monolingual: Fig. subject to discussion by the group; submitted as a point of discussion. _ The chairman said we could not discuss salaries since the topic was no longer on the table.
examples: The chairman said we could not discuss salaries since the topic was no longer on the table.

on the take.monolingual: taking bribes. (Underworld.) _ I heard that the mayor is on the take. _ Everyone in city hall is on the take.
examples: I heard that the mayor is on the take.

on the throne.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of royalty] currently reigning. _ King Samuel was on the throne for two decades.
examples: King Samuel was on the throne for two decades.

on the up-and-up.monolingual: legitimate; open and aboveboard. _ Is this deal on the up-and-up? What’s the catch? _ Everything I do is on the up-and-up. I am totally honest.
examples: Everything I do is on the up-and-up.

on the wagon.monolingual: Fig. not drinking alcohol. _ No, I don’t care for a cocktail. I’m on the wagon. _ Bob’s old drinking buddies complained that he was no fun when he went on the wagon.
examples: No, I don’t care for a cocktail.

on the wane.monolingual: becoming less; fading away. _Her inf luence in on the wane, but she is still the boss.
examples: Her inf luence in on the wane, but she is still the boss.

on the warpath.monolingual: very angry. _The boss is on the warpath again. Watch out! _I am on the warpath about setting goals and standards again.
examples: The boss is on the warpath again.

on the whole.monolingual: generally; considering everything. _ On the whole, this was a very good day. _ Your work—on the whole—is quite good.
examples: On the whole, this was a very good day.

on the wing.monolingual: Fig. while flying; while in flight. (Usually refers to birds, fowl, etc., not people or planes.) _ There is nothing as pretty as a bird on the wing. _ The hawk caught the sparrow on the wing.
examples: There is nothing as pretty as a bird on the wing.

on the wrong track.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of a train] following the wrong set of tracks. _ We had to back up, because somehow we got on the wrong track.
examples: We had to back up, because somehow we got on the wrong track.

on thin ice.monolingual: 1. Lit. on ice that is too thin to support one. _ Billy is on thin ice and is in great danger.
examples: Billy is on thin ice and is in great danger.

on tiptoe.monolingual: standing or walking on the front part of the feet (the balls of the feet) with no weight put on the heels. (This is done to gain height or to walk quietly.) _ I had to stand on tiptoe in order to see over the fence. _I came in late and walked on tipt
examples: I had to stand on tiptoe in order to see over the fence.

on top of something.monolingual: 1. Fig. up-to-date on something; knowing about the current state of something. _ Ask Mary. She’s on top of this issue. _ This issue is constantly changing. She has to pay attention to it to stay on top of things.
examples: Ask Mary. She’s on top of this issue.

on top of the world.monolingual: Fig. feeling wonderful; glorious; ecstatic. _ Wow, I feel on top of the world. _ Since he got a new job, he’s on top of the world.
examples: Wow, I feel on top of the world.

*on track.monolingual: on schedule; progressing as planned. (*Typically: be ~; get someone or something ~; have someone or something ~; keep someone or something ~; put someone or something ~; set someone or something ~.) _ Try to keep these procedures on track this time.
examples: Try to keep these procedures on track this time.

on trial.monolingual: 1. [of someone] in a legal case before a judge. _ The criminal was on trial for over three months. _I am not on trial. Don’t treat me like that!
examples: The criminal was on trial for over three months.

on vacation.monolingual: away, taking time off work; on holiday. _ Where are you going on vacation this year? _ I’ll be away on vacation for three weeks.
examples: I’ll be away on vacation for three weeks.

on view.monolingual: visible; on public display. _ The painting will be on view at the museum. _ I’ll pull the shades so that we won’t be on view.
examples: The painting will be on view at the museum.

on with someone.monolingual: [of a date or appointment] agreed to and confirmed with someone. _Is the Friday date still on with you? _ It’s on with me.
examples: It’s on with me.

once and for all.monolingual: finally; permanently. _ Sue: I’m going to get this place organized once and for all! Alice: That’ll be the day! _ “We need to get this straightened out once and for all,” said Bob, for the fourth time today.
examples: “We need to get this straightened out once and for all,” said Bob, for the fourth time today.

once bitten, twice shy..monolingual: Prov.When something or someone has hurt you once, you tend to avoid that thing or person. _ Jill: Let’s go ride the roller coaster. Jane: No, thanks. I got really sick on one of those once—once bitten, twice shy. _ I once sent in money for something
examples: Jill: Let’s go ride the roller coaster.

once in a blue moon.monolingual: Cliché very seldom. _ Jill: Does your husband ever bring you f lowers? Ellen: Once in a blue moon. _ Once in a blue moon, I buy a fashion magazine, just to see what people are wearing.
examples: Jill: Does your husband ever bring you f lowers? Ellen: Once in a blue moon.

once upon a time.monolingual: Cliché once in the past. (A formula used to begin a fairy tale.) _Once upon a time, there were three bears. _Once upon a time, I had a puppy of my own.
examples: Once upon a time, there were three bears.

*the once-over.monolingual: a quick, visual examination. (*Typically: get ~; give someone ~.) _ Every time John walks by I get the once-over. Does he like me? _ I went to the doctor yesterday, but I only had a once-over.
examples: Every time John walks by I get the once-over.

once-over-lightly.monolingual: 1. Fig. a quick and careless treatment. (A noun. Said of an act of cleaning, studying, examination, or appraisal.) _Bill gave his geometry the once-overlightly and then quit studying. _ Ann, you didn’t wash the dishes properly. They only got a once-o
examples: Bill gave his geometry the once-overlightly and then quit studying.

one and all.monolingual: everyone. _ “Good morning to one and all,” said Jane as she walked through the outer office. _Let’s hope that this turns out to be a wonderful party for one and all.
examples: “Good morning to one and all,” said Jane as she walked through the outer office.

the one and only.monolingual: the famous and talented (person). (Used in theatrical introductions. See also my one and only. ) _And now—the one and only—Jane Smith! _Let’s have a big hand for the one and only Bob Jones!

one and the same.monolingual: Cliché the very same person or thing. _ John Jones and J. Jones are one and the same. _ Men’s socks and men’s stockings are almost one and the same.
examples: John Jones and J.

*one for the road.monolingual: a drink; a drink before a journey or before leaving a bar. (*Typically: down ~; drink ~; have ~; take ~.) _Let’s have one for the road. _Don’t down one for the road if you are going to be the driver.
examples: Let’s have one for the road.

one good turn deserves another..monolingual: Prov. If someone does you a favor, you should do a favor for that person in return. _ Jill: Thanks for the ride. Jane: It’s the least I can do after you helped me wash the car last week. One good turn deserves another. _ Child: I don’t want to help G
examples: Jill: Thanks for the ride.

one little bit.monolingual: any at all; at all. _ Jean could not be persuaded to change her mind one little bit. _ I don’t want to hear anything more about it. Not even one little bit.
examples: Jean could not be persuaded to change her mind one little bit.

one moment, please..monolingual: Please wait briefly. (A polite way of acknowledging that you noticed someone’s request.) _ John: Can you help me? Clerk: One moment, please. I will be with you shortly. _ Bill (answering the phone): Hello? Bob: Hello. Can I speak to Tom? Bill: One mo
examples: John: Can you help me? Clerk: One moment, please.

one of these days.monolingual: someday; in some situation like this one. _ One of these days, someone is going to steal your purse if you don’t take better care of it. _ You’re going to get in trouble one of these days.
examples: One of these days, someone is going to steal your purse if you don’t take better care of it.

*one’s bearings.monolingual: the knowledge of where one is; the knowledge of how one is oriented to one’s immediate environment. (*Typically: get ~; find ~; have ~; lose ~; tell one ~.) _ After he fell, it took Ted a few minutes to get his bearings. _Jean found her compass and g
examples: After he fell, it took Ted a few minutes to get his bearings.

one’s best bib and tucker.monolingual: Rur. one’s best clothing. _ I always put on my best bib and tucker on Sundays. _ Put on your best bib and tucker, and let’s go to the city.
examples: I always put on my best bib and tucker on Sundays.

one’s best shot.monolingual: Fig. one’s best attempt (at something). _ That was his best shot, but it wasn’t good enough. _I always try to give something my best shot.
examples: That was his best shot, but it wasn’t good enough.

one’s better half.monolingual: Fig. one’s spouse. (Usually refers to a wife.) _ I think we’d like to come for dinner, but I’ll have to ask my better half. _ I have to go home now to my better half. We are going out tonight.
examples: I think we’d like to come for dinner, but I’ll have to ask my better half.

one’s claws are showing.monolingual: one is acting catty; one is saying spiteful and cruel things. _ Gloria: Did you see what she was wearing? I wouldn’t be caught dead in it! Sally: Gloria, my dear, your claws are showing.
examples: Gloria: Did you see what she was wearing? I wouldn’t be caught dead in it! Sally: Gloria, my dear, your claws are showing.

one’s days are numbered.monolingual: Fig. one is facing death or dismissal. _If I don’t get this contract, my days are numbered at this company. _ Uncle Bill has a terminal disease. His days are numbered.
examples: If I don’t get this contract, my days are numbered at this company.

one’s deepest sympathy.monolingual: one’s very sincere sympathy. _ I am so sorry about the death of your father. You have my deepest sympathy. _ She sent her deepest sympathy to the family.
examples: I am so sorry about the death of your father.

one’s ears are red.monolingual: Fig. [for someone’s ears] to be red from embarrassment. _ I’m so embarrassed. Wow, are my ears red! _ My ears are red! I can’t believe I said that.
examples: I’m so embarrassed.

one’s ears are ringing.monolingual: Fig. [for someone’s ears] to have a ringing sound because of an illness or other condition; very loud music, or some other very loud sound. _ After the explosion, my ears were ringing for hours. _My ears are ringing because I have a sinus infection.
examples: After the explosion, my ears were ringing for hours.

one’s fair share.monolingual: the amount of something that one is due relative to what other people are receiving. _Let him take more. He didn’t get his fair share. _ I want my fair share. You cheated me! Give me some more!
examples: Let him take more.

one’s for the asking.monolingual: Fig. [can become] one’s property if one asks for it. _ I have a cherry pie here. A slice is yours for the asking if you want it. _ Uncle Mac said we could have his old car if we wanted it. It was ours for the asking.
examples: I have a cherry pie here.

one’s frame of mind.monolingual: Fig. one’s mood or mental state. _ My frame of mind is sort of low at the moment. I’ve had a very bad day.
examples: My frame of mind is sort of low at the moment.

one’s future looks bright..monolingual: Fig. One has a promising future. _Tom’s future looks bright and he will do well if he keeps working hard.
examples: Tom’s future looks bright and he will do well if he keeps working hard.

one’s goose is cooked.monolingual: one is finished; one has been found out and is in trouble. _ It’s over. His goose is cooked! _ If I get caught, my goose is cooked.
examples: If I get caught, my goose is cooked.

one’s heart stands still.monolingual: Fig. one’s heart (figuratively) stops beating because of strong emotions. _ When I first saw you, my heart stood still. _ My heart will stand still until you answer.
examples: When I first saw you, my heart stood still.

one’s home away from home.monolingual: a place, other than one’s home, where one can feel at home. _ Please make our house your home away from home when you are in town.
examples: Please make our house your home away from home when you are in town.

one’s last resting place.monolingual: Euph. one’s grave. _ Daddy has gone to his last resting place. _ I want to be beside her in her last resting place.
examples: Daddy has gone to his last resting place.

one’s luck runs out.monolingual: Fig. one’s good luck stops. _My luck ran out, so I had to come home. _ She will quit gambling when her luck runs out.
examples: My luck ran out, so I had to come home.

one’s mind went blank.monolingual: Fig. someone’s mind has experienced total forgetfulness. _ He knew all his lines in rehearsal, but his mind went blank when he went before an audience.
examples: He knew all his lines in rehearsal, but his mind went blank when he went before an audience.

*one’s money’s worth.monolingual: Fig. everything that one has paid for; the best quality for the money paid. (*Typically: get ~; have ~.) _ Weigh that package of meat before you buy it. Be sure you’re getting your money’s worth. _I didn’t get my money’s worth with my new camera, so
examples: Weigh that package of meat before you buy it.

one’s name is mud.monolingual: Fig. one is in trouble or humiliated. _ If I can’t get this contract signed, my name will be mud. _ His name is mud ever since he broke the crystal vase.
examples: If I can’t get this contract signed, my name will be mud.

one’s next of kin.monolingual: one’s closest living relative or relatives. _The police notified the dead man’s next of kin. _My next of kin lives 800 miles away.
examples: The police notified the dead man’s next of kin.

one’s next-door neighbor.monolingual: the person living in the house or apartment closest to one’s own. _My next-door neighbor came over to borrow a shovel. _ I will be visiting our next-door neighbor if you need me.
examples: My next-door neighbor came over to borrow a shovel.

one’s number is up.monolingual: Fig. one’s time to die—or to suffer some other unpleasantness—has come. _John is worried. He thinks his number is up. _ When my number is up, I hope it all goes fast.
examples: John is worried.

one’s old stamping ground.monolingual: Fig. the place where one was raised or where one has spent a lot of time. (There are variants with stomping and grounds.) _ Ann should know about that place. It’s near her old stamping ground. _I can’t wait to get back to my old stomping grounds.
examples: Ann should know about that place.

*one’s own worst enemy.monolingual: Fig. consistently causing oneself to fail; more harmful to oneself than other people are. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ Ellen: My boss is my enemy. She never says anything good about me. Jane: Ellen, you’re your own worst enemy. If you did your job
examples: Ellen: My boss is my enemy.

*one’s sea legs.monolingual: Fig. one’s ability to tolerate the movement of a ship at sea. (*Typically: get ~; have ~.) _ Jean was a little awkward on the cruise at first, but in a few days she got her sea legs and was fine. _You may feel a little sick until you get your sea leg
examples: Jean was a little awkward on the cruise at first, but in a few days she got her sea legs and was fine.

*one’s second wind.monolingual: 1. Lit. one’s stabilized breathing after exerting oneself for a short time. (*Typically: get ~; have ~.) _ John was having a hard time running until he got his second wind. _ Bill had to quit the race because he never got his second wind.
examples: John was having a hard time running until he got his second wind.

one’s sunset years.monolingual: Euph. one’s old age. _ Many people in their sunset years love to travel. _ Now is the time to think about financial planning for your sunset years.
examples: Many people in their sunset years love to travel.

*one’s walking papers.monolingual: Fig. a notice that one is fired from one’s job. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give one ~.) _ Well, I’m through. I got my walking papers today. _ They are closing down my department. I guess I’ll get my walking papers soon.
examples: Well, I’m through.

one’s way of life.monolingual: one’s lifestyle; one’s pattern of living. _ That kind of thing just doesn’t fit into my way of life. _Our way of life includes contributing to worthy causes.
examples: That kind of thing just doesn’t fit into my way of life.

one’s word is one’s bond.monolingual: Fig. one’s statement of agreement is as sound as a posting of a performance bond. _ Of course, you can trust anything I agree to verbally. My word is my bond. There’s no need to get it in writing.
examples: Of course, you can trust anything I agree to verbally.

the one that got away.monolingual: Fig. the big fish that got away, especially as the subject of a fisherman’s story. _ The one that got away is always bigger than the one that got caught.
examples: The one that got away is always bigger than the one that got caught.

one thing leads to another..monolingual: One event sets things up for another event, and so on. (As an explanation of how little things lead to big problems.) _I kept spending more and more money until I was broke. You know how one thing leads to another. _ He bought a car, then a house, th
examples: I kept spending more and more money until I was broke.

one to a customer.monolingual: Fig. each person can have or receive only one. (As in sales restrictions where each customer is permitted to buy only one.) _ “Only one to a customer!” said the chef as he handed out the hamburgers. _ Is it one to a customer, or can I take two now?
examples: “Only one to a customer!” said the chef as he handed out the hamburgers.

one too many.monolingual: Euph. one drink of liquor too many, implying drunkenness. _I think I’ve had one too many. It’s time to stop drinking. _ Don’t drive if you’ve had one too many.
examples: I think I’ve had one too many.

one way or another.monolingual: somehow. _ Tom: Can we fix this radio, or do I have to buy a new one? Mary: Don’t fret! We’ll get it repaired one way or another. _John: I think we’re lost. Alice: Don’t worry. We’ll get there one way or another.
examples: Tom: Can we fix this radio, or do I have to buy a new one? Mary: Don’t fret! We’ll get it repaired one way or another.

one-horse town.monolingual: Fig. a very small town; a small and backward town. _ I refuse to spend a whole week in that onehorse town! _ I grew up in a one-horse town, and I liked it very much.
examples: I grew up in a one-horse town, and I liked it very much.

one-man show.monolingual: 1. Lit. a performance put on by one person. _ It was a one-man show, but it was very entertaining. _For a one-man show, it was very long.
examples: It was a one-man show, but it was very entertaining.

one-night stand.monolingual: 1. Lit. a performance lasting only one night. _ The band did a series of one-night stands down the East Coast. _ You can’t make a living doing one-night stands.
examples: The band did a series of one-night stands down the East Coast.

one-track mind.monolingual: Fig. a mind that thinks entirely or almost entirely about one subject. _ Adolescent boys often have one-track minds. All they’re interested in is the opposite sex. _ Bob has a one-track mind. He can only talk about football.
examples: Adolescent boys often have one-track minds.

online.monolingual: Fig. connected to a computer or network. _ As soon as I get online, I can check the balance of your account. _ I was online for an hour before I found out what I wanted to know.
examples: As soon as I get online, I can check the balance of your account.

only have eyes for someone.monolingual: Fig. [to be] loyal to only one person, in the context of romance. _Oh, Jane! I only have eyes for you! _ Don’t waste any time on Tom. He only has eyes for Ann.
examples: Don’t waste any time on Tom.

the only way to go.monolingual: the best way to do something; the best choice to make. _ Get a four-wheel drive car. It’s the only way to go. _ That’s it! A new house. It’s the only way to go.
examples: Get a four-wheel drive car.

*onto a good thing.monolingual: having found something useful, promising, or profitable. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ This is a great scheme. I know I’m onto a good thing. _I’m onto a good thing. I’m sure I am.
examples: This is a great scheme.

ooze with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to flow or seep with something; to be covered with some oozing substance. _ The wound oozed with blood. _The roast beef oozed with juices.
examples: The wound oozed with blood.

open a conversation.monolingual: to start a conversation. _ I tried to open a conversation with him, but he had nothing to say. _ She opened a conversation with an inquiry into my health, which got me talking about my favorite subject.
examples: I tried to open a conversation with him, but he had nothing to say.

open for business.monolingual: [of a shop, store, restaurant, etc.] operating and ready to do business. _ The store is now open for business and invites you to come in. _ The construction will be finished in March, and we will be open for business in April.
examples: The store is now open for business and invites you to come in.

open into something.monolingual: to open inward to something. _The passageway opened into a dining room. _Our kitchen opens into a bright breakfast nook.
examples: The passageway opened into a dining room.

*an open mind.monolingual: a mind or attitude that is open to new ideas and opinions. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; keep ~.) _ Please try to be nice and keep an open mind. It’s all not as bad as you think.
examples: Please try to be nice and keep an open mind.

open oneself to criticism.monolingual: to do something that makes one vulnerable to criticism. _By saying something so stupid in public, you really opened yourself to criticism.
examples: By saying something so stupid in public, you really opened yourself to criticism.

open pandora’s box.monolingual: Fig. to uncover a lot of unsuspected problems. _When I asked Jane about her problems, I didn’t know I had opened Pandora’s box. _You should be cautious with people who are upset. You don’t want to open Pandora’s box.
examples: When I asked Jane about her problems, I didn’t know I had opened Pandora’s box.

an open secret.monolingual: something that is supposed to be known only by a few people but is known in fact to a great many people. _ Their engagement is an open secret. Only their friends are supposed to know, but in fact, the whole town knows. _ It’s an open secret that Max
examples: Their engagement is an open secret.

open someone up†.monolingual: Fig. to perform a surgical operation requiring a major incision on someone. _The doctor had to open George up to find out what was wrong. _ They opened up George, seeking the cause of his illness.
examples: The doctor had to open George up to find out what was wrong.

open something out†.monolingual: to unfold or expand something; to open and spread something out. _ When she opened the fan out, she saw it was made of plastic. _ The peacock opened out its tail feathers and delighted the children.
examples: When she opened the fan out, she saw it was made of plastic.

open something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to unwrap something; to open something. _Yes, I want to open my presents up. _I can’t wait to open up my presents. _ Open up this door!
examples: Yes, I want to open my presents up.

open the door to someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to permit someone to enter a room, building, etc. _ The butler opened the door to the guests and they all entered. _ I opened the door to Mr. Wilson.
examples: The butler opened the door to the guests and they all entered.

open the door to something.monolingual: Fig. to invite something to happen. _The armistice opened the door to peace talks. _ The door was opened to further discussion.
examples: The armistice opened the door to peace talks.

open to criticism.monolingual: vulnerable to criticism. _Anything the president does is open to criticism.
examples: Anything the president does is open to criticism.

open to question.monolingual: [an action or opinion] inviting question, examination, or refutation. _Everything he told you is open to question and you should look into it.
examples: Everything he told you is open to question and you should look into it.

open to something.monolingual: Fig. agreeable to hear or learn about new ideas and suggestions. _The store owner was open to suggestions from her employees. _We are always open to new ideas.
examples: The store owner was open to suggestions from her employees.

open up.monolingual: 1. Lit. open your door; open your mouth. (Usually Open up!) _ I want in. Open up! _ Open up! This is the police.
examples: Open up! This is the police.

open up to something.monolingual: to become more accepting of someone or something. _ Finally, he opened up to the suggestion that he should leave. _ Finally the boss opened up to the notion of Tom as a manager.
examples: Finally, he opened up to the suggestion that he should leave.

open with someone or something.monolingual: to begin a season, session, series, or performance with someone or something. _The conference will open with a series of invited speakers. _The performance opened with Donna, who played the f lute.
examples: The conference will open with a series of invited speakers.

an open-and-shut case.monolingual: a simple and straightforward situation without complications. (Often said of criminal cases where the evidence is convincing.) _ The murder trial was an open-and-shut case. The defendant was caught with the murder weapon. _ Bob’s death was an open-an
examples: The murder trial was an open-and-shut case.

opening gambit.monolingual: Fig. an opening movement, tactic, or statement which is made to secure a position that is to one’s advantage. _ The rebel army’s opening gambit was to bomb the city’s business district. _ The prosecution’s opening gambit was to call a witness who lin
examples: The rebel army’s opening gambit was to bomb the city’s business district.

operate against someone or something.monolingual: to work against someone or something; to have a negative effect on someone or something. _ All of this operates against our idea of fixing the garage up as a family room. _ The new vacation policy operates against my plan to take all of July off.
examples: All of this operates against our idea of fixing the garage up as a family room.

operate from something.monolingual: to work out of something or some place. _I’m in business for myself. I operate from my home. _ We operate from a garage in the back of City Hall.
examples: I’m in business for myself.

operate on someone.monolingual: to perform a surgical operation on someone. _ They decided not to operate on her. _ She wasn’t operated on after all.
examples: They decided not to operate on her.

operate on something.monolingual: 1. to work on something; to work with the insides of something. (As a surgeon might operate.) _ He tried to operate on his watch and ruined it. _ Todd operated on the door lock and fixed it.
examples: He tried to operate on his watch and ruined it.

opportunity knocks but once..monolingual: Prov. You will only have one chance to do something important or profitable. (You can say opportunity knocks to signal that someone’s chance to do something important is here right now.) _ When Nancy got a scholarship offer from a college far away, h
examples: When Nancy got a scholarship offer from a college far away, her parents encouraged her to go, even though they didn’t like the thought of her moving so far from home.

opportunity makes a thief..monolingual: Prov. Anyone would steal, given a chance to do so without being punished. _ Mr. Cooper thought of himself as a moral man. But opportunity makes a thief, and with the safe unguarded he had the opportunity to steal thousands of dollars undetected.
examples: Mr. Cooper thought of himself as a moral man.

opposed to something.monolingual: in opposition to something. _I am strongly opposed to your suggestion. _ He is morally opposed to war.
examples: I am strongly opposed to your suggestion.

the opposite sex.monolingual: the other sex; (from the point of view of a female) males; (from the point of view of a male) females. (Also with member of, as in the example.) _Ann is crazy about the opposite sex. _ Bill is very shy when he’s introduced to the opposite sex. _ Do m
examples: Ann is crazy about the opposite sex.

opt for something.monolingual: to choose a particular option. _ I opted for the orange one. _ I opt for not going out at all.
examples: I opted for the orange one.

or else.monolingual: or suffer the consequences. (An inspecific threat of bad consequences.) _ Do what I tell you, or else. _ Don’t be late for work, or else!
examples: Do what I tell you, or else.

or what?.monolingual: a way of adding emphasis to a yes-or-no question the speaker has asked. (In effect, if it wasn’t what I said, what is it?) _ Bob: Now, is this a fine day or what? John: Looks okay to me. _ Tom: Look at Bill and Mary. Do they make a fine couple or wha
examples: Bob: Now, is this a fine day or what? John: Looks okay to me.

or words to that effect.monolingual: Fig. or similar words meaning the same thing. _ John: It says right here in the contract, “You are expected to attend without fail,” or words to that effect. Mary: That means I have to be there, huh? John: You got it! _ Sally: She said that I wasn’t
examples: John: It says right here in the contract, “You are expected to attend without fail,” or words to that effect.

the order of the day.monolingual: something necessary or usual at a certain time. _Warm clothes are the order of the day when camping in the winter. _ Going to bed early was the order of the day when we were young.
examples: Warm clothes are the order of the day when camping in the winter.

order someone off the field.monolingual: [for a game official] to command a player to leave the playing area. _The referee will order you off the field. _ He ordered us off the field.
examples: The referee will order you off the field.

order something in†.monolingual: to have something, usually food, brought into one’s house or place of business. _ Do you want to order pizza in? _ Shall I order in pizza?

orient someone to something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to help someone locate a compass direction or other similar location. _Try to orient Karen to the light so I can photograph her. _ It took time, but I oriented myself to north at last.
examples: Try to orient Karen to the light so I can photograph her.

originate from something.monolingual: to come from something or some place. _ Did you originate from around here? _ I originated from a different area of the country. _ Some of our customs originate from old beliefs.
examples: I originated from a different area of the country.

originate in something.monolingual: to have had a beginning in something or some place. _ The river originates in the Andes Mountains. _ All your troubles originate in your lungs.
examples: The river originates in the Andes Mountains.

originate with someone or something.monolingual: to have been started by someone, something, or during a time period or event. _Did this policy originate with you? _This idea originated with the committee.
examples: This idea originated with the committee.

ornament something with something.monolingual: to decorate something with something. _The driver ornamented his truck with lots of chrome. _The room was ornamented with velvet drapes, wood paneling, family portraits—a den of Victorian virtue.
examples: The driver ornamented his truck with lots of chrome.

the other place.monolingual: Euph. hell. _ If you’re good, you’ll go to heaven, and if you’re bad, you’ll go to the other place. _ If she keeps up her drinking and gambling, she’s headed to the other place for sure.
examples: If you’re good, you’ll go to heaven, and if you’re bad, you’ll go to the other place.

other times, other manners..monolingual: Prov. Different generations or eras have different customs. _ Amy thought her grandchildren addressed their friends in startlingly rude terms. “But then,” she ref lected, “other times, other manners.” _ Jane: The young folks today are so shocking. Wh
examples: Amy thought her grandchildren addressed their friends in startlingly rude terms.

oust someone from something.monolingual: to force someone to leave something or some place; to throw someone out of something or some place. _ They ousted the boys from the bar. _ The underage kids were ousted from the tavern quickly.
examples: They ousted the boys from the bar.

*out and about.monolingual: outside the house; outdoors. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _Beth has been ill, but now she’s out and about. _ As soon as I feel better, I’ll be able to get out and about.
examples: Beth has been ill, but now she’s out and about.

out at some place.monolingual: located at a distant place. _ Tom’s out at the farm and there’s no phone there, so you can’t talk to him. _ Jed is out at the cabin on a hunting trip.
examples: Tom’s out at the farm and there’s no phone there, so you can’t talk to him.

out for blood.monolingual: Fig. aggressively seeking to harm or get revenge; angry and looking for the cause of one’s distress. _ The opposite team is out for blood, but we have a good defense.
examples: The opposite team is out for blood, but we have a good defense.

*out from something.monolingual: some distance away from something. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; go ~.) _ I would like to be farther out from the city. _I need to get out from the town.
examples: I would like to be farther out from the city.

out front.monolingual: 1. in the front of one’s house. _ Our mailbox is out front. _ We have a spruce tree out front and a maple tree in the back.
examples: Our mailbox is out front.

*out in force.monolingual: Fig. appearing in great strength. (*Typically: be ~; come ~; go ~. See also out in large numbers.) _ What a night! The mosquitoes are out in force. _ The police went out in force over the holiday weekend.
examples: What a night! The mosquitoes are out in force.

out in left field.monolingual: Fig. offbeat; unusual and eccentric. _ Sally is a lot of fun, but she’s sort of out in left field. _ What a strange idea. It’s really out in left field.
examples: Sally is a lot of fun, but she’s sort of out in left field.

*out in the cold.monolingual: 1. Lit. outdoors where it is cold. (*Typically: be ~; keep someone or some creature ~; leave someone or some creature ~; put someone or some creature ~.) _ Open the door! Let me in! Don’t keep me out in the cold! _ Who left the dog out in the cold al
examples: Who left the dog out in the cold all night? 2.

*out in the open.monolingual: 1. Lit. visible in an open space; exposed in an open area. (*Typically: be ~; bring something ~; come ~; get ~; get something ~.) _ The trucks are out in the open where we can see them. _They came out in the open.
examples: The trucks are out in the open where we can see them.

out of action.monolingual: not operating temporarily; not functioning normally. _ The pitcher was out of action for a month because of an injury. _ I will be out of action for a while.
examples: The pitcher was out of action for a month because of an injury.

out of character.monolingual: 1. unlike one’s usual behavior. _Ann’s remark was quite out of character. _ It was out of character for Ann to act so stubborn.
examples: Ann’s remark was quite out of character.

out of circulation.monolingual: 1. Lit. no longer available for use or lending. (Usually said of library materials, certain kinds of currency, etc.) _I’m sorry, but the book you want is temporarily out of circulation. _How long will it be out of circulation?
examples: I’m sorry, but the book you want is temporarily out of circulation.

out of commission.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a ship] to be not currently in use or under command. _ This vessel will remain out of commission for another month. _ The ship has been out of commission since repairs began.
examples: This vessel will remain out of commission for another month.

*out of context.monolingual: [of an utterance or the report of an action] removed from the surrounding context of the event, thereby misrepresenting the intent of the utterance or report. (*Typically: be ~; lift something ~; quote someone or something ~; take something ~.) _ You

*out of debt.monolingual: no longer owing a debt. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; get oneself ~.) _ I’ve taken a second job so I can get myself out of debt.
examples: I’ve taken a second job so I can get myself out of debt.

out of earshot.monolingual: Fig. too far from the source of a sound to hear the sound. _ I was out of earshot and could not hear the conversation. _ Mary waited until her children were out of earshot before mentioning the presents she got them.
examples: I was out of earshot and could not hear the conversation.

*out of focus.monolingual: blurred or fuzzy; seen indistinctly. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; go ~.) _ What I saw through the binoculars was sort of out of focus. _ The scene was out of focus.
examples: What I saw through the binoculars was sort of out of focus.

*out of gas.monolingual: 1. Lit. without gasoline (in a car, truck, etc.). (*Typically: be ~; run ~.) _ We can’t go any farther. We’re out of gas. _ This car will be completely out of gas in a few more miles.
examples: We can’t go any farther.
