*out of harm’s way.monolingual: Fig. not liable to be harmed; away from any causes of harm. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; get someone ~.) _We should try to get all the civilians out of harm’s way.
examples: We should try to get all the civilians out of harm’s way.

out of hock.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of something] bought back from a pawn shop. _ When I get my watch out of hock, I will always be on time.
examples: When I get my watch out of hock, I will always be on time.

out of it.monolingual: Fig. not alert; giddy; uninformed. _Bill is really out of it. Why can’t he pay attention? _Don’t be out of it, John. Wake up! _ Ann is really out to lunch these days.
examples: Bill is really out of it.

out of left field.monolingual: suddenly; from an unexpected source or direction. _ Most of your ideas are out of left field. _All of his paintings are right out of left field.
examples: Most of your ideas are out of left field.

out of luck.monolingual: without good luck; having bad fortune. _ If you wanted some ice cream, you’re out of luck. _ I was out of luck. I got there too late to get a seat.
examples: If you wanted some ice cream, you’re out of luck.

out of necessity.monolingual: because of necessity; due to need. _ I bought this hat out of necessity. I needed one, and this was all there was. _ We sold our car out of necessity.
examples: I bought this hat out of necessity.

*out of nowhere.monolingual: appearing suddenly, without warning. (*Typically: appear ~; come ~; materialize ~.) _ A huge bear appeared out of nowhere and roared and threatened us. _Suddenly, a truck came out of nowhere. _Without warning, the storm came out of nowhere.
examples: A huge bear appeared out of nowhere and roared and threatened us.

*out of one’s depth.monolingual: Fig. involved in something that is beyond one’s capabilities. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ You know, you are really out of your depth in this project. _ I am sure I am out of my depth in organic chemistry.
examples: You know, you are really out of your depth in this project.

*out of one’s element.monolingual: Fig. not in a natural or comfortable situation. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ When it comes to computers, I’m out of my element. _Sally’s out of her element in math.
examples: When it comes to computers, I’m out of my element.

*out of one’s skull.monolingual: Sl. intoxicated. (*Typically: be ~; go ~.) _ Oh, man, I drank till I was out of my skull. _ Two beers and he went out of his skull.
examples: Oh, man, I drank till I was out of my skull.

out of order.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of something or things] out of the proper sequence. _ She noticed that the books on the shelf were out of order. _ All these cards were alphabetized, and now they’re out of order.
examples: She noticed that the books on the shelf were out of order.

*out of patience.monolingual: annoyed and impatient after being patient for a while. (*Typically: be ~; run ~.) _ I finally ran out of patience and lost my temper. _ The boss is finally out of patience with me.
examples: I finally ran out of patience and lost my temper.

*out of place.monolingual: 1. Lit. not in the proper place. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; knock something ~.) _ The book I wanted was out of place, and I almost did not find it. _How did the furniture in this room get out of place?
examples: The book I wanted was out of place, and I almost did not find it.

*out of practice.monolingual: performing poorly due to a lack of practice. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; go ~.) _ I used to be able to play the piano extremely well, but now I’m out of practice. _ The baseball players lost the game because they were out of practice.
examples: I used to be able to play the piano extremely well, but now I’m out of practice.

out of print.monolingual: [for a book] to be no longer available from the publisher. _ The book you want just went out of print, but perhaps I can find a used copy for you. _ It was published nearly ten years ago, so it’s probably out of print.
examples: The book you want just went out of print, but perhaps I can find a used copy for you.

out of reach.monolingual: 1. Lit. not near enough to be reached or touched. _ Place the cookies out of reach, or the children will eat them all. _The mouse ran behind the piano, out of reach. The cat just sat and waited for it.
examples: Place the cookies out of reach, or the children will eat them all.

out of season.monolingual: 1. not now available for sale. _Sorry, oysters are out of season. We don’t have any. _ Watermelon is out of season in the winter.
examples: Sorry, oysters are out of season.

out of service.monolingual: inoperable; not currently operating. _ Both elevators had been put out of service, so I had to use the stairs. _ The washroom is temporarily out of service.
examples: Both elevators had been put out of service, so I had to use the stairs.

*out of sight.monolingual: 1. not visible; too far away to be seen. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; go ~; keep ~; stay ~.) _The cat kept out of sight until the mouse came out. _ “Get out of sight, or they’ll see you!” called John.
examples: The cat kept out of sight until the mouse came out.

*out of someone’s hands.monolingual: 1. Lit. no longer in someone’s grasp. (*Typically: get ~; pull something ~; take something ~.) _ The police officer took the gun out of Fred’s hands. _ The heavy tray was pulled out of my hands just in time.
examples: The police officer took the gun out of Fred’s hands.

*out of sorts.monolingual: not feeling well; grumpy and irritable. (*Typically: be ~; feel ~; get ~.) _ I’ve been out of sorts for a day or two. I think I’m coming down with something. _The baby is out of sorts. Maybe she’s getting a new tooth.
examples: I’ve been out of sorts for a day or two.

out of spite.monolingual: with the desire to harm someone or something. _ Jane told some evil gossip about Bill out of spite. _ That was not an accident! You did it out of spite.
examples: Jane told some evil gossip about Bill out of spite.

out of stock.monolingual: not immediately available in a store; [for goods] to be temporarily unavailable. _ Those items are out of stock, but a new supply will be delivered on Thursday. _ I’m sorry, but the red ones are out of stock. Would a blue one do?
examples: Those items are out of stock, but a new supply will be delivered on Thursday.

*out of sync.monolingual: uncoordinated; unsynchronized. (An abbreviation for synchronization. *Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ Our efforts are out of sync. _ My watch and your watch are out of sync.
examples: Our efforts are out of sync.

out of the ballpark.monolingual: Fig. beyond the amount of money suggested or available. _Your estimate is completely out of the ballpark. Just forget it.
examples: Your estimate is completely out of the ballpark.

*out of the closet.monolingual: 1. Fig. revealing one’s secret interests. (*Typically: be ~; come ~; get ~.) _ Tom Brown came out of the closet and admitted that he likes to knit. _ It’s time that all of you lovers of chamber music came out of the closet and attended our concerts.
examples: Tom Brown came out of the closet and admitted that he likes to knit.

out of the hole.monolingual: Fig. out of debt. _ I get paid next week, and then I can get out of the hole. _ I can’t seem to get out of the hole. I keep spending more money than I earn.
examples: I get paid next week, and then I can get out of the hole.

out of the ordinary.monolingual: unusual. _ It was a good meal, but not out of the ordinary. _ Your report was nicely done, but nothing out of the ordinary.
examples: It was a good meal, but not out of the ordinary.

out of the picture.monolingual: Fig. no longer relevant to a situation; departed; dead. _ Now that Tom is out of the picture, we needn’t concern ourselves about his objections. _ With her husband out of the picture, she can begin living as she pleases.
examples: Now that Tom is out of the picture, we needn’t concern ourselves about his objections.

out of the question.monolingual: Fig. not allowed; not permitted. _ I’m sorry, but your taking my car is out of the question. _ You can’t go to Florida this spring. We can’t afford it. It’s out of the question.
examples: I’m sorry, but your taking my car is out of the question.

out of the red.monolingual: Fig. out of debt; into profitability. _ This year our company is likely to get out of the red before fall. _If we can cut down on expenses, we can get out of the red fairly soon.
examples: This year our company is likely to get out of the red before fall.

out of the running.monolingual: Fig. no longer being considered; eliminated from a contest. _ After the first part of the diving meet, three members of our team were out of the running. _ After the scandal was made public, I was out of the running. I pulled out of the election.
examples: After the first part of the diving meet, three members of our team were out of the running.

out of the woods.monolingual: Fig. past a critical phase; out of the unknown. _When the patient got out of the woods, everyone relaxed. _ I can give you a better prediction for your future health when you are out of the woods.
examples: When the patient got out of the woods, everyone relaxed.

*out of the woodwork.monolingual: Fig. out into the open from other places or a place of concealment. (*Typically: bring someone or something ~; come ~; creep ~.) _ When the cake appeared, all the office people suddenly came out of the woodwork.
examples: When the cake appeared, all the office people suddenly came out of the woodwork.

out of thin air.monolingual: Fig. out of nowhere; out of nothing. _ Suddenly—out of thin air—the messenger appeared. _You just made that excuse up out of thin air.
examples: Suddenly—out of thin air—the messenger appeared.

out of this world.monolingual: 1. Fig. wonderful and exciting. _This pie is out of this world. _ My boyfriend is just out of this world.
examples: This pie is out of this world.

out of town.monolingual: temporarily not in one’s own town. _ I’ll go out of town next week. I’m going to be at a conference. _ I take care of Mary’s cat when she’s out of town.
examples: I’ll go out of town next week.

out of turn.monolingual: not at the proper time; not in the proper or expected order. _ We were permitted to be served out of turn because we had to leave early. _ Bill tried to register out of turn and was sent away.
examples: We were permitted to be served out of turn because we had to leave early.

out of work.monolingual: unemployed; having lost one’s job. _ Todd was out of work for almost a year. _ Too many people were out of work, and the economy got into trouble.
examples: Todd was out of work for almost a year.

*out on a limb.monolingual: 1. Lit. out on a limb of a tree where it is dangerous. (*Typically: be ~; go ~.) _It’s okay to climb the tree, but don’t go out on a limb and fall off.
examples: It’s okay to climb the tree, but don’t go out on a limb and fall off.

out on bail.monolingual: out of jail after a court appearance and pending trial because bail bond money has been paid. (The money will be forfeited if the person who is out on bail does not appear for trial at the proper time.) _ Bob got out on bail waiting for his trial. _
examples: Bob got out on bail waiting for his trial.

out on the town.monolingual: Fig. celebrating at one or more places in a town. _ I’m really tired. I was out on the town until dawn. _We went out on the town to celebrate our wedding anniversary.
examples: I’m really tired.

out, please..monolingual: Please let me get out. (Said by someone trying to get out of an elevator. Compare this with Coming through(, please).) _ The elevator stopped again, and someone at the back said, “Out, please.” _Jane: Out, please. This is my f loor. John: I’ll get ou
examples: The elevator stopped again, and someone at the back said, “Out, please.

out to get someone.monolingual: Fig. intending to harm someone in particular. _ I know they are out to get me! They hate me!

out to win.monolingual: determined to win. _ Bobby is out to win at all costs! He can’t face losing.
examples: Bobby is out to win at all costs! He can’t face losing.

out west.monolingual: in the western part of the United States. _ We lived out West for nearly ten years. _ Do they really ride horses out West?
examples: We lived out West for nearly ten years.

out-of-pocket expenses.monolingual: Fig. the actual amount of money spent. (Alludes to the money one person pays while doing something on someone else’s behalf. One is usually paid back this money.) _My out-of-pocket expenses for the party were nearly $175. _My employer usually reimbur
examples: My out-of-pocket expenses for the party were nearly $175.

outside of something.monolingual: except for something; besides something. _ Outside of the cost of my laundry, I have practically no expenses. _Outside of some new shoes, I don’t need any new clothing.
examples: Outside of the cost of my laundry, I have practically no expenses.

*over a barrel.monolingual: Fig. out of one’s control; in a dilemma. (*Typically: get someone ~; have someone ~; put someone ~.) _ He got me over a barrel, and I had to do what he said. _ Ann will do exactly what I say. I’ve got her over a barrel.
examples: He got me over a barrel, and I had to do what he said.

over and above something.monolingual: Fig. more than something; in addition to something. _ I’ll need another twenty dollars over and above the amount you have already given me. _ You’ve been eating too much food over and above what is required for good nutrition. That’s why you’re gaini
examples: I’ll need another twenty dollars over and above the amount you have already given me.

over and out..monolingual: I am finished talking. (From two-way radio communications.) _That’s all. Good day. Over and out.
examples: That’s all. Good day.

over easy.monolingual: Fig. [of eggs] turned carefully during cooking. _ I want mine cooked over easy. _ Over easy eggs are better than scrambled.
examples: I want mine cooked over easy.

over my dead body!.monolingual: Inf. Fig. a defiant phrase indicating the strength of one’s opposition to something. (A joking response is “That can be arranged.”) _Sally: Alice says she’ll join the circus no matter what anybody says. Father: Over my dead body! Sally: Now, now. You
examples: Sally: Alice says she’ll join the circus no matter what anybody says.

over the counter.monolingual: Fig. [of medication bought or sold] without a prescription. (Hyphenated when prenominal. See also under the counter.) _ This is a good product. You can buy it over the counter. _I don’t put much trust in over-the-counter medications.
examples: This is a good product.

over the edge.monolingual: Fig. excessive; out of control. _ His performance was over the edge. Too long, too dirty, and too loud!
examples: His performance was over the edge.

*over the hill.monolingual: 1. Fig. Inf. escaped from prison or the military. (*Typically: be ~; go ~.) _ Two privates went over the hill last night. _ They broke out of jail and went over the hill.
examples: Two privates went over the hill last night.

over the hump.monolingual: 1. Fig. over the hard part; past the midpoint. _ Things should be easy from now on. We finally got over the hump. _ When you get over the hump, life is much better.
examples: Things should be easy from now on.

over the top.monolingual: 1. Fig. having gained more than one’s goal. _Our fund-raising campaign went over the top by $3,000. _We didn’t go over the top. We didn’t even get half of what we set out to collect.
examples: Our fund-raising campaign went over the top by $3,000.

*over the wall.monolingual: reaching freedom from a prison. (*Typically: be ~; go ~.) _ Max tried to go over the wall, but they caught him. _Lefty was over the wall for a week before that caught him.
examples: Max tried to go over the wall, but they caught him.

overflow into something.monolingual: to spill over into something. _ The river overf lowed into the surrounding farmland. _The water in the bowl overf lowed into the sink.
examples: The river overf lowed into the surrounding farmland.

overflow with someone or something.monolingual: to have so much or so many people or things that they spill over. _ The kitchen overf lowed with the guests. _ My cup overf lowed with coffee and spilled on the counter.
examples: The kitchen overf lowed with the guests.

owing to.monolingual: because of something; due to the fact of something. _ Owing to the lateness of the evening, I must go home. _ We were late owing to the heavy traffic.
examples: Owing to the lateness of the evening, I must go home.

own up to someone.monolingual: to confess or admit something to someone. _ Finally, he owned up to his mother about breaking the vase. _ We had hoped he would own up to us sooner.
examples: Finally, he owned up to his mother about breaking the vase.

pace something off†.monolingual: to mark off a distance by counting the number of even strides taken while walking. _The farmer paced a few yards off and pounded a stake into the soil. _ He paced off a few yards.
examples: The farmer paced a few yards off and pounded a stake into the soil.

pace something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to measure a distance by counting the number of even strides taken while walking. _He paced the distance out and wrote it down. _ He paced out the distance from the door to the mailbox.
examples: He paced the distance out and wrote it down.

pack down.monolingual: [for something] to settle down in a container. _ The cereal has packed down in the box so that it seems that the box is only half full. _Everything was packed down carefully inside.
examples: The cereal has packed down in the box so that it seems that the box is only half full.

pack it in.monolingual: 1. Fig. to quit trying to do something; to give up trying something and quit. _ I was so distressed that I almost packed it in. _ I’ve had enough! I’m going to pack it in.
examples: I was so distressed that I almost packed it in.

a pack of lies.monolingual: a series of lies. _ The thief told a pack of lies to cover up the crime. _ John listened to Bill’s pack of lies about the fight and became very angry.
examples: The thief told a pack of lies to cover up the crime.

pack someone or something together†.monolingual: to press or squeeze people or things together. _ The ushers packed the people together as much as they dared. _They packed together all the people standing in the room. _ They packed the cups together too tightly and some broke.
examples: The ushers packed the people together as much as they dared.

pack something away†.monolingual: to pack something up and put it away. _ Pack this mirror away where it will be safe. _ Please pack away this mirror carefully.
examples: Pack this mirror away where it will be safe.

pack something down†.monolingual: to make something more compact; to press something in a container down so it takes less space. _The traffic packed down the snow. _Pack the grass down in the basket so the basket will hold more.
examples: The traffic packed down the snow.

pack something in something.monolingual: to surround or enclose something in something. _ They packed his wounded hand in ice, then took him to the hospital. _Pack the vase in shredded paper before you close the box.
examples: They packed his wounded hand in ice, then took him to the hospital.

pack them in.monolingual: Fig. to draw a lot of people. _It was a good night at the theater. The play really packed them in. _ The circus manager knew he could pack them in if he advertised the lion tamer.
examples: It was a good night at the theater.

pack up.monolingual: to prepare one’s belongings to be transported by placing them into a container; to gather one’s things together for one’s departure. _ If we are going to leave in the morning, we should pack up now. _ I think you should pack up and be ready to leave
examples: If we are going to leave in the morning, we should pack up now.

a package deal.monolingual: Fig. a collection or group of related goods or services sold as a unit. _ I got all these tools in a package deal for only $39.95. _ What about giving me all three shirts as a package deal?
examples: I got all these tools in a package deal for only $39.

pad out.monolingual: Sl. to go to bed or to sleep. _ Man, if I don’t pad out by midnight, I’m a zombie. _ Why don’t you people go home so I can pad out?
examples: Man, if I don’t pad out by midnight, I’m a zombie.

pad something out†.monolingual: Fig. to make something appear to be larger or longer by adding unnecessary material. _ If we pad the costume out here, it will make the person who wears it look much plumper. _ Let’s pad out this paragraph a little.
examples: If we pad the costume out here, it will make the person who wears it look much plumper.

pad the bill.monolingual: Fig. to put unnecessary or additional items on a bill to make the total cost higher. _The plumber had padded the bill with things we didn’t need. _ I was falsely accused of padding the bill.
examples: The plumber had padded the bill with things we didn’t need.

paddle one’s own canoe.monolingual: Fig. to do something by oneself; to be alone. _ I’ve been left to paddle my own canoe too many times. _Sally isn’t with us. She’s off paddling her own canoe.
examples: I’ve been left to paddle my own canoe too many times.

a pain in the neck.monolingual: Fig. a bother; an annoyance. _ This assignment is a pain in the neck. _ Your little brother is a pain in the neck.
examples: This assignment is a pain in the neck.

paint on something.monolingual: to apply paint to the surface of something. _ He painted on the fence a while and then went inside to rest. _ Please don’t paint on the area that is not sanded down.
examples: He painted on the fence a while and then went inside to rest.

paint over something.monolingual: to cover something up with a layer of paint. _Sam painted over the rusty part of the fence. _ The work crew was told to paint over the graffiti.
examples: Sam painted over the rusty part of the fence.

paint something in†.monolingual: to paint something extra onto a painted area. _ I know that there is supposed to be a big white spot here. We will have to paint it in. _We will have to paint in the spot.
examples: I know that there is supposed to be a big white spot here.

paint something out†.monolingual: to cover something up or obliterate something by applying a layer of paint. _ The worker painted the graffiti out. _ They had to paint out the graffiti.
examples: The worker painted the graffiti out.

pair off.monolingual: [for two people or other creatures] to form a couple or pair. _ All of them paired off and worked as teams to solve the puzzle. _ Everyone should pair off and discuss the issue for a while.
examples: All of them paired off and worked as teams to solve the puzzle.

pale at something.monolingual: to become weak, frightened, or pale from fear of something or the thought of something. _ Bob paled at the thought of having to drive all the way back to get the forgotten suitcase. _We paled at the notion that we would always be poor.
examples: Bob paled at the thought of having to drive all the way back to get the forgotten suitcase.

pale beside someone or something.monolingual: Fig. to appear to be weak or unimportant when compared to someone or something. _ He is competent, but he pales beside Fran. _ My meager effort pales beside your masterpiece.
examples: He is competent, but he pales beside Fran.

pan for something.monolingual: to search for a precious metal, usually gold, by using a pan to locate the bits of metal in sand and gravel in a stream bed. _ When I was in Alaska, I panned for gold in a little stream set aside for tourists. _ The old prospector spent many hours pa
examples: When I was in Alaska, I panned for gold in a little stream set aside for tourists.

pan over someone or something.monolingual: to turn or rotate a film or television camera so that the picture moves across a view of someone or something. _ The camera panned over the skyline, picking up interesting cloud formations. _ It panned over Roger as if he weren’t there—which is exact
examples: The camera panned over the skyline, picking up interesting cloud formations.

pander to someone or something.monolingual: to cater toward undesirable tastes or people with undesirable tastes. _ All your writing seems to pander to persons with poor taste. _ You are pandering to the moral dregs of society.
examples: All your writing seems to pander to persons with poor taste.

panic at something.monolingual: to lose control in a frightening or shocking situation. _ Try not to panic at what you see. It will be a shock. _ Don’t panic at the price of food. It will be worse next week.
examples: Try not to panic at what you see.

panic someone by something.monolingual: to make someone lose control by doing something. _ She panicked Denise by describing the event too vividly. _ She panicked her horse by jerking the reins too tightly.
examples: She panicked Denise by describing the event too vividly.

pant for air.monolingual: to breathe fast and hard in need of air. _The dog was panting for air. _ I was panting for air after my long climb.
examples: The dog was panting for air.

pant for someone or something.monolingual: Fig. to desire or long for someone or something. _ My heart is panting for you! _ I am just panting for some interesting news.
examples: I am just panting for some interesting news.

pant something out†.monolingual: to tell something while panting for breath. _Laura had been running but she was able to pant the name of the injured person out. _ She panted out the name.
examples: Laura had been running but she was able to pant the name of the injured person out.

paper over something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to put a layer of wallpaper on a wall. _We papered over the wall, giving the room a bright, new look. _ We papered over the old plaster on the wall.
examples: We papered over the wall, giving the room a bright, new look.

*a paper trail.monolingual: Fig. a series of records that is possible to examine to find out the sequence of things that happen. (*Typically: have ~; leave ~; make ~.) _The legal department requires all these forms so that there is a paper trail of all activity.
examples: The legal department requires all these forms so that there is a paper trail of all activity.

par for the course.monolingual: typical; about what one could expect. (This refers to golf courses, not school courses.) _ So he went off and left you? Well that’s about par for the course. He’s no friend. _ I worked for days on this proposal, but it was rejected. That’s par for th
examples: So he went off and left you? Well that’s about par for the course.

parcel someone or something out†.monolingual: Fig. to divide up and send or give away people or things. _Carla parceled all the uniforms out so everyone would have one to wear for the parade. _ We will parcel out the children for the summer.
examples: Carla parceled all the uniforms out so everyone would have one to wear for the parade.

parcel something up†.monolingual: to wrap something up in a package. _Would you parcel the papers up and set them in the corner? _ Parcel up the files and place them on top of the file cabinet.
examples: Parcel up the files and place them on top of the file cabinet.

pardon me for living!.monolingual: Inf. a very indignant response to a criticism or rebuke. _ Fred: Oh, I thought you had already taken yourself out of here! Sue: Well, pardon me for living! _ Tom: Butt out, Mary! Bill and I are talking. Mary: Pardon me for living!
examples: Tom: Butt out, Mary! Bill and I are talking.

pardon someone for something.monolingual: 1. to excuse someone for doing something. _ Will you please pardon me for what I did? _ I can’t pardon her for that.
examples: I can’t pardon her for that.

parlay something into something.monolingual: Fig. to exploit an asset in such a way as to increase its value to some higher amount. _She is trying to parlay her temporary job into a full-time position. _ Alice parlayed her inheritance into a small fortune by investing in the stock market.
examples: She is trying to parlay her temporary job into a full-time position.

parley with someone.monolingual: Fig. to talk with someone. _ I need to parley with my brother before making a financial commitment. _ We need to parley with each other sometime soon.
examples: I need to parley with my brother before making a financial commitment.

part from someone.monolingual: to leave someone. _I just hate parting from you. _ I must part from her now.
examples: I just hate parting from you.

part over something.monolingual: [for people] to separate because of something. _ We had to part over our disagreement. _ They parted over a very small matter.
examples: We had to part over our disagreement.

part someone’s hair.monolingual: 1. Lit. to divide someone’s hair into separate sections while combing it. _The barber asked me where I parted my hair.
examples: The barber asked me where I parted my hair.

part with someone or something.monolingual: to give up or let go of someone or something. _ She did not want to part with her friend. _ I could never part with my books.
examples: She did not want to part with her friend.

partake in something.monolingual: to participate in something. _ Valerie does not care to partake in those childish games. _ I would like to partake in the fun.
examples: Valerie does not care to partake in those childish games.

partake of something.monolingual: 1. to have a portion of something, such as food or drink. _Would you care to partake of this apple pie with me? _ I would like to partake of that fine dinner I see set out on the table.
examples: I would like to partake of that fine dinner I see set out on the table.

*partial to someone or something.monolingual: favoring or preferring someone or something. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ The boys think their teacher is partial to female students. _ I am partial to vanilla ice cream.
examples: The boys think their teacher is partial to female students.

partially sighted.monolingual: Euph. not able to see well. _ Carrie is partially sighted, but she is not able to see well enough to read. _ I am not blind. I am partially sighted.
examples: Carrie is partially sighted, but she is not able to see well enough to read.

the particulars of something.monolingual: specific details about something. _ My boss stressed the important particulars of the project. _ What are the particulars of your request?
examples: My boss stressed the important particulars of the project.

a parting of the ways.monolingual: a point at which people separate and go their own ways. (Often with come to a, arrive at a, reach a, etc.) _ Jane and Bob finally came to a parting of the ways. _ Bill and his parents reached a parting of the ways.
examples: Jane and Bob finally came to a parting of the ways.

partition something into something.monolingual: to divide or separate something into something [smaller]. _I will partition this room into two separate spaces. _Do you think you can partition this box into four compartments so we can store files by quarter?
examples: I will partition this room into two separate spaces.

partition something off†.monolingual: to divide off a section of something. _ They planned to partition the basement off. _ We will partition off a larger area.
examples: They planned to partition the basement off.

partners in crime.monolingual: 1. Fig. persons who cooperate in committing a crime or a deception. (Usually an exaggeration.) _The sales manager and the used-car salesmen are nothing but partners in crime.
examples: The sales manager and the used-car salesmen are nothing but partners in crime.

the party line.monolingual: Fig. the official ideas and attitudes that are adopted by the leaders of a particular group and that the other members are expected to accept. _ Tom has left the club. He refused to follow the party line. _Many politicians agree with the party line w
examples: Tom has left the club.

the party’s over..monolingual: Fig. A happy or fortunate time has come to an end. _ We go back to school tomorrow. The party’s over. _ The staff hardly worked at all under the old management, but they’ll find the party’s over now.
examples: We go back to school tomorrow.

a party to something.monolingual: a participant in something; someone who is involved in something. _ I refuse to be a party to your dishonest plan!

pass as someone or something.monolingual: to succeed in being accepted as someone or something. _ The spy was able to pass as a regular citizen. _ The thief was arrested when he tried to pass as a priest.
examples: The spy was able to pass as a regular citizen.

pass for someone or something.monolingual: to be accepted as someone, some type of person, or something. _ You could pass for your twin brother. _This painting could almost pass for the original.
examples: You could pass for your twin brother.

pass for something.monolingual: to pay for something; to treat someone by paying for something. _Come on. Let’s go out. I’ll pass for dinner. _ I’ll pass for drinks if you want.
examples: Come on. Let’s go out.

pass from something.monolingual: to fade away from something; to go away gradually. _ The larger trees had passed from the scene years ago. _ The exact details passed from Harry’s memory some time ago.
examples: The larger trees had passed from the scene years ago.

pass gas.monolingual: Euph. to release intestinal gas through the anus. _ Someone on the bus had passed gas. It smelled awful. _ Something I ate at lunch made me pass gas all afternoon.
examples: Someone on the bus had passed gas.

pass in review.monolingual: [for marchers] to move past an important person for a visual examination. _ All the soldiers passed in review on the Fourth of July. _ As they passed in review, each of them saluted the officers on the reviewing stand.
examples: All the soldiers passed in review on the Fourth of July.

pass into something.monolingual: to move into something; to fade away into something. _ Thoughts about the accident, little by little, passed into oblivion. _All her old school chums passed into oblivion.
examples: Thoughts about the accident, little by little, passed into oblivion.

pass muster.monolingual: Fig. to measure up to the required standards. _ I tried, but my efforts didn’t pass muster. _ If you don’t wear a jacket and tie, you won’t pass muster at that fancy restaurant. They won’t let you in.
examples: I tried, but my efforts didn’t pass muster.

pass on someone or something.monolingual: to accept or approve someone or something. _ She refused to pass on Ted, so he will not be appointed. _The committee passed on the proposal, so work can now begin.
examples: She refused to pass on Ted, so he will not be appointed.

pass out.monolingual: to faint; to lose consciousness. _ Oh, look! Tom has passed out. _ When he got the news, he passed out.
examples: Oh, look! Tom has passed out.

pass sentence on someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a judge] to read out the sentence of punishment for a convicted criminal. _It is my job as judge to pass sentence on you. _The judge was about to pass sentence on Max—ten years in prison.
examples: It is my job as judge to pass sentence on you.

pass someone or something by†.monolingual: to miss someone or something; to overlook someone or something. _ The storm passed by the town leaving it unharmed. _ The teacher passed me by and chose the next person in line.
examples: The storm passed by the town leaving it unharmed.

pass someone or something up†.monolingual: 1. to fail to select someone or something. _ The committee passed Jill up and chose Kelly. _ They passed up Jill.
examples: The committee passed Jill up and chose Kelly.

pass something forward.monolingual: to send something toward the front of a group of people. (Each person hands it to the next.) _ Please pass this forward to the front of the room. _ Would you pass this book forward, please?
examples: Please pass this forward to the front of the room.

pass something on†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to hand or give something (to another person). _ Have a piece of toffee and pass the box on. _Please pass on this book to the next person on the list.
examples: Have a piece of toffee and pass the box on.

pass something to someone.monolingual: to hand or send something to someone, usually by way of a number of other people. _ Please pass this paper to Betty. _ Who passed this to me?
examples: Please pass this paper to Betty.

pass the buck.monolingual: Fig. to pass the blame (to someone else); to give the responsibility (to someone else). _ Don’t try to pass the buck! It’s your fault, and everybody knows it. _ Some people try to pass the buck whenever they can.
examples: Don’t try to pass the buck! It’s your fault, and everybody knows it.

pass through someone.monolingual: to be digested through the bowels of someone. _ This fruit should pass through you in no time at all. _ He will be better when the offending food passes through him.
examples: This fruit should pass through you in no time at all.

pass through something.monolingual: to travel through something or some place. _ I passed through the countryside and breathed the good clean air. _ Perhaps I will stop and visit Joe the next time I pass through Adamsville.
examples: I passed through the countryside and breathed the good clean air.

pass under something.monolingual: to move or travel beneath something. _The ship slowly passed under the bridge. _Harry counted the cars as they passed under the bridge.
examples: The ship slowly passed under the bridge.

passport to something.monolingual: Fig. something that allows something good to happen. _ John’s new girlfriend is his passport to happiness. _ Anne’s new job is a passport to financial security.
examples: John’s new girlfriend is his passport to happiness.

past caring.monolingual: Fig. [of someone] beyond caring about someone or something that is hopeless. _I don’t care what you do! I’m past caring!

*a past master at something.monolingual: Fig. someone proven extremely good or skillful at an activity. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ Mary is a past master at cooking omelets. _ Pam is a past master at the art of complaining.
examples: Mary is a past master at cooking omelets.

past someone’s or something’s prime.monolingual: Fig. beyond the most useful or productive period. _ Joan was a wonderful singer, but she’s past her prime now. _ This old car’s past its prime. I’ll need to get a new one.
examples: Joan was a wonderful singer, but she’s past her prime now.

paste someone one.monolingual: Sl. to land a blow on someone. _ I pasted him one right on the nose. _ Next time you do that, I’ll paste you one!
examples: I pasted him one right on the nose.

paste something down†.monolingual: to secure something down [onto something] with paste or glue. _The poster will look better if you will paste the loose edges down. _ Please paste down the edges.
examples: The poster will look better if you will paste the loose edges down.

paste something on someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to affix something to someone with paste or glue. _We had to paste a mustache on her for the last scene of the play. _ They pasted beards on themselves too.
examples: We had to paste a mustache on her for the last scene of the play.

paste something up†.monolingual: 1. to repair something with paste. _ See if you can paste this book up so it will hold together. _ Paste up the book and hope it holds together for a while.
examples: See if you can paste this book up so it will hold together.

a pat answer.monolingual: a quick, easy answer; a simplified or evasive answer. _Don’t just give them a pat answer. Give some more explanation and justification. Otherwise you will just end up answering a lot more questions.
examples: Don’t just give them a pat answer.

pat something down†.monolingual: to tap something down with the open hand. _ I heaped some soil over the seeds and patted it down. _ I patted down the soil.
examples: I heaped some soil over the seeds and patted it down.

patch a quarrel up†.monolingual: Fig. to put an end to a quarrel; to reconcile quarreling parties. _ Tom and Fred were able to patch their quarrel up. _I hope we can patch up this quarrel.
examples: Tom and Fred were able to patch their quarrel up.

patch someone up†.monolingual: to give medical care to someone. _ That cut looks bad, but the doc over there can patch you up. _ The doc patched up my friend.
examples: That cut looks bad, but the doc over there can patch you up.

patch something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to repair something in a hurry; to make something temporarily serviceable again. _Can you patch this up so I can use it again? _ I’ll patch up the hose for you.
examples: I’ll patch up the hose for you.

the path of least resistance.monolingual: Fig. the easiest course to follow; the easiest route. (Often with follow the or take the.) _John will follow the path of least resistance. _I like challenges. I won’t usually take the path of least resistance.
examples: John will follow the path of least resistance.

patience is a virtue..monolingual: Prov. It is good to be patient. _ Jill: I wish Mary would hurry up and call me back! Jane: Patience is a virtue. _Fred: The doctor has kept us waiting for half an hour! If he doesn’t call us into his office pretty soon, I may do something violent. El
examples: Jill: I wish Mary would hurry up and call me back! Jane: Patience is a virtue.

*patient as job.monolingual: very patient. (Alludes to the biblical figure Job. *Also: as ~.) _ If you want to teach young children, you must be as patient as Job. _ The director who is working with that temperamental actor must have the patience of Job.
examples: If you want to teach young children, you must be as patient as Job.

the patter of tiny feet.monolingual: the sound of young children; having children in the household. _ I really liked having the patter of tiny feet in the house. _ Darling, I think we’re going to be hearing the patter of tiny feet soon.
examples: I really liked having the patter of tiny feet in the house.

pattern something after something.monolingual: to use something as an example or model when making something. _I patterned my house after one I saw in England. _ She wanted to pattern her coat after her mother’s.
examples: I patterned my house after one I saw in England.

pattern something on something.monolingual: to use something as a model for something else. _ Try to pattern your sales speech on Jane’s. She’s got it just right. _ We patterned our approach on Bob’s.
examples: Try to pattern your sales speech on Jane’s.

pay a call.monolingual: Euph. to go to the toilet; to leave to go to the toilet. _ Excuse me. I have to pay a call. _ Tom left to pay a call. He should be back soon.
examples: Excuse me. I have to pay a call.

pay a call on someone.monolingual: to visit someone. _ Grandmother always paid us a call on Sundays. _Let’s pay a call on Mary at the hospital.
examples: Grandmother always paid us a call on Sundays.

pay as you go.monolingual: to pay costs as they occur; to pay for goods as they are bought (rather than charging them). _ You ought to pay as you go. Then you won’t be in debt. _ If you pay as you go, you’ll never spend too much money.
examples: You ought to pay as you go.

pay by something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to use something as a medium of payment. _ Will you pay by cash or check? _ The bill was paid by check.
examples: The bill was paid by check.

pay court to someone.monolingual: Fig. to solicit someone’s attention; to woo someone. _ The lawyer was thought to be paying court to too many politicians. _ The lobbyist paid court to all the inf luential members of Congress.
examples: The lawyer was thought to be paying court to too many politicians.

pay for something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to pay out money for something. _ Did you pay for the magazine, or shall I? _ No, I’ll pay for it.
examples: No, I’ll pay for it.

pay heed to someone.monolingual: to listen to and accommodate someone. _ You had better pay heed to your father! _ They are not paying heed to what I told them.
examples: They are not paying heed to what I told them.

pay in advance.monolingual: to pay (for something) before it is received or delivered. _I want to make a special order. Will I have to pay in advance? _ Yes, please pay in advance.
examples: I want to make a special order.

pay into something.monolingual: to pay money into an account. _ I intend to pay into my vacation account until I have enough for a nice vacation. _We paid a lot into our savings account this month.
examples: I intend to pay into my vacation account until I have enough for a nice vacation.

pay off.monolingual: to yield profits; to result in benefits. _ My investment in those stocks has really paid off. _ The time I spent in school paid off in later years.
examples: My investment in those stocks has really paid off.

pay on something.monolingual: to make a payment against a bill. _ You have to pay on this every month or we will repossess it. _ How much do you plan to pay on the car per month?
examples: You have to pay on this every month or we will repossess it.

pay one’s dues.monolingual: 1. Lit. to pay the fees required to belong to an organization. _ If you haven’t paid your dues, you can’t come to the club picnic. _How many people have paid their dues?
examples: If you haven’t paid your dues, you can’t come to the club picnic.

pay one’s own way.monolingual: to pay for one’s own transportation, entrance fees, tickets, room, board, etc. _ I wanted to go to Florida this spring, but my parents say I have to pay my own way.
examples: I wanted to go to Florida this spring, but my parents say I have to pay my own way.

pay someone a compliment.monolingual: Fig. to give someone a compliment. _ Tom paid Bill a compliment when he told him he was intelligent. _ Mary was very gracious when Anne paid her a compliment.
examples: Tom paid Bill a compliment when he told him he was intelligent.

pay someone back†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to return money that was borrowed from a person. _You owe me money. When are you going to pay me back? _ You must pay John back. You have owed him money for a long time. _ You have to pay back everyone you owe money to.
examples: You owe me money.

pay someone off†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to pay what is owed to a person. _ I can’t pay you off until Wednesday when I get my paycheck. _ I have to use this money to pay off Sarah.
examples: I can’t pay you off until Wednesday when I get my paycheck.

pay someone respect.monolingual: to honor someone; to have and show respect for someone. _ You really should pay your boss more respect. _We have to pay our parents a lot of respect.
examples: You really should pay your boss more respect.

pay someone’s way.monolingual: to pay the costs (of something) for a person. _My aunt is going to pay my way to Florida—only if I take her with me!

pay something down†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to make a deposit of money on a purchase. _You will have to pay a lot of money down on a car that expensive. _I only paid down a few thousand dollars.
examples: You will have to pay a lot of money down on a car that expensive.

pay something off†.monolingual: to pay all of a debt; to pay the final payment for something bought on credit. _ This month I’ll pay the car off. _ Did you pay off the gas bill yet?
examples: This month I’ll pay the car off.

pay something out†.monolingual: to unravel or unwind wire or rope as it is needed. _ One worker paid the cable out, and another worker guided it into the conduit. _ The worker paid out the cable.
examples: One worker paid the cable out, and another worker guided it into the conduit.

pay something up†.monolingual: to pay all of whatever is due; to complete all the payments on something. _ Would you pay up your bills, please? _ Your dues are all paid up.
examples: Your dues are all paid up.

pay the penalty.monolingual: 1. Lit. to pay a fine for doing something wrong. _ You ran the red light and now you will have to pay the penalty.
examples: You ran the red light and now you will have to pay the penalty.

pay the piper.monolingual: Fig. to face the results of one’s actions; to receive punishment for something. _You can put off paying your debts only so long. Eventually you’ll have to pay the piper. _ You can’t get away with that forever. You’ll have to pay the piper someday.
examples: You can put off paying your debts only so long.

pay the price.monolingual: 1. Lit. to pay the price that is asked for goods or services. (Usually implying that the price is high.) _If this is the quality of goods that you require, you will have to pay the price.
examples: If this is the quality of goods that you require, you will have to pay the price.

pay through something.monolingual: to make payment through an intermediary, such as a bank. _ I will pay the bill through my bank in New York. _ Sam had to pay through his brokerage account.
examples: I will pay the bill through my bank in New York.

pay to do something.monolingual: to be beneficial to do something; to be profitable. _It doesn’t pay to drive downtown when you can take the train. _ It pays to take an umbrella with you if it’s supposed to rain.
examples: It doesn’t pay to drive downtown when you can take the train.

pay up.monolingual: to pay what is owed. (Often a command: Pay up!) _ I want my money now. Pay up! _ If you don’t pay up, I’ll take you to court.
examples: I want my money now.

peace of mind.monolingual: Fig. a tranquility that results from not having worries, guilt, or problems. _If peace of mind is more important to you than earning a lot of money, maybe you should consider teaching.
examples: If peace of mind is more important to you than earning a lot of money, maybe you should consider teaching.

peal out.monolingual: [for bells or voices] to sound forth musically. _ The bells pealed out to announce that the wedding had taken place. _ All six of the bells seemed to peal out at once.
examples: The bells pealed out to announce that the wedding had taken place.

peck at something.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a bird] to poke someone or something with its beak. _The bird pecked at the ground, snatching up the ants. _ I tried to hold on to the bird but it pecked at me hard.
examples: The bird pecked at the ground, snatching up the ants.

peck something up†.monolingual: [for a bird] to eat something up by pecking at it. _The chickens pecked all the grain up. _The birds pecked up the grain.
examples: The chickens pecked all the grain up.

peek at someone or something.monolingual: to sneak a glimpse at someone or something. _ Now, don’t peek at me while I am changing my shirt. _ I peeked at the dessert you made. It looks delicious.
examples: Now, don’t peek at me while I am changing my shirt.

peek over something.monolingual: 1. to examine something with a quick glance. _ I really can’t say how good the story was. I only peeked over it. _I peeked over your manuscript, and it looks good.
examples: I really can’t say how good the story was.

peek under something.monolingual: to sneak a little glance beneath something. _ I peeked under the table, hoping to see the dog waiting there for the part of my dinner I wasn’t going to eat. _ Peek under the chair and see if the cat is there.
examples: I peeked under the table, hoping to see the dog waiting there for the part of my dinner I wasn’t going to eat.

peel out.monolingual: [for a driver] to speed off in a car with a screeching of tires. _ Dave got in his car and peeled out, waking the neighbors. _ I wish he would stop peeling out!
examples: Dave got in his car and peeled out, waking the neighbors.

*a peep.monolingual: a quick look at someone or something. (*Typically: have ~; take ~.) _ Have a peep into the refrigerator and see if we need any milk. _ I took a peep at the comet through the telescope.
examples: Have a peep into the refrigerator and see if we need any milk.

peep at someone or something.monolingual: to get a glimpse of someone or something, as if looking through a hole. _ I peeped at Tom through the venetian blinds. _Look in the microscope and peep at this bacterium.
examples: I peeped at Tom through the venetian blinds.

peep over something.monolingual: to raise up and sneak a glance over some barrier; to look over the top of something. _ The child peeped over the wall to get a look at the yard next door. _ Grandfather peeped over his glasses to look at the television set for a moment.
examples: The child peeped over the wall to get a look at the yard next door.

peep through something.monolingual: to take a quick glance through something, such as a hole, telescope, etc. _ Sam peeped through the keyhole and saw that the room was dark. _Peep through the telescope and have a look at the moon!
examples: Sam peeped through the keyhole and saw that the room was dark.

peep under something.monolingual: to take a quick little glance under something. _ Would you please peep under the table and see if my shoes are there? _ Dave peeped under the bed, looking for the cat.
examples: Dave peeped under the bed, looking for the cat.

peer about.monolingual: to stare around; to look at everything about. _She came into the room and peered about. _Mary peered about, looking for a place to sit.
examples: She came into the room and peered about.

peer at someone or something.monolingual: to look at someone or something closely; to stare at and examine someone or something. _The child peered at me for a while in a strange way. _ The owl peered at the snake for a moment before grabbing it.
examples: The child peered at me for a while in a strange way.

peer over something.monolingual: to stare out or look over something, such as one’s glasses. _The old man peered over his glasses and looked off into the distance. _She peered over the wall to see what she could see.
examples: The old man peered over his glasses and looked off into the distance.

peer through something.monolingual: 1. to view or look through glasses, spectacles, binoculars, etc. _ From the way she peered through her glasses at me, I knew I was in trouble. _ Claire stood on the balcony, peering through her binoculars.
examples: From the way she peered through her glasses at me, I knew I was in trouble.

peer under something.monolingual: to look underneath something. _ She peered under the bed, hoping to find her slippers. _ When she peered under the bed, she found nothing but lint.
examples: She peered under the bed, hoping to find her slippers.

peg out.monolingual: Sl. to die. _ I was so scared, I thought I would peg out for sure. _ Uncle Herman almost pegged out last week.
examples: I was so scared, I thought I would peg out for sure.

peg something down†.monolingual: to fasten something to the ground with pegs. _ After he had finished pegging the tent down, he built a fire. _ He pegged down the tent before building a fire.
examples: After he had finished pegging the tent down, he built a fire.

penalize someone for something.monolingual: to punish someone for something. _ It’s not fair to penalize her for being late. _ You needn’t penalize yourself for the failure. It wasn’t all your fault.
examples: It’s not fair to penalize her for being late.

pencil someone or something in†.monolingual: to write in something with a pencil. (Implies that the writing is not final.) _This isn’t a firm appointment yet, so I will just pencil it in. _ I penciled in a tentative answer.
examples: This isn’t a firm appointment yet, so I will just pencil it in.

penetrate into someone or something.monolingual: to pierce into someone or something; to stick deep into someone or something. _The lance penetrated into the knight, right through his armor. _ The bullet penetrated into the wall.
examples: The lance penetrated into the knight, right through his armor.

penetrate something with something.monolingual: to pierce something with something. _I could not even penetrate the steel door with a cold chisel. _ It was easy to penetrate the lid with a can opener.
examples: I could not even penetrate the steel door with a cold chisel.

penetrate through something.monolingual: to pierce all the way through something. (Some people will view the through as redundant.) _ The bullet could not penetrate through the metal plating. _ It did not have enough force to penetrate through the steel.
examples: The bullet could not penetrate through the metal plating.

a penny for your thoughts!.monolingual: Prov. What are you thinking about?; I would give you a penny if you tell me your thoughts. _ Noticing that Janet looked pensive, Bill said, “A penny for your thoughts!” _You seem very pleased with yourself today. A penny for your thoughts!
examples: You seem very pleased with yourself today.

penny-wise and pound-foolish.monolingual: Prov. thrifty with small sums and foolish with large sums. (Describes someone who will go to a lot of trouble to save a little money, but overlooks large expenses to save a little money. Even in the United States, the reference is to British pounds s
examples: Sam: If we drive to six different grocery stores, we’ll get the best bargains on everything we buy.

pension someone off†.monolingual: to retire someone with a pension. _ The company tried to pension me off before I was ready to retire. _ They pensioned off the long-time workers.
examples: The company tried to pension me off before I was ready to retire.

people something with someone.monolingual: to provide population for something or some place, using someone or some kind of people. _ The government decided to people the frontier with a variety of races. _The island had been peopled with marooned sailors.
examples: The government decided to people the frontier with a variety of races.

pep someone or something up†.monolingual: to make someone or something more vigorous. _Nancy needs to take some vitamins to pep her up. _The coffee break pepped up the tired workers. _ Better food might pep your cat up.
examples: Nancy needs to take some vitamins to pep her up.

perch on something.monolingual: 1. [for a bird] to stand at rest on something. _ A robin perched on the branch by my window. _ We saw a parrot perched on some kind of f lowering tree.
examples: A robin perched on the branch by my window.

percolate through something.monolingual: [for a liquid] to seep down through something. _ The water percolated through the coffee grounds too slowly for Fred, who was just dying for a hot cup of the stuff. _The water percolated through the subsoil and appeared again at the bottom of the hil
examples: The water percolated through the coffee grounds too slowly for Fred, who was just dying for a hot cup of the stuff.

perhaps a little later..monolingual: Not now, but possibly later. _ Waiter: Would you like your coffee now? Bob: Perhaps a little later. Waiter: All right. _ Sally: Hey, Bill, how about a swim? Bob: Sounds good, but not now. Perhaps a little later. Sally: Okay. See you later.
examples: Waiter: Would you like your coffee now? Bob: Perhaps a little later.

perish from something.monolingual: to die from a particular cause, such as a disease. _Nearly all the fish perished from the cold. _ I was afraid that I would perish from hunger.
examples: Nearly all the fish perished from the cold.

perish in something.monolingual: to die because of involvement in something. _Four people perished in the f lames. _Our cat perished in an accident.
examples: Four people perished in the f lames.

perish the thought..monolingual: Fig. Do not even consider thinking of such a (negative) thing. _ If you should become ill— perish the thought—I’d take care of you. _ I’m afraid that we need a new car. Perish the thought.
examples: If you should become ill— perish the thought—I’d take care of you.

perish with something.monolingual: to feel bad enough to die because of something, such as heat, hunger, etc. (Often an exaggeration.) _ I was just perishing with hunger when we arrived at the restaurant. _ Mary felt as if she would perish with the intense heat of the stuffy little ro
examples: I was just perishing with hunger when we arrived at the restaurant.

perk someone up†.monolingual: to make someone more cheery or refreshed. _ A nice cup of coffee would really perk me up. _ A cup of coffee will perk up the sleepiest person.
examples: A nice cup of coffee would really perk me up.

perk something up†.monolingual: to refresh or brighten something; to make something more lively. _ A bit of bright yellow here and there will perk this room up a lot. _We need something to perk up the second act of the play.
examples: A bit of bright yellow here and there will perk this room up a lot.

perk up.monolingual: to become invigorated; to become more active. _After a bit of water, the plants perked up nicely. _About noon, Andy perked up and looked wide-awake.
examples: After a bit of water, the plants perked up nicely.

permeate something with something.monolingual: to saturate something with something. _ The comedian permeated his act with smutty jokes. _ The evening air was permeated with the smell of jasmine.
examples: The comedian permeated his act with smutty jokes.

permeate through something.monolingual: to seep in and saturate something. _The coffee spilled on the desk and permeated through all the papers and stuff. _ The strong odor permeated through the walls and nearly suffocated us.
examples: The coffee spilled on the desk and permeated through all the papers and stuff.

permit someone up to something.monolingual: to allow someone to come up to something or some place. _ The teacher would not permit the smallest children up to the edge. _ They would not permit us up to the gate before our turn came.
examples: The teacher would not permit the smallest children up to the edge.

persecute someone for something.monolingual: to harass or repress someone for something. _ They were persecuting the native people for being underdeveloped. _ They were persecuted for being simple and unsuspecting.
examples: They were persecuting the native people for being underdeveloped.

persevere at something.monolingual: to keep trying to do something. _I will persevere at my studies and I’m sure I will succeed. _ Todd persevered at his job and got promoted in no time.
examples: I will persevere at my studies and I’m sure I will succeed.

persevere in something.monolingual: to persist in [doing] something. _I will persevere in my efforts to win election. _Kelly persevered in her studies and graduated with honors.
examples: I will persevere in my efforts to win election.

persevere with something.monolingual: to continue to try to accomplish something. _ Do you really think it is wise to persevere with your plan? _ Sally persevered with her scheme to earn a million dollars.
examples: Sally persevered with her scheme to earn a million dollars.

persist in doing something.monolingual: to continue doing something. _ John persists in thinking that he’s always right. _ Tom persists in demanding that I agree to his terms.
examples: John persists in thinking that he’s always right.

persist with something.monolingual: to continue the state of something; to extend an action or state. _ Please do not persist with your demands that I agree to your terms. _ If you persist with this intrusion, I’m going to call the police.
examples: Please do not persist with your demands that I agree to your terms.

person of color.monolingual: a person of an African, Asian, or Native American race. (The plural is people of color.) _ The apartment manager clearly discriminated against people of color. He would only rent to whites. _ As a person of color, I felt threatened by the racist joke
examples: The apartment manager clearly discriminated against people of color.

*a perspective on something.monolingual: a way of looking at a situation and determining what is important. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; gain ~; give someone ~.) _The jury did not have a good perspective on the crime since some of the evidence had to be ignored. _ Studying history gives one
examples: The jury did not have a good perspective on the crime since some of the evidence had to be ignored.

persuade someone of something.monolingual: to convince someone of something. _Laura was unable to persuade me of the truth of her statement. _ We were all persuaded of the need for higher taxes.
examples: Laura was unable to persuade me of the truth of her statement.

persuade someone to do something.monolingual: to convince someone to do something. _ Are you sure I can’t persuade you to have another piece of cake? _Richard was easily persuaded to have another piece of his favorite cake.
examples: Richard was easily persuaded to have another piece of his favorite cake.

pertain to someone or something.monolingual: to relate to someone or something; to have something to do with someone or something. _ I don’t think that anything discussed in this meeting pertained to me. _ It really doesn’t pertain to the matter at hand.
examples: I don’t think that anything discussed in this meeting pertained to me.

pester someone into something.monolingual: to annoy someone into doing something. _We are trying to pester her into accepting the position. _ I don’t want to be pestered into losing my temper!
examples: We are trying to pester her into accepting the position.

pester someone out of something.monolingual: 1. to annoy someone out of doing something. _ Dave pestered Mary out of going away for the weekend. _ He pestered her out of leaving without him.
examples: Dave pestered Mary out of going away for the weekend.

pester someone with something.monolingual: to annoy someone with something. _Don’t pester me with your constant questions! _ I was pestered with phone call after phone call.
examples: I was pestered with phone call after phone call.

pet hate.monolingual: Fig. something that is disliked intensely and is a constant or repeated annoyance. _ My pet hate is being put on hold on the telephone. _ Another pet hate of mine is having to stand in line.
examples: My pet hate is being put on hold on the telephone.

pet peeve.monolingual: Fig. a frequent annoyance; one’s “favorite” or most often encountered annoyance. _ My pet peeve is someone who always comes into the theater after the show has started. _Drivers who don’t signal are John’s pet peeve.
examples: My pet peeve is someone who always comes into the theater after the show has started.

peter out.monolingual: [for something] to die or dwindle away; [for something] to become exhausted gradually. _ When the fire petered out, I went to bed. _My money finally petered out, and I had to come home.
examples: When the fire petered out, I went to bed.

phone someone up†.monolingual: to call someone on the telephone. _ I don’t know what he will do. I will phone him up and ask him. _ Phone up your brother and ask his advice.
examples: I don’t know what he will do.

physician, heal thyself..monolingual: Prov. Do not rebuke someone for a fault or problem you have yourself. (Biblical.) _ Ellen: You’re such a spendthrift. You should go on a strict budget. Fred: But you manage money even worse than I do! Physician, heal thyself. _ Jane: You look like yo
examples: Ellen: You’re such a spendthrift.

pick a lock.monolingual: to open a lock without using a key. _The robber picked the lock with a nail file. _ The thief picked the lock on the safe and stole the money.
examples: The robber picked the lock with a nail file.

pick and choose.monolingual: to choose very carefully from a number of possibilities; to be selective. _ You must take what you are given. You cannot pick and choose. _ Meg is so beautiful. She can pick and choose from a whole range of boyfriends.
examples: You must take what you are given.

pick at someone or something.monolingual: to be very critical of someone or something; to pick on someone or something. _Why are you always picking at me? _The critics picked at the little things, missing the serious problems.
examples: The critics picked at the little things, missing the serious problems.

pick at something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to try to pull away bits of something. _ Don’t pick at the bookbinding. It will fall apart.
examples: Don’t pick at the bookbinding.

the pick of something.monolingual: the best of the group. _ This playful puppy is the pick of the whole lot. _ These potatoes are the pick of the crop.
examples: This playful puppy is the pick of the whole lot.

pick on someone or something.monolingual: to harass or bother someone or something, usually unfairly. _ Please stop picking on me! I’m tired of it. _ You shouldn’t pick on the cat.
examples: Please stop picking on me! I’m tired of it.

pick someone or something apart†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to pick at and pull someone or something to pieces. _ The vultures attacked the hunger-weakened man and tried to pick him apart. _ They tried to pick apart the body. _ Harry picked his piece of cake apart, looking to get all the nuts out.
examples: The vultures attacked the hunger-weakened man and tried to pick him apart.

pick someone or something off†.monolingual: Fig. to kill someone or something with a carefully aimed gunshot. _ The hunter picked the deer off with great skill. _The killer tried to pick off the police officer.
examples: The hunter picked the deer off with great skill.

pick someone up†.monolingual: 1. to attempt to become acquainted with someone for romantic or sexual purposes. _Who are you anyway? Are you trying to pick me up? _No, I never picked up anybody in my life!
examples: No, I never picked up anybody in my life! 2.

pick something away†.monolingual: to pull or pinch something loose from something. _ Mary picked the meat away from the bones. _ He picked away the burrs.
examples: Mary picked the meat away from the bones.

pick something over†.monolingual: Fig. to look through something carefully, looking for something special. _ The shoppers who got here first picked everything over, and there is not much left. _ They picked over all the merchandise.
examples: The shoppers who got here first picked everything over, and there is not much left.

pick something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to lift up or raise something from a lower place. _ Please help me pick this stuff up off the pavement. _ Pick up every bit of it!
examples: Please help me pick this stuff up off the pavement.

pick up.monolingual: 1. to tidy up. _ When you finish playing, you have to pick up. _ Please pick up after yourself.
examples: When you finish playing, you have to pick up.

pick up on something.monolingual: to become alert to something; to take notice of something; to learn or catch on to something. _ She’s real sharp. She picks up on everything. _ The cop picked up on the car with the expired license plates.
examples: She’s real sharp.

pick up speed.monolingual: to increase speed. _ The train began to pick up speed as it went downhill. _The car picked up speed as we moved into the left lane.
examples: The train began to pick up speed as it went downhill.

pick up the pace.monolingual: to speed up the tempo; to increase the rate that something is being done. _We are going to have to pick up the pace of activity around here if we are to get the job done.
examples: We are going to have to pick up the pace of activity around here if we are to get the job done.

picked over.monolingual: rejected; worn, dirty, or undesirable. _ This merchandise looks worn and picked over. I don’t want any of it. _ Everything in the store is picked over by the end of the month.
examples: This merchandise looks worn and picked over.

picture perfect.monolingual: Fig. looking exactly correct or right. (Hyphenated as a modifier.) _At last, everything was picture perfect. _ Nothing less than a picture-perfect party table will do.
examples: At last, everything was picture perfect.

picture someone in something.monolingual: 1. to form a mental picture of someone wearing something. _ I can just picture Tony in that baseball uniform. _ Can you picture yourself in a dress like this?
examples: I can just picture Tony in that baseball uniform.

piddle around.monolingual: Fig. to waste time doing little or nothing. _ Stop piddling around and get busy. _ I’m not piddling around. I am experimenting.
examples: Stop piddling around and get busy.

piddle something away†.monolingual: Fig. to waste away money or a period of time. _Please don’t piddle all your money away. _ Jane piddled away most of the day.
examples: Please don’t piddle all your money away.

pie in the sky.monolingual: 1. Fig. a future reward after death, considered as a replacement for a reward not received on earth. _ Don’t hold out for pie in the sky. Get realistic. _ If he didn’t hope for some heavenly pie in the sky, he would probably be a real crook.
examples: Don’t hold out for pie in the sky.

piece of cake.monolingual: Fig. something easy to do. _ No problem. When you know what you’re doing, it’s a piece of cake. _ Glad to help. It was a piece of cake. _ Rescuing frightened cats is my specialty. Piece of cake!
examples: No problem. When you know what you’re doing, it’s a piece of cake.

piece something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to add patches or pieces to something to make it complete. _ There is not quite enough cloth to make a shirt, but I think I can piece it out with some scraps of a complementary color for the collar. _ We managed to piece out the material that
examples: There is not quite enough cloth to make a shirt, but I think I can piece it out with some scraps of a complementary color for the collar.

piece something together†.monolingual: to fit something together; to assemble the pieces of something, such as a puzzle or something puzzling, and make sense of it. _ The police were unable to piece the story together. _The detective tried to piece together the events leading up to the cr
examples: The police were unable to piece the story together.

pierce through something.monolingual: to poke through something; to penetrate something. _ He pierced through the meat with a fork and then put it in a spicy marinade. _Mary pierced the yarn through with the knitting needles.
examples: He pierced through the meat with a fork and then put it in a spicy marinade.

a piercing scream.monolingual: Fig. a very loud and shrill scream. _ Suddenly, there was a piercing scream from the next room. _ Bob heard Susan’s piercing scream and ran to help her.
examples: Suddenly, there was a piercing scream from the next room.

pile something up†.monolingual: 1. to crash or wreck something. _Drive carefully if you don’t want to pile the car up. _ The driver piled up the car against a tree.
examples: Drive carefully if you don’t want to pile the car up.

pile up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for things] to gather or accumulate. _The newspapers began to pile up after a few days. _ Work is really piling up around here.
examples: The newspapers began to pile up after a few days.

pilfer from someone or something.monolingual: to steal from someone or a group. _ The petty thief had pilfered from several merchants in town. _Someone has pilfered from the petty-cash drawer.
examples: The petty thief had pilfered from several merchants in town.

pin someone’s ears back†.monolingual: 1. Fig. to beat someone, especially about the head. _ Don’t talk to me like that or I will pin your ears back! _ Max wanted to pin back Lefty’s ears for making fun of him.
examples: Max wanted to pin back Lefty’s ears for making fun of him.

pin something back†.monolingual: to hold something back by pinning. _ I will pin the curtains back to let a little more light in. _ Jane pinned back the curtains.
examples: I will pin the curtains back to let a little more light in.

pin something on someone.monolingual: Fig. Inf. to blame something on someone; to frame someone for a crime; to make it appear that an innocent person has actually committed a crime. _ Don’t try to pin that crime on me! I didn’t do it. _The gang member tried to pin the crime on a rival g
examples: Don’t try to pin that crime on me! I didn’t do it.

pinch someone for something.monolingual: Sl. to arrest someone for something. _ The cops pinched Max for driving without a license. _ Max was pinched for speeding.
examples: The cops pinched Max for driving without a license.

pinch something back†.monolingual: to pinch off a bit of the top of a plant so it will branch and grow more fully. _ You should pinch this back so it will branch. _ Pinch back the new leaves at the top.
examples: You should pinch this back so it will branch.

pinch-hit for someone.monolingual: 1. Fig. to bat for someone else in a baseball game. _ Wally Wilson will pinch-hit for Gary Franklin. _Rodney Jones is pinch-hitting for Babe DiMaggio.
examples: Wally Wilson will pinch-hit for Gary Franklin.

pins and needles.monolingual: Fig. a tingling feeling in some part of one’s body, especially the arms and legs. _ I’ve got pins and needles in my legs. _ Mary gets pins and needles if she crosses her arms for long.
examples: I’ve got pins and needles in my legs.

pipe down.monolingual: to become quiet; to cease making noise; to shut up. (Especially as a rude command.) _ Pipe down! I’m trying to sleep. _ Come on! Pipe down and get back to work!
examples: Pipe down! I’m trying to sleep.

a pipe dream.monolingual: Fig. a wish or an idea that is impossible to achieve or carry out. (From the dreams or visions induced by the smoking of an opium pipe.) _ Going to the West Indies is a pipe dream. We’ll never have enough money. _ Your hopes of winning a lot of money
examples: Going to the West Indies is a pipe dream.

pipe something away†.monolingual: to conduct a liquid or a gas away through a pipe. _ We will have to pipe the excess water away. _ They piped away the water.
examples: We will have to pipe the excess water away.

piping hot.monolingual: [of food] extremely hot. _ On a cold day, I like to eat piping hot soup. _ Be careful! This coffee is piping hot!
examples: On a cold day, I like to eat piping hot soup.

piss someone off†.monolingual: Inf. to make someone angry. (Crude. Potentially offensive, even though it is widely used. Use with discretion.) _ She really pissed me off! _ That’s enough to piss off anybody.
examples: That’s enough to piss off anybody.

the pit of one’s stomach.monolingual: Fig. the middle of one’s stomach; the location of a “visceral response.” _I got a strange feeling in the pit of my stomach when they told me the bad news.
examples: I got a strange feeling in the pit of my stomach when they told me the bad news.

pitch a tent.monolingual: to erect a tent at a campsite. _ The campers pitched their tent in a clearing in the woods. _ I pitched my tent next to a large oak tree.
examples: The campers pitched their tent in a clearing in the woods.

pitch black.monolingual: very black; as black as pitch. _The hearse was pitch black. _ The bandit rode on a pitch black horse and wore black clothing.
examples: The hearse was pitch black.

pitch camp.monolingual: to set up or arrange a campsite. _We pitched camp near the stream. _ Two campers went ahead of us to pitch camp while it was still light.
examples: We pitched camp near the stream.

pitch dark.monolingual: very dark; as dark as pitch. _I couldn’t see anything outside because it was pitch dark. _ The room was pitch dark, and I couldn’t find the light switch!
examples: I couldn’t see anything outside because it was pitch dark.
