pitch forward.monolingual: to jerk or thrust forward. _ Suddenly the car pitched forward, jerking the passengers around. _ We pitched forward inside the car as we went over the bumpy road.
examples: Suddenly the car pitched forward, jerking the passengers around.

pitch something away†.monolingual: to toss or throw something away. _ He pitched the broken stick away, and looked around for something stronger. _ He pitched away the stick.
examples: He pitched the broken stick away, and looked around for something stronger.

pitch something out†.monolingual: to throw something away; to discard something. _This cottage cheese is so old, I’m going to pitch it out. _ They pitched out the bad food.
examples: This cottage cheese is so old, I’m going to pitch it out.

pivot on something.monolingual: to rotate on something; to spin around, centered on something. _This part spins around and pivots on this little red spot, which is what they call a jewel. _ If the lever will not pivot on the bar, it needs some lubrication.
examples: This part spins around and pivots on this little red spot, which is what they call a jewel.

place an order.monolingual: to submit an order. _My secretary placed an order for a new computer. _ I placed my order only yesterday.
examples: My secretary placed an order for a new computer.

place of business.monolingual: a place where business is done; a factory or office. _ Our place of business opens at 9:00 a.m. each day. _ You will have to come to our place of business to make a purchase.
examples: Our place of business opens at 9:00 a.

a place of concealment.monolingual: a hiding place. _ She brought her little safe out of a place of concealment where it had been for decades.
examples: She brought her little safe out of a place of concealment where it had been for decades.

place something aside†.monolingual: to set something aside or out of the way. _ Place this one aside and we’ll keep it for ourselves. _ Place aside some of the smaller ones for later.
examples: Place this one aside and we’ll keep it for ourselves.

place something at a premium.monolingual: to force up the value of something so that its price is higher. _ The rapid changes in the market placed all the medical stocks at a premium. _ The goods had been placed at a premium by the changing market conditions.
examples: The rapid changes in the market placed all the medical stocks at a premium.

place something back.monolingual: 1. to move something backwards. _Place this chair back a little. It is in the walkway. _Would you please place the boxes back so there is more room to get through?
examples: Place this chair back a little.

place something in something.monolingual: to put something inside something. _ Place the rabbit in the pen with the others. _ Please place your dishes in the sink when you finish.
examples: Place the rabbit in the pen with the others.

plan for someone.monolingual: to prepare enough [of something] for someone. _ Fred just called and said he can show up for dinner after all. Please plan for him. _Tony wasn’t planned for, and there is no place for him to sit.
examples: Fred just called and said he can show up for dinner after all.

plan for something.monolingual: 1. to prepare for something. _ I need to take some time and plan for my retirement. _ We carefully planned for almost every possibility.
examples: I need to take some time and plan for my retirement.

plan on someone.monolingual: to be ready for someone; to anticipate someone’s arrival. _Don’t plan on Sam. He has a cold and probably won’t come. _ We are planning on Ted and Bill.
examples: Don’t plan on Sam.

plan on something.monolingual: to prepare for something; to be ready for something; to anticipate something. _ If I were you, I would plan on a big crowd at your open house. _ This was not planned on.
examples: If I were you, I would plan on a big crowd at your open house.

plan something out†.monolingual: to make thorough plans for something. _ Let us sit down and plan our strategy out. _ We sat down and planned out our strategy.
examples: Let us sit down and plan our strategy out.

plane something away†.monolingual: to smooth off bumps or irregularities with a plane. _Please plane the bumps away so that the board is perfectly smooth. _ Sam planed away the bumps.
examples: Please plane the bumps away so that the board is perfectly smooth.

plane something down†.monolingual: to smooth something down with a plane; to remove some material from something with a plane. _ I will have to plane the door down before I hang it again. _ I planed down the edge of the door for you.
examples: I will have to plane the door down before I hang it again.

plane something off†.monolingual: to remove bumps, nicks, or scrapes by planing. _ Plane the rough places off so the surface will be as smooth as possible. _ Sam planed off the bumps.
examples: Plane the rough places off so the surface will be as smooth as possible.

plank over something.monolingual: to cover something over with planking. _ The county planked over the old bridge so bicyclists could use it.
examples: The county planked over the old bridge so bicyclists could use it.

plant something in something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to set out a plant in something; to sow seeds in something. _Are you going to plant tomatoes in these pots? _ What have you planted in the garden?
examples: What have you planted in the garden? 2.

plant something on someone.monolingual: 1. to hide incriminating evidence on a person for later discovery and use in prosecution. (Drugs. Allegedly a police practice used to entrap drug offenders.) _ The cops planted crack on Richard and then arrested him for carrying it. _ Don’t touch me!
examples: The cops planted crack on Richard and then arrested him for carrying it.

plaster one’s hair down†.monolingual: Fig. to use water, oil, or cream to dress the hair for combing. (The result looks plastered to the head.) _ Tony used some strange substance to plaster his hair down. _He plastered down his hair with something that smells good.
examples: Tony used some strange substance to plaster his hair down.

plaster over something.monolingual: to cover over something with plaster. _ I think that we will just plaster over the cracks in the wall.
examples: I think that we will just plaster over the cracks in the wall.

plaster something up†.monolingual: to close something up with plaster; to cover over holes or cracks in a wall with plaster. _ He plastered the cracks up and then painted over them. _ You have to plaster up the cracks.
examples: He plastered the cracks up and then painted over them.

plaster something with something.monolingual: to spread some substance onto something. _Jane plastered each slice of bread with butter and then heaped on a glob of jam. _ She plastered the wall with a thin coat of fine white plaster.
examples: Jane plastered each slice of bread with butter and then heaped on a glob of jam.

play a bit part.monolingual: to perform a small part in a play or a movie. _ She played a few bit parts in minor Broadway plays, and then got the lead in an exciting new musical.
examples: She played a few bit parts in minor Broadway plays, and then got the lead in an exciting new musical.

play a joke on someone.monolingual: to make a joke that tricks someone. _The children played a joke on their teacher. _I don’t like it when you play jokes on me.
examples: The children played a joke on their teacher.

play against someone or something.monolingual: to compete against someone or something in a team sport. _ We won’t be ready to play against the other team this weekend. _ We refuse to play against you until the field is in better condition.
examples: We won’t be ready to play against the other team this weekend.

play at something.monolingual: to pretend to be doing something. _You are not fixing the car, you are just playing at repair work! _ Stop playing at doing the dishes and get the job done.
examples: Stop playing at doing the dishes and get the job done.

play ball with someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to toss a ball back and forth with someone. _ Carla is out playing ball with the little kids. _ Will you play ball with us?
examples: Carla is out playing ball with the little kids.

play dead.monolingual: to pretend to be dead. _When the bear attacked me, I just dropped down and played dead.
examples: When the bear attacked me, I just dropped down and played dead.

play down to someone.monolingual: to condescend to one’s audience. _ Why are you playing down to the audience? They will walk out on you! _Don’t play down to the people who have paid their money to see you.
examples: Don’t play down to the people who have paid their money to see you.

play fair.monolingual: to do something by the rules; to play something in a fair and just manner. _John won’t play with Bill anymore because Bill doesn’t play fair. _ You moved the golf ball with your foot! That’s not playing fair!
examples: John won’t play with Bill anymore because Bill doesn’t play fair.

play first chair.monolingual: 1. to be the leader of a section of instruments in an orchestra or a band. (More literal than the following sense.) _Sally learned to play the violin so well that she now plays first chair in the orchestra. _ I’m going to practice my f lute so I can
examples: Sally learned to play the violin so well that she now plays first chair in the orchestra.

play footsie with someone.monolingual: 1. to get romantically or sexually involved with someone. (Refers literally to secretly pushing or rubbing feet with someone under the table.) _ Someone said that Ruth is playing footsie with Henry. _ Henry and Ruth are playing footsie with each othe
examples: Someone said that Ruth is playing footsie with Henry.

play for keeps.monolingual: to do things with permanent effect; to be serious in one’s actions. (From the game of marbles, where the winner actually keeps all the marbles won.) _ Are we playing for keeps or can we give everything back at the end of the game? _ We are playing fo
examples: We are playing for keeps, so be careful of what you do.

play for something.monolingual: 1. to gamble for something; to use something as the medium of exchange for gaming or gambling. _ Let’s just play for nickels, okay? _We will play for dollar bills.
examples: We will play for dollar bills.

play for time.monolingual: Fig. to stall; to act in such a way as to gain time. _ I’ll play for time while you sneak out the window. _ The lawyers for the defense were playing for time while they looked for a witness.
examples: I’ll play for time while you sneak out the window.

play freeze-out.monolingual: to open windows and doors, or turn down a thermostat, making someone cold. _ Wow, it’s cold in here! Who’s playing freeze-out? _Is someone trying to play freeze-out?

play hard to get.monolingual: Fig. to be coy, intentionally shy, and fickle. (Usually refers to someone of the opposite sex.) _ Why can’t we go out? Why do you play hard to get? _ Sally annoys all the boys because she plays hard to get.
examples: Sally annoys all the boys because she plays hard to get.

play hooky.monolingual: to fail to attend school or some other event. _ Why aren’t you in school? Are you playing hooky? _ I don’t have time for the sales meeting today, so I think I’ll just play hooky.
examples: I don’t have time for the sales meeting today, so I think I’ll just play hooky.

play in something.monolingual: 1. to play a musical instrument in some musical organization. _ I used to play in a band. _ I wanted to play in the orchestra but I wasn’t good enough.
examples: I used to play in a band.

play in the big leagues.monolingual: Fig. to be involved in something of large or important proportions. (Alludes to playing a professional sport at the highest level.) _ You had better shape up if you want to play in the big leagues. _ The conductor shouted at the oboist, “You’re playi
examples: You had better shape up if you want to play in the big leagues.

play innocent.monolingual: to pretend to be innocent and not concerned. _ There is no need to play innocent. I know you broke the lamp! _ John is playing innocent, and he knows more than he is telling us.
examples: There is no need to play innocent.

play into someone’s hands.monolingual: Fig. [for a person one is scheming against] to assist one in one’s scheming without realizing it. _ John is doing exactly what I hoped he would. He’s playing into my hands. _ John played into my hands by taking the cash he found in my desk. I caught
examples: John is doing exactly what I hoped he would.

play it cool.monolingual: 1. Inf. to do something while not revealing insecurities or incompetence; to act blasé. _ Play it cool, man. Look like you belong there. _If the boss walks in, just play it cool.
examples: Play it cool, man.

play it safe.monolingual: to be or act safe; to avoid taking a risk. _ You should play it safe and take your umbrella. _ If you have a cold or the f lu, play it safe and go to bed.
examples: You should play it safe and take your umbrella.

play like someone or something.monolingual: to pretend to be someone or a type of a person. _ Sam is playing like Mr. Watson, the teacher. _He is playing like a teacher and helping Mary with her homework.
examples: Sam is playing like Mr.

play on.monolingual: to continue to play. _ The band played on and the dance continued until the wee hours of the morning. _ We played on and on until the last guests left the party.
examples: The band played on and the dance continued until the wee hours of the morning.

play on someone’s heartstrings.monolingual: Fig. to attempt to get sympathy from someone. _ She is crying so she can play on your heartstrings and try to get you to take her home.
examples: She is crying so she can play on your heartstrings and try to get you to take her home.

play on something.monolingual: to have an effect on something; to manage something for a desired effect. (The on can be replaced by upon.) _ The clerk played on my sense of responsibility in trying to get me to buy the book. _ See if you can get her to confess by playing on her se
examples: The clerk played on my sense of responsibility in trying to get me to buy the book.

play one’s trump card.monolingual: 1. Lit. [in certain card games] to play a card that, according to the rules of the game, outranks certain other cards and is thus able to take any card of another suit. _Bob played his trump card and ended the game as the winner.
examples: Bob played his trump card and ended the game as the winner.

play out.monolingual: [for a process] to run out; to finish. _ The whole incident is about to play out. Then it all will be forgotten. _ When the event plays out, everything will return to normal.
examples: The whole incident is about to play out.

play politics.monolingual: 1. Lit. to negotiate politically. _ Everybody at city hall is playing politics as usual. _If you’re elected as a member of a political party, you’ll have to play politics.
examples: Everybody at city hall is playing politics as usual.

play possum.monolingual: Fig. to pretend to be inactive, unobservant, asleep, or dead. (The possum refers to an opossum.) _ I knew that Bob wasn’t asleep. He was just playing possum. _ I can’t tell if this animal is dead or just playing possum.
examples: I knew that Bob wasn’t asleep.

play someone against someone else.monolingual: to cause someone to dispute with someone else. _ Don tried to play George against David, but they figured out what he was up to. _ Alice never managed to play Tom against Fred.
examples: Don tried to play George against David, but they figured out what he was up to.

play someone for a fool.monolingual: Fig. to treat someone like a fool; to assume someone is naive or stupid. _ Don’t play me for a fool. I won’t have it. _ You are playing me for a fool! Stop it!
examples: Don’t play me for a fool.

play someone or something down†.monolingual: to lessen the effect or importance of someone or something. _John is a famous actor, but the director tried to play him down as just another member of the cast. _ Her lawyer tried to play down her earlier arrest.
examples: John is a famous actor, but the director tried to play him down as just another member of the cast.

play someone or something up†.monolingual: to make someone or something seem to be more important. _ The director tried to play Ann up, but she was not really a star. _ Try to play up the good qualities of our product.
examples: The director tried to play Ann up, but she was not really a star.

play something as something.monolingual: to deal with something as if it were something else. _ I will play this matter as a simple case of mistaken identity. _ We will play this lapse as an instance of forgetfulness and not make too much of it.
examples: I will play this matter as a simple case of mistaken identity.

play something off†.monolingual: to play a game to break a tied score. _ They decided not to play the tie off because it had grown so late. _ They went ahead and played off the tie after all.
examples: They decided not to play the tie off because it had grown so late.

play something out†.monolingual: 1. to play something, such as a game, to the very end. _ I was bored with the game, but I felt I had to play it out. _ She played out the rest of the game.
examples: I was bored with the game, but I felt I had to play it out.

play something over.monolingual: to replay something, such as a game, a videotape, an audio recording, etc. _There was an objection to the way the referee handled the game, so they played it over. _ Let’s play that song over again.
examples: There was an objection to the way the referee handled the game, so they played it over.

play something through†.monolingual: to play something, such as a piece of recorded music, all the way through. _ I played the album through, hoping to find even one song I liked. _ As I played through the album, I didn’t hear anything I liked.
examples: I played the album through, hoping to find even one song I liked.

play something up†.monolingual: to emphasize something; to be a booster of something. _ The press played the scandal up so much that everyone became bored with it. _ They really played up the scandal.
examples: The press played the scandal up so much that everyone became bored with it.

play the devil with something.monolingual: Fig. to cause disruption with something; to foul something up. _ Your being late really played the devil with my plans for the day. _ This weather is really playing the devil with my arthritis.
examples: Your being late really played the devil with my plans for the day.

play the field.monolingual: to date many different people rather than just one. _ When Tom told Ann good-bye, he said he wanted to play the field. _ He said he wanted to play the field while he was still young.
examples: When Tom told Ann good-bye, he said he wanted to play the field.

play the fool.monolingual: Fig. to act in a silly manner in order to amuse other people. _ The teacher told Tom to stop playing the fool and sit down. _ Fred likes playing the fool, but we didn’t find him funny last night.
examples: The teacher told Tom to stop playing the fool and sit down.

play the heavy.monolingual: Fig. to act the part of a mean person; to do the unpleasant tasks that no one else wants to do. (Refers originally to playing the role of someone evil in a movie, etc.) _ I’m a nice guy, but at work, I am required to play the heavy. The boss makes me
examples: I’m a nice guy, but at work, I am required to play the heavy.

play through.monolingual: [for golfers] to pass someone on the golf course. _ Do you mind if we play through? We have to get back to the courtroom by two o’clock. _ We let them play through because they were moving so fast.
examples: Do you mind if we play through? We have to get back to the courtroom by two o’clock.

play to someone or something.monolingual: 1. to perform something for someone or a group. _The cast played to one of their classmates who was confined to the hospital. _ Gerald Watson will play to a small gathering of wealthy socialites this Saturday evening.
examples: The cast played to one of their classmates who was confined to the hospital.

play tricks on someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to pull pranks on someone. _ You had better not play any tricks on me! _ Stop playing tricks on people!
examples: Stop playing tricks on people! 2.

play up to someone.monolingual: to flatter someone; to try to gain influence with someone. _ It won’t do any good to play up to me. I refuse to agree to your proposal. _ I played up to him and he still wouldn’t give in to me.
examples: It won’t do any good to play up to me.

play with a full deck.monolingual: 1. Lit. to play cards with a complete deck, containing all the cards. _Are we playing with a full deck or did some card drop on the f loor? I haven’t seen the three of hearts all evening!
examples: Are we playing with a full deck or did some card drop on the f loor? I haven’t seen the three of hearts all evening! 2.

play with fire.monolingual: 1. Lit. to use fire as a toy; to experiment with flames and fire. _ Jimmy! I’ve told you never to play with fire!
examples: Jimmy! I’ve told you never to play with fire! 2.

play with someone or something.monolingual: 1. to play games with someone or a group. _ I love to play Ping-Pong. Will you play with me? _ They won’t play with our team. We are too good.
examples: I love to play Ping-Pong.

play-by-play description.monolingual: a description of an event given as the event is taking place. (Usually in reference to a sporting event.) _And now here is Bill Jones with a playby- play description of the baseball game. _ John was giving me a play-by-play description of the argumen
examples: And now here is Bill Jones with a playby- play description of the baseball game.

played out.monolingual: too exhausted to continue. _At the end of the race, Donna was played out. _ After the race, we were played out for the rest of the day.
examples: At the end of the race, Donna was played out.

plead for someone.monolingual: to beg for someone to be spared. _Tom pleaded for Dave, but it was no use. Dave was found guilty. _She pleaded for her husband, but the judge sentenced him to ten years in prison.
examples: Tom pleaded for Dave, but it was no use.

plead for something.monolingual: to beg for something. _ I don’t want to have to plead for what’s already mine. _ The children were pleading for ice cream, so we got some for them.
examples: I don’t want to have to plead for what’s already mine.

plead guilty to something.monolingual: to state that one is guilty of a crime before a court of law. _ Gerald refused to plead guilty to the crime and had to stand trial. _ Max pleaded guilty to the charge and then f led town.
examples: Gerald refused to plead guilty to the crime and had to stand trial.

plead to something.monolingual: to enter an admission of guilt to a specific crime. _ Max pleaded to the lesser charge of larceny. _ Lefty pleaded to the grand larceny charge.
examples: Max pleaded to the lesser charge of larceny.

plead with someone.monolingual: to beg something of someone; to make an emotional appeal to someone. _ Do I have to plead with you to get you to do it? _You can plead with me as much as you want. I won’t permit you to go.
examples: You can plead with me as much as you want.

*pleased as punch.monolingual: delighted; very pleased. (*Also: as ~.) (This refers to Punch from the “Punch and Judy” shows.) _ Child: Do you think Grandma will like the picture I’m making for her? Father: I think she’ll be as pleased as Punch. _Fred was pleased as Punch to disco
examples: Child: Do you think Grandma will like the picture I’m making for her? Father: I think she’ll be as pleased as Punch.

pleased for someone or something.monolingual: happy for someone or a group. _ I am very pleased for you. _ We were all pleased for the committee. The members got all the praise they deserved. _ Everyone could see how pleased Sam was for himself and his whole family.
examples: I am very pleased for you.

*pleased with someone or something.monolingual: happy and satisfied with someone or something. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ I am quite pleased with you. You did a fine job. _ We are pleased with your work.
examples: I am quite pleased with you.

pledge something to someone.monolingual: to promise something to someone. _ I pledged one hundred dollars to Ralph for his cause. _We pledged a lot of money to our favorite charity.
examples: I pledged one hundred dollars to Ralph for his cause.

plenty of something.monolingual: lots of something; an abundance of something; enough of something. _I have plenty of candy. Do you want some? _ This project is giving me plenty of trouble.
examples: I have plenty of candy.

plight one’s troth to someone.monolingual: to become engaged to be married to someone. (Literary or jocular.) _ I chose not to plight my troth to anyone who acts so unpleasant to my dear aunt. _ Alice plighted her troth to Scott.
examples: I chose not to plight my troth to anyone who acts so unpleasant to my dear aunt.

plod along.monolingual: to move along slowly but deliberately. _ I’m just plodding along, but I am getting the job done. _ The old man plodded along, hardly able to stand. _ The movie plodded along putting most of the audience to sleep.
examples: I’m just plodding along, but I am getting the job done.

plod away at something.monolingual: to keep trying to do something. _ He continues to plod away at writing his novel. It’s been three years now. _ How long have you been plodding away at that book?
examples: He continues to plod away at writing his novel.

plod through something.monolingual: to work one’s way through something laboriously. _I just plodded through my work today. I had no energy at all. _ This is certainly a lot of papers to have to plod through.
examples: I just plodded through my work today.

plonk something down†.monolingual: to slap something down; to plop something down. _ He plonked a dollar down and demanded a newspaper. _ He plonked down his beer mug on the bar.
examples: He plonked a dollar down and demanded a newspaper.

plot against someone or something.monolingual: to make a scheme against someone or something. _ All the counselors plotted against the czar. _ We plotted against the opposing party.
examples: All the counselors plotted against the czar.

plot something on something.monolingual: to draw a route or outline on something. _ He plotted the course they would be taking on a map of the area. _ The captain plotted the course on a chart of the upper reaches of the Nile.
examples: He plotted the course they would be taking on a map of the area.

plot something out†.monolingual: to map something out; to outline a plan for something. _I have an idea about how to remodel this room. Let me plot it out for you. _ I plotted out my ideas for the room.
examples: I have an idea about how to remodel this room.

the plot thickens..monolingual: Things are becoming more complicated or interesting. _The police assumed that the woman was murdered by her ex-husband, but he has an alibi. The plot thickens. _John is supposed to be going out with Mary, but I saw him last night with Sally. The plot
examples: The police assumed that the woman was murdered by her ex-husband, but he has an alibi.

plot with someone.monolingual: to scheme with someone. _Mary looks as though she is plotting with Jerry to make some sort of mischief. _I am not plotting with anyone. I am planning everything myself.
examples: Mary looks as though she is plotting with Jerry to make some sort of mischief.

plow into someone or something.monolingual: to crash into someone or something; to bump hard into someone or something. _ The car plowed into the ditch. _ The runner plowed into another player.
examples: The car plowed into the ditch.

plow something in†.monolingual: to work something into soil by plowing. _ Lay the fertilizer down and plow it in. _ Plow in the fertilizer as soon as you can.
examples: Lay the fertilizer down and plow it in.

plow something up†.monolingual: to uncover something by plowing. _ The farmer plowed some old coins up and took them to the museum to find out what they were. _ He plowed up some valuable coins.
examples: The farmer plowed some old coins up and took them to the museum to find out what they were.

plow through something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to move through something such as snow or mud with a plow. _The huge truck plowed through the snow-covered streets so traffic could move again.
examples: The huge truck plowed through the snow-covered streets so traffic could move again.

pluck at someone or something.monolingual: to pull or pick at someone or something. _ Kelly plucked at Ed, picking off the burrs that had caught on his clothing. _ Kelly plucked at the strings of the guitar.
examples: Kelly plucked at Ed, picking off the burrs that had caught on his clothing.

pluck up someone’s courage.monolingual: to bolster someone’s, including one’s own, courage. _ I hope you are able to pluck up your courage so that you can do what has to be done. _ Some good advice from a friend helped pluck up my courage.
examples: I hope you are able to pluck up your courage so that you can do what has to be done.

plug something up†.monolingual: to stop or fill up a hole, crack, or gap. _ Take out the nail and plug the hole up with something. _ You have to plug up the cracks to keep out the cold.
examples: Take out the nail and plug the hole up with something.

plumb loco.monolingual: Rur. completely crazy. (Loco is from a Spanish word meaning “mad.”) _You’re plumb loco if you think I’ll go along with that. _ All those people were running around like they were plumb loco.
examples: You’re plumb loco if you think I’ll go along with that.

plummet to earth.monolingual: to fall rapidly to earth from a great height. _ The rocket plummeted to earth and exploded as it struck. _ As the plane plummeted to earth, all the people on the ground were screaming.
examples: The rocket plummeted to earth and exploded as it struck.

plummet to something.monolingual: to drop or fall to some level or low point. _Stock prices plummeted to record low levels. _The rock plummeted to the river at the base of the cliff.
examples: Stock prices plummeted to record low levels.

plump for someone or something.monolingual: to support or promote someone or something. _ Henry spent a lot of energy plumping for Bill, who was running for vice president. _ She spent a lot of time plumping for our candidate.
examples: Henry spent a lot of energy plumping for Bill, who was running for vice president.

plump something down†.monolingual: 1. to drop a heavy load of something. _ She plumped the load of groceries onto the bench and looked through her purse for the keys. _ Jill plumped down her packages.
examples: She plumped the load of groceries onto the bench and looked through her purse for the keys.

plump something up†.monolingual: to pat or shake something like a pillow into a fuller shape. _Todd plumped his pillow up and finished making the bed. _ He plumped up his pillow.
examples: Todd plumped his pillow up and finished making the bed.

plunge down something.monolingual: to run or fall down something. _ The car plunged down the hill and ran into a tree at the bottom. _The bicyclist plunged down the side of the hill at a great speed.
examples: The car plunged down the hill and ran into a tree at the bottom.

plunge from something.monolingual: to fall or flee from something or some place. _ The eagle plunged from the sky to the lake to capture its prey. _Lily plunged from the room in embarrassment.
examples: The eagle plunged from the sky to the lake to capture its prey.

plunge to something.monolingual: 1. to fall or drop down to something. _The temperature plunged to zero last night. _The burning car plunged to the f loor of the canyon.
examples: The temperature plunged to zero last night.

plunk someone or something down†.monolingual: to place, drop, or plop someone or something down hard. _ He picked her up and plunked her down in a chair and began to shout at her. _ Sally plunked down the book in anger.
examples: He picked her up and plunked her down in a chair and began to shout at her.

ply someone with something else.monolingual: to try to supply or give something to someone. (Implies an attempt to influence or fawn upon someone.) _ We plied the mayor with gifts and favors, but it got us nowhere. _ Don’t try to ply the police officer with gifts. That is considered a bribe.
examples: We plied the mayor with gifts and favors, but it got us nowhere.

pock something with something.monolingual: to cause dents or small craters by shooting or throwing something at something. _The hail pocked the roof of the car with dents. _The side of the house was pocked with tiny dents where the hail had struck.
examples: The hail pocked the roof of the car with dents.

a pocket of resistance.monolingual: Fig. a small group of people who resist change or domination. _ The accounting department seems to be a pocket of resistance when it comes to automating.
examples: The accounting department seems to be a pocket of resistance when it comes to automating.

poetic justice.monolingual: appropriate, ideal, or ironic punishment. _ It was poetic justice that Jane won the race after Mary tried to get her banned from the race. _The car thieves tried to steal a car with no gas. That’s poetic justice.
examples: It was poetic justice that Jane won the race after Mary tried to get her banned from the race.

poetic license.monolingual: liberties or license of the type taken by artists, especially poets, to violate patterns of rhyme, harmony, structure, etc. _I couldn’t tell whether he kept making spelling mistakes or if it was just poetic license.
examples: I couldn’t tell whether he kept making spelling mistakes or if it was just poetic license.

point at someone or something.monolingual: 1. [for someone] to direct an extended finger at someone or something; to point one’s finger at someone or something. _ You should not point at people. _Harry pointed at the mess Jerry had made and scowled.
examples: You should not point at people.

point down to something.monolingual: to aim downward to something. _ The sign pointed down to the little bell sitting on the counter. _ The room clerk pointed down the stairs to a little cafe on the lower level.
examples: The sign pointed down to the little bell sitting on the counter.

the point of no return.monolingual: the halfway point; the point at which it is too late to turn back. (Often with past.) _The f light was past the point of no return, so we had to continue to our destination. _ The entire project is past the point of no return; we will have to continu
examples: The f light was past the point of no return, so we had to continue to our destination.

point of view.monolingual: a way of thinking about something; [someone’s] viewpoint; an attitude or expression of self-interest. _ From my point of view, all this talk is a waste of time. _ I can understand her point of view. She has made some good observations about the probl
examples: From my point of view, all this talk is a waste of time.

point someone or something out†.monolingual: to select or indicate someone or something (from a group). _Everyone pointed the error out. _ She pointed out the boy who took her purse.
examples: Everyone pointed the error out.

point something up†.monolingual: 1. Fig. to emphasize something; to emphasize one aspect of something. _ This is a very important thing to learn. Let me point it up one more time by drawing this diagram on the board. _ This points up what I’ve been telling you.
examples: This is a very important thing to learn.

point the finger at someone.monolingual: Fig. to blame someone; to identify someone as the guilty person. _ Don’t point the finger at me! I didn’t take the money. _ The manager refused to point the finger at anyone in particular and said that everyone was sometimes guilty of being late.
examples: Don’t point the finger at me! I didn’t take the money.

point to someone or something.monolingual: to aim at someone or something. _ Who is she pointing to? _ He pointed to the door.
examples: He pointed to the door.

point to something.monolingual: to indicate, reveal, or suggest something. _ All the evidence seems to point to his guilt. _ The signs point to a very cold winter.
examples: All the evidence seems to point to his guilt.

point to something as something.monolingual: to identify something as something. _ All the indications pointed to Jill as the next president.
examples: All the indications pointed to Jill as the next president.

point toward someone or something.monolingual: to direct an extended finger toward someone or something. _ The teacher pointed toward Laura and asked her to come to the front of the room. _ Randy pointed toward the door and frowned at the dog.
examples: The teacher pointed toward Laura and asked her to come to the front of the room.

poise oneself for something.monolingual: to get ready for something. _ She poised herself for her dive. _ Fred poised himself for a fall, but everything worked out all right.
examples: She poised herself for her dive.

poise over someone or something.monolingual: to hover or hang over someone or something. _ She spent the entire afternoon poised over her desk, pouting. _ The dog poised over the downed duck, waiting for the hunter.
examples: She spent the entire afternoon poised over her desk, pouting.

poised for something.monolingual: ready for something; in the right position and waiting for something. _ The cat stared at the mouse, poised for action. _ The army was poised for battle.
examples: The cat stared at the mouse, poised for action.

poised to do something.monolingual: ready to do something; in the right position to do something. _ The cat is poised to jump on the mouse. _ The army is poised to attack at dawn.
examples: The cat is poised to jump on the mouse.

poison something with something.monolingual: to render something poisonous with something. _ She poisoned the soup with arsenic. _They are poisoning our water supply with pollutants.
examples: She poisoned the soup with arsenic.

poke along.monolingual: to move along slowly; to lag or tarry. _ Get moving. Stop poking along. _ I was just poking along, taking my time, not paying attention to what was going on around me.
examples: Get moving. Stop poking along.

poke at someone or something.monolingual: to thrust or jab at someone or something. _ Stop poking at me! _ Don’t poke at the turtle. It might bite you.
examples: Don’t poke at the turtle.

poke someone in something.monolingual: to strike or jab someone in some body part. _ Billy poked Bobby in the tummy and made him cry. _ She poked herself in the eye accidentally.
examples: Billy poked Bobby in the tummy and made him cry.

polarize something into something.monolingual: to divide a group into two segments. _ Your actions have just polarized the students into two opposing groups! _ We polarized the entire population into two factions.
examples: We polarized the entire population into two factions.

*poles apart.monolingual: very different; far from coming to an agreement. (Alludes to the distance between the north and south poles. *Typically: be ~; become ~; grow ~.) _ Mr. and Mrs. Jones don’t get along well. They are poles apart. _ They’ll never sign the contract becau
examples: Mr. and Mrs. Jones don’t get along well.

polish something off†.monolingual: to eat, consume, exhaust, or complete all of something. _ Who polished the cake off ? _ Who polished off the cake?

polish something up†.monolingual: to rub something until it shines. _ Polish the silver up and make it look nice and shiny. _ If you will polish up the silver, I will put it away.
examples: Polish the silver up and make it look nice and shiny.

a political football.monolingual: Fig. an issue that becomes politically divisive; a problem that doesn’t get solved because the politics of the issue get in the way. _ The question of campaign contributions has become a political football. All the politicians who accept questionable
examples: The question of campaign contributions has become a political football.

politics makes strange bedfellows..monolingual: Prov. People who would normally dislike and avoid one another will work together if they think it is politically useful to do so. _Jill: I never would have thought that genteel, aristocratic candidate would pick such a rabble-rousing, rough-mannered
examples: Jill: I never would have thought that genteel, aristocratic candidate would pick such a rabble-rousing, rough-mannered running mate.

pollute something with something.monolingual: to adulterate something with something; to dirty something with something. _ You should not pollute the stream with chemicals. _Someone polluted the sewer with automotive oil.
examples: You should not pollute the stream with chemicals.

pontificate on something.monolingual: to speak and act dogmatically and pompously. _ Must you pontificate on your own virtues so much? _ The speaker was pontificating on the virtues of a fat-free diet.
examples: The speaker was pontificating on the virtues of a fat-free diet.

pooch out.monolingual: to stick or bulge out, as with a belly. _ His chubby tummy pooched out when he relaxed.
examples: His chubby tummy pooched out when he relaxed.

poop out.monolingual: Inf. to quit; to wear out and stop. _ He pooped out after about an hour of hard work. _ I think I’m going to poop out pretty soon.
examples: He pooped out after about an hour of hard work.

poop someone or something out.monolingual: Inf. to cause someone to become exhausted or give out. _ All that exercise really pooped everyone out. _ A full day of play at the beach had pooped the dog out. _ The activity pooped out the dog.
examples: All that exercise really pooped everyone out.

poor but clean.monolingual: Cliché having little money but clean and of good habits, nonetheless. (Either extremely condescending or jocular. Some people would consider it offensive.) _ My salary isn’t very high, and I only have one old car. Anyway, I’m poor but clean. _ When F
examples: My salary isn’t very high, and I only have one old car.

pop for something.monolingual: Inf. to pay for a treat (for someone). _ Let’s have some ice cream. I’ll pop for it. _ It’s about time you popped for coffee.
examples: Let’s have some ice cream.

pop off.monolingual: 1. Sl. to make an unnecessary remark; to interrupt with a remark; to sound off. _ Please don’t pop off all the time. _ Bob keeps popping off when he should be listening.
examples: Please don’t pop off all the time.

pop one’s cork.monolingual: 1. Fig. to suddenly become mentally disturbed; to go crazy. _ I was so upset that I nearly popped my cork. _They put him away because he popped his cork.
examples: I was so upset that I nearly popped my cork.

pop someone off†.monolingual: Inf. to kill someone. _ Max was told to pop Lefty off because he was trying to muscle in on the gang’s turf. _ Max intended to pop off Lefty.
examples: Max was told to pop Lefty off because he was trying to muscle in on the gang’s turf.

pop someone on something.monolingual: Inf. to strike someone on some body part. _If you don’t sit down, I’ll pop you on the chin! _ Max popped Lefty on the nose.
examples: Max popped Lefty on the nose.

pop something up†.monolingual: to remove something by making it jump or burst upwards. _ Henry popped the lid up and helped himself to the strawberry preserves. _ He popped up the lid and cleaned out the jam jar.
examples: Henry popped the lid up and helped himself to the strawberry preserves.

pop the question.monolingual: [for a man] to ask a woman to marry him. (Could also be used by a woman asking a man.) _ She waited for years for him to pop the question. _ Finally she popped the question.
examples: She waited for years for him to pop the question.

pop up.monolingual: 1. [for a baseball batter] to hit a baseball that goes high upward rather than outward. _ The catcher came to bat and popped up. _I hope I don’t pop up this time.
examples: The catcher came to bat and popped up.

pore over something.monolingual: to look over something carefully. _ She pored over the reports, looking for errors. _ I need to take a few hours to pore over these contracts and see if they are ready to be signed.
examples: She pored over the reports, looking for errors.

portion something out†.monolingual: to give out shares of something. _ Who will portion the cake out? _ She portioned out the chocolate carefully, making sure everyone got an equal share.
examples: She portioned out the chocolate carefully, making sure everyone got an equal share.

pose a question.monolingual: to ask a question; to imply the need for asking a question. _ Genetic research poses many ethical questions. _My interviewer posed a hypothetical question.
examples: Genetic research poses many ethical questions.

pose as someone.monolingual: to pretend to be someone else. _ The impostor posed as the president of the company. _My twin posed as me while I went on vacation.
examples: The impostor posed as the president of the company.

pose as someone or something.monolingual: to pretend to be someone or a type of person. _ I posed as Gerald and got the job. _ I posed as a nurse and got a job at a summer camp.
examples: I posed as Gerald and got the job.

pose for someone or something.monolingual: to assume a posture appropriate to the subject of a photograph or painting. _ Paul wanted me to pose for him, but I declined. _Will you pose for my painting?
examples: Paul wanted me to pose for him, but I declined.

*possessed by something.monolingual: obsessed or driven by something. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ Ned was possessed by a desire to become the best at everything he did. _ Jan acts as if she is possessed by the need to be right all the time.
examples: Ned was possessed by a desire to become the best at everything he did.

*possessed of something.monolingual: having something; possessing something. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ She is possessed of a large amount of money. _ Todd wishes he were possessed of a large car and a fine house.
examples: She is possessed of a large amount of money.

post someone somewhere.monolingual: to place someone, as if on guard, at something or some place. _ The police chief posted a guard at the hospital door. _The boss posted himself at the water cooler to catch up on the gossip.
examples: The police chief posted a guard at the hospital door.

post something on something.monolingual: to fasten a notice onto something. _Please post this notice on the door where everyone will see it. _ I will post this photo on the bulletin board.
examples: Please post this notice on the door where everyone will see it.

post something to someone.monolingual: to mail something to someone. _I posted it to him over a month ago. I can’t imagine where it is now. _ The letter was posted last week.
examples: I posted it to him over a month ago.

post something up†.monolingual: to record a transaction in an account. _I’ll post this charge up right away, and then you can check out. _ Please post up the charges a little later.
examples: I’ll post this charge up right away, and then you can check out.

postage and handling.monolingual: charges for shipping [something] and for wrapping and handling the item. _The cost of the book was quite reasonable, but the postage and handling was outrageous. _ They did not charge postage and handling because I prepaid the order.
examples: The cost of the book was quite reasonable, but the postage and handling was outrageous.

postpone something until something.monolingual: to delay something until something happens or until a later time. _ Can we postpone our meeting until tomorrow? _ The picnic was postponed until Saturday.
examples: The picnic was postponed until Saturday.

posture as someone or something.monolingual: to pretend to be someone or a particular type of person. _ Why is the secretary posturing as the manager and giving out assignments? _ Carla entered the ballroom, posturing as a grand duchess of somewhere or another.
examples: Carla entered the ballroom, posturing as a grand duchess of somewhere or another.

a pot of gold.monolingual: 1. Lit. a container filled with gold, as in myth guarded by a leprechaun. _ I was hoping to find a pot of gold in the cellar, but there were only cobwebs.
examples: I was hoping to find a pot of gold in the cellar, but there were only cobwebs.

pot something up†.monolingual: to put plants into pots. _ If you would like one of these tomato plants, I’ll pot one up for you. _Jan potted up a plant for me.
examples: If you would like one of these tomato plants, I’ll pot one up for you.

pound a beat.monolingual: Fig. to walk a regular route. _ The cop pounded the same beat for years and years. _ Pounding a beat will wreck your feet.
examples: The cop pounded the same beat for years and years.

pound along something.monolingual: 1. Fig. to walk or run along something awkwardly or heavily. _As the horse pounded along the street, the rider tried hard to get it to slow down. _Tom pounded along the pavement, looking a bit angry.
examples: As the horse pounded along the street, the rider tried hard to get it to slow down.

pound for pound.monolingual: [Usually of value, quality, strength, etc.] considering the amount of weight involved. _Pound for pound, a dog fed properly is much stronger than a dog that has to fend for itself. _ Pound for pound, there is more food value in beef than in chicken.
examples: Pound for pound, a dog fed properly is much stronger than a dog that has to fend for itself.

*a pound of flesh.monolingual: Fig. a payment or punishment that involves suffering and sacrifice on the part of the person being punished. (*Typically: give someone ~; owe someone ~; pay someone ~; take ~.) _ He wants revenge. He won’t be satisfied until he takes his pound of f l
examples: He wants revenge.

pound on someone or something.monolingual: to beat or hammer on someone or something. _She kept pounding on him until he released her. _ Will you please stop pounding on that drum?
examples: She kept pounding on him until he released her.

pound one’s ear.monolingual: Sl. to sleep. _ I’ve got to spend more time pounding my ear. _ She went home to pound her ear an hour or two before work.
examples: I’ve got to spend more time pounding my ear.

pound someone’s head in†.monolingual: Fig. to beat someone, especially about the head. _ Fred looked like he wanted to pound Mike’s head in; he was so mad! _ You want me to pound in your head?

pound something down†.monolingual: to hammer, flatten, or batter something. _ Please pound that nail down so that no one gets hurt on it. _ Yes, please pound down that nail!
examples: Please pound that nail down so that no one gets hurt on it.

pound something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to flatten something by pounding. _He pounded the gold leaf out very thin. _He pounded out the gold leaf.
examples: He pounded the gold leaf out very thin.

pound something up†.monolingual: to break something up by pounding. _ Pound the crackers up into crumbs and use them to coat the chicken before you fry it. _ Pound up the crackers and put the crumbs in a jar.
examples: Pound the crackers up into crumbs and use them to coat the chicken before you fry it.

pound the pavement.monolingual: Fig. to walk through the streets looking for a job. _I spent two months pounding the pavement after the factory I worked for closed. _Hey, Bob. You’d better get busy pounding those nails unless you want to be out pounding the pavement.
examples: I spent two months pounding the pavement after the factory I worked for closed.

pour along something.monolingual: to rush along something in great numbers or in a great amount. _ Hundreds of people poured along the street during the lunch hour. _ The rainwater poured along the gutter, heading toward the sewer basin.
examples: Hundreds of people poured along the street during the lunch hour.

pour forth.monolingual: to gush out; to gush forth. _ The milk gushed out of the hole in the container. _A tremendous amount of water poured forth when the fire hydrant was knocked over.
examples: The milk gushed out of the hole in the container.

pour money down the drain.monolingual: Fig. to waste money; to throw money away. _ What a waste! Buying that old car is just pouring money down the drain. _ Don’t buy any more of that low-quality merchandise. That’s just throwing money down the drain.
examples: What a waste! Buying that old car is just pouring money down the drain.

pour oneself into something.monolingual: 1. Fig. to get deeply involved with something. _ He distracted himself from his grief by pouring himself into his work. _She poured herself into the project and got it done on time.
examples: He distracted himself from his grief by pouring himself into his work.

pour out one’s soul.monolingual: Fig. to confess something [to someone]; to reveal one’s deepest concerns. _ Every time she calls me up, she takes an hour or more to pour out her soul.
examples: Every time she calls me up, she takes an hour or more to pour out her soul.

pour something through something.monolingual: to cause something to flow through something, such as a filter. _ The chemist poured the mixture through the filter or opening. _ I can’t get the syrup into the bottle without pouring it through a funnel.
examples: The chemist poured the mixture through the filter or opening.

pour through something.monolingual: to flow freely through something. _The water poured through the leak in the window frame. _ The rain poured through the hole in the roof.
examples: The water poured through the leak in the window frame.

pour with rain.monolingual: to rain heavily. (Said of the sky, day, morning, night, the weather, etc.) _ The sky was pouring with rain and the sun never shone from dawn to dusk. _ It poured with rain the entire night.
examples: The sky was pouring with rain and the sun never shone from dawn to dusk.

pouring rain.monolingual: very heavy rain. _The children’s clothes were soaked after they played out in the pouring rain. _I waited in the pouring rain for the next bus.
examples: The children’s clothes were soaked after they played out in the pouring rain.

pout about someone or something.monolingual: to be sullen about someone or something. _There is no need to pout about the cat. She’ll come back. _ Sally is pouting about her lost dog.
examples: There is no need to pout about the cat.

powder up.monolingual: Sl. to drink heavily; to get drunk. _ Let’s go out and powder up. _ He’s at the tavern powdering up.
examples: Let’s go out and powder up.

the power behind the throne.monolingual: Fig. the person who actually controls the person who is apparently in charge. _ Mr. Smith appears to run the shop, but his brother is the power behind the throne. _They say that the vice president is the power behind the throne.
examples: Mr. Smith appears to run the shop, but his brother is the power behind the throne.

a power play.monolingual: Fig. a strategy using one’s power or authority to carry out a plan or to get one’s way. _ In a blatant power play, the manager claimed he had initiated the sales campaign.
examples: In a blatant power play, the manager claimed he had initiated the sales campaign.

power something up†.monolingual: to start something, such as an engine. _ You should power the engine up and let it run awhile before you drive away. _Power up the engine and mow the grass.
examples: You should power the engine up and let it run awhile before you drive away.

power something with something.monolingual: to provide something as the source of energy for something to operate. _The government decided to power its vans with natural gas engines. _ We will power the generators with coal as long as it is cheap.
examples: The government decided to power its vans with natural gas engines.

power up.monolingual: to start an engine. _ Well, let’s power up so we will be ready to leave with the others. _ It’s time to power up and get going.
examples: Well, let’s power up so we will be ready to leave with the others.

the powers that be.monolingual: the people who are in authority. _ The powers that be have decided to send back the immigrants. _ I have applied for a license, and the powers that be are considering my application.
examples: The powers that be have decided to send back the immigrants.

practice makes perfect..monolingual: Prov. Cliché Doing something over and over again is the only way to learn to do it well. _ Jill: I’m not going to try to play the piano anymore. I always make so many mistakes. Jane: Don’t give up. Practice makes perfect. _ Child: How come you’re so
examples: Jill: I’m not going to try to play the piano anymore.

practice what you preach..monolingual: Prov. Cliché You yourself should do the things you advise other people to do. _Dad always told us we should only watch an hour of television every day, but we all knew he didn’t practice what he preached.
examples: Dad always told us we should only watch an hour of television every day, but we all knew he didn’t practice what he preached.

prance around.monolingual: to dance, jump, or strut around. _ The little deer were prancing around, enjoying the spring air. _ Stop prancing around and get to work.
examples: The little deer were prancing around, enjoying the spring air.

prance around something.monolingual: to dance or jump in celebration around something or throughout some place. (Compare this with waltz around something.) _ The kids pranced around the room, celebrating. _ They pranced around the table that held the ice cream and cake.
examples: The kids pranced around the room, celebrating.

pray for someone or something.monolingual: 1. to beseech God, or some other deity, on behalf of someone or something. _ I will pray for you to recover from your illness quickly. _ As the fire spread throughout the old church, the congregation prayed for its preservation.
examples: I will pray for you to recover from your illness quickly.

pray over something.monolingual: 1. to say grace over a meal. _Do you pray over your meals? _ We prayed over dinner just after we sat down to eat.
examples: We prayed over dinner just after we sat down to eat.

pray to someone or something.monolingual: to utter prayers of praise or supplication to some divine or supernatural being or something. _ I pray to God that all this works out. _ The high priest prayed to the spirits of his ancestors that the rains would come.
examples: I pray to God that all this works out.

pray to the porcelain god.monolingual: Sl. to kneel at the toilet bowl and vomit from drunkenness. _Wally spent a while praying to the porcelain god last night. _ I think I have to go pray to the porcelain god.
examples: Wally spent a while praying to the porcelain god last night.

preach about something.monolingual: to give a moral or stern discourse on something. _Please don’t preach about the evils of fried food. I like the stuff, and people eat it all the time and don’t die! _ She was preaching about the value of a fat-free diet.
examples: Please don’t preach about the evils of fried food.

preach against someone or something.monolingual: to exhort against someone or something. _The evangelist preached against the operator of the town’s only saloon. _The principal kept preaching against drinking and drugs.
examples: The evangelist preached against the operator of the town’s only saloon.

preach at someone.monolingual: to lecture or moralize at someone. _ Don’t preach at me! I don’t need any of your moralizing. _ I really don’t wish to be preached at.
examples: Don’t preach at me! I don’t need any of your moralizing.

preach to someone.monolingual: to give a moral discourse to someone. _ Please don’t preach to me. I know that I did wrong. _ When you preach to us like that, we don’t pay any attention to you.
examples: Please don’t preach to me.

*precedence over someone or something.monolingual: the right to come before someone or something else; greater importance than someone or something else. (*Typically: take ~; have ~; be given ~.) _ Ambulances have precedence over regular cars at intersections. _My manager’s concerns take precedence o
examples: Ambulances have precedence over regular cars at intersections.

precipitate into something.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a chemical] to go out of solution into solid form. _The sodium chloride precipitated into a salt. _Will this compound precipitate into anything if I cool it?
examples: The sodium chloride precipitated into a salt.

precipitate something into something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to cause a chemical to go out of a solution into a solid form. _ Adding just one salt grain at the right time will precipitate the salt dissolved into the water into large crystals. _ One grain precipitated the dissolved salt into crystals.
examples: Adding just one salt grain at the right time will precipitate the salt dissolved into the water into large crystals.

preface something by something.monolingual: to begin something by saying, writing, or reading something. _I would like to preface my prepared remarks by making a personal observation. _ Her remarks were prefaced by the reading of a poem.
examples: I would like to preface my prepared remarks by making a personal observation.

preface something with something.monolingual: to begin something with a particular message. _ She prefaced her speech with a recitation of one of her favorite poems. _Alice prefaced her remarks with a few personal comments.
examples: She prefaced her speech with a recitation of one of her favorite poems.

prefer something against someone.monolingual: to file legal charges against someone [with the police]; to file a complaint or a charge against someone. _ The neighbors preferred charges against the driver of the car who ruined their lawns. _ I will not prefer charges against the driver, since it
examples: The neighbors preferred charges against the driver of the car who ruined their lawns.

prefix something to something.monolingual: to place something at the beginning of a word or part of a word. _ If you prefix a re- to some verbs, you get an entirely different meaning. _ You can’t prefix anything to some verbs.
examples: If you prefix a re- to some verbs, you get an entirely different meaning.

a prelude to something.monolingual: an act or event that comes before and signals another act or event. _Her rudeness to her boss was a prelude to her resignation. _ The Munich Pact was a prelude to World War II.
examples: Her rudeness to her boss was a prelude to her resignation.

prepare someone for something.monolingual: to build someone up for shocking news. _I went in and had a talk with her to prepare her for the report. _ You should prepare yourself for the worst.
examples: I went in and had a talk with her to prepare her for the report.

prescribe something for someone.monolingual: to order a medication to be given to or sold to someone. _I asked the doctor to prescribe a painkiller for me. _What can you prescribe for me for this illness?
examples: I asked the doctor to prescribe a painkiller for me.

prescribe something for something.monolingual: to suggest or recommend something for a particular disease. _Could you prescribe something for my cold? _What can you prescribe for this illness?

preside at something.monolingual: to manage or act as chair at a meeting or a ceremony. _ The mayor presided at the meeting, assuring that the speeches would be very short. _ She presided at the ceremony.
examples: The mayor presided at the meeting, assuring that the speeches would be very short.

preside over something.monolingual: to be in control of the order and procedures of a meeting or ceremony. _ The vice president will have to preside over the next meeting. _ I will be glad to preside over the discussion.
examples: The vice president will have to preside over the next meeting.

press against someone or something.monolingual: to push or bear upon someone or something. _ I pressed against Henry, trying gently to get him to move out of the way. _ Don’t press against the glass door!
examples: I pressed against Henry, trying gently to get him to move out of the way.

press for something.monolingual: 1. to urge for something to be done; to request something. _The mayor is pressing for an early settlement to the strike. _ I will press her for an answer. _ The citizens are pressing for an investigation of the incident.
examples: The mayor is pressing for an early settlement to the strike.

press forward.monolingual: to move forward; to struggle forward; to continue. _Do not be discouraged. Let us press forward. _ We must press forward and complete this work on time.
examples: Do not be discouraged.

press on something.monolingual: to push or depress something, such as a button, catch, snap, etc. _ Press on this button if you require room service. _ Don’t press on this because it rings a loud bell.
examples: Press on this button if you require room service.

press something together.monolingual: to use pressure to close or unite things. _ He pressed his lips together and would say no more. _ Why are his lips pressed together so tightly?
examples: He pressed his lips together and would say no more.

pressure someone into something.monolingual: to force someone into doing something. _ Please don’t try to pressure me into taking that promotion. _ You can’t pressure me into it. I won’t do it!
examples: Please don’t try to pressure me into taking that promotion.

pretend to something.monolingual: to claim to have a skill or quality. _ I can hardly pretend to the artistry that Wally has, but I can play the piano a bit. _ I can’t pretend to that level of skill.
examples: I can hardly pretend to the artistry that Wally has, but I can play the piano a bit.

*pretty as a picture.monolingual: very pretty. (*Also: as ~.) _Sweet little Mary is as pretty as a picture. _ Their new house is pretty as a picture.
examples: Sweet little Mary is as pretty as a picture.

pretty is as pretty does..monolingual: Prov. It is more important to treat people well than to be good-looking; just because you are good-looking does not mean you are a good person. (Said only of girls and women.) _ Janice may have a pretty face, but pretty is as pretty does; the way she
examples: Janice may have a pretty face, but pretty is as pretty does; the way she behaves isn’t pretty at all.

pretty oneself or something up†.monolingual: Rur. to make oneself or something more attractive; to tidy oneself or something up. _ I tried to pretty myself up for him, but he didn’t notice. _ Let’s try to pretty up this room.
examples: I tried to pretty myself up for him, but he didn’t notice.

a pretty pickle.monolingual: Fig. a difficult situation. (Pickle = a bad situation.) _ Well, this is a pretty pickle you’ve gotten us into.
examples: Well, this is a pretty pickle you’ve gotten us into.

pretty please?.monolingual: an emphasised form of please? _ Pretty please? I need an answer! _ Can I have my book back? Pretty please?

prevail against someone or something.monolingual: to win out over someone or something; to dominate someone or something. _ You will not prevail against me! _ I am sure that our team will prevail against the challengers.
examples: I am sure that our team will prevail against the challengers.

prevent someone from doing something.monolingual: to keep someone from doing something. _You can’t prevent me from doing it! _ We must try to prevent her from going back there.
examples: We must try to prevent her from going back there.

prevention is better than cure..monolingual: Prov. It is better to try to keep a bad thing from happening than it is to fix the bad thing once it has happened. _ If we spend more money on education, so that children learn to be responsible citizens, we won’t have to spend so much money on priso
examples: If we spend more money on education, so that children learn to be responsible citizens, we won’t have to spend so much money on prisons.

prey on something.monolingual: [for an animal] to feed on another animal as a matter of habit or preference. _ Owls prey on mice. _ Many birds prey on snakes.
examples: Owls prey on mice.

*a price on one’s head.monolingual: a reward for one’s capture. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; put ~; place ~.) _ We captured a thief who had a price on his head, and the sheriff gave us the reward. _ The crook was so mean, he turned in his own brother, who had a price on his head.
examples: We captured a thief who had a price on his head, and the sheriff gave us the reward.

price something down†.monolingual: to lower the price of something. _ When they start pricing this stuff down at the end of the season, I’ll come in and buy something. _ I hope to price down the merchandise soon.
examples: When they start pricing this stuff down at the end of the season, I’ll come in and buy something.

price something out.monolingual: to list and total all the component prices of goods and services for a complex project. _ I have finished listing all the materials required for the project, and now I have to price it out so that we can decide if we can afford it.
examples: I have finished listing all the materials required for the project, and now I have to price it out so that we can decide if we can afford it.

price something up†.monolingual: to raise the price of something. _They have priced oranges up so high that I can’t afford any. _ Why do they price up these common foods so high?
examples: They have priced oranges up so high that I can’t afford any.

pride and joy.monolingual: Fig. something or someone that one is very proud of. (Often in reference to a baby, a car, a house, etc. Fixed order.) _ And this is our little pride and joy, Roger. _ Fred pulled up in his pride and joy and asked if I wanted a ride.
examples: And this is our little pride and joy, Roger.

prime mover.monolingual: Fig. the force that sets something going; someone or something that starts something off. _ The assistant manager was the prime mover in getting the manager sacked. _Discontent with his job was the prime mover in John’s deciding to retire early.
examples: The assistant manager was the prime mover in getting the manager sacked.

prime something with something.monolingual: to enable something to start working or functioning with something. _ Larry primed the pump with a little water, and it began to do its work. _We will prime the market for our new product with a free coupon offer.
examples: Larry primed the pump with a little water, and it began to do its work.

the primrose path.monolingual: Fig. earthly delights that come to an end. _ She led him down the primrose path until she got tired of him.
examples: She led him down the primrose path until she got tired of him.

print something in something.monolingual: 1. to make block letters in a specific location on a paper. _ Please print your name in the box. _ Would you please print the information in the space provided?
examples: Please print your name in the box.

print something out†.monolingual: 1. to write something out by using block letters. _ Please print it out. I can’t read your handwriting. _ Print out your name, please.
examples: Please print it out.

print something up†.monolingual: to set something in type and print it; to print something by any process. _ This looks okay to me. Let’s print it up now. _ Print up the final version.
examples: This looks okay to me.

privy to something.monolingual: Fig. knowledgeable about something secret or private. _ The reporter became privy to the senator’s evil plan. _ Why are you privy to this secret information?
examples: The reporter became privy to the senator’s evil plan.

probe into something.monolingual: to investigate something. _ The police will probe into the matter and report to the commissioner. _ We will take some time and probe into that for you.
examples: The police will probe into the matter and report to the commissioner.

probe something for something.monolingual: to poke around in something for something. _ He probed his memory for some clue as to where he had been on that date. _ Sam probed the darkened space for the tool that he had mislaid.
examples: He probed his memory for some clue as to where he had been on that date.

proceed against someone or something.monolingual: 1. to begin to move against someone or something. _The entire platoon proceeded against the single enemy soldier who refused to surrender. _ The army proceeded against the fortress as planned.
examples: The entire platoon proceeded against the single enemy soldier who refused to surrender.

proceed with something.monolingual: to move ahead with something; to continue something. _ Now, we will proceed with the reading of the minutes of the last meeting. _When will you proceed with the needed action?
examples: Now, we will proceed with the reading of the minutes of the last meeting.

prod at someone or something.monolingual: to poke at someone or something. _ The boys prodded at the prone body of the man to see if he was dead or sleeping. _ If you prod at the turtle, it will never come out of its shell.
examples: The boys prodded at the prone body of the man to see if he was dead or sleeping.

prod someone into something.monolingual: to motivate someone into doing something; to provoke someone into action. _ Do I have to prod you into going? Can’t you volunteer for once? _ We will prod her into getting it done on time.
examples: We will prod her into getting it done on time.

produce something for something.monolingual: 1. to make something for some purpose. _ This production line produces brackets for the installation of the circuit boards in the next production line. _We produce the seats for the trucks that they assemble on the other side of town.
examples: This production line produces brackets for the installation of the circuit boards in the next production line.

produce something from something.monolingual: to create something from something; to make something out of something. _ We are able to produce a high-quality writing paper from the scraps we trim off the edges of the books as we bind them. _Jane produces an excellent jelly from the grapes she gr
examples: We are able to produce a high-quality writing paper from the scraps we trim off the edges of the books as we bind them.

progress to something.monolingual: to reach all the way to something or some place. _The crisis has progressed to its final stage. _ Things had progressed to a serious stage where nothing more could be done for him.
examples: The crisis has progressed to its final stage.

progress toward something.monolingual: to move partway toward some goal. _ Nancy is progressing toward her degree quite nicely. _ We are progressing toward the end of the project.
examples: Nancy is progressing toward her degree quite nicely.

progress with something.monolingual: to continue to move toward something or completing something. _ I can’t seem to progress with this project. _ How are you progressing with the building of your model ship?
examples: I can’t seem to progress with this project.

prohibit someone from something.monolingual: 1. to prevent someone from doing something. _The committee voted to prohibit people from leaving before the meeting was over. _ They prohibit anyone from being seated after the first act has started.
examples: The committee voted to prohibit people from leaving before the meeting was over.

prohibit something from something.monolingual: 1. to prevent something from happening or from doing something. _ My mother prohibits me from going out with friends on school nights. _ Why do you want to prohibit the cars from traveling on this street during rush hour?
examples: My mother prohibits me from going out with friends on school nights.

project into something.monolingual: to extend into something. _ The end of the grand piano projected into the next room, but she had to have a grand, nonetheless. _The front of the car projected into the flower bed when it was parked, but that was all right.
examples: The end of the grand piano projected into the next room, but she had to have a grand, nonetheless.

project something onto someone.monolingual: to imagine that someone else experiences one’s feelings, especially one’s guilt or anger. _ Since you project your anger onto your best friends, you imagine you have gathered a number of angry people around you. _ You should not project your feelings
examples: Since you project your anger onto your best friends, you imagine you have gathered a number of angry people around you.

promise something to someone.monolingual: to pledge something to someone. _I promised this vase to my niece. _Is this book promised to anyone?
examples: I promised this vase to my niece.

prone to something.monolingual: likely to [do] something; apt to have something. _My boss is prone to anger when my work isn’t done on schedule. _ My sister is prone to sneezing because of her allergies.
examples: My boss is prone to anger when my work isn’t done on schedule.

propose a toast.monolingual: to make a toast before a celebratory drink. _ I’d like to propose a toast in honor of your birthday. _At the wedding reception, the bride’s father proposed a toast to the new couple.
examples: I’d like to propose a toast in honor of your birthday.

propose something to someone.monolingual: to suggest something to someone. _ I have an idea I would like to propose to you. _ Sam wanted to propose a new plan to Sarah.
examples: I have an idea I would like to propose to you.

propose to someone.monolingual: to suggest marriage to someone, usually a male to a female. _ Guess who proposed to me last night? _ Do you think that Sam will propose to Mary?

prospect for something.monolingual: to search for something, especially for metals or minerals. _ The old men said they were prospecting for gold. _ What are they prospecting for out in the desert?
examples: The old men said they were prospecting for gold.

prosper from something.monolingual: to gain wealth from something. _ Carla prospered from trading on the options exchange. _ I hope you prosper from your new enterprise.
examples: Carla prospered from trading on the options exchange.

protrude from someone or something.monolingual: to stick out from someone or something. _Even in the dark, I knew he was hurt because I could see the knife protruding from him. _ A knife protruded from the victim’s back.
examples: Even in the dark, I knew he was hurt because I could see the knife protruding from him.

prove oneself as something.monolingual: to demonstrate that one can serve in a certain office or capacity. _It’s time to promote her. She has proved herself as a teller. _ I proved myself as an investor by making a lot of money in the stock market.
examples: It’s time to promote her.

prove something to someone.monolingual: to substantiate a claim about something to someone; to make someone believe or accept a statement about something. _ What do I have to do to prove my innocence to you? _Nothing you say will prove it to me.
examples: Nothing you say will prove it to me.

prove to be something.monolingual: to be shown to be someone or something; to be found to be someone or something. _ Susan proved to be a good friend when she lent me some money. _ The food proved to be spoiled when I smelled it.
examples: Susan proved to be a good friend when she lent me some money.
