provide against something.monolingual: to plan against something happening. _ Have you provided against the possible collapse of the agreement? _ We have not provided against financial disaster.
examples: We have not provided against financial disaster.

provide for someone or something.monolingual: to supply the needs of someone or something. _Don’t worry, we will provide for you. _ We will provide for the committee in the budget.
examples: Don’t worry, we will provide for you.

provide someone with something.monolingual: to supply something to someone. _ I will provide you with an escort to your car. _Jane provided herself with just enough food to get through the weekend.
examples: I will provide you with an escort to your car.

provide something under something.monolingual: to supply something in keeping with a contract, rule, guideline, agreement, etc. _ We have agreed to provide two tons of coal per month under our contract. Do you want more? _We will agree to provide ample insurance for our employees under union guid
examples: We have agreed to provide two tons of coal per month under our contract.

provided that.monolingual: on the condition that. _ I will come, provided that I am invited. _I will help you, provided that you pay me.
examples: I will come, provided that I am invited.

provoke someone into something.monolingual: to incite someone into doing something. _ The soldiers sought to provoke the demonstrators into starting a riot. _They provoked us into leaving.
examples: The soldiers sought to provoke the demonstrators into starting a riot.

prune something away†.monolingual: to cut away something unwanted or unneeded. _Please prune the lower branches of the trees away. They are starting to annoy pedestrians. _We pruned away the dead branches.
examples: Please prune the lower branches of the trees away.

prune something of something.monolingual: to clear, clean, or groom something of something by pruning. _ Sally was out in the orchard pruning the apple trees of dead branches. _ They pruned the roses of their unneeded branches.
examples: Sally was out in the orchard pruning the apple trees of dead branches.

pry around.monolingual: to sneak or prowl around looking for something. _Why are you prying around? Mind your own business! _ Please don’t pry around. You might find out something you don’t want to know.
examples: Please don’t pry around.

pry into something.monolingual: to snoop into something; to get into someone else’s business. _ Why are you prying into my affairs all the time? _I wish you wouldn’t pry into my personal life.
examples: I wish you wouldn’t pry into my personal life.

pry something up†.monolingual: to raise something with or as with a lever. _ See if you can pry that trapdoor up. _ Pry up that lid.
examples: See if you can pry that trapdoor up.

psych out.monolingual: 1. Inf. to have a nervous or emotional trauma; to go mad for a brief time. _ Another day like this one and I’ll psych out for sure. _ He looked at the bill and psyched out.
examples: Another day like this one and I’ll psych out for sure.

psych someone out†.monolingual: 1. Inf. to get someone very excited; to cause someone to lose mental control. _ Wow! What you just said really psyched me out! _ He psyched out his friends.
examples: He psyched out his friends.

psych someone up†.monolingual: Inf. to get someone excited or mentally prepared for something. _ I psyched myself up to sing in front of all those people. _ The coach psyched up the team for the game.
examples: I psyched myself up to sing in front of all those people.

psych up.monolingual: Inf. to get mentally ready for something. _I have to psych up before the big game tonight. _We want to psych up so we can play a good game.
examples: I have to psych up before the big game tonight.

publish or perish.monolingual: Fig. [for a professor] to try to publish scholarly books or articles to prevent getting released from a university or falling into disfavor in a university. (Also occurs as other parts of speech. See the examples.) _Alice knew she would have to publi
examples: Alice knew she would have to publish or perish if she took the teaching job.

pucker something up†.monolingual: to cause something to wrinkle up, especially the edges of the mouth, as when tasting something very sour. _ She puckered her lips up and pouted for a while. _ She puckered up her lips when she tasted the lemon juice.
examples: She puckered her lips up and pouted for a while.

pucker up.monolingual: 1. Lit. to tighten one’s lips together into a circle as if to kiss. _He puckered up and kissed her once, and then again.
examples: He puckered up and kissed her once, and then again.

puff along.monolingual: 1. [for someone] to run along, puffing to breathe. _Sam puffed along, jogging on his morning route. _ As Wally puffed along, he thought again about going on a diet.
examples: Sam puffed along, jogging on his morning route.

puff out.monolingual: to swell out. _ The frog’s throat puffed out, and we expected to hear a croak. _ The sail puffed out, and the boat began to move.
examples: The frog’s throat puffed out, and we expected to hear a croak.

puff someone or something up†.monolingual: to boost or promote someone or something. _Judy puffed Nell up so much that Nell could not begin to live up to her reputation. _ Don’t puff up your own accomplishments so much.
examples: Judy puffed Nell up so much that Nell could not begin to live up to her reputation.

puff something out†.monolingual: to cause something to swell out or expand outward. _ The frog puffed its throat out and croaked. _ The frog puffed out its throat and croaked a mighty croak.
examples: The frog puffed its throat out and croaked.

puff up.monolingual: to swell up. _Her finger puffed up and she thought she might have an infection. _ His eyelids had puffed up during the night.
examples: Her finger puffed up and she thought she might have an infection.

pull a boner.monolingual: Inf. to do something stupid or silly. _ Boy, I really pulled a boner! I’m so dumb. _ If you pull a boner like that again, you’re fired!
examples: Boy, I really pulled a boner! I’m so dumb.

pull a fast one.monolingual: Inf. to succeed in an act of deception. _ She was pulling a fast one when she said she had a headache and went home. _ Don’t try to pull a fast one with me! I know what you’re doing.
examples: She was pulling a fast one when she said she had a headache and went home.

pull a job.monolingual: Sl. to carry out a crime, especially a robbery. (Police and underworld. Note the variations in the examples.) _Richard decided that it was not a good time to pull a bank job. _Willie and Richard left town after they pulled the job.
examples: Richard decided that it was not a good time to pull a bank job.

pull a muscle.monolingual: to strain a muscle and suffer the attendant pain. _ I pulled a muscle in my back and can’t play golf today.
examples: I pulled a muscle in my back and can’t play golf today.

pull all the stops out†.monolingual: Fig. to use everything available; to not hold back. (Alludes to pulling out all of the stops on an organ so that it will sound as loud as possible.) _ The mayor decided to pull out all the stops and campaign in every district. _Todd pulled all the st
examples: The mayor decided to pull out all the stops and campaign in every district.

pull around to something.monolingual: to drive around to something or some place. _Please pull around to the back and deliver the furniture there. _ We told the driver to pull around to the service entrance.
examples: Please pull around to the back and deliver the furniture there.

pull at someone.monolingual: to vie for someone’s attention or concern. _ There are too many demands pulling at me. I need to cut down on my responsibilities. _ I don’t see how I can function with so many different things pulling at me.
examples: There are too many demands pulling at me.

pull at someone or something.monolingual: to tug at someone or something. _ The child kept pulling at her mother to get her attention. _ Don’t keep pulling at your hair. It will come out.
examples: The child kept pulling at her mother to get her attention.

pull for someone or something.monolingual: to support and cheer for someone, a group, or something. _We’re pulling for you. We know you can do it! _ All the students were pulling for the team.
examples: We’re pulling for you.

pull in one’s ears.monolingual: Fig. to stop listening in on someone or something. (The opposite of prick up one’s ears.) _Now, pull in your ears. This is none of your business. _ Pull in your ears and mind your own business.
examples: Now, pull in your ears.

pull in some place.monolingual: [for a wheeled vehicle] to steer or drive to a point off the main route. _ Let’s pull in at the next motel and get some rest. _I want to pull in at a service station and have my tires checked.
examples: Let’s pull in at the next motel and get some rest.

pull on something.monolingual: to tug something. _I pulled on the rope, hoping to get it loose. _ Please help me pull on the anchor chain so we can raise the anchor.
examples: I pulled on the rope, hoping to get it loose.

pull one over on someone.monolingual: to deceive someone. _ Don’t try to trick me! You can’t pull one over on me.
examples: Don’t try to trick me! You can’t pull one over on me.

pull one’s punches.monolingual: 1. [for a boxer] to strike with light blows to enable the other boxer to win. _ Bill has been barred from the boxing ring for pulling his punches. _ “I never pulled punches in my life!” cried Tom.
examples: Bill has been barred from the boxing ring for pulling his punches.

pull oneself together.monolingual: 1. Fig. to compose oneself; to gather one’s wits about one. _ I have to pull myself together and try it again. _ Now try to pull yourself together and get through this crisis.
examples: I have to pull myself together and try it again.

pull someone about.monolingual: 1. Lit. to drag someone around. _ The boys were pulling one another about and playing very rough. _ Don’t pull your little brother about so!
examples: The boys were pulling one another about and playing very rough.

pull someone apart.monolingual: 1. Lit. to separate people who are entangled. _The teacher pulled the fighting boys apart and sent them home. _ They hugged each other so tightly that no one could have pulled them apart.
examples: The teacher pulled the fighting boys apart and sent them home.

pull someone aside†.monolingual: to grasp and pull a person to one side. _I pulled the child aside and scolded him for trying to sneak into the theater. _ I pulled aside the child to say something to him.
examples: I pulled the child aside and scolded him for trying to sneak into the theater.

pull someone down†.monolingual: Fig. to degrade someone; to humiliate someone. _ I’m afraid that your so-called friends are pulling you down behind your back. _ There is no need to pull down everyone.
examples: I’m afraid that your so-called friends are pulling you down behind your back.

pull someone or something apart†.monolingual: to separate or dismember someone or something. _The murderer pulled his victim apart and sought to dispose of the parts. _ He pulled apart his victim. _ Nick pulled the parts of the box apart.
examples: The murderer pulled his victim apart and sought to dispose of the parts.

pull someone or something around†.monolingual: to drag or haul someone or something around. _ The woman had pulled her children around all day while she did the shopping. All of them were glad to get home. _ Nick pulled around his wagon and collected discarded aluminum cans.
examples: The woman had pulled her children around all day while she did the shopping.

pull someone or something under.monolingual: 1. Lit. to drag someone or something beneath the surface of something. _ The strong undertow pulled John under the surface. _ The whirlpool nearly pulled the boat under.
examples: The strong undertow pulled John under the surface.

pull someone or something up†.monolingual: to drag or haul someone or something upward or to an upright position. _ Bob had slipped down into the creek, so I reached down and pulled him up. _I pulled up Bob and nearly fell in myself. _Nick pulled the cushion up and propped it against the back
examples: Bob had slipped down into the creek, so I reached down and pulled him up.

pull someone’s leg.monolingual: Fig. to kid, fool, or trick someone. _ You don’t mean that. You’re just pulling my leg. _ Don’t believe him. He’s just pulling your leg.
examples: You don’t mean that.

pull someone’s or something’s teeth.monolingual: Fig. to reduce the power or efficacy of someone or something. _ The mayor tried to pull the teeth of the new law. _ The city council pulled the teeth of the new mayor.
examples: The mayor tried to pull the teeth of the new law.

pull someone up short.monolingual: to cause someone to stop short. _ My scream pulled him up short. _The sudden thought that everything might not be all right pulled Tom up short.
examples: My scream pulled him up short.

pull something down†.monolingual: 1. to demolish something; to raze something. _Why do they want to pull the building down? Why not remodel it? _ They are going to pull down the old building today.
examples: They are going to pull down the old building today.

pull something on†.monolingual: to draw on an article of clothing. _ He pulled his pants on. _ He pulled on his pants quickly and ran outside while putting on his shirt.
examples: He pulled his pants on.

pull something on someone.monolingual: to play a trick on someone; to deceive someone with a trick. (The word something is often used.) _You wouldn’t pull a trick on me, would you? _ Who would pull something like that on an old lady?

pull something out of someone.monolingual: to draw or force information out of someone. _The cops finally pulled a confession out of Max. _ I thought I would never pull her name out of her.
examples: The cops finally pulled a confession out of Max.

pull something to.monolingual: to close something, usually a door of some type. _ The door is open a little. Pull it to so no one will hear us. _ Please pull the door to.
examples: The door is open a little.

pull something together.monolingual: 1. Lit. to close something, such as a pair of drapes or sliding doors. _Please pull the doors together when you finish in the closet. _Would you pull the drapes together before you turn on the lights?
examples: Please pull the doors together when you finish in the closet.

pull something toward oneself.monolingual: to draw something closer to oneself. _ He pulled his plate toward himself and began eating like a starving man. _Mary pulled the basket of fruit toward herself and chose a nice juicy peach.
examples: He pulled his plate toward himself and began eating like a starving man.

pull up a chair..monolingual: Please get a chair and sit down and join us. (Assumes that there is seating available. The speaker does not necessarily mean that the person spoken to actually has to move a chair.) _Tom: Well, hello, Bob! Bob: Hi, Tom. Pull up a chair. _The three me
examples: Tom: Well, hello, Bob! Bob: Hi, Tom.

pull up stakes.monolingual: 1. Lit. to pull up tent stakes to take down a tent in preparation to leaving. _ Let’s pull up stakes and head home before the storm hits.
examples: Let’s pull up stakes and head home before the storm hits.

pull up to something.monolingual: to drive up close to something. _ I pulled up to the drive-in window and placed my order. _ When the taxi pulls up to the curb, open the door and get in.
examples: I pulled up to the drive-in window and placed my order.

pulse through someone or something.monolingual: to flow or surge through someone or something. _ A jolt of electricity pulsed through Sam, causing him to jerk his hand away from the wire. _ They repaired the power lines and electricity began to pulse through the wires again.
examples: A jolt of electricity pulsed through Sam, causing him to jerk his hand away from the wire.

pump someone for something.monolingual: Inf. to try to get information about something out of someone. _ The representative of the other company pumped Harry for information, but he refused to say anything. _ Are you trying to pump me for company secrets?
examples: The representative of the other company pumped Harry for information, but he refused to say anything.

pump something through something.monolingual: to force something, such as a gas or fluid, through something. _They pumped crude oil through this pipeline, all the way to the south shore. _They pumped fresh air through the sewers while the workers were working inside.
examples: They pumped crude oil through this pipeline, all the way to the south shore.

pump something up†.monolingual: 1. to inflate something. _ Do you have something with which I can pump my basketball up? _ I pumped up the ball just an hour ago.
examples: I pumped up the ball just an hour ago.

punch a hole in something.monolingual: to make a hole in something with something. _John punched a hole in the wall with his fist. _ Mary punched a hole in the paper with her pencil.
examples: John punched a hole in the wall with his fist.

punch in.monolingual: to record one’s arrival at one’s workplace at a certain time. _ What time did you punch in? _ I punched in at the regular time.
examples: I punched in at the regular time.

punch out.monolingual: to record that one has left one’s workplace at a certain time. _ Why didn’t you punch out when you left last night? _ I punched out at the regular time.
examples: I punched out at the regular time.

punch someone in something.monolingual: to strike someone in some body part. _Tony punched Nick in the side. _Why didn’t you punch that mean guy in the nose?
examples: Tony punched Nick in the side.

punch someone on something.monolingual: to strike someone on some body part, typically the shoulder. (Not with the intention of causing harm.) _ Sally punched Frank on the shoulder just to show they were still friends. _Tom punched Fred on the shoulder in a friendly way.
examples: Sally punched Frank on the shoulder just to show they were still friends.

punch someone out†.monolingual: Sl. to overcome or beat someone by punching. _ He threatened to punch me out. _ The thug punched out the cop and ran down an alley.
examples: He threatened to punch me out.

punch someone’s lights out.monolingual: Sl. to knock someone out with a fist. _You had better stop that, or I will punch your lights out! _ Do you want me to punch your lights out?

punch something down†.monolingual: to press something down. _ Punch this lever down and then try to place your telephone call. _ Punch down this lever and push this button.
examples: Punch this lever down and then try to place your telephone call.

punch something in†.monolingual: to crush or smash something in. _ Who punched the cereal box in? _ Who punched in the cereal box?

punch something into something.monolingual: to stick or press something into something. _She punched her finger into the cake and ruined my lovely icing job. _ He finally punched a spoon into the cereal box to get it open.
examples: She punched her finger into the cake and ruined my lovely icing job.

punch something up†.monolingual: to register a figure on a cash register or calculator. _Jake punched the total up, and the register drawer opened. _ He punched up the total too carelessly.
examples: Jake punched the total up, and the register drawer opened.

punctuate something with something.monolingual: 1. to add a particular punctuation mark to a piece of writing. _ You have punctuated this ad with too many exclamation points. _ This letter is punctuated with dashes to emphasize the key points.
examples: You have punctuated this ad with too many exclamation points.

punish someone by something.monolingual: to discipline someone by doing something. _The headmaster punished the children by forcing them to go to bed early. _ She punished herself by not eating.
examples: The headmaster punished the children by forcing them to go to bed early.

punish someone for something.monolingual: to discipline someone for [doing] something. _ Someone will punish you for what you did. _ Please don’t punish me for doing it. I’m sorry.
examples: Someone will punish you for what you did.

punish someone with something.monolingual: to use something to discipline someone. _ The captain punished the sailor with the lash. _Sally threatened to punish Timmy with a spanking.
examples: The captain punished the sailor with the lash.

punk out.monolingual: Sl. to chicken out (of something); to withdraw from something in cowardice. _He was supposed to ask her out, but he punked out at the last minute. _ Come on! Stick with it! Don’t punk out!
examples: He was supposed to ask her out, but he punked out at the last minute.

puppy love.monolingual: Fig. mild infatuation; infatuation as in a crush. (Used especially of adolescent relationships.) _Is it really love or just puppy love? _ Look at them together. It may be puppy love, but it looks wonderful.
examples: Look at them together.

purchase something for someone.monolingual: to buy something for someone else; to buy something to give to someone. _ Tony purchased a number of toys for the children in the orphanage. _ Who did you purchase this gift for?
examples: Tony purchased a number of toys for the children in the orphanage.

*pure as the driven snow.monolingual: pure and chaste. (Often used ironically. *Also: as ~.) _Jill: Sue must have gone to bed with every man in town. Jane: And I always thought she was as pure as the driven snow. _ Robert was notoriously promiscuous, but tried to convince all his girlfri
examples: Jill: Sue must have gone to bed with every man in town.

purge something away†.monolingual: to wash or flush something away. _We will purge the rusty water away and then start up the pump again. We will have fresh, clean water again in no time. _ Laura purged away the rusty water.
examples: We will purge the rusty water away and then start up the pump again.

purse something up†.monolingual: to bunch or pucker something up. (Usually the lips.) _ When he tasted the lemon juice, he pursed his lips up and spat it out. _ Don pursed up his lips as if to spit it out.
examples: When he tasted the lemon juice, he pursed his lips up and spat it out.

push along.monolingual: to move along; to travel along as with a purpose. _We must push along. We have a long way to travel before morning. _ They pushed along at a steady clip until they arrived at their destination.
examples: We must push along.

push at someone or something.monolingual: to apply pressure to and try to move someone or something. _She pushed at him, trying to get him to get out of the way, but he wouldn’t budge. _ Mary pushed at the door, trying to open it against the wind. _ There is no need for you to push at me so
examples: She pushed at him, trying to get him to get out of the way, but he wouldn’t budge.

push down on something.monolingual: to press down on something, such as a button, stamp, lever, etc. _ Push down on this button if you want room service. _ Don’t push down on the door handle too hard. It will break. push push for something to request or demand something. _ The citizens
examples: Push down on this button if you want room service.

push forward.monolingual: to move forward; to move onward toward a goal. _We have lots to do. We must push forward! _They are pushing forward, hoping to complete the project on time.
examples: We have lots to do.

push on someone or something.monolingual: to put pressure on someone or something. _Don’t push on me! I can’t move any faster than the person in front of me! _ Push on this button if you want the steward to come. _ Push on the door a little. It will open.
examples: Push on this button if you want the steward to come.

push out.monolingual: to spread out; to expand outward. _ The sides of the box pushed out, and I was afraid it would break. _ His little tummy pushed out when he was full.
examples: The sides of the box pushed out, and I was afraid it would break.

push someone around.monolingual: Fig. to harass someone physically; to jostle someone. _ I wish you would stop pushing me around all the time. _ Stop pushing Max around if you know what’s good for you.
examples: I wish you would stop pushing me around all the time.

push someone or something along.monolingual: to apply pressure to move someone or something along. _ The mother tried to push her child along, but he wouldn’t go. _ Jane pushed the cart along, down the supermarket aisle.
examples: The mother tried to push her child along, but he wouldn’t go.

push someone or something aside†.monolingual: to shove someone or something to one side. _ Martha pushed Bill aside and went in ahead of him. _ He pushed aside the papers and laid his books on the desk.
examples: Martha pushed Bill aside and went in ahead of him.

push someone or something down†.monolingual: to force someone or something downward. _Every time he tried to get up, the other boys pushed him down again. _ I pushed down the button and the machine began to operate.
examples: Every time he tried to get up, the other boys pushed him down again.

push someone or something forward.monolingual: to shove or move someone or something to the front. _ Mary’s mother pushed her forward where she would be seen. _Let me push the piano bench forward for you.
examples: Mary’s mother pushed her forward where she would be seen.

push someone or something over†.monolingual: to make someone or something fall over or fall down. _When you ran into me, you nearly pushed me over. _ You nearly pushed over your friend.
examples: When you ran into me, you nearly pushed me over.

push someone or something up†.monolingual: to raise or lift someone or something. _ Jake is sliding down again. Push him up. _ Push up the window, please.
examples: Jake is sliding down again.

push someone to something.monolingual: to try to drive or force a person to do something. _ After the bankruptcy the board pushed the president to resign. _ We pushed her to reconsider, but her mind was made up.
examples: After the bankruptcy the board pushed the president to resign.

push someone too far.monolingual: Fig. to antagonize someone too much; to be too confrontational with someone. _ I guess I pushed him too far, because he began shouting at me and threatening to hit me.
examples: I guess I pushed him too far, because he began shouting at me and threatening to hit me.

push something in†.monolingual: to crush something in; to make something cave in. _ He ran at the door and pushed it in. _ He pushed in the door.
examples: He ran at the door and pushed it in.

push something to.monolingual: to close or nearly close something, such as a door. _ The door is open a little. Please push it to. _ Todd came in and pushed the door to.
examples: The door is open a little.

push the envelope.monolingual: Fig. to expand the definition, categorization, dimensions, or perimeters of something. _ The engineers wanted to completely redesign the product, but couldn’t push the envelope because of a very restricted budget.
examples: The engineers wanted to completely redesign the product, but couldn’t push the envelope because of a very restricted budget.

push toward someone or something.monolingual: to move or struggle toward someone or something. _ The crowd pushed toward the convicted man, but the police held them back. _ The horses pushed toward the corral gate.
examples: The crowd pushed toward the convicted man, but the police held them back.

push up on something.monolingual: to raise something upward; to push something up from below. _Larry pushed up on the trapdoor and lifted it so he could climb out. _ Push up on this lever if you want the lights to get brighter.
examples: Larry pushed up on the trapdoor and lifted it so he could climb out.

pussyfoot around.monolingual: Fig. to go about timidly and cautiously. (Alludes to a cat walking carefully.) _Stop pussyfooting around! Get on with it! _I wish that they would not pussyfoot around when there are tough decisions to be made.
examples: I wish that they would not pussyfoot around when there are tough decisions to be made.

put a cap on something.monolingual: Fig. to put a limit on something. _ We need to put a cap on spending in every department. _ The city put a cap on the amount each landlord could charge.
examples: We need to put a cap on spending in every department.

put a damper on something.monolingual: Fig. to have a dulling or numbing influence on something. _ The bad news really put a damper on everything. _ The rainy weather put a damper on our picnic.
examples: The bad news really put a damper on everything.

put a hold on something.monolingual: to place restriction on something so that it is reserved, delayed, or inactivated. _ The bank put a hold on my credit card until I paid my bill. _The committee agreed to put a hold on the troublesome piece of business.
examples: The bank put a hold on my credit card until I paid my bill.

put a premium on something.monolingual: to make something harder or more expensive to obtain or do. _ The recent action of the bank directors put a premium on new home loans. _ The scarcity of steel put a premium on the cost of new cars.
examples: The recent action of the bank directors put a premium on new home loans.

put a spin on something.monolingual: to twist a report or story to one’s advantage; to interpret an event to make it seem favorable or beneficial to oneself or one’s cause. _ The mayor tried to put a positive spin on the damaging polls. _ The pundit’s spin on the new legislation was hig
examples: The mayor tried to put a positive spin on the damaging polls.

put an animal down†.monolingual: Euph. to take the life of an animal mercifully. _We put down our old dog last year. _It’s kind to put fatally ill animals down.
examples: We put down our old dog last year.

put an animal out†.monolingual: to send an animal, such as a pet, outdoors. _ Did you put the cat out? _ Yes, I put out the cat.
examples: Yes, I put out the cat.

put balls on something.monolingual: Sl. to make something more masculine or powerful; to give something authority and strength. (Potentially offensive. Use only with discretion.) _ Come on, sing louder. Put some balls on it. _ This story is too namby-pamby. Put some balls on it.
examples: Come on, sing louder.

put hair on someone’s chest.monolingual: Fig. to do or take something to invigorate or energize someone, always a male, except in jest. _ Here, have a drink of this stuff! It’ll put hair on your chest. _ That stuff is powerful. It will really put hair on your chest.
examples: Here, have a drink of this stuff! It’ll put hair on your chest.

put ideas into someone’s head.monolingual: Fig. to suggest something— usually something bad—to someone (who would not have thought of it otherwise). _Bill keeps getting into trouble. Please don’t put ideas into his head. _ Bob would get along all right if other kids didn’t put ideas into his
examples: Bill keeps getting into trouble.

put in for something.monolingual: to apply for something; to make a request for something. _ I put in for a transfer, but I bet I don’t get it. _She put in for a new file cabinet, but she never got one.
examples: I put in for a transfer, but I bet I don’t get it.

put on an act.monolingual: to pretend that one is something other than what one is. _ Be yourself, Ann. Stop putting on an act. _ You don’t have to put on an act. We accept you the way you are.
examples: Be yourself, Ann.

put on weight.monolingual: to gain weight; to get fat. _ I think I am putting on a little weight. I had better go on a diet. _ He has put on a lot of weight since last year.
examples: I think I am putting on a little weight.

put one in one’s place.monolingual: to rebuke someone; to remind one of one’s (lower) rank or station. _ The boss put me in my place for criticizing her. _Then her boss put her in her place for being rude.
examples: The boss put me in my place for criticizing her.

put one off one’s stride.monolingual: 1. Lit. to cause one to deviate from a rhythmic stride while walking, running, or marching. _A rabbit ran across the path and put me off my stride.
examples: A rabbit ran across the path and put me off my stride.

put one on one’s guard.monolingual: to make one wary or cautious. _ The menacing growl by the watchdog put me on my guard. _ Every time the boss comes around, it puts me on my guard.
examples: The menacing growl by the watchdog put me on my guard.

put one on one’s honor.monolingual: Fig. to inform one that one is trusted to act honorably, legally, and fairly without supervision. _ I’ll put you on your honor when I have to leave the room during the test. _They put us on our honor to take no more than we had paid for.
examples: I’ll put you on your honor when I have to leave the room during the test.

put one’s best foot forward.monolingual: Fig. to act or appear at one’s best; to try to make a good impression. _When you apply for a job, you should always put your best foot forward. _ I try to put my best foot forward whenever I meet someone for the first time.
examples: When you apply for a job, you should always put your best foot forward.

put one’s dibs on something.monolingual: to lay a claim to something; to announce one’s claim to something. _ She put her dibs on the last piece of cake. _ I put my dibs on the seat by the window.
examples: She put her dibs on the last piece of cake.

put one’s face on.monolingual: Fig. [for a woman] to apply cosmetics. _ Martha’s gone to put her face on. _ We’ll be on our way once my wife has put her face on.
examples: Martha’s gone to put her face on.

put one’s feet up†.monolingual: to sit down, lean back, and rest; to lie down. _He was really exhausted and had to go put his feet up. _ Time to put up my feet and get some rest.
examples: He was really exhausted and had to go put his feet up.

put one’s finger on something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to touch something with one’s finger. _ I put my finger on the button and pressed. _ Put your finger on this spot and push hard.
examples: I put my finger on the button and pressed.

put one’s hair up†.monolingual: to arrange one’s hair into a ponytail, bun, etc. (with curlers, hairpins, etc.). _ I can’t go out because I just put my hair up. _ I put up my hair every night.
examples: I can’t go out because I just put my hair up.

put one’s hand up†.monolingual: to raise one’s hand to get attention from whomever is in charge. _ The student put his hand up to ask a question of the teacher. _ She put up her hand to ask a question.
examples: The student put his hand up to ask a question of the teacher.

put one’s house in order.monolingual: Fig. to put one’s business or personal affairs into good order. (As if one were cleaning one’s house. See also put one’s own house in order.) _ There was some trouble in the department office and the manager was told to put his house in order. _ Ever
examples: There was some trouble in the department office and the manager was told to put his house in order.

put one’s thinking cap on†.monolingual: Fig. to start thinking in a serious manner. (Usually used with children.) _ It’s time to put our thinking caps on, children. _ All right now, let’s put on our thinking caps and do some arithmetic.
examples: It’s time to put our thinking caps on, children.

put oneself out.monolingual: to inconvenience oneself. _ I just don’t know why I put myself out for you! _ No, I did not put myself out at all. It was no trouble, in fact.
examples: No, I did not put myself out at all.

put out.monolingual: to generate [lots of something]. _ What a great machine. It really puts out! _ The new laser printer really puts out!
examples: What a great machine.

put paid to something.monolingual: to consider something closed or completed; to mark or indicate that something is no longer important or pending. (As if one were stamping a bill “paid”.) _ At last, we were able to put paid to the matter of who is to manage the accounts.
examples: At last, we were able to put paid to the matter of who is to manage the accounts.

put people or things together.monolingual: to join or combine people or things. _We will put Sam and Trudy together at the dinner table. _ Let’s put all the crystal goblets together.
examples: We will put Sam and Trudy together at the dinner table.

put people’s heads together.monolingual: to join together with someone to confer. _ Let’s put our heads together and come up with a solution to this problem. _ Mary and Ted put their heads together, but failed to provide anything new.
examples: Let’s put our heads together and come up with a solution to this problem.

put pressure on something.monolingual: to apply weight or pressure to something. _Put pressure on the wound to stop the bleeding. _Put some pressure on the papers to f latten them out.
examples: Put pressure on the wound to stop the bleeding.

put some teeth into something.monolingual: Fig. to increase the power or efficacy of something. _ The mayor tried to put some teeth into the new law. _The delivery clause in the contract is too weak. Put some teeth into it.
examples: The mayor tried to put some teeth into the new law.

put someone off†.monolingual: 1. to delay dealing with someone until a later time. _ I hate to keep putting you off, but we are not ready to deal with you yet. _ I had to put off the plumber again. He really wants his money.
examples: I hate to keep putting you off, but we are not ready to deal with you yet.

put someone off the scent.monolingual: Fig. to distract someone or a group from following a scent or trail. (From put a dog off the scent; the scent or trail can be purely figurative. _The clever maneuvers of the bandits put the sheriff ’s posse off the scent. _The mob laundered the drug
examples: The clever maneuvers of the bandits put the sheriff ’s posse off the scent.

put someone on hold.monolingual: Fig. to stop all activity or communication with someone. _John put Ann on hold and started dating Mary. _ “You can’t just put me on hold!” cried Ann.
examples: John put Ann on hold and started dating Mary.

put someone on the spot.monolingual: Fig. to ask someone forthright questions; to demand that someone produce as expected. _ Don’t put me on the spot. I can’t give you an instant answer. _The boss put Bob on the spot and demanded that he do everything he had promised.
examples: Don’t put me on the spot.

put someone or something forward.monolingual: 1. Lit. to move someone or something forward. _The director put all the players forward during the last scene, leaving more room for the chorus to come on for the finale. _ Could you put your left foot forward a little?
examples: The director put all the players forward during the last scene, leaving more room for the chorus to come on for the finale.

put someone or something over.monolingual: to succeed in making someone or something be accepted. _ The public relations expert helped put John over to the public. _ Do you think we can put this new product over?
examples: The public relations expert helped put John over to the public.

put someone out†.monolingual: to distress or inconvenience someone. _ I’d like to have a ride home, but not if it puts you out. _ Don’t worry. It won’t put out anybody.
examples: I’d like to have a ride home, but not if it puts you out.

put someone out to pasture.monolingual: Fig. to retire someone. (Based on put a horse out to pasture.) _ Please don’t put me out to pasture. I have lots of good years left. _ This vice president has reached retirement age. It’s time to put him out to pasture.
examples: Please don’t put me out to pasture.

put someone’s eye out†.monolingual: to puncture or harm someone’s eye and destroy its ability to see. _ Careful with that stick or you’ll put your eye out. _ He fell on a stick and almost put out his eye!
examples: Careful with that stick or you’ll put your eye out.

put someone through something.monolingual: to cause someone to have to endure something. _The doctor said he hated to put me through all these tests, but that it was medically necessary.
examples: The doctor said he hated to put me through all these tests, but that it was medically necessary.

put someone through the wringer.monolingual: Fig. to give someone a difficult time; to interrogate someone thoroughly. (Alludes to putting something through an old-fashioned clothes wringer.) _ The lawyer really put the witness through the wringer! _ The teacher put the students through the wri
examples: The teacher put the students through the wringer.

put someone to shame.monolingual: 1. to embarrass someone; to make someone ashamed. _ I put him to shame by telling everyone about his bad behavior.
examples: I put him to shame by telling everyone about his bad behavior.

put someone to sleep.monolingual: to bore someone. _ That dull lecture put me to sleep. _Her long story just put me to sleep.
examples: That dull lecture put me to sleep.

put someone under.monolingual: Fig. to anesthetize someone. _ They put him under with ether. _ After you put her under, we will begin the operation.
examples: They put him under with ether.

put someone up†.monolingual: to provide lodging for someone. _I hope I can find someone to put me up. _ They were able to put up John for the night.
examples: I hope I can find someone to put me up.

put someone up against someone.monolingual: to place someone into competition with someone else. _ The coach put his best wrestler up against the champ from the other team. _ The varsity put themselves up against the alumni team in a game to benefit charity.
examples: The coach put his best wrestler up against the champ from the other team.

put someone up to something.monolingual: to cause someone to do something; to give someone the idea of doing something. _ Who put you up to throwing the party? _ Nobody put me up to it. I thought it up myself.
examples: Nobody put me up to it.

put someone up with someone.monolingual: to house someone with someone. _ I will put her up with my cousin, who has an extra bedroom. _ We will put up the lady with us.
examples: I will put her up with my cousin, who has an extra bedroom.

put something aside†.monolingual: to set or place something to the side. _ I put the magazine aside and began reading a book. _ Put aside your work for a minute and listen to what I have to tell you.
examples: I put the magazine aside and began reading a book.

put something at a premium.monolingual: to make something available only at an extra cost or through extra effort. _ The scarcity of fresh vegetables at this time of year puts broccoli at a premium. _ The high demand for apples puts them at a premium.
examples: The scarcity of fresh vegetables at this time of year puts broccoli at a premium.

put something at an amount.monolingual: to price something at a certain amount of money; to estimate something at a certain figure. _ I would put the charges at about two hundred dollars. _ She put the damages at nearly two hundred thousand dollars.
examples: I would put the charges at about two hundred dollars.

put something away†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to return something to its proper storage place. _ When you are finished with the hammer, please put it away. Don’t leave it out. _ Put away this mess!
examples: When you are finished with the hammer, please put it away.

put something behind one.monolingual: Fig. to try to forget about something. _ I look forward to putting all my problems behind me. _ She will be happier when all this can be put behind her.
examples: I look forward to putting all my problems behind me.

put something forward†.monolingual: to state an idea; to advance an idea. _ Toward the end of the meeting, Sally put an idea forward. _ He put several suggestions forward.
examples: Toward the end of the meeting, Sally put an idea forward.

put something in a nutshell.monolingual: Fig. to state something very concisely. (Alludes to the small size of a nutshell and the amount that it would hold.) _The explanation is long and involved, but let me put it in a nutshell for you. _ To put it in a nutshell: you are fired!
examples: The explanation is long and involved, but let me put it in a nutshell for you.

put something in mothballs.monolingual: 1. Lit. to put something into storage in mothballs. _ He put his winter coat in storage with mothballs each fall and had to air it out for a week each spring.
examples: He put his winter coat in storage with mothballs each fall and had to air it out for a week each spring.

put something in quotes.monolingual: to put quotation marks around writing or printing. _Please put this word in quotes, since it means something special the way you have used it here. _ They put it in quotes so people would know it means something different.
examples: Please put this word in quotes, since it means something special the way you have used it here.

put something into practice.monolingual: to make a suggested procedure the actual procedure. _ That is a good policy. I suggest you put it into practice immediately. _I plan to put the new technique into practice as soon as I can.
examples: That is a good policy.

put something into words.monolingual: Fig. to form an idea into sentences that can be spoken or written. _ I find it hard to put my thoughts into words. _ She put it into words quite nicely.
examples: I find it hard to put my thoughts into words.

put something off†.monolingual: to postpone something; to schedule something for a later time. _ I have to put off our meeting until a later time. _I put off a visit to the dentist as long as I could.
examples: I have to put off our meeting until a later time.

put something on hold.monolingual: to postpone something; to stop the progress of something. _They put the project on hold until they got enough money to finish it. _ Sorry, but we must put your plan on hold.
examples: They put the project on hold until they got enough money to finish it.

put something on paper.monolingual: Fig. to write something down. _ You have a great idea for a novel. Now put it on paper. _ I’m sorry, I can’t discuss your offer until I see something in writing. Put it on paper, and then we’ll talk.
examples: You have a great idea for a novel.

put something on the cuff.monolingual: Fig. to buy something on credit; to add to one’s credit balance. _I’ll take two of those, and please put them on the cuff. _I’m sorry, Tom. We can’t put anything more on the cuff.
examples: I’ll take two of those, and please put them on the cuff.

put something on the map.monolingual: Fig. to make some place famous or popular. _ The good food you serve here will really put this place on the map. _Nothing like a little scandal to put an otherwise sleepy town on the map.
examples: The good food you serve here will really put this place on the map.

put something on the street.monolingual: Sl. to tell something openly; to spread news. _ There is no need to put all this gossip on the street. Keep it to yourself. _ Now, please don’t put this on the street, but I am going to get married.
examples: There is no need to put all this gossip on the street.

put something out†.monolingual: 1. to emit something. _ The factory put a lot of fumes out. _It put out nasty fumes.
examples: The factory put a lot of fumes out.

put something over†.monolingual: to accomplish something; to put something across. _ This is a very hard thing to explain to a large audience. I hope I can put over the main points. _This is a big request for money. I go before the board of directors this afternoon, and I hope I can
examples: This is a very hard thing to explain to a large audience.

put something plainly.monolingual: to state something firmly and explicitly. _ To put it plainly, I want you out of this house immediately. _ Thank you. I think you’ve put your feelings quite plainly.
examples: To put it plainly, I want you out of this house immediately.

put something to bed.monolingual: Fig. to complete work on something and send it on to the next step in production, especially in publishing. (From put someone to bed.) _ This week’s edition is finished. Let’s put it to bed. _ Finish the editing of this book and put it to bed.
examples: This week’s edition is finished.

put something together.monolingual: 1. Lit. to assemble something. _ How long will it take to put dinner together? _ This model was put together incorrectly.
examples: This model was put together incorrectly.

put something up†.monolingual: 1. to build a building, a sign, a fence, a wall, etc. _ We’ll put a garage up next month. _ The city put up a fence next to our house.
examples: We’ll put a garage up next month.

put the arm on someone.monolingual: Fig. to apply pressure to someone. _ John’s been putting the arm on Mary to get her to go out with him. _ John has been putting the arm on Bill to get him to cooperate.
examples: John’s been putting the arm on Mary to get her to go out with him.

put the brakes on someone.monolingual: Fig. to block someone’s activities; to cause someone to stop doing something. (Based on put the brakes on something.) _ The boss put the brakes on Gerald, who was trying too aggressively to get promoted. _ We are going to have to put the brakes on yo
examples: The boss put the brakes on Gerald, who was trying too aggressively to get promoted.

put the brakes on something.monolingual: to halt or impede some process. _ The manager had to put the brakes on the Wilson project due to lack of funds. _We will put the brakes on this project because it is costing too much money.
examples: The manager had to put the brakes on the Wilson project due to lack of funds.

put the heat on†.monolingual: to turn on central heating; to increase the amount of heat in a room or house. _ It’s going to get cold tonight. I’d better put the heat on. _ Let’s put on the heat to take off the chill.
examples: It’s going to get cold tonight.

put the squeeze on someone.monolingual: Inf. to attempt to get money out of someone. _ The mob put the squeeze on all the merchants, threatening to break their windows if they didn’t pay. _ Are you trying to put the squeeze on me for more money?
examples: The mob put the squeeze on all the merchants, threatening to break their windows if they didn’t pay.

put to it.monolingual: strained or exhausted. _ Man, I’m really put to it! What a day! _ John was put to it to get there on time.
examples: John was put to it to get there on time.

put two and two together.monolingual: to figure something out from the information available. _Well, I put two and two together and came up with an idea of who did it. _ Don’t worry. John won’t figure it out. He can’t put two and two together.
examples: Well, I put two and two together and came up with an idea of who did it.

put up one’s dukes.monolingual: Fig. to be prepared to fight. _ He’s telling you to put up your dukes. _ Put up your dukes and be a man!
examples: He’s telling you to put up your dukes.

put up or shut up!.monolingual: 1. Inf. a command to prove something or stop talking about it; Do something or stop promising to do it! _I’m tired of your telling everyone how fast you can run. Now, do it! Put up or shut up! _ Now’s your chance to show us that you can run as fast a
examples: I’m tired of your telling everyone how fast you can run.

put upon by someone.monolingual: to be made use of to an unreasonable degree. (Typically passive.) _My mother was always put upon by her neighbors. She was too nice to refuse their requests for help. _ Jane feels put upon by her live-in mother-in-law.
examples: My mother was always put upon by her neighbors.

put weight on†.monolingual: Fig. to gain weight; to grow fat. _ The doctor says I need to put some weight on. _ I have to go on a diet because I’ve been putting on a little weight lately.
examples: The doctor says I need to put some weight on.

putt along.monolingual: to move along rapidly, usually in a motorized vehicle. (“Putt-putt” is the sound made to mimic engines, especially small engines.) _The little car was putting along down the highway, when one of the tires went f lat. _ We were putting along very smoo
examples: The little car was putting along down the highway, when one of the tires went f lat.

*putty in someone’s hands.monolingual: Fig. [of someone] easily influenced by someone else; excessively willing to do what someone else wishes. (Putty is soft and malleable. *Typically: be ~; seem like ~.) _ Bob’s wife is putty in his hands. She never thinks for herself. _ Jane is putty i
examples: Bob’s wife is putty in his hands.

a put-up job.monolingual: Inf. a deception; a deceptive event. _ That’s really phony; a put-up job if I ever saw one. _ No put-up job is clever enough to fool me.
examples: That’s really phony; a put-up job if I ever saw one.

putz around.monolingual: Inf. to fiddle around; to mess around. _Stop putzing around and get to work. _ Those guys spend most of their time just putzing around.
examples: Stop putzing around and get to work.

puzzle over someone or something.monolingual: to consider or ponder someone or something. _ Anne is a bit strange. I’ve spent some time puzzling over her. _ While I was puzzling over why she had slapped me, she did it again.
examples: Anne is a bit strange.

puzzle something out†.monolingual: to figure something out. _ It took me a while to puzzle it out. _ I can’t puzzle out the meaning of this argument.
examples: It took me a while to puzzle it out.

quail at someone or something.monolingual: to show fear at someone or something; to shrink from someone or something. _Todd quailed at the thought of what he had to do. _The students quailed at the teacher who had been so hard on them in the past.
examples: Todd quailed at the thought of what he had to do.

quail before someone or something.monolingual: to cower before or at the threat of someone or something. _ The students quailed before the angry principal. _ They quailed before the thought of punishment.
examples: The students quailed before the angry principal.

quake with something.monolingual: to shake as with fear, terror, etc. _ Alice was quaking with fear as the door slowly opened. _ Todd quaked with terror when he saw the vicious dog at the door.
examples: Alice was quaking with fear as the door slowly opened.

qualify as something.monolingual: to fulfill the requirements to be something. _Tom qualified as a mechanic. _I have been qualified as a mechanic since I was twenty.
examples: Tom qualified as a mechanic.

qualify for something.monolingual: to meet the requirements for something. _I’m sorry, you do not qualify for this job. _I don’t qualify for it.
examples: I’m sorry, you do not qualify for this job.

qualify someone as something.monolingual: to cause someone to fulfill the requirements for something. _ Does this course qualify me as a stockbroker? _She qualified herself as a realtor.
examples: She qualified herself as a realtor.

qualify someone for something.monolingual: to enable someone to meet the requirements for something. _His years with the company qualified him for pension. _ Does this ticket qualify me for the drawing?
examples: His years with the company qualified him for pension.

quality time.monolingual: time spent with someone allowing interaction and closeness. _ He was able to spend a few minutes of quality time with his son, Buxton, at least once every two weeks.
examples: He was able to spend a few minutes of quality time with his son, Buxton, at least once every two weeks.

quarrel with something.monolingual: to argue against something; to have a complaint about something. _ I can’t quarrel with that. _Does anyone want to quarrel with that last remark?
examples: I can’t quarrel with that.

the queen’s english.monolingual: “Official” British English. _ He can’t even speak The Queen’s English! Despicable!

queer for something.monolingual: Inf. in the mood for something; desiring something. (Old.) _ I’m queer for a beer right now. _ She’s queer for him because of his money.
examples: I’m queer for a beer right now.

quest for someone or something.monolingual: to seek after someone or something. _Martin is off questing for a book on baroque organ building. _ She is questing for a better way to do it.
examples: Martin is off questing for a book on baroque organ building.

a question of something.monolingual: a matter of something; a problem of something. _ It’s not a matter of not wanting to go to the opera. It’s a question of money.
examples: It’s not a matter of not wanting to go to the opera.

quick and dirty.monolingual: Fig. [done] fast and carelessly; [done] fast and cheaply. _I am not interested in a quick and dirty job. I want it done right. _ The contractor made a lot of money on quick and dirty projects that would never last very long.
examples: I am not interested in a quick and dirty job.

quick like a bunny.monolingual: really quick. _ Now’s your chance. Do it! Quick like a bunny!
examples: Now’s your chance.

quick off the mark.monolingual: quick starting or reacting. (Compare this with slow off the mark.) _ Boy, you were quick off the mark there! _ If you can be really quick off the mark, you can soon find the answer.
examples: If you can be really quick off the mark, you can soon find the answer.

quick on the uptake.monolingual: quick to understand or learn something. _Just because I’m not quick on the uptake, it doesn’t mean I’m stupid. _Mary understands jokes before anyone else because she’s so quick on the uptake.
examples: Just because I’m not quick on the uptake, it doesn’t mean I’m stupid.

a quick study.monolingual: a person who is quick to learn things. (Compare this to a slow study.) _ Jane, who is a quick study, caught the joke immediately and laughed before everyone else.
examples: Jane, who is a quick study, caught the joke immediately and laughed before everyone else.

quicker than hell.monolingual: Inf. very fast. _ You got over here quicker than hell. _Be careful in the stock market. You can lose all your money quicker than hell.
examples: You got over here quicker than hell.

quiet down.monolingual: to become quiet; to become less noisy. _ Please quiet down. _ Ask them to quiet down.
examples: Please quiet down.

quip about someone or something.monolingual: to joke about someone or something. _ The kids were quipping about the principal’s hairpiece. _It is rude to quip about an elderly person.
examples: The kids were quipping about the principal’s hairpiece.

quit a place.monolingual: to leave a place. _In the autumn, Melinda quit Paris and traveled south to warmer climes.
examples: In the autumn, Melinda quit Paris and traveled south to warmer climes.

quit on someone.monolingual: 1. [for something] to quit while someone is using it. _ This stupid car quit on me. _ I hope this thing doesn’t quit on me.
examples: This stupid car quit on me.

quit over someone or something.monolingual: to stop working or doing something because of someone or something; to quit because of a dispute over someone or something. _Please don’t quit over a silly thing like that. _ She quit over one of her fellow workers.
examples: Please don’t quit over a silly thing like that.

quit while one is ahead.monolingual: to stop doing something while one is still successful. _When will I learn to quit while I’m ahead? _ Get into the market. Make some money and get out. Quit while you’re ahead.
examples: Get into the market.

quite a something.monolingual: definitely something; a good example of something. _ The captain of the swim team is quite a swimmer. _ That’s quite a bruise you have there.
examples: The captain of the swim team is quite a swimmer.

quite something.monolingual: something very good or remarkable. _ You should see their new house. It’s quite something. _Meg’s mother has bought a new hat for the wedding and it’s quite something.
examples: You should see their new house.

quiver with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to shake or shiver from something, such as cold, fear, anticipation, etc. _On seeing the bear, the dogs quivered with fear. _ Todd quivered with the cold.
examples: On seeing the bear, the dogs quivered with fear.

quote a price.monolingual: to name or state in advance the charge for doing or supplying something. _ The mechanic quoted a price of $100 to repair my car. _ The carpenter quoted a price for fixing the stairs.
examples: The mechanic quoted a price of $100 to repair my car.

quote, unquote.monolingual: a parenthetical expression said before a word or short phrase indicating that the word or phrase would be in quotation marks if used in writing. _ So I said to her, quote, unquote, it’s time we had a little talk.
examples: So I said to her, quote, unquote, it’s time we had a little talk.

race against someone or something.monolingual: to attempt to win a trial of speed against someone or something. _ I don’t want to race against Kelly. She is too fast. _ I had to race against time to get there before the baby got worse.
examples: I don’t want to race against Kelly.

race against time.monolingual: 1. a rush; a rush to beat a deadline. _ We were in a race against time to beat the deadline. _It was a race against time, but we made it.
examples: We were in a race against time to beat the deadline.

race around.monolingual: to run or move around in a great hurry. _ Stop racing around and calm down! _ I have been racing around all morning, trying to get some things done.
examples: I have been racing around all morning, trying to get some things done.

race for something.monolingual: to run or drive fast to get to something in a hurry. _ I raced for the door to see who was there. _ The children raced for the best seats in front of the television set.
examples: I raced for the door to see who was there.

race into someone or something.monolingual: to bump or crash into someone or something. _ The boys raced into the side of the car, and one of them was hurt. _ We raced into Mary and knocked her over.
examples: The boys raced into the side of the car, and one of them was hurt.

race into something.monolingual: to run into a place. _ The children raced into the room and headed straight for their presents. _ Please don’t race into the garden. You will trample the f lowers.
examples: The children raced into the room and headed straight for their presents.

race someone for something.monolingual: to compete against someone for a prize; to try to outrun someone to get to something first. _ I will race you for the grand prize. _ Ned raced his sister for the breakfast table every morning.
examples: I will race you for the grand prize.

race someone to some place.monolingual: to compete against someone to see who gets to a place first. _I will race you to the door. _ Tim wanted to race me to the corner.
examples: I will race you to the door.

race through someone or something.monolingual: to run or chase through a group of people or a place. _The children raced through the group of ladies standing by the door. _The dogs raced through the room, upsetting a lamp.
examples: The children raced through the group of ladies standing by the door.

race through something.monolingual: to perform some task very rapidly. _ They raced through their prayers and jumped into bed. _The children raced through dinner, in a hurry to get outside to play.
examples: They raced through their prayers and jumped into bed.

race to someone or something.monolingual: to run to someone or something. _ The girls raced to the front room. _ We all raced to Mary, who had the candy.
examples: The girls raced to the front room.

race with someone or something.monolingual: to enter a speed contest with someone or something. _I refuse to race with Carla. She is much too fast for me. _ I can’t race with a horse!
examples: I refuse to race with Carla.

rack out.monolingual: Sl. to go to bed and to sleep. _ I’m really tired. I’ve got to go rack out for a while. _I racked out until nearly noon.
examples: I’m really tired.

rack something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to place something onto or into its rack. _ You had better rack the billiard balls up when you finish this game. _ Please rack up the balls.
examples: You had better rack the billiard balls up when you finish this game.

racked with pain.monolingual: suffering from severe pain. _My body was racked with pain, and I nearly passed out. _ My head was racked with pain.
examples: My body was racked with pain, and I nearly passed out.

radiate from someone or something.monolingual: to spread out from someone or something, as with rays. _ Happiness radiated from Mary. She was so proud! _ The heat radiated from the wall next to the furnace room.
examples: Happiness radiated from Mary.

raffle something off†.monolingual: to give something away by a drawing or raffle. _ They will raff le a television set off. _ They are going to raff le off a television set this weekend at the school.
examples: They will raff le a television set off.

rag out.monolingual: Sl. to dress up. _ I like to rag out and go to parties. _ I hate to rag out. I like comfortable clothes.
examples: I like to rag out and go to parties.

rage against someone or something.monolingual: to vent one’s anger about someone or something; to criticize someone or something severely. _She exhausted herself raging against Judy. _ Mary is raging about the office politics again.
examples: She exhausted herself raging against Judy.

rage at someone or something.monolingual: to direct one’s anger at someone or something. _ Why are you raging at me? What on earth did I do? _ Nothing can be solved by raging at the police department.
examples: Nothing can be solved by raging at the police department.

rage out of control.monolingual: to become uncontrollable. _ The fire raged out of control and threatened the residential area. _ If we didn’t do something quickly, the fire would be raging out of control.
examples: The fire raged out of control and threatened the residential area.

rage over someone or something.monolingual: to fight furiously over someone or something. _The two managers both wanted to hire the same prospective employee. They raged over her for nearly an hour. _ The bears raged over that one fish for a long time.
examples: The two managers both wanted to hire the same prospective employee.

rage through something.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a fire] to burn rapidly through an area or a building. _ The fire raged through the unoccupied building. _ When the fire began to rage through the forest, we knew we had better head for the river.
examples: The fire raged through the unoccupied building.

rail against someone or something.monolingual: to complain vehemently about someone or something. _ Why are you railing against me? What did I do? _ Leonard is railing against the tax increase again.
examples: Leonard is railing against the tax increase again.

railroad someone into something.monolingual: to force someone into doing something in great haste. _ The salesman tried to railroad me into signing the contract. _ You can’t railroad me into doing anything!
examples: The salesman tried to railroad me into signing the contract.

rain cats and dogs.monolingual: Fig. to rain very hard. _ It’s raining cats and dogs. Look at it pour! _ I’m not going out in that storm. It’s raining cats and dogs.
examples: It’s raining cats and dogs.

rain or shine.monolingual: no matter whether it rains or the sun shines. _ Don’t worry. I’ll be there rain or shine. _ We’ll hold the picnic—rain or shine.
examples: Don’t worry. I’ll be there rain or shine.

rain something out†.monolingual: [for the weather] to spoil something by raining. _Oh, the weather looks awful. I hope it doesn’t rain the picnic out. _ It’s starting to sprinkle now. Do you think it will rain out the ball game?
examples: Oh, the weather looks awful.

raise cain.monolingual: to make a lot of trouble; to raise hell. (A Biblical reference, from Genesis 4.) _ Fred was really raising Cain about the whole matter. _ Let’s stop raising Cain.
examples: Fred was really raising Cain about the whole matter.

raise one’s sights.monolingual: Fig. to set higher goals for oneself. (Alludes to someone lifting the sights of a gun in order to fire farther.) _ When you’re young, you tend to raise your sights too high. _ On the other hand, some people need to raise their sights.
examples: When you’re young, you tend to raise your sights too high.

raise someone from something.monolingual: to help someone up from a lowly state. _ They hoped for some windfall to raise them from their poverty. _ They raised me from the depressed state I was in.
examples: They hoped for some windfall to raise them from their poverty.

raise someone from the dead.monolingual: Fig. to bring a dead person back to life. (When used figuratively, usually refers to something very bad or offensive.) _How great are your magic powers? Can you raise people from the dead? _They say her singing could raise people from the dead.
examples: They say her singing could raise people from the dead.

raise someone or something up†.monolingual: to lift someone or something up. _The aides raised the patient up while the nurse spread clean linen beneath him. _ Jane raised up the lid.
examples: The aides raised the patient up while the nurse spread clean linen beneath him.

raise someone to something.monolingual: to promote or advance someone to a higher rank. _ The boss raised her to vice president after one year. _ I hope she raises me to head clerk.
examples: The boss raised her to vice president after one year.

raise something with someone.monolingual: to bring up a matter with someone. _ I will raise that question with Mary when she comes in. _ Please raise the question with the boss.
examples: I will raise that question with Mary when she comes in.

raise the bar.monolingual: Fig. to make a task a little more difficult. (As with raising the bar in high jumping or pole vaulting.) _ Just as I was getting accustomed to my job, the manager raised the bar and I had to perform even better.
examples: Just as I was getting accustomed to my job, the manager raised the bar and I had to perform even better.

raise up.monolingual: to lift oneself up; to get up or begin to get up. _ She raised up and then fell back onto her bed. She was too weak to get up. _ I could not raise up enough to see out the window.
examples: She raised up and then fell back onto her bed.

raised in a barn.monolingual: brought up to behave like a barnyard animal; having crude behavior. _ Close the door behind you! Were you raised in a barn? _ Don’t wipe your nose on your sleeve. Were you raised in a barn?
examples: Don’t wipe your nose on your sleeve.

rake something around†.monolingual: to spread something around with a rake. _She raked the leaves around, spreading them over the f lower beds as natural fertilizer. _I need to rake around the soil and stir it up.
examples: She raked the leaves around, spreading them over the f lower beds as natural fertilizer.

rake something in†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to draw or pull something inward with a rake. _ Jane is raking in the leaves into a big pile.
examples: Jane is raking in the leaves into a big pile.

rake something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to gather and clean up something with a rake. _Would you please rake these leaves up before it rains? _ Please rake up the leaves.
examples: Please rake up the leaves.

rake through something.monolingual: Fig. [for someone] to rummage through something, as if with a rake. _ She quickly raked through the mass of loose papers, looking for the right one. _ I will have to rake through everything in this drawer to find a red pencil.
examples: She quickly raked through the mass of loose papers, looking for the right one.

rally around someone or something.monolingual: Fig. to unite or assemble in support of someone or something. _ All the other workers rallied around Fred in his fight with management. _ They rallied around the principle that Fred stood for.
examples: All the other workers rallied around Fred in his fight with management.

rally to someone or something.monolingual: to unite in support of someone or something. _ The students rallied to Betty, their elected president. _ We all rallied to the cause.
examples: The students rallied to Betty, their elected president.

ralph something up†.monolingual: Sl. to vomit something. (Teens and collegiate.) _ The doctor gave him some stuff that made him ralph it up. _ He ralphed up his dinner.
examples: The doctor gave him some stuff that made him ralph it up.

ram into someone or something.monolingual: to crash into someone or something. _ Mary accidentally rammed into a fence as she rode along. _ The car rammed into the tree and was totally wrecked.
examples: Mary accidentally rammed into a fence as she rode along.

ram something down†.monolingual: to pack something down by pounding, as with a ram. _ The worker used a pole to ram the earth down and pack it tight. _The worker rammed down the earth.
examples: The worker used a pole to ram the earth down and pack it tight.

ram through something.monolingual: to crash or pound through something. _ The car rammed through the back of the garage. _ I was afraid that the truck would ram through the fence.
examples: The car rammed through the back of the garage.

ramble on.monolingual: 1. to wander about aimlessly. (As with a traveler or a winding path.) _ The road rambled on through mile after mile of wilderness.
examples: The road rambled on through mile after mile of wilderness.

range from something to something.monolingual: to vary from one thing to another. _ The winter weather ranges from bad to terrible in this part of the north. _The appraisals of the property ranged from high to low.
examples: The winter weather ranges from bad to terrible in this part of the north.

range over something.monolingual: to cover an area; to travel about in one area. _ The buffalo ranged over vast areas of prairie, grazing and breeding. _ These animals range over a very large territory.
examples: The buffalo ranged over vast areas of prairie, grazing and breeding.

rank above someone.monolingual: to outrank someone; to rank higher than someone. _ I think that I rank above you, so I will sit by the window. _ The boss ranks above everyone and demands that everyone recognize the fact.
examples: I think that I rank above you, so I will sit by the window.

rank among something.monolingual: to be included in a particular group. _ In my opinion, Kelly ranks among the very best. _ Tom ranks among the most widely known of the contemporary writers.
examples: In my opinion, Kelly ranks among the very best.

rank and file.monolingual: 1. Lit. regular soldiers, not the officers. _ I think there is low morale among the rank and file, sir. _ The rank and file usually do exactly as they are told.
examples: I think there is low morale among the rank and file, sir.

rank as something.monolingual: to have a particular rank; to serve in a particular rank. _ She ranks as a fine pianist in my book. _ Don ranks as the top economist of the day.
examples: She ranks as a fine pianist in my book.

rank on someone.monolingual: Sl. to attack someone verbally; to gossip about someone. _ Please stop ranking on my family! _ Tom keeps ranking on Jennifer, and she is really mad about it.
examples: Tom keeps ranking on Jennifer, and she is really mad about it.

rank someone among something.monolingual: to judge someone to be essentially equal to a specific group of people. _ I don’t rank Kelly among the best drivers in the world. _Our committee ranked Fred among the best of the current applicants.
examples: I don’t rank Kelly among the best drivers in the world.

rank someone with someone.monolingual: to judge someone to be equal with someone. _ Would you rank Tom with Donna? _ Fred ranked himself with Tom when it came to diving.
examples: Fred ranked himself with Tom when it came to diving.

rank with someone or something.monolingual: to be equal to someone or something. _Do you think Sarah ranks with Albert? _No one ranks with Albert. _ The food at that restaurant ranks with that of the best places in New York.
examples: No one ranks with Albert.

rant against someone or something.monolingual: to rave and yell against someone or something. _ She spent most of the morning ranting against her mother-in-law. _ Leonard spent the entire morning ranting against the government.
examples: She spent most of the morning ranting against her mother-in-law.

rant at someone or something.monolingual: to rave and yell at someone or something. _ Stop ranting at me! _ The boss would never rant at the office staff.
examples: The boss would never rant at the office staff.

rap with someone.monolingual: Sl. to have a chat with someone or a group of people. (Old.) _Come in, sit down, and rap with me for a while. _Let’s get together and rap with one another sometime.
examples: Come in, sit down, and rap with me for a while.

rarin’ to go.monolingual: extremely keen to act or do something. _Jane can’t wait to start her job. She’s rarin’ to go. _Mary is rarin’ to go and can’t wait for her university term to start.
examples: Jane can’t wait to start her job.

rasp something out†.monolingual: to carve or smooth something out with a rasp. _ You should use this tool to rasp the inside of the bowl out. Use sandpaper to make the inside smoother. _ Rasp out the inside carefully.
examples: You should use this tool to rasp the inside of the bowl out.

rat around.monolingual: Sl. to waste time loafing around; to kick around. (Collegiate.) _I didn’t do anything but rat around all summer. _ If kids don’t have jobs, they just rat around.
examples: I didn’t do anything but rat around all summer.

rat on someone.monolingual: Inf. to report someone’s bad behavior to someone in authority; to tattle on someone. _ John ratted on me, and I got in trouble. _ If he rats on me, I’ll hit him!
examples: John ratted on me, and I got in trouble.

rat out.monolingual: Sl. to quit; to fink out (on someone or something). _ It’s too late to rat out. _ He tried to rat out at the last minute.
examples: It’s too late to rat out.

rat race.monolingual: Fig. a fierce struggle for success, especially in one’s career or business. _ Bob got tired of the rat race. He’s retired and gone to the country. _ The money market is a rat race, and many people who work in it get out quickly because of the stress.
examples: Bob got tired of the rat race.

rate something at something.monolingual: to assign a particular level of rating to something. _ I rate this brand at about a B-. _ The broker rated this stock at a buy.
examples: I rate this brand at about a B-.

rate with someone.monolingual: to be in someone’s favor; to be thought of highly by someone. _Ann is great. She really rates with me. _ She doesn’t rate with me at all.
examples: Ann is great. She really rates with me.

rattle around in something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to make a rattling noise inside something. _ What is rattling around in this package? _There is something rattling around in my glove compartment.
examples: There is something rattling around in my glove compartment.

rattle away.monolingual: to chatter endlessly and aimlessly. _ The two old men sat there and rattled away at one another. _ Tom rattled away at Jane for a few minutes and then left the house.
examples: The two old men sat there and rattled away at one another.
