right on!.monolingual: Sl. Exactly!; That is exactly right! _ After the speaker finished, many people in the audience shouted, “Right on!” _ One member of the crowd called out, “Right on!”

right on time.monolingual: at the correct time; no later than the specified time. _ Bill always shows up right on time. _ If you get there right on time, you’ll get one of the free tickets.
examples: Bill always shows up right on time.

right side up.monolingual: with the correct (top) side upwards, as with a box or some other container. _ Keep this box right side up, or the contents will be crushed. _ Please set your coffee cup right side up so I can fill it.
examples: Keep this box right side up, or the contents will be crushed.

the right stuff.monolingual: the right or correct character or set of skills to do something well. _She’s got the right stuff to be a winner.
examples: She’s got the right stuff to be a winner.

*the right-of-way.monolingual: the legal right to occupy a particular space on a public roadway. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~; yield ~.) _ I had a traffic accident yesterday, but it wasn’t my fault. I had the right-of-way. _ Don’t pull out onto a highway if you haven
examples: I had a traffic accident yesterday, but it wasn’t my fault.

rile someone up†.monolingual: to get someone excited and angry. _ He yelled at them and riled them up. They left quite angry. _ He riles up everyone he talks to.
examples: He yelled at them and riled them up.

ring a bell.monolingual: Fig. [for something] to cause someone to remember something or for it to seem familiar. _ I’ve never met John Franklin, but his name rings a bell. _ Whenever I see a bee, it rings a bell. I remember when I was stung by one.
examples: I’ve never met John Franklin, but his name rings a bell.

ring around something.monolingual: to circle something. _The children ringed around the maypole, dancing and singing. _ The mourners had ringed around the coffin for the final ceremony.
examples: The children ringed around the maypole, dancing and singing.

ring back.monolingual: to call back on the telephone. _ No, there’s no message. I’ll ring back later. _ She’s not here now. I suggest you ring back after dinner.
examples: No, there’s no message.

ring in the new year.monolingual: Fig. to celebrate the beginning of the new year at midnight on December
examples: We are planning a big party to ring in the new year.

ring off the hook.monolingual: Fig. [for a telephone] to ring incessantly and repeatedly. _ What a busy day! The telephone has been ringing off the hook all day long. _The telephone has been ringing off the hook ever since the ad appeared in the paper.
examples: What a busy day! The telephone has been ringing off the hook all day long.

ring out.monolingual: [for a loud sound] to go out. _ The bells rang out at the end of the wedding ceremony. _Loud cheers rang out at the end of the game. _A shot rang out and started all the dogs barking.
examples: The bells rang out at the end of the wedding ceremony.

ring out the old.monolingual: Fig. to celebrate the end of a year while celebrating the beginning of a new one. _ I don’t plan to ring out the old this year. I’m just going to go to bed. _ We never ring out the old because it’s too dismal.
examples: I don’t plan to ring out the old this year.

ring someone back†.monolingual: to call someone back on the telephone. _I will have to ring back the store at a later time. _Please ring me back when you have a moment.
examples: I will have to ring back the store at a later time.

ring someone up†.monolingual: to call someone on the telephone. _ I will ring her up when I get a chance. _ I have to ring up a whole list of people.
examples: I will ring her up when I get a chance.

ring something up†.monolingual: to record the cost of an item on a cash register. _ Please ring this chewing gum up first, and I’ll put it in my purse. _The cashier rang up each item and told me how much money I owed.
examples: Please ring this chewing gum up first, and I’ll put it in my purse.

ring the bell.monolingual: Inf. to be just what is needed; to hit the spot. _ This cold water really rings the bell. _ A good hot bowl of soup would ring the bell about now.
examples: This cold water really rings the bell.

ring the curtain up†.monolingual: 1. Fig. to raise the curtain in a theater. (Alludes to sending the signal to raise the curtain.) _ The stagehand rang the curtain up precisely on time. _ Let’s ring up the curtain. It’s time to start the show.
examples: The stagehand rang the curtain up precisely on time.

ring true.monolingual: Fig. to sound or seem true or likely. (From testing the quality of metal or glass by striking it and evaluating the sound made.) _ The student’s excuse for being late doesn’t ring true. _ Do you think that Mary’s explanation for her absence rang true
examples: The student’s excuse for being late doesn’t ring true.

ring with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to resound with something. _ The morning air rang with the sound of church bells. _The canyon rang with the sound of gunfire.
examples: The morning air rang with the sound of church bells.

rinse someone or something down†.monolingual: to wash or clean someone or something with water or other fluid. _I rinsed him down for an hour and still didn’t get the smell of skunk off him. _ I had to rinse down the driveway.
examples: I rinsed him down for an hour and still didn’t get the smell of skunk off him.

rinse someone or something off†.monolingual: to wash or clean someone or something by flushing with water or other fluid. _ Mother rinsed the baby off and dried him with a soft towel. _ She rinsed off the baby.
examples: Mother rinsed the baby off and dried him with a soft towel.

rinse something out†.monolingual: 1. to clean cloth or clothing partially by immersing it in water and squeezing it out. _ Can you please rinse this rag out? It’s all dirty. _Please rinse out your clothes to make sure there is no soap left in them.
examples: Can you please rinse this rag out? It’s all dirty.

rinse something out of something.monolingual: to remove something from something by flushing it with water. _See if you can rinse the dirt out of this jacket. _ I can’t rinse out the dirt.
examples: See if you can rinse the dirt out of this jacket.

rinse something with something.monolingual: to flush something with some fluid. _ You should rinse your clothes in milk or tomato juice to remove the smell of the skunk. _Please rinse the stain with cold water.
examples: You should rinse your clothes in milk or tomato juice to remove the smell of the skunk.

a riot of color.monolingual: Cliché a selection of many bright colors. _ The landscape was a riot of color each autumn.
examples: The landscape was a riot of color each autumn.

rip into someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to attack someone or something by ripping. _The raccoons ripped into the trash bags, scattering papers and stuff all over the street. _ The horrid murderer ripped into the helpless victim.
examples: The raccoons ripped into the trash bags, scattering papers and stuff all over the street.

rip off.monolingual: [for something] to tear or peel off. _ My pocket ripped off, and my money is gone now! _ A piece of the bumper ripped off my car.
examples: A piece of the bumper ripped off my car.

rip on someone.monolingual: Sl. to give someone a hard time; to hassle someone. _ Stop ripping on me! What did I do to you? _ Tim is ripping on Mary and she is getting really mad.
examples: Tim is ripping on Mary and she is getting really mad.

ripsnorter.monolingual: Rur. a remarkable person or thing; a hilarious joke. _Old Fred is a real ripsnorter. _Her new car is a ripsnorter, I tell you. _ Let me tell you a ripsnorter about a farmer and his cow.
examples: Old Fred is a real ripsnorter.

rip someone off†.monolingual: Inf. to steal [something] from someone; to cheat someone. _ That merchant ripped me off! _ She rips off everyone.
examples: She rips off everyone.

rip someone or something apart†.monolingual: to tear someone or something apart into pieces. _ The automobile accident ripped the car apart. _ Don’t rip apart the newspaper!
examples: The automobile accident ripped the car apart.

rip someone or something up†.monolingual: to tear someone or something into bits; to mutilate someone or something. _ Careful! That machine will rip you up if you fall in. _ I ripped up the contract and threw the pieces in the trash.
examples: Careful! That machine will rip you up if you fall in.

rip something down†.monolingual: to tear something down. (Alludes to something that has been posted or mounted.) _ The cus- todian ripped all the posters down at the end of the day. _ He ripped down the posters.
examples: The cus- todian ripped all the posters down at the end of the day.

rip something up†.monolingual: to take something up by force and remove it. (Usually refers to something on the floor or ground, such as carpeting or pavement.) _ They are going to rip all the broken sidewalk up. _ The workers ripped up the pavement and loaded the pieces into a tr
examples: They are going to rip all the broken sidewalk up.

a ripe old age.monolingual: a very old age. _Mr. Smith died last night, but he lived to a ripe old age—99. _ All the Smiths seem to reach a ripe old age.
examples: Mr. Smith died last night, but he lived to a ripe old age—99.

ripen into something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to ripen and become something recognizable. _ This little green ball will ripen into an apple.
examples: This little green ball will ripen into an apple.

a ripple of excitement.monolingual: a series of quiet but excited murmurs. _ A ripple of excitement spread through the crowd. _ As the president came near, a ripple of excitement indicated that people could really see him.
examples: A ripple of excitement spread through the crowd.

a ripple of protest.monolingual: quiet remarks protesting something; a small amount of subdued protest. _ There was only a ripple of protest about the new tax law. _ The rude comedian hardly drew a ripple of protest.
examples: There was only a ripple of protest about the new tax law.

ripple through something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to move through a liquid so as to cause ripples or tiny waves. _ The canoe rippled through the still water. _A tiny snake rippled through the water of the swamp.
examples: The canoe rippled through the still water.

rise above something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to move up above something. _ The huge sun rose above the horizon and spread its red glow across the sea.
examples: The huge sun rose above the horizon and spread its red glow across the sea.

rise and shine!.monolingual: Fig. Get out of bed and be lively and energetic! (Often a command.) _Come on, children! Rise and shine! We’re going to the beach. _Father always calls “Rise and shine!” in the morning when we want to go on sleeping.
examples: Come on, children! Rise and shine! We’re going to the beach.

rise from someone or something.monolingual: to emanate from someone or something in the manner of a cloud of dust or a cheer. _After the singer finished, a loud cheer rose from the crowd. _ A cloud of smoke rose from the burning barn.
examples: After the singer finished, a loud cheer rose from the crowd.

rise from the ashes.monolingual: Fig. [for a structure] to be rebuilt after destruction. _ The entire west section of the city was destroyed and a group of new buildings rose from the ashes in only a few months. _ Will the city rise again from the ashes? No one knows.
examples: The entire west section of the city was destroyed and a group of new buildings rose from the ashes in only a few months.

rise from the ranks.monolingual: Fig. to achieve position or office, having worked up from the masses. _ He rose from the ranks to become president of the company. _ Most of the officers of the company have risen from the ranks.
examples: He rose from the ranks to become president of the company.

rise in something.monolingual: to increase in something. _ I hope that this land rises in value over the next few years. _Her expensive antique car actually rose in value during the first year.
examples: I hope that this land rises in value over the next few years.

rise to one’s feet.monolingual: to stand up. _ The entire audience rose to its feet, applauding wildly. _We rose to our feet when the bride came down the aisle.
examples: The entire audience rose to its feet, applauding wildly.

rise to the bait.monolingual: Fig. to respond to an allurement; to fall for an enticement or fall into a trap. (Alludes to a fish coming up from deep water to seize bait.) _ You can get him here easily. Tell him that there will be lots of food and he will rise to the bait. _ He r
examples: You can get him here easily.

rise to the challenge.monolingual: Fig. to accept a challenge. (Usually in reference to success with the challenge.) _You can depend on Kelly to rise to the challenge. _We were not able to rise to the challenge and we lost the contract.
examples: You can depend on Kelly to rise to the challenge.

rise to the occasion.monolingual: Fig. to meet the challenge of an event; to try extra hard to do a task. _ John was able to rise to the occasion and make the conference a success. _ It was a big challenge, but he rose to the occasion.
examples: John was able to rise to the occasion and make the conference a success.

rise to the top.monolingual: to move or float to something, such as the top, surface, etc. _ The cream will rise to the top. _ The lighter oil rose to the top and we scooped it up and saved it.
examples: The cream will rise to the top.

rise up.monolingual: 1. to come up; to ascend. _ The water is rising up fast. You had better get to higher ground. _ As the water rose up, it covered the fields and streets.
examples: The water is rising up fast.

rival someone in something.monolingual: to have a quality or status that is comparable to that of someone else. _ I would say that Jane rivals Dave in the ability to find the essential elements of a problem and deal with them swiftly. _ No one rivals Ted in pitching a baseball.
examples: I would say that Jane rivals Dave in the ability to find the essential elements of a problem and deal with them swiftly.

rivet someone’s attention.monolingual: Fig. to keep someone’s attention fixed [on something]. _ The movie riveted the audience’s attention. _ Professor Jones’s lecture riveted the students’ attention.
examples: The movie riveted the audience’s attention.

riveted to the ground.monolingual: Fig. [of someone or someone’s feet] unable to move. _ I was riveted to the ground out of fear. _ My feet were riveted to the ground and I could not move an inch.
examples: I was riveted to the ground out of fear.

road hog.monolingual: Fig. someone who drives carelessly and selfishly. _ Look at that road hog driving in the middle of the road and stopping other drivers from passing him. _ That road hog nearly knocked the children over. He was driving too fast.
examples: Look at that road hog driving in the middle of the road and stopping other drivers from passing him.

roar at someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to bellow or bawl at someone or something. _ Don’t roar at me! Control your temper. _The lion roared at the hyena, who ran off.
examples: Don’t roar at me! Control your temper.

roar away.monolingual: to speed away, making a loud clamor. _ The car roared away into the night with tires screeching. _ The train roared away, carrying Andy to Canada.
examples: The car roared away into the night with tires screeching.

roar something out†.monolingual: to bellow something out loudly. _ Walter roared his protest out so everyone knew how he felt. _ Jane roared out her criticism.
examples: Walter roared his protest out so everyone knew how he felt.

rob peter to pay paul.monolingual: Fig. to take or borrow from one in order to give or pay something owed to another. _Why borrow money to pay your bills? That’s just robbing Peter to pay Paul. _ There’s no point in robbing Peter to pay Paul. You will still be in debt.
examples: Why borrow money to pay your bills? That’s just robbing Peter to pay Paul.

rob someone blind.monolingual: 1. Fig. to steal freely from someone. _ Her maid was robbing her blind. _I don’t want them to rob me blind. Keep an eye on them.
examples: Her maid was robbing her blind.

rob someone of something.monolingual: to deprive someone of something, not necessarily by theft. _What you have done has robbed me of my dignity! _If you do that, you will rob yourself of your future.
examples: If you do that, you will rob yourself of your future.

rob the cradle.monolingual: Fig. to marry or date someone who is much younger than oneself. _ I hear that Bill is dating Ann. Isn’t that sort of robbing the cradle? She’s much younger than he is. _ Uncle Bill—who is nearly eighty—married a thirty-year-old woman. That is really
examples: I hear that Bill is dating Ann.

rock around.monolingual: to tilt or totter about. _ The boat rocked around, tossing the passengers to and fro. _ The road was bumpy and the huge car rocked around.
examples: The boat rocked around, tossing the passengers to and fro.

rock someone to something.monolingual: to help someone, usually an infant, get to sleep by rocking in a rocking chair, cradle, or carriage. _ It is best to rock the baby to sleep after you feed her. _ Somehow she learned to rock herself to sleep.
examples: It is best to rock the baby to sleep after you feed her.

rock the boat.monolingual: 1. Lit. to do something to move a boat from side to side, causing it to rock. (Often in a negative sense.) _ Sit down and stop rocking the boat. You’ll turn it over!
examples: Sit down and stop rocking the boat.

rocket something into something.monolingual: to send something somewhere— usually into space—by rocket. _The government rocketed the satellite into space. _Someone suggested rocketing our waste into space.
examples: The government rocketed the satellite into space.

a rocky road.monolingual: a difficult period of time. _Bob’s been going down quite a rocky road since his divorce.
examples: Bob’s been going down quite a rocky road since his divorce.

roll about.monolingual: to move about, turning or rotating, as a wheel or a ball. _ The ball rolled about awhile and then came to rest. _His eyes rolled about in amazement before he spoke.
examples: The ball rolled about awhile and then came to rest.

roll along.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for wheels or something on wheels] to move along, smoothly and rapidly. _ The wheels of the cart rolled along, making a grinding noise as they went. _ Our car rolled along rapidly toward our destination.
examples: The wheels of the cart rolled along, making a grinding noise as they went.

roll around.monolingual: to move about, rotating, turning over, turning, or moving on wheels. _The baby rolled around on the f loor, giggling and cooing. _The toy truck won’t roll around anymore.
examples: The baby rolled around on the f loor, giggling and cooing.

roll away.monolingual: to move away, rotating, turning over, turning, or moving on wheels. _The ball rolled away and fell down a storm sewer. _The cart rolled away, and we had to chase it down the hill.
examples: The ball rolled away and fell down a storm sewer.

roll back.monolingual: [for something] to return, rotating or turning or moving on wheels. _ I rolled the ball away, thinking it would roll back. It didn’t. _ I struck the golf ball out of the sand trap, but it rolled back.
examples: I rolled the ball away, thinking it would roll back.

roll by.monolingual: 1. Lit. to pass by, rotating, as a wheel or a ball; to move past, rolling on wheels. _ The wheel of a car rolled by, all by itself. It must have come off a car somewhere down the road. _The traffic rolled by relentlessly.
examples: The wheel of a car rolled by, all by itself.

roll down.monolingual: to move downward, rotating, as a wheel or a ball, or to move downward on wheels. _ I pushed the wagon up the driveway, and it rolled down again. _ Don’t place the cart at the top of the hill. It will roll down.
examples: I pushed the wagon up the driveway, and it rolled down again.

roll down something.monolingual: to move downward, along something, rotating, as a wheel or a ball, or moving downward on wheels. _ The ball rolled down the hall to the end. _ The cart went rolling down the hill all by itself.
examples: The ball rolled down the hall to the end.

roll in.monolingual: Fig. to come in large numbers or amounts, easily, as if rolling. (Alludes to the arrival of many wheeled conveyances.) _We didn’t expect many people at the party, but they just kept rolling in. _Money is simply rolling in for our charity.
examples: We didn’t expect many people at the party, but they just kept rolling in.

roll in something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to rotate about in something. _ What is that dog rolling in? _ We had fun rolling in the leaves.
examples: We had fun rolling in the leaves.

roll on.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to continue rolling. _ The ball rolled on and on. _ The cart came rolling down the hill and rolled on for a few yards at the bottom.
examples: The ball rolled on and on.

roll one’s sleeves up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to turn one’s sleeves upward, exposing the arms. _He rolled his sleeves up and began to wash the dishes. _ Don rolled up his sleeves so he would be cooler.
examples: He rolled his sleeves up and began to wash the dishes.

roll over.monolingual: to turn over; to rotate one half turn. _ The old man rolled over and started snoring again. _Please roll over and give me some more space in the bed.
examples: The old man rolled over and started snoring again.

roll over and play dead.monolingual: Fig. to just give up and be unable to cope with life or a problem. _Why can’t I complain about this? Am I supposed to roll over and play dead?

roll over something.monolingual: [for something that rolls] to pass over something. _ The wheelbarrow rolled over the hose, making the water squirt off and on. _After all the traffic had rolled over Timmy’s ball, there was very little left to it.
examples: The wheelbarrow rolled over the hose, making the water squirt off and on.

roll prices back†.monolingual: Fig. to reduce prices. _ The store rolled all its prices back for the sale. _ The protesters demanded that the big oil companies roll back their prices.
examples: The store rolled all its prices back for the sale.

roll someone or something over.monolingual: to turn someone or something over. _Bobby rolled Billy over and began tickling him ruthlessly in the tummy. _Mary rolled the stone over, hoping to find a snake underneath.
examples: Bobby rolled Billy over and began tickling him ruthlessly in the tummy.

roll something away†.monolingual: to cause something to move away, rotating, turning over, turning, or moving on wheels. _ Jane rolled the ball away and it was lost. _Jane rolled away the ball.
examples: Jane rolled the ball away and it was lost.

roll something back†.monolingual: to return something to someone by rotating it, as with a wheel or a ball, or moving it back on wheels. _ I intercepted the ball and rolled it back. _ Jane rolled back the ball.
examples: I intercepted the ball and rolled it back.

roll something down†.monolingual: 1. to move something down, making it rotate like a wheel or a ball, or moving it on wheels. _ Don’t carry the ball down; roll it down! _ I rolled down the ball as you asked.
examples: I rolled down the ball as you asked.

roll something down something.monolingual: to cause something to move down along something, rotating it like a wheel or a ball. _ Claire rolled the bowling ball down the alley for a strike. _ Roll the barrel down the ramp carefully. It is heavy.
examples: Claire rolled the bowling ball down the alley for a strike.

roll something in†.monolingual: to bring something in by rotating it like a wheel or a ball or by moving it on wheels. _ She put the round table on its edge and rolled it in. Then she went out and got the chairs before the rain started. _ The waiters rolled in the table with the we
examples: She put the round table on its edge and rolled it in.

roll something in something.monolingual: to turn something over and over in something, as if to coat the thing being rolled. _ Tony rolled each of the meatballs in f lour and popped them into the hot oil. _ Roll each of these cookies in powdered sugar.
examples: Tony rolled each of the meatballs in f lour and popped them into the hot oil.

roll something out†.monolingual: 1. to bring or take something out by rolling it; to push something out on wheels. _ Jane rolled her bike out to show it off. _ Alice rolled out her bicycle for us to see.
examples: Jane rolled her bike out to show it off.

roll something over†.monolingual: Fig. to renew a financial instrument as it expires. _ Do you plan to roll this certificate of deposit over? _ Are you going to roll over your certificates of deposit?

roll something up†.monolingual: to coil or rotate something into a coil or roll of something. _ I rolled the poster up and put it back in its mailing tube. _ I have to roll up this paper.
examples: I rolled the poster up and put it back in its mailing tube.

roll with the punches.monolingual: Fig. to absorb the force of a blow, as in boxing. _ You have to learn to roll with the punches. Accept what is dealt to you. _Paul could never roll with the punches. He always had to get even.
examples: You have to learn to roll with the punches.

*rolling in the aisles.monolingual: Fig. [of an audience] wild with laughter. (*Typically: get them ~; have them ~; leave them ~.) _I have the best jokes you’ve ever heard. I’ll have them rolling in the aisles. _ What a great performance. We had them rolling in the aisles.
examples: I have the best jokes you’ve ever heard.

romp around.monolingual: to run and bounce around playfully. _The horses were in the meadow, romping around in the crisp autumn air. _ The children need to get out and romp around.
examples: The horses were in the meadow, romping around in the crisp autumn air.

romp through something.monolingual: to run through something fast and playfully. _ The conductor romped through the slow movement of the symphony as if it were a march. _ The cast romped through the last act, knowing that the play would be closed that very night.
examples: The conductor romped through the slow movement of the symphony as if it were a march.

roof something over†.monolingual: to build a roof over something; to provide something with a roof. _ After the destructive storm they had to roof the shed over so that the cow would have some shelter. _ We will roof over the patio and turn the area into a porch.
examples: After the destructive storm they had to roof the shed over so that the cow would have some shelter.

room and board.monolingual: food to eat and a place to live; the cost of food and lodging. _ That college charges too much for room and board. _ How much is your room and board?
examples: That college charges too much for room and board.

room together.monolingual: [for two or more people] to share a room, as in a college dormitory. _ Sarah and I roomed together in college. _ We don’t want to room together anymore.
examples: Sarah and I roomed together in college.

room with someone.monolingual: to share a room with someone, as in college. _ I need someone to room with me next year. _ No one wants to room with Kelly.
examples: I need someone to room with me next year.

root for someone or something.monolingual: to cheer and encourage someone or something. _ Are you rooting for anyone in particular, or are you just shouting because you’re excited? _ I’m rooting for the home team.
examples: I’m rooting for the home team.

*the root of the problem.monolingual: an understanding of the causes or basis of a problem. (*Typically: determine ~; figure out ~; find ~; get to ~; get at ~.) _ It will take a little more study to get to the root of the problem. _ Let’s stop avoiding the issue and get at the root of th
examples: It will take a little more study to get to the root of the problem.

root something in something.monolingual: to start a plant growing roots in something. _ I tried to root the plants in sand, but they died. _ You have to root this kind of tree in very rich soil.
examples: I tried to root the plants in sand, but they died.

root something out†.monolingual: to get rid of something completely; to destroy something to its roots or core. _ No government will ever root out crime completely. _ The principal wants to root out troublemakers at the local school.
examples: No government will ever root out crime completely.

root something up†.monolingual: [for a pig] to find something in the ground by digging with its nose. _ The pigs will root your plants up if they get out of their pen. _ The pigs will root up your plants if they get out of their pen.
examples: The pigs will root your plants up if they get out of their pen.

rooted in something.monolingual: based on something; connected to a source or cause. _ The civil war was rooted in old cultural hatred. _ This fictional book was rooted in actual events.
examples: The civil war was rooted in old cultural hatred.

*rooted to something.monolingual: [of someone] firmly attached to something. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ She is firmly rooted to her homeland and has no intention of emigrating. _ The farmer is rooted to the land and will not leave.
examples: She is firmly rooted to her homeland and has no intention of emigrating.

*rooted to the spot.monolingual: Fig. unable to move because of fear or surprise. (*Typically: appear to be ~; be ~; become ~.) _Jane stood rooted to the spot when she saw the ghostly figure. _Mary stood rooted to the spot when the thief snatched her bag.
examples: Jane stood rooted to the spot when she saw the ghostly figure.

rope someone into doing something.monolingual: Fig. to persuade or trick someone into doing something. _I don’t know who roped me into doing this, but I don’t want to do it. _ See if you can rope somebody into taking this to the post office.
examples: I don’t know who roped me into doing this, but I don’t want to do it.

rope something off†.monolingual: to isolate something with a rope barrier. _The police roped the scene of the accident off. _The police roped off the scene of the accident.
examples: The police roped the scene of the accident off.

rope something together†.monolingual: to tie or bind up a thing or things with rope. _ Rope this carton together and put it in the trunk of the car. _Rope together these two packages and take them to the truck.
examples: Rope this carton together and put it in the trunk of the car.

*the ropes.monolingual: Fig. knowledge of how to do something; how to work something. (*Typically: know ~; learn ~; show someone ~; teach someone ~.) _ I’ll be able to do my job very well when I know the ropes. _ John is very slow to learn the ropes.
examples: I’ll be able to do my job very well when I know the ropes.

rot away.monolingual: to decompose; to decompose and fall away. _ The fallen trees rotted away and surrendered their nutrients to the soil. _ As the wood rotted away, it became rich humus.
examples: The fallen trees rotted away and surrendered their nutrients to the soil.

rot off.monolingual: to decompose. _If you don’t clean and repaint that old windowsill, it will rot off. _ A few old branches finally rotted off, but the ancient tree looked as if it would survive the wet spell.
examples: If you don’t clean and repaint that old windowsill, it will rot off.

rot out.monolingual: to decompose and fall out. _If you don’t clean your teeth regularly, they’ll rot out! _ Some of the rafters in the shed rotted out, but we replaced them easily.
examples: Some of the rafters in the shed rotted out, but we replaced them easily.

rotate on something.monolingual: to spin on something; to pivot on something. _ This wheel rotates on this little red jewel on the main frame of the watch. _ The record rotates on this device, which is called a turntable.
examples: This wheel rotates on this little red jewel on the main frame of the watch.

a rotten apple.monolingual: a single bad person or thing. _ There always is a rotten apple to spoil it for the rest of us. _ Tom sure has turned out to be the rotten apple.
examples: There always is a rotten apple to spoil it for the rest of us.

rotten luck.monolingual: Fig. bad luck. _ Of all the rotten luck! _ I’ve had nothing but rotten luck all day.
examples: I’ve had nothing but rotten luck all day.

rotten to the core.monolingual: Fig. really bad; corrupt. _ That lousy punk is rotten to the core. _ The entire administration is rotten to the core.
examples: That lousy punk is rotten to the core.

rough it.monolingual: to live without luxury; to live simply; to camp out. _ During the blackout, we roughed it without electricity. _ The campers roughed it in the remote cabin for a week.
examples: During the blackout, we roughed it without electricity.

rough someone up†.monolingual: to beat someone up; to maltreat someone. _Am I going to have to rough you up, or will you cooperate? _ The crooks roughed up the old lady before taking her purse.
examples: The crooks roughed up the old lady before taking her purse.

rough something in†.monolingual: to construct or draw something initially, temporarily, or crudely. _ The carpenter roughed the doorways in without consulting the plans. _ The carpenter roughed in the doorways without consulting the plans.
examples: The carpenter roughed the doorways in without consulting the plans.

rough something out†.monolingual: to make a rough sketch of something. _ I will rough it out and have one of the staff artists attend to the details. _ Jane roughed out a picture of the proposed building.
examples: I will rough it out and have one of the staff artists attend to the details.

rough something up†.monolingual: to scrape or rub something in a way that makes it rough. _ All you have to do is rough the ground up, sow the seeds, and then water them. _ Rough up the surface a little before you paint it.
examples: All you have to do is rough the ground up, sow the seeds, and then water them.

rough stuff.monolingual: unnecessary roughness; physical violence or threats of violence. _ Okay, let’s cut out the rough stuff! _ There was too much rough stuff in the football game.
examples: There was too much rough stuff in the football game.

round someone or something up†.monolingual: to locate and gather someone or something. _Please round the suspects up for questioning. _ The police rounded up the two possible suspects.
examples: Please round the suspects up for questioning.

round something down†.monolingual: to reduce a fractional part of a number to the next lowest whole number. _ You can round this figure down if you want. It won’t affect the total all that much. _Please round down all figures having fractions less than one-half.
examples: You can round this figure down if you want.

round something off†.monolingual: to change a number to the next higher or lower whole number. _ You should round 8.122 off. _ I rounded off 8.789 to 9.
examples: You should round 8.

round something out†.monolingual: to complete or enhance something. _ We will round the evening out with dessert at a nice restaurant. _ They rounded out the meal with dessert.
examples: We will round the evening out with dessert at a nice restaurant.

round something up†.monolingual: 1. to collect a group of people or things; to organize people or things into a group. _ The cowboys rounded up the cattle for market. _ See if you can round some helpers up.
examples: The cowboys rounded up the cattle for market.

a rounding error.monolingual: a large amount of money that is relatively small in comparison to a much larger sum. _ To a large company like Smith & Co., a few thousand dollars is just a rounding error. It’s not a lot at all.
examples: To a large company like Smith & Co.

round-trip ticket.monolingual: a ticket (for a plane, train, bus, etc.) that allows one to go to a destination and return. _ A round-trip ticket is usually cheaper than two one-way tickets. _ How much is a round-trip ticket to San Francisco?
examples: A round-trip ticket is usually cheaper than two one-way tickets.

rouse someone from something.monolingual: to awaken someone from something; to cause someone to come out of something. _ I roused Tom from his nap and sent him on his way. _ We could not rouse her from her deep sleep.
examples: I roused Tom from his nap and sent him on his way.

rouse someone out of something.monolingual: to awaken someone out of a state, such as sleep. _It was almost impossible to rouse George out of his sleep. _They could not rouse us out of our drowsy state.
examples: It was almost impossible to rouse George out of his sleep.

rouse someone to something.monolingual: to stir someone to something. _I will rouse the workers to action. They will work or have to find other jobs. _ The speech by the president roused the citizens to action.
examples: I will rouse the workers to action.

route something to someone.monolingual: to send something along a particular path to someone. _Try to route this to Walter, who is on a ship at sea. I’ll get the name of the ship for you. _ I will route a copy of the invoice to you.
examples: Try to route this to Walter, who is on a ship at sea.

a royal pain.monolingual: a great annoyance. _ This guy’s a royal pain, but we have to put up with him because he’s the boss.
examples: This guy’s a royal pain, but we have to put up with him because he’s the boss.

the royal treatment.monolingual: very good treatment; very good and thoughtful care of a person. _ I was well cared for. They gave me the royal treatment. _ I got the royal treatment when I stayed at that expensive hotel.
examples: I was well cared for.

rub salt in a wound.monolingual: Fig. to deliberately make someone’s unhappiness, shame, or misfortune worse. _ Don’t rub salt in the wound by telling me how enjoyable the party was. _ Bill is feeling miserable about losing his job and Bob is rubbing salt into the wound by saying ho
examples: Don’t rub salt in the wound by telling me how enjoyable the party was.

rub someone out†.monolingual: Sl. to kill someone. (Underworld.) _The gunman was eager to rub somebody out. _The crooks tried to rub out the witness.
examples: The gunman was eager to rub somebody out.

rub someone’s nose in it.monolingual: Fig. to remind one of something one has done wrong; to remind one of something bad or unfortunate that has happened. (Alludes to a method of housebreaking pets.) _ When Bob failed his exam, his brother rubbed his nose in it. _ Mary knows she shouldn’
examples: When Bob failed his exam, his brother rubbed his nose in it.

rub something away†.monolingual: to remove something by chafing or rubbing. _See if you can rub some of the dirt away. _Rub away the dirt if you can.
examples: See if you can rub some of the dirt away.

rub something out†.monolingual: to obliterate something by rubbing. _ See if you can rub those stains out. _ Rub out the graffiti on the side of the car if you can.
examples: See if you can rub those stains out.

rub something over something.monolingual: to cover something with something, spreading it by rubbing. _The chef rubbed the herbal butter over the skin of the turkey. _ Please rub the lotion over my back.
examples: The chef rubbed the herbal butter over the skin of the turkey.

rub something together.monolingual: to press two things together and move them back and forth. _ Sam rubbed his fingers together, indicating that he needed some money before he could continue. _ Mary rubbed her hands together to get them warmed up.
examples: Sam rubbed his fingers together, indicating that he needed some money before he could continue.

rub something up†.monolingual: to raise something, such as the nap of a rug, by rubbing. _ When you run the vacuum cleaner across the f loor, you rub the nap of the rug up and get the dirt out. _ Don’t rub up the nap.
examples: When you run the vacuum cleaner across the f loor, you rub the nap of the rug up and get the dirt out.

ruffle its feathers.monolingual: [for a bird] to point its feathers outward. _ The bird ruff led its feathers when it was annoyed. _My parrot ruff les its feathers whenever it is ready to preen itself.
examples: The bird ruff led its feathers when it was annoyed.

ruffle someone’s feathers.monolingual: Fig. to irritate or annoy someone. _ I didn’t mean to ruff le his feathers. I just thought that I would remind him of what he promised us.
examples: I didn’t mean to ruff le his feathers.

ruffle something up†.monolingual: to raise something, such as feathers, up or outward. _ The bird ruff led its feathers up and started to preen. _ It ruff led up its feathers.
examples: The bird ruff led its feathers up and started to preen.

rug rat.monolingual: Sl. a small child, especially an infant or toddler. (Also a term of address.) _ You got any rug rats at your house? _ Hey, you cute little rug rat, come over here.
examples: Hey, you cute little rug rat, come over here.

rule against someone or something.monolingual: to give a judgment against someone or something. _The judge ruled against the prosecutor. _ The judge ruled against my motion.
examples: The judge ruled against the prosecutor.

a rule of thumb.monolingual: a general principle developed through experiential rather than scientific means. _ As a rule of thumb, I move my houseplants outside in May. _ Going by a rule of thumb, we stop for gas every 200 miles when we are traveling.
examples: As a rule of thumb, I move my houseplants outside in May.

rule on something.monolingual: to give a decision or judgment about something. _ How long will it be before the court rules on your petition? _ The boss will rule on your request tomorrow.
examples: The boss will rule on your request tomorrow.

rule over someone or something.monolingual: to serve as the boss or chief over someone or something. _ I guess you could say that the boss rules over me. _ The president of a democracy doesn’t really rule over the country.
examples: I guess you could say that the boss rules over me.

rule someone or something out†.monolingual: to prevent, disqualify, overrule, or cancel someone or something. _ John’s bad temper rules him out for the job. _ The rainy weather ruled out a picnic for the weekend.
examples: John’s bad temper rules him out for the job.

rule the roost.monolingual: Fig. to be the boss or manager, especially at home. _ Who rules the roost at your house? _ Our new office manager really rules the roost.
examples: Our new office manager really rules the roost.

rule with a velvet glove.monolingual: Fig. to rule in a very gentle way. _ She rules with a velvet glove, but she gets things done, nonetheless. _ He may appear to rule with a velvet glove, but he is really quite cruel.
examples: She rules with a velvet glove, but she gets things done, nonetheless.

rule with an iron fist.monolingual: Fig. to rule in a very stern manner. _The dictator ruled with an iron fist and terrified the citizens. _ My boss rules with an iron fist. I’m looking for a new job.
examples: The dictator ruled with an iron fist and terrified the citizens.

rummage through something.monolingual: to move things about haphazardly while searching through something. _ I rummaged through my top drawer, looking for any two socks that matched. _Mary spent some time rummaging through the toolbox before she found what she was looking for.
examples: I rummaged through my top drawer, looking for any two socks that matched.

rumor has it that....monolingual: there is a rumor that.... _ Rumor has it that Fred is seeing Mary and that they are engaged.
examples: Rumor has it that Fred is seeing Mary and that they are engaged.

rump session.monolingual: a meeting held after a larger meeting. _ A rump session continued after the meeting was adjourned. _ A lot of business was conducted in the rump session.
examples: A rump session continued after the meeting was adjourned.

rumple someone or something up†.monolingual: to bring disorder to someone[’s clothing] or something; to wrinkle someone or something. _One of the little boys knocked another boy down and rumpled him up. _ He rumpled up Dan’s shirt.
examples: One of the little boys knocked another boy down and rumpled him up.

run a comb through something.monolingual: to comb one’s hair quickly. _ Run a comb through your hair after you come back in the house. _She ran a comb through Timmy’s hair, and tried to make him look presentable.
examples: Run a comb through your hair after you come back in the house.

run a make on someone.monolingual: to perform an identity check on someone. _ The cops ran a make on Lefty and learned about his prison record. _ We tried to run a make on him and came up with nothing.
examples: The cops ran a make on Lefty and learned about his prison record.

run a red light.monolingual: to pass through an intersection having a red traffic light without stopping. _ Sam got a ticket for running a red light.
examples: Sam got a ticket for running a red light.

run a tab.monolingual: to accumulate charges on a bill at a bar or tavern. _ They won’t let me run a tab here. I have to pay for each drink as I order it.
examples: They won’t let me run a tab here.

run across something.monolingual: to cross something while running. _The joggers all ran across the bridge together. _The mice ran across the f loor, not knowing that a cat was watching them.
examples: The joggers all ran across the bridge together.

run after someone.monolingual: to chase someone of the opposite sex hoping for a date or some attention. _ Is John still running after Ann? _ No, Ann is running after John.
examples: No, Ann is running after John.

run against someone.monolingual: to compete against someone for elective office. _ Eisenhower ran against Adlai Stevenson in
examples: Eisenhower ran against Adlai Stevenson in 1952.

run along.monolingual: to leave. _Please run along and leave me alone. _ I have to run along now. Good-bye.
examples: Please run along and leave me alone.

run around.monolingual: 1. to run here and there. _Why are you running around? Sit down and be quiet. _Please stop running around. You are making me nervous.
examples: Why are you running around? Sit down and be quiet.

run around with someone.monolingual: to be friends with someone; to go places with regular friends. _ John and I were great friends. We used to run around with each other all the time. _ Mary ran around with Jane for about a year.
examples: John and I were great friends.

run as something.monolingual: to run for office in a certain party. _ Do you suppose I can run as an independent? _ Fred ran as a Democrat and won a seat in the legislature.
examples: Fred ran as a Democrat and won a seat in the legislature.

run at someone or something.monolingual: to run toward someone or something; to charge someone or something. _ The bull started to run at us, but changed its mind—thank heavens. _ The huge crocodile ran at the goat, but the goat leapt away.
examples: The bull started to run at us, but changed its mind—thank heavens.

run away with someone.monolingual: 1. to flee in the company of someone. _Frank arrived on the scene, saw what had happened, and ran away with the other boys. _ Tom ran away with Bill to a place where they could hide.
examples: Frank arrived on the scene, saw what had happened, and ran away with the other boys.

run away with something.monolingual: 1. to flee with something in one’s possession. _ The crook ran away with the watch. _ Someone ran away with that lady’s purse.
examples: The crook ran away with the watch.

run back.monolingual: to come back, running. _ She ran to the barn and then ran back. _ Tom ran back, very much afraid.
examples: She ran to the barn and then ran back.

run back over something.monolingual: to review something. _ Would you please run back over that last part again? _Let me run back over the hard part for you.
examples: Let me run back over the hard part for you.

run behind.monolingual: to be late; to run late. _ We are running behind. You had better hurry. _Things are running behind, and we will not finish on time.
examples: We are running behind.

run behind someone or something.monolingual: to travel along behind someone or something, running. _ I will run behind you in the race. _ Mary ran behind the bicycle until she could not run anymore.
examples: I will run behind you in the race.

run counter to something.monolingual: to be in opposition to something; to run against something. (This has nothing to do with running.) _ Your proposal runs counter to what is required by the manager. _ His idea runs counter to good sense.
examples: Your proposal runs counter to what is required by the manager.

run down.monolingual: 1. to come down, running or very quickly; to go down, running or very quickly. _ I need to talk to you down here. Can you run down? _I will run down and talk to you.
examples: I need to talk to you down here.

run down some lines.monolingual: 1. Sl. to converse (with someone). _ I was running down some lines with Fred when the bell rang. _ Hey, man, let’s run down some lines.
examples: I was running down some lines with Fred when the bell rang.

run down to some place.monolingual: to travel to a place. (By running or any other means.) _I have to run down to the store and get some bread. _ I want to run down to the bank, but my car is out of gas.
examples: I have to run down to the store and get some bread.

run for it.monolingual: to escape by running. _ The dogs were coming after me fast. There was nothing I could do but run for it. _ I ran for it when I saw the police coming.
examples: The dogs were coming after me fast.

run for one’s life.monolingual: to run away to save one’s life. _The dam has burst! Run for your life! _ The captain told us all to run for our lives.
examples: The captain told us all to run for our lives.

*a run for one’s money.monolingual: 1. Fig. the results or rewards one deserves, expects, or wants. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ I get a run for my money at the club tennis tournament. _I had a run for my money in the stock market.
examples: I get a run for my money at the club tennis tournament.

run for something.monolingual: 1. to travel quickly by running to a place of safety. _The picnickers ran for the shelter when the rain started to fall. _ Tom and Jane ran for the house as soon as they heard your call.
examples: The picnickers ran for the shelter when the rain started to fall.

run from someone or something.monolingual: to flee someone or something, usually on foot. _She ran from the mugger who had accosted her. _ Mary ran from the dog and jumped over a fence to safety.
examples: She ran from the mugger who had accosted her.

run from something to something.monolingual: to travel on foot from one thing or place to another, running. _ Do you think you can run from the bank downtown to the post office on Maple Street? _I ran from door to door, telling people what had happened.
examples: I ran from door to door, telling people what had happened.

run in something.monolingual: to compete in something, such as a race or an election. _ I will run in the one-hundred-yard dash. _ I will not run in a race this time. _ Who will run in this year’s election?
examples: I will run in the one-hundred-yard dash.

run in the family.monolingual: [for a characteristic] to appear in many (or all) members of a family. _My grandparents lived well into their nineties, and it runs in the family. _ My brothers and I have red hair. It runs in the family.
examples: My grandparents lived well into their nineties, and it runs in the family.

run into a stone wall.monolingual: Fig. to come to a barrier against further progress. _We’ve run into a stone wall in our investigation. _Algebra was hard for Tom, but he really ran into a stone wall with geometry.
examples: We’ve run into a stone wall in our investigation.

run into someone or something.monolingual: to bump into someone or something. _ I didn’t mean to run into you. I’m sorry. _ Mary ran into the fence and scraped her elbow.
examples: I didn’t mean to run into you.

run it down.monolingual: Sl. to tell the whole story; to tell the truth. _ Come on! What happened? Run it down for me! _ I don’t care what happened. Run it down. I can take it.
examples: I don’t care what happened.

run its course.monolingual: [for something] to continue through its cycle of existence, especially a disease. _ Sorry. There is no medicine for it. It will just have to run its course.
examples: Sorry. There is no medicine for it.

run like clockwork.monolingual: to run very well; to progress very well. _I want this office to run like clockwork—with everything on time and everything done right. _ The plans for the party were made and we knew that we could depend on Alice to make sure that everything ran like
examples: I want this office to run like clockwork—with everything on time and everything done right.

run off.monolingual: 1. to flee. _The children rang our doorbell and then ran off. _They ran off as fast as they could.
examples: The children rang our doorbell and then ran off.

run off at the mouth.monolingual: Sl. to talk too much. _ I wish you would stop running off at the mouth. _Tom runs off at the mouth too much. I wish he would temper his remarks.
examples: I wish you would stop running off at the mouth.

run off in all directions.monolingual: Fig. [for people] to set out to do something or go somewhere in an aimless and disorganized fashion. (Can also apply to one person. See also ride off in all directions.) _ The people in the marketing department need some organization. They are always
examples: The people in the marketing department need some organization.

run off something.monolingual: to drive or travel off something, such as rails, tracks, a road, etc. _ The train ran off its rails and piled up in a cornfield. _ We almost ran off the road during the storm.
examples: The train ran off its rails and piled up in a cornfield.

run on.monolingual: 1. to continue running. _I wanted to stop her and ask her something, but she just ran on. _ The joggers had a chance to stop and rest, but they just ran on.
examples: I wanted to stop her and ask her something, but she just ran on.

run on all cylinders.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for an engine] to run well and smoothly. _ This car is now running on all cylinders, thanks to the tune-up. _ You can hear if an engine is not running on all cylinders.
examples: This car is now running on all cylinders, thanks to the tune-up.

run one’s eye over something.monolingual: Fig. to gaze at the whole of something; to glance at all of something. _ She ran her eyes over the lines of the automobile and nodded her approval. _ He ran his eyes over the drawing and decided that he had to have it.
examples: She ran her eyes over the lines of the automobile and nodded her approval.

run one’s feet off.monolingual: Fig. to run very hard and fast. _ I ran my feet off and I’m really tired now that the race is over. _ I almost ran my feet off getting over here to see you!
examples: I ran my feet off and I’m really tired now that the race is over.

run one’s rhymes.monolingual: Sl. to say what you have to say; to give one’s speech or make one’s plea. _ Go run your rhymes with somebody else! _ I told him to run his rhymes elsewhere.
examples: I told him to run his rhymes elsewhere.

run out of some place.monolingual: to leave a place quickly, on foot; to flee a place. _ He ran out of the room as fast as he could. _We ran out of the building as soon as we felt the first signs of the earthquake.
examples: He ran out of the room as fast as he could.

run out of steam.monolingual: Fig. to lose momentum and fail. _ Toward the end of the lecture, he seemed to run out of steam, leaving us with no summary or conclusion.
examples: Toward the end of the lecture, he seemed to run out of steam, leaving us with no summary or conclusion.

run out of time.monolingual: to have used up most of the allotted time; to have no time left. _You have just about run out of time. _ I ran out of time before I could finish the test.
examples: You have just about run out of time.

run over.monolingual: 1. to come by for a quick visit. _ Can you run over for a minute after work? _I will run over for a minute as soon as I can.
examples: I will run over for a minute as soon as I can.

run over someone or something.monolingual: to drive, steer, or travel so as to pass over someone or something. _The bus ran over the fallen man. _ That car almost ran over my toe.
examples: The bus ran over the fallen man.

run over something with someone.monolingual: to review something with someone. _I would like to run over this with you one more time. _ I want to run over the proposal with Carl again.
examples: I would like to run over this with you one more time.

run over to something.monolingual: to go to something or some place, running or by any independent mode of transportation. _ Would you run over to the store and get me some eggs? _ I have to run over to the bank to cash a check.
examples: I have to run over to the bank to cash a check.

run over with something.monolingual: to drop over for a visit, bringing something. _ Do you mind if I run over with the cup of sugar I borrowed last week? _ Mary ran over with the papers you requested.
examples: Mary ran over with the papers you requested.

run rampant.monolingual: to run, develop, or grow out of control. _ The children ran rampant through the house. _Weeds have run rampant around the abandoned house.
examples: The children ran rampant through the house.

run scared.monolingual: to behave as if one were going to fail. _ The mayor was running scared, but won anyway. _ When we lost that big contract, everyone in the office was running scared. We thought we’d be fired.
examples: The mayor was running scared, but won anyway.

run someone in†.monolingual: to arrest one and take one to the police station. _The cop ran George in so they could question him extensively. _ They ran in George to protect him from the rioters.
examples: The cop ran George in so they could question him extensively.

run someone or something down†.monolingual: 1. to collide with and knock down someone or something. _ The drunken driver ran three pedestrians down. _ Mary ran down a stop sign.
examples: The drunken driver ran three pedestrians down.

run someone ragged.monolingual: Fig. to keep someone or something very busy. _ This busy season is running us all ragged at the store. _ What a busy day. I ran myself ragged.
examples: This busy season is running us all ragged at the store.

run someone through something.monolingual: 1. to make or guide someone though an area while running. _They ran us through a maze as part of our training. _ We ran the little boys through the park so they could get some exercise.
examples: They ran us through a maze as part of our training.

run something back†.monolingual: to wind something back to the beginning. _ Run the tape back and listen to it again. _ Run back the tape and listen again.
examples: Run the tape back and listen to it again.

run something down†.monolingual: to use something having batteries, a motor, or an engine until it has no more power and it stops. _ Who ran my electric toothbrush down? _ Someone ran down my batteries.
examples: Someone ran down my batteries.

run something off†.monolingual: 1. to get rid of something, such as fat or energy, by running. _ The little boys are very excited. Send them outside to run it off. _They need to run off their energy.
examples: The little boys are very excited.

run something onto something.monolingual: to drive or guide something onto the surface of something. _ He ran the car onto the grass and washed it. _ Please run your bicycle onto the porch and I will try to fix it for you.
examples: He ran the car onto the grass and washed it.

run something through something.monolingual: 1. to drive or propel something through the midst of something or a group. _ The cowboys ran the cattle right through the crowd of people standing at the station. _ He ran his truck through the bushes at the end of the driveway.
examples: The cowboys ran the cattle right through the crowd of people standing at the station.

run something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to raise or hoist something, such as a flag. _ Harry ran the f lag up the f lagpole each morning. _Will you please run up the f lag today?
examples: Harry ran the f lag up the f lagpole each morning.

run the gamut.monolingual: to cover a wide range [from one thing to another]. _ She wants to buy the house, but her requests run the gamut from expensive new carpeting to completely new landscaping. _ His hobbies run the gamut from piano repair to portrait painting.
examples: She wants to buy the house, but her requests run the gamut from expensive new carpeting to completely new landscaping.

run the good race.monolingual: to do the best that one could; to live life as well and as fully as possible. _ He didn’t get what he wanted, but he ran the good race. _ Joan ran the good race, and she will be remembered by all of us.
examples: He didn’t get what he wanted, but he ran the good race.

run the show.monolingual: to be in charge; to be in command. _Who’s running this show? _ No, I don’t want to have to run the show again.
examples: No, I don’t want to have to run the show again.

run through something.monolingual: 1. to pass through an area, running. _ Stop running through the living room! _ We ran through the park as part of our exercise.
examples: We ran through the park as part of our exercise.

run to someone or something.monolingual: to travel quickly on foot to someone or something; to go to someone or something with some urgency. _ Mary ran to Alice and greeted her. _ I ran to the door and f led.
examples: Mary ran to Alice and greeted her.

run to something.monolingual: to amount to a certain amount of money. _ In the end, the bill ran to thousands of dollars. _ His account ran to more than I expected.
examples: In the end, the bill ran to thousands of dollars.

run up to some place.monolingual: to travel to a place quickly or for a brief time. _ Let’s run up to the lake for the weekend.
examples: Let’s run up to the lake for the weekend.

run with someone or something.monolingual: to stay in the company of someone or some group. _ Fred was out running with Larry when they met Vernon. _ Let’s go out and run with the other guys this morning.
examples: Fred was out running with Larry when they met Vernon.

run with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to run, showing a particular characteristic. _ Sally runs with speed and grace. _ Fred runs with tremendous speed.
examples: Sally runs with speed and grace.

*the runaround.monolingual: a series of excuses, delays, and referrals. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _You’ll get the runaround if you ask to see the manager. _ I hate it when they give me the runaround.
examples: You’ll get the runaround if you ask to see the manager.

running high.monolingual: [for feelings] to be in a state of excitement or anger. _ Feelings were running high as the general election approached. _ The mood of the crowd was running high when they saw the mother slap her child.
examples: Feelings were running high as the general election approached.

run-of-the-mill.monolingual: common or average; typical. _ The restaurant we went to was nothing special—just run-of-themill. _ The service was good, but the food was run-of-themill or worse.
examples: The restaurant we went to was nothing special—just run-of-themill.

rush at someone or something.monolingual: to run at or charge toward someone or something. _The dog rushed at us and scared us to death. _Mary rushed at the door, but it slammed shut before she got there.
examples: The dog rushed at us and scared us to death.

rush for something.monolingual: to hurry to something. _ All the people rushed for the exits when the game was over. _ We rushed for the picnic tables as soon as they said that lunch was ready.
examples: All the people rushed for the exits when the game was over.

rush hour.monolingual: the period of time when heavy traffic is moving into or out of a city. _ This is the slowest rush hour I have ever been in. Traffic is almost in gridlock.
examples: This is the slowest rush hour I have ever been in.

rush someone into something.monolingual: to hurry someone into doing something. _We rushed Harry into taking the job. _Sally has always hated that dress. Sam rushed her into buying it.
examples: We rushed Harry into taking the job.

rush someone to the hospital.monolingual: to take someone to the hospital very quickly. _ They had to rush her to the hospital because she had stopped breathing. _We rushed Uncle Harry to the hospital after he complained of chest pains.
examples: They had to rush her to the hospital because she had stopped breathing.

rush something into print.monolingual: to print up something hastily. _The story was so timely that the newspaper editor rushed it into print without checking all the details. _We will rush the book into print as soon as the author finishes.
examples: The story was so timely that the newspaper editor rushed it into print without checking all the details.

rush through something.monolingual: to hurry to get something finished; to race through something. _ Please don’t rush through this business. Get it right. _Timmy rushed through dinner so he could go out and play.
examples: Please don’t rush through this business.

rush to conclusions.monolingual: to try to reach a conclusion too fast, probably with insufficient evidence; to jump to conclusions. _ I hope that you don’t rush to any conclusions. I can explain this. _ I’m afraid you are rushing to conclusions when you speak of canceling the perfo
examples: I hope that you don’t rush to any conclusions.

rush to someone or something.monolingual: to hurry to get to someone, something, or some event. _ I rushed to the injured man to try to help him. _We all rushed to the office to see what had happened.
examples: I rushed to the injured man to try to help him.

rust away.monolingual: to dissolve away into rust. _In a few years, this car will rust away if you don’t take care of it. _ The bridge is rusting away, little by little.
examples: In a few years, this car will rust away if you don’t take care of it.

rust belt.monolingual: Fig. the industrial north of the United States. (Patterned on sun belt.) _The economy in the rust belt is slowing down. _ The salt they put on the roads in the winter made my car all rusty. I guess that’s why they call this area the rust belt.
examples: The economy in the rust belt is slowing down.

rust out.monolingual: to develop holes or weak places owing to rust. _ Our hot water heater rusted out and f looded the basement.
examples: Our hot water heater rusted out and f looded the basement.

rustle something up†.monolingual: Rur. to manage to prepare a meal, perhaps on short notice. _ I think I can rustle something up for dinner. _ Please rustle up something to eat.
examples: I think I can rustle something up for dinner.

sack out.monolingual: to go to bed or go to sleep. _ It’s time for me to sack out. _ Let’s sack out early tonight.
examples: It’s time for me to sack out.

sack something up†.monolingual: to put something into bags or sacks. _ Please sack the groceries up and put them in the cart. _ I will sack up your groceries.
examples: Please sack the groceries up and put them in the cart.

sacked out.monolingual: asleep. _ Mary is sacked out in her room. _ Here it is ten o’clock, and you are still sacked out!
examples: Mary is sacked out in her room.

sacred cow.monolingual: Fig. something that is regarded by some people with such respect and veneration that they do not like it being criticized by anyone in any way. (From the fact that the cow is regarded as sacred in India and is not eaten or mistreated.) _A university
examples: A university education is a sacred cow in the Smith family.

sadder but wiser.monolingual: Cliché unhappy but knowledgeable [about someone or something—after an unpleasant event]. _ After the accident, I was sadder but wiser, and would never make the same mistake again. _ We left the meeting sadder but wiser, knowing that we could not ever
examples: After the accident, I was sadder but wiser, and would never make the same mistake again.

saddle an animal up†.monolingual: to put a saddle on a horse or some other beast of burden. _Please saddle my horse up. I have to leave. _ Would you saddle up my horse for me?
examples: Please saddle my horse up.

saddle up.monolingual: 1. Lit. to prepare one’s horse for riding by putting a saddle on it. _ Let’s saddle up and go for a ride.
examples: Let’s saddle up and go for a ride.

saddled with someone or something.monolingual: Fig. burdened with someone or something. _ I’ve been saddled with the children all day. Let’s go out tonight. _ I don’t want to be saddled with your work.
examples: I’ve been saddled with the children all day.

safe and sound.monolingual: unharmed and whole or healthy. _ It was a rough trip, but we got there safe and sound. _ I’m glad to see you here safe and sound.
examples: It was a rough trip, but we got there safe and sound.

safeguard against someone or something.monolingual: to protect against someone or something. _We will try to safeguard against accidents. _How can I safeguard against prowlers?
examples: We will try to safeguard against accidents.

safety in numbers.monolingual: safety achieved by being concealed in or united with large numbers of people or other creatures. _ We stayed close together, thinking that there was safety in numbers. _ The elderly people went out together for a walk, knowing that there was safety i
examples: We stayed close together, thinking that there was safety in numbers.

sag down.monolingual: to droop downward. _The branch sagged down and nearly touched the ground. _ When the rain got the drapes wet, they sagged down and touched the f loor.
examples: The branch sagged down and nearly touched the ground.

sag under something.monolingual: to droop under the burden of something. _ The porch roof sagged under the weight of the snow. _ The springs of the car sagged under the weight of all the passengers.
examples: The porch roof sagged under the weight of the snow.

sage advice.monolingual: very good and wise advice. _My parents gave me some sage advice when I turned
examples: My parents gave me some sage advice when I turned 18.

sail against something.monolingual: to operate a boat or ship, so as to move against the wind. _ It takes skill and training to sail against the wind. _ The huge cruise ship sailed against the wind all the way to St. Thomas.
examples: It takes skill and training to sail against the wind.

sail around.monolingual: to travel by water in a boat or ship. _ We sailed around for about an hour and then went back to the shore. _ Let’s go out and sail around before dinner.
examples: We sailed around for about an hour and then went back to the shore.

sail for some place.monolingual: to depart in a boat or ship for some place. _ This ship sails for Bridgetown, Barbados, at noon today. _ We will sail for home early in the morning.
examples: This ship sails for Bridgetown, Barbados, at noon today.

sail into someone.monolingual: Fig. to attack someone; to chastise someone. (Based on sail into someone or something.) _ The angry coach sailed into the players. _ The teacher sailed into Timmy for breaking the window.
examples: The angry coach sailed into the players.

sail into someone or something.monolingual: 1. to crash into someone or something with a boat or ship. _ The boat sailed into the dock, causing considerable damage. _ I was in my skiff when a larger boat sailed into me.
examples: The boat sailed into the dock, causing considerable damage.

sail under false colors.monolingual: 1. Lit. to sail with false identification. (Pirates often sailed under the national flag of the ship they planned on attacking.) _ The ship, sailing under false colors, suddenly started to pursue our ship. _ Bluebeard the pirate was known for sailing
examples: The ship, sailing under false colors, suddenly started to pursue our ship.

sail up a river.monolingual: to travel upstream on a river in a boat or ship. _We sailed up the Amazon River in a large, seagoing ship. _ It was not possible to sail up the Mississippi as far as we wanted.
examples: We sailed up the Amazon River in a large, seagoing ship.

sally forth.monolingual: to go forth; to leave and go out. _ The soldiers sallied forth from behind the stone wall. _Well, it’s time to sally forth and drive to work.
examples: The soldiers sallied forth from behind the stone wall.

the salt of the earth.monolingual: Fig. the most worthy of people; a very good or worthy person. (A biblical reference, Matthew 5:13.) _ Mrs. Jones is the salt of the earth. She is the first to help anyone in trouble. _ Frank’s mother is the salt of the earth. She has five children of
examples: Mrs. Jones is the salt of the earth.

salt something away†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to store and preserve a foodstuff by salting it. _ The farmer’s wife salted a lot of fish and hams away for the winter. _ She salted away a lot of food.
examples: The farmer’s wife salted a lot of fish and hams away for the winter.

salt something down†.monolingual: to place salt on something, such as icy roads. _ I won’t go out until midmorning, after they have salted the roads down. _ I hope they salt down the roads soon.
examples: I won’t go out until midmorning, after they have salted the roads down.

salt something with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to put a variety of salt or a salt substitute onto some food. _ Oscar salts his food with a salt substitute. _Did you salt your meat with salt or something else?
examples: Oscar salts his food with a salt substitute.

salute someone with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to greet someone with a formal hand salute. _ He failed to salute the officer with the proper salute and was reprimanded. _ David saluted the captain with the appropriate salute and passed on by.
examples: He failed to salute the officer with the proper salute and was reprimanded.

same difference.monolingual: the same; no difference at all. _ Pink, fuchsia, what does it matter? Same difference. _ Whether you go or I go, it’s the same difference.
examples: Pink, fuchsia, what does it matter? Same difference.

same here..monolingual: Me too!; I agree! _Bob: I’ll have chocolate ice cream! Bill: Same here. _ Mary: I’ll vote for the best candidate. Tom: Same here!
examples: Bob: I’ll have chocolate ice cream! Bill: Same here.

the same old story.monolingual: something that occurs or has occurred in the same way often. _Jim’s got no money. It’s the same old story. He’s spent it all on clothing. _The company is getting rid of workers. It’s the same old story—a shortage of orders.
examples: Jim’s got no money.

the same to you..monolingual: The same comment applies to you. (This can be a polite or a rude comment.) _ Bill: Have a pleasant evening. Bob: Thank you. The same to you. _ Mary: You’re the most horrible person I’ve ever met! John: The same to you!
examples: Bill: Have a pleasant evening.

sand something down†.monolingual: 1. to make something smooth by rubbing it with sandpaper. (To act on the main body of the object, not the imperfections.) _ You should sand the board down before you paint it. _ Please sand down the board.
examples: You should sand the board down before you paint it.

the sands of time.monolingual: Fig. the accumulated tiny amounts of time; time represented by the sand in an hourglass. _The sands of time will make you grow old like everyone else. _ My only enemy is the sands of time.
examples: The sands of time will make you grow old like everyone else.

saturday night special.monolingual: a small, easily obtainable pistol. _ There was another killing last night with a Saturday night special. _ That’s the tenth shooting done with a Saturday night special this week.
examples: There was another killing last night with a Saturday night special.

saunter along.monolingual: to walk along slowly; to ramble along. _ Bob sauntered along, looking as if he didn’t have a care in the world. _ I was just sauntering along, minding my own business, when all of a sudden a mugger jumped out and swiped my purse.
examples: Bob sauntered along, looking as if he didn’t have a care in the world.

save it!.monolingual: Inf. Stop talking.; Shut up!; Tell it to me later. _ I’ve heard enough. Save it! _ Save it! You talk too much!
examples: I’ve heard enough.

save one’s breath.monolingual: Fig. to refrain from talking, explaining, or arguing. _ There is no sense in trying to convince her. Save your breath. _Tell her to save her breath. He won’t listen to her.
examples: There is no sense in trying to convince her.

save something up†.monolingual: to save something; to accumulate something. _ I’m saving up cans for recycling. _ If you’d only save your money up, you could buy anything you want.
examples: I’m saving up cans for recycling.

save the day.monolingual: to produce a good result when a bad result was expected. _ The team was expected to lose, but Sally made three points and saved the day. _ Your excellent speech calmed the crowd and saved the day.
examples: The team was expected to lose, but Sally made three points and saved the day.

saved by the bell.monolingual: Cliché saved by the timely intervention of someone or something. (Alludes to a boxer who is saved from being counted out by the bell that ends a round.) _ I was going to have to do my part, but someone knocked on the door and I didn’t have to do it.
examples: I was going to have to do my part, but someone knocked on the door and I didn’t have to do it.

saving grace.monolingual: Cliché the one thing that saves or redeems someone or something that would otherwise be a total disaster. _ Her saving grace is that she has a lot of money. _ The saving grace for the whole evening was the good music played by the band.
examples: Her saving grace is that she has a lot of money.

savor of something.monolingual: to taste like something. _ This casserole savors of nutmeg. _ The meat savors of too much garlic.
examples: This casserole savors of nutmeg.

saw into something.monolingual: to cut into something with a saw. _ The carpenter sawed into the beam and had it cut in two in no time at all. _ Be careful not to saw into the table.
examples: The carpenter sawed into the beam and had it cut in two in no time at all.

saw something down†.monolingual: to cut something down with a saw. _ We are going to have to saw that dead tree down before it falls on the house. _ I’ll saw down the tree.
examples: We are going to have to saw that dead tree down before it falls on the house.

saw through something.monolingual: to cut through something with a saw. _ I can’t saw through this wood. It’s too hard! _ I can saw through it!
examples: I can’t saw through this wood.

say a mouthful.monolingual: Fig. to say a lot; to say something very important or meaningful. _ When you said things were busy around here, you said a mouthful. It is terribly busy. _ You sure said a mouthful, Bob. Things are really busy.
examples: When you said things were busy around here, you said a mouthful.
