say cheese!.monolingual: Inf. an expression used by photographers to get people to smile, which they must do while saying the word cheese. _“All of you please stand still and say cheese!” said the photographer. _“Is everybody ready? Say cheese!” asked Mary, aiming the camera
examples: “All of you please stand still and say cheese!” said the photographer.

say grace.monolingual: to say a prayer of gratitude before or after a meal. _ Grandfather always says grace at Thanksgiving. _ A local preacher said grace at the banquet.
examples: Grandfather always says grace at Thanksgiving.

say no more..monolingual: Inf. I agree.; I will do it.; I concede, no need to continue talking. _ John: Someone ought to take this stuff outside. Bill: Say no more. Consider it done. _ Mary: Shouldn’t we turn here if we plan to visit Jane? Alice: Say no more. Here we go.
examples: John: Someone ought to take this stuff outside.

say something for something.monolingual: [for something] to imply something good about something. _ The speed with which we were able to sell the house says something for the state of the real estate market. _ The number of new cars on the road says something for the state of the nation’s e
examples: The speed with which we were able to sell the house says something for the state of the real estate market.

say something out loud.monolingual: to say something so it can be heard; to say something that others might be thinking, but not saying. _ Yes, I said it, but I didn’t mean to say it out loud. _ If you know the answer, please say it out loud.
examples: Yes, I said it, but I didn’t mean to say it out loud.

say something to oneself.monolingual: 1. Lit. to mutter something to oneself so that no one else can hear. _ He said something to himself, but I didn’t catch what it was. _ I said the answer to myself and no one else was supposed to hear it.
examples: He said something to himself, but I didn’t catch what it was.

say something to someone.monolingual: to tell something to someone. _ He didn’t say anything to me. _Did someone say something to you?
examples: He didn’t say anything to me.

say something to something.monolingual: to say yes or no to a proposal, request, etc. _ I hope you will say yes to my proposal. _ Nothing was said to your request at the last meeting.
examples: I hope you will say yes to my proposal.

say the word.monolingual: to give a signal to begin; to say yes or okay. _ I’m ready to start any time you say the word. _ We’ll all shout “Happy Birthday!” when I say the word.
examples: I’m ready to start any time you say the word.

say what?.monolingual: Inf. What did you say?; Please repeat what you said. _ Sally: Would you like some more salad? Fred: Say what? Sally: Salad? Would you like some more salad? _ John: Put this one over there. Sue: Say what? John: Never mind, I’ll do it.
examples: John: Put this one over there.

say when..monolingual: Inf. Tell me when I have given you enough of something, usually a liquid. (Sometimes answered simply with When.) _ Tom (pouring milk into Fred’s glass): Say when, Fred. Fred: When. _ John: Do you want some more juice? Mary: Yes. John: Okay. Say when.
examples: Tom (pouring milk into Fred’s glass): Say when, Fred.

says you!.monolingual: Inf. That’s just what you say!; You don’t know what you are talking about! _ Fred: You are fat and ugly. Tom: Says you! _ Mary: People who go around correcting other people were found to be very annoying in a recent survey. Bill: Says you!
examples: Fred: You are fat and ugly.

scab over.monolingual: [for a wound] to form a scab. _The wound soon scabbed over and the injury was well on its way to healing. _ I hope this shaving cut scabs over before I have to leave for work.
examples: The wound soon scabbed over and the injury was well on its way to healing.

scale something down†.monolingual: to reduce the size or cost of something. _ The bad economy forced us to scale the project down. _ Liz scaled down the project.
examples: The bad economy forced us to scale the project down.

scale something to something.monolingual: to design or adjust the size of one thing to match or complement the size of another thing. _ The architect sought to scale the office building to the buildings surrounding it. _ The playhouse will have to be scaled to the main house.
examples: The architect sought to scale the office building to the buildings surrounding it.

scamper along.monolingual: [for a child or small animal] to run along nimbly. _ The rabbit scampered along, unaware that a fox was following it. _ It is time for Timmy to scamper along home.
examples: The rabbit scampered along, unaware that a fox was following it.

scamper away.monolingual: [for a child or small animal] to run away nimbly. _ The rabbit scampered away across the lawn. _ The children scampered away when they heard the teacher coming.
examples: The rabbit scampered away across the lawn.

scar over.monolingual: [for an injury] to form and leave a scar. _ The wound will scar over, but your arm will never be the same as it was before the accident.
examples: The wound will scar over, but your arm will never be the same as it was before the accident.

scare someone or something up†.monolingual: Rur. to search for and find someone or something. _ Go out in the kitchen and scare some food up. _ I’ll see if I can scare up somebody to fix the broken chair.
examples: Go out in the kitchen and scare some food up.

scare someone out of something.monolingual: to startle someone; to frighten someone into losing something, such as a year’s worth of growth, ten years of life, etc. _You nearly scared me out of my skin! _ The bad news scared Roger out of ten years’ growth.
examples: The bad news scared Roger out of ten years’ growth.

scare someone stiff.monolingual: Fig. to frighten someone severely. (Stiff = dead.) _ That loud noise scared me stiff. _ The robber jumped out and scared us stiff.
examples: That loud noise scared me stiff.

scare something out of someone.monolingual: to frighten someone very badly. (The something can be the living daylights, the wits, the hell, the shit, etc. Use discretion with shit.) _ Gee, you scared the living daylights out of me! _ The police tried to scare the truth out of her. _ The door b
examples: The police tried to scare the truth out of her.

scared silly.monolingual: frightened very much. _ I was scared silly by the loud explosion. _We were scared silly to go into the park after dark.
examples: I was scared silly by the loud explosion.

scared stiff.monolingual: Fig. badly frightened. _ We were scared stiff by the robber. _ I was scared stiff when the dog growled at me.
examples: We were scared stiff by the robber.

scarf out.monolingual: Sl. to overeat. _ I scarf out whenever we have pizza. _My brother scarfs out every day—around the clock!
examples: I scarf out whenever we have pizza.

scarf something down†.monolingual: Sl. to eat something, perhaps in a hurry; to swallow something, perhaps in a hurry. _ Are you going to scarf this whole thing down? _ Here, scarf down this sandwich.
examples: Here, scarf down this sandwich.

scheme against someone or something.monolingual: to plot or conspire against someone or something. _A group of generals was plotting against the government. _ They schemed against the king until he caught them and put an end to it.
examples: A group of generals was plotting against the government.

scheme for something.monolingual: to plot and plan for something, perhaps using deception. _She is scheming for a raise. _Ted is always scheming for a way to miss work.
examples: She is scheming for a raise.

the school of hard knocks.monolingual: Fig. the school of life’s experiences, as opposed to a formal, classroom education. _ I didn’t go to college, but I went to the school of hard knocks. I learned everything by experience.
examples: I didn’t go to college, but I went to the school of hard knocks.

school of thought.monolingual: a particular philosophy or way of thinking about something. _ One school of thought holds that cats cause allergic reactions. _ I come from the school of thought that believes people should always be polite.
examples: One school of thought holds that cats cause allergic reactions.

school someone in something.monolingual: to train, discipline, or coach someone in something. _ The voice coach schooled the singer in excellent breathing techniques. _We were schooled in oratory and debate. _ She schooled herself in patience.
examples: The voice coach schooled the singer in excellent breathing techniques.

scoff at someone or something.monolingual: to show ridicule or scorn for someone or something. _The directors scoffed at her when she presented her plan. _ They scoffed at my new hat, not realizing how stylish it was.
examples: The directors scoffed at her when she presented her plan.

scold someone about something.monolingual: to rebuke or chastise someone about something. _ How many times have I scolded you about that? _Please don’t scold me about something I didn’t do.
examples: Please don’t scold me about something I didn’t do.

scold someone for something.monolingual: to rebuke or chastise someone for doing something. _ The manager scolded the worker for misplacing the door key. _ The teacher scolded all the students for their bad behavior.
examples: The manager scolded the worker for misplacing the door key.

scoop something up†.monolingual: to gather and remove something by scooping, dipping, or bailing. _Karen scooped the nuts up and put them in a bag. _ Jill scooped up all the money she had won and left the poker table.
examples: Karen scooped the nuts up and put them in a bag.

scoot over.monolingual: to slide sideways while seated. _Scoot over and let me sit down. _If you scoot over, we can get another person in this row.
examples: Scoot over and let me sit down.

scope someone or something out†.monolingual: Sl. to look someone or something over; to check someone or something out. _ Hey, scope the new car out! _ Dave was scoping out all the girls.
examples: Dave was scoping out all the girls.

score against someone or something.monolingual: to make a point or goal against someone or some team. _ Because of his bad ankle, Fred was unable to score against his defender. _ We never scored against the visiting team.
examples: Because of his bad ankle, Fred was unable to score against his defender.

score something for something.monolingual: 1. to arrange music for one or more musical instruments; to arrange music for a particular type of voice or voices. _ The arranger scored the music for two pianos. _ The arranger scored the song for a four-part chorus.
examples: The arranger scored the music for two pianos.

scour something out†.monolingual: to clean something out by scouring. _ Would you scour the pans out? _ Please scour out the pans—don’t just wash them.
examples: Please scour out the pans—don’t just wash them.

scour something out of something.monolingual: to clean something out of something by scouring. _ Did you scour the rust out of the pan? _Please scour the burned material out of the bowl.
examples: Please scour the burned material out of the bowl.

scout someone or something out†.monolingual: to search for and discover someone or something. _ I will scout a new salesclerk out for you if you want. _ I’ll scout out a new clerk for you.
examples: I will scout a new salesclerk out for you if you want.

scout someone or something up†.monolingual: to search for and find someone or something. _ I’ll scout up a costume for the Halloween party. _ Can you scout a date up for Friday night?
examples: I’ll scout up a costume for the Halloween party.

scowl at someone or something.monolingual: to make a frown of disapproval or displeasure at someone or something. _ Why are you scowling at me? I didn’t do anything wrong! _Mary scowled at her noisy cat.
examples: Mary scowled at her noisy cat.

scramble for someone or something.monolingual: to push and struggle to get to someone or something. _All the teenagers scrambled for the rock star but couldn’t catch him. _The children scrambled for the candy as it fell from the piñata.
examples: All the teenagers scrambled for the rock star but couldn’t catch him.

scrape something together†.monolingual: to gather things together by scraping. _The waiter scraped all the crumbs together and removed them from the table with a little gadget. _ Karen scraped together all the trimmings and set them aside.
examples: The waiter scraped all the crumbs together and removed them from the table with a little gadget.

scratch at something.monolingual: to scratch something. _You shouldn’t scratch at a chigger bite because it might get infected. _ Don’t scratch at it!
examples: You shouldn’t scratch at a chigger bite because it might get infected.

scratch someone or something out†.monolingual: to mark out the name of someone or something. _I scratched John out and wrote in George instead. _ I scratched out John and forgot about him.
examples: I scratched John out and wrote in George instead.

scratch someone or something up†.monolingual: to damage or mar someone or something by scratching. _ Being thrown clear of the car in the accident didn’t break any bones, but it scratched her up a lot. _Who scratched up my coffee table?
examples: Being thrown clear of the car in the accident didn’t break any bones, but it scratched her up a lot.

scratch someone’s back.monolingual: 1. Lit. to scratch, usually with the fingers, the parts of someone’s back that they cannot reach. _ Please scratch my back between my shoulder blades.
examples: Please scratch my back between my shoulder blades.

scratch something away†.monolingual: to rub or scrape something off by scratching. _ Look at the finish on this furniture. The cat has almost scratched it away! _That cat scratched away the finish on the table!
examples: Look at the finish on this furniture.

scratch the surface.monolingual: 1. Lit. to scratch something just on the surface, not extending the mark below the finish into the wood, stone, marble, below. _There is no serious damage done to the bench. You only scratched the surface.
examples: There is no serious damage done to the bench.

scream at someone or something.monolingual: to yell or screech at someone or something. _ Why are you screaming at me? _ Go scream at the dog, not me!

scream for something.monolingual: to yell or shriek for something. _ The teenage audience applauded and screamed for more. _ The children said they were screaming for ice cream.
examples: The teenage audience applauded and screamed for more.

scream someone down†.monolingual: to scream loudly at someone; to outscream someone. (Compare this with shout someone down.) _ The angry crowd screamed down the politician. _ They screamed her down and drove her from the platform.
examples: The angry crowd screamed down the politician.

scream something out†.monolingual: to say something in a very loud voice. _ She screamed his name out for everyone to hear. _ Liz screamed out the winner’s name.
examples: She screamed his name out for everyone to hear.

scream with something.monolingual: to scream because of something, such as pain, anger, rage, etc. _Frank screamed with pain when the car door closed on his fingers. _ The teacher screamed with rage when the student talked back.
examples: Frank screamed with pain when the car door closed on his fingers.

screw around.monolingual: 1. Inf. to mess around; to waste time. _ Stop screwing around and get to work! _ I’m not screwing around, I’m thinking.
examples: I’m not screwing around, I’m thinking.

screw off.monolingual: Inf. to waste time. _ Stop screwing off and get busy! _ I’m not screwing off. This is my lunch hour.
examples: I’m not screwing off.

screw someone around.monolingual: Inf. to harass or bother someone. _Don’t screw me around, man! I bite back! _Max got tired of being screwed around by Lefty.
examples: Max got tired of being screwed around by Lefty.

screw someone or something up†.monolingual: Inf. to interfere with someone or something; to mess up someone or something. _ Try again and don’t screw it up this time. _ You really screwed up my brother by not being on time.
examples: Try again and don’t screw it up this time.

screw someone out of something.monolingual: Inf. to cheat someone out of something. _ I think you screwed me out of ten bucks on that deal. _ Max screwed me out of what was due me.
examples: I think you screwed me out of ten bucks on that deal.

screw someone over†.monolingual: Sl. to give someone a very bad time; to scold someone severely. _Those guys really screwed you over. What started it? _Don’t think you can screw over me and my friends. I won’t let you.
examples: Those guys really screwed you over.

screw someone up†.monolingual: Inf. to confuse someone mentally. _ Please don’t screw me up again! _You screwed up my train of thought.
examples: You screwed up my train of thought.

screw something down†.monolingual: to secure something to the floor or a base by the use of screws. _You had better screw these seats down or someone will knock them over. _Please screw down the shelf.
examples: You had better screw these seats down or someone will knock them over.

screw something into something.monolingual: to twist something that is threaded into something. _ I screwed all the screws into the back of the computer and turned it on. _ Please screw this bracket into the wall.
examples: I screwed all the screws into the back of the computer and turned it on.

screw something up†.monolingual: to attach something to a higher place by the use of screws. _ The bracket holding the shelf up has come loose. Will you please screw it up again? _ Please screw up this loose bracket.
examples: The bracket holding the shelf up has come loose.

screw up.monolingual: 1. Inf. to mess up. _ I hope I don’t screw up this time. _The waiter screwed up again.
examples: I hope I don’t screw up this time.

screw up one’s courage.monolingual: Fig. to build up one’s courage. _ I guess I have to screw up my courage and go to the dentist. _ I spent all morning screwing up my courage to take my driver’s test.
examples: I guess I have to screw up my courage and go to the dentist.

screwed, blued, and tattooed.monolingual: 1. Sl. taken advantage of _ I got a bad deal. I got screwed, blued, and tattooed. _ When John bought his wreck of a car, he got screwed, blued, and tattooed.
examples: I got a bad deal.

screwed up.monolingual: Inf. ruined; messed up. _ This is a really screwed up schedule. Let’s start over again. _ Your schedule is completely screwed up.
examples: This is a really screwed up schedule.

scribble something down†.monolingual: to write something down fast and not too neatly. _ He scribbled the figure down and raced for the telephone. _Liz scribbled down the telephone number.
examples: He scribbled the figure down and raced for the telephone.

scrimp on something.monolingual: to try to economize on the use of something; to fail to use enough of something. _ Please don’t scrimp on the quality of the food. _ There is enough money. You don’t have to scrimp on anything.
examples: Please don’t scrimp on the quality of the food.

scrounge someone or something up†.monolingual: Fig. to find someone or something somewhere; to dig someone or something up. _ I can’t think of anyone just now, but I will scrounge someone up. _ They scrounged up an escort for Liz.
examples: I can’t think of anyone just now, but I will scrounge someone up.

scrub someone or something down†.monolingual: to clean someone or something thoroughly by rubbing. _The mother scrubbed the baby down gently and put lotion on her. _ Please scrub down this f loor.
examples: The mother scrubbed the baby down gently and put lotion on her.

scrub someone or something off†.monolingual: to clean someone or something by rubbing. _ Mother scrubbed Timmy off. _ Liz scrubbed off the countertop.
examples: Mother scrubbed Timmy off.

scrub something away†.monolingual: to clean something away by rubbing. _ See if you can scrub that rust away. _ Scrub away that rust if you can.
examples: See if you can scrub that rust away.

scrub up.monolingual: 1. Lit. to clean oneself up. _ You have to scrub up before dinner. _ Please go scrub up before you come to the table.
examples: You have to scrub up before dinner.

scrunch down.monolingual: to squeeze or huddle down into a smaller shape. _ Mary scrunched down, trying to hide behind the chair. _ The children scrunched down so they wouldn’t be seen.
examples: Mary scrunched down, trying to hide behind the chair.

scrunch down into something.monolingual: to squeeze down into a small area or container. _ Fred scrunched down into his seat, hoping no one would see him there. _ Don’t scrunch down into your seat. It’s bad for your posture.
examples: Fred scrunched down into his seat, hoping no one would see him there.

scrunch something up†.monolingual: to crush or crunch up. _I pounded the biscuits and scrunched them up into crumbs. _ He scrunched up the note and threw it upon the fire.
examples: I pounded the biscuits and scrunched them up into crumbs.

scuff something up†.monolingual: to scrape or scratch something. _Who scuffed my f loor up? _Please don’t scuff up my freshly polished f loors!

scuffle with someone.monolingual: to struggle or have a fight with someone. _ The two prisoners scuffled with each other a little till a guard came along and saw them. _The cowboys scuff led with the deputies when they came out of the saloon.
examples: The two prisoners scuffled with each other a little till a guard came along and saw them.

scurry along.monolingual: to run or scamper along fast. _The children scurried along, trotting to school. _ We scurried along the trail, keeping watch out for things that might trip us up.
examples: The children scurried along, trotting to school.

scuttle across something.monolingual: to hurry across something. (Said especially of a small animal.) _ A tiny mouse scuttled across the kitchen f loor and startled me. _A rabbit scuttled across my path.
examples: A tiny mouse scuttled across the kitchen f loor and startled me.

scuttle away.monolingual: [for a small animal] to run away. _ The otters scuttled away as we approached. _ A skunk scuttled away quickly—thank heavens.
examples: The otters scuttled away as we approached.

scuzz someone out†.monolingual: Sl. to nauseate someone. _He had this unreal face that almost scuzzed me out! _ It’s not nice to scuzz out people like that, especially when you hardly know them.
examples: It’s not nice to scuzz out people like that, especially when you hardly know them.

a sea change.monolingual: Fig. a major change or transformation. _ This is not the time for a sea change in our manufacturing division. There are too many orders at the moment.
examples: This is not the time for a sea change in our manufacturing division.

seal someone’s fate.monolingual: Fig. to determine finally the fate of someone. _ His lying and cheating sealed his fate. He was convicted and sent to prison.
examples: His lying and cheating sealed his fate.

seam something with something.monolingual: to join the edges of something together with something. _ The worker seamed the two parts of the carpet with a special tool. _She seamed the material with a strip of cloth to strengthen the seam.
examples: The worker seamed the two parts of the carpet with a special tool.

the seamy side of life.monolingual: Fig. the most unpleasant or roughest aspect of life. (A reference to the inside of a garment where the seams show.) _ Doctors in that area really see the seamy side of life. _ Mary saw the seamy side of life when she worked as a volunteer in the home
examples: Doctors in that area really see the seamy side of life.

search after someone or something.monolingual: to look for someone or something. (Perhaps over a long period of time.) _ We searched after a suitable candidate for weeks. _I am searching after a part for my ’57 Chevy.
examples: We searched after a suitable candidate for weeks.

search for someone or something.monolingual: to look very hard for someone or something. _ I searched for Ted everywhere, but he was already gone. _ I have searched for my glasses high and low.
examples: I searched for Ted everywhere, but he was already gone.

search me..monolingual: Inf. I do not know.; You can search my clothing and my person, but you won’t find the answer to your question anywhere near me. (The two words have equal stress.) _ Jane: What time does Mary’s f light get in? Sally: Search me. _ John: What kind of pa
examples: Jane: What time does Mary’s f light get in? Sally: Search me.

search someone for something.monolingual: to feel, touch, pat, frisk, or examine electronically a person’s body, looking for something hidden underneath the clothes. _ The police searched the suspect for hidden weapons. _ The airport guard used an electronic instrument to search the passenge
examples: The police searched the suspect for hidden weapons.

search someone or something out†.monolingual: to seek and find someone or something. _I will search Fred out. I know he’s here somewhere. _ We have to search out the key to the safedeposit box.
examples: I will search Fred out.

search through something.monolingual: to examine all the things found in something. _ I searched through my books for the answer. _ My drawers were searched through thoroughly.
examples: I searched through my books for the answer.

season something with something.monolingual: to make something more flavorful with specific spices and herbs. _ I always season my stews with lots of freshly ground black pepper. _The chili was seasoned with cumin and allspice, among other things.
examples: I always season my stews with lots of freshly ground black pepper.

secede from something.monolingual: to withdraw from something. _ Which was the first state to secede from the Union? _ We do not want to secede from the organization, but we will if we must.
examples: We do not want to secede from the organization, but we will if we must.

second-guess someone.monolingual: to try to predict what some person will do before it is known to anyone, including the person. _ There is no point in trying to second-guess Bob. He is completely unpredictable.
examples: There is no point in trying to second-guess Bob.

second hand.monolingual: from another person or source, not directly from personal experience or observation. _ I wasn’t present at the meeting. I heard about it at second hand. _ Frank tells stories about the Gulf War, but he got them second hand. He wasn’t actually in the
examples: I wasn’t present at the meeting.

*second nature to someone.monolingual: easy and natural for someone. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ Swimming is second nature to Jane. _ Flying a helicopter is no problem for Bob. It’s become second nature to him.
examples: Swimming is second nature to Jane.

second to none.monolingual: better than everything else. _This is an excellent car—second to none. _ Her suggestion was second to none, and the manager accepted it eagerly.
examples: This is an excellent car—second to none.

security against something.monolingual: something that keeps something safe; something that protects; a protection. _Insurance provides security against the financial losses owing to theft, loss, or damage. _ A good education is a security against unemployment.
examples: Insurance provides security against the financial losses owing to theft, loss, or damage.

seduce someone from something.monolingual: to lure someone away from something. _ The crooked agent seduced Jerry from his usual honest behavior. _ Frank was seduced from his proper ways by the offer of money.
examples: The crooked agent seduced Jerry from his usual honest behavior.

see about someone or something.monolingual: to investigate someone or something; to check on something that someone has said. _ I don’t know who is going on the trip. You ask Jill, and I’ll see about Jerry. _ I will see about your request.
examples: I don’t know who is going on the trip.

see after someone or something.monolingual: to take care of someone or something. (The same as but less common than look after someone or something.) _Would you please see after Walter? He looks a little pale. _ I will see after the committee while they are meeting.
examples: Would you please see after Walter? He looks a little pale.

see around something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to see what is on the other side of or partially concealed by something. _I could not see around the truck in front of me. _ Do you think I can see around corners?
examples: I could not see around the truck in front of me.

see beyond something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to be able to perceive into the distance beyond something. _Can you see beyond the big tree there, where the barn is on the horizon? _ I can’t see beyond the end of the road. I think I need glasses.
examples: I can’t see beyond the end of the road.

see double.monolingual: to see two of everything instead of one, owing to a medical disorder. _ When I was driving, I saw two people on the road instead of one. I’m seeing double. There’s something wrong with my eyes. _ Mike at first thought he was seeing double when he saw
examples: When I was driving, I saw two people on the road instead of one.

see if i care!.monolingual: Inf. I do not care if you do it! _Mary: That does it! I’m going home to Mother! John: See if I care! _Sue: I’m putting the sofa here, whether you like it or not. Bill: Go ahead! See if I care!
examples: Sue: I’m putting the sofa here, whether you like it or not.

see over something.monolingual: to be able to have a view over something such as a wall, fence, etc. _ I couldn’t see over the fence, but I could hear what was going on. _ We could not see over the wall.
examples: I couldn’t see over the fence, but I could hear what was going on.

see red.monolingual: to be angry. _ Whenever I think of the needless destruction of trees, I see red. _Bill really saw red when the tax bill arrived.
examples: Whenever I think of the needless destruction of trees, I see red.

see someone across something.monolingual: to accompany someone across a dangerous area. _ Paul saw his mother across the field, which contained a number of hazards. _ Timmy offered to see the elderly lady across the street.
examples: Paul saw his mother across the field, which contained a number of hazards.

see someone as something.monolingual: to consider someone or something; to deem someone or something as something. _ The manager saw the skilled employee as a godsend. _John saw the new salesman as a threat to his territory.
examples: The manager saw the skilled employee as a godsend.

see someone down to something.monolingual: to accompany or escort someone to a lower level. _I will see you down to the front door. _ Would you please see Mrs. Bracknell down to the door?
examples: I will see you down to the front door.

see someone home.monolingual: to accompany someone home. _ Bill agreed to see his aunt home after the movie. _ You don’t need to see me home. It’s perfectly safe, and I can get there on my own.
examples: Bill agreed to see his aunt home after the movie.

see someone off†.monolingual: to accompany one to the point of departure for a trip and say good-bye upon departure. _ We went to the train station to see Andy off. _ We saw off all the scouts going to camp.
examples: We went to the train station to see Andy off.

see someone off something.monolingual: to accompany someone who is leaving something; to escort someone away from something. _I saw the elderly lady off the station platform safely. _ The emcee saw the contestants off the stage.
examples: I saw the elderly lady off the station platform safely.

see someone to some place.monolingual: to escort someone to a place; to make sure that someone gets some place safely; to accompany someone to a place. _ I saw Mary to her apartment, and then got back in my car and left. _ Bill saw his cousin to the train station, and then they parted.
examples: I saw Mary to her apartment, and then got back in my car and left.

see someone to something.monolingual: to accompany or escort someone to something or some place. _ Let me see you to the station. _ Would you please see your aunt to her car?
examples: Let me see you to the station.

see someone up to something.monolingual: to accompany or escort someone to a higher level. _ That is the end of the tour of the wine cellar. I will see you up to the exit. _Ted saw Mary up to her apartment.
examples: That is the end of the tour of the wine cellar.

see something against something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to view something against something else. _ I can’t see the cars against the evening sky if their lights aren’t on. _The cars can’t be seen against the evening sky.
examples: I can’t see the cars against the evening sky if their lights aren’t on.

see something as something else.monolingual: to visualize or fantasize something as something else. _ I see this as a wonderful way to interest some new people in our organization. _ We all see this as a golden opportunity to get to know one another better.
examples: I see this as a wonderful way to interest some new people in our organization.

see something through.monolingual: to follow through on something until it is completed. _Mary is prepared to see the project through. _ It’s going to be an unpleasant experience, but I hope you’ll see it through.
examples: Mary is prepared to see the project through.

see stars.monolingual: Fig. to seem to see flashing lights after receiving a blow to the head. _ I saw stars when I bumped my head on the attic ceiling. _ The little boy saw stars when he fell headfirst onto the concrete.
examples: I saw stars when I bumped my head on the attic ceiling.

see the light.monolingual: Fig. to understand something clearly at last. _ After a lot of studying and asking many questions, I finally saw the light. _ I know that geometry is difficult. Keep working at it. You’ll see the light pretty soon.
examples: After a lot of studying and asking many questions, I finally saw the light.

see the sights.monolingual: to see the important things in a place; to see what tourists usually see. _We plan to visit Paris and see the sights. _ Everyone left the hotel early in the morning to see the sights.
examples: We plan to visit Paris and see the sights.

see through someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for one’s vision] to penetrate something clear or opaque or a person. _Of course, I can see through the window! _ With x-rays, they can see through your body!
examples: With x-rays, they can see through your body! 2.

see to someone or something.monolingual: to take care of someone or something. _Tom will see to the horses. Come to the house and freshen up. _ I hear the doorbell. Will someone please see to answering the door?
examples: Tom will see to the horses.

see ya, bye-bye..monolingual: Inf. Bye. _ Bill: I have to be off. Bob: See ya, bye-bye. _ Mary: See ya, bye-bye. Sue: Toodle-oo.
examples: Bill: I have to be off.

see you around..monolingual: Inf. I will see you again somewhere. _ Bob: Bye for now. Jane: See you around. _ Tom: See you around, Fred. Fred: Sure, Tom. See you.
examples: Bob: Bye for now.

seeing is believing..monolingual: Prov. It is hard to believe something you have not seen. (Implies that you will not believe the thing under discussion until you have actually seen it.) _ Jill: They say Melissa has become a wonderful housekeeper now that she has her own apartment. J
examples: Jill: They say Melissa has become a wonderful housekeeper now that she has her own apartment.

seeing that....monolingual: considering...; since... _Seeing that she has no money, Sally won’t be going shopping. _ Seeing that it’s raining, we won’t go to the beach.
examples: Seeing that she has no money, Sally won’t be going shopping.

seeing things.monolingual: imagining that one sees someone or something that is not there. _ Lisa says that she saw a ghost, but she was just seeing things. _ I thought I was seeing things when Bill walked into the room. Someone had told me he was dead.
examples: Lisa says that she saw a ghost, but she was just seeing things.

seek after someone or something.monolingual: to keep looking for someone or something. _ I will continue to seek after the thief who stole my car. _The thief was seeking after a late-model sedan.
examples: I will continue to seek after the thief who stole my car.

seek and ye shall find..monolingual: Prov. If you search hard enough for something, you will find it. (Biblical. Can imply that the only thing you need to do to get something is look for it.) _ The bookstore on the corner is an excellent one. Any book you want, just seek and ye shall fi
examples: The bookstore on the corner is an excellent one.

seek professional help.monolingual: Euph. to get psychiatric or psychological treatment. _If you are seriously thinking of sui- cide, now is the time to seek professional help. _His friends suggested that he seek professional help.
examples: If you are seriously thinking of sui- cide, now is the time to seek professional help.

seek someone or something out†.monolingual: to search for and find someone or something. _ We will seek someone out to do the work for us. _ Liz sought out a helper for Karen.
examples: We will seek someone out to do the work for us.

seem like someone or something.monolingual: to appear to be like some kind of person or something. _You seemed like such a nice person when I met you. _ This seems like a nice day.
examples: You seemed like such a nice person when I met you.

seep away.monolingual: [for a fluid] to escape little by little, as through a leak. _All the oil seeped away, leaving none in the engine. _ The water seeped away after a while.
examples: All the oil seeped away, leaving none in the engine.

seep through something.monolingual: [for a fluid] to permeate something and escape. _The oil seeped through the gasket onto the ground. _Some water seeped through the ceiling, ruining our carpet as well as the ceiling.
examples: The oil seeped through the gasket onto the ground.

seethe with someone or something.monolingual: to swarm or seem to “boil” with someone or something. _The wedding reception was seething with guests and well-wishers. _The room was just seething with f lies and other f lying creatures.
examples: The wedding reception was seething with guests and well-wishers.

seethe with something.monolingual: [for someone] to be agitated with anger, hatred, scorn, disgust, etc. _ Laura was seething with rage as she entered the tax office. _ We were seething with disgust at the rude way they treated the people who had just moved in.
examples: Laura was seething with rage as she entered the tax office.

segue into something.monolingual: to make a smooth transition into something. (From filmmaking and broadcasting. Rhymes with egg - day.) _ At this point in the script, you should segue into the next scene. _ Don’t segue here, this is where a commercial goes.
examples: At this point in the script, you should segue into the next scene.

seize onto someone or something.monolingual: to grab onto someone or something. _The beggar seized onto the well-dressed gentleman and demanded money. _Tony seized onto the doorknob and gave it a hard jerk.
examples: The beggar seized onto the well-dressed gentleman and demanded money.

seize something up†.monolingual: to grab or take something. _The crow seized the freshly hatched chick up and f lew away. _ The huge bird seized up the tiny chick.
examples: The crow seized the freshly hatched chick up and f lew away.

seize the opportunity.monolingual: to take advantage of an opportunity when offered. _ My uncle offered me a trip to Europe, so I seized the opportunity. _ Whenever you have a chance, you should seize the opportunity.
examples: My uncle offered me a trip to Europe, so I seized the opportunity.

seize up.monolingual: to freeze or halt; to grind suddenly to a stop. _ The engine seized up, and the car coasted to a stop. _ My knee seized up in the middle of a football game.
examples: The engine seized up, and the car coasted to a stop.

seized with something.monolingual: Fig. affected suddenly by something, such as laughter, coughing, sneezing, fits of rage, etc. _Suddenly, I was seized with a fit of coughing. _Mary was seized with laughter at the sight of Ted in a clown suit.
examples: Suddenly, I was seized with a fit of coughing.

select from someone or something.monolingual: to make a choice from a group of people or things. _ You will have to select from the people we have asked to interview with you today. _ They told me that I had to select from what you have in stock.
examples: You will have to select from the people we have asked to interview with you today.

select someone from something.monolingual: to choose someone from a group of people. _ You will have to select a new secretary from the available pool of workers. _ I selected Ted from the applicants I had at the time.
examples: You will have to select a new secretary from the available pool of workers.

self-praise is no recommendation..monolingual: Prov. If you praise yourself, people will think that you are boastful and will not respect you. _ After listening to the lawyer brag about his achievements for a solid half hour, I decided I would find someone else to handle my case. Self-praise is n
examples: After listening to the lawyer brag about his achievements for a solid half hour, I decided I would find someone else to handle my case.

sell at something.monolingual: [for something] to be marketed at a particular price. _ This coat formerly sold at twice this price. _ Next month, this will sell at a 60 percent markup.
examples: This coat formerly sold at twice this price.

sell like hotcakes.monolingual: Fig. [for something] to be sold very fast. _ The delicious candy sold like hotcakes. _ The fancy new cars were selling like hotcakes.
examples: The delicious candy sold like hotcakes.

sell out.monolingual: [for an item] to be sold until there is no more. _ All the plastic hangers have sold out.
examples: All the plastic hangers have sold out.

sell someone or something short.monolingual: Fig. to underestimate someone or something; to fail to see the good qualities of someone or something. _ This is a very good restaurant. Don’t sell it short. _When you say that John isn’t interested in music, you’re selling him short. Did you know he
examples: This is a very good restaurant.

sell something at something.monolingual: 1. to market something at a particular price. _Do you think we can sell these things at four dollars each? _ We cannot sell these at ten times what we paid for them!
examples: We cannot sell these at ten times what we paid for them! 2.

sell something for a song.monolingual: Fig. to sell something for very little money. (As in trading something of value for the singing of a song.) _I had to sell my car for a song because I needed the money in a hurry. _I have two geometry books and I would sell one of them for a song.
examples: I had to sell my car for a song because I needed the money in a hurry.

sell something off†.monolingual: to sell all of something. _We ended up with a large stock of out-of-style coats and we had to sell them all off at a loss. _ We sold off all the excess stock.
examples: We ended up with a large stock of out-of-style coats and we had to sell them all off at a loss.

sell something on credit.monolingual: to sell something now and let the purchaser pay for it later. _ I’m sorry, we don’t sell groceries on credit. It’s strictly cash-and-carry. _ There is a shop around the corner that sells clothing on credit.
examples: I’m sorry, we don’t sell groceries on credit.

sell something out†.monolingual: to sell all of something. _ Have they sold their supply out yet? _ The stores sold out their stocks of that game long before Christmas.
examples: The stores sold out their stocks of that game long before Christmas.

a selling point.monolingual: a feature of a product or idea that is worth mentioning when trying to sell the product or idea. _The fact that the book had large type is an important selling point.
examples: The fact that the book had large type is an important selling point.

send after someone or something.monolingual: to request that someone or something be brought; to send for someone or something. _You really ought to send after a doctor. _Let’s send after a taxi to take us to the airport.
examples: You really ought to send after a doctor.

send ahead for something.monolingual: to send a message for something to be ready or available when one arrives. _ I will send ahead for a taxi to meet us at the station. _ We sent ahead for room reservations at the hotel.
examples: I will send ahead for a taxi to meet us at the station.

send for someone or something.monolingual: to make a request that someone or something be brought. _ Mr. Franklin sent for his secretary. _ I think we should send for an ambulance.
examples: Mr. Franklin sent for his secretary.

send one about one’s business.monolingual: to send someone away, usually in an unfriendly way. _ Is that annoying man on the telephone again? Please send him about his business. _ Ann, I can’t clean up the house with you hanging around. I’m going to have to send you about your business.
examples: Is that annoying man on the telephone again? Please send him about his business.

send one to one’s death.monolingual: to order one to go on a mission or journey that will result in one’s death. _ The general sent many fine young men to their deaths that day. _ They were sent to their death by the act of a madman.
examples: The general sent many fine young men to their deaths that day.

send someone away with something.monolingual: to make someone leave and carry something away. _ I sent him away with a message for his mother. _ She sent Ted away with a little booklet about manners.
examples: I sent him away with a message for his mother.

send someone back for something.monolingual: to cause someone to return to get something. _ He came without it, so I sent him back for it. _Ted sent Roger back for the rest of the groceries.
examples: He came without it, so I sent him back for it.

send someone below.monolingual: to send someone to one of the lower decks of a ship. _ The first mate sent the sailor below to shovel coal into the boiler. _ The captain sent Mr. Wallace below, where he would be out of the way during the storm.
examples: The first mate sent the sailor below to shovel coal into the boiler.

send someone down for something.monolingual: to request someone to go to a place on a lower level to get something. _ I sent the butler down for another bottle of wine. _I sent the butler down for more of this vintage.
examples: I sent the butler down for another bottle of wine.

send someone in for someone.monolingual: to send someone into a game as a replacement for someone else. _ The coach sent Jill in for Alice, who was beginning to tire. _ Ted sent Bill in for Wally.
examples: The coach sent Jill in for Alice, who was beginning to tire.

send someone off.monolingual: to participate in saying good-bye to someone who is leaving. _ We had a party to send Tom off on his retirement. _Bob’s parents sent him off from the airport.
examples: We had a party to send Tom off on his retirement.

send someone or something along†.monolingual: to help someone or something continue along; to send someone. _ I knew it was time for Johnny to go home, so I sent him along. _I will send along the baggage later.
examples: I knew it was time for Johnny to go home, so I sent him along.

send someone or something around†.monolingual: to cause someone or something to go from place to place. _ I sent my secretary around to look for the missing book. _ I will send around some papers for you to sign.
examples: I sent my secretary around to look for the missing book.

send someone or something away†.monolingual: to cause someone, a group, or something to leave. _ I sent the salesman away. _ The store sent away all late deliveries.
examples: I sent the salesman away.

send someone or something back†.monolingual: to cause someone or something to return. _ He came to apologize, but I sent him back. _ Send back these goods. They are defective.
examples: He came to apologize, but I sent him back.

send someone or something down†.monolingual: to dispatch someone or something to some place on a lower level. _ They wanted someone downstairs to help with the moving, so I sent John down. _ I sent down John to help.
examples: They wanted someone downstairs to help with the moving, so I sent John down.

send someone or something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to order someone to go upward to a higher level; to arrange for something to be taken upward to a higher level. _ I’ll send up Gary. _ They are hungry on the tenth f loor. Let’s send some sandwiches up.
examples: I’ll send up Gary.

send someone packing.monolingual: Fig. to send someone away; to dismiss someone, possibly rudely. _I couldn’t stand him anymore, so I sent him packing. _ The maid proved to be so incompetent that I had to send her packing.
examples: I couldn’t stand him anymore, so I sent him packing.

send someone to glory.monolingual: 1. Fig. to kill someone. _One shot sent him to glory. _ You want me to send you to glory or something?
examples: One shot sent him to glory.

send someone up†.monolingual: Fig. to mock or ridicule, particularly by imitation. _ Last week, he sent the prime minister up. _ In his act, he sends up famous people.
examples: Last week, he sent the prime minister up.

send someone up the wall.monolingual: Fig. to annoy and irritate someone; to drive someone crazy. _ Don’t scratch your fingers on the blackboard. It sends me up the wall! _ That noise sends me up the wall!
examples: Don’t scratch your fingers on the blackboard.

send something by something.monolingual: to dispatch something by a particular carrier. _ I will send it to you by special messenger. _ We sent the package by air freight.
examples: I will send it to you by special messenger.

send something c.o.d..monolingual: to send merchandise to someone who will pay for it when it is delivered. (C.O.D. means “cash on delivery” or “collect on delivery.”) _I asked them to send the book C.O.D. _ This person has ordered a copy of our upcoming release. Send it C.O.D.
examples: I asked them to send the book C.

send something from something.monolingual: to dispatch something from something or some place. _ Ted sent the package from the downtown post office. _ The gifts were sent off in a large box from the company’s shipping dock.
examples: Ted sent the package from the downtown post office.

send up a trial balloon.monolingual: to suggest something and see how people respond to it; to test public opinion. _ Mary had an excellent idea, but when we sent up a trial balloon, the response was very negative. _Don’t start the whole project without sending up a trial balloon.
examples: Mary had an excellent idea, but when we sent up a trial balloon, the response was very negative.

send word to someone.monolingual: to get a message to someone by any means. _I will send word to her as soon as I have something to report. _ Tom sent word to Bill just in time.
examples: I will send word to her as soon as I have something to report.

a sense of humor.monolingual: the ability to appreciate good humor and jokes; the ability to create jokes and say funny things. _Does he have a sense of humor? He looks like he has never laughed in his life.
examples: Does he have a sense of humor? He looks like he has never laughed in his life.

sensitize someone to something.monolingual: 1. to make a person have an allergic reaction to something. _ Frequent exposure to the chemical sensitized Harry to it and made him get a rash. _ He became sensitized to pet dander.
examples: Frequent exposure to the chemical sensitized Harry to it and made him get a rash.

separate but equal.monolingual: segregated but of equal value or quality. (A doctrine once sanctioned by the U.S. Supreme Court regarding racial segregation.) _ The separate but equal doctrine was abandoned years ago. _They were provided with facilities that were said to be separat
examples: The separate but equal doctrine was abandoned years ago.

serious about someone.monolingual: in love with someone; romantically interested in someone. _ I’m afraid I’m getting serious about Bill. _Bill, unfortunately, is pretty serious about Mary.
examples: I’m afraid I’m getting serious about Bill.

serve as a guinea pig.monolingual: Fig. [for someone] to be experimented on; to allow some sort of test to be performed on one. (Alludes to the use of guinea pigs for biological experiments.) _ Try it on someone else! I don’t want to serve as a guinea pig! _Jane agreed to serve as a g
examples: Jane agreed to serve as a guinea pig.

serve as someone or something.monolingual: to act in the capacity of someone or something. _I served as the mayor’s assistant for a number of years. _ This brick will not serve as a doorstop.
examples: I served as the mayor’s assistant for a number of years.

serve on something.monolingual: to carry out one’s duty or responsibility on something, such as a committee or a board. _Will you be able to serve on this committee next year also? _ Sarah refused to serve on the committee again.
examples: Sarah refused to serve on the committee again.

serve someone right.monolingual: [for an act or event] to punish someone fairly (for doing something). _John copied off my test paper. It would serve him right if he fails the test. _ It’d serve John right if he got arrested.
examples: John copied off my test paper.

serve someone with something.monolingual: to officially deliver something, such as a subpoena, to someone. _ He served her with papers from the circuit court. _ Has Tom been served with the subpoena?
examples: He served her with papers from the circuit court.

serve something around†.monolingual: to distribute something to eat or drink to everyone present. _ Please serve the snacks around so that everyone gets some. _ Serve around the birthday cakes, would you?
examples: Please serve the snacks around so that everyone gets some.

serve something for something.monolingual: to distribute something to eat or drink for a particular purpose. _We served smoked salmon for an appetizer. _ What will you serve for a main course?
examples: We served smoked salmon for an appetizer.

serve something in something.monolingual: to present something to eat or drink in a particular container. _ Kelly served the lemonade in paper cups. _What will you serve the soup in?
examples: Kelly served the lemonade in paper cups.

serve something on someone.monolingual: to officially deliver something, such as a subpoena, to someone. _ A prosecuting attorney served the subpoena on Max. _ The document was served on the plaintiff by a sheriff ’s deputy.
examples: A prosecuting attorney served the subpoena on Max.

serve something out†.monolingual: to carry out one’s duty or responsibility for the whole time, all the way to the end. _She was unable to serve her term out. _ The convict served out his sentence in solitary confinement.
examples: She was unable to serve her term out.

serve something to someone†.monolingual: 1. to present someone with something to eat or drink. _ The host served the snacks to everyone and left the room to work on the salad. _ The snacks were served to everyone in attendance.
examples: The host served the snacks to everyone and left the room to work on the salad.

serve something up†.monolingual: to distribute or deliver food for people to eat. _ The cook served the stew up and then passed around the bread. _ Can you serve up the food now?
examples: The cook served the stew up and then passed around the bread.

serve time.monolingual: to spend a certain amount of time in jail. _ The criminal served ten years in jail. _ After the felon served his time, he was released from prison.
examples: The criminal served ten years in jail.

serve under someone or something.monolingual: to carry out one’s responsibility under the direction or in the employment of someone. _ I served under the president of the company as special assistant. _ Jane served under the previous administration as an investigator.
examples: I served under the president of the company as special assistant.

serve with someone.monolingual: to perform military service alongside or with someone. _I served with Harry when we were both in the army. _ At the reunion, I met a lot of the guys I served with in the navy.
examples: I served with Harry when we were both in the army.

set a precedent.monolingual: to establish a pattern; to set a policy that must be followed in future cases. _ I’ll do what you ask this time, but it doesn’t set a precedent. _We’ve already set a precedent in matters such as these.
examples: I’ll do what you ask this time, but it doesn’t set a precedent.

set a trap.monolingual: to adjust and prepare a trap to catch an animal. _Bill set a mousetrap and baited it with cheese. _The old man set a trap to catch an annoying squirrel.
examples: Bill set a mousetrap and baited it with cheese.

set about doing something.monolingual: to begin to do something. _ When are you going to set about fixing the roof ? _ We will set about painting the house when the weather gets a little cooler.
examples: We will set about painting the house when the weather gets a little cooler.

set foot in some place.monolingual: to enter into some place; to begin to enter some place. _ The judge ordered him never to set foot in her house again. _ I would never set foot in a place like that.
examples: The judge ordered him never to set foot in her house again.

set for life.monolingual: prepared to exist for the rest of one’s life; having adequate supplies for the rest of one’s life. _ As soon as I win the lottery, I will be set for life. I’ll never have to work again!
examples: As soon as I win the lottery, I will be set for life.

set in.monolingual: to begin; to become fixed for a period of time. _ A severe cold spell set in early in November. _When high temperatures set in, the use of electricity went up considerably.
examples: A severe cold spell set in early in November.

set in one’s ways.monolingual: leading a fixed lifestyle; living according to one’s own established patterns. _ At her age, she’s getting sort of set in her ways. _If you weren’t so set in your ways, you’d be able to understand young people better.
examples: At her age, she’s getting sort of set in her ways.

a set of pipes.monolingual: Fig. a very loud voice; a good singing voice. _She has a nice set of pipes. _With a set of pipes like that, she’s a winner.
examples: She has a nice set of pipes.

a set of wheels.monolingual: Fig. a car. _ I need a new set of wheels. _ Man, look at that set of wheels that chick has!
examples: I need a new set of wheels.

set off on something.monolingual: to begin on a journey or expedition. _ When do you plan to set off on your journey? _ We will set off on our adventure tomorrow morning.
examples: We will set off on our adventure tomorrow morning.

set one’s heart against something.monolingual: Fig. to turn against something; to become totally against something. _ Jane set her heart against going to Australia. _ I set my heart against her departure.
examples: Jane set her heart against going to Australia.

set one’s house in order.monolingual: Fig. to make certain that one’s affairs are in proper legal order. _ Before we can ask for a bank loan, we have to set our house in order. _ I found an accountant who would help me set my house in order.
examples: Before we can ask for a bank loan, we have to set our house in order.

set out to do something.monolingual: to begin to do something; to intend to do something. _ Jill set out to weed the garden, but pulled up a few valuable plants in the process. _I set out to repair the door, not rebuild the whole porch.
examples: Jill set out to weed the garden, but pulled up a few valuable plants in the process.

set sail for some place.monolingual: to leave in a ship or boat for some place. (Not limited to ships having sails.) _We set sail for Grenada at noon. _ When do we set sail for Nantucket?
examples: We set sail for Grenada at noon.

set someone about something.monolingual: to make someone begin doing something. _ I set the boys about raking up the leaves. _ She set herself about repairing the damaged machine.
examples: I set the boys about raking up the leaves.

set someone off†.monolingual: 1. Fig. to cause someone to become very angry; to ignite someone’s anger. (Based on set something off Q.) _That kind of thing really sets me off! _Your rude behavior set off Mrs. Franklin.
examples: Your rude behavior set off Mrs.

set someone on fire.monolingual: Fig. to excite someone; to make someone passionate. (Based on set fire to someone or something.) _ Her oratory set everyone on fire. _ Ted’s presentation didn’t exactly set me on fire, but it was a good summary of the project.
examples: Her oratory set everyone on fire.

set someone’s teeth on edge.monolingual: 1. Fig. [for a scraping sound] to irritate someone’s nerves. _ That noise sets my teeth on edge! _ Tom’s teeth were set on edge by the incessant screaming of the children.
examples: Tom’s teeth were set on edge by the incessant screaming of the children.

set someone straight.monolingual: to make certain that someone understands something exactly. (Often said in anger or domination.) _ Please set me straight on this matter. Do you or do you not accept the responsibility for the accident? _I set her straight about who she had to ask fo
examples: Please set me straight on this matter.

set someone up†.monolingual: to lead—by deception—a person to play a particular role in an event; to arrange an event—usually by deception—so that a specific person suffers the consequences for the event; to frame someone. _I had nothing to do with the robbery! I was just standi
examples: I had nothing to do with the robbery! I was just standing there.

set something aside†.monolingual: to place something in a place that is to one side or out of the way. _ Betty set the manuscript aside until she had more time to work on it. _ Liz set aside her book for a while.
examples: Betty set the manuscript aside until she had more time to work on it.

set something at something.monolingual: to fix something at a particular value or amount. _ Please set the thermostat at a lower temperature. _ Who set the refrigerator at freezing?
examples: Please set the thermostat at a lower temperature.

set something beside something.monolingual: to place something near or next to something. _ Please set the chair beside the window. _ I set the suitcase beside the door so I would not forget it.
examples: Please set the chair beside the window.

set something down as something.monolingual: to regard something as something. _I set his behavior down as an event that would not repeat itself. _Please just set the whole afternoon down as an exercise in patience.
examples: I set his behavior down as an event that would not repeat itself.

set something for something.monolingual: to adjust something for a particular setting. _ I set the thermostat for a lower temperature. _ Please set the air conditioning for about 75 degrees.
examples: I set the thermostat for a lower temperature.

set something forth†.monolingual: to explain something; to present some information. _ She set her ideas forth in an organized and interesting manner. _Please set forth your thoughts quickly and concisely.
examples: She set her ideas forth in an organized and interesting manner.

set something forward.monolingual: 1. to move something to a more forward position. _Please set the chair forward a little bit. It is in the walkway. _ If you set the vase forward, it will show up better against the dark background.
examples: Please set the chair forward a little bit.

set something in a place.monolingual: to locate the action of a play or movie in a place. _ The author set the second act in a wooded glade. _ The opera was set in a forest outside Moscow.
examples: The author set the second act in a wooded glade.

set something in motion.monolingual: to start something moving. _ The mayor set the project in motion by digging the first shovelful of soil. _ I cannot set the procedure in motion until I receive a purchase order.
examples: The mayor set the project in motion by digging the first shovelful of soil.

set something off†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to ignite something, such as fireworks. _ The boys were setting firecrackers off all afternoon. _ They set off rocket after rocket.
examples: The boys were setting firecrackers off all afternoon.

set something over something.monolingual: to place something in a position above something else. _ Toby set the plate over the hole in the tablecloth. _Please place the kettle over the fire.
examples: Toby set the plate over the hole in the tablecloth.

set something to music.monolingual: to write a piece of music to accompany a set of words. _The musician set my lyrics to music. _ The rock band set the poem to music.
examples: The musician set my lyrics to music.

set something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to put something together; to erect something. _My parents bought me a dollhouse, but I had to set it up myself. _ It took nearly an hour to set up the tent.
examples: My parents bought me a dollhouse, but I had to set it up myself.

set the record straight.monolingual: Fig. to put right a mistake or misunderstanding; to make sure that an account, etc., is correct. _The manager thought Jean was to blame, but she soon set the record straight. _Jane’s mother heard that Tom is a married man, but he set the record strai
examples: The manager thought Jean was to blame, but she soon set the record straight.

set the stage for something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to arrange a stage for an act or scene of a production. _ The stage crew set the stage for the first act. _ They set the stage for the second scene while the orchestra played.
examples: The stage crew set the stage for the first act.

set the table.monolingual: to place plates, glasses, napkins, etc., on the table before a meal. (The opposite of clear the table.) _ Jane, would you please set the table? _ I’m tired of setting the table. Ask someone else to do it.
examples: I’m tired of setting the table.

set the world on fire.monolingual: Fig. to do exciting things that bring fame and glory. (Frequently with the negative.) _I’m not very ambitious. I don’t want to set the world on fire. _ You don’t have to set the world on fire. Just do a good job.
examples: I’m not very ambitious.

set to.monolingual: to begin to fight; to attack or commence someone or something. _The two boys set to almost as soon as they met each other. _They set to and fought for about ten minutes, cursing and screaming.
examples: The two boys set to almost as soon as they met each other.

*set to do something.monolingual: ready to do something. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ I’m all set to go. Are you ready? _ We are set to leave at a moment’s notice.
examples: I’m all set to go.

set type.monolingual: to arrange type for printing; to prepare finished pages for printing. _ Have you finished setting the type for page one yet? _ John sets type for a living.
examples: John sets type for a living.

set up shop somewhere.monolingual: to establish one’s place of work somewhere. _ Mary set up shop in a small office building on Oak Street. _ The police officer said, “You can’t set up shop right here on the sidewalk!”
examples: Mary set up shop in a small office building on Oak Street.

set upon someone or something.monolingual: to attack someone or something violently. _The dogs set upon the bear and chased it up a tree. _ Bill set upon Tom and struck him hard in the face.
examples: The dogs set upon the bear and chased it up a tree.

settle down.monolingual: 1. to calm down. _ Now, children, it’s time to settle down and start class. _ If you don’t settle down, I’ll send you all home.
examples: Now, children, it’s time to settle down and start class.

settle for something.monolingual: to agree to accept something (even though something else would be better). _ We wanted a red one, but settled for a blue one. _Ask your grocer for Wilson’s canned corn—the best corn in cans. Don’t settle for less.
examples: We wanted a red one, but settled for a blue one.

settle in.monolingual: to become accustomed to one’s new surroundings; to get used to living in a place or a new dwelling. _ I need a little time to settle in, then I can think about buying a car.
examples: I need a little time to settle in, then I can think about buying a car.

settle on something.monolingual: to decide on something. _We’ve discussed the merits of all of them, and we’ve settled on this one. _ I can’t settle on one or the other, so I’ll buy both.
examples: We’ve discussed the merits of all of them, and we’ve settled on this one.

settle someone’s affairs.monolingual: to deal with one’s business matters; to manage the business affairs of someone who can’t. _ When my uncle died, I had to settle his affairs. _ I have to settle my affairs before going to Mexico for a year.
examples: When my uncle died, I had to settle his affairs.

settle someone’s hash.monolingual: Sl. to calm someone down, perhaps by threats or by violence. _ If he comes in here, I’ll settle his hash. _ Now, that ought to settle your hash.
examples: If he comes in here, I’ll settle his hash.

settle up with someone.monolingual: to pay someone what one owes; to pay one one’s share of something. _ I must settle up with Jim for the bike I bought for him. _Bob paid the whole restaurant bill and we all settled up with him later.
examples: I must settle up with Jim for the bike I bought for him.

a seven-day wonder.monolingual: Fig. a person or a process supposedly perfected in only seven days. (Sarcastic.) _ Tommy is no seven-day wonder. It took him 6 years to get through high school!
examples: Tommy is no seven-day wonder.

the seven-year itch.monolingual: a real or imagined longing for other women in a man’s seventh year of marriage. _ Looks like Jack has the seven-year itch. _ The seven-year itch is just a rumor.
examples: Looks like Jack has the seven-year itch.

sever ties with someone.monolingual: Fig. to end a relationship or agreement suddenly or completely. _ The company severed its ties with the dishonest employee. _ John has severed all ties with his parents.
examples: The company severed its ties with the dishonest employee.

sew someone or something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to stitch together an opening in someone or something. _ The surgeon sewed the patient up and pronounced the operation a success. _ This is torn. Can you sew up this rip?
examples: The surgeon sewed the patient up and pronounced the operation a success.

shackle someone with something.monolingual: to fetter or hobble someone with something, such as chains, etc. _ The sheriff shackled the prisoner with handcuffs and leg irons. _ The prisoners were shackled with leg irons.
examples: The sheriff shackled the prisoner with handcuffs and leg irons.

shades of someone or something.monolingual: Fig. reminders of someone or something; a thing that is reminiscent of someone or something. _ When I met Jim’s mother, I thought “shades of Aunt Mary.” _ “Shades of grade school,” said Jack as the university lecturer rebuked him for being late.
examples: When I met Jim’s mother, I thought “shades of Aunt Mary.

a shady deal.monolingual: Fig. a questionable and possibly dishonest deal or transaction. _ The lawyer got caught making a shady deal with a convicted felon.
examples: The lawyer got caught making a shady deal with a convicted felon.

shagged out.monolingual: Sl. exhausted. _ What a day! I’m shagged out! _ You guys look sort of shagged out.
examples: You guys look sort of shagged out.

a shaggy-dog story.monolingual: a kind of funny story that relies for its humor on its length and its sudden ridiculous ending. _Don’t let John tell a shaggy-dog story. It’ll go on for hours. _ Mary didn’t get the point of Fred’s shaggy-dog story.
examples: Don’t let John tell a shaggy-dog story.

shake a leg.monolingual: 1. to hurry; to move faster. (Often as a command.) _ Let’s shake a leg, you guys. We gotta be there in twenty minutes. _ She told me to shake a leg, so I hurried the best I could.
examples: Let’s shake a leg, you guys.

shake someone down†.monolingual: 1. to blackmail someone. (Underworld.) _ Fred was trying to shake Jane down, but she got the cops in on it. _The police chief was trying to shake down just about everybody in town.
examples: Fred was trying to shake Jane down, but she got the cops in on it.

shake someone or something off†.monolingual: Fig. to get rid of someone; to get free of someone who is bothering you. _ Stop bothering me! What do I have to do to shake you off ? _ I wish I could shake off John. He’s such a pest!
examples: I wish I could shake off John.

shake someone or something up†.monolingual: to jostle or knock someone or something around; to toss someone or something back and forth. _ We rode over a rough road, and that shook us up. _ The accident shook up John quite a bit.
examples: We rode over a rough road, and that shook us up.

shake someone up†.monolingual: to shock or upset someone. _The sight of the injured man shook me up. _Your rude remark really shook up Tom.
examples: The sight of the injured man shook me up.

shake something off†.monolingual: to get rid of something that is on one by shaking. _ I tried to shake the spider off. _The dog shook off the blanket Billy had put on him.
examples: I tried to shake the spider off.

shake something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to shake a container to mix its contents together well. _ Please shake this up before using it. _ I shook up the medicine bottle like it says on the label.
examples: Please shake this up before using it.

shame on you!.monolingual: a phrase scolding someone for being naughty. (Typically said to a child or to an adult for a childish infraction.) _John: I think I broke one of your figurines. Mary: Shame on you! John: I’ll replace it, of course. Mary: Thanks, I sort of liked it. _
examples: John: I think I broke one of your figurines.

shank it.monolingual: Sl. to use one’s legs to get somewhere; to walk. _ My car needs fixing so I had to shank it to work today. _ I like to shank it every now and then.
examples: My car needs fixing so I had to shank it to work today.

shank’s mare.monolingual: Fig. travel on foot. _You’ll find that shank’s mare is the quickest way to get across town. _Is there a bus, or do I have to use shank’s mare?
examples: You’ll find that shank’s mare is the quickest way to get across town.

shape someone up†.monolingual: to get someone into good physical shape; to make someone behave or perform better. _I’ve got to shape myself up to improve my health. _The trainer was told that he’d have to shape up the boxer before the fight.
examples: I’ve got to shape myself up to improve my health.

shape up.monolingual: 1. to improve; to reform. _ I want to get things shaped up around here. _ I guess I’d better shape up if I want to stay in school.
examples: I want to get things shaped up around here.

shape up or ship out..monolingual: Fig. Either improve one’s performance (or behavior) or leave. (Used as a command.) _ Okay, Tom. That’s the end. Shape up or ship out! _ John was late again, so I told him to shape up or ship out.
examples: Okay, Tom. That’s the end.

share and share alike.monolingual: Cliché having or taking equal shares. _I kept five and gave the other five to Mary—share and share alike. _ The two roommates agreed that they would divide expenses—share and share alike.
examples: I kept five and gave the other five to Mary—share and share alike.

share someone’s pain.monolingual: to understand and sympathize with someone’s pain or emotional discomfort. (Said in order to sound sympathetic.) _I am sorry about the loss of your home. I share your pain. _We sympathize about the loss of your mother. We share your pain.
examples: I am sorry about the loss of your home.

share someone’s sorrow.monolingual: to grieve as someone else grieves. _ We all share your sorrow on this sad, sad day. _ I am sorry to hear about the death in your family. I share your sorrow.
examples: We all share your sorrow on this sad, sad day.

a sharp tongue.monolingual: Fig. an outspoken or harsh manner; a critical manner of speaking. _ He has quite a sharp tongue. Don’t be totally unnerved by what he says or the way he says it.
examples: He has quite a sharp tongue.

a sharp wit.monolingual: Fig. a good and fast ability to make jokes and funny comments. _Terry has a sharp wit and often makes cracks that force people to laugh aloud at inappropriate times.
examples: Terry has a sharp wit and often makes cracks that force people to laugh aloud at inappropriate times.

*a shellacking.monolingual: 1. Fig. a physical beating. (*Typically: get ~; take ~; give someone ~.) _ The boxer took a shellacking and lost the fight. _I got a shellacking when I broke the window.
examples: The boxer took a shellacking and lost the fight.

shift one’s ground.monolingual: Fig. to change one’s opinions or arguments, often without being challenged or opposed. _ At first Jack and I were on opposite sides, but he suddenly shifted ground and started agreeing with me. _Jim has very fixed views. You won’t find him shifting h
examples: At first Jack and I were on opposite sides, but he suddenly shifted ground and started agreeing with me.

shine up to someone.monolingual: Fig. to try to gain someone’s favor by being extra nice. _ John is a nice guy, except that he’s always trying to shine up to the professor. _ Mary never tries to shine up to the manager.
examples: John is a nice guy, except that he’s always trying to shine up to the professor.

shipping and handling.monolingual: the costs of handling a product and transporting it to a customer. _ Shipping and handling charges were included in the price. _ The cost of the goods is low and shipping and handling added only a few dollars.
examples: Shipping and handling charges were included in the price.

shirk one’s duty.monolingual: to neglect one’s job or task. _ The guard was fired for shirking his duty. _You cannot expect to continue shirking your duty without someone noticing.
examples: The guard was fired for shirking his duty.

shit happens..monolingual: Sl. Bad things just happen and are unavoidable. (Potentially offensive. Use only with discretion.) _ Too bad that your new car got dented, but shit happens. _ Shit happens. There’s nothing that can be done about it.
examples: Too bad that your new car got dented, but shit happens.

*the shock of one’s life.monolingual: Fig. a serious (emotional) shock. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give one ~.) _ I opened the telegram and got the shock of my life. _ I had the shock of my life when I won $5,000.
examples: I opened the telegram and got the shock of my life.

shook up.monolingual: upset; shocked. _ Relax, man! Don’t get shook up! _ I always get shook up when I see a bad accident.
examples: I always get shook up when I see a bad accident.

shoot first, ask questions later..monolingual: Prov. Assume that everyone you encounter is hostile to you.; Take action, even though you do not know enough to be sure if it is the right action. _ If the foreman saw that one of the workers was working slowly, he didn’t stop to find out if the work
