examples: If the foreman saw that one of the workers was working slowly, he didn’t stop to find out if the worker was sick or unhappy; he just fired him.

shoot for something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to aim for or at something. (Usually in reference to basketball.) _ The center shot for the basket just before the end of the game. _Wally shot for the basket but missed.
examples: The center shot for the basket just before the end of the game.

shoot from the hip.monolingual: 1. Lit. to fire a gun that is held at one’s side, beside one’s hip. (This increases one’s speed in firing a gun but is much less accurate.) _ When I lived at home on the farm, my father taught me to shoot from the hip. _ I quickly shot the snake befo
examples: When I lived at home on the farm, my father taught me to shoot from the hip.

shoot one’s mouth off†.monolingual: Inf. to boast or talk too much; to tell secrets. _ Don’t pay any attention to Bob. He’s always shooting his mouth off. _ Oh, Sally! Stop shooting off your mouth! You don’t know what you’re talking about.
examples: Don’t pay any attention to Bob.

shoot one’s wad.monolingual: Sl. to spend all or nearly all one’s cash on hand. _I shot my wad on junk food. _I can’t afford a cab. I shot my wad at the restaurant.
examples: I shot my wad on junk food.

shoot oneself in the foot.monolingual: Fig. to cause oneself difficulty; to be the author of one’s own misfortune. _ I am a master at shooting myself in the foot. _ Again, he shot himself in the foot by saying too much to the press.
examples: I am a master at shooting myself in the foot.

shoot someone down in flames.monolingual: Fig. to ruin someone; to bring about someone’s downfall. _ It was a bad idea, okay, but you didn’t have to shoot me down in flames at the meeting. _ I didn’t mean to shoot you down in f lames.
examples: It was a bad idea, okay, but you didn’t have to shoot me down in flames at the meeting.

shoot something down†.monolingual: Fig. to foil a plan through criticism; to counter an idea with criticism. (Based on shoot someone, something, or an animal down.) _He raised a good point, but the others shot him down almost immediately. _ Liz shot down Jeff ’s best idea.
examples: He raised a good point, but the others shot him down almost immediately.

shoot something out†.monolingual: 1. to stick, throw, or thrust something outward. _ The diamond shot bright shafts of light out when the sun fell on it. _ The little girl shot out her tongue at the teacher.
examples: The diamond shot bright shafts of light out when the sun fell on it.

shoot the breeze.monolingual: Fig. to chat casually and without purpose. _ We spent the entire afternoon just shooting the breeze. _ It was good to shoot the breeze with you, Mary.
examples: We spent the entire afternoon just shooting the breeze.

shoot the cat.monolingual: Sl. to empty one’s stomach; to vomit. _ I must have shot the cat a dozen times during the night. _ Shooting the cat is no fun when you’re weak and dizzy.
examples: I must have shot the cat a dozen times during the night.

shoot the works.monolingual: 1. to do everything; to use everything; to bet all one’s money. _ Okay, let’s go out to dinner and shoot the works. _ Don’t shoot the works! Save some for a cab.
examples: Okay, let’s go out to dinner and shoot the works.

shoot up.monolingual: Sl. to take drugs by injection. _ Wallace was caught by the cops shooting up in the high school rest room.
examples: Wallace was caught by the cops shooting up in the high school rest room.

shopping list.monolingual: 1. Lit. a list of things one needs to buy. _ I made up a shopping list for groceries that we are out of. _ Don’t forget to take the shopping list with you to the store.
examples: I made up a shopping list for groceries that we are out of.

shore someone up†.monolingual: Fig. to (figuratively) prop up or support someone. _ Mary’s solid character and personality helped shore her up during her recent problems with the law. _ Everyone co-operated to shore up John when his mother died.
examples: Mary’s solid character and personality helped shore her up during her recent problems with the law.

shore something up†.monolingual: to prop up or support something. _ The fence fell over, so we shored it up with more posts. _ The storm weakened the foundation of our house, and we had to have workers shore up the house.
examples: The fence fell over, so we shored it up with more posts.

short and sweet.monolingual: Cliché brief (and pleasant because of briefness). _ That was a good sermon—short and sweet. _I don’t care what you say, as long as you make it short and sweet.
examples: That was a good sermon—short and sweet.

short for something.monolingual: [of a form] being a shortened form of a word or phrase. _Photo is short for photograph. _Dave is short for David.
examples: Photo is short for photograph.

short of something.monolingual: not having enough of something. _ I wanted to bake a cake, but I was short of eggs. _Usually at the end of the month, I’m short of money.
examples: I wanted to bake a cake, but I was short of eggs.

short reckonings make long friends..monolingual: Prov. If you borrow something from a friend, pay it back as soon as possible so that the two of you remain friendly. _ Now that you’ve finished using Bert’s saw, take it right back to him. Short reckonings make long friends. (a) short shrift a brief
examples: Now that you’ve finished using Bert’s saw, take it right back to him.

*short with someone.monolingual: abrupt and a little bit rude in speaking to a person. (*Typically: be ~; become ~; get ~.) _ Please don’t be short with me. I am doing the best that I can.
examples: Please don’t be short with me.

a shot in the arm.monolingual: 1. Lit. an injection of medicine. _The doctor administered the antidote to the poison by a shot in the arm.
examples: The doctor administered the antidote to the poison by a shot in the arm.

a shot in the dark.monolingual: Fig. a very general attempt; a wild guess. _ It was just a shot in the dark. I had no idea I was exactly correct. _ Come on, try it. Even a shot in the dark may win.
examples: It was just a shot in the dark.

shot through with something.monolingual: Fig. containing something; interwoven, intermixed, or filled with something. _ The rose was a lovely pink shot through with streaks of white. _ John’s comments are often shot through with sarcasm.
examples: The rose was a lovely pink shot through with streaks of white.

a shotgun wedding.monolingual: Fig. a forced wedding. (From imagery of the bride’s father having threatened the bridegroom with a shotgun to force him to marry the bride because he made her pregnant.) _ Mary was six months pregnant when she married Bill. It was a real shotgun wedd
examples: Mary was six months pregnant when she married Bill.

should have stood in bed.monolingual: Fig. an expression used on a bad day, when one should have stayed in one’s bed. _ What a horrible day! I should have stood in bed. _ The minute I got up and heard the news this morning, I knew I should have stood in bed.
examples: What a horrible day! I should have stood in bed.

shoulder to shoulder.monolingual: Fig. side by side; with a shared purpose. _ The two armies fought shoulder to shoulder against the joint enemy. _ The strikers said they would stand shoulder to shoulder against the management.
examples: The two armies fought shoulder to shoulder against the joint enemy.

shouldn’t happen to a dog.monolingual: Fig. an expression of something that is so bad that no creature deserves it. _ Poor guy. That shouldn’t happen to a dog. _ This cold I got shouldn’t happen to a dog.
examples: Poor guy. That shouldn’t happen to a dog.

shout about someone or something.monolingual: 1. to yell about someone or something. _ Alice is shouting about Tom, the guy who stood her up. _ What are you shouting about?
examples: Alice is shouting about Tom, the guy who stood her up.

shout someone or something down†.monolingual: to overwhelm someone or something by shouting. _Mary was trying to speak, but Sally shouted her down. _ Ann brought up a very important suggestion, but Bob shouted it down. _ The lecturer had to shout down the entire audience to be heard.
examples: Mary was trying to speak, but Sally shouted her down.

shove one’s way somewhere.monolingual: to make a path through a crowd by pushing. _ The impatient man shoved his way through the crowd. _ The reporter shoved her way to the front of the crowd.
examples: The impatient man shoved his way through the crowd.

shove someone around†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to push someone around. _ The bigger boys shoved him around easily because he is so small. _ Karen shoved around the little kids until they got mad at her.
examples: The bigger boys shoved him around easily because he is so small.

show and tell.monolingual: a session where objects are presented and described. (Essentially a kindergarten or grade school activity, but often used figuratively.) _ It was a short lecture with lots of show and tell. _ I can’t take another show and tell session.
examples: It was a short lecture with lots of show and tell.

show good faith.monolingual: to demonstrate good intentions or good will. _ I’m certain that you showed good faith when you signed the contract. _Do you doubt that she is showing good faith?
examples: I’m certain that you showed good faith when you signed the contract.

a show of hands.monolingual: a display of raised hands [in a group of people] that can be counted for the purpose of votes or surveys. _We were asked to vote for the candidates for captain by a show of hands. _Jack wanted us to vote on paper, not by a show of hands, so that we c
examples: We were asked to vote for the candidates for captain by a show of hands.

show off.monolingual: to do things in a way that is meant to attract attention. _Please stop showing off! You embarrass me. _ John is always showing off to his girlfriend.
examples: Please stop showing off! You embarrass me.

show one’s hand.monolingual: Fig. to reveal one’s intentions to someone. (From card games.) _ I don’t know whether Jim is intending to marry Jane or not. He’s not one to show his hand. _If you want to get a raise, don’t show the boss your hand too soon.
examples: I don’t know whether Jim is intending to marry Jane or not.

show signs of something.monolingual: to show hints or indications of something. _I let the horse run at full speed until it began to show signs of tiring. _ Sally is showing signs of going to sleep.
examples: I let the horse run at full speed until it began to show signs of tiring.

show someone one’s stuff.monolingual: Fig. to show someone how well one can do something. _ We’ll audition Kate now. Okay, Kate, show us your stuff.
examples: We’ll audition Kate now.

show someone or something off†.monolingual: to display someone or something so that the best features are apparent. _ Bill drove around all afternoon showing his new car off. _Mrs. Williams was showing off her baby to the neighbors.
examples: Bill drove around all afternoon showing his new car off.

show someone up†.monolingual: to make someone’s faults or shortcomings apparent. _ John is always trying to show someone up to make himself look better. _John’s excellent effort really showed up Bill, who didn’t try very hard at all.
examples: John is always trying to show someone up to make himself look better.

show someone up† as something.monolingual: to reveal that someone is really something (else). _The investigation showed her up as a fraud. _ The test showed up the candidate as unqualified.
examples: The investigation showed her up as a fraud.

show something to good advantage.monolingual: to display the best features of something; to display something so that its best features are apparent. _ Put the vase in the center of the table and show it to good advantage. _ Having and using a large vocabulary shows your intelligence to good adv
examples: Put the vase in the center of the table and show it to good advantage.

show up.monolingual: to appear; to arrive. _ Where is John? I hope he shows up soon. _ When will the bus show up? _ Weeds began to show up in the garden.
examples: Where is John? I hope he shows up soon.

a shrinking violet.monolingual: Fig. someone who is very shy and not assertive. _ I am not exactly a shrinking violet, but I don’t have the guts to say what you said to her.
examples: I am not exactly a shrinking violet, but I don’t have the guts to say what you said to her.

shrouds have no pockets..monolingual: Prov. You cannot take any material goods with you when you die. _ You should use your money to enjoy yourself while you’re alive. Shrouds have no pockets.
examples: You should use your money to enjoy yourself while you’re alive.

shuck something off†.monolingual: 1. to take something off. _ Tom shucked his jacket off and sat on the arm of the easy chair. _ He shucked off his jacket.
examples: Tom shucked his jacket off and sat on the arm of the easy chair.

shuffle off this mortal coil.monolingual: Euph. to die. (Often jocular or formal euphemism. Not often used in consoling someone.) _Cousin Fred shuff led off this mortal coil after suffering a heart attack. _ When I shuff le off this mortal coil, I want to go out in style—bells, f lowers, and
examples: Cousin Fred shuff led off this mortal coil after suffering a heart attack.

shut someone or something out†.monolingual: to exclude someone or something; to refuse entrance to someone or something. _ We tried to get into the stadium, but they shut us out because there was no more room. _ My parents shut out their children when they made important decisions.
examples: We tried to get into the stadium, but they shut us out because there was no more room.

shut someone up†.monolingual: to silence someone. _ Oh, shut yourself up! _ Will you please shut up that crying baby!

shut up!.monolingual: Inf. Be quiet! (Impolite.) _ Bob: And another thing. Bill: Oh, shut up, Bob! _ Andy: Shut up! I’ve heard enough! Bob: But I have more to say! _ “Shut up! I can’t hear anything because of all your noise!” shouted the director.
examples: Bob: And another thing.

shut up about it..monolingual: Inf. Do not tell anyone about it. _Bill: I heard that you had a little trouble with the police. Tom: Just shut up about it! Do you hear? _Andy: Didn’t you once appear in a movie? Alice: Shut up about it. No one has to know.
examples: Bill: I heard that you had a little trouble with the police.

*sick as a dog.monolingual: Cliché very sick; sick and vomiting. (*Also: as ~.) _We’ve never been so ill. The whole family was sick as dogs. _ Sally was as sick as a dog and couldn’t go to the party.
examples: We’ve never been so ill.

*sick at heart.monolingual: Fig. distressed and depressed. (*Typically: be ~; become ~; make someone ~.) _I became sick at heart just looking at all the homeless children.
examples: I became sick at heart just looking at all the homeless children.

sick in bed.monolingual: remaining in bed while (one is) ill. _ Tom is sick in bed with the f lu. _ He’s been sick in bed for nearly a week.
examples: Tom is sick in bed with the f lu.

side against someone.monolingual: to be against someone; to take sides against someone. _ I thought you were my friend! I never thought you would side against me! _The two brothers were always siding against their sister.
examples: The two brothers were always siding against their sister.

side by side.monolingual: (of two or more people or things) lined up so their sides are adjacent. _We walked side by side across the lawn.
examples: We walked side by side across the lawn.

side with someone.monolingual: to join with someone; to take someone else’s part; to be on someone’s side. _ Why is it that you always side with him when he and I argue? _ I never side with anybody. I form my own opinions.
examples: I never side with anybody.

sift something from something.monolingual: to remove something from something by sifting. _Fran sifted all the impurities from the f lour before using it. _Timmy sifted all the leaves from the sand in his sandbox.
examples: Fran sifted all the impurities from the f lour before using it.

sift something through something.monolingual: to make something pass through something such as a sieve. _ She sifted the powdered sugar through a strainer. _Please sift the soil through this screen and watch for bits of pottery.
examples: She sifted the powdered sugar through a strainer.

sift through something.monolingual: to examine all parts of something. _ The fire inspector sifted through the rubble, looking for clues to the start of the fire. _ We sifted through all the papers in the old trunk, but we did not find what we were looking for.
examples: The fire inspector sifted through the rubble, looking for clues to the start of the fire.

sigh about something.monolingual: to release a deep breath, indicating anxiety, distress, or relief about something. _ What are you sighing about? _ She sighed about her illness and then shifted her thoughts to something else.
examples: She sighed about her illness and then shifted her thoughts to something else.

sigh for someone.monolingual: to release a deep breath, indicating anxiety about one’s emotional attachment for someone. _ Dave spent a lot of his time sighing for Laura, on whom he had a crush. _ Laura has been sighing for some as-yetunnamed young man.
examples: Dave spent a lot of his time sighing for Laura, on whom he had a crush.

a sight for sore eyes.monolingual: Fig. a welcome sight. _ Oh, am I glad to see you here! You’re a sight for sore eyes. _ I’m sure hungry. This meal is a sight for sore eyes.
examples: Oh, am I glad to see you here! You’re a sight for sore eyes.

sign for someone.monolingual: to sign something, using one’s own signature in place of someone else’s signature; to sign something, using another person’s name, adding the phrase “by [one’s own name].” _ He’s not here. I will sign for him. Where do I sign? _ Who will sign for Mr.
examples: He’s not here. I will sign for him.

sign for something.monolingual: to sign a piece of paper indicating that one has received something. _ Would you sign for this, please? _ Ted signed for the package and opened it up.
examples: Ted signed for the package and opened it up.

sign in.monolingual: to indicate that one has arrived somewhere and at what time by signing a piece of paper or a list. _ Please sign in so we will know you are here. _ Did you remember to sign in this time?
examples: Please sign in so we will know you are here.

a sign of the times.monolingual: something that signifies the situation evident in the current times. _ Your neighbor’s unmowed grass is just a sign of the times. Nobody really cares any longer.
examples: Your neighbor’s unmowed grass is just a sign of the times.

sign off.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a broadcaster] to announce the end of programming for the day; [for an amateur radio operator] to announce the end of a transmission. _Wally signed off and turned the transmitter off. _ Channel 43 failed to sign off at the scheduled time
examples: Wally signed off and turned the transmitter off.

sign off on something.monolingual: to sign a paper, indicating that one has finished with something or agrees with the state of something. _The publisher signed off on the book and sent it to be printed. _ I refuse to sign off on this project until it is done correctly.
examples: The publisher signed off on the book and sent it to be printed.

sign on.monolingual: to announce the beginning of a broadcast transmission. _The announcer signed on and then played “The Star-Spangled Banner.” _ We usually sign on at six in the morning.
examples: The announcer signed on and then played “The Star-Spangled Banner.

sign on the dotted line.monolingual: 1. Lit. to indicate one’s agreement or assent by placing one’s signature on a special line provided for that purpose. (The line may be solid or dotted.) _ I agreed to the contract, but I haven’t signed on the dotted line yet. _When you have signed on
examples: I agreed to the contract, but I haven’t signed on the dotted line yet.

sign one’s own death warrant.monolingual: Fig. to do something (knowingly) that will most likely result in severe trouble. (As if one were ordering one’s own execution.) _ I wouldn’t ever gamble a large sum of money. That would be signing my own death warrant. _The killer signed his own deat
examples: I wouldn’t ever gamble a large sum of money.

sign out.monolingual: to indicate that one is leaving a place or going out temporarily by signing a piece of paper or a list. _ I forgot to sign out when I left. _ Please sign out every time you leave.
examples: I forgot to sign out when I left.

sign someone in†.monolingual: to record that someone has arrived somewhere and at what time by recording the information on a paper or a list. _ I will sign you in. What is your name? _ Do I have to sign in everyone?
examples: I will sign you in.

sign someone on†.monolingual: to employ someone; to recruit someone as an employee. _How many workers did the manager sign on? _ The construction company signed on ten new workers.
examples: The construction company signed on ten new workers.

sign something away†.monolingual: to sign a paper in which one gives away one’s rights to something. _Valerie signed her rights away. _ She signed away her claim to the money.
examples: Valerie signed her rights away.

sign something for someone.monolingual: 1. to sign one’s signature on a paper in place of someone else’s signature. _ Would you please sign this for me? _ I can’t sign it right now. Would you sign it for me?
examples: I can’t sign it right now.

sign something in†.monolingual: to record that something has been received at a particular time by recording the information on a paper or a list. _ I have to sign this package in, then I will be right with you. _ Should I sign in this shipment now?
examples: I have to sign this package in, then I will be right with you.

signal for someone.monolingual: to make a sign for someone to come. _I signaled for the waiter and got the check. _Ted signaled for the parking lot attendant.
examples: I signaled for the waiter and got the check.

signal for something.monolingual: to make a sign that something should be done. _ I caught the waiter’s eye and signaled for the check. _ The director signaled for applause.
examples: I caught the waiter’s eye and signaled for the check.

signed, sealed, and delivered.monolingual: Fig. formally and officially signed; [for a formal document to be] executed. _ Here is the deed to the property—signed, sealed, and delivered. _ I can’t begin work on this project until I have the contract signed, sealed, and delivered.
examples: Here is the deed to the property—signed, sealed, and delivered.

silence gives consent..monolingual: Prov. If you do not object to what someone says or does, you can be assumed to agree with or condone it. _Jill: What did Fred say when you told him we were thinking about leaving the office early? Jane: He didn’t say anything. Jill: Then he must not
examples: Jill: What did Fred say when you told him we were thinking about leaving the office early? Jane: He didn’t say anything.

silence is golden..monolingual: Prov. Silence is often good or desirable. _ Jerry has two teenage children who listen to music using their headphones all day. He knows that silence is golden. _ Hush! Silence is golden.
examples: Jerry has two teenage children who listen to music using their headphones all day.

*silly as a goose.monolingual: very foolish. (*Also: as ~.) _ Edith is as silly as a goose. She thinks that reading aloud to her houseplants will help them grow. _The ad in the newspaper said this lotion would make my hair grow back, but I’ve been using it for a whole month and my
examples: Edith is as silly as a goose.

silt up.monolingual: [for a body of water] to become filled with silt. _ The river moved too fast to silt up. _ The lake silted up in a very few years.
examples: The river moved too fast to silt up.

simmer down.monolingual: 1. Lit. to decrease in intensity. (As boiling dies down when the heat is lowered or removed.) _ The hectic activity of the day finally simmered down. _ When things simmer down in the fall, this is a much nicer place.
examples: The hectic activity of the day finally simmered down.

sin against someone or something.monolingual: to offend or desecrate someone or something sacred or revered. _The critic said that Walter sinned against the poet when he read the poem in a sarcastic manner. _ I would say that Walter sinned against poetry, not just one poet.
examples: The critic said that Walter sinned against the poet when he read the poem in a sarcastic manner.

since time immemorial.monolingual: since a very long time ago. (Literally, since time before recorded history.) _ My hometown has had a big parade on the Fourth of July since time immemorial. _Since time immemorial, the trees have blossomed each spring.
examples: My hometown has had a big parade on the Fourth of July since time immemorial.

since when?.monolingual: Inf. When was that decided?; That’s news to me.; When was that done? _Tom: You’ve been assigned to the night shift. John: Since when? _ Jane: Fred is now the assistant manager. Pete: Since when? Jane: Since I appointed him, that’s when.
examples: Tom: You’ve been assigned to the night shift.

sing of someone or something.monolingual: to tell about or sing a song about someone or something. _ The folksinger sang of Paul Bunyan. _ They all sang of happier times in the past.
examples: The folksinger sang of Paul Bunyan.

sing out.monolingual: to sing louder. _ Sing out, please. This is a very large hall. _ The sopranos will have to sing out more.
examples: Sing out, please.

sing someone to sleep.monolingual: to sing softly and sweetly to someone until sleep comes. _The mother sang her baby to sleep. _ Please sing Timmy to sleep. He is very restless.
examples: The mother sang her baby to sleep.

sing something out†.monolingual: to sing or announce something loudly. _ The teacher sang the names out loud and clear. _ She sang out “The Star-Spangled Banner” in a loud voice.
examples: The teacher sang the names out loud and clear.

sing to someone or something.monolingual: to sing a song and direct it at someone or something. _ The singer sang to a man in the front row, and he was very embarrassed by it. _Claire sang to an older audience and put many of them to sleep.
examples: The singer sang to a man in the front row, and he was very embarrassed by it.

sing together.monolingual: [for people] to coordinate their singing. _ Let’s sing together now. Everyone should watch the conductor and follow the beat. _ You have to sing together if you want your words to be understood.
examples: Let’s sing together now.

single file.monolingual: a line of things or people, one person or one thing wide. _ Please get into single file. _ You have to march single file.
examples: Please get into single file.

sink below something.monolingual: to descend below a certain level. _ The boat sank below the surface of the water and was gone. _ The temperature sank below the freezing mark again today.
examples: The boat sank below the surface of the water and was gone.

sink down.monolingual: to sink or submerge. _The sun sank down and darkness spread across the land. _ She sat in the chair and sank down, enjoying her moment of relaxation.
examples: The sun sank down and darkness spread across the land.

sink in.monolingual: 1. Lit. to sink, submerge, or descend into something. _ How long will it take the water to sink in? _ It might take days for the oil to sink in, so you have time to clean it up.
examples: It might take days for the oil to sink in, so you have time to clean it up.

sink into despair.monolingual: to become depressed; to become completely discouraged. _ After facing the hopelessness of the future, Jean Paul sank into despair. _ Mary sank into despair upon learning of the death of her grandmother.
examples: After facing the hopelessness of the future, Jean Paul sank into despair.

sink into oblivion.monolingual: Fig. to fade into obscurity. _She may be famous now, but in no time she will sink into oblivion. _ In his final years, Wally Wilson sank into oblivion and just faded away.
examples: She may be famous now, but in no time she will sink into oblivion.

sink or swim.monolingual: Fig. to fail or succeed. (Alludes to the choices available to someone who has fallen into the water.) _ After I’ve studied and learned all I can, I have to take the test and sink or swim. _ It’s too late to help John now. It’s sink or swim for him.
examples: After I’ve studied and learned all I can, I have to take the test and sink or swim.

*a sinking feeling.monolingual: the feeling that everything is going wrong; a bad feeling in the base of one’s stomach. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _I get a sinking feeling whenever I think of the night of the accident.
examples: I get a sinking feeling whenever I think of the night of the accident.

sit around.monolingual: to relax sitting; to waste time sitting. _ Don’t just sit around! Get moving! _ I need to sit around every now and then and reorganize my thoughts.
examples: I need to sit around every now and then and reorganize my thoughts.

sit around something.monolingual: to be seated at the edge or perimeter of something. _They sat around the campfire for hours. _ We used to sit around the big kitchen table and talk.
examples: They sat around the campfire for hours.

sit at something.monolingual: to be seated in front of something, such as a table. _ He sat at the table, taking his tea. _ Please sit at your desk and finish your work before taking a break.
examples: He sat at the table, taking his tea.

sit back.monolingual: to push oneself back in one’s seat; to lean against the back of one’s seat. _ Please sit back. I can’t see around you. _ I sat back and made myself comfortable, assuming that the movie would bore me to sleep.
examples: Please sit back.

sit bolt upright.monolingual: to sit up straight. _ Tony sat bolt upright and listened to what the teacher was saying to him. _After sitting bolt upright for almost an hour in that crowded airplane, I swore I would never f ly again.
examples: Tony sat bolt upright and listened to what the teacher was saying to him.

sit by someone.monolingual: to sit next to someone. _ May I sit by you? _ Come over here and sit by me.
examples: Come over here and sit by me.

sit down.monolingual: to be seated; to sit on something, such as a chair. _ Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. _ Can I sit down here?
examples: Please sit down and make yourself comfortable.

sit down on something.monolingual: to be seated on something. _ Please sit down on this chair and wait until you are called. _ I don’t want to sit down on this hard bench.
examples: Please sit down on this chair and wait until you are called.

sit down to something.monolingual: to sit down at a table to do something, such as eat a meal or attend to some business. _ I look forward to going home and sitting down to a quiet supper. _ Ted looked forward to sitting down to a big Thanksgiving dinner.
examples: I look forward to going home and sitting down to a quiet supper.

sit for an exam.monolingual: to take an exam to qualify for a license, such as a bar exam. _ When do you sit for the bar exam? _ I will sit for the exam next week.
examples: I will sit for the exam next week.

sit for one’s portrait.monolingual: to serve as the subject of a portrait being done by a painter or photographer. _ I sat for the picture for two hours. _Do you mind sitting for the painter all day? It will be easier if you get it over with all at once.
examples: I sat for the picture for two hours.

sit for someone.monolingual: 1. to care for someone in the role of babysitter. _ I sit for Timmy sometimes. I like him. He’s a good little kid. _ Mary doesn’t sit for anyone anymore. It leaves no time for a social life.
examples: I sit for Timmy sometimes.

sit on one’s ass.monolingual: Inf. to sit idle; to sit around doing nothing. (Use ass with discretion.) _Don’t just sit on your ass! Get busy! _He just sat on his ass, watching what was going on.
examples: He just sat on his ass, watching what was going on.

sit on one’s hands.monolingual: Fig. to do nothing; to fail to help. _When we needed help from Mary, she just sat on her hands. _ We need the cooperation of everyone. You can’t sit on your hands!
examples: When we needed help from Mary, she just sat on her hands.

sit on someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to place oneself in a sitting position on someone or something. _ The enormous woman knocked the crook out and sat on him until the police came. _ I need to sit on this chair for a minute and catch my breath.
examples: The enormous woman knocked the crook out and sat on him until the police came.

sit on the fence.monolingual: Fig. not to take sides in a dispute; not to make a clear choice between two possibilities. (Fig. on the image of someone straddling a fence, representing indecision.) _When Jane and Tom argue, it is best to sit on the fence and not make either of the
examples: When Jane and Tom argue, it is best to sit on the fence and not make either of them angry.

sit out.monolingual: to elect not to participate in something. _ I think I will not join in this game. I’ll sit out. _ I’ll sit out for this round.
examples: I think I will not join in this game.

sit right with someone.monolingual: Fig. [for something] to be acceptable or understandable to someone. (Very close to sit well with someone.) _ What you just said doesn’t really sit right with me. Let’s talk about it. _ It didn’t sit right with the boss.
examples: What you just said doesn’t really sit right with me.

sit something out†.monolingual: not to participate in something; to wait until something is over before participating. _Oh, please play with us. Don’t sit it out. _ I’m tired of playing cards, so I think I’ll sit out this game.
examples: Oh, please play with us.

sit still for something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to remain seated without fidgeting during something. _ The child could hardly be expected to sit still for the opera. _ Timmy would not sit still for his haircut.
examples: The child could hardly be expected to sit still for the opera.

sit through something.monolingual: to remain seated and in attendance for all of something, even though it is boring or poorly done. _I can’t stand to sit through that class one more time! _ Do I have to sit through the whole lecture?

sit tight.monolingual: to wait; to wait patiently. (This does not necessarily refer to sitting.) _Just relax and sit tight. I’ll be right with you. _ We were waiting in line for the gates to open when someone came out and told us to sit tight because it wouldn’t be much lo
examples: Just relax and sit tight.

sit up.monolingual: 1. to rise from a lying to a sitting position. _ When the alarm went off, he sat up and put his feet on the f loor. _ She couldn’t sleep, so she sat up and read a book.
examples: When the alarm went off, he sat up and put his feet on the f loor.

sit up and take notice.monolingual: to become alert and pay attention. _ A loud noise from the front of the room caused everyone to sit up and take notice. _The company wouldn’t pay any attention to my complaints. When I had my lawyer write them a letter, they sat up and took notice.
examples: A loud noise from the front of the room caused everyone to sit up and take notice.

sit up with someone.monolingual: to stay with someone through the night, especially with a sick or troubled person or with someone who is waiting for something. _ I had to sit up with my younger sister when she was ill. _ I sat up with Bill while he waited for an overseas telephone
examples: I had to sit up with my younger sister when she was ill.

sit well with someone.monolingual: to be acceptable to someone. _Your explanation of your absence doesn’t sit well with the president. _ The whole affair didn’t sit well with the manager.
examples: Your explanation of your absence doesn’t sit well with the president.

sit with someone.monolingual: 1. to stay with someone; to sit up with someone. _My uncle sat with me my first day in the hospital.
examples: My uncle sat with me my first day in the hospital.

*a sitting duck.monolingual: Fig. someone or something vulnerable to attack, physical or verbal. (Alludes to a duck floating on the water, not suspecting that it is the object of a hunter or predator. *Typically: be ~; like ~; looking like ~.) _ You look like a sitting duck out
examples: You look like a sitting duck out there.

sitting on a gold mine.monolingual: Fig. in control of something very valuable; in control of something potentially very valuable. _ When I found out how much the old book was worth, I realized that I was sitting on a gold mine. _Mary’s land is valuable. She is sitting on a gold mine.
examples: When I found out how much the old book was worth, I realized that I was sitting on a gold mine.

sitting on a powder keg.monolingual: Fig. in a risky or explosive situation; in a situation where something serious or dangerous may happen at any time. (A powder keg is a keg of gunpowder.) _ Things are very tense at work. The whole office is sitting on a powder keg. _ The fire at the
examples: Things are very tense at work.

*sitting pretty.monolingual: living in comfort or luxury; living in a good situation. (*Typically: be ~; leave someone ~.) _ My uncle died and left enough money for me to be sitting pretty for the rest of my life. _Now that I have a goodpaying job, I’m sitting pretty.
examples: My uncle died and left enough money for me to be sitting pretty for the rest of my life.

six feet under.monolingual: Fig. dead and buried. _ Fred died and is six feet under. _They put him six feet under two days after he died.
examples: Fred died and is six feet under.

a sixth sense.monolingual: a supposed power to know or feel things that are not perceptible by the five senses of sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. _ My sixth sense told me to avoid going home by my usual route. Later I discovered there had been a fatal accident on it.
examples: My sixth sense told me to avoid going home by my usual route.

the sixty-four-dollar question.monolingual: Fig. the most important question; the question that everyone wants to know the answer to. _ Who will win? Now, that is the sixty-fourdollar question. _ Now for the sixty-four-dollar question. What’s the stock market going to do this year?
examples: Who will win? Now, that is the sixty-fourdollar question.

size someone or something up†.monolingual: to observe someone or something to get information; to check someone or something out. _ The comedian sized the audience up and decided not to use his new material. _ I like to size up a situation before I act.
examples: The comedian sized the audience up and decided not to use his new material.

skate around.monolingual: to skate here and there in no particular direction. _ Let’s go over to the pond and skate around. _ We will skate around for a while until we get too cold.
examples: Let’s go over to the pond and skate around.

skate around someone or something.monolingual: 1. to skate to one side or the other of someone or something. _Somehow I managed to skate around the child without knocking her down. _ I skated around the tree limb and avoided an accident.
examples: Somehow I managed to skate around the child without knocking her down.

skate on something.monolingual: to skate on a particular surface. _You can’t skate on that ice! It’s too thin. _Don’t skate on the ice until it has been scraped smooth.
examples: You can’t skate on that ice! It’s too thin.

skate on thin ice.monolingual: Fig. to be in a risky situation. (Fig. on the image of someone taking the risk of ice skating on thin ice.) _ I try to stay well informed so I don’t end up skating on thin ice when the teacher asks me a question. _ You are skating on thin ice when yo
examples: I try to stay well informed so I don’t end up skating on thin ice when the teacher asks me a question.

skate over something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to move over something, skating. _ I love to be the first one to skate over newly frozen ice. _ I skated over the pond too soon and the ice cracked while I was on it.
examples: I love to be the first one to skate over newly frozen ice.

sketch something in†.monolingual: to draw in the image of someone or something. _ I sketched a figure of a woman in so that she appears to be standing beneath the tree. _ I’ll sketch in the house in the upper left corner.
examples: I sketched a figure of a woman in so that she appears to be standing beneath the tree.

sketch something out†.monolingual: to create a rough idea or image of something by sketching or some other means. (Does not necessarily require an actual sketch.) _ Sally sketched the furniture arrangement out so we could get an idea of what it was to look like. _ Would you sketch out
examples: Sally sketched the furniture arrangement out so we could get an idea of what it was to look like.

skid across something.monolingual: to slip or glide across something, such as ice or wet pavement. _ The car skidded across the pavement and crashed into a tree. _Our bus skidded across the icy bridge and ran into a ditch on the other side.
examples: The car skidded across the pavement and crashed into a tree.

skid into someone or something.monolingual: to slip or glide into someone or something. _The bicycle skidded into a pedestrian. _ The car skidded into a guard rail.
examples: The bicycle skidded into a pedestrian.

skim over something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to glide across something. _ The sailboat skimmed over the waves like a bird. _The bird skimmed over the treetops, darting and dodging.
examples: The sailboat skimmed over the waves like a bird.

skim through something.monolingual: to go through something hastily; to read through something hastily. _ She skimmed through the catalogs, looking for a nice gift for Gary. _I will skim through your manuscript and see whether it looks promising.
examples: She skimmed through the catalogs, looking for a nice gift for Gary.

skimp on something.monolingual: to use too little of something; to save something by using less of it than needed for something. _Please don’t skimp on the gravy. I like my potatoes swimming in it. _ They skimped on quality a little when they furnished the lobby.
examples: Please don’t skimp on the gravy.

skin someone alive.monolingual: Fig. to be very angry with someone; to scold someone severely. (Fig. on being angry enough to do this kind of bodily harm to someone.) _I was so mad at Jane that I could have skinned her alive. _ If I don’t get home on time, my parents will skin me a
examples: I was so mad at Jane that I could have skinned her alive.

*skinny as a beanpole.monolingual: very thin; very skinny. (*Also: as ~.) _ I exercised and dieted until I was skinny as a beanpole.
examples: I exercised and dieted until I was skinny as a beanpole.

skinny-dip.monolingual: to swim naked. _ The boys were skinnydipping in the creek when Bob’s mother drove up.
examples: The boys were skinnydipping in the creek when Bob’s mother drove up.

skip it!.monolingual: Inf. Never mind!; Forget it! (Shows impatience or disappointment.) _ John: I need some help on this project. Mary: What? John: Oh, skip it! _Jane: Will you be able to do this, or should I get someone with more experience? Bob: What did you say? Jane:
examples: John: I need some help on this project.

skip out with something.monolingual: Fig. to leave and take something with one; to steal something. _The hotel guest skipped out with the towels. _Someone skipped out with the petty cash box.
examples: The hotel guest skipped out with the towels.

skip over someone or something.monolingual: not to choose someone or something next in line. _ She skipped over me and chose the next one in line. _ I skipped over the red ones and took a blue one.
examples: She skipped over me and chose the next one in line.

skip rope.monolingual: to jump over an arc of rope that is swung beneath one’s feet then over one’s head, repeatedly. _The children skipped rope on the playground. _ The boxer skipped rope while training.
examples: The children skipped rope on the playground.

skip through something.monolingual: to go through a book or a stack of papers without dealing with every page. _ I skipped through the book, just looking at the pictures. _Ted skipped through the report, not bothering to read it.
examples: I skipped through the book, just looking at the pictures.

skirmish with someone or something.monolingual: to have a minor fight with someone, a group, or something. _ Tim skirmished a bit with his brother and then ran into the house. _I don’t want to skirmish with the committee.
examples: Tim skirmished a bit with his brother and then ran into the house.

skirt around someone or something.monolingual: Fig. to move around and avoid someone or something. (Something can be a topic of conversation.) _We talked the whole evening and managed to skirt around Fred. _ We had to skirt around the subject.
examples: We talked the whole evening and managed to skirt around Fred.

the sky’s the limit..monolingual: Inf. there is no upper limit. _ I can afford it. The sky’s the limit. _ You can do anything you set your mind to, Billy. The sky’s the limit.
examples: I can afford it.

slack off.monolingual: 1. to taper off; to reduce gradually. _ Business tends to slack off during the winter months. _ The storms begin to slack off in April.
examples: Business tends to slack off during the winter months.

slam dunk.monolingual: 1. Lit. [in basketball] a goal scored by shooting the ball down from above the rim. _He was wide open and scored on an easy slam dunk.
examples: He was wide open and scored on an easy slam dunk.

slam into someone or something.monolingual: to crash into someone or something. _The race car—out of control—slammed into the stands. _ The bus slammed into a truck.
examples: The race car—out of control—slammed into the stands.

slam someone or something down†.monolingual: to drive or strike someone or something downward. _The wrestler slammed his opponent down hard. _ He slammed down his opponent and injured him.
examples: The wrestler slammed his opponent down hard.

slam the brakes on†.monolingual: to push on a vehicle’s brakes suddenly and hard. (The can be replaced by a possessive pronoun.) _ The driver in front of me slammed her brakes on and I nearly ran into her. _Don’t slam on your brakes when the road is wet.
examples: The driver in front of me slammed her brakes on and I nearly ran into her.

slant against something.monolingual: to rest obliquely against something. _The bookcase slants against the wall, and it should be straight. _ The lumber was left slanted against the garage.
examples: The bookcase slants against the wall, and it should be straight.

slant toward someone or something.monolingual: to incline toward someone or something. _ The scenery slanted toward the actors and looked as if it would fall. _ Everything in your sketch slants toward the right.
examples: The scenery slanted toward the actors and looked as if it would fall.

slap against someone or something.monolingual: [for something] to flap or strike against someone or something. _ The f lag kept slapping against Ed, making it hard for him to remain at attention. _ The awning slapped against the side of the house.
examples: The f lag kept slapping against Ed, making it hard for him to remain at attention.

a slap in the face.monolingual: an insult; an act that causes disappointment or discouragement. _ Losing the election was a slap in the face for the club president. _Failing to get into a good college was a slap in the face to Tim after his years of study.
examples: Losing the election was a slap in the face for the club president.

*a slap on the wrist.monolingual: 1. Lit. a hit on the wrist as a mild punishment for putting one’s hands where they shouldn’t be or taking something. (*Typically: get ~; give someone ~.) _ When Billy tried to grab another cookie, he got a slap on the wrist.
examples: When Billy tried to grab another cookie, he got a slap on the wrist.

slap someone down†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to cause someone to fall by striking with the open hand. _ She became enraged and slapped him down when he approached her again. _ Liz slapped down the insulting wretch.
examples: She became enraged and slapped him down when he approached her again.

slap someone in something.monolingual: Fig. Inf. to put or throw someone in jail or prison. _ The sheriff slapped the crooks in jail. _ Do you want me to slap you in jail?
examples: The sheriff slapped the crooks in jail.

slap someone on something.monolingual: to slap a particular part of someone. _ Gerald was always slapping his friends on the back. _ He slapped himself on the knee and laughed very loudly.
examples: Gerald was always slapping his friends on the back.

slap something down†.monolingual: to strike downward with something flat in one’s hand. _ She slapped the dollar bill down in great anger and took her paper cup full of water away with her. _ Karen slapped down the money that the bailiff demanded.
examples: She slapped the dollar bill down in great anger and took her paper cup full of water away with her.

slap something on someone.monolingual: Inf. to serve someone with a legal paper or citation. _ The strange man came into the office and slapped a subpoena on Mary. _I will slap a citation on you for speeding if you don’t stop arguing.
examples: The strange man came into the office and slapped a subpoena on Mary.

*slated for something.monolingual: scheduled for something. (As if a schedule had been written on a slate. *Typically: be ~; have someone ~.) _ John was slated for Friday’s game, but he couldn’t play with the team. _ Ann is slated for promotion next year.
examples: John was slated for Friday’s game, but he couldn’t play with the team.

*slated to do something.monolingual: scheduled to do something. (*Typically: be ~; have someone ~.) _ Mary is slated to go to Washington in the fall. _ We are slated to leave in November.
examples: Mary is slated to go to Washington in the fall.

slave over something.monolingual: Fig. to stand over something, working at it very hard, typically cooking over a hot stove. _ I’ve been slaving over this hot stove for hours to cook this meal! _ Ted slaved over his special dessert for hours.
examples: Ted slaved over his special dessert for hours.

*a slave to something.monolingual: Fig. someone who is under the control of something; someone whose time or attention is controlled or “owned by” by something. (Fig. on being a slave to a person. *Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ Mary is a slave to her job. _Bill is a slave to his drug
examples: Mary is a slave to her job.

sled down something.monolingual: to ride down something on a sled. _ I love to sled down the hill in the winter. _ This hill is too steep to sled down safely.
examples: I love to sled down the hill in the winter.

sled over something.monolingual: to travel over something, such as snow, in a sled. _ We sledded rapidly over the fresh snow, scooting down the hill. _ We wanted to sled over the new snow, but we had to wait until Uncle Herman had taken a picture of it for his scrapbook.
examples: We sledded rapidly over the fresh snow, scooting down the hill.

sleep around the clock.monolingual: to sleep for a full twenty-four hours; to sleep for a very long time. _I was so tired I could have slept around the clock. _When I got home, I lay down and slept around the clock.
examples: I was so tired I could have slept around the clock.

sleep in.monolingual: to oversleep; to sleep late in the morning. _If you sleep in again, you’ll get fired. _ I really felt like sleeping in this morning.
examples: If you sleep in again, you’ll get fired.

sleep on something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to recline on something and slumber. _ I like to sleep on a firm bed. _ Mary had to sleep on the f loor because her sister was visiting.
examples: I like to sleep on a firm bed.

sleep out.monolingual: to sleep outside or away from one’s home. _ Can I sleep out tonight? _ Didn’t you sleep out last night?

sleep something away†.monolingual: to spend or waste a specific period of time sleeping. _ You can’t sleep the whole day away! _ Jim slept away his whole vacation.
examples: Jim slept away his whole vacation.

sleep something off†.monolingual: to sleep while the effects of liquor or drugs pass away. _ John drank too much and went home to sleep it off. _Bill is at home sleeping off the effects of the drug they gave him.
examples: John drank too much and went home to sleep it off.

sleep through something.monolingual: to remain sleeping through some event. _I didn’t hear the storm. I guess I slept through it. _ Wally slept through the entire opera—even the loud part.
examples: I didn’t hear the storm.

sleep tight.monolingual: to sleep warm and safe. (Usually said with good night to someone going to bed.) _Sleep tight, Bobby. See you in the morning.
examples: Sleep tight, Bobby.

sleep together.monolingual: 1. [for two or more people] to share a bed. _ Do you mean that Fred and Dave have to sleep together? _My brother and I used to have to sleep together.
examples: My brother and I used to have to sleep together.

sleep with someone.monolingual: 1. to share a bed with someone. _ Do I have to sleep with my little brother? _Many little boys have to sleep with their brothers.
examples: Many little boys have to sleep with their brothers.

a sleeping giant.monolingual: a great power that is still and waiting. _ The huge country to the south is a sleeping giant, waiting for its chance to become sufficiently industrialized to have real prosperity. _ The U.S. was a sleeping giant at the outbreak of both world wars.
examples: The huge country to the south is a sleeping giant, waiting for its chance to become sufficiently industrialized to have real prosperity.

a slice of the cake.monolingual: a share of something. _ There’s not much work around and so everyone must be content with a slice of the cake. _The company makes huge profits and the workers want a slice of the cake.
examples: There’s not much work around and so everyone must be content with a slice of the cake.

slice someone or something up†.monolingual: to cut someone or something up into slices. _ The blades of the lawn mower can slice you up if you get too close. _ The sharp blades sliced up Bobby’s rubber ball.
examples: The blades of the lawn mower can slice you up if you get too close.

slice something off†.monolingual: to cut something off with slicing motions. _Sue sliced the dead branches off with a tree saw. _ Karen sliced off a nice piece of turkey.
examples: Sue sliced the dead branches off with a tree saw.

slice through something.monolingual: to cut through something with slicing motions. _ The chef sliced through the ham as if it were butter. _ The knife was too dull to slice through the tomato.
examples: The chef sliced through the ham as if it were butter.

*slick as a whistle.monolingual: quickly and cleanly; quickly and skillfully. (*Also: as ~.) _ Tom took a broom and a mop and cleaned the place up as slick as a whistle. _ Slick as a whistle, Sally pulled off the bandage.
examples: Tom took a broom and a mop and cleaned the place up as slick as a whistle.

slick something down†.monolingual: to brush or comb down hair, usually with some sort of dressing or water. _He used something gooey—grease or something—to slick his hair down. _ Please slick down your hair. You look a mess.
examples: He used something gooey—grease or something—to slick his hair down.

slick something up†.monolingual: to tidy up something or some place. _ I have to slick this house up a little. _ Please slick up this room before company gets here.
examples: I have to slick this house up a little.

slide along.monolingual: to slip or glide along. _ The sled slid along at a good clip down the gently sloping hill. _We slid along on the icy roads and had a hard time stopping and turning.
examples: The sled slid along at a good clip down the gently sloping hill.

slide around.monolingual: to slip or skid around. _ Many cars slide around on the roads when they are icy. _ The pedestrians were sliding around on the icy pavement.
examples: Many cars slide around on the roads when they are icy.

slide by.monolingual: to get along with a minimum of effort. _ She didn’t do a lot of work—she just slid by. _ Don’t just slide by. Put in some effort.
examples: She didn’t do a lot of work—she just slid by.

slide down from something.monolingual: to slip down on something from a higher place. _ Beth slid down from the top of the mound. _The boys slid down from the roof of the shed and got their pants all dirty.
examples: Beth slid down from the top of the mound.

slide down something.monolingual: to slip down something, such as a pole. _ The fire captain slid down the pole and ran to the engine. _ Please don’t slide down the stairs. You’ll ruin the carpet.
examples: The fire captain slid down the pole and ran to the engine.

slide into something.monolingual: to slip or glide into something, as a car going into a ditch. _It was raining hard, and car after car slid into the ditch at the sharp turn near Wagner Road. _ Mary’s car slid right into the side of a bus.
examples: It was raining hard, and car after car slid into the ditch at the sharp turn near Wagner Road.

slide out of something.monolingual: to slip or glide out of something without much effort. _ Mary slid out of the car and ran to the front door. _The CD-ROM slid out of the computer.
examples: Mary slid out of the car and ran to the front door.

slide over something.monolingual: to slip or glide over something. _The car almost slid over the edge of the cliff. _ We almost slid over the edge.
examples: The car almost slid over the edge of the cliff.

slide something around.monolingual: to push, twist, or turn something around. (The thing must be movable, but not often on wheels.) _ Please slide the carton around and look at the address on the other side. _ Can you slide the refrigerator around so I can clean the back of it?
examples: Please slide the carton around and look at the address on the other side.

slightly rattled.monolingual: 1. Inf. upset; confused. _ Tom was slightly rattled by the policeman at the door. _ I’m slightly rattled. I’ll get over it.
examples: Tom was slightly rattled by the policeman at the door.

a slim chance.monolingual: a slight chance; a small chance. _ There is a slim chance that I will arrive on Monday, but Tuesday is more likely.
examples: There is a slim chance that I will arrive on Monday, but Tuesday is more likely.

slim down.monolingual: to become thinner; to lose weight. _You have really slimmed down a lot since I last saw you. _ I need to eat less so I can slim down. _ He slimmed down quite a bit after he had his health problem.
examples: You have really slimmed down a lot since I last saw you.

slim someone down†.monolingual: to cause someone to lose weight. _ They started to slim her down in the hospital, but she gained the weight back as soon as she got out. _ The dietitian slimmed down all the patients under his care.
examples: They started to slim her down in the hospital, but she gained the weight back as soon as she got out.

sling something out†.monolingual: 1. to toss or heave something outward. _ The fishermen slung their nets out into the water. _ They slung out their nets.
examples: The fishermen slung their nets out into the water.

sling the cat.monolingual: Sl. to empty one’s stomach; to vomit. _Suddenly Ralph left the room to sling the cat, I guess. _ That stuff will make you sling the cat.
examples: Suddenly Ralph left the room to sling the cat, I guess.

slink around.monolingual: to creep or slither around furtively. _ The cat slunk around, waiting for a chance to get at the bird. _ Don’t slink around like that. Someone is likely to take you for a robber.
examples: The cat slunk around, waiting for a chance to get at the bird.

slink away.monolingual: to creep or slither away furtively. _ The fox slunk away, leaving the henhouse as quietly as such a thing is possible. _ I hope that the skunk will slink away as quietly as it came.
examples: The fox slunk away, leaving the henhouse as quietly as such a thing is possible.

slink off.monolingual: to creep away furtively. _ Carl was embarrassed and tried to slink off, but the ushers spotted him. _The boys slunk off from the picnic and smoked some cigarettes.
examples: Carl was embarrassed and tried to slink off, but the ushers spotted him.

slip around.monolingual: to slide or skid around. _ The pedestrian slipped around and finally fell on the ice. _The dog slipped around on the ice and finally made it to shore.
examples: The pedestrian slipped around and finally fell on the ice.

slip between the cracks.monolingual: Fig. [for someone or something] to be forgotten or neglected. (Fig. on something being lost by falling between floorboards.) _ Where is Alice? I guess we neglected her and she slipped between the cracks. _This issue seems to have slipped between the
examples: Where is Alice? I guess we neglected her and she slipped between the cracks.

slip down.monolingual: to slide or glide downward. _ His socks kept slipping down. _ He lost so much weight that his pants almost slipped down.
examples: His socks kept slipping down.

slip from something.monolingual: to fall away from something; to lose one’s step or grasp and fall from something. _ He slipped from the top step and fell down the other three. _ Ted slipped from the stool and fell on the f loor.
examples: He slipped from the top step and fell down the other three.

a slip of the tongue.monolingual: an error in speaking in which a word is pronounced incorrectly, or in which the speaker says something unintentionally. _I didn’t mean to tell her that. It was a slip of the tongue. _ I failed to understand the instructions because the speaker made a
examples: I didn’t mean to tell her that.

slip on something.monolingual: to step on and slide on something. _ Valerie slipped on a banana peel and hurt her back. _Don’t slip on that wet spot on the f loor!
examples: Valerie slipped on a banana peel and hurt her back.

slip one’s mind.monolingual: [for something that was to be remembered] to be forgotten. _I meant to go to the grocery store on the way home, but it slipped my mind. _ My birthday slipped my mind. I guess I wanted to forget it.
examples: I meant to go to the grocery store on the way home, but it slipped my mind.

slip one’s trolley.monolingual: Sl. to become a little crazy; to lose one’s composure. _ I was afraid I would slip my trolley. _ He slipped his trolley and went totally bonkers.
examples: I was afraid I would slip my trolley.

slip out.monolingual: 1. [for someone] to exit quietly without bothering anyone. _ I slipped out during intermission.
examples: I slipped out during intermission.

slip past someone or something.monolingual: to sneak or move past someone or something unnoticed. _It is impossible to slip past the armed guards and metal detectors. _Do you think I can slip past the doorway without being seen?
examples: It is impossible to slip past the armed guards and metal detectors.

slip someone a mickey.monolingual: to secretly put a Mickey Finn in someone’s alcoholic drink. (This drug either makes the victim ill or causes immediate diarrhea.) _ Somebody slipped Barlowe a Mickey and sent him into action. _ For a ten-spot, the bartender slipped Slim a Mickey.
examples: Somebody slipped Barlowe a Mickey and sent him into action.

slip someone five.monolingual: Sl. to shake someone’s hand. _ Billy slipped me five, and we sat down to discuss old times. _ Come on, man, slip me five!
examples: Billy slipped me five, and we sat down to discuss old times.

slip something back†.monolingual: 1. to pull or place something back. _Alice slipped the gearshift lever back and away they went. _She slipped back the gearshift and sped away.
examples: Alice slipped the gearshift lever back and away they went.

slip something down†.monolingual: to slide something downward. _ I slipped my pants down a little so the doctor could give me a shot in what they call your “hip.” _ He slipped down his pants a little.
examples: I slipped my pants down a little so the doctor could give me a shot in what they call your “hip.

slip something off†.monolingual: to let an item of clothing slide off one’s body; to remove an item of clothing easily or casually. _ He slipped his coat off and put it on a chair. _ She slipped off her shoes and relaxed.
examples: He slipped his coat off and put it on a chair.

slip something on†.monolingual: to put on an article of clothing, possibly in haste or casually. _ I will go in and slip my bathing suit on and join you in a minute. _She slipped on her shoes and we left.
examples: I will go in and slip my bathing suit on and join you in a minute.

slip through someone’s fingers.monolingual: 1. Lit. to slide through and out of one’s grasp. _The glass slipped through his fingers and crashed to the ground. _The rope slipped through his fingers and followed the anchor to the bottom of the lake.
examples: The glass slipped through his fingers and crashed to the ground.

slip through something.monolingual: to slide or slither through something narrow or crowded. _ Gerald slipped through the narrow opening and got away. _ The dog slipped through the door and ran out into the street.
examples: Gerald slipped through the narrow opening and got away.

slip up.monolingual: to make an error. _ I hope you don’t slip up again. Try to be more careful.
examples: I hope you don’t slip up again.

slip up on something.monolingual: to make an error in something. _ I guess I slipped up on that last job. _Fred slipped up on compiling that list—there are a lot of names missing.
examples: I guess I slipped up on that last job.

slip up something.monolingual: to climb something, slipping along the way. _ The hikers slipped up the wet slope. _ Ted slipped up the stairs, tracking mud and water as he went along.
examples: The hikers slipped up the wet slope.

*slippery as an eel.monolingual: devious and untrustworthy, but impossible to catch. (*Also: as ~.) _ Don’t sign a lease with that landlord; I think he’s as slippery as an eel. _ The con artist was slippery as an eel. Although he defrauded many people, he never went to prison.
examples: Don’t sign a lease with that landlord; I think he’s as slippery as an eel.

a slippery customer.monolingual: 1. Fig. a clever and deceitful customer. _ Watch out for that guy with the big padded coat. He may snatch something. He’s a real slippery customer.
examples: Watch out for that guy with the big padded coat.

a slippery slope.monolingual: a dangerous pathway or route to follow; a route that leads to trouble. _ The matter of euthanasia is a slippery slope with both legal and moral considerations.
examples: The matter of euthanasia is a slippery slope with both legal and moral considerations.

slither along.monolingual: to slink or crawl along. _ The snake slithered along, unmindful of our presence. _ A pair of otters slithered along playfully.
examples: The snake slithered along, unmindful of our presence.

slither away.monolingual: to sneak or crawl away, like a snake. _ The little lizards slithered away soundlessly. _ The snake slithered away while Maggie was still screaming.
examples: The little lizards slithered away soundlessly.

slob up.monolingual: Sl. to eat. _What time do you people slob up around here? _Fred stopped slobbing up long enough to change the channel on the TV set.
examples: Fred stopped slobbing up long enough to change the channel on the TV set.

slobber over someone or something.monolingual: Fig. to drool with delight or eagerness at the thought of someone or something. (Based on slobber over something. See also slobber (all) over someone or something.) _Fred was slobbering over Donna as she lay sunbathing in a tiny bikini. _ Jamie was s
examples: Fred was slobbering over Donna as she lay sunbathing in a tiny bikini.

slobber over something.monolingual: to drool with delight or eagerness before or while eating something. _ The dog was slobbering over a chunk of meat when the cat came in and hissed at the dog.
examples: The dog was slobbering over a chunk of meat when the cat came in and hissed at the dog.

slog through something.monolingual: to wade or trudge through something, such as mud or snow. _ Do I have to slog through the snow to go to school? Can’t you drive me? _ When I was your age, I slogged through snow twice this deep to get to school.
examples: When I was your age, I slogged through snow twice this deep to get to school.

slop around.monolingual: 1. [for someone] to splash around in a body of liquid, such as a bath. _ Timmy was in his bath, slopping around and singing. _ Bob is out in the pool, slopping around.
examples: Timmy was in his bath, slopping around and singing.

slop over.monolingual: [for a liquid] to splash out of or overflow a container. _ The milk slopped over and messed up the carpet. _ Her cup slopped over and spilled its contents on the kitchen table.
examples: The milk slopped over and messed up the carpet.

slop something around†.monolingual: to spill portions of a liquid here and there. _ Don’t slop the milk around as you pour it. _ Please don’t slop around the paint while you work.
examples: Don’t slop the milk around as you pour it.

slop something over something.monolingual: to spill or splash some liquid onto something. _ He slopped the starting f luid over the charcoal and lit it. _The artist slopped some grape juice over the canvas and proceeded to spread it around in an artistic fashion.
examples: He slopped the starting f luid over the charcoal and lit it.

slope away from something.monolingual: to slant downward and away from something. _ The lawn sloped away from the patio toward the riverbank. _ The porch sloped away from the house at a very slight angle.
examples: The lawn sloped away from the patio toward the riverbank.

slosh over.monolingual: [for a liquid] to splash over its container. _ The water in the wading pool sloshed over and made the grass slippery. _Don’t fill the glass too full. It will slosh over.
examples: The water in the wading pool sloshed over and made the grass slippery.

slosh something around†.monolingual: to cause a liquid to rush or splash in a container. _ The chef sloshed the dressing around a few times and poured it on the salad. _ The chef sloshed around the dressing and poured it on the salad.
examples: The chef sloshed the dressing around a few times and poured it on the salad.

slosh through something.monolingual: [for a person] to wade or splash through something. _The little kids sloshed through every puddle on their way home. _ We sloshed through the stream, ruining our shoes and soaking our cuffs.
examples: The little kids sloshed through every puddle on their way home.

slouch around.monolingual: to move around with a stooped or bent body. (One may slouch because of age, illness, fatigue, depression, fear, or with the intention of not being observed.) _ She is slouching around because she is tired. _ Don’t you slouch around when you are tired
examples: She is slouching around because she is tired.

slouch behind something.monolingual: to remain behind something, slouching with depression, fear, or the intent of not being observed. _Jim slouched behind a chair where no one could see him. _A weary clerk slouched behind the counter, wanting a nap more than anything else.
examples: Jim slouched behind a chair where no one could see him.

slouch down.monolingual: to slump or droop down. _ Don’t always slouch down, Timmy! Stand up straight. _ I slouch down because I am tired.
examples: Don’t always slouch down, Timmy! Stand up straight.

slouch over.monolingual: to lean or crumple and fall to one side; [for someone] to collapse in a sitting position. _ He slouched over and went to sleep in his chair. _ When he slouched over, I thought something was wrong.
examples: He slouched over and went to sleep in his chair.

slough something off†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to brush or rub something off. _ The snake sloughed its old skin off. _ It sloughed off its skin.
examples: The snake sloughed its old skin off.

slow down.monolingual: to decrease speed; to go slower. _Please slow down. You are going too fast.
examples: Please slow down.

slow going.monolingual: the rate of speed when one is making slow progress. _ It was slow going at first, but I was able to finish the project by the weekend. _ Getting the heavy rocks out of the field is slow going.
examples: It was slow going at first, but I was able to finish the project by the weekend.

slow off the mark.monolingual: 1. Lit. slow in starting or reacting. (Compare this with quick off the mark.) _ If you are always that slow off the mark you will never win the race. _ Boy, you were slow off the mark there!
examples: If you are always that slow off the mark you will never win the race.

a slow study.monolingual: a person who is slow to learn things. (Compare this to a slow study.) _ Fred, who is a slow study, never caught on to the joke.
examples: Fred, who is a slow study, never caught on to the joke.

slow up.monolingual: to go slower; to reduce speed in order for someone or something to catch up. _ Slow up a little! I can’t keep up with you! _ Please slow up. I can’t follow your lecture when you talk so fast.
examples: Please slow up.

slower and slower.monolingual: at a decreasing rate of speed; slow and then even slower. _The car is going slower and slower and will stop soon. _ The dog’s breathing got slower and slower as it went to sleep.
examples: The car is going slower and slower and will stop soon.

slug it out.monolingual: to fight something out; to argue intensely about something. _ They finally went outside to slug it out. _ We’ll just have to sit down in the conference room and slug it out.
examples: They finally went outside to slug it out.

sluice something down†.monolingual: to rinse something down; to flood the surface of something with water or other liquid to clean it. _John sluiced the driveway down. _Karen sluiced down the garage f loor.
examples: John sluiced the driveway down.

sluice something out†.monolingual: to rinse something out; to flood the inside of something to clean it. _ Sluice the wheelbarrow out, will you? _ Please sluice out the wheelbarrow.
examples: Please sluice out the wheelbarrow.

slump down.monolingual: [for someone] to collapse and fall down; [for someone] to crumple. _The shot hit Max and he slumped down. _ Suddenly, Mr. Wilson slumped down in pain.
examples: The shot hit Max and he slumped down.

slump over.monolingual: [for someone] to collapse and fall over forward in a sitting position. _ Just after the gunshot, Bruno slumped over and slid from his chair.
examples: Just after the gunshot, Bruno slumped over and slid from his chair.

slur over something.monolingual: Lit. to avoid saying difficult or crucial words by mumbling them; to speak over words unclearly. _ The speaker slurred over so many words that we didn’t know what she was saying. _ Unfortunately, Ted slurred over many of the important parts of his sp
examples: The speaker slurred over so many words that we didn’t know what she was saying.

slush up.monolingual: to become messy with slush. _ As the winter storm increases in intensity, the roads will slush up and become impassable. _ After an hour of snow and rain, the roads were so slushed up that we could not travel.
examples: As the winter storm increases in intensity, the roads will slush up and become impassable.

a smack in the face.monolingual: Fig. something that will humiliate someone, often when it is considered deserved; an insult. _ Being rejected by Jane was a real smack in the face for Tom, who thought she was fond of him. _Meg thought she was the best-qualified candidate for the job
examples: Being rejected by Jane was a real smack in the face for Tom, who thought she was fond of him.

smack of something.monolingual: to be reminiscent of something; to imply something. _ The whole scheme smacked of dishonesty and deception. _ All of this story smacks of illegal practices.
examples: The whole scheme smacked of dishonesty and deception.

smack someone down†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to knock a person down or cause a person to retreat with a slap or a blow. _ He tried to touch her again and she smacked him down. _ She smacked down the rude fellow.
examples: He tried to touch her again and she smacked him down.

smack the road.monolingual: Sl. to leave; to hit the road. _ Time to smack the road! Let’s go! _ Let’s smack the road. I have to get up early.
examples: Let’s smack the road.

small change.monolingual: Fig. an insignificant person. (Also a rude term of address.) _Look, small change, why don’t you just move along? _ The guy you think is small change happens to own this building you seem to be guarding so well.
examples: The guy you think is small change happens to own this building you seem to be guarding so well.

a small fortune.monolingual: a rather sizeable amount of money. _ This set of wheels cost me a small fortune. _I’ve got a small fortune tied up in test equipment.
examples: This set of wheels cost me a small fortune.

small fry.monolingual: 1. Lit. newly hatched fish; small, juvenile fish. _ The catch was bad today. Nothing but small fry.
examples: The catch was bad today.

small potatoes.monolingual: something or someone insignificant; small fry. _ This contract is small potatoes, but it keeps us in business till we get into the real money. _Small potatoes are better than no potatoes at all.
examples: This contract is small potatoes, but it keeps us in business till we get into the real money.

smart ass.monolingual: someone who makes wisecracks and acts cocky. (Potentially offensive. Use only with discretion.) _ Some smart ass came in here and asked for a sky hook. _ Don’t be such a smart ass!
examples: Some smart ass came in here and asked for a sky hook.

smart at something.monolingual: to suffer the pains of something. _ Over an hour later she was still smarting at his cruel remarks. _ For many days Ted smarted at the scolding he got.
examples: Over an hour later she was still smarting at his cruel remarks.

smart from something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to get a stinging pain from something. _His arm smarted from many mosquito bites. _Her legs smarted from the scratches she got from walking through the briars.
examples: His arm smarted from many mosquito bites.

smart guy.monolingual: someone who acts cocky or rude. _ All right, smart guy, see if you like this one. _ Some smart guy put chewing gum on this bench.
examples: All right, smart guy, see if you like this one.

smart money.monolingual: money belonging to smart or clever people. _Most of the smart money is going into utility stocks right now. _ Watch and see what the smart money is doing.
examples: Most of the smart money is going into utility stocks right now.

smart mouth.monolingual: someone who makes wisecracks; a cocky person who speaks out of turn. _Don’t be a smart mouth with me! _Mr. Atkins is going to get a reputation as a smart mouth.
examples: Mr. Atkins is going to get a reputation as a smart mouth.
