smart under something.monolingual: to suffer stinging pain under something. _The sailor’s back smarted under the blows of the lash. _ Ted smarted under the lash for his wrongdoings.
examples: The sailor’s back smarted under the blows of the lash.

smarten up.monolingual: to get smarter; to become more alert and knowing. _ You had better smarten up if you want to survive around here. _ I knew he would smarten up sooner or later.
examples: You had better smarten up if you want to survive around here.

a smash hit.monolingual: a play, movie, musical, etc., that is a big success. _ Her first book was a smash hit. The second was a disaster. _ A smash hit doesn’t always make people rich.
examples: Her first book was a smash hit.

smash into something.monolingual: to crash into something; to bump or crash into something. _ Judy smashed into the coffee table and hurt her leg. _ The car smashed into the side of a bus and caused a lot of damage.
examples: Judy smashed into the coffee table and hurt her leg.

smash out of something.monolingual: to break [one’s way] out of something. _ The prisoner smashed out of his cell and ran. _ The horse smashed out of its stable.
examples: The prisoner smashed out of his cell and ran.

smash someone’s face in†.monolingual: 1. Fig. to crush someone’s face. _The accident smashed Harry’s face in, and he had to have extensive surgery. _ The accident smashed in his face.
examples: The accident smashed Harry’s face in, and he had to have extensive surgery.

smash something in†.monolingual: to crush something inward; to make something collapse inward by striking it. _Andy gave one good kick and smashed the box in. _ Liz smashed in the window.
examples: Andy gave one good kick and smashed the box in.

smash something up†.monolingual: to break something up; to destroy something. _ I hope the children don’t smash any of the good china up if we use it tonight. _ The driver fell asleep and smashed up the car.
examples: I hope the children don’t smash any of the good china up if we use it tonight.

smash through something.monolingual: to break [one’s way] through some sort of barrier. _ The f leeing car smashed through the police barrier. _ Max got angry and smashed through the office door.
examples: The f leeing car smashed through the police barrier.

smell a rat.monolingual: to suspect that something is wrong; to sense that someone has caused something wrong. _I don’t think this was an accident. I smell a rat. Bob had something to do with this. _ The minute I came in, I smelled a rat. Sure enough, I had been robbed.
examples: I don’t think this was an accident.

smell blood.monolingual: Fig. to be ready for a fight; to be ready to attack; to be ready to act. (Like sharks, which are sent into a frenzy by the smell of blood.) _ Lefty was surrounded, and you could tell that the guys from the other gang smelled blood. _ The lawyer heard
examples: Lefty was surrounded, and you could tell that the guys from the other gang smelled blood.

smell fishy.monolingual: to seem suspicious. _ Barlowe squinted a bit. Something smells fishy here, he thought. _Something about the deal smelled fishy—too good to be true.
examples: Barlowe squinted a bit.

smell like a rose.monolingual: Fig. to seem innocent. _ I came out of the whole mess smelling like a rose, even though I caused all the trouble. _ The politician survived the scandal smelling like a rose, but I knew different.
examples: I came out of the whole mess smelling like a rose, even though I caused all the trouble.

smell of something.monolingual: to have the smell of something; to smell like something. _This house smells of onions. _Her cooking always smells of entirely too much garlic.
examples: This house smells of onions.

smell something up†.monolingual: to cause a bad or strong odor in a place or on something. _Your cooking sure smelled this place up! _ The spoiled meat really smelled up the house!

smile at someone.monolingual: to make a smiling face at someone. _ I love the way you smile at me. _ I am glad you smile at me occasionally.
examples: I love the way you smile at me.

smile on someone or something.monolingual: to be favorable to someone or something. _ Fate smiled on me and I got the job. _ Lady luck smiled on our venture and we made a profit.
examples: Fate smiled on me and I got the job.

smile when you say that..monolingual: Inf. I will interpret that remark as a joke or as kidding. _ John: You’re a real pain in the neck. Bob: Smile when you say that. _Sue: I’m going to bop you on the head! John: Smile when you say that!
examples: John: You’re a real pain in the neck.

smiling like a cheshire cat.monolingual: Fig. smiling very broadly. (Alludes to a grinning cat in Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland.) _ There he stood, smiling like a Cheshire cat, waiting for his weekly pay.
examples: There he stood, smiling like a Cheshire cat, waiting for his weekly pay.

smirk at someone or something.monolingual: to smile in a smug or sneering way at someone or something. _ Why are you smirking at me like that? _Jane looked at the report and smirked at it.
examples: Jane looked at the report and smirked at it.

smite someone with something.monolingual: to strike someone with something. (Literary or biblical.) _ The silver knight approached the black knight and smote him with his sword. _ Please go and smite the dragon with your sword.
examples: The silver knight approached the black knight and smote him with his sword.

smoke and mirrors.monolingual: deception and confusion. (Said of statements or more complicated rhetoric used to mislead people rather than inform. Alludes to the way a magician uses optical illusion to create believability while performing a trick. Fixed order.) _Most people know
examples: Most people know that the politician was just using smoke and mirrors to make things look better than they really were.

smoke like a chimney.monolingual: to smoke a great deal of tobacco or other smokable substances. _ My uncle smoked like a chimney when he was living. _ Somebody who smokes like a chimney in a restaurant ought to be thrown out.
examples: My uncle smoked like a chimney when he was living.

smoke something up†.monolingual: to cause something or a place to become smoky. _Get out of here with that cigarette! I don’t want you smoking my house up! _ The burning beans sure smoked up the house.
examples: The burning beans sure smoked up the house.

smoke-filled room.monolingual: a room where a small group of people make important decisions. (Usually used in reference to political parties.) _The smoke-filled rooms are still producing the candidates for most offices, despite all the political reforms. _ The deal was cut in a s
examples: The smoke-filled rooms are still producing the candidates for most offices, despite all the political reforms.

the smoking gun.monolingual: Fig. the indisputable sign of guilt. (Fig. on a murderer being caught just after shooting the victim.) _Mr. South was left holding the smoking gun. _The chief of staff decided that the the aide should be found with the smoking gun.
examples: Mr. South was left holding the smoking gun.

smooth something away†.monolingual: to remove something, such as wrinkles or other unevenness, by pressing or smoothing. _ Jeff put the cloth on the table and smoothed the wrinkles away with his hand. _ Jeff smoothed away the wrinkles.
examples: Jeff put the cloth on the table and smoothed the wrinkles away with his hand.

smooth something back†.monolingual: to flatten and position something by pressing or smoothing. _ He smoothed his hair back out of his eyes. _ Jeff smoothed back his hair.
examples: He smoothed his hair back out of his eyes.

smooth something down†.monolingual: to make something flat or smooth by pressing. _She smoothed her skirt down, f luffed her hair, and went into the boardroom. _ Karen smoothed down the bedclothes.
examples: She smoothed her skirt down, f luffed her hair, and went into the boardroom.

snake along.monolingual: to move along in a curving line, looking like a snake; to move along in a line, moving as a snake moves. _ The train snaked along, gaining speed as it went downhill. _The line of people waiting to buy tickets snaked along slowly.
examples: The train snaked along, gaining speed as it went downhill.

snake in the grass.monolingual: a sneaky and despised person. _How could I ever have trusted that snake in the grass? _ John is such a snake in the grass.
examples: John is such a snake in the grass.

snakebite medicine.monolingual: Inf. inferior whiskey; strong whiskey; homemade whiskey. _ That old-time snakebite medicine is good for what ails you. _ Snakebite medicine is a tremendous protection against snakebites if you can get the snake to drink the stuff before it bites you.
examples: That old-time snakebite medicine is good for what ails you.

snap at someone.monolingual: to speak sharply or angrily to someone. (Based on snap at someone or something.) _ Don’t snap at me. What did I do? _ Why did you snap at me? I did nothing wrong.
examples: Don’t snap at me.

snap at someone or something.monolingual: to bite at someone or something. _ The dog snapped at my pants leg, but I escaped the attack unharmed. _ The fox snapped at the chicken and finally caught hold of it. _ The dog snapped at the judge and was disqualified.
examples: The dog snapped at my pants leg, but I escaped the attack unharmed.

snap at something.monolingual: Fig. to seize an opportunity. _ It is such a good deal, I knew you would snap at it. _Just as I thought, Ted snapped at my final offer.
examples: It is such a good deal, I knew you would snap at it.

snap into something.monolingual: [for something] to be put or fit into an opening with an audible snap. _ The larger edge of the card snaps into the slot at the base. _ This part snaps right into the other part.
examples: The larger edge of the card snaps into the slot at the base.

snap it up!.monolingual: Inf. Hurry up! _ John: Come on, Fred. Snap it up! Fred: I’m hurrying! I’m hurrying! _ Sally: Snap it up! You’re going to make us late. John: That’s exactly what I had in mind.
examples: John: Come on, Fred.

snap one’s cookies.monolingual: Sl. to vomit; to regurgitate. _ I think I’m gonna snap my cookies. _ Some jerk snapped his cookies on the sidewalk.
examples: I think I’m gonna snap my cookies.

snap out of something.monolingual: Fig. to become suddenly freed from a condition. (The condition can be a depression, an illness, unconsciousness, etc.) _ I was very depressed for a week, but this morning I snapped out of it. _ It isn’t often that a cold gets me down. Usually I can s
examples: I was very depressed for a week, but this morning I snapped out of it.

snap someone’s head off.monolingual: Fig. to speak very sharply to someone. (Based on snap at someone.) _How rude! Don’t snap my head off! _ Mary snapped Ted’s head off because he had come in late.
examples: Mary snapped Ted’s head off because he had come in late.

snap something back†.monolingual: to cause something to jerk back. _ The force of the crash snapped his head back and injured his neck. _ The crash snapped back his head.
examples: The force of the crash snapped his head back and injured his neck.

snap something off†.monolingual: to break off something brittle. _ Liz snapped a bit of the rock off and put it in her bag. _ Carl snapped off a piece of the candy and gave it to Timmy.
examples: Liz snapped a bit of the rock off and put it in her bag.

snap something on†.monolingual: to attach something to something else, causing an audible snap. _ Dawn took two pills from the bottle and snapped the lid on. _ She snapped on the lid.
examples: Dawn took two pills from the bottle and snapped the lid on.

snap something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to grasp something quickly. _ Karen snapped her pencil up and strode out of the room. _ Harry walked through the kitchen and snapped up two cookies on the way.
examples: Karen snapped her pencil up and strode out of the room.

snap to it!.monolingual: Inf.Move faster!; Look alert! _Bill: Snap to it! Mary: Don’t rush me! _ John: Get in line there. Snap to it! Sally: What is this, the army? You just wait till I’m ready!
examples: John: Get in line there.

snarl someone or something up†.monolingual: to tangle someone or something; to mess something up. _The wind snarled my hair up terribly. _ The wind snarled up my hair.
examples: The wind snarled my hair up terribly.

snarl something out†.monolingual: to utter something by snarling or growling. _Lefty snarled a naughty word out at the police. _Walt the pickpocket snarled out a curse as the cop grabbed his coat collar.
examples: Lefty snarled a naughty word out at the police.

snatch at someone or something.monolingual: to grasp at someone or something. _ The mugger snatched at Jane just as she sprayed Mace on him. _ He snatched at the Mace, but it was too late.
examples: The mugger snatched at Jane just as she sprayed Mace on him.

snatch something out of something.monolingual: to grab something out of something. _ The police officer snatched the gun out of Don’s hand. _Mary snatched the piece of chicken out of the fire as soon as it fell in.
examples: The police officer snatched the gun out of Don’s hand.

snatch something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to grasp something and lift it up. _ Tom snatched the last cookie up and popped it into his mouth. _ He snatched up the last piece of cake.
examples: Tom snatched the last cookie up and popped it into his mouth.

snazz something up†.monolingual: Sl. to make something classy or exciting. _ Come on, let’s try to snazz this up. _ What can I do to snazz up my face?
examples: Come on, let’s try to snazz this up.

sneak around someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to creep around or past someone or something. _The cat sneaked around Molly and ran out the door. _ We had to sneak around the corner so we wouldn’t be seen.
examples: The cat sneaked around Molly and ran out the door.

sneer at someone or something.monolingual: to make a haughty or deprecating face at someone or something; to show one’s contempt for someone or something. _I asked her politely to give me some more room, and she just sneered at me. _ Jamie sneered at the report that Ken had submitted.
examples: I asked her politely to give me some more room, and she just sneered at me.

sneeze at someone.monolingual: to sneeze in someone’s direction. _ Please don’t sneeze at me! Cover your nose and mouth! _ You should never sneeze at anyone. It is very bad manners.
examples: You should never sneeze at anyone.

sneeze at something.monolingual: Fig. to indicate one’s disapproval of something; to belittle someone or something. _I wouldn’t sneeze at that amount of money if I were you. It’s better than nothing. _ I though it was a good offer, but the customer just sneezed at it.
examples: I wouldn’t sneeze at that amount of money if I were you.

sneeze into something.monolingual: to aim a sneeze into something. _ You should always sneeze into a handkerchief. _ Please sneeze into a tissue or something.
examples: You should always sneeze into a handkerchief.

sneeze on someone or something.monolingual: to aim a sneeze onto someone or something, probably by accident. _ Don’t sneeze on me! _Don’t sneeze on anything. Cover your nose and mouth!
examples: Don’t sneeze on anything.

sniff at someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to try to get the smell of someone or something by smelling. _ The dog sniffed at the visitor. _ The cat sniffed at almost every inch of the rug that the dog had walked on.
examples: The dog sniffed at the visitor.

sniff someone or something out†.monolingual: to locate someone or something by sniffing or as if by sniffing. _The dog sniffed the intruder out and the police captured him. _The dog sniffed out the mole in the lawn.
examples: The dog sniffed the intruder out and the police captured him.

snipe at someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to fire a weapon at someone or something from a concealed position. _ Someone with a rif le sniped at the troops as they went through the jungle. _ A rif leman was busy sniping at the platoon.
examples: Someone with a rif le sniped at the troops as they went through the jungle.

snitch on someone.monolingual: to tattle on someone. _ You wouldn’t snitch on me, would you? _ Timmy snitched on his older brother.
examples: Timmy snitched on his older brother.

snoop into something.monolingual: to pry into something or someone else’s affairs. _ I wish you would stop snooping into my business! _ Whose affairs are they snooping into now?

snort at someone or something.monolingual: to show one’s displeasure with someone or something by snorting. _ The customer snorted at the waiter for his surliness. _ The customer snorted at the prices and walked out.
examples: The customer snorted at the waiter for his surliness.

snow bunny.monolingual: 1. someone learning to ski. _This little slope is for snow bunnies. _Most of the snow bunnies come here to socialize.
examples: This little slope is for snow bunnies.

a snow job.monolingual: a systematic deception; a deceptive story that tries to hide the truth. _You can generally tell when a student is trying to do a snow job. _ This snow job you call an explanation just won’t do.
examples: You can generally tell when a student is trying to do a snow job.

snow someone or something in†.monolingual: [for heavy snowfall] to block someone or something in a place. _ The sudden storm snowed us in. _The storm snowed in most of the people in town.
examples: The sudden storm snowed us in.

snowball into something.monolingual: Fig. [for something] to become larger or more serious by growing like a snowball being rolled. _ This whole problem is snowballing into a crisis very rapidly. _ The argument soon snowballed into a fullblown riot.
examples: This whole problem is snowballing into a crisis very rapidly.

snowed in.monolingual: trapped (somewhere) because of too much snow. _ The snow was so deep that we were snowed in for three days. _ Being snowed in is no problem if you have enough food.
examples: The snow was so deep that we were snowed in for three days.

snowed under.monolingual: overworked; exceptionally busy. _ Look, I’m really snowed under at the moment. Can this wait? _ He really has been snowed under with work.
examples: Look, I’m really snowed under at the moment.

snuff someone out†.monolingual: Sl. to kill someone. _ Max really wanted to snuff the eyewiteness out, once and for all. _ Lefty wanted to snuff out his partner.
examples: Max really wanted to snuff the eyewiteness out, once and for all.

snuff something out†.monolingual: to extinguish something, such as a flame. _ She snuffed all the candles out and went to bed. _ Karen snuffed out the f lames one by one.
examples: She snuffed all the candles out and went to bed.

so be it..monolingual: This is the way it will be. _ If you insist on running off and marrying her, so be it. Only don’t say I didn’t warn you! _Mary has decided that this is what she wants. So be it.
examples: If you insist on running off and marrying her, so be it.

so do i..monolingual: I do too. _Mary: I want some more cake. Sally: So do I. _Bob: I have to go home now. Tom: So do I. Bob: Bye.
examples: Mary: I want some more cake.

so far, so good..monolingual: All is going well so far. _We are half finished with our project. So far, so good. _ The operation is proceeding quite nicely—so far, so good.
examples: We are half finished with our project.

so gross!.monolingual: Sl. How disgusting! _He put chocolate syrup on his pie! So gross! _ He’s barfing! So gross!

so it goes..monolingual: Inf. That is the kind of thing that happens.; That is life. _ Too bad about John and his problems. So it goes. _ I just lost a twenty-dollar bill, and I can’t find it anywhere. So it goes.
examples: Too bad about John and his problems.

so long..monolingual: Good-bye. _So long, see ya later. _It’s been good talking to you. So long.
examples: So long, see ya later.

so mad i could scream.monolingual: very mad. _ I am just so mad I could scream! Why is he such a jerk? _ She makes me so mad I could scream.
examples: She makes me so mad I could scream.

so much for that..monolingual: That is the end of that.; We will not be dealing with that anymore. _ John tossed the stub of a pencil into the trash. “So much for that,” he muttered, fishing through his drawer for another. _ Mother: Here, try some carrots. Child (brushing the spoo
examples: John tossed the stub of a pencil into the trash.

so much the better.monolingual: even better; all to the better. _Please come to the picnic. If you can bring a salad, so much the better. _ The f lowers look lovely on the shelf. It would be so much the better if you put them on the table.
examples: Please come to the picnic.

so’s your old man!.monolingual: Inf. The same to you!; Drop dead! (Old. A catch phrase indicating basic disagreement or hostility.) _Bill: You’re acting like an idiot! Tom: So’s your old man! _ I don’t know what you said, but so’s your old man!

so soon.monolingual: early; before the regular time; ahead of schedule. _ I got there early because my bus arrived so soon. _ Because the meeting ended so soon, I had some extra time.
examples: I got there early because my bus arrived so soon.

so, sue me..monolingual: If you are so angry, why don’t go ahead and sue me. (A rude way of brushing off an angry person.) _ A: You ran into my car! You didn’t even look where you were going! B: So, sue me.
examples: A: You ran into my car! You didn’t even look where you were going! B: So, sue me.

so to speak.monolingual: as one might say; said a certain way, even though the words are not exactly accurate. _ John helps me with my taxes. He’s my accountant, so to speak. _I just love my little poodle. She’s my baby, so to speak.
examples: John helps me with my taxes.

soak one’s face.monolingual: Sl. to drink heavily. _ They’re down at the tavern soaking their faces. _Well, I guess I’ll go soak my face in a few beers.
examples: They’re down at the tavern soaking their faces.

soak someone to the skin.monolingual: [for water, rain, or other liquid] to work its way through someone’s clothing to the skin. _ The storm soaked us all to the skin. _ She soaked herself to the skin in the storm.
examples: The storm soaked us all to the skin.

soak something in something.monolingual: to leave something immersed in a liquid, intending for it to be absorbed. _ Soak your feet in Epsom salts to make them feel better. _I had to soak my elbow in ice water to take down the swelling.
examples: Soak your feet in Epsom salts to make them feel better.

soak something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to gather up moisture or a liquid, using an absorbent cloth, paper, etc. _ Alice soaked the spill up with a sponge. _She soaked up the spilled milk.
examples: Alice soaked the spill up with a sponge.

soak through something.monolingual: [for liquid] to work its way through something, such as cloth or paper. _Please wipe up that mess before it soaks through the tablecloth. _It’s too late. The grape juice has soaked through the carpet into the mat.
examples: Please wipe up that mess before it soaks through the tablecloth.

soaked to the skin.monolingual: wet clear through one’s clothing to the skin. _ I was caught in the rain and got soaked to the skin. _ Oh, come in and dry off! You must be soaked to the skin.
examples: I was caught in the rain and got soaked to the skin.

so-and-so.monolingual: a despised person. (This expression is used in place of other very insulting terms. Often modified, as in the examples.) _You dirty so-and-so! I can’t stand you! _ Don’t you call me a so-and-so, you creep!

soap someone or something down†.monolingual: to cover someone or something thoroughly with soap or suds. _Mother soaped Timmy down and rinsed him off in warm water. _ She soaped down the f loor.
examples: Mother soaped Timmy down and rinsed him off in warm water.

sob oneself to sleep.monolingual: to cry until one falls asleep. _ He sobbed himself to sleep for days after his grandpa died. _ The child sobbed himself to sleep night after night.
examples: He sobbed himself to sleep for days after his grandpa died.

sob something out†.monolingual: to speak something out while sobbing. _ Wally sobbed his story out while the police made notes. _ He sobbed out his sad tale.
examples: Wally sobbed his story out while the police made notes.

sob something to someone.monolingual: to cry and tell one’s troubles to someone. _He is always sobbing his sad tale to anyone who will listen. _ Timmy sobbed his story to the teacher.
examples: He is always sobbing his sad tale to anyone who will listen.

sob story.monolingual: Fig. a sad story that is likely to draw tears. _I’ve heard nothing but sob stories today. Isn’t anybody happy? _ She had quite a sob story, and I listened to the whole thing.
examples: I’ve heard nothing but sob stories today.

*sober as a judge.monolingual: 1. Cliché very formal, somber, or stuffy. (*Also: as ~.) _ You certainly look gloomy, Bill. You’re sober as a judge. _ Tom’s as sober as a judge. I think he’s angry.
examples: You certainly look gloomy, Bill.

sober someone up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to take actions that will cause a drunken person to become sober. _ Some coffee ought to sober him up. _He tried to sober himself up because he had to drive home. _ They tried to sober up the guys who had been out all night.
examples: Some coffee ought to sober him up.

sober up.monolingual: to recover from alcohol or drug intoxication. _ Barlowe had one hour to sober up and get to the station. _ It took him a while to sober up.
examples: Barlowe had one hour to sober up and get to the station.

sock it to someone.monolingual: 1. to punch someone; to punch one’s fist at someone. _ Max really socked it to Lefty! _ Lefty socked it to Roger and knocked him down.
examples: Lefty socked it to Roger and knocked him down.

sock someone or something in†.monolingual: [for fog] to cause someone or something to remain in place. _ The heavy fog socked us in for six hours. _ The fog socked in the airport for an hour.
examples: The heavy fog socked us in for six hours.

sock something away†.monolingual: to place something, such as money, into reserve; to store something in a secure place. _ I try to sock a little money away each month for my vacation. _ I will sock away some money.
examples: I try to sock a little money away each month for my vacation.

socked in.monolingual: fogged in. _ The airport was completely socked in. _ We couldn’t take off because we were socked in.
examples: The airport was completely socked in.

soft in the head.monolingual: Fig. stupid; witless. _ George is just soft in the head. He’ll never get away with his little plan. _ You’re soft in the head if you think I’ll go along with that.
examples: George is just soft in the head.

*soft on someone.monolingual: 1. Fig. romantically attracted to someone. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _Fred is soft on Martha, I’ve heard. _ He looked like he was getting a little soft on Sally.
examples: Fred is soft on Martha, I’ve heard.

soft sell.monolingual: a polite attempt to sell something; a very gentle sales pitch. _ Some people won’t bother listening to a soft sell. You gotta let them know you believe in what you are selling. _ I tried the soft sell, but that didn’t work.
examples: Some people won’t bother listening to a soft sell.

soft soap.monolingual: 1. flattering talk; sweet talk. _ I don’t mind a little soft soap. It won’t affect what I decide, though. _Don’t waste my time with soft soap. I know you don’t mean it.
examples: I don’t mind a little soft soap.

soft touch.monolingual: 1. a gentle way of handling someone or something. _ Bess has a soft touch and can bring both sides together. _Kelly lacks the kind of soft touch needed for this kind of negotiation.
examples: Bess has a soft touch and can bring both sides together.

soften someone up†.monolingual: Fig. to prepare to persuade someone of something. _ I will talk to Fred and soften him up for your request. _ I will soften up your father before you ask him about it.
examples: I will talk to Fred and soften him up for your request.

soften something up†.monolingual: to take actions that will make something softer. _Soften the butter up before you add it to the batter. _ Please soften up the ice cream before you try to serve it.
examples: Soften the butter up before you add it to the batter.

soften up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to become softer. _The butter softened up in the heat of the day. _ The candles will probably soften up and bend over in this hot weather.
examples: The butter softened up in the heat of the day.

soft-pedal something.monolingual: to play something down; to deemphasize something. (Alludes to the soft pedal on the piano, which reduces the volume.) _Try to soft-pedal the problems we have with the cooling system. _ I won’t softpedal anything. Everyone must know the truth.
examples: Try to soft-pedal the problems we have with the cooling system.

sold on someone or something.monolingual: convinced of the value of someone or something. _I’m not yet sold on your idea. _ The crowd was sold on Gary. Nothing he had done or could do would cool their enthusiasm.
examples: I’m not yet sold on your idea.

sold out.monolingual: [of a product] completely sold with no more items remaining; [of a store] having no more of a particular product. _ The tickets were sold out so we couldn’t go to the concert. _ I wanted new shoes like yours, but they were sold out.
examples: The tickets were sold out so we couldn’t go to the concert.

solicit for someone or something.monolingual: to seek money or other contributions for someone or something, such as a charitable cause. _ I am soliciting for crippled children. Would you care to contribute? _Are you soliciting for a local cause?
examples: I am soliciting for crippled children.

solicit someone for something.monolingual: to attempt to persuade someone to give something, such as money, for a specific purpose. _ The school band solicited the owners of the business for a contribution. _ Fred solicited everyone in his department for at least a dollar.
examples: The school band solicited the owners of the business for a contribution.

*solid as a rock.monolingual: Cliché very solid; dependable. (*Also: as ~.) _Jean has been lifting weights every day, and her arm muscles are solid as a rock. _This company has always built power tools that are as solid as a rock.
examples: Jean has been lifting weights every day, and her arm muscles are solid as a rock.

*some elbow room.monolingual: Fig. room to move about in; extra space to move about in. (*Typically: allow ~; get ~; have ~; give someone ~; need ~.) _This table is too crowded. We all need some elbow room.
examples: This table is too crowded.

*some loose ends.monolingual: Fig. some things that are not yet finished; some problems not yet solved. (*Typically: are ~; have ~; leave~; tie ~ up†; take care of ~.) _ I have to stay in town this weekend and tie up some loose ends.
examples: I have to stay in town this weekend and tie up some loose ends.

*some shut-eye.monolingual: some sleep. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; use ~; need ~.) _I need to get home and get some shut-eye before I do anything else. _We all could use some shut-eye.
examples: I need to get home and get some shut-eye before I do anything else.

someone of note.monolingual: a person who is famous. _ We invited a speaker of note to lecture at the next meeting. _ The baseball player of note was inducted into the Hall of Fame.
examples: We invited a speaker of note to lecture at the next meeting.

someone’s bread and butter.monolingual: Fig. someone’s basic income; someone’s livelihood—the source of one’s food. _ I can’t miss another day of work. That’s my bread and butter. _ I worked as a bartender for a year, and it was the tips that were my bread and butter.
examples: I can’t miss another day of work.

someone’s claim to fame.monolingual: someone’s reason for being wellknown or famous. _Her claim to fame is that she can recite the entire works of Shakespeare.
examples: Her claim to fame is that she can recite the entire works of Shakespeare.

someone’s dirty laundry.monolingual: Fig. someone’s unpleasant secrets. _ I don’t want to hear about her dirty laundry. Why do you feel it necessary to gossip about things like this?
examples: I don’t want to hear about her dirty laundry.

someone’s fate is sealed.monolingual: Fig. the destiny of somene has been determined. _ When the driver finally saw that the bridge was out, he knew his fate was sealed.
examples: When the driver finally saw that the bridge was out, he knew his fate was sealed.

someone’s hands are tied.monolingual: Fig. someone is not able to help or intervene. _ I’m sorry. There’s nothing I can do. My hands are tied.
examples: I’m sorry. There’s nothing I can do.

someone’s level best.monolingual: one’s very best effort. _ I will do my level best to find your husband. _ Don’t go to a whole lot of trouble. Your level best is good enough.
examples: I will do my level best to find your husband.

someone’s point is well taken.monolingual: someone’s idea or opinion is accepted and appreciated. _Your point is well taken and I will see that it is not forgotten.
examples: Your point is well taken and I will see that it is not forgotten.

someone’s train of thought.monolingual: Fig. someone’s pattern of thinking or sequence of ideas; what one was just thinking about. _ My train of thought is probably not as clear as it should be. _ I cannot seem to follow your train of thought on this matter. Will you explain it a little mo
examples: My train of thought is probably not as clear as it should be.

someone’s true colors.monolingual: Fig. a person’s true attitude, opinions, and biases. _ When he lost his temper at his wife, I began to see his true colors.
examples: When he lost his temper at his wife, I began to see his true colors.

someone’s word is good.monolingual: someone can be believed and trusted. _ You can believe her. Her word is good.
examples: You can believe her.

someone’s word of honor.monolingual: someone’s trustworthy pledge or promise. _He gave me his word of honor that he would bring the car back by noon today.
examples: He gave me his word of honor that he would bring the car back by noon today.

something about someone or something.monolingual: something alluring or curious about someone or something. _ There is something about Jane. I just can’t figure her out. _ I love Mexican food. There’s just something about it.
examples: There is something about Jane.

something is better than nothing..monolingual: Prov. It is better to get only some of what you want than to get nothing at all. better than nothing.) _ Fred: I only got $50 for all those books I sold. Jane: Something is better than nothing. _ Jill: Is your camera very good? Jane: It’s better than
examples: Fred: I only got $50 for all those books I sold.

something is killing someone.monolingual: Fig. something is causing someone pain. _ Wow, my feet are killing me!

something never fails.monolingual: a particular thing always works. _ My old folk remedy for hiccups never fails.
examples: My old folk remedy for hiccups never fails.

something of sorts.monolingual: an inferior example of a kind of something. _ Well, it’s a solution of sorts, I suppose. _ It was a novel of sorts, but not what I’d ever have chosen.
examples: Well, it’s a solution of sorts, I suppose.

something of the sort.monolingual: something of the kind just mentioned. _The tree isn’t exactly a spruce tree, just something of the sort. _ Jane has a cold or something of the sort.
examples: The tree isn’t exactly a spruce tree, just something of the sort.

something or other.monolingual: something unspecified; one thing or another. _I can’t remember what Ann said—something or other. _A messenger came by and dropped off something or other at the front desk.
examples: I can’t remember what Ann said—something or other.

something’s got to give..monolingual: Emotions or tempers are strained, and there is going to be an outburst. _ Alice: There are serious problems with Mary and Tom. They fight and fight. Sue: Yes, something’s got to give. It can’t go on like this. _ Bill: Things are getting difficult at
examples: Alice: There are serious problems with Mary and Tom.

something’s up.monolingual: something is going to happen; something is going on. _Everybody looks very nervous. I think something’s up. _From the looks of all the activity around here, I think something’s up.
examples: Everybody looks very nervous.

*something to shout about.monolingual: Fig. something that causes one to show pride or enthusiasm about someone or something. (*Typically: be ~; have ~.) _ Getting into med school is really something to shout about. _She’s something to shout about.
examples: Getting into med school is really something to shout about.

something to that effect.monolingual: something like that just mentioned. _ She said she wouldn’t be available until after three, or something to that effect. _ I was told to keep out of the house—or something to that effect.
examples: She said she wouldn’t be available until after three, or something to that effect.

son of a bitch.monolingual: 1. Inf. a very horrible person. (Use with caution. Usually intended as a strong insult. Never used casually.) _ Bill called Bob a son of a bitch, and Bob punched Bill in the face. _ This guy’s a son of a bitch. He treats everybody rotten.
examples: Bill called Bob a son of a bitch, and Bob punched Bill in the face.

son of a sea biscuit.monolingual: Euph. a person, usually a male. (Sometimes a substitute for son of a bitch.) _Why, good to see you, you old son of a sea biscuit. _ You son of a sea biscuit! You make me so mad I could slug you.
examples: Why, good to see you, you old son of a sea biscuit.

*soon as possible.monolingual: at the earliest time. (*Also: as ~.) _I’m leaving now. I’ll be there as soon as possible. _Please pay me soon as possible.
examples: I’m leaving now.

sooner or later.monolingual: eventually; in the short term or in the long term. _ He’ll have to pay the bill sooner or later. _ She’ll get what she deserves sooner or later.
examples: He’ll have to pay the bill sooner or later.

sooner than you think..monolingual: an expression stating that something will happen sooner than a time expected or just mentioned. _ Sally: I’m going to have to stop pretty soon for a rest. Mary: Sooner than you think, I’d say. I think one of our tires is low. _ Tom: The stock market
examples: Sally: I’m going to have to stop pretty soon for a rest.

the sooner the better..monolingual: The sooner something [referred to] gets done, the better things will be. _ Bob: When do you need this? Mary: The sooner the better. _ Bob: Please get the oil changed in the station wagon. The sooner the better. Alice: I’ll do it today.
examples: Bob: When do you need this? Mary: The sooner the better.

sop something up†.monolingual: to mop or soak up a liquid. _ Use this rag to sop the spilled milk up. _The rag will sop up the mess a little at a time.
examples: Use this rag to sop the spilled milk up.

sorrow over someone or something.monolingual: to grieve or feel sad about someone or something. _ There is no need to sorrow over Tom. He will come back. _ He is sorrowing over the business he has lost because of the weather.
examples: There is no need to sorrow over Tom.

sort oneself out.monolingual: to pull oneself together; to figure out what to do about one’s problems. (Fig. on sort something out W.) _ I need a few days to sort myself out. _ I need some time to sort myself out.
examples: I need a few days to sort myself out.

sort something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to sort something; to arrange according to class or category. _ Let’s sort these cards out. _ Would you please sort out your socks?
examples: Let’s sort these cards out.

*sound as a bell.monolingual: in perfect condition or health; undamaged. (*Also: as ~.) _ The doctor says that the old man’s heart’s as sound as a bell. _ I thought the vase was broken when it fell, but it was sound as a bell.
examples: The doctor says that the old man’s heart’s as sound as a bell.

*sound as a dollar.monolingual: 1. Cliché very secure and dependable. (*Also: as ~.) _ This investment is as sound as a dollar. _I wouldn’t put my money in a bank that isn’t sound as a dollar.
examples: This investment is as sound as a dollar.

sound asleep.monolingual: completely asleep; in a deep sleep. _ I was sound asleep when the fire broke out.
examples: I was sound asleep when the fire broke out.

sound like a broken record.monolingual: to say the same thing over and over again. (Fig. on a scratch in a phonograph record causing the needle [or stylus] to stay in the same groove and play it over and over.) _ He’s always complaining about the way she treats him. He sounds like a broken
examples: He’s always complaining about the way she treats him.

sound off.monolingual: to speak something loudly; to call out one’s name or one’s place in a numerical sequence. _ All right, sound off, you guys! _ Each one sounded off.
examples: Each one sounded off.

sound someone out†.monolingual: to try to find out what someone thinks (about something). _I don’t know what Jane thinks about your suggestion, but I’ll sound her out. _Please sound out everyone in your department.
examples: I don’t know what Jane thinks about your suggestion, but I’ll sound her out.

sound something out†.monolingual: to pronounce the letters or syllables of a word as a means of figuring out what the word is. (Usually said to a child.) _This word is easy, Bobby. Try to sound it out.
examples: This word is easy, Bobby.

soup’s on!.monolingual: Rur. The meal is ready to eat. (Said for any food, not just soup.) _Tom: Soup’s on! Bill: The camp chef has dished up another disaster. _ John: Soup’s on! Come and get it! Mary: Well, I guess it’s time to eat again.
examples: Tom: Soup’s on! Bill: The camp chef has dished up another disaster.

soup something up†.monolingual: to increase the power of something. _ He souped his car up so it will do nearly 120 miles per hour. _ If only I could soup up this computer to run just a little faster.
examples: He souped his car up so it will do nearly 120 miles per hour.

souped up.monolingual: made more powerful. _ That souped-up car of John’s sure makes a lot of noise. _Why do all cars driven by males under the age of twenty have to be souped up?
examples: That souped-up car of John’s sure makes a lot of noise.

*sour as vinegar.monolingual: 1. [of something] very sour. (*Also: as ~.) _This milk is as sour as vinegar. _The juice they gave us is sour as vinegar.
examples: This milk is as sour as vinegar.

sour grapes.monolingual: Fig. something that one cannot have and so disparages as if it were never desirable. _ Of course you want to buy this expensive jacket. Criticizing it is just sour grapes, but you still really want it.
examples: Of course you want to buy this expensive jacket.

sow one’s wild oats.monolingual: to do wild and foolish things in one’s youth. (Often assumed to have some sort of sexual meaning.) _Jack was out sowing his wild oats last night, and he’s in jail this morning. _ Mrs. Smith told Mr. Smith that he was too old to be sowing his wild oat
examples: Jack was out sowing his wild oats last night, and he’s in jail this morning.

space out.monolingual: to become giddy or disoriented. _ Judy spaced out during the meeting and I didn’t understand a word she said. _ I have a tendency to space out at the end of a hard day.
examples: Judy spaced out during the meeting and I didn’t understand a word she said.

space someone out†.monolingual: to cause someone to become giddy. _ The circus clowns just spaced me out. _ The hilarious spectacle spaced out the entire audience.
examples: The circus clowns just spaced me out.

spade something up†.monolingual: to turn over the soil in a garden plot with a spade. _ Please go out and spade the garden up so I can plant the potatoes and onions. _I will spade up the garden when I have time.
examples: Please go out and spade the garden up so I can plant the potatoes and onions.

spar with someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to box with someone for practice. _ The champ needs someone to spar with every day. _ Ted was sparring with his brother when the phone rang and saved him from further exertion.
examples: The champ needs someone to spar with every day.

spare someone something.monolingual: to exempt someone from having to listen to or experience something. _ I’ll spare you the details and get to the point. _Please, spare me the story and tell me what you want.
examples: I’ll spare you the details and get to the point.

spare tire.monolingual: 1. a thickness in the waist; a roll of fat around one’s waist. _ I’ve got to get rid of this spare tire. _ The spare tire started when I was twenty-six.
examples: I’ve got to get rid of this spare tire.

spark something off†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to ignite something flammable or explosive. _ The lightning sparked a fire off. _ The match sparked off a raging inferno.
examples: The lightning sparked a fire off.

sparkle with something.monolingual: to glitter or twinkle because of something. _ The crystal goblets sparkled with the light from the f lickering candles. _ Her eyes sparkled with the ref lection of the candles.
examples: The crystal goblets sparkled with the light from the f lickering candles.

spatter on someone or something.monolingual: [for a liquid or something moist] to splash onto someone or something. _ When Kelly painted the hallway, a lot of paint spattered on the f loor. _ The hot fat spattered on me.
examples: When Kelly painted the hallway, a lot of paint spattered on the f loor.

spatter someone or something up†.monolingual: to get drops of a liquid or bits of something moist onto someone or something. _ The painter spattered his partner up when he dropped the paint bucket accidentally. _ The falling paint bucket spattered up the wall.
examples: The painter spattered his partner up when he dropped the paint bucket accidentally.

spatter something around†.monolingual: to scatter bits or drops of a liquid or something moist here and there. _Ted spattered paint around everywhere when he redecorated his kitchen. _ Don’t spatter around the paint.
examples: Ted spattered paint around everywhere when he redecorated his kitchen.

spaz around.monolingual: Sl. to waste time; to mess around. _You kids are always spazzing around. Why don’t you do something useful? _ We’re just spazzing around. Leave us alone.
examples: You kids are always spazzing around.

spaz down.monolingual: Sl. to relax. _ Spaz down, man! Chill out! _ We tried to get the crowd to spaz down, but they were very excited.
examples: We tried to get the crowd to spaz down, but they were very excited.

spaz out.monolingual: 1. Sl. to overreact to something; to become overly excited about something. _ I knew you would spaz out! But my grades are not that bad! _Come on, don’t spaz out!
examples: Come on, don’t spaz out! 2.

speak about someone or something.monolingual: to mention or discuss someone or something. _ And now I will speak about Abraham Lincoln. _Let us speak about what happened yesterday.
examples: And now I will speak about Abraham Lincoln.

speak against someone or something.monolingual: 1. to criticize someone or something. _Many people are speaking against the mayor. She will not be reelected. _ Please don’t speak against cats in my presence.
examples: Many people are speaking against the mayor.

speak down to someone.monolingual: to address someone in simpler terms than necessary; to speak condescendingly to someone. _ There is no need to speak down to me. I can understand anything you are likely to say. _ Sorry. Sometimes I tend to speak down to people over the telephone.
examples: There is no need to speak down to me.

speak for oneself.monolingual: to speak on one’s own behalf. _ I can speak for myself. I don’t need you to speak for me. _ Speak for yourself. What you say does not represent my thinking.
examples: I can speak for myself.

speak for someone or something.monolingual: 1. to testify or argue for someone or something. _ I would be happy to speak for you in court. Just tell me when. _ My attorney will speak for our position.
examples: I would be happy to speak for you in court.

speak from something.monolingual: to draw authority or credibility in one’s speaking from something such as knowledge or experience. _ Believe me, I speak from experience. _ Listen to her. She speaks from a lot of knowledge and training.
examples: Believe me, I speak from experience.

speak ill of someone.monolingual: to say something bad about someone. _ I refuse to speak ill of any of my friends. _ Max speaks ill of no one and refuses to repeat gossip.
examples: I refuse to speak ill of any of my friends.

speak of someone or something.monolingual: 1. to mention or discuss someone or something. _Were we speaking of Judy? I don’t recall. _ We were speaking of the new law.
examples: Were we speaking of Judy? I don’t recall.

speak off-the-cuff.monolingual: Fig. to speak without preparing a speech; to speak extemporaneously; to render a spoken opinion or estimate. (As if one’s notes had been written hastily on one’s cuff.) _She is capable of making sense and being convincing even when she speaks off-the
examples: She is capable of making sense and being convincing even when she speaks off-the-cuff.

speak one’s mind.monolingual: Fig. to say frankly what one thinks (about something). _ Please let me speak my mind, and then you can do whatever you wish. _ You can always depend on John to speak his mind. He’ll let you know what he really thinks.
examples: Please let me speak my mind, and then you can do whatever you wish.

speak out.monolingual: to speak loudly; to speak to be heard. _ Please speak out. We need to hear you. _They won’t hear you in the back row if you don’t speak out.
examples: Please speak out.

speak out of turn.monolingual: Fig. to say something unwise or imprudent; to say something at the wrong time. _Excuse me if I’m speaking out of turn, but what you are proposing is quite wrong. _ Bob was quite honest, even if he was speaking out of turn.
examples: Excuse me if I’m speaking out of turn, but what you are proposing is quite wrong.

speak someone’s language.monolingual: Fig. to say something that one agrees with or understands. _I gotcha. Now you’re speaking my language. _ Mary speaks Fred’s language. They get along fine.
examples: I gotcha. Now you’re speaking my language.

speak the same language.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for two or more people] to communicate in a shared language. _ These two people don’t speak the same language and need an interpreter.
examples: These two people don’t speak the same language and need an interpreter.

speak to someone.monolingual: to talk to someone. _ I am angry with him and I refuse to speak to him. _ Were you speaking to me?
examples: I am angry with him and I refuse to speak to him.

speak to something.monolingual: [for something] to address, indicate, or signal something. _ This event speaks to the need for good communication. _ Your present state of employment speaks to your need for a better education.
examples: This event speaks to the need for good communication.

speak up.monolingual: 1. Lit. to speak more loudly. _ They can’t hear you in the back of the room. Please speak up. _What? Speak up, please. I’m hard of hearing.
examples: They can’t hear you in the back of the room.

speak volumes.monolingual: Fig. [for something that is seen] to reveal a great deal of information. _ The unsightly yard and unpainted house speaks volumes about what kind of people live there.
examples: The unsightly yard and unpainted house speaks volumes about what kind of people live there.

speak with a forked tongue.monolingual: Fig. to tell lies; to try to deceive someone. _ Jean’s mother sounds very charming, but she speaks with a forked tongue. _People tend to believe Fred because he seems plausible, but we know he speaks with a forked tongue.
examples: Jean’s mother sounds very charming, but she speaks with a forked tongue.

speaking for oneself.monolingual: an expression indicating that one is expressing only one’s own opinion. _Speaking for myself, I am ready to cancel the contract. _ Sally is speaking for herself. She is not expressing our opinions.
examples: Speaking for myself, I am ready to cancel the contract.

specialize in something.monolingual: to limit oneself to or be specially trained to practice one particular thing. _ I specialize in tropical medicine. _ What do you specialize in?
examples: I specialize in tropical medicine.

speculate about someone or something.monolingual: to make guesses about someone or something; to hypothesize about someone or something. _I refuse to speculate about Sally. I don’t presume to guess what she will do. _ We don’t speculate about the future.
examples: I refuse to speculate about Sally.

speculate in something.monolingual: to make risky business deals in the buying and selling of something. _ Jeff made a fortune speculating in cotton. _ I do not wish to speculate in anything. It is too risky.
examples: Jeff made a fortune speculating in cotton.

speculate on something.monolingual: to make a hypothesis about something. _I really don’t want to speculate on what might happen next. _Would you care to speculate on what might happen if you quit your job?
examples: I really don’t want to speculate on what might happen next.

speed someone or something up†.monolingual: to cause someone or something to move faster. _We tried to speed him up, but he is just a very slow person. _We sped up the process, but it still took too long.
examples: We tried to speed him up, but he is just a very slow person.

speed up.monolingual: to go faster. _ Please speed up. We are late.
examples: Please speed up.

*speeds of some amount.monolingual: a variety of speeds (of movement) of a certain level. (*Typically: clock someone at ~; have ~; hit ~; reach ~.) _The cops clocked him at speeds of up to one hundred miles per hour.
examples: The cops clocked him at speeds of up to one hundred miles per hour.

spell disaster.monolingual: Fig. to indicate or predict disaster. _What a horrible plan! It would spell disaster for all of us!

spell someone down†.monolingual: to win over someone in a spelling match. _ Frank spelled everyone else down and won the spelling bee. _ He spelled down almost everyone.
examples: Frank spelled everyone else down and won the spelling bee.

spell something for someone.monolingual: to spell a word or name for someone’s benefit. _ I don’t recognize that word. Would you please spell it for me? _It is a difficult name. I will have to spell it for you.
examples: I don’t recognize that word.

spell something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to spell something (with letters). _I can’t understand your name. Can you spell it out? _ Please spell out all the strange words so I can write them down correctly.
examples: I can’t understand your name.

spell trouble.monolingual: to signify future trouble; to mean trouble. _This letter that came today spells trouble. _The sky looks angry and dark. That spells trouble.
examples: This letter that came today spells trouble.

spend something for something.monolingual: to pay out an amount of money for something. _I spent nearly forty dollars for that vase! _ How much did you spend for this house—if I may ask?

spend time in something.monolingual: to stay in something or some place for a period of time. _I spent time in Barbados when I was younger. _ I am afraid that you will have to spend some time in the hospital until the infection is cleared up.
examples: I spent time in Barbados when I was younger.

spending money.monolingual: cash, as opposed to money in the bank. _I’m a little short of spending money at the present. Could I borrow ten dollars? _ I don’t have any spending money either.
examples: I’m a little short of spending money at the present.

spew something out†.monolingual: to have something gush forth. _The faucet spewed a little yellowish water out and stopped altogether. _ The faucet spewed out some yellowish water.
examples: The faucet spewed a little yellowish water out and stopped altogether.

spew something up†.monolingual: to gush something upward. _ The geyser spewed hot water and steam up every hour on the hour. _The fountain spewed up a thin stream of cool, clear water.
examples: The geyser spewed hot water and steam up every hour on the hour.

spice something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to make some food or drink more spicy. _Judy spiced the cider up by adding cinnamon and nutmeg. _ She spiced up the chili too much.
examples: Judy spiced the cider up by adding cinnamon and nutmeg.

spiel something off†.monolingual: to recite a list of things very rapidly; to recite something very rapidly. _I used to be able to spiel the names of the presidents off. _Liz spieled off her gift list to the clerk.
examples: I used to be able to spiel the names of the presidents off.

spiff something up†.monolingual: to polish and groom something very well; to make something clean and tidy. _ See if you can spiff this place up a little. _ I will spiff up the room a little.
examples: See if you can spiff this place up a little.

spiffed out.monolingual: Sl. to be dressed in one’s finest clothes and well-groomed. _He got himself all spiffed out for the wedding reception. _ Man, are you ever spiffed out!
examples: He got himself all spiffed out for the wedding reception.

spiffed up.monolingual: dressed up, groomed, and polished up nicely; clean and tidy. _ See if you can get yourself a little spiffed up before we go out to dinner. We wouldn’t want the Wilmington-Thorpes to think you only have one suit. _The house doesn’t have to be too spif
examples: See if you can get yourself a little spiffed up before we go out to dinner.

spill one’s guts.monolingual: Sl. to tell all; to confess. _I had to spill my guts about the broken window. I didn’t want you to take the blame. _Mary spilled her guts about the window. She confessed that she was trying to shield Bob.
examples: I had to spill my guts about the broken window.

spill over.monolingual: 1. [for a container] to overflow. _ I hope your bucket of water doesn’t spill over. _ The milk glass spilled over because it was filled too full.
examples: I hope your bucket of water doesn’t spill over.

spin a yarn.monolingual: Fig. to tell a tale. _ Grandpa spun an unbelievable yarn for us. _ My uncle is always spinning yarns about his childhood.
examples: Grandpa spun an unbelievable yarn for us.

spin around.monolingual: 1. to turn around to face a different direction. _ Jill spun around to face her accuser. _ Todd spun around in his chair so he could see who was talking to him.
examples: Jill spun around to face her accuser.

spin doctor.monolingual: someone who gives a twisted or deviously deceptive version of an event. (Usually in the context of manipulating the news for political reasons.) _ Things were going bad for the candidate, so he got himself a new spin doctor. _A good spin doctor could
examples: Things were going bad for the candidate, so he got himself a new spin doctor.

spin off.monolingual: [for something] to part and fly away from something that is spinning; [for something] to detach or break loose from something. _ The blade of the lawn mower spun off, but fortunately no one was injured. _The rustedon nut spun off easily after I got i
examples: The blade of the lawn mower spun off, but fortunately no one was injured.

spin one’s wheels.monolingual: to waste time; to remain in a neutral position, neither advancing nor falling back. (Fig. on a car that is running but is not moving because its wheels are spinning in mud, etc.) _ I’m just spinning my wheels in this job. I need more training to get
examples: I’m just spinning my wheels in this job.

spin out.monolingual: [for a vehicle] to go out of control, spinning. _ You nearly spun out on that last turn! _Cars were spinning out all over the highway when the ice storm hit.
examples: Cars were spinning out all over the highway when the ice storm hit.

spin something off†.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something rotating] to release a part that flies away. _ The propeller spun one of its blades off and then fell apart all together. _ It spun off one of its blades.
examples: The propeller spun one of its blades off and then fell apart all together.

spiral down.monolingual: to descend in a spiral path. _ The ancient trail spiraled down the mountain peak. _ A path spiraled down and at the bottom was a small refreshment stand.
examples: The ancient trail spiraled down the mountain peak.

spiral up.monolingual: to ascend in a spiral path. _ The smoke spiraled up to the sky. _ The trail spiraled up the slope to the top.
examples: The smoke spiraled up to the sky.

spit and polish.monolingual: orderliness; ceremonial precision and orderliness. _ I like spit and polish. It comes from being in the military. _ There is no such thing as too much spit and polish.
examples: I like spit and polish.

spit at someone or something.monolingual: to expectorate on someone or something or in the direction of someone or something. _The angry crowd cursed and spit at the prisoner as he was being taken back to jail. _ Max actually spit at the police station door as he was dragged in.
examples: The angry crowd cursed and spit at the prisoner as he was being taken back to jail.

spit something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to cast something from the mouth. _ The food was so terrible that I spit it out. _ I spit out the sweet potatoes.
examples: The food was so terrible that I spit it out.

spit something up†.monolingual: Euph. to vomit something. _She almost spit her dinner up. _ Sally was afraid she was going to spit up her dinner.
examples: She almost spit her dinner up.

spit up.monolingual: Euph. to vomit. _ The food was so bad, she was afraid she would spit up. _ Mommy, I have to spit up!
examples: The food was so bad, she was afraid she would spit up.

splash down.monolingual: [for a space capsule] to land in the water. _ The capsule splashed down very close to the pickup ship.
examples: The capsule splashed down very close to the pickup ship.

splash on someone or something.monolingual: to scatter [a liquid] on someone or something. _ Try to keep from splashing on anybody. _ Don’t splash on the wall!
examples: Try to keep from splashing on anybody.

splash over.monolingual: [for a volume of liquid] to overflow its container. _ A lot of the coffee splashed over before I got to the table with the cup. _ Don’t fill it so full and it won’t splash over.
examples: A lot of the coffee splashed over before I got to the table with the cup.

splash someone or something up†.monolingual: to scatter a liquid onto someone or something. _ Don’t get that stuff all over. Don’t splash the place up! _ She splashed up the kitchen when she washed the dishes.
examples: Don’t get that stuff all over.

splash something about.monolingual: to scatter or slosh a liquid about. _ Please don’t splash that about. It will stain anything you spill it on. _ Don’t splash that stuff about!
examples: Please don’t splash that about.

splatter someone or something up†.monolingual: to cover someone or something with drops of a liquid. _The painter splattered his coworker up with both red and blue. _Don’t splatter up the wall!
examples: The painter splattered his coworker up with both red and blue.

splay out.monolingual: to spread out; to extend out at an angle. _ His feet splayed out so much that it was hard to see how he could stand up. _ The legs of the table splayed out and gave it sturdy support.
examples: His feet splayed out so much that it was hard to see how he could stand up.

splice something together†.monolingual: to connect things together, usually by twisting or tying a joint between the two. _ I spent over an hour splicing the two ends of the ropes together, and it didn’t hold for even a minute. _ He carefully spliced together the two ropes.
examples: I spent over an hour splicing the two ends of the ropes together, and it didn’t hold for even a minute.

split hairs.monolingual: Fig. to quibble; to try to make petty distinctions. _ They don’t have any serious differences. They are just splitting hairs. _ Don’t waste time splitting hairs. Accept it the way it is.
examples: They don’t have any serious differences.

split in something.monolingual: to divide into a certain number of groups. (The something can be half, thirds, two, quarters, etc.) _ Lightning struck the big tree and the trunk split in half. _ The vase dropped and split in quarters.
examples: Lightning struck the big tree and the trunk split in half.

split people up†.monolingual: to separate two or more people (from one another). _ If you two don’t stop chattering, I’ll have to split you up. _I will have to split up that twosome in the corner.
examples: If you two don’t stop chattering, I’ll have to split you up.

*a split second.monolingual: an instant; a tiny period of time. (*Typically: for ~; in ~.) _The lightning struck, and in a split second the house burst into f lames. _ For a split second, it looked like she would fall.
examples: The lightning struck, and in a split second the house burst into f lames.

split something into something.monolingual: to divide or sever something into something. _Jeff split the log into four parts. _Please split this log in half so it will burn better.
examples: Jeff split the log into four parts.

split the difference.monolingual: to divide the difference evenly (with someone else). _ You want to sell for $120, and I want to buy for $100. Let’s split the difference and close the deal at $110. _ I don’t want to split the difference. I want $120.
examples: You want to sell for $120, and I want to buy for $100.

a splitting headache.monolingual: Fig. a severe headache, as if one’s head were splitting open. _I’m sorry, I can’t. I have a splitting headache. Maybe Fred will play bridge with you. _This splitting headache has been going on for hours.
examples: I’m sorry, I can’t.

splurge on someone or something.monolingual: to spend a lot of money on someone or something. _ I really splurged on my wife for her birthday. _ Mary really splurged on that dinner!
examples: I really splurged on my wife for her birthday.

spoiled rotten.monolingual: Fig. indulged in; greatly spoiled. _ This kid is spoiled rotten! _ I was spoiled rotten when I was a child, so I’m used to this kind of wasteful luxury.
examples: I was spoiled rotten when I was a child, so I’m used to this kind of wasteful luxury.

spoiling for a fight.monolingual: argumentative; asking for a fight. _ They were just spoiling for a fight, and they went outside to settle the matter. _ She was grouchy, and you could tell she had been spoiling for a fight all day.
examples: They were just spoiling for a fight, and they went outside to settle the matter.

spoken for.monolingual: taken; reserved (for someone). _ I’m sorry, but this piece of cake is already spoken for. _ Pardon me. Can I sit here, or is this seat spoken for?
examples: I’m sorry, but this piece of cake is already spoken for.

sponge someone or something down†.monolingual: to remove the [excess] moisture from someone or something; to wipe someone or something with a sponge. _ The fight manager sponged his boxer down. _ I will sponge down the countertop.
examples: The fight manager sponged his boxer down.

sponge something away†.monolingual: to absorb, wipe up, and wipe away something, as with a sponge. _ Try sponging the stain away with some soda water. _ I will sponge away the mess.
examples: Try sponging the stain away with some soda water.

sponge something from someone.monolingual: to beg or borrow money or food from someone. _Gary tried to sponge a few bucks from me. _ I can’t continue sponging food from my relatives.
examples: Gary tried to sponge a few bucks from me.

sponge something from something.monolingual: to remove moisture from something, as with a sponge. _Liz sponged the sauce from her blouse. _ We gently sponged the splattered paint from the carpet.
examples: Liz sponged the sauce from her blouse.

sponge something up†.monolingual: to absorb or take up moisture, as with a sponge. _ I had to sponge the spilled milk up from the f loor, the chair, the table, and the baby. What a mess! _ Liz sponged up the water.
examples: I had to sponge the spilled milk up from the f loor, the chair, the table, and the baby.

spook someone or something.monolingual: to startle or disorient someone or something. _ A snake spooked my horse, and I nearly fell off. _Your warning spooked me, and I was upset for the rest of the day.
examples: A snake spooked my horse, and I nearly fell off.

spoon something out†.monolingual: to serve something out, as with a spoon; to give something out, as with a spoon. _The cook spooned the beans out, giving plenty to each camper. _The cook spooned out the beans.
examples: The cook spooned the beans out, giving plenty to each camper.

spoon something up†.monolingual: to serve something that requires finding and bringing up out of a pot with a spoon. _The cook spooned the hard-cooked eggs up one by one. _ The cook spooned up chunks of meat from the stew.
examples: The cook spooned the hard-cooked eggs up one by one.

spoon-feed someone.monolingual: Fig. to treat someone with too much care or help; to teach someone with methods that are too easy and do not stimulate the learner to independent thinking. _ The teacher spoon-feeds the students by dictating notes on the novel instead of getting the
examples: The teacher spoon-feeds the students by dictating notes on the novel instead of getting the children to read the books.

the sport of kings.monolingual: horse racing. _ The sport of kings has sure impoverished a lot of commoners.
examples: The sport of kings has sure impoverished a lot of commoners.

sport with someone or something.monolingual: to tease or play with someone or something. _ What a tease you are! You are just sporting with me! _ The dog was sporting with a turtle down by the stream.
examples: The dog was sporting with a turtle down by the stream.

a sporting chance.monolingual: a reasonably good chance. _ If you hurry, you have a sporting chance of catching the bus. _ The firm has only a sporting chance of getting the export order.
examples: If you hurry, you have a sporting chance of catching the bus.

spot someone as something.monolingual: to recognize someone to be something; to realize that someone is something. _I spotted you as a troublemaker from the very beginning. _ The guard spotted Max as a potential thief the moment he saw him.
examples: I spotted you as a troublemaker from the very beginning.

spout from something.monolingual: [for a liquid] to gush from something. _A plume of water vapor spouted from the blowhole of the whale. _Water spouted from the top of the fountain and flowed down the sides.
examples: A plume of water vapor spouted from the blowhole of the whale.

spout something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to exude a liquid. _ The hose spouted the cooling water out all over the children. _ It spouted out cooling water.
examples: The hose spouted the cooling water out all over the children.

sprain one’s ankle.monolingual: to become pregnant. _ She has, ah, sprained her ankle. _ From the looks of her, she must have sprained her ankle some months ago.
examples: She has, ah, sprained her ankle.

sprawl out.monolingual: to spread oneself out casually while lounging. (Usually done one time, not habitually. Compare this with sprawl about.) _He sprawled out and took up most of the space. _ I need more room so I can sprawl out.
examples: He sprawled out and took up most of the space.

spread like wildfire.monolingual: Fig. [for something] to spread rapidly. _ Rumors spread like wildfire when people are excited. _This disease will spread like wildfire when it gets going.
examples: Rumors spread like wildfire when people are excited.

spread oneself too thin.monolingual: Fig. to do so many things at one time that you can do none of them well. _It’s a good idea to get involved in a lot of activities, but don’t spread yourself too thin. _ I’m too busy these days. I’m afraid I’ve spread myself too thin.
examples: It’s a good idea to get involved in a lot of activities, but don’t spread yourself too thin.

spread out.monolingual: to separate and distribute over a wide area. _ The sheriff told the members of the posse to spread out and continue their search. _The wine spread out and stained a large area of the carpet.
examples: The sheriff told the members of the posse to spread out and continue their search.

spread over someone or something†.monolingual: [for something] to cover someone or something gradually. _ The shade slowly spread over the picnickers. _ Dusk spread its final shadows over the land.
examples: The shade slowly spread over the picnickers.

spread someone or something around†.monolingual: to distribute people or things over an area. _ Spread the good singers around so they can help the others in the choir. _Liz spread around the seeds so they would dry.
examples: Spread the good singers around so they can help the others in the choir.

spread something around†.monolingual: to distribute news or gossip. _ Please don’t spread this around, but Don ran away from home! _ Don’t spread around that story!

spread something on thick.monolingual: to distribute a thick layer of something. _ This paint will cover well if you spread it on thick. _ If you spread the paint on thick, you will only need one coat.
examples: This paint will cover well if you spread it on thick.

spread something out†.monolingual: to open, unfold, or lay something over a wider area. _ Spread the wet papers out so they will dry. _ She spread out the papers to dry them.
examples: Spread the wet papers out so they will dry.

spread something with something.monolingual: to cover something with a coat of something. _ Using the roller, Judy spread the wall with a thick coat of pink paint. _ Spread the lasagna with a layer of cheese mixture and cover that with another layer of lasagna.
examples: Using the roller, Judy spread the wall with a thick coat of pink paint.

spread the word.monolingual: to tell many people some kind of information. _I need to spread the word that the meeting is canceled for this afternoon.
examples: I need to spread the word that the meeting is canceled for this afternoon.

spread to someone or something.monolingual: to expand or extend to reach someone or something. _ The epidemic finally spread to me and my family. _ The business slowdown spread to the West Coast.
examples: The epidemic finally spread to me and my family.

spring at someone or something.monolingual: to jump at someone or something. _ The cat sprang at me but could not sink in its claws. _ The spider sprang at the moth and captured it.
examples: The cat sprang at me but could not sink in its claws.

spring into action.monolingual: Fig. to suddenly begin moving or doing something. _ As soon as the boss came in the door, everyone sprang into action. _ Every morning, I jump out of bed and spring into action.
examples: As soon as the boss came in the door, everyone sprang into action.

spring out at someone.monolingual: to jump out at someone. _A grasshopper sprang out at me when I peered into the hollow log. _ I was afraid that something would spring out at me, so I opened the cellar door carefully.
examples: A grasshopper sprang out at me when I peered into the hollow log.

spring out of something.monolingual: to jump out of something. _The cat sprang out of the closet when I opened the door. _ The boys sprang out of the cold water as fast as they could.
examples: The cat sprang out of the closet when I opened the door.

spring something on someone.monolingual: 1. to surprise someone with something. _ I hate to spring this on you at the last moment, but I will need some money to travel on. _ Please don’t spring any other demands on me.
examples: I hate to spring this on you at the last moment, but I will need some money to travel on.

spring to attention.monolingual: to move quickly to assume the military posture of attention. _ The recruit sprang to attention.
examples: The recruit sprang to attention.

spring to life.monolingual: Fig. to become suddenly alive or more alive. _The party sprang to life after midnight. _The city sprang to life at dawn.
examples: The party sprang to life after midnight.

spring to one’s feet.monolingual: Fig. to stand up quickly. _He sprang to his feet and demanded that the chair recognize him. _ The audience sprang to its feet and cheered madly when the soprano finished.
examples: He sprang to his feet and demanded that the chair recognize him.

spring to someone’s defense.monolingual: Fig. to go quickly to defend someone. (Can be against physical or verbal attack.) _ Fred was attacked and Ralph sprang to his defense. _ We sprang to Mary’s defense when she was accused of doing wrong.
examples: Fred was attacked and Ralph sprang to his defense.

spring up.monolingual: to appear or develop suddenly; to sprout, as with a seedling. _ We knew it was really spring when all the f lowers sprang up. _It seems as if the tulips sprang up overnight. _ The dog’s ears sprang up when the refrigerator opened.
examples: We knew it was really spring when all the f lowers sprang up.

sprout up.monolingual: to grow upward quickly, as do newly sprouted seedlings. _ The seeds sprouted up in the warm rains. _ Many of the newly planted seeds failed to sprout up on time.
examples: The seeds sprouted up in the warm rains.

sprout wings.monolingual: Fig. to behave so well as to resemble an angel. _ The kid is not about to sprout wings, but he probably won’t get into jail again. _ He was so good and helpful, I thought he would sprout wings.
examples: The kid is not about to sprout wings, but he probably won’t get into jail again.

spruce someone or something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to tidy up and groom someone or something. _ Laura’s mother took a few minutes to spruce her daughter up for the party. _ She spruced up her room each day.
examples: Laura’s mother took a few minutes to spruce her daughter up for the party.

spur someone on†.monolingual: to urge someone onward; to egg someone on. (Fig. on applying spurs to a horse.) _ The crowd spurred the runners on throughout the race. _ The cheering spurred on the runners.
examples: The crowd spurred the runners on throughout the race.

spurt something out†.monolingual: to eject something in a stream. _The octopus spurted its ink out as the scuba diver approached it. _ It spurted out all its ink.
examples: The octopus spurted its ink out as the scuba diver approached it.

sputter out.monolingual: [for a flame] to go out in little puffs. _ The candle f lame f lickered and sputtered out. _ The fire sputtered out after midnight and we all got very cold before down.
examples: The candle f lame f lickered and sputtered out.

sputter something out†.monolingual: to utter something while stuttering or faltering. (As when one is physically or mentally disoriented.) _She was so excited she could hardly sputter her name out. _ He could only sputter out a few words.
examples: She was so excited she could hardly sputter her name out.
