squabble about someone or something.monolingual: to quarrel and disagree about someone or something. _ Please stop squabbling about Jeff, or I’ll put him on my team so neither of you can have him. _ There is no need to squabble about the last piece of pie. There’s more in the kitchen.
examples: Please stop squabbling about Jeff, or I’ll put him on my team so neither of you can have him.

squabble over someone or something.monolingual: to fight over someone or something. _Please don’t squabble over me. I don’t want to be chosen by any of you! _ Stop squabbling over money and go out and get a job.
examples: Please don’t squabble over me.

squabble with someone.monolingual: to argue with someone. _Please don’t squabble with your sister! _ I wish that everyone would stop squabbling with me!

squabble with something.monolingual: to argue about something. _ I won’t squabble with what you said, but you are wrong. _ One political party will squabble with any issue the other party brings up.
examples: I won’t squabble with what you said, but you are wrong.

squander something away†.monolingual: to waste something; to use up something valuable wastefully. _ Where is all the money I gave you last month? Did you squander it all away? _ Frank squandered away all his assets.
examples: Frank squandered away all his assets.

a square deal.monolingual: a fair and honest transaction; fair treatment. _All the workers want is a square deal, but their boss underpays them. _ You always get a square deal with that travel company.
examples: All the workers want is a square deal, but their boss underpays them.

square someone away†.monolingual: to get someone or something arranged or properly taken care of. _See if you can square Bob away in his new office. _When you are squared away, come back and we’ll talk.
examples: See if you can square Bob away in his new office.

square something off†.monolingual: to make something square; to trim something until it is square. _You will have to square this corner off a bit so it will match the part it will be attached to. _ Please square off this corner.
examples: You will have to square this corner off a bit so it will match the part it will be attached to.

square something up†.monolingual: to cause something to have right angles. _Please square the door frames up better before you nail them in. _ Can you square up this box a little better?
examples: Please square the door frames up better before you nail them in.

square something with someone.monolingual: to make certain that something is approved by a particular person. _I am sure I can square this matter with Sally. _ Sam intended to square everything with Henry when he had time.
examples: I am sure I can square this matter with Sally.

square up with someone.monolingual: to pay someone what one owes; to pay one’s share of something to someone. _ I’ll square up with you later if you pay the whole bill now. _ Bob said he would square up with Tom for his share of the gas.
examples: I’ll square up with you later if you pay the whole bill now.

square with someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to settle a disagreement with someone. _ I will try to square with Fred before the end of the school year. _Max refused to square with Lefty and they are still feuding.
examples: I will try to square with Fred before the end of the school year.

square with something.monolingual: Fig. [for a statement] to agree, match, or correspond to something. _Your answer doesn’t square with mine. _ The figures I have don’t square with those the government has.
examples: Your answer doesn’t square with mine.

squared away.monolingual: arranged or properly taken care of. _ Is Ann squared away in her dorm room yet? _ I will talk to you when I am squared away.
examples: I will talk to you when I am squared away.

squash someone or something up†.monolingual: to grind someone or something up; to mash someone or something up. _ You had better stay out of the traffic, or some big truck will squash you up! _ The truck squashed up the tiny car.
examples: The truck squashed up the tiny car.

squash something down†.monolingual: to crush something down; to pack something down. _Squash the ice cream down so the air will be pushed out. _ Who squashed down my hat?
examples: Squash the ice cream down so the air will be pushed out.

squawk about something.monolingual: to complain about something. _ Stop squawking about how much money you lost. I lost twice as much. _ What are you squawking about now?
examples: Stop squawking about how much money you lost.

squeak something through.monolingual: Fig. to manage just to get something accepted or approved. _ I just managed to squeak the proposal through. _ Tom squeaked the application through at the last minute.
examples: I just managed to squeak the proposal through.

squeal with something.monolingual: Fig. to shriek or squeak, exhibiting some characteristic emotion or experience, such as delight, pain, glee, etc. _ The baby saw the bright picture and squealed with delight. _ Timmy squealed with excitement when he saw the presents and the birthday
examples: The baby saw the bright picture and squealed with delight.

squeeze someone or something together.monolingual: to press people or things together. _The driver squeezed us together so he could get more people in the taxi. _ See if you can squeeze the vegetables together a little so we can get more in the basket.
examples: The driver squeezed us together so he could get more people in the taxi.

squeeze someone or something up†.monolingual: to press people or things close together. _ The usher tried to squeeze us up so she could seat more people. _ Don’t squeeze up the cars too tight in the parking area.
examples: The usher tried to squeeze us up so she could seat more people.

squeeze something from something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to press something out of something; to press on something until something comes out. _ Betty squeezed some toothpaste from the tube. _ Don’t squeeze so much mustard from the bottle.
examples: Betty squeezed some toothpaste from the tube.

squeeze through something.monolingual: to manage to press oneself through an opening. _ I think I can squeeze through the window and get out of this place. _ The cat squeezed through a hole in the fence and got away.
examples: I think I can squeeze through the window and get out of this place.

squiff out.monolingual: Sl. to collapse from drink. _Hank squiffed out at midnight, right on the dot. _She kept from squiffing out and barely made it home.
examples: Hank squiffed out at midnight, right on the dot.

squint at someone or something.monolingual: to look at someone or something with the eyes partly closed. (When squinting, the eyes are partly closed by pressing the upper and lower eyelids toward one another.) _ Why are you squinting at me? _ I had to squint at the small print in order to read
examples: I had to squint at the small print in order to read it.

squint out of something.monolingual: 1. to cast one’s gaze from something, such as a place of concealment, with one’s eyes partly closed. _The prisoner squinted out of the little hatch in the door to his cell. _You could see that many people were squinting out of the windows, trying to
examples: The prisoner squinted out of the little hatch in the door to his cell.

squirm with something.monolingual: to fidget or move around restlessly, showing irritation of some type. _The children squirmed with impatience, but they kept quiet. _I squirmed with discomfort, hoping that the time on the aircraft would pass rapidly.
examples: The children squirmed with impatience, but they kept quiet.

squirrel something away†.monolingual: Fig. to hide something or store something in the way that a squirrel stores nuts for use in the winter. _ I squirreled a little money away for an occasion such as this. _Liz squirreled away a lot of money while she was working.
examples: I squirreled a little money away for an occasion such as this.

squirt from something.monolingual: [for a liquid] to be ejected in a spurt from something. _ The water squirted from the hose. _ Juice squirted from the orange when I squeezed it.
examples: The water squirted from the hose.

stab at someone or something.monolingual: to thrust at someone or something with something sharp, such as a knife. _ The horrid man stabbed at me and missed. _ The stork stabbed at the frog with its beak.
examples: The horrid man stabbed at me and missed.

stab someone in something.monolingual: to stab someone in a particular place. _ Max stabbed a prison guard in the belly and left him to die. _Tom stabbed himself in the thigh by accident.
examples: Max stabbed a prison guard in the belly and left him to die.

stab someone in the back.monolingual: 1. Lit. to thrust a knife into someone’s back. _ Max planned to stab his hostage in the back if he screamed. _ The murderer stabbed his victim in the back and f led.
examples: Max planned to stab his hostage in the back if he screamed.

stack something up†.monolingual: to make a stack of things. (Also without the up.) _Where should I stack them up? _Please stack up these boxes.
examples: Please stack up these boxes.

stack up.monolingual: [for something] to accumulate, as in stacks. _ Your work is stacking up. You will have to work late to finish it. _I hate to let my work stack up. I have to do it sooner or later.
examples: Your work is stacking up.

stagger around.monolingual: to go about tottering or wobbling, especially as if drunk. _ The wounded man staggered around and then fell. _ A lot of people came out of the party and staggered around.
examples: The wounded man staggered around and then fell.

stagger from something.monolingual: to move out of a place, tottering. _The drunk staggered from the tavern and fell into the gutter. _The wounded man staggered from the door and called for help.
examples: The drunk staggered from the tavern and fell into the gutter.

stagger under something.monolingual: to struggle or totter under a serious burden, either a heavy object or a serious problem or responsibility. _The welfare budget is staggering under the burden of having to care for many people. _Sam staggered under the heavy load and finally fell.
examples: The welfare budget is staggering under the burden of having to care for many people.

stain something with something.monolingual: 1. to cause a blemish or blotch on something with something. (Usually an accident.) _ Judy stained the carpet with some grape juice. _ You will stain your clothing with that food if you drop any of it.
examples: Judy stained the carpet with some grape juice.

stake someone or something out†.monolingual: 1. to position a person so that someone or something can be observed or followed. _ The cops staked the car out and made the arrest. _Barlowe staked out the apartment building and watched patiently for an hour.
examples: The cops staked the car out and made the arrest.

stake someone to something.monolingual: to make a loan of something to someone. _ I will stake you to a hundred bucks if that will help. _ Jed refused to stake Tex to a loan.
examples: I will stake you to a hundred bucks if that will help.

stake something off†.monolingual: to mark out the boundaries of an area of land with stakes. _ The prospectors staked an area off for themselves. _ The prospectors staked off an area in which they would look for gold.
examples: The prospectors staked an area off for themselves.

stalk out of some place.monolingual: to stride out of a place indignantly. _Jeff stalked out of the store and went straight to the police. _ Mary got angry and stalked out of the meeting.
examples: Jeff stalked out of the store and went straight to the police.

stall for time.monolingual: to cause a delay intentionally. _You are just stalling for time. Please hurry. _ She is stalling for time, hoping someone will rescue her.
examples: You are just stalling for time.

stall someone or something off†.monolingual: to put off or delay someone or something. _The sheriff is at the door. I’ll stall him off while you get out the back door. _ You can stall off the sheriff, but you can’t stall off justice.
examples: The sheriff is at the door.

stammer something out†.monolingual: to manage to say something, but only haltingly. _ Fred stammered the words out haltingly. _ He stammered out the name of the winner.
examples: Fred stammered the words out haltingly.

stamp a fire out†.monolingual: to extinguish a fire by stamping on it. _ Quick, stamp that fire out before it spreads. _ Tom stamped out the sparks before they started a fire.
examples: Quick, stamp that fire out before it spreads.

stamp on someone or something.monolingual: to strike down hard on someone or something with the bottom of the foot. _The attacker stamped on his victim after he had knocked him down. _ Walter stamped on a spider.
examples: The attacker stamped on his victim after he had knocked him down.

stamp someone out†.monolingual: Sl. to get rid of or kill someone. (Fig. on stamp something out.) _You just can’t stamp somebody out on your own! _ The victim wanted to stamp out the robbers without a trial.
examples: The victim wanted to stamp out the robbers without a trial.

stamp something onto something.monolingual: to affix an informative label onto something, as with a rubber stamp. _ She stamped her name and address onto all her books. _ Tom stamped his identification onto all his papers and books.
examples: She stamped her name and address onto all her books.

stampede out of some place.monolingual: [for a crowd of people or other creatures] to move rapidly out of a place, as if in panic. _ The patrons stampeded out of the smoky theater. _ The cattle stampeded out of the corral.
examples: The patrons stampeded out of the smoky theater.

stand and deliver.monolingual: to give up something to someone who demands it. (Originally used by highway robbers asking for passengers’ valuables.) _ And when the tax agent says “Stand and deliver” you have to be prepared to pay what is demanded. _The robber stopped the coach an
examples: And when the tax agent says “Stand and deliver” you have to be prepared to pay what is demanded.

stand around.monolingual: to wait around, standing; to loiter. _Please don’t stand around. Get busy! _ Why are all these people standing around doing nothing?
examples: Please don’t stand around.

stand aside.monolingual: 1. Lit. to step aside; to get out of the way. _ Please stand aside while the bridal party passes by. _ The guests stood aside while the bride and groom left.
examples: Please stand aside while the bridal party passes by.

stand at something.monolingual: 1. to stand in front of something; to stand in the vicinity of something. _ I stood at the window, watching the traffic. _ Tom stood at the door, counting people as they came in.
examples: I stood at the window, watching the traffic.

stand by.monolingual: to wait and remain ready. (Generally heard in communication, such as broadcasting, telephones, etc.) _ Your transatlantic telephone call is almost ready. Please stand by. _ Is everyone ready for the telecast? Only ten seconds— stand by.
examples: Your transatlantic telephone call is almost ready.

stand by someone.monolingual: to support someone; to continue supporting someone even when things are bad. _ Don’t worry. I’ll stand by you no matter what. _ I feel as though I have to stand by my brother even if he goes to jail.
examples: Don’t worry. I’ll stand by you no matter what.

stand by someone or something.monolingual: to stand next to someone or something. _ Jeff, please stand by Judy. I want to take your picture. _ Can I stand by the window and watch the birds?
examples: Jeff, please stand by Judy.

stand corrected.monolingual: to admit that one has been wrong. _ I realize that I accused him wrongly. I stand corrected. _ We appreciate now that our conclusions were wrong. We stand corrected.
examples: I realize that I accused him wrongly.

stand down.monolingual: 1. to step down, particularly from the witness stand in a courtroom. _ The bailiff told the witness to stand down. _ Please stand down and take your seat.
examples: The bailiff told the witness to stand down.

stand for something.monolingual: 1. to permit something; to endure something. _ The teacher won’t stand for any whispering in class. _We just can’t stand for that kind of behavior.
examples: The teacher won’t stand for any whispering in class.

stand off some place.monolingual: [for a ship] to wait some distance from a point on shore. _ The ship stood off at some distance, waiting for its berth. _We stood off about a mile from shore and went to land in small boats called tenders.
examples: The ship stood off at some distance, waiting for its berth.

stand on ceremony.monolingual: to hold rigidly to protocol or formal manners. (Often in the negative.) _Please help yourself to more. Don’t stand on ceremony. _We are very informal around here. Hardly anyone stands on ceremony.
examples: Please help yourself to more.

stand on one’s dignity.monolingual: to remain dignified in spite of difficulties. _ I will stand on my dignity to the very end. _ She stood on her dignity and ignored all the nonsense going on around her.
examples: I will stand on my dignity to the very end.

stand on one’s head.monolingual: 1. Lit. to stand or balance vertically with one’s head and hands—rather than one’s feet— touching the floor. _Can you stand on your head? _Todd stood on his head as a form of exercise.
examples: Todd stood on his head as a form of exercise.

stand on something.monolingual: 1. to step or tread on something, perhaps by accident. _I didn’t mean to stand on the cat’s tail. _ Please don’t stand on the nice carpet with muddy shoes.
examples: I didn’t mean to stand on the cat’s tail.

stand over someone or something.monolingual: to hover over someone or something; to monitor or keep close watch on someone or something. _ Please don’t stand over me while I work! _ Dave stood over the machine, making sure it did what it was supposed to do.
examples: Dave stood over the machine, making sure it did what it was supposed to do.

stand someone in good stead.monolingual: [for something] to be of great use and benefit to someone. _ I know that my large vocabulary will always stand me in good stead at college. _ Any experience you can get in dealing with the public will stand you in good stead no matter what line of wo
examples: I know that my large vocabulary will always stand me in good stead at college.

stand someone or something off.monolingual: to repel the attack of someone or something; to defend against someone or something; to stave someone or something off. _ It was all we could do to stand them off. _ The soldiers stood off the attackers as long as they could.
examples: It was all we could do to stand them off.

stand someone to a treat.monolingual: to pay for a treat for someone. _Come on. Let’s go out and eat. I’ll stand you to a treat. _ It seems as if I am always standing someone to a treat.
examples: Come on. Let’s go out and eat.

stand someone up†.monolingual: 1. to place someone into a standing position. _I tried to stand him up, but he was just too tired. _Let’s try to stand up Timmy and get him awake.
examples: I tried to stand him up, but he was just too tired.

stand something on its head.monolingual: Fig. to stir up, baffle, or surprise a group or organization. _The new owners came into the company and stood it on its head. Nothing will ever be the same. _The mayor set out to stand the town on its head, but after one month, it was business as usu
examples: The new owners came into the company and stood it on its head.

stand tall.monolingual: to be brave and proud. _ I can still stand tall. I’m innocent. _ Our athletes stand tall in the knowledge that they did their best.
examples: I can still stand tall.

stand the test of time.monolingual: Prov. to be well regarded; to last for a long time. _Bill and Nancy just celebrated their fiftieth wedding anniversary. Their marriage has stood the test of time. _The singer’s work was not popular while she was alive, but it has stood the test of ti
examples: Bill and Nancy just celebrated their fiftieth wedding anniversary.

stand to lose something.monolingual: to be likely to lose something or have it taken away. _ I stand to lose hundreds of dollars if I am not there on time.
examples: I stand to lose hundreds of dollars if I am not there on time.

stand to reason.monolingual: to seem reasonable. _ It stands to reason that it’ll be colder in January than it is in November. _ It stands to reason that Bill left in a hurry, although no one saw him go.
examples: It stands to reason that it’ll be colder in January than it is in November.

stand together.monolingual: 1. to stand in a group. _ All the members of the family stood together for a photograph. _Please stand together so I can count you.
examples: All the members of the family stood together for a photograph.

stand trial.monolingual: to be the accused person in a trial before a judge; to be on trial. _ He had to stand trial for perjury and obstruction of justice.
examples: He had to stand trial for perjury and obstruction of justice.

stand up.monolingual: 1. to arise from a sitting or reclining position. _He stood up and looked across the valley. _She had been sitting for so long that it was a pleasure to stand up.
examples: He stood up and looked across the valley.

stand up and be counted.monolingual: to state one’s support (for someone or something). _ If you believe in more government help for farmers, write your representative—stand up and be counted. _ I’m generally in favor of what you propose, but not enough to stand up and be counted.
examples: If you believe in more government help for farmers, write your representative—stand up and be counted.

stand up in court.monolingual: [for a case] to survive a test in a court of law. _Do you think that this case will stand up in court? _ These charges will never stand up in court. They are too vague.
examples: These charges will never stand up in court.

stand up with someone.monolingual: to attend someone who is being married. (Usually refers to males.) _ I agreed to stand up with my buddy at his wedding. _Tom stood up with Harry when the latter got married.
examples: I agreed to stand up with my buddy at his wedding.

stand well with someone.monolingual: to be acceptable or agreeable to someone. _ That idea doesn’t stand well with the management. _ I hope my suggestions stand well with you.
examples: That idea doesn’t stand well with the management.

stand with someone.monolingual: to unite with someone, as in defense. _ Don’t worry. I’ll stand with you to the end. _ He stood with her and they faced the threat together.
examples: Don’t worry. I’ll stand with you to the end.

a standing joke.monolingual: a subject that regularly and over a period of time causes amusement whenever it is mentioned. _ Uncle Jim’s driving was a standing joke. He used to drive incredibly slowly. _Their mother’s inability to make a decision was a standing joke in the Smith
examples: Uncle Jim’s driving was a standing joke.

star as someone or something.monolingual: [for someone] to be a featured performer, representing a particular person, or play in a particular role. _ Judy starred as Evita in the broadway production of the same name. _ Mary starred as an aging countess.
examples: Judy starred as Evita in the broadway production of the same name.

star in something.monolingual: to be a featured actor in a play, movie, opera, etc. _ Roger starred in an off-Broadway play last season. _ Mary always wanted to star in her own movie, but it was not to be.
examples: Roger starred in an off-Broadway play last season.

star-crossed lovers.monolingual: ill-fated lovers. _ I suppose that Romeo and Juilet are star-crossed lovers.
examples: I suppose that Romeo and Juilet are star-crossed lovers.

stare at someone or something.monolingual: to look fixedly at someone or something. _ Why are you staring at me? _ I was staring at the scenery behind you.
examples: I was staring at the scenery behind you.

stare into something.monolingual: to gaze fixedly into something. _She just sat there, staring into space. _ Tom stared into the water, hoping to see a fish or maybe a turtle.
examples: She just sat there, staring into space.

stare someone down†.monolingual: to pressure someone to capitulate, back down, or yield by staring. _ Don’t try to stare me down. I have nerves of steel. _ I tried to stare down my opponent, but it didn’t work.
examples: Don’t try to stare me down.

stark raving mad.monolingual: Cliché totally insane; completely crazy; out of control. (Often an exaggeration.) _When she heard about what happened at the office, she went stark raving mad. _ You must be start raving mad if you think I would trust you with my car!
examples: When she heard about what happened at the office, she went stark raving mad.

*stars in one’s eyes.monolingual: Fig. an obsession with celebrities, movies, and the theater. (Alludes to movie stars. *Typically: get ~; have ~; give one ~.) _Many young people have stars in their eyes at this age. _ Anne has stars in her eyes. She wants to go to Hollywood.
examples: Many young people have stars in their eyes at this age.

start as something.monolingual: to begin in some original condition or status. _ Every forest fire starts as a small spark. _ The argument started as a small disagreement.
examples: Every forest fire starts as a small spark.

start for some place.monolingual: to begin a journey to some place. _ When shall we start for Springfield? _ We will start for Detroit before dawn.
examples: We will start for Detroit before dawn.

start from scratch.monolingual: to start from the very beginning; to start from nothing. _Whenever I bake a cake, I start from scratch. I never use a cake mix in a box. _ I built every bit of my own house. I started from scratch and did everything with my own hands.
examples: Whenever I bake a cake, I start from scratch.

start from some place.monolingual: 1. [for someone] to begin a journey at some place. (The emphasis is on the location of the start of the journey.) _ We started from California. _ Where will you start from?
examples: We started from California.

start off.monolingual: to begin; to set out on a journey. _ When do you want to start off ? _ We will start off as soon as we can get everything packed.
examples: We will start off as soon as we can get everything packed.

start off from some place.monolingual: to begin a journey from some place. (The emphasis is on the inception of the journey.) _ We will start off from Detroit and drive to Chicago. _ He started off from work rather than home.
examples: We will start off from Detroit and drive to Chicago.

start on someone or something.monolingual: 1. to begin dealing with someone or something. _ We have finished talking about Gary, and now we will start on Bob. _ We will start on dessert after you have finished your broccoli.
examples: We have finished talking about Gary, and now we will start on Bob.

start out.monolingual: to begin. _Whenever you are ready, we will start out. _ We can’t start out until Tom is here.
examples: Whenever you are ready, we will start out.

start out as something.monolingual: to begin one’s career as something. _I started out as a clerk and two years later I’m still a clerk! _ I wanted to start out as an assistant manager.
examples: I wanted to start out as an assistant manager.

start over.monolingual: to begin again. _I have messed this up so much that there is nothing to do now but start over. _ When you start over, try to do it right this time.
examples: I have messed this up so much that there is nothing to do now but start over.

start someone over.monolingual: to cause someone to begin again; to lead someone to begin again. _ The orchestra messed up the first few bars, so the conductor started them over again. _ I hope the conductor doesn’t start us over again. This is getting boring to play.
examples: The orchestra messed up the first few bars, so the conductor started them over again.

start something up†.monolingual: to start something, such as a car or some procedure. (Also without up.) _ It was cold, but I managed to start up the car without any difficulty. _ We can’t start the project up until we have more money.
examples: It was cold, but I managed to start up the car without any difficulty.

start something up† with something.monolingual: to use something in the process of starting something else. _ Do you have to start this old car up with a crank? _ Do you start up this car with a crank?

start up.monolingual: to begin; to begin running, as with an engine. _ The car started up without a problem. _The engines of the plane started up one by one.
examples: The car started up without a problem.

startle someone out of something.monolingual: to frighten someone very badly. (The something that may be lost may be expressed as wits, senses, ten years’ growth, etc.) _The explosion star- tled Polly out of her senses. _ I frightened myself out of ten years’ growth.
examples: The explosion star- tled Polly out of her senses.

starve for some food.monolingual: to be very hungry for something. _ I am just starved for some fresh peaches. _We were starved for dinner by the time we finally got to eat.
examples: I am just starved for some fresh peaches.

starve for someone or something.monolingual: Fig. to have a strong desire or need for someone or something. (Based on starved for some food.) _ I am starved for Jane. I miss her so! _ Claire was starved for affection.
examples: I am starved for Jane.

stash something away†.monolingual: to hide something; to set something aside for use at a later time. _Please stash this away somewhere. You may need it someday. _ You should stash away some money for later.
examples: Please stash this away somewhere.

stash something in something.monolingual: to put or shove something into something; to store or hide something in something. _ You should stash your food in a place that is safe from bears when you go camping. _ I stashed my clothes in my suitcase and called a taxi.
examples: You should stash your food in a place that is safe from bears when you go camping.

state of mind.monolingual: basic attitude or outlook at a point in time. _ She was in a terrible state of mind when she was interviewed for a job.
examples: She was in a terrible state of mind when she was interviewed for a job.

state of the art.monolingual: using the most recent technology. (Hyphenated before nouns.) _ Our company’s computer setup is strictly state of the art. _This state-of-the-art radio is capable of filling the whole room with sound.
examples: Our company’s computer setup is strictly state of the art.

station someone at something.monolingual: to position or place someone near something. _ The manager stationed a receptionist at the door. _Would you station a guard at the back door to keep people out?
examples: The manager stationed a receptionist at the door.

stave someone or something off†.monolingual: to hold someone or something off; to defend against the attack of someone or something. _ The citizen was not able to stave the mugger off. _The army staved off the attackers for three hours without letup.
examples: The citizen was not able to stave the mugger off.

stave something in†.monolingual: to crush something in. (The past tense is usually stove with ships, and otherwise, staved.) _ The rocks on the reef staved the hull of the ship in. _ The angry sailor staved in the cask of rum.
examples: The rocks on the reef staved the hull of the ship in.

stave something off†.monolingual: to delay or postpone something unwanted, such as hunger, foreclosure, death, etc. _ He could stave his thirst off no longer. Despite the enemy sentries, he made a dash for the stream. _The lost hiker could not stave off her hunger any longer.
examples: He could stave his thirst off no longer.

stay at some place.monolingual: 1. to remain at a place. _Have you ever tried to make a cat stay at one place? _ Please stay at home until I call you.
examples: Please stay at home until I call you.

stay at something.monolingual: to keep working at something. _ You should stay at something until you finish it. _ She couldn’t seem to stay at her place of work for a whole day.
examples: You should stay at something until you finish it.

stay behind.monolingual: [for someone] to remain in a place when others have left. _ I will stay behind and tell the late arrivers where you have gone. _Fred always stayed behind to clean up.
examples: I will stay behind and tell the late arrivers where you have gone.

stay by someone or something.monolingual: to remain close to someone or something. _Please stay by me until we get through this crowd of rough-looking people. _Stay by the wall and move along slowly.
examples: Please stay by me until we get through this crowd of rough-looking people.

stay down.monolingual: to remain in a prone, squatting, or sitting position. _Stay down until the danger is over. _Stay down so they won’t see you.
examples: Stay down until the danger is over.

stay for something.monolingual: to remain in a place to participate in something. _ Would you please stay for dinner? _ I am sorry, but we cannot stay for dinner.
examples: I am sorry, but we cannot stay for dinner.

stay on something.monolingual: 1. to remain on something, such as a horse, road, stool, etc. _ The first time I rode, I could hardly stay on the horse. _It was so slippery that I had trouble staying on the road.
examples: The first time I rode, I could hardly stay on the horse.

stay put.monolingual: not to move; to stay where one is. _We’ve decided to stay put and not to move to Florida. _If the children just stay put, their parents will come for them soon.
examples: We’ve decided to stay put and not to move to Florida.

stay to something.monolingual: to remain in a place for something, such as dinner. _ I hope you will stay to dinner. _ I stayed to lunch because they were having fried shrimp.
examples: I hope you will stay to dinner.

stay up late.monolingual: to remain awake and out of bed later than usual. _ I am in the practice of staying up late. _ I can’t stay up late three nights in a row.
examples: I am in the practice of staying up late.

stay with someone or something.monolingual: to remain in the company of someone or something. _ Please stay with me for a little while. _ How long did you stay with the company?
examples: Please stay with me for a little while.

stay within something.monolingual: to remain inside something. _You will have to stay within the immediate area until things return to normal in the town. _ Our dog just can’t seem to stay within our yard.
examples: You will have to stay within the immediate area until things return to normal in the town.

*steady as a rock.monolingual: Cliché very steady and unmovable; very stable. (*Also: as ~.) _ His hand was steady as a rock as he made each incision. _You must remain as steady as a rock when you are arguing with your supervisor.
examples: His hand was steady as a rock as he made each incision.

steal a base.monolingual: Fig. to sneak from one base to another in baseball. _ The runner stole second base, but he nearly got put out on the way. _Tom runs so slowly that he never tries to steal a base.
examples: The runner stole second base, but he nearly got put out on the way.

steal from someone or something.monolingual: to rob someone or something. _ You wouldn’t steal from a poor man, would you? _ Max didn’t feel bad about stealing from a bank.
examples: Max didn’t feel bad about stealing from a bank.

steal out of some place.monolingual: to sneak quietly out of some place. _ The critic stole out of the theater, unable to endure any more of the abysmal play. _ I stole out of the lecture and went back to my room.
examples: The critic stole out of the theater, unable to endure any more of the abysmal play.

steal over someone or something.monolingual: 1. [for a covering of some sort] to move slowly over someone or something. (As with the sun or the shade of a cloud.) _The shade stole over the sunbathers and ended their day. _ Darkness stole over the land.
examples: The shade stole over the sunbathers and ended their day.

steal someone’s heart.monolingual: Fig. to capture someone’s affections; to cause someone to fall in love with oneself. _ When I first met him, I knew he would steal my heart away. And he did.
examples: When I first met him, I knew he would steal my heart away.

steal someone’s thunder.monolingual: Fig. to lessen someone’s force or authority. _ What do you mean by coming in here and stealing my thunder? I’m in charge here! _ Someone stole my thunder by leaking my announcement to the press.
examples: Someone stole my thunder by leaking my announcement to the press.

steal something off someone.monolingual: to rob something from someone. _ I think that guy who walked past me stole my wallet off me! _Max stole a lot of money off tourists last season.
examples: Max stole a lot of money off tourists last season.

steam across something.monolingual: [for a ship] to cross a body of water under power. (Originally referred to steam engines, but now can be any sort of engine.) _ How long does it take to steam across the Atlantic these days? _We steamed across the bay in less than an hour.
examples: We steamed across the bay in less than an hour.

steam someone’s beam.monolingual: Sl. to make someone angry. _ Being stood up really steams my beam! _ Come on, don’t steam your beam. Remember how hard times are now.
examples: Come on, don’t steam your beam.

steam someone up†.monolingual: 1. Sl. to get someone excited. _Steam yourselves up and get in there and win this game! _ The coach can really steam up those guys.
examples: The coach can really steam up those guys.

steam something up†.monolingual: to cause something to be covered with water vapor due to the presence of steam. _ Our breaths steamed the windows up. _The hot shower steamed up the mirror.
examples: Our breaths steamed the windows up.

steam up.monolingual: 1. Lit. to become covered with a film of steam or water vapor. _ The windows steamed up and we had to wipe them so we could see out. _ The window has steamed up, and I can’t see.
examples: The windows steamed up and we had to wipe them so we could see out.

a steely gaze.monolingual: Cliché an intense, staring gaze. _The principal turned a steely gaze toward the frightened student and suddenly smiled.
examples: The principal turned a steely gaze toward the frightened student and suddenly smiled.

steep someone in something.monolingual: Fig. to immerse someone in some kind of knowledge or other experience; to saturate someone with some kind of experience or training. (Fig. on steep something in something.) _ Her parents steeped her in good literature and music. _ She steeped herself
examples: Her parents steeped her in good literature and music.

steep something in something.monolingual: to soak something in a liquid. _ I steeped the shirt in red dye. _ You have to steep these herbs in steamy hot water for five minutes.
examples: I steeped the shirt in red dye.

steer into something.monolingual: to turn or drive into something. _ Try to steer into the right parking space this time. _ Poor Wally steered into the curb.
examples: Try to steer into the right parking space this time.

steer something for something.monolingual: to aim oneself or one’s vehicle toward something. _Jeff steered the car for the entrance to the tunnel and stepped on the gas. _ The driver steered the bus for the center lane just in time.
examples: Jeff steered the car for the entrance to the tunnel and stepped on the gas.

steer through something.monolingual: to maneuver through something that is confusing or treacherous. _ Do you think you can steer through this f looded tunnel? _ I can’t steer through this mess of leaves and mud on the road.
examples: I can’t steer through this mess of leaves and mud on the road.

steer toward someone or something.monolingual: to turn or drive toward someone or something. _ He steered toward the empty parking space, but someone got there before he did. _ Steer toward the house with the red door.
examples: He steered toward the empty parking space, but someone got there before he did.

stem from something.monolingual: [for an event] to result from something. _ These problems all stem from your mismanagement. _Our difficulties stem from the bad weather we have been having.
examples: These problems all stem from your mismanagement.

step forward.monolingual: 1. Lit. to move forward one step or several steps. _ The volunteer stepped forward. _ I stepped forward and someone moved up behind me immediately.
examples: The volunteer stepped forward.

step into someone’s shoes.monolingual: Fig. to take over a job or some role from someone. _I was prepared to step into the boss’s shoes, so there was no disruption when he left for another job. _ There was no one who could step into Alice’s shoes when she left, so everything came to a sto
examples: I was prepared to step into the boss’s shoes, so there was no disruption when he left for another job.

step off.monolingual: to come off something by taking a step. _ She came to the bottom step and stepped off. _ Ed was afraid to dive in from the side of the pool, so he just stepped off.
examples: She came to the bottom step and stepped off.

step on someone or something.monolingual: to tread on someone or something. _ Ouch! You stepped on me! _ Don’t step on the f looring in that spot. It’s weak.
examples: Don’t step on the f looring in that spot.

step out into something.monolingual: to go out from a place into a different set of conditions. _ Julie stepped out of her previous job into a whole new world. _ Wally stepped out into the bright sunlight.
examples: Julie stepped out of her previous job into a whole new world.

step out of line.monolingual: 1. Lit. to move out of a line of people. _ If you step out of line, you will lose your place in it. _ I had to step out of line to sit down on the curb and rest for a minute.
examples: If you step out of line, you will lose your place in it.

step outside.monolingual: 1. to go outside, as if to get some fresh air. _ I need to step outside for a minute to get a breath of air. _ Tom and Harry stepped outside for a moment.
examples: I need to step outside for a minute to get a breath of air.

step over someone or something.monolingual: to walk so as to avoid stepping on someone or something. _I stepped over Tom, who was napping on the f loor. _ Please step over the things on the f loor. We are doing the spring cleaning.
examples: I stepped over Tom, who was napping on the f loor.

step right up.monolingual: to come right to where the speaker is; to come forward to the person speaking. (Used by people selling things, as at carnival sideshows.) _Please step right up and buy a ticket to see the show. _ Don’t be shy! Step right up and buy one of these.
examples: Please step right up and buy a ticket to see the show.

step something down†.monolingual: to reduce the intensity or amount of something by one step or grade. _ See if you can step the lights down a little. _ Step down the lights just a little more.
examples: See if you can step the lights down a little.

step something off†.monolingual: to measure a distance by counting the paces required to cover it. _ She stepped the distance off and noted it on her pad. _ Liz stepped off the number of feet from the window to the opposite wall.
examples: She stepped the distance off and noted it on her pad.

step something up†.monolingual: 1. to make something more active. _ I hope we can step the pace of business up in the next few days. _We can step up business considerably by putting out a larger sign.
examples: I hope we can step the pace of business up in the next few days.

step up.monolingual: to increase. _ Industrial production stepped up a large amount this last quarter. _ Traffic has stepped up since the road was paved.
examples: Industrial production stepped up a large amount this last quarter.

step up to something.monolingual: to walk to something, especially a counter or a bar. _ Jake stepped up to the ticket counter and bought a single ticket for the balcony. _ When Wally stepped up to the ticket window, he learned that the show was sold out.
examples: Jake stepped up to the ticket counter and bought a single ticket for the balcony.

step up to the plate.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a batter in baseball] to move near home plate in preparation for striking the ball when it is pitched. _The batter stepped up to the plate and glared at the pitcher.
examples: The batter stepped up to the plate and glared at the pitcher.

step-by-step.monolingual: 1. Lit. [walking] one step at a time. _ The old man slowly moved across the lawn step-by-step.
examples: The old man slowly moved across the lawn step-by-step.

stew in one’s own juice.monolingual: Fig. to be left alone to suffer one’s anger or disappointment. _ John has such a terrible temper. When he got mad at us, we just let him go away and stew in his own juice. _ After John stewed in his own juice for a while, he decided to come back and
examples: John has such a terrible temper.

stick around.monolingual: [for a person] to remain in a place. _ The kids stuck around for a time after the party was over. _Oh, Ann. Please stick around for a while. I want to talk to you later.
examples: The kids stuck around for a time after the party was over.

stick at something.monolingual: to keep trying to do something; to stay on a task or job. _ I hope he can stick at this job. _ He doesn’t seem to be able to stick at anything for very long.
examples: I hope he can stick at this job.

stick in someone’s mind.monolingual: to remain in someone’s thinking. _ The events of that day stuck in my mind for a very long time. _The image of her smiling face stuck in Henry’s mind for a long time.
examples: The events of that day stuck in my mind for a very long time.

stick in something.monolingual: to remain embedded in something; to remain held in something. _ Do you think this will stick in the hole, or is it too small? _ A fish bone stuck in his throat for a while.
examples: A fish bone stuck in his throat for a while.

stick it to someone.monolingual: Inf. to give someone a problem; to confront someone. _ They stuck it to me about the stoppedup drain. _He was late, and the boss really stuck it to him.
examples: They stuck it to me about the stoppedup drain.

stick man.monolingual: Sl. a police patrol officer (who carries a stick). _The stick man is due here in about three minutes. Hurry. _ I was a stick man for a few years till my feet went bad.
examples: The stick man is due here in about three minutes.

stick one’s tongue out†.monolingual: Fig. to cause one’s tongue to project outward. (A gesture of contempt.) _ Don’t stick your tongue out at me! _ She stuck out her tongue at me!

stick out.monolingual: to project outward. _ You can’t lock your suitcase because there is a bit of cloth sticking out. _Some cloth stuck out of the top of the drawer.
examples: You can’t lock your suitcase because there is a bit of cloth sticking out.

stick out a mile.monolingual: Fig. to project outward very obviously. _My nose sticks out a mile! I hate it! _ His stomach sticks out a mile. What do you suppose is in there?
examples: His stomach sticks out a mile.

stick out against something.monolingual: to be highly visible against a background of something. _Your cold, red nose sticks out against your white, frozen face. _ The red vase sticks out against the pale blue wallpaper.
examples: Your cold, red nose sticks out against your white, frozen face.

stick shift.monolingual: 1. having to do with a nonautomatic transmission or a car that has one. _ I prefer a stick shift car— I don’t know why. _ The stick shift models are cheaper— that’s why.
examples: I prefer a stick shift car— I don’t know why.

stick someone or something up†.monolingual: to rob someone or a business establishment. (Presumably with the aid of a gun.) _ Max tried to stick the drugstore up. _ Max stuck up the store.
examples: Max tried to stick the drugstore up.

stick something down†.monolingual: to fasten something down, as with glue or paste. _ Get some glue and stick down this wallpaper, please. _ Stick this wallpaper down, would you?
examples: Get some glue and stick down this wallpaper, please.

stick something out†.monolingual: to endure something; to stay with something. (The something can be vaguely expressed using it.) _ I will stick it out as long as I can. _ She stuck out the abuse as long as she could; then she started looking for another job.
examples: I will stick it out as long as I can.

stick something out† to someone.monolingual: to hold something, such as one’s hand, out where someone can grasp it. _She stuck her hand out to him, intending that he shake it. _Ted stuck out his hand to Bill, but withdrew it suddenly.
examples: She stuck her hand out to him, intending that he shake it.

stick something together.monolingual: 1. to glue or paste something together. _Use glue to stick these pieces together. _Please stick the pieces of the broken vase together with glue.
examples: Use glue to stick these pieces together.

stick something up†.monolingual: 1. to fasten something to a place where it can be seen; to put something on display, especially by gluing, tacking, or stapling. _ Stick this notice up. Put a copy on every bulletin board. _ Please stick up this notice.
examples: Stick this notice up.

stick to one’s guns.monolingual: Fig. to remain firm in one’s convictions; to stand up for one’s rights. (Fig. on a soldier remaining in place to fire a gun even when all appears to be lost.) _ I’ll stick to my guns on this matter. I’m sure I’m right. _ Bob can be persuaded to do it
examples: I’ll stick to my guns on this matter.

stick to one’s ribs.monolingual: Fig. [for food] to last long and fortify one well; [for food] to sustain one even in the coldest weather. _ This oatmeal ought to stick to your ribs. You need something hearty on a cold day like this. _I don’t want just a salad! I want something that
examples: This oatmeal ought to stick to your ribs.

stick to someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to adhere to someone or something; to remain affixed to someone or something. _ The tape stuck to me and I couldn’t get it off. _ This stamp won’t stick to the envelope.
examples: The tape stuck to me and I couldn’t get it off.

stick to someone’s fingers.monolingual: Fig. to remain in someone’s possession; to be stolen by someone. _ Other people’s watches tend to stick to Max’s fingers. _ Watch that clerk. Your change tends to stick to his fingers.
examples: Other people’s watches tend to stick to Max’s fingers.

stick together.monolingual: 1. Lit. to adhere to one another. _ The noodles are sticking together. What shall I do? _ You need to keep the pieces separate while you fry them or else they will stick together.
examples: The noodles are sticking together.

stick up.monolingual: to stand upright or on end; to thrust upward. _ The ugly red f lower stuck up from the bouquet. _ Why is the worst-looking f lower sticking up above all the rest?
examples: The ugly red f lower stuck up from the bouquet.

stick with it..monolingual: Do not give up. Stay with your task. _ Bill: I’m really tired of calculus. Father: Stick with it. You’ll be a better person for it. _ Bill: This job is getting to be such a pain. Sue: True, but it pays well, doesn’t it? Stick with it.
examples: Bill: I’m really tired of calculus.

stick-in-the-mud.monolingual: Fig. a dull and old-fashioned person. _Don’t be such an old stick-in-the-mud. _Some stick-inthe- mud objected to the kind of music we wanted to play in church.
examples: Don’t be such an old stick-in-the-mud.

*stiff as a poker.monolingual: rigid and inflexible; stiff and awkward. (Usually used to describe people. *Also: as ~.) _ This guy’s dead. He’s cold and as stiff as a poker. _ John is not a very good dancer; he’s stiff as a poker.
examples: This guy’s dead.

stiffen something up†.monolingual: to make something rigid or tense. _ He added a little starch to the rinse water to stiffen his collars up a bit. _ The cold draft has stiffened up my neck.
examples: He added a little starch to the rinse water to stiffen his collars up a bit.

stiffen up.monolingual: to become stiff. _ The bread dough stiffened up as it got cold. _ My knees began to stiffen up after I sat still for an hour.
examples: The bread dough stiffened up as it got cold.

stigmatize someone as something.monolingual: to brand or label someone as something. _ The opposition will try to stigmatize you as a spendthrift. _Tony was stigmatized as a poor loser.
examples: The opposition will try to stigmatize you as a spendthrift.

*still as death.monolingual: Cliché immobile; completely still. (The reference to death gives this expression ominous connotations. *Also: as ~.) _George sat as still as death all afternoon. _When the storm was over, everything was suddenly still as death.
examples: George sat as still as death all afternoon.

still waters run deep..monolingual: Prov. Quiet people are often very thoughtful. _ Jill: I get the impression that Nathan is not very smart. He never says anything. Jane: Don’t be so sure. Still waters run deep, you know.
examples: Jill: I get the impression that Nathan is not very smart.

sting someone for something.monolingual: Sl. to cheat someone of a particular amount; to make someone pay for something. _ That guy stung me for twenty bucks! _ Toby was stung for the lunch bill.
examples: Toby was stung for the lunch bill.

sting someone with something.monolingual: to use something to sting someone. _The bee stung me with its stinger. _The wasp can sting you with its poisonous barb.
examples: The bee stung me with its stinger.

stink on ice.monolingual: Sl. to be really rotten. (So rotten as to reek even when frozen.) _This show stinks on ice. _The whole idea stank on ice.
examples: This show stinks on ice.

stink something up†.monolingual: to make something or some place smell very bad. _ Your cooking really stunk the place up! _ The rotten eggs will stink up the whole house.
examples: The rotten eggs will stink up the whole house.

stink with something.monolingual: to smell very bad with the smell of something. _The room stinks with a garlicky smell. _Our garden stinks with the smell of something rotting.
examples: The room stinks with a garlicky smell.

stinking rich.monolingual: Fig. very rich. _ I’d like to be stinking rich for the rest of my life. _Tiffany is stinking rich, and she acts like it.
examples: I’d like to be stinking rich for the rest of my life.

stinking with something.monolingual: Fig. having lots of something. _ Mr. Wilson is just stinking with cash. _ Those guys are stinking with jewelry.
examples: Mr. Wilson is just stinking with cash.

stir someone up†.monolingual: Fig. to get someone excited; to get someone angry. (Fig. on stir something up.) _The march music really stirred the audience up. _ The march stirred up the audience.
examples: The march music really stirred the audience up.

stir something around.monolingual: to agitate or mix a liquid substance by moving it in a circular motion. _ Stir the mixture around to mix it up. _ You should stir the dressing around a bit before you serve it.
examples: Stir the mixture around to mix it up.

stir something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to mix something by stirring. _ Please stir the pancake batter up before you use it. _Please stir up the batter.
examples: Please stir the pancake batter up before you use it.

stir up a hornet’s nest.monolingual: Fig. to create a lot of trouble. (Fig. on stir something up W.) _If you say that to her, you will be stirring up a hornet’s nest. _There is no need to stir up a hornet’s nest.
examples: If you say that to her, you will be stirring up a hornet’s nest.

*stir-crazy.monolingual: crazy from being confined. (*Typically: be ~; become ~; go ~; get ~; make someone ~. Stir is a slang word for prison.) _ I am going to go stir-crazy if I don’t get out of this office.
examples: I am going to go stir-crazy if I don’t get out of this office.

stitch something up†.monolingual: to sew something together; to mend a tear or ripped seam. _ I tore my shirt. Would you stitch it up, please? _ Please stitch up my shirt.
examples: I tore my shirt.

stock in trade.monolingual: whatever goods, skills, etc., are necessary to undertake an activity of some kind. _ Of course I am glad to help. Packing household goods is my stock in trade.
examples: Of course I am glad to help.

stoke something up†.monolingual: 1. to poke or add fuel to a fire to make it burn hotter. _ Grandpa had to go down each winter morning to stoke the fire up. _ He stoked up the furnace every morning during the winter.
examples: Grandpa had to go down each winter morning to stoke the fire up.

*stoked on someone or something.monolingual: Sl. excited by someone or something. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ I am really stoked on that movie. _ She was really stoked on Tom.
examples: I am really stoked on that movie.

stoked out.monolingual: Sl. exhausted. _I ran all the way and got stoked out. _Alex is totally stoked out from working in the hot sun.
examples: I ran all the way and got stoked out.

stomp on someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to stamp someone down. _The angry crowd knocked him down and stomped on him. _ The crowd stomped on the mugger.
examples: The angry crowd knocked him down and stomped on him.

stone dead.monolingual: Rur. dead; unquestionably dead; long dead. _ The cat was stone dead and stiff as a board by the time we got to him. _ Old Tom is stone dead and in the ground.
examples: The cat was stone dead and stiff as a board by the time we got to him.

a stone’s throw away.monolingual: Fig. a short distance; a relatively short distance. _ John saw Mary across the street, just a stone’s throw away. _ Philadelphia is just a stone’s throw away from Camden, New Jersey.
examples: John saw Mary across the street, just a stone’s throw away.

stoop down.monolingual: to dip, duck, or squat down. _I had to stoop down to enter the tiny door. _ Stoop down so you don’t bump your head.
examples: I had to stoop down to enter the tiny door.

stoop over.monolingual: to bend over. _ Carl stooped over to pick up his napkin and lost his balance. _ As he stooped over, he lost his balance and fell.
examples: Carl stooped over to pick up his napkin and lost his balance.

stoop to doing something.monolingual: to degrade oneself or condescend to doing something; to do something that is beneath one. _ Whoever thought that the manager of the department would stoop to sweeping up? _ I never dreamed that Bill would stoop to stealing.
examples: I never dreamed that Bill would stoop to stealing.

stop at something.monolingual: 1. to go as far as something and then stop. _ I will stop at the end of the road. _ The road stopped at the base of a mountain.
examples: I will stop at the end of the road.

stop behind someone or something.monolingual: to bring oneself or one’s vehicle to a stop behind someone or something. _ I stopped behind Fred at the red light. _Fred stopped behind a minivan.
examples: I stopped behind Fred at the red light.

stop dead in one’s tracks.monolingual: Fig. to stop completely still suddenly because of fear, a noise, etc. _ I stopped dead in my tracks when I heard the scream. _The deer stopped dead in its tracks when it heard the hunter step on a fallen branch.
examples: I stopped dead in my tracks when I heard the scream.

stop for someone.monolingual: to halt one’s vehicle to allow someone to get in. _ I stopped for Jeff, but he didn’t want a ride. _ I didn’t have time to stop for you. I hope you will forgive me.
examples: I stopped for Jeff, but he didn’t want a ride.

stop for something.monolingual: to halt one’s vehicle because of something or the need of something. _ I had to stop for a red light. _ We stopped for some gas.
examples: I had to stop for a red light.

stop, look, and listen.monolingual: to exercise caution, especially at street corners and railroad crossings, by stopping, looking to the left and to the right, and listening for approaching vehicles or a train. _Sally’s mother trained her to stop, look, and listen at every street corn
examples: Sally’s mother trained her to stop, look, and listen at every street corner.

stop on a dime.monolingual: Fig. to come to a stop in a very short distance. _ This thing will stop on a dime. _ Imagine a bus that could stop on a dime.
examples: This thing will stop on a dime.

stop on something.monolingual: to go as far as something [on the floor or the ground] and then stop. _ Please stop on the line. _ You are supposed to stop on the white line or behind it.
examples: Please stop on the line.

stop short of a place.monolingual: not to go as far as something. _The bus stopped short of the end of the road. _The speeding car stopped short of the sidewalk where children were playing.
examples: The bus stopped short of the end of the road.

stop short of doing something.monolingual: not to go as far as doing something. _Fortunately Bob stopped short of hitting Tom. _ The boss criticized Jane’s work but stopped short of firing her. _Jack was furious but stopped short of hitting Tom.
examples: Fortunately Bob stopped short of hitting Tom.

stop someone cold.monolingual: to halt someone immediately. _When you told us the bad news, it stopped me cold.
examples: When you told us the bad news, it stopped me cold.

stop someone from doing something.monolingual: to prevent someone from doing something. _ I can’t stop her from running away. _ They couldn’t stop themselves from eating.
examples: I can’t stop her from running away.

stop up.monolingual: [for something] to become clogged. _ The sink stopped up again!

store something away†.monolingual: to put something away for future use; to set something aside. _Store the extra rice away for use next week. _ Please store away the extra food.
examples: Store the extra rice away for use next week.

store something in something.monolingual: to set something aside in something. _ Can I store my bicycle in your garage? _ Do you mind if I store my coat in your locker?

store something up†.monolingual: to build up and lay away a supply of something. _ The bears will store fat up for the long winter. _ They store up fat for the winter.
examples: The bears will store fat up for the long winter.

storm around.monolingual: Fig. to go about in a fury. _ What is he storming around about? _ Martin was storming around all morning because he lost his car keys.
examples: Martin was storming around all morning because he lost his car keys.

storm at someone or something.monolingual: Fig. to direct one’s anger at someone or something. _ She stormed at him because he was late again. _ Richard was storming at the cat again.
examples: She stormed at him because he was late again.

a storm is brewing..monolingual: 1. There is going to be a storm. _ Look at the clouds. A storm is brewing. _ A storm is brewing in the west.
examples: Look at the clouds.

stow away.monolingual: to conceal oneself in a vehicle, originally a ship, in order to travel without paying. _ Don got to this country by stowing away on a cargo ship.
examples: Don got to this country by stowing away on a cargo ship.

stow something away†.monolingual: to pack something away. _ I have to stow my clothes away before I go to bed. _ Please stow away your things and get right to work.
examples: I have to stow my clothes away before I go to bed.

straddle the fence.monolingual: Fig. to support both sides of an issue. (As if one were partly on either side of a fence.) _ The mayor is straddling the fence on this issue, hoping the public will forget it. _The legislator wanted to straddle the fence until the last minute, and th
examples: The mayor is straddling the fence on this issue, hoping the public will forget it.

the straight and narrow.monolingual: Fig. a straight and law-abiding route through life. (Referring to a morally rigid and correct course of behavior. Fixed order.) _ You should have no trouble with the police if you stick to the straight and narrow. _ Roger was the kind who followed th
examples: You should have no trouble with the police if you stick to the straight and narrow.

*straight as an arrow.monolingual: 1. Cliché [of something] very straight. (*Also: as ~.) _ The road to my house is as straight as an arrow, so it should be very easy to follow.
examples: The road to my house is as straight as an arrow, so it should be very easy to follow.

the straight dope.monolingual: the true information; the full story. _ He gave us the straight dope. _ I want the straight dope. I can take it.
examples: He gave us the straight dope.

*a straight face.monolingual: Fig. a face free from smiles or laughter. (*Typically: have ~; keep ~.) _ It’s hard to keep a straight face when someone tells a funny joke.
examples: It’s hard to keep a straight face when someone tells a funny joke.

straight from the shoulder.monolingual: Fig. very direct, without attenuation or embellishment. _ Okay, I’ll give it to you straight from the shoulder. _Right straight from the shoulder: clean out your desk; you’re through.
examples: Okay, I’ll give it to you straight from the shoulder.

straight low.monolingual: Sl. the absolute truth. (From lowdown = the story; the truth.) _ Can you give me the straight low on this mess? _Nobody ain’t gonna tell no warden the straight low; you can be sure of that.
examples: Nobody ain’t gonna tell no warden the straight low; you can be sure of that.

straight man.monolingual: someone who sets up jokes or gags so that someone else can say the punch line. _ I need a straight man to set up all my jokes. _ I’m tired of being a straight man for a has-been comic.
examples: I need a straight man to set up all my jokes.

straight out.monolingual: frankly; directly. _Bob told Pam straight out that he didn’t want to marry her. _ Jim was told straight out to start working harder.
examples: Bob told Pam straight out that he didn’t want to marry her.

straight shooter.monolingual: Fig. an honest person. _ I trust Mike; he’s a straight shooter. _We need a straight shooter in office who will work for the people rather than some lobbyists.
examples: I trust Mike; he’s a straight shooter.

straight talk.monolingual: direct and honest talk. _ It’s about time for a little straight talk around here. _ If they want straight talk and can handle straight talk, give ’em straight talk.
examples: It’s about time for a little straight talk around here.

straight up.monolingual: 1. Sl. upright. _ A fine guy—really straight up. _ She is one of the most straight up brokers in town.
examples: A fine guy—really straight up.

straighten out.monolingual: 1. to become straight. _ The road finally straightened out. _The train tracks straightened out on the plain.
examples: The road finally straightened out.

straighten someone or something up†.monolingual: 1. to put someone or something into an upright position. _ The fence is tilted. Please straighten that post up when you get a chance. _ Bill, you’re slouching again. Straighten up your back.
examples: The fence is tilted.

straighten someone out†.monolingual: 1. to make someone’s body straight or orderly. _The undertaker straightened Sam out in his coffin. _ Straighten out your body so I can massage your back.
examples: The undertaker straightened Sam out in his coffin.

straighten something out†.monolingual: 1. to make something straighter. _ I can’t straighten these heavy boxes out. _ Please straighten out this line of people.
examples: I can’t straighten these heavy boxes out.

straighten up.monolingual: 1. to sit or stand more straight. _ Billy’s mother told him to straighten up or he’d fall out of his chair. _John straightened up so he’d look taller.
examples: Billy’s mother told him to straighten up or he’d fall out of his chair.

straighten up and fly right.monolingual: Fig. to improve one’s behavior or attitude and perform better. (Originally referred to an airplane.) _ If you want to keep out of trouble, you had better straighten up and f ly right. _ Straighten up and f ly right or I will send you to the principal
examples: If you want to keep out of trouble, you had better straighten up and f ly right.

strain after something.monolingual: [for a singer] to work very hard to reach a very high or a very low note. _ Don’t strain after the note. Let it come naturally, like a cooling breeze. _ She was straining after each note as if it hurt her to sing, which it probably did.
examples: Don’t strain after the note.

strain at the leash.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a dog] to pull very hard on its leash. _ It’s hard to walk Fido, because he is always straining at the leash. _I wish that this dog would not strain at the leash. It’s very hard on me.
examples: It’s hard to walk Fido, because he is always straining at the leash.

strain for an effect.monolingual: to work very hard to try to achieve some effect. _ The actors were straining so hard for an effect that they forgot their lines. _ Don’t strain for effect so much. The authors of this drama knew what they were doing, and it’s in the lines already.
examples: The actors were straining so hard for an effect that they forgot their lines.

strain something through something.monolingual: to filter a liquid or a watery substance by pouring it through something. _ Tony strained the strawberry jelly through cheesecloth. _ We will have to strain the clabber to take out the curds.
examples: Tony strained the strawberry jelly through cheesecloth.

strand someone on something.monolingual: to abandon someone on something from which there is no escape. _The shipwreck stranded our little group on a deserted beach. _ We were stranded on the little island by a storm.
examples: The shipwreck stranded our little group on a deserted beach.

strap someone or something down†.monolingual: to tie or bind someone or something down to something. _ The nurses strapped Gary down in preparation for the operation. _ They strapped down the patient and gave him a sedative.
examples: The nurses strapped Gary down in preparation for the operation.

*strapped for something.monolingual: needing something, usually money. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ I am really strapped for cash. Can you lend me some? _Ted is strapped for money and cannot pay his bills.
examples: I am really strapped for cash.

a straw man.monolingual: a weak proposition posited only to be demolished by a simple countering argument. _ So you can knock down your own straw man! Big deal. The question is how can you deal with real problems.
examples: So you can knock down your own straw man! Big deal.

stray onto something.monolingual: to wander onto an area, such as a parcel of land. _ Your cows strayed onto my land and ate my marigolds! _If your horse strays onto my land one more time, it’s my horse!

streak across something.monolingual: to move across something very fast. _ A comet streaked across the night sky. _ Tom streaked across the street to get a cup of coffee.
examples: A comet streaked across the night sky.

stretch away to some place.monolingual: to extend as far as some place. _ The forest stretched away to the horizon. _ The river stretched away to the sea.
examples: The forest stretched away to the horizon.

stretch one’s legs.monolingual: Fig. to walk around and loosen one’s leg muscles after sitting down or lying down for a time. _We wanted to stretch our legs during intermission. _ After sitting in the car all day, the travelers decided to stretch their legs.
examples: We wanted to stretch our legs during intermission.

stretch out.monolingual: [for one] to extend and stretch one’s body to its full length. _ She lay down, stretched out, and relaxed for the first time in days. _I need a bigger bed. I can’t stretch out in this one.
examples: She lay down, stretched out, and relaxed for the first time in days.

stretch someone or something out†.monolingual: to extend or draw out someone or something. _ Molly stretched the baby out to change his clothes. _ She stretched out the baby, who had rolled into a ball.
examples: Molly stretched the baby out to change his clothes.

strew something with something.monolingual: to cover something with bits of something. _ Who strewed the sidewalk with rice and confetti? _ The yards were strewn with leaves and branches after the storm.
examples: The yards were strewn with leaves and branches after the storm.

*stricken with something.monolingual: afflicted or overwhelmed with something. (*Typically: be ~; become ~; get ~.) _ Albert was stricken with a strange disease. _ Fred was stricken with remorse because of his rude remarks. _ Tom was stricken with the f lu after his trip to Russia.
examples: Albert was stricken with a strange disease.

strictly business.monolingual: 1. a matter or issue that is all business and no pleasure. _ This meeting is strictly business. We don’t have time for any leisure activity.
examples: This meeting is strictly business.

stride out of some place.monolingual: to walk with long steps out of some place. _ The angry customer strode out of the shop without purchasing anything. _We strode out of the restaurant, pledging never to go there again.
examples: The angry customer strode out of the shop without purchasing anything.

strike a match.monolingual: to light a match by rubbing it on a rough surface. _ Mary struck a match and lit a candle. _ When Sally struck a match to light a cigarette, Jane said quickly, “No smoking, please.”
examples: Mary struck a match and lit a candle.

strike a pose.monolingual: to position oneself in a certain posture. _ Bob struck a pose in front of the mirror to see how much he had bulked up. _ Lisa walked into the room and struck a pose, hoping she would be noticed.
examples: Bob struck a pose in front of the mirror to see how much he had bulked up.

strike at someone or something.monolingual: to hit at or toward someone or something. _ She struck at him, but he parried the blows. _ The bear struck at the branch, hoping to break it and get at the honey.
examples: She struck at him, but he parried the blows.

strike for something.monolingual: to conduct a work stoppage in order to gain something. _ The workers were striking for longer vacations. _ We are striking for higher pay.
examples: The workers were striking for longer vacations.

strike home with someone.monolingual: [for something] to awaken recognition and acceptance in a person. _ What you said really strikes home with me. _ Her comments struck home with her audience.
examples: What you said really strikes home with me.

strike it rich.monolingual: to acquire wealth suddenly. _If I could strike it rich, I wouldn’t have to work anymore. _ Sally ordered a dozen oysters and found a huge pearl in one of them. She struck it rich!
examples: If I could strike it rich, I wouldn’t have to work anymore.

strike out.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a baseball batter] to be declared out after making three strikes. (Baseball.) _And so Drew Wilson strikes out for his second time in this game! _He struck out in the second inning, and the manager took him out then.
examples: He struck out in the second inning, and the manager took him out then.

strike out for some place.monolingual: to begin a journey to some place; to set out on a journey for some place. _ We struck out for Denver, hoping to get there in a few hours. _ The hikers struck out for the cabin but were delayed by a sudden storm.
examples: We struck out for Denver, hoping to get there in a few hours.

strike over something.monolingual: to mark out printed words by putting x’s over them or a line through them. _ Please don’t strike over your errors. Erase them altogether. _Betty struck over most of the misspellings.
examples: Please don’t strike over your errors.

strike someone as something.monolingual: 1. [for a thought or behavior] to affect someone a certain way. _John’s rude behavior struck me as surprising. _Mary’s attitude struck me as childish.
examples: John’s rude behavior struck me as surprising.

strike someone funny.monolingual: Fig. to seem funny to someone. _ Sally has a great sense of humor. Everything she says strikes me funny. _ Why are you laughing? Did something I said strike you funny?
examples: Sally has a great sense of humor.

strike someone or something down†.monolingual: to knock someone or something down by striking. _ Max struck Lefty down with one blow. _ He struck down the weeds with a scythe.
examples: Max struck Lefty down with one blow.

strike someone’s fancy.monolingual: to appeal to someone. _ I’ll have some ice cream, please. Chocolate strikes my fancy right now. _ Why don’t you go to the store and buy a CD that strikes your fancy?
examples: I’ll have some ice cream, please.

strike something down†.monolingual: [for a court] to invalidate a ruling or law. _The higher court struck the ruling of the lower court down. _ The court struck down the ruling.
examples: The higher court struck the ruling of the lower court down.

strike something into something.monolingual: to knock something, such as a ball, into something. _Johnny struck the ball into the vacant lot. _ Ted struck golf ball after golf ball into the water.
examples: Johnny struck the ball into the vacant lot.

strike something out†.monolingual: to cross something out of a section of printing or writing. _This is wrong. Please strike it out. _ Strike out this sentence.
examples: This is wrong. Please strike it out.

strike something up†.monolingual: to begin something; to cause something to begin. (Typically, the playing of a band, a conversation, or a friendship.) _ We tried to strike a conversation up—to no avail. _ I struck up a conversation with Molly.
examples: We tried to strike a conversation up—to no avail.

strike the right note.monolingual: Fig. to achieve the desired effect; to do something suitable or pleasing. _ Meg struck the right note when she wore a dark suit to the interview. _The politician’s speech failed to strike the right note with the crowd.
examples: Meg struck the right note when she wore a dark suit to the interview.

strike up a conversation.monolingual: to start a conversation (with someone). _ I struck up an interesting conversation with someone on the bus yesterday. _It’s easy to strike up a conversation with someone when you’re traveling.
examples: I struck up an interesting conversation with someone on the bus yesterday.

strike up a friendship.monolingual: to become friends (with someone). _ I struck up a friendship with John while we were on a business trip together. _If you’re lonely, you should go out and try to strike up a friendship with someone you like.
examples: I struck up a friendship with John while we were on a business trip together.

strike up the band.monolingual: 1. Lit. to cause a (dance) band to start playing. _ Strike up the band, maestro, so we all can dance the night away.
examples: Strike up the band, maestro, so we all can dance the night away.

string someone along.monolingual: to maintain someone’s attention or interest, probably insincerely. _ You are just stringing me along because you like to borrow my car. You are not a real friend. _ Rachel strung her along for the sake of old times.
examples: You are just stringing me along because you like to borrow my car.
