string someone up†.monolingual: to hang someone. _ The sheriff swore he would string Tex up whenever he caught him. _He never strung up Tex.
examples: The sheriff swore he would string Tex up whenever he caught him.

string something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to unwind, stretch, or straighten something, such as wire, and extend it. _ The workers strung the wires out before installing them. _They strung out the wires first.
examples: The workers strung the wires out before installing them.

string something together.monolingual: to connect things, such as beads, together, as with string. _ I spent all afternoon stringing beads together. _ My pearls broke and I had to take them to a jeweler to have them strung together again.
examples: I spent all afternoon stringing beads together.

strip down.monolingual: to remove one’s clothing. _ The doctor told Joe to strip down for his examination. _ Joe stripped down for the examination.
examples: The doctor told Joe to strip down for his examination.

strip for something.monolingual: to take off one’s clothing for something. _ Todd went into the locker room and stripped for his shower. _ All the recruits stripped for their medical examination.
examples: Todd went into the locker room and stripped for his shower.

strip something in†.monolingual: to insert something into a line of print by gluing or a strip of paper. _ You will have to strip the accent in. _ Strip in a grave accent right here.
examples: You will have to strip the accent in.

strip to something.monolingual: to take off one’s clothing down to a particular level, usually to one’s skin, the waist, or some euphemistic way of expressing nudity or near nudity. _ Tom stripped to the waist and continued to labor in the hot sun. _ Tom stripped to the bare essent
examples: Tom stripped to the waist and continued to labor in the hot sun.

strive after something.monolingual: to try very hard to obtain something. _ I am always striving after perfection. _ Ted was striving after a promotion and finally got it.
examples: I am always striving after perfection.

strive against something.monolingual: to work against something. _ He worked hard, striving against failure at every turn. _ Things were difficult. I had to strive against quitting almost every day.
examples: He worked hard, striving against failure at every turn.

strive for something.monolingual: to try to obtain or bring about something. _ I am striving for the best possible result. _ Mary strives for perfection in everything she does.
examples: I am striving for the best possible result.

strive to do something.monolingual: to try hard to do something. _ She strove very hard to do what she had set out to do. _ Please strive to do it as best you can.
examples: She strove very hard to do what she had set out to do.

strive toward something.monolingual: to work toward a goal. _I always strive toward perfection. _ Mary strove toward doing her best at all times.
examples: I always strive toward perfection.

a stroke of genius.monolingual: an act of genius; a very clever and innovative idea or task. _ Your idea of painting the rock wall red was a stroke of genius.
examples: Your idea of painting the rock wall red was a stroke of genius.

a stroke of luck.monolingual: Fig. a bit of luck; a lucky happening. _ I had a stroke of luck and found Tom at home when I called. He’s not usually there. _ Unless I have a stroke of luck, I’m not going to finish this report by tomorrow.
examples: I had a stroke of luck and found Tom at home when I called.

stroke someone’s ego.monolingual: Fig. to flatter and praise someone. _If you have trouble with him, just take a few minutes and stroke his ego. You’ll soon have him eating out of your hand.
examples: If you have trouble with him, just take a few minutes and stroke his ego.

stroll around.monolingual: to walk around casually. _ I think I will stroll around a bit this evening. _ Would you like to stroll around a little and see the sights?
examples: I think I will stroll around a bit this evening.

stroll through something.monolingual: to walk casually through something or some place. _Would you like to stroll through the park with me? _ Let’s stroll through a few shops and see what the prices are like here.
examples: Let’s stroll through a few shops and see what the prices are like here.

the strong, silent type.monolingual: a strong, quiet man. _Clark looks like the strong, silent type. Actually he is slightly deaf and that’s fat, not muscle.
examples: Clark looks like the strong, silent type.

strong-arm tactics.monolingual: force; the use of force. _ No more strong-arm tactics. You need to be more subtle. _ Strongarm tactics are out. The boss says be gentle and don’t hurt anybody.
examples: No more strong-arm tactics.

struggle against someone or something.monolingual: to strive or battle against someone or something. _ There is no point in struggling against me. I will win out. _He struggled against the disease for a year before he died.
examples: There is no point in struggling against me.

struggle along under something.monolingual: to make do as well as one can under a particular burden. _ I will have to struggle along under these poor conditions for quite a while. _ I am sorry you have to struggle along under such burdens.
examples: I will have to struggle along under these poor conditions for quite a while.

struggle for something.monolingual: to strive to obtain something. _ I was struggling for a law degree when I won the lottery. _ I had to struggle for everything that came my way.
examples: I was struggling for a law degree when I won the lottery.

struggle on with something.monolingual: to make do as well as one can with something. _ I will have to struggle on with the car that I have. _We will struggle on with what we have, hoping for better someday.
examples: I will have to struggle on with the car that I have.

struggle to do something.monolingual: to strive or battle to do something. _ She struggled hard to meet her deadlines. _ We had to struggle to make ends meet.
examples: She struggled hard to meet her deadlines.

struggle to the death.monolingual: 1. Lit. a bitter struggle ending in death. _ The wolf and the elk fought in a struggle to the death.
examples: The wolf and the elk fought in a struggle to the death.

struggle with someone for something.monolingual: to fight with someone to obtain something. _ Max struggled with Lefty for the gun, and it went off. _ Timmy struggled with Bobby for the bicycle, and finally David took it away from both of them.
examples: Max struggled with Lefty for the gun, and it went off.

struggle with someone or something.monolingual: to fight or battle with someone or something. _ Fred struggled with Tom for a while and finally gave in. _Tom struggled with the disease for a while and finally succumbed to it.
examples: Fred struggled with Tom for a while and finally gave in.

strum something on something.monolingual: to brush or play with the fingers some stringed instrument, such as a guitar. _She strummed a nice little melody on her guitar. _ He strummed the accompaniment on the guitar.
examples: She strummed a nice little melody on her guitar.

strung out.monolingual: 1. extended in time; overly long. _ Why was that lecture so strung out? She talked and talked. _ It was strung out because there was very little to be said.
examples: Why was that lecture so strung out? She talked and talked.

strut around.monolingual: to stride around pompously. _ Stop strutting around in your new jeans and get to work! _ Tex was strutting around, showing off his new boots.
examples: Tex was strutting around, showing off his new boots.

strut one’s stuff.monolingual: Sl. to walk proudly and show off one’s best features or talents. _ Get out there on that stage and strut your stuff! _ I’m going to strut my stuff and become a star.
examples: I’m going to strut my stuff and become a star.

strut out of some place.monolingual: to stride pompously or showily out of some place. _ The clowns strutted out of the tent and joined the parade through the big top. _Tex strutted out of the saloon and got on his horse.
examples: The clowns strutted out of the tent and joined the parade through the big top.

stub something out†.monolingual: to put out something, such as a cigarette or cigar, by crushing the burning end against a hard object. _ Max stubbed his cigar out and tossed it into the street. _ He stubbed out his cigar.
examples: Max stubbed his cigar out and tossed it into the street.

stuck in traffic.monolingual: to be caught in a traffic jam. _I am sorry I am late. I was stuck in traffic. _ Our taxi was stuck in traffic and I thought I would never get to the airport on time.
examples: I am sorry I am late.

*stuck on someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. attached, as if by glue, to someone or something. (*Typically: be ~; become ~; get ~.) _The gum is stuck on me. How do I get it off ? _ The gum is stuck on the f loor.
examples: The gum is stuck on me.

stuck on something.monolingual: Fig. to be locked into an idea, cause, or purpose. _ Mary is really stuck on the idea of going to France this spring. _You’ve proposed a good plan, Jane, but you’re stuck on it. We may have to make some changes. Fig. to be confused by something, such
examples: Mary is really stuck on the idea of going to France this spring.

stuck with someone or something.monolingual: burdened with someone or something; left having to care for or deal with someone or something. _Please don’t leave me stuck with your aunt. She talks too much. _ My roommate quit school and left me stuck with the telephone bill.
examples: Please don’t leave me stuck with your aunt.

study for something.monolingual: to try to learn in preparation for an examination. _ I have to study for my calculus exam. _ Have you studied for your exam yet?
examples: I have to study for my calculus exam.

stuff and nonsense.monolingual: foolishness; foolish talk. _ Come on! Don’t give me all that stuff and nonsense! _ I don’t understand this book. It’s all stuff and nonsense as far as I am concerned.
examples: I don’t understand this book.

stuff someone’s head with something.monolingual: to fill someone’s brain with certain kinds of thoughts. _ Who has been stuffing your head with that nonsense? _ Tex thought that the government was stuffing peoples’ heads with all sorts of propaganda.
examples: Tex thought that the government was stuffing peoples’ heads with all sorts of propaganda.

stuff something down someone’s throat.monolingual: Fig. to force someone to hear, learn, endure, etc., some kind of information. _ I don’t like the nonsense they are stuffing down our throats. _ Please don’t try to stuff those lies down our throats.
examples: I don’t like the nonsense they are stuffing down our throats.

stuff something down something.monolingual: to force something down inside of something. _ Don stuffed the caulif lower leaves down the garbage disposal and turned it on. _ Timmy stuffed the leaves down the hole and covered them with dirt.
examples: Don stuffed the caulif lower leaves down the garbage disposal and turned it on.

stuff something up†.monolingual: to plug something by stuffing something in its opening. _ He stuffed the hole up with old newspapers. _ Liz stuffed up the hole with paper.
examples: He stuffed the hole up with old newspapers.

stuff something up something.monolingual: to force something upward or up into something. _He tried to hide the book by stuffing it up the chimney. _ Sam stuffed the money he found up the downspout, where he thought no one would find it.
examples: He tried to hide the book by stuffing it up the chimney.

stuff the ballot box.monolingual: to fill a ballot box with illegal votes or with more votes than the number of actual voters. _ The politician was charged with stuffing the ballot box. _ The ballot box was stuffed with lots of votes for the crooked politician.
examples: The politician was charged with stuffing the ballot box.

stumble on someone or something.monolingual: to trip over someone or something. _ There were three of us sleeping in the small tent. Each of us would stumble on the others whenever we went out or came in. _ I stumbled on the curb and twisted my ankle.
examples: There were three of us sleeping in the small tent.

stumble over someone or something.monolingual: to trip over someone or something. _ Tom stumbled over Bill, who was napping on the f loor. _Don’t stumble over the laundry basket.
examples: Tom stumbled over Bill, who was napping on the f loor.

stumble through something.monolingual: to get through a sequence of something awkwardly and falteringly. _ The cast stumbled through the first act and barely finished the second. _ Mary stumbled through her speech and f led from the stage.
examples: The cast stumbled through the first act and barely finished the second.

a stumbling block.monolingual: Fig. something that prevents or obstructs progress. _ We’d like to buy that house, but the high price is a stumbling block. _ Jim’s age is a stumbling block to getting another job. He’s over sixty.
examples: We’d like to buy that house, but the high price is a stumbling block.

stump for someone.monolingual: to go about making political speeches in support of someone. _ The vice president was out stumping for members of Congress who were running this term. _ Since all the politicians were out stumping for one another, there was no one in the capital to v
examples: The vice president was out stumping for members of Congress who were running this term.

stump someone.monolingual: to confuse or puzzle someone. _ I have a question that will really stump you. When was the Achaean League established?
examples: I have a question that will really stump you.

sub for someone or something.monolingual: to substitute for someone or something. _I have to sub for Roger at work this weekend. _ Will pliers sub for the wrench you wanted?
examples: I have to sub for Roger at work this weekend.

subdivide something into something.monolingual: to divide something into parts. _ They subdivided the land into several valuable parcels. _Sam tried to subdivide his large lot into three smaller lots, but the zoning commission wouldn’t let him do it.
examples: They subdivided the land into several valuable parcels.

subject to something.monolingual: likely to have something, such as a physical disorder. _ The sick man was subject to dizzy spells. _ I am subject to frequent headaches.
examples: The sick man was subject to dizzy spells.

subjugate someone to someone.monolingual: to suppress someone in someone else’s favor. _ The army sought to subjugate everyone to the king.
examples: The army sought to subjugate everyone to the king.

submit to something.monolingual: to surrender to something; to agree to something. _He submitted to the cross-examination. _ She will probably refuse to submit to surgery.
examples: He submitted to the cross-examination.

subpoena someone to do something.monolingual: to formally deliver a document forcing someone to do something for a legal process. _The attorney subpoenaed a number of witnesses to testify. _I subpoenaed four witnesses to appear but none of them showed up.
examples: The attorney subpoenaed a number of witnesses to testify.

subscribe to something.monolingual: 1. to agree with a policy. _I don’t subscribe to the scheme you have just described. _You don’t have to subscribe to the policy to accept it.
examples: I don’t subscribe to the scheme you have just described.

subsist on something.monolingual: to exist on something; to stay alive on something. _ We can barely subsist on this amount of money. We need more! _ They are able to do no more than subsist on what Mrs. Harris is paid.
examples: We can barely subsist on this amount of money.

substitute for someone or something.monolingual: to serve as a replacement for someone or something. _I have to substitute for Roger at work this weekend. _ Do you think that this will substitute for the one you wanted?
examples: I have to substitute for Roger at work this weekend.

subtract something from something else.monolingual: to deduct or take away something from something else. _ Please subtract the cost of the meal from my fee. _ I demanded that they subtract the extra charge from my bill.
examples: Please subtract the cost of the meal from my fee.

succeed as something.monolingual: to flourish or prosper as a type of person. _ I hope I succeed as a bank teller. _ Jamie succeeded as an investigator.
examples: I hope I succeed as a bank teller.

succeed at something.monolingual: to prosper or flourish in some task. _ I hope I can succeed at the task you have assigned me. _ I am sure you will succeed at it.
examples: I hope I can succeed at the task you have assigned me.

succeed in something.monolingual: to prosper or flourish in some position or office. _ I hope you succeed in your new job. _ We knew you would succeed in doing what you wanted to do.
examples: I hope you succeed in your new job.

succeed someone as something.monolingual: to take the place of someone as something; to supplant someone in something. _ Jeff will succeed Claude as president of the organization. _ You are not allowed to succeed yourself as president.
examples: Jeff will succeed Claude as president of the organization.

succeed to something.monolingual: to fall heir to something; to take something over. _Carl will succeed to the throne when he is of age. _Mary succeeded to the throne at the age of three months.
examples: Carl will succeed to the throne when he is of age.

succumb to something.monolingual: to yield to something, especially a temptation, fatal disease, a human weakness, etc. _ He finally succumbed to his pneumonia. _She did not succumb to the disease until she was very old.
examples: He finally succumbed to his pneumonia.

such and such.monolingual: someone or something whose name has been forgotten or should not be said. _ Mary said that such and such was coming to her party, but I forgot their names. _If you walk into a store and ask for such and such and they don’t have it, you go to a differ
examples: Mary said that such and such was coming to her party, but I forgot their names.

such as it is.monolingual: Cliché in the imperfect state that one sees it; in the less-than-perfect condition in which one sees it. _ This is where I live. This is my glorious home—such as it is. _I’ve worked for days on this report, and I’ve done the best that I can do. It’s
examples: This is where I live.

such is life!.monolingual: That is the way things happen! (Usually in reference to an unfortunate outcome.) _Oh, well. Everything can’t be perfect. Such is life! _So I failed my test. Such is life! I can take it again some time.
examples: Oh, well. Everything can’t be perfect.

suck someone or something down†.monolingual: [for a vacuum or water currents] to pull someone or something downward. _The savage currents sucked the swimmers down to their death. _ The current sucked down the f loating trees.
examples: The savage currents sucked the swimmers down to their death.

suck someone or something under.monolingual: [for a current or waves] to pull someone or something beneath the surface of the water. _ The strong rip tide almost sucked me under! _ It almost sucked our boat under.
examples: It almost sucked our boat under.

suck someone’s hind tit.monolingual: Sl. to be forced to do someone’s bidding no matter how unpleasant or impossible. (Fig. on the idea of the last of a litter of animals to get its mother’s milk. Potentially offensive. Use only with discretion.) _ What am I supposed to do—suck his hind
examples: She acts like everybody has to suck her hind tit to keep their jobs.

suck something from something.monolingual: to draw something out of something by the application of a vacuum. _Freddie used his straw to suck the last of the cola from the can. _ The machine sucked the water from the bottom of the barrel.
examples: Freddie used his straw to suck the last of the cola from the can.

suck something in†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to draw something into one’s mouth by sucking. _ She sucked the milk shake in so hard she nearly collapsed the straw. _Liz sucked in the fresh air.
examples: She sucked the milk shake in so hard she nearly collapsed the straw.

suck something up†.monolingual: to pick something up by suction, as with a vacuum cleaner, or through a straw. _Will this vacuum suck all this dirt up? _The vacuum cleaner sucked up all the dirt.
examples: The vacuum cleaner sucked up all the dirt.

suck up to someone.monolingual: Sl. to attempt to gain influence with or favor from someone. _ In school, Richard was always sucking up to the teacher. _ Don’t suck up to me. It won’t do any good.
examples: In school, Richard was always sucking up to the teacher.

sucker list.monolingual: Fig. a list of potential dupes; a list of people who might be taken in by deception. _ I’m sure on their sucker list. They are trying to get me to give a lecture and receive a free clock or something. _ Here’s the sucker list. Call them all and try t
examples: I’m sure on their sucker list.

sue for something.monolingual: to file a lawsuit in order to get something. _ If you so much as harm a hair on my head, I will sue for damages. _Ted sued for back pay in his dispute with a former employer.
examples: If you so much as harm a hair on my head, I will sue for damages.

sue someone for something.monolingual: to file a lawsuit against someone in order to get something. _ I will sue you for damages if you do anything else to my car! _ She sued her employer for failure to provide a safe workplace.
examples: She sued her employer for failure to provide a safe workplace.

suffer a setback.monolingual: to have a minor or temporary failure. _ We suffered a setback when much of our vineyard was damaged by a fungus.
examples: We suffered a setback when much of our vineyard was damaged by a fungus.

suffer from something.monolingual: to endure or experience unpleasantness, a disease, or a health condition. _ Jeff is suffering from the f lu. _ I’m afraid that you must suffer from the disease until it has run its course. _ Toby is really suffering from the cold.
examples: Jeff is suffering from the f lu.

suffer under someone.monolingual: to endure the punishments or bad treatment of someone. _The citizens suffered badly under the rule of the cruel king. _ We suffered under Carlos and we will suffer under his successor.
examples: The citizens suffered badly under the rule of the cruel king.

suffice for someone or something.monolingual: to be sufficient for someone or something. _ This serving will suffice for me. Did you get enough? _ Will this suffice for you?
examples: This serving will suffice for me.

suffix something onto something.monolingual: to add an inflection or other part of a word onto another word. _ The students were told to suffix the correct plural marker onto all the nouns in the list. _ What do you get when you suffix -ed onto a verb like talk?
examples: The students were told to suffix the correct plural marker onto all the nouns in the list.

suffuse something with something.monolingual: to saturate something with something, usually a color. _ The sun suffused the afternoon sky with orange and yellow. _ The bright light suffused the leaves with a golden glow.
examples: The sun suffused the afternoon sky with orange and yellow.

suggest itself to someone.monolingual: [for an idea] to seem to present itself to someone. _ A new scheme suggested itself to Alice as she looked at the records of the last attempt. _ As you read this, does anything suggest itself to you?
examples: A new scheme suggested itself to Alice as she looked at the records of the last attempt.

suggest something to someone.monolingual: to make a suggestion of something to someone. _ The waiter suggested the roast beef to all his customers. _What did you suggest to the people at the other table? They look quite pleased with their meal.
examples: The waiter suggested the roast beef to all his customers.

*suggestive of something.monolingual: reminiscent of something; suggesting something. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ Bill’s homemade soup is suggestive of his mother’s. _ The new movie was suggestive of an old one I had seen on TV.
examples: Bill’s homemade soup is suggestive of his mother’s.

suit someone’s fancy.monolingual: to appeal to someone’s imagination, fantasy, or preferences. _ Does this handbag suit your fancy, or would you prefer something larger? _ I think a big bowl of ice cream would suit my fancy quite nicely.
examples: I think a big bowl of ice cream would suit my fancy quite nicely.

suit yourself..monolingual: Inf. You decide the way you want it.; Have it your way. _Mary: I think I want the red one. Tom: Suit yourself. _John (reading the menu): The steak sounds good, but it’s hard to pass up the fried chicken. Sally: Suit yourself. I’ll have the steak.
examples: Mary: I think I want the red one.

*suited for something.monolingual: appropriate for something. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ Do you think I am suited for this kind of work? _Those clothes are not suited for outdoor work.
examples: Those clothes are not suited for outdoor work.

sum and substance.monolingual: a summary; the gist. _ Can you quickly tell me the sum and substance of your proposal? _ In trying to explain the sum and substance of the essay, Thomas failed to mention the middle name of the hero.
examples: In trying to explain the sum and substance of the essay, Thomas failed to mention the middle name of the hero.

summon something up†.monolingual: to call forth particular qualities, such as strength, courage, wisdom, etc. _ She summoned her courage up and went into the room. _ Liz summoned up all her courage.
examples: She summoned her courage up and went into the room.

the sun belt.monolingual: Fig. the southern U.S. states, where it is generally warm and sunny. _ I want to retire to the sun belt. _ The population of the sun belt is exploding.
examples: I want to retire to the sun belt.

sunday best.monolingual: one’s best clothing, which one would wear to church. _ We are in our Sunday best, ready to go. _ I got mud on my Sunday best.
examples: We are in our Sunday best, ready to go.

sunday driver.monolingual: a slow and leisurely driver who appears to be sightseeing and enjoying the view, holding up traffic in the process. (Also a term of address.) _I’m a Sunday driver, and I’m sorry. I just can’t bear to go faster. _Move over, you Sunday driver!
examples: I’m a Sunday driver, and I’m sorry.

sunday-go-to-meeting clothes.monolingual: Rur. one’s best clothes. _ John was all dressed up in his Sunday-go-to-meeting clothes. _ I hate to be wearing my Sunday-go-to-meeting clothes when everyone else is casually dressed.
examples: John was all dressed up in his Sunday-go-to-meeting clothes.

sunny-side up.monolingual: Fig. [of eggs] with yolks facing up and not turned over or cooked through; straight up. _ I’ll have my eggs sunny-side up, with toast and coffee. _People who like sunny-side up eggs wouldn’t dream of eating a whole raw egg.
examples: I’ll have my eggs sunny-side up, with toast and coffee.

supply and demand.monolingual: the availability of things or people as compared to the need to utilize the things or people; the availability of goods compared to the number of willing customers for the goods. _ Sometimes you can find what you want by shopping around and other tim
examples: Sometimes you can find what you want by shopping around and other times almost no store carries the items you are looking for.

supposed to do something.monolingual: expected or intended to do something; obliged or allowed to do something. _ You’re supposed to say “excuse me” when you burp. _ Mom says you’re supposed to come inside for dinner now.
examples: You’re supposed to say “excuse me” when you burp.

*sure as hell.monolingual: Inf. very sure. (Use discretion with hell. *Also: as ~.) _ As sure as hell, Ill be there on time. _ As sure as hell he did it!
examples: As sure as hell, Ill be there on time.

sure as shooting!.monolingual: Inf. Absolutely yes! (An elaboration of Sure.) _Bill: Are you going to be there Monday night? Bob: Sure as shooting! _Bob: Will you take this over to the main office? Bill: Sure as shooting!

sure thing..monolingual: Inf. I certainly will. _ Sue: Will you be at the reception? Bob: Sure thing. _Bill: You remember my cousin, Tom, don’t you? Bob: Sure thing. Hi, Tom.
examples: Sue: Will you be at the reception? Bob: Sure thing.

surf and turf.monolingual: fish and beef; lobster and beef. (A dinner serving incorporating both expensive seafood and an expensive cut of beef. Alludes to the sea and to the pasture. Fixed order.) _Walter ordered the surf and turf, but Alice ordered only a tiny salad. _ No su
examples: Walter ordered the surf and turf, but Alice ordered only a tiny salad.

surf the net.monolingual: to browse around in the contents of the Internet. _ I spend an hour a day or more surfing the Net.
examples: I spend an hour a day or more surfing the Net.

surge up.monolingual: to rush or gush upwards. _ A spring of fresh water surged up under the stone and f lowed out on the ground. _ The oil surged up and blew out into the open air in a tall black column.
examples: A spring of fresh water surged up under the stone and f lowed out on the ground.

surprise someone by something.monolingual: to astonish someone by doing or being something. _ You surprised me by your forthrightness. _ No one was surprised by the way it happened.
examples: You surprised me by your forthrightness.

surprise someone with something.monolingual: to astonish someone by presenting or showing something. _ I surprised her with a bouquet of roses. _ He surprised Roger with a new car.
examples: I surprised her with a bouquet of roses.

surrender to someone or something.monolingual: to give in to someone or something; to yield to someone or something. _ The robber surrendered to the cops. _ I will never surrender to my baser passions.
examples: The robber surrendered to the cops.

the survival of the fittest.monolingual: the idea that the most able or fit will survive (while the less able and less fit will perish). (This is used literally as a principle of the theory of evolution.) _ In college, it’s the survival of the fittest. You have to keep working in order to s
examples: In college, it’s the survival of the fittest.

susceptible to something.monolingual: 1. easily persuaded; easily influenced. _ The students were susceptible to the allure of drugs. _The young revolutionaries were susceptible to propaganda.
examples: The students were susceptible to the allure of drugs.

suspect someone of something.monolingual: to think or believe that someone has done something. _I suspect the clerk of stealing. _Ted was suspected of leaving the door unlocked when he left last Friday.
examples: I suspect the clerk of stealing.

suspend someone from something.monolingual: to prevent someone from participating in something. (Usually as a form of discipline.) _ The principal suspended the student from classes for a week. _Ted was suspended from school for three days.
examples: The principal suspended the student from classes for a week.

suspend something by something.monolingual: to hang something by something. _ The workers carefully positioned the stone that was suspended by a steel cable. _ Will suspended the decoration by a fine thread.
examples: The workers carefully positioned the stone that was suspended by a steel cable.

suss someone out†.monolingual: Sl. to try to figure someone out. _ I can’t seem to suss Tom out. What a strange guy. _ I don’t have any luck sussing out people I don’t know well.
examples: I can’t seem to suss Tom out.

sustain someone in something.monolingual: to stand by or support someone through some problem. _ She knew she could count on her friends to sustain her in times of trouble. _ We will sustain you in the difficult times the best we can.
examples: She knew she could count on her friends to sustain her in times of trouble.

swab something down†.monolingual: to wash or scrub something, such as the deck of a ship. _ The sailors were told to swab the deck down each day. _ Swab down the deck!
examples: The sailors were told to swab the deck down each day.

swallow one’s pride.monolingual: Fig. to forget one’s pride and accept something humiliating. _ I had to swallow my pride and admit that I was wrong. _ When you’re trying to master a new skill, you find yourself swallowing your pride quite often.
examples: I had to swallow my pride and admit that I was wrong.

swallow someone or something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to eat or gobble up someone or something. _ The fairy-tale wolf threatened to swallow the pig up in one bite. _ The wolf swallowed up the meat in one bite.
examples: The fairy-tale wolf threatened to swallow the pig up in one bite.

swallow something down†.monolingual: to swallow something. _Here, take this pill and swallow it down. _ Liz swallowed down the pill.
examples: Here, take this pill and swallow it down.

swan song.monolingual: Fig. the last work or performance of a playwright, musician, actor, etc., before death or retirement. _ His portrayal of Lear was the actor’s swan song. _ We didn’t know that her performance last night was the singer’s swan song.
examples: His portrayal of Lear was the actor’s swan song.

swap with someone.monolingual: to exchange someone or something with someone. _ I like yours better. I’ll swap with you. _ If you don’t want the sandwich you have, I will swap with you.
examples: I like yours better.

swarm around someone or something.monolingual: to gather or crowd around someone or something, in the manner of a swarm of bees. _The little children swarmed around the lady with the candy. _ The bees swarmed around the f lowers.
examples: The little children swarmed around the lady with the candy.

swarm out of something.monolingual: to move out of something in great numbers. _ The bees swarmed out of the hive. _ People swarmed out of the park at the end of the game.
examples: The bees swarmed out of the hive.

swarm through something.monolingual: to gather in a crowd and move through something or some place. _ The shoppers swarmed through the store, buying everything in sight. _ The locusts swarmed through the field, eating the entire harvest.
examples: The shoppers swarmed through the store, buying everything in sight.

swarm with someone or something.monolingual: to be abundant or crowded with moving people or things. _The playground was swarming with children, and I couldn’t find my own. _ The picnic blanket swarmed with ants.
examples: The playground was swarming with children, and I couldn’t find my own.

sway back and forth.monolingual: to swing or bend from one direction to another. _ The pendulum swayed back and forth, counting off the seconds. _ Mary was swaying back and forth, keeping time to the music.
examples: The pendulum swayed back and forth, counting off the seconds.

sway from side to side.monolingual: to swing or bend from one side to the other. _ The car swayed from side to side as we started out, indicating that something was seriously wrong. _He swayed from side to side with the rhythm of the music.
examples: The car swayed from side to side as we started out, indicating that something was seriously wrong.

sway someone to something.monolingual: to convince someone to do something. _ I think I can sway her to join our side. _ We could not sway Ted to our position.
examples: I think I can sway her to join our side.

swear at someone or something.monolingual: to curse someone or something. _ Please don’t swear at the children. _ Scott swore at the police station as he drove by.
examples: Please don’t swear at the children.

swear by someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to utter an oath on someone or something. _ I swear by Jupiter that I will be there on time. _ She swore by her sainted mother that she would never do it again. _ The sheriff swore by his badge that he would lock her up if she ever did it aga
examples: I swear by Jupiter that I will be there on time.

swear like a trooper.monolingual: to curse and swear with great facility. (The trooper here refers to a soldier.) _ Mrs. Wilson was known to swear like a trooper on occasion. _The clerk started swearing like a trooper, and the customer started crying.
examples: Mrs. Wilson was known to swear like a trooper on occasion.

swear someone to something.monolingual: to cause someone to take an oath pledging something, such as silence or secrecy, about something. _ I swore Larry to secrecy, but he told anyway. _ We were sworn to silence about the new product.
examples: I swore Larry to secrecy, but he told anyway.

swear something out† against someone.monolingual: to file a criminal complaint against someone. _Walter swore a warrant out against Jeff. _ He swore out a warrant against Tony.
examples: Walter swore a warrant out against Jeff.

swear something to someone.monolingual: to pledge or promise something to someone. _ I had to swear my allegiance to the general before I could become one of his bodyguards. _ We swore our loyalty to our country.
examples: I had to swear my allegiance to the general before I could become one of his bodyguards.

swear to something.monolingual: to claim that what one says is absolutely true. _ It is true. I swear to it. _ I think I have remembered it all, but I couldn’t swear to it.
examples: It is true. I swear to it.

sweat for something.monolingual: Fig. to work very hard for something. _I sweat for every dollar I bring in. _Ted really sweats for his salary.
examples: I sweat for every dollar I bring in.

sweat something off†.monolingual: Fig. to get rid of excess fat or weight by exercising or taking a steam bath to produce sweat. _ I think I can sweat a lot of this fat off. _Tony tried to sweat off some of his excess weight.
examples: I think I can sweat a lot of this fat off.

sweep along.monolingual: to glide along smoothly, as if flying. _ The sailboat swept along, pushed by the strong wind. _ The fallen leaves blew up against the fence, swept along by a strong wind.
examples: The sailboat swept along, pushed by the strong wind.

sweep off.monolingual: to exit quickly. _ He stopped only brief ly, then swept off again. _ Mary swept off, leaving Ted standing there confused.
examples: He stopped only brief ly, then swept off again.

sweep out of some place.monolingual: to exit from some place quickly with style or grace. _ The famous actress swept out of the room in a grand fashion. _ She swept out of her dressing room and walked on stage just as her cue was uttered.
examples: The famous actress swept out of the room in a grand fashion.

sweep over someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to pass over and cover someone. _ The waves swept over us and nearly drowned us. _ The f lood swept over the farmers who would not leave their homes.
examples: The waves swept over us and nearly drowned us.

sweep someone or something aside†.monolingual: to push or brush someone or something aside. _The guards swept the spectators aside as the king’s coach approached. _ They swept aside the spectators.
examples: The guards swept the spectators aside as the king’s coach approached.

sweep someone or something away†.monolingual: to dispose of someone or something by pushing or brushing away. _ The waves nearly swept us away. _ The waves caused by the storm swept away all the debris on the beach.
examples: The waves nearly swept us away.

sweep something back†.monolingual: to push or move something backward in the shape of a curve. _ He took the brush and swept his hair back in a huge wave. _ She swept back her hair in a striking arrangement.
examples: He took the brush and swept his hair back in a huge wave.

sweep something down†.monolingual: to clean something by sweeping. _ Please sweep this f loor down whenever you make a mess here. _ Jeff will sweep down the f loor before he goes home.
examples: Please sweep this f loor down whenever you make a mess here.

sweep something out†.monolingual: to clean something out by sweeping. _Someone has to sweep the garage out. _Don’t sweep out this room. I’ll do it.
examples: Someone has to sweep the garage out.

sweep something under the carpet.monolingual: 1. Lit. to hide dirt by brushing it away under the edge of a carpet. _ He was in such a hurry with the cleaning that he just swept the dirt under the carpet. _ She swept the dirt under the carpet, hoping no one would find it.
examples: He was in such a hurry with the cleaning that he just swept the dirt under the carpet.

sweep something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to clean up and remove something, such as dirt, by sweeping. _ Please sweep these crumbs up. _ Can you sweep up these crumbs?
examples: Please sweep these crumbs up.

sweep up.monolingual: to clean up by sweeping. _ Would you sweep up this time? _ Please give me a few minutes to sweep up before you come to visit.
examples: Please give me a few minutes to sweep up before you come to visit.

sweep up after someone.monolingual: to clean up the dirt left on the floor by someone. _ Do you mind sweeping up after the kids? _ I had to sweep up after your party and I am not happy about it!

sweet and sour.monolingual: a combination of fruity sweet and sour, but not necessarily salty, flavors. (Typically referring to certain Chinese-American foods.) _ I prefer sweet-andsour pork to anything else on the menu. _ Alice does not care for sweet-and-sour dishes, but she
examples: I prefer sweet-andsour pork to anything else on the menu.

sweet nothings.monolingual: affectionate but unimportant or meaningless words spoken to a loved one. _ Jack was whispering sweet nothings in Joan’s ear when they were dancing. _ The two lovers sat in the cinema exchanging sweet nothings.
examples: Jack was whispering sweet nothings in Joan’s ear when they were dancing.

*sweet on someone.monolingual: Rur. fond of someone. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ Tom is sweet on Mary. He may ask her to marry him. _ Mary’s sweet on him, too.
examples: Tom is sweet on Mary.

sweeten someone up†.monolingual: to make someone more pleasant. _ I had hoped that a week in the Caribbean would sweeten him up. _ The trip sweetened him up, but not for long.
examples: I had hoped that a week in the Caribbean would sweeten him up.

sweeten something up†.monolingual: to make something taste sweeter. _ Where is the sugar? I need to sweeten this up a little. _ A little sugar will sweeten up the coffee.
examples: Where is the sugar? I need to sweeten this up a little.

sweeten the pot.monolingual: Fig. to increase the amount of money bet in a card game with hopes of encouraging other players to bet more enthusiastically. _ John sweetened the pot hoping others would follow.
examples: John sweetened the pot hoping others would follow.

sweet-talk someone.monolingual: Rur. to talk convincingly to someone with much flattery. _ I didn’t want to help her, but she sweet-talked me into it. _ He sweet-talked her for a while, and she finally agreed to go to the dance with him.
examples: I didn’t want to help her, but she sweet-talked me into it.

swell out.monolingual: to bulge outward; to expand outward. _ The sides of the box swelled out because it was too full. _ The west wall of the garage swelled out just before the building collapsed.
examples: The sides of the box swelled out because it was too full.

swell up.monolingual: to enlarge; to inflate; to bulge out. _ I struck my thumb with a hammer and it swelled up something awful.
examples: I struck my thumb with a hammer and it swelled up something awful.

swell with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to expand from a particular cause. _ My knee joints swelled with arthritis. _ His nose swelled after it was struck by the door.
examples: My knee joints swelled with arthritis.

*a swelled head.monolingual: Fig. a state of being conceited. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ John got a swelled head after he won the prize. _ Don’t get a swelled head from all this success.
examples: John got a swelled head after he won the prize.

swerve into someone or something.monolingual: to turn sharply and directly into someone or something. (Usually an accident.) _ The car almost swerved into a pedestrian. _ The bus swerved into a truck.
examples: The car almost swerved into a pedestrian.

swift and sure.monolingual: fast and certain. (As with the flight of a well-aimed arrow.) _ The response of the governor to the criticism by the opposing party was swift and sure. _ The boxer’s punch was swift and sure and resulted in a quick knockout and a very short match.
examples: The response of the governor to the criticism by the opposing party was swift and sure.

swill something down†.monolingual: to drink something, especially an alcoholic drink, in great gulps. _ The guy took a quart of beer and swilled it down in a few seconds. _ He swilled down a quart of beer.
examples: The guy took a quart of beer and swilled it down in a few seconds.

swim around.monolingual: to swim here and there. _ I just like to get into the pool and swim around. _I saw only one fish swimming around in your aquarium.
examples: I just like to get into the pool and swim around.

swim before someone’s eyes.monolingual: Fig. [for something, such as spots or visions] to appear in one’s field of vision. _ I was getting feverish and spots swam before my eyes. _ Visions of total destruction swam before my eyes as the bus skidded in the snow.
examples: I was getting feverish and spots swam before my eyes.

swim for it.monolingual: to escape by swimming. _ I escaped from the guard, dived into the river, and swam for it. _ Max swam for it, but he didn’t get away.
examples: I escaped from the guard, dived into the river, and swam for it.

swim for someone or something.monolingual: to travel toward someone or something by swimming. _I swam for George, who was farther out, holding onto a f loat. _ I am going to swim for the island.
examples: I swam for George, who was farther out, holding onto a f loat.

swim in something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to swim in a body of water. _ Is it safe to swim in this water? _ Can we swim in your pool?
examples: Can we swim in your pool? 2.

swim into something.monolingual: to enter something swimming. _ They swam into a lovely grotto. _ Ted swam into the cove and got out on the beach.
examples: They swam into a lovely grotto.

swim toward someone or something.monolingual: to swim in the direction of someone or something. _ Jeff swam toward the drowning man and helped him. _I swam toward the boat.
examples: Jeff swam toward the drowning man and helped him.

swim with something.monolingual: to swim in the same direction as the movement of water. _Fred had no trouble swimming with the current. _Please swim with the current and not against it.
examples: Fred had no trouble swimming with the current.

swimming in something.monolingual: Fig. having lots of something. _ Right now we are swimming in merchandise. In a month it will be gone. _The Wilmington-Thorpes are just swimming in money.
examples: Right now we are swimming in merchandise.

swimming with someone or something.monolingual: Fig. engulfed with someone or something. _ The scene of the crime was swimming with cops and reporters. _ The hotel was swimming with out-of-town visitors.
examples: The scene of the crime was swimming with cops and reporters.

swing at someone or something.monolingual: to strike at someone or something. _Max swung at the cop—a serious mistake. _ The batter swung at the ball and missed.
examples: Max swung at the cop—a serious mistake.

swing for something.monolingual: Fig. [for someone] to die by hanging for committing a crime. _The sheriff swore that Tex would swing for the killing. _ Max said he would not swing for something that Lefty had done.
examples: The sheriff swore that Tex would swing for the killing.

swing from something.monolingual: to hang or dangle from something. _The child was swinging from an exercise bar on her swing set. _ Ted was swinging from the edge of the cliff, waiting to be rescued.
examples: The child was swinging from an exercise bar on her swing set.

swing into high gear.monolingual: to begin operating at a fast pace; to increase the rate of activity. _ During the winter season we swing into high gear around here. _The chef swings into high gear around six o’clock in preparation for the theater crowd.
examples: During the winter season we swing into high gear around here.

swing into something.monolingual: to enter something by swinging. _ The monkey swung into its cage, and I quickly locked the cage door. _ I grabbed a rope and swung into the cave, where my pursuer couldn’t see me.
examples: The monkey swung into its cage, and I quickly locked the cage door.

swing something.monolingual: Fig. to make something happen. _I hope I can swing a deal that will make us all a lot of money. _ We all hope you can swing it.
examples: I hope I can swing a deal that will make us all a lot of money.

swing to something.monolingual: to change to a different position or attitude. _ The mood of the country is swinging to conservatism. _ Soon the attitudes of the people will swing to the opposite side.
examples: The mood of the country is swinging to conservatism.

swing with someone or something.monolingual: Sl. to appreciate someone or something. _ Man, I can really swing with that color. Glorious! _I can really swing with John. He and I are real close.
examples: Man, I can really swing with that color.

swirl about someone or something.monolingual: [for something, such as dust or a fluid] to circle and wind about someone or something. _ The snow swirled about me as I walked along. _ The smoke swirled about the tiny campfire.
examples: The snow swirled about me as I walked along.

swirl around.monolingual: [for dust or a fluid] to circle around. _The liquid swirled around in the f lask as Toby shook it up. _ Dust swirled around the room in the sunlight.
examples: The liquid swirled around in the f lask as Toby shook it up.

swish around.monolingual: [for a fluid] to slosh or rush around. _All that water I drank is swishing around in my stomach. _ I can hear the water swishing around in the pipes.
examples: All that water I drank is swishing around in my stomach.

switch around.monolingual: to change, swing, or turn around. _ The horse switched around and ran the other way. _ I switched around and sat looking the other way for a while.
examples: The horse switched around and ran the other way.

switch into something.monolingual: to change [one’s clothes] into something else. _ Let me switch into something a little more dressy if we are going to a nice restaurant. _I have to switch into something more comfortable.
examples: Let me switch into something a little more dressy if we are going to a nice restaurant.

switch off.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to turn itself off. _ At midnight, all the lights switched off automatically. _ The television switched off after I went to sleep.
examples: At midnight, all the lights switched off automatically.

switch on.monolingual: 1. [for something] to turn itself on. _ Exactly at midnight, the lights switched on. _ The radio switched on early in the morning to wake us up.
examples: Exactly at midnight, the lights switched on.

switch someone or something around†.monolingual: to change, swing, or turn someone or something. _I was prepared for a late f light out of Miami, but they switched me around at the last minute. _ They switched around my f lights.
examples: I was prepared for a late f light out of Miami, but they switched me around at the last minute.

switch someone or something off†.monolingual: to cause someone or something to be quiet or stop doing something. _ I got tired of listening to her, so I punched the button and switched her off. _ I switched off the television set.
examples: I got tired of listening to her, so I punched the button and switched her off.

switch someone or something through.monolingual: to connect someone or something with something else. _I will switch you through the priority network. _ The operator switched the call through.
examples: I will switch you through the priority network.

switch something on†.monolingual: to close an electrical circuit that causes something to start functioning or operating. _ Please switch the fan on. _ I switched on the fan.
examples: Please switch the fan on.

switch something out†.monolingual: to remove something from an electrical circuit to turn it off. _Please switch the light out. _ I switched out the light.
examples: Please switch the light out.

switch something to something else.monolingual: to change something to something else. _ It was hot so I switched the thermostat from heating to cooling. _ Mary switched the controls to automatic so she wouldn’t have to worry about them constantly.
examples: It was hot so I switched the thermostat from heating to cooling.

switch to something.monolingual: to change to something. _I am going to switch to a cheaper brand of tissues. _ We switched to a different long-distance telephone company to save some money.
examples: I am going to switch to a cheaper brand of tissues.

switched on.monolingual: 1. Sl. alert and up-to-date; with it. _ My brother is switched on and has lots of friends. _ I’m not switched on. In fact, I am pretty dull.
examples: My brother is switched on and has lots of friends.

swoon over someone or something.monolingual: to seem to faint or pass out about someone or something. _The kids swooned over the rock star like the kids of thirty years ago. _ Evangeline swooned over the frightful news.
examples: The kids swooned over the rock star like the kids of thirty years ago.

synchronize something with something els.monolingual: to set or adjust something to coordinate its timing with something else. _Would you please synchronize your watch with mine? _ We could never synchronize our schedules so that we could get together.
examples: We could never synchronize our schedules so that we could get together.

tab someone for something.monolingual: to choose someone for something. _ The director tabbed Sam for a walk-on part. _ I wanted her to tab me for a part.
examples: The director tabbed Sam for a walk-on part.

table a motion.monolingual: to postpone the discussion of something during a meeting. _Mary suggested that they should table the motion. _The motion for a new policy was tabled until the next meeting.
examples: Mary suggested that they should table the motion.

tack something down†.monolingual: to fasten something down with small nails. _ Someone had better tack this carpet down. _ Please tack down this carpet.
examples: Someone had better tack this carpet down.

tack something up†.monolingual: to fasten something onto something with tacks. _ The drapes started to fall, so we tacked them up again. _ Please tack up these posters.
examples: The drapes started to fall, so we tacked them up again.

tag someone out†.monolingual: [in baseball] to touch with the ball, and thereby put someone out. _The shortstop tagged the runner out and retired the side. _ He tagged out the runner.
examples: The shortstop tagged the runner out and retired the side.

tail after someone.monolingual: Fig. to follow after someone. _Why do you always have to tail after me? _ There is someone tailing after you.
examples: There is someone tailing after you.

tail off.monolingual: to dwindle to nothing. _The number of people filing for unemployment insurance is beginning to tail off. _ As the storms tailed off, we began to realize how much damage had been done.
examples: The number of people filing for unemployment insurance is beginning to tail off.

the tail wagging the dog.monolingual: a situation where a small part is controlling the whole of something. _ John was just hired yesterday, and today he’s bossing everyone around. It’s a case of the tail wagging the dog. _Why is this small matter taking so much time? Now it’s the tail w
examples: John was just hired yesterday, and today he’s bossing everyone around.

taint something with something.monolingual: to spoil or debase something with something. _ The f lood tainted the drinking water with disease germs. _The food had been tainted with germs.
examples: The f lood tainted the drinking water with disease germs.

take a beating.monolingual: to be beaten, bested, or defeated. _ The candidate took a beating in the primaries. _The team took quite a beating.
examples: The candidate took a beating in the primaries.

take a bow.monolingual: to bow and acknowledge credit for a good performance. _At the end of the concerto, the pianist rose and took a bow. _ The audience applauded wildly and demanded that the conductor come out and take a bow again.
examples: At the end of the concerto, the pianist rose and took a bow.

take a dirt nap.monolingual: Sl. to die and be buried. _ I don’t want to end up taking a dirt nap during this operation. _ Isn’t Tom a little young to take a dirt nap?
examples: I don’t want to end up taking a dirt nap during this operation.

take a hand in something.monolingual: to help with something; to participate in something. _ Would you take a hand in this work? We need your efforts. _ Ted refused to take a hand in the preparations for the evening meal.
examples: Would you take a hand in this work? We need your efforts.

take a hint.monolingual: to understand a hint and behave accordingly. _ I said I didn’t want to see you anymore. Can’t you take a hint? I don’t like you. _Sure I can take a hint, but I’d rather be told directly.
examples: I said I didn’t want to see you anymore.

take a leak.monolingual: Inf. to urinate. (Crude. Use caution with the topic. Usually in reference to a male.) _ I gotta go take a leak. Back in a minute. _ He just went out to take a leak.
examples: I gotta go take a leak.

take a nap.monolingual: to have a brief period of sleep. _I took a short nap just after lunch. _The baby takes a long nap each afternoon.
examples: I took a short nap just after lunch.

take a new turn.monolingual: [for something] to begin a new course or direction. _When I received the telegram with the exciting news, my life took a new turn. _I began taking the medicine at noon, and by evening the disease had begun to take a new turn. I was getting better!
examples: When I received the telegram with the exciting news, my life took a new turn.

take a powder.monolingual: Sl. to leave; to leave town. (Underworld.) _ Why don’t you take a powder? Go on! Beat it! _ Willie took a powder and will lie low for a while.
examples: Willie took a powder and will lie low for a while.

take a spill.monolingual: to have a fall; to tip over. (Also with bad, nasty, quite, etc. Also with have.) _Ann tripped on the curb and took a nasty spill. _ John had quite a spill when he fell off his bicycle.
examples: Ann tripped on the curb and took a nasty spill.

take a swing at someone.monolingual: to attempt to punch someone. _ He took a swing at me! _ Tom took a swing at Bob, but Bob ducked out of the way.
examples: Tom took a swing at Bob, but Bob ducked out of the way.

take a vacation.monolingual: to go somewhere for a vacation; to stop work to have a vacation. _Sue took a vacation at the Grand Canyon last year. _ I need to take a vacation and relax.
examples: Sue took a vacation at the Grand Canyon last year.

take advantage of someone.monolingual: 1. to deceive someone. _ I knew that you wouldn’t take advantage of me! I trusted you. _ Please don’t take advantage of me the way you took advantage of Carl.
examples: I knew that you wouldn’t take advantage of me! I trusted you.

take after someone.monolingual: to resemble a close, older relative. _ Don’t you think that Sally takes after her mother? _ No, Sally takes after her Aunt Ann.
examples: No, Sally takes after her Aunt Ann.

take an oath.monolingual: to make an oath; to swear to something. _ You must take an oath that you will never tell anyone about this. _When I was a witness in court, I had to take an oath that I would tell the truth.
examples: You must take an oath that you will never tell anyone about this.

take attendance.monolingual: to make a record of persons attending something. _ The teacher took attendance before starting the class. _ I will take attendance each day.
examples: The teacher took attendance before starting the class.

take care of someone.monolingual: 1. to tip someone. _ I took care of the doorman as we left. _ Did you remember to take care of the waiter?
examples: I took care of the doorman as we left.

take care of something.monolingual: to deal with something; to handle or manage a problem or detail. _ Would you please take care of this little problem? _ This is an easy thing to take care of. I will fix it immediately.
examples: This is an easy thing to take care of.

take cover.monolingual: to seek shelter from gunfire or other projectiles. _ As soon as the firing started, we took cover behind a huge boulder.
examples: As soon as the firing started, we took cover behind a huge boulder.

take credit for something.monolingual: to allow people to believe that one has done something praiseworthy, whether or not one has actually done it. _I can’t take credit for the entire success. Toby helped a lot. _ Mary took credit for everything that Dave did.
examples: I can’t take credit for the entire success.

take five.monolingual: Sl. to take a five-minute rest period; to take a short break. _Okay, everybody. Take five! _Hey, Bob. I’m tired. Can we take five?
examples: Okay, everybody.

take fuel on†.monolingual: to refuel; to be refueled. (Usually said of a large conveyance, such as a ship or a plane.) _We need to land at the next major airport to take fuel on. _ We will land somewhere to take on fuel.
examples: We need to land at the next major airport to take fuel on.

take inventory.monolingual: to make an inventory list. _They are taking inventory in the warehouse, counting each item and writing the number on a list. _ The hardware store closed once a year in order to take inventory.
examples: They are taking inventory in the warehouse, counting each item and writing the number on a list.

take issue with someone.monolingual: to argue with someone. _ I heard your last statement and I have to take issue with you. _ Tom took issue with Maggie about the cost of the house.
examples: I heard your last statement and I have to take issue with you.

take issue with something.monolingual: to disagree with or argue about something. _ I have to take issue with that statement. _ I want to take issue with the last statement you made.
examples: I have to take issue with that statement.

take it away!.monolingual: Inf. Start up the performance!; Let the show begin! (Typically a public announcement of the beginning of a musical performance.) _ And now, here is the band playing “Song of Songs.” Take it away! _Sally will now sing us a song. Take it away, Sally!
examples: And now, here is the band playing “Song of Songs.

take it easy..monolingual: 1. Inf. Good-bye and be careful. _ Mary: Bye-bye. Bill: See you, Mary. Take it easy. _ Sue: Take it easy, Tom. Tom: Bye, Sue. See you soon.
examples: Mary: Bye-bye. Bill: See you, Mary.

take it easy on something.monolingual: Fig. to use less of something (rather than more). _Take it easy on the soup. There’s just enough for one serving for each person. _Please take it easy! There are hardly any left.
examples: Take it easy on the soup.

take it from me!.monolingual: Inf. Believe me! _It’s true! Take it from me! _Take it from me. This is a very good day for this part of the country.
examples: Take it from me.

take it from the top.monolingual: Fig. to begin [again] at the beginning, especially the beginning of a piece of music. (Originally in reference to the top of a sheet of music.) _ The conductor stopped the band and had the players take it from the top again. _ Let’s take it from the
examples: The conductor stopped the band and had the players take it from the top again.

take it like a man.monolingual: [for a male] to suffer misfortune stoically. (Compare this with take it.) _She said some really cutting things to him, but he took it like a man. _ I knew he could take it like a man.
examples: She said some really cutting things to him, but he took it like a man.

take it on the lam.monolingual: Sl. to get out of town; to run away. (Underworld.) _ Both crooks took it on the lam when things got hot. _Walt knew that the time had come to take it on the lam.
examples: Both crooks took it on the lam when things got hot.

take it or leave it..monolingual: Inf. Take this one or none; you have no choice. _ Bill: That’s my final offer. Take it or leave it. Bob: Aw, come on! Take off a few bucks. _ Bill: Aw, I want eggs for breakfast, Mom. Mother: There’s only cornf lakes left. Take it or leave it.
examples: Bill: That’s my final offer.

take it slow.monolingual: to go slowly and carefully. _ Just relax and take it slow. You’ve got a good chance. _You’ll make it. Take it slow and keep your spirits up.
examples: Just relax and take it slow.

take it that....monolingual: to understand it to be thus... _Am I to take it that you think this is the end of our relationship?

take it to one’s grave.monolingual: to carry a secret with one until one dies. _ I will never tell anyone. I’ll take your secret to my grave. _ She took the answer to the mystery to her grave.
examples: I will never tell anyone.

take it to the street.monolingual: Sl. to tell everyone about your problems. _If there’s something bothering her, she’s gonna take it to the street, first thing. _ Come on, don’t take it to the street.
examples: If there’s something bothering her, she’s gonna take it to the street, first thing.

take it with one.monolingual: Fig. to take possessions with you when you die. (Usually negative.) _ Spend a little on yourself. You can’t take it with you, you know. _He knew he couldn’t take it with him, so he spent it all.
examples: Spend a little on yourself.

take its course.monolingual: to continue along its way; [for a disease] to progress the way it normally progresses until it is cured naturally. _ There is really no good medicine for this. This disease simply has to take its course.
examples: There is really no good medicine for this.

take kindly to something.monolingual: to be agreeable to something. _ My father doesn’t take kindly to anyone using his tools. _ I hope they’ll take kindly to our request.
examples: My father doesn’t take kindly to anyone using his tools.

take leave of one’s senses.monolingual: Fig. to become irrational. (Often verbatim with one’s.) _ What are you doing? Have you taken leave of your senses? _What a terrible situation! It’s enough to make one take leave of one’s senses.
examples: What a terrible situation! It’s enough to make one take leave of one’s senses.

take my word for it..monolingual: Believe me.; Trust me, I am telling you the truth. _Bill: Take my word for it. These are the best power tools you can buy. Bob: But I don’t need any power tools. _Rachel: No one can cook better than Fred. Take my word for it. Bill: Really? Fred: Oh,
examples: Bill: Take my word for it.

take names.monolingual: Sl. to make a list of wrongdoers. (Often figuratively, referring to a schoolteacher making a list of the names of misbehaving students to be sent to the principal.) _The boss is madder than hell, and he’s taking names. _ Gary is coming by to talk abo
examples: The boss is madder than hell, and he’s taking names.

take no prisoners.monolingual: 1. Lit. to kill the enemy rather than seize the enemy as prisoners. _ The soldiers’ orders were to take no prisoners.
examples: The soldiers’ orders were to take no prisoners.

take off.monolingual: 1. Fig. to leave the ground and begin to fly. (As with a bird or an airplane.) _ When do we take off ? _ The eagle took off and headed toward the mountains.
examples: The eagle took off and headed toward the mountains.

take off from something.monolingual: to take flight from something or some place. _The plane took off from the busy airport right on schedule. _We will take off from the airport on one side of town, f ly across the city, and land at our destination within 15 minutes.
examples: The plane took off from the busy airport right on schedule.

take office.monolingual: to begin serving as an elected or appointed official. _When did the mayor take office? _All the elected officials took office just after the election.
examples: All the elected officials took office just after the election.

take one at one’s word.monolingual: to believe what someone says and act accordingly. _ She told me to go jump in the lake, and I took her at her word. _You shouldn’t take her at her word. She frequently says things she doesn’t really mean.
examples: She told me to go jump in the lake, and I took her at her word.

take one’s cue from someone.monolingual: to use someone else’s behavior or reactions as a guide to one’s own. (From the theatrical cue as a signal to speak, etc.) _ If you don’t know which spoons to use at the dinner, just take your cue from John. _The other children took their cue from Tom
examples: If you don’t know which spoons to use at the dinner, just take your cue from John.

take one’s gloves off†.monolingual: Fig. to stop being calm or civil and show an intention of winning a dispute by any means. (As if boxers were to remove their gloves in order to inflict more damage. See also The gloves are off.) _Both of them took their gloves off and really began ar
examples: Both of them took their gloves off and really began arguing.

take one’s lumps.monolingual: Inf. to accept the result or punishment one deserves. _ You’ve got to learn to take your lumps if you’re going to be in politics. _ I hate taking my lumps. I’d rather pretend nothing had happened.
examples: You’ve got to learn to take your lumps if you’re going to be in politics.

take one’s medicine.monolingual: Fig. to accept the consequences or the bad fortune that one deserves. (Alludes to having to take unpleasant-tasting medicine.) _ I know I did wrong, and I know I have to take my medicine. _Billy knew he was going to get spanked, and he didn’t want to
examples: I know I did wrong, and I know I have to take my medicine.

take one’s own life.monolingual: to kill oneself; to commit suicide. _ Bob tried to take his own life, but he was stopped in time. _ Later, he was sorry that he had tried to take his own life.
examples: Bob tried to take his own life, but he was stopped in time.

take one’s time.monolingual: to go as slow as one wants or needs to; to use as much time as is required. _There is no hurry. Please take your time. _ Bill is very careful and takes his time so he won’t make any mistakes.
examples: There is no hurry.

take one’s turn.monolingual: [when playing a game] to make one’s move or play one’s cards; [when alternating with someone, waiting for one’s opportunity or place in a sequence] to perform one’s task. _Somebody please wake Max up so he can take his turn.
examples: Somebody please wake Max up so he can take his turn.

take oneself off some place.monolingual: to go away to some place more private. _I need to take myself off someplace and think all this over. _ She kept her sanity by taking herself off to her bedroom for a few hours each day.
examples: I need to take myself off someplace and think all this over.

take out a loan.monolingual: to get a loan of money, especially from a bank. _Mary took out a loan to buy a car. _We will have to take out a loan to remodel the kitchen.
examples: Mary took out a loan to buy a car.

take pains over something.monolingual: Fig. to deal with something with great care. _She certainly takes pains over her work. _You will have to take pains over this if you want it to be done right.
examples: She certainly takes pains over her work.

take place.monolingual: to happen. _ When will this party take place? _ It’s taking place right now.
examples: It’s taking place right now.

take refuge in something.monolingual: to hide in something; to seek safety or the comfort of being safe in something. _ The rabbits took refuge in a hole in the ground. _ The children took refuge in the house as soon as the storm began.
examples: The rabbits took refuge in a hole in the ground.

take root.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a plant] to develop roots in soil or some other growing medium. _ The new plants should take root in a few weeks and start growing.
examples: The new plants should take root in a few weeks and start growing.

take shape.monolingual: [for something, such as plans, writing, ideas, arguments, etc.] to begin to be organized and specific. _ My plans are beginning to take shape. _As my manuscript took shape, I started showing it to publishers.
examples: My plans are beginning to take shape.

take sides.monolingual: to choose one side of an argument. _ They were arguing, but I didn’t want to take sides, so I left. _ I don’t mind taking sides on important issues.
examples: They were arguing, but I didn’t want to take sides, so I left.

take some doing.monolingual: to require considerable effort and care. _ It’ll take some doing, but it’ll get done. _ It’s not impossible. It’ll just take some doing.
examples: It’ll take some doing, but it’ll get done.

take someone apart†.monolingual: 1. Sl. to beat someone up. _ Don’t talk to me that way, or I’ll take you apart. _He was so mad that I thought he was going to take apart all of us.
examples: Don’t talk to me that way, or I’ll take you apart.

take someone around†.monolingual: to show someone the premises; to introduce someone to the people on the premises. _ Mr. Franklin needs a plant tour. Would you take him around? _ Would you kindly take around our guests?
examples: Mr. Franklin needs a plant tour.

take someone aside†.monolingual: to remove someone temporarily from the group for the purposes of discussing something privately. _ I’m sorry he insulted you. I’ll take him aside and take talk to him about it. _ I took aside my secretary and explained the procedure.
examples: I’m sorry he insulted you.

take someone below.monolingual: to guide someone to a lower deck on a ship. _ The captain told the first mate to take the passengers below. _ Please take Mr. Wilson below, where he will not be in the way.
examples: The captain told the first mate to take the passengers below.

take someone for a ride.monolingual: 1. Lit. to carry someone about, usually for recreation, in a car, plane, boat, etc. _ Would you take us for a ride in your boat? _ Please take me for a ride in your new car.
examples: Please take me for a ride in your new car.

take someone for dead.monolingual: to assume that someone who is still alive is dead. _ When we found her, we took her for dead, but the paramedics were able to revive her. _He was taken for dead and abandoned.
examples: When we found her, we took her for dead, but the paramedics were able to revive her.

take someone for something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to escort someone to and through some activities, such as a walk, a swim, a ride, etc. _ Can I take you for a ride? _ He took me for a walk in the park, and then we came home.
examples: He took me for a walk in the park, and then we came home.

take someone hostage.monolingual: to kidnap or seize someone to be a hostage. _The terrorists planned to take the ambassador hostage. _ The entire family was taken hostage by the robber.
examples: The terrorists planned to take the ambassador hostage.

take someone in† as something.monolingual: to make someone a member of an organization. _We took her in as an associate at first. _ I took in Karen as an associate.
examples: We took her in as an associate at first.

take someone in hand.monolingual: Fig. to take control of someone; to assume the responsibility of guiding someone. _ Someone is going to have to take Tim in hand and help him out. _Alice decided that she would take the new worker in hand.
examples: Someone is going to have to take Tim in hand and help him out.

take someone into one’s confidence.monolingual: to trust someone with confidential information; to tell a secret to someone and trust the person to keep the secret. _ We are good friends, but I didn’t feel I could take her into my confidence. _I know something very important about Jean. Can I take
examples: We are good friends, but I didn’t feel I could take her into my confidence.

take someone off†.monolingual: Sl. to kill someone. (Underworld.) _ The mob took the witness off a week before the trial. _Barlowe didn’t want to have to take off Lefty, but he was afraid he might talk.
examples: The mob took the witness off a week before the trial.

take someone on.monolingual: 1. to enter into a fight or argument with someone. _I pretended to agree because I really didn’t want to take him on.
examples: I pretended to agree because I really didn’t want to take him on.

take someone or something aboard.monolingual: to load someone or something onto a ship. _ The ship was in its berth, taking passengers aboard. _ The ship took many tons of cargo aboard.
examples: The ship was in its berth, taking passengers aboard.

take someone or something along†.monolingual: to bring someone or something along with one. _ Can I take my friend along on the hike? _ You should take along your own drinking water.
examples: You should take along your own drinking water.

take someone or something down†.monolingual: to move someone or something to a lower position or level. _The boss is downstairs and wants to meet our visitor. Will you take her down? _The way down to the lobby is confusing. Let me take down our visitor. _ Let me take the sandwiches down.
examples: The boss is downstairs and wants to meet our visitor.

take someone or something off†.monolingual: Sl. to rob someone or something. (Underworld.) _Weren’t you in that bunch that took the bank off in Philly? _ No, we never took off no bank, did we, Lefty?

take someone or something on†.monolingual: to accept the task of handling a difficult person or thing. _I’ll take it on if nobody else will do it. _ Nobody wanted to take on Mrs. Franklin, but it had to be done.
examples: I’ll take it on if nobody else will do it.

take someone or something over†.monolingual: to take charge (of someone or something); to assume control of someone or something. _ The new manager will take the office over next week. _Will you please take over your children? I can’t seem to control them.
examples: The new manager will take the office over next week.

take someone or something wrong.monolingual: to misunderstand someone or something. _ Please don’t take me wrong, but I believe that your socks don’t match. _ You’ll probably take this wrong, but I have to say that I’ve never seen you looking better.
examples: Please don’t take me wrong, but I believe that your socks don’t match.

take someone out†.monolingual: 1. to date someone. _ I hope he’ll take me out soon. _She wanted to take out her guest for the evening.
examples: I hope he’ll take me out soon.

take someone out† to dinner.monolingual: to take someone as one’s guest to a meal at a restaurant. _Can I take you out to dinner sometime? _ We will take out the visitors to dinner tonight.
examples: We will take out the visitors to dinner tonight.

take someone’s blood pressure.monolingual: to measure a person’s blood pressure. _The doctor takes my blood pressure every time I am in the office. _ Bob takes his blood pressure at home every day.
examples: The doctor takes my blood pressure every time I am in the office.
