take someone’s breath away.monolingual: 1. Lit. to cause someone to be out of breath due to a shock or hard exercise. _ Running this fast takes my breath away. _ Mary frightened me and took my breath away.
examples: Running this fast takes my breath away.

take someone’s head off.monolingual: Fig. to scold or berate someone severely. _ There is no need to take his head off about such a simple matter.
examples: There is no need to take his head off about such a simple matter.

take someone’s life.monolingual: to kill someone. (Can include onself.) _ It’s the executioner’s job to take people’s lives.
examples: It’s the executioner’s job to take people’s lives.

take someone’s part.monolingual: Fig. to take a side in an argument; to support someone in an argument. _ My sister took my mother’s part in the family argument. _You are always taking the part of the underdog!
examples: My sister took my mother’s part in the family argument.

take someone’s pulse.monolingual: to measure the frequency of the beats of a person’s pulse. _I can take my own pulse. _The nurse took my pulse and said I was fine.
examples: I can take my own pulse.

take someone’s temperature.monolingual: to measure a person’s body temperature with a thermometer. _ I took my temperature and I found that I am running a fever. _ The nurse took my temperature and said I was okay.
examples: I took my temperature and I found that I am running a fever.

take someone to court.monolingual: to sue someone; to force someone to appear in court. _ I will take you to court if you persist in pestering my client. _ Don was taken to court in a negligence suit.
examples: I will take you to court if you persist in pestering my client.

take someone to one side.monolingual: Fig. to lead someone to a relatively private place, to say something private or give private instructions. _ Gary took Fran to one side to talk to her. _ I will take Sue to one side and have a word with her about this matter.
examples: Gary took Fran to one side to talk to her.

take someone to task.monolingual: to scold or reprimand someone. _ The teacher took John to task for his bad behavior. _ I lost a big contract, and the boss took me to task in front of everyone.
examples: The teacher took John to task for his bad behavior.

take someone to the cleaners.monolingual: 1. Sl. to take a lot of someone’s money; to swindle someone. _ The lawyers took the insurance company to the cleaners, but I still didn’t get enough to pay for my losses. _ The con artists took the old man to the cleaners.
examples: The lawyers took the insurance company to the cleaners, but I still didn’t get enough to pay for my losses.

take someone up†.monolingual: to discuss or deal with someone. _ What are we going to do about Bill? Are we going to take Bill up today at the board meeting? _ Let’s take up the applicants in our next meeting.
examples: Let’s take up the applicants in our next meeting.

take someone up on something.monolingual: to accept an offer that someone has made. _ That’s a good offer. I’ll take you up on it. _ Tom took Sue up on her offer of dinner.
examples: That’s a good offer.

take something aloft.monolingual: to take an aircraft into the air. _The pilot took the plane aloft and tested it out. _When will you take this aloft for a test f light?
examples: The pilot took the plane aloft and tested it out.

take something apart†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to disassemble something. _ Bobby took his bicycle apart. _ You take apart everything that is mechanical.
examples: Bobby took his bicycle apart.

take something around†.monolingual: to take something from various people or places. _Would you take the pictures around and show them to everyone? _ I will take around this stack of pictures and show them to each person.
examples: I will take around this stack of pictures and show them to each person.

take something at face value.monolingual: to accept something exactly the way it appears to be. _I don’t know whether I can take her story at face value, but I will assume that she is not lying. _The committee took the report at face value and approved the suggested changes.
examples: I don’t know whether I can take her story at face value, but I will assume that she is not lying.

take something back†.monolingual: to retract a statement; to rescind one’s remark. _ You had better take back what you said about my sister. _I won’t take what I said back! She’s a twit!
examples: You had better take back what you said about my sister.

take something down†.monolingual: 1. to take some large or complicated things apart. _ They plan to take all these buildings down and turn the land into a park. _Do they plan to take down the television broadcasting tower?
examples: They plan to take all these buildings down and turn the land into a park.

take something from someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to remove something from someone’s possession. _ Jimmy took Tim’s cookie from him. _ Please don’t take my money from me.
examples: Jimmy took Tim’s cookie from him.

take something from something.monolingual: to subtract something from something; to remove something from something. _Take ten from twenty and see what you have left. _ If you take the lettuce out of the salad, what do you have left?
examples: Take ten from twenty and see what you have left.

take something into one’s head.monolingual: Fig. to get an obsession or overpowering idea into one’s thinking. _ George took this strange idea into his head about fixing the car himself. _I don’t know why she took that strange idea into her head.
examples: George took this strange idea into his head about fixing the car himself.

take something lying down.monolingual: Fig. to endure something unpleasant without fighting back. _ He insulted me publicly. You don’t expect me to take that lying down, do you? _I’m not the kind of person who’ll take something like that lying down.
examples: He insulted me publicly.

take something off†.monolingual: to remove something, such as an article of clothing. _Please take your coat off and stay awhile. _ Please take off your coat.
examples: Please take your coat off and stay awhile.

take something on faith.monolingual: to accept or believe something on the basis of little or no evidence. _ Please try to believe what I’m telling you. Just take it on faith. _Surely you can’t expect me to take a story like that on faith.
examples: Please try to believe what I’m telling you.

take something on the chin.monolingual: 1. Lit. to absorb a blow on the chin. _ The boxer tried to duck but took the blow on the chin.
examples: The boxer tried to duck but took the blow on the chin.

take something on trust.monolingual: to accept that something is true through trust. _ I don’t know if it’s so, but I’ll take it on trust. _You will have to take it on trust because I can’t prove it.
examples: I don’t know if it’s so, but I’ll take it on trust.

take something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to carry something outside. _ Please take the trash out. _I’ll take out the trash.
examples: Please take the trash out.

take something out in trade.monolingual: Fig. to accept someone’s goods or services in payment of a bill. _ The grocer told the plumber that he would pay the plumber by allowing him to take his bill out in trade. _ I don’t have any cash right now. Can you take what I owe you out in trade?
examples: The grocer told the plumber that he would pay the plumber by allowing him to take his bill out in trade.

take something over†.monolingual: 1. to assume responsibility for a task. _ It looks as if I’m going to have to take the project over. _ I will take over the project.
examples: It looks as if I’m going to have to take the project over.

take something personally.monolingual: to interpret a remark as if it were mean or critical about oneself. _ Don’t take it personally, but you really need a haircut. _ I want to tell you something, but please don’t take it personally.
examples: Don’t take it personally, but you really need a haircut.

take something public.monolingual: 1. to make something known to the public. _ You gotta take it public—put it on the street— even when it’s none of your business. _ Don’t take it public. You’ll just get talked about.
examples: You gotta take it public—put it on the street— even when it’s none of your business.

take something to heart.monolingual: Fig. to consider that some comment is significant to oneself. _ Mary listened to Bob’s advice and took it all to heart. _ All Sue’s advice was taken to heart by the show committee.
examples: Mary listened to Bob’s advice and took it all to heart.

take something to pieces.monolingual: Inf. to disassemble something. _ I will have to take the vacuum cleaner to pieces to find out what’s wrong with it. _The machine was taken to pieces again in an effort to find where the leftover part belonged.
examples: I will have to take the vacuum cleaner to pieces to find out what’s wrong with it.

take something under advisement.monolingual: to hear an idea and think about it carefully. _ It’s a good idea, but I’ll have to take it under advisement. _The suggestion was taken under advisement, and a reply was not expected for at least a month.
examples: It’s a good idea, but I’ll have to take it under advisement.

take something up†.monolingual: 1. [for someone or a group] to deliberate something. _ When will the board of directors take this up? _ Let’s take up that matter now.
examples: Let’s take up that matter now.

take something up to someone.monolingual: to deliver something to a person on a higher level. _ I will take this up to the boss and try to get it approved. _ Please take this up to Sue on the next f loor and see what she thinks about it.
examples: I will take this up to the boss and try to get it approved.

take something with one.monolingual: to take something [away] with one. _ I am going to take this food with me. _ Can I take one of these catalogs with me?
examples: I am going to take this food with me.

take something with something.monolingual: to eat or swallow something, such as medicine, with something. _ You have to take this medicine with milk or soda water. _I will take this pill with milk.
examples: You have to take this medicine with milk or soda water.

take the coward’s way out.monolingual: Euph. to kill oneself. _ When faced with financial disaster, Sarah took the coward’s way out. _ I can’t believe that Bill would take the coward’s way out. His death must have been an accident.
examples: When faced with financial disaster, Sarah took the coward’s way out.

take the cure.monolingual: to enter into any treatment program or treatment center. (Especially those dealing with drugs and alcohol.) _ I wanted to take the cure, but I just couldn’t bring myself to do it. _ It’s hard to get those addicted to realize that they are the ones wh
examples: I wanted to take the cure, but I just couldn’t bring myself to do it.

take the easy way out.monolingual: to get free of something by taking the path of least resistance. _You can depend on Kelly to take the easy way out of a tough situation. _ I’m not the type that takes the easy way out.
examples: You can depend on Kelly to take the easy way out of a tough situation.

take the fall.monolingual: Sl. to get arrested for a particular crime. (Especially when others are going unpunished for the same crime. _ Walt and Tony pulled the job off together, but Tony took the fall. _You did it, and I won’t take the fall!
examples: Walt and Tony pulled the job off together, but Tony took the fall.

take the floor.monolingual: 1. Fig. to stand up and address the audience. _ When I take the f loor, I’ll make a short speech. _ The last time you had the f loor, you talked for an hour.
examples: When I take the f loor, I’ll make a short speech.

take the pledge.monolingual: Fig. to promise to abstain from drinking alcohol. _ I’m not ready to take the pledge yet, but I will cut down. _My aunt tried to get me to take the pledge.
examples: I’m not ready to take the pledge yet, but I will cut down.

take the plunge.monolingual: to marry someone. _ I’m not ready to take the plunge yet. _ Sam and Mary took the plunge.
examples: I’m not ready to take the plunge yet.

take the pulse of something.monolingual: Fig. to sample or survey something to learn about its progress or state. _Two executives came in to take the pulse of the local business unit.
examples: Two executives came in to take the pulse of the local business unit.

take the slack up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to tighten a rope that is holding something loosely. _ Take the slack up if you can. _ This clothesline is too loose. Do something to take up the slack.
examples: Take the slack up if you can.

take the stage.monolingual: Fig. to become the center of attention; to become the focus of everyone’s attention. _ Later in the day, the problems in the warehouse took the stage, and we discussed them until dinnertime.
examples: Later in the day, the problems in the warehouse took the stage, and we discussed them until dinnertime.

take the stand.monolingual: to go to and sit in the witness chair in a courtroom. _ I was in court all day, waiting to take the stand. _ The lawyer asked the witness to take the stand.
examples: I was in court all day, waiting to take the stand.

take things easy.monolingual: 1. to live well and comfortably. _ I’ll be glad when I can make enough money to take things easy. _I make enough to take things easy.
examples: I’ll be glad when I can make enough money to take things easy.

take time out.monolingual: to spend time away from studying or working. _ He’s taking time out between high school and starting at the university. _Mary’s taking time out from her job to work abroad for a year.
examples: He’s taking time out between high school and starting at the university.

take to one’s bed.monolingual: to go to bed, as with an illness. _ I feel a little ill, so I’ll take to my bed for a day or so. _ Sam took to his bed with a fever.
examples: I feel a little ill, so I’ll take to my bed for a day or so.

take to one’s heels.monolingual: Fig. to run away. _ The little boy said hello and then took to his heels. _The man took to his heels to try to get to the bus stop before the bus left.
examples: The little boy said hello and then took to his heels.

take too much on†.monolingual: to undertake to do too much work or too many tasks at one time. _ Don’t take too much on, or you won’t be able to do any of it well. _Ann tends to take on too much and get exhausted.
examples: Don’t take too much on, or you won’t be able to do any of it well.

take turns with someone.monolingual: to alternate [doing something] with someone. _ We both can’t be there at the same time. I’ll take turns with you. _You have to take turns with your brother.
examples: We both can’t be there at the same time.

take umbrage at something.monolingual: to feel that one has been insulted by something. _ The employee took umbrage at not getting a raise. _Mary took umbrage at the suggestion that she was being unreasonable.
examples: The employee took umbrage at not getting a raise.

take up residence some place.monolingual: to make a residence of a place. _ Ed took up residence in a small efficiency apartment. _ It looks as if a family of mice has taken up residence in the cupboard.
examples: Ed took up residence in a small efficiency apartment.

take up the challenge.monolingual: to respond to a challenge and do what the challenge asks. _ I am not prepared to take the challenge up. _ Dave took up the challenge without much urging.
examples: I am not prepared to take the challenge up.

take up with someone.monolingual: to become close with someone; to become friends with someone. _ I think that Albert may have taken up with the wrong people. _I did not want Lefty to take up with Max, but he did, and look where it’s gotten him.
examples: I think that Albert may have taken up with the wrong people.

take your seat..monolingual: Please sit down. (Often plural.) _Please take your seats so we can begin.
examples: Please take your seats so we can begin.

taken aback.monolingual: Cliché surprised and confused. _ When Mary told me the news, I was taken aback for a moment. _ When I told my parents I was married, they were completely taken aback.
examples: When Mary told me the news, I was taken aback for a moment.

taken for dead.monolingual: appearing to be dead; assumed to be dead. _ I was so ill with the f lu that I was almost taken for dead. _ The accident victims were so seriously injured that they were taken for dead at first.
examples: I was so ill with the f lu that I was almost taken for dead.

taken with someone or something.monolingual: highly attracted to someone or something. _ She was really quite taken with the young man who escorted her to the ball. _ The audience was taken with the stage setting.
examples: She was really quite taken with the young man who escorted her to the ball.

take-off artist.monolingual: Sl. a thief. (Underworld.) _ A take-off artist known as the Cat is cleaning out closets and jewelry boxes all over town. _ He’s not a sales agent. He’s a takeoff artist, pure and simple.
examples: A take-off artist known as the Cat is cleaning out closets and jewelry boxes all over town.

taking calls.monolingual: willing to receive telephone calls. _I’m sorry, but she’s not taking calls at the moment. Can I have her call you later?
examples: I’m sorry, but she’s not taking calls at the moment.

tale of woe.monolingual: a sad story; a list of personal problems; an excuse for failing to do something. _ I listened to her tale of woe without saying anything. _ This tale of woe that we have all been getting from Kelly is just too much.
examples: I listened to her tale of woe without saying anything.

talk a blue streak.monolingual: Fig. to talk very much and very rapidly. _ Billy didn’t talk until he was two, and then he started talking a blue streak. _ I can’t understand anything Bob says. He talks a blue streak, and I can’t follow his thinking.
examples: Billy didn’t talk until he was two, and then he started talking a blue streak.

talk about someone or something.monolingual: to discuss someone or something. _ I don’t want to talk about Jerry anymore. _ Let’s not talk about it now.
examples: I don’t want to talk about Jerry anymore.

talk about someone or something!.monolingual: If you think that thing or person is remarkable, then... _ Talk about ugly buildings! This one is horrendous.
examples: Talk about ugly buildings! This one is horrendous.

talk around something.monolingual: to talk, but avoid talking directly about the subject. _ You are just talking around the matter! I want a straight answer! _ He never really said anything. He just talked around the issue.
examples: He never really said anything.

talk at someone.monolingual: to say words at someone; to talk to someone in a desultory manner. _ You are just talking at her and she isn’t paying attention. _ Talk to me, not at me. I want to communicate with you.
examples: You are just talking at her and she isn’t paying attention.

talk big.monolingual: to brag; to make grandiose statements. _She talks big but can’t produce anything. _ He has some deep need to talk big, but it’s just talk—no action.
examples: She talks big but can’t produce anything.

talk down to someone.monolingual: to speak to someone in a patronizing manner; to speak to someone in the simplest way. _ The manager insulted everyone in the office by talking down to them. _Please don’t talk down to me. I can understand anything you have to say.
examples: The manager insulted everyone in the office by talking down to them.

talk in circles.monolingual: Fig. to talk in a confusing or roundabout manner. _I couldn’t understand a thing he said. All he did was talk in circles. _We argued for a long time and finally decided that we were talking in circles.
examples: I couldn’t understand a thing he said.

talk is cheap..monolingual: Prov. It is easier to say you will do something than to actually do it. (Saying this in response to someone who promises you something implies that you do not believe that person will keep the promise.) _ My boss keeps saying she’ll give me a raise,
examples: My boss keeps saying she’ll give me a raise, but talk is cheap.

talk like a nut.monolingual: to say stupid things. _ You’re talking like a nut! You don’t know what you are saying. _Don’t talk like a nut! We can’t afford a trip to Florida!
examples: You’re talking like a nut! You don’t know what you are saying.

the talk of a place.monolingual: someone or something who is the subject of a conversation somewhere, such as the town, the office, the community, etc. _ The handsome new teacher was the talk of the town. _ John’s new car is the talk of the office.
examples: The handsome new teacher was the talk of the town.

talk of someone or something.monolingual: to speak about someone or something. _ Weren’t we talking of old Mrs. Watson just now? _ We were just talking of old times—happier times.
examples: Weren’t we talking of old Mrs.

talk on.monolingual: to continue to talk. _ The lecturer talked on for hours. _ How can anyone talk on so long without saying anything useful?
examples: The lecturer talked on for hours.

talk on someone or something.monolingual: to speak on the subject of someone or something. _ Today, I will talk on Abraham Lincoln. _ Ann is going to talk on the subject of manners.
examples: Today, I will talk on Abraham Lincoln.

talk one’s head off.monolingual: Fig. Inf. to talk endlessly; to argue vigorously. _ I talked my head off trying to convince them. _ Don’t waste time talking your head off to them.
examples: I talked my head off trying to convince them.

talk oneself out.monolingual: to talk until one can talk no more. _ She talked herself out and was silent for the rest of the day. _ I talked until I talked myself out.
examples: She talked herself out and was silent for the rest of the day.

talk over someone’s head.monolingual: Fig. to say things that someone cannot understand; to speak on too high a level for one’s audience. _ The speaker talked over our heads and we learned nothing. _ It is not a good idea to talk over your audience’s heads.
examples: The speaker talked over our heads and we learned nothing.

talk over something.monolingual: to use something, such as a microphone, intercom, or telephone, to talk. _I don’t mind talking over the telephone. _ I will talk to Jeff over the intercom and see what he thinks about the idea.
examples: I don’t mind talking over the telephone.

talk shop.monolingual: to talk about business or work matters at a social event (where such talk is out of place). _ All right, everyone, we’re not here to talk shop. Let’s have a good time. _ Mary and Jane stood by the punch bowl, talking shop.
examples: All right, everyone, we’re not here to talk shop.

talk someone down†.monolingual: 1. to win at debating someone. _ Liz was able to talk her opponent down. _She talked down her opponent.
examples: Liz was able to talk her opponent down.

talk someone or something up†.monolingual: to promote or speak in support of someone or something. _ I’ve been talking the party up all day, trying to get people to come. _ They keep taking up the candidate as if he represented a real change.
examples: I’ve been talking the party up all day, trying to get people to come.

talk someone out of something.monolingual: to convince someone to give up or change something. _They were trying to talk me out of my decision. _ Timmy tried to talk Mary out of her ice cream cone.
examples: They were trying to talk me out of my decision.

talk someone ragged.monolingual: Fig. to talk to someone too much; to bore someone. _That was not an interview. She talked me ragged. _ He always talks me ragged, but I always listen.
examples: That was not an interview.

talk someone’s ear off.monolingual: Fig. to talk to someone endlessly; to bore someone with too much talk. _ My aunt always talks my ear off when she comes to visit. _ Stay away from Mr. Jones. He will talk your ear off if he gets a chance.
examples: My aunt always talks my ear off when she comes to visit.

talk someone’s head off.monolingual: 1. Fig. [for someone] to speak too much. _ Why does John always talk his head off ? Doesn’t he know he bores people? _ She talks her head off and doesn’t seem to know what she’s saying.
examples: She talks her head off and doesn’t seem to know what she’s saying.

talk something out†.monolingual: to settle something by discussion. _ Let’s not get mad. Let’s just talk it out. _ Please, let’s talk out this matter calmly.
examples: Let’s not get mad.

talk something over†.monolingual: to discuss something. _ Come into my office so we can talk this over. _We talked over the plans for nearly an hour.
examples: Come into my office so we can talk this over.

talk something through†.monolingual: 1. to discuss something in detail. _ Let’s talk the issue through and get it decided.
examples: Let’s talk the issue through and get it decided.

talk something up†.monolingual: to promote or advertise something by saying good things about it to as many people as possible. _Let’s talk the play up around campus so we can get a good audience. _ I will talk up the play all I can.
examples: Let’s talk the play up around campus so we can get a good audience.

talk through one’s hat.monolingual: Fig. to brag or exaggerate; to talk nonsense. _ That can’t be so! You are just talking through your hat! _ Pay no attention to Mary. She is just talking through her hat.
examples: Pay no attention to Mary.

talk turkey.monolingual: Fig. to talk business; to talk frankly. _ Okay, Bob, we have business to discuss. Let’s talk turkey. _ John wanted to talk turkey, but Jane just wanted to joke around.
examples: Okay, Bob, we have business to discuss.

talked out.monolingual: tired of talking; unable to talk more. _ I can’t go on. I’m all talked out. _ She was talked out in the first hour of discussion.
examples: I can’t go on. I’m all talked out.

*a tall order.monolingual: a request that is difficult to fulfill. (*Typically: be ~; give someone ~.) _ That’s a tall order. Do you think anyone can do it? _Well, it’s a tall order, but I’ll do it.
examples: That’s a tall order.

tally something up†.monolingual: to add something up. _ Please tally everything up and tell me the total. _ Let’s tally up everything and ask for donations.
examples: Please tally everything up and tell me the total.

tally with something.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for one set of figures] to match another set of figures. _Your figures don’t tally with mine. Let’s add them up again. _ The total Sam got didn’t tally with what the tax agent had come up with.
examples: Your figures don’t tally with mine.

tamp something down†.monolingual: to pat or pack something down. _ Tamp the soil down over the seeds after you plant them. _ Please tamp down the soil firmly.
examples: Tamp the soil down over the seeds after you plant them.

tamper with someone or something.monolingual: to fiddle with someone or something; to meddle with someone or something. _ I’ve got him believing just what I want him to believe. Don’t tamper with him. _ Please don’t tamper with the thermostat.
examples: I’ve got him believing just what I want him to believe.

tan someone’s hide.monolingual: to spank someone. _Billy’s mother said she’d tan Billy’s hide if he ever did that again. _ “I’ll tan your hide if you’re late!” said Tom’s father.
examples: Billy’s mother said she’d tan Billy’s hide if he ever did that again.

tangle someone or something up†.monolingual: to entangle someone or something. _ Please don’t tangle me up in your ropes. _ I tangled up my feet in the cords on the f loor.
examples: Please don’t tangle me up in your ropes.

tap at something.monolingual: to make one or more light blows on something. _ Fred tapped at the door, but no one heard him. _ Who is tapping at my window?
examples: Fred tapped at the door, but no one heard him.

tap on something.monolingual: to make one or more light blows on something. _Who is that tapping on my windowpane? _I wish you would stop tapping on the tabletop.
examples: I wish you would stop tapping on the tabletop.

tap out.monolingual: 1. Sl. to lose one’s money in gambling or in the securities markets. _I’m gonna tap out in about three more rolls—just watch. _ I really tapped out on that gold-mining stock.
examples: I’m gonna tap out in about three more rolls—just watch.

tap something down†.monolingual: to pound something down with light blows. _ Please tap that nail down so no one gets hurt on it. _ Tap down the tack, if you would.
examples: Please tap that nail down so no one gets hurt on it.

tap something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to clean something, as the ashes out of a pipe, by tapping. _ He took the pipe out of his mouth and tapped the ashes out. _ He tapped out the soil from the f lower pot.
examples: He took the pipe out of his mouth and tapped the ashes out.

tap something with something.monolingual: to make light blows on something with something. _ Alice tapped the table with her keys in an annoying fashion. _Just tap the nail lightly with your hammer.
examples: Alice tapped the table with her keys in an annoying fashion.

tap-dance like mad.monolingual: Sl. to appear busy continuously; to have to move fast or talk cleverly to distract someone. _ When things get tough, the whole Congress tap-dances like mad. _ Any public official knows how to tap-dance like mad when the press gets too nosy.
examples: When things get tough, the whole Congress tap-dances like mad.

tar and feather someone.monolingual: to punish or humiliate someone by coating them with tar and feathers. _ The people of the village tarred and feathered the bank robber and chased him out of town. _ They threatened to tar and feather me if I ever came back into their town.
examples: The people of the village tarred and feathered the bank robber and chased him out of town.

tarred with the same brush.monolingual: Fig. sharing the same characteristic( s); having the same good or bad points as someone else. _ Jack and his brother are tarred with the same brush. They’re both crooks. _The Smith children are tarred with the same brush. They’re all lazy.
examples: Jack and his brother are tarred with the same brush.

taste blood.monolingual: Fig. to experience something exciting, and perhaps dangerous, for the first time. _ She had tasted blood once, and she knew that the life of a race-car driver was for her. _ Once you taste blood, you’re hooked.
examples: She had tasted blood once, and she knew that the life of a race-car driver was for her.

*a taste for something.monolingual: a desire for a particular food, drink, or experience. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~; acquire ~.) _The Smiths have a taste for adventure and take exotic vacations. _ When she was pregnant, Mary often had a taste for pickles.
examples: The Smiths have a taste for adventure and take exotic vacations.

taste like more.monolingual: to taste very good; to taste so good as to make one want to eat more. _ This pie is great. It tastes like more. _ Mom’s cooking always tastes like more.
examples: This pie is great.

taste like something.monolingual: to have the same taste as something. _ This stuff tastes like watermelon. _ What do you think this tastes like?
examples: This stuff tastes like watermelon.

taste of something.monolingual: 1. to have a taste similar to something; to have the hint of a certain flavor. _This ice cream tastes of apricots. _ Why does this wine taste of vinegar?
examples: This ice cream tastes of apricots.

a taste of something.monolingual: an experience; an example. _Bill gave Sue a taste of her own rudeness. _ My friend used a parachute and got a taste of what it’s like to be a bird.
examples: Bill gave Sue a taste of her own rudeness.

tastes differ..monolingual: Prov. Different people like different things. _ Fred: Bill always goes out with such stupid girls. I can’t understand why. Alan: Tastes differ.
examples: Fred: Bill always goes out with such stupid girls.

taunt someone about something.monolingual: to mock, tease, or torment someone about something. _ Stop taunting me about something that happened years ago! _ Terry was being taunted about his gaudy tie, so he took it off.
examples: Terry was being taunted about his gaudy tie, so he took it off.

taunt someone into something.monolingual: to mock, tease, or torment someone into doing something. _ The gang taunted Liz into taking unnecessary chances. _ Don was taunted into leaving the room.
examples: The gang taunted Liz into taking unnecessary chances.

taunt someone with something.monolingual: to tease or tantalize someone with something. _ Jerry taunted Fran with the plate of fudge. _ Please don’t taunt me with food I shouldn’t eat.
examples: Jerry taunted Fran with the plate of fudge.

tax-and-spend.monolingual: spending freely and taxing heavily. (Referring to a legislative body that repeatedly passes expensive new laws and keeps raising taxes to pay for the cost. Fixed order.) _I hope that people do not elect another tax-and-spend Congress this time. _ The
examples: I hope that people do not elect another tax-and-spend Congress this time.

teach someone a lesson.monolingual: to get even with someone for bad behavior. _John tripped me, so I punched him. That ought to teach him a lesson. _ That taught me a lesson. I won’t do it again.
examples: John tripped me, so I punched him.

*the teacher’s pet.monolingual: the teacher’s favorite student. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ Sally is the teacher’s pet. She always gets special treatment. _ The other students don’t like the teacher’s pet.
examples: Sally is the teacher’s pet.

a team player.monolingual: someone who works well with the group; someone who is loyal to the group. _Ted is a team player. I am sure that he will cooperate with us.
examples: Ted is a team player.

tear a place apart†.monolingual: Fig. to search somewhere to the point of destruction. _The cops came with a search warrant and tore your room apart. _ If you don’t come up with the money you kept for us, we’ll tear apart your house!
examples: The cops came with a search warrant and tore your room apart.

tear across something.monolingual: to move rapidly across some area. _ The boys tore across the lawn to the swimming pool. _ As the plane tore across the sky it made a horrendous roar.
examples: The boys tore across the lawn to the swimming pool.

tear along.monolingual: to go along very fast, as in running, driving, cycling, etc. _The cars tore along the road, raising dust and making noise. _ Andy tore along on his bicycle, trying to see how fast he could go.
examples: The cars tore along the road, raising dust and making noise.

tear at someone or something.monolingual: to rip at someone or something; to try to tear someone or something up. _The badger tore at me, but I dodged it and ran away fast. _ Timmy tore at the package, struggling to get the paper off.
examples: The badger tore at me, but I dodged it and ran away fast.

tear down something.monolingual: to race down something very fast. _ The girls tore down the hallway as fast as they could run. _ They tore down the stairs and ran out the door.
examples: The girls tore down the hallway as fast as they could run.

tear into some place.monolingual: to run or race into a place. _The kids tore into the house and knocked over a lamp. _ Kelly tore into the boss’s office and put the papers on the desk.
examples: The kids tore into the house and knocked over a lamp.

tear into someone.monolingual: Fig. to scold someone severely; to attack someone with criticism. _I was late, and the boss tore into me like a mad dog. _ I don’t know why she tore into me. I was at work when the window was broken.
examples: I was late, and the boss tore into me like a mad dog.

tear into someone or something.monolingual: to attack someone or something; to attack someone or something with the intent of eating someone or something. _ The wolves tore into the hunter and injured him severely. _ The kids tore into the cake and ate it all.
examples: The wolves tore into the hunter and injured him severely.

tear into something.monolingual: Fig. to begin eating food with gusto. _The family tore into the mountain of food like they hadn’t eaten since breakfast—which was true, in fact. _ Jimmy tore into the turkey leg and cleaned it off in no time.
examples: The family tore into the mountain of food like they hadn’t eaten since breakfast—which was true, in fact.

tear someone apart†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to rip someone apart savagely. _ Max threatened to tear Tom apart. _The bear tore apart the hiker.
examples: Max threatened to tear Tom apart.

tear someone or something down†.monolingual: to criticize or degrade someone or something. _ Tom is always tearing Jane down. I guess he doesn’t like her. _It’s not nice to tear down the people who work in your office. _ Why are you always tearing my projects down?
examples: Tom is always tearing Jane down.

tear someone up†.monolingual: Fig. to cause someone much grief. _The news of Tom’s death really tore Bill up. _ Bad news tears up some people. Other people can take it calmly.
examples: The news of Tom’s death really tore Bill up.

tear something apart†.monolingual: 1. to pull or rip something apart. _ The bear tore the tent apart. _The lions tore apart the wildebeest in minutes, and began eating it.
examples: The bear tore the tent apart.

tear something down†.monolingual: to dismantle or destroy something. _They plan to tear the old building down and build a new one there. _ They’ll tear down the building in about two weeks.
examples: They plan to tear the old building down and build a new one there.

tear something from something.monolingual: to rip or peel something from something. _ He tore the wrapping from the gift. _ The monkey tore the peel from the banana and took a bite of it.
examples: He tore the wrapping from the gift.

tear something on something.monolingual: to rip something on something sharp or jagged. _I tore my pants on the corner of the desk. _ Mary tore her new skirt on something sharp on the side of the car.
examples: I tore my pants on the corner of the desk.

tear something up†.monolingual: to rip someone or something to pieces. _ The two drunks tore the bar up in their brawling. _ The dog tore up the newspaper.
examples: The two drunks tore the bar up in their brawling.

tease someone into doing something.monolingual: to force someone to do something through teasing or tormenting. _ Sam teased her into doing what he wanted. _ Perhaps you can tease him into leaving, but he won’t go if you ask him.
examples: Sam teased her into doing what he wanted.

tee off.monolingual: 1. Lit. to start the first hole in a game of golf. _ It’s time to tee off. Let’s get on the course. _ What time do we tee off ?
examples: It’s time to tee off.

tee someone off†.monolingual: Sl. to make someone angry. _ That really teed me off! _ Well, you sure managed to tee off everybody!

teed off.monolingual: Inf. angry. _I’m not teed off! I’m enraged. _I was so teed off I could have spit!
examples: I’m not teed off! I’m enraged.

teem with someone or something.monolingual: to swarm with someone or something; to be abundant with someone or something. _ The porch was teeming with f lies, so we couldn’t eat there. _ The beach teemed with people enjoying the sunny weather.
examples: The porch was teeming with f lies, so we couldn’t eat there.

teething troubles.monolingual: 1. Lit. pain and crying on the part of a baby whose teeth are growing in. _Billy has been whining because of teething troubles.
examples: Billy has been whining because of teething troubles.

telegraph one’s punches.monolingual: 1. Fig. to signal, unintentionally, what blows one is about to strike. (Boxing.) _Wilbur used to telegraph his punches until his trainer worked with him. _ Don’t telegraph your punches, kid! You’ll be f lat on your back in twenty seconds.
examples: Wilbur used to telegraph his punches until his trainer worked with him.

telescope into something.monolingual: [for one cylindrical part of something] to fit down inside another part, thereby reducing the length of the whole. _This part telescopes into this part. _The tent poles telescoped into a small, compact unit.
examples: This part telescopes into this part.

tell all.monolingual: to tell everything, even the secrets. _Some reporter got hold of the actress’s maid who offered to tell all for a fee.
examples: Some reporter got hold of the actress’s maid who offered to tell all for a fee.

tell it like it is..monolingual: Inf. Speak frankly.; Tell the truth no matter who is criticized or how much it hurts. _ Come on man, tell it like it is! _ Well, I’ve got to tell it like it is.
examples: Well, I’ve got to tell it like it is.

tell it to the marines!.monolingual: Inf. I do not believe you (maybe the marines will)! _ Your excuse is preposterous. Tell it to the marines. _I don’t care how good you think your reason is. Tell it to the marines!
examples: Your excuse is preposterous.

tell of someone or something.monolingual: to speak of someone or something. _ The messenger told of great destruction, hunger, and disease in the northern part of the country. _ I want you to tell of Jane and how she is doing.
examples: The messenger told of great destruction, hunger, and disease in the northern part of the country.

tell on someone.monolingual: to report someone’s bad behavior; to tattle on someone. _ If you do that again, I’ll tell on you! _ Please don’t tell on me. I’m in enough trouble as it is.
examples: Please don’t tell on me.

tell one to one’s face.monolingual: to tell [something] to someone directly. _ I’m sorry that Sally feels that way about me. I wish she had told me to my face. _ I won’t tell Tom that you’re mad at him. You should tell him to his face.
examples: I’m sorry that Sally feels that way about me.

tell people or things apart†.monolingual: to distinguish one from another. _I can’t tell Bob and Bill apart. _I find it easy to tell apart Bill and Bob. _ The two cakes look different, but in taste, I can’t tell this one and that one apart.
examples: I can’t tell Bob and Bill apart.

tell someone off†.monolingual: to scold someone; to attack someone verbally. (This has a sense of finality about it.) _I was so mad at Bob that I told him off. _ By the end of the day, I had told off everyone else, too.
examples: I was so mad at Bob that I told him off.

tell someone on someone.monolingual: to tattle to someone about someone. _ I’m going to tell your mother on you! _ I’ll tell the teacher on you!

tell something from something.monolingual: to know something because of something, such as evidence, signs, experience, etc. _ I can tell that she’s lying from the way she holds her eyebrows. _ I can’t tell anything from what you told me.
examples: I can tell that she’s lying from the way she holds her eyebrows.

tell tales out of school.monolingual: to tell secrets or spread rumors. _ I wish that John would keep quiet. He’s telling tales out of school again. _ If you tell tales out of school a lot, people won’t know when to believe you.
examples: I wish that John would keep quiet.

tell things apart.monolingual: to distinguish one thing or a group of things from another thing or group of things. _ This one is gold, and the others are brass. Can you tell them apart? _ Without their labels, I can’t tell them apart.
examples: This one is gold, and the others are brass.

tell time.monolingual: 1. Lit. to keep or report the correct time. _This clock doesn’t tell time very accurately. _ My watch stopped telling time, so I had to have it repaired.
examples: This clock doesn’t tell time very accurately.

temper something with something.monolingual: 1. Fig. to harden something, such as metal, with something. _ You have to temper the metal pieces with very high heat. _ The sheet of metal was tempered by the application of great pressure.
examples: You have to temper the metal pieces with very high heat.

tempt someone into something.monolingual: to lure or seduce someone into something. _Could I tempt you into going swimming? _ She would not be tempted into eating the rich and fattening cake.
examples: She would not be tempted into eating the rich and fattening cake.

tempt someone to do something.monolingual: to entice someone to do something. _ You can’t tempt me to eat any of that cake! _ I wasn’t even tempted to go into town with the others.
examples: I wasn’t even tempted to go into town with the others.

tempt someone with something.monolingual: to entice someone with something. _Can I tempt you with a bit of chocolate cake? _ I was tempted with a free book if I sent in my name, but I decided against it.
examples: I was tempted with a free book if I sent in my name, but I decided against it.

tend to do something.monolingual: to have a tendency to do something. _ Jill tends to play with her hair while she works. _ Sam tends to say things like that when he is upset.
examples: Jill tends to play with her hair while she works.

tend toward something.monolingual: to have a tendency to display a certain characteristic. _ Roger tends toward the dramatic. _ We all tend toward bad humor during bad weather.
examples: Roger tends toward the dramatic.

the tender age of....monolingual: the young age of... _ She left home at the tender age of 17 and got married to a rock singer.
examples: She left home at the tender age of 17 and got married to a rock singer.

tender something for something.monolingual: to offer something (of value) for something. _ The shareholders were asked to tender one of their shares for two of the offering company’s. _ I decided not to tender my shares.
examples: The shareholders were asked to tender one of their shares for two of the offering company’s.

test for something.monolingual: to try to find out about something by testing. _We are testing for weak places in your roof. That’s the noise you hear up there. _They are testing for some sort of infection.
examples: We are testing for weak places in your roof.

test someone in something.monolingual: to test someone in a particular subject. _ The committee decided to test her in her knowledge of the laws of the state. _ We were all tested in math and English.
examples: The committee decided to test her in her knowledge of the laws of the state.

test something out†.monolingual: to try something out; to test something to see if it works. _ I can’t wait to test my new laptop out. _ I will test out the new brakes on the car.
examples: I can’t wait to test my new laptop out.

testify against someone or something.monolingual: to be a witness against someone or something. _Who will testify against him in court? _I cannot testify against the company I work for.
examples: I cannot testify against the company I work for.

testify for someone.monolingual: to present evidence in favor of someone; to testify on someone’s behalf. _I agreed to testify for her at the trial. _Max testified for Lefty, but they were both convicted.
examples: I agreed to testify for her at the trial.

testify to something.monolingual: to swear to something. _I will testify to your whereabouts if you wish. _I think I know what happened, but I would not testify to it.
examples: I will testify to your whereabouts if you wish.

thank god for small favors..monolingual: Rur. Be thankful that something good has happened in a bad situation. _Charlie: We’re out of gas, but I think I see a gas station up ahead. Tom: Thank God for small favors. _He had a heart attack, but it was right there in the doctor’s office, so the
examples: Charlie: We’re out of gas, but I think I see a gas station up ahead.

thank one’s lucky stars.monolingual: Fig. to be thankful for one’s luck. _ You can thank your lucky stars that I was there to help you. _I thank my lucky stars that I studied the right things for the test.
examples: You can thank your lucky stars that I was there to help you.

thank someone for something.monolingual: to show or state one’s gratitude to someone for something. _ We would all like to thank you for coming tonight. _Thank you for inviting me.
examples: We would all like to thank you for coming tonight.

thank you for calling..monolingual: Thank you for calling on the telephone. (Said when the call is helpful or a bother to the caller.) _Mary: Good-bye. Sue: Good-bye, thanks for calling. _ John: Okay. Well, I have to get off the phone. I just wanted you to know what was happening with
examples: Mary: Good-bye. Sue: Good-bye, thanks for calling.

thank you for sharing..monolingual: Inf. a sarcastic remark made when someone tells something that is unpleasant, overly personal, disgusting, or otherwise annoying. _Thank you for sharing. I really need to hear about your operation. _ Thank you for sharing, Bob. I hope your parents’ d
examples: Thank you for sharing.

thank you kindly..monolingual: Thank you very much. _ Tom: May I give you a lift? Jane: Why, yes. Thank you kindly. _Mary: That’s a nice suit, and you wear it well. Charlie: Thank you kindly, ma’am.
examples: Tom: May I give you a lift? Jane: Why, yes.

*thankful for small blessings.monolingual: grateful for any small benefits or advantages one has, especially in a generally difficult situation. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ We have very little money, but we must be thankful for small blessings. At least we have enough food. _ Bob was badl
examples: We have very little money, but we must be thankful for small blessings.

thanks a bunch.monolingual: Inf. thanks. _ Thanks a bunch for your help. _ He said “thanks a bunch” and walked out.
examples: Thanks a bunch for your help.

thanks a million..monolingual: Inf. Thank you a lot._Bill: Oh, thanks a million. You were very helpful. Bob: Just glad I could help. _ John: Here’s your book. Jane: Thanks a million. Sorry I needed it back in such a rush.
examples: Bill: Oh, thanks a million.

thanks awfully..monolingual: Thank you very much. _ John: Here’s one for you. Jane: Thanks awfully. _ Mary: Here, let me help you with all that stuff. Sue: Thanks awfully.
examples: John: Here’s one for you.

thanks, but no thanks..monolingual: Inf. Thank you, but I am not interested. (A way of turning down something that is not very desirable.) _Alice: How would you like to buy my old car? Jane: Thanks, but no thanks. _ John: What do you think about a trip over to see the Wilsons? Sally: T
examples: Alice: How would you like to buy my old car? Jane: Thanks, but no thanks.

thanks loads..monolingual: Inf. Thanks a lot. _ Mary: Here, you can have these. And take these too. Sally: Thanks loads. _John: Wow! You look great! Sally: Thanks loads. I try.
examples: Mary: Here, you can have these.

thanks to someone or something.monolingual: due to someone or something; because of someone or something. (This does not necessarily suggest gratitude.) _ Thanks to the storm, we have no electricity. _ Thanks to Mary, we have tickets to the game. She bought them early before they were sold out
examples: Thanks to the storm, we have no electricity.

that ain’t hay..monolingual: Inf. That is not a small amount of money. (The highly informal word ain’t is built into the expression.) _I paid forty dollars for it, and that ain’t hay! _Bob lost his wallet with $200 in it—and that ain’t hay.
examples: Bob lost his wallet with $200 in it—and that ain’t hay.

that ain’t no lie..monolingual: Rur. What was said is true. (The highly informal word ain’t is built into the expression.) _ Tom: Sure is hot today. Jane: That ain’t no lie. _ I’m plumb exhausted, and that ain’t no lie.
examples: Tom: Sure is hot today.

that makes two of us..monolingual: Inf. The same is true for me. _ So you’re going to the football game? That makes two of us. _ Bill: I just passed my biology test. Bob: That makes two of us!
examples: So you’re going to the football game? That makes two of us.

that’s a fine how-do-you-do..monolingual: Inf. That is a terrible situation. _ Well, that’s a fine how-do-you-do! I tried to call Mary, and her number is disconnected! _That’s a fine howdo- you-do. I come home and find the kids are playing catch with my best crystal bowl.
examples: That’s a fine howdo- you-do.

that’s all for someone..monolingual: Inf. Someone will get no more chances to do things correctly. _ That’s all for you, Tom. I’ve had all I can take from you. One disappointment after another. _ You’ve gone too far, Mary. That’s all for you. Good-bye!
examples: That’s all for you, Tom.

that’s enough!.monolingual: Inf. No more!; Stop that! _Sue: Here, I’ll stack another one on top. Mary: That’s enough! It will fall. _ John: I could go on with complaint after complaint. I could talk all week, in fact. Bob: That’s enough!
examples: Sue: Here, I’ll stack another one on top.

that’s enough for now..monolingual: No more of that for now.; Please stop for a while. _ Mary: Here, have some more cake. Do you want a larger piece? Bill: Oh, no. That’s enough for now. _Bill: Shall I cut a little more off this tree, lady, or save the rest till spring? Jane: No, that’
examples: Mary: Here, have some more cake.

that’s for dang sure!.monolingual: Rur. That is quite certain! (The formulaic response to That’s for sure!. The accent is always on the dang.) _ Tom: That’s for sure! Jane: That’s for dang sure! _ Sally: We’ll be there and that’s for sure! Bill: Yup! That’s for dang sure!

that’s funny..monolingual: That is strange or peculiar. _Bill: Tom just called from Detroit and says he’s coming back tomorrow. Mary: That’s funny. He’s not supposed to. _Sue: The sky is turning very gray. Mary: That’s funny. There’s no bad weather forecast.
examples: Bill: Tom just called from Detroit and says he’s coming back tomorrow.

that’s it!.monolingual: 1. Inf. That does it!; That’s the last straw! _ That’s it! I’m leaving! I’ve had enough! _ Okay. That’s it! I’m going to report you to human resources!

examples: The ventriloquist threw his voice.

throw one’s weight around.monolingual: Fig. to attempt to boss people around; to give orders. _ The district manager came to our office and tried to throw his weight around, but no one paid any attention to him. _ Don’t try to throw your weight around in this office. We know who our boss
examples: The district manager came to our office and tried to throw his weight around, but no one paid any attention to him.

throw oneself at someone’s feet.monolingual: 1. Lit. to bow down humbly at someone’s feet; to prostrate oneself before someone. _In his guilt and horror, he threw himself at the feet of his master and begged forgiveness.
examples: In his guilt and horror, he threw himself at the feet of his master and begged forgiveness.

throw oneself into something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to jump into something, such as a body of water. _ He stood on the bridge and threw himself into the river because he was unhappy with life.
examples: He stood on the bridge and threw himself into the river because he was unhappy with life.

throw people together.monolingual: to bring or put two or more people together. _The crisis threw complete strangers together, and they became fast friends before it was over. _They were thrown together by fate.
examples: The crisis threw complete strangers together, and they became fast friends before it was over.

throw someone a curve.monolingual: 1. Lit. to pitch a curveball to someone in baseball. (See pitch someone a curve(ball).) _ The pitcher threw John a curve, and John swung wildly against thin air. _ During that game, the pitcher threw everyone a curve at least once.
examples: The pitcher threw John a curve, and John swung wildly against thin air.

throw someone for a loss.monolingual: to cause someone to be uncertain or confused. (Often passive.) _ The stress of being in front of so many people threw Ann for a loss. She forgot her speech. _It was a difficult problem. I was thrown for a loss for an answer.
examples: The stress of being in front of so many people threw Ann for a loss.

throw someone off.monolingual: to interrupt and confuse someone; to mislead someone. _ The interruption threw me off, and I lost my place in the speech. _ Little noises throw me off. Please try to be quiet. _ Your comment threw me off.
examples: The interruption threw me off, and I lost my place in the speech.

throw someone off balance.monolingual: 1. Lit. to cause someone to falter (and probably fall). _ The cyclist bumped into me and threw me off balance. _ I was thrown off balance by the gust of wind.
examples: The cyclist bumped into me and threw me off balance.

throw someone or something around†.monolingual: to toss or cast someone or something around. _ The belligerent fellow at the bar threatened to throw me around a little if I didn’t get out of his way. _ Don’t throw around your empty cans.
examples: The belligerent fellow at the bar threatened to throw me around a little if I didn’t get out of his way.

throw someone or something aside†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to cast someone or something to the side. _ He threw his child aside just as the car was about to run him down. _ Don’t just throw aside the wrapper!
examples: He threw his child aside just as the car was about to run him down.

throw someone or something back†.monolingual: to return someone or something by tossing. _The sailor climbed out of the water into the boat, and his mates grabbed him and threw him back. That was their idea of fun. _ Karen threw back the undersize fish.
examples: The sailor climbed out of the water into the boat, and his mates grabbed him and threw him back.

throw someone over.monolingual: to end a romance with someone. _ Jane threw Bill over. I think she met someone she likes better. _ Bill was about ready to throw her over, so it’s just as well.
examples: Jane threw Bill over.

throw someone’s name around.monolingual: Fig. to impress people by saying you know a famous or influential person. _ You won’t get anywhere around here by throwing the mayor’s name around. _ When you get to the meeting, just throw my name around a bit, and people will pay attention to you.
examples: You won’t get anywhere around here by throwing the mayor’s name around.

throw someone to the dogs.monolingual: Fig. to abandon someone to enemies or evil. _He served the evil empire well, but in the end, they threw him to the dogs.
examples: He served the evil empire well, but in the end, they threw him to the dogs.

throw someone to the wolves.monolingual: Fig. to sacrifice someone to save the rest; to abandon someone to harm. (Fig. on the image of giving one person to the wolves to eat so the rest can get away.) _ Don’t try to throw me to the wolves. I’ll tell the truth about the whole affair! _ The i
examples: Don’t try to throw me to the wolves.

throw something across something.monolingual: to toss something over something, from one side of it to the other. _ Can you throw this stone across the river? _ Walter threw the ball across the court to Michael.
examples: Walter threw the ball across the court to Michael.

throw something away†.monolingual: to toss something out; to dispose of something. _ Should I throw this away? _ Don’t throw away anything that might be useful.
examples: Don’t throw away anything that might be useful.

throw something back† at someone.monolingual: Fig. to return a problem or difficulty to the person from whom it came. _ He said that the problem was mine alone, and he threw it back at me. _ I tried to get someone else to take care of it, but it was thrown back at me.
examples: He said that the problem was mine alone, and he threw it back at me.

throw something back† to someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. to return something to someone by throwing. _ Liz threw the ball back to Kelly. _She threw back the ball.
examples: Liz threw the ball back to Kelly.

throw something down†.monolingual: to cast something down onto the ground; to cast something to a lower level. _ Dave took one look at the box and threw it down. _ He threw down the box.
examples: Dave took one look at the box and threw it down.

throw something down something.monolingual: to hurl something downward through something, such as a stairway, a duct, a drain, a hole. _ Max threw the weapon down the storm sewer. _ Someone threw the bucket down the well.
examples: Max threw the weapon down the storm sewer.

throw something into sharp relief.monolingual: Fig. [for something] to make something plainly evident or clearly visible. _ The dull, plain background threw the ornate settee into sharp relief. _ The red vase was thrown into sharp relief against the black background.
examples: The dull, plain background threw the ornate settee into sharp relief.

throw something off†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to cast something, such as a coat, off one’s body. _ He threw his jacket off and dived into the icy water. _He threw off his jacket.
examples: He threw his jacket off and dived into the icy water.

throw something up†.monolingual: 1. to build or erect something in a hurry. _ They sure threw that building up in a hurry. _ They threw up the building in only a few weeks.
examples: They sure threw that building up in a hurry.

throw something up to someone.monolingual: to confront someone with something. _ I threw the whole matter up to her, but she had nothing to say about it. _ I can’t figure out what to do. I will just throw the whole business up to the boss.
examples: I threw the whole matter up to her, but she had nothing to say about it.

throw the book at someone.monolingual: Fig. to charge or convict someone with as many crimes as is possible. _I made the police officer angry, so he took me to the station and threw the book at me. _ The judge threatened to throw the book at me if I didn’t stop insulting the police office
examples: I made the police officer angry, so he took me to the station and threw the book at me.

throw up.monolingual: to vomit. _ I was afraid I would throw up, the food was so horrible. _This food is bad enough to make you throw up.
examples: I was afraid I would throw up, the food was so horrible.

throw up one’s toenails.monolingual: Sl. to vomit heavily. _ I was so sick. I nearly threw up my toenails. _Frank was in the bathroom, throwing up his toenails.
examples: I was so sick. I nearly threw up my toenails.

thrust and parry.monolingual: Fig. to enter into verbal combat [with someone]; to compete actively [with someone]. (Fig. on the sport of fencing.) _I spent the entire afternoon thrusting and parrying with a committee of so-called experts in the field of insurance. _ I do not inte
examples: I spent the entire afternoon thrusting and parrying with a committee of so-called experts in the field of insurance.

thrust out.monolingual: to stick out; to stab outward; to protrude outward. _A deck thrust out from the back of the house, offering a lovely view of the stream far below. _ As he grew angrier, his chin thrust out farther and farther.
examples: A deck thrust out from the back of the house, offering a lovely view of the stream far below.

thrust someone or something aside†.monolingual: to push someone or something out of the way or to one side. _ Walter thrust Fred aside and dashed by him into the room. _ He thrust aside Fred and came into the room.
examples: Walter thrust Fred aside and dashed by him into the room.

thrust someone or something back†.monolingual: to push someone or something backward and away. _Tom moved forward, but the guard thrust him back. _He thrust back the door, which had closed on his foot.
examples: Tom moved forward, but the guard thrust him back.

thrust something down†.monolingual: to jab something downward. _ Max thrust the knife down and speared a piece of chicken. _ He thrust down the fork like a spear.
examples: Max thrust the knife down and speared a piece of chicken.

thrust something down something.monolingual: to jab or stab something down into something. _ The keeper quickly thrust the medicine down the lion’s throat. _ The chimney sweep thrust his brush down the chimney.
examples: The keeper quickly thrust the medicine down the lion’s throat.

thrust something forward.monolingual: to jab something forward. _ She thrust her jaw forward and walked into the room. _ Roger thrust his hand forward just in time to stop the child from crossing the street.
examples: She thrust her jaw forward and walked into the room.

thrust through something.monolingual: to drive or push through something forcefully. _ The front end of the car thrust through the side of the house. _The stock clerk’s knife thrust through the box, ruining the packages of noodles inside.
examples: The front end of the car thrust through the side of the house.

thrust up through something.monolingual: to stick or stab upward through something. _ The tallest of the trees thrust up through the canopy of leaves far overhead. _ We heard a ripping sound and saw the tent pole thrust up through the top of the tent.
examples: The tallest of the trees thrust up through the canopy of leaves far overhead.

thud against someone or something.monolingual: to thump against someone or something, making a dull noise on impact. _ The pumpkin thudded against Jerry, breaking open and messing up his clothes. _The ball thudded against the wall and bounced back.
examples: The pumpkin thudded against Jerry, breaking open and messing up his clothes.

thud into someone or something.monolingual: to bump into someone or something, making a dull noise on impact. _ The door blew open and thudded into Marie, giving her a bump on the knee. _ The ball thudded into the side of the house.
examples: The door blew open and thudded into Marie, giving her a bump on the knee.

a thumbnail sketch.monolingual: a brief or small picture or description. _The manager gave a thumbnail sketch of her plans. _ The student wrote a thumbnail sketch of his project.
examples: The manager gave a thumbnail sketch of her plans.

thumbs down.monolingual: 1. a sign of disapproval. _The board gave our proposal a thumbs down. _ The administration’s tax bill got a thumbs down in Congress.
examples: The board gave our proposal a thumbs down.

thumbs up.monolingual: 1. a sign of approval. _It was a thumbs up on the new filtration plant at Thursday’s village board meeting. _ There was no thumbs up for the mayor as she faced certain defeat in today’s balloting.
examples: It was a thumbs up on the new filtration plant at Thursday’s village board meeting.

thump on someone or something.monolingual: to pound on someone or something. _ Tim was angry with Roger and thumped on him a little, but decided to forgive him. _ Andy thumped on the bass drum for an hour.
examples: Tim was angry with Roger and thumped on him a little, but decided to forgive him.

thump something down†.monolingual: to throw something down so it makes a pounding noise. _ Nancy thumped the parcel down and caught her breath. _She thumped down the parcel.
examples: Nancy thumped the parcel down and caught her breath.

thunder across something.monolingual: Fig. to move across something, making a rumbling sound. _The jets thundered across the sky, heading for their home base. _ As the race car thundered across the track, people strained to get a better view.
examples: The jets thundered across the sky, heading for their home base.

thunder past someone or something.monolingual: Fig. to move past someone or something, rumbling. _ As the traffic thundered past, I wondered why there was so much of it. _ The train thundered past the sleeping town.
examples: As the traffic thundered past, I wondered why there was so much of it.

thunder something out†.monolingual: Fig. to respond with words spoken in a voice like thunder. _ He thundered the words out so everyone could hear them. _He thundered out the words.
examples: He thundered the words out so everyone could hear them.

tick away.monolingual: [for seconds or minutes] to go by as the clock ticks. _ The seconds ticked away as the fateful time got closer. _ As time ticked away, the surgeons worked feverishly to repair the walls of Roger’s heart.
examples: The seconds ticked away as the fateful time got closer.

tick someone off†.monolingual: to make someone angry. _ That really ticks me off! _ Doesn’t that tick off everyone?

ticket someone for some place.monolingual: to supply a ticket for someone to go to some place. _ The airlines clerk ticketed me for Houston and checked in my baggage. _ I was ticketed for both f lights, saving me some time.
examples: The airlines clerk ticketed me for Houston and checked in my baggage.

tickle someone pink.monolingual: Fig. to please or entertain someone very much. _ Bill told a joke that really tickled us all pink. _ I know that these flowers will tickle her pink.
examples: Bill told a joke that really tickled us all pink.

tickle someone’s fancy.monolingual: to interest someone; to make someone curious. _ I have an interesting problem here that I think will tickle your fancy. _ This doesn’t tickle my fancy at all. This is dull and boring.
examples: I have an interesting problem here that I think will tickle your fancy.

tickle the ivories.monolingual: to play the piano. _I used to be able to tickle the ivories real nice. _ She sat down to tickle the ivories for a while.
examples: I used to be able to tickle the ivories real nice.

tickled pink.monolingual: Fig. very much pleased or entertained. _ I was tickled pink to have you visit us. _We were tickled pink when your f lowers arrived.
examples: I was tickled pink to have you visit us.

the tide turned.monolingual: 1. Lit. the tide changed from high tide to low tide or vice versa. _ The tide turned before the ship had sailed out of the harbor.
examples: The tide turned before the ship had sailed out of the harbor.

tidy something up†.monolingual: to clean something up; to make something more orderly. _ Please tidy this room up. _ I’ll tidy up the kitchen later.
examples: Please tidy this room up.

tidy up.monolingual: to clean up [oneself or a place]. _ Please tidy up. This place is a mess. _ Please tidy up. You are a mess.
examples: Please tidy up.

tie in with something.monolingual: [for a piece of information] to complement other information. _ These figures tie in with what I just said. _The crime lab report ties in with our current theory.
examples: These figures tie in with what I just said.

tie someone or something down†.monolingual: to fasten someone or something down by tying or binding. _ The robbers tied Gary down so he couldn’t get up and get away. _ They tied down Gary.
examples: The robbers tied Gary down so he couldn’t get up and get away.

tie someone or something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to bind someone or something securely. _ The sheriff tied the crooks up and took them to a cell. _ He tied up the bandit. _ I tied the package up and put a label on it.
examples: The sheriff tied the crooks up and took them to a cell.

tie someone’s hands.monolingual: 1. Lit. to use rope or string to tie someone’s hands together. _The robber tied my hands and I couldn’t call the police.
examples: The robber tied my hands and I couldn’t call the police.

tie someone to something.monolingual: Fig. to associate someone with something; to make a connection between someone and something. _ The police are trying to tie Lefty to the burglary. _ They’ll never tie me to that bunch of crooks!
examples: The police are trying to tie Lefty to the burglary.

tie something back†.monolingual: to bind or fasten something back out of the way. _ George tied the curtains back to let a little more light in. _ Let me tie back the vines out of the way.
examples: George tied the curtains back to let a little more light in.

tie something in a knot.monolingual: to bend something, such as a rope, upon itself to make a knot. _ I ended up tying the rope in a knot. _ The rope was tied in a knot and no one could get it undone.
examples: I ended up tying the rope in a knot.

tie something off†.monolingual: to tie the ends of something losing fluid, as blood vessels to prevent bleeding. _ The surgeons tied all the blood vessels off—one by one—as they were exposed. _ They tied off all the vessels very quickly.
examples: The surgeons tied all the blood vessels off—one by one—as they were exposed.

tie something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to tie strings or cords on something in order to close or contain it. _Please tie this pack- age up securely so I can mail it. _Tie up your shoes!
examples: Please tie this pack- age up securely so I can mail it.

tie the knot.monolingual: 1. Fig. to marry a mate. _ We tied the knot in a little chapel on the Arkansas border. _They finally tied the knot.
examples: We tied the knot in a little chapel on the Arkansas border.

tie traffic up†.monolingual: Fig. to cause road traffic to stop. _ If you tie traffic up for too long, you’ll get a traffic ticket. _Please don’t stop on the roadway. It’ll tie up traffic.
examples: If you tie traffic up for too long, you’ll get a traffic ticket.

tied down.monolingual: Fig. restricted by responsibilities. _ I love my home, but sometimes I don’t like being tied down. _I don’t feel tied down, even though I have a lot of responsibility.
examples: I love my home, but sometimes I don’t like being tied down.

tied up.monolingual: Fig. busy. _ How long will you be tied up? _ I will be tied up in a meeting for an hour.
examples: I will be tied up in a meeting for an hour.

*tight as a tick.monolingual: 1. very tight. (Fig. on the image of a tick swollen tight with blood or of a tick stuck tightly in someone’s skin. *Also: as ~.) _ This lid is screwed on tight as a tick. _The windows were closed—tight as a tick—to keep the cold out.
examples: This lid is screwed on tight as a tick.

*tight as dick’s hatband.monolingual: Fig. very tight. (*Also: as ~.) _ I’ve got to lose some weight. My belt is as tight as Dick’s hatband. _ This window is stuck tight as Dick’s hatband.
examples: I’ve got to lose some weight.

a tight race.monolingual: a close race. _ It was a tight race right up to the final turn when my horse pulled ahead and won easily.
examples: It was a tight race right up to the final turn when my horse pulled ahead and won easily.

tighten one’s belt.monolingual: Fig. to manage to spend less money; to use less of something. _ Things are beginning to cost more and more. It looks like we’ll all have to tighten our belts. _ Times are hard, and prices are high. I can tighten my belt for only so long.
examples: Things are beginning to cost more and more.

tighten something up†.monolingual: to make something tighter. _ Tighten your seat belt up. It looks loose. _ Can you tighten up all the bolts?
examples: Tighten your seat belt up.

tighten up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to get tighter. _ The door hinges began to tighten up, making the door hard to open and close. _ His grip around the handle tightened up and he refused to let go.
examples: The door hinges began to tighten up, making the door hard to open and close.

till hell freezes over.monolingual: Inf. forever. (Use caution with hell.) _ That’s all right, boss; I can wait till hell freezes over for your answer. _ I’ll be here till hell freezes over.
examples: That’s all right, boss; I can wait till hell freezes over for your answer.

till kingdom come.monolingual: Fig. until the end of the world; forever. _ Do I have to keep assembling these units till kingdom come? _ I’ll hate her guts till kingdom come.
examples: I’ll hate her guts till kingdom come.

tilt at windmills.monolingual: Fig. to fight battles with imaginary enemies; to fight against unimportant enemies or issues. (As with the fictional character, Don Quixote, who attacked windmills.) _ Aren’t you too smart to go around tilting at windmills? _ I’m not going to fight t
examples: I’m not going to fight this issue.

tilt something back†.monolingual: to move something so it leans back. _ Alice tilted her chair back and nearly fell over. _ She tilted back her chair and relaxed.
examples: Alice tilted her chair back and nearly fell over.

tilt to something.monolingual: to lean or slant toward something or in a particular direction. _ The picture tilts to the left. _ Her head was tilted to the left because she was trying to see around the corner.
examples: The picture tilts to the left.

tilt toward someone or something.monolingual: 1. Lit to lean toward someone or something. _The table is tilting toward Roger. _ The old shed tilted toward the west.
examples: The table is tilting toward Roger.

*time for someone or something.monolingual: the time to deal with someone or something. (Often with the negative. *Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~; make ~; find ~.) _I’m sorry, I don’t have time for you today. _I don’t think I have time for a game of chess. _ I have time for one short
examples: I’m sorry, I don’t have time for you today.

time in.monolingual: to record one’s arrival time. _ Did you remember to time in this morning? _ When did she time in?

time is a great healer..monolingual: Prov. Emotional pain will grow less as time passes. _ You may think your heart is broken and you can never possibly love again, but time is a great healer.
examples: You may think your heart is broken and you can never possibly love again, but time is a great healer.

time is money..monolingual: (My) time is valuable, so don’t waste it. _I can’t afford to spend a lot of time standing here talking. Time is money, you know! _ People who keep saying time is money may be working too hard.
examples: I can’t afford to spend a lot of time standing here talking.

time is of the essence..monolingual: Timing and meeting all the deadlines are essential and required. (Often seen in contractual agreements.) _ The final payment is due on the first day of December, by midnight. Time is of the essence.
examples: The final payment is due on the first day of December, by midnight.

the time is ripe..monolingual: Prov. It is the most favorable time to do something. _ You ought to buy a house this year. Prices are so low, and you have enough money saved for a down payment. The time is ripe. _Since Joe was in a good mood, I judged that the time was ripe to ask
examples: You ought to buy a house this year.

time is up..monolingual: Fig. The allotted time has run out. _You must stop now. Your time is up. _ Time’s up! Turn in your tests whether you’re finished or not.
examples: You must stop now.

*time off.monolingual: a period of time that is free from employment. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~; take (some)~.) _I’ll have to get time off for jury duty. _I have time off to go downtown and shop.
examples: I’ll have to get time off for jury duty.

*time off for good behavior.monolingual: 1. Lit. a reduction in one’s prison sentence because of good behavior. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ Bob will get out of jail tomorrow rather than next week. He got time off for good behavior.
examples: Bob will get out of jail tomorrow rather than next week.

time out.monolingual: 1. to record one’s departure time. _ Did you remember to time out when you left work? _I timed out at the regular time.
examples: I timed out at the regular time.

time’s a-wastin’.monolingual: Rur. Time is running out.; It is getting late. _Hurry up! Time’s a-wastin’! _How come you’re still in bed? Time’s a-wastin’!

time someone in†.monolingual: to record someone’s arrival time. _ I timed you in at noon. Where were you? _My job is to time in people.
examples: I timed you in at noon.

time someone out†.monolingual: to record someone’s departure time. _ Harry had to time everyone out because the time clock was broken. _ I had to time out everyone.
