examples: Harry had to time everyone out because the time clock was broken.

*time to catch one’s breath.monolingual: Fig. enough time to relax or behave normally. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give one ~.) _When things slow down around here, I’ll get time to catch my breath. _Sally was so busy she didn’t even have time to catch her breath.
examples: When things slow down around here, I’ll get time to catch my breath.

time will tell..monolingual: Something will become known in the course of time. _I don’t know if things will improve. Time will tell. _Who knows what the future will bring? Only time will tell.
examples: I don’t know if things will improve.

time works wonders..monolingual: Prov. The passing of time can resolve many problems. _ I thought I would never forgive my ex-husband for leaving me, but now, ten years later, I feel pretty well disposed toward him. Time works wonders. _You’ll change your mind eventually. Time works
examples: I thought I would never forgive my ex-husband for leaving me, but now, ten years later, I feel pretty well disposed toward him.

times are changing..monolingual: a response to a surprising piece of news from someone. _Sue: They paid nearly five hundred thousand for their first house! Rachel: Well, I shouldn’t be so surprised. Times are changing, I guess. _ “Times are changing,” warned Mary. “You can’t expect
examples: Sue: They paid nearly five hundred thousand for their first house! Rachel: Well, I shouldn’t be so surprised.

a tin ear.monolingual: Fig. a poor ear for music; a poor hearing ability when it comes to music and distinguishing pitches. _ I think I had better not try to sing along with you. I have a tin ear and would ruin your performance.
examples: I think I had better not try to sing along with you.

tinge something with something.monolingual: to give something a bit of the character, color, state of mind, light, etc., of something. _ The dust in the air had tinged the sunset with orange. _ The evening air was tinged with the smell of jasmine.
examples: The dust in the air had tinged the sunset with orange.

the tip of the iceberg.monolingual: Fig. only the part of something that can be easily observed, but not the rest of it, which is hidden. (Referring to the fact that the majority of an iceberg is below the surface of the water.) _ The problems that you see here now are just the tip of
examples: The problems that you see here now are just the tip of the iceberg.

tip one’s hand.monolingual: to reveal what one is going to do; to reveal one’s secrets. (From card playing.) _ I didn’t tip my hand at all. I left them guessing. _ They tried to get me to tip my hand.
examples: I didn’t tip my hand at all.

tip over.monolingual: to topple over and fall. _ Roger shook the table slightly, and the vase tipped over. _ The truck was overloaded and looked so heavy that I thought it would tip over.
examples: Roger shook the table slightly, and the vase tipped over.

tip someone over.monolingual: to cause someone to fall. _ Oh! You almost tipped me over! _ Todd fell against Maggie and tipped her over.
examples: Todd fell against Maggie and tipped her over.

tip someone with something.monolingual: to pay a tip of a certain amount to someone. _ I tipped the headwaiter with a twenty or we would still be waiting. _How much did you tip the waitress with?
examples: I tipped the headwaiter with a twenty or we would still be waiting.

tip something over†.monolingual: to cause something to fall over. _ Did you tip this chair over? _ Who tipped over the chair?

tip something up†.monolingual: to tilt something so it dumps. _ Jason tipped the wheelbarrow up and dumped the dirt out. _ He tipped up the glass, dumping the orange juice on the table.
examples: Jason tipped the wheelbarrow up and dumped the dirt out.

tip the scales at something.monolingual: to weigh a particular weight. _Albert tips the scales at nearly 200 pounds. _The champ weighed in and tipped the scales at 180.
examples: Albert tips the scales at nearly 200 pounds.

tire of someone or something.monolingual: to grow weary of someone or something. _She tired of him and left him. _I am beginning to tire of the furniture in the living room.
examples: She tired of him and left him.

tire out.monolingual: to become exhausted. _ I tire out easily. _ When I had the f lu, I found that I tired out easily.
examples: I tire out easily.

tire someone out†.monolingual: to exhaust someone. _ The extra work tired him out a lot. _Too much work will tire out the horses.
examples: The extra work tired him out a lot.

tits and ass.monolingual: a public display of [the human female] breasts and buttocks. (Referring to television, film, and stage performances in which women breasts and buttocks or in which these body parts are emphasized or made prominent. Use caution with the expression. Fi
examples: We have a really fine choice on television tonight.

to a great extent.monolingual: Cliché mainly; largely. _ To a great extent, Mary is the cause of her own problems. _ I’ve finished my work to a great extent. There is nothing important left to do.
examples: To a great extent, Mary is the cause of her own problems.

to and fro.monolingual: [of movement] toward and away from something. _The puppy was very active—running to and fro— wagging its tail. _ The lion in the cage moved to and fro, watching the people in front of the cage.
examples: The puppy was very active—running to and fro— wagging its tail.

to be safe.monolingual: to be cautious; to be careful; [to do something just] in case it is necessary; to be very well prepared. _ Just to be safe, you should take some extra water with you. _ Other people like to drive over the speed limit, but I prefer to be safe.
examples: Just to be safe, you should take some extra water with you.

to beat the band.monolingual: very briskly; very fast. _ He’s selling computers to beat the band since he started advertising. _ She worked to beat the band to get ready for this.
examples: He’s selling computers to beat the band since he started advertising.

to boot.monolingual: in addition. _For graduation, I got a new suit and a coat to boot. _She got an F on her term paper and flunked the final to boot.
examples: For graduation, I got a new suit and a coat to boot.

to date.monolingual: up to the present time. _ How much have you accomplished to date? _ I’ve done everything I’m supposed to have done to date.
examples: I’ve done everything I’m supposed to have done to date.

to die for.monolingual: Sl. important or desirable enough to die for; worth dying for. _ This chocolate cake is to die for! _ We had a beautiful room at the hotel and the service was to die for.
examples: We had a beautiful room at the hotel and the service was to die for.

to each his own..monolingual: Prov. Each person has the right to make choices. _ A: Bob likes chopped prunes on ice cream! B: To each his own.
examples: A: Bob likes chopped prunes on ice cream! B: To each his own.

to have a hollow leg.monolingual: Fig. to have a great capacity or need for food or drink. _Bobby can drink more beer than I can afford. I think he has a hollow leg!
examples: Bobby can drink more beer than I can afford.

to one’s heart’s content.monolingual: Fig. as much as one wants. _ John wanted a week’s vacation so he could go to the lake and fish to his heart’s content. _ I just sat there, eating chocolate to my heart’s content.
examples: John wanted a week’s vacation so he could go to the lake and fish to his heart’s content.

to say the least.monolingual: at the very least; without overemphasizing the subject; to put it mildly. _ We were not at all pleased with her work—to say the least. _ When they had an accident, they were upset to say the least.
examples: We were not at all pleased with her work—to say the least.

to some extent.monolingual: to some degree; in some amount; partly. _ I’ve solved this problem to some extent. _ I can help you understand this to some extent.
examples: I’ve solved this problem to some extent.

to someone’s liking.monolingual: fitting someone’s personal preferences. _I had my house painted, but the job was not to my liking. _ Large meals with lots of fat are not to Bob’s liking.
examples: I had my house painted, but the job was not to my liking.

to someone’s way of thinking.monolingual: in someone’s opinion. _ This isn’t satisfactory to my way of thinking. _ To my way of thinking, this is the perfect kind of vacation.
examples: This isn’t satisfactory to my way of thinking.

to the core.monolingual: all the way through; basically and essentially. (Usually with some negative sense, such as evil, rotten, etc.) _ Bill said that John is evil to the core. _ This organization is rotten to the core.
examples: Bill said that John is evil to the core.

to the last.monolingual: to the very end; to the conclusion. _ All of us kept trying to the last. _ It was a very boring play, but I sat through it to the last.
examples: All of us kept trying to the last.

to the letter.monolingual: exactly as instructed; exactly as written. _ I didn’t make an error. I followed your instruction to the letter. _We didn’t prepare the recipe to the letter, but the cake still turned out very well.
examples: I didn’t make an error.

to the max.monolingual: Sl. as much as possible, maximally. _ She is happy to the max. _ They worked to the max their whole shift.
examples: She is happy to the max.

to the nth degree.monolingual: to the maximum amount. _ Jane is a perfectionist and tries to be careful to the nth degree. _This scientific instrument is accurate to the nth degree.
examples: Jane is a perfectionist and tries to be careful to the nth degree.

to whom it may concern.monolingual: Cliché to the person to whom this applies. (A form of address used when you do not know the name of the person who handles the kind of business you are writing about.) _ The letter started out, “To whom it may concern.” _ When you don’t know who to w
examples: The letter started out, “To whom it may concern.

to wit.monolingual: namely; that is; that is to say. _ The criminal was punished; to wit, he received a 20-year sentence. _ Many students, to wit Mary, Bill, Sue, and Anne, complained about their teacher.
examples: The criminal was punished; to wit, he received a 20-year sentence.

today here, tomorrow the world..monolingual: Prov. Successful in this location now, with later recognition in the rest of the world. (Describes something whose influence seems certain to spread. The name of an appropriate locality is usually substituted for here.) _ I thought that silly fashion
examples: I thought that silly fashion in clothes was unique to California, but it seems to be spreading.

toddle along.monolingual: 1. to walk along in an unconcerned manner. _ Kathleen was just toddling along, minding her own business.
examples: Kathleen was just toddling along, minding her own business.

toil for someone.monolingual: 1. to work on behalf of someone or for someone’s benefit. _I don’t mind toiling for her as long as she thanks me. _ I don’t know why I toil for you. You are totally ungrateful.
examples: I don’t mind toiling for her as long as she thanks me.

toil for something.monolingual: 1. to work toward a particular goal or ideal. _ I am willing to toil for something I believe in. _ She spent the afternoon toiling for her favorite charity.
examples: I am willing to toil for something I believe in.

toil over someone or something.monolingual: to work hard on someone or something. _ The doctors toiled over the patient for hours. _Ken toiled over his model plane well into the night.
examples: The doctors toiled over the patient for hours.

toil up something.monolingual: to work hard to climb something steep. _ The hikers toiled up the slope slowly. _ As the bus toiled up the hill, we worried that the engine might be overheating.
examples: The hikers toiled up the slope slowly.

a token gesture.monolingual: an action or a decision that is so small or inconsequential as to be only symbolic. _ Offering to pay for my dinner was only a token gesture. That does little to make up for my inconvenience.
examples: Offering to pay for my dinner was only a token gesture.

toll for someone.monolingual: [for a bell] to ring for someone. _ Who are the bells tolling for? _The bells are tolling for Mr. Green, who died last night.
examples: The bells are tolling for Mr.

tomorrow is another day..monolingual: Prov. Things may improve tomorrow; tomorrow you will have a chance to solve the problems that are upsetting you today. (Often used to encourage someone to relax and wait until tomorrow to do or worry about something.) _Child: This math homework is ho
examples: Child: This math homework is horrible! I can’t do it! Mother: Put it away for tonight and go to bed.

tomorrow never comes..monolingual: Prov. When the day arrives that you are now calling “tomorrow,” you will call that day “today” and a different day will be called “tomorrow.” (Therefore, you should not resolve to do something tomorrow, since that day will never arrive.) _ Jill: When
examples: Jill: When are you going to go to lunch with me? Jane: Tomorrow.

tone someone or something up†.monolingual: to make someone or something stronger or more fit, muscularly. _ I suggested an exercise that would tone him up and make him feel better. _ The exercises toned up his tummy muscles. _ I need to get busy and tone myself up.
examples: I suggested an exercise that would tone him up and make him feel better.

tone something down†.monolingual: to cause something to have less of an impact on the senses of sight or sound; to lessen the impact of something prepared for public performance or consumption. _ This is rather shocking. You had better tone it down a bit. _ Tone down this paragraph.
examples: This is rather shocking.

tongue-in-cheek.monolingual: Fig. insincere; joking. _ Ann made a tongue-in-cheek remark to John, and he got mad because he thought she was serious. _ The play seemed very serious at first, but then everyone saw that it was tongue-in-cheek, and they began laughing.
examples: Ann made a tongue-in-cheek remark to John, and he got mad because he thought she was serious.

*a tongue-lashing.monolingual: Fig. a severe scolding. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ I really got a tonguelashing when I got home. _ Ted will have a tongue-lashing at home.
examples: I really got a tonguelashing when I got home.

tons of something.monolingual: lots of something. _We got tons of fried chicken, so help yourself. _ You are in tons of trouble.
examples: We got tons of fried chicken, so help yourself.

too big for one’s britches.monolingual: Rur. too haughty for one’s status or age. _ Bill’s getting a little too big for his britches, and somebody’s going to straighten him out. _ You’re too big for your britches, young man! You had better be more respectful.
examples: Bill’s getting a little too big for his britches, and somebody’s going to straighten him out.

too close for comfort.monolingual: Cliché [for a misfortune or a threat] to be dangerously close. _ That car nearly hit me! That was too close for comfort. _ When I was in the hospital, I nearly died from pneumonia. Believe me, that was too close for comfort.
examples: That car nearly hit me! That was too close for comfort.

*too funny for words.monolingual: extremely funny. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ Tom is usually too funny for words at parties. _ The joke Tom told was really too funny for words.
examples: Tom is usually too funny for words at parties.

*too good to be true.monolingual: almost unbelievable; so good as to be unbelievable. (*Typically: be ~; become ~; get ~.) _ The news was too good to be true. _ When I finally got a big raise, it was too good to be true.
examples: The news was too good to be true.

too little, too late.monolingual: Prov. Not enough help to save the situation, and arriving too late. _After a lifetime of bad diet and no exercise, Lorna tried to save her health by improving her habits, but it was too little, too late. _ Fred: I know how to keep my business from go
examples: After a lifetime of bad diet and no exercise, Lorna tried to save her health by improving her habits, but it was too little, too late.

*too much.monolingual: overwhelming; excellent. (*Typically: be ~; get to be ~.) _ It’s wonderful. It’s just too much! _ You are so kind. This is too much.
examples: It’s wonderful.

too rich for someone’s blood.monolingual: 1. too expensive for one’s budget. _ This hotel is too rich for my blood. _ Europe is getting too rich for our blood.
examples: This hotel is too rich for my blood.

tool something up†.monolingual: to equip a factory or production line with particular tools and machines, as for new products. _ The manager closed down the factory so she could tool it up for the new models. _She tooled up the factory in record time.
examples: The manager closed down the factory so she could tool it up for the new models.

tool up.monolingual: to become equipped with tools. _ I need some money so I can tool up to do the job. _ The factory tooled up to make the new cars in only two weeks.
examples: I need some money so I can tool up to do the job.

top brass.monolingual: the highest leader(s); the boss(es). (Originally military.) _The top brass turned thumbs down on the proposal. _You’ll have to check it out with the top brass. She’ll be home around five.
examples: The top brass turned thumbs down on the proposal.

top notch.monolingual: the absolute best. (Hyphenated before a nominal.) _Julie’s singing in the musical is top notch. _He prepared a top-notch meal before the movie and dessert for afterward.
examples: Julie’s singing in the musical is top notch.

the top of the heap.monolingual: Fig. a position superior to everyone else. _ For some reason, Jerry has to be at the top of the heap. _She fought her way to the top of the heap and means to stay there.
examples: For some reason, Jerry has to be at the top of the heap.

top something off.monolingual: to add to the difficulty of something. _ Jane lost her job, and to top that off, she caught the f lu. _ I had a bad day, and to top it off, I have to go to a meeting tonight.
examples: Jane lost her job, and to top that off, she caught the f lu.

top something up†.monolingual: to add a bit of something to replenish the amount that was used. _ Let me top your drink up. _ Can I top up your glass?
examples: Let me top your drink up.

top something with something.monolingual: to decorate or finish something by adding something. _They topped the new garage with a weather vane. _ Molly-Jo topped each sundae with a big red cherry.
examples: They topped the new garage with a weather vane.

topple down.monolingual: [for a stack of something] to crumple and fall down. _The chimney toppled down in the earthquake. _ The woodpile toppled down during the night and scared us all to death.
examples: The chimney toppled down in the earthquake.

topple over.monolingual: [for something very tall] to fall over. _I was afraid that Jimmy’s stack of blocks would topple over. _The stack of books toppled over and ended up as a jumbled mess on the f loor.
examples: I was afraid that Jimmy’s stack of blocks would topple over.

topple something down†.monolingual: to cause a stack of something to crumple and fall down. _ The earthquake toppled the chimney down. _ The hurricane toppled down the weakest buildings.
examples: The earthquake toppled the chimney down.

torment someone into doing something.monolingual: to force someone to agree to do something through threats or maltreatment. _ You can’t torment me into doing something I don’t want to do! _ Alice was tormented into going on the picnic.
examples: Alice was tormented into going on the picnic.

torture someone into something.monolingual: to force someone to do something through the use of torture. (More severe than torment someone into something.) _The agents threatened to torture me into telling the secrets, so I gave in immediately, of course. _ Max tried to torture the old prospec
examples: The agents threatened to torture me into telling the secrets, so I gave in immediately, of course.

toss a salad.monolingual: to mix various salad ingredients together. _ The chef tossed the salad. _I tossed the salad just before my guests arrived.
examples: The chef tossed the salad.

toss one’s cookies.monolingual: Sl. to vomit. _ Don’t run too fast after you eat or you’ll toss your cookies. _ Oh, I feel terrible. I think I’m going to toss my cookies.
examples: Don’t run too fast after you eat or you’ll toss your cookies.

toss someone or something around†.monolingual: to throw someone or something around. _ The waves tossed him around and almost dashed him on the rocks. _The waves tossed around all the little boats.
examples: The waves tossed him around and almost dashed him on the rocks.

toss someone or something aside†.monolingual: to throw someone or something aside or out of the way. _The kidnapper tossed the child aside and reached for his gun. _The soldier tossed aside the helpless civilian and ran into the house. _ Fred tossed the can aside and Alice picked it up.
examples: The kidnapper tossed the child aside and reached for his gun.

toss someone or something away†.monolingual: to throw someone or something away; to discard someone or something. _You can’t just toss me away! I’m your husband! _ She tossed away her husband of twenty years. _ She tossed the cigarette away.
examples: She tossed away her husband of twenty years.

toss someone or something back†.monolingual: 1. to throw or force someone or something backward. _ The blast tossed me back into the room. _ The blast tossed back the emergency personnel.
examples: The blast tossed me back into the room.

toss something around†.monolingual: Fig. to discuss something. _ I have a few things to discuss. Can we meet later and toss them around? _ We tossed around a few ideas after dinner.
examples: I have a few things to discuss.

toss something back and forth.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for two or more people] to toss something to each other alternately. _ Carol and Kelly tossed the ball back and forth for a few minutes. _We will toss the ball back and forth until we get tired.
examples: Carol and Kelly tossed the ball back and forth for a few minutes.

toss something down†.monolingual: Fig. to drink down a drink quickly. _ He tossed a beer down and left the bar. _ Sam tossed down a couple of shots.
examples: He tossed a beer down and left the bar.

toss something off†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to throw something off (of oneself ). _ Bob coughed so hard he tossed his blanket off. _ Tom tossed off his jacket and sat down to watch television.
examples: Bob coughed so hard he tossed his blanket off.

toss something together.monolingual: to assemble something hastily. _This report is useless. You just tossed it together! _ This meal was just tossed together, but it was delicious.
examples: This report is useless.

toss something up†.monolingual: to throw something upward to a higher place or up into the air. _ He tossed the coin up, calling “heads” and hoping for the best. _ He tossed up the coin.
examples: He tossed the coin up, calling “heads” and hoping for the best.

total something up†.monolingual: to add up the total of something. _ Please total the bill up and let me see the cost. _ Total up the bill and give it to me.
examples: Please total the bill up and let me see the cost.

totally awesome.monolingual: Sl. very, very impressive. _ His motorcycle is totally awesome. It must have cost a fortune.
examples: His motorcycle is totally awesome.

tote something up†.monolingual: to add something up. _The clerk toted the bill up and asked for an enormous sum. _ Tote up your expense report quickly and submit it to accounts payable.
examples: The clerk toted the bill up and asked for an enormous sum.

touch at some place.monolingual: Fig. [for a ship or an airplane] to visit or call at a port. _We touched at Aruba for about an hour. _ Our little boat touched at a number of different islands during the two-week cruise.
examples: We touched at Aruba for about an hour.

touch down.monolingual: [for an airplane] to come in contact with the ground; to land. _ Flight twelve is due to touch down at midnight. _ When will this plane touch down?
examples: Flight twelve is due to touch down at midnight.

a touch of something.monolingual: 1. a mild case of some illness. _ I have a touch of the flu and need some more bed rest.
examples: I have a touch of the flu and need some more bed rest.

touch on something.monolingual: Fig. to mention something; to talk about something briefly. _ In tomorrow’s lecture I’d like to touch on the matter of taxation. _ The teacher only touched on the subject. There wasn’t time to do more than that.
examples: In tomorrow’s lecture I’d like to touch on the matter of taxation.

touch someone or something off†.monolingual: Fig. to ignite or excite someone or something; to excite anger or chaos. _ She is very excitable. The slightest thing will touch her off. _ The appearance of the fox touched off a furor in the henhouse.
examples: She is very excitable.

touch something to something.monolingual: to bring something into contact with something. _ She touched her hand to her ear to indicate to the speaker to talk louder. _ The magician touched his wand to the hat and a rabbit jumped out.
examples: She touched her hand to her ear to indicate to the speaker to talk louder.

touch something up†.monolingual: to fix up the minor flaws in something; to repair a paint job on something. _It’s only a little scratch in the finish. We can touch it up easily. _ Tom touched up the scrape with a little paint.
examples: It’s only a little scratch in the finish.

touch-and-go.monolingual: very uncertain or critical. _ Things were touch-and-go at the office until a new manager was hired. _ Jane had a serious operation, and everything was touchand- go for two days after her surgery.
examples: Things were touch-and-go at the office until a new manager was hired.

touched by someone or something.monolingual: Fig. emotionally affected or moved by someone or something. _Sally was very nice to me. I was very touched by her. _ I was really touched by your kind letter.
examples: Sally was very nice to me.

a tough break.monolingual: a bit of bad fortune. _ I’m sorry to hear about your accident. Tough break. _John had a lot of tough breaks when he was a kid, but he’s doing okay now.
examples: I’m sorry to hear about your accident.

a tough call.monolingual: a difficult judgment to make. _ It’s a tough call, but I choose Fred and Mary. Sorry Tom and Carole. _ We’re still undecided on whether to buy a place or rent— it’s a tough call.
examples: It’s a tough call, but I choose Fred and Mary.

a tough cookie.monolingual: a person who is difficult to deal with. _ He’s a tough cookie, but I can handle him. _ There was a tough cookie in here this morning who demanded to see the manager.
examples: He’s a tough cookie, but I can handle him.

a tough customer.monolingual: someone who is difficult to deal with. _ Some of those bikers are really tough customers. _ Walt is a tough customer. Just keep away from him.
examples: Some of those bikers are really tough customers.

tough going.monolingual: progress that is difficult. _It was tough going for the first few miles, but the trail became much easier as we got farther into the forest.
examples: It was tough going for the first few miles, but the trail became much easier as we got farther into the forest.

tough guy.monolingual: a strong and severe man; a man who might be part of the underworld. _He was your typical tough guy— jutting chin, gruff voice—but he was just our decorator checking up on the drapes. _So, you want to be a tough guy, huh?
examples: He was your typical tough guy— jutting chin, gruff voice—but he was just our decorator checking up on the drapes.

*tough on someone.monolingual: severe and demanding in dealing with someone. (*Typically: act ~; be ~; become ~; get ~.) _ My boss is very tough on me, but I need the structure and discipline.
examples: My boss is very tough on me, but I need the structure and discipline.

tough something out.monolingual: to carry on with something despite difficulties or setbacks. _ Sorry, you’ll just have to tough it out. _I think I can tough this job out for another month.
examples: Sorry, you’ll just have to tough it out.

toughen someone or something up†.monolingual: to cause someone or something to be stronger, more uncompromising, or more severe. _ A few days behind the service counter at the dis- count store will toughen her up quickly. _ Having to deal with complaints toughened up the clerk quickly. _She trie
examples: A few days behind the service counter at the dis- count store will toughen her up quickly.

toughen up.monolingual: to become tougher, stronger, or more severe. _ She will toughen up after a while. You have to be tough around here to survive. _ You are going to have to toughen up if you want to play on the team.
examples: She will toughen up after a while.

tout someone or something around.monolingual: to promote and boost someone or something publicly. _He is touting his favorite candidate around, hoping to get a few votes for her. _Roger is touting his book around, trying to boost sales.
examples: He is touting his favorite candidate around, hoping to get a few votes for her.

tout suite!.monolingual: right away; with all haste. (Pronounced “toot sweet.” From French toute de suite.) _ John: Come on, get this finished! Bob: I’m trying. John: Tout suite! Get moving! _ “I want this mess cleaned up, tout suite!” shouted Sally, hands on her hips and st
examples: John: Come on, get this finished! Bob: I’m trying.

tow someone or something away†.monolingual: to pull something, such as a car or a boat, away with another car, boat, etc. (The someone refers to the property of someone, not the person.) _If I don’t get back to my car, they will tow me away. _ The truck towed away my car. _ A big truck came an
examples: If I don’t get back to my car, they will tow me away.

towel someone or something down†.monolingual: to rub someone or something dry with a towel. _ The mother toweled her child down and dressed her in clean clothes. _ She toweled down the child gently. _ Towel down the dog. He’s wet and shaking.
examples: The mother toweled her child down and dressed her in clean clothes.

towel someone or something off†.monolingual: to dry someone or something with a towel. _ The young mother toweled the baby off with a soft, warm towel. _ She toweled off the baby.
examples: The young mother toweled the baby off with a soft, warm towel.

tower above someone or something.monolingual: to stand or be much taller than someone or something. (Often used in exaggeration.) _The basketball player towered above everyone else in the room. _ The new building towered above all the others in town.
examples: The basketball player towered above everyone else in the room.

a tower of strength.monolingual: Fig. a person who can always be depended on to provide support and encouragement, especially in times of trouble. _ Mary was a tower of strength when Jean was in the hospital. She looked after her whole family. _Jack was a tower of strength during th
examples: Mary was a tower of strength when Jean was in the hospital.

tower over someone or something.monolingual: to stand much taller than someone or something. _ Tom towers over his older brother, Stan. _ Tom towered over the little desk he had been assigned to.
examples: Tom towers over his older brother, Stan.

town-and-gown.monolingual: the relations between a town and the university located within the town; the relations between university students and the nonstudents who live in a university town. (Usually in reference to a disagreement. Fixed order.) _ There is another town-and-g
examples: There is another town-and-gown dispute in Adamsville over the amount the university costs the city for police services.

toy with someone.monolingual: to tease someone; to deal lightly with someone’s emotions. _ Ann broke up with Tom because he was just toying with her. He was not serious at all. _ Don’t toy with me! I won’t have it!
examples: Ann broke up with Tom because he was just toying with her.

toy with something.monolingual: to play with something; to fiddle with something. _ You are just toying with me! _ Please don’t toy with the stereo controls.
examples: Please don’t toy with the stereo controls.

trace around something.monolingual: to press something against paper and draw a line around the edges that are in contact with the paper. _ Trace around this piece of material and cut out a new pattern. _If you trace around the edges carefully, you will end up with a good drawing of th
examples: Trace around this piece of material and cut out a new pattern.

trace over something.monolingual: 1. to draw over something lightly. _Trace over the drawing to make it a little darker. _I had to trace over it twice to make it visible.
examples: Trace over the drawing to make it a little darker.

track someone or something down†.monolingual: to search out where someone or something is. _ I don’t know where Anne is. I’ll try to track her down. _ I’ll track down Anne for you.
examples: I don’t know where Anne is.

track something up†.monolingual: to mess something up by spreading around something dirty or messy with one’s shoes or feet. _ Please don’t track the f loor up! _ Claire tracked up the f loor.
examples: Claire tracked up the f loor.

trade at some place.monolingual: to buy and sell at some place; to shop at someplace. _Do you trade at that store anymore? _We don’t trade there because their prices are too high.
examples: We don’t trade there because their prices are too high.

trade on something.monolingual: to use a fact or a situation to one’s advantage. _Tom was able to trade on the fact that he had once been in the army. _ John traded on his poor eyesight to get a seat closer to the stage.
examples: Tom was able to trade on the fact that he had once been in the army.

a trade secret.monolingual: 1. Lit. a secret way of making or selling a product; a business secret. _The exact formula of the soft drink is a trade secret.
examples: The exact formula of the soft drink is a trade secret.

trade something off†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to get rid of something in an exchange. _ I traded my car off. _ I traded off my old car for a new one.
examples: I traded my car off.

trade something with someone.monolingual: to exchange something with someone. _ Would you trade seats with me? I want to sit there. _ Can I trade books with you? This one is dull.
examples: Would you trade seats with me? I want to sit there.

trade up from something.monolingual: to exchange a specific lower-level product for a higher-level product. _I decided to trade up from my little car to a much larger one. _I can’t afford what I have, let alone be able to trade up to anything.
examples: I decided to trade up from my little car to a much larger one.

trade with someone or something.monolingual: to do business with someone or something. _ I don’t like the owner of that shop. I won’t trade with him anymore. _ Thank you for trading with us all these years. _ We don’t trade with that company because their prices are too high.
examples: I don’t like the owner of that shop.

traffic in something.monolingual: to deal in something; to trade in something, usually something illegal. _ Max had been trafficking in guns for years before they caught him. _The president of the country was trafficking in drugs for years.
examples: Max had been trafficking in guns for years before they caught him.

a traffic jam.monolingual: vehicle traffic that is so heavy and slow that it can no longer move. _Going to the airport, we got stuck in a traffic jam for nearly and hour and missed our plane.
examples: Going to the airport, we got stuck in a traffic jam for nearly and hour and missed our plane.

trail over something.monolingual: to lie behind, flowing out over something. _Her long gown trailed over the marble f loor. _The flowering vine trailed over the wall, making a lovely little garden area.
examples: Her long gown trailed over the marble f loor.

train for something.monolingual: to practice or drill for some task. _ I am training for the marathon. _We all have to train for the upcoming football season.
examples: I am training for the marathon.

train someone in something.monolingual: to drill and practice someone in a particular skill or body of knowledge. _ Her mentor trained her in the art of argumentation. _I will try to train you in the skills needed to perform this task.
examples: Her mentor trained her in the art of argumentation.

train someone on something.monolingual: to educate someone in the use of something. _We trained him on the high diving board, but he isn’t ready for competition yet. _She trained herself on the computer so she could write a book.
examples: We trained him on the high diving board, but he isn’t ready for competition yet.

train up to something.monolingual: to practice or drill up to a certain level of proficiency. _ I don’t have enough stamina for the marathon now, but I am training up to it. _ Alice trained up to the long-distance swim for years.
examples: I don’t have enough stamina for the marathon now, but I am training up to it.

tramp across something.monolingual: to march or stamp across an area. _ The kids tramped across the yard and wore a path. _ Please don’t tramp across my garden.
examples: The kids tramped across the yard and wore a path.

tramp through something.monolingual: to march or stamp a passage through something. _ The kids tramped through every puddle in town on their way to school. _ Don’t tramp through every mud puddle you see.
examples: The kids tramped through every puddle in town on their way to school.

trample someone or something down†.monolingual: to crush down someone or something with the feet. _Stay out of crowds at rock concerts. Those kids will trample you down if they get excited. _ The cows trampled down the stalks of corn.
examples: Stay out of crowds at rock concerts.

trample something out†.monolingual: to create a pathway by marching or stamping the same trail over and over. _The mail carriers have trampled a path out through my marigolds! _ Jim trampled out a path in my garden.
examples: Jim trampled out a path in my garden.

transcribe something in something.monolingual: 1. to transliterate one alphabet into another. _ Can you translate these romanized Korean words into the Korean script? _We had to transcribe the entire novel into Cyrillic.
examples: We had to transcribe the entire novel into Cyrillic.

transfer to something.monolingual: to have oneself reassigned to something. _ I am transferring to the accounting department. _ Andy wanted to transfer to a different school.
examples: I am transferring to the accounting department.

transgress against someone or something.monolingual: to make an offense against someone or something. (Stilted and formal.) _I did not mean to transgress against you. _We did not transgress against the rules of the college.
examples: I did not mean to transgress against you.

trap someone in something.monolingual: to catch someone in an inconsistency or contradiction. _ The lawyer trapped the witness in his inconsistencies. _She trapped herself in her own argument.
examples: The lawyer trapped the witness in his inconsistencies.

trap someone into something.monolingual: to get one into such a position that one has little choice but to do something unwanted. _You’ll never trap me into going out with Roger! _ I was trapped into going there.
examples: I was trapped into going there.

travel across something.monolingual: to make a journey across something or some place. _ We have to travel across the desert to get there. _ I do not want to travel across that rickety bridge on the way back.
examples: We have to travel across the desert to get there.

travel broadens the mind..monolingual: Prov. When you travel, you learn things about the people and places you see. _Marie: I never realized how well-off most Americans are until I visited India. Jane: So it’s true that travel broadens the mind, huh? _ Everyone who gets the chance should
examples: Marie: I never realized how well-off most Americans are until I visited India.

travel by something.monolingual: 1. to make a journey, using a particular conveyance. _ I will go by train, since I don’t like to travel by plane. _We traveled by car, since that is the cheapest.
examples: I will go by train, since I don’t like to travel by plane.

travel for someone or something.monolingual: to go from place to place selling for someone or a company. _Walter travels for his uncle, who runs a toy factory. _ She travels for a company that makes men’s clothing.
examples: Walter travels for his uncle, who runs a toy factory.

travel on something.monolingual: 1. to make a journey on a particular conveyance. _ Do you like to travel on the train? _ I do not care to travel on the bus.
examples: I do not care to travel on the bus.

travel over something.monolingual: 1. to go over something as part of a journey. _ We had to travel over an old bridge over the Mississippi to get to my sister’s house. _We will travel over a long narrow strip of land to get to the marina.
examples: We had to travel over an old bridge over the Mississippi to get to my sister’s house.

travel through something.monolingual: 1. to make a journey through some area or country. _ We will have to travel through Germany to get there. _ Do you want to travel through the desert or through the mountains?
examples: We will have to travel through Germany to get there.

travel with someone.monolingual: 1. to associate with someone; to move about in association with someone. _ She travels with a sophisticated crowd. _ I am afraid that Walter is traveling with the wrong group of friends.
examples: She travels with a sophisticated crowd.

travel with something.monolingual: to have something with one as one travels. _ I always travel with extra money. _ I hate to travel with three suitcases. That is more than I can handle.
examples: I always travel with extra money.

a travesty of justice.monolingual: a miscarriage of justice; an act of the legal system that is an insult to the system of justice. _The jury’s verdict was a travesty of justice. _The lawyer complained that the judge’s ruling was a travesty of justice.
examples: The jury’s verdict was a travesty of justice.

treat someone to something.monolingual: to provide and pay for something for someone as a gift or as entertainment. _ I will be delighted to treat you to dinner. _ After the play, they treated themselves to pie and coffee.
examples: I will be delighted to treat you to dinner.

trek across something.monolingual: to hike or march across something. _ The scouts trekked across the fields of the small farming community. _ I don’t look forward to trekking across the desert.
examples: The scouts trekked across the fields of the small farming community.

trek to some place.monolingual: to hike or march to some place. _I have to trek all the way to the store because my car is in the shop. _ We trekked to the cabin and made that our base camp for the whole two weeks.
examples: I have to trek all the way to the store because my car is in the shop.

tremble at something.monolingual: to shake with fear or anticipation at the thought of something. _ David trembled at the thought of having to go to Russia by himself. _ Carl trembled at the idea of winning first place.
examples: David trembled at the thought of having to go to Russia by himself.

tremble from something.monolingual: to shake or vibrate in response to something like an explosion or an earthquake. _ The house trembled from the blast. _ I could feel the bridge trembling from the minor earthquake that I was hearing about on the radio.
examples: The house trembled from the blast.

tremble with something.monolingual: to tremble because of something. _ The children trembled with fear during the storm. _ David trembled with rage when he saw his slashed tires.
examples: The children trembled with fear during the storm.

trend toward something.monolingual: to move gradually toward something. _Fashions are trending toward the gaudy and flamboyant. _ Attitudes are trending toward the more conservative.
examples: Fashions are trending toward the gaudy and flamboyant.

trial and error.monolingual: trying repeatedly for success. _ I finally found the right key after lots of trial and error. _ Sometimes trial and error is the only way to get something done.
examples: I finally found the right key after lots of trial and error.

trial balloon.monolingual: a test of someone’s or the public’s reaction. _It was just a trial balloon, and it didn’t work. _The trial balloon was a great success.
examples: It was just a trial balloon, and it didn’t work.

trials and tribulations.monolingual: Cliché problems and tests of one’s courage or perseverance. _I suppose I have the normal trials and tribulations for a person of my background, but some days are just a little too much for me. _ I promise not to tell you of the trials and tribulation
examples: I suppose I have the normal trials and tribulations for a person of my background, but some days are just a little too much for me.

trick or treat!.monolingual: Give me a treat of some kind or I will play a trick on you! (The formulaic expression said by children after they ring someone’s doorbell and the door is answered on Halloween. It is now understood to mean simply that the child is requesting a treat
examples: “Trick or treat!” cried Jimmy when the door opened.

trickle away.monolingual: [for a liquid] to seep or dribble away. _ All the water trickled away down the drain. _ After the last of the spilled milk had trickled away, Timmy began to cry.
examples: All the water trickled away down the drain.

*the tricks of the trade.monolingual: special skills and knowledge associated with any trade or profession. (*Typically: know ~; learn ~; show someone ~; teach someone ~.) _I know a few tricks of the trade that make things easier. _ I learned the tricks of the trade from my uncle.
examples: I know a few tricks of the trade that make things easier.

tried and true.monolingual: trustworthy; dependable. (Hyphenated before nominals.) _ The method I use to cure the hiccups is tried and true. _ Finally, her old tried-and-true methods failed because she hadn’t fine-tuned them to the times.
examples: The method I use to cure the hiccups is tried and true.

trifle with someone or something.monolingual: to act without seriousness or respect toward someone or something. _ Don’t talk that way to me! I am not to be trifled with. _ I wish that Ann wouldn’t trif le with our efforts at reform.
examples: Don’t talk that way to me! I am not to be trifled with.

trigger someone off†.monolingual: to cause someone to become angry. (Fig. on trigger something off.) _Your rude comments triggered her off. _ Your comments triggered off Bob’s temper.
examples: Your rude comments triggered her off.

trigger something off†.monolingual: to set something off, such as an explosion. _We were afraid that the sparks from the engine would trigger an explosion off. _ The sparks triggered off an explosion.
examples: We were afraid that the sparks from the engine would trigger an explosion off.

trim something down†.monolingual: to reduce the size of something. _ You will have to trim the picture down to get it into the frame. _ Trim down the picture before you frame it.
examples: You will have to trim the picture down to get it into the frame.

trim something from something.monolingual: to cut something away from something. _I trimmed the fat from the steaks. _We had to trim a lot of the fat from the meat after we got it home.
examples: I trimmed the fat from the steaks.

trim something with something.monolingual: to decorate something with something. _ She trimmed the dress with lace. _ Bobby and Timmy trimmed the tree with colorful ornaments.
examples: She trimmed the dress with lace.

trip along.monolingual: to move along happily. _The kids tripped along on their way to school. _ We were just tripping along, not having any notion of what was about to happen.
examples: The kids tripped along on their way to school.

trip someone up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to cause someone to trip; to entangle someone’s feet. (Someone includes oneself.) _The rope strewn about the deck tripped him up. _ The lines tripped up the crew.
examples: The rope strewn about the deck tripped him up.

trip the light fantastic.monolingual: Jocular to dance. _ Shall we go trip the light fantastic?

triumph over someone or something.monolingual: to achieve victory over someone or something. _Our team triumphed over all the others. _ Our army triumphed over theirs.
examples: Our team triumphed over all the others.

troop across someone or something.monolingual: [for a mass of creatures] to move across someone or something. _The huge herds of wildebeest began to troop across the plain in search of food. _ The ants trooped across Karen as she lay in the sand.
examples: The huge herds of wildebeest began to troop across the plain in search of food.

trot after someone.monolingual: to follow along after someone, as done by a small dog. _ The puppy trotted along after the kids wherever they went. _My little brother would always come trotting after us, annoying us a lot.
examples: The puppy trotted along after the kids wherever they went.

trot along.monolingual: to step along in a lively fashion. _ The horses trotted along in time with the music. _The horses were trotting along, going exactly where we led them.
examples: The horses trotted along in time with the music.

trot someone or something out†.monolingual: to bring out and display someone or something. _ The boss trotted the new vice president out for us to meet. _ The boss trotted out his daughter and introduced her as a new vice president. _Fred trotted out his favorite project for everyone to see.
examples: The boss trotted the new vice president out for us to meet.

trot something out†.monolingual: Fig. to mention something regularly or habitually, without giving it much thought. (Fig. on the image of trotting out a pony for display.) _ When James disagreed with Mary, she simply trotted her same old political arguments out. _Bob always trots ou
examples: When James disagreed with Mary, she simply trotted her same old political arguments out.

trouble someone for something.monolingual: to ask someone to pass something or give something. (Usually a question.) _ Could I trouble you for the salt? _ Could I trouble you for some advice?

trouble someone to do something.monolingual: to ask someone to do something. (Usually a question.) _Could I trouble you to pass the salt? _Could I trouble you to give me some advice?

trouble someone with something.monolingual: to bother someone with something, such as a question or a problem. _ I hate to trouble you with this, but could you help me adjust my binoculars? _ Don’t trouble yourself with this matter.
examples: Don’t trouble yourself with this matter.

trudge along.monolingual: to plod along on foot. _ It seemed as if we trudged along for miles. _ As we trudged along, we forgot how cold it was.
examples: It seemed as if we trudged along for miles.

trudge through something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to walk through snow, sand, or something similar. _We trudged through the hot sand all the way down the beach. _I used to have to trudge through snow like this all winter to get to school.
examples: We trudged through the hot sand all the way down the beach.

*true as steel.monolingual: very loyal and dependable. (*Also: as ~.) _ Through all my troubles, my husband has been as true as steel. _ Pedro was a staunch friend, true as steel.
examples: Through all my troubles, my husband has been as true as steel.

true something up†.monolingual: to straighten something up; to put something into true plumb. _ Please true this door frame up better before you hang the door. _ Can you true up this wall a little?
examples: Please true this door frame up better before you hang the door.

true to form.monolingual: exactly as expected; following the usual pattern. (Often with running, as in the example.) _As usual, John is late. At least he’s running true to form. _ And true to form, Mary left before the meeting was adjourned.
examples: As usual, John is late.

true to one’s word.monolingual: keeping one’s promise. _ True to his word, Tom showed up at exactly eight o’clock. _ We’ll soon know if Jane is true to her word. We’ll see if she does what she promised.
examples: True to his word, Tom showed up at exactly eight o’clock.

trump something up†.monolingual: 1. to promote or boost something. _ They think they have to trump something up to get people to see it. _ They trumped up the movie so much that many people were disappointed when it finally came out.
examples: They think they have to trump something up to get people to see it.

trumped up.monolingual: 1. heavily promoted; overly praised. (Hyphenated before nominal.) _I don’t care for trumpedup stuff like that movie. _ That movie was so trumped up. I expected to see something much better than it turned out to be.
examples: I don’t care for trumpedup stuff like that movie.

truss someone or something up†.monolingual: to bind, tie, or bundle someone or something up. _The attendants trussed Walter up and took him to a padded cell. _ They trussed up Walter tightly. _ Ann trussed the bundle up and sent it off.
examples: The attendants trussed Walter up and took him to a padded cell.

trust in someone or something.monolingual: to believe in someone or something. _Trust in me. I know what I am saying. _Can I trust in the figures in this report?
examples: Trust in me. I know what I am saying.

trust me!.monolingual: I am telling you the truth. Please believe me. _ Tom said with great conviction, “Trust me! I know exactly what to do!” _ Mary: Do you really think we can keep this party a secret until Thursday? Sally: Trust me! I know how to plan a surprise party.
examples: Mary: Do you really think we can keep this party a secret until Thursday? Sally: Trust me! I know how to plan a surprise party.

trust someone for something.monolingual: to depend on someone for payment for something. _I will lend you one hundred dollars. I know I can trust you for it. _ I loaned Ted a lot of money. It’s all right. I can trust him for it.
examples: I will lend you one hundred dollars.

trust someone to do something.monolingual: to believe that someone can be relied on to do something. _ You can trust her to be here on time. _ I can’t trust myself to eat wisely.
examples: You can trust her to be here on time.

the truth will out..monolingual: Prov. The truth will always be discovered. (Can be used to remark that someone who had been concealing the truth is now revealing it, as in the second example.) _ The embezzler may think that someone else will be blamed for his crime, but the truth w
examples: The embezzler may think that someone else will be blamed for his crime, but the truth will out.

try for something.monolingual: to try to win or achieve something. _ I am going to try for the silver trophy in this year’s race. _ Will you try for a place on the team?
examples: I am going to try for the silver trophy in this year’s race.

try me..monolingual: Ask me.; Give me a chance. _ A: I don’t suppose you know what the Achaean League is. B: Try me.
examples: A: I don’t suppose you know what the Achaean League is.

try someone for something.monolingual: to put someone through a court trial for some crime or wrongdoing. _ The prosecutor wanted to try Harry for fraud. _ Anne was tried for shoplifting.
examples: The prosecutor wanted to try Harry for fraud.

try someone or something out†.monolingual: to test someone or something for a while; to sample the performance of someone or something. _ We will try her out in the editorial department and see how she does. _We will try out this employee in another department for a while.
examples: We will try her out in the editorial department and see how she does.

try someone’s patience.monolingual: to strain someone’s patience; to bother someone as if testing the person’s patience. (Try means test here.) _ My loud neighbors are trying my patience today. _ You really try my patience with all your questions!
examples: My loud neighbors are trying my patience today.

try something on with someone.monolingual: to get someone’s opinion about an idea or plan. _ Let me try this idea on with you. _ She tried the new idea on with the boss, but the response was not good.
examples: Let me try this idea on with you.

try something out† on someone.monolingual: to see how someone responds to something or some idea. _Let me try this idea out on you and see what you think. _ Let me try out this new medicine on her.
examples: Let me try this idea out on you and see what you think.

tub of lard.monolingual: a fat person. (Insulting.) _ Who’s that tub of lard who just came in? _ That tub of lard can hardly get through the door.
examples: That tub of lard can hardly get through the door.

tuck into something.monolingual: to begin eating something vigorously. _ The kids really tucked into the stew. _ I could see from the way that they tucked into their meal that they were really hungry.
examples: The kids really tucked into the stew.

tuck something away†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to hide or store something away. _ Tuck this away where you can find it later. _ Can you tuck away this money somewhere?
examples: Tuck this away where you can find it later.

tuck something up†.monolingual: to raise up some part of one’s clothing and attach it temporarily. _ She tucked her skirt up and waded through the f looded basement. _ She tucked up her skirt.
examples: She tucked her skirt up and waded through the f looded basement.

tucker someone out.monolingual: to tire someone out. _ All this work has tuckered me out. _ The heavy work tuckered the staff out early in the day.
examples: All this work has tuckered me out.

tug at someone or something.monolingual: to pull at someone or something. _ Stop tugging at me! I’ll talk to you in a minute. _ The dog tugged at my pants cuff.
examples: Stop tugging at me! I’ll talk to you in a minute.

tumble along.monolingual: to roll or bounce along. _The ball tumbled along, across the lawn and into the street. _ As the boulder tumbled along, it crushed everything in its path.
examples: The ball tumbled along, across the lawn and into the street.

tumble down.monolingual: to fall down; to topple. _The old barn was so rickety that it almost tumbled down on its own. _ The pile of books tumbled down all over the f loor.
examples: The old barn was so rickety that it almost tumbled down on its own.

tumble from something.monolingual: to fall from something. _The food tumbled from the tray and fell to the f loor. _ The books tumbled from the shelf during the earthquake.
examples: The food tumbled from the tray and fell to the f loor.

tumble into bed.monolingual: to get into or fall into bed. _ Liz went home and tumbled into bed.
examples: Liz went home and tumbled into bed.

tumble into someone or something.monolingual: to fall down and roll into someone or something. (Either accidentally or on purpose.) _ Liz tripped and tumbled into the table. _ She tumbled into Ken.
examples: Liz tripped and tumbled into the table.

tumble out of something.monolingual: to fall, topple, or drop out of something. _ Don’t let the baby tumble out of the chair! _The children tumbled out of the car and ran for the school building.
examples: The children tumbled out of the car and ran for the school building.

tumble over.monolingual: to fall over. _ The vase tumbled over and broke. _ I held Timmy up to keep him from tumbling over.
examples: The vase tumbled over and broke.

tumble over someone or something.monolingual: to trip or stumble over someone or something and fall down. _ I tumbled over Fred, who was napping under the tree. _ I tumbled over a chair and fell down.
examples: I tumbled over Fred, who was napping under the tree.

tune out.monolingual: Fig. to cease paying attention to anything at all. _I wasn’t interested, so I just tuned out. _I think that most of the audience tuned out during the last part of the lecture.
examples: I wasn’t interested, so I just tuned out.

tune someone or something out†.monolingual: to put someone or something out of one’s consciousness; to cease paying attention to someone or something. _I had to tune the radio out in order to concentrate. _ I tuned out what the speaker was saying and daydreamed for a while.
examples: I had to tune the radio out in order to concentrate.

tune something in†.monolingual: to adjust a radio or television set so that something can be received. _Could you tune the newscast in? _ Please tune in the station a little better.
examples: Please tune in the station a little better.

tune something up†.monolingual: Fig. to adjust an engine to run the best and most efficiently. _ You need to tune this engine up. _ Please tune up this engine so it will run more economically.
examples: You need to tune this engine up.

tune up.monolingual: [for one or more musicians] to bring their instruments into tune. _ You could hear the orchestra behind the curtain, tuning up. _We have to tune up before the concert.
examples: You could hear the orchestra behind the curtain, tuning up.

tuned in.monolingual: aware; up-to-date. _ Jan is tuned in and alert to what is going on around her. _ Hey, Jill! Get tuned in, why don’t you?
examples: Jan is tuned in and alert to what is going on around her.

tunnel through something.monolingual: to make a tunnel or passageway through something or a group of people. _Roger had to tunnel through the crowd to get to the rest room. _ The workers tunneled through the soft soil to reach the buried cable.
examples: Roger had to tunnel through the crowd to get to the rest room.

tunnel under someone or something.monolingual: to dig a tunnel under someone or something. _All the time she was standing in the yard talking about the moles, they were tunneling under her. _They took many months to tunnel under the English Channel.
examples: All the time she was standing in the yard talking about the moles, they were tunneling under her.

tunnel vision.monolingual: 1. Lit. a visual impairment wherein one can only see what is directly ahead of oneself. _ I have tunnel vision, so I have to keep looking from side to side.
examples: I have tunnel vision, so I have to keep looking from side to side.

turn a place upside down.monolingual: Fig. to search a place thoroughly. _The cops turned the whole house upside down but never found the gun. _I had to turn the place upside down to find my car keys.
examples: The cops turned the whole house upside down but never found the gun.

turn a profit.monolingual: to earn a profit. _The company plans to turn a profit two years from now.
examples: The company plans to turn a profit two years from now.

turn a trick.monolingual: Sl. to perform an act of prostitution. (Use caution with the topic.) _ She can turn a trick and be on the streets again in six minutes f lat. _She’s upstairs, turning a trick.
examples: She can turn a trick and be on the streets again in six minutes f lat.

turn in.monolingual: 1. [for something] to fold or point inward. _ Do my toes turn in too much? _ The legs of the table turned in at the bottom, giving a quaint appearance to the piece of furniture.
examples: The legs of the table turned in at the bottom, giving a quaint appearance to the piece of furniture.

turn into someone or something.monolingual: to change into someone or something. _ After work is over, he turns into a fairly nice person. _The room turned into a very pleasant place when the lights were dimmed.
examples: After work is over, he turns into a fairly nice person.

the turn of the century.monolingual: the time when the year changes to one with two final zeros, such as from 1899 to
examples: My family moved to America at the turn of the century.

turn off.monolingual: [for something] to go off; to switch off. _ All the lights turn off automatically.
examples: All the lights turn off automatically.

turn off something.monolingual: to walk or turn a vehicle one way or another so that one leaves the road or route to another. _ You are supposed to turn off the highway at the yellow mailbox.
examples: You are supposed to turn off the highway at the yellow mailbox.

turn on.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to switch on and start running. _The lights turned on right at dusk. _At what time do the street lights turn on?
examples: The lights turned on right at dusk.

turn on a dime.monolingual: Fig. [for a vehicle] to turn in a very tight turn. _This car can turn on a dime. _I need a vehicle that can turn on a dime.
examples: This car can turn on a dime.

turn on someone.monolingual: to attack someone. _I thought the strange dog was friendly, but suddenly it turned on me and bit me. _ Bob knows a lot about lions, and he says that no matter how well they are trained, there is always the danger that they’ll turn on you.
examples: I thought the strange dog was friendly, but suddenly it turned on me and bit me.

turn on the waterworks.monolingual: Fig. to begin to cry. _ Every time Billy got homesick, he turned on the waterworks. _ Sally hurt her knee and turned on the waterworks for about twenty minutes.
examples: Every time Billy got homesick, he turned on the waterworks.

turn one’s hand to something.monolingual: to begin to or to be able to do something. _ I would like to turn my hand to Chinese cooking. _ He gave up accounting and turned his hand to writing poetry.
examples: I would like to turn my hand to Chinese cooking.

turn onto something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to walk or steer one’s vehicle onto a road, highway, or path. _Turn onto the main road and go west about a mile. _ As she turned onto the familiar highway, she realized that she had left her purse in the store.
examples: Turn onto the main road and go west about a mile.

turn out.monolingual: [for something] to aim outward. _ Her toes turned out just right for a ballet dancer. _ The legs of the chair turned out just a little, adding a bit of stability.
examples: Her toes turned out just right for a ballet dancer.

turn out somehow.monolingual: to end in a particular way, such as well, badly, all right, etc. _I hope everything turns out all right. _ The party did not turn out well.
examples: I hope everything turns out all right.

turn over a new leaf.monolingual: Fig. to begin again, fresh; to reform and begin again. (Fig. on turning to a fresh page. The leaf is a page—a fresh, clean page.) _ I have made a mess of my life. I’ll turn over a new leaf and hope to do better. _ Why don’t you turn over a new leaf a
examples: I have made a mess of my life.

turn some place inside out.monolingual: Fig. to search some place thoroughly. _ I will find that book if I have to turn this place inside out! _ I turned the room inside out and still didn’t find it.
examples: I turned the room inside out and still didn’t find it.

turn someone aside†.monolingual: to divert someone from the flow of people. _ The attendant turned the poorly dressed man aside. _ The attendant turned aside all the persons who arrived late.
examples: The attendant turned the poorly dressed man aside.

turn someone down†.monolingual: to issue a refusal to someone. _ We had to turn Joan down, even though her proposal was okay. _ We turned down Joan, even though her credentials were good.
examples: We had to turn Joan down, even though her proposal was okay.

turn someone off†.monolingual: to dull someone’s interest in someone or something. _ The boring prof turned me off to the subject. _ The preacher set out to turn off the congregation to sin.
examples: The boring prof turned me off to the subject.

turn someone on†.monolingual: to excite or interest someone. _ Fast music with a good beat turns me on. _ That stuff doesn’t turn on anyone.
examples: Fast music with a good beat turns me on.

turn someone or something back†.monolingual: to cause someone or something to stop and go back; to cause someone or something to retreat. _ The border guards turned us back because we had no passports. _ They turned back the bus because the bridge was down.
examples: The border guards turned us back because we had no passports.

turn someone or something over†.monolingual: to rotate someone or something so that the side that was on the bottom is now on the top. _ The nurses turned the patient over so they could give her some medicine. _ They turned over the unconscious patient.
examples: The nurses turned the patient over so they could give her some medicine.

turn someone or something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to increase the volume of a device emitting the sound of someone or something. _ I can’t hear the lecturer. Turn her up. _ Turn up the radio, please.
examples: I can’t hear the lecturer.

turn someone out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to send someone out of somewhere. _ I didn’t pay my rent, so the manager turned me out. _I’m glad it’s not winter. I’d hate to turn out someone in the snow.
examples: I didn’t pay my rent, so the manager turned me out.

turn someone’s head.monolingual: Fig. [for flattery or success] to distract someone; to cause someone not to be sensible. _ Don’t let our praise turn your head. You’re not perfect! _ Her successes had turned her head. She was now quite arrogant.
examples: Don’t let our praise turn your head.

turn someone’s stomach.monolingual: Fig. to upset one’s stomach. _ The violent movie turned my stomach. _ The rich, creamy food turned John’s stomach.
examples: The violent movie turned my stomach.

turn someone’s water off†.monolingual: Sl. to deflate someone; to silence someone. _ He said you were stupid, huh? Well, I guess that turns your water off! _That really turned off her water.
examples: That really turned off her water.

turn something aside†.monolingual: to evade something. _ Ann turned the awkward questions aside. _ She turned aside the questions she didn’t want to answer.
examples: Ann turned the awkward questions aside.

turn something down†.monolingual: 1. to bend or fold something down. _ He turned his coat collar down when he got inside the house. _Timmy had turned down his cuffs and caught one of them in his bicycle chain.
examples: He turned his coat collar down when he got inside the house.

turn something off†.monolingual: to switch something off so that it stops running or operating. _ Please turn the light off. _ Turn off the lights as you leave.
examples: Please turn the light off.

turn something on†.monolingual: to switch on something to make it run. _ I turned the microwave oven on and cooked dinner. _ I turned on the lights when the sun went down.
examples: I turned the microwave oven on and cooked dinner.

turn something out†.monolingual: 1. to manufacture or produce something in numbers. _ The factory turns too few cars out. _ The factory turns out about seventy-five cars a day.
examples: The factory turns too few cars out.

turn something to good account.monolingual: to use something in such a way that it is to one’s advantage; to make good use of a situation, experience, etc. _Pam turned her illness to good account and did a lot of reading. _ Many people turn their retirement time to good account and take up int
examples: Pam turned her illness to good account and did a lot of reading.

turn something to one’s advantage.monolingual: to make an advantage for oneself out of something (which might otherwise be a disadvantage). _ Sally found a way to turn the problem to her advantage. _ The ice cream store manager was able to turn the hot weather to her advantage.
examples: Sally found a way to turn the problem to her advantage.

turn something up†.monolingual: 1. to bend or fold something up. _ Please turn your cuffs up. They are getting muddy. _He turned up his coat collar to keep the rain off his neck.
examples: Please turn your cuffs up.

turn something upside down.monolingual: Fig. to throw things all about in a thorough search for someone or something. _ We turned this place upside down, looking for the lost ring. _ Please don’t turn everything upside down, looking for your book.
examples: We turned this place upside down, looking for the lost ring.

turn the corner.monolingual: Fig. to pass a critical point in a process. _The patient turned the corner last night. She should begin to show improvement now. _ The project has turned the corner. The rest should be easy.
examples: The patient turned the corner last night.

turn the other cheek.monolingual: Fig. to ignore abuse or an insult. _ When Bob got mad at Mary and yelled at her, she just turned the other cheek. _ Usually I turn the other cheek when someone is rude to me.
examples: When Bob got mad at Mary and yelled at her, she just turned the other cheek.

turn the other way.monolingual: Fig. to look away and ignore someone or something. _When I tried to talk to her, she turned the other way and made it clear that she was angry.
examples: When I tried to talk to her, she turned the other way and made it clear that she was angry.

turn the tide.monolingual: Fig. to cause a reversal in the direction of events; to cause a reversal in public opinion. _ It looked as if the team were going to lose, but near the end of the game, our star player turned the tide. _At first, people were opposed to our plan. Afte
examples: It looked as if the team were going to lose, but near the end of the game, our star player turned the tide.

turn to.monolingual: Fig. to begin to get busy. _Come on, you guys! Turn to! Let’s get to work. _If you people will turn to, we can finish this work in no time at all.
examples: Come on, you guys! Turn to! Let’s get to work.

turn turtle.monolingual: Fig. to turn upside down. _ The sailboat turned turtle, but the sailors only got wet. _ The car ran off the road and turned turtle in the ditch.
examples: The sailboat turned turtle, but the sailors only got wet.

turn up.monolingual: 1. [for part of something] to point upward. _The ends of the elf ’s funny little shoes turned up.
examples: The ends of the elf ’s funny little shoes turned up.

turn up one’s toes.monolingual: Sl. to die. _ When I turn up my toes, I want a big funeral with lots of f lowers. _ Our cat turned up his toes during the night. He was nearly ten years old.
examples: When I turn up my toes, I want a big funeral with lots of f lowers.

turnabout is fair play..monolingual: Prov. It is fair for one to suffer whatever one has caused others to suffer. _ So, you don’t like being made fun of! Well, turnabout is fair play.
examples: So, you don’t like being made fun of! Well, turnabout is fair play.

turned off.monolingual: uninterested. _ I’m sort of turned off to stuff like that these days. Part of getting older, I guess. _ I can’t pay attention if I’m turned off, now can I?
examples: I’m sort of turned off to stuff like that these days.

*a turning point.monolingual: Fig. a time when things may change; a point at which a change of course is possible or desirable. (Originally nautical. Fig. on the image of a ship approaching a point where a change of course has been planned. (*Typically: be at ~; come to ~; reach
examples: Things are at to a turning point.

tussle with someone or something.monolingual: 1. to struggle or battle with someone or something. _Tim tussled with Roger for a while, and then they made peace. _ I tussled with the trunk, trying to get it into the attic.
examples: Tim tussled with Roger for a while, and then they made peace.

twelve good men and true.monolingual: Fig. a jury composed of trustworthy men. _ He was convicted by a jury of twelve good men and true. Not a wino in the lot.
examples: He was convicted by a jury of twelve good men and true.

twiddle one’s thumbs.monolingual: Fig. to pass the time by twirling one’s thumbs. _ What am I supposed to do while waiting for you? Sit here and twiddle my thumbs? _Don’t sit around twiddling your thumbs. Get busy!
examples: Don’t sit around twiddling your thumbs.

twiddle with something.monolingual: to play with something; to play with something, using one’s fingers; to fiddle with something. _ I asked Jason to stop twiddling with the pencils. _ Someone is twiddling with the stereo controls.
examples: I asked Jason to stop twiddling with the pencils.

twilight years.monolingual: Fig. the last years before death. _ In his twilight years, he became more mellow and stopped yelling at people.
examples: In his twilight years, he became more mellow and stopped yelling at people.

twine around something.monolingual: to weave or coil around something. _ The snake twined around the branch. _ As the vine grew, it twined around the lamppost.
examples: The snake twined around the branch.

twinkle with something.monolingual: [for someone’s eyes] to sparkle because of something. _ Her eyes twinkled with laughter. _Tom’s eyes twinkled with recognition when he saw Gwen again.
examples: Her eyes twinkled with laughter.

twist around.monolingual: to turn around part way at the waist, without moving one’s feet or legs. _ Nancy twisted around to get a better look at who was sitting behind her. _ I had to twist around to see who was there.
examples: Nancy twisted around to get a better look at who was sitting behind her.

twist someone’s arm.monolingual: Fig. to pressure someone. (Fig. on the image of hurting someone until they agree to cooperate.) _I had to twist her arm a little, but she agreed. _Do I have to twist your arm, or will you cooperate?
examples: I had to twist her arm a little, but she agreed.

twist something into something.monolingual: to change or distort something into something else, as if by twisting. _Kelly twisted the balloons into the shape of a dog. _ Ann twisted the silver wires into an earring.
examples: Kelly twisted the balloons into the shape of a dog.

twist something out of something.monolingual: to remove something from something by twisting. _ Flo twisted the cork out of the bottle and smelled the wine. _ Roger twisted the bulb out of its socket and replaced it with a good one.
examples: Flo twisted the cork out of the bottle and smelled the wine.

twist up.monolingual: 1. to move upward in a twisting path. _ The smoke twisted up into the sky. _ As the car twisted up the narrow path, we got a good view of the valley.
examples: The smoke twisted up into the sky.

two jumps ahead of someone.monolingual: Fig. a good way ahead of someone. _Her market research kept her two jumps ahead of her competitors. _ I was just starting to think of vacation plans, not realizing that my wife was two jumps ahead of me. She had already made hotel reservations.
examples: Her market research kept her two jumps ahead of her competitors.

two of a kind.monolingual: Fig. people or things of the same type or that are similar in character, attitude, etc. _Jack and Tom are two of a kind. They’re both ambitious. _ The companies are two of a kind. They both pay their employees badly.
examples: Jack and Tom are two of a kind.

*two strikes against one.monolingual: 1. two strikes on a baseball batter, three being the number that will put the batter “out.” (Such a player is in a vulnerable position. *Typically: get ~; have ~.) _Sammy has two strikes against him and might just strike out.
examples: Sammy has two strikes against him and might just strike out.
