two-fisted.monolingual: Fig. [of a male] aggressive and feisty. _ Perry is a real, two-fisted cowboy, always ready for a fight or a drunken brawl.
examples: Perry is a real, two-fisted cowboy, always ready for a fight or a drunken brawl.

a two-time loser.monolingual: a confirmed loser. _ Poor Richard is a two-time loser. _ Martin is a two-time loser, or at least he looks like one.
examples: Poor Richard is a two-time loser.

two-time someone.monolingual: Sl. to cheat on or betray one’s spouse or lover by dating or seeing someone else. _ When Mrs. Franklin learned that Mr. Franklin was two-timing her, she left him. _ Ann told Bob that if he ever two-timed her, she would cause him a lot of trouble.
examples: When Mrs. Franklin learned that Mr.

a two-way street.monolingual: a reciprocal situation. _ This is a twoway street, you know. You will have to help me someday in return. _ Friendship is a two-way street.
examples: This is a twoway street, you know.

type over something.monolingual: to type one letter over another. _Just type over the o with an e. No one will notice.
examples: Just type over the o with an e.

type something out†.monolingual: to make some information presentable by typing or keying it. _ Please type this out before you submit it to the board for approval. _Can you type out this report before quitting time?
examples: Please type this out before you submit it to the board for approval.

type something up†.monolingual: to type a handwritten document; to type a document, perhaps using a computer. _I will give this to you as soon as I type it up. _Please type up this document.
examples: I will give this to you as soon as I type it up.

*ugly as a toad.monolingual: [of a living creature] very ugly. (*Also: as ~.) _Maria may be a beautiful woman, but when she was a child she was as ugly as a toad. _ The shopkeeper was ugly as a toad, but he was kind and generous, and everyone loved him.
examples: Maria may be a beautiful woman, but when she was a child she was as ugly as a toad.

*ugly as sin.monolingual: Cliché extremely ugly. (*Also: as ~.) _Why would anyone want to buy that dress? It’s as ugly as sin! _ Harold is ugly as sin, but his personality is very charming.
examples: Harold is ugly as sin, but his personality is very charming.

unaccustomed to someone or something.monolingual: not used to someone or something. _ The poor family was unaccustomed to going to fancy restaurants. _ Bill was unaccustomed to mailing his own letters.
examples: The poor family was unaccustomed to going to fancy restaurants.

unbosom oneself to someone.monolingual: Fig. to reveal one’s inner thoughts and secrets to someone. _ He unbosomed himself to his best friend. _Todd unbosomed himself to almost everyone he met.
examples: He unbosomed himself to his best friend.

unburden oneself to someone.monolingual: Fig. to tell someone about one’s trouble or anxiety. _ I didn’t mean to unburden myself to you. I’m just so upset. _ She unburdened herself to her mother.
examples: I didn’t mean to unburden myself to you.

*under a spell.monolingual: Fig. enchanted; under the control of magic. (*Typically: be ~; have someone ~; put someone ~.) _ Her soft voice and faint perfume put Buxton under a spell. Then enchantment was broken when he found his wallet missing.
examples: Her soft voice and faint perfume put Buxton under a spell.

*under arrest.monolingual: arrested and in the custody of the police in preparation for the filing of a charge. (*Typically: be ~; put someone ~.) _Stop where you are! You are under arrest! _ Am I under arrest, officer? What did I do?

under construction.monolingual: Fig. being built or repaired. _ We cannot travel on this road because it’s under construction. _ Our new home has been under construction all summer. We hope to move in next month.
examples: We cannot travel on this road because it’s under construction.

*under control.monolingual: Fig. manageable; restrained and controlled; not out of control. (*Typically: be ~; bring someone or something ~; get someone or something ~; have someone or something ~; keep someone or something ~.) _ We finally got things under control and function
examples: We finally got things under control and functioning smoothly.

*under fire.monolingual: Fig. during an attack; being attacked. (*Typically: be ~; resign ~; think ~.) _There was a scandal in city hall, and the mayor was forced to resign under fire. _ John is a good lawyer because he can think under fire.
examples: There was a scandal in city hall, and the mayor was forced to resign under fire.

under normal circumstances.monolingual: Fig. normally; usually; typically. _ “We’d be able to keep the dog at home under normal circumstances,” said Mary to the vet. _“Under normal circumstances you’d be able to return to work in a week,” explained the doctor.
examples: “We’d be able to keep the dog at home under normal circumstances,” said Mary to the vet.

under oath.monolingual: Fig. bound by an oath; having taken an oath. _ You must tell the truth because you are under oath. _ I was placed under oath before I could testify in the trial.
examples: You must tell the truth because you are under oath.

*under one’s belt.monolingual: 1. Fig. eaten or drunk and in one’s stomach. (Fig. on the image of swallowed food ending up under one’s belt. *Typically: get something ~; have something ~.) _ I need to have something filling under my belt. I’ve had it with just soup. _I want to get
examples: I need to have something filling under my belt.

*under one’s breath.monolingual: Fig. [spoken] so softly that almost no one can hear it. (*Typically: curse ~; curse someone or something ~; mutter ~; mutter something ~; say something ~.) _John was muttering something under his breath, and I don’t think it was very pleasant. _I’m g
examples: John was muttering something under his breath, and I don’t think it was very pleasant.

under one’s own steam.monolingual: Fig. by one’s own power or effort. _I missed my ride to class, so I had to get there under my own steam. _ John will need some help with this project. He can’t do it under his own steam.
examples: I missed my ride to class, so I had to get there under my own steam.

*under someone’s thumb.monolingual: Fig. under someone’s control and management. (*Typically: get someone ~; have someone ~; hold someone ~; keep someone ~.) _You can’t keep your kids under your thumb all their lives. _ I don’t want to have these people under my thumb. I’m not the mana
examples: You can’t keep your kids under your thumb all their lives.

under the circumstances.monolingual: Fig. in a particular situation; because of the circumstances. _ I’m sorry to hear that you’re ill. Under the circumstances, you may take the day off. _ We won’t expect you to come to work for a few days, under the circumstances.
examples: I’m sorry to hear that you’re ill.

under the counter.monolingual: Fig. [bought or sold] in secret or illegally. (Compare this to over the counter.) _ The drugstore owner was arrested for selling liquor under the counter. _ The clerk sold dirty books under the counter.
examples: The drugstore owner was arrested for selling liquor under the counter.

under the sun.monolingual: Fig. anywhere on earth at all. _ This is the largest cattle ranch under the sun. _ Isn’t there anyone under the sun who can help me with this problem?
examples: This is the largest cattle ranch under the sun.

under the table.monolingual: 1. Sl. intoxicated. _ Jed was under the table by midnight. _By 3:00 in the morning, everyone was under the table.
examples: Jed was under the table by midnight.

under the weather.monolingual: 1. ill. _ I feel sort of under the weather today. _Whatever I ate for lunch is making me feel a bit under the weather.
examples: I feel sort of under the weather today.

under the wire.monolingual: Fig. just barely in time or on time. _ I turned in my report just under the wire. _ Bill was the last person to get in the door. He got in under the wire.
examples: I turned in my report just under the wire.

*under way.monolingual: Fig. moving; running; started. (*Typically: be ~; get something ~; have something ~.) _The time has come to get this game under way. _ Now that the president has the meeting under way, I can relax.
examples: The time has come to get this game under way.

*under wraps.monolingual: Fig. concealed; suppressed. (*Typically: be ~; have ~; hold ~; keep ~.) _ We kept the candidate’s conviction under wraps until after the election. _The plan we had under wraps had to be scrapped anyway.
examples: We kept the candidate’s conviction under wraps until after the election.

undertake to do something.monolingual: to try to do something; to take the responsibility of doing something. _ The carpenter undertook to repair the door frame. _ I will undertake to fix it.
examples: The carpenter undertook to repair the door frame.

the unexpected always happens..monolingual: Prov. The things you do not foresee will happen to you; when you plan, you cannot think of everything that might happen. _ It took us an hour to drive to the restaurant, and when we got there, it was closed. I would never have expected a restaurant t
examples: It took us an hour to drive to the restaurant, and when we got there, it was closed.

unfamiliar territory.monolingual: an area of knowledge unknown to the speaker. _ We are in unfamiliar territory and I don’t know the answer. _ Astronomy is unfamiliar territory for me, and I cannot answer any questions about the stars.
examples: We are in unfamiliar territory and I don’t know the answer.

unfold into something.monolingual: 1. [for something folded up] to unfold into something. _ The greeting card unfolded into a little paper house. _ It unfolded into a cute scene.
examples: The greeting card unfolded into a little paper house.

unfold something into something.monolingual: to spread something out into something. _The child unfolded the page into a model village. _I unfolded the brochure into a large colorful sheet of advertising.
examples: The child unfolded the page into a model village.

union is strength..monolingual: Prov. If people join together, they are more powerful than if they work by themselves. _ The students decided to join together in order to present their grievances to the faculty, since union is strength. _We cannot allow our opponents to divide us.
examples: The students decided to join together in order to present their grievances to the faculty, since union is strength.

unite against someone or something.monolingual: to join against someone or something. _ We will unite against the opposing forces. _ We must unite against the incumbent legislators.
examples: We will unite against the opposing forces.

unite for something.monolingual: to join together for some purpose. _ All the forces united for the attack. _ We will unite for a great party.
examples: All the forces united for the attack.

unite in something.monolingual: to come together in something. _ Let us unite in our efforts. _ We will unite in song.
examples: Let us unite in our efforts.

unite someone in something.monolingual: to join two or more people in something, usually marriage. _ The preacher united the couple in matrimony. _ A judge united them in marriage.
examples: The preacher united the couple in matrimony.

unite with someone.monolingual: to join with someone; to go or come together with someone. _ I was pleased to unite with my family for the holidays. _ The brothers united with their sister after many years of separation.
examples: I was pleased to unite with my family for the holidays.

*an unknown quantity.monolingual: Fig. a person or thing about which no one is certain. (*Typically: be ~; become ~.) _ John is an unknown quantity. We don’t know how he’s going to act. _ The new clerk is an unknown quantity. Things may not turn out all right.
examples: John is an unknown quantity.

unload something from something.monolingual: to take things off of something; to remove the burden from something. _ Please unload the groceries from the car. _ I unloaded the groceries from the bags.
examples: Please unload the groceries from the car.

unsung hero.monolingual: Fig. a hero who has gotten no praise or recognition. _ The time has come to recognize all the unsung heroes of the battle for low-cost housing.
examples: The time has come to recognize all the unsung heroes of the battle for low-cost housing.

until all hours.monolingual: Fig. until very late. _Mary is out until all hours, night after night. _ If I’m up until all hours two nights in a row, I’m just exhausted.
examples: Mary is out until all hours, night after night.

*up a blind alley.monolingual: Fig. at a dead end; on a route that leads nowhere. (*Typically: be ~; go ~.) _ I have been trying to find out something about my ancestors, but I’m up a blind alley. I can’t find anything. _The police are up a blind alley in their investigation of th
examples: I have been trying to find out something about my ancestors, but I’m up a blind alley.

*up a storm.monolingual: Fig. [doing or making] a great amount with fury or intensity. (*Typically: cook ~; gab ~; sing ~; kick ~; talk ~.) _Whenever we get together, we always talk up a storm. _ Everyone was gabbing up a storm and didn’t hear the chairman come in.
examples: Whenever we get together, we always talk up a storm.

up a tree.monolingual: 1. confused; without an answer to a problem; in difficulty. _This whole business has me up a tree. _I’m up a tree, and I need some help.
examples: This whole business has me up a tree.

*up against someone or something.monolingual: in opposition to someone or something, as in a contest. (*Typically: be ~; come ~; go ~; run ~; team ~.) _ Let’s team up against Paul and Tony in the footrace. _ We came up against a very strong team.
examples: Let’s team up against Paul and Tony in the footrace.

*up against something.monolingual: 1. Fig. resting firmly against something. (*Typically: be ~; place something ~.) _The car is up against the back of the garage! Back out a little!
examples: The car is up against the back of the garage! Back out a little! 2.

*up against the wall.monolingual: Fig. in serious difficulties. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; push someone ~.) _ Let’s face it, we’re up against the wall this time. _ It’s when you’re up against the wall that your true character shows.
examples: Let’s face it, we’re up against the wall this time.

up and at ’em.monolingual: Fig. up and taking action. _ Dad woke me at seven, saying, “Up and at ’em!” _It’s six-thirty. Time for us to be up and at ’em.
examples: It’s six-thirty.

up and away.monolingual: Fig. [of a bird or an airplane] up into the air and into flight. _After a few seconds of speeding down the runway, our f light to Tucson was up and away. _ Just before the cat pounced on the sparrows, they were up and away and the cat was left with e
examples: After a few seconds of speeding down the runway, our f light to Tucson was up and away.

up and running.monolingual: Fig. [of a machine] functioning. _ As soon as we can get the tractor up and running, we will plant the corn crop.
examples: As soon as we can get the tractor up and running, we will plant the corn crop.

*up before someone.monolingual: Fig. standing in front of someone to receive something. (Especially in front of a judge. *Typically: be ~; come ~; stand ~.) _ Have you been up before me before? _ I have never been up before any judge.
examples: I have never been up before any judge.

*up for auction.monolingual: Fig. to be sold at an auction. (*Typically: be ~; come ~; go ~; put something ~.) _ The old farm where I lived as a child is up for auction.
examples: The old farm where I lived as a child is up for auction.

up for grabs.monolingual: 1. Fig. available for anyone; not yet claimed. _The election is up for grabs. Everything is still very chancy. _I don’t know who will get the promotion. It’s up for grabs.
examples: The election is up for grabs.

*up for reelection.monolingual: Fig. to be running for reelection to an office or position. (*Typically: be ~; come ~.) _ The governor is up for reelection in the fall. _ Lily is up for reelection this fall.
examples: The governor is up for reelection in the fall.

*up for sale.monolingual: Fig. available for purchase. (*Typically: be ~; come ~; put something ~.) _ When this lot comes up for sale, let me know. _ Is this property up for sale?
examples: When this lot comes up for sale, let me know.

up front.monolingual: 1. in the forefront; under fire (at the front). _ You guys who are up front are gonna get the most fire. _ You two go up front and see if you can help.
examples: You guys who are up front are gonna get the most fire.

*up in arms.monolingual: 1. Fig. in armed rebellion. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _The entire population is up in arms. _They are up in arms, ready to fight.
examples: The entire population is up in arms.

up north.monolingual: to or at the northern part of the country or the world. _ I don’t like living up North. I want to move down South where it’s warm. _When you say “up North,” do you mean where the polar bears live or just in the northern states?
examples: I don’t like living up North.

up stakes.monolingual: to prepare for leaving and then leave. (Up has the force of a verb here. The phrase suggests pulling up tent stakes in preparation for departure.) _ They just upped stakes and left without saying good-bye. _ It’s that time of the year when I feel lik
examples: They just upped stakes and left without saying good-bye.

up the pole.monolingual: Fig. intoxicated. _ You sound a little up the pole. Why don’t you call back when you’re sober? _ She’s up the pole and shouldn’t drive.
examples: You sound a little up the pole.

up the river.monolingual: Sl. in prison. (Underworld.) _ Gary was up the river for a couple of years, but that doesn’t make him an outcast, does it? _The judge who sent him up the river was indicted for accepting bribery. If Gary had only known sooner!
examples: The judge who sent him up the river was indicted for accepting bribery.

up the wall.monolingual: Fig. in a very bad situation; very upset or anxious. _ He’s really up the wall about Mary’s illness. _ We were all up the wall until the matter was resolved.
examples: He’s really up the wall about Mary’s illness.

up to no good.monolingual: Fig. doing something bad. _ I could tell from the look on Tom’s face that he was up to no good. _ There are three boys in the front yard. I don’t know what they are doing, but I think they are up to no good.
examples: I could tell from the look on Tom’s face that he was up to no good.

*up to one’s knees.monolingual: Fig. deep in something, such as paperwork or water. (The idea is that it is hard to move or make progress. *Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ We’re up to our knees with orders and getting more all the time. _ The orders are up to our knees.
examples: We’re up to our knees with orders and getting more all the time.

up to par.monolingual: Fig. as good as the standard or average; up to standard. _ I’m just not feeling up to par today. I must be coming down with something. _The manager said that the report was not up to par and gave it back to Mary to do over again.
examples: I’m just not feeling up to par today.

*up to the minute.monolingual: Fig. current. (*Typically: be ~; bring something ~.) _This report is up to the minute and fresh from the wire services.
examples: This report is up to the minute and fresh from the wire services.

up-and-coming.monolingual: Fig. enterprising and alert. _ Jane is a hard worker—really up-and-coming. _ Bob is also an upand- coming youngster who is going to become well known.
examples: Jane is a hard worker—really up-and-coming.

upbraid someone for something.monolingual: to scold someone for doing something. _ The judge upbraided David severely for his crime. _ Walter upbraided his son for denting the car.
examples: The judge upbraided David severely for his crime.

upgrade to something.monolingual: to move up to a higher grade or rank. _I would like to upgrade to a first-class seat. _Please upgrade me to a better room.
examples: I would like to upgrade to a first-class seat.

upon impact.monolingual: Fig. at the place or time of an impact. _The car crumpled upon impact with the brick wall. _ The man who fell from the top of the building died on impact.
examples: The car crumpled upon impact with the brick wall.

upper crust.monolingual: Fig. the higher levels of society; the upper class. (From the top, as opposed to the bottom, crust of a pie.) _Jane speaks like that because she pretends to be from the upper crust, but her father was a miner. _James is from the upper crust, but he i
examples: Jane speaks like that because she pretends to be from the upper crust, but her father was a miner.

uproot someone from some place.monolingual: Fig. to cause someone to move from a well-established home or setting. _ You should not uproot people from the land in which they were born. _ I just couldn’t uproot myself from my home.
examples: You should not uproot people from the land in which they were born.

uproot something from some place.monolingual: to take up a plant or tree, roots and all. _ Wally uprooted the bush from the backyard and replanted it on the other side of the house. _ Who uprooted a rosebush from my garden?
examples: Wally uprooted the bush from the backyard and replanted it on the other side of the house.

upset someone’s plans.monolingual: Fig. to ruin someone’s plans. _ I hope it doesn’t upset your plans if I’m late for the meeting. _ No, it won’t upset my plans at all.
examples: I hope it doesn’t upset your plans if I’m late for the meeting.

upset the apple cart.monolingual: Fig. to mess up or ruin something. _ Tom really upset the apple cart by telling Mary the truth about Jane. _ I always knew he’d tell secrets and upset the apple cart.
examples: Tom really upset the apple cart by telling Mary the truth about Jane.

the upshot of something.monolingual: Fig. the result or outcome of something. _ The upshot of my criticism was a change in policy. _ The upshot of the argument was an agreement to hire a new secretary.
examples: The upshot of my criticism was a change in policy.

*upside-down.monolingual: Fig. in a financial state such that one owes more money on a car, truck, house, etc., than its resale value. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _When I tried to trade in the car, I found that I was upside-down and couldn’t close the deal without more money.
examples: When I tried to trade in the car, I found that I was upside-down and couldn’t close the deal without more money.

*up-to-date.monolingual: modern or contemporary. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _Is the room up-to-date, or is it standard? _ Your knowledge is not really up-to-date on this matter.
examples: Your knowledge is not really up-to-date on this matter.

up-to-date.monolingual: modern; up to the current standards of fashion; having the most current information. _I’d like to see a more up-to-date report on Mr. Smith. _ This is not an up-to-date record of the construction project.
examples: I’d like to see a more up-to-date report on Mr.

up-to-the-minute.monolingual: the very latest or most recent. _ I want to hear some up-to-the-minute news on the hostage situation. _I just got an up-to-the-minute report on Tom’s health.
examples: I want to hear some up-to-the-minute news on the hostage situation.

urban legend.monolingual: Fig. a myth or piece of folklore that is totally false. _ That story about the rats in the sewer being as big as dogs is an urban legend. It’s just not so.
examples: That story about the rats in the sewer being as big as dogs is an urban legend.

urge someone along.monolingual: to encourage someone to continue or go faster. _ We urged them along with much encouragement. _ They won’t do well, but we urged them along anyway.
examples: We urged them along with much encouragement.

urge someone forward.monolingual: to encourage someone to move forward. _ The generals urged the troops forward. _ Sally urged Timmy forward into the classroom.
examples: The generals urged the troops forward.

urge someone to do something.monolingual: to try to get someone to do something. _ I urge you to give skiing a try. _ Ken urged Lily to finish her dinner.
examples: I urge you to give skiing a try.

use foul language.monolingual: Euph. to swear. _ There’s no need to use foul language. _ When she gets angry, she tends to use foul language.
examples: There’s no need to use foul language.

use some elbow grease.monolingual: Fig. use some effort, as in scrubbing something. (As if lubricating one’s elbow would make one more efficient. Note the variations in the examples.) _ Come on, Bill. You can do it. Just use some elbow grease. _ I tried elbow grease, but it doesn’t he
examples: Come on, Bill. You can do it.

use someone up.monolingual: Fig. to use all the effort or talent a person has. _ His career simply used him up. _ I used myself up. I’m done. I can’t function anymore.
examples: His career simply used him up.

use something before something.monolingual: 1. to consume or use something before using something else. _ Use this jar before that one. This one is older. _I used the old one before the one you just bought.
examples: Use this jar before that one.

use something by something.monolingual: to consume or complete the use of something by a specified time. _ Please use this jar of mayonnaise by the last day of the month. _Use this one by next week.
examples: Please use this jar of mayonnaise by the last day of the month.

use something up†.monolingual: to consume or use all of something. _ Use the f lour up. I have more in the cupboard. _ Use up every bit of it. Go ahead.
examples: Use the f lour up.

use something with something.monolingual: to use something in a particular manner. _ Use this tool with a lot of skill and caution. _ Use this one with great care.
examples: Use this tool with a lot of skill and caution.

use strong language.monolingual: Euph. to swear, threaten, or use abusive language. _ I wish you wouldn’t use strong language in front of the children. _ If you feel that you have to use strong language with the manager, perhaps you had better let me do the talking.
examples: I wish you wouldn’t use strong language in front of the children.

*used to someone or something.monolingual: Fig. accustomed to someone or something; familiar and comfortable with someone or something. (*Typically: be ~; become ~; get ~.) _ I am used to eating better food than this. _ I am used to the doctor I have and I don’t want to change.
examples: I am used to eating better food than this.

user friendly.monolingual: Fig. easy to use. (Hyphenated before nominals.) _ The set-up instructions for the printer were very user friendly. _ I have a user-friendly computer that listens to my voice and does what I tell it.
examples: The set-up instructions for the printer were very user friendly.

usher someone to something.monolingual: to escort or lead someone to something, such as a seat, the door, etc. _The well-dressed gentleman ushered the bride to the altar. _Her father ushered her to the altar.
examples: The well-dressed gentleman ushered the bride to the altar.

vacuum something out†.monolingual: to clean an enclosed area out with a vacuum cleaner. _ Please vacuum this car out now! _ Can you vacuum out the car?

value something at something.monolingual: to consider something to be worth a certain amount. _The museum curator valued the vase at one million dollars. _ I value this vase at one million dollars.
examples: The museum curator valued the vase at one million dollars.

vanish away.monolingual: to disappear. (The away is considered redundant.) _ The pizza vanished away in no time at all. _ The city lights vanished away as dawn broke.
examples: The pizza vanished away in no time at all.

vanish from something.monolingual: to disappear from something or some place. _ The money vanished from the desk drawer. _ My glasses have vanished from sight again.
examples: The money vanished from the desk drawer.

vanish into something.monolingual: to disappear by going into something. _ All the deer vanished into the forest. _ Money seems to vanish into a black hole.
examples: All the deer vanished into the forest.

vanish into thin air.monolingual: Cliché to disappear without leaving a trace. _ My money gets spent so fast. It seems to vanish into thin air. _ When I came back, my car was gone. I had locked it, and it couldn’t have vanished into thin air!
examples: My money gets spent so fast.

vary from something to something.monolingual: to fluctuate over the range from something to something. _ The colors vary from red to orange. _ It varies from warm to very hot during the summer.
examples: The colors vary from red to orange.

vary with something.monolingual: 1. to be at variance with someone’s figures or a sum or estimate. _My figures vary with yours considerably. _Her estimate varies with yours by a few dollars.
examples: My figures vary with yours considerably.

vault into something.monolingual: to jump or dive into something. _ The diver vaulted into the pool. _ He vaulted into bed and pulled up the covers.
examples: The diver vaulted into the pool.

vault over someone or something.monolingual: to jump or leap over someone or something. _Molly vaulted over Ted and kept on running. _ She vaulted over the trunk.
examples: Molly vaulted over Ted and kept on running.

veer toward someone or something.monolingual: to turn sharply or swerve toward someone or something. _The car suddenly veered toward me. _ The horse veered toward the side of the bridle path.
examples: The car suddenly veered toward me.

veg out.monolingual: to cease working and take it easy; to vegetate. _ Someday, I just want to veg out and enjoy life. _I think I’ll just veg this weekend.
examples: Someday, I just want to veg out and enjoy life.

vegged out.monolingual: debilitated by drugs or alcohol. _Ernie is vegged out and has quit his job and everything. _Won’t be long till Larry is vegged out altogether.
examples: Ernie is vegged out and has quit his job and everything.

vent one’s spleen.monolingual: Fig. to get rid of one’s feelings of anger caused by someone or something by attacking someone or something else. _ Jack vented his spleen at his wife whenever things went badly at work. _ Peter vented his spleen on his car by kicking it when it brok
examples: Jack vented his spleen at his wife whenever things went badly at work.

venture forth.monolingual: 1. Fig. to set out; to go forward; to go out cautiously. _ George ventured forth into the night. _ I think I will venture forth. It looks safe.
examples: George ventured forth into the night.

verge into something.monolingual: to change gradually into something. _ The reds verged into a violet color that seemed to glow. _ The cool morning verged imperceptibly into a steamy midday.
examples: The reds verged into a violet color that seemed to glow.

verify something with someone.monolingual: to check with someone to make sure that something is the truth. _I will have to verify your story with the storekeeper. _ I verified your story with the other witness.
examples: I will have to verify your story with the storekeeper.

very good..monolingual: 1. It is good. _John: How do you like your lobster? Alice: Mmm. Very good. _ Jane: What did you think of the movie? Fred: Very good. Jane: Is that all? Fred: Yeah.
examples: John: How do you like your lobster? Alice: Mmm.

the very last.monolingual: Fig. the end; an absolute end of something. _ At the very last of the movie, the hero gets killed. _ Bill stayed at the party until the very last.
examples: At the very last of the movie, the hero gets killed.

the very thing.monolingual: Fig. the exact thing that is required. _The vacuum cleaner is the very thing for cleaning the stairs. _ I have the very thing to remove that stain.
examples: The vacuum cleaner is the very thing for cleaning the stairs.

vest someone with something.monolingual: to grant power, rights, or ownership to someone. _ Who vested you with the power to order me around? _The dictator vested himself with the power to imprison almost anyone.
examples: The dictator vested himself with the power to imprison almost anyone.

*a vested interest in something.monolingual: Fig. a personal or biased interest, often financial, in something. (*Typically: have ~; give someone ~.) _Margaret has a vested interest in wanting her father to sell the family firm. She has shares in it and would make a large profit. _ Bob has a ve
examples: Margaret has a vested interest in wanting her father to sell the family firm.

the villain of the piece.monolingual: Fig. someone or something that is responsible for something bad or wrong. (Fig. on the villainous role in a drama.) _I wonder who told the newspapers about the local scandal. I discovered that Jane was the villain of the piece. _We couldn’t think who
examples: I wonder who told the newspapers about the local scandal.

vim and vigor.monolingual: Cliché energy; enthusiasm. _ Show more vim and vigor! Let us know you’re alive. _ She’s sure got a lot of vim and vigor.
examples: Show more vim and vigor! Let us know you’re alive.

vindicate someone of something.monolingual: to clear or acquit someone of something. _ The police sought to vindicate Donald of the charges. _ They vindicated themselves of the charges with a clear alibi.
examples: The police sought to vindicate Donald of the charges.

virtual reality.monolingual: Fig. computer imaging that attempts to mimic real scenes or places. _The movie had so much virtual reality that the regular photographic scenes began to look funny.
examples: The movie had so much virtual reality that the regular photographic scenes began to look funny.

virtue is its own reward..monolingual: Prov. You should not be virtuous in hopes of getting a reward, but because it makes you feel good to be virtuous. _ Bill: If I help you, will you pay me? Fred: Virtue is its own reward.
examples: Bill: If I help you, will you pay me? Fred: Virtue is its own reward.

a visit from the stork.monolingual: Fig. a birth. (According to legend, babies are brought to their parents by a stork.) _ I hear that Maria is expecting a visit from the stork. _ The young couple had a visit from the stork.
examples: I hear that Maria is expecting a visit from the stork.

visit the plumbing.monolingual: Euph. to go to the bathroom. _ I think I’d better visit the plumbing before we go. _ I want you kids to visit the plumbing before we get in the car.
examples: I think I’d better visit the plumbing before we go.

visit with someone.monolingual: to pay a social call on someone. _ I would like to come by and visit with you for a while. _I will enjoy visiting with you.
examples: I would like to come by and visit with you for a while.

visually impaired.monolingual: Euph. blind or partly blind. _ I am visually impaired, but I like TV just as much as the next person. _ The disease left him visually impaired.
examples: I am visually impaired, but I like TV just as much as the next person.

volunteer as something.monolingual: to submit oneself as a person ready or willing to do something. _Would you be willing to volunteer as a marcher? _ I will volunteer as a helper in the hospital.
examples: I will volunteer as a helper in the hospital.

volunteer for something.monolingual: 1. to submit oneself for some task without being asked. _I volunteered for the job. _I didn’t volunteer for this.
examples: I volunteered for the job.

vomit something out†.monolingual: Fig. [for something] to spill forth a great deal of something. _ The volcano vomited the lava out for days. _ It vomited out hot lava for months.
examples: The volcano vomited the lava out for days.

vomit something up†.monolingual: to bring up something from the stomach by vomiting. _The dog vomited the chocolate cake up. _ Fido vomited up the rabbit.
examples: The dog vomited the chocolate cake up.

vote a split ticket.monolingual: Fig. to cast a ballot on which one’s votes are divided between two or more parties. _I always vote a split ticket since I detest both parties. _ Mary voted a split ticket for the first time in her life.
examples: I always vote a split ticket since I detest both parties.

vote a straight ticket.monolingual: Fig. to cast a ballot on which all one’s votes are for members of the same political party. _ I’m not a member of any political party, so I never vote a straight ticket. _ I usually vote a straight ticket because I believe in the principles of one pa
examples: I’m not a member of any political party, so I never vote a straight ticket.

vote against someone or something.monolingual: to cast a ballot against someone or something. _Are you going to vote against the provision? _ I plan to vote against David.
examples: I plan to vote against David.

vote for someone or something.monolingual: to cast a ballot in favor of someone or something. _Did you vote for Alice? _I plan to vote for the tax freeze. _ Of course, I voted for myself! Wouldn’t you?
examples: I plan to vote for the tax freeze.

a vote of confidence.monolingual: Fig. a poll taken to discover whether or not a person, party, etc., still has the majority’s support. _The government easily won the vote of confidence called for by the opposition. _ The president of the club resigned when one of the members called
examples: The government easily won the vote of confidence called for by the opposition.

a vote of thanks.monolingual: Fig. a speech expressing appreciation and thanks to a speaker, lecturer, organizer, etc., and inviting the audience to applaud. _ John gave a vote of thanks to Professor Jones for his talk. _ Mary was given a vote of thanks for organizing the dance.
examples: John gave a vote of thanks to Professor Jones for his talk.

vote someone or something down†.monolingual: to defeat someone or something in an election. _The community voted the proposal down. _ They voted down the proposal.
examples: The community voted the proposal down.

vote something through†.monolingual: to get something through a set of procedures by voting in favor of it. _They were not able to vote the bill through. _ They voted through the bill.
examples: They were not able to vote the bill through.

vote with one’s feet.monolingual: Fig. to express one’s dissatisfaction with something by leaving, especially by walking away. _ I think that the play is a total f lop. Most of the audience voted with its feet during the second act. _ I am prepared to vote with my feet if the meeting
examples: I think that the play is a total f lop.

vouch for someone or something.monolingual: to support or back someone or something; to endorse someone or something. _ I can vouch for Tom. _ Irene will vouch for my honesty.
examples: I can vouch for Tom.

wade across something.monolingual: to walk across something covered by water. _ Let’s wade across the stream at this point. _ If I wade across it, I will get wet.
examples: Let’s wade across the stream at this point.

wade through something.monolingual: 1. to walk with effort through a substance, such as water, mud, garbage, etc. _ The soldiers waded through the mud on the way to battle. _ They waded through the mess to get to where they were going.
examples: The soldiers waded through the mud on the way to battle.

wag one’s chin.monolingual: Rur. to talk. _ She loves to visit. She’ll wag her chin for hours. _He was on the phone, wagging his chin to his buddy.
examples: She loves to visit.

wager on someone or something.monolingual: to bet on someone or something. _ I wouldn’t want to wager on the outcome. _ I’ll wager on Bill, the fastest runner in town.
examples: I wouldn’t want to wager on the outcome.

wait one’s turn.monolingual: Fig. to keep from doing something until everyone ahead of you has done it. _ You can’t cross the intersection yet. You must wait your turn. _I can’t wait my turn. I’m in a tremendous hurry.
examples: You can’t cross the intersection yet.

wait something out†.monolingual: to wait until something ends. _ I will wait the summer out, and if nothing happens, I’ll write again. _ I can wait out the storm inside.
examples: I will wait the summer out, and if nothing happens, I’ll write again.

wait-and-see attitude.monolingual: Fig. a skeptical attitude; an uncertain attitude in which someone will just wait to see what happens before reacting. _ John thought that Mary couldn’t do it, but he took a wait-and-see attitude. _ His wait-and-see attitude seemed to indicate that he
examples: John thought that Mary couldn’t do it, but he took a wait-and-see attitude.

waiting in the wings.monolingual: Fig. ready or prepared to do something, especially to take over someone else’s job or position. _ Mr. Smith retires as manager next year, and Mr. Jones is just waiting in the wings. _Jane was waiting in the wings, hoping that a member of the hockey t
examples: Mr. Smith retires as manager next year, and Mr.

wake the dead.monolingual: Fig. to be so loud as to wake those who are “sleeping” the most soundly: the dead. _You are making enough noise to wake the dead. _ Stop hollering! You’ll wake the dead!
examples: You are making enough noise to wake the dead.

wake up.monolingual: to awaken; to become alert. _Wake up! We have to get on the road. _ It’s time to wake up!
examples: Wake up! We have to get on the road.

walk a tightrope.monolingual: Fig. to be in a situation where one must be very cautious. _ I’ve been walking a tightrope all day. I need to relax. _ Our business is about to fail. We’ve been walking a tightrope for three months.
examples: I’ve been walking a tightrope all day.

walk across something.monolingual: to move across something on foot. _ We walked across the bridge carefully. _ Jerry walked across the field and examined the fence on the other side.
examples: We walked across the bridge carefully.

walk along.monolingual: to move along on foot. _ I was just walking along when my heel broke off. _ I’m in no hurry. I’ll just walk along at my own speed.
examples: I was just walking along when my heel broke off.

walk along something.monolingual: to move beside something on foot. _Let’s not walk along the road. It’s too dangerous. _Walk along the wall where it’s safer.
examples: Let’s not walk along the road.

walk around.monolingual: to move around walking; to pace around. _ I need to walk around and get some fresh air. _ Why don’t we walk around for a while before we go in?
examples: I need to walk around and get some fresh air.

walk around something.monolingual: 1. to avoid something by passing around it. _Let’s walk around this muddy place in the path.
examples: Let’s walk around this muddy place in the path.

walk down something.monolingual: to go down something on foot. _ She walked down the path and turned to the right. _ Todd was walking down the road when they caught up with him.
examples: She walked down the path and turned to the right.

walk off.monolingual: to walk away; to leave on foot abruptly. _ She didn’t even say good-bye. She just walked off. _ He walked off and never looked back.
examples: She didn’t even say good-bye.

walk off the job.monolingual: 1. Fig. to abandon a job abruptly. _ I was so mad I almost walked off the job. _ Fred almost walked off the job when he saw how bad things were.
examples: I was so mad I almost walked off the job.

walk on.monolingual: to continue walking. _ Walk on. Go all the way to the end. _ I knew I wasn’t there yet, so I just walked on.
examples: Walk on. Go all the way to the end.

walk on air.monolingual: Fig. to be very happy; to be euphoric. _ Ann was walking on air when she got the job. _ On the last day of school, all the children are walking on air.
examples: Ann was walking on air when she got the job.

walk on eggshells.monolingual: 1. Fig. to walk very carefully; to take steps gingerly. _ Since he stumbled and fell against the china cabinet, Bill has been walking on eggshells.
examples: Since he stumbled and fell against the china cabinet, Bill has been walking on eggshells.

walk out with someone.monolingual: to exit something or some place with someone on foot. _After the play, Jane and I walked out together and had a nice talk. _We walked out with Mr. Wilson, who had sat next to us during the show.
examples: After the play, Jane and I walked out together and had a nice talk.

walk right in.monolingual: to enter on foot without hesitation. _ He went up to the door, opened it, and walked right in. _Please just walk right in!
examples: He went up to the door, opened it, and walked right in.

walk soft.monolingual: to be unobtrusive; to be gentle and humble. _ I try to walk soft and not rock the boat. _The guy’s a tyrant. He walks soft just to mislead people.
examples: I try to walk soft and not rock the boat.

walk someone out.monolingual: to accompany someone out, walking. _ I’ll walk you out. The exit is hard to find. _ Please let me walk you out so you don’t get lost.
examples: I’ll walk you out.

walk someone’s feet off.monolingual: Fig. to walk too much and tire out someone’s feet, including one’s own. _ I’ve gone all over town today. I walked my feet off, looking for just the right present for Jill. _ I need to know where I am going before I leave so I won’t walk my feet off.
examples: I’ve gone all over town today.

walk someone through something.monolingual: 1. to lead or accompany someone through an opening, arch, doorway, etc. _Mike walked Mary through the arch into a lovely garden. _Todd walked Rita through the doorway, into the ballroom.
examples: Mike walked Mary through the arch into a lovely garden.

walk tall.monolingual: Fig. to be brave and self-assured. _ I know I can walk tall because I’m innocent. _ You go out on that stage and walk tall. There is no reason to be afraid.
examples: I know I can walk tall because I’m innocent.

walk the floor.monolingual: Fig. to pace nervously while waiting. _ While Bill waited for news of the operation, he walked the f loor for hours on end. _Walking the f loor won’t help. You might as well sit down and relax.
examples: While Bill waited for news of the operation, he walked the f loor for hours on end.

walk the plank.monolingual: Fig. to suffer punishment at the hand of someone. (Fig. on the image of pirates making their blindfolded captives die by walking off the end of a plank jutting out over the open sea.) _Fred may think he can make the members of my department walk the
examples: Fred may think he can make the members of my department walk the plank, but we will fight back.

walk through something.monolingual: Fig. to rehearse something in a casual way; to go through a play or other performed piece, showing where each person is to be located during each speech or musical number. _Let’s walk through this scene one more time.
examples: Let’s walk through this scene one more time.

walk together.monolingual: [for two or more people] to walk as a group. _ Let’s all walk together so we can talk to one another. _ We walked together for a while.
examples: Let’s all walk together so we can talk to one another.

walk up something.monolingual: 1. to move up an incline or stairs on foot. _Sally will have to walk up the stairs by herself.
examples: Sally will have to walk up the stairs by herself.

walk with someone.monolingual: to walk in the company of someone. _ Why don’t you walk with me for a while? _ Can I walk with you?

walk with something.monolingual: 1. to walk with the aid of something, such as a cane, crutches, etc. _ You can recognize her easily. She walks with a cane. _ Dan walks with the help of a crutch.
examples: You can recognize her easily.

wall someone or something in†.monolingual: to contain someone or something behind or within a wall. (Implies a constriction of space, but not necessarily an inescapable area. See wall something up.) _ The count walled his prisoner in permanently. _Jane decided to wall in the little garden at
examples: The count walled his prisoner in permanently.

wall someone or something off†.monolingual: to separate or segregate someone or something by building a wall. _ She sat right across from me at her desk, listening to every phone call I made. Finally, the manager walled her off so we now can carry on our business in privacy. _They walled off t
examples: She sat right across from me at her desk, listening to every phone call I made.

wall something up†.monolingual: 1. to seal something up behind a wall. _We simply walled the old furnace up. It was cheaper than removing it. _They walled up the old furnace.
examples: We simply walled the old furnace up.

wallow in something.monolingual: Fig. to experience an abundance of something. (Fig. on wallow (around) in something.) _ Roger and Wilma are just wallowing in money. _ Claire spent the entire day wallowing in self-pity. _ The villagers are all wallowing in superstition.
examples: Roger and Wilma are just wallowing in money.

walls have ears..monolingual: Prov. Someone may be listening. (A warning that you think your conversation is being overheard.) _ Jill: Did I tell you what I found out about Fred? He— Jane: Shhh! Walls have ears. _ Don’t say anything about our business dealings in here. Walls have
examples: Jill: Did I tell you what I found out about Fred? He— Jane: Shhh! Walls have ears.

waltz around something.monolingual: Fig. to move around or through a place happily or proudly. _She waltzed around the room, very pleased with herself. _ Who is that person waltzing around, trying to look important?
examples: She waltzed around the room, very pleased with herself.

waltz off.monolingual: Fig. to depart briskly and easily. _ They said good-bye and waltzed off.
examples: They said good-bye and waltzed off.

waltz through something.monolingual: Fig. to get through something easily. _ I waltzed through my comps and started on my research in my second year of grad school. _I tried to waltz through my assignment, but it was too hard.
examples: I waltzed through my comps and started on my research in my second year of grad school.

wander from something.monolingual: to stray from something, such as a path, a set of rules, etc. _ Please do not wander from the path I have set for you. _ If you wander from our guidelines, your finished product may not be acceptable.
examples: Please do not wander from the path I have set for you.

wangle out of something.monolingual: Fig. to get out of having to do something; to argue or deceive one’s way out of a responsibility. _ Don’t try to wangle out of this mess. You must stay and fix the problems you made. _ Mary managed to wangle out of staying late again.
examples: Don’t try to wangle out of this mess.

want for nothing.monolingual: Fig. not to lack anything; to have everything one needs or desires. _The Smiths don’t have much money, but their children seem to want for nothing. _Lisa’s husband spoils her. She wants for nothing.
examples: The Smiths don’t have much money, but their children seem to want for nothing.

want for something.monolingual: Fig. to lack something; to need something. _ I certainly don’t want for advice. In fact, I have had too much. _ We don’t want for helpers around here.
examples: I certainly don’t want for advice.

want someone for something.monolingual: 1. to desire someone for some job or purpose. _I want Fred for my team. _We all want you for a candidate.
examples: I want Fred for my team.

want someone or something back.monolingual: to desire the return of someone or something. _Timmy wanted his mother back very badly. _ I want my money back!
examples: Timmy wanted his mother back very badly.

war against someone or something.monolingual: to fight against someone or something; to oppose someone or something. _ That country is always warring against its neighbors. _ Why do you want to war against the city council?
examples: That country is always warring against its neighbors.

war over someone or something.monolingual: to fight about who is to get someone or something. _ Stop warring over Tom. He refuses to play on either team. _ There is no point in warring over the contract.
examples: Stop warring over Tom.

war with someone.monolingual: to fight or dispute with someone. _ Ruth is always warring with someone, usually about something trivial. _ Please don’t war with me!
examples: Ruth is always warring with someone, usually about something trivial.

ward someone or something off†.monolingual: to hold someone or something off; to fight someone or something off. _ The army was able to ward the attackers off repeatedly. _We couldn’t ward off the attackers any longer.
examples: The army was able to ward the attackers off repeatedly.

*warm as toast.monolingual: very warm and cozy. (*Also: as ~.) _ The baby will be warm as toast in that blanket. _ We were as warm as toast by the side of the fire.
examples: The baby will be warm as toast in that blanket.

warm body.monolingual: a person; just any person (who can be counted on to be present). _ See if you can get a couple of warm bodies to stand at the door and hand out programs. _ You mean among all these warm bodies nobody knows calculus?
examples: See if you can get a couple of warm bodies to stand at the door and hand out programs.

warm someone or something up†.monolingual: to make someone or something warmer; to take the chill off someone or something. _ I put him by the fire to warm him up a little. _ We warmed up our feet before the fire. _ Could you warm up my coffee, please?
examples: I put him by the fire to warm him up a little.

warm someone up†.monolingual: 1. to make someone warmer. _Stand by the fire and warm yourself up. _Warm up the kids and then give them some cookies.
examples: Stand by the fire and warm yourself up.

warm something over†.monolingual: 1. to reheat food to serve it as leftovers. _ I’ll just warm the rest over for lunch tomorrow. _ Jane warmed over yesterday’s turkey.
examples: I’ll just warm the rest over for lunch tomorrow.

warm the bench.monolingual: Fig. [for a player] to remain out of play during a game—seated on a bench. _John spent the whole game warming the bench. _Mary never warms the bench. She plays from the beginning to the end.
examples: John spent the whole game warming the bench.

warmed over.monolingual: not very original; rehashed. _ I am not interested in reading warmed over news on a computer screen. _ The lecture sounded sort of warmed over, but it wasn’t too dull.
examples: I am not interested in reading warmed over news on a computer screen.

warn someone of something.monolingual: to advise someone that something bad is likely to happen. _ I wish you had warned us of what was going to happen. _ Please warn John of the heavy traffic he may run into.
examples: I wish you had warned us of what was going to happen.

warn someone off†.monolingual: to advise a person to stay away. _ We placed a guard outside the door to warn people off until the gas leak could be fixed. _ The guards warned off everyone in the vicinity.
examples: We placed a guard outside the door to warn people off until the gas leak could be fixed.

warts and all.monolingual: Cliché even with the flaws. _ It’s a great performance—warts and all. _ Yes, we admire each other very much, warts and all.
examples: It’s a great performance—warts and all.

wash away.monolingual: to be carried away by water or some other liquid. _ The bridge washed away in the f lood. _ All the soil washed away and left the rocks exposed.
examples: The bridge washed away in the f lood.

wash out.monolingual: 1. Inf. to fail and be removed from something, such as school. _ I studied all I could, but I still washed out. _I don’t want to wash out. It’s my whole future.
examples: I studied all I could, but I still washed out.

wash over someone.monolingual: Fig. [for a powerful feeling] to flood over a person. _ A feeling of nausea washed over me. _ A strong feeling of satisfaction washed over me.
examples: A feeling of nausea washed over me.

wash overboard.monolingual: [for someone or something] to be carried overboard (off the deck of a ship) by water. _ Our chairs washed overboard in the storm. _ I was afraid that the dog would wash overboard, so I took her below.
examples: Our chairs washed overboard in the storm.

wash someone or something away†.monolingual: [for a flood of water] to carry someone or something away. _The f lood washed the boats away. _The high water washed away much of the sand along the shoreline.
examples: The f lood washed the boats away.

wash someone or something off†.monolingual: to clean someone or something by washing. _ She washed the muddy children off with a hose and put their clothes right into the washing machine. _ Jane washed off the children.
examples: She washed the muddy children off with a hose and put their clothes right into the washing machine.

wash someone or something overboard.monolingual: [for water] to flood up and carry someone or something off the deck of a ship into the sea. _ The high seas washed two of the sailors overboard. _ The storm washed our chairs overboard.
examples: The high seas washed two of the sailors overboard.

wash someone or something up†.monolingual: 1. to clean up someone or something by washing. _ Please wash the baby up as long as you are changing the diaper. _ I’ll wash up the baby. _ Sam will wash himself up before dinner.
examples: Please wash the baby up as long as you are changing the diaper.

wash someone up†.monolingual: to terminate someone in something. _ This error is going to wash you up as an account executive. _ That washed me up. _ Problems like this have washed up quite a few careers.
examples: This error is going to wash you up as an account executive.

wash something away†.monolingual: to clean something by scrubbing and flushing away the dirt. _ Fresh water will wash the seawater away. _ Let’s wash away these muddy footprints.
examples: Fresh water will wash the seawater away.

wash something down something.monolingual: to get rid of something by flooding it down the sewer, drain, sink, etc. _Wash all the soap suds down the drain and clean the sink, please. _ Please wash all that stuff down the drain.
examples: Wash all the soap suds down the drain and clean the sink, please.

wash something of something.monolingual: to get something cleaned of something by washing. _ I washed my hair of the smell of cigarette smoke I was saturated with in the meeting. _ I have to get home and wash my trousers of this stain.
examples: I washed my hair of the smell of cigarette smoke I was saturated with in the meeting.

washed out.monolingual: Inf. exhausted; tired. _ I feel too washed out to go to work today. _ Poor Ted really looks washed out.
examples: I feel too washed out to go to work today.

washed up.monolingual: Fig. finished. _ “You’re through, Tom,” said the manager, “Fired—washed up!” _Wilbur is washed up as a bank teller.
examples: Wilbur is washed up as a bank teller.

waste away.monolingual: to wither or dwindle away. _Our money just seemed to waste away. _ As she grew older, she just sort of wasted away.
examples: Our money just seemed to waste away.

waste not, want not..monolingual: Prov. Cliché If you do not waste anything, you will always have enough. _Always save the fabric scraps left over from your sewing projects; you can use them to make something else. Waste not, want not. _ Sam never let his leftovers spoil in the refri
examples: Always save the fabric scraps left over from your sewing projects; you can use them to make something else.

a waste of space.monolingual: something that is completely without value. _ The wrecked furniture in here is just a waste of space. _ This broken-down car is a waste of space!
examples: The wrecked furniture in here is just a waste of space.

waste one’s breath.monolingual: Fig. to waste one’s time talking; to talk in vain. _Don’t waste your breath talking to her. She won’t listen. _ You can’t persuade me. You’re just wasting your breath.
examples: Don’t waste your breath talking to her.

waste someone.monolingual: Sl. to kill someone. _ The thief tried to waste the bank guard after the bank robbery. _ The crook said, “Try that again, and I’ll waste you!”
examples: The thief tried to waste the bank guard after the bank robbery.

waste something away†.monolingual: to use something up wastefully; to dissipate something. _ He wasted all his money away and had to live in poverty. _ They wasted away everything and regretted it later.
examples: He wasted all his money away and had to live in poverty.

watch for someone or something.monolingual: to keep looking for someone or something to appear. _Watch for me. I’ll be wearing a red carnation in my hair. _ I will watch for the bus.
examples: Watch for me. I’ll be wearing a red carnation in my hair.

watch it!.monolingual: 1. Inf. Be careful. _ Rachel: Watch it! There’s a broken stair there. Jane: Gee, thanks. _ Mary: Watch it! There’s a pothole in the street. Bob: Thanks.
examples: Rachel: Watch it! There’s a broken stair there.

watch one’s step.monolingual: 1. be careful of one’s walking or stepping. _ It’s slippery here. Watch your step.
examples: It’s slippery here.

watch over someone or something.monolingual: to keep guard over someone or something; to care for someone or something. _ Could you please watch over my little girl while I go to the store? _ I will watch over your house while you are away.
examples: I will watch over your house while you are away.

a watched pot never boils..monolingual: Prov. Something you are waiting for will not happen while you are concentrating on it. _ Don’t just sit there staring at the phone while you wait for Lucy to call. A watched pot never boils. _ I’d better do something besides look out the window waiti
examples: Don’t just sit there staring at the phone while you wait for Lucy to call.

water something down†.monolingual: 1. to dilute something. _ Who watered the orange juice down? _ Jim watered down the orange juice.
examples: Jim watered down the orange juice.

watering hole.monolingual: 1. Lit. a place where there is water for animals (and people) to drink. _ The elephants came down to the watering hole and chased away the lions so they could drink in peace.
examples: The elephants came down to the watering hole and chased away the lions so they could drink in peace.

wave someone or something aside†.monolingual: to make a signal with the hand for someone or something to move aside. _The police officer waved us aside and would not let us turn into our street. _ The officer waved aside the spectators. _ She waved all the traffic aside.
examples: The police officer waved us aside and would not let us turn into our street.

wave someone or something off†.monolingual: to make a signal with the hand for someone or something to remain at a distance. _ There was someone standing in front of the bridge, waving everyone off. The bridge must have collapsed. _ He waved off all the traffic.
examples: There was someone standing in front of the bridge, waving everyone off.

wave someone or something on†.monolingual: to make a signal with the hand for someone or something to move on or keep moving. _The traffic cop waved us on. _The cop waved on the hordes of pedestrians.
examples: The traffic cop waved us on.

wave something around†.monolingual: to raise something up and move it around so that everyone can see it. _ When Ruth found the money, she waved it around so everyone could see it. _ She kept waving around the dollar she found in the street.
examples: When Ruth found the money, she waved it around so everyone could see it.

wax and wane.monolingual: Fig. to increase and then decrease, as the phases of the moon. _ As the moon waxes and wanes, so does the height of the tide change. _Voter sentiment about the tax proposal waxes and wanes with each passing day.
examples: As the moon waxes and wanes, so does the height of the tide change.

wax eloquent.monolingual: Fig. to speak with eloquence. _Perry never passed up a chance to wax eloquent at a banquet.
examples: Perry never passed up a chance to wax eloquent at a banquet.

wax poetic.monolingual: Fig. to speak poetically. _I hope you will pardon me if I wax poetic for a moment when I say that your lovely hands drift across the piano keys like swans on a lake.
examples: I hope you will pardon me if I wax poetic for a moment when I say that your lovely hands drift across the piano keys like swans on a lake.

the way it plays.monolingual: Sl. the way it is; the way things are. _The world is a rough place, and that’s the way it plays. _ It’s tough, but it’s the way it plays.
examples: The world is a rough place, and that’s the way it plays.

way out.monolingual: 1. extreme; arcane. _Some of your ideas are really way out. _What a way-out hairdo.
examples: Some of your ideas are really way out.

we aim to please..monolingual: Fig.We try hard to please you. (Usually a commercial slogan, but can be said in jest by one person, often in response to Thank you.) _ Mary: This meal is absolutely delicious! Waiter: We aim to please. _ Tom: Well, Sue, here’s the laundry detergent y
examples: Mary: This meal is absolutely delicious! Waiter: We aim to please.

weak sister.monolingual: a timid person, usually a male. _It looks like Dave is the weak sister on the team. _ We’ve got to pull together and stop playing like a bunch of weak sisters.
examples: It looks like Dave is the weak sister on the team.

a wealth of something.monolingual: Fig. a large amount of something. _There’s a wealth of information on parrots at the library. _ The junkyard had a wealth of used car parts.
examples: There’s a wealth of information on parrots at the library.

wear down.monolingual: Fig. to break down with wear; to erode. _The steps had worn down so much that each one was curved and slanted dangerously.
examples: The steps had worn down so much that each one was curved and slanted dangerously.

wear off.monolingual: [for the effects of something] to become less; to stop gradually. _ The effects of the painkiller wore off and my tooth began to hurt. _ I was annoyed at first, but my anger wore off.
examples: The effects of the painkiller wore off and my tooth began to hurt.

wear on someone.monolingual: Fig. to bother or annoy someone. _ We stayed with them only a short time because my children seemed to wear on them. _ Always being short of money wears on a person after a while.
examples: We stayed with them only a short time because my children seemed to wear on them.

wear out.monolingual: to become worn from use; to become diminished or useless from use. _My car engine is about to wear out. _ It takes a lot of driving to wear out an engine.
examples: My car engine is about to wear out.

wear out one’s welcome.monolingual: Fig. to stay too long (at an event to which one has been invited); to visit somewhere too often. _ Tom visited the Smiths so often that he wore out his welcome. _ At about midnight, I decided that I had worn out my welcome, so I went home.
examples: Tom visited the Smiths so often that he wore out his welcome.

wear someone down†.monolingual: 1. Fig. to exhaust someone. _ This hot weather wears me down. _ The steamy weather wore down the tourists and made them stay in their hotels.
examples: This hot weather wears me down.

wear someone out†.monolingual: Fig. to exhaust someone; to make someone tired. _ The coach made the team practice until he wore them out. _If he wears out everybody on the team, nobody will be left to play in the game.
examples: The coach made the team practice until he wore them out.

wear someone to a frazzle.monolingual: Fig. to exhaust someone. _ Her work wears her to a frazzle. _ Taking care of all those kids must wear you to a frazzle.
examples: Her work wears her to a frazzle.

wear something away†.monolingual: to erode something. _The constant rains wore the side of the cathedral away. _ The flooding wore away the topsoil.
examples: The constant rains wore the side of the cathedral away.

wear something down†.monolingual: to grind something away; to erode something. _ The constant rubbing of the door wore the carpet down. _The rubbing of the door wore down the carpet.
examples: The constant rubbing of the door wore the carpet down.

wear something out†.monolingual: to make something worthless or nonfunctional from use. _ I wore my shoes out in no time at all. _ I wore out my shoes in less than a month.
examples: I wore my shoes out in no time at all.

wear through something.monolingual: to grind or rub through something. _My heel finally wore through the carpeting beneath the accelerator of my car. _ The constant rubbing of hands wore through the paint on the railing.
examples: My heel finally wore through the carpeting beneath the accelerator of my car.

weary of someone or something.monolingual: to become tired of or bored with someone or something. _ I am beginning to weary of you. Isn’t it time you were going? _ We soon wearied of chicken twice a week.
examples: I am beginning to weary of you.

weary someone with something.monolingual: to tire or bore someone with something. _ He wearied her with his constant requests. _ Please don’t weary me with your complaints.
examples: He wearied her with his constant requests.

weather permitting.monolingual: Fig. if the weather allows it. _ Weather permitting, we will be there on time. _ The plane lands at midnight, weather permitting.
examples: Weather permitting, we will be there on time.

weather the storm.monolingual: 1. Fig. to experience and survive a storm. _ We decided to stay in the building and weather the storm there with the other visitors.
examples: We decided to stay in the building and weather the storm there with the other visitors.

weave around.monolingual: to move about, changing directions at random. _The drunken driver wove around all over the road. _ He was weaving around everywhere.
examples: The drunken driver wove around all over the road.

weave something from something.monolingual: 1. to make a fabric from some type of fiber. _ They weave this cloth from a fine plant fiber. _ This cloth is woven from silk threads.
examples: They weave this cloth from a fine plant fiber.

weave something into something.monolingual: 1. to form fibers into a fabric. _ They could weave the threads into simple cloth with a primitive loom. _We will weave this wool into a rug.
examples: They could weave the threads into simple cloth with a primitive loom.

weave through something.monolingual: to move through something by turning and dodging. _ The car wove through traffic, almost hitting a number of other cars. _We wove through the jungle vines, trying to avoid touching the poisonous ones.
examples: The car wove through traffic, almost hitting a number of other cars.

wed someone to someone.monolingual: to marry someone to someone else. _Her parents wedded her to a young prince when she was only twelve. _ They cannot wed her to anyone if she has already married someone of her own choosing.
examples: Her parents wedded her to a young prince when she was only twelve.

wed someone to something.monolingual: Fig. to join someone firmly to a concept. (Fig. on wed someone to someone.) _Don’t try to wed me to your way of doing things. I have my own way. _ Don’t wed yourself to that idea.
examples: Don’t try to wed me to your way of doing things.

wedded to something.monolingual: Fig. mentally attached to something; firmly committed to something. (Fig. on wed(ded) to someone.) _The manager was wedded to the idea of getting new computers. _ The mayor was wedded to the new budget plan.
examples: The manager was wedded to the idea of getting new computers.

weed someone or something out†.monolingual: Fig. to remove someone or something unwanted or undesirable from a group or collection. (Fig. on removing weeds from the soil.) _ We had to weed the less productive workers out one by one. _ The auditions were held to weed out the actors with the lea
examples: We had to weed the less productive workers out one by one.

week in, week out.monolingual: Fig. every week, week after week. _ We have the same old food, week in, week out. _ I’m tired of this job. I’ve done the same thing—week in, week out— for three years.
examples: We have the same old food, week in, week out.

weep about someone or something.monolingual: to cry about someone or something; to mourn someone or something. _ She was weeping about her grandfather, who had passed away in the night. _ There is no use weeping about spilled milk.
examples: She was weeping about her grandfather, who had passed away in the night.

weep for joy.monolingual: Fig. to cry out of happiness. _ She was so happy, she wept for joy. _ We all wept for joy at the safe return of the child.
examples: She was so happy, she wept for joy.

weep over someone or something.monolingual: to cry about someone or something. _ No need to weep over me. I’ll do all right. _ There is no point in weeping over something you can’t do anything about.
examples: No need to weep over me.

weigh against someone or something.monolingual: Fig. to count against someone or something; [for some fact] to work against someone or something. _I hope my many absences do not weigh against me on the final grade. _ This will weigh against you.
examples: I hope my many absences do not weigh against me on the final grade.

weigh on someone’s mind.monolingual: Fig. [for something] to be in a person’s thoughts; [for something] to be bothering someone’s thinking. _ This problem has been weighing on my mind for many days now. _ I hate to have things weighing on my mind. I can’t sleep when I’m worried.
examples: This problem has been weighing on my mind for many days now.

weigh someone down†.monolingual: Fig. [for a thought] to worry or depress someone. _ All these problems really weigh me down. _Financial problems have been weighing down our entire family.
examples: All these problems really weigh me down.

weigh someone or something down†.monolingual: to burden someone or something. _ The heavy burden weighed the poor donkey down. _ The load of bricks weighed down the truck.
examples: The heavy burden weighed the poor donkey down.

weigh someone’s words.monolingual: 1. Fig. to consider carefully what someone says. _ I listened to what he said, and I weighed his words very carefully. _Everyone was weighing his words. None of us knew exactly what he meant.
examples: I listened to what he said, and I weighed his words very carefully.

weigh something against something.monolingual: to ponder something by balancing it against something. _ I weighed going to town against staying here and sleeping and I decided to stay here. _ When I weigh your suggestion against my own ideas, I realize that I must follow my own conscience.
examples: I weighed going to town against staying here and sleeping and I decided to stay here.

weigh something out†.monolingual: to weigh something as it is distributed. _The merchant weighed the cuts of meat out for each of the waiting women. _ They weighed out the grain carefully.
examples: The merchant weighed the cuts of meat out for each of the waiting women.

weigh something up†.monolingual: to find out the weight of something. _ I can’t tell you how much this will cost until I weigh it up. _ Liz weighed up the meat and jotted down the price.
examples: I can’t tell you how much this will cost until I weigh it up.

weird out.monolingual: Sl. to become emotionally disturbed or unnerved; to flip out. _ The day was just gross. I thought I would weird out at noon. _ I weirded out at the news of Frankie’s death.
examples: The day was just gross.

weirded out.monolingual: Sl. disturbed or unnerved by drugs or events. _ I was totally weirded out and couldn’t control myself. _ After the blowup, Fred was really weirded out.
examples: I was totally weirded out and couldn’t control myself.

welcome aboard..monolingual: Fig. Welcome to employment at our company. _Glad to meet you. Welcome aboard.
examples: Glad to meet you.

welcome someone or something back†.monolingual: to greet the return of someone or something. _We are delighted to welcome you back to our house. _ The students welcomed back the teacher who had been ill.
examples: We are delighted to welcome you back to our house.

welcome someone to something.monolingual: to greet someone who has come into something or some place. _ I am very pleased to welcome you to Adamsville! _ They welcomed us to the party and showed us where to put our coats and hats.
examples: They welcomed us to the party and showed us where to put our coats and hats.

welcome someone with something.monolingual: to present something to someone as a sign of greeting. _ The natives welcomed us with garlands of f lowers. _I welcomed the visitors with gifts and good wishes.
examples: The natives welcomed us with garlands of f lowers.

welcome to do something.monolingual: free to do something; allowed to do something. _ The audience is welcome to ask questions at the end of the speech. _ You are welcome to help yourself to anything in the kitchen.
examples: The audience is welcome to ask questions at the end of the speech.

welcome to our house..monolingual: an expression said by a host or hostess when greeting guests and bringing them into the house. _ Andy: Hello, Sally. Welcome to our house. Come on in. Sally: Thanks. It’s good to be here. _ Tom: Welcome to our house. Make yourself at home. Henry: Tha
examples: Andy: Hello, Sally.

well begun is half done..monolingual: Prov. Beginning a project well makes it easier to do the rest.; Once you have begun a project well, you do not need to put in much more effort to finish it. _ Jill: I’m afraid I’ll never be able to finish writing this report. Jane: You’ve already wri
examples: Jill: I’m afraid I’ll never be able to finish writing this report.

well, bust my buttons!.monolingual: Rur. What a surprise! _ Well, bust my buttons! It’s good to see you! _ Well, bust my buttons! You did all the dishes!

well done!.monolingual: Fig. You did that nicely! _ Sally: Well done, Tom. Excellent speech. Tom: Thanks. _ In the lobby after the play, Tom was met with a chorus of well-wishers saying, “Well done, Tom!”
examples: Sally: Well done, Tom.

well in hand.monolingual: Fig. under control. _ Is that matter well in hand? _ We have everything well in hand. Don’t worry.
examples: We have everything well in hand.

*well into something.monolingual: Fig. far into something or far along in something. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ It was well into the morning before she awoke. _ The car was well into the tunnel when it broke down.
examples: It was well into the morning before she awoke.

well over.monolingual: [for a liquid] to fill up and spill over. _ The laundry tub finally welled over as it became too full. _The milk glass began to well over, and Timmy began to cry.
examples: The laundry tub finally welled over as it became too full.

well said..monolingual: Fig. You said that very well, and I agree. _ As Sally sat down, Mary complimented her, “Well said, Sally. You made your point very well.” _ John: And I for one will never stand for this kind of encroachment on my rights again! Mary: Well said! Bob: W
examples: As Sally sat down, Mary complimented her, “Well said, Sally.

well, shut my mouth!.monolingual: Rur. I am very surprised! _Well, shut my mouth! I didn’t know you were in town! _ Tom: The governor’s on the phone and wants to talk to you. Jane: Well, shut my mouth!
examples: Tom: The governor’s on the phone and wants to talk to you.
