well up in years.monolingual: Euph. aged; old. _Jane’s husband is well up in years. He is nearly seventy-five. _ Joan’s well up in years but healthy.
examples: Jane’s husband is well up in years.

well up with something.monolingual: to fill up or gush with something, such as water. _Her eyes welled up with tears. _The basement drain welled up with the f loodwaters.
examples: Her eyes welled up with tears.

well-to-do.monolingual: Fig. wealthy and of good social position. (Often with quite, as in the examples.) _ The Jones family is quite well-to-do. _ There is a gentleman waiting for you at the door. He appears quite well-to-do.
examples: The Jones family is quite well-to-do.

welsh on someone.monolingual: to renege on a bet or an agreement made with someone. (Also spelled welch.) _You had better not welsh on me if you know what is good for you. _ Max welshed on the mob boss and made a lot of trouble for himself.
examples: You had better not welsh on me if you know what is good for you.

welter in something.monolingual: 1. to roll about or wallow in something; to be immersed in or surrounded by something. _ Most breeds of pigs will welter happily in mud. _I hate having to welter in the heat.
examples: Most breeds of pigs will welter happily in mud.

a wet blanket.monolingual: Fig. a dull or depressing person who spoils other people’s enjoyment. _ Jack’s fun at parties, but his brother’s a wet blanket. _ I was with Anne and she was being a real wet blanket.
examples: Jack’s fun at parties, but his brother’s a wet blanket.

wet one’s whistle.monolingual: Rur. to take a drink. _He stopped at the bar to wet his whistle. _ I don’t need a big glass of water. Just enough to wet my whistle.
examples: He stopped at the bar to wet his whistle.

wet someone or something down†.monolingual: to put water onto someone or something. _ Mother wet the children down with a hose while she was washing the car. _ Karen wet down the children with the hose. _We wet the new concrete down to help it cure in all the heat.
examples: Mother wet the children down with a hose while she was washing the car.

whack someone or something up†.monolingual: Sl. to damage someone or something. _ Bob got mad at Greg and whacked him up. _ Clara whacked up her car yesterday.
examples: Bob got mad at Greg and whacked him up.

whack something off†.monolingual: 1. Sl. to complete something easily or quickly. _If you want a pair of these, I can whack them off for you in a few minutes. _ The artisan whacked off a set of the earrings in a few minutes.
examples: If you want a pair of these, I can whack them off for you in a few minutes.

whack something up†.monolingual: Sl. to chop something up. _In about an hour, he had whacked the tree up into small logs. _Have you whacked up the chicken for frying yet?
examples: In about an hour, he had whacked the tree up into small logs.

wham bam thank you ma’am.monolingual: Rur. a bump in the road. _We hit a wham bam thank you ma’am and lost one of our hubcaps. _Watch out for the wham bam thank you ma’am at the corner of Third Street.
examples: We hit a wham bam thank you ma’am and lost one of our hubcaps.

what about it?.monolingual: Inf. So what?; Do you want to argue about it? (Contentious.) _ Bill: I heard you were the one accused of breaking the window. Tom: Yeah? So, what about it? _ Mary: Your piece of cake is bigger than mine. Sue: What about it?
examples: Bill: I heard you were the one accused of breaking the window.

what about you?.monolingual: 1. Fig. What is your choice? (Compare this with How about you?) _ Tom: I’m having the pot roast and a cup of coffee. What about you? Mary: I want something fattening and unhealthy. _ Sally: I prefer green and purple for this room. What about you? Mar
examples: Tom: I’m having the pot roast and a cup of coffee.

what are you drinking?.monolingual: 1. Fig. a phrase inquiring what someone is already drinking so that the person who asks the question can offer another drink of the same thing. _ Bill: Hi, Tom. Nice to see you. Can I get you something to drink? Tom: Sure. What are you drinking? Bill
examples: Bill: Hi, Tom. Nice to see you.

what are you driving at?.monolingual: Fig. What are you implying?; What do you mean? _ What are you driving at? What are you trying to say? _ Why are you asking me all these questions? What are you driving at?

what are you having?.monolingual: Fig. What food or drink are you planning to order? (Either part of a conversation or a request from food service personnel. In a restaurant, sometimes the host or hostess will signal to a guest to order first by saying this. Sometimes a guest will as
examples: Waiter: Would you care to order now? Tom: What are you having? Mary: You order.

what brings you here?.monolingual: Fig. What is your reason for being here? (A polite request for this information. More polite than “Why are you here?”) _ Tom: Hello, Mary. What brings you here? Mary: I was invited, just like you. _ Doctor: Well, John, what brings you here? John: I’v
examples: Tom: Hello, Mary.

what can i say?.monolingual: Inf. I have no explanation or excuse. What do you expect me to say? _ Bill: Why on earth did you lose that big order? Sally: What can I say? I’m sorry! _ Bob: You’re going to have to act more aggressive if you want to make sales. You’re just too timi
examples: Bob: You’re going to have to act more aggressive if you want to make sales.

what can i tell you?.monolingual: 1. Lit. What kind of information do you want? _ Bill: I have a question. Bob: What can I tell you? Bill: When do we arrive at Chicago? _ Mary: I would like to ask a question about the quiz tomorrow. Bill: What can I tell you? Mary: The answers, if yo
examples: Bill: I have a question.

what difference does it make?.monolingual: Does it really matter?; Does it cause any trouble? _What if I choose to leave home? What difference does it make? _So Jane dropped out of the club. What difference does it make?
examples: So Jane dropped out of the club.

what do you know?.monolingual: Inf. a typical inquiry on greeting someone. (A specific answer is not expected. Often pronounced “Wha-da-ya know?”) _Bob: Hey, Tom! What do you know? Tom: Look who’s here! Hi, Bob! _ John: What do you know? Mary: Nothing. How are you? John: Okay.
examples: John: What do you know? Mary: Nothing.

what do you say?.monolingual: 1. Inf. Hello, how are you? _ Bob: What do you say, Tom? Tom: Hey, man. How are you doing? _Bill: What do you say, man? Fred: What’s the good word, you old so-and-so?
examples: Bob: What do you say, Tom? Tom: Hey, man.

what do you think?.monolingual: What is your opinion? _Mary: This is our new company stationery. What do you think? Bill: Stunning. Simply stunning. _ Mary: We’re considering moving out into the country. What do you think? Sue: Sounds good to me.
examples: Mary: This is our new company stationery.

what does that prove?.monolingual: Fig. So what?; that does not mean anything. (A defensive expression. The heaviest stress is on that. Often with so, as in the examples.) _Tom: It seems that you were in the apartment the same night that it was robbed. Bob: So, what does that prove? T
examples: Tom: It seems that you were in the apartment the same night that it was robbed.

*what for.monolingual: 1. Fig. a scolding; a stern lecture. (*Typically: get ~; give someone ~.) _Billy’s mother gave him what for because he didn’t get home on time. _ I will really give you what for if you don’t straighten up.
examples: Billy’s mother gave him what for because he didn’t get home on time.

what gives?.monolingual: Inf. What happened?; What went wrong?; What’s the problem? _Bill: Hi, you guys. What gives? Bob: Nothing, just a little misunderstanding. Tom’s a little angry. _ Bob: Where’s my wallet? What gives? Tom: I think one of those roughnecks who just walked
examples: Bill: Hi, you guys.

what happened?.monolingual: What went wrong here? _ Bob (approaching a crowd): What happened? Tom (with Bob): What’s wrong? Bystander: Just a little mix-up. A car wanted to drive on the sidewalk, that’s all. _ There was a terrible noise, an explosion that shook the house. Bob l
examples: Bob (approaching a crowd): What happened? Tom (with Bob): What’s wrong? Bystander: Just a little mix-up.

what if...?.monolingual: What would be the result if something were true? _ What if you had all the money you want? _ What if everyone thought you were great?

what if i do?.monolingual: Does it matter to you if I do it?; What difference does it make if I do it? _Tom: Are you really going to sell your leather coat? Bob: What if I do? _ Jane: You’re not going to go out dressed like that, are you? Sue: So what if I do?

what if i don’t?.monolingual: Does it matter to you if I do not do it?; What difference does it make if I do not do it? _ Bob: You’re certainly going to tidy up a bit before going out, aren’t you? Tom: What if I don’t? _ Father: You are going to get in by midnight tonight or you’
examples: Father: You are going to get in by midnight tonight or you’re grounded.

what is it?.monolingual: What do you want from me?; Why do you want to get my attention? _ Tom: John, can I talk to you for a minute? John: What is it? _Sue: Jane? Jane: What is it? Sue: Close the door, please.
examples: Sue: Jane? Jane: What is it? Sue: Close the door, please.

what makes someone tick.monolingual: Fig. something that motivates someone; something that makes someone behave in a certain way. (Fig. on what makes something tick.) _ William is sort of strange. I don’t know what makes him tick. _ When you get to know people, you find out what makes t
examples: William is sort of strange.

what makes something tick.monolingual: Fig. the sense or mechanism that makes something run or function. (With reference to the ticking of a clock representing the functioning of the clock.) _ I don’t know what makes it tick. _ I took apart the radio to find out what made it tick.
examples: I don’t know what makes it tick.

what makes you think so?.monolingual: 1. Lit. Why do you think that?; What is your evidence for that conclusion? _ Tom: This bread may be a little old. Alice: What makes you think so? Tom: The green spots on the edges. _ Bob: Congress is in session again. Tom: What makes you think so? Bo
examples: Tom: This bread may be a little old.

what number are you calling?.monolingual: an expression used when one suspects that a telephone caller may have gotten the wrong number. _ Bob (on the telephone): Hello? Mary: Hello, is Sally there? Bob: Uh, what number are you calling? Mary: I guess I have the wrong number. Sorry. Bob: No p
examples: Bob (on the telephone): Hello? Mary: Hello, is Sally there? Bob: Uh, what number are you calling? Mary: I guess I have the wrong number.

what of it?.monolingual: Inf. What does it matter?; Why treat it as if it were important?; Why do you think that this is any of your business? (A bit contentious.) _ John: I hear you’ve been having a little trouble at the office. Bob: What of it? _ Sue: You missed a spot sha
examples: John: I hear you’ve been having a little trouble at the office.

what price something?.monolingual: What is the value of something?; What good is something? (Said when the value of the thing referred to is being diminished or ignored.) _Jane’s best friend told us all about Jane’s personal problems. What price friendship? _ Jack simply declared hims
examples: Jane’s best friend told us all about Jane’s personal problems.

*what’s coming to one.monolingual: what one deserves. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give one ~.) _ If you cheat, you’ll get in trouble. You’ll get what’s coming to you. _They gave Billy what was coming to him.
examples: If you cheat, you’ll get in trouble.

what’s cooking?.monolingual: Inf. What is happening?; How are you? _Bob: Hi, Fred! What’s cooking? Fred: How are you doing, Bob? _ Bob: Hi, Fred! What’s cooking? Bill: Nothing. Anything happening with you?
examples: Bob: Hi, Fred! What’s cooking? Bill: Nothing.

what’s done cannot be undone..monolingual: Prov. You cannot change what has already happened. _ Jill: I wish I hadn’t insulted Maria. Jane: What’s done cannot be undone. _Jill soon regretted telling Mike that she loved him, but she knew that what’s done cannot be undone.
examples: Jill: I wish I hadn’t insulted Maria.

what’s done is done..monolingual: Prov. It is final and in the past. _ It’s too late to change it now. What’s done is done. _What’s done is done. The past cannot be altered.
examples: It’s too late to change it now.

what’s eating someone?.monolingual: Inf. Fig. What is bothering someone? _ Tom: Go away! Bob: Gee, Tom, what’s eating you? _ Bill: Tom’s so grouchy lately. What’s eating him? Bob: Beats me!
examples: Bill: Tom’s so grouchy lately.

what’s in a name?.monolingual: Prov. The name of a thing does not matter as much as the quality of the thing. (From Shakespeare’s play, Romeo and Juliet.) _ Sue: I want to buy this pair of jeans. Mother: This other pair is much cheaper. Sue: But it doesn’t have the designer brand
examples: Sue: I want to buy this pair of jeans.

what’s in it for me?.monolingual: Inf. What is the benefit for me in this scheme? _ Bob: Now that plan is just what is needed. Bill: What’s in it for me? What do I get out of it? _ Sue: We signed the Wilson contract yesterday. Mary: That’s great! What’s in it for me?
examples: Bob: Now that plan is just what is needed.

what’s it to you?.monolingual: Inf. Why does it matter to you?; It’s none of your business. (A bit contentious.) _Tom: Where are you going? Jane: What’s it to you? _ Mary: Bill’s pants don’t match his shirt. Jane: Does it matter? What’s it to you?
examples: Mary: Bill’s pants don’t match his shirt.

what’s keeping someone?.monolingual: What is delaying someone? (The someone is replaced by a person’s name or a pronoun.) _ Bob: Wasn’t Mary supposed to be here? Bill: I thought so. Bob: Well, what’s keeping her? Bill: How should I know? _ Bill: I’ve been waiting here for an hour for Sa
examples: Bob: Wasn’t Mary supposed to be here? Bill: I thought so.

what’s new?.monolingual: Inf. What things have happened since we last met? _Mary: Greetings, Jane. What’s new? Jane: Nothing much. _ Bob: What’s new? Tom: Not a whole lot.
examples: Mary: Greetings, Jane.

what’s new with you?.monolingual: Inf. a typical greeting, often a response to What’s new? _ Mary: What’s new with you? Sally: Oh, nothing. What’s new with you? Mary: The same. _Fred: Hi, John! How you doing? John: Great! What’s new with you?
examples: Mary: What’s new with you? Sally: Oh, nothing.

what’s on tap for today?.monolingual: Inf. What is on the schedule for today?; What is going to happen today? (As a beer that is on tap and ready to be served.) _ Tom: Good morning, Fred. Fred: Morning. What’s on tap for today? Tom: Trouble in the morning and difficulty in the afternoon.
examples: Tom: Good morning, Fred.

what’s poppin’?.monolingual: Sl. Hello, what is happening? _ What’s poppin’? Anything new? _ What’s poppin’, G?

what’s that?.monolingual: What did you say? _ Tom: We’re leaving tomorrow. Jane: What’s that? _ What’s that? Did you say “Iowa” or “Idaho”?
examples: Tom: We’re leaving tomorrow.

what’s the catch?.monolingual: Sl. What is the drawback?; It sounds good, but are there any hidden problems? _ Sounds too good to be true. What’s the catch? _ This looks like a good deal. What’s the catch?
examples: Sounds too good to be true.

what’s the damage?.monolingual: Sl. What are the charges?; How much is the bill? _ Bill: That was delicious. Waiter, what’s the damage? Waiter: I’ll get the check, sir. _ Waiter: Your check sir. Tom: Thanks. Bill: What’s the damage, Tom? Let me pay my share. Tom: Nonsense, I’ll get
examples: Bill: That was delicious.

what’s the drill?.monolingual: 1. Inf. What is going on here? _ Bill: I just came in. What’s the drill? Tom: We have to carry all this stuff out to the truck. _ “What’s the drill?” asked Mary. “Why are all these people sitting around like this?”
examples: Bill: I just came in.

what’s the good of something?.monolingual: What is the point of something?; Why bother with something? _ What’s the good of my going at all if I’ll be late? _ There is no need to get there early. What’s the good of that?
examples: There is no need to get there early.

what’s the problem?.monolingual: 1. Lit. What problem are you presenting to me? _ Bill (coming in): I need to talk to you about something. Tom: What’s the problem, Bill? _“What’s the problem?” said Mary, peering at her secretary over her glasses.
examples: Bill (coming in): I need to talk to you about something.

what’s the scoop?.monolingual: Inf. What is the news?; What’s new with you? _ Bob: Did you hear about Tom? Mary: No, what’s the scoop? _ “Hi, you guys!” beamed John’s little brother. “What’s the scoop?”
examples: “Hi, you guys!” beamed John’s little brother.

what’s up?.monolingual: Inf. Hello. What is happening? _ What’s up? How’re you doing? _ Hey, Chuck! What’s up?

what’s up, doc?.monolingual: Cliché What’s happening around here?; What are you doing? _ Your bike’s spread out all over the garage. What’s up, Doc?
examples: Your bike’s spread out all over the garage.

what’s with someone or something?.monolingual: Why is someone or something in that condition?; What’s going on with someone or something? _ Mary: What’s with Tom? He looks depressed. Bill: He broke up with Sally. _“What’s with this stupid coffee maker? It won’t get hot!” groused Alice.
examples: Mary: What’s with Tom? He looks depressed.

what’s wrong?.monolingual: There is something wrong here. What has happened? _ Mary: Oh, good grief! Bill: What’s wrong? Mary: I forgot to feed the cat. _ Sue (crying): Hello, Sally? Sally: Sue, what’s wrong? Sally: Oh, nothing. Tom left me.
examples: Mary: Oh, good grief! Bill: What’s wrong? Mary: I forgot to feed the cat.

what’s your age?.monolingual: Sl. Hello, how are you? _ Tim: What’s your age? Joe: Hey, Tim, what’s going on with you? _ Yo, Sam! What’s your age?

what the deuce?.monolingual: Sl. What has happened?; What? (Deuce is an old word for devil.) _ What the deuce! Who are you? _ What the deuce! Who did this?

what the heck!.monolingual: Inf. It doesn’t matter! (Often with the force of an exclamation.) _ Oh, what the heck! Come on in. It doesn’t matter. _Oh, what the heck! I’ll have another beer. Nobody’s counting.
examples: Oh, what the heck! Come on in.

what was the name again?.monolingual: Please tell me your name again. (More typical of a clerk than of someone just introduced.) _ Clerk: What was the name again? Bill: Bill. _ “What was the name again? I didn’t write it down,” confessed Fred.
examples: Clerk: What was the name again? Bill: Bill.

what with something.monolingual: because of something. _ What with the children being at home and my parents coming to stay, I have too much to do. _The Smiths find it difficult to manage financially, what with Mr. Smith losing his job and Mrs. Smith being too ill to work.
examples: What with the children being at home and my parents coming to stay, I have too much to do.

what would you say if...?.monolingual: an expression introducing a request for an opinion or a judgment. _Bill: What would you say if I ate the last piece of cake? Bob: Go ahead. I don’t care. _ Mary: What would you say if we left a little early? Sally: It’s okay with me.
examples: Bill: What would you say if I ate the last piece of cake? Bob: Go ahead.

whatever turns you on..monolingual: 1. Inf. Whatever pleases or excites you is okay. _ Mary: Do you mind if I buy some of these f lowers? Bill: Whatever turns you on. _ Mary: I just love to hear a raucous saxophone play some smooth jazz. Bob: Whatever turns you on, baby.
examples: Mary: Do you mind if I buy some of these f lowers? Bill: Whatever turns you on.

wheedle someone into something.monolingual: to get someone to agree to do something by begging or flattery. _ She is always trying to wheedle us into coming for a visit. _ You can’t wheedle me into doing that!
examples: She is always trying to wheedle us into coming for a visit.

wheel and deal.monolingual: to take part in clever (but sometimes dishonest or immoral) business deals. _ John loves to wheel and deal in the money markets. _ Jack got tired of all the wheeling and dealing of big business and retired to run a pub in the country.
examples: John loves to wheel and deal in the money markets.

wheel around.monolingual: to turn around quickly; to change direction quickly. _ She wheeled around quickly to face him. _ Suddenly, Roger wheeled around and started chasing Wally.
examples: She wheeled around quickly to face him.

wheel someone or something around†.monolingual: to push or steer around someone or something on wheels. _I had to wheel my great-uncle around all day when we visited the zoo. _ I wheeled around my uncle so he could enjoy the park. _ I wheeled the heavy shopping cart around the grocery store.
examples: I had to wheel my great-uncle around all day when we visited the zoo.

wheel someone or something away†.monolingual: to push away someone or something on wheels. _The nurse wheeled the old man away, into the shelter of the porch. _She wheeled away the old man.
examples: The nurse wheeled the old man away, into the shelter of the porch.

wheel someone or something off†.monolingual: to push or steer someone or something on wheels some distance away. _The nurse wheeled the old man off. _ Karen wheeled off the patient.
examples: The nurse wheeled the old man off.

wheeze something out†.monolingual: to say something, while wheezing; to say something, using a wheeze for a voice. (As if one is out of breath.) _ He was out of breath from running and was only able to wheeze a few words out. _Liz wheezed out a quick hello.
examples: He was out of breath from running and was only able to wheeze a few words out.

when do we eat?.monolingual: What time is the next meal served? (Indicates that the speaker is hungry, but considered impolite.) _Bill: This is a lovely view, and your apartment is great. When do we eat? Mary: We’ve already eaten. Weren’t you just leaving? Bill: I guess I was. _
examples: Bill: This is a lovely view, and your apartment is great.

when it comes to something.monolingual: as for something; speaking about something. _ When it comes to fishing, John is an expert. _When it comes to trouble, Mary really knows how to cause it.
examples: When it comes to fishing, John is an expert.

when least expected.monolingual: when one does not expect something. _ An old car is likely to give you trouble when least expected. _ My pencil usually breaks when least expected.
examples: An old car is likely to give you trouble when least expected.

when one’s ship comes in.monolingual: Fig. when one becomes rich and successful. _ When my ship comes in, we’ll live in one of these huge mansions on the hill, my lass. _ When your ship comes in, Otto, I’ll probably die of amazement!
examples: When my ship comes in, we’ll live in one of these huge mansions on the hill, my lass.

when the chips are down.monolingual: Fig. at the final, critical moment; when things really get difficult. _ When the chips are down, I know that I can depend on Jean to help out. _I knew you would come and help when the chips were down.
examples: When the chips are down, I know that I can depend on Jean to help out.

when the dust settles.monolingual: 1. Lit. when the dust falls out of the air. _ When the dust settles, we will have to begin sweeping it up.
examples: When the dust settles, we will have to begin sweeping it up.

when the time is ripe.monolingual: Fig. at exactly the right time. _ I’ll tell her the good news when the time is ripe. _When the time is ripe, I’ll bring up the subject again.
examples: I’ll tell her the good news when the time is ripe.

where in the world...?.monolingual: Inf. Where? (An intensive form of where. See examples for variations.) _ Where in the world have you been? _ Where in the world did I put my glasses?

where is the restroom?.monolingual: the appropriate way of asking for the toilet in a public place. _ Bob: ’Scuse me. Waiter: Yes, sir. Bob: Where is the restroom? Waiter: To your left, sir. _ Mary: Where is the restroom, please? Clerk: Behind the elevators, ma’am.
examples: Bob: ’Scuse me.

where it’s at.monolingual: Sl. what one is aiming for; what is needed. (This does not refer to a place.) _ Keep on trying. That’s where it’s at! _ Good strong friends. That’s where it’s at.
examples: Keep on trying.

where one is coming from.monolingual: one’s point of view. _I think I know what you mean. I know where you’re coming from. _ Man, you don’t know where I’m coming from! You don’t understand a single word I say.
examples: I think I know what you mean.

where’s the beef?.monolingual: Inf. Where is the substance?; Where is the important content? _That’s really clever and appealing, but where’s the beef ? _ Where’s the beef ? There’s no substance in this proposal.
examples: Where’s the beef ? There’s no substance in this proposal.

where’s the fire?.monolingual: Inf. Where are you going in such a hurry? (Typically said by a police officer after stopping a speeding driver.) _ Officer: Okay, where’s the fire? Mary: Was I going a little fast? _ “Where’s the fire?” Bob called ahead to Sue, who had gotten well ah
examples: “Where’s the fire?” Bob called ahead to Sue, who had gotten well ahead of him in her excitement.

where someone is at.monolingual: Sl. what mental condition someone is in. _ I know where you’re at. I know what you are talking about. _ You said it! I know just where you’re at!
examples: I know where you’re at.

where someone lives.monolingual: Inf. at one’s core; in one’s personal situation. _ That really hits you where you live, doesn’t it? _ Yes, that gets me where I live.
examples: Yes, that gets me where I live.

where someone’s head is at.monolingual: Inf. the state of one’s mental well-being. _ As soon as I figure where my head is at, I’ll be okay. _ He doesn’t know where his head is at.
examples: As soon as I figure where my head is at, I’ll be okay.

where the action is.monolingual: where important things are happening. _ I want to be where the action is. _ Right there in city hall. That’s where the action is.
examples: I want to be where the action is.

where the sun don’t shine.monolingual: Sl. in a dark place, namely the anus. _I don’t care what you do with it. Just put it where the sun don’t shine. _ For all I care you can shove it where the sun don’t shine.
examples: I don’t care what you do with it.

where will i find you?.monolingual: Please give me directions for finding you. (Said when people are arranging a meeting somewhere.) _ Sue: Where will I find you? Bob: I’ll be sitting in the third row somewhere. _ Tom: We’ll get to the farm about noon. Where will we find you? Sally: Pr
examples: Sue: Where will I find you? Bob: I’ll be sitting in the third row somewhere.

whet someone’s appetite.monolingual: Fig. to cause someone to be interested in something and to be eager to have, know, learn, etc., more about it. _ Seeing that film really whetted my sister’s appetite for horror films. She now sees as many as possible. _ My appetite for theater was wh
examples: Seeing that film really whetted my sister’s appetite for horror films.

whether or not.monolingual: either if something is the case or if something is not the case; one way or the other. _ I’ll drive to New York tomorrow whether or not it rains. _ I’m going to the mall whether you come with me or not.
examples: I’ll drive to New York tomorrow whether or not it rains.

*a whiff of something.monolingual: 1. Lit. the smell or odor of something. (*Typically: get ~; catch ~; have ~; take ~; give someone ~.) _ Did you get a whiff of the turkey roasting? Yummy. _ I caught a whiff of something rather unpleasant in the attic. I think there is a dead mouse u
examples: Did you get a whiff of the turkey roasting? Yummy.

whine about someone or something.monolingual: to whimper or complain about someone or something. _ Please don’t whine about Sally. She is sorry she couldn’t come to your party, but it’s not the end of the world. _The dog is whining about its hurt paw.
examples: Please don’t whine about Sally.

whine something out†.monolingual: to say something in a whine; to say something, using a whine for a voice. _ She whined her complaint out so everyone could hear it. _Jake whined out his usual complaints.
examples: She whined her complaint out so everyone could hear it.

whip around.monolingual: 1. to reverse suddenly. (As with the tip of a whip.) _ The rope suddenly whipped around and struck me in the face. _ A branch whipped around and tore my shirt.
examples: The rope suddenly whipped around and struck me in the face.

whip into something.monolingual: Fig. to go quickly into something or some place. _ They whipped into the parking space before I could get there. _I whipped into the store to pick up a few things.
examples: They whipped into the parking space before I could get there.

whip someone into a state.monolingual: Fig. to excite, arouse, or foment someone into some state. (Based on whip someone into doing something.) _The governor’s speech whipped the audience into a frenzy. _ The angry cries from the audience whipped the speaker into a rage.
examples: The governor’s speech whipped the audience into a frenzy.

whip someone into doing something.monolingual: to beat someone into doing something. _ The cruel captain whipped his men into going on with the journey. _ You can’t whip me into betraying my friends.
examples: The cruel captain whipped his men into going on with the journey.

whip someone or something around†.monolingual: to cause someone or something to reverse direction quickly. _ The roller coaster whipped around the riders, right and left, until they were almost sick. _ The sharp turn whipped me around, but I wasn’t hurt.
examples: The roller coaster whipped around the riders, right and left, until they were almost sick.

whip someone or something on†.monolingual: to force someone or something to continue by whipping or beating. _ The rider whipped his horse on, faster and faster. _ The stage coach driver whipped on the team of horses.
examples: The rider whipped his horse on, faster and faster.

whip someone up†.monolingual: to excite or stir up someone. _ Well, you’ve certainly whipped them up with that speech. _Harry whipped up the crowd with a few good jokes.
examples: Well, you’ve certainly whipped them up with that speech.

whip something into something.monolingual: to beat one soft ingredient into another. _ Whip the butter into the egg and make a smooth paste. _ First, you must whip the egg whites into the cream.
examples: Whip the butter into the egg and make a smooth paste.

whip something off†.monolingual: 1. Inf. to do or create something quickly. _ If you need another receipt, I can whip one off in a jiffy. _ She whipped off another set of earrings for the tourist.
examples: If you need another receipt, I can whip one off in a jiffy.

whip something out†.monolingual: 1. Inf. to complete making or working on something quickly. _I think I can whip one out for you very quickly. _ The factory whips out twenty of these every minute.
examples: I think I can whip one out for you very quickly.

whip something up†.monolingual: to prepare, create, or put something together. _ I haven’t written my report yet, but I’ll whip one up before the deadline. _I will whip up the most beautiful arrangement you have ever seen.
examples: I haven’t written my report yet, but I’ll whip one up before the deadline.

whip through something.monolingual: Fig. to work through something very fast. _Do this carefully. Don’t just whip through it. _ She whipped through her homework and went outside to play.
examples: Do this carefully.

a whipping boy.monolingual: Fig. someone who is punished for someone else’s misdeeds. _ The president has turned out to be the whipping boy for his party.
examples: The president has turned out to be the whipping boy for his party.

whirl around.monolingual: to turn around very quickly. _I tapped him on the shoulder and he whirled around to see who it was. _ Todd whirled around and grabbed Max by the wrists.
examples: I tapped him on the shoulder and he whirled around to see who it was.

whirl someone or something around†.monolingual: to turn someone or something around quickly. _ I grabbed him by the shoulder and whirled him around to face me. _I whirled around the book display and found what I wanted.
examples: I grabbed him by the shoulder and whirled him around to face me.

whisk someone around†.monolingual: to move someone around rapidly from place to place. _ I didn’t get much chance to see the city. They just whisked me around. _ We whisked around the visitor from place to place.
examples: I didn’t get much chance to see the city.

whisk someone or something away†.monolingual: to move someone or something out of the way rapidly. _The firemen came and whisked the students away to a safe place. _ The agents whisked away a number of people.
examples: The firemen came and whisked the students away to a safe place.

whisper about someone or something.monolingual: to speak about someone or something in a quiet, breathy voice, as if telling secrets. _ I hope they aren’t whispering about me. _ Everyone is whispering about the incident in the lunchroom.
examples: I hope they aren’t whispering about me.

whisper something around.monolingual: to spread secrets or gossip around. _Now, don’t whisper this around, but Sam is going to run away from home. _ If you whisper this around, you will spoil the surprise.
examples: Now, don’t whisper this around, but Sam is going to run away from home.

whistle at someone or something.monolingual: to indicate approval or disapproval of someone or something by whistling. _The men whistled at the beautiful woman who walked by. _ Everyone whistled at the enormous roast of beef the cook’s assistant carried in.
examples: The men whistled at the beautiful woman who walked by.

whistle for someone or something.monolingual: to summon someone or something by whistling. _I stood on the corner and whistled for a cab, but they all ignored me. _ I whistled for the dog, but it did not appear.
examples: I stood on the corner and whistled for a cab, but they all ignored me.

whistle in the dark.monolingual: Fig. to guess aimlessly; to speculate as to a fact. _Am I close, or am I just whistling in the dark? _ She was whistling in the dark. She has no idea of what’s going on.
examples: She was whistling in the dark.

white elephant.monolingual: something that is large and unwieldy and is either a nuisance or expensive to keep up. _Bob’s fatherin- law has given him an old Rolls Royce, but it’s a real white elephant. He has no place to park it and can’t afford the gas for it. _ Those antique
examples: Bob’s fatherin- law has given him an old Rolls Royce, but it’s a real white elephant.

white knuckle something.monolingual: to survive something threatening through strained endurance, that is to say, holding on tight. _ The f light from New York was terrible. We had to white knuckle the entire f light.
examples: The f light from New York was terrible.

whittle at something.monolingual: to cut or carve at something. _ He just sat there, whittling at a chunk of wood. _I am not carving anything, I am just whittling at some wood.
examples: He just sat there, whittling at a chunk of wood.

whittle someone down to size.monolingual: Fig. to reduce someone’s ego; to cause someone to have better, more respectful behavior. (Fig. on whittle something down (to size).) _ After a few days at camp, the counselors had whittled young Walter down to size. _ It took some doing, but they whi
examples: After a few days at camp, the counselors had whittled young Walter down to size.

whittle something away†.monolingual: to cut or carve something away. _The carver whittled the wood away until only a small figure was left. _ He whittled away the wood.
examples: The carver whittled the wood away until only a small figure was left.

whittle something out of something.monolingual: to carve something out of something. _ The young man whittled a small boat out of wood. _ Can you whittle an elephant out of this chunk of wood?
examples: The young man whittled a small boat out of wood.

whiz past someone or something.monolingual: to move or travel past someone or something at a high speed. _ The train whizzed past one little town after another. _I whizzed past Chuck because I did not recognize him.
examples: The train whizzed past one little town after another.

who cares?.monolingual: Does anyone really care?; It is of no consequence. _ John: I have some advice for you. It will make things easier for you. Bob: Who cares? John: You might. _ Sue: You missed a spot shaving. Fred: Who cares?
examples: John: I have some advice for you.

who is this?.monolingual: Who is making this telephone call?; Who is on the other end of this telephone line? _ Tom (answering the phone): Hello? Fred: Hello. Do you have any fresh turkeys? Tom: Who is this? Fred: Isn’t this the Harrison Poultry Shop? Tom: No. Fred: I guess I
examples: Tom (answering the phone): Hello? Fred: Hello.

who knows?.monolingual: Who knows the answer to that question? _ Tom: When will this train get in? Rachel: Who knows? _ Andy: Why can’t someone put this stuff away? Rachel: Who knows? Why don’t you put it away?

who’s your friend?.monolingual: Sl. Who is that following along behind you? _John: Hi, Tom. Who’s your friend? Tom: Oh, this is my little brother, Willie. John: Hi, Willie. _ Looking at the little dog almost glued to Bob’s pants cuff, Sally asked, “Who’s your friend?”
examples: John: Hi, Tom. Who’s your friend? Tom: Oh, this is my little brother, Willie.

who was it?.monolingual: Who called on the telephone or who was at the door? (Assumes that the caller is not waiting on the telephone or at the door.) _ Sue (as Mary hangs up the telephone): Who was it? Mary: None of your business. _ Bill (as he leaves the door): What a pest
examples: Sue (as Mary hangs up the telephone): Who was it? Mary: None of your business.

whoa, nellie!.monolingual: Rur. Wait! Stop! _ Tom: When I get that money, I’m gonna get me my own place, and then you and I can get married, and— Jane: Whoa, Nellie! When did I say I was going to marry you? _ Whoa, Nellie! Did you measure them boards before you started cuttin’

whole bag of tricks.monolingual: Fig. everything; every possibility, argument, or technique. _ Well now. I’ve used my whole bag of tricks, and we still haven’t solved this. _ It may take my whole bag of tricks to do it, but I’ll try.
examples: Well now. I’ve used my whole bag of tricks, and we still haven’t solved this.

the whole enchilada.monolingual: Inf. the whole thing; everything. (From Spanish.) _Nobody, but nobody, ever gets the whole enchilada. _ Richard wants the whole enchilada.
examples: Nobody, but nobody, ever gets the whole enchilada.

the whole kit and caboodle.monolingual: Inf. a group of pieces of equipment or belongings. (The word caboodle is used only in this expression.) _ When I bought Bob’s motorhome, I got furniture, refrigerator, and linen—the whole kit and caboodle. _ The salesman managed to sell John the whol
examples: When I bought Bob’s motorhome, I got furniture, refrigerator, and linen—the whole kit and caboodle.

the whole nine yards.monolingual: Sl. the entire amount; everything, as far as possible. _For you I’ll go the whole nine yards. _ You’re worth the whole nine yards.
examples: For you I’ll go the whole nine yards.

a whole nother thing.monolingual: Rur. a completely different matter. (Often “corrected” to a whole other thing. The word nother is a shortening of another.) _ Borrowing! That’s a whole nother thing! I thought you said stealing!

the whole shebang.monolingual: everything; the whole thing. _ Mary’s all set to give a fancy dinner party. She’s got a fine tablecloth, good crystal, and silverware, the whole shebang. _ How much do you want for the whole shebang?
examples: Mary’s all set to give a fancy dinner party.

the whole wide world.monolingual: Fig. everywhere; everywhere and everything. _ It’s the best in the whole wide world. _ I’ve searched the whole wide world for just the right hat.
examples: It’s the best in the whole wide world.

the whole works.monolingual: everything; the complete amount. _ I cashed my paycheck and lost the whole works playing the ponies.
examples: I cashed my paycheck and lost the whole works playing the ponies.

whoop it up.monolingual: to celebrate, especially with cheers and whoops. _It was a very noisy party. Everyone was whooping it up well past midnight. _ The campaign workers whooped it up for their candidate. _ I can’t get out there and whoop it up for something I don’t belie
examples: It was a very noisy party.

why don’t you?.monolingual: a question tag that is put onto the end of a command. _ Andy: Move aside, why don’t you? Bob: Okay. Sorry. I didn’t know I was in the way. _ “Just keep bugging me, why don’t you?” threatened Wally. _Andy: Try it again, why don’t you? Sue: I hope I ge
examples: Andy: Move aside, why don’t you? Bob: Okay.

why not?.monolingual: 1. Lit. Please explain your negative answer. _ Mother: No, you can’t. Mary: Why not? _Sue: Could I have another piece of cake? Mary: No. Sue: Why not? Mary: I want it.
examples: Mother: No, you can’t.

*wide of the mark.monolingual: 1. Lit. far from the target. (*Typically: be ~; fall ~.) _Tom’s shot was wide of the mark. _ The pitch was quite fast but wide of the mark. _ The arrow fell wide of the mark.
examples: Tom’s shot was wide of the mark.

wide open.monolingual: 1. as fast as possible; at full throttle. _ I was driving along wide open when I became aware of a f lashing red light. _ It was wide open and still wouldn’t do better than eighty.
examples: I was driving along wide open when I became aware of a f lashing red light.

wig out.monolingual: Sl. to become intoxicated. _ One more drink and Wally will wig out. _This guy has wigged out. Get him out of here.
examples: One more drink and Wally will wig out.

wiggle out of something.monolingual: 1. Lit to get out of something or some place; to squirm out of something or some place. _ The kitten was able to wiggle out of the cage in which it had been put. _ The squirrel wiggled out of the trap we caught it in.
examples: The kitten was able to wiggle out of the cage in which it had been put.

wild about someone or something.monolingual: very excited about someone or something. _I’m just wild about comedies. _John is wild about antique cars.
examples: I’m just wild about comedies.

wild and woolly.monolingual: Inf. exciting. _ Things get a little wild and woolly on a Friday evening at Wally’s place. _The ride home was a little wild and woolly.
examples: Things get a little wild and woolly on a Friday evening at Wally’s place.

a wild-goose chase.monolingual: a worthless hunt or chase; a futile pursuit. _ I wasted all afternoon on a wild-goose chase. _ John was angry because he was sent out on a wild-goose chase.
examples: I wasted all afternoon on a wild-goose chase.

will come of something.monolingual: will result from something. _ I don’t think that much will come of this. _ Nothing at all will come of it.
examples: I don’t think that much will come of this.

will do..monolingual: Inf. I will do it. _Will do. I’ll get right on it. _Fix the stuck window? Will do.
examples: Will do. I’ll get right on it.

will i see you again?.monolingual: a question asked toward the end of a date implying that further dating would please the speaker. (This question leaves it open to the other party to confirm that the interest is mutual by requesting a further date. Compare this with Can I see you aga
examples: Tom: I had a wonderful time tonight, Mary.

will something away†.monolingual: to give something away in a will. _ The old man simply willed all his money away. He said he wouldn’t need it when he was dead. _She had willed away all of her treasures to her grandchildren.
examples: The old man simply willed all his money away.

will stop at nothing.monolingual: Cliché will do everything possible (to accomplish something); will be unscrupulous. _ Bill would stop at nothing to get his way. _ Bob is completely determined to get promoted. He’ll stop at nothing.
examples: Bill would stop at nothing to get his way.

win at something.monolingual: to triumph at some competition. _ Will I ever be able to win at golf ? _ She always wins at poker.
examples: She always wins at poker.

win by a nose.monolingual: Fig. to win by the slightest amount of difference. (Can be literal in horses races.) _I ran the fastest race I could, but I only won by a nose. _Sally won the race, but she only won by a nose.
examples: I ran the fastest race I could, but I only won by a nose.

win something at something.monolingual: to win a prize in some sort of competition. _ I won this silly doll at the ring-toss game. _ Did you win anything at the fair?
examples: I won this silly doll at the ring-toss game.

win through something.monolingual: to succeed by a certain method or procedure. _ Winning is no good if you have to win through dishonesty. _ Sally won through her own hard work.
examples: Winning is no good if you have to win through dishonesty.

wince at something.monolingual: to shrink back because of something, such as pain. _ She winced at the pain but did not cry out. _After he had just winced at the pain for a while, he finally screamed.
examples: She winced at the pain but did not cry out.

wind around.monolingual: [for something, such as a road] to make a turn or turns around. _ The road wound around and ended up at the lake. _ The path wound around and came to a stop at the cabin door.
examples: The road wound around and ended up at the lake.

wind around someone or something.monolingual: to twist or coil around someone or something. _ The python wound around the rabbit, suffocating it. _ The vines wound around the gatepost.
examples: The python wound around the rabbit, suffocating it.

wind back.monolingual: [for something, such as a road] to turn so that it heads in the direction from whence it came. _The road we got lost on wound back and we were not able to reach the lake on time. _ When we were lost, we found a stream in the woods, but it wound back
examples: The road we got lost on wound back and we were not able to reach the lake on time.

wind down.monolingual: to start running or operating slower. _Things will begin to wind down at the end of the summer. _ As things wind down, life will be a lot easier. _ The clock wound down and finally stopped.
examples: Things will begin to wind down at the end of the summer.

wind into something.monolingual: to coil up into something. _ The snake wound into a tight coil. _ The rubber bands wound into a knot and were worthless.
examples: The snake wound into a tight coil.

wind someone up.monolingual: 1. Inf. Fig. to get someone excited. _ That kind of music really winds me up!
examples: That kind of music really winds me up! 2.

wind something around something.monolingual: to twist or coil something around something. _ Wind this cloth around your hand to stop the bleeding. _ Wind the string around this stick so it won’t get all tangled up.
examples: Wind this cloth around your hand to stop the bleeding.

wind something down†.monolingual: to slow something down; to make something less hectic. _ Let’s wind this party down and try to get people to go home. It’s really late. _ We tried to wind down the party, but it kept running.
examples: Let’s wind this party down and try to get people to go home.

wind something in†.monolingual: to reel something in. _ She wound in the rope that was tied to the anchor. _ Liz wound in the cable that raised the awning.
examples: She wound in the rope that was tied to the anchor.

wind something off†.monolingual: to unreel or unwind something. _He wound the rope off, little by little, until he had as much as he needed. _ Karen wound off as much as she needed.
examples: He wound the rope off, little by little, until he had as much as he needed.

wind something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to tighten the spring in something, such as a watch or a clock. _Please wind your watch up now—before it runs down. _Wind up your watch before you forget.
examples: Please wind your watch up now—before it runs down.

wind through something.monolingual: [for a pathway] to twist or turn through an area. _ The trail wound through the jungle, avoiding the densest places. _ A path wound through the woods, leading us to the main road.
examples: The trail wound through the jungle, avoiding the densest places.

wind up somehow.monolingual: to end up in some fashion. _ I don’t want to wind up broke and depressed. _ You don’t want to wind up like Ted, do you?
examples: I don’t want to wind up broke and depressed.

a window of opportunity.monolingual: Fig. a brief time period in which an opportunity exists. _ This afternoon, I had a brief window of opportunity when I could discuss this with the boss, but she wasn’t receptive.
examples: This afternoon, I had a brief window of opportunity when I could discuss this with the boss, but she wasn’t receptive.

wine and dine someone.monolingual: to treat someone to an expensive meal of the type that includes fine wines; to entertain someone lavishly. _The lobbyists wined and dined the senators one by one in order to inf luence them. _ We were wined and dined every night and given the best ho
examples: The lobbyists wined and dined the senators one by one in order to inf luence them.

wing it.monolingual: to improvise; to do something extemporaneously. _I lost my lecture notes, so I had to wing it. _Don’t worry. Just go out there and wing it.
examples: I lost my lecture notes, so I had to wing it.

wink at someone.monolingual: to close one eye at a person as a sign of friendliness or flirtation. _She winked at him and he was shocked. _ I hope she winks at me again.
examples: She winked at him and he was shocked.

wink at something.monolingual: to pretend not to see something; to condone something wrong. _ The police officer winked at my failure to make a complete stop. _I cannot wink at blatant infractions of the law!
examples: The police officer winked at my failure to make a complete stop.

wink something away†.monolingual: to blink the eyes to try to clear them of tears, dirt, etc. _ He looked up at me and tried to wink away his tears, but he was just too upset. _ Jane winked away her tears.
examples: He looked up at me and tried to wink away his tears, but he was just too upset.

winner take all.monolingual: a situation where the one who defeats others takes all the spoils of the conflict. _ The contest was a case of winner take all. There was no second place or runner-up.
examples: The contest was a case of winner take all.

wipe it off!.monolingual: Inf. Wipe that smile off your face! _ It’s not funny. Wipe it off! _ Wipe it off! Nothing funny here, soldier.
examples: It’s not funny.

wipe out.monolingual: 1. Inf. to crash. _ I wiped out on the curve. _ The car wiped out on the curve.
examples: I wiped out on the curve.

wipe someone or something off†.monolingual: to clean something off someone or something by wiping. _ She wiped the baby off and put clean clothes on him. _ Please wipe off your shoes. _ John fell in the mud and Sam wiped him off.
examples: She wiped the baby off and put clean clothes on him.

wipe someone out†.monolingual: 1. Sl. to kill someone. _Max intended to wipe Lefty’s gang out. _ Lefty wiped out Max’s gang.
examples: Max intended to wipe Lefty’s gang out.

wipe something away†.monolingual: to clean or mop something away. _Wipe all this mud away and scrub the f loor clean. _Jake wiped away the mud.
examples: Wipe all this mud away and scrub the f loor clean.

wipe something down†.monolingual: to rub or mop something down. _ Wipe the counter down and keep it clean! _ Don will wipe down the counter.
examples: Don will wipe down the counter.

wipe something off†.monolingual: 1. to remove something (from something else) by wiping or rubbing. _ There is mud on your shirt. Please wipe it off. _I must wipe off the ketchup from my shirt.
examples: There is mud on your shirt.

wipe something out†.monolingual: Sl. to use up all of something. _ I wiped the cookies out—not all at once, of course. _ Who wiped out the strawberry preserves?
examples: I wiped the cookies out—not all at once, of course.

wipe something up†.monolingual: 1. to clean something up by wiping. _Please wipe that spilled milk up. _Jim wiped up the spill.
examples: Please wipe that spilled milk up.

wire for something.monolingual: to send for something by telegram. _ I wired for money, but it hasn’t come yet. _ I will have to wire for further advice.
examples: I wired for money, but it hasn’t come yet.

wire something back to someone.monolingual: to send something, such as a reply or money, back to someone by telegram. _ Please wire your answer back to me by tomorrow. _ The reply wasn’t wired back in time.
examples: Please wire your answer back to me by tomorrow.

wire something in†.monolingual: to send something into a central point by telegram. _ I can’t mail my story to my editor in time, so I will have to wire it in. _ I’ve got to wire in this story.
examples: I can’t mail my story to my editor in time, so I will have to wire it in.

wire something together.monolingual: to bind the pieces of something together with wire; to bind things together with wire. _ I wired the car’s exhaust pipe together, hoping to get a few more miles out of it. _I will wire it together to keep it from dragging on the roadway.
examples: I wired the car’s exhaust pipe together, hoping to get a few more miles out of it.

wire something up†.monolingual: 1. to repair or reattach something with wire, especially something electrical. _I will wire this light fixture up and it will work like new. _ As soon as I wire up this again, it will work very well.
examples: I will wire this light fixture up and it will work like new.

wired into someone or something.monolingual: Sl. closely concerned with someone or something; really involved with someone or something. _ Mary is really wired into classical music. _ Sam and Martha are totally wired into one another.
examples: Mary is really wired into classical music.

*wise to someone or something.monolingual: fully aware of someone or something. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; put someone ~.) _ The cops are wise to the plan.
examples: The cops are wise to the plan.

wish for someone or something.monolingual: to wish to have someone or something. _ She spent most of her life wishing for Prince Charming, who would come along and sweep her off her feet. _ She still wishes for escape.
examples: She spent most of her life wishing for Prince Charming, who would come along and sweep her off her feet.

wish list.monolingual: a list of things one wishes to have. _ I put a new car at the top of my wish list. _I have a DVD player on my wish list.
examples: I put a new car at the top of my wish list.

wish someone or something away†.monolingual: to wish that someone or something would go away. _ You can’t just wish him away. You’ll have to ask him to leave! _ Don’t try to wish away the difficulties of your life.
examples: You can’t just wish him away.

wishful thinking.monolingual: believing that something is true or that something will happen just because one wishes that it were true or would happen. _ Hoping for a car as a birthday present is just wishful thinking. Your parents can’t afford it. _Mary thinks that she is going
examples: Hoping for a car as a birthday present is just wishful thinking.

with a heavy heart.monolingual: Cliché sadly. _ With a heavy heart, she said good-bye. _We left our summer cottage on the last day with a heavy heart.
examples: With a heavy heart, she said good-bye.

with a vengeance.monolingual: Cliché with determination and eagerness. _ The angry soldier attacked the enemy with a vengeance. _ Bill ate all his dinner and gobbled up his dessert with a vengeance.
examples: The angry soldier attacked the enemy with a vengeance.

with a will.monolingual: with determination and enthusiasm. _ The children worked with a will to finish the project on time. _ The workers set about manufacturing the new products with a will.
examples: The children worked with a will to finish the project on time.

with all the trimmings.monolingual: with all the extra things, especially with food. _ We had a lovely Thanksgiving dinner with all the trimmings. _I look forward to roast turkey with all the trimmings.
examples: We had a lovely Thanksgiving dinner with all the trimmings.

with bated breath.monolingual: Cliché while holding one’s breath. _ We stood there with bated breath while the man hung on the side of the bridge. _ They listened with bated breath for the announcement about the winner.
examples: We stood there with bated breath while the man hung on the side of the bridge.

*with child.monolingual: Euph. pregnant. (Biblical. *Typically: be ~; get a woman ~.) _The first thing he did after he got married was to get his wife with child. _She deliberately set out to get herself with child, as they say.
examples: The first thing he did after he got married was to get his wife with child.

with each passing day.monolingual: as days pass, one by one; day by day. _ Things grow more expensive with each passing day. _ We are all growing older with each passing day.
examples: Things grow more expensive with each passing day.

with ease.monolingual: without effort. _ The smart student passed the test with ease. _ The gymnast did a back f lip with ease.
examples: The smart student passed the test with ease.

with flying colors.monolingual: Cliché easily and excellently. _ John passed his geometry test with f lying colors. _ Sally qualified for the race with f lying colors.
examples: John passed his geometry test with f lying colors.

with impunity.monolingual: without risk of punishment; with immunity from the negative consequences of an act; while being exempt from punishment. _ The diplomat parked in illegal parking spaces with impunity. _ Bob used his brother’s property with impunity.
examples: The diplomat parked in illegal parking spaces with impunity.

with it.monolingual: 1. Inf. alert and knowledgeable. _ Jane isn’t making any sense. She’s not really with it tonight. _ Jean’s mother is not really with it anymore. She’s going senile. _ Peter’s not with it yet. He’s only just come round from the anesthetic.
examples: Jane isn’t making any sense.

with my blessing.monolingual: a phrase expressing consent or agreement; yes. _Bob: Can I take this old coat down to the rummage sale? Sue: With my blessing. _ Mary: Shall I drive Uncle Tom to the airport a few hours early? Sue: Oh, yes! With my blessing!
examples: Bob: Can I take this old coat down to the rummage sale? Sue: With my blessing.

with or without?.monolingual: Do you wish your tea or coffee to be with or without sugar or with or without milk? _ How do you like your tea? With or without? _Do you drink your coffee with or without?

with pleasure..monolingual: a phrase indicating eager consent to do something. _Fred: Would you please take this note over to the woman in the red dress? Waiter: With pleasure, sir. _ Sue: Would you kindly bring in the champagne now? Jane: With pleasure.
examples: Fred: Would you please take this note over to the woman in the red dress? Waiter: With pleasure, sir.

with relish.monolingual: with pleasure or enjoyment. _John put on this new coat with great relish. _ We accepted the offer to use their beach house with relish.
examples: John put on this new coat with great relish.

with the naked eye.monolingual: with eyes that are not aided by telescopes, microscopes, or binoculars. _ The moon is quite visible with the naked eye. _ Bacteria are too small to be seen with the naked eye.
examples: The moon is quite visible with the naked eye.

withdraw from something.monolingual: 1. to depart from something physically. _ I withdrew from the smoky room and ran to the open window to get some air. _ I withdrew from the unpleasant-looking cafe and looked for something more to my liking.
examples: I withdrew from the smoky room and ran to the open window to get some air.

withdraw into oneself.monolingual: to become introverted; to concern oneself with one’s inner thoughts. _ After a few years of being ignored, she withdrew into herself. _ I have to struggle to keep from withdrawing into myself.
examples: After a few years of being ignored, she withdrew into herself.

withdraw into something.monolingual: to pull back into something. _ The turtle withdrew into its shell. _ The mouse withdrew into its hole.
examples: The turtle withdrew into its shell.

withdraw someone from something.monolingual: 1. to pull someone out of something physically. _She withdrew the child from the water just in time. _ I had to withdraw my child from the kindergarten room. He was having such a good time, he wouldn’t leave on his own.
examples: She withdrew the child from the water just in time.

withdraw something into something.monolingual: to pull something back into something. _ The turtle withdrew its head into its shell. _ It then withdrew its feet into the shell also.
examples: The turtle withdrew its head into its shell.

wither away.monolingual: to shrivel up; to shrink up. _Soon, the wart withered away. _ Many of our roses withered away in the hot sun.
examples: Soon, the wart withered away.

wither up.monolingual: to shrivel up. _ It was so hot that the leaves of the trees withered up.
examples: It was so hot that the leaves of the trees withered up.

*within one’s grasp.monolingual: 1. Lit. where one can grasp something with one’s hand. (*Typically: be ~; get ~; get something ~.) _The rope was within his grasp, but he was too weak to reach for it.
examples: The rope was within his grasp, but he was too weak to reach for it.

*within one’s rights.monolingual: acting legally in one’s own interest. (*Typically: be ~; act ~.) _ I know I am within my rights when I make this request. _ You are not within your rights!
examples: I know I am within my rights when I make this request.

within reason.monolingual: reasonable; reasonably. _You can do anything you want within reason. _I’ll pay any sum you ask— within reason.
examples: You can do anything you want within reason.

within walking distance.monolingual: close enough to walk to. _ Is the train station within walking distance? _ My office is within walking distance from here.
examples: My office is within walking distance from here.

without a doubt.monolingual: a phrase expressing certainty or agreement; yes. _ John: This cheese is as hard as a rock. It must have been in the fridge for weeks. Fred: Without a doubt. _ Mary: Taxes will surely go up before I retire. Jane: Without a doubt!
examples: John: This cheese is as hard as a rock.

without a hitch.monolingual: Fig. with no problem(s). _ Everything went off without a hitch. _ We hoped the job would go off without a hitch.
examples: Everything went off without a hitch.

without batting an eye.monolingual: Lit. Fig. without showing alarm or response; without blinking an eye. _ I knew I had insulted her, and she turned to me and asked me to leave without batting an eye. _ Right in the middle of the speech—without batting an eye—the speaker walked off th
examples: I knew I had insulted her, and she turned to me and asked me to leave without batting an eye.

without fail.monolingual: for certain; absolutely. _I’ll be there at noon without fail. _ The plane leaves on time every day without fail.
examples: I’ll be there at noon without fail.

without further ado.monolingual: Cliché without further talk. (An overworked phrase usually heard in public announcements.) _ And without further ado, I would like to introduce Mr. Bill Franklin! _ The time has come to leave, so without further ado, good evening and good-bye.
examples: And without further ado, I would like to introduce Mr.

without half trying.monolingual: Rur. effortlessly. _He was so strong, he could bend an iron bar without half trying. _ I wish I had his ability to cook. He makes the most delicious dishes without half trying.
examples: He was so strong, he could bend an iron bar without half trying.

without missing a beat.monolingual: Lit. Fig. without pausing for any potential interruption. _He kept right on giving his speech without missing a beat, despite the interruptions. _ She went right on drumming without missing a beat.
examples: He kept right on giving his speech without missing a beat, despite the interruptions.

without question.monolingual: absolutely; certainly. _ She agreed to help without question. _ She said, “I stand ready to support you without question.”
examples: She agreed to help without question.

without rhyme or reason.monolingual: Cliché without purpose, order, or reason. (See variations in the examples. Fixed order.) _The teacher said my report was disorganized. My paragraphs seemed to be without rhyme or reason. _Everything you do seems to be without rhyme or reason.
examples: The teacher said my report was disorganized.

witness for someone or something.monolingual: to serve as a witness for some person or some deed. _ They could find no one to witness for the accused person. _ The police found someone to witness for the hour of the crime.
examples: They could find no one to witness for the accused person.

witness to something.monolingual: to serve as a witness to some act or deed. _ I was witness to the beating. _ We were not witness to any of the activities you have described.
examples: I was witness to the beating.

woe is me!.monolingual: I am unfortunate.; I am unhappy. (Usually humorous.) _ Woe is me! I have to work when the rest of the office staff is off. _ Woe is me. I have the flu and my friends have gone to a party.
examples: Woe is me! I have to work when the rest of the office staff is off.

a wolf in sheep’s clothing.monolingual: Fig. a dangerous person pretending to be harmless. _ Carla thought the handsome stranger was gentle and kind, but Susan suspected he was a wolf in sheep’s clothing. _ Mimi: Why shouldn’t I go out with David? He’s the nicest man I’ve ever met. Alan: H
examples: Carla thought the handsome stranger was gentle and kind, but Susan suspected he was a wolf in sheep’s clothing.

wolf something down†.monolingual: Fig. to eat something very rapidly and in very large pieces. (As a wolf might eat.) _ Don’t wolf your food down! _ Liz would never wolf down her food.
examples: Liz would never wolf down her food.

woman of ill repute.monolingual: Euph. a prostitute. _ His favorite companion was a woman of ill repute. _ If you can’t be faithful to your husband, you’re no better than a woman of ill repute.
examples: His favorite companion was a woman of ill repute.

wonder about someone or something.monolingual: to be curious or in doubt about someone or something. _ I wonder about Carl and what he is up to. _Sometimes I wonder about life on other planets. _ Jenny’s performance record made me wonder about her chances for success.
examples: I wonder about Carl and what he is up to.

wonder at someone or something.monolingual: to be amazed at or in awe of someone or something. (Stilted.) _We all wondered at Lee and the way he kept his spirits up. _ The people wondered at the bright light that lit up the sky.
examples: We all wondered at Lee and the way he kept his spirits up.

won’t hold water.monolingual: to be inadequate, insubstantial, or illconceived. _ Sorry, your ideas won’t hold water. Nice try, though. _The prosecution’s case wouldn’t hold water, so the defendant was released.
examples: Sorry, your ideas won’t hold water.

won’t you come in?.monolingual: the standard phrase used to invite someone into one’s home or office. _Bill: Won’t you come in? Mary: I hope I’m not early. _ Tom stood in the doorway of Mr. Franklin’s office for a moment. “Won’t you come in?” said Mr. Franklin without looking up.
examples: Bill: Won’t you come in? Mary: I hope I’m not early.

word by word.monolingual: one word at a time. _ We examined the contract word by word to make sure everything was the way we wanted. _We compared the stories word by word to see what made them different.
examples: We examined the contract word by word to make sure everything was the way we wanted.

word for word.monolingual: in the exact words; verbatim. _ I memorized the speech, word for word. _ I can’t recall word for word what she told us.
examples: I memorized the speech, word for word.

a word to the wise.monolingual: a good piece of advice; a word of wisdom. _ If I can give you a word to the wise, I would suggest going to the courthouse about an hour before your trial. _Here is a word to the wise. Keep your eyes open and your mouth shut.
examples: If I can give you a word to the wise, I would suggest going to the courthouse about an hour before your trial.

work against someone or something.monolingual: 1. [for someone] to struggle against someone or something. _ She worked hard against the passage of the law. _Dave worked against Betty.
examples: She worked hard against the passage of the law.

work among someone or something.monolingual: to do one’s work among some people or things. _ I wanted to work among the Indians, but I set up my medical practice in the inner city. _ I want to get a job in forestry and work among the trees.
examples: I wanted to work among the Indians, but I set up my medical practice in the inner city.

work around someone or something.monolingual: to manage to do one’s work while avoiding someone or something. _He is being a problem, but he will have to leave pretty soon. You’ll just have to work around him for now. _ You have to work around the piano. It is too heavy to move.
examples: He is being a problem, but he will have to leave pretty soon.

work as something.monolingual: to work in the capacity of something. _ I worked as a waiter for a year when I was in college. _ I will work as a stockbroker for a while, and then move on to something else.
examples: I worked as a waiter for a year when I was in college.

work at something.monolingual: 1. to work in a particular trade or craft. _ He works at carpentry when he has the time. _ Julie works at editing for a living.
examples: He works at carpentry when he has the time.

work for someone.monolingual: 1. to be employed by someone. _ She works for Scott Wallace. _Who do you work for?
examples: She works for Scott Wallace.

work for something.monolingual: 1. to work for a group, company, etc. _ Everyone at the picnic works for the same employer. _ We work for the telephone company.
examples: Everyone at the picnic works for the same employer.

work itself out.monolingual: [for a problem] to solve itself. _ Eventually, all the problems worked themselves out without any help from us. _ This will work itself out. Don’t worry.
examples: Eventually, all the problems worked themselves out without any help from us.

work of art.monolingual: 1. Lit. a piece of art. _She purchased a lovely work of art for her living room.
examples: She purchased a lovely work of art for her living room.

work on someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a physician] to treat someone; [for a surgeon] to operate on someone. _ The doctor is still working on your uncle. There is no news yet. _ They are still working on the accident victims.
examples: The doctor is still working on your uncle.

work on something.monolingual: to repair, build, or adjust something. _The carpenter worked on the fence for three hours. _Bill is out working on his car engine.
examples: The carpenter worked on the fence for three hours.

work one’s way along something.monolingual: to move or labor alongside something or a route. _ She worked her way along the ledge and finally came to a wide space where she could relax. _ They worked themselves along the jungle path, chopping and cutting as they went.
examples: She worked her way along the ledge and finally came to a wide space where she could relax.

work oneself up.monolingual: to allow oneself to become emotionally upset. _ Todd worked himself up, and I thought he would scream. _Don’t work yourself up over Sally. She’s not worth it.
examples: Todd worked himself up, and I thought he would scream.

work oneself up into something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to struggle to raise oneself upward into something or some place. _I worked myself up into the top of the tree. _I worked myself up into the rafters of the barn and couldn’t get down.
examples: I worked myself up into the top of the tree.

work out.monolingual: 1. [for something] to turn out all right in the end. _ Don’t worry. Everything will work out. _ This will work out. Don’t worry.
examples: Don’t worry. Everything will work out.

work out for the best.monolingual: [for a bad situation] to turn out all right in the end. _ Don’t worry. Everything will work out for the best. _ I think that nothing ever works out for the best.
examples: Don’t worry. Everything will work out for the best.

work someone or something over†.monolingual: to give someone or something a thorough examination or treatment. _ The doctor really worked me over but couldn’t find anything wrong. _ They worked over the patient but found nothing.
examples: The doctor really worked me over but couldn’t find anything wrong.

work someone over†.monolingual: 1. to threaten, intimidate, or beat someone. _Walt threatened to work Sam over. _Max had worked over Sam, and Sam knew that this was no idle threat.
examples: Walt threatened to work Sam over.

work someone up†.monolingual: to get someone ready for something, especially medical treatment. _The staff worked up three patients for surgery that morning. _ The doctor told the nurse to work Mr. Franklin up for surgery.
examples: The staff worked up three patients for surgery that morning.

work something down†.monolingual: to lower or reduce something, especially an amount of money. _Over a few months, they worked the price down, and the house soon was sold. _They worked down the price so much that the house was a steal.
examples: Over a few months, they worked the price down, and the house soon was sold.

work something off†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to get rid of anger, anxiety, or energy by doing physical activity. _ I was so mad! I went out and played basketball to work my anger off. _He works off nervousness by knitting.
examples: I was so mad! I went out and played basketball to work my anger off.

work something over†.monolingual: to rework something. _ He saved the play by working the second act over. _Would you work over this report and see if you can improve it?
examples: He saved the play by working the second act over.

work something under something.monolingual: to manipulate something beneath something. _ She worked the knife blade under the window and tried to pry the window up. _ Work the envelope under the office door. She will find it when she opens the door in the morning.
examples: She worked the knife blade under the window and tried to pry the window up.

work something up†.monolingual: to prepare something, perhaps on short notice. _There are some special clients coming in this weekend. We need to make a presentation. Do you think you can work something up by then? _I will work up something for this weekend.
examples: There are some special clients coming in this weekend.

work something up† into something.monolingual: to develop something into something. _ I will work this story up into a screenplay in a few months. _ I can work up this idea into a good novel.
examples: I will work this story up into a screenplay in a few months.

work things out.monolingual: to improve one’s state gradually by solving a series of problems. _If we sit down and talk this over, I am sure we can work things out.
examples: If we sit down and talk this over, I am sure we can work things out.

work through channels.monolingual: Fig. to try to get something done by going through the proper procedures and persons. _ You can’t accomplish anything around here if you don’t work through channels. _ I tried working through channels, but it takes too long. This is an emergency.
examples: You can’t accomplish anything around here if you don’t work through channels.

work together.monolingual: [for people or things] to cooperate or function together. _Come now! Let’s all work together and get this done on time! _ We will work together on this and enjoy it more.
examples: We will work together on this and enjoy it more.

work toward something.monolingual: 1. to progress toward a goal, such as a promotion. _ He was working toward a position with the new company. _ She was working toward a law degree when the accident happened.
examples: He was working toward a position with the new company.

work under someone.monolingual: to have one’s work supervised by someone. _ I work under Michael, who is head of the department. _ Who do you work under?
examples: I work under Michael, who is head of the department.

work under something.monolingual: to work underneath something. _ I have to work under the car for a while. Please don’t start it. _ The plumber had to work under the house to fix the pipes.
examples: I have to work under the car for a while.

work up to something.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to build or progress to something. (Usually concerning the weather.) _ The sky is working up to some kind of storm. _ The weather is working up to something severe.
examples: The sky is working up to some kind of storm.

work with someone or something.monolingual: to manipulate or work on someone or something. _ Let me work with him for a while. I’ll convince him. _ I want to work with this engine and see if I can get it started.
examples: Let me work with him for a while.

work with something.monolingual: to do work with some tool or instrument. _ She is working with a chisel now. In a minute she will switch to a tiny knife. _Do you know how to work with a voltmeter?
examples: She is working with a chisel now.

a working stiff.monolingual: Fig. someone who works, especially in a nonmanagement position. (Originally and typically referring to males.) _But does the working stiff really care about all this economic stuff ? _ All the working stiffs want is a raise.
examples: All the working stiffs want is a raise.

the world is one’s oyster..monolingual: Fig. One rules the world.; One is in charge of everything. _I feel like the world is my oyster today. _ The world is my oyster! I’m in love!
examples: I feel like the world is my oyster today.

*worlds apart.monolingual: Fig. greatly separated by differing attitudes, needs, opinions, or temperaments. (*Typically: be ~; grow ~; live ~; think ~.) _ They are worlds apart. I can’t imagine how they ever decided to get married.
examples: They are worlds apart.

worm something out of someone.monolingual: to draw or manipulate information out of someone. _ I managed to worm the name of the doctor out of her before she ran off. _You can’t worm the names out of me!
examples: I managed to worm the name of the doctor out of her before she ran off.

worry about someone or something.monolingual: to fret or be anxious about the welfare of someone or something. _Please don’t worry about me. I’ll be all right. _ Don’t worry about the bill. I’ll pay it.
examples: Please don’t worry about me.

worry over someone or something.monolingual: to fret or be anxious about someone or something. _ She worried over dinner, but it came out all right. _Jerry is worried over his daughter, Alice.
