examples: She worried over dinner, but it came out all right.

worry something out of someone.monolingual: to annoy some information out of someone. _ They finally worried the correct number out of me. _ You can’t worry the information out of her. It will require force.
examples: They finally worried the correct number out of me.

worry through something.monolingual: to think and fret through a problem. _I can’t talk to you now. I have to worry through this tax problem. _We worried through the financial problem over a three-day period.
examples: I can’t talk to you now.

worrywart.monolingual: someone who worries all the time. _Don’t be such a worrywart. _ I’m sorry I’m such a worrywart.
examples: Don’t be such a worrywart.

the worse for wear.monolingual: 1. Euph. intoxicated. _You were the worse for wear last night. _ The three came stumbling in, the worse for wear again.
examples: You were the worse for wear last night.

worship someone as something.monolingual: to revere or honor one as if one were something divine or special. _ He worships her as a goddess. _ She worships her father as a god.
examples: He worships her as a goddess.

*the worst of something.monolingual: the poorest share of something; the worst part of something. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give someone ~.) _ I knew I would get the worst of the deal because I was absent when the goods were divided up. _ I’m sorry that you got the worst of it.
examples: I knew I would get the worst of the deal because I was absent when the goods were divided up.

the worst-case scenario.monolingual: Cliché the worse possible future outcome. _ Now, let’s look at the worst-case scenario. _ In the worst-case scenario, we’re all dead.
examples: Now, let’s look at the worst-case scenario.

worth its weight in gold.monolingual: Fig. very valuable. _This book is worth its weight in gold. _ Oh, Bill. You’re wonderful. You’re worth your weight in gold.
examples: This book is worth its weight in gold.

worth one’s salt.monolingual: Fig. worth (in productivity) what it costs to keep or support one. _ We decided that you are worth your salt, and you can stay on as office clerk. _ You’re not worth your salt. Pack up!
examples: We decided that you are worth your salt, and you can stay on as office clerk.

worth someone’s while.monolingual: worth one’s time and trouble. _ The job pays so badly it’s not worth your while even going for an interview. _It’s not worth Mary’s while going all that way just for a one-hour meeting.
examples: The job pays so badly it’s not worth your while even going for an interview.

worthy of the name.monolingual: deserving to be so called; good enough to enjoy a specific designation. _ There was not an actor worthy of the name in that play. _ Any art critic worthy of the name would know that painting to be a fake.
examples: There was not an actor worthy of the name in that play.

would rather.monolingual: would more willingly; would more readily. _ I would rather have an apple than a pear. I don’t like pears. _ I’d rather live in the north than the south, because I like snow.
examples: I would rather have an apple than a pear.

would you believe!.monolingual: Inf. Isn’t that unbelievable?; How shocking! _Tom: Jane has run off and married Fred! Sally: Would you believe! _Jane: Then the manager came out and asked us to leave. Would you believe? Mary: It sounds just awful. I’d send them a letter of complaint
examples: Jane: Then the manager came out and asked us to leave.

would you excuse me?.monolingual: 1. a polite question that essentially announces one’s departure. (Compare this with Could I be excused?; Excuse me.) _ Jane: Would you excuse me? I have to get home now. Andy: Oh, sure. I’ll see you to the door. _ Rising to leave, Jane said, “Would y
examples: Jane: Would you excuse me? I have to get home now.

would you please?.monolingual: a polite phrase that agrees that what was offered to be done should be done. _ Bill: Do you want me to take this over to the bank? Mary: Would you please? _ Tom: Can I take your coat? Sally: Would you please?

wouldn’t dream of doing something.monolingual: would not even consider doing something. _ I wouldn’t dream of taking your money! _ I’m sure that John wouldn’t dream of complaining to the manager.
examples: I’m sure that John wouldn’t dream of complaining to the manager.

wrack and ruin.monolingual: Cliché complete destruction or ruin. _ They went back after the fire and saw the wrack and ruin that used to be their house. _ Drinking brought him nothing but wrack and ruin.
examples: They went back after the fire and saw the wrack and ruin that used to be their house.

wrap around someone or something.monolingual: to enclose or fold about someone or something. _ The snake wrapped around the helpless man and it was soon all over. _ The flames wrapped around the barn and swallowed it up.
examples: The snake wrapped around the helpless man and it was soon all over.

wrap one’s car around something.monolingual: to drive one’s car into something at fairly high speed. _ She wrapped her car around a light pole. _ If he hadn’t wrapped his car around a tree, he’d be here with us tonight.
examples: She wrapped her car around a light pole.

wrap something around someone.monolingual: to fold or drape something onto someone. _ He wrapped a towel around himself and went to answer the telephone. _ She wrapped a blanket around her little boy to keep him warm.
examples: He wrapped a towel around himself and went to answer the telephone.

wrap something up†.monolingual: to complete work on something; to bring something to an end. _ I will wrap the job up this morning. I’ll call you when I finish. _ I can wrap up this little project in a week.
examples: I will wrap the job up this morning.

wrench something from someone.monolingual: to grab or twist something out of someone’s grasp. _ The policeman wrenched the gun from Lefty’s hand and called for his partner. _Max wrenched the wallet from Jed’s hand and f led with it.
examples: The policeman wrenched the gun from Lefty’s hand and called for his partner.

wrench something out of something.monolingual: to yank or twist something out of something. _ The policeman wrenched the gun out of Lefty’s hand and told Lefty to put his hands up. _Tom wrenched the bone out of the dog’s mouth and threw it away.
examples: The policeman wrenched the gun out of Lefty’s hand and told Lefty to put his hands up.

wrestle something from someone.monolingual: to get something away from someone after a physical struggle. _ Wally wrestled the gun away from Max and threw it out the window. _ I could not wrestle my wallet from the thief.
examples: Wally wrestled the gun away from Max and threw it out the window.

wrestle something into something.monolingual: to struggle with something large to get it into something or some place. _ She wrestled the packages into the backseat of the car. _I wrestled the suitcases into the rack over my seat.
examples: She wrestled the packages into the backseat of the car.

wrestle with someone.monolingual: to contend with someone in a physical wrestling match. _You are too big to wrestle with him! _ I want to wrestle with someone my own size.
examples: I want to wrestle with someone my own size.

wrestle with something.monolingual: 1. to struggle with something large to move it about. _ He wrestled with the piano and finally got it to move. _ The two men were wrestling with the heavy trunk for nearly ten minutes, trying to get it up the stairs.
examples: He wrestled with the piano and finally got it to move.

wring something out†.monolingual: to squeeze or twist something dry of liquid. _ He wrung the rag out and wiped up more of the spilled milk. _Liz wrung out the rag and wiped up more of the spilled milk.
examples: He wrung the rag out and wiped up more of the spilled milk.

wring something out of someone.monolingual: to pressure someone into telling something. _ The police will wring the truth out of her. _ After a lot of questioning, they wrung the information out of Fred.
examples: The police will wring the truth out of her.

wrinkle something up†.monolingual: to make something get wrinkles and creases. _ I love the way you wrinkle your nose up. _ Don’t wrinkle up your jacket.
examples: I love the way you wrinkle your nose up.

wrinkle up.monolingual: [for something] to draw up in wrinkles; [for something] to become wrinkled. _ His nose wrinkled up as he smelled the burning pie. _ The cloth wrinkled up in the intense heat.
examples: His nose wrinkled up as he smelled the burning pie.

write about someone or something.monolingual: to write a narrative or description of someone or something. _I wanted to write about wild canaries, but there is not much to say. _ Sally writes about famous people.
examples: I wanted to write about wild canaries, but there is not much to say.

write against someone or something.monolingual: to oppose someone or something in writing. _ John writes against the current administration too harshly. _Almost everyone enjoys writing against the CIA.
examples: John writes against the current administration too harshly.

write away.monolingual: to write a lot; to continue writing. _ There he was, writing away, not paying attention to anything else. _ I spent the entire afternoon writing away, having a fine, productive time.
examples: There he was, writing away, not paying attention to anything else.

write away for something.monolingual: to send for something in writing, from a distant place. _I wrote away for a book on the rivers of the world. _ You will have to write away for another copy of the instruction manual.
examples: I wrote away for a book on the rivers of the world.

write back to someone.monolingual: to write a letter to someone in return for a letter received from someone. _ I wrote back to her at once, but I have heard no more from her. _ Please write back to me when you have a chance.
examples: I wrote back to her at once, but I have heard no more from her.

write down to someone.monolingual: to write to someone condescendingly. _ You should never write down to your audience if you want to be convincing. _ I have to write down to them, because they are very young.
examples: You should never write down to your audience if you want to be convincing.

write for something.monolingual: 1. to write and request something. _ I wrote for clarification but received none. _ Julie wrote for another copy of the instruction book.
examples: I wrote for clarification but received none.

write of someone or something.monolingual: to write about the general topic of someone or something. _ He wrote of the beauty of nature and the way we are destroying it. _ She wrote of Henry, her ancient house cat.
examples: He wrote of the beauty of nature and the way we are destroying it.

write on and on.monolingual: to write too much; to write endlessly. _ You tend to write on and on. Try to focus on one point and leave it at that. _ I think you write on and on just to fill up space.
examples: You tend to write on and on.

write someone down as something.monolingual: to list someone’s name, noting something. _ I’ll write you down as a contributor. _ Can I write you down as a charter member?
examples: I’ll write you down as a contributor.

write someone for something.monolingual: to send a written request to someone for something. _ Henry wrote Harry for a firm quote, but Harry never responded. _ Did you write me for permission?
examples: Henry wrote Harry for a firm quote, but Harry never responded.

write someone or something off†.monolingual: to drop someone or something from consideration. _ The manager wrote Tom off for a promotion. _I wrote off that piece of swampy land as worthless. It can’t be used for anything.
examples: The manager wrote Tom off for a promotion.

write someone or something up†.monolingual: to write an article about someone or something. _ A reporter wrote me up for the Sunday paper. _ I wrote up a local business and sent the story to a magazine, but they didn’t buy the story.
examples: A reporter wrote me up for the Sunday paper.

write something back to someone.monolingual: to write a letter answering someone. _I wrote an answer back to her the same day that I received the letter. _Will you please write something back to Julie? She complains that you are ignoring her. _ I wrote a letter back to Harry, explaining what ha
examples: I wrote an answer back to her the same day that I received the letter.

write something down†.monolingual: to make a note of something; to record something in writing. _ Please write this down. _ Please write down what I tell you.
examples: Please write this down.

write something off†.monolingual: to absorb a debt or a loss in accounting. _ The bill couldn’t be collected, so we had to write it off. _ The bill was too large, and we couldn’t write off the amount. We decided to sue.
examples: The bill couldn’t be collected, so we had to write it off.

write something out†.monolingual: 1. to spell or write a number or an abbreviation. _Don’t just write “7,” write it out. _Please write out all abbreviations, such as Doctor for Dr.
examples: Don’t just write “7,” write it out.

write something to someone.monolingual: 1. to send specific information to someone in writing. _I wrote the facts to John, and he thanked me for the information. _ They wrote all the details to me, and I filed them.
examples: I wrote the facts to John, and he thanked me for the information.

write something to something.monolingual: to write something that is supplementary to something else. _ Molly wrote an epilogue to her story covering the time up till now. _ I will write the introduction to the book this afternoon.
examples: Molly wrote an epilogue to her story covering the time up till now.

write something up†.monolingual: to prepare a bill, order, or statement. _ Please write the order up and send me a copy. _ As soon as I finish writing up your check, I’ll bring you some more coffee.
examples: Please write the order up and send me a copy.

write to someone.monolingual: to compose a letter or e-mail and send it to someone. _I will write to her again, but I don’t expect to hear anything. _ Please write to me as soon as you can.
examples: I will write to her again, but I don’t expect to hear anything.

writer’s block.monolingual: the temporary inability for a writer to think of what to write. _ I have writer’s block at the moment and can’t seem to get a sensible sentence on paper.
examples: I have writer’s block at the moment and can’t seem to get a sensible sentence on paper.

writhe under something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to squirm with pain from being beaten with something. _ The sailor writhed under the sting of the lash. _ The child writhed under the pain of his spanking.
examples: The sailor writhed under the sting of the lash.

*the wrong number.monolingual: 1. Lit. an incorrect telephone number. (*Typically: get ~; have ~; dial ~; give someone ~.) _He got the wrong number and hung up. _When a young child answered, I knew I had the wrong number.
examples: He got the wrong number and hung up.

wrote the book on something.monolingual: Fig. to be very authoritative about something; to know enough about something to write the definitive book on it. (Always in past tense.) _Ted wrote the book on unemployment. He’s been looking for work in three states for two years. _ Do I know about
examples: Ted wrote the book on unemployment.

*wrought up.monolingual: disturbed or excited. (Wrought is an old past tense and past participle meaning “worker.” *Typically: be ~; get ~.) _She is so wrought up, she can’t think. _ I am sorry you are so wrought up.
examples: She is so wrought up, she can’t think.

x marks the spot..monolingual: This is the exact spot. (Sometimes the speaker will draw an X in the spot while saying this.) _ This is where the rock struck my car—X marks the spot. _ Now, please move that table over here. Yes, right here—X marks the spot.
examples: This is where the rock struck my car—X marks the spot.

x someone or something out†.monolingual: to mark out something printed or in writing, with Xs. _ Sally X’d the incorrect information out. _ Sally X’d out the incorrect information. _ You should X Tom out. He’s not coming. _Please X out this line of print.
examples: Sally X’d the incorrect information out.

x’d out.monolingual: 1. eliminated; crossed-out. _ But the Babbits are X’d out. _ Put the X’d out Babbits back where they were.
examples: But the Babbits are X’d out.

yack one’s head off.monolingual: Fig. to talk a great deal. _Jane yacked her head off and ended up with a sore throat. _ Don’t yack your head off!
examples: Jane yacked her head off and ended up with a sore throat.

yack something up†.monolingual: Inf. to talk a great deal [about someone or something]. (The something is often it.) _ She yacked the concert up endlessly. _ Sally yacked up the concert, trying to get people to attend. _ Yack it up and see if you can get people to attend.
examples: She yacked the concert up endlessly.

yank at someone or something.monolingual: to pull or tug at someone or something. _Please don’t yank at the drapery cord. _Stop yanking at me!
examples: Please don’t yank at the drapery cord.

yank on something.monolingual: to pull or tug on something. _ Don’t yank on my hair! _ Yank on this rope to send a signal to the worker on the f loor above.
examples: Yank on this rope to send a signal to the worker on the f loor above.

yank someone around.monolingual: Sl. to harass someone; to give someone a hard time. _Listen, I don’t mean to yank you around all the time, but we have to have the drawings by Monday. _ Please stop yanking me around.
examples: Listen, I don’t mean to yank you around all the time, but we have to have the drawings by Monday.

yank someone or something apart†.monolingual: 1. to pull, tear, or rip someone or something to pieces. _ Please don’t yank the book apart! _ He yanked apart the book! _ He threatened to yank his opponent apart.
examples: He threatened to yank his opponent apart.

yank someone or something around.monolingual: to pull or jerk someone or something around. _ Don’t yank Billy around so. You’ll hurt him! _ Please don’t yank the chairs around. Move them carefully.
examples: Don’t yank Billy around so.

yank someone’s chain.monolingual: Sl. to harass someone; to give someone a hard time. (As if one were a dog wearing a choker collar, on a leash.) _ Stop yanking my chain! _ Do you really think you can just yank my chain whenever you want?

yank something off†.monolingual: to pull or jerk off something, such as a piece of clothing. _ She yanked her jacket off. _ She yanked off her jacket and threw it on the chair.
examples: She yanked her jacket off.

yank something up†.monolingual: to pull or jerk something up. _ He yanked his pants up. _ He yanked up his pants and threw on his shirt.
examples: He yanked his pants up.

yap about someone or something.monolingual: to talk casually about someone or something; to gossip or complain about someone or something. _ Stop yapping about Molly. _ Claire is always yapping about her salary.
examples: Stop yapping about Molly.

yap at someone.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a small dog] to bark at someone or something. _ The dog yapped at the cat in great frustration. _ I am tired of that dog yapping at me all the time!
examples: The dog yapped at the cat in great frustration.

year after year.monolingual: for many years, one after another. _ We go to the same place for our vacation year after year. _ I seem to earn the same salary year after year.
examples: We go to the same place for our vacation year after year.

year in, year out.monolingual: year after year; for years. _ I seem to have hay fever year in, year out. I never get over it. _ John wears the same old suit, year in, year out.
examples: I seem to have hay fever year in, year out.

yearn for someone or something.monolingual: to long for someone or something; to desire someone or something strongly. _ Sam sat alone in his room, yearning for Mary. _ Mary yearned for a big bowl of high-butterfat ice cream.
examples: Sam sat alone in his room, yearning for Mary.

yell at someone or something.monolingual: to shout at someone or something, usually in anger. _ Please don’t yell at me. _ There is no point in yelling at a cat.
examples: Please don’t yell at me.

yell out.monolingual: to cry out; to shout loudly. _ The pain caused the child to yell out. _ I yelled out, but no one heard me.
examples: The pain caused the child to yell out.

yen for someone or something.monolingual: to long for someone or something. _ I yen for a great big bowl of highly fattening ice cream. _ Frank yenned for Sally.
examples: I yen for a great big bowl of highly fattening ice cream.

yesterday wouldn’t be too soon..monolingual: Immediately.; Right away. (An answer to the question “When do you want this?”) _Mary: Mr. Franklin, when do you want this? Fred: Well, yesterday wouldn’t be too soon. _ Alice: When am I supposed to have this finished? Sue: Yesterday wouldn’t be too s
examples: Mary: Mr. Franklin, when do you want this? Fred: Well, yesterday wouldn’t be too soon.

yield something to someone.monolingual: 1. to give the right-of-way to someone. _ You must yield the right-of-way to pedestrians. _ You failed to yield the right-of-way to the oncoming car.
examples: You must yield the right-of-way to pedestrians.

yield to someone.monolingual: 1. to let someone go ahead; to give someone the right-of-way. _Please yield to the next speaker. _ She yielded to the next speaker.
examples: Please yield to the next speaker.

a yoke around someone’s neck.monolingual: Fig. something that oppresses people; a burden. _ John’s greedy children are a yoke around his neck. _ The Smiths have a huge mortgage that has become a yoke around their necks.
examples: John’s greedy children are a yoke around his neck.

yoke people or things together.monolingual: to connect two people together with a yoke; to connect two animals together with a yoke. _Todd yoked the oxen together for the parade. _ Sam yoked Fred and Tom together so they could pull the load.
examples: Todd yoked the oxen together for the parade.

you ain’t just whistlin’ dixie..monolingual: Rur. You are right. _ Tom: Sure is hot today. Bill: Yeah, you ain’t just whistlin’ Dixie. It’s a scorcher. _ Charlie: That was a good movie. Jane: You ain’t just whistlin’ Dixie. It was the best I’ve ever seen.
examples: Tom: Sure is hot today.

you ain’t seen nothing yet!.monolingual: Rur. The best, most exciting, or cleverest part is yet to come! (The use of ain’t is a fixed part of this idiomatic expression.) _Alice: Well, the first act was simply divine. Sue: Stick around. You ain’t seen nothing yet! _ Mary: This part of the ci
examples: Alice: Well, the first act was simply divine.

you are more than welcome..monolingual: 1. You are very welcome to be here. _ Please make yourself at home. You are more than welcome.
examples: Please make yourself at home.

you asked for it!.monolingual: 1. You are getting what you requested. _The waiter set a huge bowl of ice cream, strawberries, and whipped cream in front of Mary, saying apologetically, “You asked for it!” _ Bill: Gee, this escargot stuff is gross! Mary: You asked for it!
examples: Bill: Gee, this escargot stuff is gross! Mary: You asked for it! 2.

you betcha!.monolingual: Inf. Yes!; You can be sure of it! (Literally, You bet, you.) _ Will I be there? You betcha. _ Can I? You betcha!
examples: Will I be there? You betcha.

you called?.monolingual: 1. a phrase used when returning a telephone call, meaning “What did you want to talk about when you called before?” _ Bill (answering the phone): Hello? Bob: This is Bob. You called? _Tom: You called? It’s Tom. Mary: Hi, Tom. Yes, I wanted to ask you
examples: Bill (answering the phone): Hello? Bob: This is Bob.

you cannot please everyone..monolingual: Prov. Cliché No matter what you do, there will always be some people who do not like it. _ Nancy: My mother wants me to have a big wedding in the church, but my fiancé’s mother insists that we should have an informal ceremony. What am I going to do?
examples: Nancy: My mother wants me to have a big wedding in the church, but my fiancé’s mother insists that we should have an informal ceremony.

you can’t mean that!.monolingual: Inf. Surely you do not mean what you said! _ Bill: I hate you! Mary: You can’t mean that. _ Sally: The cake burned and there’s no time to start another before the party. Mary: You can’t mean that!
examples: Bill: I hate you! Mary: You can’t mean that.

you don’t say..monolingual: 1. Inf. a general response to something that someone has said. (Expresses a little polite surprise or interest, but not disbelief.) _ Bill: I’m starting work on a new job next Monday. Bob: You don’t say. _ Sally: The Jones boys are keeping a pet snak
examples: Bill: I’m starting work on a new job next Monday.

you first..monolingual: an invitation for someone to precede the speaker. (See the examples.) _ Bill: Let’s try some of this goose liver stuff. Jane: You first. _Bill: The water sure looks cold. Let’s jump in. Bob: You first.
examples: Bill: Let’s try some of this goose liver stuff.

you got it!.monolingual: 1. Inf. I agree to what you asked!; You will get what you want! _You want a green one? You got it! _This one? You got it!
examples: This one? You got it! 2.

you got me there..monolingual: Inf. I do not know the answer to your question. (Also with subjects other than second person.) _You got me there. I don’t know. _You got me there. I have no idea what the answer is.
examples: You got me there.

you heard someone..monolingual: Don’t argue. You heard your instructions from someone. (The someone can be a person’s name, a title, or a pronoun.) _ Andy: You heard the man. Get moving. Henry: Don’t rush me! _Bill: What makes her think she can tell me what to do? Bob: She’s the bo
examples: Andy: You heard the man.

you just don’t get it!.monolingual: Inf. You really don’t see what people are trying to tell you! (Also with subjects other than second person.) _ You just don’t get it! People avoid you because you offend them.
examples: You just don’t get it! People avoid you because you offend them.

you make me laugh!.monolingual: Inf. Fig. What you said is totally ridiculous.; You are totally ridiculous. (Compare this with Don’t make me laugh!) _ Bill: I have this plan to make electricity from garbage. Sally: What a dumb idea! You make me laugh! _Bill: I’m really sorry. Give
examples: Bill: I have this plan to make electricity from garbage.

you think you’re so smart!.monolingual: Inf. You act as if you know far more than you do. (Also with subjects other than second person.) _ You think you’re so smart! You don’t know anything! _ Boy! He thinks he’s so smart!

you’ll be sorry you asked..monolingual: Inf. The answer to the question you just asked is so bad that you will be sorry you asked it. (Compare this with (Are you) sorry you asked?) _ Father: What are your grades going to be like this semester? Sally: You’ll be sorry you asked. _Mary: How m
examples: Father: What are your grades going to be like this semester? Sally: You’ll be sorry you asked.

*young at heart.monolingual: having a youthful spirit no matter what one’s age. (*Typically: act ~; be ~; keep someone ~; stay ~.) _ I am over 70 but I still feel young at heart.
examples: I am over 70 but I still feel young at heart.

your place or mine?.monolingual: Inf. an expression asking someone about whose dwelling should be the site of a rendezvous. (Often associated with a sudden or spontaneous sexual encounter.) _Bill: So, do you want to go somewhere? Mary: Your place or mine? _ Bill: I was thinking of w
examples: Bill: I was thinking of watching a movie at home.

you’re dern tootin’!.monolingual: Rur. You are absolutely right! (Never the full form tooting.) _ Tom: Are you really going to take up boxing? Bob: You’re dern tootin’! _Father: Do you really want to buy that droopy-looking puppy? Bill: You’re dern tootin’!

you’re excused..monolingual: 1. You may leave the room, the table, etc. (Said in response to May I be excused?) _ Mother: Are you finished, Tom? Tom: Yes, ma’am. Mother: You’re excused. _ Bill (raising his hand): Can I leave the room? I have to go get my books off my bike. Teach
examples: Mother: Are you finished, Tom? Tom: Yes, ma’am.

you’re telling me!.monolingual: Inf. I know all too well the truth of what you are saying. _ Tom: Man, it’s hot today! Bob: You’re telling me! _ Jane: This food is really terrible. Sally: Wow! You’re telling me!
examples: Jane: This food is really terrible.

you’re the doctor..monolingual: Inf. Fig. You are in a position to tell me what to do.; I yield to you and your knowledge of this matter. (Usually jocular; the person being addressed is most likely not a physician.) _ Bill: Eat your dinner, then you’ll feel more like playing ball.
examples: Bill: Eat your dinner, then you’ll feel more like playing ball.

you’re too much!.monolingual: 1. Inf. You are too much of a problem for me. _ Andy: You’re too much! I’m going to report you to the head office! Bob: Go ahead. See if I care. _ Bob: Get out! Just go home! You’re too much! Andy: What did I do? Bob: You’re a pest!
examples: Andy: You’re too much! I’m going to report you to the head office! Bob: Go ahead.

yours truly.monolingual: 1. a closing phrase at the end of a letter, just before the signature. _ Yours truly, Tom Jones. _ Best wishes from yours truly, Bill Smith.
examples: Yours truly, Tom Jones.

youth must be served..monolingual: Prov. Young people should be allowed to have fun. _Don’t lecture the young folks because they were out dancing all night. Youth must be served. _ I don’t know where my daughter gets the energy for school, sports, and a full social life. Youth must be
examples: Don’t lecture the young folks because they were out dancing all night.

you’ve got another think coming..monolingual: You will have to rethink your position. (The second part of an expression something like, “If you think so-and-so, then you’ve got another think coming.” Also with thing rather than think.) _ Rachel: If you think I’m going to stand here and listen to
examples: Rachel: If you think I’m going to stand here and listen to your complaining all day, you’ve got another think coming! Bill: Frankly, I don’t care what you do.

you’ve got to be kidding!.monolingual: Inf. This cannot be the truth. Surely you are kidding me! _Bob: Sally is getting married. Did you hear? Mary: You’ve got to be kidding! _Bill: I think I swallowed my gold tooth! Mother: You’ve got to be kidding!
examples: Bob: Sally is getting married.

zeek out.monolingual: Sl. to lose control of oneself. _ I was in a pretty bad state. I almost zeeked out. _ Fred zeeked out and had to be calmed down.
examples: I was in a pretty bad state.

zero tolerance.monolingual: absolutely no toleration of even the smallest infraction of a rule. _Because of the zero tolerance rule, the kindergartner was expelled from school because his mother accidentally left a table knife in his lunch box.
examples: Because of the zero tolerance rule, the kindergartner was expelled from school because his mother accidentally left a table knife in his lunch box.

zigged when one should’ve zagged.monolingual: perfomed one deed when another deed would have been better; to do something inconsequentially different from another thing. _ I don’t know why she complained. I guess I zigged when I should have zagged.
examples: I don’t know why she complained.

zip along.monolingual: to move along very fast. _The motorcycle zipped along nicely. _ Let’s zip along and get there on time.
examples: The motorcycle zipped along nicely.

zip past someone or something.monolingual: to run or move past someone or something very rapidly. _The deer zipped past the hunter, who stood there, startled. _ The cars zipped past the intersection.
examples: The deer zipped past the hunter, who stood there, startled.

zip something on†.monolingual: to put on a piece of clothing and zip it up. _ She zipped her jumper on and headed toward the door. _ Zip on your jacket and let’s go.
examples: She zipped her jumper on and headed toward the door.

zip something up†.monolingual: 1. to close a zipper. _You should zip that zipper up. _You should zip up that zipper.
examples: You should zip that zipper up.

zone something as something.monolingual: to create a particular legally defined area within a governmental or other local area. _ They zoned this area as a shopping district. _ The city council zoned the vacant lot as a park.
examples: They zoned this area as a shopping district.

zone something for something.monolingual: to specify what can be built or what can be done within a particular legally defined area within a governmental area. _ Did the council zone this area for business? _They zoned this area for residences.
examples: They zoned this area for residences.

zone something off†.monolingual: to create a special regulatory zone in an area. _The council zoned part of the land off for a park. _ They zoned off land for a park.
examples: The council zoned part of the land off for a park.

zonk out.monolingual: Sl. to collapse from exhaustion; to go into a stupor from drugs or exhaustion. _ I’m gonna go home and zonk out. _ I went home after the trip and just zonked out.
examples: I’m gonna go home and zonk out.

zonk someone out†.monolingual: 1. Sl. to make someone tired or exhausted. _ All the work zonked him out. _ She zonked out the team with the long practice.
examples: All the work zonked him out.

zoom along.monolingual: to move along very rapidly. _The bus zoomed along rapidly all night long. _ Let’s zoom along while the road is clear.
examples: The bus zoomed along rapidly all night long.

zoom off.monolingual: to leave in a hurry. _ Sorry, I have to zoom off. _ We will zoom off soon.
examples: Sorry, I have to zoom off.

zoom out.monolingual: to move back to a wider angle picture using a zoom lens. _ The camera zoomed out. _ Pan out at this point in the script and give a wider view of the scene.
examples: The camera zoomed out.

zoom over someone or something.monolingual: to fly over someone or something at high speed. _ The plane zoomed over the treetops. _ A small bird zoomed over the hikers, shrieking wildly.
examples: The plane zoomed over the treetops.

zoom past someone or something.monolingual: to run or move past someone or something very rapidly. _ The runners zoomed past the spectators. _ Our train zoomed past town after town.
examples: The runners zoomed past the spectators.

zoom up.monolingual: to drive or pull up to a place. _ A car zoomed up, and seven kids got out. _ Let’s zoom up to the door and see if she’s home.
examples: A car zoomed up, and seven kids got out.

abbreviate something to something.monolingual: 1. to make specific initials or an acronym out of a word or phrase. _ The phrase was abbreviated to ABC.
examples: The phrase was abbreviated to ABC.

abbreviate something as something.monolingual: to make specific initials or an acronym out of a word or phrase. _ The phrase was abbreviated to ABC.
examples: The phrase was abbreviated to ABC.

all over.monolingual: 1. finished. _ Dinner is all over. I’m sorry you didn’t get any. _ It’s all over. He’s dead now.
examples: Dinner is all over.

amount to something.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for someone or something] to become worthwhile or successful. _ I hope Charles amounts to something some day. _ I doubt that this business will ever amount to anything really profitable.
examples: I hope Charles amounts to something some day.

answer the call.monolingual: 1. Euph. to die. _ Our dear brother answered the call and has gone to his eternal rest.
examples: Our dear brother answered the call and has gone to his eternal rest.

as long as.monolingual: 1. since; because. _ As long as you’re going to the bakery, please buy some fresh bread. _ So long as you’re here, please stay for dinner.
examples: As long as you’re going to the bakery, please buy some fresh bread.

so long as.monolingual: if; only if. _ You may have dessert so long as you eat all your vegetables. _You can go out this evening as long as you promise to be home by midnight.
examples: You may have dessert so long as you eat all your vegetables.

ask someone for something.monolingual: 1. to request something from someone. _ The diners asked the waiter for a type of wine the restaurant didn’t have. _ A special wine was asked for by a number of patrons.
examples: The diners asked the waiter for a type of wine the restaurant didn’t have.

at length.monolingual: 1. after some time; finally. _At length, the roses bloomed, and the tomatoes ripened. _ And at length, the wizard spoke.
examples: At length, the roses bloomed, and the tomatoes ripened.

at some length.monolingual: for quite a long time. _ He spoke to us about the problem at some length. _ He described the history of his village at length.
examples: He spoke to us about the problem at some length.

at one’s best.monolingual: 1. to the utmost; to the highest degree possible. _ This restaurant serves gourmet food at its best. _The singer was at her best when she performed ballads.
examples: This restaurant serves gourmet food at its best.

at its best.monolingual: to the utmost; to the highest degree possible. _ This restaurant serves gourmet food at its best. _The singer was at her best when she performed ballads.
examples: This restaurant serves gourmet food at its best.

balance the accounts.monolingual: Lit. to determine through bookkeeping that accounts are in balance, that all money is accounted for. _Jane was up all night balancing the accounts. _The cashier was not allowed to leave the bank until the manager balanced the books.
examples: Jane was up all night balancing the accounts.

balance the books.monolingual: to determine through bookkeeping that accounts are in balance, that all money is accounted for. _Jane was up all night balancing the accounts. _The cashier was not allowed to leave the bank until the manager balanced the books.
examples: Jane was up all night balancing the accounts.

blow a fuse.monolingual: 1. to burn out the fuse on an electrical circuit and lose power. _The microwave oven blew a fuse, so we had no power. _ You’ll blow a fuse if you use too many appliances at once.
examples: The microwave oven blew a fuse, so we had no power.

blow off.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to be carried off something by moving air. _ The leaves of the trees blew off in the strong wind. _My papers blew off the table.
examples: The leaves of the trees blew off in the strong wind.

blow someone or something off†.monolingual: Sl. to ignore someone or something; to skip an appointment with someone; to not attend something where one is expected. _ He decided to sleep in and blow this class off. _ It wasn’t right for you to just blow off an old friend the way you did.
examples: He decided to sleep in and blow this class off.

blow someone off†.monolingual: Sl. to ignore someone in order to end a romantic or other relationship. _ She knew that he had blown her off when he didn’t even call her for a month. _Steve blew off Rachel before he started seeing Jane.
examples: She knew that he had blown her off when he didn’t even call her for a month.

boil down to something.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a liquid] to be condensed to something by boiling. _Boil this mixture down to about half of what it was.
examples: Boil this mixture down to about half of what it was.

boil down.monolingual: Lit. [for a liquid] to be condensed to something by boiling. _Boil this mixture down to about half of what it was.
examples: Boil this mixture down to about half of what it was.

bottle something up†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to put some sort of liquid into bottles. _She bottled her homemade chili sauce up and put the bottles in a box. _She bottled up a lot of the stuff.
examples: She bottled her homemade chili sauce up and put the bottles in a box.

reach for the sky.monolingual: 1. Fig. to set one’s sights high. _ Reach for the sky! Go for it! _You should always reach for the sky, but be prepared for not attaining your goals every time.
examples: You should always reach for the sky, but be prepared for not attaining your goals every time.

remain on.monolingual: 1. to continue to stay in one place. (The on is an adverb, not a preposition.) _ Everyone else left, but I decided to remain on there. _I remained on for a while during the time they were training my replacement.
examples: Everyone else left, but I decided to remain on there.

remain on something.monolingual: to continue to be on something; to continue to serve on a body. _ Will you remain on the board of directors for another year? _ I will remain on this committee as long as I am needed.
examples: I will remain on this committee as long as I am needed.

run in circles.monolingual: 1. Lit. to run in a circular path. _The horses ran in circles around the corral for their daily exercise. _ The children ran in circles around the tree.
examples: The horses ran in circles around the corral for their daily exercise.

run around in circles.monolingual: Fig. to waste one’s time in aimless activity. _Stop running in circles and try to organize yourself so that you are more productive. _ I have been running around in circles over this matter for days.
examples: Stop running in circles and try to organize yourself so that you are more productive.

run the gauntlet.monolingual: 1. Lit. to race, as a punishment, between parallel lines of men who thrash one as one runs. _ The knight was forced to doff his clothes and run the gauntlet.
examples: The knight was forced to doff his clothes and run the gauntlet.

run the gauntlet of something.monolingual: Fig. to endure a series of problems, threats, or criticism. _ After the play, the director found himself running the gauntlet of questions and doubts about his ability.
examples: After the play, the director found himself running the gauntlet of questions and doubts about his ability.

the runt of the litter.monolingual: 1. Lit. the smallest animal born in a litter; the animal in a litter least likely to survive. _ No one wanted to buy the runt of the litter, so we kept it.
examples: No one wanted to buy the runt of the litter, so we kept it.

the runt of the family.monolingual: Fig. the smallest child in the family. _I was the runt of the litter and the butt of all the jokes.
examples: I was the runt of the litter and the butt of all the jokes.

*sewed up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [the sewing of a gap in cloth] completed. (*Typically: get something ~; have something ~.) _ Have you got that tear sewed up yet?
examples: Have you got that tear sewed up yet? 2.

*wrapped up.monolingual: Fig. settled or finished. (*Typically: get something ~; have something ~.) _I’ll take the contract to the mayor tomorrow morning. I’ll get the whole deal sewed up by noon. _ Don’t worry about the car loan. I’ll have it wrapped up in time to make the
examples: I’ll take the contract to the mayor tomorrow morning.

shake something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to clean something of dirt or crumbs by shaking. _ Please shake the tablecloth out. _ Can you shake out your coat? It’s really dusty.
examples: Please shake the tablecloth out.

shake something down†.monolingual: Fig. to test something to find out how it works or what the problems are. _I need to spend some time driving my new car to shake it out. _We need to shake down this car before I buy it.
examples: I need to spend some time driving my new car to shake it out.

*sharp as a razor.monolingual: 1. very sharp. (*Also: as ~.) _ The penknife is sharp as a razor. _ The carving knife will have to be as sharp as a razor to cut through this gristle.
examples: The penknife is sharp as a razor.

*sharp as a tack.monolingual: very sharp-witted or intelligent. (*Also: as ~.) _ The old man’s senile, but his wife is as sharp as a razor. _ Sue can figure things out from even the slightest hint. She’s as sharp as a tack.
examples: The old man’s senile, but his wife is as sharp as a razor.

slip away.monolingual: 1. to go away or escape quietly or in secret; to slip out. _ I slipped away when no one was looking. _Let’s slip off somewhere and have a little talk. _ I’ll try to slip out for an hour or two when Tom is asleep.
examples: I slipped away when no one was looking.

slip off.monolingual: to go away or escape quietly or in secret; to slip out. _ I slipped away when no one was looking. _Let’s slip off somewhere and have a little talk. _ I’ll try to slip out for an hour or two when Tom is asleep.
examples: I slipped away when no one was looking.

slip by.monolingual: 1. to move by someone or something quickly or unnoticed; to move through a tight area or past someone or something in a tight area. _The hall was narrow, and I could hardly have slipped by.
examples: The hall was narrow, and I could hardly have slipped by.

slip by someone or something.monolingual: to move by someone or something quickly or unnoticed; to move through a tight area or past someone or something in a tight area. _The hall was narrow, and I could hardly have slipped by.
examples: The hall was narrow, and I could hardly have slipped by.

slow on the draw.monolingual: 1. Lit. slow in drawing a gun. (Cowboy and gangster talk.) _ Bill got shot because he’s so slow on the draw. _The gunslinger said, “I have to be fast. If I’m slow on the draw, I’m dead.”
examples: Bill got shot because he’s so slow on the draw.

slow on the uptake.monolingual: Fig. slow to figure something out; slow-thinking. _ Sally didn’t get the joke because she’s sort of slow on the draw. _ Bill—who’s slow on the uptake—didn’t get the joke until it was explained to him.
examples: Sally didn’t get the joke because she’s sort of slow on the draw.

smooth something out†.monolingual: 1. Lit. to flatten or even something by smoothing or pressing. _Wally smoothed the bedspread out. _Wally finished making the bed by smoothing out the spread.
examples: Wally smoothed the bedspread out.

smooth something over†.monolingual: Fig. to reduce the intensity of an argument or a misunderstanding; to try to make people feel better about something disagreeable that has happened. (Fig. on Q.) _ Mary and John had a terrible argument, and they are both trying to smooth it over. _ L
examples: Mary and John had a terrible argument, and they are both trying to smooth it over.

step into something.monolingual: 1. Lit. to step into something wet, messy, or dirty. _ Don’t step in the mud! _ What is that stinky stuff you stepped into?
examples: What is that stinky stuff you stepped into? 2.

step in something.monolingual: to step into something wet, messy, or dirty. _ Don’t step in the mud! _ What is that stinky stuff you stepped into?

take a punch at someone.monolingual: to hit at someone; to poke someone. _ Max took a jab at Lefty and missed. _ Lefty took a punch at Max.
examples: Max took a jab at Lefty and missed.

that does it!.monolingual: 1. Inf. That completes it!; It is now done just right! _ When Jane got the last piece put into the puzzle, she said, “That does it!” _ John (signing a paper): Well, that’s the last one! That does it! Bill: I thought we’d never finish.
examples: John (signing a paper): Well, that’s the last one! That does it! Bill: I thought we’d never finish.

that tears it!.monolingual: Inf. That’s the last straw!; Enough is enough! _ Bill: We’re still not totally pleased with your work. Bob: That does it! I quit! _Sally: That tears it! I never want to see you again! Fred: I only put my arm around you!
examples: Bill: We’re still not totally pleased with your work.

throw someone off the track.monolingual: 1. Lit. to cause someone to lose the trail (when following someone or something. See also put someone off the track). _ The raccoon threw us off the track by running through the creek. _ The robber threw the police off the trail by leaving town.
examples: The raccoon threw us off the track by running through the creek.

throw someone off the trail.monolingual: Lit. to cause someone to lose the trail (when following someone or something. See also put someone off the track). _ The raccoon threw us off the track by running through the creek. _ The robber threw the police off the trail by leaving town.
examples: The raccoon threw us off the track by running through the creek.

tickle someone to death.monolingual: 1. Fig. to tickle someone a great deal. _ Bobby nearly tickled Tim to death. Tim was left breathless. _ We got him down and tickled him to death.
examples: Bobby nearly tickled Tim to death.

tickle someone to pieces.monolingual: Fig. to please someone a great deal. _ What you told her just tickled her to death! _ That story just tickles me to pieces.
examples: That story just tickles me to pieces.

*tight as a drum.monolingual: 1. stretched tight. (*Also: as ~.) _ Julia stretched the upholstery fabric over the seat of the chair until it was as tight as a drum. _ The skin on his scalp is tight as a drum.
examples: Julia stretched the upholstery fabric over the seat of the chair until it was as tight as a drum.

*tight as midas’s fist.monolingual: very stingy. (*Also: as ~.) _ He won’t contribute a cent. He’s as tight as a drum. _ Old Mr. Robinson is tight as Midas’s fist. Won’t spend money on anything.
examples: He won’t contribute a cent.

turn over.monolingual: 1. Lit. to rotate so that the side that was on the bottom is now on top. _ The turtle turned over and crawled away. _ She turned over to get some sun on her back.
examples: The turtle turned over and crawled away.

kick over.monolingual: Fig. [for an engine] to start or to rotate. _ My car engine was so cold that it wouldn’t even turn over. _ The engine kicked over a few times and then stopped for good.
examples: My car engine was so cold that it wouldn’t even turn over.

*under pressure.monolingual: 1. Fig. facing or enduring something such as pressure or a deadline. (*Typically: be ~; get ~.) _ I have to get back to work. I am under a deadline. _I am under a lot of pressure lately. _The management is under the gun for the mistakes made last yea
examples: I have to get back to work.

*up to speed.monolingual: 1. Fig. moving, operating, or funtioning a normal or desired rate. (*Typically: be ~; bring something ~; get ~; get something ~.) _ Terri did everything she could to bring her workers up to speed, but couldn’t. _ Can we get this production line up to
examples: Terri did everything she could to bring her workers up to speed, but couldn’t.

warm up.monolingual: 1. [for the weather or a person] to become warmer or hotter. _ I think it is going to warm up next week.
examples: I think it is going to warm up next week.

warm up for something.monolingual: Fig. to prepare for some kind of performance or competition. _The team had to warm up before the game. _ They have to warm up.
examples: The team had to warm up before the game.

look out; watch out.monolingual: Fig. to try to avoid a confrontation with someone or something. _ Watch out! That car nearly hit you! _Look out for John. He’s looking for you, and he’s really mad. _ Thanks. I’d better look out.
examples: Look out for John.

work up a sweat.monolingual: Lit. to work very hard and sweat very much. (In the way that a horse works up a lather.) _ Don’t work yourself up into a lather. We don’t need to finish this today. _ I worked myself into a sweat getting this stuff ready.
examples: Don’t work yourself up into a lather.

writhe with something.monolingual: 1. [for someone or an animal] to squirm because of something, such as pain. _ Carl writhed with pain and began to cry. _ He was writhing in pain when the paramedics arrived.
examples: Carl writhed with pain and began to cry.

writhe in something.monolingual: [for someone or an animal] to squirm because of something, such as pain. _ Carl writhed with pain and began to cry. _ He was writhing in pain when the paramedics arrived.
examples: Carl writhed with pain and began to cry.
